https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.title: The Year of the Pro-Palestine Super PAC
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.author: Akela Lacy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.text:
The recent midterm election cycle marked by historic levels of pro-Israel spending saw an emerging trend that aimed to counter their influence: a new crop of pro-Palestine PACs.
Led by American Priorities PAC, which formed in January as part of an effort by donors, including supporters of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who opposed U.S. military support for Israel, a cadre of pro-Palestine organizations spent more than $14.4 million on races this cycle. Almost all of their candidates won.
“In the midst of the genocide, we felt compelled to push every lever and engage in every way possible to push candidates and the [Democratic] party to catch up to its base,” said Margaret DeReus, who leads the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project and the Peace, Accountability, and Leadership political action committee, or PAL PAC. Both groups spent on pro-Palestine ads for the first time this cycle.
As DeReus and other leaders of the emergent pro-Palestine lobby told The Intercept, voters, especially Democratic ones, have become increasingly disillusioned with Israel and frustrated with politicians who support unchecked military aid to the country. “I don’t think there is an issue that I can think of where the party position, the mainstream party position, is so out of step with the base,” DeReus said.
The new pro-Palestine spending is a drop in the bucket compared to the more than $84 million the pro-Israel lobby poured into elections this cycle. AIPAC’s super PAC outspent pro-Palestine groups almost 6 to 1 — and that doesn’t include the more than $50 million AIPAC funneled directly to candidates. The pro-Palestine side may never match their opponents dollar for dollar.
“The point is, nobody has to outspend AIPAC,” said Beth Miller, political director at the advocacy group Jewish Voice for Peace Action. Her group doesn’t spend directly on elections and instead focuses on mobilizing anti-Zionist Jewish voters. “AIPAC is spending this much money because the message they are trying to force down voters’ throats is unpopular.”
The pro-Israel lobby long dominated the discourse on Israel policy before its flagship group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, started spending directly on elections for the first time in the 2022 cycle. But as AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups find their brand growing increasingly toxic amid public outcry over U.S. military support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, pro-Palestine money is shifting the terrain when it comes to election spending.
Simply put, Miller said, “Their message goes further because it’s popular.”
Whether the spending is for or against the pro-Israel lobby, it’s rare to see political ads that directly address U.S. policy toward Israel. For one thing, the topic can be controversial — even if the controversy is manufactured.
When Rebellion PAC, a committee founded to back the 2020 congressional campaign of left-wing commentator Cenk Uygur, ran an ad supporting Abdul El-Sayed and connecting high grocery prices to U.S. support for Israel, the fallout threatened to upend the Michigan Senate race. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., called the ad antisemitic and took it as an opportunity to air her grievances with her former primary opponent, eventually switching her endorsement to Republican Mike Rogers. The PAC originally ran a version of the ad during Uygur’s short-lived 2024 presidential bid.
Voters didn’t seem to be swayed by the controversy, and El-Sayed beat Rogers by a comfortable 7 percentage points. “The drama comes from a handful of elected officials and an establishment that, at best, takes an outdated view of how Israel and AIPAC operate,” said Greg Krieg, spokesperson for American Priorities, which was not affiliated with the Rebellion PAC ad but did produce other ad spots that criticized the U.S. relationship with Israel.
“Not every ad we ran was about Israel, obviously, but the topic came up often because it united Democrats across the party’s ideological spectrum,” Krieg said. “This is not a controversial issue at a grassroots level.”
That new, vocally pro-Palestine PACs are backing successful candidates alongside veteran left organizations is a sign of health for a nascent effort, Miller said.
The midterms were “a test case of: Will this message resonate with voters? And the answer overwhelmingly was yes,” Miller said. “This is a sign of the increasing power and mobilization of the Palestinian rights movement in the political and electoral space.”
Groups like American Priorities and PAL PAC often endorsed the same candidates as progressive bench-builders like Justice Democrats and the Working Families Party. In some cases, the Palestine solidarity movement seemed to breathe a much-needed new life into the electoral left.
The pro-Israel lobby doled out bruising defeats last cycle, after making a promise to unleash its full arsenal to oust critics of Israel from Congress. AIPAC’s super PAC spent more than $25 million to unseat then-Reps. Cori Bush, D-Mo., and Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y. — a quarter of the $100 million it spent on primaries in 2024.
Reeling from those losses, progressive and Democratic strategists went back to the drawing board. Alone, they could never hope to have the same infrastructure or wield the same influence as a group like AIPAC. But together, they could more effectively pool their resources to tap into public opinion shifting further each year in their favor.
One of the new pro-Palestine groups, American Priorities, was born out of a desire to leverage that shifting public opinion against U.S. support for Israel into electoral wins. As the first truly pro-Palestine super PAC, the group spent $8.15 million backing 15 candidates this cycle, 13 of whom won. (The group also considered spending for Angie Nixon, a Florida democratic socialist who narrowly lost her bid for U.S. Senate, but ended up putting the money into another race.)
Twelve of the 20 candidates backed by PAL PAC won their races, including El-Sayed and Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, Adam Hamawy in New Jersey, Melat Kiros in Colorado, and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania.
The growing networks allowed groups like Justice Democrats to get involved in more races. It came back from its losses and had its most successful cycle yet, electing eight of the 15 candidates it endorsed, four of whom unseated Democratic incumbents. The group spent $5.5 million in total this cycle, including $4.6 million on ads across all its races. And it went much further: Last cycle, Justice Democrats spent a combined $3.3 million alone backing Bush and Bowman before they lost.
Together, IMEU Policy Project and PAL PAC spent $2.15 million on ads and bundling for candidates. “We ran on proud anti-genocide and pro-freedom platforms,” DeReus said. “We knew that this was a cycle where that platform could win, and we wanted to be a part of making that happen.”
Meanwhile, AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups saw diminishing returns on election spending this cycle, as they battled waning public opinion and increasingly concealed their spending in races.
“Their names often tell you very little about who’s behind them or what they’re actually trying to do — and their ads almost never mention Israel,” Krieg said. “Everybody is looking at the same polling. We have voters who agree with us, so we’re willing to say plainly what we stand for and put our names on it. When you’re pushing a position that voters don’t support, you’re naturally going to be a lot less transparent about what you’re doing.”
The general public had a greater knowledge of AIPAC’s brand and its role in maintaining a pro-Israel U.S. policy this time around, said Justice Democrats spokesperson Usamah Andrabi. This cycle also saw more candidates willing to translate public agitation against U.S. support for Israel into campaigns, he said, pointing to other efforts he said helped voters understand AIPAC’s role in elections from groups like TrackAIPAC.
“Voters’ awareness and opposition to Israel’s genocide and apartheid was raised so much higher due to grassroots movements and groups that organized against it,” Andrabi said. “We were able to — across every single one of our campaigns — talk about AIPAC as AIPAC, and talk about the genocide as something we wanted to end, and connect the dots for people.”
It’s a stark contrast to 2024, when Justice Democrats met with candidates whose top concerns were avoiding AIPAC’s wrath, Andrabi said. “Even then, in 2024, we were telling these campaigns, ‘Look, there’s no going under, around, behind, over AIPAC. The only way to defeat this lobby is to go right through them,” he said. “The political courage amongst a lot of Democratic candidates and a lot of people within the Democratic Party was just not there in 2024.”
As the 2028 presidential race begins to take shape, the same pro-Palestine groups are preparing to push candidates to meet voters where they are on Israel policy.
“Particularly with Abdul’s victory in Michigan, that win capped off a year that has really proved that Palestinian rights is an asset, not just in safe blue districts, but in the most critical of swing states,” DeReus said. Even President Donald Trump knows how much of a liability being pro-Israel has become, she added, pointing to his late-breaking claim on Election Day that the U.S. would end military support to Israel.
Potential Democratic contenders in 2028 would do well to take that lesson to heart, DeReus said, as groups like hers gear up to push candidates to support an arms embargo, sanction Israel, and recognize the genocide. She said the group hopes to see someone like Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., enter the race, but that it would also support Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., should she decide to run.
In DeReus’s view, “2024 was the last presidential election we will see where Palestinian rights were disregarded.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.text:
Jose Rosito Roca Estrada and his friends were on their way to work in a van on June 27, when a car in front of them slammed on its brakes, forcing them to crash into it and ricochet backward on the busy highway.
Three more cars surrounded theirs, and an estimated 10 to 12 officers poured out. The agents screamed at the men to get out of the vehicle despite traffic whipping by, Roca Estrada and fellow passenger Elvis Manuel Mejia told The Intercept. The stalemate ended with the sound of shattering glass and an asphyxiating cloud of chemicals flooding the car.
According to a new federal lawsuit and photos from the scene shared with The Intercept, federal agents smashed the car’s back windows and “sprayed the occupants with pepper spray through the lowered side windows.”
Officers then dragged a scared and temporarily blinded Roca Estrada from the car. “I was afraid they might be robbing me,” 24-year-old Roca Estrada told The Intercept through a translator. “They did not identify themselves. I was worried they were kidnapping me because they were asking very personal questions.”
The June attack is one of six stories described in a lawsuit brought by several groups — including the American Civil Liberties Union of Virginia, the Washington Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, the Legal Aid Justice Center, and multiple law firms — alleging widespread “unlawful and dangerous” warrantless arrests by immigration officials in Virginia.
On behalf of Roca Estrada and other plaintiffs, the groups are suing the Department of Homeland Security, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Acting Director of ICE David Venturella, and ICE D.C. Field Office Director Robert Guadian. They’re asking the court in the Eastern District of Virginia to force DHS to comply with congressional limits on warrantless immigration arrests and prohibit the agency from making immigration arrests without legally required individual assessments.
“They have a mandate from the Trump administration … to get creative and make arrests, however they see fit,” said Sophia Gregg, an immigrants’ rights attorney at the ACLU of Virginia. “The agents are ill-trained, and even when they do violate the law, there are no consequences.”
Roca Estrada said that the officers demanded to search his pockets, and when he declined, an agent threw him to the ground headfirst and dug his knees into his upper back. He remembered screaming as pain began to radiate through his collarbone. An X-ray reviewed by The Intercept would later confirm it was broken.
According to Roca Estrada and the lawsuit, officers began to punch and hit him in the back, eventually twisting his arm to place him in handcuffs and into the vehicle. Roca Estrada said that nurses who examined him after the alleged assault told him that blood had filled his lungs, and the lawsuit notes he was diagnosed with a broken clavicle and a lung injury. At no point, the lawsuit alleges, did officers ask the necessary questions to determine whether Roca Estrada was deportable or whether he was a flight risk.
Immigration officers are only supposed to make warrantless immigration arrests if they have determined “probable cause” to believe a person is unlawfully present likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. But in an effort to meet the Trump administration’s nationwide quota of 3,000 immigration arrests per day, the lawsuit alleges, the Department of Homeland Security has chosen to pursue an unlawful policy and practice of “arrest-first, investigate-later” — leaving a trail of traumatized victims who should have never been arrested in the first place.
In the first year of the Trump administration, immigration arrests drastically increased in Virginia. According to the lawsuit, in 2025, ICE made “970 arrests each month in Virginia and Washington, D.C. — nearly five times the average monthly arrest volume in 2024.”
Reached by The Intercept, a DHS spokesperson said that agency had “arrested Jose Rosito Roca Estrada, an illegal alien from Guatemala,” using Roca Estrada’s full name even though The Intercept had not provided it, but denied that its officers “fractured a detainee’s collarbone.” The spokesperson did not deny that officials had deployed chemical weapons, saying, “staff relied on their training to gain compliance.”
“Claims that agents did not properly identify themselves are FALSE. When our heroic law enforcement officers conduct operations, they clearly identify themselves as law enforcement,” wrote the spokesperson. “At NO time were any of the detainees thrown to the ground during the arrest. Allegations that our officers fractured a detainee’s collarbone during the arrest are FALSE.”
Six weeks after Roca Estrada’s arrest, 18-year-old Britney Ramirez Corona was home caring for her 4-year-old sister in Norfolk, Virginia, when she found out ICE had detained her fiancé, his brother, and his brother-in-law.
It was another traffic stop, and Ramirez Corona, a U.S. citizen and recent high school graduate, had to go pick up their abandoned car. There, according to the lawsuit, an ICE officer demanded her identification, refused to let her get her wallet, and accused her of lying about who owned the vehicle. They handcuffed and pinned her, the lawsuit alleges — leaving her little sister to cry and wander into a busy road.
Eventually, ICE allowed another sister, 15, to come pick up the 4-year-old, then took Ramirez Corona into custody. She sat in “handcuffs, ankle shackles and a waist chain” for hours, according to the lawsuit, until her 15-year-old sister was able to bring her birth certificate — showing she was a natural-born U.S. citizen.
The lawsuit argues that Ramirez Corona’s arrest exemplifies an out-of-control trend of warrantless and often nonsensical arrests. Stephen Miller, then homeland security adviser and now the White House chief of staff, directed agents to “just go out there and arrest,” and the department seems to have complied.
“More than half of all the people ICE arrested in July 2026 did not have a criminal record,” the plaintiffs note. “And more than 500 people detained by ICE since January 2025 are U.S. citizens — another likely undercount — like Ms. Ramirez Corona.”
The same month that Roca Estrada says that federal agents temporarily blinded him, broke his collarbone, and beat him until his lungs filled with blood, Congress approved another $72 billion in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Immigrant advocacy groups warned ahead of the funding vote that additional money for ICE and President Donald Trump’s brutal immigration crackdown would mean more people would suffer a fate like Roca Estrada’s — or worse. The next month, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, both in their cars.
Physicians for Human Rights and the UC Berkeley Human Rights Center documented over 412 incidents of misuse of force by law enforcement agents at immigration protests from June 2025 to May 2026, including the use of chemical irritants like pepper balls and pepper spray — the same family of weapons Roca Estrada and Mejia suspect was set off in their car.
In ICE custody, 52 people have died during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, according to Human Rights Watch, while use-of-force by guards remains largely unknown.
“We have received many more reports of violent use of force against people,” said Jeff Migliozzi, the communications director for Freedom for Immigrants, which runs the National Immigration Detention Hotline, referencing hotline numbers from June and July. “The overwhelming forces of intimidation and fear and retaliation, the M.O. of ICE has not changed. But certainly, as more people are detained, there’s more incidents [of violence].”
The DHS spokesperson claimed that Roca Estrada and everyone arrested along with him were offered medical care but declined, adding that “one of the detainees indicated that he had a prior shoulder injury.”
Roca Estrada tells a very different story.
He says he spent the next month tossed between detention centers in Virginia and West Virginia. Because he was not given a sling, Roca Estrada fashioned one for his broken collarbone out of bedsheets. He said he largely went without medical care despite agonizing pain that prevented him from laying down at night.
Roca Estrada said it got so bad he nearly fainted, at which point he was taken to a hospital.
“After medical personnel offered to document his injuries and consult a forensic physician, officers abruptly removed him from the hospital and returned him to detention,” the lawsuit alleges. “For weeks thereafter, Defendants failed to provide the promised follow-up care.”
According to the lawsuit, none of this should have happened because Roca Estrada never should have been detained in the first place.
The suit alleges that immigration officers never asked the 24-year-old “about his immigration history, whether he possessed lawful status, where he worked, how long he had lived in Virginia, whom he lived with, whether he had family or community ties in the United States, or similar questions to assess whether he was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”
Other stories in the lawsuit follow a similar pattern. Catarina Rebeca Us Lopez, a 24-year-old woman from Guatemala, was detained in Centreville, Virginia, during a traffic stop around 6:00 a.m. with her husband. She alleges that masked officers blocked her car at a traffic light and forced her and her husband from the vehicle.
The officers falsely claimed that her husband had a deportation order, according to the lawsuit. But when her husband asked questions about the stop, Us Lopez alleges an agent pepper-sprayed him in the face and threatened to draw their weapons.
According to Us Lopez, officers did not “inquire about her immigration status, ask where she lived, inquire about her family, ask about her ties to the community, or otherwise conduct any individualized investigation concerning whether she was lawfully present in the United States or likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”
Instead, she claims that officers ignored her as she explained that she had work authorization and did not have a deportation order in place, and allegedly mocked her requests for answers and legal assistance.
For Roca Estrada, his physical injuries and trauma left him unable to work for a month. While he was detained, he also lost his apartment and had his personal belongings sent back to Guatemala without his consent, according to the lawsuit.
“The way that I was arrested … and the immense pain that I had to go through during this whole experience,” said Roca Estrada. “What happened to me was not just.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

A Rogue DA in No-Man’s Land
A strange case of prosecutorial misconduct during a murder investigation in the Oklahoma panhandle.
In January 2025, I accepted an odd freelance assignment. A Florida-based trucker had received an unusual speeding citation while traveling through the panhandle of Oklahoma, which she had offered as a tip to numerous local media outlets. My mission was to investigate the trucker’s claim that the ticket represented nefarious goings-on in the part of the state known as No Man’s Land, owing to its 40-year-stint as stateless territory in the 19th century.
The trucker turned out to be right. Years before, the local district attorney’s office had assigned its drug task force the ancillary duty of writing deferred-prosecution-agreement (DPA) tickets to truckers. The task force was a kind of 20th-century posse, run by the DA and fueled by civil-asset-forfeiture laws, which amounted to the legal robbery of drugs and money by law enforcement. A DPA is a reverse bribe: If truckers caught in speed traps agree to pay a hefty fine directly to the DA, the charges go away. In theory, drug task forces seize sums of money that implicate criminal organizations. Speeding tickets seemed like peanuts. But the trucker I spoke with was asked to pay $360 for a violation that carried a $160 fine—going 11 to 15 miles per hour over the speed limit of 45. Because of the load she was carrying, she told me, she was driving well below even that.
There was a bigger problem with this arrangement than the fuzzy math: DPAs for holders of commercial driver’s licenses are prohibited under federal law. In short, the tickets weren’t shady-but-legal asset forfeitures but actually illegal shakedowns, and who knew how many of them had been written? I traveled to the panhandle to interview the head of the local drug task force, a man who had once been indicted on an embezzlement charge after being accused of staging a fake robbery to explain the mysterious disappearance of $2,600 from a separate drug-task-force office in Ardmore, in southern Oklahoma. Eventually, I learned that over a period of six years, the panhandle drug task force had written approximately 6,000 DPAs, sending more than $2 million straight into the coffers of the DA’s office.
I had my story. But something strange happened as I began to write it: The head of the task force called me to say that the DA of Texas County, George “Buddy” Leach, had canceled the ticketing program outright. The executive director of the local journalism outlet that had assigned the piece to me said it might have been the first time in his 35 years that something had changed before he published an article.
The reversal was curious, and there was only one hint as to why it had happened: The head of the task force told me they had canceled the ticketing scheme because they were concerned that negative publicity would affect Leach’s ability to prosecute a high-profile murder case.
The sudden collapse of a lucrative ticketing scheme operated by a sketchy law-enforcement outfit that had more in common with the Wild West than the modern world led my investigation to unexpected places: to cattle ranches far from Oklahoma, to the highest offices of state criminal justice, and to the remnants of a violent anti-government cult born in a nether region of the country that not long ago wasn’t part of the country at all.
In April 2024, five members of a small, cultish anti-government prayer group known as God’s Misfits were arrested over the deaths of two Kansas women. Little is known about the origin or beliefs of God’s Misfits, apart from their adherence to a vague Christian ideology and that the group, consisting of a handful of members, met weekly at a private home. In 2023, one of the members who would be accused of the murders filed a manifesto-like document in a court proceeding that lashed out at the United Nations, vaccines, government regulation, and genetically modified foods.
The killings followed a fierce custody dispute and wild accusations of child sexual abuse against one of the women who were murdered. As subsequently reported by outlets ranging from The Washington Post to the BBC, the crimes came to light when the 16-year-old daughter of Cora Twombly, one of the alleged killers, contacted the police. Grisly details emerged: Twombly had forced her daughter, CW, to clean blood from a vehicle used in the crime and had once put CW, then 15, in a bulletproof vest in anticipation of a shootout that never happened.
The publication of my article about the ticketing scheme triggered a flood of tips about corruption in the Texas County DA’s office. I received too many e-mails to keep track of, and there didn’t seem to be any reason to pay special attention to the story known as the God’s Misfits Murders—or, more simply, the Kansas Moms Killings. Then I was contacted by national media outlets that were planning to cover the murders. I agreed to an interview because many of the people I had written about—Leach and the head of the drug task force—also appeared in the God’s Misfits story. But for almost a year, I remained oblivious to the details of the murders. There were plenty of other stories of corruption to keep me occupied, most prominently a car crash that involved one of the agents of the drug task force and resulted in the death of a young Guatemalan girl and her grandfather.
In the summer of 2025, I was introduced to Lisa and Coby White, CW’s stepmother and biological father. The Whites, who were themselves witnesses in the God’s Misfits case, had been awarded full custody of CW after arrests were made in April and May 2024.
The Whites told me something troubling. They had evidence, they said, that Leach, in violation of a standing protective order, had been facilitating contact between CW, whom he described as the case’s key witness, and her mother, Cora, whom he had accused of murder.
This was puzzling. I described the evidence that the Whites had told me about to an attorney I called, who was incredulous.
“Why would he want to tank his own case?” the lawyer said.
It wasn’t the first time I had stumbled across prosecutorial misconduct in Oklahoma. In 2024, I pitched an article dissecting the oral arguments in the Supreme Court case Glossip v. Oklahoma, which hinged on exculpatory evidence that state prosecutors had withheld. Glossip was an infamous death-penalty case that had attracted the attention of the likes of Dr. Phil, Sister Helen Prejean, and Kim Kardashian.
The prosecutors were caught dead to rights. Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond publicly admitted that the state had erred, and he refused to defend a decision by the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals to uphold Richard Glossip’s conviction. The Supreme Court was forced to recruit a ringer to defend an indefensible position. Predictably, the court ruled that Glossip deserved a new trial and that the OCCA should have no further say in the matter. “Because ample evidence supports the attorney general’s confession of error in this Court, there also is no need to remand for further evidentiary proceedings at the OCCA,” the 5–3 decision read. (A new trial is scheduled to begin on December 7.)
I admired the stance that Drummond took on the Glossip case; it was a far cry from the prosecutorial misconduct that appeared to be characteristic of the Oklahoma legal system. This was particularly true in No Man’s Land, where the stories of corruption I investigated through 2025 peeled back the curtain on a culture of legal impunity that Oklahoma media had tended to ignore. As I’d heard it said around the newsroom, “No one cares what happens in the panhandle.”
I communicated with Lisa and Coby White for months, hoping to gain access to the evidence they said they had, but they were hesitant. On the one hand, they knew that Leach was doing something wrong and that he was complicating their efforts to protect CW. On the other hand, they worried that their evidence might provide ammunition to defense attorneys.
Months later, they decided to trust the system rather than share evidence with a journalist. A live meeting wasn’t possible: The Whites were ranchers and lived at a significant distance from Oklahoma. It was calving season; births and the needs of newly born calves precluded a more than 10-hour drive to Oklahoma City. So they authorized me to approach Drummond’s office on their behalf and inform the authorities that they had evidence. In March 2026, a Zoom meeting was set up with the head of the AG’s criminal division, Jimmy Harmon, with a specific purpose: The Whites would describe, but not share, their evidence. If that information was found to be compelling, a subsequent in-person visit would be arranged.
During their meeting, the Whites counted off a string of uncomfortable revelations. Leach had admitted that he had deep personal ties to Cora Twombly’s family. He had initiated contact between Twombly and CW, in violation of the standing court order. He had shown little concern when Twombly, roughly eight months after she was arrested and while in jail, had established and funded a bank account for her daughter. The Whites reported alarming statements that Leach had made in their presence about the family of one of the victims, and they recalled discovering a handwritten note in which Twombly had informally addressed him as “Buddy.”
The Whites told Harmon that they and their attorneys had been left scratching their heads at Leach’s behavior. Consistent with the Oklahoma habit of ignoring corruption in the panhandle, Harmon shrugged off most of what they said, but he agreed to talk to Leach.
A month later, Leach attacked me and the whites in a panicky blog post on the DA office’s official website that would soon elicit a public rebuke from a panhandle judge. The April 14 post was an attempt to control two separate stories: both the fatal car crash that I had been investigating, and what the Whites had told Harmon about Leach’s communication with CW. The post severely mischaracterized the Zoom call and distorted basic facts of the God’s Misfits case.
“The stepmother, Lisa White, told [a] reporter that a no-contact order exists between Twombly and her daughter,” Leach wrote. “I am not aware of any such order.”
“He was in the courtroom when it was ordered,” Lisa told me, scoffing. “He knows.”
Court documents back her up, verifying that a protective order exists. Issued five days after the murders, the emergency order stated, “Petitioner/Mother, Cora White [Twombly] shall have no contact, electronic, physical or through third parties with the minor child until further Order of this Court”; just over three weeks later, the prohibition was extended.
There was no reasonable explanation for Leach’s claim that he was unaware of the order. In fact, the Whites’ first interaction with Leach, they said, came on the day the order was put in place. Leach had organized an entourage of eight officers to carry out one of the order’s few provisions: that CW be able to retrieve personal belongings from her home.
But whatever confidence the Whites might have had in Leach crumbled as Cora Twombly’s mother, Evalyn Moore, attempted to relay messages between her daughter and granddaughter.
Public-records requests unearthed letters from Moore to CW and text conversations in which Moore conveyed messages from Twombly to her daughter, disparaging Coby and Lisa White. But the problems had begun well before then, Coby said. The Whites did not initially object to the contact between CW and her grandmother, but as it became clear that Moore was discussing the case and sharing messages from CW’s mother, the Whites turned to Leach to find out whether these contacts were in violation of the protective order—the one he would claim to know nothing about.
When the Whites returned to the panhandle in December 2024, a bombshell dropped in the form of added detail about the extent of Leach’s connection to Cora Twombly: His own parents had been close friends with Twombly’s grandparents—Evalyn Moore’s parents—in Boise City.
Leach himself had described the two families as “close,” Lisa said.
During the Whites’ visit, Leach conducted a private interview with CW, who is still a minor. The Whites recounted to me what CW had told them of the more than two-hour exchange: A small portion of the conversation was dedicated to CW’s potential testimony, but most of it was about Cora Twombly and Evalyn Moore. Leach praised Twombly, telling the Whites that she was a good mom who had gotten mixed up with the wrong people.
The Whites told Leach that in the months since the murders, they had become acquainted with the family of one of the victims, Veronica Butler. Leach could not forbid contact with Butler’s family, but he expressed his preference for the family of the other victim, Jilian Kelley, because they were “good people.” He went on to malign Butler’s family. “He told us to stay very far away from them,” Lisa told me, “because they were trailer-park trash basking in their 15 minutes of fame.”
Studies on prosecutors gaming the system to secure convictions, as in the Glossip case, are far more common than studies on prosecutors going light on defendants because of personal conflicts of interest. A 2024 report on prosecutorial misconduct in Oklahoma from the Oklahoma Appleseed Center for Law & Justice in Tulsa focused on Brady violations, in which prosecutors fail to turn over evidence favorable to defendants. The report’s authors lamented a lack of prosecutorial oversight in Oklahoma, writing, “The citizens of Oklahoma have largely been asked to ignore and bypass the gross misconduct and indefensible administration of our criminal justice system for decades.”
In a 2017 Boston College Law Review article that did look at prosecutors compromised by conflicts of interest, the authors argued that prosecutors may make poor legal decisions because of political or pecuniary interests—that is, running for office or seeking fame through book sales—but they struggled to articulate a concrete solution. Even in states where an attorney general or governor is empowered to remove a district attorney—in Oklahoma, DAs do not serve at the pleasure of the AG or governor—the authors did not see removal as a viable solution. “Other executive officials are not better situated than the prosecutor who has declined to recuse himself,” they wrote. “The other officials are probably less knowledgeable about the relevant facts.”
In the God’s Misfits case, the evidence of improper contact was voluminous. Four months after the killings, Evalyn Moore had begun telling her granddaughter that the problem was not CW’s mother, arrested for murder, but her father and stepmother. “But your DAD has custody and it’s his word,” Moore wrote. “Him and Lisa are the only people in the World who wants to keep us apart!”
On Facebook Messenger, Moore relayed messages to CW that Twombly had sent to Moore from prison, claiming to speak on Leach’s authority.
November 28, 2024: “Mom says she loves you and is thinking of you.”
December 3, 2024: “Your mom talked to Judge [sic] Leach about your situation…. He is going to visit with you when you are in Guymon.”
December 8, 2024: “When Judge Leach talks to you, you have to tell him how bad things are…. The DA has no problem with you talking to me. That is what he told your mom.”
The Whites recalled a remark from one of the DA’s office staff during the December 2024 visit, claiming that Evalyn Moore was in the DA’s office frequently and appeared to have direct access to Leach. When I reached her by telephone, Moore admitted that Leach’s mother had worked as her accountant. Confronted with evidence of her text exchanges with CW, she quickly ended the call. “I don’t want anything,” Moore said. “I don’t want to talk to you.”
Leach’s April 14 blog post had taken particular note of a birthday card that Twombly had sent to CW in early 2026.
“Actually, that was the second birthday card,” Lisa said.
The blog post claimed that Leach and the Whites had reached an agreement: His office would review correspondence from Twombly and forward it to the Whites, if appropriate. “Absolutely not,” Coby said. “There is no communication that we had with Leach that could have been interpreted in this way.”
I drove 10 hours to visit the Whites and examine a one-line missive on Leach’s letterhead instructing them to deliver a birthday card to CW. “Under no circumstances would that be appropriate,” Lisa said. A year later, another card arrived. This time, tucked inside, there was a notably casual message from Twombly to Leach: “Buddy, per your request, I am sending this card for [CW] to you for your approval.”
In the weeks leading up to the announcement of her plea deal—only one of the five God’s Misfits defendants has been sentenced; two, including Twombly, have entered into plea agreements; trials for the other two are scheduled for 2027—Twombly and her mother established a bank account for CW, ostensibly to give her access to funds associated with cows owned under CW’s name. It was an unusual amount of money for a teenager, Lisa said, but Leach had dismissed any concerns: “He said, ‘Oh, isn’t that kind of her to think of her daughter?’”
The Whites’ attorneys—the couple had spent more than $30,000 on lawyers’ fees, even though they were just witnesses—saw the bank account differently. “They were like, ‘This cannot happen! It’s witness tampering. She’s buying a witness,’” Lisa said.
But there was an even more shocking statement in Leach’s imperious blog post: He claimed that Lisa had told a reporter—me—that his office intended to force CW to testify in the upcoming trials in violation of Twombly’s plea agreement. “Never said that to anybody,” Coby said.
“Why would he put us on the witness list and then throw us under the bus?” Lisa said.
Conflicts of interest aside, Leach was strongly rebuked on July 30 by Texas County District Court Judge Jon Parsley over his April 14 blog post. The post was cited in a June 19 motion from Tad Cullum, one of the God’s Misfits defendants, whose capital-murder case is set to go to trial early next year. Cullum argued that Leach had violated a 2024 gag order.
“The Court finds that the statements to media and blog post by the state did violate the express terms of the order,” Parsley said in his ruling. “The Court reprimanded the State and Ordered that they re-read the [gag order].”
Leach’s blog post remains publicly available. Leach did not respond to an interview request, and the offices of the Oklahoma attorney general and the State Bureau of Investigation refused my requests for comment.
But Leach’s actions are neither an isolated nor an atypical case. Nationwide studies reveal that prosecutorial misconduct is as difficult to define as it is to investigate and punish. A 2023 survey of judges found broad agreement on the most egregious forms of illegal or unethical prosecutorial behavior, but a frustrating lack of consensus on what other behaviors should result in investigation and possible sanction.
“Why is it that prosecutors are seldom disciplined, often in the face of ample evidence?” the survey’s authors wrote. “One reason may be that judges and others within the system do not agree on what acts of prosecutorial discretion constitute willful or intentional forms of misconduct.”
Furthermore, a number of the judges who responded to the survey suggested that whatever flaws the system may have should be addressed by the system itself. “In my opinion,” one judge said, “often the response to bad prosecutors needs to come from voters, the defense team, and the bench.”
Cora Twombly’s plea agreement was for a life sentence with a possibility of parole after 30 years for each of the two murders, with one of the sentences suspended depending on her good behavior.
“It’s a sweet deal,” Lisa White said. She believed that Leach had put his thumb on the scale to secure Twombly a better sentence than the others—such as Cullum, who’s facing the death penalty for the same crime. Under Oklahoma’s 85 percent rule, which requires the perpetrators of serious crimes to serve at least 85 percent of their sentence, Twombly could be released after serving 25.5 years.
“There’s consequences that need to be paid,” Coby White said. “She’ll be 70-some years old when she gets out.”
But Lisa questioned whether the punishment matched the crime. “I don’t know,” she said. “Does only one of the murders matter?”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: South London Gallery director Margot Heller to leave role after 25 years
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Joe Ware
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years. Over this time the institution’s physical footprint has more than tripled and visitor numbers increased tenfold, according to a gallery statement.
Heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser. She will retain a connection with the gallery, curating the Dutch artist’s Mark Manders’s first solo exhibition at a London institution, opening at SLG on 23 September 2027.
“After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career,” Heller said in a statement.
“From the day I took up the role, I saw an opportunity to build an institution that could be internationally acclaimed for its contemporary art programme, and deeply embedded in its local community. I have stayed true to that vision ever since.”
Serge Ramin, the chair of the gallery’s trustees, described Heller as “a visionary curator and cultural leader”, adding: “She leaves a museum that is artistically ambitious, rooted in its community and physically transformed.”
Heller’s tenure encompassed two major building projects with 6a architects: the conversion of a neighbouring house and construction of an education studio in 2010, followed by the opening of the former Peckham Road Fire Station in 2018.
The fire station was donated in 2014 by the artist Raqib Shaw, whose identity was initially withheld. Its conversion cost £4m. Heller told The Art Newspaper in 2018 that the gallery had not been actively seeking to expand when the building was offered.
A garden designed by Gabriel Orozco opened in 2016, while Art Block, the gallery’s free space for children and young people on the neighbouring Sceaux Gardens estate, opened at its current site in 2017.
The artist and SLG trustee Alvaro Barrington said: “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own.”
He added: “Her commissioning of the Orozco Garden should be considered one of the most important architectural interventions in the UK.”
Exhibitions Heller has worked on during her tenure include solo presentations by Steve McQueen, Rashid Johnson, Oscar Murillo, Michael Armitage and Christina Quarles. The gallery was a joint winner of Art Fund’s Museum of the Year award in 2020.
Before joining the SLG, Heller worked at Southampton City Art Gallery, becoming its director, and as director of exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery. She was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2014.
The gallery became an independent charity in 2003, having previously been managed by Southwark Council.
Joy Gregory, an artist and SLG trustee, said of Heller in a statement: “As a local resident and artist, I am enormously grateful for the extraordinary legacy she leaves behind and excited to see what she does next.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Who Decides What Matters? The Jensen Huangs of the World or the American People?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Stephen Crowley
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Who Decides What Matters? The Jensen Huangs of the World or the American People?
Why we need greater democratic control over how society’s vast wealth is invested.
Two seemingly unrelated scandals captured the country’s attention last week: Jensen Huang’s downfall as CEO of Nvidia following an alleged honey trap, and a technical glitch that led to the sudden grounding of all flights in the United States. The impacts of both scandals are stunning on their own, but their juxtaposition—of cutting-edge technology against technological obsolescence—underscores a profound imbalance at the heart of our capitalist economy.
There is much to unpack in the Nvidia scandal beyond the sex and espionage: a single individual, a centibillionaire, running a multitrillion-dollar enterprise as if it were a small business, yet one that is at the center of an AI bubble whose bursting could reverberate throughout the global economy. Nvidia’s monopolistic control over a vital technology places it at the very core of the promised AI revolution. Where will that technological revolution lead? Will AI cure cancer or lead to human extinction? The possibilities appear endless. As the acronym has it: FAFO.
Meanwhile, in the skies, actual lives are already at stake, with over 3 million people flying in and out of US airports every day. No tech revolution here: These lives rely on copper wires and (only recently retired) floppy disks, technology said to hark back to the 1980s. The risk here is not hypothetical. Besides the numerous near misses, 67 lives were lost last year in the nation’s capital when a passenger plane collided with a military helicopter.
Avoid the distraction of Trump’s incompetent appointees’ failing to reassure us about the safety of air travel, or the partisan recriminations over funding for the FAA in Washington. Both miss a larger point: Who ultimately decides what matters most?
If one were searching for a succinct definition of capitalism, two words might suffice: “Capital decides.” Capital decides where investment should flow and what is considered “valuable,” as capital inevitably seeks to amass yet more capital.
The alternative is greater democratic control over how society’s vast wealth is invested, shifting it toward the values that the public holds dear.
As I write this in Washington, DC, I hear planes taking off from that same airport where those 67 lives were lost. That airport is named, ironically enough, for Ronald Reagan, the president who fired striking air traffic controllers in 1981. The air traffic controllers then were demanding not only better pay but also an end to outdated equipment, chronic understaffing, overlong hours, and workplace stress.
The crushing of that strike decimated America’s labor movement—one of the few checks on the power of capital—and ushered in the era of neoliberalism, freeing markets from government regulation so they could invest wherever the profits are greatest. Hence the world we live in now.
How different would our world look if people could vote on how trillions are invested?
Should they go to data centers? Based on the midterm elections, the votes on that score are already in. Or should investment go to ensuring safety in the air? How about healthcare for all? Or perhaps retiring some of the $1.7 trillion in student loan debt? As we imagine the possibilities, there will be inevitable limits and trade-offs. But let the deliberations begin.
Then again, we can continue to trust the brilliance of people like Jensen Huang to make those decisions for us. Will AI lead to a bright new economic future for all or a job apocalypse? Let’s FAFO!

https://www.propublica.org/article/faith.title: I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life.
https://www.propublica.org/article/faith.author: Beth Nakamura
https://www.propublica.org/article/faith.text:
About eight years ago, I was assigned to photograph the sentencing of Travis and Sarah Mitchell, a couple with deep roots in an insular faith-healing sect outside of Portland, Oregon.
The Mitchells, as members of the Followers of Christ, adhere to a doctrine that forbids medical care. Instead, followers rely on healing through faith. So when Sarah Mitchell gave birth prematurely to twins in 2017 — and both gasped for breath in their first hours — the couple didn’t rush them to an emergency room. Instead, they turned to prayer.
One twin, Ginnifer, lived for four hours, each one a struggle. The family eventually sought medical care for her surviving twin sister, Evelyn, but only after the county’s deputy medical examiner arrived at the location of the home birth and learned, though not right away, of Evelyn’s existence. Even then, he had to seek help from police, who arrived at the Oregon City home and told reluctant family members to take the struggling infant to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.
The Mitchells pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide in the death of their infant daughter, Ginnifer, and to criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for her surviving twin, Evelyn. The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to ProPublica and The Oregonian’s recent requests to be interviewed.)
Today, my memory of the sentencing is more montage than detail. But I remember the crowded gallery, the couple in black-and-white-striped prison clothing, and their prison sentence of more than six years. Evelyn, who within days of her birth had been placed in the custody of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, another couple in the Followers of Christ, wasn’t present. She remained in the couple’s permanent care.
The Mitchells went off to prison, and I went on with my life.
Such is the grinding rhythm of the daily news cycle. So often I see people on their worst day — and then never again. Stories don’t really end, of course, but my role as a photojournalist is limited. I’m an observer rather than a participant, seeing mostly slivers of the human experience that offer only a window into the whole. It’s rare that I get to see what happens next.
Never would I have dreamed that the surviving baby in this case, Evelyn, would be someone I’d later come to know and care about through my work. But that’s precisely what happened eight years after that courtroom scene played out, when I began documenting the lives of Evelyn and her parents, the Phillipses. (In a legal filing in an ongoing case relating to Evelyn’s custody, the Mitchells criticized the Phillipses for allowing her to participate in our coverage.) The resulting story, a collaboration between ProPublica and The Oregonian, is one of several recently published about faith healing and the Followers of Christ church. It intimately explores the Phillipses’ journey out of the sect and illustrates how changes in Oregon state law — in contrast to neighboring Idaho, where the Followers have a handful of churches — have led to a reduction in child deaths.
To spend time around 9-year-old Evelyn is to behold a luminous, magnetic force of nature. It’s impossible to imagine this same girl as a premature baby so small that the only items that fit her were doll clothes purchased from the supermarket toy aisle.
Series Timeline
For months, as I documented Evelyn’s life — from her baptism to her home life to doctors’ appointments — my journalism colleagues worked on their own pieces of our project. Teresa Mahoney, video editor at The Oregonian, produced a video introduction to the story that included a sequence of footage recorded by body cameras worn by police officers who stood outside Evelyn’s grandparents’ house that night, at first nudging, then ordering, Evelyn’s family to get her to the hospital. Each time I viewed it, as I watched the officers politely letting time slip away, I’d need to regulate my own breathing as I imagined Evelyn on the other side of that door, struggling to breathe herself.
I hope that reporter Noelle Crombie’s words, Teresa’s video and my photographs allow readers to see not only the journey of the couple who are raising Evelyn as their own but also the surviving — indeed, thriving — twin I came to know. That Evelyn is alive at all is, depending on your worldview, a miracle.
My work is all about observing and capturing moments, about freezing time. Here, I was witnessing the unfolding of time. I got to see what happened next.

https://citylimits.org/rent-stabilized-e.title: Rent-Stabilized East Harlem Buildings Fail To Sell At Auction, Leaving Tenants in the Lurch
https://citylimits.org/rent-stabilized-e.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/rent-stabilized-e.text:
Share This Article
Despite the Mamdani administration’s efforts to avoid the auction block, a large portfolio of former Emerald Equities’ buildings went up for sale—but failed to attract any bids at foreclosure auction, throwing tenants into an uncertain future and raising alarm about the health of the city’s rent-stabilized housing stock.
Ideally, “we shouldn’t even be going to an auction,” organizer Sergio Sorza lamented.
Tenant leaders, community organizers, and members of the East Harlem Community Land Trust were huddled in the hallway outside a Manhattan courtroom, still abuzz with the frenzy of a dozen foreclosure auctions that concluded in rapid succession last Tuesday.
They were a bit shell-shocked.
“I’m pissed,” said Vic Washington, a tenant of a building on East 103rd Street included in the auction.
It’s part of a nearly 900-unit portfolio of 39 mostly rent-stabilized buildings, once owned by Emerald Equities’ Isaac Kassirer, many of which went up for foreclosure sale last week, despite the efforts of Washington, her tenant union, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration.
Of the 27 buildings in the portfolio up for auction over the past two weeks, 26 attracted no bids. One building on East 114th Street sold for $826,000, splitting the tenants and throwing their plans—to steer the properties to their preferred buyers, who could work to preserve the apartments—into uncertainty.
It’s another twist in the Mamdani administration’s efforts to intervene in the sales of distressed affordable housing.
“It makes it more challenging, but we’re up for the challenge,” said Washington, who also works at the El Barrio Community Land Trust.
Tenants in five Emerald Equities buildings on East 103rd Street won a rent strike in 2025 before expanding their organizing across the rest of the real estate group’s portfolio and starting a “buyer beware” campaign.
Tenants called for a responsible owner—preferably a nonprofit that would help them turn some of the apartments into affordable coops—to take over. The city took notice, and backed a bid from preservation buyer Spatial Equity.
But the city’s efforts to push for a sale failed, as the creditor, Sabal Investment Holdings, rejected Spatial Equity’s offers of $68 and $110 million in July and October, according to reporting by both City Limits and Gothamist.
If banks holding the roughly $250 million in debt on the properties hoped for a better deal at auction, it didn’t materialize Tuesday. Instead, tenants are back to the drawing board, trying to get repairs on their neglected buildings.
“We are disappointed that one of these buildings was apparently purchased by a third party, assuming this sale goes through,” said Matt Latterner, a staff attorney at Legal Services NYC working with the tenants. “We do have a tenant’s association in this building and we are prepared to stand by those tenants as they seek to get repairs and fight the illegal overcharges.”
‘Going once, going twice… back to the plaintiff.’
At foreclosure auctions, investors can bid for buildings on the cheap, looking for financial upside.
But one after the other, as Emerald Equities’ buildings were announced on consecutive Tuesdays this month, auctions closed without a bid, sending them back to the bank for just $500 apiece.
At auction, bids must clear the “upset price”—a figure that matches the size of the judgement the bank holds. Only one building, 417 East 114th St., a skinny three story walk-up that looks out over Thomas Jefferson park, sold at auction, for $1,000 above the upset price of $826,000.
It was sold to a bidder, “Matt,” who, according to court papers, bid on behalf of 135th Place LLC, a group linked to Isaac Badalov, who owns one other building in Rockaway, according to Who Owns What. Attempts to reach representatives from LLCs associated with Badalov and his business address were unsuccessful.
While the tenants hope the scarce interest from buyers leaves the door open for nonprofit ownership, it alarmed landlords.
The prices of heavily rent-stabilized buildings like those in the Emerald Equities portfolio are flagging. “Nobody wants to own these buildings,” said Kenny Burgos, CEO of the New York Apartment Association.
Burgos’s group says that New York’s rent stabilization policies, including 2019 changes to state law that made it harder for owners to deregulate buildings, have limited landlords’ ability to increase rent to keep pace with expenses and repairs.
Banks are not in the business of operating housing, Burgos said, and are looking for the best deal—but don’t realize just how little interest owners have in these buildings. “The banks are still in this disbelief stage that the values have fallen so drastically,” he said.
But tenants say it’s because Emerald Equities neglected the buildings, destroying their value. They complain about pests, mold, heat outages, and unsafe conditions across the portfolio, which had 2,300 open housing code violations as of this summer.
“I think what we’re looking at is an unprecedented reckoning for how these buildings have been managed,” said Cami Dominguez, a staff organizer with Community Voices Heard.
Washington said that Emerald Equities and the banks have no one but themselves to blame, taking out an irresponsible level of debt, hoping to be able to take some of the units out of rent stabilization—until reforms in 2019 that closed rent-raising loopholes foiled their plans.
“These banks overleveraged their hand. They over-lent to a clearly irresponsible landlord who wasn’t able to properly steward these buildings, and now the tenants are facing the brunt of that,” said Washington.
Nonprofit owners may face some of the same challenges as their for profit peers, with rising maintenance and insurance costs.
“Purchasing or rehabbing rent stabilization is hard. The amount of money in it is really hard,” said Brian Peters, executive director of the El Barrio Community Land Trust. “So anybody who’s going to commit to it, it’s got to make financial sense. And clearly, for a for-profit entity, it’s not making sense—99 percent of people [are] saying this doesn’t make sense to buy at these prices.”
The mayor’s original plan makes sense to Peters—have a preservation buyer come in, with city support, and spin off some of the buildings on East 103rd Street for a community land trust, which would own the land and govern it through a resident board, managed by El Barrio.
Putting distressed rentals in the hands of community groups and trusted nonprofits is a pillar of Mamdani’s housing plan—and he just signed a bill, the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, that may open up more opportunities for groups like Peters’ to buy.
“The goals are different. The money is different,” said Peters. “For non-profits, it’s just used to maintain the building. It’s not going anywhere.”
But groups like his need financial support from the city to be able to afford the high costs of preserving housing.
The mayor’s office has intervened strategically to try and push vulnerable portfolios of housing to preferred buyers, as they tried earlier this year with more than 5,000 rent-stabilized apartments formerly owned by Pinnacle Realty.
Those efforts have seen mixed results. Even when sales don’t go their way—as was the case with the Pinnacle units—tenant unions say their organizing helped them extract key concessions from new ownership.
But the scale of the problem in rent-stabilized housing, according to Burgos, outpaces the city’s resources to preserve them.
“Lost in all of this is that tenants get stuck in limbo,” said Burgos.
“Policy after policy ignores the underlying math,” he added. “[The mayor] will not be able to intervene and scale to every building…that is a futile effort.”
What’s next for tenants?
Going to auction throws tenants into another round of uncertainty, and each day in ownership limbo is another lived in poor conditions.
With most of the buildings back in the bank’s hands, tenants hope to resurrect their vision of a preservation buyer and a community land trust. A court-appointed receiver currently manages the buildings.
“We might not today have the power to influence the sale, but the majority of tenants coming together to understand the conditions and chart their own path forward, that’s what the tenant union is doing,” said Dominguez.
With little to show from the foreclosure, tenants are hoping that Spatial Equity’s $110 million offer now looks more appealing to the banks.
“It’s just adding extra steps, but the fight is still one and the same,” said Sorza, who works for the nonprofit Community Voices Heard.
For tenants in 417 East 114th St., the lone property that sold, the uncertainty is compounded by their uncoupling from the rest of the portfolio.
“We said ‘buyer beware’… we’re going to be on their necks,” said Washington. “Whoever buys these buildings is going to inherit a lot of violations, a lot of work that they’re going to be doing, and a whole lot of organizing that’s been behind each and every tenant in this building.”
Where the Mamdani administration and Spatial Equity want to go from here remains to be seen. Spatial Equity head Teg Sethi did not respond to requests for comment.
“The Mayor’s Office is proud to support the tenants of the East Harlem Tenants Union as they organize for better living conditions and more control over the future of their homes,” said Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants’ leader Cea Weaver in a statement.
With Pinnacle’s portfolio now in private hands and Emerald Equities’ buildings up for grabs, it’s not yet clear if the administration’s plans to steer more affordable housing into community hands will work.
“They’re developing a strategy. It’s in progress,” said Dominguez.
When new owners Summit, who bought the Pinnacle portfolio, agreed to make repairs in bankruptcy court, the Mamdani administration claimed a partial victory.
Washington said she isn’t ready to call that a win.
“Let’s get the show on the road. Let’s get these buildings fixed,” she said.
“The amount of concessions that some of my neighbors have had to make is more than enough,” Washington added. “Some of us, some of my neighbors, don’t have doors. They don’t have ceilings that are working properly. Their apartments are not comfortable. They don’t have cooking gas. They don’t have heat. I think we’ve made enough concessions.”

https://citylimits.org/betting-platform-.title: Betting Platform Kalshi Pledges $1M to NYCHA Health Careers Program, Amid Gambling Lawsuit With State
https://citylimits.org/betting-platform-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/betting-platform-.text:
Share This Article
Kalshi’s million dollar commitment will support the NYCHA Health Corps, which offers public housing residents a pathway to jumpstart health careers.
A career training program for the city’s public housing residents is getting $1 million from an unusual source: Kalshi, the prediction market company recently sued by New York State for allegedly operating as an illegal and unlicensed gambling platform.
Kalshi’s million dollar commitment establishes the Kalshi Public Housing Health Fund, and will be rolled out over the next four years to support NYCHA Health Corps, a program run by the New York City Housing Authority that provides public housing residents with experience and training in public health careers.
“I’ve been in elected office for about 14 years, and I never had a company come to me and say, ‘We want to invest $1 million in public housing,'” said Congressman Ritchie Torres, who announced the partnership with Kalshi at NYCHA’s Andrew Jackson Houses in the South Bronx earlier this month.
Public housing residents currently involved in the program describe it as a pathway to jumpstart health careers—in anything from social work, environmental justice, and even beekeeping—and as a way to give back to their communities.
Still, some advocates expressed alarm at the involvement of Kalshi, which was sued in July by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James, who accused the company of sidestepping its obligation to pay taxes owed by licensed mobile gambling platforms—taxes used to fund public services, like schools and programs for underserved youth.
Ramona Ferreyra, founder of Save Section 9, a coalition of tenants advocating to keep private management companies out of public housing, described the partnership as “wild.”
“My understanding of the issue is that Kalshi is bypassing our tax laws around gambling, and if they are doing that, it means the state is losing revenue,” Ferreyra said. “If the governor and the attorney general feel that Kalshi is causing us to lose revenue, why is a congressman partnering with them and validating their behavior?”
But Torres and public housing residents say the $1 million injection provides critical support for an important public service program.
All of the money from Kalshi will be used on living allowances for public housing residents who participate in NYCHA’s Health Corps program, according to Alex Zablocki, the executive director of the Public Housing Community Fund (PHCF), a nonprofit that NYCHA created in 2016 to facilitate public projects funded by private donors.
“What’s so special about Kalshi’s contribution is that they’re coming in with four years of funding, which gives us confidence that we can continue the program over the next few years,” Zablocki said.
Participants work up to 40 hours each week in jobs that broadly focus on chronic disease prevention, family wellbeing, and social determinants of health.
The program is in partnership with AmeriCorps, and participants receive standardized living allowances of $22,000 over a period of roughly 10 months, which is paid out every two weeks. Interested applicants can apply on NYCHA’s website here.
Now in its second year, the health program will swear in up to 35 public housing residents across the city this December, who will be placed at one of roughly 20 public agencies and nonprofit sites citywide that partner with NYCHA, including the city’s Health Department, NYC Health + Hospitals, and local nonprofits.
“The goal is to place about two-thirds of our graduates into full-time jobs, which could be at any of our health partners,” Zablocki said. Along with access to direct pathways to public health careers, participating residents can also receive professional development training.
“There’s a variety of jobs and careers, and they could also get further certifications or education, for things like social work licenses,” Zablocki said.
Tina Aurice Johnson, a 59-year-old resident of NYCHA’s General Grant Houses in West Harlem since birth, told City Limits she learned of the program through her role as an appointed member to the NYC Environmental Justice Board.
“I got involved in all the work I’ve been doing to improve my community, and help it prepare for extreme weather conditions” fueled by climate change, Johnson said.
Over the last 10 months, she was paired to work as a habitat specialist with The Bee Conservancy, an environmental non-profit that’s focused on saving bees, and manages pollinator gardens across the city.
“All the work that I did in the gardens were on NYCHA campuses,” Johnson said, adding that her role included planting, weeding and learning about bees and soil.
“Through this program I’ve learned so much about public health and I’ve begun to see it as a framework for environmental justice,” she added.
At the announcement of the partnership, Rep. Torres, who was raised in NYCHA’s Throgg’s Neck Houses in the Bronx, described the program as a way for residents to become “healthcare providers who have roots in our community,” and “who have earned the trust of our community.”
“The million dollars from Kalshi is not charity, it’s an investment in healthcare access as a human right,” Torres said.
Kalshi launched in 2021 as the first federally regulated prediction market platform, and allows users across the country to make predictions and bets on outcomes of future events—anything from rates of inflation and unemployment to the weather.
Headquartered in New York City, the company’s vision is to “allow people to capitalize on their opinions,” according to its website.
The recent lawsuit against Kalshi follows an investigation by Attorney General James, which accused the prediction market of being “an illegal, unlicensed gambling operation,” that exposes New Yorkers, including those younger than the legal gambling age of 21, “to serious personal and financial risk.”
Torres told City Limits that “prediction markets are a new technology, and with new technology comes a need for regulation.”
“The federal government has to figure out how we’re going to regulate it, how we generate tax revenue from it, and how we ensure that there’s consumer and investor protection,” the congressmember said. “Those are questions that Congress is actively thinking through.”
PHCF declined to comment on the ongoing litigation, and Kalshi did not respond to City Limits’ request for comment.
Kalshi’s $1 million commitment to the health program follows the company’s $3 million partnership with the nonprofit Housing Works, which aims to expand healthcare access and strengthen community services for thousands of New Yorkers, announced in October.

https://hellgatenyc.com/reuters-guild-st.title: Hundreds of Reuters Journalists Are Ready to Strike
https://hellgatenyc.com/reuters-guild-st.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/reuters-guild-st.text:
Reuters journalists spent Monday voting on whether or not to authorize a strike, after more than a year of bargaining and 11 months working under an expired contract. The result: an overwhelming yes. 
According to NewsGuild of New York, around 96 percent of the almost 300-person Reuters Guild unit participated, and of those voters, 94 percent voted in favor of a potential strike. 
"Our members have given us the authority to call a strike, which is not something we would do lightly," Andy Sullivan, a Reuters reporter based out of the publication's Washington, D.C. bureau, told Hell Gate. "That would involve significant financial hardship for a lot of our members—and also, we're passionate about our work. We would rather not not work, you know. But at the same time, we can't. We need to get paid more than they are offering. It's that simple."
Thomson Reuters did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
