https://www.propublica.org/article/publi.text:
A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies.
“Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them.
Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth.
ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules.
Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers.
Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land.
“These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service.
Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives.
“I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress.
Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority.
“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.”
Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities.
Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes.
The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued.
Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate.
Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.”
The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura, a new bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.
Juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration issues, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020).
Though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.
“On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper. “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.
Central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo says, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”
Sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite, which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, launched in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is currently in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.
“A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales says. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”
The Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” says Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.
Sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.
“There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” says Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”
In El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December), curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra says. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”
Independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea, exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo, will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” says Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation, which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff, a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.
Sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta, presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.
Picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other issues. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he says.
Sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo says. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”
- Sutura, 18 November-22 November, various locations, Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, El Paso, United States

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Teachers Union Fires Legal Shot Over Pension Clawback
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The United Federation of Teachers formally announced its intent to sue the main pension fund covering the city’s retired educators over a pension clawback impacting 183 disabled retired paraprofessionals.
The UFT filed a notice of claim with the city comptroller’s office against the Teachers Retirement System on Tuesday, a required move ahead of filing any lawsuit seeking damages from the city. Union president Michael Mulgrew first disclosed the filing in a delegates assembly meeting on Wednesday evening.
“Yesterday we filed a notice of claim, which you have to do when you’re suing the city of New York. We were trying to get to a resolution, and it’s just something I said, I don’t believe it can be done in a timely manner,” Mulgrew said according to a transcript of his remarks obtained by The City Reporter.
”But we’re not going to sit here and just say because TRS and others made a mistake over 20 years ago that these paraprofessionals are going to have their lives completely upset.”
It’s the latest twist in a controversy that dates to mid-June, when more than 180 retired paraprofessionals were informed by the city’s Teachers Retirement System that it would dramatically reduce their monthly payments by as much as half to recoup a portion from their checks going forward to make up for more than 20 years of overpayments.
In those letters, TRS acknowledged that the pension system, not the retirees, was responsible for the miscalculated payments. At the time, UFT officials suggested they might pursue legal action against the pension fund.
But the question of how to address the overpayments, which by some estimates cost the pension fund about $155,000 a month, have roiled the stakeholders of the fund who have competing interests and opinions on how to resolve the issue.
TRS and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have said that the city has a legal obligation to claw back the overpayments. The UFT and retiree advocates have said that recovery efforts are cruel and that the impacted paraprofessionals should be allowed to keep their pensions because the overpayments were a result of the pension fund’s own error.
“The city is one of many parties when it comes to the stewarding of these pensions,” Mamdani said in August. “The Law Department has come forward and identified this as a mistake that took place over many, many years, and the need for us to be in legal compliance to correct that moving forward.”
Law Department spokesperson Nicholas Paolucci said the notice of claim is “under review,” and a City Hall spokesperson said the Mamdani administration had no further comment. A spokesperson for TRS referred questions to the Law Department.
The teachers union has spent the last several months negotiating a resolution with TRS, which agreed to pause any pension clawbacks until January.
The notice of claim that the union filed this week offers a glimpse into the arguments it plans to make in a forthcoming lawsuit.
In the letters that it sent to the retired paraprofessionals and in public statements, TRS has acknowledged the overpayments resulted from its own error.
The UFT stressed the point in its notice of claim, claiming that under TRS’ governing laws, the pension fund has “discretion to ensure that those least able to afford it are not subject to financial harm due to TRS’s own mistakes.”
The Teachers Retirement System board of trustees is scheduled to have its monthly meeting Thursday afternoon. The board is made up of six members: city Comptroller Mark Levine, three teacher members, a representative for the education department’s Panel of Educational Policy, and an appointee from the mayor’s office.
Levine, the steward of the city’s pension funds, has not publicly said how he believes the matter should be handled and has referred all questions to TRS.
The retired paraprofessionals impacted by the payment mishap all retired early due to injuries they sustained on the job, including brutal assaults by students that required surgeries and physical therapy.
The retirees had erroneously been earning pensions equivalent to two-thirds of their final average salaries when, under state law, retirees who are eligible for Workers Compensation are owed just one-third of their salaries. In June, TRS announced that those 183 retirees should have only been receiving pensions equivalent to one-third of their salaries.
Current salaries for paraprofessionals, teachers aides who often work with children with disabilities, tops out at $56,700 per year. The impacted pensioners all retired from their jobs more than 10 years ago, when the top salaries were much lower.
Several who spoke with The City Reporter in August said they were dropping their doctors and prescriptions due to the pension clawback. One retiree living in Florida said his revised pension dropped to less than $1,000 per month, a loss compounded by more than $38,000 in overpayments the TRS informed him it would collect from future checks.
That retiree, Anthony Delgardio, retired from his job in a special education high school in Brooklyn more than 12 years ago after he was attacked by a student. He suffered a concussion and broken bones and continues to struggle with memory loss and mobility issues. When he first received the letter from TRS informing him of the pension rollback, Delgardio assumed it was a scam. He relocated to his sister’s Long Island home to cut back on expenses and is contemplating selling his home.
The City Reporter described Delgardio’s and other paraprofessionals’ dilemmas to Mamdani in September: “We will follow up on that,” he responded.
A distraught Delgardio described his grim financial situation: “I can’t even buy a toothbrush right now.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Battles Early Flu Surge as Thanksgiving Approaches
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
New York City is seeing a sharp early-season surge in flu cases with infections more than doubling from the same time last year as officials urge residents to get vaccinated ahead of Thanksgiving gatherings.
There were 6,467 reported flu cases last week, up from 2,489 at the same time last year, according to Health Commissioner Dr. Alister Martin. Nearly 12% of emergency room visits last week were related to respiratory viral illnesses, he added.
“Flu season in New York City started earlier than it has in the past few years,” Martin told reporters. “And now, while we don’t have enough information yet to make judgments about why that might be, we are tracking these developments closely.”
The warning comes after a particularly severe flu season last winter, when New York recorded more than 146,000 laboratory-confirmed cases and hospitalizations across the state hit record levels.
More than half of the city’s reported cases during last year’s flu season involved children under 18. City officials have said the surge contributed to major delays in emergency room treatment, including an average 27-hour wait for a hospital bed at Kings County Hospital, as The City Reporter previously detailed.
The hardest-hit area so far is Jamaica, Queens, where 15% of ER visits were tied to respiratory illnesses, according to the city’s Respiratory Illness Data Portal. Pelham and Fordham in The Bronx were a close second at 14%, the data shows.
Health officials aren’t sure why there has been an early spike in flu cases.
More than 360,000 children between six months and 18 years have received their flu shots in New York City this season, according to Dr. Andrea Howard, the deputy commissioner for disease control.
“That number is very similar to this time last year,” Howard said, noting the city doesn’t have complete data on adult vaccination because healthcare providers are not required to report those jabs.
The last time the city saw a surge in flu cases in late October-early November was in the 2022-2023 season.
MORE: A 27-Hour Wait for a Hospital Bed? Why Delays Are Growing at New York Hospitals
Health officials are particularly concerned because the flu, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) typically spread during indoor family gatherings and plane travel, especially when people are bunched together.
They are urging everyone six months and older to get the annual flu vaccine. Additionally, most New Yorkers six months and older should receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine and eligible New Yorkers should receive RSV immunization.
“We’re asking everyone to do their best,” Martin said.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ottoman-hist.title: What the Ottomans Tell Us About Plunder and Capitalism
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ottoman-hist.author: Y. Doğan Çetinkaya
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ottoman-hist.text:
What the Ottomans Tell Us About Plunder and Capitalism
Did colonial plunder create capitalism? Ottoman history suggests not.
Vivek Chibber’s recent interview on the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism and Vijay Prashad’s response in Monthly Review have reopened fundamental questions about capitalism’s origins, colonialism, and the transition from feudalism to capitalism in world history. Drawing on my research into Ottoman history, I want to make the case that societies beyond Europe belong in this history not simply for their contributions to the rise of capitalism in the West but for their own internal transformations.
The origins of capitalism and its subsequent development through colonialism are distinct historical problems. Ottoman history allows us to draw this distinction by examining a transition beyond the northwestern European cases at the center of this debate.
On the central question of this debate, I am closer to Chibber: I support his distinction between the emergence of capitalism and colonial plunder, and his insistence on looking to the internal transformation of feudal society for an explanation. I also accept Robert Brenner’s account of the English transition. My disagreement concerns whether capitalist relations could also emerge from within other feudal societies, before Western economic domination and along different historical paths. I agree with some of Prashad’s criticisms of political Marxism, but that agreement does not extend to his account of capitalism’s origins.
In the Ottoman Empire, too, capitalism developed out of the internal dynamics of feudal society without relying on colonial plunder, and before Western economic domination and the Industrial Revolution. This process transformed both society and the state, later laying the groundwork for internal colonization. Ottoman history thus brings into focus the distinctions between capitalism’s emergence, its colonial expansion, and the rise of the West — processes that Prashad folds into a single explanation.
Wealth Is Not Capital
Chibber’s starting point is that the accumulation of wealth and the emergence of capitalist social relations are distinct processes. A society that possesses vast financial resources does not necessarily organize its production along capitalist lines. Nor does the wealth that colonizers plundered create capitalism on its own.
Chibber acknowledges that once capitalist relations have emerged, such wealth can accelerate their development. Supporting his argument about capitalism’s origins therefore does not require denying colonialism’s importance in its subsequent history. On the contrary, it allows us to ask within which social relations, and at what historical stage, colonialism acquired that importance. The crucial advance we need to preserve in the debate over capitalism’s origins is the shift from explaining it through the quantity of wealth to explaining it through the character of the relations of production.
Here the meaning of primitive accumulation becomes clear. Before asking how enough money accumulated to finance investment, we need to explain how producers’ relationships to their means of subsistence and production changed. Capital’s power over production and labor depends on social relations that allow money to function as a social power. The emergence of those relations involves dispossession, coercion, and class struggle.
But we cannot equate all these processes with colonialism. Transformations within feudal society have their own history of dispossession and struggle. To treat colonial plunder as capitalism’s necessary starting point is to subsume the very history we need to explain under a different process. The value of Chibber’s intervention lies in bringing this social transformation back to the center of the debate over capitalism’s origins.
Just as trade existed before capitalism, so did plunder, invasion, and conquest. Their existence alone cannot explain the emergence of capitalist social relations.
We should also note that Chibber does not locate capitalism’s early development exclusively in England. He also includes Holland and other parts of the Low Countries in his account of the transformation of northwestern Europe. I accept Brenner’s account of the emergence of capitalism in England. My objection is not to its validity for England but to ruling out the possibility that capitalist relations could also emerge from feudalism’s internal dynamics in other societies.
Such transitions need not reproduce England’s historical trajectory or institutional forms. Different paths need not contradict political Marxism’s definition of capitalism: the social relations that define capitalism can emerge under different historical conditions and take different forms. This is the case I am making by bringing Ottoman history into the debate. I am not rejecting the explanation of the English transition but challenging the use of its specific forms as a yardstick that excludes other histories of capitalist development.
Chibber also points to northwestern Europe’s stronger growth as one reason to locate capitalism’s early development there. Here too we need to be clear about what the evidence allows us to conclude. It is one thing to explain why certain societies grew faster by pointing to capitalist relations; it is another to claim that capitalist relations existed only in those faster-growing societies. The second proposition does not follow from the first.
A society can become capitalist without becoming a leader in capitalist development. To identify capitalism, we need to establish whether capital accumulation has come to govern production and the conditions under which producers secure their livelihoods. Faster economic growth may be a consequence of capitalist relations, but it is not what defines them.
Nor can we equate the development of productive forces with economic growth or its pace. It involves changes in productive capacity, including productive techniques and the organization of labor, which we cannot reduce to increases in output. Northwestern Europe’s stronger growth therefore cannot by itself establish that slower-growing societies remained feudal or exclude the possibility of capitalist transitions elsewhere. The distinction between capitalism’s emergence and economic supremacy that we defend against Prashad must also hold when we assess Chibber’s account.
Origins and Expansion
Here I agree with Prashad’s critique of political Marxism’s explanatory framework. We cannot confine the history of capitalism to the history of English agriculture. But moving beyond that limit requires more than bringing in societies outside Europe solely for their contributions to Europe’s capitalist development.
In such an account, the rest of the world enters the explanation, but the transformation it sets out to explain remains Europe’s. Changes in those societies’ own relations of production disappear. Overcoming Eurocentrism requires more than adding examples of what the rest of the world supplied to the West. We must also investigate the emergence of capitalism within these societies’ own histories.
Prashad does of course discuss the transformation of labor and social reproduction in colonized societies, so I am not reducing his account to a tally of the wealth that colonizers transferred to Europe. My objection is to making colonial connections the overarching framework for explaining the emergence of capitalism. Explaining transformations under colonial domination does not also explain transitions in which domination played no constitutive role. Colonial relations cannot be the only way we connect societies in a global explanation.
Prashad makes clear that he does not see colonialism as mechanically producing capitalism. His argument is that we cannot understand capitalism as it historically developed — industrial, global, racialized, and imperial — apart from colonial dispossession. Nor does he discuss only accumulation after the Industrial Revolution: he also examines early plantations and transformations in colonial production.
Prashad writes: “If you ignore colonialism and the machine, you do not get the genesis of industrial capitalism, only the emergence of certain social relations.” Yet the Industrial Revolution was itself a historical outcome of capitalist development, and industrial capitalism a further stage in that development. These developments transformed capitalist relations that had already emerged; they cannot serve as the defining criteria for capitalism itself.
Explaining the emergence of those relations therefore addresses the question of capitalism’s origins. It is not simply an incomplete explanation of industrial capitalism. By making a later stage of capitalist development the measure of capitalism itself, Prashad shifts the question from how capitalist relations emerged to how they subsequently developed.
The emergence of those social relations is itself the transformation we need to investigate. We must distinguish their subsequent combination with colonialism, or their development into a new phase through mechanized production, from the causes of their emergence. When that distinction is precisely what is at issue, substituting capitalism’s entire subsequent history for the question of its origins does not resolve the disagreement.
My question for Prashad, then, goes beyond whether capitalism is conceivable without colonialism. The capitalist transformation I identify in the Ottoman Empire is not a thought experiment about what might have happened had colonialism never existed but a historical process we need to explain. Why should capitalist relations that developed without colonialism fall outside an account of “capitalism as it actually emerged”?
Defining the West’s colonial and industrial development as capitalism’s real history, while excluding other paths to capitalism, does not resolve the question of origins. It narrows the history we set out to explain.
The same problem arises in the relationship between primitive accumulation and colonialism. Colonial dispossession can be one means of separating producers from the means of production and accumulating capital. It does not follow that we must define primitive accumulation, as an explanation of the emergence of capitalist relations, through colonialism.
We need to distinguish the establishment of capitalist relations from their subsequent expansion into new areas and their reproduction. Colonialism can play an enormous role in this second process. But projecting that role backward changes the explanation of capitalism’s origins.
My objection to Prashad is not that he discusses colonial dispossession, but that he places this connection at the center of the question of origins. The social conditions under which capitalism emerged without colonialism then drop out of the explanation.
We therefore cannot treat the emergence of capitalism, the West’s global dominance, and the Industrial Revolution as different names for the same problem. The first asks how new relations of production emerged; the second, how the West established its dominance on a world scale; the third, how the technical and social organization of production changed radically. These processes shape one another, but an explanation of one cannot substitute for an explanation of another. Colonialism’s importance to the West’s rise or industrialization does not establish that capitalism originated in colonialism.
We are challenging the use of later developments as founding causes of relations that had already emerged. The early appearance of colonial practices does not establish this causal link either. The fact that two processes unfolded at the same time does not show that one produced the other.
Establishing that requires us to identify the mechanisms through which colonial appropriation brought capitalist relations of production into being. The strength of the Ottoman case lies in shifting the debate from a hypothetical world without colonialism to the question of how these relations actually emerged.
The Ottoman Transition
My argument is that capitalist relations in the Ottoman Empire emerged from within feudal society between roughly 1550 and 1650. After 1650, these relations reinforced one another and became increasingly decisive in shaping social reproduction. This chronology rules out explaining the origins of Ottoman capitalism as a consequence of the West’s later economic domination. It also prevents us from treating the absence of large-scale mechanized industry as proof of capitalism’s absence.
What we need to investigate is the transformation of Ottoman society from within during this period. In this light, we see not a feudal society standing still in the face of a capitalist West but a history in which productive forces developed, relations of production changed, and a new social structure took shape through class struggle.
Recent contributions to Ottoman economic and social history include Mehmet Kuru’s work on Izmir’s regional economy, Mehmet Ali Çelik’s research on çiftliks and agrarian labor, and Önder Eren Akgül’s study of capital accumulation and dispossession in western Anatolia. These studies help illuminate changes in Ottoman production, property, and class relations across different periods.
What drives this transformation is not the first appearance of trade or money, both of which already existed in feudal society. What changes is the relationship between the conditions that allow producers to continue producing and control over the surplus. When merchant capital begins to organize production through credit, the supply of raw materials, and control over output, the movement of capital comes to govern the continuity of production. Producers’ relationship to the market can shift from merely selling what they have left over to depending on it to sustain their livelihoods and production.
The interpretation I am developing in ongoing research concerns how changes in property, credit, and labor relations increasingly placed the continuation of production under capital’s control. Demonstrating this requires more than evidence of expanding trade or growing indebtedness: it requires tracing how class struggle transformed producers’ access to the means of production and subsistence. Competitive pressure is one mechanism to investigate within this process, but we cannot reduce the transformation to producers losing their holdings because they could not compete.
It is in this transformation that I look for the emergence of Ottoman capitalism. The starting point of this explanation is not wealth that colonial plunder brought in from outside but changes within existing social relations. Those changes concern not only who controls the surplus but also how it flows back into reproduction.
As the expansion of production, control over labor, and access to markets intertwine, accumulation begins to determine the conditions of social reproduction. Capital thus confronts producers not simply as a power that buys their output but as a social relation that governs the conditions under which production can continue.
The existence of trade does not prove the existence of capitalism. But it does not follow that merchant capital cannot reorganize production or help transform feudal class relations. An increase in the volume of trade is not the same as the subordination of production to capital. This is not a story of capitalism emerging spontaneously from the continuous expansion of markets but a history of qualitative change in capital’s relationship to production.
The development of productive forces is also part of this transformation. A deeper division of labor, a larger scale of production, connections between different branches of production, and the reorganization of labor all increase society’s productive power even before mechanization. This development proceeds alongside changes in relations of production and struggles over control of the surplus. The conflicting interests of peasants, artisans, merchants, local ruling elites, and the state shape the direction and form of the transformation.
To speak of feudalism’s internal dynamics is not to tell a story of technological progress unfolding on its own. It is to understand capitalism’s emergence as a history in which productive forces and relations of production develop and reshape one another through class struggle. Producers’ efforts to preserve their access to land and means of subsistence come up against the ruling classes’ attempts to extract a larger surplus. The terms of debt, taxation, and control over production take shape through these conflicts.
The outcome of the transition is not a destination that feudal society contained from the outset, but the historical product of struggles to preserve and transform existing relations. The development of productive forces, then, is neither an engine operating independently of class relations nor an outcome that appears only after capitalism has emerged, but part of the social process that explains the transition itself.
The Ottoman Empire’s fiscal transformation is part of this same history. Three changes increasingly tied control over the surplus to relations of capital and credit. The tımar system (rights the state granted to collect agrarian revenues, often in return for military service) changed, tax farming (iltizam) expanded, and the state later introduced lifetime tax farms (malikâne).
None of these institutions, taken on its own, proves the existence of capitalism. But when we examine them alongside changes in production, property, market dependence, and accumulation, they show that the state itself was changing within the same social process. This moves us away from viewing capitalism as a sphere that emerges within society after the state retreats, as much of the literature assumes. The struggles that reorganize relations between producers and those who appropriate the surplus also transform the state’s sources of revenue and its social foundations.
This history does not require the Ottoman Empire to replicate the institutions of the English transition. When we turn England’s specific forms of property and labor into universal criteria for capitalism, we fail to recognize capital’s command over production in other societies.
Treating the transition from feudalism to capitalism as a problem of world history does not mean equating capitalism with trade wherever it occurs. To speak of a transition to the same mode of production is not to insist that every society follow the same historical path. This distinction also challenges the assumption that, once capitalism had emerged, it could take root in other societies only through external diffusion.
Of course, speaking of the Ottoman Empire’s internal dynamics does not mean treating it as a society isolated from the world. Trade, war, and flows of money are part of this history. But the existence of external connections does not show that the West introduced capitalism or that colonial plunder gave birth to it. What we need to explain are the social relations within which those connections operated.
Placing the Ottoman capitalist transformation before the West’s decisive economic influence does not write the outside world out of the story; it changes the direction of causality. The West’s later influence acted on capitalist relations that had already begun to emerge. Nor does their subsequent development under conditions of external dependence prove that their origins lay elsewhere. Dependency cannot substitute for an explanation of origins.
For the same reason, late industrialization is a separate issue. If we measure the existence of capitalism by the prevalence of mechanized production, we end up defining Ottoman relations of production in terms of a technological gap with the West. Yet capitalist societies do not develop at the same pace, occupy the same international position, or enjoy the same opportunities for accumulation. Colonialism can play a decisive role in widening these inequalities and securing the supremacy of particular capitalist states.
Here we move from the question of origins to that of uneven capitalist development, where the colonial accumulation and industrial transformation that Prashad emphasizes acquire explanatory force. But this explanation does not erase histories in which capitalist relations emerged earlier and without colonial plunder. Accepting Prashad’s emphasis on colonialism does not require abandoning Chibber’s distinction concerning capitalism’s origins.
The fact that Ottoman capitalism did not originate in colonial plunder does not mean that the empire stood outside later wars and struggles over the division of the world. Its participation in those struggles and wars as a capitalist state does not show that it owed its transition to capitalism to resources it extracted from colonies abroad. We need to distinguish the state’s later political position from the origins of society’s capitalist transformation.
The same distinction applies to the empire’s long history of conquest. Earlier conquests and relations of taxation do not prove that capitalism emerged from colonial plunder. Empire and capitalist colonialism are not the same historical category. We must reassess the relationship between them as relations of production and the social character of the state change.
From Capitalist Transformation to Internal Colonization
The transformation of the Ottoman state into a capitalist state is therefore the next step in the argument. Capitalism does more than create new sources of profit for particular sections of society. Through control over property, labor, and the surplus, it also changes how the state reproduces itself.
What makes a state capitalist is not that its rulers become merchants or that it builds factories but that social relations become organized around the requirements of capital accumulation, with class struggles unfolding on that basis. Capitalist relations emerging from within Ottoman society deepen alongside the state’s fiscal and administrative transformation. The form of state that emerges from this transformation also begins to view the empire’s vast domains in a new light and to reorganize them accordingly.
It is in the wake of this transformation that I situate internal colonization — the process I call self-colonialism. The Ottoman Empire did not owe its transition to capitalism to the plunder of colonies abroad; as the state became capitalist, it already ruled vast territories and diverse communities toward which it could direct its colonial practices. Its territories in the Balkans, the Middle East, Anatolia, the Caucasus, and North Africa became the terrain on which it established new internal relations of domination. Holding these territories is not the same as reorganizing them as internal colonies, which involved a capitalist state transforming earlier imperial rule to serve new purposes within a new set of social relations.
In this transformation, the state ties civilizing rhetoric to remaking peripheral communities into populations it can govern and tax and whose labor can be controlled. Scholars have explored Ottoman colonialism from different perspectives: Nilay Özok-Gündoğa through resource extraction in Kurdistan, İlkay Yılmaz through security policies in the eastern provinces, and Ella Fratantuono through immigrant settlement. Selim Deringil and Ussama Makdisi examine the colonial outlook and civilizing claims of Ottoman elites. My question here is how these forms of domination relate to capitalism’s origins.
I argue that internal colonization follows the capitalist transformation of society and the state; as it unfolds, it can intensify dispossession and open up new opportunities for accumulation. We can thus establish the causal sequence without denying the relationship between colonialism and capitalism. Internal colonization did not create Ottoman capitalism; a capitalist transformation already underway laid the social and political groundwork that made internal colonization possible.
I am not proposing a single historical sequence valid for all societies, only specifying the direction of the causal relationship we need to explain in the Ottoman case. Here the question is not how colonialism created capitalism but how capitalist transformation reshaped state domination and laid the groundwork for colonial practices.
This sequence does not imply that capitalism emerged without violence. The dissolution of feudal relations and the formation of capitalist relations involved conflicts over producers’ rights to their means of subsistence, their labor, and the surplus they produced. But treating every act of dispossession as colonialism prevents us from distinguishing changes in class relations from the specific history of colonial domination. We need to distinguish capitalism’s origins from colonialism not to downplay colonial violence but to explain the historical connections between different forms of domination.
In the Ottoman case, this distinction allows us to trace the capitalist transformation first, then examine how it extended into internal colonization through state action. Recognizing colonialism’s immense importance to capitalist development does not require locating capitalism’s origins in it. This is the fundamental distinction on which I agree with Chibber and part ways with Prashad.
In the Ottoman Empire, capitalism emerged from within feudal society and transformed both society and the state, and internal colonization followed. This history shows that accepting the analysis of the English transition does not require ruling out capitalism’s origins in other societies.
Writing a world history of capitalism requires us to explain more than the world’s contributions to the making of the West. We must also explain how the world itself changed. We therefore cannot reduce the transition from feudalism to capitalism to an English or European story. Capitalism’s origins belong to a world history broader than the history of Western domination.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/20/m.title: Mayor Mamdani Moves To Curb Truck Impacts With Warehouse Regulations
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/20/m.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/20/m.text:
Last-mile warehouses like this one in Queens are the source of so many problems. Photo: Google Earth
The Mamdani administration says it will reduce the pollution, crashes and health risks associated with large warehouses by forcing the largest facility operators to ween themselves off dangerous diesel trucks with a menu of options.
The initiative, known as “Warehouse Indirect Source Emissions Reduction” or WISER, would affect facilities bigger than 50,000 square feet. Qualifying warehouse owners can chose how to reduce their negative impact, like buying electric trucks, delivering with cargo bikes, building e-vehicle charging infrastructure, installing solar or paying a tax on pollution, according to a draft scope of work put out by the city Department of Environmental Protection in October.
The previous administration supported the goals of the program, but “stalled” the environmental review, said Council Member Alexa Avilés (D-Sunset Park), whose bill created the initiative.
“We are delighted to see things kick off and move,” Avilés told Streetsblog. “Our city is past due if we want to meet our climate goals.”
A public meeting on Tuesday night started a roughly one-year environmental review process which is required before the Council can vote on a policy of this kind. One research analyst called it “funny,” considering the rule is meant to benefit the environment.
“We still do environmental review of programmatic changes, even ones that are intended to benefit the environment. So that’s what’s happening here,” said Sasan Saadat, senior research and policy analyst at Earthjustice, an environmental group pushing for the program. “It is basically seeing if there are any unintended environmental consequences, and it’s also to show what the impacts of a ‘no action’ scenario would be.”
But “no action” isn’t an option, the environmental groups that testified charged, especially for those who live near these facilities.
“Every morning I bike from Sunnyside, Queens to offices in Greenpoint, Brooklyn. And there are sections of my commute where more than half the vehicles passing me on a roadway are UPS and FedEx trucks,” said Willis Elkins, the executive director of the Newtown Creek Alliance. “Currently, there are 16 last-mile facilities along the Newtown Creek and even more are projected to come. We need strong regulations to address the adverse environmental health impacts.”
But these warehouses are filling a need. Ninety percent of goods in the city are delivered by truck and more than 80 percent of New Yorkers get at least a package per week. Delivery is cheaper than ever for consumers and the service is increasingly on-demand. E-commerce companies opened 21 last-mile warehouses since 2018. These warehouses, in the city’s industrial business zones, increased truck traffic on nearby streets, and with it traffic crashes, according to the city Comptroller’s office.
“Now because they are trying to deliver directly to people’s doorsteps and they’re delivering lots of goods to lots of people every day, [the warehouses] are getting cited closer and closer to where people live,” said Saadat.
There are 305 “potentially affected warehouses” in the city that could be regulated under WISER, the majority in the industrial areas of Maspeth, Queens, and nearby North Brooklyn, the South Bronx and Red Hook, Brooklyn, according to the DEP’s market assessment.
Under the WISER program, each warehouse would have to count the number of vehicles using the facility. The number of trips and type of vehicle making the trips will generate a “points obligation” for compliance. That’s where the menu of options comes in: warehouse operators select weighted mitigation strategies that equal its points obligation. Some of those mitigations could help ween the city off trucks.
“There’s a lot of opportunity here to be more creative and flexible in New York City, and think bigger picture than just getting vehicles off of diesel pollution,” said Saadat. “The compliance pathways being considered also includes acquisition and use of cargo bikes, the introduction of locker systems … investment in things like the blue highways system … and the build out of microhubs — systems where you reduce the need for truck trips altogether.”
But critics say WISER won’t tackle the root problem: overconsumption.
“WISER regulates buildings, but buildings don’t drive trucks,” said Miquela Craytor, who worked at the New York City Economic Development Corporation during the de Blasio administration and now runs a consulting business, at the public hearing. “Most warehouse owners don’t control the fleets that visit them, and many of the dirtiest trucks fuel up outside our city. This proposal and program never touches what actually puts trucks on our streets: how much we all buy, and our expectation of free, fast delivery.”
Avilés pushed back, emphasizing that there is no one solution to the city’s freight woes. WISER is just one piece of the city’s freight management puzzle. A new city Council bill would ban diesel powered refrigerated trailers at the city’s largest food distribution center, Hunts Point Market. The Department of City Planning is developing a special permit for last-mile warehouses, another Council bill would force these types of warehouses to directly hire its delivery drivers, and the city just revamped its truck routes.
“We have to do all the things because there is no silver bullet,” said Avilés. “If we purport to care about people and wan’t to keep them health and safe, we’re going to have to continue to pursue this policy.”
New Yorkers have until Dec. 17 to submit written comments.

The Landing, a much-loved Los Angeles gallery, has closed its doors, Artnews reports. The gallery operated in a 2,800-square-foot space on Jefferson Boulevard and represented a roster of both historical and living artists, including Jeremy Anderson, Yevgeniya Baras, Lenore Tawney, Ruth Asawa, and Brenda Goodman.
Gerard O’Brien, the gallery’s founder and owner, posted a short note on the Landing’s website, stating, “We are no longer programming at this location. We are deeply grateful to the artists, collectors, collaborators, and community who have been fellow participants in our engagements. It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery.”
O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an extension inside Reform Gallery, which focused on design. The name came from his placement of the new space at the top of a short staircase. O’Brien moved it into its own space, on Jefferson, in 2015 and opened with a show of painting, drawing, and sculpture by the late California artist J. B. Blunk.
In an Instagram post, he wrote, “End of an era … 22 years of Gallery spaces in Los Angeles, Reform Gallery 2004–2019 … the Landing Gallery 2012–2026 … onwards. thank you Los Angeles❣️”
Maxwell Hendler’s one-night-only exhibition on October 29 marked the gallery’s final show, preceded earlier in the year by a pair of ten-year-anniversary shows devoted to twentieth-century art and design and twenty-first-century contemporary art, respectively. The press release for the shows cited their celebration of “the feeling of the earliest days of the Landing Gallery when two years of exhibitions took place inside Reform Gallery on Melrose Avenue. Exhibiting art in a salon style in dialogue with decorative arts is how tL began.”

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: 'Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall' is a coronation. A performance at Carnegie always is.
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
Bob Dylan was only 22 years old when he first performed at Carnegie Hall’s main auditorium in 1963. But his youth didn’t deter the respect the solo concert garnered. In a glowing review, The New York Times critic Robert Shelton referred to Dylan as “unlike any poet or song writer to be heard today.”
“He is assuming the role of a radical spokesman,” Shelton wrote. “The adulatory reception of his listeners indicated that he was speaking for them, too.”
Echoes of Dylan’s early acclaim resounded throughout Carnegie Hall’s Stern Auditorium decades later, when the singer-songwriter Cameron Winter commanded the stage last December at the grand old age of 23. Winter, a drawling baritone whose talents have been lauded ever since he broke out as the lead singer of the New York rock band Geese, sat at a Steinway & Sons piano with his back to the audience as he performed stripped-down versions of songs from his 2024 debut album “Heavy Metal.” The hall reached its nearly 3,000-person capacity. But the rapt audience listened in near silence, which was only broken by jubilant applause after each of the dozen numbers on his setlist.
The concert was captured on 35mm and 16mm film by the Oscar-winning director Paul Thomas Anderson, whose resulting project — a 72-minute film simply titled “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall” — kicks off its nationwide tour of movie theaters today at BAM Rose Cinemas. The entire country is now invited to weigh in on whether Winter is, in fact, “the next Bob Dylan,” as his supporters have often pondered. Is his prestigious Carnegie Hall concert film the final stamp of approval?
Simon Vozick-Levinson understands the comparison. But as Rolling Stone's deputy music editor, who wrote a September cover story on Geese’s skyrocketing success, he also wonders whether it even makes sense to measure Winter against Dylan.
“Pretty much every songwriter who’s emerged in the last 60 years gets compared to Bob Dylan if they get good enough,” Vozick-Levinson said in a recent interview. “I think the thing that’s most notable about [Winter] is how little he sounds like any of his influences. You can hear little bits of Dylan or Tom Waits or Leonard Cohen in there, but … he sounds like himself, and that’s what’s most impressive.”
So, setting Dylan aside — what about Carnegie Hall? Plenty of artists have played on that stage, but what does it mean for Winter to have done so while recording a live album and performing for the cameras of a celebrated director in the midst of his own momentous awards season? (Anderson captured Winter’s show during a brief break from promoting “One Battle After Another,” which won the Best Picture at the Oscars three months later.)
I recently visited Carnegie Hall to meet with Kathleen Sabogal, director of the concert venue’s Rose Archives and Museum. She gave me a tour of the grandiose Stern Auditorium, descending from the balcony to the parquet level. Gazing upon the rows of lush velvet seats as an audience member, the hall can seem rather imposing. But the curved space is designed to feel intimate from the performer’s perspective. “When you’re on stage,” Sabogal said, “it kind of feels like it’s hugging you.”
Next, Sabogal accompanied me to the museum. After pointing out a few concert flyers — including one for Dylan’s first-ever formal concert, held in 1961 at the smaller, now-defunct Carnegie Chapter Hall; tickets cost $2 each — she showed me a list she had compiled of artists she believed to be Winter’s predecessors as rising stars at the main hall. Joan Baez played her first solo performance there at 21; James Taylor at 22; Neil Young at 25; Joni Mitchell at 25; Carole King at 29 — all of which unfolded between the years 1962-1971, before the explosion of rock musicians who played the hall over the following decade.
“It feels like a pinnacle,” Sabogal said. “It’s an important place to play. Also, acoustically, it’s a perfect hall for singer-songwriters … just playing the guitar or the piano.”
The show was immortalized at the urging of Ariel Rechtshaid, a Grammy-winning record producer and audio engineer who has worked with acts such as Vampire Weekend and Charli XCX. Rechtshaid, an early fan of Winter’s, was struck by the power of his playing.
When Rechtshaid saw Winter at the first of his two sold-out shows at Greenpoint’s St. John’s Lutheran Church in April 2025, he knew he admired the performer’s live sets enough to attempt to record the following night’s show.
“There was a magic in the room that compelled me to go Alan Lomax style,” Rechtshaid said, referring to the ethnomusicologist known for his field recordings of 20th-century folk music. “I showed up the next night with a tape machine and two mics.”
Rechtshaid mentioned Winter while casually hanging out with Anderson (whom he called “my boy Paul”). The filmmaker listened to Winter’s music and told Rechtshaid he was intrigued by the contrast between the studio recording of “Heavy Metal,” which features sparse instrumentation, and Winter’s live performances, which were even leaner. Anderson signed on to capture the concert after it was confirmed Winter had booked Carnegie Hall. He recruited fellow director Benny Safdie and other camera operators to shoot the December show with five Panavision 35mm cameras — cumbersome equipment that Rechtshaid and Safdie said underscored the team’s deep commitment to the task.
On the day of the concert, Anderson asked Rechtshaid whether everything looked good on stage. Rechtshaid remembered looking at the Steinway piano and wondering why it was positioned backward, facing the wall. Anderson said he wasn’t sure.
“Then it was just like, ‘Okay, I guess this is what he wants,’ you know?” Rechtshaid said. “Suddenly we’re filming Cameron at Carnegie Hall with his back to the audience.”
Sabogal, the Rose Archives director, also wondered why Winter sat this way. “But that’s the beauty of Carnegie Hall,” she said. “You don’t have to follow tradition.”
It takes an especially skilled performer to connect with nearly 3,000 people at once — let alone all the theatergoers who will join them a year later. Vozick-Levinson, of Rolling Stone, credited Winter’s enchantment of the Carnegie Hall audience to his “remarkable vulnerability and openness” as a lyricist and performer.
More than 60 years after Shelton referred to Dylan as “an angry young man with a guitar,” New York Times film critic Manohla Dargis reviewed “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.” She described Winter’s demeanor at the piano as “borderline monastic,” noting that he barely smiles or banters with the crowd. He behaves as an “especially serious classical concert pianist,” she writes.
People have spun all sorts of theories online about how Winter’s cult following came to be, given that, as Dargis notes, his music “is an acquired taste.”
But that’s what people said — and continue to say — about Dylan, too. His quirks, off-putting to some, were eventually overpowered by the strength of his songwriting. With that in mind, the younger man’s popularity doesn’t seem all that complicated. Vozick-Levinson put it simply: “It’s just that the songs really are that good.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/20/c.title: City Must Bring Back Successful Lithium-Ion Battery-Swap: Menin
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/20/c.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/20/c.text:
City Must Bring Back Successful Lithium-Ion Battery-Swap: Menin
"It is pretty shocking that no one seems to know why the program has been discontinued. It’s really unacceptable to be honest," said Menin, after asking the panel about the pilot.
A lithium-ion battery sparked this fatal fire in The Bronx. Photo: FDNY
The city Department of Transportation failed to extend a trade-in program that removed dangerous lithium-ion batteries from the streets — a failure that Mayor Mamdani must remedy, Council Speaker Julie Menin said at an “emergency” oversight hearing on Friday.
Menin called out city officials for allowing the $2-million trade-in program to sunset without a replacement. The program allowed around 400 delivery workers to swap their unsafe batteries or e-bikes for versions that are UL-certified — the gold standard for safe bikes and batteries. It is illegal in the city to sell un-certified e-bikes or batteries, but the cheaper equipment is still available through online or black market sales.
As a result, there have been 421 fires, and nine deaths, linked to the batteries so far this year, a dramatic increase from the 268 fires the city battled all of last year.
“This is a crisis of epic proportions,” Menin said at the hearing about prevent battery fires, which was announced after last month’s deadly blaze in Sunset Park. “The Council has passed bill after bill after bill and yet the problem is getting worse, not better. These incidents are more than tragic, they are entirely preventable, and the represent safety failures at the highest level.”
Menin’s comments came after FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said her agency would welcome another trade-in program.
“It is pretty shocking that no one seems to know why the program has been discontinued. It’s really unacceptable to be honest,” said Menin, after asking the panel about the pilot.
Menin reminded Bonsignore that the Mamdani administration does not need a Council mandate to run such a program.
“If we have effective strategies, we need to be proactive and keep using them. So, I want to see that buy-back program go back into effect,” she said. “That was an excellent idea. … So why would we stop it? It makes no sense to stop it, it should continue.”
DOT spokesman Vin Barone reiterated that the prior Council had mandated an end date for the program. He added that DOT is working on launching another program.
“We are actively working with the Council on an expanded program incorporating the lessons learned from the pilot,” he said.
The hearing raised questions about the city’s understanding of the battery-fire crisis. As Streetsblog reported in October, FDNY’s data suggests that the rise in fires has less to do with charging uncertified batteries and more to do with a large swath of batteries reaching their end of life. Structural fires, or fires that occur inside residential or commercial buildings, are down slightly from last year’s 167. The main increase this year is related to fires that occur outdoors, including many that occur in sanitation vehicles.
The FDNY said its efforts to stop the sale of uncertified batteries has been successful, thanks to 843 inspections at bike shops in 2025 and about half that this year. The agency said it now rarely see uncertified batteries for sale.
But Menin was unconvinced: “How can you say they [inspections] have been effective if we’re seeing these skyrocketing numbers?” she asked.
First Deputy Commissioner Daniel Flynn later told the Council that all batteries, even UL-certified ones, can become dangerous with wear and tear.
“Over time, these batteries do get beat up on our streets,” said Flynn. “They’re subjected to the elements, the salt, the extreme heat the extreme cold. … A good battery can become a bad battery If it’s beat up and the casing is broken.”
Flynn even went as far as to say that New Yorkers shouldn’t have a “false sense of security” that a certified device “is 100 percent safe.”
FDNY testified that it supported just one of the seven bills being discussed: a proposal from Council Member Susan Zhuang (D-Sunset Park), that would give the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection the teeth to close a retailer for selling uncertified batteries after two violations instead of three.
The other bills included making it illegal to possess or use an uncertified battery, which critics said would be overly punitive to delivery workers (who may not know they are buying faulty equipment), and requiring sellers to give their customers fire-safe bags to store their equipment (which FDNY said weren’t proven to be effective).
The FDNY stressed that the point of sale is the most effective way to regulate lithium-ion batteries. The agency praised a just-passed federal bill that will force the Consumer Product Safety Commission to create a federal safety standard for such batteries, which could help stop them from entering the country and proliferating through online sales. The bill was introduced by Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-Bronx) in 2023.
Experts say a federal standard is key to stopping unsafe batteries from entering cities.
“[The bill] will help prevent additional deaths, injuries, and property damage that have plagued communities across the country for far too long,” said Gabe Knight, senior safety policy analyst at Consumer Reports. “Despite broad support from consumers, first responders, delivery companies, and the U.S. e-bike industry, passage of this legislation was needlessly delayed.”
