https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Nan Goldin to debut new film exploring nature and extinction in first UK solo museum show in over two decades
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Simon Bainbridge
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
For audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.
What links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.
Rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents new and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.
The show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a new score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.
It accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.
Elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.
For Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas says. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”
• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-
14 March 2027

https://www.propublica.org/article/feder.title: They Were Just Admitted to the Bar. Now They’re Federal Prosecutors. Meet Trump’s New DOJ.
https://www.propublica.org/article/feder.author: J. David McSwane, Pratheek Rebala
https://www.propublica.org/article/feder.text:
In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration.
After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.”
It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor.
Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found.
Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S. attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar exam, public disclosures show.
That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are redacted in government personnel data. But of those ProPublica identified through bar membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a range of schools.
“The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.”
To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S. attorneys.
More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18 months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent, on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows. Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal experts say and court dockets show.
ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.”
Under Trump’s Second Administration, Newly Hired Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Less Experience Than Those Who Departed
The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington, but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors.
Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year, Bloomberg Law reported, the DOJ waived a policy requiring at least one year of experience.
While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan.
“The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’ offices.”
Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding consequences, McQuade said.
“It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.”
While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May. “Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) position.”
As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” None of the recent law school graduates responded to requests for comment.
Shifting Personnel, Shifting Caseloads
The departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in Trump’s second administration marks the largest number of exits two years into a presidential term in at least two decades.
Beyond the personnel turnover, the administration’s priorities have shifted since Trump retook the White House, an analysis of Federal Judicial Center data shows.
As immigration cases shot up nationwide, felony fraud prosecutions fell sharply in key districts. Amid an exodus of prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia, for instance, fraud cases fell 66%. Those cases dropped 14% in the Southern District of Florida, a hotbed for white-collar crime, where many prosecutors have left in protest of Trump’s retribution campaign against people deemed political enemies. Nationally, drug prosecutions have fallen about 10% in Trump’s first 18 months and fraud cases are flat.
Meanwhile, the number of people facing immigration-related charges skyrocketed by almost 50%, clogging the courts and depleting resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices nationwide. Even in border districts where immigration proceedings can dominate the caseload, prosecutions have risen dramatically. For instance, New Mexico and the Southern District of California saw 300% and 125% increases in immigration cases, respectively, the ProPublica analysis shows. In the Western District of Texas, where Bigley and at least two other recent graduates just became prosecutors, immigration cases have surged at least 36%.
The immigration caseload, including tens of thousands of unlawful-detention cases filed in civil court, has strained the department so severely that the DOJ has drafted hundreds of attorneys from other federal agencies and the military to keep up, former officials said.
Those cases coincided with violent deportation sweeps led by masked immigration agents, who killed U.S. citizens, and the nationwide protests that sprouted up in response. Many of the cases Trump’s DOJ brought against people protesting immigration authorities’ actions fell apart, a ProPublica analysis showed. The news organization also reported how the truthfulness of Trump’s prosecutors has come under question in courts across the country. The DOJ previously said its attorneys “represent the United States with integrity.”
Amid the unrest, ProPublica has tracked nearly 100,000 habeas corpus petitions filed by immigrants arguing that their detentions were unjust. In each case, an assistant U.S. attorney must defend the government’s position, a task that had some U.S. attorneys reassigning veteran lawyers — experts in financial crimes, civil rights and human trafficking — to immigration. In Washington state, an acting U.S. attorney said he’s so overbooked with unlawful-detention petitions, his office cannot handle every case.
In South Florida, where an exodus of veteran lawyers presaged a drop in fraud and financial crime cases, one former white-collar crimes prosecutor said he and his colleagues could not decline an immigration case without permission from U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who abruptly resigned this month. Before his resignation, Quiñones had led the “grand conspiracy” investigation targeting former officials Trump alleged were part of a “deep state” plot against him.
“Every case takes time, and you want to put in effort, and now you’re wasting your time on cases you don’t believe in or think are unjust,” said the former prosecutor, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he hopes to return to the Justice Department after Trump leaves office. “It affects morale.”
Ramping Up to Fill the Void
In recent months, the DOJ has ramped up efforts to recruit lawyers to replace the lost expertise, government data and the department’s recruiting materials show.
While Justice Department personnel data is kept secret, assistant U.S. attorneys are paid on a unique pay scale set by the attorney general, a quirk that dates to the 1950s and distinguishes them from other civil servants. By tracking the number of people compensated this way, it is possible to obtain broad data on the numbers of assistant U.S. attorneys.
As of January 2025, the department employed about 6,200 assistant U.S. attorneys, the data shows. Then Trump’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency took a hatchet to the Justice Department and other federal agencies. Led by the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, DOGE offered employees financial packages to resign from the federal government by September 2025. About 1 in 10 of all assistant U.S. attorney departures were part of that offer, the data suggests.
The ranks shrank much faster than the department anticipated, former officials said, and it was unable to hire sufficient replacements. By the end of January 2026, the DOJ lost over 1,300 assistant U.S. attorneys and replaced only about 470 of those attorneys.
More Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Departed the Department of Justice Under Trump Than at Any Time in at Least Two Decades
For most of the past two decades, quarterly AUSA departures held fairly steady until Trump’s reelection, when they peaked at nearly 500 departures in the second quarter of 2025.
The DOJ began turning to novice attorneys to fill the empty desks.
In early 2026, a former White House official shared a post on X, the social media platform owned by Musk, that hinted at the DOJ’s growing desperation to find new hires.
“If you are a lawyer, are interested in being an AUSA, and support President Trump and anti-crime agenda, DM me,” wrote Chad Mizelle, who had recently left his DOJ role as chief of staff to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. Mizelle did not respond to a request for comment.
In March, the department hit its lowest numbers since 2014. A month later, the University of Miami hosted an event titled “Lunch & Learn: Entry Level Opportunities with The U.S. Attorney’s Office.” The invite, targeted toward third-year law students, promised a new pathway to become a criminal prosecutor in one of the country’s busiest districts.
“The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida is now recruiting 3Ls for entry-level positions beginning immediately after graduation — an exciting expansion of opportunities for Miami Law students interested in federal prosecution,” the invitation said.
To lure new hires, the DOJ is offering signing bonuses. As of August, due in part to the hiring spree focused on greener attorneys, the department lifted its ranks to about 5,600, still a 10% drop from the end of the Biden administration.
U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee and the presumed chair once Democrats take charge, told ProPublica that the shift toward inexperience is showing in courtrooms across the country.
“They’ve sacked some of the finest lawyers in America, by tradition, and replaced them with a large group of inexperienced lawyers,” said Raskin, himself an attorney.
In his home state of Maryland, fraud cases fell 31% and drug cases nearly 16%, while immigration charges nearly doubled. “Those numbers are jaw-dropping,” he said.
“Good Time to Be a … Criminal”
Jim Fang was among the veteran prosecutors who left.
Fang’s road to becoming a criminal prosecutor was winding. After working in tech for about a decade, he switched careers, and in 2009 graduated from Georgetown Law. He worked in private practice, focusing on intellectual property law, but couldn’t shake a feeling that what he really wanted was “to take down bad guys.”
In April 2020, he got his dream job and was named a federal criminal prosecutor in the District of Nevada. He moved to Las Vegas and, aided by his 11 years handling complex areas of the law, took on tough white-collar crime cases.
After the election, Trump picked Sigal Chattah, a former Republican political candidate, to run the Nevada U.S. Attorney’s Office.
Through court records and sources, ProPublica confirmed that more than 30 staff have left under Chattah’s tenure. The Nevada district is so depleted that for months it didn’t have prosecutors in its Reno office, about 450 miles away. Las Vegas prosecutors were asked to fly there for court appearances, sources said. Chattah disputed the 30 figure but acknowledged that Las Vegas-based staff flew to Reno “to ensure that our federal and local partners had competent and aggressive prosecutors.”
The office dropped cases it had been building as Chattah pushed immigration and politically motivated prosecutions. To ease the caseload, Chattah ordered her civil defense unit, charged with fighting lawsuits demanding cash from taxpayers, to pay out all cases that could be settled for $250,000 or less, multiple sources said. “We were ordered to settle those cases even if they didn’t have merit,” one former assistant U.S. attorney said. “It was just throwing money at a problem.”
Chattah called the allegations that she issued such a directive “patently false” and pushed back on her former employees’ characterizations of her tenure.
“There were attorneys that failed to meet the expectations of competent workmanship with the Department of Justice, and chose to leave or retire, some were terminated,” she wrote. “Former AUSAs who failed to handle an expected case load were replaced with aggressive prosecutors who will keep our state safe.”
In September 2025, Fang took the DOGE offer and went back into private practice as a defense attorney. He suspects the department’s loss of financial crime experts like him will result in fewer successful prosecutions.
“It’s a good time to be a white-collar criminal,” Fang said.
Now facing off against his former colleagues, he’s mostly busy representing clients who’ve filed habeas petitions. He was recently surprised to learn that one of the new hires brought into his former office had just passed the bar. “They’re taking a gamble on them,” he said.
Fang says they may well end up being fine attorneys but added, “There’s no way I could have taken that job and done it well right out of law school.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie's 20th-century sale in New York
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Judd Tully
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.
The hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.
Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.
It wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.
Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).
The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.
The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.
Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.
The evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in May 1986 for $1m.
Gustave Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).
Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.
The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s New York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.
A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s New York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.
Impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).
The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s New York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.
French painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.
Big name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.
The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).
The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.
Backed by a house guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s New York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.
Picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.
The Koons trove, backed by house and third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s New York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.
Willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).
One of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.
It hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).
Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s New York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.
Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export issues, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.
“It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” said Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”
The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Modigliani sculpture heads Phillips's New York evening sale at $44.6m
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sarah Cascone
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $104.4m. That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).
Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, said in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”
Sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordhour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.
It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.
On the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.
The piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s New York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.
The evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.
The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.
Rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.
Helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.
The night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas. 
And while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.
Nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: 2027 Could Be a Breakthrough Year for Criminal Justice Reform
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Janos Marton
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
2027 Could Be a Breakthrough Year for Criminal Justice Reform
Will Democrats seize the moment?
Eight years after passing the historic First Step Act with overwhelming bipartisan support, Congress has a chance to reclaim its role in improving the federal prison system—the largest in America.
The new Democratic Congress has an obligation to address the deplorable conditions in the federal Bureau of Prisons, as well as the racial inequities that continue to characterize the American prison system. The last time Congress passed major reforms was with 2018’s First Step Act, during Donald Trump’s first term and at the height of the criminal justice reform movement. In the years immediately following the global pandemic, a crime uptick that now appears correlated with Covid disruptions threw cold water on all but the most modest reforms. Today, however, crime rates have reached historic lows all across the country. We have come a long way in learning how to prevent violence through community-based programs and lower recidivism rates for people coming home through better reentry support.
Politically, criminal justice hasn’t suffered setbacks the way healthcare, foreign aid, climate, and other policy areas have. The First Step Act is still standing, helping thousands come home from federal prison sooner every year. The reason for this may be hard for some liberals to believe, but it’s because important conservative voices pushed against the Stephen Miller–allied forces in the White House who wanted to weaponize crime as a political issue.
As a progressive nonprofit leader, I’ve been part of many coalitions, and none have been more effective than the bipartisan criminal justice alliance that I work with federally. We’ve defeated numerous bad bills, gotten bipartisan prison oversight legislation passed two years ago, and come tantalizingly close to passing the EQUAL Act. This would have ended the crack/powder cocaine disparity, which embarrassingly is still federal law.
Eleven Republicans in the US Senate supported us then, and more than 100 House Republicans. Think about what those numbers could mean on top of Democrats after the blue tsunami, nearly all of whom support criminal justice reform in name.
That kind of political cover should ease Democratic concerns about blowback. Not that they should be overly worked up anyway. Plenty of Republicans trotted out tired “tough on crime” messaging this cycle, and guess what? That dog don’t hunt anymore. Even in places like New York, where “bail reform” was once considered an electoral epithet, Democrats have reached historic levels of political power compared to where they were when they overhauled that state’s pretrial laws.
I’m not going to pretend that President Trump is a criminal justice champion, even though he did more on the issue in signing the First Step Act than President Biden did. But I’d rather roll the dice on how he’ll respond to, for example, legislation that expands the First Step Act than I would on how he’d react to myriad other issues.
The midterms also swept Democrats into governors’ mansions and state legislative control across the country, including a number of states that have been working toward bipartisan criminal justice reform for many years. Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin have all passed reforms in recent years under fully or partially Republican-controlled legislatures, and we now have a chance to build on this progress with longtime allies of the justice movement ascending to prominent positions within trifecta governments.
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, who is entering his final year in office, has quietly made the case as the nation’s most effective executive on this issue. Other governors are entering 2027 looking to burnish their credentials for Democratic presidential primary voters before announcing. In states where advocates have worked for years to acclimate Republicans to criminal justice reform, Democrats have a chance to lead on an issue that won’t be a bare-knuckle culture-war fight like so many others.
Finally, next year, officials from both parties will have a chance to tackle AI policy in the context of criminal justice reform. The Flock debacle this fall showed that Americans of all ideological backgrounds were properly freaked out about having a private company surveilling their every move. In a country that has historically struggled with the tension between freedom and “law and order,” politicians must now reckon with AI’s ability to supercharge surveillance to degrees we previously thought unimaginable.
We can start by eliminating the “data broker loophole,” which allows the federal government—otherwise not allowed to spy on innocent Americans—to acquire data that private companies hoover up about us when we’re using their apps.
This work, federally and in the states, will be taking place in the shadow of the 2028 Democratic presidential primary, which will informally begin in the months ahead. Many of the floated names have strong track records on criminal justice reform, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Andy Beshear, Pete Buttigieg, Cory Booker, Wes Moore, Gavin Newsom, Jon Ossoff, and JB Pritzker. That means this issue will not be fading into the background but instead should get the attention it deserves until the United States can finally build a criminal justice system that’s smaller, safer, and fairer than the one we have today.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Sara Bennett on Photographing Women With Life Sentences
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Victoria Law
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Sara Bennett, a former public defender, spent more than a decade photographing women sentenced to life, mostly for homicide, in New York State’s prisons. A new book of her photographs, Looking Inside: Women with Life Sentences, traces their lives behind prison walls and, for those who have been released after decades behind bars, their reentry into the outside world. It won the 2026 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards, Jurors’ Special Mention Prize.
Judith Clark was one of Bennett’s clients when she was an attorney. She served 38 years of a 75-to-life prison sentence before then-Governor Andrew Cuomo commuted her sentence, enabling her to receive parole. “For me, this book is a family album,” Clark wrote in the afterword. “I spent half my life with everyone in this book.”
Clark is now out of prison. Many of the other women photographed have also been released—some, like Clark, through parole. Others had their sentences reduced through New York’s Domestic Violence Survivors Justice Act, which allows people to petition the courts for resentencing if the crime they were convicted of was linked to abuse they had suffered. Meanwhile, in New York’s three women’s prisons, 174 people are serving life sentences. As of 2024, one in 11 incarcerated women, or more than 6,800 nationally, were serving life sentences.
The Nation spoke with Sara Bennett as well as two women she photographed. Their interviews have been edited for length and clarity. You can view more photos from the book in The Nation’s December issue.
—Victoria Law
Victoria Law: Why did you choose to focus on women convicted of homicide?
Sara Bennett: The reason I focused on women convicted of homicide is that they all have life sentences, which means that you never know if you’re getting out of prison. You might get a sentence of 25 years to life. That means that, after 25 years, you’re eligible for parole, but you don’t know if you’re ever going to get parole. The women I was photographing didn’t know if they were ever getting out.
Some people, like Karen, had 25 years to life. She was denied parole five times and ended up serving 35 years. When I started this project in 2014, everybody was getting denied parole. The parole board would deny you; you’d come back two years later and you’d get denied again. This happened repeatedly. It doesn’t mean that people weren’t “model prisoners.” They had gotten educations, jobs; they were running the prison—but they couldn’t get out.
I never tell the details of a person’s crime [in the book], but I wanted people to know that they were serious crimes.
VL: How did you navigate permission to photograph inside the prison?
SB: I called the Department of Corrections, said who I was and that I wanted to photograph inside prison. They said, “Yes, theoretically, it’s possible.”
As soon as the prison’s media liaison told me that theoretically, I could photograph, I reached out to women I knew inside prison. I told formerly incarcerated women outside [about the project] and asked if they knew anybody still imprisoned.
I wrote to 30 or 35 women. I went to see them and said, “This is who I am, and this is the work I’ve done. I want to do something inside prison. I would like to come and visit you, and we’ll see if you want to do this. I made a zillion trips before I started photographing.”
VL: Talk about the process of gaining the consent of the people you photographed in a place where consent often isn’t possible.
SB: That’s why I went to visit them first and tell them what I was doing. I had no idea where the work was going to go. They would have to do it because they believed in it, and they wanted to be part of it because there was nothing in it for them.
When I gave them the typical photographer consent form, they were just going to sign it. I said, “Let me tell you what this says because this consent form says that I can do anything I want with these photographs forever except for using them commercially. But otherwise, when you allow me to take your photo, you’re giving me carte blanche to do whatever I want with it, and you need to know that.”
Then I said, “Now I’m going to tell you what I’m going to do because this is who I am. If I take your photo and you decide you don’t want to be part of the project anymore, then you tell me that, and I will never use your photo again. But I can’t take it back if it’s already been in a magazine or online.”
A lot of people knew me as somebody’s lawyer. I had a good reputation as a lawyer who did a lot for my clients. I had already photographed people and had made little self-published books. They’d seen those. And so, if they wanted to be part of it, they wanted to be part of it. But you’re also right that consent is difficult when you’re in a situation where you don’t really have any power over your life. So I think a photographer really has to be cognizant of their own ethics and stay true to those ethics.
When I’m in shows and the curator says, “I want to use this, this, and this photo,” l say, “I have to ask the women.” They ask, “Don’t you have a consent form?” And I’ll say, “Yeah, I do, but I still want to ask them and make sure that they’re consenting to this one.”
VL: You had talked about allowing them to withdraw consent at any time. Did that happen?
SB: Only one person, who is still incarcerated, doesn’t want her photo out there anymore. I photographed 50 women.
VL: Talk about your decision to include their writings.
SB: I really wanted their voices to be part of the book. And their handwriting. [The handwritten pages] make people feel more connected than if they were typewritten.
VL: What are some “do”s and “don’t”s when photographing vulnerable people?
SB: I think you have to be you have to be really really respectful of the person that you’re photographing. You have to be aware that there’s a certain power dynamic and that you don’t want to fall into that power dynamic, meaning you don’t want to push them to do things that they don’t want to do.
Don’t do any harm. If you don’t know enough about the subject that you’re photographing, then find a mentor or somebody in the field who knows. When you’re photographing people who are incarcerated, for instance, there’s always the potential for legal cases to arise and anything they said in the past can be harmful. If you don’t know that, you may think that it’s helpful, but it can be very harmful to them. For example, one of the women told me in her writing that she was innocent. I know that if you go to the parole board and claim that you’re innocent, they’re probably going to deny you because they don’t believe you and think you’re not taking responsibility or showing remorse. I said to her, “If you write this, and you’re going to the parole board next year, and they see this statement; it could come back to haunt you.” But if you didn’t know that [and published it], you unintentionally are causing harm.
VL: What do you want readers to take away from this book—and these photographs?
SB: We don’t look enough at all of the harms in society. Prison is the one I focused on. I wanted to show who people in prison are, the kinds of things that they go through, the hardships they have. They’re full, interesting human beings and that’s what I wanted people to see. Then I want the viewer to decide for themselves. This is how we treat imprisoned people in this country. Do you feel OK about that? If you do feel OK, at least you’re doing it with open eyes. If you don’t feel OK about it, then do something about it.
Taylor is locked up on a 22 to life sentence since her 20s. Now in her 40s, she shared her thoughts on participating in Looking Inside over the prison’s electronic messaging system.
How did you first learn about the project?
Judy Clark [who was a mentor to many during her 38 years in prison] asked me if I wanted to participate and then I helped to find other participants. Sara had sent me one of her previous books. She is an amazing photographer. Even though she is no longer an attorney she is still advocating for the freedom of incarcerated women through her photography. She is invested, passionate and truly cares for us.
Why did you decide to participate in Looking Inside?
I love Sara’s work. She is very passionate about the work she does and committed to humanizing the women she photographs. Her work always tells a story that shifts the narrative and it helps to change the trajectory of how incarcerated women are viewed.
What does it mean to have your portrait shared with the wider world?
It makes me feel seen and not forgotten.
Anything else you’d like to add about participating in this project?
Since I participated, I have had the pleasure of seeing many of the women released. Seeing them go home back to back, I have always felt in a unique way that Sara’s advocacy through that project helped. I always wondered who was next. There are only a few women from her last project still incarcerated, and I pray for those of us still inside to soon be released.
Karen was denied parole five times, extending her 25-to-life sentence to 35 years. She was granted parole at her sixth parole hearing. Bennett photographed her the day before her release and then multiple times after she left prison, including in her first post-prison bedroom.

How did you first learn about the project? And what was your participation like?
I got a letter from Sara that said, “You don’t know me, but I’m a former criminal defense attorney. I’ve turned professional photographer and started a project called Life After Life in Prison. Judy Clark gave me your name. She said it was all over the prison that you made your sixth board and that you’ll be going home soon. I would like to photograph you before you go home, the day you go home, and afterward. I know it’s a big ask because you don’t know who I am, and I don’t. You can say no.”
I wrote her back immediately and said, “I do know who you are. I worked for the Bedford Hills superintendent as her secretary. I worked in the main building right by the front door. I used to see this lawyer coming in to see her clients. One of my friends had you, and you helped get a reduction in her sentence. You came to visit her for free. You helped her go home. So if you come see your clients in prison, I trust you enough to photograph me.”
She called the prison and made arrangements to photograph me the day before I was released. They let us go in the visiting room. There were no visits on weekdays, so it was just us and an officer. She took pictures of me sitting in a chair, waiting to pack out the next morning.
When I got released, I had nobody. Nobody met me. I came out empty-handed. I had my release papers, my ID, and my papers for parole. I got out and there was Sara crouched on the ground with her camera right by the gate. She got a picture of my first step outside with no shackles or handcuffs.
That first year I was home, she followed me everywhere. If I went to a restaurant, she came in and photographed me eating. If I went to do laundry, she photographed me putting the quarters in the machine. She photographed me at Trinity Church. She photographed me at my job interview.
What does it mean to have your portrait and writings in her book?
I love it, because if I can reach anybody else that’s living in a domestic violence situation and thinks that their only way out is to kill their abuser, I want them to learn from me. That’s only a new set of problems, so don’t do it. Don’t be me. I can get you help. There’s resources now.
Now that I have a bigger audience, I can reach people. That’s why I do everything I do with Sara, because I want to reach women who are not OK and who don’t know where to turn.
You’re the only woman in Life Inside to write about your crime. Why did you choose to do so for the book?
If I don’t talk about it, I’m part of the problem. There’s that secrecy. Some of my art is based on that secrecy. No physical violence, emotional violence, financial or sexual violence could exist unless it was secret.
My sister-in-law says to me, “You’ve been out for a long time. Why don’t you just stop?” And I say, “Because there are still people suffering and because my sisters are still in prison. I’ll keep my mouth shut when everybody’s home and nobody else is going in.”

“We Remain In This Nightmare”: Another Letter From the Hell of ICE Detention
It is now over seven months since my son, my husband, and I were detained. It feels like being stabbed in the heart again and again.
Last August, we published a message from behind the walls of an ICE detention center from Maryam Tahmasebi. Three months later, Maryam, her husband, and their teenage son are all still imprisoned—despite being legal permanent residents with no criminal record. (You can find more details about their case here.)
Today, we are publishing a new dispatch from Maryam, who is being held in the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas. We will be publishing additional pieces by her in the months ahead.
How do you keep track of time when it does not move linearly—when days last forever and decades seem to go by in a flash?
I used to think about this as a child. Waiting all day for the hour of cartoons I could watch on TV felt endless, but entire summers were over in the blink of an eye.
These days, I’m feeling the nonlinear passage of time—but for very different reasons.
It is now over seven months since my son, my husband, and I were detained and locked in ICE detention, despite having no criminal records, settled immigration status with valid permanent residency, and no charges of any personal misconduct. (You can read more details about our case in the piece I wrote for The Nation in August.) My son and I are still detained in the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas, while my husband remains separated from us, detained in the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall. And, while there are many horrors in this life of detention, the warping of time has felt especially cruel.
Over seven months. Two hundred and twenty days. Over half a year. Every one of them lived, endured, and marked by harm. In whatever scale I put these numbers, they feel surreal and terrifying. This has been, without doubt, the longest traumatic experience of our lives, and it has felt like an eternity—more than seven months of absolute hell.
Every day I think about my kind, soulful son’s childhood slipping through his fingers. I think about the months of his precious life that his father has missed. Teenage years are full of growth and new experiences, but for the last seven months, my son—a minor who has done absolutely nothing wrong—has been denied that most basic right: the right for a child to have a normal, happy life. He spent his birthday in this horrible place. He has been robbed of the high-school experiences that his friends are having. And he has been separated from his father for over half a year.
I, too, have been violently cut off from my life outside these detention walls. I taught hundreds of undergraduate students and dozens of graduate students every semester. I miss teaching even more than I miss wearing normal clothes or reading books on my phone. I haven’t been able to teach any of my undergraduate classes or my graduate courses for two semesters now. I still don’t know what happened to one of my PhD candidates, who was very close to defending her proposal. My husband has been similarly torn from his own professional academic world.
If you are wondering whether daily life here becomes normal or tolerable, the answer is no. It absolutely does not. There is not a single day that goes by that I don’t have to take a deep breath just to force myself to keep breathing. There is not a single day that I don’t rage, or that I don’t miss my husband—who can only hear our voices once every two weeks for 10 minutes. Not a single day that I don’t need to force my face into submission so as not to let my son know how I truly feel.
Yet, along with the pain, there is resolve. I am a trauma-informed psychologist. This place or the circumstances can’t take that away from me. Every day, I put on my community psychologist hat and do everything in my power, using all the tools in my toolbox, to help other families. To find ways to witness, observe, and break down the incompetent, cruel systems and the dehumanizing policies around us. To help the community that I now live within. Every day, I am also sustained by my extraordinary friends who hold my grief, hold space for my anger, and never leave me alone.
Hanging over this nightmare is one still-unanswered question: why? Who has benefited from this cruelty? Who has profited from the baseless accusations still being hurled around about me and my family? What has been gained by decimating the normal lives of two educators and their child?
And we are far from alone. I am acutely aware of the pain that children are experiencing in this prison of family detention. I see the devastation in their eyes every single day—the sadness, the fear, the distrust, the defeat.
It feels like being stabbed in the heart again and again. But even with horrors abundant and repeating every day, there are instances that stay with you for far longer and cut far deeper than you expected. One happened recently in the so-called “library.” There was a child who looked to be around 5 years old. His mother was trying to write a letter. But she kept being interrupted by her child asking, over and over again, when they were going back home.
The pain I felt in that moment stayed with me for many days. Home. Such a simple, unattainable concept for many. For children, it is a foundational part of their psychological development. It is the cornerstone of their sense of safety and belonging. Taking it away, to me, is one of the many unforgivable sins committed towards children in detention. The mother said nothing in response to the child’s pleas. I know why she kept her face blank and kept typing. What do you even say? How do you explain to a 5-year-old that home is most likely never going to be the same—that there is no going back?
After I wrote my Nation piece in August, I received so many kind responses from people of conscience who heard my plea and responded by reaching a hand out and amplifying our voices. Now I am writing this just under a week after the midterm elections—and, once again, I have been heartened. It was beautiful to see that, across the country, people voiced their disdain for the horrible ICE practices that led to the imprisonment of me, my family, and everyone else detained with us. It was inspiring to see so many people across the country express their opposition to the dehumanization and brutalization of law-abiding people, including lawful permanent residents.

But we are all still here, locked away. The murky immigration laws that allowed all of this to happen are still on the books. We all remain in this nightmare. My family and I are still experiencing unending, unendurable misery created by lies and smear campaigns and executed by a system that we have no power to fight against. What I dream of these days is the same dream I have had all through this ordeal: freedom for my family and a normal, safe life where my child can go to school, and my husband and I can go back to writing and teaching. This, however, is not only about me and my family. I am here with so many other people, and nothing in our day-to-day lives has changed. Nor will it if the pressure stops. No one can go home now and think that we are done because of an election. We are nowhere near the finish line.
Change will require laws that prevent the government from stripping people of their lawful immigration status without meaningful due process and that establish meaningful judicial oversight of immigration detention. It will happen when there are clear laws that prohibit the detention of children and separation of families, ending the horrific trauma inflicted upon thousands of people with zero criminal background every day. Shutting down one detention center, such as Dilley, without changing the laws only means families are being separated and tormented in a different place. No elected official can kick this trauma out of their backyard thinking it will go away. As long as the root cause is not addressed, this can happen in any state or any city, and it can be far worse. The collective psyche can’t hide from this.
There is so much work that needs to be done to repair the broken systems that made these atrocities possible. There is so much work that needs to be done to create better policies that prevent a repeat of any of this. While hope is now possible, healing demands far more than that. Healing sometimes needs opening the wounds and bearing the hurt of looking closely at what has happened. Healing needs us to mourn what we have lost collectively and demands commitment to the healing process.
The scale of damage is vast. The state of our immigration policies is an open wound that we can no longer afford to ignore. This is not pain experienced only by immigrant families, or witnessed only by those of us living through it. It is our collective pain. Regardless of where we live, or whether we have personally contributed to or experienced these injustices, we are all affected by their consequences. And the solution must also be collective. We must acknowledge what is happening, allow ourselves to feel the weight of it, and decide that we do not want to live in a country that treats children this way. We do not want children to be intentionally traumatized or to know the pain of losing their homes and the security of belonging. And with that decision comes action to change policies, systems, and laws.
Now, with people having elected representatives to act on their behalf, it is time for those representatives to act. We need them to put their bodies on the line. We need them to come to Dilley, to witness what is happening, to hear the families, and to advocate for those who cannot make their voices heard. Don’t forget about us. Don’t stop fighting until we are all, collectively, free.
