https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-dsps-.title: Amazon Is Ratcheting Up Its Fight With NYC Delivery Drivers
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-dsps-.author: Alex N. Press
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-dsps-.text:
Amazon Is Ratcheting Up Its Fight With NYC Delivery Drivers
Amazon is warning New Yorkers that a bill making it easier for delivery drivers to unionize will cost jobs and raise prices. The company has already put hundreds of drivers out of work by cutting ties with its contractors.
New Yorkers opening Amazon’s app on Thursday were greeted with a warning: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” A link invited them to “act now to protect low prices,” directing customers to contact their city council members about legislation that would require Amazon to directly employ its delivery drivers.
Amazon rolled out the warnings, which also appear on packages delivered in the New York area, as part of its campaign against New York City’s Delivery Protection Act (DPA), which an Amazon-funded coalition has already spent upward of $8 million opposing. Amazon is warning customers that the legislation would put small delivery companies out of business, eliminate jobs, and delay their packages. The company has not explained how it calculated the additional $5 per order.
The act’s partisans say Amazon’s threats are absurd.
“The Delivery Protection Act would require companies like Amazon to pay a $500 licensing fee every other year and comply with workplace and public safety regulations,” Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s lead sponsor, told Jacobin. “It’s simply dishonest to claim that this bill would require them to charge consumers $5 for every delivery. New Yorkers won’t let themselves be bullied by corporations and billionaires.”
“It’s a slap in the face to hardworking people everywhere,” Tony Rosario, a New York–based organizer for the Teamsters Amazon Division, told me. “You have to have some nerve to try to blame the city council for holding Amazon accountable.” He dismissed the company’s threats to leave the city should the legislation pass. “They’re not leaving New York City,” he said. The city is largely thought to be the company’s biggest market in the country.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani also responded to the warnings Thursday afternoon. “If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council’s efforts to protect workers’ rights and keep our streets safe,” he tweeted. “It’s greed.”
Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash similarly used their apps to campaign for California’s Proposition 22 in 2020, spending more than $200 million to pass a measure allowing them to continue treating drivers as independent contractors.
The legislation Amazon is fighting in New York would change who employs its sprawling delivery-driver workforce. Cabán’s bill would require operators of last-mile delivery facilities to employ their drivers and warehouse workers directly. Amazon currently contracts out much of that work to smaller companies known as Delivery Service Partners (DSPs). The bill would also impose licensing, safety, and training requirements on delivery facilities, with protections for workers whose jobs are affected by the change.
Thirty-four of the fifty-one City Council members have signed on as sponsors, and Mayor Mamdani supports the bill. Council Speaker Julie Menin, however, has yet to bring it to a vote. Councilmembers are negotiating changes to the legislation, including whether to retain the ban on subcontracting, which Amazon is particularly determined to defeat.
When the company began planning its own delivery network in 2013, executives worried that entering the transportation business would expose it to organized labor.
“A primary concern was whether getting into the transportation business would expose them to unions,” executives involved in those discussions told journalist Brad Stone. When Amazon launched the DSP program several years later, it could run its own delivery network while leaving the drivers on someone else’s payroll.
The Teamsters have spent years fighting to establish that Amazon is a joint employer of those drivers and therefore has to bargain with their union. Amazon has threatened to challenge the DPA in court, and the bill is now fueling a steady stream of criticism in the right-wing New York Post. But the legislation could still pass without the requirement that Amazon directly employ its drivers.
The current version of the bill would spare workers years of litigation at the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) to establish that Amazon is their employer and therefore must bargain with their union. That wouldn’t guarantee a collective bargaining agreement, but it would eliminate one of the company’s principal defenses against unionization.
Amazon has funded its multimillion-dollar lobbying and advertising campaign through the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, which operates publicly as New York Delivers. Its advertisements feature DSP owners and drivers warning that the legislation would eliminate small businesses and raise prices. Amazon says that more than forty DSPs in New York City employ over five thousand workers whose jobs could be threatened if the companies were prohibited from contracting with Amazon. The company has also raised the possibility of moving delivery facilities outside city limits.
The Teamsters’ Rosario said the concern is misplaced — and that the bill could help DSP owners too. “They’re being squeezed just as much as their employees are,” he said.
DSP owners are responsible for maintaining and repairing vehicles and bear much of the responsibility when drivers are injured or involved in accidents. Under the existing arrangement, Rosario said, DSPs serve as a “scapegoat” for the company.
Opposition to the bill includes the city’s chambers of commerce and the National Urban League, which has argued that the legislation would particularly harm black-owned delivery businesses. Amazon is listed among the organization’s highest-tier corporate donors, a category representing contributions of at least $1 million.
On November 16, the National Urban League and the Amazon-backed New York Delivers coalition threatened legal action if the bill passes in its current form. Their attorney argued that the legislation conflicts with federal and state law. An earlier memo prepared by Brendan McGuire, an attorney at WilmerHale retained by the Amazon-funded Five Borough Jobs Campaign, argued that the bill could violate federal restrictions on local regulation of motor carriers.
Menin, who supported an earlier version of the bill, has held off on backing the current one. She has raised concerns about potential job losses, higher prices for consumers, and whether the legislation would survive a legal challenge. A spokesman for the Mamdani administration’s Law Department told The New York Times that he was confident the final legislation would withstand legal scrutiny.
The Times also reported that Menin has considered a version of the bill that would license and regulate delivery warehouses without requiring Amazon to directly employ its drivers, though she has not ruled out retaining the subcontracting ban. The New York Post reports that councilmembers are considering requiring warehouse operators to own the delivery vehicles currently owned or leased by contractors. Other details are still being negotiated, including how large a warehouse must be to fall under the law. Sources familiar with the negotiations expect the text to be finalized next week.
“Direct employment is one of the most important provisions of the bill,” Rosario said. He said there had been some discussion of exceptions for truly independent contractors but was adamant that Amazon shouldn’t be exempt from the direct-employment requirement. “There’s no way they’re getting around that language,” he said.
Menin has insisted that the council will regulate Amazon while protecting jobs and consumer prices. On Thursday, she criticized the company’s new direct appeals to customers.
“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote on X. “We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”
“If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong,” she added.
The Teamsters called Amazon’s warnings to customers “extortion by one of the richest corporations in human history” and accused the company of caring about neither its workers nor its customers.
The legislation has attracted support from across New York City’s labor movement, including the Central Labor Council, the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union, the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, and the New York Taxi Workers Alliance. On October 22, hundreds of Amazon workers and Teamsters rallied outside city hall, joined by representatives of other unions, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Teamsters President Sean O’Brien. O’Brien accused Menin of failing to keep her promise to bring the bill to a vote.
“Keep your promises; don’t fall in love with corporate America,” O’Brien said. “Speaker Menin, you need to do what the people want — the people that put you where you’re at.”
The campaign has extended well beyond the rally, with New York City Democratic Socialists of America (NYC-DSA) playing a central role alongside Teamsters Local 804. NYC-DSA has put its electoral canvassing operation to work on the bill, organizing phone banks and sending volunteers door-to-door. By October, they had knocked on more than 11,000 doors and helped bring three councilmembers on as sponsors. In Menin’s Upper East Side district alone, more than 100 volunteers knocked on 2,500 doors in a single day.
Mamdani has continued campaigning for the legislation, too. At the October rally, he pointed to the contradiction at the center of Amazon’s employment arrangements.
“When a driver wears an Amazon vest, drives an Amazon van, [and] follows a route Amazon set and Amazon insists that driver does not work for them, what is that if not exploitation?” he said.
When reporters asked Mamdani about the possibility of dropping the ban on subcontracting and passing a narrower bill, he rejected the idea.
“I don’t think that we need to have a conversation about a new bill,” he said. “I think we have all of the answers in the bill as it currently stands.”
When I spoke with Julie Su, Mamdani’s deputy mayor for economic justice and the former acting US secretary of labor, about the bill earlier this year, she described Amazon’s arrangement as “a business model built on getting all the benefits of labor while disclaiming any responsibility for it.”
“It is an end run around a century of labor protections that have been fought for and won,” she said.
Su also took issue with Amazon’s warnings that the bill would cost workers their jobs.
“It is an age-old argument by corporations who have profited massively off the backs of exploited workers, to say that working people only have two choices: a really bad job in which you’re struggling to get by, or no job at all,” she told me. “We reject that as a false choice.”
Amazon has itself put drivers out of work by cutting ties with DSPs whose employees unionized. Last year in Queens, 105 drivers at Cornucopia Logistics lost their jobs when Amazon canceled its contract with the company. The drivers had organized with the Teamsters and accused Amazon of retaliating against them. Amazon denied it.
In Palmdale, California, Amazon cut ties with Battle-Tested Strategies, a contractor whose eighty-four drivers had organized with the Teamsters in 2023. The NLRB later accused Amazon of illegally ending the contract and refusing to bargain. Drivers at another Amazon contractor in Skokie, Illinois, struck in 2024, alleging retaliation for organizing. Amazon denied retaliating against union supporters.
The DSP arrangement has also cost New York workers jobs when union organizing wasn’t involved. Last week, the company terminated its relationship with Kaizen Management Solutions, a Manhattan contractor whose employees deliver Amazon packages on electric cargo bikes. Roughly two hundred workers learned that their employment would end November 18. Amazon said it had discovered safety violations and fraud involving the recording of drivers’ hours; some workers disputed that explanation.
“This DSP model is about Amazon’s bottom line,” one worker told Streetsblog. “The model that allegedly creates jobs just laid off 200 people right before the holidays.”
“I wish I could tell you I have another thing lined up but I don’t,” he added. “They didn’t even give me a month to figure it out.”
Rosario met Kaizen’s owner, Ezra Tilaye, at a Teamsters picket outside the Delancey Street facility earlier this week. Tilaye, who is from Guyana, seemed as blindsided by Amazon’s decision as the workers. One driver Rosario spoke with had been on the job for only three days; another had just been promoted to dispatcher. Rosario took that as evidence that Tilaye hadn’t known the contract was about to be terminated. For Rosario, the layoffs made a mockery of Amazon’s campaign to defend small businesses, particularly those owned by minorities.
“Are you protecting small businesses, or do you just not care and are pretending otherwise?” he asked.
Menin called the layoffs “terrible” and said that the city would regulate Amazon “in a very significant way.”
Amazon may not need to defeat the bill outright. The majority of councilmembers have signed on, but negotiations could still strip out the requirement that Amazon employ its drivers directly. Similar legislation has already been introduced in Chicago, and worker advocates want to pursue it in other cities. What survives the negotiations in New York could shape those efforts elsewhere.

https://gothamist.com/news/theyre-blowin.title: 'They’re blowing this': Amazon's push against NYC delivery worker bill may be backfiring
https://gothamist.com/news/theyre-blowin.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/theyre-blowin.text:
Amazon issued an ultimatum to New Yorkers on Thursday, warning its deliveries would get more expensive if lawmakers pass a bill forcing the company to hire many of its contract delivery workers as regular employees.
People across the five boroughs who opened their Amazon apps to order dish soap or dog treats were greeted by a new banner ad with the word “ATTENTION” bolded and highlighted in red.
“The NYC Council is considering Intro 518, legislation that could increase fees for New Yorkers by up to $5.00 per order,” the ad reads. “This bill would raise costs just when we need to make New York more affordable.”
But the move appears to be backfiring by antagonizing Council Speaker Julie Menin, who could soon bring the measure to a vote.
Menin, a moderate Democrat who is often viewed as an ally of the city’s business class, in recent days grew noticeably frustrated in her public statements as the e-retail giant ramped up its lobbying efforts against the bill, called the Delivery Protection Act.
“Amazon’s campaign is nothing short of a cynical ploy to trick New Yorkers,” Menin said at a press conference Thursday. “It is a last-ditch effort to try to escape the responsibility to the very workers and customers who have made the firm’s success possible.”
Supporters of the bill immediately cried foul.
“Amazon is a multitrillion-dollar company,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani posted on social media. “If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed.”
“It's a bunch of BS,” said Queens Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, the measure’s lead sponsor. “We knew that they were getting desperate.”
The Delivery Protection Act would ban the third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver packages. Although most of the company’s delivery workers wear blue Amazon vests and drive Amazon-branded vans, they work for independent contractors called delivery service partners. There are more than 40 such companies in New York City, according to Amazon, employing about 5,000 people.
Amazon argues the system empowers small businesses and ensures packages are delivered quickly and at low cost. The company points to a study they helped fund that found the Delivery Protection Act would raise costs for customers by about $400 to $660 a year.
“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written — which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement. The company has threatened to move its warehouses out of New York City if the bill passes.
The banner ad Amazon put out on its app has an “Act Now” button where customers can send emails to city councilmembers. The company said its users sent about 20,000 messages within the first six hours of the campaign launch.
Supporters of the bill argue the measure won’t increase costs for customers, but would improve livelihoods for thousands of delivery workers. Delivery drivers organized by the Teamsters union say the system allows Amazon to escape liability for unsafe work conditions and faulty vehicles. Advocates on the City Council say the bill would force accountability by making Amazon hire its own drivers.
“ There's no world where this common-sense bill would cost Amazon $5 for every single delivery,” Cabán said in an interview. “This is just an example of corporate bullying. They want to bully New Yorkers with junk fees.”
City lobbying data shows the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a group almost entirely funded by Amazon, has spent over $8 million this year opposing the bill.
The scorched-earth PR tactics echo another episode in New York City politics where a tech giant organized its users against proposed legislation.
In 2015, then-Mayor Bill de Blasio and members of the City Council tried to institute a cap limiting the number of for-hire vehicle licenses issued to companies like Uber and Lyft. Uber hired Bradley Tusk, a tech startup PR adviser and investor who managed Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s 2009 re-election campaign, to help sink the proposal.
Tusk describes in his book "The Fixer: My Adventures Saving Startups from Death by Politics," how he flooded the zone with negative TV, radio and digital ads while also ordering his team of lobbyists to “suffocate” individual councilmembers and their staffs. Similar to Amazon issuing a notice to its customers, Uber added a feature in New York known as “de Blasio view” to its app that told users to expect extensive wait times for a car if the legislation passed.
The strategy worked, and de Blasio pulled the bill before a vote. There were about 12,500 vehicles operating for Uber and Lyft in the five boroughs in 2015, according to city data. By 2019, the year lawmakers eventually capped for-hire vehicle licenses, that figure exceeded 86,000. The rapid growth of the e-hailing companies in New York correlated with more traffic congestion and the demise of the city’s yellow taxi industry.
In an interview with Gothamist, Tusk said while Amazon’s strategy may appear similar on the surface, the company was failing to deliver a credible message.
“Nobody believes that Amazon's going to stop delivering in New York,” he said. “So saying, ‘Oh, well, it might be a little more slower,’ or, ‘It might be a little more expensive’ — that doesn't move people.”
Tusk said that Menin could’ve been a sympathetic ear. Instead, he said the negative ads appeared to be driving her closer to politicians to her left, like Mamdani and Cabán, both members of the Democratic Socialists of America.
“Julie is no pushover,” Tusk said. “They’re blowing this.”
While supporters of the Delivery Protection Act like the Teamsters have called for an immediate vote on the bill, Menin has pumped the brakes, saying the legislation needs changes to address legal concerns.
Menin insists the changes won’t weaken the core intent of the bill, but protect it from potential legal challenges. A spokesperson for Cabán’s office said they expect the proposal to come to a vote by the end of the year.
“I have a very clear message for Amazon,” Menin said direct-to-camera during her Thursday press conference. “If you think that that is going to deceive New Yorkers and intimidate the City Council out of passing basic worker and consumer protections, you are dead wrong.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/huang-scanda.title: The Jensen Huang Scandal: A Gift to China Hawks and AI Giants
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/huang-scanda.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/huang-scanda.text:
The Jensen Huang Scandal: A Gift to China Hawks and AI Giants
The exact truth behind Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia remains murky. But one thing’s for sure: it’s been a huge boon to China hawks like Marco Rubio and other enormous AI firms.
Often, when people cheat on their spouses, they get kicked out of the house and strain their families. Not many can say they wiped out $1.8 trillion worth of share value and made the economy wobble.
Yet this is exactly the case with ousted Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang and the scandal surrounding his various infidelities, including to a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy. (Or is she?)
The uncertainty around that question is part of the general murkiness of this entire affair (no pun intended), one tied into a knot of three separate political threads: the economy’s outsize reliance on the artificial intelligence industry, ruthless corporate anti-competition, and the simmering new Cold War with China.
While Huang had a number of infidelities, it’s his affair with business executive Alice Huang that is central to both the global attention this has drawn and to his ouster from the company he had founded over a Denny’s meal with only $40,000 of capital, thanks to his paramour’s alleged role as a spy for the Ministry of State Security, roughly China’s equivalent to the Central Intelligence Agency. Even as the infractions piled up, it’s hard to imagine Huang — a widely admired, politically connected CEO who commanded intense loyalty from his employees — being pushed out of his own company over infidelity if not for the possibility, leaked to the press, that he fell for a Chinese government honey trap.
So it’s notable that no one seems to really know whether or not Alice Huang truly was a spy. CNN reports that US intelligence agencies aren’t actually sure, with some officials viewing media reports alleging that she is as overstating the reality. At the same time, Donald Trump, Vice President J. D. Vance, and Attorney General Todd Blanche have all publicly claimed uncertainty about this central allegation. The Singaporean government went out of its way to explicitly deny The Wall Street Journal’s reporting that its officials had been concerned about her alleged spying for Beijing and investigated it.
Most explosively, The Washington Post reported that the spy claim came from one official in particular: China hawk Marco Rubio, who personally reshaped the CIA’s more ambiguous intelligence into a memo forcefully making the spy allegation and circulated it around the administration all the way back in May, to little effect.
Let’s take a moment now to note how odd it is that the details of that memo then somehow made their way to the press. Let’s also take a moment to note how odd it is that neither this administration, which has zealously investigated and thrown the book at leakers, nor Rubio, who has called leakers “criminals” and once tried to throw some in prison for a decade, seem to particularly care about this leak.
A Win for Hawks
So what exactly is going on here? It’s too early to say for sure. But one thing we can say with certainty is that Huang was long given the side-eye by Washington’s China hawks owing to his unabashed advocacy for doing business with China, his closeness with the president, and the fact that he had used that closeness to get Trump to let Nvidia skirt US export controls and sell its chips to China. For those hawks, who Huang publicly lambasted as carrying a “badge of shame,” this was a grave offense and a threat to national security, with the possibility that China could use the advanced chips to win the “AI race” that this crowd is obsessed with.
Another certainty is that these same hawks have wasted no time in seizing on the affair to push for harder-line policies against China, at a time when Trump had been edging toward a more conciliatory posture with the country, drawing growing pushback from Washington. The Trump administration has now tightened export controls on AI chips in the wake of this scandal, and a consensus is now emerging in Congress to go beyond this. China hawks are making a renewed push to tighten them even further, with parts of a fourth bill doing so now set to be added to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for 2027.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, reportedly the main figure within the administration resisting a crackdown on the export of Nvidia chips, is being publicly undermined by one of his own fellow cabinet members, facing the possibility of being investigated, and may see his head roll over the episode, all as lawmakers demand he clamp down on the chip exports. China hawks “are thrilled right now” and are “gonna win the day,” one Trump official told The Washington Sun, while an economist who backs the stricter controls told the outlet that with Lutnick and Nvidia “sidelined, the center of gravity has shifted to Rubio-world,” since they “were the main opposition to any sort of export controls.”
A Win for AI Monopolists
China hawks aren’t the only ones who stand to benefit from Huang’s ouster. The battle over China’s access to high-end AI chips is, in part, a proxy for a whole other battle being fought within the industry.
The removal of Huang is viewed as a blow to the movement behind open-source AI models — those that the general public can download and tinker with, as opposed to closed-source models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude, where the developer has exclusive control but chooses to make the model available for public use. Open-source models also happen to be mostly the kind developed by Chinese companies, whose cheaper models US companies are increasingly turning to.
Huang also happened to be a major champion for — and, more importantly, financial backer of — such models, probably because the proliferation of more AI models also means more business for Nvidia. One venture capitalist who invested in some of the same start-ups as Nvidia told the Financial Times that Huang getting the boot means “we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers.”
That put him at odds with companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, whose commercial interest lies in trying to dominate the AI market and preventing the spread of open-source models that would make people less reliant on their products. Anthropic has long been an outspoken proponent of the export controls on AI chips that Huang chafed against, breaking from other industry players over the issue by backing the three restrictionist bills included in the NDAA for 2027.
OpenAI, meanwhile, pulled back on its advocacy for export controls, both as Huang’s dealmaking saw it become more financially intertwined with Nvidia and to align more closely with Trump as he came under Huang’s influence, costing China hawks what they had counted as an important industry ally. But Huang’s ouster has “loosened them up a bit,” a source told Politico, with OpenAI now back to arguing in favor of those same three export control bills in the defense authorization bill for next year.
In fact, it goes much further than this. Because filings show that both of these closed-source firms have thrown a small mountain of money into lobbying various arms of the federal government on this issue, including the very two organs — the State Department and the National Security Council (NSC) — that happen to be headed by Marco Rubio, China-hawk-in-chief and the main figure responsible for the spy claims about Huang’s mistress.
Starting from the third quarter of this year, dating from July to the end of September — the period that came after Rubio reportedly circulated his spy allegation memo in May — OpenAI spent a whopping $1.5 million lobbying on issues that included “foreign AI capabilities and national-security risks,” lining up with Politico’s reporting that the firm had started voicing its support for export controls to Congress in recent months. This was a notable shift from 2025: that year, OpenAI’s in-house lobbying outfit had spent substantially less than this amount per quarter and hadn’t lobbied the State Department, nor does that phrase appear as a lobbying issue in that year’s filings.
In other words, it’s not just that OpenAI started pushing for restricting the export of chips right after Rubio circulated his questionable memo linking Nvidia’s CEO to Chinese spying, and that it was that CEO’s removal that had “loosened them up” to do it. They also lobbied Rubio’s own department, and did it just months before that memo mysteriously leaked to the press, forcing his ouster.
There is a similar pattern with the other closed-source AI giant, Anthropic, which, in that same July-to-September period paid several Trumpworld lobbying firms to work on this matter.
One was Navigators Global, which that very same quarter started lobbying Congress on behalf of the AI firm on the export control provisions in the NDAA. Navigators Global’s cofounder happened to be Rubio’s very first chief of staff when he was a senator, while one of the lobbyists who worked on this issue is Andy Keiser, who for fourteen years served in various roles for ex-congressman Mike Rogers, the Trump ally who ran for Michigan’s Senate seat this year and in 2024.
Sit for a moment with the fact that Anthropic was pushing this issue using a lobbying firm closely connected to the very figure arguably most responsible for driving Huang’s ouster.
It’s a similar case with Ballard Partners, founded by a longtime Florida lobbyist who counts Rubio as a friend and where Trump’s recently ousted chief of staff Susie Wiles was managing partner for years before joining up with Trump in 2019 — a firm so connected that one departed Trump official has charged it “controlled” White House policy. In the third quarter, it started lobbying for Anthropic on “advocacy regarding US policy regarding AI” to the tune of $380,000, including at Rubio’s NSC, for which it employed two recently departed Trump national security personnel, one of whom had just worked at Rubio’s State Department.
Another specifically Rubio-connected lobbying firm used by Anthropic for this was Continental Strategy, one of whose managing partners is Alberto Martinez — a “trusted advisor” to Rubio who worked in various roles for the former senator over the course of a decade, including chief of staff and senior strategist on his first Senate race — and which promoted Wiles’s daughter a day after Trump hired her. Martinez was among the lobbyists Continental used to lobby agencies that included Rubio’s NSC (from April to the end of June) and then Rubio’s State Department (in this just-passed third quarter) on “AI development and national security,” for which it was paid a total of $300,000 by Anthropic for these periods. Both Ballard and Continental’s roles were first reported by ZeroHedge, but this is based on my own separate analysis of Anthropic’s 2026 lobbying disclosures.
It’s remarkable that at the same time the interests of Rubio-led China hawks and firms like Anthropic were crossing over, the company was literally employing Rubio’s own former loyalists to lobby the government bodies he was in charge of.
This is on top of the $230,000 that Anthropic paid over the past year’s three quarters to Fierce Government Relations — a firm with a couple of Trump-connected employees — to lobby Congress and the Office of the President on export controls and the NDAA bills; another $180,000 over the same period to Aquia for the same issues; $60,000 to the Democratic firm Avenue Solutions to lobby Congress on the NDAA starting in the third quarter; and the nearly $6 million it spent in-house in that period to lobby on issues that included these topics. In that last case, it used a longtime staffer of Sen. Patty Murray, who had been demanding in recent months that Trump impose these stricter export controls.
So in summary, the two closed-source AI firms that view China’s AI industry as a threat to their own bottom line have done the following: lobbied heavily for these China-squeezing export controls this year; appear to have in some cases ramped up their lobbying on this after Rubio circulated the sensational but unproven claim that led to Huang’s booting; hired former staffers from Trumpworld to do that lobbying; and in particular, hired lobbying firms and used lobbyists with long-standing connections to Rubio specifically to do it.
The picture that emerges is of the unmistakable — some might say convenient — convergence of interests between Washington’s China hawks and AI giants, and the downright eerie overlap between the offices and personnel of what are in theory meant to be two different entities. Even more convenient, all of this has come to a head just as one of these AI giants, Anthropic, was set to embark on its initial public offering, which it did yesterday, raising $81 billion in the largest stock-market debut on record.
Like I said: convenient.
A Bet Without Consent
Less convenient is another thing we can say for sure, which is that, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO aside, this entire saga is causing heart rates to spike.
That’s because Nvidia — and, owing to his domination of the company and personal role in every deal it struck, Huang himself — is a load-bearing force for an industry straining to stay standing up, passing out the necessary capital for flagship AI firms, start-ups, the building of data centers, and the neo-cloud firms that provide the computing power for firms that can’t build their own. In fact, Nvidia effectively came to the rescue of one of those neo-clouds, CoreWeave, when its bonds recently entered distressed territory after skeptical investors started dumping the company’s debt en masse.
Huang’s ouster throws the industry into uncertainty as it waits to see, first, if any one person is able to actually fill Huang’s shoes, and second, if the person who does has the same kind of appetite for risk that he did. So far, indications are that the interim CEO does not, and with the firm about to be dragged through an acre of thorns in the form of congressional hearings and other scrutiny, it would not be surprising if it embarks on a more conservative approach going forward.
That doesn’t necessarily mean that the AI industry is headed toward an imminent crash. But this is all spectacularly bad timing given the spate of setbacks and growing investor doubts it’s been weathering, the last one being an incoming US Congress dominated by politicians who ran and won on restricting the data centers that AI firms need to keep being built to stay financially viable.
At this point, you might stop to marvel at the absurdity that — because of the way we’ve structured our economy, the way it’s intertwined with US foreign policy, and the corrupting distortion of the Washington revolving door and influence-peddling — one man’s horniness threatens to bring down the US economy and ramp up conflict between two nuclear-armed powers. It’s just one of several layers of absurdity to a situation and industry that, without ever being consulted on it, we have all as a society been roped into staking our collective future on.
Huang is not the first or last CEO who will have a personal scandal that can be exploited by shadowy forces with their own ulterior motives. But because of the nature of the AI industry, whichever executive draws embarrassing headlines next, it’s gossip that we’re all going to have to care deeply about.

https://gothamist.com/news/group-looking.title: Group looking to open NYC's primaries tries again, over Mamdani's pushback
https://gothamist.com/news/group-looking.author: Brigid Bergin
https://gothamist.com/news/group-looking.text:
A group seeking to end New York City’s closed primaries filed a new batch of 75,000 petitions with the City Clerk this week, marking its latest push to open city primaries to voters of all parties.
New York City is famously blue, with registered Democrats outnumbering Republicans six to one. So the city’s Democratic primaries tend to be the unofficial general elections for many candidates, cutting out a wide swath of voters who are not registered Democrats.
The group Unite NY is trying to put a question on the ballot asking voters to change that system ahead of the next mayoral election in 2029. They argue the current closed primary system disenfranchises more than 1 million city voters each cycle during a crucial step in the municipal election system.
But they have a big opponent in Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has said he thinks the city’s current primary system is working well. He won his party’s nod last June with 56% of the vote, beating former Gov. Andrew Cuomo by nearly 13 percentage points.
Their proposal would make the June primary a preliminary election, open to all registered voters, who would then use ranked-choice voting to pick up to five candidates in order of preference. The top three finishers would advance to a final election in November that would also use ranked-choice voting.
The change would likely mean a general election with multiple Democratic candidates because of the party’s significant enrollment advantage. This is often the case in neighboring New Jersey cities like Newark and Jersey City that operate nonpartisan municipal elections.
“ Voters who pay taxes should participate in all elections, period,” said Anthony Thomas, the executive director of Unite NY. “And right now, we've got 1.1 million and growing New Yorkers who can't participate,” he said, a reference to the number of registered voters who are not affiliated with a political party. Those voters are referred to by the Board of Elections as “blanks.”
Proposals to reform the city’s partisan election system have been debated for decades, particularly among the city’s independent voters. And as the ranks of unaffiliated city voters continue to swell, good government groups have also voiced support for opening primaries to all registered voters.
But the Mamdani administration, which was swept into office with record-high voter turnout, has remained opposed to these changes. This is Unite NY’s second attempt this year to force a question on the ballot about opening up all city elections to unaffiliated voters.
Typically, voters weigh in on ballot questions set by a charter revision commission, made up of appointees by the mayor or the City Council. Mamdani appointed a commission earlier this year that ended up putting five ballot questions before voters. Voters adopted all five earlier this month.
But another way for New Yorkers to get a question on the ballot is to gather thousands of signatures from registered voters here in the city.
Last July, Unite NY filed more than 45,000 petitions trying to force a question onto the ballot about the city’s election system. A month later, the city clerk tossed the group’s first set of petitions after the Board of Elections said they contained an insufficient number of valid signatures. Unite NY filed a lawsuit over the decision and asked the court to order the board to review the signatures line by line. The parties were last in court in October for oral arguments.
A spokesman for the city Law Department said it was still awaiting a decision in that case. The city clerk did not respond to a request for comment on the new batch of petitions. The Board of Elections declined to comment, citing the ongoing litigation.
Unite NY is a nonpartisan political organization that has been advocating for election reforms statewide for nearly a decade. The group was founded by Martin Babinec, a technology entrepreneur and venture capitalist who lives in the small city of Little Falls in Central New York, more than 200 miles from New York City. Voting records indicate Babinec, who is registered as unaffiliated with a party, spent hundreds of thousands of his own dollars on the cause.
Government reform advocates in the city say Unite NY is ultimately fighting to strengthen the city’s democracy.
“Unaffiliated voters are actually the fastest-growing segment of the electorate,” said Ben Weinberg, director of Public Policy at Citizens Union, which supports open primaries. “They're young. They're diverse. They're politically engaged. They want to vote in the primaries, but under the current system, we are not letting them be part of our local democracy.”
He pointed to recent voter analysis from the New York City Campaign Finance Board that found that voters under 30 made up nearly a quarter of the unaffiliated voters, which means those voters could not participate in the primary election.
Reinvent Albany, another nonpartisan nonprofit focused on government reform, found New York City is an outlier among the 100 biggest cities when it comes to holding closed primaries for its municipal elections. Only six big cities — Buffalo, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Charlotte, Baltimore and New York City — hold closed primaries.
The mayor’s opposition seems to be unchanged. Even though Mamdani won his own party’s nod last year, Cuomo, a fellow Democrat, was still able to challenge Mamdani on an independent ballot line named “Fight and Deliver” in the general election by collecting petitions.
Then-Mayor Eric Adams, who was the first sitting mayor in modern New York City history to be criminally indicted, also appeared on the ballot on two independent lines. A Gothamist investigation found fake and fraudulently obtained signatures on his petitions.
Cuomo won 41.3% of the final vote, to Mamdani’s 50.8%. Adams, who suspended his campaign just weeks before the election, won only 3%.
When asked for comment, mayoral spokesperson Dora Pekec referred to remarks Mamdani made over the summer shortly after Unite NY filed its first set of petitions seeking to force a ballot question. At the time, he was asked whether he thought this was an effort to keep a candidate like him from winning a primary.
“I am quite content with the system of primaries that we have thus far,” Mamdani said in July. “I think that we've seen it's a system that's been in effect for quite some time. And it's also a system that doesn't preclude greater participation.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/billionaire-.title: Billionaires Always Want to Maintain Control
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/billionaire-.author: Sophie Bandarkar
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/billionaire-.text:
Billionaires Always Want to Maintain Control
California’s billionaire tax was defeated this time. But Mark Zuckerberg’s deal with Meta in anticipation of Proposition 40 teaches us two things: billionaire wealth can be converted into cash, and tech elites value control even more than wealth.
In October, Meta released a filing saying that Mark Zuckerberg had threatened to leave California in anticipation of Proposition 40, the billionaire wealth tax on the 2026 state ballot, which was defeated 53 to 47 percent. According to the document, Zuckerberg told the board he was “evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California,” and that any steps toward doing so, including listing his residential real estate on the market, “would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees.”
In response, the board quickly mobilized to negotiate a deal: Meta agreed to issue a new class of nonvoting (“Class C”) stock, which will be distributed to all shareholders in January 2027. This would have allowed Zuckerberg to sell his shares to convert a portion of his wealth into the billions in cash he would need to meet his potential tax liability, without losing his near-supermajority voting share. In exchange, he agreed to stay in the state for at least eight years and keep his $1 annual salary.
Conveniently, the new stock will also allow Meta to raise capital for artificial intelligence investments without changing the decision-making composition of the company. In the fallout of the proposition’s defeat, it’s useful to reflect on what the Meta deal can help us understand for the long-term movement to tax the ultrarich’s wealth.
What Proposition 40 Was
Prop 40 was designed as a onetime 5 percent tax, payable over five years, on the net worth of California residents with over $1 billion who lived in the state as of January 1, 2026. The proposition was written by legal and economics faculty and introduced by the health care workers’ union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers (SEIU-UHW). The goal of the tax was to raise around $100 billion, which would offset roughly 90 percent of the federal budget cuts to health programs, including Medi-Cal, since the beginning of the second Trump administration — and in particular, since the passing of the 2025 “Big Beautiful Bill,” which takes effect this January.
According to research by economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, California’s billionaire wealth reached around $2.3 trillion by mid-2026, which is roughly equal to the total income reported by every Californian in a year. This wealth is both extremely concentrated and recent: it’s increased by 144 percent in just three years. The approximately 250 billionaires who would qualify only pay about 0.2 percent of their wealth in California income tax each year, representing 2.4 percent of total California income tax revenue. The four richest billionaires, Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang, pay only 0.07 percent of their wealth.
If Proposition 40 had passed, it would have been the first tax of its kind and the culmination of decades of advocacy by policymakers and researchers across the world working to expose how dramatically economic inequality has grown and the degree of billionaires’ tax avoidance. This is particularly salient in California, the fourth-largest economy in the world and home to fifty-eight of the Fortune 500 companies. Companies in the Bay Area alone represent 35 percent of the market cap of the world’s top hundred companies. This makes the state an ideal place to experiment with taxing the ultrawealthy.
Why It Failed
The initiative failed for myriad, well-documented reasons. Primarily, it faced a concerted and incredibly well-funded opposition campaign. Its opponents, mostly ultrawealthy donors, spent $378.4 million against the measure (compared to the yes campaign’s budget of $33.5 million). Google cofounder and Donald Trump supporter Sergey Brin alone donated $102 million, and also funded two additional Propositions (41 and 42) designed to block the tax if it passed. California Governor Gavin Newsom opposed the measure and endorsed Proposition 42, stating, “Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level.”
According to Rigel Robinson, former Berkeley city councilmember and Democratic public policy consultant,
It would be a mistake to see the electoral outcome of Proposition 40 as a clear rejection of its goal from voters. There was the enormous and well-funded opposition campaign, and competing and confusing ballot measures designed to nullify the measure. Proposition 42, which was put on the ballot to prevent Proposition 40 (and future versions of it) from taking effect even if it did pass, was sold to voters as a protection for retirement savings.
However, in California and across the country, candidates won on a message of seizing power from billionaires and championing affordability. In many ways, this is the sort of message Bernie Sanders tried to bring to the Democratic agenda a decade ago.
Voters across the country have demonstrated that redistribution and economic justice are clear priorities, and we cannot let the outcome of this proposition diminish the ground won.
There were also concerns about the legality and mechanics of the legislation — in particular, that it was introduced as a onetime proposition, was not national, and was technically a retroactive tax, since it applied to anyone living in the state as of January 2026. And as Fred Glass explained in Jacobin, California’s labor and progressive forces were unable to form a unified front in support of the measure.
While disappointing, it’s helpful to historicize the initiative and the broader movement to tax the assets of the ultrawealthy alongside other fights for redistribution. The federal income tax, for example, took several attempts before successfully passing. It took the Sixteenth Amendment passing in 1913 to make it permanent. SEIU-UHW has already said it plans to try again in 2028, and Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna have introduced a bill at the federal level this spring.
Billionaire Wealth Is Money Today
From the Meta deal, we can learn two things. First, it is possible for tech leadership to convert their wealth into liquidity. One of the most persistent arguments against taxing the ultrawealthy is that their money isn’t “real,” since it’s mostly in shares of companies whose value rises and falls with the market. Because of this, it shouldn’t be treated as income.
Stocks are legal claims on future production whose prices are set by expected returns. It is not uncommon for the companies who issue them to have not yet produced anything profitable or concrete. SpaceX’s shares were the most valuable in history at the time of their initial public offering (IPO), even though its AI division had lost $2 for every dollar of revenue it earned in 2025.
In other words, a stock is a title of ownership to a slice of the surplus value a company will produce. In the Marxian sense, this is an example of fictitious capital and inherently speculative. However, “speculative” does not mean unreal. As Dimitris P. Sotiropoulos, John Milios, and Spyros Lapatsioras write in A Political Economy of Contemporary Capitalism and its Crisis: Demystifying Finance, fictitious capital is not detached from real production but a necessary phase within its totality, and claims on future income can become commodities in their own right. These can be traded, priced, and converted into money at any time. A stock is not just a promise of future wealth; it is wealth (and command over the labor of others) today.
Modern finance for the AI sector also has a remarkable capacity to innovate and reinvent itself, and the financial engineering to create the Class C share is another demonstration of the sector’s remarkable capacity to adapt to secure endless capital for the AI rush.
Another Front of Contestation
Second, tech executives are most concerned with losing control of their companies. As economist and tax expert Gabriel Zucman told me, “the existence of super-voting shares and the Zuckerberg and Proposition 40 episode more generally highlight that what matters most to billionaires, even more than their wealth, is their power to exert control over the giant businesses they own. This is indeed their greatest power.” He also commented on X that the opposition to the wealth tax could not be driven by concerns about losing money, since the onetime 5 percent liability would “merely bring billionaire’s fortunes back to where they stood a few weeks ago, at the beginning of September.”
Meta is not an isolated case, and a dual-class share system (which allows companies to sell shares to the public, while a small group keeps most of the votes) has been on the rise. When SpaceX went public, Elon Musk floated only 3–4 percent of the company and retained 42 percent of its shares, but 85 percent of its voting share through his “super-voting stock.” Anthropic’s IPO includes five types of stock, which specifically gives the cofounders the ability to keep a say over the controlling vote even if they give away 98 percent of their shares. The most valuable companies in the world are increasingly owned by a handful of individuals insulated from markets, shareholders, and other public mechanisms of accountability.
As Fred Glass wrote, Proposition 40 is a lost battle, not a lost war. Amid the manufactured panic over the tax, Zuckerberg seized the political moment to negotiate a deal with his company. The outcome of their agreement deepens our understanding of how to anticipate and oppose the coordinated class response against taxing extreme wealth. First, the shares of future value held by tech billionaires are not just abstractions but real money today, necessary to the current cycle of reproduction. And second, billionaires will fight hardest to protect not their fortune but their control.
The Left’s political project has to include a new front of contestation beyond fighting for shares of the returns tech companies produce. Countering the enclosure of the AI economy will require reclaiming democratic control over the infrastructures of this intelligence in the first place.
