The Trump administration did not open a formal investigation into Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO, before Donald Trump urged the board to reinstate him, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Instead, Todd Blanche, the attorney general, concluded the Justice Department (DOJ) had no evidence to indicate Huang broke any laws based on the department’s ongoing investigations into two of Nvidia’s clients, including Megaspeed International – the company suspected of smuggling chips into China.
Blanche was vague with reporters on Tuesday, refusing to directly say whether the DOJ had conducted an investigation, instead claiming law enforcement “looked into” the situation to make a final determination.
The probe of Nvidia’s clients found no evidence that Huang acted as an agent of China or provided sensitive information about semiconductors to China, sources told Reuters.
Donald Trump insisted, on Wednesday, that stocks were down “because of the November Third Election results” rather than waning confidence in AI and tech companies, new tariff proposals or rising inflation.
“Stocks are down sharply because of the November Third Election results. I wasn’t on the Ballot, but if I was, the results, just like all three times before, would have been much different, and the Stock Market, and your 401-k’s, would be BOOMING. I told you so!!!” Trump wrote, indirectly blaming the Democratic Party’s sweeping wins earlier this month.
However, other facts appear to be contributing to the stock market’s performance.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index also fluctuated in the wake of drama over Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang. Despite being reinstalled as the company’s leader, the Nasdaq was down by more than two percentage points.
US finds no evidence China directed executive to spy on Nvidia CEO - report
US officials found no evidence that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the Wall Street Journal (paywall) reports, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.
The briefing comes after Donald Trump controversially cleared the way for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement earlier this week, after assuring Nvidia that its CEO posed no national-security ‌threat.
The controversy began ‌with concerns over Alice Huang’s alleged Chinese intelligence links ‌and whether her relationship with Jensen Huang affected suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China.
Officials said Alice Huang contacted China’s spy agency during the affair but found no indication that she ‌provided significant intelligence, the WSJ reports.
The report said current evidence suggests that Alice Huang and Jensen Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but not a coordinated play by China, adding that new information could, however, change that assessment.
Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and ‌chamber leaders, according to the Journal.
The BBC has lodged an urgent appeal to have Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against it thrown out, after internal surprise at a judge’s decision to allow the case to go to trial.
The corporation is currently heading to court next year over a Panorama documentary that spliced together two parts of Trump’s speech made before the 6 January insurrection at the US Capitol.
While the broadcaster has apologised over the edit, which featured in the 2024 programme Trump: A Second Chance, it has always denied that the film defamed Trump. It has also said it was never broadcast in Florida, where Trump’s legal action is being heard.
The federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz, a Trump appointee, ruled earlier this month that the lawsuit could proceed, denying the BBC’s attempt to have the case thrown out. However, the BBC has now appealed to a higher court, the United States court of appeals for the 11th circuit, restating that the Florida court has no jurisdiction to hear the case.
In a legal submission seen by the Guardian, the BBC’s lawyers state that the documentary “never aired in the United States”. It argues that Kuntz found the Florida court held jurisdiction over the BBC “despite the complete lack of evidence that anyone accessed it there, as both Florida law and this circuit’s precedent require.”
The move is a sign of the BBC’s desperation to have the case dismissed, given the time, expense and political headache it is causing, while it is also making huge cuts at home and holding talks with the UK government over its future funding.
“We are surprised and disappointed by the court’s decision that this case should be heard in Florida,” said a BBC spokesperson. “As we have made clear from the start, the BBC broadcast this documentary in the UK – and UK only. We did not show it in Florida, nor did any other broadcaster.
“Given the urgency of this issue, we are now requesting a higher court review the ruling.”
Fifty three newly elected members of Congress told Harvard University on Tuesday that they will boycott an informal orientation program at Harvard’s Kennedy School next month in support of the school’s striking graduate students union.
In a letter to the university’s administrators, the incoming House Democrats expressed thanks for their invitations to the Bipartisan Program for Newly Elected Members of Congress, in which more than 800 members have participated in since 1972.
“However, as much as we would like to attend, we have been informed that to attend your event we would be required to cross a union picket line,” the new lawmakers wrote. “From our understanding, thousands of UAW members who belong to the Harvard Graduate Students Union (HGSU-UAW Local 5118) are on strike, seeking basic provisions like a cost of living increase. In addition, thousands of members of the Harvard Academic Workers (HAW-UAW) have been bargaining for a first contract for over two years and recently went on a week-long strike.”
“While we appreciate the invitation to Harvard’s Institute of Politics, we will not cross a picket line. So long as these workers are on strike, any trip we take to Harvard would be to stand in solidarity with our striking union siblings,” they added.
Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran national whose mistaken deportation turned him into a symbol of Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, has landed in Spain.
Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after leaving the United States of his own volition. Prior to his departure, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents met him at the airport and removed his ankle monitor, according to We Are CASA, a Maryland-based advocacy group.
The interaction, the group noted, was “a powerful symbol that ends a chapter marked by illegal deportation, imprisonment, abuse at Cecot, retaliatory prosecution, and government surveillance.”
As he made his way through the Madrid airport, Ábrego García did not speak to reporters, instead raising his fist in the air as he climbed into a waiting van.
Kilmar Ábrego García arrives at the airport in Madrid, Spain on 25 November 2026. Photograph: Fernando Villar/EPA
In a statement provided by We Are CASA, he described his departure from the US as proof that justice was still capable of prevailing over the most powerful government in the world.
“In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible,” he said.
Swiss government expects 15% tariff deal to be respected by US
The Swiss government has said that it assumes new tariff proposals by the office of the US Trade Representative are consistent with an agreement between the two countries last year setting a 15% cap on US tariffs on Swiss goods.
In a statement quoted by Reuters, the economy ministry said it expected the deal announced on 14 November 2025 to be respected.
As my colleague Lauren Aratani notes, tariffs have proven unpopular with US voters, who handed Democrats a decisive victory in the midterm elections that will give the party control of Congress. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs currently in effect have added an additional $900 in costs for each US household.
The rising cost of living was the number one issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a Harris Poll survey for the Guardian. An earlier Harris poll found seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices.
US inflation hits highest since May after prices climb 3.8% over the last year
Lauren Aratani
Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, according to new inflation data released today, the highest since May and the last inflation reading before a crucial US Federal Reserve board meeting next month.
Prices rose 0.3% from September to October amid soaring energy prices, according to the Personal Consumption Expenditure index, the Fed’s preferred inflation measure from the commerce department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis.
The data comes after the Bureau of Labor Statistics separately reported prices climbed 0.4% from September to October, higher than economists had anticipated.
Energy prices, including gas prices at the pump, have cooled, going from a high of $4.41 a gallon in early October to $3.61 a gallon by mid-November, according to AAA.
In early December, the Fed will hold the last of its interest rate-setting meetings for the year, and officials are widely expected to hike interest rates for the second time this year. The Fed has set a target inflation rate of 2%, a level not seen since February 2021. Higher interest rates make it more expensive to borrow money, slowing price increases and raising the price of loans like mortgages and student debt.
Though officials held rates steady at the last board meeting in late October, minutes from the meeting showed that some expressed concern about inflation’s stickiness.
“A few of them warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later,” the minutes said.
The move would come at a tumultuous time for the US economy. A new survey from the Conference Board released on Tuesday showed consumer confidence had ticked up in November to its highest level since January 2025, probably driven by the shake-up from the midterm elections.
At the same time, US stocks have been fluctuating from a mixture of uncertainty over datacenter regulations, continuing scandals coming out of Nvidia and overall investor concern about the seemingly limitless amount of money being spent on building AI and the infrastructure to support it.
Further to that, the European Commission expects any measures imposed by the United States to respect the 15% tariff ceiling for EU goods imports, a Commission spokesperson told Reuters, after the Trump administration’s proposed new Section 301 tariffs.
“Under the Joint ‌Statement, the ‌15% all-inclusive ceiling applies to EU ‌goods. We expect any measure from this investigation to respect it in full, including when combined with existing duties,” ‌the spokesperson said, referring to the statement setting out last year’s EU-US tariff deal.
He also said that the European Commission regretted the lack of joint action on global overcapacity, adding that it strongly rejected the premise that ‌Europe is a source of structural overcapacity.
'We regret the lack of joint action': EU hits back at Trump's plans for more tariffs
Lisa O’Carroll
The European Union has hit back at Donald Trump’s plans for more tariffs which come almost a year after his previous “liberation day” levies were struck down by the US supreme court.
Washington’s proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan, South Korea and the EU to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global ‌trade tensions.
According to a statement by the US trade representative “the EU’s unreasonable cars, policies and practices” include “industrial plans to expand manufacturing”; policies to “promote production an exports”, “sustained market access barriers” and “preferential lending” to target domestic sectors.
These increase the US economic security risks especially in cars, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, it says.
The current tariff plan is to impose a 15% levy on EU imports, pegging it at the same level agreed with the EU and Trump’s course last July.
“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” the EU said, a possible reference to imports flooding in from China.
The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Nasa knocked an asteroid off course. New closeup photos shed light on aftermath
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Linda Geddes
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Humanity may not yet have a means of fending off a Vogon constructor fleet – the destroyers of Earth in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy – but its prospects of surviving an encounter with a rogue asteroid are looking considerably brighter.
Four years after Nasa deliberately slammed a spacecraft into a roughly 160-metre-wide asteroid called Dimorphos to knock it off course, scientists have released the first closeup images of the aftermath.
They suggest the asteroid now has one face flattened with a stadium-sized crater and is tumbling chaotically. Meanwhile, hundreds of previously unknown boulders encircle Dimorphos and its larger companion asteroid, Didymos.
As well as shedding new light on what happened to the asteroid after the collision, the images, captured by the European Space Agency’s (Esa) Hera spacecraft, could help scientists design more effective missions to deflect potentially hazardous space rocks in the future.
“Nasa’s Dart [Double Asteroid Redirection Test] mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid’s orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself,” said the Hera mission manager, Ian Carnelli, at Esa. “By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.”
Nasa’s mission aimed to test-drive a planetary defence system that could prevent humanity from going the same way as the dinosaurs, should an asteroid or comet threaten Earth.
Neither Dimorphos nor its larger companion asteroid, Didymos, posed such a threat, but their movements provided scientists with a convenient means of assessing whether the strategy of trying to knock an asteroid off course might work.
On 26 September 2022, the roughly half-tonne Dart spacecraft ploughed into Dimorphos at more than 13,000mph, blasting a vast cloud of rocky debris into space.
Observations by telescopes on Earth revealed that the mission had succeeded in shortening the time it took Dimorphos to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. Before the collision, Nasa officials had said a change of 73 seconds or more would be considered a success.
But how much of the asteroid was displaced and precisely how it responded to the collision have remained open questions.
To investigate, Esa launched its Hera mission on 7 October 2024. After a two-year journey, the car-sized spacecraft reached the asteroid pair this month and has been surveying them from a distance of 15-18 miles (25-30km).
“Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same,” said Dr Patrick Michel, Hera principal investigator and director of research at the CNRS Côte d’Azur observatory in France. “Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once. The face struck by Dart has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid’s entire width.”
While the rest of Dimorphos appears to be relatively unchanged, the impact has also left Dimorphos “tumbling wildly in its orbit”, added Dr Michael Kueppers, the Esa’s Hera mission scientist.
“Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few metres in size,” Kueppers said.
Dr Michaël Marsset, an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory in Germany, described the release of the images as “a major milestone for both planetary defence and asteroid science”.
Unlike naturally occurring asteroid collisions, scientists knew precisely the mass, velocity and trajectory of the projectile and now had images of the asteroid before and after the impact, he said. “This offers a unique opportunity to study the physics of impacts at the scale of an asteroid.”
The Dart impact may also have exposed pristine material beneath Dimorphos’s weathered surface, offering scientists a rare glimpse of its interior, Marsset added.
Over the coming months, Hera will venture progressively closer to the asteroids and deploy two shoebox-sized satellites, one of which will use radar to peer inside Dimorphos.
The ultimate aim of these investigations is to transform asteroid deflection from a successful one-off experiment into a reliable means of planetary defence.
“The initial idea of deflecting an asteroid is not as straightforward as it sounds,” said Dr Ian Whittaker, a senior lecturer in physics at Nottingham Trent University. Although the momentum transferred by a spacecraft colliding with an asteroid should alter its motion, much also depends on how the asteroid responds to the impact, including how much material is blasted into space.“These images will help with understanding what is present after the impact and make for more accurate calculations in the future,” he said.
Asteroids are also remarkably diverse, ranging from relatively solid bodies to loose piles of rocks held together by their own weak gravity, said Marsset. “If we ever have to deflect another asteroid, this time on a collision course with Earth, we need to know what we are shooting at.”
The other major challenge is detecting potentially hazardous asteroids sufficiently early. Given years or decades of warning, even a tiny change in an asteroid’s velocity could be enough to make it miss Earth. “If it is discovered only months before impact, our options become considerably more limited,” Marsset said.
However, he added that major advances in asteroid detection were expected from the Vera C Rubin Observatory in Chile and Nasa’s forthcoming Near-Earth Object Surveyor space telescope. “These two complementary surveys will greatly improve our ability to discover potentially hazardous asteroids and, crucially, give us more time to respond.”
Whereas Douglas Adams’s Earth inhabitants were given mere minutes’ warning of their destruction, such advances could afford us both the time and the technology to avert our own.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
The Houthi-held seaport is a critical lifeline for millions of Yemenis but has taken significant damage over the course of recent conflicts.
The Saudi-led coalition has launched renewed attacks on Houthi targets at Yemen’s port of Hodeidah as the armed group fights Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The strikes come amid significant Houthi territorial gains in recent weeks and escalating attacks by the group on Saudi Arabia.
Hodeidah, which has repeatedly been attacked over the past decade, is critical to both Yemen’s economy and the supply of essential goods to millions of people in Houthi-controlled areas.
Here’s what we know:
How important is the port of Hodeidah?
The port of Hodeidah, situated on Yemen’s western Red Sea coast, is the country’s principal commercial seaport and has been under Houthi control since 2014.
It serves as a major entry point for food, fuel and other commercial goods as well as humanitarian assistance, supplying the densely populated northern and western regions of Yemen, including the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa.
The port had eight berths and the capacity to accommodate 6,500 standard shipping containers in 2023. However, attrition due to Yemen’s more than a decade of conflict has reduced the number of operational berths and damaged cranes and storage facilities.
Despite this, in September 2025, the United Nations Mission to Support the Hodeidah Agreement estimated that the port handled about 70 percent of commercial imports and 80 percent of humanitarian aid coming into Yemen, calling it a “lifeline”.
“The closure or disruption [of the port] under the current circumstances would delay the arrival of food, medicine and fuel; increase transport costs and prices; and exacerbate the suffering of families already facing an acute humanitarian crisis,” said Abdusattor Esoev, Yemen Chief of Mission for the International Organization for Migration.
“At a time when millions of people in Yemen depend on humanitarian assistance and face severe food insecurity, Hodeidah remains a critical lifeline. The port is essential for bringing in food, fuel, medicines and other basic goods needed by civilians across northern Yemen,” said Francesca Quinto, the programme manager for Yemen for Doctors Without Borders.
However, the Houthis have long been accused of using Hodeidah’s port for both civilian and military purposes. Investigations have found that the group exploits commercial port facilities to smuggle in weapons from Iran, its chief ally.
“The ports of Hodeidah are key to commercial flows. However, the Houthis’ increasing militarisation of vital civilian infrastructure by smuggling and storing arms, fuel and narcotics is undermining the humanitarian functions they serve in wartime,” Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera.
Tawfiq al-Hamidi, a Yemeni lawyer and human rights activist, told Al Jazeera that the port has been misused by the group for smuggling despite its importance for Yemen’s population.
“Nevertheless, efforts must be made to protect the port as a civilian facility, and the Houthi movement must provide genuine guarantees,” he said.
Has the port been attacked before?
Yes. Since the start of Yemen’s civil war in September 2014, the port and its surrounding area have repeatedly come under attack from the Saudi-led coalition, the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. Pro-Yemeni government forces also tried to capture it in a 2018 offensive.
About 70 percent of Yemenis live in Houthi-controlled areas in the country’s west, where most goods arrive from the rest of the world through Red Sea ports. Humanitarian aid continues to enter through other ports, including Mocha and a major government-held port in Aden, but renewed fighting has made the overland flow of this aid to the country’s interior difficult. Humanitarian operations in Houthi-controlled areas have also been severely curtailed because of the detention of UN staff by the group.
In March 2015, shortly after launching its military intervention in support of the Yemeni government, the Saudi-led coalition began a partial maritime blockade on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.
A UN-brokered nationwide truce in April 2022 led to an easing of restrictions on fuel imports through Hodeidah. Further restrictions on commercial imports were lifted in early 2023, which also helped to revitalise the port.
But that recovery was then jeopardised by a campaign of US, British and Israeli strikes on Houthi-controlled areas beginning in 2024 and lasting into the next year, in retaliation for Houthi drone and missile attacks on Israel and Red Sea shipping, carried out ostensibly in the name of supporting Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave.
Why is Saudi Arabia attacking the port now?
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announced on Wednesday that it had launched new strikes against the Houthis at the port, days after it warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Houthis have promised not to let strikes against the port go unanswered.
Since the return of full-scale war to Yemen in September, the Houthis have made sweeping territorial gains across Yemen, pushing back the forces of the internationally recognised government.
A government counteroffensive launched in early October has failed to stem Houthi advances despite heavy air support. Government forces are now scrambling to defend Aden, the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
“Broadly speaking, the strikes [on Hodeidah’s port] were a response to the shift on the battlefield in favour of the Houthis,” Ali al-Dhahab, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, told Al Jazeera.”
“They were aimed at undermining and crippling their economic and logistical capabilities, including infrastructure, such as ports and airports, as well as their military capabilities,” he said.
Escalating Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia targeting airports, oil infrastructure and commercial buildings also played a role in the decision, al-Dhahab said, mentioning Thursday’s attack on the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in Riyadh.
The following day, the Saudi-led coalition urged civilians near Hodeidah’s port to evacuate without providing specifics.
What could happen next?
Before Wednesday’s strikes, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree reiterated a threat of retaliation on Saudi seaports on the Red Sea, naming Jeddah’s port in particular.
Nabil Al-Bukairi, a Yemeni researcher and policy expert, told Al Jazeera that Saudi Arabia’s strikes on the port should not be taken as a warning. “I believe the strikes have gone beyond being merely symbolic,” he said.
“Continued bombardment would inevitably lead to its closure and render it inoperable once its infrastructure and logistical capabilities have been targeted,” he warned.
Even without a closure, strikes that disrupt the operations of the facility risk delays of critical aid as Yemen’s war shows no sign of an imminent end.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/the-g.title: The gold-filled mountains of Chad that hold the key to Libya's crisis and Sudan's war
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/the-g.author: MEE correspondent
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/the-g.text:
The gold-filled mountains of Chad that hold the key to Libya's crisis and Sudan's war
Deep inside the Tibesti mountains of northern Chad, in the central Sahara, the town of Miski sits surrounded by a succession of never-ending wadis.
A couple of families live at the top of each of these valleys and in August, when the rainy season comes, the wadis become a river that washes through the mountains. When the rains go, the valleys become green and camels feed on them.
A remote volcanic range characterised by rugged, bare rock, rivers of lava and volcanoes that climb to 3,000 metres, the Tibesti, which runs through northern Chad across the border into southern Libya, is sometimes called the roof of the Sahara.
These mountains are home to the Tubu, an indigenous community whose territory also includes a part of southern Libya, northern Niger and northwestern Sudan.
And the valleys that surround the town of Miski contain vast deposits of a precious metal that throughout human history has been prized almost above anything else: gold.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The mountains, too, are filled with antimony, a toxic heavy metal that is putting the ecosystem of this indigenous community at severe risk and is also exported in great quantities.
For decades, the gold that sits in this remote place has been one of the drivers of armed conflict between the Tubu and the Libyan, then Chadian states.
Now, the Tubu find themselves caught up in a web of warfare and illicit trade that stretches out from Chad into Libya, Sudan and over the sea to the United Arab Emirates, from where arms and supplies are flown to proxy armies, militias and paramilitaries.
On 14 October, armed clashes broke out in Miski.
The day after fighting began, the Chadian army’s general staff accused Miski’s self-defence committee - a local armed group descended from the Tubu institution of village guardianship - of breaking a peace agreement struck between them and the army last year by attacking the National Brigade for the Control of Mining Activities.
The army gave the Tubu group an ultimatum: lay down your arms at once or be treated as rebels. In response, the committee accused the brigade of firing first and of opening new mining fronts in grazing lands, in violation of the Bardai peace accord signed last year.
The gold ends up in Dubai…'yet we do not have a single clinic in Miski or a single paved road in the whole of the Tibesti'
- Tubu commander
One Tubu commander in Miski told Middle East Eye that last year Chad had exported over $1bn worth of gold and more than 15,000 tonnes of antimony, all sourced from the Tibesti mountains.
Almost all this gold ends up in the UAE, in the gold market of Dubai.
“And yet we do not have a single clinic in Miski or a single paved road in the whole of the Tibesti,” the commander said. “We won’t let this continue.”
Since the armed clashes broke out in October, the Chadian army has moved considerable numbers of troops and armoured vehicles into the Tibesti.
The situation on the ground, according to one Chadian army officer who spoke to MEE, is difficult for government troops. “We are fighting the mines and the mountains in Miski,” he said.
This fighting has not stopped: scores of people have died in the clashes and the Chadian army has conducted multiple drone strikes across the mountain range.
Weapons corridor
Miski’s uprising appears, on the surface, to be a local fight over gold - and in a large part, it is.
But it is unfolding inside a region that has become one of the most consequential, least scrutinised arms corridors in Africa: a route that, according to United Nations investigators and extensive reporting from Middle East Eye, has carried weapons, fuel and fighters from the UAE through Libya and Chad to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan.
These weapons are part of a network of arms and mercenaries that spans swathes of north and central Africa, utilised not just in Sudan but by organised criminal groups and armed entities across the Sahel.
Between October 2024 and the end of 2025, according to a UN Panel of Experts report, heavy cargo aircraft made 458 flights between military airports in the UAE or the Emirati base at Bosaso in the breakaway Somali region of Puntland and eastern Libya.
Some 239 of these landed at Kufra, a town about 300km from the Sudan border that was transformed, in the months before the RSF took el-Fasher in October 2025, into a fortified logistics hub complete with new hangars and scheduled flights.
Separately, as reported by MEE and confirmed by UN experts, the UAE was using Amdjarass, in eastern Chad, to land cargo planes.
Senior Egyptian army sources told MEE earlier this year that the Emiratis have a military operations room inside Amdjarass airport to coordinate with the RSF.
Just over 100km from the border with Darfur, the vast western region of Sudan controlled by the RSF, Amdjarass is a Zaghawa-dominated town that is the home region of Chad’s president, Mahamat Idriss Deby, and the site of a lavish state infrastructure programme that residents of Tibesti, 1,300km away and without a single paved road or a functioning hospital between them, have started to openly resent.
Abu Dhabi continues to deny supplying the Rapid Support Forces.
Haftar’s expanding footprint
In November 2025, Chad and the UAE-backed Haftar family’s Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), de facto commanded by Khalifa Haftar’s son Saddam, formed a joint border force covering roughly 1,050km of shared frontier.
The Haftars are not just in control of eastern Libya: leaked details of US adviser Massad Boulos’s plan to unify Libya propose Saddam Haftar as president of a government that would continue to be led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.
Chad’s government has two reasons to want this partnership, and they reinforce each other.
One is logistical: Chad and Haftar can cement their relationship in the eastern Libyan corridor that carries Emirati arms to the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan.
The other is that a joint border force hems in the Tubu, who have supplied the armed resistance to Mahamat Deby’s government and to Haftar’s forces alike.
Jalel Harchaoui, an analyst focusing on Libya and political economy, told Middle East Eye that when the deal was initially struck, the Tubu were not part of the thinking.
“It was to ensure better security along the route between Chad and Libya, especially with the passage via Ma’tan as-Sarra in Libya down through Chad to Amdjarass and then on to Darfur,” he said.
This “security problem” included armed groups attacking the convoys headed to Darfur to supply the RSF, Harchaoui said. There was also the need to build further cooperation between Emirati allies who were not natural bedfellows.
“Saddam Haftar and Mahamat Deby don’t get along, so there was a need to please the UAE by doing a joint force. And the agreement was never that the joint force would be pushed to the west, it was really to cover the northeastern corner of Chad,” Harchaoui said.
That changed earlier this year, when Saddam Haftar “ran into trouble” with armed Tubu groups like the Southern Liberation Operations Room (Slor), which is led by Mohamed Wardougou, a Libyan Tubu, and often hides out in northern Niger.
Haftar asked Chad to move forces to the west, arguing correctly, according to Harchaoui, “that Wardougou’s activism served as a shot in the arm for the anti-Deby Chadian group Front for Change and Concord in Chad (Fact) in northern Niger”.
History of revolt
This move played into the Tubu’s long record of rising up against the central governments of Chad, going back to the country’s independence from France in 1960.
Their most recent armed revolt, in April 2021, culminated in the death on the front line of President Idriss Deby Itno, who had decided at the age of 68 to command his forces in person. His son Mahamat succeeded him.
In Libya too, the Tubu rose against Muammar Gaddafi, and after his fall in 2011, they held sway over vast stretches of southern Libya until 2021, when Haftar’s forces pushed into the areas they had controlled. The containment effort carries a human cost well beyond Tibesti.
In Libya, Tubu communities describe a steady tightening around their citizenship, with human rights researchers long having flagged discriminatory practices such as treating the Tubu as second-class citizens and stopping them from obtaining passports and IDs.
'We do not want to be part of a bigger game… We just want peace and justice and foremost, transparency in mining and the development of our region'
- Tubu defence committee member
On 14 October, the same day gunfire broke out in Miski, Libya’s attorney general in Tripoli said he was prepared to strip the 28,000 families registered at Murzuq, in the Fezzan region of southwest Libya, of their Libyan nationality, citing alleged forgery.
Because the overwhelming majority of Libya’s Tubu are registered through that one civil registry, the announcement reads as an existential threat: if carried through, most of Libya’s Tubu would become stateless.
On the border between Libya and Niger, Wardougou’s Slor group has fought a running battle with Haftar’s forces, using northern Niger as a rear base. The Slor’s declared aim is to remove Haftar’s men from southern Libya.
In July, photographs circulated online showing Chadian soldiers at Libya’s Wigh airbase, near the Nigerien border - evidence, the group’s leadership says, that Chad is fighting on Haftar’s behalf.
On 20 October, the LAAF arrested a former Chadian minister and senior opposition figure, Hassan Soukaya, as he tried to cross from Libya into Niger, and handed him to the Chadian army.
Days later, Niger’s government publicly accused the Chadian military, with alleged French support, of carrying out a drone strike on 24 October near the Salvador Pass that killed two civilians. The attack was reportedly meant to target Slor positions in Libya, but hit Nigerien territory by accident.
The UAE-Israel desert axis
On 19 October, Israel’s second-ever ambassador to Chad landed in N’Djamena to present her credentials to Deby.
Since taking power after his father’s death in 2021, Deby has made a point of binding Chad ever closer to the UAE and Israel: diplomatic relations with Israel were restored in 2022, and the first Israeli ambassador in more than half a century - since Chad broke off ties in 1972 - was received shortly afterwards. Despite this, in November 2023, Chad recalled its ambassador from Israel, citing “the unprecedented tide of deadly violence” inside Gaza.
Chadian alignment with the UAE is not only military. As previously reported by MEE, the Emiratis offered Deby “more than a billion dollars” to “flip Chad towards supporting the RSF” after the war in Sudan began, according to former CIA analyst Cameron Hudson.
That figure now looks like loose change. In May 2025, in Abu Dhabi, Chad unveiled Chad Connexion 2030, a $30bn national development strategy to remake the infrastructure of a landlocked country from the ground up.
The UAE was, by a wide margin, its most important bilateral underwriter, securing $20.5bn in total backing and signing 18 contracts of its own worth over $6.2bn.
Among the headline projects: an 800-km Etihad rail line to Cameroon’s port of Douala, a 50 MWp solar plant by Global South Utilities, industrial zones, Abu Dhabi Ports logistics hubs, and critical-mineral exploration permits.
The partnership has tightened Chad’s dependence on the UAE and has become, in effect, the economic lifeline of Deby’s administration. To the west, Chad is already at odds with its neighbour Niger, which has drawn closer to Algeria.
In late October, Algeria deployed troops to Niger, the first time it had done this outside its borders since 1973. The move came days after Niger’s military government survived a coup attempt on 28 August.
Algeria’s move into Niger, according to the retired Algerian diplomat Amar Belani, is designed to counter what he described as “a destabilisation strategy actively involving the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, Israel and certain French proxies.”
The current geopolitical shifts, Belani went on, together with all they entail by way of rivalry and intervention by foreign actors, mean that “new tools, such as a show of presence including at the military level, are no longer a taboo and will be utilised to draw and reinforce Algeria’s red lines.”
Borderlands unrest
What is forming, in other words, is not one war but two rival blocs assembling around unrest in the desert borderlands.
On one side: the Sudanese Armed Forces (which receives backing from Egypt and Turkey), Niger, Algeria, and the Tubu in Libya and Chad. On the other: the RSF, the Haftars, the UAE, Ethiopia and the Chadian state, with the French leaning towards this camp.
And the local fights and the larger one are no longer separate. A mining dispute in a town of a few thousand people tucked away deep in the remote mountains of Chad has become entangled with an arms corridor sustaining one of the world’s deadliest wars, with a succession contest inside Libya’s eastern military establishment, and a Sahelian realignment redrawing alliances from Algiers to Khartoum.
“We do not want to be part of a bigger game,” one member of the Tubu defence committee in Miski told MEE. “We just want peace and justice and foremost, transparency in mining and the development of our region.”
But whether it remains a local counter-insurgency or becomes the spark for something larger will depend less on what happens in the mountains of Tibesti than on decisions being made in Abu Dhabi, Benghazi and Paris.

https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n44-a.author: Martin Groch, Louis Van Ginneken

News, influence et création de conflits
En Belgique francophone, une poignée de jeunes diffusent de l’info et commentent l’actu sur les réseaux sociaux. De quoi faire paniquer vieux journalistes et parlementaires.
« On a commencé comme ça, pour informer sur les élections européennes qui étaient ouvertes pour la première fois aux jeunes de 16 ans. » En 2024, Noah Heine est encore étudiant du secondaire à Habay (Luxembourg), lorsqu’un ami et lui inaugurent la page Instagram @Politiquensemble. Succès de zinzin : le compte gagne 40 000 abonnés en à peine un an. « Et puisque ça a bien fonctionné, on a continué sur l’actualité au sens large », poursuit l’étudiant en droit de 20 ans. Le compte, depuis rebaptisé @Lexplik, publie des vidéos courtes titrées Voici tout ce qui change en Belgique le 1 er juillet ou On fait le point sur la tenue (ou non) des examens en FWB. « Le but, c’est d’expliquer et de vulgariser l’actu », en reprenant les bases. « Parce que, ça parait con, mais il y a plein de gens qui ne savent pas ce qu’est le Conseil des ministres, par exemple. » Alors, Noah Heine s’y attèle chaque jour, pour quelque 60 000 personnes sur Instagram, 75 000 sur TikTok et 40 000 autres sur Facebook. « J’aime pas trop le terme de newsinfluenceur parce que ça sous-entend qu’on est là pour influencer. Mais c’est comme ça qu’on nous appelle. » Qui est ce « nous » qui préfère être appelé « créateurs de contenus d’info » ?
En Belgique, leurs comptes se nomment Asckipe, Yurbise, En Bref, Bruxelles Dévie ou Quelcharabia. Leur succès est assez récent tandis qu’en France, HugoDécrypte officie depuis dix ans. Derrière ces pages, des jeunes d’une vingtaine d’années s’emparent de sujets d’actu en épousant les codes propres aux plateformes numériques (vidéos face cam au format vertical ou carrousels de slides). Toute autre tentative de définition des créateurs de contenus d’info s’avère périlleuse, tant lesdits contenus varient d’un compte à l’autre, voire au sein d’une même page.
Avec @Quelcharabia, Camille Terlinden résume « le charabia de l’actualité » et partage, chaque semaine, le sens d’un mot (cette semaine, c’est « rubicond »). Noah Bundula présente d’emblée @Asckipe comme « le compte que tu ne peux pas ranger dans une case » et aborde de grands sujets du moment avec malice (« Nous avons un gouvernement de victimes »), tandis que Noah Heine et ses comparses « essayent d’être impartiaux ». Adrien Goffin, alors étudiant en journalisme, a créé @Enbref en 2025 pour documenter les violences policières et les manifestations, qu’il considère trop peu traitées dans la presse. « Je suis là pour ajouter une plus-value parce que je pense que plus on est nombreux dans l’environnement médiatique, plus c’est qualitatif pour le citoyen. » Ses publications entrainent 2 millions de likes, commentaires et repartages par mois en moyenne, mais peuvent scorer jusqu’à 20 millions. Qui a dit que les jeunes se désintéressaient de l’actu ?
Des médias sans journalistes
Ces créateurs partagent un dernier point commun : ils se présentent pour la plupart comme des médias. Pour autant, sont-ils journalistes ? Ni Adrien Goffin ni Noah Heine ne le revendiquent. Peut-être parce que, comme d’autres créateurs cités, ils sont étudiants ou l’étaient au moment de lancer leurs comptes, qu’ils alimentent de manière bénévole (jusqu’à 20 h par semaine pour Lexplik). Tous deux se soucient malgré tout de respecter la déontologie du métier « apprise sur le tas ». Cette volonté de professionnalisation s’est faite au fur et à mesure et dans un contexte de crispations grandissantes dans le secteur. Car si certains produisent leurs propres contenus originaux, la plupart remâchent des infos puisées dans des journaux (payants), voire en proposent une lecture très personnelle. Des journalistes du Soir ont ainsi vu leurs productions pompées et partagées gratuitement sur les réseaux sociaux, sans toujours être cités. « La forme est protégée, mais pas le droit d’avoir accès à ce qui se passe, observe Noah Heine. Je trouve légitime d’expliquer l’info dans un format différent. » Mais s’il n’y a pas d’apport significatif par rapport à une information exclusive d’un média, il s’agit de plagiat, selon les critères du Conseil de déontologie journalistique (CDJ). L’Association des journalistes professionnels (AJP) a, de son côté, déploré des citations erronées et des modifications du sens de certaines infos.
@Yurbise se définit comme « média insolent ». Et il l’est. Sur son compte Instagram, suivi par 52 000 personnes, il s’offusque à grands coups de superlatifs des actions de nos gouvernements et se montre très critique vis-à-vis des médias. Lorsque Sarah Frères, présidente de l’AJP, a souligné certaines erreurs factuelles sur ce compte et rappelé que, « sans le travail des journalistes professionnels, il n’aurait pas beaucoup de contenu à partager », le créateur de Yurbise, Jérémie Nzita Mambu, lui a répondu tout en sarcasme et par story interposée : « Je n’existais pas il y a un an, mais c’est déjà moi le grand déstabilisateur de votre profession. » Avant d’ajouter : « Si les citoyens ne vous font plus confiance… qui en porte la responsabilité ? Un gamin de 21 ans ? Ou des décennies de drames internes, d’entre-soi, d’erreurs, de filtrage des sujets, de silences gênants, de minimisations, de fausses équivalences, de déconnexion avec la réalité ? » Conflit finalement constructif puisque des corrections sont, depuis, souvent apportées aux publications de Yurbise et les sources sont systématiquement mentionnées.
Rappels déontos
La posture critique de Yurbise, pas toujours à côté de la plaque, mais invariablement irrévérencieuse, irrite aussi une de ses cibles de prédilection : le Mouvement réformateur (MR). Le 4 novembre, en commission Média au parlement de la FWB, le député libéral Chris Massaki mentionne directement Yurbise et pointe « qu’ils n’offrent pas toujours les garanties d’indépendance, de vérification des sources et de déontologie que l’on attend de la presse professionnelle ». Chris Massaki demande à la ministre Jacqueline Galant quels leviers permettraient de « mieux encadrer ce phénomène émergent, sans porter atteinte à la liberté d’expression ni à l’indépendance éditoriale ».
Dans sa réponse, la ministre évoque une possible « régulation », qui a fait bondir plusieurs créateurs. Une carte blanche et, cinq mois plus tard, trois auditions sont organisées au Parlement pour démêler ce phénomène aussi nouveau qu’incompris. Yurbise, Asckipe, En Bref y sont conviés, aux côtés du CDJ, de l’AJP, du Conseil supérieur de l’audiovisuel (CSA), du Conseil supérieur de l’éducation aux médias (CSEM), des rédacteurs en chef de La Libre et du Soir ainsi que des professeurs de journalisme de l’IHECS et l’ULB.
« Lorsque des acteurs comme nous émergent, la première réaction n’est pas de chercher à comprendre leur manière de faire, mais plutôt de les cadrer, de les classer et parfois même de les mettre sous suspicion », a reproché Adrien Goffin, lors de sa prise de parole. Car une question plane durant ces auditions : faut-il créer un statut spécifique pour les créateurs de contenus d’info ? Piste balayée d’une même main par tous les auditionnés. Les créateurs de contenus d’info peuvent se dire journalistes s’ils respectent les règles de la profession : publier des infos vérifiées, de manière indépendante, dans le respect des personnes et agir loyalement. En cas de manquement à ces principes, chacun est libre de soumettre une plainte au CDJ (députés et ministres compris). Car l’instance de régulation peut se considérer comme compétente même lorsque le créateur ne se dit pas journaliste, mais partage de l’information ou qu’il publie sur un réseau social. Elle a ainsi considéré, en 2023, qu’une plainte envers Michel Henrion pour non-respect du droit de réplique était fondée, alors même qu’elle concernait des publications Facebook et Twitter. Le journaliste avait accepté d’épingler cette décision en haut de ses fils Twitter et Facebook pendant 48 heures, alors qu’il n’y était pas tenu.
Plutôt que tailler un cadre spécifique aux créateurs, Amandine Degand, chercheuse et professeure à l’IHECS, suggère plutôt de « les inviter à créer une charte qui leur imposerait de citer leurs sources, mentionner les partenariats et, pourquoi pas, de faire preuve d’humilité ». Le compte Lexplik a récemment publié sa propre charte éditoriale, sur son site.
Indépendants, mais de qui ?
Ces formats cartonnent parce qu’ils sont incarnés par des créateurs qui s’adressent de manière directe et simple à leur audience : la recette n’est pas si différente de celle du JT. Sauf qu’ils le font directement sur les plateformes qui hébergent nos vies sociales. « La proximité perçue avec les créateurs, leur authenticité revendiquée ainsi que la dimension émotionnelle et narrative des contenus jouent un rôle déterminant dans l’adhésion », analyse le Conseil supérieur de l’éducation aux médias (CSEM). Mais en se vautrant dans les plateformes, les créateurs de contenus d’info doivent jouer le jeu algorithmique, qui favorise les contenus interpelants et clivants. Avec le risque que cela abime la qualité, la véracité ou l’objectivité de leurs productions. Mais aussi leur éthique journalistique. Car sans monétisation via les plateformes ou soutien financier de leurs followers, la tentation est grande d’accepter les collaborations commerciales. Asckipe se sentira peut-être moins libre de critiquer Win for Life depuis leur collaboration commerciale du 28 juin 2026. Adrien Goffin, qui refusait les partenariats comme les dons, s’est résolu à rejoindre le parti Écolo en tant que chargé de communication. Une fonction pourtant incompatible avec le métier de journaliste, qui exige une indépendance, entre autres politique. Il continuera à animer En Bref tout en étant transparent sur son embauche, assure-t-il.
Malgré ces fragilités, les créateurs de contenus s’imposent comme des acteurs à part entière du paysage médiatique. Le passage de chaque président de parti sur le compte du vulgarisateur politique Elio Acar, au moment des élections de 2024, en est un signe. Effrayés par le vieillissement de leurs audiences et flairant l’opportunité de jouvence, de nombreux médias belges ou internationaux ont entamé des rapprochements avec des créateurs. Camille Terlinden, déjà chroniqueuse sur LN24, a rejoint cet été Sudinfo pour des capsules régulières. En 2025, Tarmac (RTBF) a fait appel à Elio Acar pour un format « qui décrypte les préoccupations des jeunes ». Et, le 20 juin 2026, la RTBF a annoncé l’ouverture de son Auvio Studio, mis à la disposition des créateurs. En plus de l’accès gratuit au matériel et à l’infrastructure, le média public leur propose un accompagnement technique et éditorial, pour développer leur projet. Reste à déterminer qui a à apprendre de qui.
- Le Conseil de déontologie journalistique a rappelé (2020) que la reprise d’une info ne pouvait être un simple copié-collé. ↩
- Jérémie Nzita Mambu n’a pas souhaité répondre aux questions de Médor. ↩
- Comme le sont les journalistes et médias membres de l’Association pour l’autorégulation de la déontologie journalistique (l’AADJ, qui met en place le Conseil de déontologie). ↩
