https://gothamist.com/news/these-new-yor.title: These New Yorkers ditched their smartphones for a month. No, seriously.
https://gothamist.com/news/these-new-yor.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/these-new-yor.text:
In an event space atop a warehouse in East Williamsburg, people lined up to check their phones at the door.
Being phone-free for the night was a requirement for those who wanted to party with the roughly 100 New Yorkers who had just given up their smartphones for a month. Friends and families were invited to celebrate along with them — and see a showcase of hobbies and art projects that were picked up during the month instead of screens.
In one corner of the dimly lit room, people practiced their yo-yo skills. Someone else passed out bowls of homemade chicken soup. Others, lubricated by Modelos and boxed wine, made artsy stickers formed from pictures of a black and white cat. But the main attraction was the dance floor, which thudded to the beat of a DJ, who spun actual vinyl.
“Free your phone and ur a-- will follow,” the party invite advertised.
The participants, mostly in their 20s and 30s, are part of a growing group of New Yorkers who have declared that they’re unsatisfied with their relationships with their smartphones and are looking to set new boundaries with technology. The Month Offline organizers host weekly meetups where participants find community IRL (in real life) rather than online.
The group challenge, which started last year in Washington, D.C, took off quickly in New York, according to Lydia Peabody, one of the organizers. Seemingly overnight, the waitlist to participate in New York’s Month Offline became hundreds of names long, she said.
Peabody said she was initially surprised that demand was so high in a city as plugged in as New York. But, it makes sense, she later concluded: Being on your phone all the time is isolating.
“People need this space to not feel alone,” she said.
During the October effort, phone-free crews met weekly in small groups, or pods, based on where they live. The idea, Peabody explained, is that as New Yorkers detox from their smartphones, they can lean on their neighbors and get to know each other in the process.
Groups congregated across boroughs, in neighborhoods like the East Village, Astoria and Fort Greene.
“It's kinda like Alcoholics Anonymous for smartphones and social media,” said Axel Berlin, who participated in the Month Offline challenge in Chelsea.
‘People do feel overwhelmed’
Caitlin Begg studies movements like these for a living.
The sociologist and founder of Authentic Social, a research lab that focuses on the intersection of sociology and technology, said more and more people are looking to change their relationships with their phones.
According to survey results Begg recently presented at a Princeton University TEDx Talk, the average person uses eight different methods of communication daily, including social media, Slack and other apps. More than 90% of respondents reported checking their smartphones within 15 minutes of waking up.
“People do feel overwhelmed,” Begg said. “That’s just a lot.”
Taking a break from your phone in hyperlocal groups, Begg said, makes particular sense in a city like New York.
“ We live in such an incredibly vibrant city,” Begg said, “and because of work constraints or just being in the routine of life, sometimes people are just going from place to place… you know, a slop bowl place and back to their apartment.”
She added, getting off your phone is “about pushing people past their comfort zone, and I think pods really encourage that pro-social behavior.”
Joining the the 'flipside' scene
On a balmy evening earlier this fall, dozens of New Yorkers congregated in the plaza of Tompkins Square Park to kick off their detoxes.
The organizers, using a megaphone, encouraged those in the audience — plus passersby who stopped to listen — to join what they called “the flipside,” by switching to low-tech flip phones that could be borrowed for free during the challenge.
(The phones are provided by dumb.co, a flip phone company that some of the Month Offline organizers started after the Month Offline challenge took off. For those looking for a permanent switch, the $20 phone is also available for purchase – and advertised on flyers across New York City.)
The leaders of the group told Gothamist that this isn’t just a trend — it’s an act of resistance to big tech, Silicon Valley and a social life increasingly organized around group chats and other digital platforms. It’s time to go back to analog, they told Gothamist.
“Building the capacity for technological resistance on literally the neighborhood level, I think is the most important place to build it,” said Damian Thomas, who led the Astoria pod and is the director of the Unplatform Project, a tech literacy initiative to get people to divest from big tech.
In Tompkins Square, under the park’s street lights, the facilitators of each neighborhood pod met with those who signed up to participate. Throughout the course of October, the leaders would host pods in their living rooms, bookstores or other neighborhood hangouts.
The Month Offline organization is working to democratize their program, so people across the world can start their own pod. The group published a DIY guide equipped with a curriculum for weekly meetups, including exercises on communication, memory and navigating urban space without GPS.
But pod facilitators told Gothamist that the weekly meetings are run with their own flair.
Thomas, whose group met weekly at the Museum of the Moving Image in Astoria, said at one meeting that he assigned his group to find a new movie, show or book without recommendations from social media. During another week, everyone had to find a new spot in their neighborhood without the help of Google Maps.
Quinn Winters, who helped lead the Greenpoint pod, said he realized that New York seems smaller when you’re not staring down at a screen all the time.
“Now I'm seeing the same people over and over again, and I'm actually able to wave and say hi,” Winters said.
But being without a smartphone is a unique challenge in a city that runs on apps like Google Maps, Apple Pay and DoorDash.
“Someone pointed out very reasonably like, ‘Oh, I use the Citi Bike to get around all the time, and I realized that I didn't have a smartphone on me, so I couldn't check one out,’” Thomas said.
He added, “People rely on the Citi Bike system to get around. That's a way that our public infrastructure now is locking people into the usage of these devices.”
Some people who signed up for the challenge didn’t complete it.
Facilitators of several pods told Gothamist that attendance to the weekly meetings was lower than they hoped — if there were 10 people in a pod, sometimes only six would show up.
Berlin, from the Chelsea pod, told Gothamist that, frankly, unplugging is hard.
“I think it's very likely that people, people got dragged back into their smartphone lifestyle,” he said.
Begg, the researcher, said giving up your smartphone isn’t for everyone; being able to do so is a privilege in modern society, and not everyone’s life allows the break.
“[Throwing] your phone in the river … from an economic standpoint, it's just not realistic for most people,” Begg said. “They have to support their families. There's childcare and things and other things that are wrapped up in the smartphone.”
Short of ditching their phone altogether, Begg said, there are other things people can do to set boundaries with their devices, like sleeping with their phones outside of their bedrooms or switching back to landlines at home.
Some participants said flip phones have everything they need, especially because they now come equipped with basic navigation systems. Others told Gothamist that being without smartphones isn’t sustainable long term, but they want to have new boundaries, like only taking them out to FaceTime with family.
At the East Williamsburg party, the white brick walls were decorated with an alternative to doom scrolling on social media: actual scrolls, made from butcher paper, with musings and reflections from each pod scribbled in crayon and markers.
On a neighboring wall, the group’s constitution, written boldly in Sharpie, was on display.
“We the participants of [Month Offline] declare that we ought to be free and independent human beings, that we are absolved of all dependence on big tech and other attention grabbing algorithms,” the butcher paper read. “Here is to boredom, wrong turns, to fruitful friction, to life beyond the screen.”
Winters, from the Greenpoint pod, stood beside an art installation where people wrote their secrets on slips of paper that would later be set on fire.
He said being off his phone frees up a part of his brain. Some people write books during their phone-free month, he said. Others simply choose to spend more time with their friends and families — or, in this case, their neighbors.
“More and more, I'm realizing the isolating part of New York is really a choice,” Winters said. “You can isolate yourself, but you can also choose to engage with the people nearby you."
Winters said taking a break from his phone has changed the way he moves through a city — even as those around him are glued to their screens.
“Every time that someone else is pulling out their phone to check their emails, I'm looking around and seeing what's in the sky,” he said.
This story was updated with additional details regarding the flip phones used by some Month Offline participants.

https://gothamist.com/news/new-film-capt.title: New film captures ICE agents' banter amid NYC courthouse arrests
https://gothamist.com/news/new-film-capt.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/new-film-capt.text:
Emma V.F. is among the legion of photographers, videographers and other journalists who have chronicled the human drama unfolding in New York City’s main immigration court, located in the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building, where masked federal agents have plied the halls for more than a year arresting immigrants leaving court hearings.
V.F. filmed scores of arrests at the sprawling government complex at 26 Federal Plaza in Lower Manhattan, where a federal judge later temporarily barred U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from making routine civil immigration arrests. She also captured something rarer still: the small talk among the omnipresent ICE agents at the facility.
Her new documentary short, “Water Cooler,” splices together snippets of the mundane, day-to-day chatter among the agents and airs them alongside footage of some of the many immigrants being arrested in the hallways and thereafter being sent off to ICE detention centers. V.F calls the film an exploration of the “banality of evil."
The compilation provides a rare airing of the personal musings of agents — all recorded in a public place — as they execute what President Donald Trump has billed as the largest mass deportation effort in the nation’s history.
The documentary had its New York City premiere at the festival DOC NYC earlier this month, and will be screened again at DCTV’s Firehouse Cinema in Manhattan on Dec. 2 at 7 p.m.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, in a statement referred to the filmmaker as an "activist" and said her work "smears ICE."
V.F. expressed a different view in an interview with Gothamist. Here is a transcript of the conversation, edited for length and clarity:
What were your main impressions from watching and recording ICE agents for weeks?
V.F.: From literally the first day I went just to observe without my camera, I was really struck by the fact that the agents were just standing around having these very mundane conversations that felt to me very indifferent about what they were doing, what they were there to do. And the fact that they were having these very openly right next to all the journalists, that really surprised me, and was not something I knew about from just being a viewer and reader of the news.
So, right away I thought, if I can capture elements of this, there's something there, this kind of banality-of-evil theme that feels really interesting and important to memorialize in some way. It feels like this dark history is happening in these very kind of claustrophobic hallways. So that was my goal.
The thing that struck me was this complete lack of acknowledgement on the part of the ICE agents of what they were there to do, until they were arresting someone. Like, you wouldn't know from their conversations that they were tearing families apart and potentially ruining lives. Just this ability that they have to have these very water cooler conversations, very kind of like standard small talk, felt really eerie and upsetting to me.
How did you make sense of that discrepancy between their conversations and the arrests they were making?
On a human level, I don't know that I have. I think that's why I wanted to make the film in this way. I don't know how to grapple with that as a human being, that people can be this heartless.
I think as a filmmaker, it really immediately felt clear to me, especially because of, I should say, references like “The Zone of Interest” (a historical drama) that had come out a few years before, about the banality of evil during the Holocaust. It felt clear to me that this was something that could be compelling if edited the right way. And so I really embraced juxtaposing these very kind of normal, quiet conversations with these scenes of state violence to try to make that point.
Did any particular scenes stand out to you, when you were there observing and filming?
I think the conversation that cemented for me that I was making a short film and that there was something noteworthy going on was the conversation where this female supervisor is talking about how she always gets broken appliances. Her appliances are always broken when she orders the things online. And she kind of flippantly says that she has PTSD from that. And that was very early on in the filming process that that conversation happened.
So I think it was both the combination of the fact that it happened at all, that she said this very ironic thing, when she is in fact inflicting trauma on people as an agent of the government — it boggled my mind, it still does — and also the fact that she said it knowing I was feet away from her recording. I wonder if that was a bit of a trolling me moment. But either way, I think it shows the true colors very clearly and is a part of the film that the audience holds onto as well.
What was your dynamic with the ICE agents? Were they aware you were filming them?
I know for a fact that they knew I was filming them because I actually filmed them talking about me at one point. There's a shot at the very end of the film where there are five agents standing kind of far away from me in a hallway, and they all turn and look at me at once, and that's because they're saying, "Oh, homegirl's still recording us. What do you think she does with this footage? Do you think she just goes home and watches us?" And they're like making jokes about the fact that I'm filming. And then they actually joke about harming me in some way. I don't know exactly what they said, but they start talking about how, like, "Why don't you just go over there and by the time the investigation's over you'll be long gone."
So I know that they knew I was filming and I know they didn't appreciate it. But I think they also knew I was well within my rights. Anyone can film ICE agents on the job in a public place. So I always tried to be respectful and safe, but I knew that I was well within my journalistic and filmmaking rights to be doing that.
What do you hope audiences take away from the film?
I guess my answer has changed a little since the Blue Wave. I've always hoped that people would feel invigorated to either call for abolishing ICE, or learn how to be a volunteer or learn know-your-rights trainings, like any of these things that are kind of the obvious impact of storytelling about ICE from this point of view.
But I think especially now in this moment when so many people on the left are rightfully very excited and very happy, I think I feel like it's a really valuable film to remind people, ICE is part of the executive branch and that hasn't changed, and if anything, we've seen the president elevate Stephen Miller to White House Chief of Staff, and Stephen Miller has been one of the key policymakers in all this. So I think, I hope that the film will remind everyone who shares these values to really stay vigilant and stay calling for change and decency and humanism.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-citi-bike.title: NYC Citi Bike member rides to be capped at $3.65 after Mamdani inks new deal with Lyft
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-citi-bike.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-citi-bike.text:
Citi Bike members will soon pay less for electric bike rides under a new agreement between Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration and Lyft, which operates the bike-share program.
The deal will also freeze annual membership prices and other fees for members through May 2029.
Starting Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for an e-bike ride lasting up to 45 minutes. The cap also applies to reduced-fare members and shorter rides that already cost less will remain at their current price.
Annual membership prices, member per-minute e-bike fees and charges for rides that exceed 45 minutes will be frozen at current rates until May 26, 2029, when Lyft’s contract with the city expires.
“Getting around New York City shouldn't come with a price tag that keeps climbing by the minute,” Mamdani wrote in a release announcing the agreement. “Because a more affordable city is one where getting around it doesn’t break the bank.”
Citi Bike members currently pay 27 cents per minute for e-bike rides, or $12.15 for a 45-minute ride, except for rides entering or leaving Manhattan, which are capped at $5.40. The annual membership fee is $239 and rides on regular bikes lasting up to 45 minutes are included.
Under the new agreement, members could save as much as $8.50 on a single e-bike ride, according to City Hall. The new cap replaces the existing $5.40 cap for rides entering or leaving Manhattan, as well as a one-time allotment of 60 e-bike minutes for members.
The agreement doesn't prohibit Lyft from increasing Citi Bike prices for non-members, who currently pay $4.99 for a ride up to 30 minutes on analog bikes and an additional 41 cents per-minute for e-bike rides.
The city has also agreed to help install electric charging infrastructure at more than 130 Citi Bike stations starting next year. This will allow the e-bikes to recharge while docked, rather than having Lyft workers swap out depleted batteries. City officials said the changes will reduce operating costs and make more e-bikes available to riders.
City Councilmember Lincoln Restler introduced a bill two years ago to rein in the rising cost of Citi Bike rides.
“ This is such a tremendous victory for Citi Bike riders,” Restler said. “The city had given Lyft a monopoly, essentially, with the Citi Bike program and the cost spiraled out of control in such a way where it felt like New Yorkers were being taken advantage of.”
Citi Bike raised prices six times from 2022 through January 2026, with Lyft recently blaming tariffs and inflation for the need to raise rates.
“We’re grateful to Mayor Mamdani and Commissioner Flynn for working with us to make Citi Bike an even more sustainable, reliable, and affordable option for New Yorkers,” Patrick Knoth, general manager of Citi Bike, wrote in a statement.

https://taz.de/Palaestinensische-Frauen-.title: Palästinensische Frauen in Israel: Die Tabubrecherin
https://taz.de/Palaestinensische-Frauen-.author: Tamar Ziff
https://taz.de/Palaestinensische-Frauen-.text:
Palästinensische Frauen in Israel: Die Tabubrecherin
Abeer Zeibak Haddad sah schon früh Gewalt gegen Frauen in ihrer Umgebung. Als Dokumentarfilmerin bricht sie heute das Schweigen, das das Thema umgibt.
Abeer Zeibak Haddad war schon immer eine Kämpferin, wie sie selbst sagt. Als palästinensische Israeli, die in Nazareth aufwuchs, war sie erschüttert von dem Tabu, das Gewalt gegen Frauen umgab. Mit 17 engagierte sie sich ehrenamtlich in einer Schutzunterkunft in Haifa für Frauen, die häusliche Gewalt erlitten hatten. Seitdem widmet sie fast ihr ganzes Leben diesem Thema – als Regisseurin und Dozentin zu Gewalt gegen Frauen und Femizide in der arabisch-palästinensischen Gesellschaft.
Haddad spricht von ihrem Zuhause in Jaffa aus, wo sie heute lebt, und klingt am Telefon begeistert. „Gestern Abend haben wir ‚Women of Freedom‘ in Shfar’am (eine mehrheitlich arabische Stadt im Norden Israels, d. Red.) gezeigt. Der Film kam schon 2016 heraus – doch nach zehn Jahren wird er immer noch gezeigt.“
Ihr Film befasst sich mit dem, was gemeinhin als „Ehrenmorde“ bezeichnet wird, doch Haddad lehnt diesen Begriff ab. „Ein Mord ist ein Mord – darin liegt keine Ehre“, sagt sie. „Wenn ich über den Film schreibe oder Vorträge halte, verwende ich den Begriff ‚Mord an Frauen‘, um diesen Begriff nicht weiter zu verfestigen.“
„Women of Freedom“ ist Haddads zweiter Film. Sie brauchte fast vier Jahre, um ihn fertigzustellen, was sie mit der anhaltenden Zurückhaltung begründete, über Morde an Frauen in der arabischen Gesellschaft zu sprechen und sich damit auseinanderzusetzen. Ihr vorheriger Film, „Duma“, war der erste arabischsprachige Dokumentarfilm überhaupt, der sexuelle Gewalt gegen Frauen in der arabischen Gesellschaft Israels thematisierte.
Sie gab nicht auf
„Ich habe 2008 mit der Arbeit an dem Film begonnen. Man sagte mir: Du wirst auf keinen Fall Frauen finden, die bereit sind, darüber zu sprechen.“ Doch sie gab nicht auf. „Duma“ kam 2011 heraus und wurde seitdem vielfach in ganz Israel, im Westjordanland und im Ausland gezeigt, insbesondere an Gymnasien und Universitäten.
Für Haddad sind Filme ein wichtiges pädagogisches Instrument. Einige Schüler, die den Film als Teenager gesehen hatten, besuchten sie Jahre später und erzählten ihr, wie sehr sie ihr Film beeinflusst habe, sagt sie. Sie führt dies darauf zurück, dass sie selbst Teil der Gesellschaft ist, die sie kritisiert und verändern möchte.
Haddad glaubt, dass die arabische Gesellschaft sich diesem Thema zwar langsam, aber immer mehr öffnet. Ihre Filme dürften einen großen Teil dazu beigetragen haben. Doch das Ausmaß der Gewalt hat nicht abgenommen – und natürlich gebe es noch immer Widerstand dagegen, sich damit auseinanderzusetzen. Noch immer mangelt es an angemessener Aufklärung, und Haddad sieht auch eine Komplizenschaft innerhalb von Familien und Gemeinschaften, sowohl von Seiten der Männer als auch seitens der Frauen.
Nach außen hin wird Gewalt gegen arabische Frauen – und gegen arabische Israelis im Allgemeinen – von der israelischen Polizei nicht ernst genommen und nicht ordnungsgemäß untersucht. Laut aktuellen Berichten der jüdisch-arabischen gemeinnützigen Organisation The Abraham Initiatives findet die Polizei bei weniger als 15 Prozent der Morde an Arabern den Täter, verglichen mit rund 65 Prozent bei Morden an Juden.
Explosive Welle tödlicher Gewalt
Haddad sagt, dass die Polizei und die israelische Gesellschaft Gewalt in ihrer Gemeinschaft oft als „arabisches Problem“ betrachten, was zu geringeren Mitteln für Polizeischutz und angemessene allgemeine Bildung führt. Das Zusammenspiel dieser Faktoren hat in den vergangenen Jahren zu einer explosiven Welle tödlicher Gewalt in arabischen Gemeinden in Israel geführt.
Haddad wird weltweit zu Konferenzen zum Thema Frauenrechte und Gewalt gegen Frauen eingeladen und gilt in Israel nach wie vor als Expertin und Vorreiterin auf diesem Gebiet. Ihr nächstes Projekt, so sagt sie, sei ein historischer Film über feministische Aktivistinnen in Jaffa vor 1948. „Uns wird immer erzählt, dass Frauen in dieser Zeit nur in der Küche standen oder so“, sagt sie. „Aber das stimmt einfach nicht.“

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Toddlers are not just little people. Their culture deserves respect | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs.
As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I immediately went down an online rabbit hole and discovered various other people have made similar jokes. It’s a common issue.
And it’s not just unsolicited singing: a lot of weird things are a sign of great disrespect in small-child culture. When they are clearly exhausted, for example, you must not, under any circumstances, say: “You are clearly exhausted.” This is considered rude and uncalled for. When they tell the postman about your bowel movements, you must smile politely rather than shush them. And when they find a decaying leaf on the filthy pavement and hand it to you, you must not say: “Yuck, that probably has dog pee on it.” Instead, you must marvel over how beautiful it is, and guard it with your life until they forget about it and it has crumbled to pieces in your pocket.
While I could do without my singing being critiqued, I do enjoy being given little street treasures. One of the greatest joys of parenthood is watching your child marvel over the mundane. To bastardise William Blake, little kids really are able to “see a world in a grain of sand / And a heaven in a wild flower”. As Blake also wrote in Auguries of Innocence (a real banger): “He who respects the infant’s faith / Triumphs over Hell and Death.” So, until she grows out of it, I shall be respecting my child’s faith. Next time my five-year-old screams when I attempt to sing along to Frozen, I’m not going to take it personally – I’m just going to let it go.

https://taz.de/Ermittlungen-gegen-Terror.title: Ermittlungen gegen „Terror 18“: Bundesanwaltschaft knüpft sich nächste Jungnazi-Gruppe vor
https://taz.de/Ermittlungen-gegen-Terror.author: Konrad Litschko
https://taz.de/Ermittlungen-gegen-Terror.text:
Ermittlungen gegen „Terror 18“: Bundesanwaltschaft knüpft sich nächste Jungnazi-Gruppe vor
Sie drohten in Chats mit Gewalt, wollten Brandanschläge verüben. Nun geht die Bundesanwaltschaft gegen die Neonazis von „Terror 18“ vor.
Sie sind sehr jung, posierten mit Hitlergruß, prahlten mit Gewalt. Nun ist die Jungnazi-Gruppe „Terror 18“, erst vor wenigen Wochen gegründet, ein Fall für die Bundesanwaltschaft. Die oberste Ermittlungsbehörde veranlasste am Mittwoch bundesweit mehrere Durchsuchungen und nahm drei Gruppenmitglieder fest; drei weitere befanden sich bereits in Haft. Der Vorwurf: Bildung einer terroristischen Vereinigung.
Die Gruppe hatte sich über eine geschlossene WhatsApp‑Gruppe zusammengefunden. Vor allem Teenager aus Mecklenburg-Vorpommern und Schleswig-Holstein, aber auch aus anderen Bundesländern versammelten sich dort. Gut 40 Mitglieder sollen es gewesen sein. Das Gruppenlogo war mit SS-Totenkopf oder Sturmgewehr versehen, in Chats wurde zu „Antifa jagen“ aufgerufen oder zu Gewalt gegen Geflüchtete.
„Lass mal was anzünden (…) dann verbrennen die alle und das ist sogar viel besser, dann müssen wir sie nicht schlagen“, schrieb ein Mitglied. Es müsse „wenigstens einen toten K*naken geben“. Verabredet wurde sich auch zum „Pedo Hunting“, zur Jagd auf vermeintliche Pädophile.
Und es blieb nicht bei Worten. Ende Oktober war ein 15-jähriges Mitglied, Marcello P., in Wahlstedt in Schleswig-Holstein mit einem Benzinkanister losgezogen – zuvor hatte er in der Chatgruppe einen Anschlag auf eine lokale Geflüchtetenunterkunft angekündigt, wie die Antifa-Recherchegruppe Exif öffentlich machte. Antifaschisten stoppten den Jugendlichen nahe seines Wohnhauses, die Polizei nahm ihn fest. Auch das Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz soll in der Chatgruppe mitgelesen und die Polizei gewarnt haben.
Anschlag in Schwerin verhindert
Wenig später wurden zwei weitere „Terror 18“-Mitstreiter festgenommen: zunächst der mutmaßliche Gruppengründer Dwayne S., ein 18-Jähriger aus der Nähe von Schwerin, später dann Jarik Fabian W. aus Winsen in Niedersachsen, der Marcello P. mit angestachelt und bei sich vor Ort ebenso eine Unterkunft mit einem Stein beworfen haben soll. Die Gruppe hatte auf Social-Media-Kanälen auch danach getönt, man werde weitermachen.
Die taz hatte schon Anfang November berichtet, dass die Gruppe noch mindestens einen weiteren Brandanschlag plante: auf das linke Wohnprojekt Komplex in Schwerin. Die Polizei hatte die Tat zwar verhindert, die Bewohner*innen aber beklagten, sie seien nicht über den Tatplan informiert worden.
Die Bundesanwaltschaft geht nun von noch weiteren geplanten Brandanschlägen aus und von Gewalttaten „bis hin zu gezielten Tötungen von Ausländern und politischen Gegnern“.
Festgenommen wurden am Mittwoch deshalb Kalle K., Lasse G. und Shawn Z. in Brandenburg, Niedersachsen und Schleswig-Holstein, allesamt Teenager. Sie sollten anschließend Haftrichtern vorgeführt werden. Ob diese tatsächlich in allen Fällen Haftbefehle in Vollzug setzen, war wegen des jungen Alters der Beschuldigten ungewiss.
Zusätzliche Durchsuchungen gab es in insgesamt zehn Orten in Brandenburg, Niedersachsen, Bayern, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern und Sachsen. Ermittelt wird hier gegen vier weitere Beschuldigte, die die Gruppe unterstützt oder geplante Straftaten nicht angezeigt haben sollen. Durchsucht wurde dabei nach taz-Informationen auch ein 13-Jähriger, der noch nicht strafmündig ist. Im Einsatz waren rund 70 Polizeibeamte.
Die Bundesanwaltschaft war zuletzt schon gegen die Jungnazi-Gruppe „Letzte Verteidigungswelle“ vorgegangen, die bereits mit Anschlägen auftrat. Auch hier lautete der Vorwurf: Terror. Das Oberlandesgericht Hamburg verhängte im August gegen acht Beschuldigte Jugendstrafen von bis zu fünf Jahren Haft.
Unter den „Terror 18“-Mitgliedern war nun auch mindestens ein bekennender AfD-Fan. Fotos zeigen den Schweriner Amon G. auf zwei Kundgebungen der Partei im August und September in Schwerin, auch bei einem Aufmarsch der AfD‑Jugend. Die Partei hatte dazu eine taz-Anfrage unbeantwortet gelassen.

https://taz.de/Umweltschutz-und-Landwirt.title: Umweltschutz und Landwirtschaft: Pestizidrecht schützt Böden Studie zufolge zu wenig
https://taz.de/Umweltschutz-und-Landwirt.author: Jost Maurin
https://taz.de/Umweltschutz-und-Landwirt.text:
Umweltschutz und Landwirtschaft: Pestizidrecht schützt Böden Studie zufolge zu wenig
Forscher:innen stellen Defizite beim Schutz der Böden vor Pestiziden fest. Die Regeln seien veraltet und bei Verstößen gebe es kaum Konsequenzen.
Die deutschen Gesetze schützen Böden einer neuen Studie zufolge nur unzureichend vor Pestiziden. Die Vorschriften zur Anwendung der Mittel hätten eine „sehr begrenzte Steuerungswirkung“, schreiben Katharine Heyl, Jessica Stubenrauch und Felix Klickermann vom Helmholtz-Zentrum für Umweltforschung (UFZ) in der Fachzeitschrift Environmental Management. Sie seien zu ungenau und kaum durchsetzbar.
Der Einsatz von Pestiziden ist eine von mehreren Methoden, mit denen Landwirt:innen ihre Pflanzen vor Schädlingen schützen können. Die Chemikalien tragen aber dazu bei, dass Pflanzen- und Tierarten aussterben. Zudem haben sich manche Mittel im Nachhinein als gesundheitsschädlich erwiesen.
Als Beispiel für mangelhafte Regulierung nennen die Forscher:innen die im Pflanzenschutzgesetz vorgeschriebene „gute fachliche Praxis“, die unter anderem einen möglichst umweltschonenden Pestizideinsatz sicherstellen soll. Die Grundsätze seien seit 2010 nicht aktualisiert worden, neuere Erkenntnisse über die Belastung der Böden fehlten deshalb. Verstöße gegen die gute fachliche Praxis seien zudem nicht unmittelbar sanktionierbar. „Kontrolle und Durchsetzung sind daher praktisch unmöglich“, schreiben die Autor:innen, solange eine Behörde keine konkreten Maßnahmen angeordnet habe.
Wie selten kontrolliert wird, zeigen Zahlen des Bundesamts für Verbraucherschutz und Lebensmittelsicherheit, auf die sich die Studie stützt: 2023 wurden demnach nur 1,5 Prozent der Betriebe überprüft, bei 21 Prozent dieser Kontrollen gab es Verstöße gegen Vorschriften zur Pestizidanwendung. Bei einer Kontrollserie 2025 verstieß rund ein Drittel der überprüften Betriebe (230 von 687) gegen Gewässerabstände oder produktspezifische Anwendungsbestimmungen.
Bundesagrarministerium „prüft“ die Studie
Auch das Bundesbodenschutzgesetz bietet nach Einschätzung der Wissenschaftler keinen ausreichenden Schutz. Auf Agrarflächen gingen die spezielleren Regeln des Pflanzenschutzrechts vor. Das führe zu einer „bedauerlichen Situation“, schreiben die Autor:innen: Der Vorrang des Spezialrechts gelte selbst dann, „wenn die Bodenschutzmaßnahmen in den Spezialgesetzen hinter dem Standard des Bundesbodenschutzgesetzes zurückbleiben“.
Ähnlich fällt die Kritik am Bundesnaturschutzgesetz aus. Nach einem Urteil des Bundesverwaltungsgerichts von 2016 enthalten die Vorgaben für eine naturverträgliche Landwirtschaft nur unverbindliche Leitlinien. Die UFZ-Forscher schließen sich dieser Bewertung an. Außerhalb von Natura-2000-Gebieten leiste das deutsche Naturschutzrecht deshalb keinen ausreichenden Beitrag zur Verringerung der Pestizidrisiken, schreiben sie. In und in der Nähe dieser EU-Schutzgebiete müssen die Mitgliedstaaten dagegen nach europäischem Recht schädlichen Pestizideinsatz zumindest einschränken, sofern keine rechtlich zulässige Ausnahme greift.
In nationalen Naturschutzgebieten ist der Einsatz zwar grundsätzlich verboten. Doch Ausnahmen, etwa zur Abwehr erheblicher wirtschaftlicher Schäden oder zur Sicherung von Bahnstrecken, schwächten die Verbote und erschwerten ihre Durchsetzung.
Die Forscher empfehlen, die gute fachliche Praxis zu aktualisieren und verbindlich zu machen, mit überprüfbaren Anforderungen sowie Kontroll- und Sanktionsmöglichkeiten für die Behörden. Außerdem schlagen sie Pufferzonen zwischen Naturschutzgebieten und Agrarflächen vor. Zusätzlich halten sie eine Pestizidsteuer für nötig, deren Höhe sich nach der Umweltgefährlichkeit der Wirkstoffe richtet. Eine pauschale Abgabe hingegen könnte dazu führen, dass Landwirte weniger, aber giftigere Mittel einsetzen, so die Wissenschaftler. Die Einnahmen könnten Umweltleistungen der Landwirtschaft finanzieren.
Das von dem CSU-Politiker Alois Rainer geleitete Bundesagrarministerium teilte der taz in einer Stellungnahme zu der Kritik nur mit: „Die genannte Studie ist dem Bundesministerium für Landwirtschaft, Ernährung und Heimat (BMLEH) bekannt. Sie wird derzeit im BMLEH geprüft.“

https://taz.de/Gen-Z-Proteste-und-Gewalt.title: Gen-Z-Proteste und Gewalt: Karneval der Freiheit
https://taz.de/Gen-Z-Proteste-und-Gewalt.author: Robert Misik
https://taz.de/Gen-Z-Proteste-und-Gewalt.text:
Gen-Z-Proteste und Gewalt: Karneval der Freiheit
Ja, der Typus des übermotivierten Engagierten kann nerven. Doch brauchen Bewegungen ihre Energie, um die Ohnmacht der Vereinzelung zu überwinden.
D ie Protestler wurden als ungewaschene Langhaarige geschmäht, die konservative Presse und andere mediale Leitkulturen konnten sich gar nicht mehr einkriegen: „Rote Unruhestifter“, „Politgammler“, „Volksfeinde“ machte die Bild-Zeitung aus. Gegenstand des bürgerlichen Nervenzusammenbruchs waren Hippies, die 68er-Bewegung und natürlich deren Frontleute wie Rudi Dutschke und Daniel Cohn-Bendit. Sechzig Jahre ist das jetzt her. Heute lachen wir über die autoritären Leitartikler von damals.
Jetzt protestiert die Jugend unserer Tage auch wieder. Und die alten Feindmuster sind wiedergekehrt. Nur dass die Jugend nicht mehr als langhaarig und ungewaschen diffamiert wird, sondern als gewalttätige Plünderer, Chaoten, als Antisemiten und – natürlich – als testosterongetriebene „migrantische Milieus“. Grotesker Treppenwitz der Geschichte: Es soll vorkommen, dass nicht wenige derer, die vor sechzig Jahren selbst als „Politgammler“ diffamiert wurden, jetzt bei der Elitenpanik mitmachen. Man hat sich in der Altbauwohnung schön eingerichtet.
Die Sozialfigur des migrantischen männlichen Jugendlichen erinnert als soziale Wahnvorstellung manchmal an die Angstfantasie der gesetzten bürgerlichen Milieus des 19. Jahrhunderts: Die gruselten sich über jene, die man seinerzeit die „gefährlichen Klassen“ nannte.
„Der Begriff der gefährlichen Klassen (französisch: classes dangereuses) stammt aus dem 19. Jahrhundert und bezeichnete im Zuge der Industrialisierung die schnell wachsende, eigentumslose Armuts- und Unterschicht in den Großstädten“, weiß schon die KI. Prägend für die Diskurse ist „bürgerliche Angst“. Denn: „Die bürgerliche Oberschicht und der Staat fürchteten, dass sich Teile der verelendeten Bevölkerung der staatlichen Kontrolle entziehen, kriminell werden oder soziale Unruhen und Revolutionen anzetteln.“
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Die Phase der (post-)pubertären Unsicherheit reicht heute weit hinein ins Lebensalter zwischen dreißig und vierzig. Einstieg ins Berufsleben? Holprig. Wohnungen? Faktisch nicht zu bekommen und sowieso unleistbar. Das Leben selbst? Unleistbar. Prekäre Jobs reichen vielleicht für ein Zimmer, jeder Jobsverlust bedroht die Existenz. Früher konnte man für kleines Geld ein Bohemeleben führen. Heute kommt man mit weniger als 1.500 Euro kaum durch den Monat. Ein bisschen rumlungern und sich ausprobieren? Das ging früher, wenn der Wohnraum gerade mal 200 D-Mark kostete.
Was glaubt die heutige Mehrheitsgesellschaft eigentlich: Dass man die Leben der Jungen ruinieren kann, das Weltklima zerstören, die Lebenshaltungskosten in die Höhe treiben kann, dass man die Idee von einem eigenen Wohnraum in eine irreale Fantasie verwandeln kann? Dass man alle auf Dauer mit der Peitsche der Prekarität gefügig halten kann und sie schön den Rücken krümmen und einen Knicks machen? Glaubt sie das wirklich?
Die Revolte ist nicht ein Aufstand gegen die moralische Ordnung, sondern umgekehrt ein Aufstand dagegen, dass die moralische Ordnung gebrochen worden ist. Die wahren Plünderer ziehen nicht mit Kapuzenpulli durch die Straßenzüge. Nicht die Proteste sind radikal, sondern die Verhältnisse, gegen die sie sich wenden. Radikal ist die skrupellose Schurkerei, mit der die Wichtigtuer, Gutvernetzten, die Tech-Oligarchen und die besonders gut organisierte Kriminalität der Geldsäcke die Welt ruinieren und den Jungen die Zukunft stehlen.
Trivial ist der Vorhalt, dass Proteste auch Halbstarke anziehen können, bei denen der Erlebnishunger die politische Strategie überwiegt. Radikalinski-Getue und Spinnertum gehen gelegentlich Hand in Hand, und kaum ein gesellschaftlicher Fortschritt wurde je erkämpft ohne ein paar nervige Narren am Rand.
Der Sozialwissenschaftler Tareq Sydiq hat vor kurzem das Buch „Die neue Protestkultur“ herausgebracht. Proteste haben es schwer, sie werden niedergeschlagen, sie werden ignoriert, sie verlieren mit der Zeit ihren Elan – warum haben sie „trotz allem regelmäßig Erfolg?“, fragt Sydiq. Protestbewegungen sind dann erfolgreich, „wenn sie es schaffen, heterogene Gruppen zu mobilisieren, weil sie damit unterschiedliche Milieus ansprechen“, so Sydiq.
Und wer einmal an Protesten teilgenommen hat, wird auch künftig leichter mobilisierbar sein. So entstehen politisch aktive Milieus mit langfristiger Wirkung. Besonders wirksam sind sie, wenn Verbände entstehen, die die Aktivitäten verstetigen, und wenn damit ein „Marsch durch die Institutionen“ gelingt. Sind sie friedlich, nützen sie dem Anliegen, werden sie gewalttätig, stoßen sie auch Verbündete ab. Sie können Parteien treiben und anstacheln. Nicht immer können Regierende den Protest aussitzen.
Ausbruch aus Demütigung
Dabei ist noch die Randale – als Sprache der Sprachlosen, als Ausnahmezustand von unten – nicht nur Spektakel, von Lust am Exzess getrieben, sondern immer auch eine Art Karneval der Freiheit. Was den einen als sinnlose Zerstörung erscheint, ist manchmal auch temporärer Ausbruch aus Demütigung, Kommandiert-Werden und der Erfahrung chronischer Respektlosigkeit.
Bewegungen haben auch etwas Ansteckendes. Sie überwinden die Ohnmacht der Vereinzelung, geben Schwung und Gemeinschaftsgefühl, können den Nebel der Depression vertreiben. Politische Bewegungen sind Erfahrungsräume des Politischen, und das unmittelbarer als die Ortsverbände von Parteien. In ihnen lernt man Dinge, die kein Lehrbuch vermitteln kann und die die Engagierten prägen.
Bevor sie die Welt verändern, verändern sie die Aktiven. Im besten Fall ist solches Engagement Einübung in Lebenskunst. Der Typus des übermotivierten Engagierten kann einem zweifelsohne oft ordentlich auf die Nerven gehen: Gern gilt ihm der, welcher nicht alles exakt genauso erregt sieht wie er selbst, nicht als potenzieller Verbündeter, sondern als Gegner.
Der übermotivierte Engagierte hat nicht immer automatisch recht, aber das elitäre Naserümpfen über das Engagement hat immer unrecht.

https://taz.de/Ungarns-Magyar-besucht-di.title: Ungarns Magyar besucht die Ukraine: Volleyball statt Eiszeit
https://taz.de/Ungarns-Magyar-besucht-di.author: Florian Bayer
https://taz.de/Ungarns-Magyar-besucht-di.text:
Ungarns Magyar besucht die Ukraine: Volleyball statt Eiszeit
Ungarns Regierungschef Peter Magyar trifft den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj in Transkarpatien. Die Beziehungen tauen zumindest ein bisschen auf.
Ungarns Regierungschef Péter Magyar hat am Dienstag das westukrainische Transkarpatien besucht und dort den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj getroffen. Mit dabei war Außenministerin Anita Orbán (nicht verwandt mit dem früheren Premier). Magyar sprach von einem historischen Tag und einer großen Chance, ein neues Kapitel aufzuschlagen, „das gute Nachbarn brauchen“. Selenskyj erklärte, die Ukraine sei bereit, „einen konstruktiven Dialog und eine Beziehung“ mit Ungarn aufzubauen.
Unter Magyars Vorgänger Viktor Orbán hatten sich die Nachbarländer stark entfremdet, nun nähern sie sich wieder an. Es ist der erste Besuch eines ungarischen Ministerpräsidenten in Transkarpatien seit 2015. Selenskyj kritisierte die frühere Führung in Budapest. In der politischen Elite habe es keinen Respekt gegeben, man habe die Menschen „aufgehetzt“.
Der Tag begann in der Gebietshauptstadt Uschhorod an der slowakischen Grenze. Auf dem Kalvarienfriedhof legten beide Staatschefs Kränze für gefallene Soldaten nieder. Hauptort war aber Berehowe, ungarisch Beregszász, das Zentrum der ungarischen Minderheit. Dort besuchten Magyar und Selenskyj ein mit ungarischem Geld renoviertes Krankenhaus und das ungarischsprachige Kossuth-Lyzeum, wo sie die Anzüge ablegten und mit Schülern Volleyball spielten. Am Abend traf Magyar Vertreter der ungarischen Gemeinschaft.
In Transkarpatien lebten bei der Volkszählung 2001 gut 150.000 ethnische Ungarn. Durch Abwanderung, vor allem seit Kriegsbeginn, dürften es heute weniger als 100.000 sein. Orbán nutzte die Minderheit immer wieder politisch. Auch Magyar macht ihre Rechte zur Bedingung für Ungarns Zustimmung zum EU-Beitritt der Ukraine. Dass das ukrainische Parlament im Oktober ein Minderheitengesetz beschloss, habe das Vertrauen gestärkt, so Magyar. Zugleich dämpfte er die Erwartungen. Ein beschleunigtes Beitrittsverfahren „gibt es nicht“, Ungarns eigener Beitritt habe 13 Jahre gedauert. Selenskyj nannte den EU-Weg seines Landes „unumkehrbar“.
Weiterhin keine Waffen aus Ungarn an die Ukraine
Magyar betonte die Unterstützung des von Russland überfallenen Landes. „Das ungarische Volk verurteilt entschieden die schreckliche russische Aggression, die seit fast fünf Jahren gegen Zivilisten und Soldaten tobt“, sagte er. Für einen Frieden brauche die Ukraine internationale Sicherheitsgarantien. Er erinnerte an das Budapester Memorandum von 1994, mit dem Kyjiw seine Atomwaffen abgab.
Seit Orbáns Abwahl im April hat sich Ungarn der Ukraine wieder angenähert. Im Juni und im Oktober gab Budapest sein Veto gegen weitere Beitrittskapitel auf, vier von sechs Verhandlungsclustern sind nun geöffnet. Ungarn will zudem die humanitäre Hilfe ausbauen: Magyar brachte Medizintechnik, Medikamente, Generatoren und Fahrzeuge im Wert von einer Milliarde Forint mit, rund 2,7 Millionen Euro. Auch kündigte Magyar einen neuen Sozialfonds für die Ungarn in Transkarpatien an. Waffen will Ungarn weiterhin nicht liefern.
Besprochen wurde zudem Zusammenarbeit bei Energie und Handel. Selenskyj sprach von großem Bedarf an Diesel und bot Mais an. Nach der Dürre fehlen Ungarn rund zwei Millionen Tonnen, weswegen die Agrarminister beider Länder nun über befristete Einfuhren verhandeln. Die Grenzübergänge sollen zudem erneuert und um neue ergänzt, die Bahnstrecke Kyjiw-Budapest ausgebaut und elektrifiziert werden. Beim Wiederaufbau sieht Magyar Ungarn logistisch in einer Schlüsselrolle.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Rafael Behr
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.
That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.
I don’t pretend to understand much of what Bernhard Riemann proposed in 1859. I know it relates to primes – whole integers greater than 1 that are divisible only by 1 and themselves – and the pattern of their distribution along the infinite number line. But you don’t need to know what a zeta function is to recognise that the solution to a near-170-year-old problem is a big deal in maths, or that the role of AI in completing the quest is a big deal for humanity.
Around two years ago, large language models that mesmerised users with their verbal dexterity sucked at maths. They made basic arithmetic errors. Now they resolve unfathomably hard problems with ease. In Alpöge’s breathless account of the process, Claude “flew, and danced, and sparkled” towards its conclusion. It left him “in awe”.
Other mathematicians whose discipline is being eaten by machines report more complex feelings. In October, OpenAI published hundreds of AI-generated papers containing proofs to unsolved problems, stunning faculties that had been toiling over the relevant questions for years. Some called it the “mathocalypse”.
There is still a long process of verification to run. Humans have to check that the machines haven’t taken rogue shortcuts, but early indications back the AI. Researchers are witnessing intricate edifices of abstract cognition, their life’s work, crushed under silicon bulldozers.
Many are upset, angry. Some are excited by the future possibilities, some more sceptical or feeling a combination of emotions that an LLM can describe and imitate but not, as far as we know, experience.
Mathematicians are not the first people to worry that a rising technological tide will wash away their livelihood. But their position is unusual in ways that go beyond the conventional fear of obsolescence.
Maths describes fundamental laws of the universe. Nothing is truer than a mathematically proven truth. The limit of what advanced mathematicians know delineates the frontier of human knowledge – or it has done until now. The soaring rate of computational capability raises the prospect of machines exploring dimensions that humans cannot comprehend, generating proofs that have to be taken on trust. What kind of knowledge even is it if no organic mind knows how it came to be known?
In the past, when great mysteries have been solved, the method has been as thrilling as the result. Andrew Wiles cracked Fermat’s Last Theorem by building bridges between previously disconnected realms of maths, opening new vistas of theoretical space for further exploration. It was an arduous ascent to higher truth. AI-generated proofs are windowless lifts that hoist you to the summit with little sense of how you got there.
They are also weird, according to people who can decrypt them. Hannah Fry, Cambridge maths professor, broadcaster, author and one of the world’s best communicators of hard concepts to a lay audience, called one of the recent OpenAI proofs “almost hilariously ugly”.
That might sound like a marginal quibble if the underlying logic is sound, but the aesthetic of an answer is not a minor consideration in maths. The human mind is gratified by the elegance of a solution. It is hard to celebrate an insight extracted by tens of thousands of AI agents torturing equations day and night, burning tens of millions of dollars of computing power, just so a tech company with an eye on its prospective stock market valuation can say it got to the answer before any human.
To that objection, AI evangelists say the mathematicians are being precious. If an LLM found a safe treatment for a previously incurable disease, doctors would prescribe it even if they didn’t understand how it worked. Does it matter if humans get left behind as the frontiers of knowledge are pushed forwards?
The answer depends on who controls the pace of advance and their motives. Tech boosters talk about godlike intelligence emerging when autonomous AI models start coding their successors on a trajectory of exponential self-improvement. The mathematical breakthroughs of recent weeks don’t tip us over that threshold but they bring it into view.
That a scenario is conceivable doesn’t make it inevitable. But it would be complacent to assume that soaraway superintelligence won’t happen just because it sounds far-fetched, or because tech bros are given to hyperbole, or because their businesses are perched on a Jenga tower of debt.
It can be true that AI investment is a bubble and also that the technology is capable of superseding humanity. When the first dotcom boom turned to bust at the turn of the millennium, it didn’t reveal the internet to be all worthless hype. Railways were a transformative technology for the US despite cycles of irrational exuberance, track laid to nowhere and spectacular bankruptcies.
The precedent of past industrial revolutions suggests today’s AI pioneers will be a coalition of canny entrepreneurs, philanthropic idealists, suckers, charlatans and sociopaths. Their product will offer benefits and harms; economic gains and toxic contamination. The industry will resist regulatory constraints. Resistance will take the form of increasingly blatant corruption. It will be overcome only when scandals generate a backlash of sufficient force.
In an optimistic reading of the current moment, the feeling of vertiginous peril indicates proximity to the top of the cycle. We are at the apex of hubris, when the people who are profiting most from the absence of restraint insist that laws of economic and political gravity no longer apply, shortly before discovering that they do.
This is why brute-forcing famous mathematical conundrums matters so much to the AI labs. Proving that the machines can transcend every conceivable human achievement is a way to sustain the idea that this time is different, that an AI-powered Icarus can soar beyond the sun. And this is the ugliness that despondent mathematicians discern in those proofs. It is the difference between exploration to advance knowledge and a land grab in pursuit of power.
- Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

https://taz.de/Menschenrechtspreis/!6232.title: Menschenrechtspreis: Palästinensischer Anwalt für Kinderrechte wird geehrt
https://taz.de/Menschenrechtspreis/!6232.author: Serena Bilanceri
https://taz.de/Menschenrechtspreis/!6232.text:
Menschenrechtspreis: Palästinensischer Anwalt für Kinderrechte wird geehrt
Amnesty International hat den Anwalt Khaled Quzmar für seinen Einsatz für Kinder in Haft ausgezeichnet. Die israelische Regierung bringt seinen Verein mit Terror in Verbindung.
Seit fast vier Jahrzehnten beschäftigt sich Khaled Quzmar mit einem besonders schwierigen, ja fast grausamen Thema: Kindern in Haft. Jetzt erhält er für seine Arbeit den Menschenrechtspreis der Organisation Amnesty International.
Quzmar ist Anwalt, spezialisiert auf die Verteidigung von Minderjährigen, die vor Gericht landen. Fast sein ganzes Leben lang vertritt er im von Israel besetzten Westjordanland Palästinenser:innen, die sich vor Militärgerichten verantworten müssen. Denn im Westjordanland gilt für sie, anders als für israelische Siedler:innen, das Militärrecht. Etwa 350 Kinder befinden sich derzeit in Haft. Und die Verwaltungshaft erlaubt es den israelischen Behörden, Menschen ohne Anklage jahrelang in Gewahrsam zu halten. Unter ihnen befanden sich laut Daten von Unicef, die sich auf Angaben des israelischen Gefängnisdienstes stützen, im September 2026 mindestens 164 Minderjährige.
Auch für sie setzt sich Quzmar ein. Immer wieder berichten seine jungen Klienten von Schlägen und Misshandlungen im Gefängnis. An die Erzählungen hat sich der Anwalt selbst nach 40 Jahren nicht gewöhnt. „Das sind Kinder, sie haben diese Brutalität nicht verdient“, sagt er.
Er selbst hat sich für den Beruf des Juristen entschieden, als sein eigener Bruder festgenommen wurde. Damals war Quzmar 13 Jahre alt und lebte noch in einem kleinen Dorf im westlichen Westjordanland. Während des Besuchs im Gefängnis durfte er den Bruder nicht in die Arme schließen, sondern lediglich seine Hand durch das Drahtgitter berühren. Seinen Anwalt ließen die Sicherheitskräfte hingegen hinein.
Also ließ er sich nach dem Schulabschluss an der algerischen Universität in Oran für Rechtswissenschaften einschreiben, denn eine juristische Fakultät gab es damals im Westjordanland nicht. Er kehrte dann in den 80er Jahren zurück und bildete sich später in Irland weiter. Zunächst engagierte er sich im Verein Defense for Children International-Palestine. Seit Juni 2026 ist er Geschäftsführer des Palestinian Centre for Child Rights.
Quzmar, der auf Bildern immer einen nachdenklichen Blick unter den markanten Augenbrauen hat, ist eine kontroverse Figur: In den palästinensischen Gebieten wird er gefeiert, in Israel harsch kritisiert. Die israelische Armee führte 2021 eine Razzia im Büro von Defense for Children International durch, die Regierung bezeichnete sie kurze Zeit später als „Terrororganisation“.
Sie soll Verbindungen zur verbotenen Volksfront zur Befreiung Palästinas gehabt haben, was Quzmar bestreitet. Überzeugende Beweise legte Israel nicht vor, so weigerten sich Deutschland und acht weitere EU-Länder, die NGO als Terrororganisation einzustufen. Ein Jahr später bestellte der israelische Inlandsgeheimdienst Schin Beth den Anwalt auf eine Militärbasis, in der er zwei Stunden lang verhört wurde. Anschließend kam er wieder frei.
Seit dem Hamas-Massaker am 7. Oktober und dem Krieg in Gaza ist Quzmars Arbeit noch schwieriger geworden. „Um Informationen über inhaftierte Kinder zu bekommen, muss ich Briefe an die Gefängnisse in Israel schreiben und monatelang auf eine Antwort warten“, erzählt er. Insgesamt, das belegen Berichte von Menschenrechtsorganisationen sowie eine Recherche der taz, haben sich die Haftbedingungen palästinensischer Insassen deutlich verschlechtert – auch die von Minderjährigen. Trotz der Schwierigkeiten lässt sich Quzmar nicht entmutigen. „Du musst in die Kinder investieren, damit sie in Zukunft führen können“, sagt er.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong.
So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’”
The two never discussed the incident. In the meantime, Araújo developed a sense of hyperawareness for potentially fragile safety, often double-checking the locks of her family’s home. Occasionally, she overheard her parents talk about the morning in the park, or the subsequent rape trial, or the fact that the perpetrator was released from prison when Araújo was 15. She often struggled to sleep. Then, in 2014, another incident – a stranger groped her in a theater – tipped her “functional hypervigilance” into a dark spiral. After 20 years, she finally asked her father about what they had both witnessed; she learned, for the first time, that the perpetrator had pulled a knife on her father, who tracked him at a distance until police arrived. “I asked him why he didn’t explain it to me on the day, when I asked what was going on, and he said he didn’t want to scare me,” she recalled. “But with his best intentions, of exactly how he wanted to protect me and love me, the exact opposite occurred. I became much more scared.”
In the days after that phone call, Araújo wrote a “vomit draft” in a near-literal sense, a regurgitation of that long-ago poison. “I needed to purge it out of me,” she said. The result was Josephine, which arrives, more than a decade and many revisions later, in theaters this month after a heralded festival fun; the film won both the grand jury prize and audience award at Sundance, where it left me stunned – by its refusal to blur what Josephine sees, by its bravura performances and by its precise evocation of a child’s mind ruptured by darkness she can’t yet comprehend. Like Araújo, Josephine learns the word “rape” from the incident (and then sneaking her mom’s phone to search “raip”). Writing from Josephine’s perspective became a question of: “Can I transport the audience back to being de-assimilated, to a time before they knew what sexual violence was?” Araújo said. “I learned about it in a very specific and very harsh way, but everyone learned it at some point. And so how did it then inform how we moved our bodies through the world, how we thought about our own safety?”
The film is “fictionalized, but factual”, tracing a different arc of aftermath to Araújo’s, one contained to Josephine’s immediate fear and confusion – in the days after the incident, Josephine begins to view all boys or displays of adult intimacy with hostility – and her parents’ fumbling attempts to help her. Both Gemma Chan, as her mother, Claire, and especially Tatum are superb as parents whose own coping mechanisms for male violence – calm dissociation on the one hand, fighting back on the other – cloud their well-meaning but inadequate responses to their daughter. Damien insists, without merit, that something like that will never happen to Josephine. Like Araújo’s own father, he enrolls her in self-defense classes. Claire attempts therapy, then gently tries to distract.
Damien and Claire’s counterproductive efforts “are not because they don’t love their daughter”, said Araújo. “Channing and I talked about this extensively, because he has a daughter himself – how do you talk to your daughter about sexual assault?” The inability to confront such a verboten topic from either side – the loving parent, the innocent child – forms the backbone of the film. For parents, “the lack of control must feel horrifying, because you love this person so much and yet you can’t control them starting to learn and experience the darkness of this world.” Neither parent can conceive that at night, Josephine imagines the perpetrator from the park in an aqua polo (Philip Ettinger) lurking about her room.
Viewers know the perpetrator from the film’s shattering first scene, which breaks with recent cinematic convention to elide the horror of sexual assault, allowing the viewer to fill in the blanks (see: Women Talking, She Said and Sorry, Baby), with a graphic account of just what Josephine witnesses from the bushes. It’s every film-maker’s choice, how they want to portray it,” said Araújo of the decision to stage a rape in full (the scene was shot so that Reeves, of course, sees nothing). “I just felt like if we didn’t fully see what Josephine sees, the audience would lose connection to her fear, and where she goes for the rest of the film.”
The decision was also partly informed by Araújo’s time training as a witness advocate in San Francisco, focusing on accompanying victims to obtain rape kits at a hospital within 72 hours of an assault, and her time working shifts for the LA Rape and Battering Hotline. “So many times, I heard from people that they wish they had fought back more, that they wish that they had done something differently, that if they had done this, maybe they could have stopped it.” As a witness advocate, Araújo says: “We are trained to remind survivors that their first goal was to keep themselves alive. So often when survivors fight back, it does get more violent. And I really wanted to honor that experience, because sexual violence is violent.”
Thanks to the help of screenwriters’ grants, Araújo shadowed multiple sexual assault cases through the San Francisco Hall of Justice, which informed the film’s second half, in which Josephine is called upon as the sole witness for the perpetrator’s rape trial. Two judges, two public defenders and two prosecutors read over the script to ensure accuracy to the California legal system, including the fact that female public defenders are often assigned to defend men charged with rape; in the film, the perpetrator’s lawyer attempts to undermine Josephine’s confidence and suggests that she witnessed consensual role-playing. “I’ve had such a challenging time throughout my life trying to wrap my head around him pleading not guilty,” said Araújo. “I never testified in court, and I think part of why I wrote that in was to say what I know is true.”
Araújo is resistant to discuss Josephine in terms of healing or progress. “I don’t think that anyone ever fully heals or has this big, beautiful catharsis from anything having to do with sexual violence,” she said. “I think you become a different person, and that person can continue.” But it’s “no surprise” that the film’s release, after years of development and revision, funding secured and pulled and resecured with the help of Tatum’s star wattage, coincides with a release of some fear. “This year, I’m sleeping through the night,” she said. “That’s very meaningful in my life.”
- Josephine is out in US and UK cinemas now and in Australia on 18 February

https://www.humanite.fr/medias/blast/soi.title: Soirée de lancement de Combat n°2 : contre le RN, « rien n’est joué »
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/blast/soi.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/blast/soi.text:
Ce mercredi 25 novembre, notre journal a accueilli dans ses locaux, la soirée de lancement du numéro 2 du hors-série de Combat. Avec quatre autres médias, Blast, les Inrocks, Streetpress et Nova, le collectif vient de publier « Le vrai visage du RN », en kiosque depuis mardi 24 novembre.
À Saint-Denis, les locaux de l’Humanité ont accueilli la soirée de lancement du deuxième hors-série collectif contre l’extrême droite : « Le vrai visage du RN ». https://www.humanite.fr/politique/associ.text:
En menaçant les associations de supprimer leurs subventions publiques arbitrairement, au prétexte flou d’une « politisation », la candidate du Rassemblement national assume sa volonté de mettre au pas les contre-pouvoirs pour basculer dans une démocratie illibérale. Syndicats, agences, collectivités, médias, justice sont également dans le viseur.
Un « ramassis de gauchistes » ? Sur LCI, le 16 novembre, c’est par cette expression que Marine Le Pen a qualifié la Ligue des droits de l’homme (LDH) pour justifier son intention de supprimer les subventions attribuées à l’organisation née durant l’affaire Dreyfus et interdite par Vichy.
Mais, en réalité, c’est potentiellement l’ensemble des associations que comptent le pays et leurs 13 millions de bénévoles que la candidate d’extrême droite place sous la menace, dans son projet plus global de s’attaquer à l’ensemble des contre-pouvoirs, pour faire glisser la démocratie française vers l’illibéralisme.
La candidate du Rassemblement national (RN) entend couper les subventions de l’État aux « associations politisées », dénomination suffisamment large pour procéder à des retraits arbitraires. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: US Army declares Iowa lead azide detonation ‘tremendously successful’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
US Army declares Iowa lead azide detonation ‘tremendously successful’
Army hails Iowa’s lead azide detonation, claiming no traces of airborne lead have been detected so far.
United States Army officials have hailed Wednesday’s mission to destroy 68 drums of volatile lead azide — a sensitive munitions explosive — at a military base in Iowa as a success, saying it had “wildly exceeded their expectations”.
Speaking at a news conference in Middletown, a southeastern rural city adjacent to the ammunition plant where the operation was carried out, Major General Eric Shirley, the Army official in charge of the disposal effort, said overhead footage showed that “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed”.
The controlled detonation at 10:15am (16:15 GMT) destroyed approximately 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I.
“There was no secondary explosions. There was no kick-out. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley said, adding that the operation was “tremendously successful”.
Officials also said that extensive mitigation measures, including earthworks, foam barriers and gel blocks, had helped to absorb the shockwaves and toxic fallout.
However, Democratic Illinois House Representative Mike Quigley voiced dissatisfaction over how military leaders handled the operation, calling the holiday-eve scheduling and lack of communication “unconscionable”.
In a statement on X, the congressman wrote: “It is unfair that our military leaders are releasing 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide on our friends in Iowa the day before Thanksgiving.”
‘Zero detection of airborne lead’
Following days of heightened alarm over lead dust contamination and its environmental repercussions, federal officials announced that preliminary data from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sensors had detected no airborne lead particles.
Ongoing monitoring efforts continue in the immediately affected blast zone.
A post on the agency’s social media account shortly after the operation said that “ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region”.
Chemists have noted that lead, as a nonbiodegradable element, cannot be chemically decomposed or destroyed. It persists in the environment, with airborne particles capable of travelling considerable distances before settling on soil and potentially leaching into groundwater.
Detonating large stores of the unstable explosive would decompose the compound into its basic elements – nitrogen gas and metallic lead.
Lead is a potent neurotoxin that poses its sharpest threat to children and pregnant women, with links to learning disabilities, impaired neurological function, mental health challenges, reproductive harm, hearing loss and other impairments.
“The EPA can do millions of tests, but they [must also] test for the breakdown products and the stabilisers and plasticisers [containing] lead azide [which] are endocrine disruptors; some are cancer-causing chemicals,” said Scott Smith, an independent environmental testing expert who was heavily involved in air testing after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment and industrial incidents.
The Army Sustainment Command said it would release a final breakdown of the affected area — including lead-dust dispersion and surface-deposition maps — after the operation.
“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanely possible the risk to the health and the safety of the people in Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Shirley.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Steelers reportedly cut Rodgers after QB accuses coach McCarthy of sleeping during meetings
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Tom Lutz
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Aaron Rodgers launched an extraordinary attack on his head coach, Mike McCarthy, on Wednesday after the Pittsburgh Steelers benched him in favor of backup quarterback Mason Rudolph.
ESPN have reported that the Steelers have released Rodgers after his outburst. If no other team claim Rodgers on waivers, he will become an unrestricted free agent. Several teams, including the Indianapolis Colts and New England Patriots, are in need of a starting quarterback at the moment.
McCarthy, who was also Rodgers’ coach with the Green Bay Packers, had said on Monday that the 42-year-old was still the team’s starter despite recent struggles. On Tuesday night, the Steelers changed course and said Rodgers, one of the greatest players in NFL history, would be deactivated for Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos.
On Wednesday, Rodgers appeared on The Pat McAfee Show and set fire to whatever remained of his relationship with the coach. Rodgers first said he would not return to the Steelers, stating: “That ship has sailed”. He then accused McCarthy of falling asleep during meetings.
“Last Wednesday, we were in a quarterback meeting. Mike came in late, sat down, and within 10 minutes began snoring. Woke himself up, was rattling his papers,” Rodgers said. “We all looked around. Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again. And less than five minutes after that, he walks out of the room like nothing happened.”
Rodgers added that he only found out about McCarthy’s decision when his teammate Pat Freiermuth told him. Rodgers said Freiermuth had called him and said “I can’t believe they’re doing this.” To which Rodgers replied: “Doing what?”
Rodgers, who said this summer that he will retire at the end of the season, also alleged that McCarthy appeared to think he was still coaching the Packers during Sunday’s defeat to the Philadelphia Eagles. “The nail in the coffin for so many of us was at halftime, towards the end of it, we’re kind of on the offense on one side of defense on the other side,” said Rodgers. “And there’s some rambling or something [from McCarthy] and without even a heads up, he says, ‘All right, one, two, three Packers.’ That’s what he broke it down on in the locker room … [We] looked around going, ‘What the fuck? What is going on? Where’s his head at at this point?’” ESPN reported that multiple sources agreed with Rodgers’ version of events.
Rodgers said he had spoken regularly to McCarthy over the last few days, and the coach had not mentioned the possibility of being benched. He did, however, say they had discussed McCarthy sleeping during meetings. “[I told McCarthy], we can’t even have an honest conversation. I’m telling you, you snored in the meeting twice, in a quarterback meeting, that’s unacceptable,” Rodgers said. “And you’re telling me you’ve never slept at a facility before. And I’m telling you, I have a hundred witnesses and collaborating people who would support what I’m saying. I’m not saying that to fucking bury you.
“I’m saying that because this behavior and these habits are not healthy and they’re not becoming of someone intimately involved in the game plan. And that’s my whole point. And so, I left it with him that if you try and bench me or don’t change the play call, then you should just release me because I feel like at this point, I’m doing what’s right for the organization”. Rodgers said after his comments to McCarthy that the coach decided he was “getting rid of me”.
The Steelers (6-4) have lost their last two games but are still clinging on to the final playoff place in the AFC. NFL Next Gen Stats gives them a 62% chance of making the postseason, although the model does not take into account players flambéing their own team’s coach on live television.
Rodgers is considered one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time, someone whose single Super Bowl win does not match his natural talent. He is all but guaranteed to be a first-ballot Hall of Famer. His NFL records include highest passer rating for a quarterback with a minimum of 1,500 attempts (102.5), highest passer rating in a single season (122.5 in 2011) and lowest interception in a season (0.3% in 2018).
This season, however, has arguably been the worst of Rodgers’ career. His QBR of 45.6 ranks him 26th out of 30 qualified quarterbacks, ahead of only Deshaun Watson, Baker Mayfield, Justin Herbert and Daniel Jones. His completion rate of 60.9% is the second-lowest for any season of his career in which he has started more than one game and he leads the league in yards lost in sacks.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.
Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.
Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.
There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.
According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.
“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.
“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”
The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.
The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.
On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.
Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn, has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.
He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.
Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.
“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”
Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.
More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.
“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”
