https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Documenting Women Out of Their Cells
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Sara Bennett
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Sara Bennett, a former public defender, spent more than a decade photographing women sentenced to life, mostly for homicide, in New York State’s prisons. A new book of her photographs, Looking Inside: Women With Life Sentences, traces their lives behind prison walls and, for those who have been released after decades behind bars, their reentry into the outside world. Most of the women in the book were released through parole. Others had their sentences reduced through New York’s Domestic Violence Survivors Justice Act, which allows people to petition the courts for resentencing if the crime they were convicted of was linked to abuse they had suffered. Meanwhile, in New York’s three women’s prisons, 174 people are serving life sentences. As of 2024, one in 11 incarcerated women, or more than 6,800 nationally, were serving life sentences. Reprinted here are some of Bennett’s photos of those women from Looking Inside.
—Victoria Law
Looking Inside was published by Kehrer Verlag in 2026. Bennett’s photos will be on display in 2027 at Baxter St at the Camera Club of New York in Manhattan.
To most people, the archive is just a portal on their computer. But it’s also a physical space made by a person who has never cared more about the preservation of digital history....

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as new director
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Senay Boztas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has announced that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.
Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he said he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.
“The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”
The Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.
This success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.
But Gruijthuijsen said he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he says. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”
Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.
From one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental shows of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he says.
From the Finns, he will also bring an important lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he says: “Less talking, more doing.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Emily Carr and E.J. Hughes lead the way at Heffel's $10m autumn auctions
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Larry Humber
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.
“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, said at the end of the evening.
The back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).
Hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.
The second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.
A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).
A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.
Among the night’s other big-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.
J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.
Arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a new auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.
The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in New York
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Judd Tully
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.
Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.
Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.
Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.
Price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.
Still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a new home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).
A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.
The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of important 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.
Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.
Gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in New York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.
Gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in New York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.
A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).
A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a new auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.
Though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.
The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime New York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.)
Among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.
Large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.
The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.
Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.
Measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and important champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.
The evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the New York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.)
Apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca said. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”
The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/inflation-au.title: Inflation Is About Resources — and Power
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/inflation-au.author: Oskar Brandt
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/inflation-au.text:
Inflation Is About Resources — and Power
Inflation policy is a fight over real resources: who controls them, who gets access to them, and who pays when prices rise.
After prices began rising and rising in the wake of COVID-19 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, some blamed welfare and public spending for the inflation. Yet in many economies, weak demand and falling public investment after 2008 held back investment and productive capacity. Austerity can also weaken productivity and future growth. In the United States, changes to trade policy during Donald Trump’s first presidency added to uncertainty about the economic situation. Trade policy uncertainty between 2017 and 2018 may have lowered investment by 1 to 2 percent. During the pandemic, automakers canceled orders and halted production. Demand returned before factories, suppliers, and transport networks could restart. The Cleveland Fed documented how factory shutdowns, parts shortages, and shipping delays during the pandemic disrupted supply chains. The oil crisis of 1973 is a reminder of how a real supply shock can also become a lasting case for austerity.
Joe Biden’s American Rescue Plan expanded the child tax credit. Child poverty fell from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021, then rose to 12.4 percent in 2022 after Congress let the expansion expire. From 2019 to 2023, low-wage workers’ real pay grew by 13.2 percent. Real manufacturing-construction spending rose by 85 percent from January 2021 to a six-decade high in part as a result of new investment laws. These gains helped poor families, workers, and industry, though they cannot all be attributed to Biden’s policies.
US inflation also fell earlier than in the eurozone. Consumer price index (CPI) inflation peaked at 9.1 percent in June 2022 and fell to 3 percent by June 2023, while eurozone inflation was still 5.5 percent. Global supply pressures eased, energy prices fell, and the Federal Reserve raised rates sharply. Still, stronger wages and public investment can coincide with falling inflation. The gains for poor families, however, can disappear when that policy ends.
Sweden brings the question into focus in 2026. In its March 2026 forecast, the Swedish Agency for Financial and Public Management projected a general government deficit of SEK180 billion for the year. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) describes the fiscal policy as expansionary but expects headline inflation to remain below target. Inflation can rise when spending meets shortages of labor or natural resources, limited production, or firms with the power to raise prices. But spending and higher purchasing power do not cause inflation by themselves. The result depends on resources, production, prices, and import dependence. The deficit forecast and the IMF’s outlook show why.
Production Is Power
Imagine a low-paid worker with rent due and a child to feed two weeks until payday. A pay raise may help, but it cannot create affordable homes or medicine. When the costs of essentials rise faster than incomes, people with little room in their budgets absorb the shock first. Inflation policy decides who loses purchasing power, whose costs get protected, and whose prices remain beyond public control.
A government that issues its own floating currency creates money as it spends and withdraws money from the private economy through taxes. But it still faces real limits: labor, technology, materials, energy, and ecological capacity. Reliance on imports, foreign-currency debt, and exchange rate pressure can tighten those limits. If spending exceeds what producers can supply, prices may rise. A deficit alone cannot tell us where that point lies. An economy with available workers and room to raise productivity can absorb spending without necessarily generating inflation.
Banks create money when they lend. Each loan creates a matching deposit; as the loan is repaid, that deposit money disappears. But money cannot summon nurses, electricity, medicines, homes, or skilled workers. Private credit can sustain demand when wages and public spending lag, but households and firms cannot increase debt indefinitely. When borrowers repay loans more quickly than banks issue new ones, this bank-created money contracts. Austerity can exacerbate this fall in demand. If households and businesses try to pay down debt at the same time, a financial crisis can ensue.
Globalization gave rich countries access to abundant goods and helped keep some prices down, but it tied factories to long shipping routes and distant suppliers. Military power can protect routes, resources, and property rights, but it also depends on domestic industrial capacity and state support for its industries. Japan, South Korea, and China built technical capacity through public investment, industrial policy, directed credit, protection, and managed trade, while many Western economies have become dependent on finance, services, and imported goods. This has weakened the West’s ability to sustain the military power that keeps globalization in place.
Globalization also exposed the costs of weakening domestic industry. Trade shocks left factory workers with lasting job losses and lower incomes. Research has linked layoffs to far-right support, unequal exposure to economic shocks to racial animus and right-wing voting in the United States, and local trade shocks to authoritarian values.
A company that dominates its market sector can raise prices with less fear of losing customers. Across industries in fifteen European economies, the average market share of the four largest firms rose from 26 percent in 2000 to 32 percent in 2019; average markups rose about 7 percent. A US manufacturing study found that mergers were associated with higher markups and little evidence of higher plant productivity. Firms can also use monopsony power to hold down wages and hiring. In a study of French labor markets, a 10 percent increase in labor market concentration was associated with nearly 0.9 percent lower wages for new hires and 12.4 percent fewer hires.
Shocks Give Price-Setters Cover
COVID caused real supply problems. Lockdowns disrupted production. Households saved more, while spending shifted from services to goods. Auto demand plummeted in 2020, causing carmakers to cut their chip orders. In turn, chipmakers shifted production to other customers, and when auto demand returned, they could not quickly meet carmakers’ renewed need. Shortages can make it easier for powerful firms to raise prices. When rivals face the same shock and customers expect increases, price hikes can spread even without a cartel.
In 2022, profits rose faster than production across the eurozone and accounted for the largest share of price increases. Real cost shocks, like those associated with the recent US wars of 2025–26, can nonetheless coexist with wider margins. In food markets, financial speculation and stockpiling can drive price rises beyond what shortages alone would explain, especially when war creates expectations of shortages.
When COVID arrived, manufacturers expected a prolonged recession and cut production, capacity, and orders. Demand and employment recovered faster than expected, leaving shortages of semiconductors, lumber, and other inputs. Fiscal expansion did not invent these bottlenecks; it revealed them. Repeated periods of weak demand can close factories, disperse skilled workers, and delay investment, making supply slower to recover.
In the 1960s, large industrial firms had built capacity but struggled to sell everything they produced. Some responded by buying unrelated businesses, selling off or outsourcing production, and relying more on short-term finance. This shift away from production gave financial markets greater influence over industrial decisions. In the decades that followed, private debt could temporarily sustain productive capacity despite weak wage growth, but when borrowing slowed, spending and sales fell. Debt-led crises also enabled investors to buy distressed property, companies, and assets from poor households cheaply, at a high social cost.
Debt and Austerity
Some Mesopotamian rulers in antiquity periodically canceled debts, freed people from debt bondage, and restored property, in part to check mass indebtedness and land concentration. These measures were episodic, not part of a regular, universal system. Debt was contested in Ancient Greece too, as seen in Solon’s reforms. Rome faced recurring credit crises and public-land conflict. Debt crises and land struggles shaped the politics of the late Roman Republic.
The two world wars showed that markets could be governed. During World War I, the US War Industries Board coordinated production. After the war, advocates of austerity in Britain and Italy promoted balanced budgets and hard-money policies and accepted high unemployment as ways to restore economic hierarchies at labor’s expense. During World War II, the United States used price ceilings, rationing, taxes, wage policies, credit controls, and resource allocation to restrain inflation, raise revenue, and direct production toward the war effort.
One historical estimate put the price level more than 30 percent below where it would have been without general price controls. Controls did not abolish scarcity. Many goods were rationed or simply unavailable, but alongside public management of demand and physical resources, the controls worked. World War II was one of the few times that the US came close to full productive capacity. During the war, labor shortages and stronger unions also improved many workers’ bargaining position.
A study of 166 elections in 16 OECD countries from 1980 to 2016 found austerity associated with increased electoral abstention and support for nonmainstream parties. Austerity weakens workers’ bargaining power and public services, reduces demand and investment, and can undermine social stability.
The late 1990s surpluses, combined with the trade deficit, pushed the US private sector into record deficits. Household debt grew much faster than income as Washington paid down public debt. Levy researchers later linked private sector deficits to the global crisis of 2008. Post-COVID inflation had different causes, including supply bottlenecks, a shift toward goods, and energy shocks.
Lessons From Past Shocks
Inflation was already rising in the United States before the 1973 oil shock. The US chose to escalate the Vietnam War. The war diverted workers, fuel, and materials from civilian production and sent dollars abroad. In 1971, Richard Nixon ended the dollar’s convertibility into gold. The dollar continued to serve as a major world currency without a promise of redemption in gold. Fiat money still faces real limits: the availability of oil, labor, materials, and productive capacity.
During the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil states imposed an embargo and cut production. Separately, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) raised prices. Iran’s shah, a US ally, pushed for higher oil revenues to finance the country’s military buildup. Nixon had promised to sell him the arms he wanted. A contemporary account argued that Washington encouraged Middle Eastern producers to raise prices from 1971; Washington had earlier accommodated the shah’s push for higher prices, but during the crisis it opposed the Arab embargo and resisted OPEC’s proposed 100 percent price hike.
The United States did not create the whole crisis. But US leaders accepted higher oil revenues for a strategic ally. Meanwhile, oil companies, banks, and arms firms gained from the new flows of money, while workers and households paid higher prices. Leaders later used the crisis to attack welfare and full employment, even though the oil shock did not prove that public spending caused inflation.
The shift toward policies that tolerated high unemployment, wage restraint, and public spending cuts was a political choice, not an automatic result of the oil shock. Naomi Klein has traced disaster capitalism to Milton Friedman’s argument that crises can open the way for sweeping economic change. She shows how leaders and businesses have used this approach repeatedly, from Chile and post-Soviet Russia to the Iraq occupation and Hurricane Katrina, to push privatization and expand corporate control.
This selfsame policy choice — the choice between using inflation to justify austerity, or addressing its causes and effects — is reflected in Sweden’s response to the latest energy shock.
The Swedish Case
The war in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz this past year, raising Swedish motor fuel prices by 25 percent. Yet Eurostat’s November release put Swedish inflation at just 0.6 percent, compared with 4 percent in the eurozone. On the Riksbank’s target measure, which holds mortgage interest rates fixed, Swedish inflation rose from 0.7 percent in August to 1.5 percent in September before easing to 1.1 percent in October. Excluding energy, it was just 0.1 percent in October.
Some measures that widened Sweden’s deficit also lowered prices. The November budget projected a 2026 deficit of SEK158 billion, or 2.3 percent of GDP. After Sweden halved the value-added tax (VAT) on groceries in April, food prices fell 5.5 percent that month; a government review found that retailers passed on most of the cut. The government also subsidized half-price monthly transit passes from July through December. The Riksbank estimates that without the temporary measures’ direct effects on prices, September inflation would have been 3.0 percent, twice the actual rate.
Growth continued alongside low inflation. Real GDP grew 1.6 percent, and the European Commission raised its forecast for 2026 growth to 2.8 percent. Household spending, investment, and net exports also lifted growth. The available figures give no separate estimate of how much the relief measures added to output or productivity.
The labor market recovery has been slower. A labor force survey put trend unemployment at 8.7 percent in the third quarter, even as employment rose. Sweden has also cut support for people in employment programs for more than 300 days. The government expects the cuts to speed up the return to work. But when households on tight budgets cut their spending, local businesses lose sales; and if financial pressure pushes people into jobs that make poor use of their skills, productivity could suffer. Sweden’s 2026 figures do not yet tell us how large these effects are.
The Riksbank expects inflation to exceed 2 percent in 2027 as the recovery strengthens and higher energy and import costs feed through. The government forecasts 2.8 percent in 2028 when the grocery VAT is due to return to 12 percent. Further disruption in Hormuz, the war in Ukraine, and new trade barriers could also raise costs and weaken demand for Swedish exports.
Sweden can issue kronor, but what it can buy depends on the fuel, labor, and equipment available. Higher interest rates can slow spending and hiring, but they won’t bring another tanker through Hormuz. Cheaper fares leave commuters with more money in their pockets today, and better public transport gives them a way to use less imported fuel tomorrow.
A state cannot buy resources that do not exist. But concentrated firms may raise prices before resources run out, while austerity can destroy demand and productive capacity. Inflation reflects pressure on real resources, but power determines who controls them and who pays when prices rise.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-s.title: Under Capitalism, Socialism Will Never Disappear
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-s.author: Alex McCarron
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-s.text:
Under Capitalism, Socialism Will Never Disappear
The Left won the midterms not by inventing a new politics but by reopening old fights the Right thought it had won. As long as capitalism exists, socialism can’t be consigned to the past.
If socialists and progressives had a good night on November 3, it wasn’t so much because they brought new ideas to the election, but because it was a chance to relitigate fights the Right thought it had won years ago: universal health care, Palestinian solidarity, and the expansion of the labor movement. We even got a rematch between George W. Bush–era Islamophobia and two of the Muslim Americans who had to live in its shadow, Adam Hamawy and Abdul El-Sayed.
Many have lauded Zohran Mamdani’s novel use of the term “affordability” for the recent shift in political common sense. But while his branding is new, his politics are not. Mamdani has never styled himself as a new kind of politician. He seems to be constantly locating himself in history, comparing himself to Milwaukee’s sewer socialists and New Dealers like Fiorello La Guardia. This makes sense when you consider that his policies represent decades of struggle: the project of expanding democracy into the workplace dates to the late nineteenth century, and the fight to guarantee health care as a right dates to the early twentieth.
Critics often ask why socialists are bringing a nineteenth-century ideology to bear on twenty-first century problems. The simple answer is that it seems to be what’s working. Since the turn of the twenty-first century, a series of global social movements have sought a new kind of political orientation, one that would allow for a break with the politics of the last century and the historical culs-de-sac they crashed into. Every few years brings a new form of right, center, and left politics: Occupy, Abundance, the Yellow Vests, the Movement of Squares, prison abolitionism. These movements all respond to real problems, but what’s new about them is mostly just branding. Few offer genuinely new critiques or build lasting political constituencies or institutions. Their strength is being novel enough to draw a crowd, drive a news cycle, or launch an academic career. Such innovations move to the same rhythm as capitalism’s own churning drive to simulate invention, revolution, and disruption across the economy.
At the same time, one sees the appeal. We can’t exactly blame radicals for wanting a disruption of their current institutions. Everywhere you look, leftists are trying to overcome the NGOization of the Left and searching for a common ground between their alienated, specialized critiques. Ecologists want to talk about the environmental catastrophe of the genocide in Gaza, while anti-racists want to connect their work to the extreme weather events that disproportionally effect the Global South. This is the basic drive of left-wing politics: to establish continuities between spheres of knowledge and to build connections between people.
The 20th Century Never Died
To find that meeting place in socialism is to recognize that what is happening to you has been happening to you for a very long time. Embracing the old language means realizing that you’re settling unfinished business rather than facing a new foe. Comparing the capitalist class to the aristocracy that came before it enables a person to see how arbitrary and contingent ruling-class power really is. One can understand why Bernie Sanders traded loaded terms like “bourgeoisie” and “proletariat” for the “1 percent” and “99 percent.” But it was just as important that he held onto “democratic socialism.” The term signaled that he was continuing a struggle and adding to an existing tradition of critique rather than declaring a year zero for left politics.
We are likely to be haunted for years by how dynamic, inventive, and exciting the twentieth century was. Every decade brought a new way of dressing, a new style of painting, and new stage in the maturation of cinema and popular music. Our hunger for political novelty is not just a reflection of market forces. It’s also a long shadow of that era of continuous revolution in politics and culture.
Look closely, though, and you’ll find many of the twentieth-century movements that sought a break with tradition did so while grabbing hold of another tradition buried even deeper in history. Le Corbusier claimed his form of architecture would clear “the charnel house of past ages” that our homes had become, but he did so by marrying the mathematical proportions of the Parthenon to the logic of mass production. As much as Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso wanted to carry Paul Cézanne’s project into the future, they were also looking for a way to reconnect Western painting to the animism of African sculpture. The French New Wave paid an equally backhanded compliment to the “naive” genre films of Americans like Raoul Walsh and Sam Fuller, whose primitivism could liberate French filmmakers from their own pretensions and refinement.
As Long as There’s Capitalism, There Will Be Socialists
Even Karl Marx had this moment of paradox. In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, he writes that “the social revolution of the nineteenth century cannot take its poetry from the past but only from the future.” A few lines later, he quotes the Gospel of Luke 9:60: “Let the dead bury their dead.” Marx was inveighing against the tendency of revolutionaries to reach for the words and costumes of past eras when faced with the task of changing the world: Rome for the French Revolution, the Old Testament for the English Civil War. This awkward LARPing is what turns history’s repetitions into farce. Yet Marx’s famous line about history occurring “first as tragedy, the second time as farce” is itself framed as an amendment to Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. Even the poetry of the future has a few allusions in it.
The difference between the French revolutionaries’ idealized Rome and today’s democratic socialism is that socialism is no more a thing of the past than capitalism is. Capitalism constantly calls the concept back into existence, raising its own gravediggers out of the grave, over and over again. As long as capitalism exists, it will exploit workers and destroy the planet, and the masses will find a way to fight back. Our present sits on a much longer timeline than the twenty-four-hour news cycle has accustomed us to. One day we’ll have new words and new costumes, but those belong to a new world, and we’re not there yet.

https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-hig.title: New York’s highest court upholds key protection for low-income renters with Section 8
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-hig.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-hig.text:
New York’s highest court on Monday upheld a state law that bans discrimination against tenants who use government housing subsidies to pay their rent, capping a closely watched legal fight over access to apartments for low-income tenants.
The Court of Appeals sided with state Attorney General Letitia James after she sued an Ithaca landlord who refused to lease apartments to renters with federal Section 8 housing vouchers — reversing lower court rulings that the state’s so-called source of income discrimination law was unconstitutional. The earlier rulings in the 2022 lawsuit delivered temporary victories to the landlord, Jason Fane, his real estate firm Ithaca Renting Company and its associated limited liability companies.
The company owns an apartment complex known as Commons West and argued that the Section 8 program — which pays the majority of the rent for some low-income tenants nationwide — came with inspection requirements that they deemed warrantless searches.
But in an order reversing those rulings, Chief Judge Rowan Wilson wrote that the “landlords’ theory here is extraordinary and unprecedented.”
In a written statement, James said the ruling “affirms that landlords cannot deny housing to New Yorkers simply because they are using Section 8 to pay rent.”
The landlord’s attorney, Curtis Johnson, said his client may ask the U.S. Supreme Court to review the decision.
“The question of whether a state can compel participation in a federal program that conditions participation on coerced consent to searches is important and affects landlords across New York,” he said.
The case threatened to upend New York City’s own protections against source of income discrimination, or refusing to lease an apartment to someone because they use government assistance to pay rent. The city enacted the law in 2008.
City officials and housing advocates say discrimination against voucher holders remains a chronic problem. The city’s Commission on Human Rights consistently reports source of income discrimination as its most frequent complaint, deeming it a proxy for other forms of bias, like discrimination based on race or against families with children. Landlords counter that government programs are plagued by onerous rules and requirements that delay the time before a tenant can move in.
“Today’s decision is a major victory for New Yorkers who rely on rental assistance to find and keep a home,” said attorney Diane Houk from the firm Emery Celli, who submitted a brief to the court on behalf of fair-housing advocacy groups.
Tenants qualify for voucher programs like Section 8 and the city’s CityFHEPS program based on their earnings. They typically pay no more than 30% of income on rent, while the subsidy program covers the remainder. About 123,000 households in New York City use the Section 8 program to pay a portion of their rent, while more than 60,000 New York City households use CityFHEPS, according to city data.
The Court of Appeals ruling comes the same day that Mayor Zohran Mamdani launched a new initiative to crack down on individual brokers and agents who discriminate against renters. Mamdani said the city will begin referring the brokers to the state’s licensing agency, the Department of State, for potential punishment.
“When a New Yorker is denied an apartment because they use a housing voucher, that isn’t just an obstacle in their housing search — it is illegal discrimination,” Mamdani said. “If you repeatedly discriminate against New Yorkers, you shouldn’t be able to do business as usual. We will use every tool available to protect renters and hold repeat offenders accountable.”
This story has been updated with more information.

https://gothamist.com/news/reported-flu-.title: Reported flu cases surge across New York ahead of Thanksgiving
https://gothamist.com/news/reported-flu-.author: Caroline Lewis
https://gothamist.com/news/reported-flu-.text:
As New Yorkers get ready to gather with family and friends for Thanksgiving this week, an early flu surge is threatening to throw a wrench in holiday plans.
More than 43,000 New Yorkers statewide have caught the flu since early October, compared to about 7,000 cases at this point during flu season last year, state health department data shows.
City health officials are urging New Yorkers to take precautions to avoid spreading the virus to loved ones over the long weekend — including sitting out the festivities if they’re not feeling well.
“We encourage everyone to stay home when they’re sick, to wash their hands often, cover their coughs and sneezes and consider wearing a mask in crowded spaces,” Dr. Andrea Howard, the city’s deputy commissioner of disease control, said during an appearance on WNYC’s All Things Considered.
She added that getting vaccinated is the “best tool to protect ourselves” during flu season.
In a recent notice about the flu, the city health department recommended vaccination for everyone over 6 months old — and urged New Yorkers to get their flu shots sooner rather than later, since it can take up to two weeks for immunity to build up following vaccination.
The number of confirmed flu cases in New York state rose steadily for several weeks, reaching more than 12,000 cases in the first week of November, before dipping slightly the following week, state data shows.
In New York City, the flu surge has followed a similar pattern. More than 6,000 cases were reported the week ending Nov. 14.
Flu symptoms can last a few days to a couple of weeks and may include a fever, chills, body aches, a sore throat and runny nose, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Some cases of the flu can become severe and lead to hospitalization or death.
Hospitalizations are currently on the rise in New York as cases mount. More than 886 New Yorkers statewide were hospitalized the second week of November, state data shows. The rate of hospitalizations for the flu is highest among adults over 65 and children under 4.
“As we gather, let’s look out for our older relatives, young children, and others who may be more vulnerable to serious illness,” Dr. Alister Martin, the city health commissioner said in a statement on the surge.
New York is not alone in grappling with the flu ahead of Thanksgiving this year. National data shows the virus arrived earlier than usual, according to the CDC.
But that doesn’t necessarily mean this year’s surge will be more severe overall, since every flu season looks different, Howard said.
The city has a map of locations where New Yorkers can get shots for the flu, COVID and RSV.

https://gothamist.com/news/former-nypd-d.title: Former NYPD detective ordered held in jail in fatal George Washington Bridge shooting
https://gothamist.com/news/former-nypd-d.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/former-nypd-d.text:
A New York City judge on Monday ordered a former NYPD detective to be held in jail until his trial in the killing of a man during an apparent road rage incident on the George Washington Bridge.
A Manhattan grand jury indicted Victor Romero on a second-degree murder charge for the Oct. 20 killing, according to the district attorney’s office.
Dozens of people came to court to support the man who was killed, Koran Irvine. They marched through the hallways outside the courtroom before the court appearance, and cheered after the judge ordered Romero held in jail.
Romero, 62, who was an NYPD detective before he retired in 2001, has pleaded not guilty. His attorney, Joel Cohen, declined to comment Monday.
Prosecutors said Romero fired at Irvine’s car on the George Washington Bridge after their vehicles nearly collided as they both approached the upper-level onramp.
After the shooting, prosecutors say, Romero may have tried to obstruct the investigation into the killing by wiping down the driver’s side of his car at a gas station and by cleaning the inside center console of the car.
Prosecutors said Romero gave police a revolver after the shooting, saying that was the gun he usually carried with him. However they say the murder weapon was a different gun: a 9mm pistol they found in Romero’s home.

https://gothamist.com/news/th.title: Rain on the parade: Expect a wet and windy Thanksgiving Day in NYC
https://gothamist.com/news/th.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/th.text:
The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade may be a wet and windy ordeal.
New York City is expecting rainfall, heavy winds and coastal flooding this Thursday, as families across the five boroughs prepare their Thanksgiving meals, according to the National Weather Service forecasts.
As is tradition, thousands will flock to Manhattan’s 6th Avenue to watch the Macy’s parade hoist up several-hundred-pound balloons. But NWS meteorologist Dave Radell warned of rain and wind that could shake up the festivities.
“The wind gusts are going to be ramping up really during the parade … If we start getting sustained winds certainly above 20, 30, 35 miles an hour, that is certainly going to have an impact on the parade itself,” Radell said.
The weather service also forecasts 1 to 2 inches of rainfall starting late Wednesday evening and continuing throughout Thursday. In parts of the city’s south shore, including beach areas of South Brooklyn and Queens, as well as Suffolk and Nassau counties, Radell said there could be a “couple of high tide cycles” that may create moderate coastal flooding.
“So for folks going to the parade, expect a windy and wet experience,” he added.
While Thursday’s storm will be particularly wet, it shouldn't top off any historical Thanksgiving records. The wettest Thanksgiving in terms of rainfall on record was in 2006, with 1.72 inches. Before that, 1985 tied with 1935 at 1.5 inches of rain.
As for the warmest Thanksgiving, in both 2007 and 1933, the temperature reached the upper 60s and almost 70 degrees. This Thursday’s forecast is much cooler, with highs in the 50s.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: We’re in a flaking epidemic. No wonder no one wants to host gatherings | Chelsea Flagan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Chelsea Fagan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
You might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely, especially if they’re young.
The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing. (For reference, chronic loneliness has a comparable impact on long-term health to smoking.)
And if you’re looking for a culprit, there are many to blame: the dissolution of third spaces and encroachment of car culture, the declining participation in social networks such as churches and unions, and the harsh economic conditions that have people working longer hours for less money with each passing year.
And data shows that sheer disposable income is not as strongly correlated with social life as one might think: we are often completely eschewing the budget-friendly forms of contact that used to be standard in favor of being alone and scrolling on our phones.
But, as someone who literally wrote the book on getting together, and doing so across all income and age brackets, I would like to posit another reason why the American social fabric has so rapidly dissolved.
It’s not just that phones make it more appealing to scroll aimlessly than to have a conversation – it’s that they’ve made us more selfish, less community-minded people. Nearly every time I post a video about hosting, for example, my comments are filled with the same refrain: What’s the point of spending all this time and effort if no one actually shows up?
And the concern that you might go through all the trouble of planning a party just to sit in an empty room surrounded by food and decorations is not irrational.
When I posted this recent video about the psychic damage inflicted on a host by no-showing on an RSVP, it quickly racked up thousands of commenters sharing their experiences with the phenomenon. I am tagged daily in videos of people who did what I firmly believe we all should do: they took the risk of trying to get people together in real life, and they were left feeling humiliated by the realization that their party was simply an inconvenience that could be tossed overboard at the last minute.
And with social media and party apps making it easier than ever to invite anyone you’ve ever met, and to perpetually “maybe” your entire calendar so you can make a game-time call as to what invitation you deem worthy (as this excellent Substack explores), we have entered a dual crisis. Fewer people than ever are willing to host, and when they do, it’s a massive gamble: who will actually show up?
While there are, very occasionally, legitimate reasons to bail on a gathering at the last minute, we’ve also gotten very good at leveraging the language of mental health to lean into our most selfish impulses.
We speak in terms of boundaries and self-care about actions that don’t just devastate the person on the other side of our unreliability, but also sap at our own mental health, as community is arguably more important to it than our own immediate comfort.
The truth is, whether it’s exercising, spending time outside, showing up to a social commitment, or opting for more nutritious food over some quick takeout, it is often in doing the less immediately comfortable or enjoyable thing that we are truly caring for ourselves and those around us.
And when it comes to gathering, the social isolation factor is very real: making and keeping platonic bonds is a skill, and the longer you are out of practice, the harder and more scary it becomes to start again. People are losing friends, and the process can accelerate until the entire concept of socializing feels like a threat.
It has never been easier in those moments to get under a blanket, make up a thin excuse for not showing up to a commitment, and reassure yourself that you have engaged in a powerful, therapeutic exercise by choosing to watch a screen again instead of literally anything else.
We increasingly speak of gathering in terms of self-sacrifice and effort, but, as this meme deftly satirizes, the thing we’re talking about – making friends and then hanging out with them – is supposed to be the fun part. It’s supposed to be the reward for all the work we do, both professionally and in our daily lives.
Instead, the act has slipped so far from our cultural routines in just two generations that we no longer understand it as a leisure activity. (The performance of ultra-perfect hosting and homemaking on social media doesn’t help, but that’s a subject for another day.)
Simply put, we have so radically devalued not just what it means to spend time with people we love, but to show respect for the people who facilitate it, that we have enabled a full-blown flake epidemic. And while I’m not willing to say that being a chronic flaker makes you a bad person, I am willing to say that it should not be acceptable – to you, or to anyone else.
There are so many problems to fully address our hosting and loneliness crises, but none are more immediately solvable on a personal level than holding ourselves accountable. If we say we are going to do something, it is our responsibility to actually show up.
No, it doesn’t matter that you don’t really feel like it, or that it’s raining outside: grab an umbrella, put on a smile (and maybe pick up a nice little hostess gift on the way), and go be a part of the community we all desperately need to rebuild.
- Chelsea Fagan is an author and the co-founder of The Financial Diet

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Justiça do Trabalho mantém condenação da Volkswagen por escravizar trabalhador em fazenda no Pará
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Diego Junqueira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A Volkswagen do Brasil foi condenada nesta terça-feira (24) pela Justiça do Trabalho no Pará, em segunda instância, por submeter o trabalhador Raul Batista de Souza a condições análogas à escravidão na Fazenda Vale do Rio Cristalino, propriedade mantida pela montadora no Sul do Pará nas décadas de 1970 e 1980. A empresa pode recorrer.
A 3ª Turma do TRT-8 (Tribunal Regional do Trabalho da 8ª Região) manteve, por 2 votos a 1, a condenação da montadora em primeira instância, que fixou indenização de R$ 2 milhões por danos morais e existencial. Nos próximos dias, o tribunal vai analisar recursos da empresa em outras duas ações semelhantes, nas quais a companhia também foi condenada em primeira instância.
Entre as décadas de 1970 e 1980, a montadora alemã era a principal sócia da Companhia Vale do Rio Cristalino (CVRC), empresa responsável por uma fazenda de 139 mil hectares comprada com apoio do governo militar, que investiu cerca de R$ 500 milhões em recursos públicos (em valores atuais). Conhecida como Fazenda Volkswagen, a propriedade era dedicada à extração de madeira e à criação de gado.
As ações defendem que a submissão a trabalho escravo é um crime imprescritível, segundo a jurisprudência do TST (Tribunal Superior do Trabalho) e da Corte Interamericana de Direitos Humanos. As ações requerem indenização de R$ 2 milhões por trabalhador.
Nesta terça, o desembargador Marcus Augusto Losada Maia, relator da ação, afirmou que violações como as sofridas pelo trabalhador Raul Batista de Souza não podem ser esquecidas.
“Esse tipo de conduta não pode nem deve ser esquecida, e estará sempre submetido ao crivo da avaliação de cada um sobre o que é humanidade, sobre o que é respeitar a pessoa humana, o que é respeitar o trabalhador e a trabalhadora”, disse. O desembargador também afirmou que cada empresa é responsável pelo que acontece dentro de seus estabelecimentos.
“Dar esse tipo de tratamento a uma pessoa humana é afastar por completo esse sentimento de civilidade”, acrescentou.
Maia votou pela manutenção da condenação da empresa, sendo acompanhado pela desembargadora Ida Selene. O voto divergente foi da desembargadora Mary Anne Acatauassú Camelier Medrado.
“Estou sentindo que a justiça foi feita”, afirmou Raul Batista de Souza à Repórter Brasil em junho, após a decisão de primeira instância. “Espero que fique tudo bem, para tirar um pouco do peso de cima da gente”, disse o ex-trabalhador, que atuou na Fazenda Volkswagen em 1986, quando tinha 17 anos.
Procurada pela Repórter Brasil, a empresa disse que não comenta ações em andamento, mas declarou que atua há 73 anos no Brasil, com “respeito absoluto” às leis brasileiras e aos direitos humanos. “A empresa repudia qualquer forma de trabalho forçado, degradante ou análogo à escravidão e reitera sua dedicação histórica à promoção de um ambiente laboral digno”, diz o posicionamento (leia o texto na íntegra ao final da reportagem).
Essa é a segunda vez que a Volkswagen do Brasil é condenada em segunda instância pelos episódios ocorridos na Fazenda Volkswagen. Em fevereiro, o TRT-8 condenou a montadora em ação civil pública movida pelo MPT (Ministério Público do Trabalho), determinando pagamento de R$ 165 milhões por danos morais coletivos. A condenação se refere à exploração sistemática de centenas de trabalhadores na mesma propriedade rural durante as décadas de 1970 e 1980.
Tanto na ação coletiva quanto nos processos individuais, a Justiça rejeitou os argumentos da montadora de que os crimes estariam prescritos ou de que a empresa seria apenas acionista minoritária.
Entenda o julgamento sobre a Fazenda Volkswagen
Entre as décadas de 1970 e 1980, a montadora alemã foi sócia e administradora da Companhia Vale do Rio Cristalino (CVRC), responsável por uma fazenda de 139 mil hectares no sul do Pará, comprada com apoio do governo militar. A propriedade, na qual foram investidos cerca de R$ 500 milhões em recursos públicos (em valores atuais), era dedicada à extração de madeira e à criação de gado.
Nas ações, os trabalhadores afirmam ter sido submetidos a um sistema de servidão por dívida, no qual eram aliciados por intermediários em outros estados, com promessas de bons salários, para atuarem no Pará com derrubada de mata, montagem do pasto e obras internas.
Ao chegarem à propriedade, os trabalhadores dizem ter sido informados de que o custo da viagem e um suposto adiantamento haviam se convertido em dívidas. Tudo o que consumiam — de alimentos a ferramentas e roupas de trabalho — precisaria ser comprado a preços abusivos na cantina controlada pelos próprios aliciadores, o que fazia a dívida aumentar.
Os trabalhadores alegam nas ações que eram impedidos de sair da fazenda por conta das dívidas crescentes, mesmo quando enfrentavam problemas de saúde, como a malária. Também afirmam terem sido vigiados constantemente por pistoleiros a serviço dos “gatos”, como são conhecidos os intermediários responsáveis pelo recrutamento de mão de obra.
Na decisão de primeira instância, o magistrado rejeitou os argumentos da Volkswagen de prescrição das acusações, em razão de se tratar de “violações gravíssimas aos direitos humanos e à dignidade da pessoa humana”. A decisão reconhece, nos casos, a servidão por dívida, a jornada exaustiva, a restrição da liberdade de locomoção e as condições degradantes de trabalho e alojamento.
No processo, a Volkswagen alegou que não teria responsabilidade sobre os episódios, pois seria apenas acionista da empresa, e não sua controladora, e também porque os acordos dos trabalhadores eram com os intermediários, que eram contratados para atuarem na derrubada de floresta e na abertura de pastos.
Para o juiz, contudo, documentos internos da empresa acessados durante o processo confirmaram que a Volkswagen do Brasil era não apenas acionária da fazenda, como sua gestora. “A própria ata de instalação registra a posse de dirigentes diretamente vinculados à Volkswagen nos principais cargos executivos da CVRC”, diz a sentença.
“Mais do que simples aporte financeiro, a documentação evidencia efetiva participação da reclamada na constituição, administração e direção do empreendimento agropecuário”, escreveu o magistrado. Segundo a decisão de primeira instância, a empresa teria se beneficiado economicamente da exploração dos trabalhadores.
Ainda de acordo com o magistrado, “a robustez da prova oral produzida nestes autos é reforçada por expressivo conjunto de registros documentais históricos contemporâneos aos fatos”, incluindo “radiotelegramas e comunicações oficiais encaminhados por agentes públicos a autoridades do Estado brasileiro, noticiando a existência de trabalho escravo, retenção de trabalhadores e servidão por dívida na Fazenda Vale do Rio Cristalino.”
Posicionamento da Volkswagen do Brasil:
“A Volkswagen do Brasil não se manifestará sobre discussões judiciais em andamento. Adicionalmente, a empresa ressalta que, com um legado de 73 anos, a Volkswagen do Brasil reafirma seu compromisso permanente com o respeito absoluto à Constituição Federal, às leis brasileiras e aos princípios internacionais de direitos humanos, que orientam sua atuação como uma das maiores empregadoras do país. A empresa repudia qualquer forma de trabalho forçado, degradante ou análogo à escravidão e reitera sua dedicação histórica à promoção de um ambiente laboral digno, ético e responsável.”

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.title: Weltcup-Auftakt | Das deutsche Biathlon-Team will die Handbremse lösen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.author: Lars Becker
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.text:
- Sport
- Weltcup-Auftakt
Das deutsche Biathlon-Team will die Handbremse lösen
Beim Saison-Auftakt in Kontiolahti wollen die deutschen Biathletinnen mit ihrer neuen Bundestrainerin den langen Weg zurück zu alter Stärke antreten.
Neue Damen-Bundestrainerin, neuer Sportdirektor, neues Glück? Das deutsche Biathlon wagt nach der schlechtesten Olympia-Bilanz seit 50 Jahren mit nur einer Medaille im Februar in Antholz den Neuanfang. Sportdirektor Bernd Eisenbichler, der die Nachfolge des zum Biathlon-Weltverband IBU abgewanderten Felix Bitterling als Sportdirektor angetreten hat, möchte vor der am Donnerstag im finnischen Kontiolahti beginnenden Weltcup-Saison keine großen Zielvorgaben machen: »Am Anfang geht es darum, wieder Selbstverständnis und Selbstvertrauen nach der letzten Saison zu entwickeln.« Aber natürlich sei es der Anspruch, vor allem im Nationencup und den Staffeln ums Podium mitzulaufen.
Ein Selbstläufer wird das nicht. Die Männer stecken unter Regie des auch erst seit Februar 2025 amtierenden Cheftrainers Tobias Reiter mitten im Generationswechsel. Führungsfigur Philipp Nawrath wird bald 34, auch Philipp Horn ist bereits 32 Jahre alt. Nach einigen Jahren mit latenten Nachwuchsproblemen gibt es inzwischen aber wieder einige verheißungsvolle Talente im deutschen Team: Mit Fabian Kaskel (22) und Elias Seidl (22) messen sich zwei davon beim Weltcup-Auftakt ab Donnerstag mit der Weltelite.
Flungers schwierige Mission
Bei den deutschen Frauen hat mit der inzwischen schwangeren Franziska Preuß die Führungsfigur der vergangenen Jahre ihre Karriere beendet. Sie studiert Architektur in Rosenheim und erwartet mit ihrem Lebenspartner, dem einstigen Top-Biathleten Simon Schempp, ein Kind. Nur drei Podestplätze holten die deutschen Frauen im vergangenen Winter – mit diesem schwierigen Erbe hat Sandra Flunger ihre Mission im deutschen Biathlon-Team angetreten. Die 44 Jahre alte Österreicherin soll die deutschen Frauen als Nachfolgerin von Kristian Mehringer auf dem Bundestrainerposten zurück zu alter Stärke führen. Eine schwierige Aufgabe, schließlich sind die Zeiten deutscher Seriensiegerinnen wie Magdalena Neuner und Laura Dahlmeier längst vergangen.
Einen Vorteil hat die schwierige Gemengelage vor dem Weltcup-Auftakt in Finnland für Flunger: Die Erwartungen sind moderat. Genau wie Sportdirektor Eisenbichler versucht auch Flunger, die Latte für ihre deutschen Frauen möglichst niedrig zu legen. »Ich glaube, es wäre falsch, jetzt etwas Großes auszurufen«, sagt die Frau, die vor allem durch ihre achtjährige erfolgreiche Arbeit in der Schweiz in den Fokus des deutschen Teams gerückt ist. Zum Schluss war sie im Nachbarland Cheftrainerin für Männer und Frauen. Als deutsche Bundestrainerin wartet nun in einer der auch wirtschaftlich wichtigsten Biathlon-Nationen eine Aufgabe in einer viel größeren Dimension auf sie. Finanzielle Möglichkeiten, öffentliche Aufmerksamkeit und die Zahl der Athletinnen sind hier viel größer, als sie es zuvor in der Schweiz erlebt hat.
Keine Angst vor Fehlern
Die 44-Jährige ist die Aufgabe mit der ihr eigenen Zurückhaltung, aber auch Konsequenz angegangen. Als eines der Hauptziele hatte sie mit Blick auf die latenten Probleme am Schießstand angegeben, die »Handbremse« bei ihren Frauen lösen zu wollen. Die neue Cheftrainerin forderte mehr Mut und Geschwindigkeit beim Schießen ein: »Angst vor Fehlern zu haben, ist nicht der richtige Weg.« Als neue Führungsfigur in ihrem Team nach dem Abschied von Franziska Preuß kristallisiert sich die erfahrene Janina Hettich-Walz heraus, die bei den Deutschen Meisterschaften gleich dreimal Gold gewann.
Flunger bewundert, wie die 30-jährige Hettich-Walz ihre Mutterrolle mit dem Sport verbindet. Die zweite routinierte Athletin Vanessa Voigt (29) bereitete sich auf eigenen Wunsch abseits der Mannschaft auf die Weltcup-Saison vor. Beide Leistungsträgerinnen loben den Weg, den Flunger im Team eingeschlagen hat. Voigt findet es gut, dass eine Frau an der Spitze des Teams stehe, die eine andere Ansprache als ihr Vorgänger habe. Hettich-Walz glaubt, dass Flunger die großen Potenziale im deutschen Team hervorheben könne.
Ein prominenter Name fehlt
An Talenten mangelt es bei den deutschen Frauen tatsächlich nicht. In Flungers erstem Weltcup-Aufgebot sind vier der sechs Athletinnen um die fünfmalige Junioren-Weltmeisterin Julia Tannheimer Jahrgang 2002 oder jünger. Allerdings fehlt im Youngster-Quartett ein prominenter Name: Die 22 Jahre alte Selina Grotian, die bereits einen Weltcup und zwei WM-Medaillen gewonnen hat, darf nur im zweitklassigen IBU-Cup starten. Ein Zeichen, dass bei der schwierigen Mission der neuen Cheftrainerin nur Leistung und keine alten Verdienste zählen.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Cruz com suástica no Amapá mobiliza missão de direitos humanos e busca de reparação histórica por presença nazista na Amazônia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Uma missão de direitos humanos realiza, entre esta quarta-feira (25) e sexta-feira (27), em Laranjal do Jari, no sul do Amapá, uma audiência pública e reuniões com o poder público para debater a reparação histórica pela presença nazista na Amazônia. A iniciativa do Conselho Nacional dos Direitos Humanos (CNDH) e do Observatório Brasileiro sobre Discurso de Ódio, Extremismo e Neonazismo (Oben) busca aprofundar a discussão sobre o reconhecimento formal das responsabilidades dos Estados alemão e brasileiro por esse passado.
O símbolo mais visível desse capítulo é uma cruz de madeira de quase três metros de altura, marcada com uma suástica, que identifica o túmulo de Joseph Greiner, integrante de uma expedição alemã realizada durante o regime de Adolf Hitler.
A missão é desenvolvida no âmbito da Relatoria Especial de Enfrentamento ao Discurso de Ódio, Extremismo e Neonazismo do CNDH, em parceria com o Instituto Brasileiro de Análises Sociais e Econômicas (Ibase). Participam o relator especial do CNDH, Carlos Nicodemos, e Maria Fernanda Fernandes, consultora da relatoria e coordenadora-geral do Oben.
“A missão em Laranjal do Jari representa uma ampliação da atuação da Relatoria Especial de Enfrentamento ao Discurso de Ódio, ao Extremismo e ao Neonazismo e de seu mecanismo, o Oben, a partir da perspectiva de incidência em um território que carrega, em sua memória, a influência direta do nazismo. A iniciativa atuará especialmente nas frentes da educação, da cultura e da memória em direitos humanos, contribuindo para o reconhecimento dessas violações e para a reparação histórica”, explica Maria Fernanda Fernandes.
A audiência pública deve reunir lideranças da região, representantes de comunidades locais e movimentos sociais para discutir o significado histórico da cruz, a memória da expedição e os caminhos para a reparação. Nas reuniões com a prefeitura e representantes do poder público, estão em pauta a queda do monumento em 2022, sua reinstalação e as responsabilidades institucionais pela preservação da memória local.
Para a presidenta do CNDH, Ivana Cláudia Leal de Souza, a discussão diz respeito também ao presente. “Não há democracia plena sem verdade, memória e justiça. Para o CNDH, falar em reparação histórica na Amazônia é tirar essas violações da invisibilidade e reafirmar o dever do Estado de combater qualquer resquício de ideologias supremacistas ou antidemocráticas no Brasil de hoje”, afirma.
Expedição nazista
A cruz fica em um pequeno cemitério às margens do Rio Jari, próximo à cachoeira de Santo Antônio, a cerca de uma hora de barco de Laranjal do Jari, município a 287 quilômetros de Macapá. Em alemão, a inscrição diz: “Joseph Greiner morreu aqui de febre em 2 de janeiro de 1936 a serviço da pesquisa alemã”. Depois do sepultamento, a área passou a ser usada como cemitério pelas comunidades do território.
Greiner integrava a chamada Expedição Jari, liderada por Otto Schulz-Kampfhenkel, que percorreu a região entre 1935 e 1937. Oficialmente, a missão fazia pesquisas sobre a fauna, a flora e a geografia amazônica, mas estudos apontam interesses estratégicos da Alemanha nazista na região. Segundo historiadores, o objetivo era reunir informações para a implantação de uma colônia alemã na América do Sul, com vistas a uma possível invasão da Guiana Francesa.
O plano nunca foi levado adiante. Ao longo da expedição, os alemães levantaram dados ambientais e sobre a cultura indígena. Registros da época mostram a relação do grupo com o povo Aparai. Doenças como malária e difteria atingiram os integrantes da comitiva. Greiner, que, segundo historiadores, vivia no Brasil desde a adolescência e foi recrutado como capataz para facilitar a comunicação, morreu de uma febre não especificada.
Em 2022, a cruz foi encontrada caída após uma cheia do Rio Jari. A prefeitura levou o monumento para a sede do município, onde ele foi restaurado por um escultor, e em 2023 o reinstalou no local de origem, sobre uma nova base, como registro histórico do município.
