Anwalt der Kinder
Der diesjährige Menschenrechtspreis von Amnesty International in Deutschland geht an den palästinensischen Rechtsanwalt Khaled Quzmar.
Khaled Quzmar ist ein typischer Alltagsheld: Was er tut, sieht man meist nicht, doch ist seine Arbeit fundamental für die, die davon profitieren. Seit Jahrzehnten setzt er sich für die Belange von Kindern in den von Israel besetzten palästinensischen Gebieten ein, streitet als Rechtsanwalt für deren Rechte gegen ein übermächtiges Besatzungsregime, das auch bei Kindern und Jugendlichen vor Gefängnis, Schikanen und Folter nicht zurückschreckt.
Und seine Aktivität ärgert die Besatzer offenbar so sehr, dass der israelische Geheimdienst ihn vorladen ließ, mit Gefängnis drohte. An den Druck und die Diffamierungen ist der in Ramallah ansässige Quzmar zwar gewöhnt, doch aufgrund der anhaltenden Repressionen musste er im Frühjahr dieses Jahres die von ihm geleitete NGO Defense For Children International – Palestine (DCI-P) nach über 35 Jahren auflösen. Seit Juni 2026 fungiert er als Geschäftsführender Direktor der Organisation Palestinian Center for Child Rights. Für sein langjähriges Engagement als Menschenrechtsanwalt erhält er in diesem Jahr den Menschenrechtspreis der internationalen NGO Amnesty International in Deutschland.
»Khaled Quzmar gibt seit fast 40 Jahren unermüdlich und allen Widerständen zum Trotz der vulnerabelsten Bevölkerungsgruppe Palästinas eine Stimme: den Kindern. Ihre erschütternde Lebenssituation ist die direkte Folge systematischer Menschenrechtsverletzungen und Unterdrückung, die sich in den letzten Jahren noch einmal deutlich verschärft hat«, erklärte in einer Pressemitteilung Julia Duchrow, Generalsekretärin von Amnesty International in Deutschland.
Aus den Erzählungen von Khaled Quzmars meist minderjährigen Mandanten lässt sich verstehen, was diese in israelischen Gefängnissen durchmachen müssen. So beschreibt ein heute 18-Jähriger in einer Reportage des Amnesty-Journals nach seiner Haftentlassung, was er im Knast erlebt hat: »Im Gefängnis gab es jeden Tag Schläge. Die Wärter kamen in unsere Zelle, ordneten an, uns bis auf die Unterhose zu entkleiden und auf den Fußboden zu legen. Dann schlugen sie uns mit einem Stromkabel.«
Khaled Quzmar hat ihn als Anwalt gegen gravierende Anschuldigungen verteidigt: Der bei der Festnahme noch Minderjährige soll Bomben fabriziert haben. Beweise gab es demnach keine, trotzdem musste er mit einer Gefängnisstrafe von zehn Jahren rechnen. Nach Quzmars Aussagen sei es gelungen, »das Gericht milde zu stimmen«, sodass er »nur« 13 Monate habe absitzen müssen. »Das sind Kinder, sie haben diese Brutalität nicht verdient«, sagt Quzmar. Die Militärgerichte, vor denen Jugendliche im Westjordanland regelmäßig angeklagt werden, würden sich nicht darum scheren, ob ein Anwalt bei der Verhandlung dabei sei. Und vor einem Militärgericht müsse der Angeklagte den Beweis führen, dass er KEIN Terrorist sei.
Nach Angaben von Amnesty International sind derzeit mindestens 350 Minderjährige in israelischen Gefängnissen teils für viele Jahre inhaftiert, nicht selten verurteilt aufgrund von erzwungenen »Geständnissen«, die unter Druck, Gewalt und ohne rechtlichen Beistand abgegeben werden. Ein besonders perfides Mittel der israelischen Justiz ist die sogenannte Administrativhaft, von der mehr als die Hälfte der inhaftierten Minderjährigen betroffen sein soll. Das heißt, sie können ohne Anklage auf unbestimmte Zeit festgehalten werden.
Khaled Quzmars Wunsch, den Rechtsanwaltsberuf zu ergreifen, hat mit der Verhaftung seines Bruders zu tun. Als er diesen im Gefängnis besuchte, durfte er ihn nicht umarmen, ein Anwalt dagegen wurde zu ihm durchgelassen. Damit stand Quzmars Berufswunsch fest: Das Jura-Studium absolvierte er in Algerien, da es in Palästina seinerzeit keine juristische Fakultät gab. Ab 1987 arbeitete er dann als Rechtsanwalt, genau in dem Jahr, als im Westjordanland die erste Intifada begann: Bald hatte er pro Tag 30 bis 40 Fälle, auch viele Kinder und Jugendliche, die Steine auf Panzer geworfen hatten. Er lernte Hebräisch, um mit Richtern und Staatsanwälten verhandeln zu können, und sattelte noch einen Master-Studiengang in Internationalem Recht drauf – in Irland.
Der 62-jährige Quzmar hat zwei Töchter sowie zwei Söhne, von denen einer ebenfalls als Rechtsanwalt arbeitet. In Ramallah lebt die Familie nahe einer israelischen Siedlung. Früher habe es keine Probleme mit den Siedlern gegeben, sagte er in der Reportage des Amnesty-Journals. »Aber seit dem 7. Oktober 2023 leben wir in Angst.«
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.title: What Is Internet Cinema?
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.text:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.
During last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare. The Gallery, a nomadic curatorial platform, had set up an exhibition, titled “WeWork (oralmoral)”, in one of the building’s vacant office spaces. In celebration of the show’s closing the curators were screening films, some of which fall into the category of what is being called “internet cinema,” a burgeoning movement, or method, that has been in the making since late 2020.
Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening. Someone in front of me was hastily scrawling the lineup of the screenings on paper with a black marker and passing them around as fast as he produced them. One passed back to me. The first film on the list was Zarina Nares’ I am going to die (this is my sign) (2025). The projector was fiddled with and a rectangle of white with a buffer symbol appeared on the blank wall in front of the seated crowd.
	A chorus of female voices rose up, all in some general distress, and while I couldn’t see these women, by the tone, I could tell they were speaking into a front-facing camera. The chorus cut out to a single voice, which spoke over dashcam footage of a car crash: “You’re having problems at work, your boyfriend broke up with you, your parents are mad at you, everything is going wrong, your car broke down – that is a good sign. Like, that is the very best sign.”
What followed was a montage of TikTok videos featuring motivational advice. One video bled into another, linked by the formulaic hooks used by podcast bros, emotional car seat influencers, clips of celebrities’ acceptance speeches, athletes in interviews, or passionate pastors, all of which was set to music. One after another these TikToks reveal ‘the one thing that you need to learn’ in a high-speed carousel of intense emotion that feels increasingly forced as it becomes clear how many of these impassioned speeches are copies of one another.
“Internet cinema isn’t necessarily about the internet or its aesthetic but about its logic, how it functions and how it makes us feel,” Zarina Nares said in a phone call. On the process of making I am going to die, she added that “Clearly, I watched enough advice videos for too long that I kept getting more. Once you watch so many you see the formula behind them, whether it’s a certain cadence of speaking or certain music.”
Internet cinema was first defined in a 2007 paper by Chuck Tryon titled “New Media Studies and the New Internet Cinema.” The technologies and formats that concerned Tryon —iPods and camera phones, software like Final Cut Pro, and home movies—are far dated, but his paper was prescient, having tapped into impulses and concerns that reflect contemporary internet cinema: a do-it-yourself ethos that blurs the line between amateur and artist; the popularization of “niche exhibition;” and a “self-reflexive style” that works “to call attention to the narrative codes and technological specs that shape cultural productions.”
Contemporary internet cinema has its roots in the COVID-era, which saw an explosion of participation in internet culture and production, that often bled out into one particular place: Dimes Square, a patch of Manhattan where Chinatown and the Lower East Side meet.
	One of the most memorable dramas that played out at the time was puppeteered by a then-anonymous internet figure who went by the name Angelicism01. This figure posted creeds about extinction on Substack, and gained infamy for growing a cult-like following among young women in New York (who had never met him). With the help of various film makers, he made a three-hour long movie called Film01 which includes fast paced montages of memes, tweets, videos of natural disasters and terrorist attacks, alongside long scenes featuring the ‘it-girls’ he had recruited. Writer Madeline Cash described Film01 in the art publication Spike as “an unsophisticated collage of localized content that mimics, rather than intervenes or questions, our digital conditions,” which ultimately did nothing more than tap “into the scene’s libidinal narcissism.”
Yet, with some distance, Film01 has proven to be a productive experiment. One of Angelicism01’s collaborators, the filmmaker Dana Dawud, found internet footage to splice into the film, created short edits that became a part of the larger film, and remotely directed certain sequences. Dawud would go on to launch Open Secret, an international screening series of internet cinema that has since played a large part in consolidating disconnected artists and practices under the term.
At the same time that young women were running around Dimes Square at Angelicism01’s request, people were locked away at home with TikTok. More than ever, people around the world were subjecting themselves to hours and hours of scrolling on this relatively new video content platform.
“When you’re doom scrolling, there is, technically speaking, no specific author to this montage that you’re watching. So, it’s as if you’re exposed to radical experimental cinema all the time by a completely cynical industrial apparatus,” said 0nty, the co-author of “Dialogues on CoreCore & the Contemporary Online Avant-Garde” during a Zoom interview also attended by his co-author Mischa Dols. “The question is, how do you even begin to think about this problem? And I think internet cinema is an answer,” 0nty said.
0nty and Dols describe internet cinema as a method, rather than a genre or an aesthetic, which seeks to expose or comment on the way that the internet functions through editing found footage.
It’s worth noting that some works under the umbrella of internet cinema do feature the production of new images. Dahlia Bloomstone’s 20,000 Tokens (2025) is a screen recording of the artist chatting with men and exposing herself on the webcam site Chaturbate (the video is spliced with a glitching 3D-rendering of a blonde avatar in a black void). For The Sight is a Wound (2024), Parham Ghalamdar filmed himself burning his own paintings, as a statement on how tthe seemingly endless documentation of the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza has made images useless. Yet the particular process of editing found footage is usually highlighted in definitions of internet cinema because this method represents the folk practice that preceded internet cinema: corecore.
	
	Core, or rather, -core, is a suffix that denotes some kind of bundle of aesthetics and moods. Cottagecore, for example, is a reference to an image universe of milkmaid tops, galoshes, a straw basket full of wildflowers, a shingled cottage, butter made with wooden tools, but also, beyond images, a wish for simple, optimistic, pastoral life. But corecore emerged not as a specific aesthetic but as a way of making video content through editing together music, clips from movies, podcasts, and other TikToks.
These videos are often melancholic ruminations of the deep and unrecognized suffering of young men, the terrible sublimity of being alone with your screen, an alienated awareness of hurtling towards extinction while scrolling on your parents’ sofa. Watching compilations of corecore I reminded me intensely of my time on Tumblr as a teenager.
On Tumblr, the practice of posting and reblogging images, fragments of text, and GIFs under an “aesthetic” was a way of cultivating and nurturing a feeling: a world of images that created a visual language for all that we thought life could be. Painful, dramatic love; intensity chased by the doom of its own ephemerality; cold, beautiful suffering. In the pivot to video platforms, corecore takes that tendency to collect images and feelings and turns it into a form much more contained and shareable than a blog: the film.
	Removed from the usual logics of personal branding and sponsorship deals, it became an exciting trend for those who take internet-based cultural production seriously. Corecore, as a mass movement of people making films on the same devices they watch them on, represented the realization of an old dream of experimental cinema: film as a truly collective practice.
“Authorship gets really muddy, you have content creators and video artists making films on the same platforms. Dana [Dawud] has compared internet cinema to the way that SoundCloud functions, where people can steal your edit, steal your beat, steal a sample, and then it gets lost who put it online first, and that’s okay,” said Edison Niebla Rodriguez, a curator who also creates video art with his wife, Dayana Matasheva, under the name Demon Lovers Inc. “Obviously, it’s kind of at odds with video art which is very hard for people to see because of the way that the art market functions.”
That said, video art has been a major inspiration for artists working in internet cinema. Arthur Jafa’s Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death (2016) in particular is often cited as a kind of totem of legitimacy for internet cinema. The film is a montage of civil rights–era footage and grainy videos of Black Americans circulated online: reaction memes, women twerking, women getting slammed to the ground by police, men getting shot by police, arms raised in the air. It’s profound love and profound despair, but also a comment on how images of Black people circulate online. When I first saw it, I was struck by how internet it felt: the video was playing on a laptop, which had been filmed by a phone camera. Of course, it turned out I’d been watching a bootleg, and that extra frame wasn’t part of the original.
	Dawud’s film Palcorecore (2024) can be read in Jafa’s lineage. Like Jafa, Dawud cuts together found footage in an act of memory, love, and grief. The footage shows Palestinians flying kites, breakdancing, rapping, riding horses, and playing by the sea. Children surround a tank; a mute man desperately mimes a murder he witnessed. “The internet exists to document its own martyrdom,” a computerized voice says, playing on the fact that the Arabic word for martyr comes from the root meaning “to witness.” “We are martyrs together,” the voice says: we are witnesses together.
“What interests me about internet cinema is that it creates a history of internet artists, the thoughts and languages they develop online, and the possibility of establishing a continuity between what they produce on the internet and how it can be given a temporal form through cinema,” wrote Dawud in an email. “Internet cinema doesn’t merely document an existing culture; it participates in the creation of its history. It is a way for the internet to historicize itself.”
Ultimately, internet cinema is less a practice than a name: one that gives form to a whole range of ways of making online that are often lost in the tumult of the internet’s incessant production. If there is one thing that separates the art world from online cultural production, it is that the art world is nothing if not a form of memory. In its obsession with provenance, catalogues, and archives, it is a network of stewardship. Internet cinema is a means of making an object of what is so fleeting online, by turning the internet into a film.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Selo ‘Não é Não’ certifica bar e mobiliza rede de proteção às mulheres na Paraíba
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Bar do Baiano, em João Pessoa, será referência em uma iniciativa de prevenção à violência contra as mulheres. Na sexta-feira (27), às 18h30, o estabelecimento, no bairro dos Bancários, receberá o “Selo Não é Não – Mulheres Seguras”, após participar de uma capacitação voltada ao acolhimento e à proteção de mulheres em situações de assédio e violência. A ação é promovida pelo Ministério das Mulheres e pela ONU Mulheres, por meio do Projeto das Articuladoras Territoriais na Paraíba, representado por Patrícia Oliveira, coordenadora, e Marcella Arbia, especialista, em parceria com movimentos sociais do estado.
Segundo Arbia, o Protocolo Não é Não vai para além dos grandes eventos, envolvendo diretamente os proprietários de bares e os trabalhadores do setor de entretenimento
“Aqui na Paraíba, neste ano, o Ministério das Mulheres lançou novamente a iniciativa do Protocolo Não é Não. Para que o protocolo seja aplicado, é necessário que os estabelecimentos participem da capacitação para receber o Selo Não é Não. O selo é concedido após um treinamento realizado por uma pessoa indicada pelo próprio estabelecimento, que aprende como prevenir situações de violência contra as mulheres e como agir diante desses casos”, explicou.
Para Patrícia Oliveira, a iniciativa é importante para garantir que bares, casas de shows e boates adotem protocolos de segurança para proteger mulheres vítimas de violência e saibam como acionar a rede de proteção diante dessas situações.
“A importância reside exatamente no cumprimento, pelos estabelecimentos, sejam bares, casas de shows ou boates, da instituição de um protocolo de segurança para as mulheres vítimas de violência. É fundamental que esses espaços estejam preparados para acolher e proteger as mulheres. Sobretudo, precisam saber como acionar a rede de proteção quando uma mulher passar por esse tipo de situação”, destacou.
Capacitação e rede de proteção
De acordo com Arbia, um representante do estabelecimento participou de um curso on-line de 36 horas. Além do certificado, o bar recebe um cartaz identificando o espaço como seguro para mulheres.
“É importante que as mulheres saibam que estão em um ambiente mais seguro, onde os funcionários fizeram o curso e sabem como agir diante de uma situação de violência. Eles precisam saber a quem recorrer e quais procedimentos adotar para proteger a mulher. Queremos que o Bar do Baiano seja um exemplo para que outros estabelecimentos também adotem o protocolo”, comentou ela.
A entrega reunirá instituições da rede de proteção, incluindo a Delegacia Especializada no Atendimento à Mulher (Deam), a Patrulha Maria da Penha, o Procon – órgão responsável pela aplicação do protocolo – as secretarias de mulheres estadual e municipal e conselhos. Bares interessados poderão procurar os movimentos de mulheres, as secretarias ou as articuladoras territoriais. O curso também pode ser acessado pelo portal do Ministério das Mulheres.
O que prevê a lei federal
A Lei Federal nº 14.786/2023 estabelece medidas de prevenção ao constrangimento e à violência em casas noturnas, boates, shows e espetáculos musicais em locais fechados com venda de bebidas alcoólicas. Entre as medidas estão acolhimento da vítima, afastamento do agressor e capacitação de funcionários.
Na Paraíba, a Lei nº 12.724/2023, de autoria da deputada Silvia Benjamin (Republicanos), determina a divulgação da campanha “Não é Não” em shows, festas e eventos realizados ou patrocinados pelo governo da Paraíba, incluindo campanhas educativas e presença de órgãos para receber denúncias.
Contexto nacional
Segundo o Ministério das Mulheres, a iniciativa integra uma mobilização nacional prevista para 27 de novembro de 2026, com a certificação de bares nas capitais brasileiras por meio do Selo “Não é Não”. A ação busca incentivar a adesão de estabelecimentos ao protocolo federal, ampliar a capacitação de funcionários e fortalecer a prevenção ao assédio e à violência contra as mulheres em ambientes de lazer.

https://taz.de/Verurteilter-YouTuber-JP-.title: YouTuber JP Kraemer: Ganz konkrete Männer
https://taz.de/Verurteilter-YouTuber-JP-.author: Gunnar Hinck
https://taz.de/Verurteilter-YouTuber-JP-.text:
YouTuber JP Kraemer : Ganz konkrete Männer
Ein Youtube-Star wird wegen Gewalt an seiner Partnerin verurteilt – und macht Business as usual. Die nötige Antwort wäre ein kollektiver Aufschrei.
D er Youtuber und Autotuner JP Kraemer dürfte unter taz-LeserInnen eher unbekannt sein, doch hat er eine riesige Fangemeinde. 2,7 Millionen Menschen folgen ihm auf seinem Videokanal. Und Eltern, die 12-jährige Söhne haben oder hatten, dürften an seinen Videos nicht vorbeikommen. JP Kraemer kann in seinen Videos witzig und charmant sein und, ganz wichtig für fahrradfahrende Eltern, er nimmt die Autowelt nicht so ernst wie andere Kfz-Fanatiker.
Doch der Dortmunder ist ein verurteilter Straftäter. Im Oktober wurde er zu einer Geldstrafe in sechsstelliger Höhe verurteilt (wegen seiner florierenden Einkünfte haben die RichterInnen einen entsprechend hohen Tagessatz festgelegt). JP Kraemer hat seine damalige Frau wie ein Boxer niedergeschlagen. Heraus kam die Tat nur, weil eine Überwachungskamera in seiner Autowerkstatt die Gewaltattacke filmte. Da konnte die Tat nicht mehr geleugnet werden.
Ausgerechnet einen Tag vor dem Internationalen Tag zur Beseitigung von Gewalt an Frauen veröffentlichte er ein Video. Man kann es nur als Tiefpunkt eines Umgangs mit dem eigenen Gewaltproblem und Frauenbild bezeichnen: Er habe sehr viele Fehler gemacht, aber, na klar, habe er aus seinen „Fehlern gelernt“. Und: „Es wird so nicht mehr vorkommen“, wobei sich die Frage anschließt, ob es auf andere Weise noch mal vorkommen wird.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Leute wie JP Kraemer dürfen weitermachen, als sei nichts passiert, und weiterhin werden ihn Hunderttausende Jungs und junge Männer dafür bewundern, wie cool er an Autos herumschraubt. Und das toxische Frauenbild wird gleich mitgeliefert.
Schweigeminuten für die Opfer, wie am Mittwoch im Bundestag geschehen, sind wichtig und richtig. Das reicht aber nicht. Politik und Zivilgesellschaft sollten es klar verurteilen, wenn Gewalttäter weiter viel Geld mit ihrer Bekanntheit verdienen – und auch deren Namen nennen. Gewalt an Frauen ist nichts Abstraktes, sondern sie kommt von ganz konkreten Männern.

Mönchengladbach bekommt den Abschiebeknast
Trotz Protesten stimmt der Bauausschuss dem Vorhaben zu. Dabei hatte sich die Stadt 2020 zum »sicheren Hafen« für Geflüchtete erklärt.
In Mönchengladbach will das Land Nordrhein-Westfalen eine Abschiebehaftanstalt, im Politikerdeutsch »Unterbringungseinrichtung für Ausreisepflichtige« (UfA), errichten. Seit Langem gehen Bürger immer wieder gegen das Vorhaben auf die Straße. Doch am Dienstagabend hat der Bauausschuss des Stadtrats mit den Stimmen von AfD, CDU, FDP/Volt und SPD grünes Licht für den Bebauungsplan gegeben. Lediglich Linke und Bündnis90/Die Grünen stimmten dagegen. Damit ist eigentlich schon die letzte Hürde für das Quasi-Gefängnis genommen, das auf dem Gelände des früheren Nato-Hauptquartiers der britischen Armee, des JHQ Rheindahlen, entstehen soll.
Nicht abfinden mit dieser Entscheidung will sich ein Bündnis von Gegnern. Noch kurz vor der entscheidenden Sitzung hatte es den Bauausschuss aufgefordert, sich dem Vorhaben entgegenzustellen. Mara Sauer, Sprecherin des Bündnisses, erinnert gegenüber »nd« daran, dass sich Mönchengladbach vor sechs Jahren zum »sicheren Hafen« für Geflüchtete erklärt habe. Für das Bündnis »Abschiebegefängnis verhindern – in Düsseldorf, Mönchengladbach und überall« passt das nicht zusammen. »Ein sicherer Hafen baut keinen Abschiebeknast«, heißt es in einem Schreiben an die Mitglieder der Bezirksvertretung und des Bauausschusses.
In diesem Brief an die Kommunalpolitiker hatte das Bündnis den Rat der Stadt aufgefordert, das Bauleitplanverfahren nicht auf den Weg zu bringen und stattdessen alle verbleibenden baurechtlichen und politischen Möglichkeiten auszuschöpfen, um die UfA zu verhindern. Auch das Jugendparlament der Stadt hat sich geschlossen gegen den Bau ausgesprochen. Es verweist auf die Situation von in Abschiebehaft Genommenen. Bis zu 18 Monate könnten Menschen dort festgehalten werden, nur um ihre reibungslose »Rückführung« sicherzustellen.
Während der Sitzung des Bauausschusses protestierte ein gutes Dutzend Gegner*innen im Saal singend gegen das Abschiebegefängnis. Zu den Klängen von »Freude schöner Götterfunken« hallte es durch den Sitzungssaal des Stadtrats: »Nein zu UfAs, Frontex, Pushbacks, ja zu Solidarität. Wir steh’n für den sich’ren Hafen, den die Stadt hier grad verrät.« Wenig Freude an dieser musikalischen Einlage hatten Politik und Verwaltung – sie riefen die Polizei.
Abschiebung in Haft und Folter
Dass Abschiebungen immer wieder zu Haft und Folter führen können, zeigt der Fall von Dilmurod Ergashev aus Tadschikistan. Zwei Jahre nach seiner Abschiebung hob das Verwaltungsgericht Düsseldorf am 17. November den Bescheid auf, auf dessen Grundlage der Transport erfolgt war. Ergashev war sofort nach seiner Ankunft in Tadschikistan verhaftet und anschließend zu acht Jahren Haft verurteilt worden. »Mit dem Urteil des Verwaltungsgerichts Düsseldorf ist es nun klipp und klar: Der Bescheid des Bundesamts für Migration und Flüchtlinge vom Juli 2024 ist rechtswidrig und wurde aufgehoben«, sagt Sebastian Rose von der Initiative Abschiebungsreporting NRW zu »nd«. Der Kreis Kleve hätte Ergashev »auf alleiniger Grundlage dieses Bescheides niemals« abschieben dürfen, betont er.
Sobald die Düsseldorfer Entscheidung rechtskräftig ist, könnte sie nach Einschätzung von Ergashevs Unterstützern den Weg für eine verwaltungsrechtliche Rückgängigmachung der Abschiebungsfolgen und mögliche Amtshaftungsansprüche eröffnen. »Bedauerlich ist allerdings, dass der zuständige Einzelrichter am Verwaltungsgericht Düsseldorf durch seine formale Entscheidung von einer inhaltlichen Bewertung der Inhaftierung und Verurteilung eines Oppositionsaktivisten in Tadschikistan abgesehen hat«, kritisiert Rose.
Gleichzeitig sei es wichtig, dass die wesentlichen Fakten nun im Urteil dokumentiert seien. Dazu gehörten der Haftort Ergashevs in einem Gefängnis in Chudschand und die Verurteilung durch ein tadschikisches Gericht am 27. Februar 2025. Er begrüße es, dass die Fakten zu Verurteilung und Inhaftierung des Betroffenen nun durch das Düsseldorfer Urteil »amtlich bestätigt sind und von niemandem mehr ernsthaft in Zweifel gezogen werden können«, so Rose.
Die Anwältin Ergashevs will sich nun für eine mögliche Rückkehr ihres Mandanten an den Kreis Kleve und die deutsche Botschaft in der tadschikischen Hauptstadt Duschanbe wenden. Rose fordert die deutschen Behörden auf, sich für den Mann einzusetzen: »Sobald Herr Ergashev freigelassen wird, muss ihm die umgehende Möglichkeit der Rückkehr nach Deutschland gegeben werden, wenn er das möchte.« Der Kreis Kleve solle bereits jetzt eine Vorab-Zustimmung für die Erteilung eines Visums ausstellen.
Der Fall Ergashev ist indes kein Einzelfall. Erst jüngst sei mit Asadullo Boboev ein weiterer tadschikischer Oppositioneller aus dem Kreis Kleve abgeschoben worden, sagt Rose. Berichten zufolge sei er dort sogar zu einer Haftstrafe von 17 Jahren verurteilt worden.
Die Kostenschätzungen für die »UfA« erhöhen sich derweil immer weiter. War im vergangenen Jahr noch von 200 Millionen Euro für die 140 Haftplätze die Rede, so nannte die Landesregierung im September schon eine Summe von 313 Millionen. Ende Juli war zudem bekannt geworden, dass das Land Nordrhein-Westfalen mit dem Bund einen Kaufvertrag über die benötigten Flächen auf dem JHQ-Gelände geschlossen hat.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.title: Five Questions for Advisors on the November Marquee Sales: Guarantees, Spotty Bidding, and a $190 M. Van Gogh
https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.author: Harrison Jacobs
https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.text:
Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance, the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.
It’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-important November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach. But before we turn to Miami, a quick post-mortem on the marquee sales just passed.
Perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder. Do you measure it by overall totals? By sell-through rate? By the number of bidders, or the number of guaranteed lots? By the ratio of hammer prices to estimates? Each figure tells a slightly different story, leaving plenty for our resident market whisperers to debate. But before we turn this week’s column over to the advisers, let’s set out some basic figures.
According to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022. Sotheby’s led the pack with $1.16 billion, clearing $1 billion and taking more than half of the three houses’ combined total for the second straight year. (Its share rose to 57 percent from 53 percent. Christie’s share dropped to 38 percent from 43 percent, while Phillips’s ticked up to 5 percent from 4 percent, pushed by the $44.6 million Modigliani sculpture.)
And yes, the $384 million gap between Sotheby’s and Christie’s is roughly what the Blaquier-Arrieta collection brought in on its own: $412 million on just 12 lots. Winning those big consignments really does matter.
But for all those gaudy totals, there was a definite sense watching the week’s sales that bidding was uneven, thin, and at times absent entirely. Blame fickle collectors, sure, but it seems the auction houses pushed their estimates to the limit. Per ARTDAI, hammer prices across the various-owner sales in November 2025 came in 17 percent above the low estimates and at roughly 80 percent of the high estimates. This season, hammer prices for the same sales (i.e. excluding the Blaquier-Arrieta single-owner sale) were flat against the low estimates and just 69 percent of the highs. As Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart said after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale last week, “Our estimates weren’t shy.”
But does an aggressive auction house make for a weak market? Or is this the same market we’ve seen for the last few cycles—one that is choosy, blue-chip and provenance-driven, and competitive for the right objects—just approached differently by the specialists? That’s what we asked the advisers, along with their takes on everything from the spread of guarantees to that $190 million van Gogh.
Answers have been edited for clarity and concision.
- What Was the Single Most Revealing Moment of the Week For You? Evan Beard, Beard & Co: Our having to repeatedly chase Impressionist and Modern Day Sale works well above the high estimates with a fairly low hit rate tells us that the “flight to safety” is more than just a tired cliché. Even second- and third-tier Impressionists performed very well. Liz Sterling, Sterling | Teel Capital: The strong result for the Jeff Koons Bob-Tail [at Sotheby’s] was a pleasant reminder that no matter how highly orchestrated evening sales have become, there are still surprises. Equally, the results for the small Robert Ryman and Robert Rauschenberg from the Agnes Gund collection clearly demonstrate that there is still connoisseurship in the market. Nina del Rio, del Rio | Byers: I have always believed the market is driven by the number of participants; more bidders = higher prices, more volatility, and less predictability. The current moment feels more predictable, safe, and tempered—which would signal fewer bidders. Estimates were full, reflecting strong performance over the past few seasons, and the buyers are still there for the majority of material, which is European Impressionism and modernism and American postwar abstraction, but there was less competition and flatter prices as a result. However, I was surprised by the sober bidding on the truly rare material, which represented a singular (once-in-a-lifetime) opportunity for buyers. Monday evening after the Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary auction, I told ARTnews I was excited for the Blaquier sale on Wednesday because of the rarity and quality of the works; well, I was wrong that rarity would translate into bidder competition and runaway prices. The fact is, each work was priced at the top end of the artists’ (very mature) markets—leaving little room for price discovery, and bidding was thin and tempered as a result. Did buyers perceive these prices as the very top end of the market? Yes, I think so, which meant little to no competition for great works. Maria Brito: Believe it or not, the moment that caught my attention happened in Stockholm, with the sale of Hilma af Klint’s Ser III No. 5. It hammered at 108 million Swedish kronor against a high estimate of 8 million, an extraordinary 13.5 times the estimate! Here is an artist whose importance to the history of abstraction has been celebrated by major museums for years, but whose market barely existed because so few of her abstract paintings ever became available. And suddenly collectors were fighting to pay nearly $13 million for one. We saw something similar with Aaron Douglas’s Harriet Tubman in New York, which sparked a seven-minute bidding war involving eight bidders and sold for $14.48 million against a high estimate of $3.5 million. I think this tells us something fascinating about today’s market. There is enormous capital available for historically significant, genuinely rare works, particularly by artists whose contributions have been undervalued. Collectors are willing to reconsider established price hierarchies, and when they really want something, they’re not shy about spending. Allan Schwartzman, Schwartzman&: For me, there were several standout points: the fever for hot young artists at auction has passed; Robert Rauschenberg remains the most important innovator of the last 75 years, and yet his market remains undeservedly quiet; and behind that, Gilbert & George are a crazy bargain; even though their work is photographic, they are unique and should be commanding the prices of the great painters of their generation. Erica Samuels, Samuels Creative: Beyond prices, this week highlighted a distinct mood across the field. There is a strong sense of collegiality—advisors, dealers, and auction houses are actively working together to ensure success for their clients amid a generally sideways market. The market relies as much on goodwill as it does on capital, and both were evident this week. Despite broader tech and financial shifts, such as the Anthropic IPO, this remains a human-driven market centered on human-made art. Danielle Forest Brandi, Beaumont Nathan: There were a few revealing moments for us, but among them was the spectacular result for Monet’s La Barque. The price of $6.9 million was, on the one hand, a surprising result for a work that measured only 2 by 3 inches, but on the other hand, a good case study for how collectors are behaving at the top end of the market. Looking at that alone, it’s perhaps an irrational result, but when you think about the rarity of the object, the story, and how good that picture will look on someone’s wall, i.e., styled alongside their Chinese porcelain collection and Nakashima furniture, it starts to make sense. That’s how collectors are thinking right now; it’s the beauty of the art market and what makes collecting different from other pursuits.
- 47 Percent of Christie’s Evening Lots Carried Guarantees, Compared With 77 percent at Sotheby’s. What Do Those Numbers Tell You About How Each House Is Approaching This Season? Evan Beard: Two key themes drove the high third-party guarantee rate this season: (1) Much of the material came from single-owner sales that carried house guarantees—Blaquier, Baum, Clive Davis, etc.—so the houses had to put the risk off on third parties. (2) Consignor expectations were elevated coming off a strong spring season, which pushed estimates to a level that the houses felt more comfortable locking in guarantees rather than risk a lot going unsold. Guarantees are fundamental at this point. They’re a behavior tool to get an early bid from a buyer and a behavioral tool to give comfort to a consignor. Both sides still have the chance at upside. Guarantees are an important lubricant. Nina del Rio: Estimates were high across both auction houses, reflecting the past six years of consistent demand and solid performance—especially for European modernism and postwar American abstraction. The auction houses agree to full estimates to compete for consignments. My guess is that Christie’s was less willing to offer house guarantees which were not backed by irrevocable bids at the start of the consignment-getting season. And Sotheby’s had a bit more faith that they would find an IB [irrevocable bid] later in the process. In brief, I believe Sotheby’s appetite for risk—and possibly their confidence in the market—was a bit stronger this season. Maria Brito: Sotheby’s just announced its biggest-ever week of fine art sales at $1.31 billion, which is extraordinary. But let’s look underneath those numbers. Almost a third of that total came from just 12 paintings in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, all guaranteed, and the majority hammered below their low estimates. Sotheby’s guaranteed 77 percent of its evening lots compared with 47 percent at Christie’s, suggesting a much more aggressive approach to securing major consignments. Guarantees are essential to attracting exceptional property, and third-party guarantors can absorb much of the risk. But a guaranteed sale tells us little about competitive demand. What interests me is how many collectors were willing to bid beyond the guaranteed price. The money is clearly there. The willingness to compete at any price is another matter. Allan Schwartzman: The numbers speak for themselves; I don’t have any great insights here. Erica Samuels: Each house has a different appetite for risk and adapts its strategy based on the specific estate or group of works. So I think comparing things side by side is tricky because it’s not apples to apples. While guaranteeing lots significantly affects outcome variations, there is clear demand right now for artists like Warhol (Flowers, Soup Can), Celmins, and Albers in postwar, as well as Tanguy, Kandinsky, and Monet in the modern. Danielle Forest Brandi: The IB market is relatively saturated at the moment, and there is a lot of competition. To be in the game, you need to be quick, decisive, and on the inside track. Collectors are clearly enjoying the ability to gain a competitive advantage through the IB mechanism, and it shapes behavior enormously. We find that collectors who don’t get the IB early on may not bid without it. That said, this season showed us that when the guarantees are set too high, it can take the energy out of the room and make it harder for works to inspire competitive bidding.
- The van Gogh Set A Record At $190.4 M., the Highest Price for a Work Sold This Season, Yet It Hammered Below Estimate After Only a Few Bids. How Are You Reading The Relationship Between Estimates and Bidding This Season? Evan Beard: Elevated estimates repel potential bids. Blaquier estimates crowded out potential bids. Most works get auctioned three times in a season: the auction between the houses for the material; the auction among potential guarantors; and, finally, the auction among the general public. The first two auctions erode the margin for the houses. Keeping estimates low while winning consignments is always a tricky dance. Liz Sterling: I think a lot of works found their market this season regardless of where the presale estimate was set. Where presale estimates were overly aggressive, the auction houses worked hard to match reserves to bids and get works sold. Conversely, works that were conservatively estimated, such as the Aaron Douglas and Edward Hopper at Sotheby’s, saw competition and achieved prices well in excess of their presale estimates. Nina del Rio: The markets for the high-profile works this season, which were largely European Impressionist and modern, and American Abstract Expressionist, are all relatively mature, and the top end of the artists’ prices have largely been realized. Couple this with full estimates (which the auction houses had to offer sellers to win the business) and it leaves little room for price discovery, even for the exceedingly rare Blaquier van Gogh. I believe this affected competition for the van Gogh, the entire Blaquier sale, and several other highlights across all the auction houses. However, I can’t help but wonder whether the last-minute claim on the van Gogh took other bidders out of the mix? Just a thought … and certainly not unique to me. Maria Brito: I think we’re reading too much into the number of bidders. In 2022, when the global art market reached its second-highest level in history, Orchard with Cypresses from the Paul Allen collection sold for $117.2 million with exactly three bidders. This week’s van Gogh also attracted three bidders, but fetched $190.4 million, more than 60 percent above the previous record. I consider Châtaigniers en fleurs a substantially better painting. Yes, it hammered at $165 million, below Sotheby’s $180 million expectation, but that doesn’t make the result disappointing. We also cannot ignore the Nazi-era provenance controversy, settled barely a day before the auction. Whether it deterred potential bidders is impossible to know. At this level of the market, buyers have extraordinary financial resources, but they still have their own ideas about value. Allan Schwartzman: It brought a huge price. There were few bids because the auction houses sometimes have to stretch to get headline material. Many works that are competitively offered sell on few bids because the auction houses have already conducted an auction between themselves to get those works. This does not necessarily reflect a thin market. Erica Samuels: I enjoy the philosophical roundabout of auction house estimates. There are different categories: the attractive, come-hither estimate; the punchy estimate; the estimate right in line with the market. It’s pretty nuanced, and you have to be careful about reading too much into them. An estimate is not a price tag. It’s a range, a suggestion. And to a certain extent, there’s a part of the auction world you only understand if you’re out there seeing a lot of things. Some artworks couldn’t sell privately, so they come to auction to try a broader audience. They may not find a buyer at any estimate. But let’s be honest, it’s quite thin at the top. $190 million is a lot of money for any buyer to spend. No wonder it sold to a very seasoned professional. Danielle Forest Brandi: The discrepancy between headline prices and estimates was a defining feature of the week. In recent years, the houses drove down estimates in an effort to revive competition, but it seems that pricing has crept back up. The thinness we saw with bidding was more indicative of these ambitious estimates than the market overall.
- The Modern Sales Produced the Week’s Biggest Prices, While Contemporary Results Were More Mixed. How Would You Describe the Contemporary Market Right Now, and What’s Driving Collectors’ Appetites There? Evan Beard: From 2020 to 2023, we were in a pretty intense risk-on speculation cycle where emerging contemporary was hot, so a lot of that material got flipped to auction. We’re in a risk-off cycle now. So very few emerging contemporary lots need to go to auction because they are easily accessible privately. The pendulum will swing back, albeit for a new group of hot young artists. Nina del Rio: There was a lot of American postwar and contemporary material on the market last week, but few really great, major examples in the auctions. Rothko, de Kooning, Richter, Frankenthaler, and Stella (among others) were well represented with fully priced seven- and eight-figure examples, but nothing outstanding or market-making vs. the great European material on offer. (It is worth noting that women artists from the same postwar period performed better, but were still uneven—Kusama and Agnes Martin in particular.) De Kooning and Rothko are interesting case studies. While de Kooning was well represented, especially by the 1975 oil from the Hedreen collection at Sotheby’s and the Whitney’s de Kooning at Christie’s, both were fully estimated, and neither had the potential to push the artist’s market. Four Rothko paintings on paper were offered last week; one very good example sold well above estimate, and the other three examples, which were arguably not as strong, sold below estimate or were unsold. Maria Brito: The contemporary market is suffering from serious fatigue. There are simply too many artists, too much work being produced, and too much material circulating. Collectors have become desensitized and increasingly skeptical, particularly after watching so many artists’ prices rise dramatically and then collapse. Compare that with Impressionism and modern art, where the universe of historically established artists is considerably smaller and the supply of important works is finite. There’s a level of scarcity and historical validation that gives buyers confidence. Contemporary art is a much more crowded field, and there’s simply not enough demand to support everyone at the prices we’ve become accustomed to seeing. Of course, exceptional artists and exceptional works will continue to command extraordinary prices, but collectors are increasingly questioning what’s genuinely worth pursuing. And I think that’s healthy. Allan Schwartzman: The fever for hot young artists at auction is over for now. This is for several reasons: prices for most young artists for whom there was hysterical (read: speculative) buying at auction could not and did not live up to such lofty numbers; a new generation of artists has not emerged for which the market has the same speculative appetite (and that’s a good thing); and sometimes the market for young artists is very different at auction than at the galleries that represent artists and develop those markets. Erica Samuels: Collectors are looking for historical depth far more than in previous seasons. A new wave of younger collectors is definitely entering the market. They are educated, critical thinkers who ask great questions, which makes for an exciting path forward. They want collections that move across generations of artists, not just one moment. Danielle Forest Brandi: With some exceptions, the contemporary offering across both houses this season felt a bit tired in [the] view [of myself and my colleagues at Beaumont Nathan], especially in comparison to the Impressionist and modern. The depth and cultural authority of blue-chip modernism seems to offer an assuring sense of solidity and substance that is perhaps universally needed right now. Of course, tastes change, the market moves on, and in time the contemporary world will come back as that market continues to recalibrate. But in the meantime, it seems to us that collectors are more interested in the past than the present.
- The Auction Houses Talk a Lot About Attracting Younger Collectors and New Wealth. Who Did You See Buying This Week? Evan Beard: Anyone who tells you that Gen Z is driving the art market in any meaningful way is either misinformed or trying to sell you a dream. The market is driven by a group of private equity, hedge fund, real estate, and tech entrepreneurs in their 50s and 60s. It’s the usual suspects. And each new year a few new big buyers enter the fray. New wealth grows up and ultimately buys art. But young collectors are not a major driver at auction at the moment. How many Gen Z collectors are on the ARTnews Top 200 collectors list? Or the Forbes 400 list? Or any list? Their day is coming, though. We’ve got some young risers we’re working with. Nina del Rio: I would be guessing if I had an answer to this question. Here’s what I know: buyer access to great quality primary market material, while still difficult and often reserved for museums, is less difficult than in the past. I believe the younger collectors are buying great material from galleries (as they should). There is less great material by living artists at auction, and the speculation in that auction market has quieted considerably. Maria Brito: I didn’t see clear evidence of a major generational shift this week, but the reality is that we rarely know who the ultimate buyers are. So much of the bidding happens through advisors, dealers, and telephone representatives. The auction houses know who’s behind those paddles. The rest of us are largely guessing. There’s certainly growing participation from younger collectors, but we should distinguish between buying a $20,000 print and bidding $100 million on a painting. Younger wealth is entering the market, but I haven’t seen compelling evidence from this week’s sales that it has fundamentally changed who’s buying at the very top. Allan Schwartzman: I was not in the room to observe live bidding. Danielle Forest Brandi: Impressionism was clearly the dominant category during the November sales, across different levels of the market. We are seeing a growing generation of collectors who are engaged with this area and other historical categories, seeking established blue-chip names or, the inverse, overlooked artists in history like the female Surrealists. Prices across many historical areas of the market have come down from where they once were, making accessible entry points for newer collectors who want to buy things that have substance and will hold up over time.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network sued the agency in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns.
The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel.
At a hearing early last month, AliKhan seemed skeptical of the FCC’s reasoning for the early renewal order.
In her ruling, the judge said that ABC is “likely to succeed on their first amendment claim” of retaliation.
In addition to granting ABC’s request for a preliminary injunction, the judge denied the FCC’s request to dismiss the case. But she also denied ABC’s request to prevent the FCC from taking “any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten plaintiffs with sanctions in an effort to alter their exercise of editorial discretion”.
In her ruling, the judge acknowledged the seriousness of the possible penalties facing ABC – and the chilling effect produced by an early license renewal order on a news organization’s first amendment rights. “Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face – loss of their broadcast licenses – the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness,” she wrote. “Any broadcaster of ordinary firmness – wealthy or not – would not hesitate to think twice if faced with such an existential threat to its business.”
The judge highlighted Trump’s long-standing animus against ABC as a clear factor in the FCC’s actions. “Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now,” she wrote, adding that the chairperson, Brendan Carr, “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders”.
As for the timing of the early renewal order request, coming soon after Trump’s criticism of Kimmel, the judge wrote: “Against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr’s call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.”
The judge also noted the odd timing of the early renewal order, coming more than a year after the FCC began investigating ABC. And she acknowledged as credible the network’s concern that the agency’s license review process could run indefinitely.
“The existence of other mechanisms to solicit public input, coupled with the untenable timeline, casts serious doubt on the argument that Defendants are using the early license renewal proceedings to enhance public participation,” she wrote. “All told, the ‘significant mismatch’ between Defendants’ decision to order the proceedings when they did and their stated rationale for doing so presents an air of pretext the court will not ignore.”
In a statement, an ABC News spokesperson said: “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration.”
Anna M Gomez, the lone FCC commissioner appointed by a Democratic president, also celebrated the judge’s ruling. “This decision shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights,” she said in a statement. “For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct. That brings badly needed accountability to a Commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control. Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I’ve said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side.”
“While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law – as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear,” a FCC spokesperson said in a statement. “The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Governo Sánchez anuncia pacote de medidas sociais às vésperas das eleições espanholas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Raissa Neves
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O governo da Espanha, liderado por Pedro Sánchez, anunciou nesta quarta-feira (25/11), Dia Internacional para a Eliminação da Violência contra as Mulheres, um conjunto de medidas sociais e de igualdade a quatro dias das eleições gerais de 29 de novembro. As iniciativas incluem mudanças nas licenças parentais, benefícios econômicos e novas regras relacionadas à interrupção voluntária da gravidez.
Uma das principais decisões amplia o período de licença remunerada após o nascimento de filhos. O benefício passará de 19 para 20 semanas para cada progenitor e de 32 para 34 semanas nas famílias monoparentais. A medida, segundo a ministra do Trabalho e segunda vice-presidente do governo, Yolanda Díaz, busca promover uma divisão mais equilibrada das responsabilidades familiares.
A desigualdade nesse campo também aparece no relatório “Estado da Paternidade na Espanha 2026”, elaborado pela Convive Fundación Cepaim. De acordo com o levantamento, 40% das mães deixaram de trabalhar para cuidar dos filhos, enquanto o percentual entre os pais é de 26%.
O pacote inclui ainda reduções tributárias para trabalhadores autônomos, a prorrogação do imposto extraordinário sobre os bancos e a diminuição pela metade da proporção de alunos por professor na educação infantil, destinada a crianças de zero a três anos.
Governo enfrenta disputa sobre direitos reprodutivos
Na área da saúde, uma nova regulamentação pretende uniformizar as informações clínicas e jurídicas oferecidas às mulheres que decidem interromper a gravidez. Apresentado pela ministra da Igualdade, Ana Redondo, o decreto também estabelece restrições à participação de médicos que tenham integrado registros de objetores de consciência nos últimos três anos em comitês clínicos regionais.
A iniciativa ocorre em meio a questionamentos sobre as diferenças de acesso ao aborto na rede pública entre as comunidades autônomas, apontadas em relatório do Ministério da Saúde.
Paralelamente, o governo central decidiu recorrer ao Tribunal Constitucional contra uma legislação da Comunidade de Madri, presidida por Isabel Díaz Ayuso. A norma condiciona determinados benefícios fiscais e o reconhecimento como família numerosa à continuidade da gravidez após a 14ª semana, além de exigir comunicação quando a gestação não chega ao fim.
Para o Executivo espanhol, as disposições ultrapassam as competências regionais e interferem na autonomia das mulheres.
Oposição critica pacote em meio à campanha eleitoral
A proximidade da votação transformou as medidas em mais um ponto de confronto entre governo e oposição. Em Barcelona, Sánchez pediu apoio ao Partido Socialista Operário Espanhol (PSOE) e criticou o Partido Popular (PP) e o Vox por questionarem a integridade do processo eleitoral.
O líder do PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, classificou os anúncios como uma tentativa de obter vantagens eleitorais e voltou a defender a extinção do Ministério da Igualdade. Já o Vox, de Santiago Abascal, manteve sua oposição às leis de combate à violência de gênero e se afastou das mobilizações do 25 de Novembro.
Enquanto os partidos disputam espaço na campanha, organizações feministas realizaram manifestações em Madri e em outras cidades espanholas para exigir políticas permanentes de enfrentamento à violência contra as mulheres. O país registra 47 mulheres assassinadas por parceiros ou ex-parceiros, segundo os dados apresentados no contexto das mobilizações.
A Frente Ampla e o Podemos também defenderam o fortalecimento das políticas de igualdade, com destaque para o combate à desigualdade salarial e para a ampliação do acesso aos serviços de cuidado. As manifestações reforçaram a cobrança para que a proteção dos direitos das mulheres, a “igualdade de gênero” e a garantia dos “direitos reprodutivos” não fiquem restritas ao calendário eleitoral.

https://taz.de/Smart-Glasses-Verbraucher.title: Nutzung von Smart Glasses: Klagen gegen Überwachungsbrillen
https://taz.de/Smart-Glasses-Verbraucher.author: Svenja Bergt
https://taz.de/Smart-Glasses-Verbraucher.text:
Nutzung von Smart Glasses: Klagen gegen Überwachungsbrillen
Verbraucherschützer:innen ziehen wegen Metas Smart Glasses vor Gericht. Risiken gebe es nicht nur für Menschen, die ungewollt gefilmt werden.
Mit zwei Klagen geht der Verbraucherzentrale Bundesverband gegen Smart Glasses vor. Die Organisation hat eigenen Angaben zufolge Klage eingereicht gegen das Unternehmen hinter der Marke Ray-Ban, Hersteller und Verkäufer von Metas Smart Glasses. Außerdem sei eine Klage gegen den IT-Konzern Meta selbst geplant.
Smart Glasses sind Brillen, die unter anderem Kamera und Lautsprecher eingebaut haben und mit dem Smartphone vernetzt sind. Wer sie trägt, kann zum Beispiel Musik hören, ohne Kopfhörer nutzen zu müssen. Wer sie trägt, kann aber auch unauffällig Bilder und Videos von der Umgebung aufnehmen. Zwar soll standardmäßig eine LED anzeigen, wenn die Aufnahmefunktion aktiviert ist. Diese ist aber nicht immer gut sichtbar. Zudem gibt es Berichte über erfolgreiche Manipulationen, die eine Aufnahme ohne leuchtende LED ermöglichen. Als Smart Glasses erkennbar sind die Brillen der aktuellen Generation nicht. Sie wirken wie handelsübliche Korrektur- oder Sonnenbrillen.
Die Verbraucherschützer:innen kritisieren nun: Ray-Ban und Meta würden beim Vertrieb ihrer Smart Glasses gegen Informationspflichten und Datenschutzvorschriften verstoßen. „Smart Glasses ermöglichen unbemerkte Bild- und Tonaufnahmen“, sagt Verbandsvorständin Ramona Pop. Für die aufgenommenen Personen sei kaum zu erkennen, ob und wie ihre Daten verarbeitet würden. Ein wenige Millimeter großes, weiß blinkendes Licht reiche nicht aus, um im öffentlichen Raum das Filmen oder Fotografieren zu signalisieren.
Die Vorwürfe im Einzelnen: Der Verbraucherzentrale Bundesverband (vzbv) wirft Ray-Ban eine Verletzung von Informationspflichten vor. Unter anderem würden Kund:innen nicht darüber informiert, dass sie die Brille im öffentlichen Raum nur mit Einschränkungen nutzen könnten, weil sie sonst gegen die Vorschriften der Datenschutz-Grundverordnung zu verstießen. So drohten den Nutzenden Bußgelder. Das kann zum Beispiel der Fall sein, wenn sie im öffentlichen Raum Dritte ohne Information und Einverständnis filmen.
Verstoß gegen Datenschutz
Bei Meta hält der vzbv die Werbeaussagen zu den Smart Glasses auf der Website für irreführend. Meta erwecke dort den Eindruck, dass alle beworbenen Funktionen der Brille ohne Weiteres im Alltag verwendet werden können. Das sei aber – siehe Datenschutz-Grundverordnung – nicht der Fall. Außerdem verstoße das Design der Brille gegen die Datenschutz-Vorgabe des „privacy by design“. Daraus lasse sich ableiten, dass die kleine, blinkende LED nicht ausreiche, um Betroffene transparent über das Filmen oder Fotografieren – was eine Erhebung personenbezogener Daten ist – zu informieren.
„Smart Glasses schaffen sowohl für Unbeteiligte als auch für Nutzerinnen und Nutzer erhebliche Datenschutzrisiken“, kritisiert Pop. Produkte müssten so gestaltet sei, dass Menschen sie datenschutzkonform nutzen könnten und die Rechte Dritter geschützt würden.
Meta verteidigt sein Produkt: Das LED-Licht könne nicht ausgeschaltet werden und die Kamera werde deaktiviert, wenn die Leuchte abgedeckt sei. „Das ist etwas, das Smartphones und andere Kameras nicht haben“, so ein Sprecher des Konzerns. EssilorLuxottica, das Unternehmen hinter der Marke Ray-Ban, teilte mit, man arbeite daran, „sicherzustellen, dass die Verbraucher verstehen, wie sie KI-Brillen respektvoll und unter Einhaltung der geltenden Gesetze und Vorschriften nutzen können“.
Die beiden Klagen sind nicht der erste Versuch, gegen die umstrittenen Brillen vorzugehen. Zwei Petitionen an die Regierung forderten unter anderem einen Vertriebsstopp für Geräte in heutiger Ausgestaltung und das Schließen von Schutzlücken für heimliche Aufnahmen. Die NGO Hate Aid hat darüber hinaus Strafanzeige gegen Meta, Ray-Ban und den weiteren Hersteller Oakley gestellt und auch gegen Optik- und Elektronikhandelsketten, die die Geräte vertreiben.
Die Hamburgische Datenschutzaufsichtsbehörde hatte bereits im September eine rechtliche Bewertung zu den Brillen veröffentlicht. Das Ergebnis: Das Filmen und Fotografieren von Menschen mit Smart Glasses von Meta sei in den meisten Fällen nicht erlaubt. Gerade in der Öffentlichkeit hätten die Gefilmten in der Praxis nicht die Möglichkeit, informiert in die Aufnahmen einzuwilligen.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.title: Berlin-Wahl | Vanessa Emde: Der Sturm zieht gerade erst auf
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.author: Marten Brehmer
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.text:
- Berlin
- Berlin-Wahl
Vanessa Emde: Der Sturm zieht gerade erst auf
Vanessa Emde ist aus der Linksfraktion im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus ausgeschlossen. Ein Ende des Streits um Nahost dürfte das kaum bedeuten.
Einen Vorgeschmack darauf, wie die nächsten Wochen in der Linken verlaufen werden, konnten Interessierte am Dienstagabend im Veranstaltungsraum »Casino« in Neukölln bekommen. »Der rot-grün-rote Senat soll vor uns zittern«, soll Hannah Bruns dort gesagt haben. Eingeladen hatte der Jugendverband Solid unter dem Titel »Palästina-Solidarität ist kein Verbrechen! Raus aus der Defensive!« Gekommen waren etwa 150 Menschen – nach einer ad-hoc-Umfrage in großer Mehrheit selbst Parteimitglieder.
Dass man den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde aus der Linksfraktion im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus nicht verhindern konnte, bezeichnete Bruns als »Klatsche«, die Vorwürfe gegen die Neuköllner Abgeordnete nannte sie eine »Verleumdungskampagne«. Gegen Bruns selbst läuft ein Parteiausschlussverfahren. Sie hatte sich in einem Fernsehinterview explizit nicht vom Terror der Hamas distanziert. Ihrer Motivation scheint der drohende Parteiausschluss wenig geschadet zu haben. »Wir dürfen uns auf keinen Fall ohnmächtig machen«, sagte sie bei der Veranstaltung, wie die »Morgenpost« dokumentierte.
Tatsächlich glaubt niemand in der Linken, dass der Dauerstreit um Nahost mit dem Rauswurf Emdes, den die Linksfraktion am Dienstagnachmittag mit Drei-Viertel-Mehrheit beschloss, enden wird. Schon allein, weil Emde weiter Parteimitglied bleiben wird. Ein Ausschlussverfahren wie bei Bruns ist für Emde nach nd-Informationen nicht geplant. Sie ist auch weiterhin eine der rund 150 Delegierten zum Landesparteitag – auch wenn sie selbst zuletzt vorzog, vor dem Tagungssaal zu demonstrieren, statt sich drin an den Beratungen zu beteiligen.
Nach ihrem Fraktionsausschluss gab sich auch Emde kämpferisch. »Ihr seid nicht allein, wir sind nicht allein – und wir werden uns organisieren«, sagte sie im Abgeordnetenhaus. Emde rief propalästinensische Linke auf, weiter Mitglied der Linkspartei zu bleiben. In zahlreichen Medien war zuletzt spekuliert worden, der radikal palästinasolidarische Flügel der Linken könnte zu der kleinen Partei Mera 25 oder zum BSW übertreten, in denen antizionistische Positionen Parteilinie sind. Hand und Fuß hat das allerdings nicht. Das wäre für die Parteiführung »ein Geschenk«, sagte Linksjugend-Vertreterin Chiara Stenger bei der Veranstaltung in Neukölln.
Auch außerhalb des Jugendverbands gibt es nicht wenige Genossen, die ähnlich ticken wie Emde. »Ihr Ausschluss folgt auf eine wochenlange Kampagne, in der falsche Antisemitismusvorwürfe instrumentalisiert wurden, auch um das palästinasolidarische Profil der Partei zu schwächen«, reagierte der Neuköllner Linke-Bezirksvorsitzende Hermann Nehls auf Emdes Ausschluss aus der Fraktion.
Mit dieser Position steht er nicht allein da. Auch in den Bezirksverbänden Mitte und Tempelhof-Schöneberg gibt es relativ starke Strömungen, die wenig Problematisches daran finden, Israel das Existenzrecht abzusprechen. In der Abgeordnetenhausfraktion stimmten sechs Abgeordnete gegen Emdes Ausschluss, vier enthielten sich. Die prominenteste Fürsprecherin hatte Emde in Vizefraktionschefin Martha Kleedörfer.
Angesichts dieser Lage änderten Fraktions- und Landesspitzen der Partei zuletzt merklich ihre Argumentation. »Die Vorwürfe, dass das Eintreten für eine Ein-Staaten-Lösung per se antisemitisch sei, weisen wir entschieden zurück. Diese Diskussion wird auch in Teilen der israelischen Linken und international geführt«, heißt es in einer Erklärung, die der Fraktionsvorstand nach der Sitzung am Dienstag versandte. Man sei »eine Partei der Palästina-Solidarität«.
Stattdessen stellte man Emdes Verhalten in den Vordergrund. Sie habe sich »jeder konstruktiven Zusammenarbeit in der Fraktion verweigert«. Man habe den Dialog gesucht, sei jedoch auf eine Verweigerungshaltung gestoßen. Die Bundesvorsitzende Ines Schwerdtner warf Emde zuletzt öffentlichkeitswirksam eine »Ego-Show« vor, um sie im nächsten Satz inhaltlich in Schutz zu nehmen. Auch in der Sitzung der Linksfraktion soll Kritik an Emdes Verhalten inhaltliche Fragen überschattet haben, wie Abgeordnete berichten.
Eine »Brücke« nennt ein Fraktionsmitglied das. Denn über die Kritik an Emdes Unzuverlässigkeit habe man sich einfacher einig werden können als über gemeinsame Position zur Nahost-Frage. Auch innerparteilich hofft man, die Wogen so zumindest bis zum Abschluss der Koalitionsverhandlungen glätten zu können.
Ob das gelingt, ist allerdings mehr als zweifelhaft. Die Landesarbeitsgemeinschaft Palästina-Solidarität organisiert in Berlin eine dreistellige Zahl von Mitgliedern, die über Chatgruppen eng vernetzt sind. Die Gruppe könnte das nutzen, um gezielt zu Parteiveranstaltungen und Gremiensitzungen zu mobilisieren. Der Fraktionsausschluss Emdes könnte für die Aktivitäten der Gruppe sogar förderlich sein.
Seit Abschluss des Waffenstillstands in Nahost im Oktober 2025 hat das Thema deutlich an öffentlicher Aufmerksamkeit verloren, auch die Mobilisierung auf der Straße ließ merklich nach. Dass die Palästina-Aktivisten mit Emde nun eine Märtyrerin gefunden haben, könnte ihnen neuen Schub verleihen.
Zugleich dürfte der Ausschluss Emdes kaum ein Ende der Anschuldigungen gegen die Linkspartei bedeuten. »Der Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde aus der Links-Fraktion ist nicht mehr als Symbolik, um die Koalitionsverhandlungen und damit die eigenen Machtperspektiven zu retten«, wird Cerstin Richter-Kotowski, Vorsitzende der Deutsch-Israelischen Gesellschaft Berlin-Brandenburg, in einer Pressemitteilung zitiert. Der Linkspartei gehörten weiter zahlreiche führende Funktionäre an, die »Hass« verbreiteten. Noch weiter ging Stephan Weh, Vorsitzender der Polizeigewerkschaft GdP, der davor warnte, mit einem Senat unter Linke-Führung würden »extrem einsatzbelastende Versammlungslagen mit Hass und Hetze auf unseren Straßen zunehmen«, wie es in einer Pressemitteilung heißt.
Mitglied der Linksfraktion ist Emde nicht mehr, im Landesparlament bleibt sie aber weiter. Während ihr Ausschluss bedeutet, dass sie die Ressourcen der Fraktion nicht mehr nutzen kann und auch in keinen Ausschüssen mehr Mitglied werden kann, hat er für sie auch Vorteile. Zehn Minuten Redezeit stehen fraktionslosen Abgeordneten pro Sitzung zu. Als Mitglied der Linksfraktion war ihr ein Auftritt vor dem Abgeordnetenhausplenum bislang verwehrt geblieben. Zuletzt hatte Emde versucht, sich neben der Palästinafrage auch als kritische Stimme in der Debatte um die Enteignung großer Wohnungskonzerne zu profilieren. Die Linke musste hier im Rahmen der Sondierungen zahlreiche Kompromisse eingehen. Bereits am Donnerstag könnte Emde bei der Sitzung des Abgeordnetenhauses erstmals das Wort ergreifen.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.
