It said that the disparity in this treatment is, in itself, antisemitic.
“Ignoring the many Jews who do not conform with the established narrative of universal support for Israel and Zionism is a position that is itself antisemitic, as it generalises about Jews, reduces them to stereotypes, denies them individuality and agency, and may even endanger their safety, by suggesting that they all support Israel's genocidal actions in Palestine,” the group said.
They said that the letter follows six months of “unsatisfactory correspondence”, which began in May.
That was when some 40 descendants of Holocaust survivors wrote to then Prime Minister Keir Starmer, the Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mark Rowley refuting allegations that pro-Palestine protests presented a threat to the Jewish community.
“Six weeks later, a junior minister for policing sent us a really anodyne letter just stating government policy,” Romberg told Middle East Eye.
“We had made the point that the only hostility that we actually face on these protests comes from Zionist counter-protesters,’ he said.
“And the letter we got back said, 'Oh, very sorry that you've had this aggression,' but seemed to imply no recognition at all that it was from the counter-protesters."
The group then wrote to incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham and said that, since then, they have received three letters from the two ministers which they described as being “dismissive in tone” and containing “generalised statements of government policy, much of it irrelevant to the issues we raised”.
They said that the ministers were slow to respond, with one taking two months to reply.
A government spokesperson told MEE in response to a request for comment that they "regularly engage with a wide range of organisations to discuss their concerns and remain committed to working with our Jewish communities".
‘We haven’t even had an acknowledgement’
Last month, the group received a letter from Jones saying that “this government recognises the diversity of our Jewish communities” and expressing commitment to “meaningful engagement with a range of different voices and perspectives”.
“We thought, good, that's healthy. Let's follow that up,” Romberg, a retired British Army colonel, said. “We're not getting anywhere with these letters. We had been waiting six months with all this, so we asked if we could have a meeting in two weeks.”
But the letter went unanswered.
“It's now been four weeks, and we haven’t even had an acknowledgement,” Romberg said.
The statement noted the “complete contrast” in the government’s attitude to pro-Israel groups, saying that they were not aware of either Burnham or his predecessor holding a single meeting with Jewish pro-Palestine or anti-Zionist organisations.
“The approach the government is taking is actually an approach that is itself in danger of being antisemitic,” Romberg told MEE.
'The approach the government is taking is actually an approach that is itself in danger of being antisemitic'
- Chris Romberg, Holocaust survivor descendant
“They seem to want to ignore Jewish groups that do not fit in with their stereotypical view of what Jews should be. That Jews should support Israel. Jews should be pro-Zionist. And when there are groups that do not fit into that narrative, then they just want to ignore them and won't engage with them.”
MEE is aware of numerous meetings in the last 12 months between government ministers and the Board of Deputies of British Jews, the Jewish Leadership Council - both of whom intervened in the appeal of the government's ban on direct action group Palestine Action - and the Community Security Trust.
In the months before the proscription of Palestine Action, Met chief Rowley met with the Jewish Board of Deputies on 6 November 2024 to discuss a series of actions by the group.
A government spokesperson said that: "As the Court of Appeal found, Palestine Action is not a civil disobedience protest group but one that carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence."
Declassified has revealed that a number of meetings between ministers and pro-Israel lobbyists were unminuted, including an off-the-record meeting between then Foreign Minister David Lammy and pro-Israeli businessman Trevor Chinn in February 2025.
Another meeting between Middle East Minister Hamish Falconer and Chinn a month later was also not recorded in transparency data.
Romberg said he had “very low expectations” that things would shift under Burnham’s government, despite the prime minister’s admission that his party “got it wrong on Gaza” and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s imposition of sanctions on settlements.
“I feel this is deflectionary. This is a recognition of electoral pressures. Words are easy,” Romberg said.
“There’s been a lot of clucking, but there haven't actually been any eggs laid,” he added.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.title: Rechte Wissenschaftspolitik | Moralapostel
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.author: Tanja Röckemann
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.text:
- Kultur
- Rechte Wissenschaftspolitik
Moralapostel
Die USA und Italien haben ein Forschungsabkommen unterzeichnet. Es ist ein Musterbeispiel für rechte Staatsräson in den Geisteswissenschaften
Was haben die USA und Italien gemeinsam? Richtig: eine rechtsradikale Regierung! Ganz folgerichtig also verkündeten beide Staaten jüngst die Unterzeichnung einer Kooperation zur »Förderung von Forschung und internationalem Austausch zwischen Institutionen und Wissenschaftlern in den Geisteswissenschaften«. (Ich gendere hier mit Absicht nicht, denn das wäre, wie sich gleich zeigen wird, gänzlich irreführend.)
Unterzeichnet wurde das Abkommen von Michael McDonald, von Trump ernannter Vorsitzender des »National Endowment for the Humanities« und Andrea Lenzi, Präsident des italienischen »Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche« – im Anschluss an eine laut »New York Times« skandalös teure und verdächtig geheim gehaltene Konferenz in einem römischen Palazzo. Tatsächlich könnte nichts die geistigen Gefilde besser verdeutlichen, in denen sich die Wissenschaftspolitik dieser beiden Staaten derzeit bewegt als die Veranstaltung mit dem Titel »Moralische Autorität und ihre klassischen Grundlagen«.
Zunächst einmal muss herausgestellt werden, dass es sich hierbei um eine absolut männerdominierte Konferenz handelte; die einzige Ausnahme unter 29 Redebeiträgen bildete die Juristin Margherita Cassano, bis vergangene Woche Präsidentin des Corte Suprema di Cassazione, des Obersten Gerichts Italiens. Die Redner der Konferenz sind, Cassano eingeschlossen, mindestens Apologeten, teils wichtige Stichwortgeber und definitiv Profiteure einer offen rassistischen, misogynen, trans- und behindertenfeindlichen sowie naturzerstörenden Regierungspolitik, die also stark zum Faschismus tendiert, der menschenfeindlichsten Herrschaftsform überhaupt. Dabei versammeln sich diese Akademiker keineswegs mit einem »Der Mensch ist dem Menschen ein Wolf«-Vibe, sondern als moralische Autoritäten.
Ein Widerspruch? Nicht wirklich. Das Römische Reich, das hier als »klassische Grundlage« dient, war eine Sklavenhaltergesellschaft; ein imperialistisches Kolonialreich; ein Patriarchat; eine ausbeuterische Macht gegenüber Mensch und Natur. Und das Römische Reich hatte demokratische Elemente. Es gab einen Senat, eine Volksversammlung, es gab das Wahlrecht für männliche Bürger. Alles in allem also kein Wunder, dass weiße rechte Männer von heute das römische Imperium und dessen Moral als Musterbeispiel für ihr eigenes Herrschaftsprojekt heranziehen.
Dass dies Wissenschaft sein soll, ist natürlich absurd. Das Geschäft dieser Männer ist nicht die ergebnisoffene Erforschung der Realität, die angesichts der unvernünftig eingerichteten Verhältnisse auf Darstellung als Kritik hinausläuft. Sondern es geht ihnen um normative, politisch motivierte Setzungen. Der größere Kontext, in dem das US-italienische Forschungsabkommen steht, ist entsprechend sowohl in den USA als auch in Italien die ausgesprochene Wissenschaftsfeindlichkeit der rechtsradikalen Regierungen. Ihnen sind die Geisteswissenschaften tendenziell am verdächtigsten – es sei denn natürlich, hier bleiben männliche Moralautoritäten unter sich.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: FIFA says personal and business information stolen in cyberattack
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
FIFA says personal and business information stolen in cyberattack
FIFA sources say no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed.
FIFA said it had been the victim of a criminal cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information, although no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed, according to media reports.
“FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information,” a FIFA spokesperson told the Reuters news agency.
FIFA strongly condemned the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data, adding that such actions were “a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy”.
FIFA did not say how many people or organisations were affected, when the attack took place or what the business information included. Its reference to publication did not say whether any data had appeared online, or where.
Al Jazeera has reached out to FIFA for comment.
Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked.
The person with knowledge of the matter told Reuters that less than 0.1 percent of the total data held by world football’s governing body was affected.
A FIFA source told The Athletic that the person – or group – responsible for carrying out the cyberattack gained access by impersonating staff rather than a systems or technical failure.
FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in July that his organisation had scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors following a widespread backlash.
The plan ‌involved raising up to $4.2bn by selling a 20 percent stake in a new unit that would run FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup.

https://taz.de/Parlamentswahl-in-Spanien.author: Reiner Wandler
https://taz.de/Parlamentswahl-in-Spanien.text:
Parlamentswahl in Spanien: Rechter Wahlkampf auf Antimigrationskurs
VOX und Partido Popular machen Migranten für alle Probleme im Wohnungs-, Gesundheits- und Bildungswesen verantwortlich. Die Sozialisten lassen sich nicht darauf ein.
Wer hat schuld am völlig überteuerten Wohnungsmarkt in Spanien? Die Immigranten. Wer überfordert das Gesundheitssystem? Nein, nicht die Sparpolitik und die Privatisierung, sondern die Immigranten. Warum ist das Schulsystem in Nöten? Wegen mangelnder Finanzierung durch die Regionen? Nein, wegen der Immigranten. So einfach ist dies zumindest für Spaniens Rechte, die darauf hofft, bei den Parlamentswahlen am Sonntag an die Macht zu kommen.
Die Immigration ist für die rechtsextreme VOX das Grundübel schlechthin – und die konservative Partido Popular (PP) zieht nach. Die einen wollen nicht nur die Grenzen schließen, wenn es sein muss, mit Armee und Marine, sondern im Zweifel auch fünf bis acht Millionen „remigrieren“, also aus dem Land verweisen. Die anderen reden davon, Immigranten aus den sozialen Absicherungen auszuschließen, wenn sie nicht arbeiten. In den Regionen und Gemeinden, in denen PP und VOX bereits gemeinsam regieren, schreiben sie bei Sozialmaßnahmen fest, Menschen mit spanischem Pass zu priorisieren. Die Zahlen, die PP und VOX in der Immigrationsdebatte nutzen, sind fast immer völlig überzogen. Das Ziel: mitten im Wahlkampf ein Problem zu schaffen, das es eigentlich nicht gibt.
Dabei ist in der öffentlichen Wahrnehmung fast vergessen, was im Juli noch die Schlagzeilen beherrschte: Damals umschwammen mindestens 70.000 Menschen aus Marokko die Grenze bei Ceuta, was zu einer Krise hochstilisiert wurde. Der Verdacht liegt allerdings nahe, dass die Menschen, die nach Ceuta kamen, von ausländischen Akteuren aufgestachelt wurden, um Sanchez unter Druck zu setzen. Spanische Behörden ermitteln entsprechend.
Die neuen Massenankünfte auf der kanarischen Insel El Hierro, wo allein im November über 12.000 Menschen in Booten ankamen – diesen Dienstag waren es über 2000 –, haben weniger öffentliches Echo als die Krise in Ceuta. Unter anderem wohl deshalb, weil die Regierung schneller reagiert und die Ankommenden auf andere Inseln umverteilt. Und weil die Inselregierung von El Hierro weitaus weniger populistisch ist als die in Ceuta. Auf El Hierro wird die Ankunft der Immigranten in erster Linie als das gesehen, was sie ist, als humanitäre Katastrophe.
Eine Million Migranten legalisiert
Spanien hat unter der Koalitionsregierung des Sozialisten Pedro Sánchez rund eine Million Immigranten legalisiert. Die lebten bereits in Spanien und hatten Jobs; allerdings keine Papiere und damit auch keine Rechte oder soziale Absicherung. Der Rechten gefällt das nicht.
Doch die Sozialisten lassen sich auf die Debatte nicht ein. Ein Großteil der linken Wählerschaft ist sich mit Sánchez einig, dass alle Menschen, egal woher sie kommen, in Spanien gerecht behandelt gehören. Sánchez betont immer wieder, dass Spanien die Immigration aus „demografischen und wirtschaftlichen Gründen“ braucht. Das Land wäre sonst überaltert, der Arbeitsmarkt hätte nicht genug Arbeitskräfte vor allem in der Landwirtschaft, der Gastronomie, auf dem Bau und bei der Pflege.
Der Grund für das spanische Wirtschaftswachstum, das deutlich über EU-Schnitt liegt, ist die liberale Immigrationspolitik. Das vermeintliche Problem mit der Immigration wird dadurch zum Diskurs, der vor allem innerhalb der Rechten dazu dient, zu beweisen, wer der bessere Patriot ist.

Abgeordnete fordern besseren Schutz von Prostituierten
Nach Vorschlägen einer Expertenkommission zur Prostitution fordern Unionspolitiker ein Verbot des Sexkaufs. Die Grünen sprechen sich dagegen aus.
Berlin. Nach der Vorlage der Expertenempfehlungen zur Reform des Prostitutionsgesetzes haben Bundestagsabgeordnete mehrerer Parteien noch weiter gehende Maßnahmen gefordert. »Einzelne Nachbesserungen reichen nicht aus: Wir brauchen einen echten Kurswechsel im Prostitutionsrecht«, sagte der Justiziar der Unionsfraktion im Bundestag, Martin Plum (CDU), der »Rheinischen Post«. Der Kauf sexueller Dienstleistungen müsse »grundsätzlich unter Strafe gestellt werden«.
Als Vorbild verwies Plum auf die Regelungen zum Sexkaufverbot in nordischen Ländern wie Schweden. Das »Nordische Modell« sei »der richtige Weg«, sagte der CDU-Politiker. »Ein Ja zur sexuellen Selbstbestimmung heißt auch ein Ja zum Sexkaufverbot.«
Die stellvertretende Vorsitzende der Grünen-Bundestagsfraktion, Misbah Khan, sprach sich wiederum gegen ein Sexkaufverbot aus. »Das Nordische Modell birgt die Gefahr, Strukturen zu verfestigen, die Ausbeutung, Menschenhandel und Gewalt begünstigen, anstatt die Situation in der Sexarbeit nachhaltig zu verbessern«, sagte sie der Zeitung.
Khan forderte zugleich: »Freier müssen stärker in die Verantwortung genommen werden.« Eine mögliche Maßnahme wäre eine Registrierungspflicht für Freier. »Sie könnte dazu beitragen, das Verantwortungsbewusstsein zu stärken und Prävention wirksamer zu gestalten«, sagte Khan.
Die am Mittwoch vorgestellten Vorschläge der Expertenkommission sehen kein Sexkaufverbot wie in Norwegen oder Schweden vor. Auch eine Registrierungspflicht für Freier gehört nicht zu den Empfehlungen. Vorgesehen sind allerdings Sanktionen gegen Freier, die sexuelle Dienstleistungen von nicht offiziell angemeldeten Prostituierten in Anspruch nehmen. AFP/nd

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Suit alleges Louisiana land deal between SpaceX and ExxonMobil violates open meetings law
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sara Sneath in New Orleans
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
After ending a lawsuit over ExxonMobil’s damage to wetlands, Louisiana officials moved quickly to approve a deal giving SpaceX access to 125,000 acres (50,600 hectares) of marsh formerly owned by the oil company. A new lawsuit now alleges they did so in violation of the state’s open meetings law.
The lawsuit, filed by three south-central Louisiana residents, follows state and Vermilion parish officials’ approval of what is estimated to be a record $27.5bn tax incentive package for SpaceX’s Starbase Louisiana project, announced over the summer. The officials violated the state’s open meetings law eight times while facilitating the agreement in attempts to “keep the public in the dark about what they are doing for SpaceX”, the lawsuit alleges.
Prior to working on the tax abatement for SpaceX, the Vermilion parish industrial development board had not been active for nearly three decades. But in July 2026, the Vermilion parish police jury appointed seven members to the board without advance notice at the same meeting where they approved the ExxonMobil settlement, which wasn’t on the meeting agenda either, according to the lawsuit. The police jury’s legal counsel, Paul Moresi, told WWL Louisiana that the officials deny the allegations in the lawsuit and followed the requirements of the state’s open meetings law.
The governor’s office then collected all copies of the settlement agreement with ExxonMobil, the details of which still remain unclear, said New Orleans attorney William Most.
“The Vermilion parish government has been violating transparency laws in totally new and unprecedented ways including using code names in public agendas and making sure they don’t keep copies of the contracts they sign so their constituents can’t read them,” Most said. “Transparency is so important because it helps prevent the state from making the same mistakes of the past and letting out-of-state corporations take our resources and hurt our citizens.”
Jackson Voss, the government affairs and policy coordinator for the Alliance for Affordable Energy, said there’s still much unknown about the deals, making it harder to know what the state is getting in return for the loss of tax revenue and potentially further damage to wetlands.
“I think that what we’ve done with this deal is subsidise both ExxonMobil and SpaceX. We’re helping two of the biggest corporations in the world to make even more money than they’re already making,” he said.
SpaceX has told locals that 30 rockets per day could be launched from the spaceport’s 10 launch pads, or about 10,000 launches per year.
Last month, a public research university in the area also entered into an agreement with SpaceX, which would allow the company to further expand the footprint of its 125,000-acre spaceport in the coastal marshlands of Vermilion parish. The University of Louisiana System Board approved the lease of five acres of UL Lafayette property to a non-profit called Ragin’ Cajun Facilities for $1 per year, as well as a sublease agreement to Space Exploration Technologies, or SpaceX.
Local residents have raised concerns about the launch site’s potential to disrupt migratory bird habitat on the cheniere surrounded by fast-eroding marshland. The lawsuit settled by ExxonMobil this summer alleged that the company was partly responsible for the severe land loss in the parish through decades of drilling activities.
Louisiana is experiencing some of the highest rates of relative sea level rise in the world, alongside alarming rates of wetland loss, estimated as a football field every 100 minutes. While the levying of the lower Mississippi River has contributed to much of the land loss in the bayou state, in Vermilion parish, wetland loss was largely caused by oil and gas activities, said coastal researcher Alex Kolker, the director of the Coastal Climates Institute.
“It’s a little different from other parts of Louisiana because you never had much of a river input,” he said. “Changes in hydrology of the Mississippi River weren’t as impactful.”
While SpaceX’s lease agreement with UL Lafayette does not say the company will launch rockets from the site, it does include a wide range of permitted uses, such as training and workforce development, warehousing and assembly, and “testing and light industrial operations”. In exchange, SpaceX agreed to invest $10m in planned improvements to the site, which was donated to the university last year for a wildlife and coastal preservation center.
Voss, with the Alliance for Affordable Energy, said that the university, as well as those responsible for the SpaceX tax deal, are making a lot of bets, without any real guarantees.
“We’re going out of our way to make sure that whatever deal is reached is the best possible for industry no matter how much it costs everyone else,” he said. “It really is like a fire sale: get what you can before it’s too late.”

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/plfss/.title: Budget de la Sécurité Sociale : députés et sénateurs échouent à s’entendre, le texte revient à l’Assemblée
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/plfss/.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/plfss/.text:
Sept députés et sept sénateurs se sont réunis, ce 26 novembre au matin, en commission mixte paritaire (CMP) pour tenter de trouver un compromis sur ce texte. Mais les points de vue se sont révélés inconciliables, et ce premier conclave budgétaire de la saison a rapidement été déclaré non conclusif.
Députés et sénateurs ont échoué, ce 26 novembre, à s’entendre en commission mixte paritaire sur le projet de budget de la Sécurité sociale pour 2027, renvoyant ainsi le texte en nouvelle lecture à l’Assemblée nationale. Le premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu avait tardivement proposé le 23 novembre, dans un courrier, des thèmes de compromis possibles, et annoncé qu’il recevrait la semaine suivante les présidents des groupes parlementaires.
Parmi les points d’achoppement, la suspension de la réforme des retraites de 2023 que le Sénat, dominé par la droite et les centristes, souhaitait rétablir dès 2027. Le projet gouvernemental, qui prévoit d’importants efforts notamment sur les dépenses de santé et les retraités, entend ramener à 12,7 milliards le déficit de la Sécurité sociale en 2027, contre 21,8 milliards en 2026. Il propose notamment la désindexation de deux tiers des pensions de retraite, normalement indexées sur l’inflation.
Le texte va revenir maintenant en nouvelle lecture à l’Assemblée dès la semaine prochaine en commission des Affaires sociales. Son arrivée dans l’hémicycle sera ensuite fixée à la semaine du 7 décembre, selon le ministère des Relations avec le Parlement.
Privé de majorité le gouvernement pourrait utiliser le 49.3, en espérant échapper à une censure. Il pourrait aussi choisir la voie des ordonnances, un dispositif inédit qui évite tout vote au Parlement, mais lui impose a priori d’en rester à la copie initiale du texte. Le délai constitutionnel de 50 jours au-delà duquel le gouvernement peut mettre en œuvre cet outil expire ce jeudi 26 novembre 2026 concernant le projet de budget de la Sécu.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles

Space X darf eine Million Satelliten ins All schicken
US-Behörden genehmigen Vorstoß von Tech-Unternehmer Elon Musk für Aufbau von Rechenzentren im Weltall. Doch es gibt technische Hürden.
Washington. Das Raumfahrtunternehmen SpaceX des Milliardärs Elon Musk darf bis zu einer Million Satelliten zur Errichtung von Weltraum-Rechenzentren für KI-Anwendungen in den Erdorbit schicken. Die US-Regulierungsbehörde FCC erteilte dem Space-X-Projekt »Starmind« laut einer Mitteilung vom Mittwoch eine entsprechende Genehmigung, die bis 2040 gilt. Musk hatte im August angekündigt, die ersten Satelliten im vierten Quartal 2027 ins All zu bringen und die Starts 2028 auszuweiten.
Die Satelliten sollen in einer niedrigen Erdumlaufbahn in geringem Abstand zueinander positioniert werden, um eine zuverlässige Datenübertragung untereinander zu ermöglichen. Sie sollen über die bereits im All befindlichen Satelliten des Space-X-Internetdienstes Starlink Daten zur Erde übertragen. Der US-Chiphersteller Nvidia soll eigens für den Einsatz im Weltraum konzipierte Prozessoren der neuesten Generation liefern.
Musk hatte im Februar für den Aufbau von Rechenzentren im All seine KI-Firma X AI und Space X zusammengelegt. Der wachsende Energiebedarf für künstliche Intelligenz (KI) könne auf der Erde nicht ohne Belastungen für Menschen und Umwelt gedeckt werden, argumentierte Musk damals.
Ein Vorteil von Rechenzentren im All ist die Möglichkeit, Sonnenenergie kontinuierlich zu nutzen. In einer geeigneten sonnensynchronen Umlaufbahn können Solarzellen nach Berechnungen von Google bis zu achtmal so viel Energie liefern wie auf der Erde. Allerdings sind noch nicht alle technischen Probleme gelöst. So müssen die Prozessoren der hohen Strahlenbelastung im All standhalten. Weitere Herausforderungen sind extreme Temperaturen und mögliche Schäden durch Weltraumschrott und Mikrometeoriten.
Auch andere Unternehmen arbeiten am Aufbau von Rechenzentren im Weltall, darunter der US-Internetkonzern Google und das Raumfahrtunternehmen Blue Origin von Amazon-Gründer Jeff Bezos. Dem Start-up Starcloud gelang es bereits Ende vergangenen Jahres, einen leistungsfähigen Grafikprozessor (GPU) an Bord eines Satelliten zu betreiben. Google gelang dies im Oktober. Agenturen/nd

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: ‘Symbolic’: Why did UK sanction Yemen’s Houthis amid attacks on Saudi?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
‘Symbolic’: Why did UK sanction Yemen’s Houthis amid attacks on Saudi?
UK sanctions Iran-backed group and its leaders, accusing them of undermining stability in the Middle East.
London, United Kingdom – The United Kingdom has slapped sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis and four of their senior leaders after accusing the Iran-backed group of renewed “aggression” inside Yemen and attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting the financial district in Riyadh this week, as they engage in a civil war with Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Fighting has escalated since July as a 2022 United Nations-brokered ceasefire collapsed. Since then, the Houthis have captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and the island of Mayyun, extending control over the Red Sea in a setback to the Saudi-backed government.
The war erupted after the Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, in late 2014, forcing President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the Hadi government as it saw the Iran-backed group’s rise in neighbouring Yemen as a security threat.
The UK government announced its sanctions on Tuesday, accusing the Houthis of undermining peace and security in Yemen and the region. It froze assets and placed travel bans on the group and its leaders, including Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi and Security and Intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani.
Chief prosecutor Sarim al-Din Mufadal, who has been accused of perpetrating “sexual violence, including rape and torture”, also faces an asset freeze and travel ban.
UK’s interests in the Middle East
“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable, and they must be held to account,” said UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who linked the sanctions to attacks on shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea, one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.
“Today’s measures send a clear message to the Houthis – we will always act in support of British values and interests,” he said in a statement.
The British move comes nearly a month after it decided to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia, a close ally going back decades that has increasingly come under missile and drone attacks in recent weeks.
Britain also sent Tornado fighters to Saudi Arabia in the wake of the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in 1990, according to the Royal Air Force Museum.
The Houthis have also targeted oil installations and a major pipeline that helped Saudi Arabia export its oil while Iran essentially blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint. Tehran said it has blocked the vital waterway, through which most of the Gulf oil and natural gas passes, in response to the US-Israel war on Iran.
The UK has naval and logistics bases in the neighbouring Gulf nations of Bahrain and Oman. In May, it agreed a free trade deal with the six Gulf Cooperation Council states.
‘To turn the screw on the Houthis’
Thomas Juneau, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, said the sanctions were imposed during a diplomatic push by Riyadh.
“Saudi Arabia has been asking other countries to list the Houthis as a terrorist entity, to turn the screw on the Houthis and to help in its campaign against the group,” he told Al Jazeera.
The sanctions, Ahmed Nagi from the International Crisis Group (ICG) said, are “intended to send a political message about where the UK stands on the current escalation and the Houthi actions”.
In January 2024, the UK and the United States jointly sanctioned four Houthi figures, including the group’s defence minister and naval commander, over attacks on Red Sea shipping, and a month later, a second package targeted the Quds Force, the overseas unit of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The same month, the UK joined the US in carrying out air strikes on Houthi positions over attacks on ships in the Red Sea, which had disrupted maritime trade. The Houthis had imposed a ban on ships linked to Israel from passing through the waterway in response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The Houthis are already under a UN arms embargo, and London is now “going further”, Nagi, who is a senior Yemen analyst at the ICG, said.
This month, the UN Security Council renewed its Yemen sanctions regime until November 2027 through a UK-led resolution.
Raiman al-Hamdani, a Yemeni researcher and analyst, said the UK, as the Security Council’s lead on Yemen, had helped shape that regime and “this latest step continues a longstanding policy rather than breaking from it.”
‘Largely symbolic’
But Nagi called the UK move “largely symbolic”.
“The four Houthi leaders targeted by the sanctions are unlikely to travel to the UK or hold assets there, so the practical impact will probably be limited.”
Al-Hamdani said the group’s income comes “largely from the black market, smuggling, taxation of local businesses and control of ports and customs, none of which a UK asset freeze touches”.
“The missile and drone programme hasn’t slowed despite years of UN, US, EU and UK listings,” he added.
Juneau from Chatham House agreed the sanctions would not change Houthi behaviour soon but said that while sanctions by individual countries other than the US have little effect alone, they can matter collectively, which is why Saudi Arabia is pressing as many countries as possible to act.
He also pointed to the Houthis’ growing influence in the Red Sea, which has concerned Saudi Arabia as well as its Western allies.
The British foreign secretary on Tuesday pointed out how Houthi actions in the Red Sea were “driving up the cost of living for the British people” and “undermining the stability of the Middle East”.
Analysts pointed out that the UK government statement is silent on the other parties to the war – the Yemeni government forces and Saudi Arabia – even as it said the Houthis’ “reckless aggression is responsible for this conflict”.
Nagi said the omission reflected how London sees the war.
“From London’s perspective, the Houthis are the ones attacking Saudi Arabia and escalating the conflict, rather than the other way around,” he said.
Juneau was blunter. “Sanctions are always political. You sanction your opponents. You don’t sanction your partners or friends,” he said.
Humanitarian concerns
Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressed concerns that the sanctions would impact aid organisations engaged in humanitarian work in Houthi-held areas.
“As Yemen relies heavily on imports, curbs affecting commercial goods could also push up food prices,” she told Al Jazeera.
“The sanctions really can have quite devastating impacts for the populations living in territories under Houthi control, even if that’s not what the UK intends by the sanctions,” she warned.
This is the case even though the UK’s sanctions already include a humanitarian exception covering aid and other activities that meet basic human needs, she said.
Moreover, the UK has not proscribed the Houthis under “antiterrorism” laws despite its other Western allies – the US, Canada and Australia – designating the Iran-backed group as a “terrorist” organisation.
Juneau called the aid agencies’ fear that proscription could hamper humanitarian deliveries “a valid concern” although some people argued the Houthis’ diversion of aid has already made such work extremely difficult.
The Houthis have repeatedly denied that they have diverted humanitarian aid.
Al-Hamdani said sanctions have not forced the Houthis to change their tactics. They do not “appear to respond to human rights criticism or listings”, he said, adding that the group “tends to treat detainees and abuses as bargaining chips to strengthen its negotiating position and demands”.
Rather, he said, sanctions “risk deepening polarisation and closing off the political settlement the war needs”.

Yemen: Warring sides exchange shelling and air strikes, as Saudi oil facilities burn
Houthi shelling southeast of Yemen's Taiz has killed a woman and wounded at least seven others, including a child, the government-run Saba news agency reported.
The news agency reported that the shelling targeted villages in the Sabir al-Mawadim and al-Misrakh districts of Jabal Sabir.
Several homes were also damaged in the attacks, while the injured were taken to hospital for treatment.
A series of air strikes by the Saudi-led coalition also targeted the capital Sanaa, according to media affiliated with the Houthi-led government.
An explosion was reported earlier in the city on Thursday following recent air strikes near the airport.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Forces loyal to the internationally recognised government also said they carried out air strikes on Houthi positions in the Al-Aqroud area of Al-Misrakh district, south of Taiz, following the attacks.
On Wednesday, the Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, as the kingdom’s deterrence and defensive capabilities continue to be challenged.
Riyadh is shooting down the majority of Houthi missiles and drones fired at it, Arab and western officials told Middle East Eye, but it has failed to protect key assets like energy facilities, financial centres and airports.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has tried to rally the US and regional states to his side but with mixed success.
The US has been reluctant to engage Houthi-aligned forces after its previous failed bombing campaign against them was ended last year.
Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Syria have all sent or committed to deliver military support to Saudi Arabia but - with the exception of Syria, which has sent drone operators - the assistance is defensive.
The Saudi crown prince met US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US forces in the Middle East, last week. MEE first reported the planned meeting, which was the third since fighting with the Houthis resumed in July.
The US, Saudi Arabia's top military supplier, has not publicly committed additional support to the kingdom, although it has troops and advisers inside the country.
Semafor reported on Wednesday that Mohammed bin Salman will travel to the US next month for the G20 summit in Miami.
Diplomats have speculated for months about whether the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia would leave the kingdom amid Houthi strikes and the chances of a new US-Israeli attack on Iran.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.text:
- Politik

Union schlägt Kompromiss bei Rente mit 63 vor
CDU-Politiker wollen Bewegung in den Rentenstreit bringen – doch erste Reaktionen lassen nicht auf einen schnellen Durchbruch hoffen.
Berlin. Nach einem Kompromissvorschlag aus der Union zur Frührente für langjährige Versicherte machen führende CDU-Politiker Druck, um den Koalitionsstreit über die Rentenreform beizulegen. CDU-Generalsekretärin Franziska Hoppermann erklärte: »Diese historische Chance müssen wir jetzt gemeinsam ergreifen und noch in diesem Jahr einen Beschluss herbeiführen, um eine starke und stabile Rente für die kommenden Generationen zu sichern.«
NRW-Ministerpräsident Hendrik Wüst sagte dem »Spiegel«, es sei nun am Koalitionspartner SPD, »die ausgestreckte Hand zu ergreifen und die Sache konstruktiv zu einem Ergebnis zu führen«. Die erste Reaktion aus der SPD fiel allerdings zurückhaltend aus. Aus Verhandlungskreisen hieß es am Mittwochabend bereits, der Vorschlag sei verworfen worden.
Im Streit über die Abschaffung der abschlagsfreien Frührente nach 45 Beitragsjahren hatten Fachpolitiker der Unionsfraktion zuvor einen Mittelweg vorgeschlagen. Die abschlagsfreie Rente könnte demnach »für Menschen mit kleinen Einkommen vollständig erhalten« bleiben. Diese Personengruppe arbeite besonders häufig in körperlich und psychisch belastenden Jobs, heißt es in dem am Abend bekanntgewordenen Papier.
SPD-Politikerin: »Honorierung von Lebensleistung«
Aus Sicht von Annika Klose, der Rentenexpertin der SPD-Bundestagsfraktion, geht der Vorschlag allerdings nicht weit genug. »Ich finde die Grenzen, die da gesetzt werden, viel zu niedrig«, sagte sie der ARD. »Uns geht es ja nicht um Almosen – also dass quasi diejenigen, die arm sind, keine Abschläge zahlen. Sondern es geht um die Honorierung von Lebensleistung.«
Aus anderen Verhandlungskreisen hieß es noch am Abend zum Unionsvorstoß: »Dieser Vorschlag entspricht nicht dem Verhandlungsstand und wurde verworfen, da er wenig Einsparungen bringt.« An den Verhandlungen ist federführend Arbeitsminister Alexander Schweitzer (SPD) beteiligt.
Die Abschaffung der abschlagsfreien Rente nach 45 Versicherungsjahren ist Teil der 33 Empfehlungen der Rentenkommission. Die schwarz-rote Bundesregierung hatte im Juni eigentlich angekündigt, die Vorschläge vollständig umzusetzen. Doch die SPD stemmt sich gegen das Ende der sogenannten Rente mit 63. Auch mehrere CDU-Ministerpräsidenten haben sich dagegen ausgesprochen. Befürworter einer umfassenden Reform beharren dagegen auf der Umsetzung auch dieses Punktes. dpa/nd

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers: US trying to cast ‘antiwar ideas as extremist’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers: US trying to cast ‘antiwar ideas as extremist’
The recently bailed activist denies US accusations of supporting Hamas, claiming he is being targeted for supporting Palestine.
Madrid, Spain – James “Fergie” Chambers, a pro-Palestine philanthropist who is the subject of an ongoing extradition request by the United States government, said he believed the US is targeting supporters of the people of Gaza worldwide.
The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas.
He is not charged with any “terrorism” offences and denies any wrongdoing.
Chambers, a self-proclaimed Marxist-Leninist and the heir to the Cox Enterprises media fortune, believes supporters of the Palestinian cause are being targeted around the globe.
“I think that when the neocolonial system starts to break apart economically, militarily, which I believe is happening, it becomes desperate. And when it becomes desperate, it becomes more violent and more violent,” he told Al Jazeera.
“And all these things sort of converge around the occupation of Palestine because we understand the occupation of Palestine as basically nothing more than an expression of US military and business interest. So that is the focal point of repression.”
He added: “In relation to the Palestinian cause and other causes, I think there is a kind of effort certainly in the US to designate [expressing] antiwar ideas as extremist and terrorist.”
‘They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas’
Chambers, who was released from prison in Madrid on bail last week after serving four months on remand, said he was being targeted by the US because of his support for the Palestinian cause.
“I’m not even accused of sending money anywhere illegal. I’m accused of wanting to, which is sort of a crazy distinction to me. They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas, no. They’ve accused me of wanting to send money to Hamas,” he said.
A keen football fan, he said he transferred the money to Club Africain, a Tunisian football team, which he sponsors.
He said he had met someone from the Iranian embassy in Tunisia at an international book fair in 2023.
“[They] tied in a narrative which says that … I allegedly visited the Iranian diplomats, which is not true. I met someone from the Iranian embassy at an international book fair, who told me that US citizens are allowed to have tourist visas. I never met an official at the embassy. I never went into the offices at the embassy.”
The 41-year-old said a forensic accountant had presented Club Africain’s accounts to the Madrid court.
As part of a deal in which his family cut ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023.
“I’m assuming the implication is that I would have met with these people and then transferred money to Tunisia to a football club with the intention of then laundering it to Hamas.”
The US Department of Justice said it did not want to comment when contacted by Al Jazeera.
Chambers said he was “very publicly” affiliated with the club, which won the Tunisian championship this year, and he made a four-year sponsorship deal.
“They had millions of euros worth of debt, which is why they contacted me to get involved. And the money was used to pay off debts, to revamp the team facilities, training facilities, youth programmes, pay overdue salaries. And then in return I had some involvement in management,” he said.
Chambers also said Tunisia was a “closed economy”.
“When you move money into Tunisia, you’re not allowed to move it out,” he said, adding that one of his “most constant emotions in all of this is just downright confusion”.
Chambers, who has given financial aid to 100 projects in 20 countries, including some in Palestine, said he was always careful to obey the law.
“There is no smoking gun. There’s no unloaded gun. There’s nowhere that I said I wanted to support any illegal groups,” he said.
Chambers said he was a target for supporting the Palestinian cause.
“I think the combination of an overall effort by the US authorities to criminalise basically the Palestinian cause in any capacity … this is a part of that,” he said. “You know the fact that I happen to have a lot of resources. And I speak out unapologetically and freely about my positions on US imperialism. These things just combined to make me a target and an example.”
Prison staff ‘saw me as being somebody who shouldn’t be there’
The father-of-four, who has been reunited with his family after being released on bail, is awaiting the court’s decision. His case has also drawn attention to concerns about the implications of the US extradition request.
During his time in jail, he said he received letters of support from many strangers as well as political parties from all sides.
“Even within the prison staff, there was a kind of consensus that people saw me as being somebody who shouldn’t be there,” he said.
However, he said he faces an uncertain future.
“I still don’t know … whether I am going to face decades of my life in a federal penitentiary in the US,” he said.
The High Court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent’s sworn statement, submitted in support of the extradition request. The proceedings have been the subject of further reporting on the extradition case in Spain.
Chambers was arrested on an Interpol Red Notice in Ibiza in July, but has since applied for asylum in Spain.
He cannot be extradited until the asylum claim is resolved, and if it is successful, he cannot be extradited from Spain to the US at all.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/wh.author: Ghada Majadli
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/wh.text:
Why solidarity with Gaza failed to stop the genocide
On 12 November, Israel attacked Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, killing six Palestinians and injuring dozens more.
Among those killed were Saif Abu Hatab, who was awaiting surgery, and Dr Rizq Abu Shaeira, a surgeon working at the hospital. Other surgeons, patients and their companions were among the injured.
Beyond the reporting and familiar condemnations from human rights organisations and UN agencies, the attack appeared to provoke little reaction, let alone meaningful political consequences for Israel.
But is this really surprising?
After Israel systematically attacked and dismantled Gaza's healthcare system from 2023 through 2025, why would another attack on another hospital warrant a different response?
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Still, this is precisely the moment to ask some serious questions about the international political order and its response to Israel's genocide in Gaza.
How have we reached a point where an attack on a hospital, killing patients and the doctors treating them, can pass almost unnoticed?
Growing indifference
Three years into the genocide, the growing numbness and indifference towards Gaza are increasingly difficult to ignore. Since the ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, more than 1,600 Palestinians have reportedly been killed and 5,833 injured, while the humanitarian situation remains catastrophic.
Much of Gaza lies in ruins, its healthcare system devastated, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians remain displaced. With winter arriving, heavy rains have flooded displacement camps, leaving families who have already lost their homes struggling to find somewhere dry and safe to sleep.
None of this was unexpected, yet Israel's continuous restrictions on essential supplies and the destruction of infrastructure have left people exposed to conditions that could have been prevented.
What is particularly disturbing is that Palestinians are now enduring these conditions with even less international attention than before.
The ceasefire has helped create the impression that the worst is over, allowing governments and political leaders to speak of rehabilitation and peace despite the continued destruction of Palestinian life.
Against the backdrop of the Israeli elections, political attention has increasingly shifted towards Israel's domestic politics, electoral alliances and the possibility of replacing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
For many, the prospect of removing the government responsible for so much destruction offers a sense of hope and political urgency. And while a change of government could bring some relief, there is a danger in treating it as a turning point for Palestinians.
The siege of Gaza did not begin with Netanyahu, Ben Gvir or Smotrich, nor did the occupation and dispossession of Palestinians.
These policies have been pursued and maintained by successive Israeli governments, including those presented as more moderate. Yet, as the debate increasingly centres on who will govern Israel next, the question of what will change for the Palestinians, and particularly for those in Gaza, risks being pushed aside.
The growing indifference towards Gaza cannot be understood simply as a consequence of declining media attention or public exhaustion.
During the first year of the genocide, millions of people took to the streets, students established encampments, workers organised, and campaigns demanding an end to military and institutional ties with Israel gained momentum.
Gaza was at the centre of global attention, and the evidence of Israel's atrocities was impossible to ignore. Yet, none of this brought the genocide to an end.
No concrete change
This is a reality we need to confront. The problem cannot simply be that people are no longer paying attention.
For a considerable period, they were paying attention, protesting and demanding action. And still, Israel continued its attacks and destruction, with the political and military support of some of the world's most powerful governments.
Gaza was at the centre of global attention, and the evidence of Israel's atrocities was impossible to ignore. Yet, none of this brought the genocide to an end
This is not to dismiss the significance of these mobilisations. Steps have indeed been taken within universities, trade unions and other institutions to challenge their complicity and cut ties with Israel.
Some campaigns have secured concrete changes, while others continue to organise towards goals that may take years to achieve.
Political struggles do not produce all their outcomes overnight, nor should their significance be measured solely by immediate results.
But acknowledging these achievements should not prevent us from recognising the enormous gap between the scale of global mobilisation and the reality facing Palestinians in Gaza.
Three years into the genocide, despite extensive documentation of atrocities, mass public opposition to the genocide and international legal proceedings, Israel has not faced consequences sufficient to stop the violence, and meanwhile, trucks carrying tents, blankets, mattresses and other essential supplies remain stranded outside Gaza, as Israeli restrictions continue to obstruct their entry.
This should trouble us profoundly, not because the mobilisations have been meaningless, but because of what their inability to stop the genocide reveals about the broader political and economic order that has enabled it to continue.
The problem is not that the world has failed to understand what is happening in Gaza. It is that this knowledge has not translated into the political will to stop it.
What is particularly alarming is how quickly Gaza fades from public attention when Palestinians are no longer being killed in large numbers, even as the conditions that have made such violence possible remain unchanged.
Mass killing cannot be the only catalyst for outrage and mobilisation, nor can our attention to Gaza depend on the scale of Palestinian suffering at any given moment.
Ongoing political commitment
This brings us to another difficult question: what does solidarity with Gaza look like after three years of genocide, political exhaustion and mobilisation that, despite its scale, has failed to bring an end to the violence?
And how can it be sustained when Palestinians are no longer being killed in the hundreds in a single day, but continue to die from frequent Israeli air strikes, the collapse of healthcare and the destruction of the basic conditions necessary for life?
Palestinians should not have to experience another massacre to bring people back into the streets. Nor should solidarity depend on a constant supply of images and testimonies of death and destruction.
While some of us have the privilege of turning away, Palestinians in Gaza must continue living through what the rest of the world can choose to stop watching
The past three years have demonstrated the limitations of a politics that relies on shock and bursts of outrage to sustain itself.
This is not an argument against demonstrations, but an invitation to think more seriously about how solidarity can become an ongoing political commitment rather than a reaction to particular moments of violence.
How do we organise for changes that may take years, while refusing to accept that Palestinians should have to wait years for their lives to be protected? How do we sustain political pressure while confronting the limitations of the strategies pursued so far?
These questions have no easy answers. But they are precisely the questions we need to confront, rather than waiting for another massacre to return Gaza to the centre of public attention. Solidarity cannot be reduced to witnessing Palestinian suffering.
It must also engage with Palestinian political demands and challenge the conditions that have made this destruction possible.
The attack on Nasser Hospital should have been intolerable. So should the continued killing of Palestinians after the ceasefire and the flooding of displacement camps.
Exhaustion is understandable, particularly after three years of witnessing such immense suffering. But exhaustion is not experienced equally.
While some of us have the privilege of turning away, Palestinians in Gaza must continue living through what the rest of the world can choose to stop watching.
Perhaps solidarity also means recognising this unequal burden, and asking how those of us with greater safety and freedom can take on more of the responsibility for sustaining political attention and action, even when the urgency of the moment has faded.
Three years into the genocide, perhaps the question is no longer simply how to bring Gaza back to the world's attention, but how to sustain a politics of solidarity that does not depend on that attention in the first place.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Sem chefes de gangue presos, modelo Bukele no Haiti repete receita que falhou no Rio, analisa correspondente
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Nas redes sociais do presidente de El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, a intervenção no Haiti parece uma sequência de vitórias. Há vídeos de blindados, imagens de drones e multidões agradecendo aos soldados salvadorenhos. Nas ruas de Porto Príncipe, a realidade é outra: as escolas estão fechadas, o comércio parou e a população passa o máximo de tempo possível dentro de casa.
O relato é de Cha Dafol, correspondente do Brasil de Fato no Haiti, em entrevista ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, nesta quarta-feira (25). Para ela, o modelo de segurança que deu fama a Bukele chega ao país caribenho sem atacar a raiz da violência. E a conta, ao final, deve ficar com os haitianos.
Hoje, segundo Dafol, cinco forças armadas atuam ao mesmo tempo na capital. São a polícia e o exército haitianos, as tropas salvadorenhas, a força internacional apoiada pela ONU (Organização das Nações Unidas) e a Vectus Global, empresa militar privada fundada por Erik Prince, ex-integrante das forças especiais da Marinha dos Estados Unidos. “Sem coordenação entre elas”, resume a correspondente. Fora da área onde vive a elite, “não há bairro muito seguro em Porto Príncipe”.
As tropas de Bukele chegaram depois que uma gangue da região metropolitana sequestrou quatro integrantes salvadorenhos da Força de Repressão das Gangues (FRG), em 18 de outubro. O envio foi uma decisão unilateral de Bukele e não tem vínculo legal com o mandato da FRG. Dafol desconfia do motivo oficial. “Acredita-se que os soldados tenham sido assassinados, na verdade. Então é realmente por isso que eu chamo de justificativa”, afirma.
A presença salvadorenha, diz ela, fez as demais forças ampliarem suas operações. Em Martissant, a Polícia Nacional do Haiti informou a morte de ao menos 34 supostos integrantes de gangues, numa ação feita com a Task Force, ligada à Vectus Global. Foi “a maior operação realizada pela polícia nos últimos anos”, segundo a correspondente. Mas o resultado esconde um problema de fundo.
“Nenhum chefe de gangue foi preso. Então não estão enfrentando o problema pela raiz. Eles estão matando pessoas, como a gente vê no próprio Brasil. No Rio de Janeiro tem muitas operações que matam gente, e isso nunca acabou com o crime. É a mesma coisa que está acontecendo aqui, por enquanto”, avalia. Ela acredita que os líderes das gangues já nem estão mais em Porto Príncipe.
A estratégia também levanta dúvidas. Martissant é estratégica porque, por ali, passam as rotas para o sul do país, mas os quatro soldados foram levados numa área do lado oposto da capital. “O que a gente está vendo é uma desinformação, mas também uma operação de comunicação”, diz Dafol. Os militares postam todos os dias, mas não há número oficial de vítimas civis, militares ou de integrantes das gangues.
O acordo de cooperação entre os dois países seguiu o mesmo caminho da opacidade. O Conselho de Ministros do Haiti o aprovou em 17 de novembro, quando o ministro da Justiça, Patrick Pélissier, visitava o Centro de Confinamento do Terrorismo (Cecot) e El Salvador já tinha mais de 2 mil militares no país. O anúncio não detalhou os termos nem o tamanho da participação salvadorenha. Segundo Dafol, o pacto “praticamente não foi comentado na mídia haitiana”.
Para a correspondente, a conta vai chegar. Integrantes do governo salvadorenho já disseram que querem compensação financeira pela missão, e quem deve pagar é “provavelmente o Estado haitiano”. Há um precedente: num contrato anterior, com uma empresa estadunidense, os centros carcerários em solo haitiano custaram ao Estado até US$ 6 bilhões em 50 anos, com cobrança de US$ 22 por preso por dia.
“Mais uma vez, a narrativa de que o Bukele é um salvador não é exatamente a realidade. Tem muito dinheiro em jogo também, e quem vai pagar essa conta vai ser o povo haitiano”, conclui Dafol.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

du site ou de l’application

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
LeBron James becomes oldest NBA player to post triple-double as 76ers win
James posted 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds as Philadelphia snapped Miami’s seven-game winning streak.
LeBron James became the oldest player in NBA history to produce a triple-double, leading Philadelphia to a 114-104 victory over the Miami Heat in the NBA Cup on Wednesday.
Four-time NBA Most Valuable Player James, who turns 42 on December 30, scored a season-high 25 points, passed off a season-high 12 assists and pulled down 10 rebounds to break his own triple-double age mark.
“Father Time always wins, but right now he’s giving Father Time hell,” Heat coach Erik Spoelstra said.
Miami grabbed a 32-29 lead after the first quarter, but James scored 14 consecutive Sixers points in a second-quarter run for a 62-53 half-time lead, and the hosts never lost the edge in the second half.
“We wanted to get back to our defensive identity,” James said. “We didn’t do that in the first quarter, but for the next 36 minutes I thought we got back to that.”
The 76ers improved the best record in the Eastern Conference to 15-4 while snapping a seven-game win streak for Miami (10-7).
Both clubs are 2-1 atop Cup East Group B, but with a win, Miami would have clinched the group and advanced to the knockout stage of the in-season tournament.
With Joel Embiid out due to illness and Jaylen Brown out after early left hamstring tightness, it fell to James to score and set up his teammates.
“That’s my favourite aspect of my game besides my IQ,” James said.
“To be able to go out there and just play like a quarterback role and watch these guys run the right routes, and it’s my job to put it on time and on target, it was fun.”
Tyrese Maxey led the 76ers with 30 points while VJ Edgecombe added 18.
“These are my young bulls right here,” James said. “They keep me going. They keep me energised.”
Giannis Antetokounmpo led Miami with 32 points and 14 rebounds.
James left the Los Angeles Lakers in the off-season and selected the 76ers from several clubs in hopes of capturing a fifth NBA crown.
Mavericks win group
The idle Dallas Mavericks became the first team to reach the Cup knockout round, clinching the West Group A title when the Phoenix Suns lost 116-104 at Houston.
Alperen Sengun had a triple-double with 23 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists for Houston, while Kevin Durant added 20 points and Devin Booker led Phoenix with 25.
At Portland, Deni Avdija scored 33 points, and Damian Lillard added 29 to lead the host Trail Blazers over San Antonio 116-111, leaving West Group C deadlocked with the Spurs, Lakers, Portland and Golden State atop it at 2-1.
“It showed our maturity,” Lillard said. “We won a tough one.”
French star Victor Wembanyama scored 44 points and grabbed 16 rebounds to lead the Spurs, who fell to 15-4 after their first road loss of the season.
Jalen Brunson and Mikal Bridges each scored 19 points as the defending NBA and NBA Cup champion New York Knicks beat visiting Cleveland 121-102 for their sixth consecutive victory.
Karl-Anthony Towns had 12 points and 10 rebounds, and Jose Alvarado scored 21 off the bench for New York. Donovan Mitchell scored 30 points, and James Harden added 28 for the Cavaliers.
Minnesota’s Jaden McDaniels scored 32 points and grabbed 10 rebounds to lead the Timberwolves in a 113-106 victory at Oklahoma City.
Minnesota’s LaMelo Ball had 19 points, eight assists and seven rebounds but left the game late with a left ankle injury.
Two-time NBA MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander led Oklahoma City with 32 points.
Julius Randle scored 28 points to lead Brooklyn’s 104-97 victory at Milwaukee, the Nets snapping a five-game losing skid.
Jaylen Wells scored 19 points to lead Memphis’ 115-97 home victory over the Los Angeles Clippers.
Golden State’s De’Anthony Melton scored 24 points to lead the Warriors over visiting Sacramento 129-110.
Matas Buzelis scored 24 points to lead Chicago over host Charlotte 107-105 as the Hornets’ losing skid reached six games.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Human flamethrower Aaron Rodgers lays bare the cultural rot at the once-great Steelers
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Alex Kirshner
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Nobody in the world, except maybe Pittsburgh Steelers owner Art Rooney II, is surprised that the franchise’s marriage of convenience with Aaron Rodgers ended in spectacular flames. Despite their own elevated idea of themselves, Pittsburgh have been one of the NFL’s messiest soap operas for a solid decade. When they linked up with the league’s messiest quarterback, it seemed certain we would get … even more mess. When they doubled down last offseason by hiring the coach with whom Rodgers had fallen out in Green Bay in the late 2010s, the mess became inevitable. We’d seen hints of the approaching drama in the season’s first 11 weeks.
“What the fuck … call it!” Rodgers yelled at McCarthy as he looked for a play in early October.
“Fucking asshole,” his head coach barked on the sideline.
But give this to the Steelers, and to Rodgers: no matter how trashy each party has been for however many years, the show they gave us on Wednesday was special – right up there with the Hindenburg’s final moments. The league’s most dramatic, selfish quarterback collided with the NFL franchise that has the most outdated and over-inflated view of itself, and the result was the greatest explosion in modern history between a team and their QB.
The story began to come to a head on Tuesday, when Rodgers and McCarthy had their latest relationship breakdown. That night, the Steelers said that Rodgers would be inactive for Friday’s game against the Broncos and that his backup, Mason Rudolph, would start. A 6-4 team don’t voluntarily start Mason Rudolph – a man whose NFL career could generously be described as mediocre – unless something has gone horribly awry, and indeed, the details of the Rodgers-McCarthy blowup ended up being absurd.
As the Steelers are messaging it through Pittsburgh media, Rodgers wanted full play-calling authority or to be released, and the team chose the latter. (That’s the report from the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette’s Gerry Dulac, a longtime team insider, citing anonymous sources.) As Rodgers told it in a genuinely surreal television interview with his friend Pat McAfee, the standoff came after the QB confronted his once-and-present head coach over some pretty wild accusations. Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep in team meetings, not watching film until at least two days after a Sunday game, failing to form relationships with defensive players (McCarthy’s background is on offense), and breaking a huddle by saying “1-2-3 Packers!” during a loss to the Eagles last weekend.
Rodgers, who isn’t known for his humility, has strange tendencies on his best days, and if you don’t find him a reliable narrator, you’re well within your rights. But McCarthy admitted to the “Packers” mishap during his own news conference on Wednesday, and various Steelers players had the chance to support their coach during media availabilities after practice and decided not to. “It’s all true,” one source told ESPN’s Brooke Pryor, whose story on Wednesday appeared to corroborate many of Rodgers’s claims about McCarthy.
During his call with McAfee, Rodgers made clear he didn’t expect players or coaches still with the Steelers to back up his version of events. Rodgers put Pat Freiermuth in a difficult spot by telling McAfee that it had been the tight end, not a Steelers higher-up, who informed him he’d been benched. “I can’t believe they’re doing this” was how Rodgers relayed Freiermuth’s words to him.
“I was just checking on a close friend,” the tight end said Wednesday. Good lord.
The Steelers releasing Rodgers may well have ended his career – he turns 43 next week, and had said this summer he plans to retire at the end of this season. The team move forward with Rudolph, who takes over a squad in contention to once again lose in the first round of the playoffs.
One of the day’s cattiest pieces of gossip was Rodgers telling McAfee that McCarthy had told a Steelers staffer he blamed the quarterback for his firing by the Packers in 2018, eight years after he and Rodgers won a Super Bowl together. We may never know for sure what’s in McCarthy’s head right now, but it was already well known that his relationship with Rodgers had deteriorated in the years after the Super Bowl win (against the Steelers, as it happens) in the 2010 season. The Steelers thought wrapping the two of them in their terrific organizational culture would smooth things over, I guess?
If only any of the 8 billion people on earth who knew this was a bad idea had told the Steelers’ leadership. But passing on Rodgers would have required the Steelers to take a risk on acquiring a younger quarterback. Instead, they rolled with the oldest one in the league, who had been in decline ever since he won back-to-back MVPs in 2020 and 2021. As an old man in a young man’s game, Rodgers was mostly immobile and borderline inept this season. A terrible receiving corps didn’t help, but a good running game covered up some of the deficiencies that come with age.
Wednesday was one of the most embarrassing days in the history of a once-great franchise that I grew up rooting on from the stands at Heinz Field. Could it be a turning point? The Steelers have needed one for a while. Longtime coach Mike Tomlin’s departure after last season could have been that turning point, but the Steelers ensured it wouldn’t be when they hired McCarthy. The now 63-year-old was out of the league after he left the Cowboys in 2025, and his main qualification for the Steelers job appeared to be that he was from Pittsburgh’s Greenfield neighborhood. This made for an emotional introductory press conference and a coaching tenure that is going downhill, fast.
The Steelers built their reputation for greatness in the 1970s, when they won four Super Bowls under founding owner Art Rooney. The family business had some down times in the 1980s but continued to be great under Rooney’s son, Dan, under whose leadership the club won two more championships in the 2005 and 2008 seasons. The Steelers’ devolution into their current status – a solid but unspectacular team that produces headlines worthy of TMZ – came after Dan’s son, Art Rooney II, assumed control of the franchise in 2017.
For a club once lauded for its stability – the Steelers had just three head coaches between 1969 and 2025 – it is obvious they are in the midst of cultural rot. They have ranked in the bottom 10 in the league most years since 2022 in the NFL Players Association’s “report cards”, which measure what players think of their teams. This year, they reached new depths by finishing dead last.
The franchise has seen a great deal of tabloid-style drama in the past 10 years, most of that under Tomlin, who kept putting a decent (but rarely good) product on the field despite the locker room chaos. (You may remember highlights such as Antonio Brown’s beef with Ben Roethlisberger, the scandal over JuJu Smith-Schuster being too online, or the time Steelers players raided Le’Veon Bell’s locker during his contract standoff with the team.) That is but a small sample of recent Steelers drama, and all of it falls well short of this week’s fiasco. Kudos to Pittsburgh on finding new frontiers in team culture every year.
Is this catastrophe public enough, or embarrassing enough, to prompt change? Ideally, Art Rooney II would sell the team to someone who has proven themselves more capable of running a large organization and isn’t just coasting off a family inheritance. But failing that, the Steelers cannot in good conscience bring back McCarthy for a second year, and they probably ought to look seriously into firing general manager Omar Khan as well. The team haven’t had a losing season since 2003, and their 6-4 start means they may not have one this year, either. But with an expensive, aging defense and an offense that just got beheaded, a long-overdue collapse and rebuild seems more plausible.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/attentat.title: Attentat de Trappes : « On aurait dû s’arrêter en tant que société » | ÇA IRA !

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/attentat.text:
Attentat de Trappes : « On aurait dû s’arrêter en tant que société » | ÇA IRA !
Publié le 26 novembre 2026
Un mois après l'attentat terroriste raciste qui a frappé Trappes le 23 octobre, coûtant la vie à Pengo Bossio Wangi et faisant sept blessés dont la jeune Ramatou (12 ans), l'Humanité reçoit Ali Rabeh, maire de Trappes, et Maboula Soumahoro, maîtresse de conférences à l'université de Tours, pour revenir sur le traumatisme profond qui traverse les habitants de Trappes et de La Verrière.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/explainers.title: Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?
https://www.middleeasteye.net/explainers.author: Daniel Tester
https://www.middleeasteye.net/explainers.text:
Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?
Yemen, where civil war broke out in 2014, has recently been rocked by the worst fighting in years. A truce agreed in 2022 between the Ansar Allah, better known as the Houthis, who control the north, and forces loyal to the government in the south disintegrated when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July.
In August and September, the Houthis mounted a quick offensive, recapturing much of the western coast, including the port of Mocha, putting it within close range of ships passing the strategically important Bab el-Mandab strait.
The Houthis are now targeting Aden, Yemen’s second city and seat of its internationally recognised government since the group took the capital Sanaa 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have tightened their decade-long siege of Taiz, blocking the road to Aden and raising the prospect of its capture.
The Saudi-backed pro-government military coalition contains a variety of armed units and local militias, each with different goals, rival leaders and origins, leading to infighting and disorganisation.
