https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Fifa staff asked to attend interviews as Infantino sell-off scheme investigated
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Nick Ames
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
A number of past and present Fifa employees have received letters requesting they attend interviews for a congressional investigation into the global governing body sparked by the Fifa Forward Enterprise scandal.
Letters were sent on Wednesday to a number of staff along with a handful of former employees who held senior positions. They have been asked by Democrats on the House judiciary committee to give evidence as efforts gather pace to examine Gianni Infantino’s failed FFE scheme along with links between Fifa and the Trump administration.
Should recipients agree, the voluntary interviews could commence as soon as next week. They would be likely to take place under the whistleblower protection act or the victim and witness protection act, although the potential interviewees will seek legal advice before agreeing to take part.
The investigation’s gathering of momentum will increase pressure on Infantino, who could be among those subpoenaed to give evidence to the committee in January. By then, the committee will be controlled by Democrats after their success in the midterms and is likely to be chaired by Jamie Raskin, who warned in July that it would “have the tools we need to get answers, expose corruption, protect sports fans against exorbitant and fraudulent charges and block this attempt to turn world soccer into a global financial shakedown”.
The White House has previously dismissed similar allegations as politically motivated. Fifa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Subpoenas could be issued to a range of individuals within Fifa, and in the organisation’s orbit, as soon as the second week of January. Those called to give evidence at a hearing could be required to disclose their knowledge of the FFE plan and other Fifa controversies, potentially handing over physical evidence.
Fifa confirmed on Thursday it had fallen victim to a criminal cyber-attack carried out by a group that posed as staff members to steal personal and business data. A group called the Handsome Boy Hacking Club claimed responsibility for the breach, understood to have taken place on 11 November.
In a letter to the Fifa council dated 25 November, seen by the Guardian, the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, said the hack had “resulted in information being illegally obtained which included data relevant to the personal profiles of key officials including Fifa Council members attending Fifa tournaments and events”. Grafström wrote that Fifa had “taken mitigating and corrective steps” and told council members that they would be contacted individually where necessary.

On the surface, American Doctor is a film about three American doctors who volunteered in Gaza's hospitals during Israel's war. But for director Poh Si Teng, the title was always a way in: a film to reach audiences in the West, about Palestinian health workers and the US-made bombs falling on them.
The film follows trauma surgeon Dr Feroze Sidhwa, Palestinian-American emergency physician Dr Thaer Ahmad and Dr Mark Perlmutter, from Gaza's hospitals to the halls of power in Washington.
In this Real Talk interview, Poh, Feroze and Thaer sit down with Mohamed Hashem to talk about the thinking behind the title, briefing Joe Biden on Rafah, and why funders saw the film as an "institutional risk".

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Javokhir Sindarov survives in first real fight of world title match
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
After two quieter draws, the world chess championship came to life on Thursday as Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov came within eight seconds of sudden death before fighting back to split the point with India’s Gukesh Dommaraju after nearly five hours. Their spirited 60-move battle at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs left their $2.5m match level at 1½–1½ heading into the first rest day.
Gukesh, playing with the black pieces, returned to the Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez, the opening he used in Tuesday’s 38-move opener. The defending champion sprang the first surprise on move five (5 … Be7), bringing out his bishop before retreating the knight that had taken Sindarov’s e-pawn, putting the challenger behind on time for the first time in the match. After 15 moves, Gukesh still had nearly 1hr 58min of his starting two hours, almost 40 minutes more than his opponent.
“We checked this, but not that deep,” Sindarov said afterwards. “I was very surprised.” Gukesh said he knew the line as far as his queen move on move 15 and felt comfortable with the position and his lead on the clock.
The queens came off on move 17, but Gukesh kept his king in the center and brought it forward as the pieces thinned out. Sindarov had just over four minutes left after his 33rd move, with seven still to make before he would get another half-hour. Gukesh sacrificed a pawn to clear the way for another, which reached d3 on move 36, two squares from promotion.
Sindarov spent more than a minute on his 39th move, bringing his bishop backward (39 Bb4) with eight seconds to spare. Gukesh took a pawn in reply, and Sindarov moved his rook to c1 to reach the time control. Both players got another half-hour added, with Gukesh’s advanced pawn still on the board.
“I think it was more stressful for him because I always had enough time on the clock,” Gukesh said. Sindarov said he had come close to missing something during the time scramble but was happy overall with how he defended.
The rooks came off on move 49, leaving Gukesh a pawn up in an ending with opposite-colored bishops. His king reached the second rank, but Sindarov’s bishop blocked the passed pawn’s path to promotion. The game ended in a draw after 4hr 49min with the pawn still on d3.
It was the third draw in as many days and the longest game of the match so far. Gukesh had been the one scrambling to make the time control in Tuesday’s first contest, when he held off Sindarov in 38 moves with black. Wednesday’s second game ended by threefold repetition after just 20 moves and 1hr 57min.
Both players are 20 years old, making this the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most prestigious title. Gukesh has struggled for form since becoming the youngest undisputed world champion in December 2024, falling from a career-high No 3 to No 26, the lowest ranking for a reigning world champion since Elo ratings were introduced in 1971. Sindarov, meanwhile, has surged from No 25 a year ago to a career-best No 4 after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup in Goa last November and going unbeaten at this year’s Candidates tournament in Cyprus, where he became the first player from Uzbekistan to earn a world title shot.
The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Sindarov entered as a prohibitive favorite, having won twice and drawn once in their three classical meetings before the match.
The match resumes on Saturday with Gukesh playing white in Game 4. The players get one point for a win and half a point for a draw. The first to reach 7½ points will be crowned champion, with rapid and blitz tiebreaks scheduled if the score remains level after 14 games. Three of the past five world championship matches have required tiebreaks.
After nearly five hours at the board, Sindarov was asked how much pressure there was to be the first to win a game. “That’s a very hard question,” he said. “I cannot think right now, so I’m sorry.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/trending/s.title: Socialist weather and dogs barking in Hebrew: America's Thanksgiving culture wars

Socialist weather and dogs barking in Hebrew: America's Thanksgiving culture wars
Americans celebrating Thanksgiving this year have been presented with two rather unexpected political developments: New York City's Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani now has control over the weather, and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee's dogs may have acquired a second language.
While millions of Americans gathered with their families on Thursday, social media users were engaged in another traditional Thanksgiving activity: fighting over politics. But this time it was socialism, Islam and Zionism that took centre stage in this debate.
The postponement of NYC's iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade because of severe weather conditions sent right-wing commentators into a frenzy, with some suggesting the decision had less to do with meteorology and more to do with Mamdani's political and religious affiliations.
It appears that, in addition to affordable housing, universal childcare and free buses, Mamdani's socialist agenda has taken over the weather in Manhattan.
Some users shared live webcam footage of Times Square in an apparent attempt to discredit weather forecasts, while others suggested that New Yorkers had been duped into believing the parade was called off because of rain.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
For others, the mayor's Democratic Socialist background offered an alternate explanation for the storm ripping through New York.
Never mind that the parade has not actually been cancelled, but postponed until Saturday.
Gotta hand it to Mamdani. The guy killed the New York City Thanksgiving Parade for the first time in 100 years, and everyone is walking around believing that it has to do with rain.
— Abe Greenwald (@AbeGreenwald) November 26, 2026
Unfortunately for proponents of the weather conspiracy, New York's precautions surrounding parade balloons considerably predate Mamdani's political career.
In 1997, strong winds caused a giant Cat in the Hat balloon to strike a lamppost, seriously injuring a spectator.
The following year, the city introduced safety regulations limiting balloon operations to sustained winds of 23mph (37kmph) and gusts of 34mph - well below the gusts of up to 65mph forecast for Thanksgiving.
The mayor responsible for introducing those measures was Republican Rudy Giuliani, which makes social media reactions like the X post depicting “the last Republican in NYC” all the more bizarre.
🇺🇸 The last republican in NYC, standing in front of Mamdani's Thanksgiving parade. One man, no tanks needed, just a mayor who postponed 100 years of tradition. #MamdaniOutNow #HappyThanksgiving https://t.co/qvnMANJmZe
— Love Majewski (@MajewskiLove1) November 26, 2026
Philadelphia also disrupted its Thanksgiving festivities due to severe weather.
Barking in Hebrew
Meanwhile, thousands of miles away, a prominent figure on the Christian-Zionist right was celebrating Thanksgiving from Israel.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee appeared alongside his wife and their two dogs in a video expressing gratitude for the opportunity to live in the biblical land.
"What an amazing privilege it is to live here at such a consequential time. And one thing is for sure, it's never boring," Huckabee said, in a particularly jarring choice of words against the backdrop of Israel's genocide in Gaza.
One user on Reddit wrote, “Never boring? Yeah, because they keep killing innocent people. They get the thrill from it.”
Comedian and YouTuber Alex Stein shared a satirical video mimicking Huckabee, his wife and their dogs. In the video, Stein satirises the ambassador’s Thanksgiving message by saying, “Jesus Christ says ‘love thy neighbour, but what did Bibi Netanyahu say? Bomb thy neighbour!’” He also praises his dog for “biting four Muslim Amazon delivery drivers just this year”, adding to the ridicule.
From our family to yours, Happy Thanksgiving! 🇮🇱🦃🇺🇸 https://t.co/Gd6cshlily
— Alex Stein #99 (@alexstein99) November 26, 2026
But the longtime supporter of Israel had another important development to share.
"Our dogs like it too, in fact, we think they now are barking in Hebrew."
The announcement left some on social media questioning whether the video was even real.
Others wondered how Huckabee's effusive praise for Israel squared with the Trump administration's much-touted "America First" agenda.
@USAmbIsrael Imagine an American sending a message on a uniquely American holiday and using it to praise Israel.
— Bill The Butcher (@317Donnely) November 25, 2026
And so, this Thanksgiving, Americans found themselves debating the political affiliations of a weather forecast and the linguistic capabilities of two dogs.
The turkeys, at least, were largely spared the culture wars.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Éric Cantona: ‘If I regret something about the kung fu kick, it’s that I would love to kick him in another place’
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Donald McRae
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
“I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”
It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil. Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United, whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.
I prepare for a possible meltdown because rare archive footage, which opens the documentary, captures a televised standoff between Cantona and a few French journalists. He objects to the fact that L’Équipe had described his kung fu kick against a Crystal Palace supporter in 1995 as “unforgivable”. After asking who is truly “unforgivable”, and highlighting the historical sins of the Catholic church, Cantona sneers: “I piss on the pope’s arse. Just as I piss on the arse of certain journalists … including you and you,” he says, pointing to two outraged writers.
Now, 30 years later, Cantona emerges in his home city of Marseille, wearing a natty trilby. Within minutes I can tell that the flower of evil is elsewhere because Cantona is in a generous mood. As he recalls that bitterly sensational clash with the French reporters he smiles: “I’m a good client for the journalists – and they are a good client for me to express myself. We play a bit like the cat and the mouse. Sometimes we have good relationships, sometimes a bad relationship. But it’s always interesting and exciting.”
This might be Cantona at his most angelic, stretching the truth about the supposed thrill of his journalistic encounters, but it’s fitting that the film starts with the 60-year-old quoting Charles Baudelaire, the 19th-century French poet who, in his Flowers of Evil collection, wrote: “I am the wound and the knife/I am the blow and the cheek/ … The victim and the executioner …”
Cantona’s brilliance and spite defined his troubled time at six French clubs between 1983 and 1992. He could have “disappeared” from football because, despite being France’s most gifted player, he had fallen out with the national manager. The young Cantona said: “I hope people realise Henri Michel is one of the most incompetent coaches in world football.”
Michel Platini, who replaced Michel, persuaded Cantona to end his fleeting retirement in 1992 by moving to England. As Cantona says: “I knew it will be my last chance … and it’s really in England where I regain this passion for football … it’s a rebirth.”
The documentary provides a compelling account of his turbulent love affair with English football – but ignores a strange prelude at Sheffield Wednesday. Cantona tells me this forgotten strand of his story with amused incredulity. “I arrived at Sheffield Wednesday and we played a friendly. We won 4-3 and I scored three goals. And then I waited to sign the contract. At the end of the week they said: ‘You have to spend one more week on trial.’ I said: ‘No. I leave.’”
Who managed Wednesday then? “Trevor Francis – who was a great player,” Cantona replies. “Howard Wilkinson heard about that and asked me to come to Leeds. I arrived in Leeds and then we became champions and it was a great time.”
That deceptively simple last sentence fails to capture the seismic impact Cantona had on English football and especially on Leeds, who won the league title for the first time in 18 years in 1992. “It was old-fashioned football,” Cantona says. “It was interesting. There was also, for me, the feeling of adding something different.”
Was it disheartening playing antiquated football? “No, because I played with wonderful players. We had a great midfield with Gary Speed, David Batty, Gary McAllister and Gordon Strachan. And quickly [the following season] I arrive at Manchester United with Alex Ferguson. The club had the Busby Babes. That was wonderful football. Manchester United has always been a club where winning in a good way is important.”
This should be the moment to ask Cantona about the contrast with the current moribund state of United but, rather than falling out over his refusal to discuss the club now, it’s enough to hear him in full flow. “This club always loved people with different personalities. They loved George Best, Brian McClair, [Norman] Whiteside, [Roy] Keane …”
Cantona was adored at Old Trafford, as he had been at Leeds before his shock departure to United for a mere £1m in November 1992. He also led United to their first Premier League title, in 1993, after a 26-year drought.
There are great clubs in Italy, Spain and Germany so could he have resurrected his career in one of these countries? Cantona shakes his head: “I love Italian football. I love Spanish football. I love Barcelona. But nothing can compare to English football and the fans, the way they sing and express themselves. It’s so powerful.”
Cantona remembers that, when he arrived in England, “in the street, nobody knew me. I felt free for the first time in my life. I could go have a drink somewhere, listen to some music and it was always peaceful.”
Ferguson recalls that he asked Guy Roux, the wise old manager who nurtured Cantona at his first club, Auxerre, how to harness his volatile talent. Roux offered two words: “Love him.”
Cantona nods: “I’m instinctive. If I feel bad I go. If I feel good, I try to create a relationship. And when I arrive in Manchester I see the ghosts of the past. I felt this very strong energy and I thought: ‘Maybe this is the place where I will have the opportunity to express myself.’ I found in Alex Ferguson the perfect manager. I was very lucky he gave me this freedom. He understood me so well so I could express myself 100%. He’s a great manager.”
Everything changed when Cantona’s temper returned – culminating in the dark moment in January 1995 when, after he was sent off against Crystal Palace, he was insulted by a rival fan as he headed towards the tunnel. Cantona launched himself at the man and, in mid-air, caught him with a scything kung fu kick.
He faced a charge of criminal assault and was sentenced to two weeks in prison, a judgment which was reduced to 120 hours of community service on appeal. Cantona was banned from football for eight months and returned to France. He looks at me coolly: “I know people expect me to say: ‘Oh, I regret it.’ No, I don’t regret it. If I regret something, it’s that I would love to kick him in another [place].” Cantona points out that perceptions are always changing. “The kung fu kick was criticised a lot, especially by journalists. But now it’s a [more positive] symbol. So I change everything.”
Did much thought go into his cryptic comment after the court hearing: “When the seagulls follow the trawler it’s because they think sardines will be thrown into the sea.”
Cantona grins. “No. I didn’t want to speak to the press, but the lawyer said: ‘You have to say something.’ I could have said: ‘I walk on the moon and tomorrow I dive deeper in the ocean.’ It was good for everybody. We all enjoyed it together.”
Ferguson, with compassion and guile, enticed Cantona back to Manchester. It was a triumph as, in a young team including David Beckham, Ryan Giggs and Paul Scholes, Cantona was a model of brooding magnificence as he inspired United to another championship.
He left the game for good the following year, in 1997, after captaining United to a fourth league title in five seasons. “I was very passionate about other things,” he says, “and I didn’t want to waste time. I wanted to do something else.”
Cantona adds: “I left football because I lost passion for the game. I had to be honest with myself, and with the fans. I’m very proud of that [honesty].”
There is a deep bond between Cantona and the older men in his life. When we spoke this month, Ferguson was 84, Cantona’s father Albert was 86, Roux was 88 and Ken Loach, the film-maker, was 90. “I met a few people in my life,” Cantona tells me, “and Guy Roux, Alex Ferguson, Ken Loach and, of course, my father, are the most wonderful people I know.”
Two days after our interview, Cantona announced the death of his dad with a heartfelt message on Instagram accompanied by a black-and-white photograph of Albert smoking a cigar: “My father. My God. My master. Rest in peace.”
The importance of his father, a painter who nourished Cantona’s interest in art and acting, is rivalled only by Ferguson. There is a deeply touching segment in the film when Ferguson reads aloud the letter of gratitude he wrote to Cantona after the footballer retired at the age of 30.
We also talk about what Cantona might have done had he not worked so much in film, art and music. “I still would have been involved in football, maybe as a manager,” he says. “It’s very interesting and I would have liked to be a manager in an artistic way, trying to create something.”
Would he have been a good manager? Cantona laughs. “I don’t know. But I will have tried to find something that nobody tried before. Something original – like Johan Cruyff at Barcelona. Or Alex Ferguson at Manchester United. It’s a big club, a rich club, it could buy anyone. But he believed in a young generation and he created a way to manage players.”
Cantona rarely watches football but when did he last see an entire game? “I’m shooting a TV series in Marseille and last month I went to the stadium to see Marseille against Olympiakos in the Europa League. It was the first time I came back to Marseille since 1991 when I was a player. They lost 1-0 but I enjoyed it because Marseille is in my veins, like English football and the fans of Manchester United.”
The world is changing so fast and, after 45 minutes, we start talking about AI and the future. “Of course,” Cantona says when I ask whether he is concerned. “I try as hard as possible to stay away [from technology]. I can show you my phone.”
He brings out an old brick. “I never had anything else,” Cantona says cheerfully. “I never had a smartphone. I don’t want it. More and more people realise that they become a prisoner of it. If you use it well, it can be good. But I’m a bit excessive. So I prefer not to have it.”
I ask Cantona about the demon inside him. What is it? “My instinct. It’s my best friend but there is always a fight with a different little voice inside. This voice is still alive.”
Cantona tips his hat one last time and grins: “We are still fighting. But I win a lot of fights.”
Cantona: Flower of Evil is in UK & Ireland cinemas 7 and 12 December only, with Éric Cantona Q&A broadcast live from Manchester. Participating cinemas here and tickets for the event here

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Fifa confirms cyber-attack exposed ‘personal and business information’
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Keely Aouga and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Fifa confirmed that hackers gained access to a “limited set of personal and business information” in a cyber-attack, amid heightened concern over digital vulnerabilities of leading organizations and institutions.
The global soccer governing body said it “condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data”, in a statement to the Associated Press on Thursday. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”
Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were Fifa files. The post has since then been removed after the account was suspended from X.
The Fifa cyber-attack is the latest high-profile digital disruption to hit a major organization in recent weeks.
Microsoft experienced a widespread outage earlier this month that caused disruption to millions of users, organizations and businesses across the globe. The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents.
The following day, the US experienced an unprecedented nationwide disruption to air travel that prompted a “ground stop” order to be issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration, which cited “communication issues” impacting air traffic control centers.
Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, later said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.
Three days later, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Such disruptions have intensified fear and concerns about the advancement of artificial intelligence, and the potential risks, even though there is no direct evidence that AI directly sparked the issues.
ESPN reported that unnamed sources said the Fifa hack accounted for less than 0.1% of data held by the organization, an that the breach was not a result of systems or technology failure on Fifa’s part, with hackers said to have gained access by impersonating staff.
As of now, it has not been shared when the cyber-attack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information.
“FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said its statement sent to the Associated Press.
The cyber-attack comes as Gianni Infantino, Fifa’s president, is under scrutiny for a proposal to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors.
Infantino admitted the project “has created divisions of a nature that are no longer in the interest of the objective”, amid widespread anger globally.
The plan has caused tensions within football around the world, leading Uefa to threaten a boycott of future Fifa tournaments if it was not shelved.
Uefa and other confederations have stepped up their search for candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term.

Iran's senior Armed Forces spokesman, Abolfazl Shekarchi, has denied that his county attacked a "vital" site in Kuwait, and said no offensive or military operation by Iranian armed forces took place in the region, Iranian state media reported on Thursday.
The Iranian denial comes after Italy said two of its citizens were killed in Iranian drone attack on Kuwait.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.title: Adorno-Vorlesungen | Konterrevolutionen des Eigentums
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.author: Ivo Eichhorn
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.text:
- Kultur
- Adorno-Vorlesungen
Konterrevolutionen des Eigentums
In den Adorno-Vorlesungen 2026 sprach Melinda Cooper über kapitalistische Vergesellschaftung, revolutionären Konservatismus und sexuelle Gewalt.
»Das Staunen darüber, daß die Dinge, die wir erleben, im zwanzigsten Jahrhundert ›noch‹ möglich sind«, notierte Walter Benjamin 1940 auf der Flucht vor dem deutschen Faschismus, »ist kein philosophisches. Es steht nicht am Anfang einer Erkenntnis, es sei denn der, daß die Vorstellung von Geschichte, aus der es stammt, nicht zu halten ist.« Auch heute scheinen die von uns erlebten Dinge oftmals aus der Vergangenheit zu stammen – nicht zuletzt aus den europäischen Faschismen des 20. Jahrhunderts.
Wie ließe sich diesem Eindruck jenseits der von Benjamin kritisierten liberalen Fortschrittsperspektive beikommen? Diese Frage stand im Zentrum der diesjährigen Frankfurter Adorno-Vorlesungen. Vom 18. bis 20. November lud das Institut für Sozialforschung in Kooperation mit dem Suhrkamp Verlag traditionsgemäß in einen Hörsaal auf dem Bockenheimer Campus. An den drei durchweg gut besuchten Abenden sprach dort die Soziologin und politische Theoretikerin Melinda Cooper unter dem Titel »Anachronism in Our Times« zu kapitalistischer Vergesellschaftung, revolutionärem Konservatismus und sexueller Gewalt.
Wiederkehr des Vergangenen
Cooper begann ihre erste Vorlesung mit dem Börsengang von SpaceX im Juni dieses Jahres. Elon Musk hält weiterhin 85 Prozent der Stimmrechte, obwohl ihm weniger als die Hälfte der Anteile gehört. Dass Eigentum seit der Wirtschaftskrise 2008 wieder zunehmend personalisiert wird und ökonomische Macht erneut Gesichter erhält, von denen Musk vielleicht das sichtbarste ist, haben einige Stimmen als Neo- oder Tech-Feudalismus zu analysieren versucht. Damit ist Cooper bei ihrem leitenden Thema angelangt: dem Eindruck, das lang Vergangene kehre zurück. Dieser Eindruck verweist ihrer Ansicht nach jedoch eher auf einen blinden Fleck im Verständnis des Kapitalismus als auf dessen Ende.
Aus einer liberalen Fortschritts- und Modernisierungsperspektive erscheinen tendenziell alle nicht-vertraglichen Verhältnisse als feudale Überbleibsel. Eine solche Mystifikation macht Cooper auch noch in Teilen der Marx’schen Theorie aus, welche Prämissen des Liberalismus unter gewandelten Vorzeichen aufnimmt. Zugleich begreift sie Marx als einen zerrissenen Denker mit mehr als nur einer Perspektive. Bei ihm finde sich ebenfalls die Erkenntnis, dass das Kapitalverhältnis durch eine Doppelbewegung gekennzeichnet ist. Demnach »produziert« die bürgerliche Gesellschaft, wie Marx an einer Stelle schreibt, »alles das in ihrer eignen Form wieder, was sie in feudaler oder absolutistischer Form bekämpft hatte«. Blickt man, wie Cooper es seit Jahren brillant vormacht, auch auf die Reproduktion des Eigentums in Vererbungspraktiken, wird etwa die Zentralität der Familie als rechtliche und gesellschaftliche Form in dieser Doppelbewegung deutlich. Die familiäre Vererbung von Vermögen wie von Privilegien und Identitäten erscheint zwar aus liberaler Sicht als feudale Elemente. Kapitalismus ist jedoch nicht auf Liberalismus zu reduzieren, sondern bringt immer wieder archaisch erscheinende Formen hervor.
In ihrer zweiten Vorlesung rekonstruierte Cooper den antistaatlichen Libertarismus in der US-Geschichte, von den Bürgerwehren zur Aufrechterhaltung weißer Vorherrschaft und Eigentumsverteidigung nach dem Bürgerkrieg bis zur Obama-Ära und Trump 2.0. Unter dem Begriff eines revolutionären Konservatismus machte sie die antistaatlichen Elemente im Bündnis zwischen Präsident Trump und Teilen der Bevölkerung verständlich. Mit Blick auf diese wird auch deutlich, inwiefern der Ausbau der ICE-Apparatur unter Trump nur vermeintlich im Widerspruch zu dessen Kampf gegen staatliche Verwaltungsbehörden steht.
Coopers Distanzierung dieser heutigen Tendenzen vom europäischen Faschismus der ersten Hälfte des 20. Jahrhunderts, den sie mit Carl Schmitts Überlegungen zum totalen Staat als etatistisch kennzeichnet, bleibt jedoch etwas unbefriedigend. Auch hier ließe sich das Verhältnis von staatlicher und gesellschaftlicher, unter Umständen antistaatlicher Gewalt als spannungsreicheres definieren. Man denke etwa an die Fasci in Italien oder die zahlreichen paramilitärischen Organisationen in der Weimarer Republik, die den Ersten Weltkrieg gegen den post-revolutionären Staat der Weimarer Republik fortsetzen wollten. Der marxistische Staatstheoretiker Nicos Poulantzas sprach diesbezüglich vom »Auftreten von Stoßtrupps und Privatmilizen, die die Kerne politischer Reorganisation darstellen«. Trotz dieses Einwands macht Coopers Genealogie die explosive Mischung aus tech-futuristischen und ultrakonservativen Elementen einsichtig, wie sie im gegenwärtigen US-Faschismus hervortritt. Der quasi-revolutionäre Gebrauch von Gewaltmitteln zum Schutz des Eigentums radikalisiert konservative Elemente kapitalistischer Gesellschaften, die aus liberaler Perspektive nur mystifiziert werden können.
Dass sich diese Elemente nicht zuletzt in den Geschlechterverhältnissen verdichten, machte Cooper in der dritten Vorlesung anhand einer ökonomischen Perspektivierung sexueller Gewalt deutlich. Hier variierte sie eine These, die in materialistisch-feministischen Debatten der 1970er Jahre etwa Colette Guillaumin entwickelt hatte, wonach Sexismus als Struktur der männlichen Aneignung von Frauen in zeitlicher, körperlicher und sexueller Hinsicht zu begreifen ist. Dass im Herzen der weiblichen Unterordnung ein Eigentumsinteresse aufzufinden ist, verdeutlichte Cooper anhand einer Rekapitulation der Rechte des Vaters und Ehemanns als Haushaltsvorstand in der frühneuzeitlichen Rechtsprechung. Sodann verfolgte sie die (rechtliche) Ausdifferenzierung des Privaten in vertraglich geregelte Arbeitsverhältnisse einerseits und familiäre, außervertragliche Abhängigkeitsverhältnisse andererseits hinein. Die letzteren erscheinen in der Folge nicht mehr als ökonomisch, was die in ihnen geleistete Arbeit und den männlichen Besitzanspruch verschleiert.
Ein erweitertes Verständnis von Ökonomie hingegen ermöglicht, die Persistenz sexueller Gewalt als Wiederherstellung des geschlechtlichen Eigentumsinteresses zu begreifen, die Cooper bis zur Ideologie heutiger Incels und vor allem zur Vergewaltigungsserie an Gisèle Pelicot und ähnlichen Fällen nachzeichnet. Der geschlechtliche Eigentumsanspruch wirkt außerhalb formaler Marktbeziehungen und reicht bis zu jenen Männern, die sonst als eigentumslos gelten. Das macht ihn leicht unsichtbar, seine Wirkungen treten im Kontinuum sexueller Gewalterfahrungen von Frauen jedoch klar hervor.
Zurück zur Kritik
Eine naheliegende Frage an Coopers Vorlesungen lautet: Verknüpfen sich die patriarchale Mikroökonomie der Haushalte und die antistaatlichen Vigilanten und Big-Tech-Milliardäre gegenwärtig zu einer präventiven Konterrevolution der bestehenden Eigentumsverhältnisse? Cooper verweigerte solche Zeitdiagnosen während ihres Aufenthalts in Frankfurt jedoch mehrfach und wollte gerade keine voreiligen Schlüsse ziehen. So verlangt die von ihr dargestellte Übereinstimmung von Logiken und Strukturen des Eigentums in verschiedenen Dimensionen weiterhin nach Deutung. Um diese Deutung vollziehen zu können, braucht es wohl eine gründlichere Kritik von Vorstellungen des allgemeinen Fortschritts und der Regression, als sie weite Teile der Kritischen Theorie Frankfurter Prägung in den letzten Jahrzehnten formuliert haben.
Es bleibt zu hoffen, dass mit der bevorstehenden Publikation von Coopers Vorlesungen in Buchform auch eine solche Gesellschaftstheorie einen Schritt näher rückt. Sie könnte – das versprechen die drei Frankfurter Abende – wirklich eine unverzichtbare Kraft zur Analyse und damit auch für den Kampf gegen den ungleichzeitigen, seltsam anachronistisch erscheinenden Faschismus unserer Zeiten sein.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trum.title: Inside the Trump Administration’s War on the International Criminal Court
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trum.author: Ashley Gate
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trum.text:
A New World Order
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has once again attacked the global system of laws, norms, and principles instituted to place limits on international armed violence. Advocating for a return to might-makes-right barbarism during a keynote speech on Friday, Rubio threatened to use military force against the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities. Warning that if the ICC was “foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their city’s charters against his legions. … ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”
Rubio’s effort to undermine the principles and rules that regulate the means and methods of warfare and the humanitarian protection of civilian populations, sick and wounded combatants, and prisoners of war is part of the Trump administration’s wide-ranging effort to upend the rules-based international order that the U.S. has championed — but often failed to abide by — since World War II.
Speaking before the conservative Federalist Society at the National Lawyers Convention in Washington, D.C., Rubio disparaged the ICC as a “fake court” and “an unelected world tribunal, which claims to supersede the laws and constitutions of sovereign states, even those who never signed up for it.”
Rubio’s tirade was the latest salvo in a long-running campaign against the ICC by President Donald Trump’s administration, which has vowed to cripple the court. In October, after former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, Trump — who has relentlessly campaigned for the award — was enraged and derided the South African jurist as “a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of.”
Hours after the award was announced, the U.S. imposed sanctions on the ICC. These latest sanctions are intended to turn the judicial organ into an economic pariah. They prohibited the court from conducting dollar-denominated transactions, froze its U.S.-based assets, and barred the judicial body from using the U.S. banking system or working with American institutions — effectively blacklisting the court.
The ICC was created by the international community to investigate and prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and the crime of aggression — when one country uses armed force against another without legal justification. The Hague, Netherlands-based court is unique as a permanent judicial organ capable of prosecuting anyone, infantry soldiers and sitting heads of state alike, for humanity’s gravest crimes if they are committed in the territories of its 125 member states. The ICC is critically a court of last resort that will only intervene when domestic jurisdictions either fail to hold their own service members and political leaders accountable, or when state parties to the court call for an investigation.
While the Trump administration’s timing in sanctioning the ICC was notable, this latest strike against the court is just one facet of the Trump administration’s yearslong campaign to — in the words of Rubio’s State Department — “dismantle” it. The effort dates back to 2020, when the first Trump administration imposed sanctions on ICC officials after the court opened an investigation into alleged U.S. war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Afghanistan.
Overturned by the Biden administration in 2021, the first round of U.S. sanctions against the court were replaced last February by a new series targeting the court’s chief prosecutor, its two deputy prosecutors, and six of its judges. All of these judges had either investigated the actions of U.S. nationals in Afghanistan or were part of the ICC’s decision to issue arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for their co-perpetration of “the war crime of starvation” and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Though the litany of prior U.S. sanctions against the court impacted the lives of those nine individuals and their families — cutting them off from their bank accounts, emails, and blocking their travel — the actions were piecemeal and did not fully upend the work of the court.
Now, all of the ICC’s U.S.-based partner organizations have six months to completely cut ties with the court or face legal retribution. What’s more, since the current global economic system is built upon the U.S. dollar, international — particularly European — organizations often preemptively abide by U.S. sanctions even if their workings fall completely outside of America’s jurisdiction. For example, when the French company Axa terminated its life and health insurance contracts with the ICC on October 1, the insurer reportedly cited the escalating campaign by the U.S. against the court.
Absent the implementation of effective countermeasures — like amending and enforcing the EU Blocking Statute, which can shield EU individuals and businesses from “unlawful” third-country sanctions — this latest move by the U.S. may not kill the ICC, but it will cut off the judicial organ’s blood supply.
Victors’ Justice?
For over 80 years, the U.S. has enjoyed the privilege of proscribing — and not necessarily abiding by — international law. American representatives served as the chief arbiters of the post-World War II Nuremberg and Tokyo military tribunals that prosecuted Nazi and Japanese war criminals, which are seen by many in the field as the birthplaces of modern international criminal law. American arbiters, notably U.S. Supreme Court Justice Robert H. Jackson, led the victors of the Second World War as they tried and prosecuted their former adversaries for novel notions of wrongdoing, including crimes against peace and crimes against humanity. These newly defined criminal acts form the bedrock of the ICC’s jurisdiction.
At the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, all 25 major Japanese leaders were convicted, with seven receiving death sentences. Judge Radhabinod Pal of India argued for the acquittal of all 25. In his dissent, he complained that the tribunal dispensed victors’ justice. He said that America’s atomic strikes on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were among the most criminal acts of the conflict, yet immune from prosecution.
Indeed, the international criminal justice system was never intended to hold the U.S. or its allies accountable. And in the decades since, consecutive U.S. administrations have wielded the nation’s political and military strength to avoid any semblance of international legal oversight.
Although relations with the court have oscillated over the course of Democratic and Republican administrations, the U.S. has always been wary of the court’s potential jurisdiction over American nationals. From the court’s conception, in which the U.S. played a role, the global hegemon has continuously shown its disdain for the court’s territorial jurisdiction. While the ICC cannot prosecute any American nationals for their actions in the U.S., it does have jurisdiction over acts undertaken, by U.S. nationals or otherwise, within the territories of its member nations including Afghanistan, Libya, and Palestine.
Under the Clinton administration in the 1990s, the U.S. was one of only seven drafting nations to initially veto the Rome Statute — the international treaty that created the ICC — due to its concerns over the court’s territorial jurisdiction. Later, in 2002, the same year the ICC was established, the George W. Bush administration signed the Hague Invasion Act into law. The act, which is still in effect, grants the president the legal backing to use military force against the court in order to free any U.S. or allied person held or imprisoned by the ICC. The Bush administration subsequently pressured dozens of countries to agree to never transfer U.S. nationals to the ICC, and threatened to cut military assistance, cease counterterrorism operations, or cut humanitarian aid if these states did not comply. Though relations with the ICC thawed somewhat under the Obama administration in the 2010s, the U.S. has never shown a substantial interest in joining the court and has worked for years to restrict its jurisdiction.
The Trump administration’s courtwide sanctions on the ICC are, however, a far leap beyond the pressure campaigns against the court and its member states by prior U.S. administrations. While the Trump administration cares little for the thin veneer of justice that prior U.S. administrations sought to maintain, the ongoing campaign to “dismantle” the ICC is just one piece of a larger effort by the current administration to ensure the U.S. military can act with impunity.
Soon after taking office, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered a mass purge of senior judge advocates general. Among their many functions, JAGs historically educated military leaders on the laws that prohibit the use of the U.S. military in domestic law enforcement and ensured commanders were aptly informed of the international legal obligations to protect civilians and prisoners of war. When asked about the mass layoffs in February 2025, Hegseth explained that the action was taken to remove potential “roadblocks to orders that are given by a commander in chief.”
In a concerted effort to further “maximum lethality,” Trump and Hegseth additionally gutted the Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence and the broader Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response program in the early months of 2025. The budding program, which the majority of U.S combatant commanders urged Hegseth to maintain, was established in 2022 to prevent, reduce, and respond to civilian casualty incidents. Stark cuts to the program’s manpower and funding coincided with a rise in civilian casualties reported in U.S. military operations in Iran, Yemen, Somalia, and in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
When taken together, the administration’s cuts to internal legal mechanisms and policy programs intended to maintain law and protect civilians, as well as its ongoing attempts to dismantle the ICC, can be seen as two aspects of a larger campaign to eradicate all avenues of military oversight.
The Fight for Justice Will Continue
The sweeping courtwide sanctions against the ICC are formidable for the same reasons they are survivable: They aim to isolate the court from its broad system of support. The international criminal justice system depends on evidence. This evidence is not found in The Hague; it is brought to it by an array of local, national, and international investigators, researchers, watchdogs, and atrocity survivors.
The evidence needed to confirm the genocide in Palestine; the U.S. bombing of the elementary school in Minab, Iran; and the extrajudicial killings of fisherman in the Caribbean would not exist without the networks of dedicated researchers, local journalists, and courageous survivors. And the work of these people, while critical to the court’s functions, will continue, even if the court is dismantled brick by brick.
The ICC has strongly condemned the U.S. sanctions. ICC President Tomoko Akane has said that the court will “continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.” Pillay has also used the publicity stemming from her Nobel Peace Prize to showcase the court’s work. She further dedicated her award to “all the survivors of international crimes” as well as the international jurists “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign.”
In his speech on Friday, Rubio took aim at those very jurists, declaring that the U.S. would never submit to the “sterile vision of radical judges or soulless global bureaucrats.” He claimed that this “global elite” was using international law as “an instrument to advance their interests under the pretense of universal principles.” This was, in fact, a stark about-face for Rubio, who was an advocate for international law during his 14 years as a U.S. senator. He even co-sponsored a resolution encouraging other nations to support the ICC’s investigations of Russian war crimes in Ukraine.
Rubio claimed that those who advocate for the restraint of law over all nations are anti-American. “For these people — the fundamental purpose of the law, American law and international law alike, is to weaken the United States,” he claimed. “It is to hinder the American government’s ability to defend American interests at home and abroad.” He continued, “There is nothing — there is nothing — in our history or the history of any other great nation that requires us to recognize the authority or legitimacy of any of these ridiculous ideas.”
Prior to Rubio’s speech, however, Pillay offered up a differing vision of America. In her estimation, Americans are not the singularly self-interested, lawless, reprobates envisioned by Rubio but a people who eschew limitless violence and value humanitarian principles. “I know,” she said, “that Americans support the principle of ending impunity for these serious crimes and that they support justice and accountability.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/ai-s.title: When the U.S. Military Implemented AI, Civilian Deaths Rose
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/ai-s.author: Namir Shabibi
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/ai-s.text:
This story is published in collaboration with Airwars.
On a balmy night in 2019, 35-year-old Barakat was on his way home, driven by friends through the ancient, mountainous Syrian village of Barisha, one among the previously abandoned Byzantine “Dead Cities.”
“I was with my best friends. They wanted to drop me off at home,” the father of five later told NPR. Barakat and his two companions had finished their day’s work as agricultural laborers at an olive press. “We had pumpkin seeds and bought coffee on the road and were having fun.”
Unknown to them, a fateful military operation was occurring nearby. Three hundred meters away, a team of U.S. special forces was raiding the compound of Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.
As the attack unfolded, most U.S. surveillance and reconnaissance assets were trained on the compound itself. Yet, known to few at the time, a new set of artificial eyes had been introduced to U.S. warfare in Iraq and Syria. Computer vision target detection, part of the Pentagon’s algorithmic warfare program known as Project Maven, enabled the military to recognize enemy personnel and vehicles through AI-assisted fusion and analysis of images and video.
As Barakat’s vehicle headed south through Barisha, Maven’s AI detected a vehicle that the U.S. military’s human eyes had missed. The ground commander then proceeded to call in the attack.
“At that moment, the helicopters arrived. Suddenly, we were hit. I didn’t know what was going on. I was just trying to escape death,” Barakat told NPR. His right arm was blown off, with his left hand partially disabled. His friends, Khaled Mustafa Qurmo and Khaled Abdel Majid Qurmo, were killed.
The U.S. military ultimately rejected Barakat’s claim of harm. The results of a second Pentagon review, opened after an NPR investigation, were never released.
A spate of articles have hailed this as the year of AI warfare — from Ukrainian drones to Israel’s algorithmic decision support systems. A recent project that I worked on tracked how the rapid and potentially dangerous introduction of AI is transforming every part of the “kill chain.”
The AI-powered attack on Barakat may have occurred seven years ago, but new research has shown that many of these systems had been fielded years earlier than previously known, prompting questions about the extent of artificial intelligence’s role in historical attacks — and how it has already impacted civilian harm.
Maven’s Dawn
The role of Maven in the 2019 Baghdadi attack was only revealed this year in journalist Katrina Manson’s book “Project Maven,” which charts the development of U.S. algorithmic warfare through the program of the same name.
Project Maven sought to create the algorithms and platforms to fuse real-time data from multiple feeds — among them drones, radar, satellites, and text — to conduct detect threats, run pattern-of-life analysis, and track targets, in the service of accelerating military targeting.
The U.S. military initially tapped Google as a technology partner for Project Maven. But Google pulled out in 2018, following protests about its involvement in AI targeting, and Palantir stepped in.
Maven’s most revolutionary aspects were twofold: the creation of a “single visualization tool” — in this case, Palantir’s Maven Smart System — to house the feeds, fuse them and turbocharge decision-making, better known as “decision support systems.”
The second transformative aspect was the training of AI algorithms on vast amounts of images and full motion video generated from drone surveillance and other aerial and space-based sensors — a collaborative effort involving multiple defense contractors, initially led by the Pentagon. Maven algorithms would then be deployed into conflict theaters and applied to data streams to detect objects or targets, in technology known as “computer vision.”
Since their introduction to the Iraq and Syria conflicts in December 2017, as reported by Manson, just how many of the U.S. strikes undertaken were aided by Project Maven algorithms remains classified. But some analysis is possible.
December 2017 also saw the introduction of Maven AI to Somalia, at Baledogle Airfield where U.S. special forces were stationed, according to Manson’s reporting. At that point, the U.S. had run a covert campaign of special force raids, kidnappings, and drone strikes in Somalia for over a decade, targeting insurgent groups opposed to its allies — most prominently al-Shabab.
Maven’s AI models were first trained on thousands of hours of drone footage from the country. Its integration lead, Colin Carroll, told Manson that Somalia was “more of a free-for-all” than other higher-profile American conflicts at the time, such as Iraq, Syria, and Afghanistan. Manson writes that “the operational risks of messing up weren’t as high,” and that Maven’s detection mistakes were “how crews got better.”
The initial aim wasn’t accuracy: Maven’s algorithms got its detections wrong more often than not, as Manson reported. Instead, the goal was to get analysts used to having their jobs made easier by the tireless, unblinking stare of computer vision. And it was a major step to the ultimate prize of getting the broader military hooked on AI — a goal that U.S. military planners appear to have met.
Earlier this year, the U.S. deputy secretary of defense wrote to Pentagon leaders to announce that Palantir’s Maven Smart System would be made a program of record, locking in use of the technology across the U.S. military.
The Pentagon remains tight-lipped about AI’s role in given strikes, save for occasional authorized leaks or disclosures to select journalists. Therefore establishing the role of AI in civilian harm in a large enough sample of cases to draw significant conclusions is nigh impossible.
But data from the civilian harm watchdog Airwars — which has tracked alleged U.S. strikes in Somalia since 2007 — gives some understanding of what happened after computer vision was integrated into U.S. targeting.
In the two years up to the introduction of Maven in December 2017, Airwars documented 64 strikes attributed to U.S. forces in Somalia. In the two years after, that number rose to 153.
This unsurprisingly coincided with a spike in civilians being harmed. In the 64 strikes in 2016 and 2017, Airwars documented a minimum of 25 civilians killed and a further eight injured. In the two years after the introduction of Maven, the civilian kill count rose to a minimum of 79 — a more than threefold increase.
There were other factors that contributed toward these trends. Shortly before Maven was fielded in 2017, President Donald Trump designated part of the country as an “area of active hostilities.” Previously, any U.S. strike in Somalia required near certainty that the intended target was present and civilians would not be harmed, but these rules were loosened. The Trump administration also reordered the military structure, making it easier for strikes to be signed off lower down the chain of command. At the same time, private contractors came to be used more extensively.
But this dramatic increase in strikes is consistent with the goals of Project Maven — which include finding more targets, and accelerating the targeting cycle.
At the very least, there is no evidence, as advocates claim, that the introduction of AI reduced harm or made targeting more accurate. In the two years before Maven’s introduction to Somalia, civilians were reported killed or injured in roughly 1 in 7 alleged U.S. strikes. In the two years after, that rose to more than 1 in 5.
In striking similarity to Barakat’s case, less than a year after Maven’s deployment in Somalia, on August 2, 2018, U.S. Africa Command struck and killed four individuals it claimed were “terrorists” in a vehicle. Amnesty International found that three civilians had been killed, prompting the command to declassify its assessment in a disclosure to The Intercept — revealing the military didn’t know the identities of those killed.
“Critical Juncture”
This week could mark a decisive moment for the use of artificial intelligence in war. At the United Nations conference on Certain Conventional Weapons, nations will decide on adopting a mandate to begin negotiations on a new treaty to regulate autonomous weapons.
“We are at a critical juncture,” said Nicole van Rooijen, executive director of the group Stop Killer Robots, a campaign group. “The vast majority of states worldwide are in favor of a new legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons systems.”
“The first and important step in setting norms for the limits of AI-enabled, accelerated use of force is the mandate to negotiate legally binding rules for autonomous weapon systems,” said Elke Schwarz, a professor of political theory at Queen Mary University of London.
Target identification AI models, such as Maven, would not be covered by current negotiations since the U.N. definition of autonomous weapons demands that a single system both autonomously select and strike a target.
“There is a whole separate [UN] process for AI in the military domain,” van Rooijen said, “and [for that] we are nowhere near a treaty process.”
What played out in Somalia in the years after Maven’s introduction — a surge in the number of strikes and associated civilian harm — is similar to trends tracked in other recent military confrontations by actors known to use AI-powered systems.
The joint U.S.–Israeli attack on Iran ushered in a new era of AI-powered warfare. In the initial 40-day assault, the U.S. and Israel declared they struck more than 17,000 targets — a pace of warfare unparalleled in modern conflict. Airwars found that on every single day, Iranian civilians were reported killed or injured, in a total of 264 tracked civilian harm incidents.
In Somalia, the current Trump administration has already launched nearly four times the number of airstrikes than that of the Biden administration in its entire period in office, with reports of grave consequences for civilians. Last November, a U.S. airstrike reportedly killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children. No investigation appears to have been launched into the attack and, when asked by The Guardian, U.S. officials declined to provide its casualty assessment of the incident.
How machine-learning algorithms have contributed to targeting errors is compounded by misleading statements by militaries using AI.
One such case was U.S. Central Command’s response to a March 2026 investigation by Airwars and The Independent into the first known victim of an airstrike in which the use of AI-assisted targeting was acknowledged. The military command claimed that it had “no way of knowing” whether the strike in Iraq had relied on machine-learning algorithms, despite its chief technology officer initially claiming that it had.
Next Chapter in AI Warfare
Meanwhile, another, quieter development is underway that seems poised to further transform AI-powered warfare. Initiated by the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, the U.S. military is planning to embrace more complex versions of already-fraught computer vision models.
The “first generation” of models applied AI object detection algorithms to images and video feeds. However, in the “next chapter,” the NGA and private contractors have been training models to spot anomalies, thus detecting not just known threats but also potential ones.
As the NGA director explained last year, it could be an adversary truck that’s out of place, or a weapons manufacturing facility that has become very busy or fallen quiet.
“Anomaly detection,” as it is known, takes computer vision one step further, by deciphering objects or targets from imagery and then applying machine reasoning to a scene to determine whether changes indicate potential threatening activity.
But computer vision-based targeting models have been plagued by inaccuracy, and therefore risks of civilian harm.
When deployed in new terrain, and where uncertain environmental conditions hinder its abilities to recognize and flag objects, the first generation of Maven models exhibited a detection accuracy below 30 percent, according to Manson’s book. At times it was less than 10 percent.
Treaty process aside, the distinction between autonomous weapons — narrowly defined — and AI-powered target identification may be one without a meaningful difference. In 2024, a Maven military exercise aimed at achieving 1,000 targeting decisions in an hour, which translates per operator as a decision to select or dismiss a target every 72 seconds.
When decision support systems serve targeting intelligence to military analysts at such intensity, the human in the loop becomes meaningless, argues Schwarz, the political theory professor.
“The use of AI target identification systems in recent conflicts in the Middle East has accelerated targeting to the point where no human decision-maker in the loop can make a truly meaningful decision, thereby becoming the proverbial cog-in-the-(killing)-machine,” she said.
“In creating an illusion of human judgment, AI-enabled targeting systems are perhaps an even more problematic technology than fully autonomous ones.”
In response to questions from Airwars and The Intercept, a Palantir spokesperson said Maven’s “superior technology is critical to both deterrence, the avoidance of wars, and the protection of civilians in the case of war.”
“Thanks to [Maven Smart System],” the spokesperson continued, “the U.S. military is now better able to protect the American people from those that seek to harm us, and is better prepared, if necessary, to win wars in a responsible, precise, and technologically-dominant manner.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
