https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Make America Function Again!
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Make America Function Again!
Who is going to fix all the things the Republicans, corporations, and tech titans broke?
The thing about bills is that they always come due. Americans are starting to see the true price of years of Republican malfeasance, corporate greed, and rushed reliance on unproven artificial intelligence systems. That price looks like e-mail outages. It looks like nationwide flight ground stops. It looks like data breaches, malware attacks, and the enshittification of every product, good, or service available for purchase.
America is not a failed state—not yet at least. In the scholarship, a “failed state” is one that has lost its monopoly on the legitimate use of force, and one that cannot provide basic public services. We’re not there yet; our extrajudicial murder force, ICE, still technically acts under the color of government authority. And the government, at the federal as well as state and local levels, still has the ability to provide services: We can maintain the electrical grid, support a transportation network, and (mostly) deliver clean drinking water to those lucky enough to have homes and not live in Michigan. We just screw up the delivery of those services with increasing and alarming frequency.
The United States is not failed, but it’s far from functional. We’re a nation held together by duct tape and super glue. Everybody can see the cracks forming, and people are starting to realize that there is nobody minding the store. There are a few heroic individuals holding their fingers in the dam, and we’re all just hoping the dam doesn’t break today.
Everyone knows the broad contours of how we got here. Republicans run for office on the claim that government cannot work, and then spend their time in power destroying government just to prove that they were right. Neoliberals help Republicans by ceding critical government functions to the private sector, which in turn ignores the public good in an all-consuming chase for greater margins and profits. Occasionally things get so bad that the people elect leaders who are modestly responsible—who fix things just enough that the next guy (and it’s pretty much always a guy) can come in and complain about taxes and Black people and get elected to wreck the government again.
The latest version of this cycle has been especially damaging because the second Trump administration was captured by people who had a plan to destroy the government (Project 2025), and Trump then went ahead and empowered Elon Musk as the chainsaw-wielding destructor. With a truly breathtaking lack of knowledge or care, Musk did serious harm to the functioning of the government by firing career professionals who actually understood how everything worked. Everybody can complain about the incompetent rogue’s gallery of cabinet secretaries Trump has appointed, but it is the loss of these institutional experts that has done the most damage to the United States’s ability to work properly. The grounding of every plane in the country is just one of the more obvious consequences of Musk and his DOGE initiative, but there are many others.
Musk is also the bridge between the dysfunction of our government and the dysfunction of our society more generally, because he is one of the eight to 10 oligarchs who have amassed power at an unbelievable scale. We live in a world where if one of these guys (and once again, they’re all guys) has a bad day, everybody has a bad day. If one of them decides to bump chips with a spy, entire industries can be manipulated. If one of them changes the algorithm, our whole perception of reality can be warped. We have global “key man risk.”
And then there’s the tech these oligarches have helped create. The problem is not that we’re reliant on technology; humans have always relied on technology, whether that technology was a spearpoint or a fish hook or Uber Eats. The problem is that the tech is no longer made to be reliable. The tech is made to make money. Everything is designed either to break or become obsolete so we have to buy a new thing.
Then that nondurable tech is integrated into a bunch of other nondurable tech so that if one thing breaks it can cause a cascade of failures. Somebody introduces a bug into a hardware system, and suddenly we cannot access our bank accounts. Somebody installs a new router, and suddenly the airplanes cannot fly. Somebody hacks into a software program and suddenly all the refrigerators in the supermarket stop working.
Oh, and just in case you think I am merely listing petty inconveniences, the National Security Agency’s internal communication system went down while I was writing this.
The monopolies controlled by the oligarchs and the integration of their tech into everything we use combine to destroy our system resiliency. If one system fails, entire systems fail. The tech bros always claim to have various contingencies, but because of conglomeration, we don’t have backups for when those contingencies fail.
On top of all of this, these same oligarchs are pushing to incorporate artificial intelligence into everything. This is a technology that few people understand, and worse, the ones who do understand it are warning us that they can’t control it. We’re also using the AI to replace human workers, so when the AI breaks, our only choice is to ask the AI how to fix it. Wonderful world we’re building here.
All of this political, corporate, and technological dysfunction has a natural endpoint: People will get hurt; people will suffer. Some might eventually die. Hell, we have managed to bring back measles. There is no clearer indication that things no longer work the way they should than people getting sick from a disease previous generations worked hard to eradicate.
What naturally follows from this gross incompetence is social unrest. Once people can’t reliably go about their daily lives without hassle, the pitchforks and torches come out. We’re seeing a little of this already. In the midterm elections, people who were willing to suffer Trump’s racism, misogyny, thievery, buffonery, incompetence, and incontinence decided to vote for Democrats for the first time in their lives because they couldn’t afford gas and eggs.
The affordability crisis is a symptom of the deeper rot in our society. Things don’t work. Things are expensive and still don’t work. Things that worked yesterday might not work tomorrow—and the update you’ve been forced to download to make it work might brick your whole system.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
A political leader could rise by running on a platform restoring functionality to our daily lives. I’d hope that such a leader would be a progressive, but I’ll remind readers that fascists and authoritarians have earned a lot of supporters over the course of history simply by making things, like trains, work. Running on an agenda of making things work properly is usually very popular, and it gets more popular the crappier things are.
I also want to be clear that I’m not talking about an institutionalist platform—I have lived through the Joe Biden era of restoring competency to government and found it lacking. I’m talking about a radical, populist platform that improves people’s daily lives and kneecaps the kleptocrats running the joint. Everybody’s flights didn’t get canceled because Sean Duffy is an incompetent boob (though he is an incompetent boob). Everybody’s flights got canceled because there was some stupid problem caused by our long failure to invest in our infrastructure—and when there was a problem, rich people were able to opt out of the entire system and charter their way home. Markwayne Mullen was literally able to fly to a football game (football teams also saw their travel prioritized, for honestly no good reason) while regular people were still sleeping in airports with their children.
Making America functional again means prioritizing the needs of people over the needs of investors. It means paying more attention to purchasing power than to quarterly profits. It means valuing durability over planned obsolescence. It means busting monopolies and restoring consumer protections. It means testing experimental technologies before they are approved for wide-scale use instead of treating every American as a beta tester or lab rat. It means being able to fill a prescription provided by your doctor without having to spend two hours on hold with your insurance company. And, for the love of humanity, it means regulating AI.
It’s one thing for stuff to break. Entropy is undefeated, but enshittification is a choice. Things are breaking because a small cadre of people have decided it’s more profitable for things to break than it is for things to last. We’re not suffering because of the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune. We’re suffering because we are paying for the fortunes of others. My computer is more expensive because AI is buying up all the RAM. My water is more expensive because AI is sucking up all the water. And all the while my e-mail sometimes doesn’t work, probably because of some AI assistant I never even asked for.
You know how most zombie movies depict “the day” the zombie plague becomes active and society is destroyed? There are always planes falling out of the sky and car crashes and fires, and the hero ends up surviving because they were functionally off the grid that day by some happenstance? The problem with these movies is that societies don’t collapse in a day (well, maybe Pompeii, but that’s an exception). They fall apart over a long period of time. Things stop working; people adjust and make workarounds, and soon enough nobody can remember what it was like when that thing worked. And within a generation or two, you go from reading a scroll in a Roman library to using the paper with the weird markings on them for kindling.
We need to make America functional again—before nobody remembers how to fix it.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: How College Students Helped Turn Texas Blue
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Lajward Zahra
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
How College Students Helped Turn Texas Blue
After years of Republican dominance, Texas Democrats won statewide with overwhelming support from young voters.
By the time Beto O’Rourke arrived at Sam Houston State University in Huntsville, Texas on October 14, Alyssa Rodriguez had spent weeks preparing for his visit. “My phone at one point was overheating from all the calls I had,” she recalled.
Rodriguez, a campus organizing intern for O’Rourke’s political advocacy group, Powered by People, and president of the university’s revived College Democrats chapter, helped coordinate his visit. She worried that only 100 students would attend the event, located in deep-red Walker County. People often think “no one’s gonna change that county,” said Rodriguez. But then an estimated 600 attendees turned up, a harbinger of student turnout at the polls the next month.
Three weeks later, Texas Democrats won their first statewide elections in more than three decades. James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton for the US Senate, while Gina Hinojosa unseated Governor Greg Abbott, becoming the state’s first Latina governor. Young voters overwhelmingly backed the Democratic candidates. According to the ABC News Voter Poll, 79 percent of Texas voters ages 18 to 29 supported Talarico, and only about half supported Democratic Senate candidate Collin Allred in 2024.
O’Rourke, the former El Paso congressman who came within three percentage points of unseating Republican Senator Ted Cruz in 2018, spent much of the year traveling to college campuses across Texas. He founded Powered by People in December 2019, shortly after ending his presidential campaign, to mobilize volunteers and support Democratic candidates across the state. The organization began focusing on college campuses in 2024 and relies on volunteers to register students to vote.
At Rice University, Matteo Devries, a junior studying political science and a campus intern for Powered by People, spent the semester staffing voter registration tables and helping organize O’Rourke’s October 22 visit to Rice in Houston.
When Democrats swept Texas’s statewide races on November 3, Devries watched the results with his cousin, who worked on political organizing in Texas, and other family members. “Oh my God, it was exhilarating. I felt incredible,” he recalled.
O’Rourke described Powered by People’s organizing strategy as one centered on maintaining personal contact with voters. Rather than passing newly registered voters’ information to a campaign or political party, volunteers ask permission to stay in touch directly, he said. They help students determine what identification they need, locate polling places, and make plans to vote.
During this midterm election cycle, Powered by People scheduled more than 130 events across 22 Texas cities.
“I’ve been on the road every single week of this semester and every week of the last semester,” O’Rourke said. “I’m there to answer students’ questions, to engage in conversations,” he added.
Those conversations, O’Rourke told me, ranged from rising prices and college tuition to the war in Iran and the difficulty of determining what information to trust on social media. He emphasized the importance of meeting young voters in person, describing those interactions as a critical alternative to the isolation and polarization of online political discourse.
Before the election, O’Rourke presciently pointed to a changing political environment for Texas Democrats. “I think the level of interest on the part of young voters is as high as I’ve ever seen it,” he said. “I also just think that the conditions are different and better for Democrats than I’ve ever seen them.”
He pointed to frustration with the Trump administration and high prices, alongside the slate of promising Democratic candidates, including Talarico and Hinojosa.
For the 2026 elections, Democrats recruited candidates for all 150 Texas House districts, including seats where Republicans had previously run unopposed. In 2018, by comparison, Democrats left 20 state and federal races uncontested.
Early voting numbers offered signs of heightened political participation. More than 7.7 million Texans cast ballots during early voting, setting a new midterm record. In Harris County, more than 104,000 people voted in person on the first day of early voting; only 63,188 voted on the opening day in 2018, when O’Rourke challenged Ted Cruz for the Senate.
At Rice, Gretchen Soika, 19, met the former congressman during his October 22 visit. Soika said reproductive healthcare and abortion access were at the top of her mind when she cast her midterm ballot. Soika remembers O’Rourke’s 2018 Senate run as one of her earliest introductions to Texas politics. His campaign signs and stickers seemed to be everywhere. “It’s inspiring to see that these people are still around and still trying to flip Texas eight years later,” she said.
Before the election, Soika described a renewed sense of optimism among her classmates, many of whom were voting for the first time That optimism persisted even among students who recognized the possibility of another Republican victory. Soika described conversations in which classmates expressing doubts about Democratic prospects were quickly interrupted by friends unwilling to entertain defeat. “Don’t say that. It needs to happen,” she recalled students responding to expressions of pessimism.
At Sam Houston State, Rodriguez described a similar sense of urgency, though her conversations with students often center on the financial pressures they face. For Rodriguez, those concerns are particularly personal. She attended Title I public schools and grew up in a low-income family that relied on SNAP and Section 8 housing assistance.
Affordability and uncertainty about life after graduation have emerged as major concerns among her classmates. “I might have to live with my parents forever because there seems to be no other option for me right now,” Rodriguez said, describing a fear among young people confronting rising costs and a difficult job market.

“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But political organizing has given Rodriguez opportunities she once struggled to imagine. As a child, she dreamed of entering politics and wanted to feel important enough for elected officials to speak with her. Now she had helped bring those conversations to students at her own university.
“I think he brought so much of that passion and of the optimism that’s been so clearly missing from this campus when it came to midterm elections, or any elections for that matter,” Rodriguez said of O’Rourke’s visit.
Devries described a similar sense of optimism surrounding O’Rourke’s visit to Rice. “A lot of people that came out were super excited to go vote. They were super excited to meet Beto,” he said.
At the weekly voter registration tables he staffed, Devries encountered students who increasingly believed their votes could make a difference in Texas. “I think the atmosphere was more lively than I’ve ever seen it before,” he said.
In a follow-up after the election, O’Rourke said Powered by People had 113,000 voters in its program this year. According to its preliminary figures provided by O’Rourke, about 70 percent of the participating voters aged 18 to 29 cast ballots, compared with 35 percent of young voters statewide.
“We made a significant difference in close state house races,” O’Rourke said, pointing to the organization’s work in 12 Texas House districts that flipped Democratic. “I feel great about it. It’s about people power, literally thousands of volunteers taking the time to meet and help turn out more than 100,000 young Texans.”
And on election night, as the first results from Texas came in, Devries was watching intently. “Damn,” he recalled thinking. “It’s actually happening.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Annabel Keenan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a new chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.
“This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”
The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.
The works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.
A selection of pieces from the collection is currently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.
“Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” says Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”
The international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka says. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.
Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.
“[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle says. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”
The donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman said in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”
The NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle says. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Working mothers face widespread discrimination in London’s commercial art world, report finds
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Anny Shaw
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The contemporary art world has become increasingly adept at putting feminism, gender equality and the politics of care at the centre of its public-facing programming. Galleries mount exhibitions exploring women's experiences, champion female artists and engage with questions of representation and social justice. But how far do those values extend to the women working behind the scenes?
Not far at all, according to the first ever peer-reviewed study on motherhood and discrimination in London’s commercial art world, published today by the European Journal of Cultural Studies and The Art Working Parents Alliance.
Based on a survey of 50 art world employees working across the UK capital’s galleries and auction houses, including 12 in-depth interviews, research by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi exposes a workplace culture in which mothering children often comes at considerable professional cost. As the report puts it: “Becoming a parent is at the root of the glass ceiling, and for many, it represents the glass cliff.”
Three-quarters of survey respondents say becoming a parent has negatively affected their career progression, while more than one in five say they had been explicitly denied promotion. One woman was told she was ineligible for promotion while on maternity leave—a breach of UK law. Just 54% received enhanced maternity pay, compared with a national workplace average of 74.1%.
And these problems are not limited to smaller companies. “We assumed this would affect small art galleries with between five and 20 staff, but we found that big, multi-national galleries are also failing,” McMillan says. As the report notes: “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”
Culture of fear and secrecy
Roberts-Komireddi believes that the “culture of secrecy” that enshrouds much of the art market—where financial transactions, benefits and networks are opaque and rarely disclosed—contributes to the discrimination women face when they become mothers. “Opacity really serves certain individuals and maintains this sense of fear, which was something I found particularly startling when we did our 12 in-depth interviews,” she says. “Fear and perceived retribution pervade these workplaces and women’s relationships to these workplaces.”
That fear is often felt as soon as women announce their pregnancies. The report documents, among other instances, a pregnant woman being made redundant while experiencing a high-risk pregnancy, an employer attempting to dissolve a pregnant employee’s role and use the money to hire a new salesperson and a woman who miscarried returning to her desk immediately after a hospital appointment because she feared taking time off would damage her career. One interviewee describes feeling that by becoming pregnant she was making herself “vulnerable and less valuable”.
The findings also point to a deeper contradiction within an industry that publicly champions equality but often operates according to an unforgiving model of constant availability, international travel and after-hours networking. The art critic and curator Hettie Judah, who is a co-founder of The Art Working Parents Alliance, describes the colliding of 6pm private views with bedtime routines as the “witching hour” clash.
The difficulties are not confined to maternity leave itself. For many, the return to work can prove more damaging. Interviewees describe coming back to find their responsibilities have been redistributed, their relationships with artists and clients disrupted, or their standing within the gallery diminished. One woman discovered that a colleague who had covered her maternity leave had been given half her role, along with the artists she had spent years representing. Another returned from leave to find there was no desk for her in the gallery’s new office.
Lack of HR
Crucially, the report reveals the lack of formal HR structures across the commercial art sector. Only half of the respondents worked for galleries with dedicated HR staff, while just 30 of the 50 said their workplace had a specific maternity or parental leave policy. In some cases, employees were left to research their own entitlements, negotiate their packages and even draft policies themselves. The report’s authors say that a lack of professional HR expertise contributed to instances of discriminatory practice and breaches of the UK Equality Act.
The consequences can be far-reaching. For many women, the choice has been stark: find a way to accommodate the demands of motherhood or compromise their careers. Three-quarters of the women interviewed made changes to their careers after becoming pregnant, with some moving into freelance or independent work, taking less senior positions or leaving the industry altogether. Only a third of survey respondents were offered flexible working on their return, while half were expected to be in the office four or five days a week. One interviewee described the culture as one in which “presentism is more important than doing the work”.
Class and wealth
The role of class and wealth is key in shaping these experiences. The report notes how some senior figures have access to live-in nannies, au pairs and domestic help, leaving them less attuned to the financial and practical pressures facing employees who must balance childcare with demanding working hours. One interviewee stated that the management team “all had night nurses, and you know, people helping at night. So, for them to understand that you’d had three hours of interrupted sleep and were expected to be at an opening, and a dinner, get home at 12:30 and then get up at 4:30 again, was impossible”.
For those on more modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make evening events and travel particularly difficult to sustain. The report suggests that the more junior and precarious the employee, the greater the likelihood of experiencing discrimination—and the fewer resources they have to challenge it.
These divisions are not simply a question of wealth, however. They also complicate assumptions about gender solidarity within an industry where women make up a significant proportion of the workforce, but senior positions are often occupied by men. As Roberts-Komireddi points out, the assumption that women will necessarily support other women can be misleading—some of the more surprising testimonies in the report describe male directors showing greater sympathy towards pregnant employees than their female counterparts.
These accounts suggest that the treatment of working mothers is shaped not simply by the gender of those in positions of authority, but by a wider workplace culture in which employees have little power to challenge established practices. Indeed, the report argues that discriminatory treatment is widespread, identifying breaches of the Equality Act in the experiences of all the women interviewed. Yet legal cases rarely make it to an employment tribunal. “In the UK, up until 1 October this year, women only had three months to bring a case to tribunal, which is not a lot of time, particularly if you’re about to give birth,” Roberts-Komireddi says. “There’s a reluctance to go down that route because it’s a long, tiring, expensive process.”
Looking ahead, the report’s authors hope to set best practice in the art industry. “If you look at huge corporations like Google, they have changed their policies in order to retain and attract mothers who make excellent staff—we could learn a lot from them,” Roberts-Komireddi says.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Van Eyck’s genius, New York auctions, Cosimo de Medici’s wine cooler—podcast
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ben Luke, Alexander Morrison, David Clack
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
One of the year’s most hotly anticipated exhibitions, Van Eyck: The Portraits, opens at the National Gallery in London this weekend after a rapturous response from the critics. Uniting all 10 of the Flemish master’s surviving portraits, including the one miraculous drawing attributed to him, it is truly a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Ben Luke takes a tour of the show with its co-curator, Emma Capron.
It is auction week in New York, with hundreds of millions of dollars of art coming under the hammer. Ben asks Melanie Gerlis, an art market columnist for the Financial Times and The Art Newspaper, about the week’s results so far.
And this episode’s Work of the Week is a maiolica wine cooler, made in 1574 by the workshop of Flaminio Fontana, in Urbino. It was made for Cosimo I de Medici, who is the subject of a small exhibition that opened this week at the Wallace Collection in London. Ben speaks to the curator of the display, Julia Van Zandvoort, about this remarkable piece.
- Van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027
- Cosimo I de’ Medici: Art and Dynasty, Wallace Collection, London, until 21 March 2027

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Finding, acquiring and showing off: how rich buyers use social media to build art collections
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Aimee Dawson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, shows that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.
Starting
While the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report says.
The data also shows that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report says. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”
Learning
When it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents said they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).
A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.
Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also showed that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.
Buying
The importance of online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among new collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.
But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.
Sharing
The report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report says. While the data showed that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".
“Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”
When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.
The auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the New York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.
Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not announced a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.
The uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).
Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).
The previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.
Nazi-era shadow
Sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”
News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the New York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?
In response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.
Urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.
Comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the New York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.
Then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.
Following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a new owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”
The terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.
As a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to New York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.
McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.
This eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.
The museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.
Objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.
The unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a new model of partnership”.
Five historic artefacts
This week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.
The items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.
The earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.
The other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.
The three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.
The five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a new display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.
However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Conservation of the ‘Sistine Chapel of the Andes’ nears completion
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Graciela Ibáñez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
One of Bolivia’s oldest churches, known as the “Sistine Chapel of the Andes” due to its impressive murals, is nearing completion of a conservation project focused on its roofs, stone buttresses and adobe walls—a process that began in May.
The US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level. Approximately 170km west of the city of Oruro, the church was declared a National Monument in 1960.
“The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper. This work follows restoration that took place more than a decade ago, funded by the German embassy in La Paz.
The restoration team has had to learn the church’s unique roof-building technique from locals, placing straw on top of hollow cane mats using a method that makes it more resilient. Hollow cane is hard to find in the highlands, so they needed to bring it in from Bolivia’s southernmost region of Tarija.
During the previous restoration, corrugated metal sheets had been added to extend the lifespan of the roofs, which cover 800 sq. m. This time, workers replaced the damaged sections. The project was delayed because of proteststhat blocked roads across the country in May and June, preventing the arrival of materials and postponing its completion by one month—from the end of October to the end of November.
'A complete catechesis'
Built by Augustinians between the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the church houses paintings of the Nativity, the Last Supper, the Crucifixion and the Last Judgment in a display of religious syncretism. “It’s a complete catechesis,” Matas says of the murals, which were made using natural dyes and finished in 1777.
There are also representations of the apostle Santiago (James), the church’s patron saint. Local Indigenous people identified him with Illapa, the Inca god of thunder. The style of the paintings ranges from Mannerism to 18th-century Baroque, with depictions of birds and flowers—an example of mestizo art.
“It’s very striking when you enter the church, because there isn’t any empty space,” Matas says. “Everything is painted.” The paintings even cover the baptistery and sacristy. “Most of the churches in the region have murals. Here, they have been well preserved,” she adds.
The building has a single entrance through a side wall, similar to other churches in the area, and is surrounded by an atrium with two gates. “Indigenous people weren’t used to entering the building for religious activities, so the atrium was spacious enough to accommodate those who wanted to be evangelised,” Matas says.
The bishop of Oruro, Krzysztof Białasik, was the one who submitted the restoration project to compete for US funding. Since 2001, the AFCP has financed more than 30 projects in Bolivia, including the restoration of colonial paintings, the protection of Baroque musical manuscripts and the creation of a digital catalogue—including archaeological artefacts, pre-Columbian textiles and colonial art—available to customs services to curb the illicit trafficking of these goods.
To celebrate the completion of the conservation of the church, a mass will be held in Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas with the bishop and the apostolic nuncio on 15 December.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘Napping together on the reeds, the swans appeared luminous’: Noah Forster’s best phone picture
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Grace Holliday
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Twenty-one-year-old Noah Forster had always thought swans were beautiful, but it was his girlfriend Cecilia is the one who made him really notice them. The pair began dating two years ago, but now live 70 miles apart; he is a welder in Newark-on-Trent, she is studying law in Leeds.
“The distance can be difficult, but we try to talk as much as possible,” Forster says. “It’s taken me a while to save up for a driver’s licence and car, so I have a daily walk from my home and across the River Trent to get the 6am train to work. We like to send photos of our day to each other, and I took this photo on an exceptionally cold and frosty morning in November, walking across the river to get to work. I saw these swans near the castle. Napping together on the reeds, they appeared luminous.”
“Me and you,” he wrote in a message to Cecilia, attaching the image. “I know she loves swans, but I also knew she was most likely sleeping herself!” he says.
Later, Cecilia encouraged him to submit the photo to be considered for the Smart Shot column. “I decided to keep the name of the image the same as the caption I sent to her, because it represents the calm and peaceful feeling you have when you are with someone you trust. I hope it makes others think about their special person who they feel safe with.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Tyson Fury looks back: ‘Once the Anthony Joshua fight is over, what will I do next? Walking the dog ain’t gonna cut it’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Harriet Gibsone
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Born in Manchester in 1988, Tyson Fury – known as the Gypsy King – is a former unified heavyweight world champion. He turned professional in 2008 and in 2015 defeated the long-reigning champion, Wladimir Klitschko, to claim the WBA, IBF, WBO and Ring magazine heavyweight titles. He made a comeback in 2020, and his long-awaited final fight is on 11 December against Anthony Joshua. He appears with his wife, Paris, and seven children in the docuseries At Home With the Furys. A documentary charting his life, Fury, is out on Netflix on 27 November.
This was taken when I was nine, back when I was cute, shy and poorly dressed. The jumper would have been knitted by my grandma. The hairstyle isn’t great but a lot better than what I have now. I loved boxing and I loved singing.
I come from a travelling background, but we never moved anywhere. We lived in a house in a village outside Manchester called Wilmslow that had a farm. Me and my three brothers would ride quads, build treehouses and make dens. Roaming around the countryside was a dream life for a young boy. Nobody knew where we were or what we were doing – there were times we could have died – but there were no worries about perverts getting us or anything like that.
Growing up, masculinity meant showing no emotion. We never discussed feelings or love. My dad was a big influence on me. I inherited his ability to talk, his size and aggression. But I was soft, too. I inherited that from my mother – a gentle, kind nature. I remember the first time I felt anxiety. I was six and hiding in the wardrobe. I had this awful feeling something bad was about to happen. I didn’t tell anyone and have no idea what triggered it.
I started going to the gym when I was six, just to mess around. By the time I was 14, I was taking it more seriously. I was always confident in boxing, but over time, I realised that it is not just raw aggression and violence, it’s an art form.
My family were not as enthusiastic about my ambitions as I was. Dad was a professional and bare-knuckle boxer. He tried to encourage me to get a normal job – to have a stable existence instead. Mum was the same. I didn’t listen. There was no other option for me.
All I did was box and train – so in many ways I was the world’s best kid. I didn’t go out partying, didn’t have any idiot friends. When I met Paris I knew she was the one straight away. She was 15. I was 16. We were children, really, but I told her: “I’m going to marry you.” She went: “What? I don’t even know you.” I replied: “I’m going to make you fall in love with me. I’m going to be world champion and we’re going to have all these kids.” I was right. I signed my first professional contract on the first day of our honeymoon. We were meant to have two weeks away. We left four days later as I had to come back to fight.
From as far back as I can remember, Wladimir Klitschko was the guy I wanted to beat. He was the world heavyweight champion when I was a kid. He was my target, but when I told people I would win, everyone laughed at me, as they always did. In 2015, I finally got my chance to prove them wrong. There was a lot going on in my life at the time – we’d had a miscarriage and a very close uncle had died. I was grieving, but I tried to push it to the back of my mind so I could focus on Wlad.
Then the fight came, and I beat him. That’s when the problems started. Almost immediately, I felt like I was spiralling out of control. I had no purpose. I didn’t want to be at the press conference, or celebrating. Me and the family went on holiday. “Enjoy this,” I said to Paris, “because it’s downhill from here.”
For that whole period I was screaming out for help, but everyone around me wanted to put me in a rematch. It was like I was a demon possessed and I needed a hospital rather than a ring. I was hearing voices – horrible, scary voices. At night my head was full of terrifying screams, to the extent I thought someone was in the room. Alcohol and drugs played a part, and I was also comfort eating – mainly sugar. It gave me joy, a short term sensation of happiness. But it wasn’t real. I was hurling myself into oblivion. If I left the house for more than an hour, Paris would call everyone we knew, as she thought I had gone to kill myself.
Two years later, everything changed. It was Halloween and I was dressed as a 400lb skeleton. I was drunk. But I had a moment of clarity. I watched these young people at the bar – kids at the beginning of their lives. I thought: “What am I doing here? I’ve been offered everything a person could want, and I’ve blown it all.”
Back at home, I took off the costume, got on my knees and started praying to God. I thought: “If I can get better, then I’ll be happy. I’d rather have nothing, live in a tent and be on benefits than go back to how I feel right now.” It seemed like I was on my knees for an eternity, but it was probably only 10 minutes, when suddenly I felt a change. I screamed out to Paris – she thought I was drunk – saying: “I’m going to make a comeback in the morning.” She’d heard it all before, but I was serious this time.
That was the start of the return mission. I went to a leading specialist and was diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar. I learned that you can never truly get away from mental health. You can only learn to manage and maintain. I started training with Ben Davison and working with promoter Frank Warren. Within a few months, I was back in the ring. Now I’m gearing up for the final hurrah. I’m 38 years old, at the end of my boxing life. What better way to go out with a bang, putting on a fight that people have been waiting a decade for?
Once that fight is over I have to decide: what will I do next? I need to find a job. Waking up in the morning and doing normal stuff ain’t going to cut it. Walking the dog or taking the kids to school is fantastic, but it’s not enough of a purpose to get up for. Once the kids are done with school, then what? It does play on my mind, but I can’t think about it as I have to focus on the fight.
Sometimes I forget the long distance I’ve travelled and everything I’ve had to overcome. That nine-year-old boy was just a nobody – an unknown person from wherever. But he knew he could be a boxer. That I would become a world champion is one thing, but to transcend the sport and do TV shows, publish bestselling books, sing with Robbie Williams, is another level. I am truly blessed – not only with the ability to work hard, but to keep the faith all the way.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-gov-hochul.title: NY Gov. Hochul vetoes bill that would have required AI accuracy warnings
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-gov-hochul.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-gov-hochul.text:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has vetoed a bill that would’ve required artificial intelligence platforms to proactively warn users that the information they receive may be inaccurate.
In a statement explaining her decision Friday, Hochul wrote that she supports “thoughtful, smart guardrails on AI” to protect consumers. But she said the bill was too far-reaching and would have applied to artistic or expressive content that isn’t meant to be factual — possibly running afoul of federal free-speech protections.
“[This] bill takes an inflexible one-size-fits-all approach to require notifications on all generative Al systems regardless of context and in doing so, the bill may present constitutional and pragmatic challenges,” Hochul wrote.
Hochul’s veto came after trade groups representing some of the world’s most prominent tech firms — including OpenAI and Meta — lobbied against the bill, warning of possible constitutional violations. Netflix and the Motion Picture Association also lobbied the governor on the measure, according to state disclosure records.
Assemblymember Clyde Vanel and state Sen. Kirsten Gonzalez, both Queens Democrats, introduced the bill after Meta’s AI platform hallucinated sexual harassment allegations against a number of state lawmakers in 2024, including the two of them.
The state Legislature passed the measure by a near-unanimous measure earlier this year.
Had Hochul signed the bill into law, the owner, operator or licensee of a generative AI platform would have been required to “clearly and conspicuously display a notice on the system’s user interface” warning that the system’s output “may be inaccurate.”
Some AI platforms, such as ChatGPT, already do that. The New York bill would’ve required all platforms to do so. X’s Grok, for example, includes a warning in its terms and services but not directly on the screen users see when they provide a written prompt.
Vanel said he believed that he had worked with the industry to come up with bill language that was “flexible enough to accommodate different types of platforms.” He said he’s hopeful he can work with the governor’s office to come up with some sort of compromise next year, when the state Legislature returns to Albany.
“The main thing is I hope we both agree that some sort of disclosure is important,” he said. “If we're disagreeing on the how, I can talk to the governor about that.”
Hochul has had an up and down relationship with AI companies.
Earlier this year, she unilaterally implemented a temporary moratorium on large-scale data centers, including those used by AI providers. She made it a key part of her reelection campaign, which came at a time when polls showed voters in New York and beyond were deeply skeptical of the facilities.
But she has not yet taken any action on a more-stringent moratorium that lawmakers approved earlier in the year, which is stridently opposed by tech firms.
Hochul has until the end of the year to sign or veto that bill.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Matchbooks are on fire at NYC restaurants
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
Cigarette smoking is on the decline, disposable lighters are cheap and easily available, and vapes are self-contained, and yet the humble matchbook has lit a fire in New York’s fine dining scene. Indeed, the retro collectible has made a full-fledged return as a restaurant giveaway and as an opulent piece of pocket-sized art.
At Manhattan’s buzzy small chain Dante, where the large format matchbooks boast gold leaf inlay, custom interior artwork and cost approximately $4 each to make, they had to stop handing them out at the front door. “ It was financially becoming quite burdensome,” said the restaurant’s co-founder Linden Pride. The matchbooks are now only available as a free add-on with purchase of their Negroni fragrance candle.
In addition to their classic appeal as miniature memorabilia from a nice meal, modern diners also find them attractive as tangible objects in an increasingly digitally-based world.
“I think in the digital age where, like, everything is online, people really want something to hold onto physically,” said Connor Pacharis, who late last year founded the website Matchbook Directory so he and his fellow phillumenists could have a place to congregate and swap sticks.
On social media and within the directory’s now nearly 900-user strong community share and trade matchbooks, which are prized for their aesthetic appeal and as compact reminders of real world experiences.
Indeed, most directory users are looking to acquire matchbooks from places they’ve visited but failed to nab a book from, or to determine which restaurants have matchbooks, so they can dine there.
“ I can go on my camera roll and I have 10,000 photos from one vacation,” said Pacharis, a San Diego-based product manager who recently visited New York, by far the most popular location in the directory. “But when I think about my New York trip, I don't really think about the photos I took. I think about my New York matchbook collection, and what a good time I had.”
City restaurateurs are aware of this burgeoning market of significantly young people, and have entered something of an aesthetic design race to keep up and stay competitive in a tough business.
When 19-year New York City restaurateur Joshua Boissy opened now-shuttered Greenpoint eatery Sauvage in 2016, they made multiple matchbooks, a choice which was “was totally psychotic, but, like, a really fun thing to do at the time; it was very unusual,” despite it not being the most cost effective. Although he’s yet to see anyone else do the multiple style shtick, luxury matchbooks are now far less of a surprising marketing stunt.
“The matchbook game has evolved a lot. We've been doing it for a while at each of our places, and I remember, you know, from 2011 when we opened Maison, matchbooks were not treated this way. They were all kind of very similar,” said Boissy, co-founder of the Lower East Side’s swanky cocktail lounge Tigre.
But in New York City fine dining “there’s always an upping of the game,” and others have since gotten in on the luxury matchbook craze, he said.
In addition to being a trendy and in-demand piece of branded merchandise, the fact that they are physical reminders of a good meal long after the bill has been paid makes them quite ideal from a marketing perspective.
"They serve as a lasting extension of our branding,” said KwangHo Lee, owner of fine-dining institutions One Bryant Park and Momoya, both of which boast delicately gilded books carefully tailored to evoke the same upscale aesthetic as their corresponding restaurants.
“In a digital world, having a physical keepsake to say ‘Hey’ with makes a lasting impression and keeps us top of mind,” added Jacob Hadjigeorgis, owner of the Upper West Side Southern food establishment Jacob’s Pickles, which boasts matchbooks inspired “by a little nostalgia for a time when restaurants had more personality in the small details.”

https://gothamist.com/news/attorney-gene.title: NYC, state sue Trump administration over ‘mixed-status’ federal housing assistance rule
https://gothamist.com/news/attorney-gene.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/attorney-gene.text:
New York Attorney General Letitia James and the city of New York sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Monday over a new rule that would strip federal housing assistance for families with mixed immigration status.
The state lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts alongside a coalition of 21 other attorneys general across the country, argued that the proposed rule change — which could strip assistance for 20,000 mixed-status families or around 78,100 people, many of whom are children — exceeds HUD’s authority and violates the Administrative Procedure Act.
The city lawsuit included a coalition of more than a dozen local governments and housing agencies.
The existing rule allowed families to live together in “HUD-assisted” housing if at least one family member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible non-citizen, such as a visa holder. The new rule states that every family member in that household must be a U.S. citizen or eligible non-citizen and each member must demonstrate their eligibility or risk losing their housing.
James said the new rule means that HUD will require people in federal housing programs to prove their citizenship through an “unreliable” process or even risk eviction.
“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. Denying a child that security because who they live with is cruel and indefensible,” James said in a statement. “With our country already in the throes of a housing crisis, it is outrageous that the federal government would push even more families out of their homes. This rule runs counter to our nation’s values and the very purpose of these housing programs.”
The state's lawsuit also argues that the federal rule change harms the states that signed on as plaintiffs in at least three ways: an increase in administrative costs for state agencies that report to HUD, increased spending on state social safety nets like right-to-shelter programs, and a reduction in income for state-financed housing developments that host tenants with federal subsidies.
The city lawsuit argued that tens of thousands of people would be removed from the program, including public housing and Section 8.
And as a result of removing people from their homes supported by federal assistance, the lawsuit argued the new rule would increase homelessness and shift much of these costs to house people to local governments.
In a statement, HUD Secretary Scott Turner said the rule change “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”
“This rule guarantees only American citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist,” Turner said.
The existing rule, called “proration,” was written into law by Congress in 1997, which helped reduce a family’s subsidy so it only covered the payment for eligible household members. The law explicitly specified that families “shall not” lose their benefits if an eligible family member lives in the same household.
James also said the rule would make it harder for millions of U.S. citizens to keep the housing they already qualify for because they’d have to provide their Social Security number and authorize a citizenship status check through a database.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age | Open letter
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Open letter
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times.
When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP.
This extreme wealth explosion has upended the balance of power, leaving choices that affect all of humanity to a few billionaires at the helm of a handful of corporations. The economic power of the ultra-wealthy is being used to consolidate their political power, creating a dynamic that is threatening democracy.
This dynamic of wealth and power is nothing new (the word “oligarchy” comes from ancient Greek), but its velocity and the scale of its cross-border impacts are unprecedented. A single decision made by the controlling shareholder of a multinational firm can wipe away jobs, deplete resources, or determine the course of a war.
Choices made by the ultra-rich ignore national borders as they disrupt work and home lives, inject their ideas into the public discourse, bend public policy to fit their desires, siphon revenue away from states, and damage our earth.
The power dynamic of this international oligarchy must be countered with a transnational coalition to defend democracy. To this end, we affirm three principles.
1 Fair taxation
The ultra-rich should pay taxes in proportion to their resources. As studies in many countries have shown, this is currently not the case. Myriad loopholes allow the wealthiest in the world to pay little or no income tax.
A tax floor, expressed as a percentage of personal wealth, would put an end to this situation. This idea was first developed in a report commissioned by the G20 in 2024, under the presidency of Brazil, which proposed setting an individual tax floor equal to 2% of wealth for all fortunes more than $100m.
Such an initiative would ensure that the ultra-rich would pay at least as large a share of their income in tax as the middle class – the bare minimum required to ensure that fiscal law complies with the principle of tax fairness.
This annual tax floor should be accompanied by a one-time “catch-up” tax on the wealth of the super-rich to settle the outstanding tax inequalities that have fueled the explosion of extreme wealth. If this exceptional levy took into account any taxes paid during the time period covered by the catch-up, only those ultra-rich individuals who had avoided meeting their fiscal obligations would be affected.
2 Media independence and pluralism
Information is not just another commodity, and access to it forms the bedrock of our democracies. The power of oligarchs to control information must be curtailed.
The purchase of media outlets and social platforms is one of the most glaring ways in which the ultra-rich capture power, ensuring themselves control over what is said, heard, learned and read. It is crucial to provide stronger support for public media and implement anti-concentration policies. In the age of big digital platforms, these anti-concentration policies should be designed on an international scale.
3 Decisions to develop and deploy artificial intelligence technologies must be democratized
Knowledge, artistic creation, and works of imagination assembled over centuries are being captured, processed and repackaged (often without permission!) by a handful of corporations to be resold as artificial intelligence to the very humanity that produced them. There is still time to refuse that hijacking.
Technologies associated with artificial intelligence come with astronomically high risks: the possibility of cyberattacks with lethal consequences, rapid and profound transformations of the labor market, the emergence of new forms of manipulation and disinformation, even the risk of human extinction. It would be folly to leave decisions about the deployment of these technologies in the hands of a few Silicon Valley billionaires.
In the field of information technology, the non-profit model has a proven track record. Some of the most popular applications and websites in the world, such as Wikipedia, Signal or Firefox, were developed by non-profit organizations. To build AI without oligarchs, companies working in this field should consider adopting the model of the non-profit foundation, with decisions piloted by those who understand them best: their own workers – the same people who, week after week, have been stepping down from their posts to warn us of the looming risk.
Today, around the world, voices are being raised to protect our democracies from the threats of oligarchy. We are calling for a transnational coalition to defend democracy because, as history has shown, our voices are most powerful when we raise them together, as interconnected citizens. It is possible for democracy to reverse the dynamic of oligarchy. It is possible to work for a world that is no longer defined by exploding inequality. Now is the time to reorient our trajectory. We hope you will join us.
