https://taz.de/Vergewaltigungsprozess-ge.title: Vergewaltigungsprozess gegen Depardieu: Immer tieferer Absturz
https://taz.de/Vergewaltigungsprozess-ge.author: Rudolf Balmer
https://taz.de/Vergewaltigungsprozess-ge.text:
Vergewaltigungsprozess gegen Depardieu: Immer tieferer Absturz
Der französische Schauspieler Gérard Depardieu muss wegen Vergewaltigung vor Gericht. Aus der Filmwelt ist er bereits verbannt.
Gérard Depardieu (77) muss sich wegen Vergewaltigung vor Gericht verantworten. Das hat am Donnerstag die französische Justiz angeordnet. Der Prozesstermin ist noch nicht bekannt. Seine Anwälte äußerten sich erleichtert, dass nicht alle Beschuldigungen der Klägerin von der Anklagekammer berücksichtigt wurden. Ohnehin erwägen sie noch eine Beschwerde vor dem Kassationsgericht gegen diesen Entscheid.
Seit Jahren war es verdächtig still geworden um Gérard Depardieu. Nach mehreren Anschuldigungen wegen Vergewaltigung, sexueller Gewalt und obszönem Verhalten ist Frankreichs berühmtester Schauspieler für die Filmproduzenten, Regisseure und bestimmt auch für einen Großteil des Publikums, das ihn so lange verehrt hat, zur Unperson geworden. Auf der Kinoleinwand hat man ihn darum schon lange nicht mehr gesehen. Zuletzt spielte 2023 noch eine Hauptrolle als desillusionierter Chefkoch, der nach Japan flüchtet.
Zuletzt wusste man nicht einmal mehr, ob er noch in Frankreich war oder in einem Haus jenseits der Grenze in Belgien, oder womöglich als „Ehrengast“ die Protektion eines befreundeten Diktators genoss.
Hilfsangebote für von sexualisierter Gewalt Betroffene
Sie sind von sexualisierter Gewalt betroffen? Unterstützung bekommen Sie von Beratungsstellen wie dem Bundesverband Frauenberatungsstellen und Frauennotrufe, HateAid, Weisser Ring e.V. oder dem Hilfetelefon „Gewalt gegen Frauen“ unter 116 016. Technische Hilfe gegen Cyberstalking bieten die Antistalking-Haecksen unter antistalking.haecksen.org.
Immer wieder in den Schlagzeilen – und vor Gericht
Eigentlich hört man nun seit Jahren nur noch von Depardieu, wenn er einen Prozesstermin hat oder neue Anschuldigungen gegen ihn bekannt werden. Und auf diese Schlagzeilen hätte das längst abgestürzte Idol einer ganzen Nation gern verzichtet. Auch Präsident Emmanuel Macron, der noch 2023 gegen eine angebliche „Treibjagd“ gegen den Filmstar protestierte und von Depardieu sagte, die Nation könne „stolz“ auf das „monstre sacré“ (als „heiliges Ungeheuer“ bezeichnete man ihn in Frankreich) sein, schweigt nun geflissentlich dazu.
Im Mai 2025 wurde Depardieu vom Pariser Strafgericht wegen sexueller Belästigung und Gewalt gegen zwei Frauen während der Dreharbeiten für den Film „Les volets verts“ („Die grünen Fensterläden“) im Jahr 2021 zu 18 Monaten Haft mit Bewährung verurteilt und in das französische Register der Sexualdelinquenten und -verbrecher eingetragen.
Depardieu reichte Berufung ein. Im selben Jahr aber wurden durch Indiskretion seine obszönen und äußerst kompromittierenden Äußerungen über ein junges Mädchen in Nordkorea publik. Depardieu stritt zunächst alles ab und reichte eine Verleumdungsklage gegen die Fernsehgesellschaft France Télévisions ein, blitzte damit aber ab.
Lawine von Enthüllungen
Doch es kam noch schlimmer: Im September 2025 wurde ein Strafverfahren wegen Vergewaltigung und sexueller Gewalt gegen die Nachwuchsschauspielerin Charlotte Arnould eingeleitet. Sie hatte bereits 2018 erklärt, sie bei einem Besuch in der Pariser Villa des Filmstars von Depardieu vergewaltigt worden. Damit löste sie eine „Lawine“ von Enthüllungen aus.
Schon 2023 hatten im Online-Magazin „Mediapart“ 13 Frauen von sexuellen Belästigungen durch Depardieu gesprochen. Die dazu eingeleiteten Ermittlungen wurden indes wegen Verjährung der Vorfälle eingestellt. Nicht so die Strafklage von Arnould, die ihm im Fall eines Schuldspruchs einen längeren Aufenthalt hinter Gittern einbringen kann.
Opportune Entschuldigungsversuche
Noch Mitte November, rund eine Woche vor dem Entscheid über den Antrag der Staatsanwaltschaft, ihm wegen der Vergewaltigungsklage vor Gericht den Prozess zu machen, versuchte Depardieu die Justiz milde zu stimmen. Er verzichtete auf die Verhandlung des Berufungsgerichts wegen der Verurteilung zu 18 Monaten von 2025. Und am 13. November veröffentlichte er via Anwalt „seine zutiefst aufrichtigen Entschuldigungen bei denjenigen, die (seinetwegen) leiden mussten“.
Das reichte allerdings nicht, um ihm einen weiteren Prozess zu ersparen, bei dem er im Höchstfall mit bis zu 15 Jahren Gefängnis bestraft werden könnte. Und dann kam am 16. November noch hinzu: Auf veröffentlichten Videos ist zu sehen, wie er in der Öffentlichkeit eine Frau mehrfach unter dem Rock anfasst. Und wegen vermutlich schwerwiegender Vorfälle während einer Szene für den Film „Thalasso“ werden Depardieu und der Schriftsteller Michel Houellebecq der gemeinsamen Vergewaltigung einer Darstellerin verdächtigt.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
The South American country’s Senate also advanced a proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of the 2027 presidential race.
Argentina’s legislature has pushed forward a series of bills that would implement changes sought by President Javier Milei, including barring the Central Bank from printing extra money for government expenses.
On Thursday, the Argentinian Chamber of Deputies gave final approval to a bill imposing restrictions on the Central Bank, defining its “primary and fundamental mission” as maintaining the value of the country’s currency.
Under past administrations, the Central Bank has printed additional funds to help cover government expenses, contributing to the country’s once sky-high inflation, which reached more than 200 percent in 2023.
Milei, a libertarian economist, swept into office that year on a promise to tame runaway inflation and slash government spending.
Under his leadership, inflation has declined, though poverty has surged. Economists also believe Argentina may be drifting into a recession, with economic activity diminished in recent months.
Still, Milei’s office celebrated the Senate’s passage of the Central Bank bill with a presidential statement.
“This marks the end of nearly two decades of political manipulation at the Central Bank,” the statement said.
The bank, founded in 1935, had experienced “91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity, and institutional decay” up to this point, it added.
The vote in the Chamber of Deputies was 141 to zero, with 99 abstentions.
The Senate previously passed the bill, though it removed language Milei had pressed for, which would have required a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress to remove Central Bank governors.
Bill seeks to suspend primary elections
Also on Thursday, Argentina’s Senate advanced a bill to reform the country’s elections by suspending its primaries.
Unlike the Central Bank reform, that bill was not final. It still needs to pass the Chamber of Deputies.
The bill, however, comes less than a year before Argentina is slated to hold its next presidential election. Milei is expected to seek re-election in the October 24 vote.
Critics see the suspension of primaries as a means for Milei to avoid early pushback in his campaign.
A dismal primary result, they say, could weaken his momentum ahead of the general election and cause unfavourable economic fluctuations. Milei has long faced public discontent over his programme of economic austerity.
Thursday’s bill would also reduce public financing for political parties and eliminate a mandatory presidential debate ahead of general elections.
Senators approved the legislation by a vote of 43 to 29. While members of Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party touted the bill as a means of simplifying Argentina’s elections, opponents warned it could erode democratic norms.
“Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating,” Buenos Aires province Governor Axel Kicillof, a potential challenger to Milei, said in a social media post.

Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
An explosive new book by veteran journalist Matthew Cole claims Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Middle East envoy, had a deep entanglement with the governments of Saudi Arabia and particularly the UAE, during the first Trump administration.
The book's most explosive claim is that Kushner was given approximately $2bn from the Saudi and Emirati governments, including $750m held at First Abu Dhabi Bank through an Emirati charity, Watani Al Emarat Foundation, ostensibly to support civic programmes in the Emirates, but in reality used for Emirati weapons purchases and covert military operations.
Kushner, who is currently acting as an envoy for Trump in Ukraine and the Middle East, has vociferously denied the claims.
But the New York Times said the allegations against Kushner should be investigated when Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.
The book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East, published last month, contains dozens of other juicy nuggets about the Middle East and the wheeling and dealing that takes place in the region. It also provides a window into the culture of the UAE’s ruling Al Nahyan family.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Cole’s sources are anonymous and MEE couldn’t independently verify all the claims but has selected several highlights below. The UAE and Saudi royal families have not commented on the claims made in the book.
Homosexual blackmail
Cole claims that in the 1990s, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan hired two Syrians to film his brother and rival for the throne, former President Khalifa bin Zayed, having gay sex in a hotel room in southern Europe. Mohammed Bin Zayed then had Russian handlers deliver the tape to the brothers’ father - and founder of the UAE - Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, to embarrass Khalifa.
Cole wrote that Zayed bin Sultan realised Mohammed was trying to blackmail his brother, but appreciated his “cunning” and was “amused”. Cole says, “Within the Al Nahyan family, Mohamed’s blackmail attempt came to be seen as an early sign of his ambition to rule the UAE”.
Khalifa had only one wife and eight children, which was relatively rare for Gulf royals in the 1990s, but has become more common today.
Although Cole’s reporting on Khalifa bin Zayed’s sexual orientation has not been verified elsewhere, there are other reports of homosexuality among Gulf royals being used against them that have appeared in recent books on the Gulf.
Cole says Mohammed bin Zayed was also seen as hostile to former Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, who was eventually sidelined by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
According to Cole, Mohammed bin Zayed lobbied the US against Mohammed bin Nayef, on the basis of his alleged homosexuality.
In the case of Mohammed bin Nayef, his sexual orientation has been reported in two well-regarded books on the Saudi kingdom: New York Times Journalist Ben Hubbard’s MBS: The Rise to Power of Mohammed bin Salman and Blood and Oil: Mohammed bin Salman's Ruthless Quest for Global Power, by journalists Bradley Hope and Justin Scheck.
Did UAE ruler drug his brother?
Khalifa bin Zayed became president of the UAE in 2004 after his father’s death. Despite his official title, he widely deferred to his brother, Mohammed bin Zayed, who was crown prince of Abu Dhabi, the UAE’s wealthiest emirate.
Khalifa bin Zayed’s decision to take a back seat to his ostensibly junior brother was often framed in the media as a willing decision that was eventually necessitated by a 2014 stroke he suffered.
Instead, Cole claims that he suffered from alcoholism and an “undiagnosed mental illness” long before. He says that when Mohamed bin Zayed was named deputy crown prince of Abu Dhabi in 2003, he was already providing medical treatments to his brother which left him unable to function.
“Khalifa’s medical treatment left him in a stupor, eventually causing nerve damage,” Cole wrote.
Cole suggests that Mohammed bin Zayed saw the treatment as a way to “undermine” his brother, and often forced the treatment on him with the help of an American nurse with whom he had a family connection.
According to the book, Mohammed bin Zayed had a sexual relationship with the nurse’s niece, Lisa, with whom he fathered an illegitimate child raised in Southern California.
Israeli tech inside UAE F-16s
The UAE is Israel’s closest Arab partner. The two were understood to have enjoyed close security ties for decades before the UAE joined the US-backed Abraham Accords in September 2020, making their relationship public.
The UAE has moved closer to Israel amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. The two countries are aligned in regional hotspots like Somaliland and Ethiopia as well.
Cole says that Mohammed bin Zayed was an admirer of Israel since at least the 1990s, despite his father’s reluctance to embrace Israel due to his sympathy with the Palestinians.
In 1998, after reading in Aviation Week about a new F-16 that the US had produced with Israeli software, Mohammed bin Zayed lobbied his father to purchase the warplanes. At the time, Mohammed bin Zayed was the UAE Armed Forces chief of staff and negotiated the purchase with the US.
With Mohammed bin Zayed’s backing, the UAE agreed to purchase 80 aircraft and install Israeli software in them. The decision came amid secret Israeli-Emirati discussions hosted by the Clinton Administration aimed at addressing Israel’s concerns that the sale would endanger its Qualitative Military Edge (QME).
Writer tortured to death
The UAE’s decision to move closer to Israel publicly also sparked a crackdown at home. Cole wrote that Emirati poet Habib Al Sayegh was tortured to death in 2019, after writing a column against normalisation with Israel.
Sayegh was an Emirati luminary who even defended the UAE and Saudi Arabia’s blockade against Qatar. He was very much a member of the UAE’s state-backed elite, working as an editor at the Al Khaleej newspaper and serving as secretary general of the Arab Writers Union, according to the book.
Sayegh, however, was vocal in elite circles about the UAE’s growing closeness to Israel. Despite warnings to remain silent, in August 2019 he wrote a column titled “Israel Is Our Real Enemy and A Dangerous Project”.
Following publication of the article, Sayegh was abducted from his home by security officers at the orders of Mohammed bin Zayed, Cole writes. He says he was tortured with a pair of pliers used to pull out several of his teeth by one security agent, while another whipped him with a “belt-like strap with a sharp metal piece attached”.
Sayegh was beaten for three days. When he died, one of Mohammed bin Zayed’s closest aides described his body as “almost unrecognizable,” Cole writes.
Sayegh’s dissent stood in the way of a major diplomatic deal that Mohammed bin Zayed was discussing with Kushner and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Saudi Arabia would eventually grow cool on normalisation with Israel, but the agreement was for the Gulf states to recognise the country and sideline the Palestinians.
Jordan was envisioned as hosting the vast majority of three million Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank, thereby reducing the territory’s population by 90 percent. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would then recognise a rump Palestinian state, Cole wrote. The state would also be awarded some land in the Negev desert and Jordanian territory.
Jared Kushner-Tom Barrack rivalry
Cole’s book not only offers a window into the lives and ambitions of Gulf rulers, but also into key figures in the Trump administration. While some of the officials are not in government today, many of them remain central officials in the Middle East.
Besides Jared Kushner, the book discusses Tom Barrack at length. Barrack, a Lebanese-American former private equity investor, is currently US ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Iraq and Syria.
Barrack came under fire in the first Trump administration for initiating contact between Trump and the rulers of the UAE and Saudi Arabia before he took office. The book discusses those ties at length, but also suggests that Barrack grew frustrated with Kushner’s rise in the administration.
According to Cole, Barrack wanted to create a Marshall Plan - a reference to the post-WWII fund that rebuilt Europe - for the Middle East, funded by Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, to help develop the region.
But Kushner would only permit Barrack to handle the “Egyptian part” of the Middle East. Barrack would later lobby the UAE to tell Kushner that the Gulf state wanted him as Middle East envoy.
“The message to Barrack was clear: Kushner wouldn’t share White House relationships with MBS and MBZ,” Cole wrote, referring to Mohammed bin Salman and Mohammed bin Zayed.
Barrack and Kushner clashed again when Saudi Arabia and the UAE launched a blockade against Qatar in June 2017. At the time, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi were aligned, although they have more recently fallen out over Yemen, the Iran war and the Red Sea.
Despite his business ties with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, Barrack also tried to maintain good ties with Qatar.
According to the book, when the UAE and Saudi Arabia lobbied Kushner to support the blockade, Barrack joined former Secretary of State Rex Tillerson in pressing Trump not to join.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US army calls detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa a success after fears of toxic plume
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The US army blew up the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives, saying the first checks show Wednesday’s controlled detonation in Iowa didn’t spread toxic dust to nearby homes and farms.
Earthen barriers were put up and foam and water were poured onto a pair of bunkers holding the 5 tons (4,500kg) of lead azide, and officials said those measures appear to have absorbed much of the blast.
The US Environmental Protection Agency air monitors were detecting no lead in the air around the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, and an alert sent to cellphones late Wednesday afternoon said it was safe to resume normal activities. Fema also issued an all clear around the plant, the US army reported.
Still, government agencies and independent researchers plan to do extensive environmental testing for lead – a heavy metal that’s especially dangerous to children and pregnant women – in the weeks ahead on water sources, farms, homes and playgrounds.
The army said the safest option had been detonating the stockpile right away because it was degrading and might explode uncontrollably at any time as the weather got colder.
Some experts cautioned that it’s too early to know whether communities are in the clear.
But Maj Gen Eric Shirley, who led the army operation, said the risk was “reduced as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible”.
Since the military announced and then delayed plans for the detonation over the past two weeks, residents and environmental groups have voiced concerns about potential health and environmental impacts and about a lack of information about what to expect.
The smoke after the blasts
An Associated Press reporter filmed the blasts from less than a mile away and upwind from the site. Following two loud booms around 9am local time, a pair of white plumes rolled high in the air before quickly dissipating.
The army attributed the smoke to the foam sprayed on the bunkers to tamp down any dust.
Bystanders who parked on the side of a road to watch came away unimpressed by the size of the explosion.
Burlington resident Tim Brandt said he wanted to feel the ground shake, but instead the detonation reminded him of the noisemakers that crack when thrown on the ground.
“It was nothing,” he told the AP. “It seemed like government put fear in a lot of people over nothing.”
The army scheduled the detonation for Wednesday because the winds were blowing to the south-west and away from populated areas including Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people along the Mississippi River.
The two controlled blasts destroyed all 68 barrels and didn’t set off any secondary explosions, Shirley said.
More lead test results needed
Donald Trump posted on social media that the army did a “great job”.
Acting secretary of the army Adam Telle along with the Republican governors of Iowa and Missouri also said it appeared to be a success and that the explosion was well contained.
However, the final results aren’t in yet, researchers said.
The EPA’s air quality data was promising, said Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters. Yet he stressed that samples need to be tested in a lab to determine if people face health risks.
“This should take days to weeks,” Whelton said. “But what we may see is different guidance issued to different communities based on how far they are from the detonation area and whether or not they were upwind or downwind.”
Colin Wellenkamp, the executive director of the Mississippi River Cities and Towns Initiative, said water treatment facilities along the Mississippi and Missouri rivers will be testing periodically to make sure that there are no detectable spikes.
Safety concerns and weather condition delays
Government officials had encouraged residents closest to the site and in range of the plume to evacuate and others to stay indoors.
Schools not already closed for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday canceled classes and many businesses closed. Some residents sealed their windows and doors as a precaution.
Doug Seyb, a livestock farmer from Donnellson, lives far enough away that he didn’t hear or feel the explosions. But he was still concerned about the accuracy of EPA air monitors.
“All of these cows are pregnant,” he said, “and we just cross our fingers that we don’t have deformed calves and stillborns.”
Army steps to quash the plume
A court ruling this week put the detonation, originally planned for last Friday, back on track. The army changed the date amid public backlash and to allow more time for safety measures and favorable wind.
The army set up “blast barriers”, with concrete and sand barriers two stories high. Ballistic gels, foams and water were added to absorb the dust.
Environmental groups who sued to halt the detonation said on Wednesday that legal action and public pressure forced the army to take more protective measures.
Had the blasts happened last week as planned, many safeguards along with clearer evacuation plans and expansive monitoring wouldn’t have been in place, they said.
“Iowa and neighboring states deserve a full accounting of why the situation was allowed to get to the point of crisis,” said Sarah Green, executive director of the Iowa Environmental Council.
Lead azide crystallizing
The stockpile was brought to Iowa from bases around the country in 2009, according to Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The lead azide was stored just in case the military needed to use it again.
During an inspection in March, staff at the ammunition plant found the chemicals had partially crystallized, making them sensitive to friction and cold temperatures and creating the risk of spontaneous detonation.
Some residents said the timing could have been better, given that it was the day before Thanksgiving, but they acknowledged it needed to be dealt with now. Others worried about the potential impact down the road.
“I don’t think lead danger goes away any time soon,” said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington. “It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this.”

https://taz.de/Nachfolge-fuer-Christine-.title: Nachfolge für Christine Lagarde: Pablo Hernández de Cos wird neuer EZB-Chef
https://taz.de/Nachfolge-fuer-Christine-.author: Eric Bonse
https://taz.de/Nachfolge-fuer-Christine-.text:
Nachfolge für Christine Lagarde: Pablo Hernández de Cos wird neuer EZB-Chef
Mit dem vorzeitigen Abgang von Christine Lagarde stand ein Personalroulette in der EZB an. Eile war auch wegen der Wahlen in Frankreich geboten.
Der Spanier Pablo Hernández de Cos soll die Nachfolge der Französin Christine Lagarde an der Spitze der Europäischen Zentralbank (EZB) in Frankfurt antreten. Darauf haben sich die Staats- und Regierungschefs der Eurozone offenbar am Donnerstag beim EU-Gipfel in Brüssel geeinigt. Eine offizielle Bestätigung stand bei Redaktionsschluss noch aus.
Neben de Cos war bis zuletzt auch noch der Niederländer Klaas Knot im Rennen um die Lagarde-Nachfolge. Die Niederlande hätten ihren Widerstand aufgegeben, hieß es am Rande des EU-Treffens, das mit einem Euro-Gipfel und einer offiziellen Verabschiedung von Lagarde begonnen hatte. Lagarde tritt Anfang Februar vorzeitig ab.
De Cos ist derzeit noch Chef der Bank für ‌Internationalen Zahlungsausgleich (BIZ); früher war er Präsident der spanischen Notenbank. Im Gegensatz zu Knot gilt der Spanier als Verfechter einer eher laxen Geldpolitik. Knot war bis 2025 Präsident der niederländischen Zentralbank. Sein strikter Kurs liegt eher auf der deutschen Linie. Allerdings hat ausgerechnet Deutschland den Weg für de Cos frei gemacht – mit der Nominierung des deutschen Ökonomen Markus Brunnermeier für das Amt des EZB-Chefvolkswirts. Brunnermeier wird so etwas wie der Hüter des heiligen Grals – er bereitet die Zinsentscheidungen der EZB vor und hat zentrale Bedeutung für die Geldpolitik.
Nach dieser Entscheidung war der Weg für de Cos an die EZB-Spitze frei, nur die Niederlande sträubten sich noch. Unklar ist, ob das Personalpaket damit komplett ist. Zuletzt war noch die Nachfolge der deutschen Wirtschaftswissenschaftlerin Isabel Schnabel offen. Die Vorschlagsfrist wurde bis zum 27. November verlängert. Als Favoritin gilt die französische Ökonomin Laurence Boone.
Die Eile bei der Neubesetzung der EZB-Spitze wird mit der französischen Präsidentschaftswahl im April 2027 begründet. Im Rennen um die Nachfolge von Staatschef Emmanuel Macron liegt derzeit die rechtsradikale Nationalistenführerin Marine Le Pen vorn. Le Pen gilt als hartnäckige Kritikerin des Euros; sie könnte die EZB blockieren, so die Sorge in Brüssel.
Bevor alles in trockenen Tüchern ist und de Cos den Chefsessel in Frankfurt übernehmen kann, müssen noch das Europaparlament und der EZB-Rat angehört werden. Nach den Stellungnahmen ernennen die Staats- und Regierungschefs die neue EZB-Spitze offiziell. Dies ist für das nächste reguläre Gipfeltreffen im Dezember geplant.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/departemen.title: Trois jeunes tués en une semaine, renfort de gendarmes et policiers… Que se passe-t-il à Mayotte ?
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/departemen.author: Théo Bourrieau
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/departemen.text:
En une semaine, trois jeunes ont perdu la vie lors d’affrontements sur l’île de Mayotte, confrontée à une tragique recrudescence des violences. Si le gouvernement a annoncé des renforts de gendarmes et policiers, la CGT regrette une réponse « exclusivement répressive » et réclame un changement de méthode.
Le délaissement total de Mayotte de la part du gouvernement a, encore une fois, des conséquences tragiques. Trois jeunes sont morts dans le département le plus pauvre de France.
Le vendredi 20 novembre, un adolescent de 17 ans, grièvement blessé à la tête et aux jambes lors d’affrontements entre bandes avant d’être pris en charge dans un état critique au centre hospitalier de Mamoudzou, a succombé à ses blessures dans la nuit. Le parquet a ouvert une enquête pour assassinat....

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: You Can See Everything overtly riffs on Vertigo. But how big is its debt to Kiarostami’s Close-Up?
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Steve Rose
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
You’re probably sick of hearing how You Can See Everything, about the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, is the buzziest, coolest, 100% freshest film of the year, but coming out of the screening last week, I couldn’t help but wonder whether Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim had been watching a lot of 90s Iranian cinema. And one film in particular: Close-Up, by Abbas Kiarostami.
If it feels as if You Can See Everything blends truth, lies, fiction and documentary in mind-bending new ways until you’re no longer sure what the hell you’re watching, then Kiarostami, who died in 2016, practically invented this mode 36 years ago. The context could not be more different – analogue 90s Tehran rather than tech-drunk 2020s California – but the themes are the same: Close-Up is a strange story of impersonation, deception and performance, made even stranger by the film-maker’s deliberate meddling.
The setup contains some uncanny parallels. Like You Can See Everything, Close-Up focuses on a convicted fraudster: Hossein Sabzian is an unemployed loner who is charged with impersonating one of Iran’s greatest film-makers, Mohsen Makhmalbaf. Posing as Makhmalbaf, Sabzian convinces a family that he’s going to make his next movie in their well-to-do home, and will even cast their sons in it. This is pre-internet, so the family can’t just Google what Makhmalbaf really looks like.
Sabzian is soon caught out and arrested – but, like Fielder, rather than maintain the arm’s-length objectivity of the documentarian, Kiarostami mischievously inserts himself into the narrative. We see him visit Sabzian in prison then, with a latitude Fielder and Oppenheim can only dream of, he gains permission to film Sabzian’s trial.
The trial, a much looser affair than a western one, is gripping in itself. Sabzian’s justification for his deception is almost as bizarre as Holmes’s. He is not a conman, he insists, he’s a cinephile, an artist. He was committing to the role of playing Makhmalbaf, and the subterfuge earned him a respect he could never achieve as his lowly self. He’s a persuasive speaker in the courtroom, but is this heartfelt testimony or masterful improv? The family aren’t convinced: “He’s still playing a role, even if a slightly different one,” the son protests. “Instead of playing Makhmalbaf, now he’s playing the sensitive soul.”
Kiarostami confounds things even further by intercutting the courtroom drama with reconstructed flashback scenes from this bizarre affair, with Sabzian and the family playing themselves, in their actual home. There are also apparently staged scenes with actors – the comically inept journalist who broke the story, for example. Notions of fact and fiction are cast adrift. Can we take anything we’re watching at face value? Is Sabzian a documentary subject or an actor, playing a director? Or perhaps a screenwriter? Kiarostami is, in effect, taking the fantasy Sabzian concocted and making it real. Even Kiarostami wasn’t sure what he’d made. Looking back on Close-Up in 2005, he said: “I wasn’t directing the actors so much as being directed by them.”
The similarities don’t stop there. You Can See Everything’s extreme closeups, for example – could they have been inspired by a movie called Close-Up? Kiarostami even explains to Sabzian (and the viewers) at one point that he is using a wide-angle lens to film the courtroom, and a different closeup lens just for him, inviting us to scrutinise Sabzian’s face in minute detail, just as Fielder does with Holmes.
And the fantastically awkward reality-folding-in-on-itself moment in Fielder’s film when Amanda Seyfried finds herself on the phone to the real Elizabeth Holmes is mirrored in Close-Up: the film concludes with a surprisingly emotional encounter between Sabzian and the real Mohsen Makhmalbaf (although Kiarostami later revealed that elements of this were also staged– make it stop!).
Has Fielder seen Close-Up? It’s more than likely. Lance Oppenheim certainly has. In an interview last month he described it as “a favourite movie of mine”. In a separate interview he said: “The two movies that made me want to make movies were Orson Welles’ F for Fake and Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up.” He’s not the only one: in 2023, Fielder’s sometime collaborators Benny and Josh Safdie judged it among their top five films of all time. “It made me think about using movies to manipulate life in its own way,” Josh said. “You’re using the real people to recreate, and then by recreating you’re understanding everything that happened in the first place, and then it’s a movie, so you really have no idea what to believe.”
Fielder has been operating in this territory for some time, not just with You Can See Everything but also with his other genre-meddling works, Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, both of which also play brilliantly with reconstruction, artifice and meta-performance.
You Can See Everything is by no means a rip-off of Close-Up. For one thing, unlike Fielder, Kiarostami doesn’t put himself in the picture, leering though the window like a stalker. And the whole vibe is very different. But what’s so bracing about both films is that sensation of destabilising uncertainty, of not really knowing what we’re watching. Is anyone being real with anyone? What makes reality “real” anyway? In our time of genre fatigue at the cinema but deepfakery and misinformation online, this mindwarping, hall-of-mirrors mode of cinema is clearly connecting with audiences, even when we think we’ve see it all before.
Right, next up: why You Can See Everything is actually a remake of Hitchcock’s Vertigo. Discuss …

https://taz.de/Konzert-fuer-DDR-Jazzer-K.title: Konzert für DDR-Jazzer Klaus Koch: Er erzählte den Jazz
https://taz.de/Konzert-fuer-DDR-Jazzer-K.author: Robert Mießner
https://taz.de/Konzert-fuer-DDR-Jazzer-K.text:
Konzert für DDR-Jazzer Klaus Koch: Er erzählte den Jazz
Im Berliner Exploratorium wird der DDR-Jazzbassist Klaus Koch gewürdigt. Weggefährten und Schüler feiern ihn zu seinem 90. Geburtstag.
Matthias Bauer sagt: „Ich sehe ihn noch genau vor mir“. Die Rede ist von Klaus Koch, Jazzbassist in der DDR und, das ist nicht unwichtig, darüber hinaus. Als „visionär, frisch und virtuos“ charakterisiert Maike Hilbig sein Spiel. „Das klingt ganz natürlich, nicht aufgesetzt, und kommt aus einem Guss“, meint Ben Lehmann. „Ich habe mich in seinem Sound wiedergefunden“, sagt Isabel Rößler.
Am 3. September hätte Koch seinen 90. Geburtstag begehen können; diesen Sonntag wird im Kreuzberger Impro-Labor Exploratorium nachgefeiert. Bauer, Hilbig, Lehmann und Rößler, alle vier selber am Bass, werden dabei sein. Bassisten haben es in der Aufmerksamkeitsökonomie schwer. Im Jazz und der improvisierten Musik immerhin gibt es ganze Soloalben von ihnen, Klaus Koch selbst veröffentlichte 1988 eins.
Das erste Album mit Klaus Koch war gleich ein Klassiker: „Solarius“ vom Rolf Kühn Quintett, ein mitteleuropäisches Joint Venture von 1965 mit den Brüdern Rolf (Klarinette, BRD), Joachim (Klavier, noch DDR), Michał Urbaniak (Saxofon), Czesław Bartkowski (Drums; beide Polen) und Klaus Koch. Einer der wenigen, „denen ich damals vertrauen konnte“, wird sich Joachim Kühn, der 1966 aus der DDR ausreiste, im Interview mit dem Jazzjournalisten Rainer Bratfisch erinnern. Aus dieser Zeit stammt auch das Album „Turning Point“, die letzte Plattenaufnahme Joachim Kühns in der DDR, eingespielt im Februar 1966 und regulär erstmals in diesem November veröffentlicht.
Der Instrumentalist scheut keine Songs
„Erzählerischer Jazz“, sagt Maike Hilbig dazu. Klaus Koch gehört zur Besetzung von „Turning Point“. Er bleibt in der DDR und wird ein viel gefragter Musiker. 1968 erscheint vom Klaus-Lenz-Sextett mit Gastsolisten die EP-Single „Protestsongs“ als Beilage einer gleichnamigen Anthologie. Manfred Krug singt internationalistische Lieder, Klaus Koch ist am Bass dabei. Der Instrumentalist scheut also keine Songs. Matthias Bauer weist darauf hin, dass Koch Mitglied des Rundfunk-Tanzorchesters von Günter Gollasch gewesen sei, des prägenden Ensembles für Tanzmusik und Swing in der DDR.
Ganz anders, an den Free Jazz Ornette Colemans erinnernd, klingt dann 1973 das Friedhelm Schönfeld-Trio auf einer Split-LP mit dem im Vergleich eher zugänglichen Hubert-Katzenbeier-Quintett: Schönfeld (Klarinette, Saxofon), Klaus Koch und am Schlagzeug Günter „Baby“ Sommer verwandeln in 20 Minuten einen elegischen Auftakt in einen expressiven Ausbruch. 1975 löst Koch Conny Bauer im Quartett Synopsis als Bassisten ab. 1979 kommt Koch mit, als die Workshop Band des Pianisten Ulrich Gumpert in einem Joint Venture von VEB Deutsche Schallplatten Berlin/DDR und der Free Music Production (FMP) in Berlin (West) ein komplettes Album einspielt.
Das Tribute-Konzert
„Avantgardist ohne Werk – Bassist Klaus Koch zum 90. Geburtstag“, Exploratorium, Berlin-Kreuzberg, 29. November
Und Klaus Koch ist einer, der sein Wissen weitergibt. Er unterrichtet an der Hochschule für Musik Hanns Eisler in Ost-Berlin. Einer seiner Schüler wird Matthias Bauer: „Ich bin ein Jahr lang zu ihm in seine Wohnung nach Pankow gefahren. Wir haben zusammen musiziert, Musik gehört und gesprochen. Von Klaus Koch konnte man Zuhören lernen.“ Am 8. November 1999 treten der ehemalige Schüler und sein Lehrer zusammen in Berlin im Podewil mit Bill Dixon (Trompete) und Tony Oxley (Schlagzeug) auf, zu 10 Jahre Mauerfall im Anschluss an das Total Music Meeting. Von dem Abend gibt es eine CD, „Berlin Abozzi“, wieder auf FMP: „Auf der Heimfahrt hat mir Klaus Koch erzählt, er habe einen tollen Bass, Baujahr 1800, den spiele er nie. Ein Jahr später, kurz nach der Veröffentlichung, ist er gestorben.“ Der Bass von Klaus Koch wohnt mittlerweile bei Matthias Bauer und wird für besondere Anlässe aktiviert. Vielleicht am Sonntag?

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/blanchim.title: À la tête du Pnaco, la magistrate Vanessa Perrée raconte les dessous de la lutte contre la grande criminalité
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/blanchim.author: Bruno Rieth
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/blanchim.text:
Le Parquet national anticriminalité organisée (Pnaco) s’apprête à achever sa première année d’existence. Crypto-rapts, atteintes aux institutions, montée en puissance des femmes dans les groupes criminels : la magistrate Vanessa Perrée, à la tête du Pnaco, revient pour « l’Humanité » sur son bilan et les mutations en cours de la grande criminalité.
Le sang-froid n’empêche pas un peu de chaleur. La conclusion s’est imposée d’elle-même à la sortie de notre entretien avec Vanessa Perrée, la patronne du Pnaco, ce parquet spécialisé dans la lutte contre le narcotrafic et les réseaux criminels créé en début d’année.
Face aux défis que pose le crime organisé, la magistrate sait garder la tête froide sans perdre en convivialité. Elle revient pour l’Humanité sur le chemin parcouru et les constats sur les évolutions du monde criminel.
Après onze mois d’existence du Parquet national anticriminalité organisée (Pnaco), quel bilan tirez-vous ?
Vanessa Perrée
Procureure de la République à la tête du Parquet national anti-criminalité organisée (PNACO)
L’originalité de notre parquet réside d’abord dans la pluridisciplinarité de son équipe, qui monte en puissance de manière progressive. Aux côtés des 26 magistrats, des 13 personnes du greffe et de l’équipe autour de moi, nous avons pu nous entourer d’assistants spécialisés : ingénieur, agents de la direction générale des finances publiques, analystes.
Nous sommes également le seul parquet de France à bénéficier d’officiers de liaison : un policier, un gendarme, un douanier et une directrice des services pénitentiaires.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Georgian police clash with Turkiye’s Besiktas fans over Palestinian flag
Match between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva suspended for 30 minutes after confrontation between fans and police in Georgia.
Georgian police have clashed with fans of Turkiye’s Besiktas after they unfurled a Palestinian flag during a Europa League game against Israel’s Hapoel Beer-Sheva.
The clashes resulted in a suspension of about 30 minutes during the 26th minute of the game held in Batumi, Georgia, but it resumed after the interruption on Thursday. Besiktas eventually won 2-1.
Turkish media outlets reported that Georgian police entered the stands and used pepper spray against fans of the Istanbul giant, prompting Danish referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.
The game was relocated by UEFA to Batumi after Turkish authorities said Istanbul could not host it for safety and security reasons. Unlike two previous Hapoel away games, spectators were allowed in the stadium.
Besiktas accused Georgian police of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.
“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the Turkish club said in a statement. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”
The Turkish Football Federation also strongly condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination in a statement on X. The federation said it would press for an investigation into the incident.
Several other Turkish Super Lig clubs, including Trabzonspor, Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, Erzurumspor, Basaksehir and Samsunspor, condemned the use of force against Besiktas fans.
Prior to the match, Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, Turkiye’s state-run Anadolu Agency reported.
A video published by Besiktas on X after the game shows their players posing for a picture behind fans carrying a banner that reads: “Rise up against the occupation. Freedom for Palestine.”
Diplomatic incident
Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci spoke to his Georgian counterpart following the game to discuss Turkiye’s concern over the incident.
According to Turkiye’s Interior Ministry, Ciftci expressed concern over the disproportionate use of force against Turkish fans and called for measures to ensure their safe return to Turkiye.
Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili reportedly said that UEFA officials had confiscated the fans’ Palestinian flags and that Georgian state authorities had played no role in the confiscation.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Jesse Eisenberg says his films contain ‘no sexuality’. But maybe his fans are just less desperate?
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Stuart Heritage
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
The imminent arrival of Jesse Eisenberg’s new film The Debut should be cause for celebration. Not necessarily because it is good – although its star Julianne Moore seems locked into an Oscar nomination at minimum – but because it means that Jesse Eisenberg has to do press for it. This is always a treat.
While the bulk of big magazine profiles about film people involve journalists breaking their spines to make the subject sound funnier or more profound than they really are, that is never particularly necessary with Eisenberg, because he appears to be a genuine oddball.
For instance, the new profile about him in the New Yorker is brimming with endless weird little details that you would never expect to read in a piece about, say, Matt Damon. For example, he says that a Freudian analyst diagnosed him with something called “arousal disgust”, a complex where simply liking something brings about waves of self-hatred. He donated a kidney to a stranger. He wrote to the Directors Guild of America to ask that his name be taken off the opening titles of The Debut, not because he disowns it but because it felt needlessly flashy.
Aaron Sorkin, meanwhile – and you have to assume that this was meant as a compliment, compared Eisenberg to Holden Caulfield, the character who inspired Mark Chapman to murder John Lennon.
But by far the most interesting nugget from the profile concerns Eisenberg’s relationship with his fans. “People are mostly fine,” he says. “It’s because there’s no sexuality to my work. I think once the public is asked to want to sleep with a person onscreen, that person’s life is fundamentally different.”
This deserves some interrogation because, on the surface, it’s a statement that presents itself like a great unspoken truth. Of course there aren’t hordes of lusty fans pulling at his clothes all the time, because he doesn’t play the sort of character that attracts those people. If you are a leading man heart-throb like Leonardo DiCaprio, then you probably have to learn how to protect yourself from people who look at you like a randy cartoon wolf or, more specifically, Jeff Bezos’ wife.
But Jesse Eisenberg tends to make smaller films, where he plays superficially asexual characters. He’s very good at playing a child of divorce. He’s undeniably great at playing clever outsiders. And if we’re talking characters with no sexual magnetism whatsoever, you need to remember that Eisenberg repeatedly plays a stage magician in film.
However, some wider context is probably necessary. In the profile, Eisenberg was specifically talking about fans interrupting him when he’s writing, this is something he does during office hours at a New York public library branch. Immediately this means that we can narrow the focus a little, because it is clear that by “fans” he is describing a very narrow subsection of fans who happen to be visiting public libraries during weekday office hours. Not to generalise too broadly, but this doesn’t feel like a particularly sexually incontinent demographic.
And, besides, in terms of roles he has played, Eisenberg is just plain wrong. There is plenty of sexuality to his work. In Richard Ayoade’s adaptation of Dostoevsky’s The Double, he plays a twin who brims with sexual confidence throughout. In the series Fleishman is in Trouble, he plays a doctor who has so much casual sex post-divorce that it has to be condensed into a montage. And in the play The Spoils – which Eisenberg wrote for himself a decade ago – his character admits to having scatological fantasies about his friend’s girlfriend.
Most damningly of all, there is the very famous interview he did with Romina Puga in 2013, which is one of the most sexually charged things you will ever clap eyes on. From start to finish, the interview is a cavalcade of flirtatious bullying in both directions, like they’re determined to neg each other into bed. Of course, we should remember that Eisenberg was a bit too relentless in this regard, and in a subsequent post entitled “Jesse Eisenberg isn’t very nice”, she describes how the encounter left her feeling humiliated.
But still, it blows a hole clean through Eisenberg’s argument. People aren’t nice to him because he isn’t sexual in movies, they’re nice to him because he makes small, clever films enjoyed primarily by people who are too shy to barge in on him when he’s clearly working in a library on a Thursday. Now, let this be the end of it, because I don’t want to convince Jesse Eisenberg that people fancy him any more than I absolutely have to.

https://taz.de/Bedrohtes-Kirchenasyl/!62.title: Bedrohtes Kirchenasyl: Abschiebespezialisten aus NRW brechen in Bremerhaven ein
https://taz.de/Bedrohtes-Kirchenasyl/!62.author: Amanda Böhm und Lotta Drügemöller
https://taz.de/Bedrohtes-Kirchenasyl/!62.text:
Bedrohtes Kirchenasyl: Abschiebespezialisten aus NRW brechen in Bremerhaven ein
Das Kirchenasyl in Bremerhaven wurde erstmals gebrochen. Verantwortlich dafür ist die Ausländerbehörde Coesfeld, die für rabiates Vorgehen bekannt ist.
Als am 18. November in Bremerhaven das Kirchenasyl gebrochen wurde, um 6 Uhr in der Früh, war Pastor Ritter gar nicht dabei. Er saß im Nebengebäude, trank seinen Kaffee, und stieß erst dazu, als das Wesentliche schon passiert war: Die Tür zu der Wohnung in der Kirchengemeinde war mit einem Brecheisen aufgehebelt worden, und „der Flüchtling, der da oben schlief, hatte den Schreck seines Lebens: Plötzlich stehen da zehn Leute in Polizeijacken rund um sein Bett“, erzählt Ritter.
Genau genommen waren nicht alle von ihnen Polizist*innen: Wolfgang Heuermann, der Leiter der Zentralen Ausländerbehörde Coesfeld, war persönlich gekommen, ebenso eine zuständige Mitarbeiterin der Behörde. Und ein Schlüsseldienst – doch weil der Heuermann nicht schnell genug arbeitete, gab er den Auftrag, die Tür mit einem Brecheisen aufzustemmen. Nur eine Person war nicht vor Ort: die 62-jährige A., wegen der die Beamt*innen aus Bremerhaven und Nordrhein-Westfalen gekommen waren. „Sie war wohl draußen spazieren“, erzählt Ritter später.
A. ist kurdische Syrerin. Geflohen ist sie über Polen, wo auch eins ihrer Kinder lebt. Zwei andere Kinder sowie die Enkel leben jedoch in Deutschland. Sie hat sehr engen Kontakt zu ihrer Familie, ihre Kinder besuchen sie regelmäßig und kümmern sich um sie. Für ihren Aufenthaltsstatus bedeutet all das jedoch nichts: Weil Polen das Land ist, in dem A. zum ersten Mal europäischen Boden betreten hat, soll sie dorthin abgeschoben werden, gemäß den Regeln des Dublin-Verfahrens.
Ziel des Kirchenasyls ist meistens, den Zeitraum zu überbrücken, bis die Überstellungsfrist des Dublin-Verfahrens nach sechs Monaten ausläuft. Dann kann die geflüchtete Person einen Asylantrag in Deutschland stellen. Auch wenn das Kirchenasyl immer häufiger gebrochen wird, respektieren die Ausländerbehörden dieses in der Regel und verzichten auf eine Abschiebung. Das können sie, denn sie haben einen Ermessensspielraum.
Birgit Naujoks, Flüchtlingsrat NRW
Auch im Bundesland Bremen hatte es Ende 2024 Versuche gegeben, das Kirchenasyl anzugreifen: Nach Aufforderung durch das Bundesamt für Migration und Flüchtlinge versuchte der damalige Innensenator Ulrich Mäurer (SPD), ein Kirchenasyl in der Zions-Gemeinde in Bremen zu räumen. Seine Polizeibehörden scheiterten mehrfach am Widerstand der Zivilgesellschaft: Über 100 Menschen hatten sich jeweils nachts vor der Gemeinde versammelt.
Das Ganze endete mit einer Art Patt: In gemeinsamen Gesprächen zum Jahresende 2024 hatten sich Kirchen und Innensenator auf eine Art Abschiebemoratorium bis Ende Januar 2025 geeinigt. Die Kirchen versprachen, weniger Menschen aufzunehmen, Bremen wollte dafür weitere Abschiebeversuche unterlassen. Aber nun wurde doch wieder ein Kirchenasyl gebrochen: Die versuchte Abschiebung von A., der erste Bruch des Kirchenasyls in der Geschichte Bremerhavens, war allerdings gar nicht vom Land Bremen beauftragt worden.
Die harte Hand des Ulrich Helmich
Die Syrerin A. ist in Nordrhein-Westfalen gemeldet, zuständig für ihren Fall ist deshalb die Zentrale Ausländerbehörde Coesfeld. Obwohl diese kommunal geführt wird, deckt sie in ihrem Aufgabenbereich ein Fünftel des 19-Millionen-Einwohner-Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen ab. Sie untersteht dem Dezernat „Sicherheit, Bauen und Umwelt“, geleitet von Ulrich Helmich, der für eine besonders harte, restriktive Handhabung von Aufenthaltsfragen bekannt ist, wie mehrere Expert:innen bestätigen. Oder, anders gesagt: sich mit herausragendem Engagement um Abschiebungen bemüht.
Schlagzeilen gemacht hatte die Behörde 2024, als sie für zahlreiche Kommunen fertige „Abschiebepakete“ für Geflüchtete aus den Westbalkanstaaten schnüren wollte – und die Kommunen, darunter Köln, diese Hilfe dann nicht annahmen.
Bei den Abschiebungen, die die Behörde selber durchführt, geht sie auf eine Weise vor, die an die US-amerikanische Behörde ICE erinnert: Am 16. Oktober zum Beispiel verschafften sich die Beamt*innen mit einem Rammbock Zutritt zu der Wohnung der Familie Rouf aus Leverkusen. Der Vater und die volljährige Tochter wurden nach Sri Lanka abgeschoben und von der Mutter und den übrigen minderjährigen Kindern, davon mehrere im Grundschulalter, getrennt. Als die Lokalpresse hinzukam, zogen sich die Beamt*innen der Ausländerbehörde Strickmasken über den Kopf, wie der Kölner Stadtanzeiger berichtete.
Das Abschiebungsreporting NRW berichtete, dass die Ausländerbehörde Coesfeld im April 2025 die vermutlich erste Abschiebung in die Ukraine seit Beginn des russischen Angriffskrieges verantwortete. Einen Monat später schob sie den schwer kranken und behinderten Luka Mgebrushvili nach Georgien ab. Weil sein Rollstuhl dabei nicht mitgenommen wurde, musste Mgebrushvili über drei Monate lang liegen.
Kein Kirchenasyl mehr sicher
Und im Mai 2026 meldete eine Kirchengemeinde aus Burgsteinfurt, Helmichs Behörde habe versucht, zwei junge Frauen aus Afghanistan aus dem Kirchenasyl abzuschieben. Die Abschiebung sei daran gescheitert, dass der Durchsuchungsantrag zu spät bei der zuständigen Richterin einging.
„Man kann schon vermuten, dass der Leiter der Ausländerbehörde persönlich nach Bremerhaven fährt, weil er nun demonstrieren will, dass das Kirchenasyl nicht mehr sicher vor ihm ist“, sagt Birgit Naujoks, Geschäftsführerin des Flüchtlingsrats Nordrhein-Westfalen.
Die 62-Jährige A. war nicht die einzige Geflüchtete, die in den Bremerhavener Kirchen Schutz bekommen hatte: Zurzeit leben 18 Menschen, darunter mehrere Kinder in Bremerhaven im Kirchenasyl. Da A. zum Zeitpunkt der versuchten Abschiebung nicht in den Gemeinderäumen war, wird nun polizeilich nach ihr gefahndet. Und in der Johanneskirche, so Ritter, fühlt sich seit vergangener Woche keine*r mehr sicher.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Israeli settlers damage Palestinian family’s homes in West Bank attack
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Israeli settlers damage Palestinian family’s homes in West Bank attack
The Tubasi family was forced out months ago and has been denied a return by settlers despite an Israeli court order.
Israeli settlers have smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the occupied West Bank after attacks stopped the family from returning.
Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the two-storey houses in the village of Jaloud, near Nablus, at about 1am on Thursday (23:00 GMT on Wednesday), before starting to damage them, Reuters reported. It added that the concrete foundations of the homes had been partially broken.
“This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators,” said Ghiath Nasser, the owners’ lawyer.
The Israeli military said the attack was “a serious criminal act” and said it was investigating, despite settlers remaining in the vicinity throughout the day.
A family forced out
The Tubasi family now live in a small house in Jaloud with a direct view of the homes they fled. “They want to demolish the houses so that we cannot return to them,” Wael Tubasi, one of the owners, said.
He said the deadline for the military to remove the settlers had passed.
“Even though there is a court order, and the army is required to remove them from the area entirely, not just return us to our homes, it’s still not being implemented,” he said.
The family said settlers set up a tent near their homes in April and began attacking them. They said settlers set fire to the homes, cut their water and electricity and blocked the roads.
After three months, settlers told the family they had an hour to leave or be killed “like the Dawabsheh family”, Wael’s mother, Aedah, said. In 2015, settlers set fire to the Dawabsheh family’s home in the village of Duma, killing an 18-month-old child and both his parents.
In September, soldiers escorted the family back to their homes under the court order. Ten minutes later, about 200 settlers attacked them, forcing the family and the soldiers to retreat, the family said. The settlers then burned the homes and broke much of the furniture.
“I’m forbidden from reaching my home, while the settlers have the right to remain inside. What rights are there?” Aedah said.
Surge in settler pogroms
The attack follows weeks of settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank. There have been an average of 53 settler attacks a week since the start of the year, according to the UN. The agency said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks causing casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season.
Over the weekend, settlers set fire to at least a dozen vehicles and several homes in five villages, and sprayed “Revenge” on walls. Last week, settlers killed an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded 10 other people in a pogrom near Jericho.
Very few cases lead to charges.
According to the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, 93.6 percent of investigations into settler pogroms are closed without indictments.

https://taz.de/Hoffnungstraeger-in-Brasi.title: Hoffnungsträger in Brasilien: Der Whatsapp-Politiker André Luis Gaspar Janones
https://taz.de/Hoffnungstraeger-in-Brasi.author: Christine Wollowski
https://taz.de/Hoffnungstraeger-in-Brasi.text:
Hoffnungsträger in Brasilien: Der Whatsapp-Politiker André Luis Gaspar Janones
Ein Anwalt aus einfachen Verhältnissen rettete mit seiner Social-Media-Kampagne Lulas Wahl. André Luis Gaspar Janones könnte Brasiliens nächster Präsident werden.
Seine Mutter wünscht sich, dass ihr Sohn Präsident wird. Wie Lula kommt er aus einfachen Verhältnissen. Wie Lula hat er Ausdauer, Talent und Durchsetzungskraft. Wie Lula liegen ihm die Menschen am Herzen, die es im Leben nicht einfach haben. Neuerdings kennt ganz Brasilien und ein Teil der Welt André Luis Gaspar Janones. Weil er mit seiner beispielhaften Whatsapp-Kampagne und dem „Heer für Lula“ entscheidenden Einfluss auf die Wiederwahl des brasilianischen Präsidenten hatte. Und weil Lula den 42-jährigen Anwalt, den er liebevoll „meinen General“ nennt, auf Staatsreisen mitnimmt, zur Klimakonferenz in die Türkei, auf die Philippinen und zuletzt nach Spanien. Janones berichtet darüber in seiner gewohnt direkten Sprache für zehn Millionen Follower auf Instagram und fast ebenso viele im Whatsapp-Kanal.
Politisches Gespür und Talent für die Kommunikation über soziale Medien beweist der Politiker 2018 als Sprachrohr der brasilienweit streikenden Lkw-Fahrer. Zuvor hatte er als Anwalt kostenlos einkommensschwache Familien vertreten, die auf dem Rechtsweg Behandlung und Medikamente im öffentlichen Gesundheitssystem einforderten. Im selben Jahr wählten ihn fast 180.000 Menschen in sein erstes Abgeordnetenmandat, obwohl er kein Geld für den Wahlkampf hatte.
In der Hauptstadt Brasília blieb er ein Außenseiter. Einer, der weder aus einer Politikerfamilie stammte, noch an Eliteunis studiert oder sich innerhalb der großen Gewerkschaften und Parteien profiliert hatte. Janones Mutter war Hausangestellte, sein Vater, 20 Jahre älter, starb zehn Monate nach seiner Geburt. Zur Uni kam der schmale blasse Junge nur mit einem Stipendium. Tagsüber arbeitete er als Kassierer in städtischen Bussen, nachts lernte er. „No pain, no gain“, tätowiert er sich auf die Lende.
Acht Millionen Follower auf Instagram
Nach vier Jahren in der Politik hat der Mann aus der Provinz acht Millionen Follower auf Instagram, fast doppelt so viele wie Lula. 2022 nominiert ihn die gemäßigte Partei Avante als Kandidaten für das Präsidentenamt. Janones zieht seine Kandidatur jedoch bald zurück, um Lula zu unterstützen, der gegen den rechtsextremen Jair Bolsonaro antritt.
Zwei Jahre später präsentiert ihm ein Gesundheits-Check die Rechnung für jahrelangen ungesunden Lebensstil: Vorstadium von Diabetes. Mit 40 Jahren ändert der Politiker sein Leben radikal, beginnt zu joggen, trainiert Boxen, stellt seine Ernährung um. Die Fitness hilft ihm, den dreiwöchigen Social-Media-Marathon durchzustehen, den er 2026 organisiert, nachdem Lula im ersten Wahlgang gegen Flávio Bolsonaro verliert.
Da sucht die Gegenseite nach dunklen Flecken auf des Abgeordneten Weste. Und findet: einen Antrag auf gerichtliche Schutzmaßnahmen wegen psychischer Gewalt von einer ehemaligen Partnerin. Der Prozess ist geheim, Janones sagt, er dürfe nichts dazu sagen. Zwei ehemalige Assistenten sagen, der Politiker habe das System der „Rachadinha“ angewendet, bei dem Assistenten eines Politikers diesem einen Teil ihres Gehalts abgeben. Janones sagt, er habe nur die Idee aufgebracht, man könne untereinander Geld für den Wahlkampf sammeln, aber die Idee nie umgesetzt. Gegen ihn liegen keine Beweise oder Verurteilungen vor.
Nach dem erneuten Wahlsieg von Lula spekulieren die Medien über einen Ministerposten für den „General“. Ein Ministeramt komme für ihn nicht infrage, sagt Janones, er sei Abgeordneter. Aber gefragt, ob er sich vorstellen kann, 2030 für das Präsidentenamt zu kandidieren, sagt er: „Ich schließe nichts aus.“ Mutter Janones wird es recht sein.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Record-breaking California tides cause major flooding of roads and businesses
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lois Beckett in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the California coast on Wednesday, sending seawater rushing into beachside communities and flooding roads and businesses.
As big waves battered the coast, the tip of a landmark pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, was slammed into the sea, local news outlets reported. The pier, which had once housed a favorite local cafe, had previously suffered structural damage and had been closed to the public, the San Francisco Chronicle reported, and collapsed after contact with ocean swells 12 times stronger than on an average November day.
Los Angeles and Santa Barbara tied or broke all-time high tide records on Wednesday, at 8.19 and 8.21ft, respectively, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). La Jolla, California, just north of San Diego, also set an all-time high tide record of 8.11ft (2.5 meters), according to the NWS, while preliminary data suggested that tides in Monterey, south of San Francisco, might also have set an all-time record at 8.03ft.
The city of Monterey closed multiple beaches to the public over safety concerns, with closures lasting until Friday. Beaches in Santa Cruz county were also closed.
“That sun may be out, but the beach and surf zone remain dangerous,” NWS San Francisco warned, citing waves around the San Francisco Bay area as high as 24ft.
“This is a preview of things to come,” California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, said in a San Francisco press conference about Wednesday’s flooding. “That’s why it’s so important that we not just situationally address and reflect on moments like this, but sustainably get under the hood and try to solve for some of these things.”
In Pacifica, giant waves and tide waters swept over beaches and piers, flooding coastal roads including Highway 1 near the famous local landmark Taco Bell Cantina, America’s poshest Taco Bell. (The iconic restaurant was unharmed by the tides, NBC Bay Area reported.)
“This El Niño is unprecedented with its strength,” the San Mateo county supervisor Ray Mueller told the Los Angeles Times. “For this to be happening when it is a beautiful day on the coast side today, in clear sunshine and no wind, is really significant.”
Multiple coastal homes in Sunset Beach, in Orange county, had flooded, the Los Angeles Times reported, but a local fire chief said the overall damage had been mitigated by how aggressively local homeowners had fortified their homes in advance.
Low-lying coastal roads around the Bay Area also saw flooding, including a stretch of road near the Golden Gate Bridge, which was temporarily closed, the Chronicle reported.
However, most of the state avoided the worst-case scenario – coastal flooding amplified by intense winter rainstorms.
“We’re past high tide, and San Francisco has made it through the worst of this round of king tides,” mayor Daniel Lurie said in a social media statement just after noon local time, saying officials were “only aware of minimal impacts across the city”.
Local officials had been preparing for weeks for the risk that flooding would disrupt travel during Thanksgiving week, one of the busiest times of the year. Experts warn that flooding risk will only worsen in the next two months.
Flooding risk at the San Francisco international airport, a major transit hub situated on low-lying coastal land, had been of particular concern. At least three airlines offered free trip changes to travelers whose journeys took them through San Francisco on Wednesday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
But the airport announced at noon that “We’re in the clear,” and said it was deactivating its emergency operations center after avoiding any impact from the high tides on Tuesday and Wednesday.
On the north coast, the NWS reported that Humboldt Bay saw its second highest tide on record, and advised residents to prepare for major coastal flooding in low lying areas. The county sheriff warned the public to stay away from beaches during the storm.
A local news outlet in Oregon shared a video on Tuesday that illustrated the risk of the west coast’s high-tide surf, showing a man and his dog almost getting swept away by unexpectedly high waves during the king tides in Cannon Beach, Oregon. Both man and dog escaped without injury, police told KVAL News.
The California governor’s office of emergency services deployed crews and equipment around the state to assist with storm response. In the Bay Area, crews could be seen preparing sandbags to help protect buildings from flooding.
California’s flooding risk this week is the result of a combination of factors, some of them driven by this year’s super El Niño weather, including the lingering effects of the massive Kelvin wave that traveled up California’s coast. The overlap of unusually high Pacific coast water levels this year with the seasonal high tides called “king tides” has sparked alarm from weather experts, who have warned that the most dangerous flooding is likely to occur if a strong winter storm with heavy wind and rain hits areas of the coast at the same time as the high tide’s peak.
So far, it seems like California has avoided the worst of that risk during the November king tide period. But the amplified king tides will return twice more, around late December and then in late January, in periods where big winter storms remain likely.
Dani Anguiano contributed reporting

https://apache.be/2026/11/11/engeland-en.title: In Engeland en Schotland bezit 1% ruim de helft van alle grond, deze burgers verzetten zich
https://apache.be/2026/11/11/engeland-en.author: Lotte Christiaens

How Conservatives Lost Their Minds Over the “Indian Question”
Indian Americans seemed to be trending towards the GOP. Then came a ton of racism.
Chris Rufo wears many hats—infamous culture warrior, fellow at the right-wing Manhattan Institute think tank, nakedly cynical enemy of diversity initiatives and Critical Race Theory, serial fabulist. And, since this is 2026, Rufo also has his own podcast, Rufo and Lomez, which he cohosts with Jonathan Keeperman on Blaze TV. This past September, an episode of Rufo and Lomez caused a wave of controversy by its title: “The Indian Question.”
The phrase is a winking provocation, a deliberate throwback to previous generations’ racialized “questions” (the “Jewish question” or the “Catholic question”). But there was nothing funny about Rufo’s message: that Indian Americans’ alleged resistance to assimilation, coupled with their collective capture of elite institutions, such as universities, threatens the cultural heritage of the United States. “Even if there might be trade-offs for keeping some amount of immigrants out who are high-skilled and might be a benefit to the economy, I like having a high-trust society,” Keeperman remarks during the podcast. “I like living somewhere where there is cultural cohesion, where I have this unspoken affinity with my neighbors.”
Of course, this is a childish view of cultural kinship and cohesion—one that fuses trust with skin color, as if all white Americans shared the same values and trusted one another the same. It’s difficult to take figures like Keeperman and Rufo seriously. The former is an erstwhile anonymous Twitter troll, and a friend to open white nationalists such as Steve Sailer. The latter is far more prominent, best known for spreading the racist lie in 2024 that immigrant Haitians in Ohio were eating their neighbors’ cats. But Rufo is nothing if not an opportunist, a shapeshifter who senses where the political winds might be blowing and moves accordingly. John Ganz astutely describes him as “a political entrepreneur… identifying conflicts developing on the right and translating cultural controversies into politically usable concepts and then into institutional campaigns.”
Rufo’s engagement with the “Indian Question” is revealing—if not for its substance, which is just faux-intellectual babble that aims to inflame, then as a sign of the present conservative approach to immigration.
By the end of the 20th century, the debate largely hinged on the axis of good “legal” and bad “illegal” immigration. The latter, it was thought, should be policed; the former wasn’t only tolerated but exalted as a monument of the American promise, a shibboleth held by Democrats and most Republicans alike. That consensus began to crack over the years of the Obama presidency, which saw Republicans repeatedly detonate efforts to substantively reform immigration laws (all while Obama presided over a historic deportation operation).
The last decade of American politics has shattered these shibboleths, thanks to a reinvigorated nativist conservative base powered by the rise of Donald Trump. These days, conservative discourse on immigration is littered with chilling, fantastical concepts such as “remigration” (the forced repatriation of immigrants and their descendants back to their home countries), and “Heritage Americans” (a category that defines “real” Americans on openly racial lines).
Figures like Rufo have long sought to harness this raucous, eliminationist spirit, and inject it into the heart of contemporary Republican Party politics. They’ve largely succeeded, and today, the status quo on immigration has been upended: Over the last year and a half, undocumented immigrants have been subjected to a fascist, murderous blitz; now “legal” immigrants have also come into the crosshairs of conservative politicians.
Two years ago, the Republican Party appeared to be on the brink of a breakthrough with Indian American voters, a historically solid Democratic bloc. Twenty-two percent of Indian American voters supported Trump’s 2020 campaign; that number shot up to 30 percent in his 2024 campaign. If Republicans could have siphoned more Indian American voters this cycle, that could have potentially affected margins of swing seats in states such as Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas. Yet, perhaps owing to the recent surge in conservative anti-Indian rhetoric, Republican gains with Indian American voters have evaporated.
Even as this new consensus was decisively rebuked in the midterms, though, it remains the dominating paradigm of American immigration—and in both interesting and pressing ways, it has touched the politics of the Indian American diaspora as well.
The present anti–Indian American phenomenon began as an outgrowth of an intra-conservative debate about the H-1B visa system, which permits tens of thousands of foreign, high-skilled workers to immigrate to the United States and work for American companies. Indian immigrants account for nearly three-quarters of H-1B visa holders, and have thus become emblematic of both the H-1B system and its alleged “abuse.” Right-wing opponents generally see the H-1B as a mechanism for job-stealing foreigners to enter America through the back door.
Some of the more enterprising firebreathers, such as Steve Bannon, talk about the program as enabling “corporate greed,” shrouding their critiques in a thin tissue of populist rhetoric (for many of this ilk, these were the first—and perhaps only—comments on corporate excess they’ve ever levied). In recent months, the Trump administration, facing historically low approval ratings and anemic enthusiasm going into the midterms, announced further restrictions to the process. As expected, the reforms roused the GOP base, jolting a fresh round of discourse around both the visa and Indian immigration.
Critiques of the H-1B system often blur into outright xenophobia—an unsurprising development when considering how much of contemporary conservative politics is powered by its white nationalist bloc. The best-known example of this came in September, when a Texas Republican candidate named Bo French reposted a photograph depicting a group of South Asian students celebrating a University of Texas–Austin football win. “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” he laments. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”
French’s comments attracted widespread condemnation, yet his sentiment was far from exceptional. In January, Aaron Reitz, a former Texas GOP candidate who currently serves as a United States Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, tweeted about the “invasion of un-assimilated & unassimilable Indians,” before calling on the Trump administration to “Deport most. Assimilate the rest.”
Another story from earlier this year, which circulated widely across the right-wing media ecosystem, highlighted the Dallas suburb of Frisco. Around 20 percent of Frisco’s residents are of Indian descent, and many of them are H-1B visa holders, a fact that prompted conservative talking heads to warn of Frisco’s “Indian takeover.” Riled-up activists flooded Frisco City Hall meetings, where they often ripped into Burt Thakur, one of the city’s council members—ironically, an Indian American Trump supporter.
On the federal stage, two of the most vocal critics alleging H-1B abuse are Vice President JD Vance and Republican Texas Representative Brandon Gill. Vance recently referred to H-1B workers as “indentured servants”; Gill, a 32-year-old with a massive and rabid online following, tweeted, “We don’t need to import 7-Eleven workers from India or anywhere across the globe. Hire Americans.”
The profound irony is that both Vance and Gill have married Indian American women; they are fathers to Indian American children. Yet both have gladly offered up their families as tributes to the white nationalist meat grinder sustaining massive swaths of their governing coalitions. Indeed, many others have made this observation in recent months, but perhaps none more noteworthy than the shrill antisemite and white supremacist Nick Fuentes, in a recent jeremiad excoriating the contemporary right’s lack of authenticity.
Vivek Ramaswamy, one of the most contemptuous figures in American politics, is a key figure in this conversation—an exemplar of the tightrope act that today’s conservatives of color are forced to walk. His Indian ancestry was a key liability during his 2024 presidential campaign, and continued to drag down his chances during his ill-fated Ohio gubernatorial campaign. Last December, he took to The New York Times to try to stake some moral high ground, writing that “it is downright unacceptable to spew poison toward Jews, Indians or any other ethnic group.”
Unfortunately for Ramaswamy, this “righteous” declaration is painfully out of step with contemporary Republican politics (to say nothing of his otherwise heinous campaign). Ahead of the election, right-wing pundit Erick Erickson described Ohio’s polling as “pretty bleak,” a fact he partly attributes to how “the white nationalists…don’t want to support Vivek Ramaswamy for governor.”
Ramaswamy ultimately lost the governor’s race by nearly eight percentage points, a humiliating defeat that will usher in Ohio’s first Democratic governor in a decade and a half. “Look at what’s happening in Dearborn, Michigan. We’re not going to let that come to our state of Ohio,” he warned at one of his final campaign speeches. It’s a Lynchian scene: a brown-skinned Hindu warning about brown-skinned Muslims, trusting that a political movement, composed of a growing number of white nationalists, will make the distinction between the “good” and the “bad” brown-skinned immigrant.
Yet this dissonance hasn’t slowed an odd set of right-wing influencers of Indian descent from unloading on the H-1B program—and in the process, slipping between the critiques of the visa and Indians writ large. Nalin Haley, son of former South Carolina governor and UN Ambassador Nimrata “Nikki” Haley, is an influencer with over 50,000 followers across social-media platforms, and has frequently called for the complete termination of the program. But his comments, too, have occasionally blasted the Indian nation-state more broadly: “They send cheap labor to the US, buy cheap oil from Iran, and cheap weapons from Russia because they have a cheap government.”
