Another influencer, one Priya Patel, who boasts a cumulative following of nearly 200,000, has also coupled her critiques of H-1B with scathing comments that implicate her own ancestry. “Not all cultures are equal, and we shouldn’t be importing the third world,” she once tweeted, before later describing India as the “third world.”
To witness these Indian Americans contort their identities to fit the shell of nativist Americanism is absurd, even carnivalesque. Perhaps they feel like they can singe off their Indian inheritances in exchange for unconditional entry into the fraternity of “America.” One quick scroll on their social-media accounts and we’re reminded just how wishful this thinking is—at any given time, you’ll find troll accounts disparaging these Indian American influencers as “jeets,” the preferred anti–South Asian slur of the online right.
In Texas, the anti-Indian fight has harmonized well with an existing Islamophobic panic around “Sharia law” currently possessing Texas conservatives. To right-wing, nativist Texans, it appears that both invasions are two sides of the same coin. In the aftermath of the midterm results, one conservative influencer commented, “This is what happens when you import Muslims and Indians into Collin County,” accompanied by a screenshot showing Collin swinging toward James Talarico (Collin contains part of Frisco, as well as Plano, another city that right-wingers have seized upon in their anti-H1B hysteria).
But the Hindu American Foundation, a noxious organization that has long served the interests of rich, right-wing Indian Americans, is trying to cleave anti-Indian hate from anti-Sharia panic. Not only does it wish to justify the latter, it also cosigns the notion that Hindus are well-suited to combat Sharia—a misguided strategy that only fans the flames of bigotry. And beyond its reprehensible moral approach, it’s a hopelessly naïve effort given the symbiotic relationship between anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim politics—a pathetic appeal that rhymes with those scenes of Ramaswamy begging white nationalists for their support.
As surreal as this entire spectacle remains, it’s not without its material consequences. According to one report by Stop AAPI Hate, the proliferation of anti-South Asian slurs online more than doubled between January 2023 and December 2025. “Threats against South Asians,” the report reads, “comprised 71% of all anti-Asian threats between August 2024 and December 2025.” Just this weekend, a right-wing activist and his followers stormed a Seattle Diwali event brandishing signs that read “Deport All Dot Heads” and “Stop Hindu Replacement of Christians.” Over recent months, following the tragic news of an undocumented Sikh truck driver’s fatal crash that killed three people, Sikh Americans were particularly targeted—both by online right-wing mobs, as well as the Department of Homeland Security. “I can’t wait till ICE swipes your ass with your H1-B and deports you via shipping container,” one anonymous right-winger tweeted to Jyot Singh, a recently elected Sikh American Georgia state representative.
Last month, a 19-year-old neo-Nazi stormed a Hindu temple in Illinois, where he intended to carry out a mass shooting. Miraculously, his rifle misfired and no one was injured. His manifesto, which allegedly derides Black, Jewish, and Indian Americans as “subhuman,” offers a clear glimpse into the ideology underpinning contemporary white supremacist radicalism. According to news reports, authorities found a gas can at the attacker’s home. The label read “Jeet Remover.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: A New Trump Rule on Tax Credits Could Impoverish Thousands of Legal Immigrants
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Bryce Covert
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
A New Trump Rule on Tax Credits Could Impoverish Thousands of Legal Immigrants
It’s the latest move in the administration’s all-out effort to deny government benefits to immigrants—even those living and working here legally.
The Trump administration recently proposed a change to tax credits that would, if finalized, significantly impoverish hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants—as well as their US citizen children. It’s the latest move in the administration’s all-out effort to deny government benefits to immigrants—both those who are undocumented and those legally living and working in the United States—in order to make life in the county as miserable as possible for them.
The proposed rule, released by the Treasury Department in August, targets four federal tax credits—the Earned Income Tax Credit, the Child Tax Credit, the American Opportunity Tax Credit, and the Adoption Credit—that give tax refunds to filers who earn below a certain threshold. The EITC and CTC are by far the largest and most commonly claimed. Over 1 million people live in families that could lose access to the CTC and 602,000 could lose access to the EITC. About 515,000 could lose both.
The immigrants who will be affected by the rule change include the recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals—people who have been living in the United States since they were very young and don’t know any other place to call home—those who have pending asylum applications with work authorization, those with Temporary Protected Status, those with visas for victims of violence and crimes, those with employment and student visas, those granted parole for less than a year, and children who have been abused or neglected by their parents. The average family losing the credits because they are DACA recipients would forgo $4,560 in tax credits per year, amounting to 13 percent of their income. “That is not a drop in the bucket for those families,” Davis said. “They are going to feel that.”
Related Articles
The EITC and CTC have long required a work-authorized Social Security number, which can only be obtained with some sort of legal status. “This is not a credit where a migrant can cross the border and start receiving it in the next day,” pointed out Carl Davis, research director at the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. But while an immigrant with one of the targeted statuses who is married to a citizen will be protected, single parents or people who are married to someone else with one of these statuses will not. Meanwhile, about 523,000 children live in families that could lose the CTC and 279,000 are in families that could lose the EITC. About 90 percent of those children are US citizens. “When a family loses access to a credit like this, it affects everyone on the return,” Davis pointed out. “The kids are going to suffer too.”
The EITC and CTC help working families avoid poverty by giving them income support. Families often use the money to fill gaps in their budgets, buying necessities like food and diapers, repairing cars, paying off owed rent, or paying for their children’s extracurriculars. “They can use the money in the way that’s most effective and most important for their families,” said Kris Cox, director of federal tax policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. These measures have proven effective. Refundable tax credits kept over 10 million people out of poverty in 2025. When the CTC was expanded in 2021, child poverty fell to the lowest level recorded.
The families targeted by the rule change pay taxes to the federal government through Social Security taxes, income taxes, sales taxes, and property taxes, meaning they are still “paying on net to the federal government,” noted Ben D’Avanzo, senior strategist for federal advocacy at the National Immigration Law Center. If the rule were finalized, they would stop getting a benefit they help to fund. It would create “a two-tiered tax system,” D’Avanzo explained, “where immigrants essentially pay higher taxes than other people, without getting the benefits in return.”
The rule could also scare immigrants away from paying taxes after years of the IRS trying to encourage them to file. For the first time, filers will have to correctly report their immigration status on their returns, and the IRS will have to verify it, even though it currently has no system for doing so. In a draft tax form for 2026, the IRS has added a box asking, “At the time you file your return, are you, and your spouse if filing jointly, a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or an alien lawfully authorized to work in the U.S.? (see instructions).” That question has “never been on there before,” Cox said. It has also drafted a new form for claiming the refundable tax credits that askes, “Are you or your spouse a U.S. citizen, U.S national, or qualified alien?”
Such questions could deter immigrants from filing their taxes, particularly after the IRS shared information on tens of thousands of people with Immigration and Customs Enforcement in 2025 (a practice courts have since blocked). “There will be some people who are just frightened about answering any questions related to their immigration status and might feel chilled answering these questions,” said Shelby Gonzales, vice president for immigration policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, even though failing to file could result in criminal penalties. Many immigrants may not know if their particular status is “qualified” for the credits or not; some might need the help of an immigration lawyer to figure it out. “If I am an immigrant, I do not have a card that says, ‘You have a qualifying immigration status,’” Gonzales pointed out. “People are not going to risk this if they don’t know for sure that they fit into one of those categories.”
“It’s unavoidable that people who are eligible for the credits, who remain eligible despite this rule” will end up without them “because of this confusion and fear,” Cox added.
The proposed rule is an outgrowth of changes made in sweeping welfare reform legislation passed in 1996, which for the first time denied this group of lawful immigrants cash welfare. They were “vilified for a conservative agenda,” said D’Avanzo, as “people who do not deserve help, do not deserve the ability to have access to support for their families.” But for the last 30 years, Congress has never applied that restriction to other benefits and programs. “This rule is really upending 30 years of precedent and policy,” Cox said.
If the rule is finalized, it’s likely to face a challenge in court. Congress “clearly thought about this issue and has crafted its own restrictions [for these tax credits], and now the administration wants to go farther,” Davis said. In 1996 Congress also passed legislation restricting the EITC to people with Social Security numbers—which these immigrants have—and there is language in current statute that says noncitizens are eligible for tax credits. “The administration is attempting to usurp Congress’s authority in setting tax law and creating its own rules,” D’Avanzo asserted, “driven not by what the law itself says but by their really deranged anti-immigrant sentiments.”
The administration also had a chance to create these changes legislatively, but it didn’t: Trump’s huge tax-focused reconciliation bill, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed last year with only Republican votes, didn’t include anything limiting tax credits for legal immigrants. At the same time, Republicans did take away some benefits—Medicaid and CHIP funding, Affordable Care Act exchange premium tax credits, Medicare, and food stamps—from a similar group of immigrants, leaving them only available to citizens, green-card holders, and a few others.

The Trump administration has already tried to apply the immigration-related restrictions of the 1996 welfare reform law to other programs, most notably Head Start. Last year, a handful of federal agencies issued guidance saying they would classify the same group of immigrants as ineligible for Head Start enrollment, as well as for access to things like mental health services, domestic violence shelters, adult education programs, and federally funded health centers, deeming these things to also be “public benefits.” The effort has been permanently blocked by the courts nationwide, in part because the judge said the agencies violated procedure in issuing the guidance. But the judge left open the possibility of agencies’ issuing rules similar to what the IRS has proposed for tax credits in an attempt to do it in a more lawful way. “It would not be surprising,” D’Avanzo said, if the agencies try again through rulemaking.
In November, the administration did the same thing to a variety of programs at the Department of Housing and Urban Development, many of which fund affordable housing and homelessness services. The administration has also finalized a rule that prohibits entire families with mixed immigration status—where one or more family members don’t have a qualifying immigration status, even if others do—from living in federally subsidized housing, including both public housing and private apartments that receive rental assistance. Nearly 80,000 people could lose their rental assistance, including 52,500 citizens.
The administration has also finalized a harsh so-called “public charge” rule that will allow immigration officials to deny people’s green-card applications. It gives these officials wide latitude to take an immigrant’s use of nearly any public benefit into account and deem that it’s a negative factor in their quest for legal status. Most of the immigrants who go through that process are not undocumented and have a pathway toward lawful permanent status, but now they will face the choice between keeping benefits that allow them and their families to eat and survive or giving them up for a shot at a green card. Between 1.4 million and 4.1 million people could end up deciding to disenroll from Medicaid and CHIP, including their 1.7 million children who are US citizens. When the Trump administration issued a similar rule during his first term, which was later blocked by the courts, it still led 31 percent of adults in families with at least one family member who did not yet have a green card to forgo benefits. It’s “another way of scaring people who remain eligible for benefit programs from accessing them,” Gonzales said.
On top of all of that, early in Trump’s second administration he rescinded a Biden-era rule that allowed DACA recipients to get health coverage on the Affordable Care Act exchanges, instead blocking them from that option.
This is “a very coordinated effort to take away eligibility for benefit programs,” Gonzales noted. And that is meant to make life as uncomfortable as possible for immigrants in this country, with and without legal status. The Trump administration is using “every lever of the federal government for making immigrants feel unwelcome and unsafe living in the United States,” D’Avanzo said. “The overarching goal is to make it as hard as possible to be an immigrant in the United States.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sophia Kishkovsky
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.
At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.
“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.
The neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.
The Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.
A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.
Berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”
The minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to plan for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.
Unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.
The strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.
A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-dinki.author: David Duhalde

David Dinkins Wasn’t Loud Enough for New York City
David Dinkins, New York’s first black mayor and a Democratic Socialists of America member, practiced a quiet, dignified form of municipal leadership — so hushed that he was easily drowned out by more reactionary and demagogic forces in the city.
In the past few weeks, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has proposed breaking up the Strategic Response Group and closing Rikers by 2032, the former established by progressive Mayor Bill de Blasio, who also revived a plan to dismantle the latter by 2027. But unfulfilled promises of police and carceral reform efforts go back to the 1990s. How much should the failures of previous mayoral administrations weigh on the decisions of Mamdani and his allies in regard to public safety and police?
This question has no easy answer. But a new book by James Barney on the tenure of New York City’s first black mayor, David Dinkins, offers insights on his efforts to rein in police excesses based on new research, especially in the local press of the era — and critically how those attempts failed, despite Mayor Dinkins’s desires and promises.
In A Fragile Alliance: David Dinkins, Coalition Politics, and the Struggle to Govern a City in Crisis, Barney, while sympathetic to Dinkins, argues that both Dinkins’s quiet leadership style and inability to create a narrative uniting his own multiracial coalition, much less the majority of the city, proved to be his undoing, dooming his reelection prospects and much of his agenda.
Barney, critical of identity politics throughout his history book, sums up his reservations here:
. . . in particular, Dinkins’s reliance on the mosaic metaphor betrayed a worldview that privileged difference. While Dinkins repeatedly noted that New York City was a “gorgeous mosaic,” in a “mosaic” each of the pieces is different. They only produce any meaning by being part of a larger piece of art. But this type of thinking was at the heart of Dinkins’s problems as a leader because it emphasized differences rather than commonalities.
Barney’s reservations about celebrating difference are at times too determinative. For instance, I doubt Dinkins could have done much to stop the disintegration of the New Deal/Great Society coalition that voted Democratic as white ethnics left the party across the country. But Barney’s concerns about the communication failures of Dinkins’s tenure were real and went beyond narrative to style.
While noble at times, the mayor’s quiet leadership style prevented New Yorkers — especially in a time without social media to get news rapidly and easily outside major media like Mamdani enjoys and uses today — from seeing their mayor’s interventions that created more peace than was seen elsewhere in America at the time, for example Los Angeles, which experienced a much deadlier upheaval triggered by the lack of convictions for the police who senselessly beat Rodney King, as well as the killing of teenager Latasha Harlins by a Korean American storeowner. This failure provided an opening to power for demagogues such as Rudy Giuliani to paint a darker picture around crime and disorder than actually existed.
While New York City’s political landscape has changed in many ways — the Staten Island secession movement, for example, is almost forgotten today — one thing Barney covers remains very much the same. The New York Police Department (NYPD) and institutions around it enjoy strong independence from civilian control that makes it difficult for any mayor to shape policy and personnel decisions commensurate with other major city agencies.
A famous instance of this was when the Sergeants Benevolent Association (SBA) tweeted out personal data of then-Mayor de Blasio’s daughter’s arrest related to the George Floyd uprising. Former SBA head Ed Mullins eventually faced disciplinary charges over this, though by then it was overshadowed by his federal indictment and conviction of stealing from his members. It is difficult to think of any other agency and its unions who would feel so emboldened to reject democratic oversight.
Dinkins, unlike most of today’s socialists and progressives, ran on a tough-on-crime agenda. He promised to hire thousands more police officers. The issue of crime polled high across racial and gender categories of voters. But Dinkins targeted his law-and-order proposals to include increasing policing in communities of color with officers of similar backgrounds. A major critic of this policy was Giuliani, who claimed this public safety policy would take police away from white neighborhoods. Giuliani’s racialized law-and-order rhetoric helped sink Dinkins.
Progressive mayors following Dinkins, such as de Blasio and Mamdani, have reckoned with the political reality that a public safety reform agenda is territory that isn’t worth attempting battle upon. And losing puts their whole left-wing agenda, not just public safety, at risk. Case in point: after Dinkins’s defeat, New York saw two decades of fiscal conservative and anti-police-reform mayors.
Crown Heights as a Turning Point
Two chapters of the book that expand on how such demagoguery on policing helped cost Dinkins his mayoralty focus on the Crown Heights riots and Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association (PBA) riots, respectively. These chapters also go beyond those two episodes of public violence to discuss how other instances of excessive police force neither led to uprisings nor successful efforts to advance civilian control of law enforcement. Barney’s research uses these events to help us understand how perceived disorder would be viewed as a key reason Dinkins lost, even though the crime rates were falling, and how his relationship with the police leadership and rank and file did not recover despite his own law-and-order narrative.
Dinkins won a surprise primary victory against three-term incumbent and bombastic erstwhile liberal Ed Koch in 1989. Barney credits Dinkins’s win through efforts to build a black-led, multiracial coalition out of the efforts in and around Jesse Jackson’s 1988 presidential campaign and subsequent Rainbow Coalition. Voter registration and mobilization, especially of black voters, to back Jackson were then used to elect Dinkins.
Those new voters proved fruitful for Dinkins’s own Rainbow Coalition. Dinkins won over half the vote in the multicandidate Democratic primary against Koch. But his candidacy against the Republican in the general was unusually closer. In New York, the Democratic Party primary more often than not is the de facto election. Not for Dinkins. He faced Giuliani, famous at the time for his federal prosecution of the mafia in New York’s Southern District, in 1989 and 1993. Each time, the victor only bested his opponent by around 2 points.
Not only were the margins similar, but Barney argues that themes in each election centered around crime, racial tension, and divisive ethnic politics. What made the difference was how a slim number of voters (turnout was roughly the same, 1.9 million in both mayoral races) eventually shifted toward a harsher response to perceptions of disorder, even as crime rates were declining.
Dinkins lost ground partly because of both the Crown Heights riot and PBA riot. Each contributed to the public perception of an ineffective Dinkins, which undermined his promises to create a safer city and less brutal policing methods.
The Crown Heights riot story officially begins on August 19, 1991, when a vehicle in a motorcade following the chief Lubavitcher (a sect of Jewish Hasidim) rabbi hit two Guyanese American children. The immediate lack of medical attention for the children by emergency medial technicians, explained by the Jewish volunteer service that initially responded to the accident lacking professional skills needed to treat the young people’s injuries, led to a retaliatory stabbing of a rabbinical student days later. The following unrest, in which 150 people were arrested and one hundred police injured, led the media to publicly question Dinkins’s ability to heal the racial and ethnic divide in the city and portray him as a weak leader.
But the conflict in Crown Heights went further back than these two incidents. The riot itself reflected the tension between the religious Jewish enclave and their black neighbors, largely of West Indian descent. In a city where fights over resources can feel zero-sum, the well-organized and self-isolating Lubavitcher community appeared to gain at others’ expense. Their leadership, politically well-connected as a result of their well-organized followers voting as a bloc, primarily looked after their own. Barney notes, for example, that the police protection for the Lubavitcher headquarters was seen as taking officers away from the crack epidemic, fostering further estrangement from their black gentile neighbors.
Dinkins, viewing this as a battle of “good and evil,” according to Barney, responded to the restive state of Crown Heights by sending in a thousand police officers to quell the violence. Black civil rights leaders and organizers such as the Reverend Al Sharpton and Sonny Carson, at times previously allied with the mayor, turned on him. Sharpton even characterized Dinkins’s action as setting up an “apartheid state.”
But a second, seemingly contradictory viewpoint sprung up from Giuliani and his allies that Dinkins actually held the police back from acting. This narrative fit well with voters that Barney says wanted to lump Dinkins, Carson, and Sharpton together. Dinkins couldn’t win.
To make things worse, Dinkins publicly stated — repeating doctors’ misdiagnosis — that the stabbed rabbinical student would recover. But his wounds were fatal. The Jewish man died a few hours after Dinkins’s remarks. The death made Dinkins look, even if unfairly, incompetent.
Barney credits much of the success the mayor did achieve in facilitating conservations between different Crown Heights faith leaders. These dialogues between Christian and Jewish leaders were rarely reported in the press. To Barney, this was just another example of Dinkins’s “quiet leadership” that, while noble, undermined public perception of governance.
Ultimately, a 1993 internal city investigation called the Girgenti Report vindicated Dinkins from the viewpoint that he had not, in fact, held back the police nor abetted the prosecution of the rabbinical student’s killing. But the report’s timing was poor for the incumbent. Barney concludes it did more to remind voters in an election year of the chaos of two years earlier than absolving Dinkins in their eyes: “For a mayor who longed to unify, Crown Heights became the moment when broad segments of the public lost confidence in Dinkins and when his vision of a gorgeous mosaic, while laudable, was found insufficient to meet New York City’s realities.”
The narrative that Dinkins held the NYPD back in Crown Heights was one of many that undermined his relationship with the police department and its officers. Another was that the overwhelming white police force felt the mayor was giving preferential treatment to people of color and criminals.
The Police Riot as a Point of No Return
In 1992, a police officer shot a Dominican immigrant in Washington Heights, which sparked a series of events that led to a police riot by September. The Washington Heights shooting seemed to be heading toward similar unrest — this time, sparked by young people who felt overpoliced. Dinkins was able to de-escalate the situation well, such that even his critics like Cardinal John O’Connor gave the mayor credit for his handling of the shooting’s aftermath.
The mayor’s initial success and efforts included allies he recruited. Dinkins had an ally in Lee P. Brown, an African American criminologist and former police chief of Houston, Texas, that took the same role under Dinkins. As commissioner, Brown supported community policing, which brought more officers who looked like the people of the neighborhoods they patrolled. Again, this policy was not favored by some white people who felt it took resources from their residential areas.
But this balance between reform and political reality in policing became unstable for both Dinkins’s coalition and the NYPD brass. At the time, the police practiced stop and frisk, an invasive and violating search practice that nearly exclusively targeted young men of color. Dinkins would come to regret this policy. Beyond the ethics, stop and frisk also fostered a schism in his coalition between the young people who felt brutalized and the older residents who wanted more police. Roscoe C. Brown Jr, a Tuskegee airman veteran quoted by Barney, summed up this division in the simple fact that black people had been victims of both crime and racist policing. Solving one requires tackling the other.
But doing so for Dinkins became impossible. Brown resigned as commissioner in 1992, because, according to Barney, even this reformer did not want to go as far as Dinkins in empowering the police watchdog city agency, the Civil Complaint Review Board. Dinkins, unlike Brown, determined the NYPD was unable to hold itself accountable. Still, Brown’s departure was from the worst rebuke Dinkins would experience by the NYPD.
On September 16, 1992, organized by the police union (PBA), nearly ten thousand off-duty officers rallied outside city hall. Fueled by alcohol and rhetoric from Giuliani and PBA union leaders saying Dinkins favored criminals over cops, some police wore anti-Dinkins shirts, and others overturned barricades.
While the media and some allies like Sharpton returned to Dinkins’s camp after this because of the racist slurs hurled at Dinkins and noxious nature of the police riot, the damage was done with enough of the public. The perception that Dinkins had lost the police overrode the actual declining crime rates with a sufficient number of voters to eventually swing the election toward Giuliani the next year. This would end a progressive holding the mayor’s office until 2014 with the election of Bill de Blasio.
NYPD Reform Returns
Today not only is the mayor a progressive but, like Dinkins, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Zohran Mamdani also shares the challenges of balancing the wishes of his coalition and campaign promises with those of political reality. Policing is no different.
Recently, Mamdani has pledged to disband the Special Response Group (SRG), a controversial police unit with both counterterrorism and protest control duties, and also backed socialist councilmember Chi Ossé’s CURB Act, which would limit tactics employed by SRG. As the SRG’s responsibilities will be reassigned to other police units, a move reportedly supported by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, limiting existing practices that police reform advocates say they are most against is critical to the success of reform.
Unlike Commissioner Lee with Dinkins, Tisch was not the incumbent mayor’s appointment but a holdover from the previous mayor. Mamdani has resisted calls from parts of his coalition to fire her; these allies identify her support of Zionism and a strong carceral state as incompatible with a socialist vision. Except for not hiring nearly six hundred more police officers after pushback from NYC-DSA and others, the recent moves against SRG nearly a year into his term are a first real push to tackle unaccountable and abusive police power.
While New York City crime stands at record lows, the experience of Dinkins should serve as a warning that statistical realities such as declining rates are sometimes no match for scare tactics. The police still have soft and unchecked power, with council allies allegedly quietly opposing the CURB Act.
Hidden opposition can become public, and allies can return. But sometimes it is too late, as Dinkins experienced after the police riot. As the title of Barney’s book reminds us, holding power can be fragile. It will take a balance of principle and strategic planning to successfully rein in the police. Or else we will set back again.
A lesson the current mayor can also learn from Dinkins is in a communication style to avoid. Instead, he should continue to present an accessible vision and visible actions so voters and other members of the public can easily understand and repeat his policy priorities.
Had Dinkins been able to enjoy the social media platforms and fluency that Mamdani does to get around mainstream gatekeepers and parochial local press, he might have been able to overcome the idea he was ineffective. But even with such tools, it requires a willingness to be public, even boastful, which people adverse to demagoguery understandably avoid.
But good intentions can be fatal. Quiet leadership, while noble, may be silent even to your supporters. And it can be used against you by your enemies. The base needs to know what you’re doing to counter the inevitable lies and distortions thrown at left-wing politicians by their reactionary political opponents.
The success of a progressive and socialist public safety agenda depends on winning the majority. That requires a tremendous amount of organizing from the grassroots, but also political leaders who can help echo a narrative that can cut through the noise trying to maintain the status quo or reserve the gains made by reformers so far.
A Fragile Alliance is worth reading for anyone trying to comprehend how the past can weigh on today’s New York. It is a valuable resource in seeing how old attack frames, especially around identity, which seem outdated but once worked against Dinkins, could return against Mamdani. But more critically, how previous efforts of mayors around police reform failed and succeeded. Learning from that history can better prepare activists to push those in power, even our allied electeds, in a more strategic direction.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/new-left-civ.text:
What the ’60s Left Gave Us
The New Left helped end a war and change American culture for the better. It also produced a strain of radicalism sometimes at odds with the working class. Adolph Reed Jr and Vivek Chibber weigh both sides of that legacy.
- Interview by
- Vivek Chibber
- Melissa Naschek
Before the Bernie Sanders presidential runs, the last big upsurge in radical American politics occurred in the 1960s. This moment is remembered for its civil rights activism and student antiwar protests, but how should we really understand the New Left’s rise and fall?
On this latest episode of the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism, Vivek Chibber and Melissa Naschek are joined by political scientist and longtime socialist organizer Adolph Reed Jr for a wide-ranging conversation about the ’60s radicals. They look at the rise of the student movement, the developments in postwar Marxism, and the birth of modern identity politics.
Confronting Capitalism with Vivek Chibber is produced by Catalyst: A Journal of Theory and Strategy and published by Jacobin. You can listen to the full episode here.
- Melissa Naschek Today we’re going to focus on the New Left and its legacy, specifically regarding race and identity politics. To start us out, Adolph, can you talk about how you became involved in politics and what your involvement in the New Left was like?
- Adolph Reed Yeah, it’s pretty prosaic. I was nineteen when Stokely Carmichael shouted black power in the Meredith March. I had already been politically aware, not just because I was precocious but also because of my family. However, I hadn’t been especially active until then. I was at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1966, and it was the crest of a period of intense campus activism and right on the edge of the beginning of another one. And like a lot of people in my demographic, the black power slogan was quite cathartic and effective. In addition, the first big escalation of the Vietnam War had occurred the previous summer in 1965, and I already had friends who had been drafted, gone over, and been killed within a two month span. The antiwar movement was kicking off on campus and I got involved in that. I was also involved with protests against the local Community Action Program. In a kind of a no-person’s-land between Chapel Hill and Carrboro, the Community Action Program decided to use funds to develop a neighborhood cleanup and beautification campaign on the principle that poor people were poor not because they didn’t have enough money, but because they were demoralized and needed a more beautiful environment, with flowers and stuff.
- Melissa Naschek This sounds like a prelude to broken windows.
- Adolph Reed Yeah, it absolutely was. So some of my friends and I started protesting the stuff that they were doing. On top of that, I did some voting rights work and some tutorial work through an organization called Youth Education Services, YES. At Chapel Hill, programs like that and other sort of do-gooder stuff worked through the campus Young Women’s Christian Association or YES, which became like a magnet for young people looking to be active in politics. And much of the leadership of the student left and even the Pan-African post-student left crowd had gone through YES in one way or another. But both the tutorial experience and voter registration drive were pretty formative for me.
- Melissa Naschek For those who don’t know, the Community Action Program was a program initiated by the 1964 Economic Opportunity Act passed by President Lyndon Johnson as part of his War on Poverty programs, which aimed to take federal dollars, invest in communities in some way, and leave it to the communities to combat poverty on their own terms. But you’re also talking about your political activism after the Voting Rights Act, which was aimed at getting more people involved in the political system.
- Adolph Reed Exactly. I think the voter registration campaign came first. At the time, the old seniority system in Congress was still in effect, so the strategy was to target the newly enfranchised black voters to vote against the incumbents who had been there for forever, had a lot of seniority, and controlled party politics. In one of these elections, there was a challenger named Jim Gardner, the owner of the first Hardee’s franchise, up against an incumbent Democrat named Harold Cooley, who was also horrible. And we were supposed to register people to go vote against Cooley by voting for this Goldwaterite Republican, who, if he won, wouldn’t have any seniority. So I did it and was knocking on people’s doors. I know this sounds like a cliché, but you know, I’d seen a lot of poverty in my life, but I’d never seen that kind of poverty before. This was worse than sharecropper’s shacks. I mean open sewage, kids outside with sores all over them, flies the size of B-52s. And after a couple of days of doing that, I thought, “Look, there’s no way I can in good conscience sell these people on the idea that they need to register to go vote for this one guy against the other one.” That was a disillusionment that led me to my father’s politics, basically. So I did that and the tutoring for as long as I could until a group of black power radicals took over the campus NAACP chapter and I was part of that. And then there were a couple of labor actions over in Greensboro. The state AFL-CIO would recruit us to go walk the picket lines at the Cone Mills corporation and that’s how I got drawn into the labor movement.
Understanding the New Left
- Melissa Naschek I think what’s so interesting and compelling about your career is that you came out of political work and then later went into academia to study politics. When I read your work, it’s clear how those experiences really shaped how you analyze and understand political developments. But let’s take a step back and look at the broader picture. When and what was the New Left?
- Adolph Reed There are narrower and broader ways to delimit what they were. First of all, there was a New Left that originated in the UK, principally during the 1950s. That emerged basically from a critical tendency within and around the Communist Party (CP). There was also something kind of comparable in the United States in the 1950s, which formed around journals like Studies on the Left and figures like C. Wright Mills and Dwight Macdonald. Some were Trotskyists or former Trotskyists.
- Vivek Chibber But much smaller. Much of the first generation of British New Leftists came out of the Communist Party, as Adolph said, and they saw themselves still as more or less Marxists. They believed the Communist Party had strayed and moved away from a vision of socialism. This was the generation of E. P. Thompson, Eric Hobsbawm, and other people around them, although Hobsbawm never left the Communist Party. In the United States, the New Left came from outside the CP, such as people like C. Wright Mills, as well as the precursors to Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), with the influence of Herbert Marcuse and people around him. And so it is a lot smaller in the United States, because the Soviet invasion of Hungary was a big catalyst in the UK, as well as Joseph Stalin’s death and the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. These all had a very big impact over there. But you would know more, Adolph. It seems to me less so over here, right?
- Adolph Reed I think that’s right. I think it was much less so, and what drove the cultural-intellectual space here that was the equivalent of the New Left there was something more like what Russell Jacoby romanticizes in The Last Intellectuals. So the combination of the continuing movement of the Trotskyist element from City College in the 1930s, as they were moving toward the National Endowment for Democracy and the right wing, basically, to becoming neoconservatives. By and large, people often said they were looking for “a non-communist left,” but what they just as likely meant was “a non-Marxist left.”
- Melissa Naschek What’s the distinction there between a non-communist versus a non-Marxist left?
- Adolph Reed Well, there’s a lot of tiptoeing wordplay around all these politics, and in the last two or three years I’ve come to feel that most of the time when Americans talk about an “anti-Stalinist Left,” what they’re really trying to distance themselves from is Marxism. And that was not necessarily the case in the UK. But in the United States, there were people like Macdonald, Mills, the liberal Partisan Review crowd, as well as Michael Harrington, the author of The Other America and the founder of one of the parents that produced the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee, and the Dissent group led by Irving Howe. All of these individuals were militantly anti-communist and combined a literary high intellectuality with a liberal sort of semi–social democratic left edge of the Democratic Party politics. What became the Students for Democratic Society, created in 1962, had originated out of the League for Industrial Democracy. And the original name, in fact, was the Student League for Industrial Democracy, but then somebody read the acronym and thought they needed to do something else — that’s not the best name, and they were always kind of a funny amalgam. For the American left in the 1950s and ’60s, there was no real class politics that defined it. This was a period in the United States when people didn’t even talk about capitalism or class. I mean, one of the unfortunate contributions of our tribe of social scientists to the hegemonic ideology was inventing the notion that the old ideological distinctions like capitalism and communism don’t make any sense anymore, and what we have now is industrial society. And Vivek’s discipline, quite like mine, from one angle was predominantly characterized by trying to make capitalism and class disappear.
- Vivek Chibber I would say, all the way through the late 1960s, postwar sociology was fundamentally backward. And it’s returning to those roots now.
- Adolph Reed So I’ve noticed.
- Vivek Chibber One of the ways in which the British and the American New Left differed is that there was a similar intellectual move away from talking about capitalism in England, but that comes out of the Labour Party. This was called revisionism within the Labour Party and was led by Anthony Crosland. And he tried to make the argument that capitalism had evolved to the point where we can think realistically about actually maneuvering beyond its class contradictions and managing it in what he would call a social democratic or egalitarian direction. This would have meant that capitalism’s defining qualities, what Karl Marx called its laws of motion, are now a thing of the past. That was an argument coming out of a section of the Labour Party. There was, of course, another very class-oriented and socialist section of the Labour Party that resisted this. In the United States, there was a kind of working-class-oriented section of the New Left as it was forming both inside the Students for a Democratic Society and outside. But very little of it was Marxist. It was pro-labor, but it didn’t really have a theory, and that’s why you had that famous speech by Paul Potter where he said, “We have to name the system.” And this was considered a controversial statement, right? Very little of it was Marxist, and they didn’t really have a theory about the system that they were challenging. This is much less so in England, because that New Left was much more imbricated within Marxism. It had a real connection to the labor movement as well. So we can say that the British New Left was trying to reform Marxism, whereas the American New Left was stumbling toward “discovering it,” and that’s the way I’ve always understood it. And the American New Left really didn’t have that much of a connection to labor until later. I think in the late 1960s or early ’70s, there was a big move toward labor inside the student-based left organizations, which was called “industrialization” back then, but that’s ten to twelve years into the biography of the New Left.
- Adolph Reed Yes, absolutely. A few years ago, I reread what may be considered SDS’s manifesto, the “Port Huron statement,” and I was struck at how much the authors of that statement had internalized all the postindustrial and post-ideological stuff. Classes disappeared from the analysis. They were as concerned as any op-ed writer in The New York Times about the problems of an affluent society and how to deal with abundance, and they were by and large people who came out of working-class families — union families, even.
Radical Goals and Politics
- Melissa Naschek So what were the most clearly articulated political goals of the New Left?
- Adolph Reed Well, one was a demand for racial justice. It wasn’t exactly clear what that would would mean concretely. Another was of course to end the war. So neither one of those was derived from a model of how the society could be different from the way it is now and could be improved, which is what you would typically think of as the vantage point of an avant-garde. Another goal, of course, was personal expression, and if you want to talk about the roots of identity politics, well, bingo. And I have memories of meetings that lasted all night long because of the principle that every voice should be heard.
- Melissa Naschek We’re talking about the period from the 1950s to the ’60s, so are there different time points at which the main political priorities of the New Left evolved?
- Adolph Reed Yeah, I think that’s right. SDS’s roots were also in the early direct-action phase of the civil rights movement. A number of the founders had already been involved in the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. But there were also a lot of prefigurative politics or a commitment to a prefigurative ideology.
- Melissa Naschek Can you explain what that means?
- Adolph Reed Well, for people who can remember, it’s like Occupy Wall Street, to the extent to which people who participated in occupations generally understood themselves to be embodying what the ideal society should be and will be, and that they were enacting the society that they wanted to see. That’s what prefigurative politics comes down to, and it’s a principle that has its roots in theology, that the way to make the world you want is through something like a demonstration effect from inside your organization.
- Vivek Chibber So you create in the organization a microcosm of what you want to see outside the organization. It sounds really nice or a great thing to do, depending on what your vision is of what an organization should be trying to do and to be. But consider a trade union. Ultimately, a trade union is a fighting organization. What you want to do in the trade union is have the meeting, make a decision, and then move on. But if it turns out that your vision is that everybody has to have a voice, you don’t leave until everybody said something, and you turn it into something very different from what the function of the organization is. And so a lot of organizations are killed around these principles.
- Adolph Reed And ironically, that’s one of the things that really took off and became a bigger and bigger problem once the New Leftists had approximated something called Marxism. And I’ve got personal stories I can share about this.
- Melissa Naschek I think hearing those would be helpful to make this a little bit more concrete.
- Adolph Reed This one is a little bit of a shaggy-dog story: I left college in the spring of 1969 after a cafeteria strike and was trying to figure out what to do. There was a guy who had been involved in setting up a couple of the first GI antiwar coffee houses, one at Fort Hood in Texas and one at Fort Jackson in South Carolina, and he started talking about the idea of doing one at Fort Bragg. So I decided to do that. But before I went down there, I went up to Fort Dix, where there was a coffee house mainly funded by people who had formed an organizing collective and were all living in a big, unheated farmhouse outside Wrightstown. The principal male in the group was coupled up with the most conventionally attractive woman in the group. And they were committed to destroying capitalism cellularly, right? I mean, not at the workplace.
- Vivek Chibber One café at a time.
- Adolph Reed Right. He was acting out a Mick Jagger thing, like chopping wood in the cold with no shirt on and firing off weapons. But on my second day, he told me that there was a Black Panther coming over from Jersey City to meet with him at the office and he wanted me to go with him. So I did. I had read that Bayard Rustin quip that there were only like a thousand members of the Black Panthers and half of them were cops — and that’s mainly the experience I had with Panthers, especially by then and especially on the East Coast. But during our meeting, our principal male — I’d literally never seen anything like this in my life before — his entire demeanor and body language changed. He kept scratching his arms, he was inarticulate in the face of the Panther, and the Panther was playing it for all his worth. In this group, there was also a former Vista worker and a former Catholic seminarian who set himself up as the psychotherapy guru. I didn’t quite realize that Maoist self-criticism could be articulated in that way, but he was basically holding confessions for everybody else on his staff. I thought, “This is nuts.” But this is really the point of this: I eventually figured out that the movement into co-ops and organizing collectives tended to deteriorate to that kind of psychologistic pathology because they weren’t able to organize. So, that fraction of the Left came to Marxism at the point when the ruling class had already basically won in 1960s.
- Vivek Chibber It’s interesting that you bring up Marxism here, Adolph. One of the things that stands out to me is that, whatever its foibles and whatever its initial confusion around how you understand the system and where you go, after the first ten or twelve years, that student left ends up stumbling into Marxism for the most part. And the reason is that, if you called yourself a radical in the 1960s, and even into the ’70s, radicalism was socialism, and socialism was Marxism. It was still the case back then. And so, whatever else there was in the ether, Marxism was still the self-identified hegemonic theory of the Left. That’s what’s so different from today. What’s different today is that you call yourself a radical, and the last place you go is Marxism. Because what’s called radicalism now has morphed into all these various sort of avatars of the crap that you’re talking about, which has to do with personal politics, personal perfection, psychologism, and most of all, the class commitments and aspirations of the elites and professional groups within blacks, women, among immigrants, all whom have taken taken over the rhetoric of radicalism. So what you have now is a radicalism that combines this personal perfection, self-help safety-ism, masked-forever kind of confessional culture on the one hand, which is a direct descendant of that student left, but with something genuinely new on the other, which is that there’s never been a time in the history of the Left when you actually made it a point to denigrate the socialist and Marxist tradition while calling yourself a radical in the name of, and in the pursuit of, professional bourgeois aspirations.
Students and Workers
- Melissa Naschek What was the New Left’s attitude toward the working class? Did it engage in working-class organizing?
- Adolph Reed Yeah, some did. But there were different tendencies. So I mentioned that when I first got involved in activist stuff, one of the first things that I and others got connected with was going to walk the picket lines for the textile workers. And there was no daylight between doing the anti-poverty stuff that we did or the anti-anti-poverty stuff we did or even the voting rights stuff we did. Everybody was doing the same kind of work, and everybody understood that the working class was the center of our activity. And then that changed gradually. The summer of 1967 was the “Summer of Love” or something like that, and that’s when you really started to get the counterculture line coming to dominate the movement. That’s when you began to see people who didn’t approach politics as an organizing project, but who approached it much more as a domain of self-expression and a display of your consumer habits and stuff like that. And that’s when you get that gloss on “The personal is political,” which was of course not the perspective that came out of the Waveland conference that gave birth to the second wave of the women’s movement. I think about even the early representations of the 1960s version of the New Left in popular culture. They were banalized in the typical way. It was all reduced to fashion and smoking weed or whatever and being free. And that’s part of what drove the massive influx into SDS after 1967. The first thing that came to my mind when I heard DSA had exploded in membership was what happened to SDS: there was a flood of emotionally powered and earnest people that came into the organization with no particular politics, and by the end of 1969, it didn’t exist anymore.
- Vivek Chibber It is interesting that of the student organizations, the socialists who came out of Trotskyism and Maoism both made a decision to dive into class organizing, right? And it was the International Socialists, the IS, that created Teamsters for a Democratic Union, which continues today. It’s still around, and it played an absolutely pivotal role in the Teamsters and in organizing them. But the unfortunate experience of the Maoists was that they went into the auto sector right at the time when all the layoffs started, and so they found themselves kind of holding the bag. So both of these tendencies existed at the time. On the one hand, what Adolph is talking about, with the flower children and the counterculture and consumption habits. But then I think there was a very serious component of that student left as well, mainly because it came to Marxism, and because there was an oral tradition that was still alive coming out of the 1930s and ’40s Old Left which transmitted to them the importance of class organizing, the trade union movement, and immersing themselves in it. You can see glimmerings today of a return to class organizing within the DSA. It’s now called salting, whereas back then it was called industrializing. So there is a kind of salting component of the DSA, but also all of those strands that Adolph is talking about in the 1960s inside Students for a Democratic Society can be seen today. But in my opinion, the weightage is now reversed. Today’s Left is far more dominated by the personalistic, identitarian self-help therapy thing, and the class component is now struggling to find its bearings.
- Adolph Reed When we were working on the Labor Party in the 1990s, one of the things that really struck me was how common people in the intermediate level of trade union leadership had come out of those sectarian Marxist groups. And it makes perfect sense to me: I mean, you do that work for a while, and you learn how to organize, and you learn what what makes sense and what doesn’t practically, but you keep the politics and you keep the goal. And from the ruling-class standpoint, it’s interesting that among the leadership of three of the major international unions in the country, until the merger stuff happened, included a president who graduated from Yale, a president who graduated from Cornell, and a president who graduated from Penn. And by the early 1970s, people at the business roundtable were already complaining that there weren’t going to be class-appropriate jobs to absorb all these people who are going to college, and all keeping access open would do is produce an adversary culture.
Anti-Imperialism Renewed
- Melissa Naschek How do you two think the Vietnam War and the antiwar movement impacted the relationship between the New Left and the working class?
- Adolph Reed Well, there’s a standard story and then there’s reality. The standard story is that the working class was patriotic and for the war. But see, the people who were telling us this were the same people from Vivek’s discipline and mine who had been “inventing” the working class as tautologically male, conservative, and Catholic. They basically invoked the same idea as Ronald Reagan’s image of Joe Six-Pack. But Penny Lewis at the City University of New York wrote a great book called Hardhats, Hippies, and Hawks that challenged this story. What she found was that, at every point during the Vietnam War going back to Dwight D. Eisenhower, support for the war increased with education and income. So the hard-hat thing was a stunt, basically. But this makes perfect sense, because whose kids were getting drafted, right? So this is another part of a concocted fantasy that the Democrats were recomposing an alliance by packaging a right-wing foreign policy as though it appealed to the concerns of the working class.
- Vivek Chibber Within the student left, the war had a dual effect, one positive and one negative. The positive one was that the war really brought the importance of imperialism into the culture of the student movement. And because a lot of the students were coming to Marxism, it took them back to the theory of imperialism in order to try to develop an account of how the Vietnam War was emblematic of or a departure from the imperial role that the United States had played in the postwar global economy. This brought them to the question: What was postwar imperialism, and to what extent was Vladimir Lenin’s theory adequate to the task of understanding it? Among those who took this up were individuals like Anwar Shaikh, who just passed away. Anwar was in large measure motivated to redevelop Marxist economics so that it could be a foundation for developing a theory of international capitalism and, potentially, imperialism. There was a deadly seriousness to this. And to my mind, the Vietnam War played a very large role in the revitalization of Marxist economics among the students, and that was very positive. But then I think there was also a negative side to the Vietnam War’s impact on the student movement. Both because of when it occurred and because of the centrality of Maoism inside the student movement; it also revived what is called “Third-Worldism.” Third-Worldism was the idea that the Western working class had essentially been bought off and corrupted by the fruits of imperialism. And so accordingly, not only was their general wealth derived from this, but they had a direct material stake in the superexploitation of workers in the Global South. This made them, at best, a kind of uninterested party in fighting imperialism, but at worst, a reactionary mass. Arghiri Emmanuel, in his very influential book, Unequal Exchange, says explicitly that workers in the West don’t just benefit from imperialism, but they exploit workers in the Global South. That thinking led, I think, to a fairly negative and dismissive attitude toward class organizing domestically, as well as an exoticization and valorization of anything happening in the Global South as the only thing that actually matters. In my opinion, this led to much of the American left conceptualizing the Global South in a profoundly reactionary way. Since after all, workers were now being called exploiters of countries in the Global South, the countries as a whole in the Global North were said to benefit from and exploit countries as a whole in the Global South. Ironically, this theorization ended up making the American left the organic intellectuals of the Third-World bourgeoisie. Because all the most backward and reactionary nationalist programs and policies in the Global South were now seen as effectuating the agency of these so-called darker nations. So, there is a quite striking legacy that comes out of the 1960s, which I believe has become hegemonic on the student left today, which exoticizes and essentializes the cultures and nations of the Global South and refuses to acknowledge that there are profound class divisions in those countries. The truth is that the first enemy of the workers in most of those countries is not American workers or even multinationals coming out of America, but their own immediate exploiters, their capitalist classes. That’s unfortunately a very debilitating legacy of that period, which was roundly criticized by the Left in the 1970s and ’80s both here and in the Global South. But because of the intervening years, with the death of Marxist political economy and class analysis, I think one big reason it’s been revived today is that it converges with the kind of identitarian race discourse we have in this country, so that it’s easily slotted into saying “whiter people in whiter nations dominate darker nations.” It’s made out to be a component of global white supremacy or something like that.
- Adolph Reed Yeah, I think that’s absolutely correct. So after Vietnam won the war, many left-inclined liberals in particular came to feel betrayed when it turned out that the Vietnam Workers Party wanted to build a state. Because what they’d always had in the back of their minds were these noble peasants.
- Vivek Chibber In my view, many of these leftists think of the people in the Global South as zoo animals.
- Adolph Reed Yeah, that’s exactly right.
- Vivek Chibber To be pitied, to be petted, but never to be recognized as basically the same as you. This reminds me of what Bayard Rustin said regarding the black middle class. He said that the white left has to understand that the black middle class is like any other middle class, and it’s going to do exactly what they do, which is craft a narrow agenda for itself and try to palm it off as a people’s agenda.
- Adolph Reed Totally. And during the 1990s anti-globalization movement, I remember debates after a South Asian economist wrote a fiery op-ed piece in the Times about how it was racist to attempt to regulate child labor. And what stunned me was that us lefties actually tried to debate among ourselves about whether we needed to acquiesce to this guy’s understanding. And I said, “What’s his job? What’s his title? Brother, who do you think he works for?” This type of thinking has been a continuous problem and it’s still around.
- Vivek Chibber It rears its head whenever issues of imperialism or empire come up, and there’s still unfortunately a big chunk of the Left, including inside the DSA, that has the view that the welfare state was built on the fruits of empire, that the white American working class is benefiting from it. What’s interesting to me is they insist on equating the Western working class with white working class, because, if you really believe that empire is what sustains the West, then black workers are as liable in the brutal exploitation of these Bangladeshis as the white ones are. You don’t really hear this implication very much because it’s all a racialized discourse.
’60s Counterculture and New Politics
- Melissa Naschek What was the relationship like between the New Left and the counterculture?
- Adolph Reed It varied a lot. On one hand, I rarely met a drug I didn’t like back then. In fact, as I reflect on it, I can hardly think of one now. But on the other hand, and I can still produce some witnesses to this too, I had no use for countercultural politics at all, and quickly came to see those people as an obstruction.
- Melissa Naschek Yeah, and when you say countercultural politics, what do you mean?
- Adolph Reed This is basically what’s called lifestyle politics. As well as the notion that there was a youth culture and something called the youth movement, which I also can produce witnesses to attest that I didn’t believe in then, when I would have been in a position to benefit from it actuarially. There was the “Age of Aquarius” stuff, the idea that there was a new consciousness that emerged in society that has to do with generational change and the new perspectives. And that flowed very naturally into the New Politics tendency within the Democratic Party.
- Melissa Naschek Can you explain what that was?
- Adolph Reed The New Politics tendency emerged from a combination of aspirant blacks, latinos, women, and environmentalists who were jockeying for organizational leadership positions within the Democratic Party. They tended to be post-class-oriented in identifying the problems, seeing Americans as consumers rather than as producers or as workers. And that tension played out around the George McGovern campaign between the Vietnam War and the Johnson administration. Lyndon Johnson’s identification with the New Deal, at least rhetorically, saddled the New Deal coalition more broadly with the baggage of the war. There was a fetishized disparagement of George Meany [the leader of the AFL-CIO], who was in fact pro-war but also tarred as a racist. The way these condensation symbols work is there’s some effective zephyr that’s there for anybody who wants to connect with. It was never directly theorized, and so there wasn’t really space to have a debate. The other national status politician who was directly associated with the New Deal and horrible racism was Mayor Richard Daley in Chicago, and his authorization of the police riot against antiwar protesters at the 1968 Democratic convention. It also fueled this untheorized notion of “us versus them,” and on a purely moral basis. Over the 1970s, Jimmy Carter became a crucial actor in this. Carter ran for governor as a candidate of segregationist nostalgia and rose to national visibility at the 1972 convention in Miami as the organic head of the Stop McGovern movement. His number one sidekick in that was a black state legislator from Atlanta named Ben Brown, who would become chair of Carter’s campaign and then later the Democratic National Committee. When Carter ran for the presidency for the first time, he billed himself on his fiscal probity and boasted about how many government departments he had cut when he was governor of Georgia. For that reason, as well as others, like his Holy-Rolling and the foolishness about being born again — my dad always said, “Well, if he had to be born again, why would he choose to be born again as Jimmy Carter?” — gave pause to a lot of northern liberal Democrats, especially Jews. I think a crucial moment in this was when the Atlanta civil rights establishment, which is where all the major non-civil-rights organizations were located, went out of their way to go all around the country to sell Carter to the liberal wing of the Democratic Party as a new kind of liberal. And what this new kind of liberal was, ultimately, was a white Southern Democrat racial liberal. And as I think more and more about it, I think that’s the moment when we can see the sign of identitarian leftism beginning to displace the vestiges, or really the residues, of the old trade-union, working-class-based Democratic coalition.
The New Left’s Legacy
- Melissa Naschek What do the two of you see as the legacy of the New Left?
- Adolph Reed I think it’s complicated. Most of the current leadership in AFL-CIO are people who have either direct or indirect connections to the New Left. That’s one of the reasons why I think this contention that the labor movement has to atone for its horrible history of sexism and racism and stuff like that is ridiculous, because all those people have been dead for a long time. And women and blacks and other non-white minorities are overrepresented among the membership of the labor movement compared to the general population. This is kind of parochial, but I’m also part of the cliché that people who came out of the Left went into the academy. And within political science, and some of the other social science disciplines too, when we found that there were big enough clusters of us holding down professorships or aspiring to professorships, it made both natural career sense and natural political sense, given our objective position, to work to make Marxism respectable in the formal academy. And I’ll say parenthetically that I’m always fearful when the political sense and the career sense converge, because it’s so easy to bullsh-t yourself. That’s the easiest thing in the world to do. But while there were some overtures from the political science and sociology mainstreams back in the day — not economics, of course, because that’s just divinity school — what turned out to be the case was that the price of intellectual respectability from one’s colleagues was breaking with an epistemic understanding of Marx’s eleventh thesis on [Ludwig] Feuerbach.
- Vivek Chibber The one that said, “Philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point, however, is to change it.”
- Adolph Reed Right, which people sometimes think of as a moral injunction. But more significantly, and I think this is one of the things that separates Marxists from non-Marxists in my view, that the intellectual foundation of the way through which we see the world rests on the principle of commitment to class struggle. And by that I don’t mean practicing at the barricades but an understanding that the world is most fundamentally moving according to the logic of Marxism.
- Melissa Naschek Well, also the idea that your intellectual work should actually be useful for people who are trying to do politics.
- Adolph Reed God forbid, right? And so structuralist Marxism emerged as a kind of halfway house for the Althusserians and some of the people around the New Left Review and stuff like that. And as sites of resistance began to atrophy outside the university, there was no basis for this epistemic principle unless you brought it with you, that the world moves by contradiction and has to change. In a moment when the ruling class’s power is greater than it’s ever been, and there are fewer and fewer real sources of opposition coming from outside the academy, many decided to take this ride. And so, for many of these radicals, the next thing they know, they were simply just structuralists. And it seems to me that the difference between a structural Marxist and a structuralist recedes toward zero, and all both of them could do was predict that things were going to keep getting worse. And it’s at that point when the better ones among them settle into a genteel alcoholism or coach their kids soccer teams or grow their gardens. And the worst of them did a lot worse. At the same time, it’s also true that within the academy — and this is probably more true in the history departments than in some other fields — as the disciplines democratized, the center of gravity of academic work began to expand more broadly. Wouldn’t you agree, Vivek?
- Vivek Chibber Yeah, absolutely. My sense is that, if I follow the same sequence of analysis as Adolph, I would say that the legacy of the New Left can be appreciated in two different domains. One is a broader culture and one is intellectual and academic. In the broader culture, I think there are a lot of positive legacies of the New Left, because of the antiwar and civil rights movements. Although, I’m not sure I want to call the civil rights movement New Left per se. I think of the civil rights movement as the last stage of the older left, because the key coterie around Martin Luther King Jr, such as A. Philip Randolph, Bayard Rustin, Tom Kahn, and Stanley Levison, were — not just generationally, but also ideologically — old-style socialists. They weren’t counterculture socialists. Nevertheless, civil rights is identified with the New Left, and it’s also true that a lot of the Freedom Riders and the students were the ones who joined the New Left. The civil rights movement had a profoundly positive influence on the culture in pushing it toward a kind of instinctive anti-racism and cosmopolitanism, and then the Vietnam War movement had yet another huge impact on that. What was the essence of the antiwar movement? It was the recognition that the Vietnamese are no less human than the Americans, and that their dignity, rights, and autonomy have to be respected. And this was also the last moment of the great independence movements in Africa as well, which had a gigantic impact on the academy and the culture more broadly. My mother came to this country right in the last stages of the Vietnam War, and she can attest to the differences from the 1970s to now as the positive elements of that antiwar movement seeped in. So while it’s true that a lot of the packaging of the 1960s is now the hippies and the counterculture and all that, the positive impact of all of those movements supporting independence and opposing imperialism, alongside the civil rights movement, injected a dose of cosmopolitanism and, in a very positive sense, multiculturalism, that is not to be denigrated and is very important. Then, however, there is the intellectual legacy of that moment and the political legacy in a more narrow sense, which is: How do we conceive of politics and social change? I think this is largely negative. It’s the aging New Left that created this new form of radicalism, which at best is sort of indifferent to working people but at worst is openly contemptuous toward them. And it crafted a vision of political change that is very narrowly conceived around the material interests and the frustrated ambitions of, as Adolph just said, this shifting center of gravity within the professional classes, away from old white men and toward these upwardly mobile women and minorities who do great for themselves, but find that they’re still not given all the goodies that the older white men are given. And instead of recognizing this as simply a kind of frustrated bourgeois politics, the New Leftists said “No, this is radical power.” I think this is mistaken and had a very negative impact. As part of that intellectual legacy, we got all the various alphabet soup “posties”: postcolonialism, postmodernism, poststructuralism. Whereas Marxism was once the theory of people who call themselves radical, these replaced it. And it’s not just that they’ve been a blight upon intellectual life.
