They are, I think, the most obvious and glaring example of the cultural and moral degeneration of the neoliberal era. But now, here’s the saving grace. That, even just in my own lifetime, the intellectual resources to criticize a lot of this intellectual detritus was also created by the New Left. I think the New Left put economics on a footing that it had never been before within the Left. I think the moral and philosophical underpinnings of socialism are a lot stronger than they used to be. There is a huge corpus of left-inspired historiography of race and colonialism that we now have thanks to them, and that, despite the packaging that the postcolonialists and the postmodernists later put on it, actually shows people’s struggles were the same everywhere. The goals were the same everywhere and the convergence around a similar set of interests was the same everywhere. This all came out of the New Left. So the legacy is mixed in the following sense. The momentum of the last ten years has been horrible, as the Left is trying to recover itself, and that negative momentum all comes out of the direct creation of the New Left as it aged and kind of sh-t on the world as it was leaving the scene. But the intellectual resources to do something and to criticize that also come out of that project. And my view is we need to recapture the moral and cultural commitments of the older left but build on the intellectual resources that the newer left has given us.
- Adolph Reed Sounds right to me. Well put.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Flooding in southwestern US underlines risks of Trump administration’s reduction of Bears Ears National Monument
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites. The concerns follow the Trump administration’s decision to reduce the monument from more than one million acres to around 120,000 acres, reversing Biden-era protections and dismantling its Indigenous-led management structure.
The decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites. The flooding hit the Four Corners area—which encompasses parts of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah—from late October to early November, causing widespread damage to roads and infrastructure.
A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah says in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable. BLM staff have been patrolling the region to assess road conditions and evaluate the status of infrastructure around areas used for recreation.
“Park rangers and archaeologists have also been assessing cultural sites to identify any potential impacts from the flooding,” the spokesperson says. “While storm events of this nature are not uncommon in this landscape and can affect sensitive cultural resources, no immediate impacts on cultural sites have been reported at this time.”
The local researcher and author Ralph “R.E.” Burrillo was in the town of Bluff, Utah, a gateway to Bears Ears National Monument, when the floods started in late October. He notes that the management plan for the new boundaries has not yet been implemented, so nothing has changed other than the “invisible line”. The longer-term implications, however, remain uncertain.
“With a monument in place, there wouldn’t be these wildcat permits for people supposedly looking to extract resources, but these are just exploratory leases,” he says. “The reality is that there isn’t that much energy to be extracted underground in Bears Ears, or people would have been going after it for decades. When anybody says the monument is locking up America’s energy potential, they are lying.”
Other monuments in the region, like the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, which has substantial deposits of coal and other minerals like uranium, chromium and copper, have a longer history of conflict over resource extraction. The Clinton administration established the monument in 1996 in part to prevent commercial development of coal extraction. Several companies had acquired coal leases in the region during the 1960s and 70s, although commercial mining never materialised.
Burrillo emphasises that the demarcation of the Bears Ears National Monument benefits two constituencies: resource developers and opponents of tribal stewardship. The Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and the Bears Ears National Monument are frequently reduced due to a “handshake deal” that grants energy lobbyists access to energy resources from one site and removes tribal jurisdiction from the latter. At this time, the main immediate threat to heritage sites in the region, Burrillo adds, remains tourism, looting and vandalism.
“What the monument did, at least potentially, was create a nexus for funding to be sent to that area for things like interdiction and law enforcement, education and interpretation, trail maintenance and collaboration with tribes,” Burrillo says. “A monument is a conduit for funding to try to protect those resources from vandals, looters and, again, tourists, who, whether intentionally or not, crawl all over the place. Without the monument, there’s no nexus for funding and that’s really a knock-on effect.”
Although flooding could affect archaeological sites, including potentially eroding petroglyphs, Burrillo says that prehistoric sites in the region are of the least concern. The region has historically flooded, with water sometimes rising to 50ft, and its archaeological sites tell a fascinating story of adaptability, with sites like ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings having been built higher than the water could ever reach. When Mormon pioneers arrived in the region in the 1870s and attempted to establish a town at Bluff, with farms and as an outpost for missioning the Navajo population, they were unsuccessful and eventually moved north.
“When you go back 500 to 2,000 years, the people didn’t have those dams. You simply had this tempestuous river that was famous for flooding more or less constantly, filling miles around the flood basin with water and mud,” Burrillo adds. “The ancestral Pueblo and their ancestors knew it and built above it. For the most part, they treated the river with more respect than we have. The archaeology is in far less danger than the modern infrastructure for that reason.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Jonathan Jones
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen.
She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching themselves, or bathing together. Here is the unfeigned, honest impact her work has had since she first put her world viscerally on camera in her early photo series The Ballad of Sexual Dependency. But there’s a difference.
A Caravaggesque young man looks with bedroom eyes at the camera. Then we cut to an actual Caravaggio painting for comparison. The resemblance is magical. And the 17th-century queer outlaw and murderer is not the only great artist whose images are collaged with Goldin’s photos. As Goldin relates on the film’s soundtrack, she saw, wandering the Louvre in a trance, her friends’ faces in sensual masterpieces including works by Correggio and Canova.
These timeless portrayals of beauty and love, in glowing paint and smooth marble, are intercut with Goldin’s erotic snaps to a rousing score. And here’s the thing. Intentionally or not, her live subjects pose their bodies in ways that mirror the old masters: lovers fondle like Cupid and Psyche, their warm living flesh as sculpted and perfect as Canova’s marble. Meanwhile, Goldin tells tales of desire from Ovid’s Metamorphoses. It turns out that this Roman poet’s kinky versions of Greek myth uncannily anticipate 21st-century boho life. She photographs a Pygmalion and Galatea she happens to know, a Narcissus in love with his own reflection.
You expect mythological references from your Twomblys and Kentridges but when an artist seen as an unvarnished recorder of opioid America mixes her world with high art and ancient mythology, it poses acute questions. What is beauty? What is art? Are they both just ways to freeze, for a moment, the passing glory of life?
In another film, Memory Lost, Goldin looks back on her and her friends’ experiences of addiction. A photo of a mattress with a huge dark hole, burnt into it by an addict’s cigarette (you guess), is juxtaposed with enraptured romantic images of red skies and wintry woodlands. There is beauty in us and all around us. But do drugs, from heroin to prescription opioids, make you see it sharper or lose sight of it in the cravings and wastings? Art is a healthier high, suggests Stendhal Syndrome, but even that can make you swoon. Goldin campaigns against opioids, but the lure of the addictive sublime pulses through her work in the Romantic spirit of American creativity from Edgar Allan Poe to Lou Reed. Even when it’s at its sweetest.
And what could be sweeter than a pussycat (unless you’re a bird)? Cat’s eyes stare at you in the film You Never Did Anything Wrong, parts one and two, that gives this show its title. They keep staring. And not just cats – owls and alligators, too. It’s a disturbing montage of glaring animal faces that makes you ponder the nature of other-species consciousness.
“You never did anything wrong”, it transpires, is an inscription from a gravestone in a pet cemetery. Another says: “We are sorry.” You may laugh. You may wonder why the pets’ owners are apologising. Then you get it. We all should be sorry. Goldin is showing us the innocence of the natural world we are destroying. Horses leaping, birds flocking, a tortoise helping a fellow tortoise get the right way up, even a pig crawling under someone’s duvet – wild and domesticated animals are all here in a rapid succession of found images. But the film clips are old, their colours untrue. All these beasts must be dead by now. That all the natural abundance here belongs to the past, that’s it going and gone, speaks obviously to our moment.
Human beings are beautiful, shows Goldin, but look what we do. We are lovely but not innocent. Yet art and life, humanity and nature, merge as you stumble dazed from one film to another. She tries to cross between worlds – to connect art and life, humans and animals, in an ecstasy of love and beauty. This exhibition is a moving and compulsive wonder by the greatest American artist since Andy Warhol. Somehow, it makes you hopeful.

https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.title: Queens Public Library restores most services nearly 3 weeks after ransomware attack
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.text:
The Queens Public Library says it has restored nearly all of its services after a ransomware attack caused a network outage almost three weeks ago, although some online features remain unavailable and officials are still investigating whether patrons' personal information was compromised.
The Nov. 4 attack had disrupted several free services that residents rely on, including Wi-Fi, public computers, book renewals and a host of digital media services. The library announced Monday that its website, mobile app, public computers, printers and digital collections are back up and running. Patrons can also search for books, manage their accounts and place holds online.
“Thanks to the extraordinary efforts of our IT team and colleagues throughout the organization, we are back online and have restored virtually all our services,” Queens Public Library President and CEO Dennis Walcott said in a statement Monday.
Walcott said library staff kept all locations open throughout the outage, sometimes recording patrons' names and borrowed materials by hand to keep books circulating.
Demand for QPL's services has continued to rise, with attendance at library programs increasing 11% from 964,018 in fiscal year 2025 to 1,071,432 in fiscal year 2026, according to the mayor's management report.
Electronic visits to QPL's website also rose 52% to 7.5 million in fiscal year 2026, although the library reported an increase in bot traffic over the last fiscal year, according to the same data.
And while most QPL services are back up and running, not every section of the library's website has been fully restored, including its online contact forms and interlibrary loan feature.
Some previous book requests and library calendar entries could also be out of date or missing altogether, officials said.
QPL also said it's been working with cybersecurity experts to investigate the attack, restore its remaining systems and strengthen its technology infrastructure. The investigation includes determining whether hackers accessed or stole patrons' personal information.
“There are encouraging indicators that no personal information was compromised, but it is too soon to draw any definitive conclusions,” the library said in its announcement Monday. “If we learn that personal information was accessed or taken, we will provide appropriate notifications directly to any impacted individuals.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: First Frieze Abu Dhabi proves successful for the region's dealers, despite geopolitical jitters
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melissa Gronlund
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) opened to a promising start. Strong sales were reported across many galleries, and the fair had an energy that spread from the stands to the garden outside at the Manarat Al Saadiyat, where guests lingered for hours over the unlikely combination of pizza and champagne.
“They’re looking after us very well here,” one established Dubai collector said. “Unlike at other fairs, where we feel pressured to buy, here we can take a breather and reflect on things. The art world is very collegiate in this region and the collectors are here to support.”
Like its name, Frieze Abu Dhabi was a mix of two halves. The successor to the long-standing Abu Dhabi Art fair that has been operating, under various names, in the UAE capital since 2007, the fair is co-run by Frieze Fairs and the UAE government’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT). Accordingly, the event blended elements of Abu Dhabi Art’s programme with those more familiar to Frieze's flagship event in Regent’s Park.
Chief among these is the Ladies’ Day—the day before the public opening that is reserved for Abu Dhabi’s sheikhas—and the pre-bound book of available works that is sent around to the city’s royals.
Meanwhile Frieze brought its art fair expertise, giving the fair a better layout and an improved allover experience. “The fair still has its Abu Dhabi Art soul but feels a lot tighter in terms of the number of galleries and the selection,” said Taymour Grahne, whose eponymous gallery moved from New York to London and has now settled in Dubai. Grahne was showing a series of mosaics by the Palestinian artist Ala Younis, which by the opening day had mostly sold.
Most of the galleries’ presentations were rooted in the Wanasa (West Asia, North Africa and South Asia) region. Standout booths included that of the Cairo gallery Art Talks/Kanafani's solo presentation of the Egyptian surrealist Samir Rafi, and the Dubai gallery Ayyam’s booth of the Dutch-Iraqi artist Sadik Kwaish Alfraiji. By the opening day, the Rafi works were about half sold.
Other Dubai galleries, who had a strong showing at the fair, equally did well, with Lawrie Shabibi selling out its marble inlay works by Hamra Abbas by the opening day for $50,000 each; Zawyeh Gallery selling about half of its collages by the Gazan artist Mohammed Joha, which had attracted much attention this year at the Venice Biennale; and Tabari Artspace, which showed two early works by another artist born in Gaza, Hazem Harb, amidst a group show, also reported selling half their booth. Most artworks were priced in the region of ten-thousands to mid-hundred thousand dollars.
A mix of blue-chip Western galleries were also in attendance. Pace were offering their fresh-to-market, large-scale paintings by the indigenous Australian artist Emily Kame Kngwarreye for between $80,000 to $750,000, although confirmed sales for these works appeared to be slow.
And in the small Frieze Masters section, a 2,000-year-old funerary stele made out of luminous alabaster, taken by a British official from what is now Yemen, was sold by the Mayfair gallerist David Aaron for "seven figures".
There were also a substantial number of new visitors to the fair, including a few starry faces like the tennis star Venus Williams. A smattering of museum heads and curators from the US, Asia and Europe also flew in, such as Michael Govan of Lacma (who was speaking at the fair), Eugene Tan of the Singapore Art Museum, and the Aspen Art Museum’s Nicola Lees, one of a number who brought along a patrons group.
And though the fair also had a number of South Asian galleries, Indian and Pakistani collectors were less present than expected, partly because the fair came right on the heels of Art Mumbai.
Perhaps as importantly, most galleries reported selling to these new collectors—both to collectors who had flown in as well as new collectors living in Abu Dhabi. The city’s population has swelled recently, particularly in the finance and tech sectors, in addition to the surge of Russians who moved to the UAE after the 2022 restrictions imposed on their country.
But the larger context of regional instability could not be ignored. Though it was hard to say how many people had stayed away because of fears of a resumption in Iran’s attacks on the UAE, it is undeniable that the frothy hype of a year ago, when the Art Basel/Doha and DCT/Abu Dhabi partnerships were announced, has settled for now. There was some sense of the fair’s energy being a product of solidarity—one collector from Beirut noted that Art Basel Paris closed early because of threats of riots, whereas the Arab art scene was pulling together under keener threats. But it would be more accurate to say that most people felt the need to get on with things rather than waiting for some far-off resolution.
This applies too for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which is scheduled to open next month after twenty years in the making. While the imminent opening partly detracted from the fair—some VIPs saw a choice between attending the fair and the early December festivities—the finished building and the buoyant museum team contributed to a sense of anticipation and substance within Abu Dhabi’s art scene.
High-level VIP tours got a preview of the building, The Art Newspaper understands, while the general VIP program was padded out with tours of the recently opened Public Art Abu Dhabi biennial, the Nomad art fair, and shows at the Cultural Foundation, the Bassam Freiha Art Foundation, and 421, as well as a number of private collections in the city—an itinerary that the city could not have supported even five years ago.
What was less visible on the trip, however, was commercial galleries. These remain almost exclusively in Dubai and fostering an independent commercial scene is a key reason for DCT’s partnership with Frieze, and also animates the city’s development of two new cultural districts, Noma on Saadiyat, led by the developer Aldar, and MiZa in Mina Zayed, led by the Sheikha Salama Foundation.
Both of these areas promise infrastructure to support artists and creative freelancers, such as studios, galleries, and co-working spaces.
These offerings will entail a loosening of control over the cultural programme in the city and—as is the case with Frieze—partnerships with private enterprise. For many who have followed the scene for a long time, this transition towards multiple stakeholders will be a key test for the capital.
“What Abu Dhabi has been doing over the last two decades is building an ecosystem, and one that is not solely institutional, but which also includes academia and smaller art spaces like 421,” says Aaron Cesar, the director of London’s Delfina Foundation. “There is now a clear path for the development of patrons and collectors—still in the making but a real possibility now, with MiZa and Noma to help complete the process. But Abu Dhabi can only do this through partnerships between public/private—that is, if they allow the voices of artists, designers, writers, and curators to come to the table with those who have money and power.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-searches.title: NYPD searches for suspect who police say stabbed a woman at random in Riverside Park
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-searches.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-searches.text:
Police are looking for a man who approached a woman in a Manhattan park Monday night and randomly stabbed her, leaving her hospitalized, according to officials.
Officers came to Riverside Park near West 96th Street around 7:40 p.m., after the victim called 911 herself to report the stabbing, police said. The 26-year-old woman had been stabbed in her torso, and police said she was taken to Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital in stable condition.
According to the NYPD, the woman was walking in the park when the suspect approached her. He did not say anything to her before stabbing her and running away, police said.
Police said the suspect was wearing all black at the time.
The incident is still under investigation, but bears some similarities to the fatal stabbing of Brooklyn jogger Katie Suarez last month.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://gothamist.com/news/digging-up-a-.title: Digging up a secret world under a Brooklyn graveyard, one teaspoon at a time
https://gothamist.com/news/digging-up-a-.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/digging-up-a-.text:
Researchers are digging-up Green-Wood Cemetery with teaspoons, looking for new species of fungus.
Since last spring, Green-Wood environmental fellows Whitney Bauck and Lauren Wilson have been sifting through the dirt as part of a larger effort to catalogue potentially thousands of unknown species of fungus.
While fungus is a vital part of the ecosystem, essential for carbon capture and the survival of plant life, researchers have only identified nearly 10% of existing varieties. Identifying the many species is the first step in studying and conserving the foundation of the planet’s ecological system – as well as ensuring that Green-Wood continues to thrive.
”It's really hard to manage and conserve and preserve an ecosystem if you don't even know what's there,” Wilson said.
Researchers are working to establish a comprehensive database in order to weed out the invasive species and protect the native species in Green-Wood from climate stresses. It’s part of a bigger effort to catalogue more types of fungus as part of a broader effort to fight climate change and protect local ecosystems from invasive species.
The relationship between fungus and plants goes way back. Early fossil evidence shows that hundreds of millions of years ago, fungus acted as the early roots systems for land plants when they evolved from their rootless aquatic ancestors.
The unseen labor of fungi also involves climate change mitigation. While billions of dollars have been invested globally for largely ineffective, man-made carbon capture technologies, fungi do the literal dirty work of capturing one-third of worldwide emissions from fossil fuels, according to the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks, a global scientific research organization dedicated to fungus.
“We're looking for technology solutions to help fight climate change, we're looking for conservation and restoration opportunities that have a climate angle,” said Michael Van Nuland, SPUN’s data science lead.
He calls fungus a natural technology “that has evolved on our planet to move carbon from plants into the soil that we need to be focusing more on.”
The Green-Wood dig
Bauck and Wilson have performed about a half-dozen digs, mostly in Brooklyn’s largest graveyard.
To obtain a sample, they measure out a square spot and mark it with mini orange cones. Then, they remove the vegetation with their fingers to expose the dirt. They use a rubber mallet to tap a 3-inch diameter pipe into the ground. When it’s 6 inches deep, the metal tube is removed gently by hand with the dirt inside.
With a sanitized plastic teaspoon, a sample is removed from the center of the tube. The specimen is sealed and sent to a lab for DNA analysis.
Along with the sample, they note location, surrounding plants, insects and soil characteristics such as color and moisture. A single teaspoon of cemetery soil contains DNA from hundreds of fungal species.
“When we get the data back from the lab, from the soil cores, it will be hundreds of fungi there,” Bauck said. “ We've found hundreds of species in New York City that had not been located here before.”
Healthy soils are chock-full of fungus. It’s an intrinsic part of soil, essentially acting as the glue that stabilizes dirt and decomposes organic matter into nutrients sent directly to trees and vegetation. Without it, most plants could not survive.
“The soil is so integral to how ecosystems work, and the fungi specifically are a key piece of that,” Van Nuland said. “If we start losing fungi, really, really serious collapse situations could start happening.”
Van Nuland said that plants are dependent on fungi for water and nutrients.
“Fungi are helping build our soils,” Van Nuland said. “They're helping all the plants that we see, the trees, the grasses, the flowers to obtain the nutrients they need.”
Identifying native species is important in monitoring the introduction of invasive species, which can outcompete the existing fungus and endanger native trees. The most dramatic example is the extinction of the American Chestnut tree by a non-native fungal blight, which was first documented at the Bronx Zoo more than a century ago.
Native trees continue to face threats from invasive species. Oak Wilt is a fungus that disrupts the transport of water and can kill red oaks in a matter of weeks. Dutch Elm and Laurel Wilt are among the lethal fungus impacting regional plant life.
”We can only protect what we've named,” Nuland said. “There are some areas where we are seeing the spread of an invasive fungus in the community, and we're watching it in real time disrupt the soil food web or disrupt the intact fungal community that exists there.”
Climate pressures are also impacting underground mycelium. Fungi have already responded to climate change. Scientists have noted that fungal species are migrating out of native ranges along with the plants they share a symbiotic relationship with. Many species are moving towards the poles and to higher elevations with the temperature shifts.
Van Nuland said that fungus is also potentially an early warning signal for climate change and desertification. It’s possible that close-monitoring of fungus can help ecologists manage and conserve plant life on the surface and mitigate catastrophic ecological impacts.
“The plants might be still persisting in an area even with intense climate pressure, but we might start seeing the fungal community start to shift even though the plants are still technically holding on,” Van Nuland said.
Wilson and Bauck have found at least 20 species that have not been documented anywhere, but expect that number to grow into the hundreds as they continue to sift through the lab data this winter. They plan to release their results next spring.

https://gothamist.com/news/fare-hikes-on.title: Fare hikes on yellow taxi cabs could keep drivers out of poverty, city report finds
https://gothamist.com/news/fare-hikes-on.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/fare-hikes-on.text:
Cab drivers could better avoid poverty through regular hikes to New York City’s yellow taxi fares, the city Taxi and Limousine Commission wrote in a report published Tuesday.
The report found the operating costs for yellow cab drivers — including the price to buy a car, maintenance, gas, medallion loan payments and insurance premiums — increased by about 16% since 2022, the last time the TLC increased the taxi meter fare. That year’s rate hike was the first one approved by the TLC in a decade, and increased the average cost of a ride by 23%.
But even with that fare hike, the average yellow cab driver now takes home from $40,000 to $58,000 a year before taxes, according to the report.
The report said regular fare hikes in line with inflation could help the city’s roughly 13,000 yellow cab drivers. It also suggested adding more flat-rate zones where customers are charged a single upfront price. The commission noted that LaGuardia Airport could be a good location for a flat-rate zone. Taxi riders at John F. Kennedy International Airport currently receive a flat rate depending on their destination.
The once lucrative yellow cab sector has suffered for more than a decade as e-hail companies like Uber flooded the city and undermined taxi drivers’ longtime monopoly on street hails. In 2018, at least eight drivers died by suicide as the value of a taxi medallion plummeted.
Over the summer, at least four yellow cab drivers died on the job. Gothamist reported that all of them suffered with poor health and were falling behind financially — and many were renters who couldn’t meet their weekly lease payments.
In issuing the report, TLC officials didn’t actually propose fare hikes. They merely noted it would be a good way to help the drivers.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned on improving the lives of working class New Yorkers, including taxi workers.
“Taxi drivers get up before dawn and work long hours to keep this city moving. They should be able to support their families on what they earn,” Mamdani said in a statement.
The report found weekly payments for taxi drivers who lease their cars, like some of the drivers who died this year, have increased by 32% since 2022. A majority of the city’s yellow cabbies drive on leases because they don’t have enough cash to buy a car and medallion up front, according to the TLC.
The report said the city’s 87,000 Uber and Lyft drivers are also struggling. Those drivers earn between $43,00 and $54,000 a year before taxes and make $6,000 less annually in tips than yellow drivers, the TLC’s analysis shows.
Bhairavi Desai, executive director of the New York Taxi Workers Alliance, said yellow cab drivers are struggling even more than what the report suggests.
“I think what the TLC’s painted is actually just a partial picture and the conditions are even more dire,” Desai said. “The yellow cab drivers are subject to more regulated expenses.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sh.title: Shahzia Sikander Sculpture in St. Louis Generates Protests and Counterprotests
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sh.author: Andy Battaglia
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sh.text:
Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).
As reported by St. Louis’s First Alert 4, protesters associating the sculpture with pro-choice abortion rights gathered outside the home base of Rung for Women, a nonprofit devoted to women’s career development that hosts it. As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.”
First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”
She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”
A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion issue and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”
Rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”
The same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander said, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”
An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.title: Smithsonian Head Assures Staff of Independence After Glimpse of White House Overhaul Plan
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.text:
Outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III reasserted the institution’s independence in a letter to his staff after a leaked document from a Trump aide laid out a sweeping overhaul of its programming and personnel.
“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in the letter, which the New York Times reviewed and first reported. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”
The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan,” was photographed on a laptop that a Trump aide was using on the Washington Metro. As first reported by ProPublica, its 25-item action list includes plans to dismiss top curators and administrators, among them Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of promoting “radical activist ideology.”
The plan also calls for a new permanent exhibit, “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance,” and another on “Great Families of American History.” It envisions a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum’s entrance, which would fulfill a request Trump made in September.
The plan appears to be a work in progress: Photos show the aide brainstorming additions in a notebook. One handwritten entry seems to read “No X-rated exhibition policy,” an apparent callback to a particularly contentious stretch of Hartig’s testimony, when lawmakers questioned her about images of bondage wear in an LGBTQ history exhibition. On Monday, ProPublica identified the staffer as an associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office behind a 162-page report that accused the Smithsonian of “extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.”
A central complaint of the report was what its authors characterized as anti-white bias at the museum, which they said showed in its promotion of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The report accused one exhibition, “Many Voices, One Nation,” of trying “to convince visitors that illegal aliens are entitled to citizenship, voting rights and ‘belonging’ in America.” (Two weeks after the report’s release, Trump signed an executive order directing that signs be installed outside the museum warning visitors of its “ideological capture.”)
The document glimpsed on the staffer’s laptop laid out new interpretive guidelines for exhibits, including an explicit end to the Smithsonian’s use of a diversity style guide. The Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions would be reviewed, and one show now on tour, “The Bias Inside Us,” would be halted. Grants to “woke third parties,” such as the American Alliance of Museums, would also be reviewed.
The Smithsonian’s online K-12 curriculum would be overhauled to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” The “Becoming US” module on immigration, for example, would be deleted and replaced with a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”
The Smithsonian, a network of 21 museums, is structured to operate independently of the White House. It’s governed by a 17-member Board of Regents: the Chief Justice of the United States, John G. Roberts Jr.; the Vice President, JD Vance; six members of Congress from both parties; and nine private citizens. Legally, the Smithsonian answers to Congress, not the White House, but federal money makes up about 60 percent of its budget. Trump proposed cutting that funding by roughly 12 percent for fiscal year 2026, a threat that ultimately went unrealized.
Bunch, who became secretary in 2019, has repeatedly asserted the institution’s legal independence as pressure from the White House has mounted. The administration has demanded that the Smithsonian turn over internal materials and pushed for the firing of Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, whom Trump had called “highly partisan.” Sajet ultimately resigned. Bunch has drawn similar attacks: a White House aide reportedly called him a “rabid partisan.”
In a May interview with the New York Times, Bunch seemed to acknowledge that recent vacancies on the Board of Regents had weakened his position, though he still appeared to have the support of a majority of the board. In September, he announced that he would retire at the end of the year.
In his letter to staff on Tuesday, Bunch wrote, “As I have said before, we welcome scrutiny of our work, and even disagreement. The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: Duran Duran was transformed by Andy Taylor’s rock edge – and never quite the same without him
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Alexis Petridis
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
It’s very easy indeed to paint Andy Taylor as the misfit within the world-beating five-man line-up of Duran Duran. The others were fans of glam and Chic: their avowed intention was to form a band that melded the sophisticated disco of the latter with the extravagant style and experimental art-pop of Roxy Music.
Taylor – who had made what he later called “that fateful journey down to Birmingham” from his home on Tyneside after spotting an ad in the Melody Maker – had tastes that tended towards rock music of a more traditional stripe, as evidenced by the artists he covered on his second solo album, 1990’s Dangerous: Thin Lizzy, Bad Company, AC/DC, Montrose.
Happy enough initially to apply the hair dye and make-up that gave Duran Duran their hip post-punk New Romantic image, by the mid-80s he looked like he’d joined the wrong band entirely. In the photos of Duran Duran taken at the Sanremo pop festival in 1985, his bandmates sport the kind of baggy, spendy designer gear common to British pop stars of the era who’ve done exceptionally well for themselves. By contrast, Andy Taylor looks like he could have been parachuted in from a heavy metal band: his hair long, his ripped vest accessorised with scarves, his belt studded, his eyes hidden behind a pair of sunglasses.
Like drummer Roger Taylor, he left Duran Duran the following year: unlike Roger Taylor, he left not because he could no longer stand the pressure of being a global teen idol and fancied a quiet life, but because he’d negotiated a solo deal with a record label that would allow him to pursue his passion for hard rock, in the company of former Sex Pistols guitarist Steve Jones.
And yet, for all he appears in retrospect have stuck out like the proverbial sore thumb, Andy Taylor was absolutely integral to the success of Duran Duran, and not merely because he was by far the most straightforwardly talented musician in the band. As soon as he arrived in Birmingham he set about transforming what one writer called their “rough, undisciplined” blend of electronics, disco-influenced rhythms and punk-y energy into cohesive songs. His leaning towards rock music gave Duran Duran a peculiar commercial edge, particularly in the US, a country that had failed to really take to punk or glam rock, and viewed disco as an aberration best forgotten.
The standard line is that Duran Duran succeeded in the US because of the rise of MTV, which took to their glamorous and expensively made videos early on. But there’s also a compelling argument that Duran Duran became bigger Stateside than any other British pop band of their era in part because Taylor’s distorted guitar – very audible indeed on Girls On Film, or Hungry Like The Wolf, the latter a song on which Taylor translated Nick Rhodes’ synth lines into something more appropriate for guitar – gave traditionally conservative radio programmers something they could understand: at least a hint of traditional rock music, amid the alienating synthesisers and preponderance of slap.
The sales figures were wildly impressive – both 1982’s Rio and its follow-up Seven And The Ragged Tiger went double-platinum in the US – but commercial success wasn’t enough to paper over the obvious fault-lines emerging within the band. Sessions for the latter album were fraught: Andy Taylor subsequently described them as “a laborious plod”, not much helped by his increasing dependence on cocaine; Rhodes tellingly noted that “everybody was pulling and tugging in different directions”.
Duran Duran went on hiatus after completing an arena tour in 1984, its members indulging in side projects. John and Andy Taylor formed The Power Station with vocalist Robert Palmer. Despite a distinctly funky undertow provided by Chic drummer Tony Thompson, their eponymous debut album leaned into the guitarist’s love of Led Zeppelin. Critically pilloried at the time as the height of mid-80s coked-out excess – decades later, it was re-evaluated for precisely the same reason – the album was successful enough to revitalise Palmer’s career: he swiftly left, tapping Andy Taylor to play on his huge solo hit Addicted To Love. Taylor jumped ship from Duran Duran the following year.
Taylor’s solo career never really took off in a comparable manner to that of the band he’d left, although it offered an intriguing index of his influences: he co-produced and wrote an album for Rod Stewart, and worked with British hard rockers Thunder, Reef and The Almighty. Duran Duran went on to have further commercial success, not least with the 1993 single Ordinary World, but they were never quite the same band without him. You could tell as much from the statement the surviving members issued following his death, which praised the “indelible fire and swagger he brought to our music”, suggested he “drove the songs that took [them] around the world”, and hymned the brief early 2000s moment when he rejoined the band, resulting in the album Astronaut and its accompanying hit single Reach Up For The Sunrise: “That time together, both onstage and in the studio, meant a tremendous amount to us all.”
“There’s a massive Andy Taylor-shaped hole in my heart,” added singer Simon Le Bon. “It’ll never close up.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ta.title: Tate Liverpool Plans Fall 2027 Reopening With Surrealism Survey
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ta.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ta.text:
Tate Liverpool will reopen in fall 2027 after a £30 million transformation with the exhibition “Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds,” a nod to the museum’s inaugural Surrealist show in 1988.
The surrealism exhibition will run from fall 2027 to spring 2028 and include works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray. According to Tate Liverpool, the show will also explore the “important role of surrealism in the history of theater and dance” through the movement’s major commissions for stage sets and costumes. Also on view will be Dorothea Tanning’s costume designs for the ballet The Witch, photographs of Sheila Legge performing as the “Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal” at the opening of the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London, and material from the archive of Ted Joans.
“Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool. This exhibition will spark imaginations, surprise visitors and reward curiosity, offering a fresh perspective on one of art’s most celebrated movements. It also brings a wonderful echo of the surrealist exhibition that opened our gallery in 1988, while taking visitors on an exciting new journey,” said Jemima Pyne, interim director of the Tate Liverpool, in a statement.
Tate Liverpool closed in October 2023 and was scheduled to reopen in 2025, but fundraising difficulties pushed the date back to 2027. The architecture firm 6a architects is redesigning the gallery’s home, an 1846 warehouse on the Royal Albert Dock, as part of a £35 million ($46.5 million) renovation.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ho.title: Hoor Al Qasimi Named Curator of 2028 Venice Biennale
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ho.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ho.text:
Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s biggest recurring art exhibition running from April 8 to November 26, 2028. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority.
The board of La Biennale di Venezia said it met on November 20 to pick Al Qasimi on the recommendation of president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. Al Qasimi will be tasked with curating the 62nd edition of the exhibition and will take on the title of director of the visual arts department.
“La Biennale di Venezia is a place where the world converges with art through its diverse visions. Throughout her career, Hoor Al Qasimi has succeeded in creating a caravanserai of geographies and the Universal, giving voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected,” said Buttafuoco in a statement on Thursday. “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people. I also recognize in her a quality of balance and composure, namely the vibrant presence of mīzān (inner harmony), which finds its strength in relationships.”
The taking of an art biennale is nothing new to Al Qasimi. In 2024, she was appointed by the Biennale of Sydney as the artistic director of the exhibition’s 25th edition, which ran from March 7 to June 8, 2026. However, the Venice Biennale is of a larger scale on an international stage. “The international art exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia has been an important platform for many of us around the world. I first visited the 50th edition in 2003 having recently stepped into my curatorial role at Sharjah Biennial,” said Al Qasimi in a statement on Monday. “For me, La Biennale continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators. I am honored to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, and the board for their confidence and trust.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Rebecca Bailey and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.
Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” the Chinese commerce ministry spokesman, He Yadong, said at a regular briefing. “China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”
Brazil was also singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled.
Brazil’s government said on Wednesday that “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.
It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.
The Trump administration said that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries. They are being imposed under a law that allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.
The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower levels ‌agreed under trade deals that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.
The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.
Trump met his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen last week but the escalation in tariffs will not be a surprise to China, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP news agency.
The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in Miami on the sidelines of the G20 in December.
“It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing.
“Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) party congress in October 2027,”Wang said.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of excess capacity.
“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Trump andd Xi.
Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” said the spokesperson Guo Jiakun.
Greer told CNBC that the administration was proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.
China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined”, said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”
The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” said the European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill.
Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.
It added it was “preparing and submitting rebuttal comments on the preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions and allegations ‌made by interested parties”.
In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in any sector, adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.
Taiwan was also earmarked for new tariffs but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing 15% tariff rate.
Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech products that account for more than 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.
Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the EU, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland and Thailand.
Tokyo’s top government spokesperson, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.
Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.
Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will probably support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
However, the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos”.
He added: “This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
With Associated Press and Reuters

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
The phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.
“The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman.
It had been a whirlwind two weeks that started with the ouster of Huang as Nvidia’s CEO after his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman some in the US government feared to be a Chinese spy. Two more alleged affairs with company employees were later revealed. Silicon Valley engineers and venture capitalists decried Huang’s departure at the time, writing an open letter to Nvidia’s board of directors saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”
Donald Trump also got involved. The president repeatedly said that he’d like to see the return of Huang calling the CEO a “fine person” and “honorable guy”.
In the meantime, Nvidia’s stock tanked, falling more than 10%, and shedding hundreds of billions in value. Nvidia, which designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence, is among the world’s top five most valuable companies.
On Monday, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang. The decision came after Trump dialed into the company’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return. In a statement, the White House said: “We have to protect our geniuses.”
Nvidia’s stock rebounded, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, who owns shares in the chip maker, took a victory lap, making up to $15m with the surge on Monday.
Silicon Valley’s venture capitalists also rejoiced. Jason Calacanis, an angel investor, Nvidia stock-holder and co-host of the tech-centric All-In podcast, wrote a flurry of posts on X. He posted an AI image of a shining long-haired Huang depicted as Jesus holding a graphics processing unit (GPU) in place of the bible, writing: “GPU Jesus has risen.”
Other tech figures took the news personally. Travis Kalanick, the disgraced Uber CEO who was pushed out by his board, was one of the top figures fighting for Huang’s reinstatement. In past weeks, he frequently posted on X, saying “Bring Jensen back”, “LFG” (Let’s fucking go), and “We’ve got your back”.
Kalanick was reportedly among a small group of venture capitalists who lobbied Trump and JD Vance to push Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, according to the FT. On Monday, Kalanick posted: “I will always sign up to serve him.”
‘We’re all being gaslit’
While a vocal cohort of Silicon Valley insiders high-fived Huang’s return, it’s been radio silence from several other of the industry’s top leaders and rank-and-file workers.
The CEOs of Google, Meta and Apple have not weighed in on the debate. When Amazon’s Jeff Bezos was asked at an event last week if he thought Huang should be reinstated, he responded: “I don’t know enough of the details … so I can’t answer that question.” Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had a similar response.
Anil Dash, an entrepreneur with a career in leading smaller tech companies, is one of the few voices in tech who has publicly criticized Huang’s reinstatement. He says it sends the wrong message to the industry – that there are no rules, boundaries or accountability.
Dash pointed to widespread rationale for Huang’s return, which is based on the CEO being singularly crucial in the AI arms race against China. Calacanis, for example, has trumpeted this justification, saying: “We can not [sic] lose the race for super intelligence to China – period, full stop.”
And now, Dash said, Huang could have been compromised by a Chinese asset, and he’s running the biggest company in the industry. “It doesn’t make any sense,” he said. “We’re all being gaslit and we’re at a certain point where we’re like, ‘No, the sky’s not green. The sky’s blue.’”
Dash says the hundreds of thousands of tech workers who live in fear of being swept up in the increasingly frequent waves of layoffs, as the industry pivots to AI, aren’t able to speak up even if they disagree with Huang’s reinstatement. They don’t know if their “boss agrees with these guys”, Dash said.
Alison Taylor, an associate professor at New York University’s Stern Business School, said that mentality extends beyond Silicon Valley to the White House, given that Trump played a part in Huang’s return. “Trump’s whole thing is retaliation,” she noted.
“The message is: if you don’t shut up and go along with it, you’re not going to survive,” Taylor said. “It’s a fuck you to everybody who believes in the rule of law and who believes in anything being fair.”
Huang apologized to Nvidia staff in a company-wide meeting on Tuesday for “some terrible mistakes” he made. The CEO also rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, adding it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.
“Everything he’s done, it’s just his affection, his admiration, his recognition of the great company that you are,” Huang said of Trump.
In a separate statement, Huang thanked leaders across the industry for their “extraordinary support”.
“I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Rodadas de negócios aproximam cooperativas brasileiras de compradores internacionais
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Kennedy Cruz
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A castanha de baru, o pequi, o arroz e o café estão entre os produtos apresentados por cooperativas brasileiras a compradores internacionais durante o Cooperar para Exportar 2026, em Brasília (DF). Promovido pela ApexBrasil, o evento segue até sexta-feira (27) e promove rodadas de negócios entre produtores e importadores interessados em conhecer a produção nacional e estabelecer parcerias comerciais.
Ao todo, participam 34 compradores de 24 países. A programação prevê cerca de 900 reuniões de negócios, com o objetivo de aproximar cooperativas brasileiras de empresas interessadas em adquirir produtos regionais para comercialização no mercado externo.
Sócio-diretor da Danfus Group, importadora e distribuidora de alimentos e bebidas brasileiras com sede em Portugal, Douglas de Lima participou do encontro em busca de novos produtos das cooperativas para levar ao mercado europeu. “Nossa expectativa é adquirir produtos regionais, como castanha de baru, castanha-do-pará, geleias, doces e leite de coco, entre outros. Queremos nos aproximar das cooperativas, conhecer melhor a produção regional brasileira e identificar produtos que possamos levar para a Europa”, afirmou o sócio-diretor da Danfus Group.
Representante da empresa ETG, da China, Jeff Zhou participou pela primeira vez de um evento da ApexBrasil. Ele destacou a importância dos encontros entre vendedores brasileiros e compradores estrangeiros. “É uma oportunidade para conhecer novos produtos, identificar possibilidades de negócios e contribuir para o desenvolvimento das relações comerciais entre o Brasil e outros países”, destacou.
Entre os produtos que despertaram o interesse de Zhou está o café. O comprador apontou o crescimento do mercado chinês da bebida como uma oportunidade de cooperação comercial com fornecedores brasileiros. “Fiquei muito interessado nos produtos de café. Como o Brasil é o maior exportador de café do mundo e o mercado chinês está crescendo muito rapidamente, acredito que há uma boa oportunidade de cooperação entre os dois países nesse setor”, disse Zhou.
A compradora Júlia Franco, da África do Sul, também participou do encontro para conhecer as cooperativas e a produção brasileira. Seu interesse está voltado especialmente ao artesanato. “Espero levar artesanato brasileiro para a África do Sul. Estou muito ansiosa para conhecer as cooperativas e descobrir tudo o que o Brasil tem de bom para apresentar”, enfatizou.
Cooperativas buscam novos mercados
Entre as cooperativas presentes está a Coopermira do Cerrado, de Mirabela (MG). A organização reúne agricultores familiares e trabalhadores do extrativismo e atua com produtos do Cerrado, como pequi, baru, fava-d’anta, jatobá e buriti. Segundo o representante Daniel Mendes, a cooperativa já comercializa seus produtos em cinco países e busca ampliar as exportações, especialmente de castanha de baru e pequi.
“Mais do que vender produtos, a gente vende a preservação do nosso bioma e a valorização das comunidades. Por meio da ApexBrasil, exportamos para cinco países. A castanha de baru é nosso principal produto de exportação, e também levamos o pequi para a Europa e os Estados Unidos”, afirmou.
O representante também destacou a presença dos produtos do Cerrado em mercados ligados às indústrias de alimentos e cosméticos. Segundo ele, a França compra óleo de pequi para a fabricação de cosméticos, produtos dermatológicos e alimentos. O país também adquire a raspa de juá produzida pela cooperativa.
Para Mendes, o desafio é conquistar novos compradores e ampliar o conhecimento sobre os produtos do Cerrado. A expectativa durante o encontro é fortalecer as vendas de baru e apresentar o pequi a outros mercados. “Precisamos reforçar a comercialização desse produto e também tentar incluir o pequi nas compras do mercado externo. Sabemos que é um desafio, porque nem todo mundo conhece o pequi e o baru, mas estamos aqui para apresentar esses produtos e conquistar novos compradores”, declarou Daniel Mendes.
Outra participante é a Cooperativa Regional Agropecuária Sul Catarinense (Conafort), do sul de Santa Catarina. A organização reúne um portfólio de aproximadamente 50 produtos, com destaque para o arroz irrigado, comercializado nas versões branco, parboilizado e integral. Para Fabiano Martins, a participação nas rodadas representa uma oportunidade de apresentar a produção dos cooperados e estabelecer contatos com empresas exportadoras.
“Quem não é visto não é lembrado. A grande importância desse evento é poder expor nossa produção e oferecer os produtos dos cooperados. Normalmente, um cooperado sozinho não consegue fazer isso, porque exige investimentos altos. De forma coletiva e organizada, fica muito mais fácil dar visibilidade aos produtos e conseguir concretizar uma exportação”, afirmou.
Preparação para exportar
Para algumas cooperativas, o acesso ao mercado internacional ainda é uma etapa em construção. É o caso da Cooperativa de Pequenos Produtores de Jaraguá do Sul, em Santa Catarina, representada por Ivanete de Souza. O grupo trabalha com hortifrutigranjeiros, sucos, geleias e banana-passa, mas ainda não realiza exportações.
Depois de participar de uma edição anterior do evento, Ivanete de Souza voltou a Brasília para acompanhar atividades de capacitação e conhecer os procedimentos necessários para comercializar os produtos no exterior. “A gente ainda não exporta. É um caminho que estamos construindo. Não é só chegar aqui, participar de uma rodada de negócios e dizer que vai começar a exportar. Existe uma série de fatores que tornam esse processo difícil para nós, pequenos produtores. Por meio da ApexBrasil e desse evento, estamos conhecendo cada etapa”, explicou.
A cooperada destacou que a preparação envolve desde questões relacionadas às embalagens até a documentação e as exigências específicas de cada mercado. “A gente sabe trabalhar com o mercado brasileiro e com as chamadas públicas do governo, mas levar nosso produto para fora é outro caminho. Existem muitas coisas que nós, como pequenas cooperativas, ainda não sabemos. Cada mercado exige documentos e procedimentos diferentes, e precisamos aprender a organizar tudo isso”, completou Ivanete de Souza.
*Conteúdo patrocinado pela ApexBrasil.

https://taz.de/Zusammenarbeit-von-AfD-un.title: Zusammenarbeit von AfD und BSW: Ein Freund, ein guter Freund
https://taz.de/Zusammenarbeit-von-AfD-un.author: Konrad Litschko und Rainer Rutz
https://taz.de/Zusammenarbeit-von-AfD-un.text:
Zusammenarbeit von AfD und BSW: Ein Freund, ein guter Freund
Beim BSW-Bundesparteitag am Wochenende droht eine Eskalation mit Ansage. Das Rumkumpeln mit der AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt geht etlichen Parteigranden gegen den Strich.
Am Mittwoch vor einer Woche lief die Sache am Ende mal wieder glatt. Im Landtag von Sachsen-Anhalt war die Wahl der Mitglieder des Parlamentarischen Kontrollgremiums angesetzt. Ein vierköpfiges Gremium, das den Verfassungsschutz des Landes kontrolliert. Dann passierte Ungewöhnliches. Im ersten Wahlgang gab das fünfköpfige BSW seinem Kandidaten Thomas Schulze genau null Stimmen. Dafür erhielten die zwei AfD-Kandidaten 44 Stimmen – 5 mehr als die AfD-Fraktion Mandate hat. Im zweiten Wahlgang erhielt Schulze dann die Stimmen der AfD – und war auch gewählt. Eine abgesprochene Wahl, offensichtlich.
Nun kontrollieren neben einem CDU-Abgeordneten nur Vertreter der AfD und des BSW den Verfassungsschutz. Ausgerechnet. Schließlich stufte der Geheimdienst die AfD als gesichert rechtsextrem ein und gilt das BSW als Russland zugeneigt. Vor allem aber zeigte der Vorgang: Die Absprachen von AfD und BSW funktionieren bestens. Was ein Vorzeichen für den 8. Dezember sein könnte – den Tag, an dem sich AfD-Spitzenkandidat Ulrich Siegmund in Sachsen-Anhalt zum ersten Ministerpräsidenten seiner Partei wählen lassen will.
Erst kürzlich erklärte Siegmund in einem Video, er werde an dem Tag, eine Woche früher als zunächst geplant, in einer Sondersitzung des Landtags als Ministerpräsident Sachsen-Anhalt antreten. Und er gehe von seiner Wahl im ersten Wahlgang aus. Dafür allerdings fehlen ihm weiterhin 3 Stimmen. Von wem die kommen, bleibt weiter unklar.
In der AfD wird dafür weiterhin Richtung CDU geschielt. Auch weil die BSW-Spitze um Fraktionschef Thomas Schulze, seine Vize Claudia Wittig und den Landesvorsitzenden John Lucas Dittrich fortwährend beteuert, sich bei der Wahl zu enthalten. Was Siegmund spätestens im dritten Wahlgang dennoch helfen könnte, sofern es noch eine weitere Enthaltung gibt. Denn dann reicht eine einfache Mehrheit. Zudem postuliert das BSW, keine Koalition mit der AfD einzugehen, die Partei auch nicht zu tolerieren – und setzt weiter auf ihre Idee eines überparteilichen Ministerpräsidenten.
„Mögliche Schnittmengen bei parlamentarischen Anträgen“
Aber sicher sein kann man sich beim BSW nicht – wie nicht nur ihr Deal mit der AfD bei der Wahl zum Kontrollgremium zeigt. Und dies auch, weil BSW-Gründerin Sahra Wagenknecht den Landesverband und dessen „Magdeburger Weg“ offenbar als Faustpfand fürs Überleben ihrer Partei einsetzt.
Wiederholt hatte sich Wagenknecht, die heute eigentlich nur noch Chefin der Grundwertekommission ihrer Partei ist, für diesen Weg starkgemacht. Nach der Sachsen-Anhalt-Wahl hatte sie sich sogar direkt mit AfD-Bundeschef Tino Chrupalla getroffen. Das bestätigte ein BSW-Sprecher der taz. Besprochen worden sei der BSW-Vorschlag eines überparteilichen Ministerpräsidenten und „mögliche Schnittmengen bei parlamentarischen Anträgen“. Weiter ins Detail ging der Sprecher nicht.
Das BSW stellt dieser Kurs dagegen längst vor eine Zerreißprobe. Deutlich hatten sich zuletzt auch Parteimitgründer und Vorstandsmitglieder wie Christian Leye oder Sevim Dağdelen dagegen ausgesprochen. Leye warf der AfD „rassistischen Müll“ vor, die Partei sei ein „politischer Gegner“. „Es ist nicht lange her, da war das im BSW klar.“ Auf dem BSW-Bundesparteitag an diesem Freitag und Samstag in Dresden könnte der Richtungsstreit nun eskalieren.
In Sachsen-Anhalt ist der BSW-Kurs dagegen längst klar. Nach der Landtagswahl am 6. September hatte die AfD alle Fraktionen zu Gesprächen geladen. Einzig das BSW nahm die Einladung an. Mindestens drei Gespräche sollen seitdem erfolgt sein, alle vertraulich. Auf AfD-Seite sollen nur Siegmund und Tobias Rausch angerückt sein, teils auch mit Sprecher Patrick Harr und Justiziar Laurens Nothdurft. Sie sollen dabei auch auf schriftliche Vereinbarungen gedrängt haben. Ihnen gegenüber vom BSW: Claudia Wittig, John Lucas Dittrich und Thomas Schulze.
Und nur mit Wagenknecht
Das BSW-Trio stimme sich dabei eng mit Sahra Wagenknecht ab, heißt es aus der Partei. Und nur mit ihr. Der Rest des Bundesvorstands soll über die Gespräche kaum bis gar nicht informiert worden sein, was dort schon länger für Unmut sorgt – aber auch machtlos hingenommen wird. Der BSW-Sprecher dagegen beteuert, dass „selbstverständlich ein enger und regelmäßiger Austausch zwischen der BSW-Fraktion in Sachsen-Anhalt mit dem Präsidium und Parteivorstand stattfindet“.
Und die Absprachen in Magdeburg funktionieren. AfD-Mann Siegmund sagte zuletzt, es gebe nur eine Fraktion im Landtag, „mit der wir konstruktiv, gut zusammenarbeiten“: das BSW. Im Landtag wurde das sichtbar. Zuerst, als dort AfD-Mann Tobias Rausch auch mit BSW-Stimmen zum Landtagspräsidenten gewählt wurde, zum ersten für die AfD bundesweit, und die BSW-Abgeordneten freudestrahlend gratulieren. Auch der AfD-Radikale Hans-Thomas Tillschneider erhielt bei der Wahl zum Vizepräsidenten Stimmen außerhalb seiner Fraktion. BSW und CDU beschuldigen sich gegenseitig, ihn gewählt zu haben. Das BSW feiert seine vermeintliche Standfestigkeit: Rausch sei wählbar gewesen, Tillschneider hingegen nicht.
Wie vertraut AfD und BSW sind, wurde kurz darauf bei einem gemeinsamen Dinner in Magdeburg offenbar, auf Einladung ausgerechnet des rechtsextremen Magazins Compact. Duzend und sich zuprostend saßen dort beide Fraktionen zusammen. BSW-Mann Schulze versprach der AfD, ein „ehrlicher Partner zu sein“. Er sei „froh, dass wir das mit euch zusammen machen werden“. Und Claudia Wittig erinnerte die AfD daran, dass sie Geschichte schreiben wolle: „Packen wir es an.“
Das Vertrauen zahlt sich aus. Wenig später erhielt AfD-Politiker Wittig den Vorsitz im Bildungsausschuss, der seiner Partei aufgrund ihrer geringen Mandatszahl gar nicht zusteht. Beide Fraktionen beriefen gemeinsam eine Sondersitzung ein, forderten ein Ende der Ukrainehilfen und verschafften weiteren Anträgen eine Mehrheit, gegen die CDU, SPD und Linke nicht mehr ankommen.
BSW-Gründerin Wagenknecht gefällt das. Man habe die „Brandmauer-Idiotie beendet“, erklärte sie erfreut nach der Rausch-Wahl und dem gemeinsamen Russlandantrag. Das kommt nicht von ungefähr: Schon im Juni hatte Wagenknecht die AfD-Bundesvorsitzenden Alice Weidel und Tino Chrupalla brieflich zu gemeinsamen Wahlkampfauftritten eingeladen und neben Unterschieden vor allem Gemeinsamkeiten betont: die Ablehnung des „propagandistischen Staatsfunk“ oder „zu enge Meinungskorridore“. Die AfD ließ das zunächst an sich abtropfen. So schien es. Das jüngste Treffen von Wagenknecht und Chrupalla zeigt jedoch, dass es längst auch auf Bundesebene einen direkten Austausch gibt.
Auch in Sachsen-Anhalt begannen die Annäherungsversuche früh. Schon im November 2024 erteilten dort die beiden BSW-Landeschefs Thomas Schulze und John Lucas Dittrich der Brandmauer zur AfD eine Absage. „Wenn von der AfD ein vernünftiger Antrag kommt – warum soll ich da nicht zustimmen?“, erklärte Dittrich. Und Schulze trat im Frühjahr 2025 auf einem BSW-Unterstützertreffen in Magdeburg gemeinsam mit dem früheren AfDler Robert Farle auf. Beide sollen sich auch privat getroffen haben. Der ehemalige DKP-Funktionär und Russlandverehrer Farle war jahrelang für die AfD Landtags- und Bundestagsabgeordneter, ehe er in Ungnade fiel und 2023 aus der Partei austrat. Beim BSW sei er nun gefeierter Gast gewesen, so schildern es mehrere frühere Mitglieder.
Andere im Landesverband störten sich dagegen an dem Auftritt und am weiteren Kurs der damaligen Doppelspitze, ihren selbstherrlichen Auftritten und dem Kaltstellen von Kritiker:innen. Vor dem Landesparteitag im November 2025 schaltete sich die Bundesspitze ein: Kurz vor dem Stichtag zur Festlegung des Delegiertenschlüssels nahm der Bundesvorstand per Eilbeschluss 130 neue Mitglieder in den Landesverband auf. Die meisten Delegierten gewannen die Kreisverbände im Norden und Westen hinzu, die hinter Dittrich und Schulze und ihrem AfD-Kurs stehen. Ihre Kritiker:innen in den Südverbänden hatten das Nachsehen.
Auf dem Parteitag folgte dann der Showdown. Einige Funktionäre wie Harald Koch, BSW-Kreischef in Mansfeld-Südharz und Ex-Linker, warnte, im Landesvorstand gebe es das Ziel, „eine Fraktion wählen zu lassen, die bereit ist, einen AfD-Ministerpräsidenten mitzuwählen“. Das sei für ihn „ein Skandal“. Koch und die anderen Kritiker unterlagen: Am Ende des Parteitags waren 5 von 8 Landesvorständen nicht mehr im Amt.
„Unfassbare Unverschämtheit“
Etwas mehr als ein halbes Jahr später, in diesem August, traten dann 21 einstige Funktionäre des Landesverbands, darunter Harald Koch, aus dem BSW aus. Zur Begründung verwiesen sie auf den autoritären Führungsstil der Parteispitze, auf Postengeschacher oder elitäre Mitgliederaufnahme zur Mehrheitsbeschaffung. Aber auch darauf: Es sei inzwischen „zu befürchten, dass diejenigen, welche das BSW wählen, letztendlich einen AfD-Ministerpräsidenten wählen“.
Zuvor hatte auch BSW-Frontfrau Claudia Wittig – formal nur Nummer 2 hinter Schulze, aber prominentestes Gesicht der Landespartei – die Nähe zur AfD gesucht. Bereits im Mai saß sie bei dem früheren CDU-Mann Alexander von Bismarck im Onlinetalk, der bei dem berüchtigten Potsdamer „Remigrations“-Treffen dabei war, ebenso wie AfD-Mann Ulrich Siegmund. Was der öffentlich-rechtliche Rundfunk so abliefere, sei eine „unfassbare Unverschämtheit“, bediente Wittig dort das „Lügenpresse“-Wording.
Wenig später war Wittig für eine Diskussion mit AfD-Mann Oliver Kirchner auf einem Compact-Sommerfest in Stößen angekündigt. Sie sagte kurzfristig ab, gab dem Magazin aber mehrere Interviews. Zwei Tage vor der Wahl saß sie doch noch mit Kirchner auf einem Podium: Auf einem „Friedensfest“ bei Magdeburg geißelten beide die „Kriegsparteien“. Auch mit Sachsens AfD-Chef Jörg Urban und dem AfD-Außenpolitiker Rainer Rothfuß diskutierte Wittig zuletzt öffentlich.
Die Hallenserin verteidigt dies mit ihrem Credo, man müsse mit allen reden. BSW-Aussteiger wie die frühere BSW-Landesvize Sylvia Winkelmann-Witkowsky sehen ein anderes Kalkül: Wittig mache alles, um aufzusteigen. „Und im Moment kann man als BSW‑Mitglied nur aufsteigen, wenn man mit der AfD kooperiert.“ Dabei sei das BSW doch angetreten, „eine Alternative zur AfD zu sein“. Mit dem aktuellen Weg werde die Partei dagegen „eine sehr kurze Laufzeit“ haben, glaubt Winkelmann-Witkowsky.
