https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-la-elect.title: Los Angeles Socialists Won Big in the Blue Electoral Wave
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-la-elect.author: Chris Kutalik
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-la-elect.text:
Los Angeles Socialists Won Big in the Blue Electoral Wave
A key but occasionally overlooked site of socialist resurgence in the United States: Los Angeles, where members of the Democratic Socialists of America won local races, the mayoralty, and a seat in Congress.
The midterm elections were truly seismic. Like many places across the country, Los Angeles made good on its protean potential from the 2026 blowout with a stronger socialist movement and a larger share of political power. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members won up and down the ballot. Nithya Raman won the mayor’s office of the country’s second-largest city in an upset victory. Marissa Roy has won the city attorney’s office, and Angela Gonzales-Torres is headed to Congress.
Together their victories put democratic socialists in two of Los Angeles’s most powerful citywide offices and sent a DSA-LA member to Congress for the very first time in a race that few expected a year ago would even be a close challenge. The formerly conservative, sleepy suburb of Burbank has elected a DSA council majority, one of the first on the West Coast.
Behind those wins is DSA’s second-largest chapter. In the last year alone, the LA chapter doubled its membership to over six thousand members, launched a citywide Shake Up LA slate, and knocked more than 110,000 doors. And it did so alongside a realignment of the city’s left-labor coalition, especially that of the powerful hotel workers union UNITE HERE Local 11, which cross-endorsed most of DSA-LA’s Shake Up City Hall slate from Nithya down to Burbank City Council, and whose thousands of members knocked doors for her.
National Earthquake
This didn’t happen in a vacuum. Nationally, Democratic candidates of all stripes won control of both chambers of Congress, while Republicans lost ground in a shocking 99 percent of roughly 2,100 counties where most ballots had been counted by the morning after the election, according to Reuters. The electorate shifted left nearly everywhere, all at once.
Within that national revolt, Los Angeles voters were also shifting left. Gonzales-Torres decisively defeated Democratic incumbent Jimmy Gomez, winning over 62 percent of the vote while running openly as a DSA member, supporting a free Palestine and the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and rejecting corporate money. Her victory gives DSA-LA its first foothold in Congress with a candidate that took clear positions against corporate power and state violence and for Palestine and the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement while building a winning electoral coalition.
Roy’s victory carries a historic mandate as well. With more than 695,000 votes and roughly 68 percent support, she received the largest vote total ever won in a Los Angeles city election at any time, according to her campaign. She campaigned uphill, against the Democratic establishment and real estate lobby’s support of the incumbent, on turning the City Attorney’s Office into LA’s largest public-interest law office: pursuing abusive corporate landlords, enforcing workers’ rights, holding polluters accountable, and challenging the Trump administration in court.
Raman’s mayoral victory expands that opening considerably. Her 2020 city council victory helped establish DSA-LA as a force in city politics. Six years later, she has defeated incumbent (and onetime New Leftist) Karen Bass to become Los Angeles’s first democratic socialist (and immigrant) mayor.
Her victory gives the socialist movement a new scale of power to advance housing, tenant protections, and public services across Los Angeles. An ongoing tension will be between her independence as an elected and the co-governance and criticism of both the LA chapter and DSA’s national leadership about her level of support for the BDS movement and other issues she may not be in lockstep with the chapter on.
The chapter has also consolidated its existing beachhead on the LA City Council. City Council Members Eunisses Hernandez and Hugo Soto-Martínez and Los Angeles Unified School District Board Member Rocío Rivas all won reelection. In the Inglewood area, Estefany Castañeda retained her seat on the Centinela Valley Union High School District board, while Yaritza Gonzalez won election to the Inglewood Unified School District board.
Red Burbank
The chapter’s reach also expanded beyond Los Angeles. In Burbank, victories for Mike Van Gorder and Nolan Southerland created a democratic socialist council majority alongside Konstantine Anthony, while Stephen Post won in West Hollywood. Estuardo Mazariegos’s race in Los Angeles’s Ninth Council District remained unresolved, with Mazariegos trailing by a mere eighty-seven votes after taking on an opponent backed by major corporate and police union spending.
Los Angeles is also part of a national advance forward by socialists. DSA reported at least eight members elected to the next House: Gonzales-Torres, Chris Rabb, Darializa Avila-Chevalier, Melat Kiros, Claire Valdez, and Donavan McKinney, alongside Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Rashida Tlaib. Its election coverage also recorded state legislative wins in Florida and Tennessee. These wins give the socialist movement more opportunities to connect local organizing with struggles over national policy.
The scale of the work behind these campaigns matters. In its largest electoral effort to date, DSA-LA endorsed thirteen candidates and mobilized more than 1,700 volunteers to fill over 4,000 canvassing shifts. Its members knocked more than 110,000 doors in chapter-led canvasses. Over the same period since the 2024 election cycle, membership grew from nearly 3,000 to more than 6,000 and has added several hundred new members since Election Day alone.
The Long Arc
The chapter’s program places this strategy in a longer history of multiracial working-class struggle, from Justice for Janitors in the 1990s to the immigrant rights marches of 2006 and the teachers’ strike of 2019. Those movements demonstrated how organized workers could reshape Los Angeles’s politics and advance demands benefiting the wider public.
Combining electoral work, movement activism (from anti-ICE mobilizations to mass transit organizing to Palestine solidarity work), and member growth points toward a way to build durable socialist organization and power. An endorsement backed by thousands of volunteer shifts creates opportunities to develop new organizers and leaders, forge relationships with neighbors, and bring people into a member-run organization.
Keeping that capacity alive takes work. New members need meaningful roles and on-ramps to activity, political education, and a voice in deciding what comes next. Campaign volunteers need opportunities to remain active after their candidate wins or loses.
There is a wide constituency for that work. Gallup’s September report found that 43 percent of Americans viewed socialism positively, the highest share in its series. In Los Angeles, late October University of California, Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies polling put democratic socialist identification at roughly a third of likely city voters. “The democratic socialist constituency is real, and it is growing,” said DSA-LA Cochairs Leslie Chang and Sean Wakasa.
The Promise
The election results alone cannot settle every argument about which message or strategy worked best. They do, however, create an opening for a Left that offers more victories, confronts concentrated wealth, and refuses to sacrifice solidarity for supposed electoral advantage.
The next test will be whether these victories open up more struggles and, most of all, change people’s lives. Roy’s promised enforcement agenda, a stronger socialist presence on city council, and Raman’s incoming mayoral administration create opportunities. Those gains, as always, will require organized pressure, alliances with unions and community groups, and members willing to remain involved in the difficult work of governing. They will also take sustained and coordinated pushing and accountability from movements and DSA locally.
The promise of the democratic road to socialism is that working people can collectively govern the institutions that shape their lives. In Los Angeles, that promise now has more members, more organizers, and more elected socialists behind it.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/tech-enshitt.title: The Enshittification of Everyday Life
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/tech-enshitt.author: Jatinder Hayre
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/tech-enshitt.text:
The Enshittification of Everyday Life
The apps promising easier access across health care, insurance, and telecomms have been a giant bait-and-switch. Digital convenience turns out to be little more than the degradation of institutional capacity and the transfer of work onto customers.
Have you tried to speak to a human being lately? Perhaps you wanted to question an energy bill, rearrange a hospital appointment, claim a benefit, or discover why your insurer had refused treatment your doctor said you needed. You will probably have been invited to download an app, create an account, and remember a password. The most recent demand is that you must interrogate a chatbot. And then, as a final act of administrative penance, you can telephone a call center, where a recorded voice assures you that your call is terribly important. Somewhere along the way, a strange inversion occurred: the institution still takes your money, increasingly so, but you perform more and more of the labor.
This sort of scenario is usually called decline, but I think that is too generous. Decline suggests something tired, neglected, perhaps capable of rescue with another budget, or, more rarely, a sufficiently earnest politician. What we have instead is a deliberate paradigm shift.
Cory Doctorow has a gloriously apt vulgarity for this: enshittification. Digital platforms court users with convenience, become indispensable, then worsen the bargain once leaving becomes harder than staying. You can delete Facebook. Try deleting your need for health care.
Privatization and austerity have produced a miserable chimera: monopoly capitalism married to managerial bureaucracy. Government commissions, contractors deliver, regulators regulate, consultants advise, managers manage. Together they form the processariat: everybody owns a part of the process; nobody quite owns the responsibility. The exhausted receptionist absorbs the anger, while staffing and spending decisions are made in the ivory tower. Meanwhile, you are still on hold.
This is “socialized inconvenience.” Once, institutions encountered complexity and employed people to deal with it; now they email the complexity to you. We photograph the meter, chase the referral, upload the evidence, and pursue which department has lost the form. Nevertheless, this is recorded as efficiency. Even the language has been enshittified: a closed desk becomes “digital transformation” and work transferred from salaried staff to unpaid customers becomes “empowerment.” Still, enshittification is subtler than collapse: things keep functioning, but with enough friction to render using them a second occupation.
Your Call Is Important to Us
As a practicing doctor, I see the more dangerous version. Being ill is work nobody pays you for: ringing at the right hour, decoding the letter, affording the fare, losing a day’s wages, explaining yourself again to somebody new. Patients increasingly become project managers of their own illnesses. The sicker the patient, the more administrative competence we seem to demand of them. The sickest people are often required to become the most capable bureaucrats.
I remember one of my own patients who underwent a biopsy of a neck lump and was found to have cancer. The biopsy was performed, the pathology was reported and the result entered the system. Yet no appointment followed, no clinician called and nobody appeared to take responsibility for what happened next. My patient simply waited, assuming that somebody, somewhere, was dealing with it. Of course, cancer does not wait to consider mitigating circumstances. On paper, each step had occurred. In reality, the one thing that mattered had not: the patient had not been followed up with. Every part of the process can function while the person at the center of it is still failed.
The American version comes with insurance paperwork. In a survey of 4,155 insured adults ages eighteen to sixty-four, 24.4 percent reported delaying or forgoing care because of administrative tasks. Respondents with disabilities reported greater burdens; those with higher incomes, fewer. They already had insurance.
The affluent can often buy their way out of the processariat altogether: a private consultation instead of the appointment queue, a taxi instead of the disrupted train, a tutor instead of navigating a struggling school, an accountant or assistant instead of another afternoon lost to forms and hold music. Those without that option remain trapped inside the machinery and pay in the resource institutions almost never count: time. Forty minutes on hold is an irritation to somebody answering emails from home — to a care worker on an unpaid lunch break, it can mean abandoning the problem altogether. Money increasingly buys something subtler than luxury — an exit from process. In 2024, across twenty-eight OECD countries, the poorest fifth were, on average, 2.5 times more likely than the richest fifth to report unmet medical needs because of cost, distance, or waiting times.
Chasing down a child’s appointment or a parent’s prescription requires human effort. The International Labour Organization’s 2018 report, drawing on sixty-four countries, estimated 16.4 billion hours of unpaid care work daily. Women performed 76.2 percent. Institutions shedding work rely on households already doing plenty.
We empirically tested whether the effort and resources an intervention requires affect who benefits from it. Income support, housing measures and regulation produced the most consistent equity gains. Programs demanding sustained personal effort, without support, often widened health inequality. Giving everybody the same instructions does not give everybody the same capacity to act on them. When people give up asking, that can look like reduced demand, although the need has gone nowhere.
Please Rate Your Health From One to Ten
Arkansas made Medicaid coverage conditional on work and reporting requirements. By the time a judge halted the policy, eighteen thousand adults had lost coverage. Researchers found no employment increase over eighteen months. In Jharkhand, India, reforms introducing biometric identification for subsidized food reduced corruption, but an estimated 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point during the reforms. The researchers traced much of the harm to how the transition was managed.
Public ownership must mean enough staff with the authority to resolve problems. Universal entitlements must be obtainable without a second occupation spent pursuing them. The worker answering from another country has no more power over the staffing budget than the patient waiting. Both have an interest in changing who controls the service. And an institution claiming an efficiency saving should have to account for the work transferred to the public.
Perhaps the most corrosive achievement of enshittification is our own habituation. We budget for the delay, expect the missed call and quietly absorb another piece of work the institution once did for us. What begins as irritation becomes adaptation. What once looked like failure is the new baseline. The processariat wins twice: first by making the service worse and then by persuading us that expecting better is somehow unreasonable.
As we wait, chase, upload, appeal and telephone, the processariat can point to its dashboards and insist that the machinery is working. Broken institutions would at least have the decency to stop. Enshittified institutions keep going, largely because we have been conscripted into keeping them going ourselves. But at what cost?

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-renters-f.title: NYC renters face ‘higher fees, reduced housing access’ due to co-signer company, lawsuit says
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-renters-f.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-renters-f.text:
New York City tenants often face a familiar predicament when they try to rent an apartment: Landlords typically require them to earn an annual income of at least 40 times the monthly rent—or find a wealthy co-signer with that kind of cash.
It can be a challenge when median asking rents hover around $5,000 in Manhattan and $4,000 in Brooklyn, according to listings site StreetEasy, but when median income sits at only about $80,000, Census data shows . For New Yorkers without a parent, aunt or family friend to co-sign the lease, a host of financial companies have entered the market offering to guarantee the rent for an upfront fee.
Now a class action lawsuit filed in Manhattan federal court charges one of the largest of those companies, TheGuarantors, with inflating renters’ costs by using exclusive agreements with landlords that prevent tenants from seeking lower prices elsewhere. The lawsuit comes as Mayor Zohran Mamdani has sought to crack down on fees facing tenants.
Department of Consumer and Worker Protection spokesperson Milo Gringlas said the agency “is aware of consumers who have allegedly been mandated by landlords to enroll in these third-party guarantor products as a condition of renting their apartments, and we remain concerned about the potential for deception and consumer harm as a result.”
Tenant Naifa Al-Anbar said in her suit, filed last Wednesday, that she was required to pay TheGuarantors for its “rental approval service” in order to rent a Manhattan apartment in June because the landlord had an exclusive agreement with the company.
Those deals lead to “higher fees, reduced housing access, and a complete throttling of consumer choice,” her lawsuit claims
Al-Anbar’s attorney, Blake Yagman, said the rent security services are crucial for many tenants in a city where rent prices continue to surge, but that TheGuarantors agreements with landlords allow it to set prices higher than other companies and prevent tenants from shopping around for cheaper options.
“When you’re engaging in exclusive dealing, you don’t have price competition,” Yagman said, adding that tenants “don't get access to be able to shop around and use another guarantor or surety system.”
The lawsuit claims tenants can pay up to 250% of one month’s rent for TheGuarantors service – or a $7,500 upfront fee for a $3,000-a-month apartment. In 2024, Gothamist reported that TheGuarantors typically charge tenants a fee ranging from 50% of their monthly rent to a price far higher. TheGuarantors’ website says the company considers each applicant’s “financial profile,” potential monthly rent and other factors before setting a price for the service.
TheGuarantors’ senior vice president for sales, Jesse Schmidt, told Gothamist that year that the company had agreements with the owners and managers of about 700,000 apartments in New York City. It is not clear how many of those agreements were exclusive deals with landlords that barred tenants from using other competitor companies.
Schmidt at the time touted his company’s product as a key resource for renters who can’t otherwise meet the landlords’ income requirements or find a co-signer.
“Students, freelancers, people in between jobs, folks who are coming from overseas and don't have U.S. credit history, these are all good examples of people who really may not have had a good option before to qualify for the home that they wanted to live in,” he said
TheGuarantors did not respond to requests for comment about the new lawsuit and its claim that exclusive deals force tenants to pay higher fees.
Yagman, the attorney representing Al-Anbar in the lawsuit, said he also once used TheGuarantors to secure an apartment after graduating from law school. He said he has researched the company and found that it has increased its prices after landing more exclusive agreements with owners and managers. He said he wants a judge to ban exclusive deals and allow tenants to have access to a range of third-party guarantor services.
The Manhattan lawsuit was filed less than a week after another third-party rent security company, CoSign, filed a separate antitrust complaint against TheGuarantors.
CoSign’s Nov. 11 lawsuit, filed in Delaware, accuses TheGuarantors of using “exclusionary contracts and smear tactics” against competitors to gain an overwhelming market share and control two of every three “rental approval services” contracts nationwide.
The Guarantors has nearly 90% of contracts in Washington, D.C., nearly 82% in New Jersey and about 78% in Pennsylvania, according to the lawsuit, which does not list data from New York.
New York City and state officials have sought to crack down on other types of tenant fees in recent years. A suite of 2019 state tenant protection laws set limits on the amount that a landlord could charge for a security deposit and established a 14-day period for landlords to return the money, or provide formal reasons for withholding it.
Last year, the City Council approved a measure prohibiting brokers from charging tenants a fee – typically set at 15% of the annual rent – unless the tenants explicitly hired them for their services. The measure, known as the Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses Act, was intended to limit upfront costs for renters and shift the burden to landlords.
And earlier this year, Mamdani launched a series of tenant resource fairs, known as “Rental Ripoff” hearings, with the stated goal of learning about fees tenants had to pay in addition to their rent.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ha.title: At the Broad, Six Decades of Art Question the Myth of Progress
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ha.author: Maximilíano Durón
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ha.text:
Two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities. For years, she’d witnessed the chasm widen between women carrying $3,500 handbags and those wearing trash bags; from her “nice neighborhood where the helicopters don’t come,” she did little to address the disparity. Still, the unrest that followed the acquittal of four LAPD officers charged with beating Rodney King seemed to have broken through the collective apathy. Angelenos, she wrote, were suddenly talking about “things that matter”: race, guilt, poverty, urban policy, to name a few. Despite history offering little reason for optimism, Scott confessed to a sense of hope: “I’m nurturing my first illusion.”
More than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay. The headlines “Seeing Ourselves” and “Has the Myth Been Shattered?” registered the same discrepancy she sensed between what she remembered as a child growing up in East LA and how the press perpetuated myths about the city’s seeming collectivity. Rosales was 11 years old in 1992, and she has a distinct memory of her mother rushing the family home from school as smoke stained the usually sun-drenched California sky. As an adult, Rosales has amassed an archive of clippings, photographs, and other ephemera of Chicanx youth culture—much of it crowdsourced through social media—that serves as both a bulwark against that dissonance and a counter to historical erasure and amnesia. “I’m not looking for answers,” she told ARTnews. “But for some kind of physical proof that things really happened, that they’re not just in our memories.”
Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights. Though it resembles a doorway, the work offers no passage; instead, viewers face their own reflections superimposed over the 1992 text, along with photographs of palm trees and police. The temporal distance between then and now collapses onto a single plane, leaving Scott’s question perpetually suspended in the present.
The work also lends its title to a just-opened exhibition at the Broad in downtown LA. Organized by assistant curator Jen Vanegas Rocha, the presentation brings together works by more than a dozen artists spanning six decades. Recent acquisitions by Rosales and Hank Willis Thomas appear alongside art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, Glenn Ligon, and Robert Longo, among others. Across prints, paintings, drawings, sculpture, and tapestry, artists appropriate text and images from various forms of public record, drawing attention to the ways media shapes perception of major sociopolitical events. Seen together, the works undermine the assumption that exposing injustice inevitably leads to redress. “There are echoes of the present in the past,” Willis Thomas said. “So is the past present or is the present past?”
The Broad’s founding director, Joanne Heyler, sees that unease as central to the exhibition’s timeliness. “The notion of a linear progression of change unfolding in a dependable, escalating way,” she said, is “becoming harder and harder to believe in.”
Consider the oldest work in the show, Andy Warhol’s Race Riot (1963), in which police dogs attack Black civil-rights demonstrators in Birmingham, Alabama. In 2026, the decades-old image calls to mind the police response to the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, as well as the more recent pro-Palestine and anti-ICE demonstrations nationwide, in which protestors were often battered and tear-gassed. Warhol lifted the photograph directly from a visual essay by Charles Moore in Life magazine, translating the confrontation into a monochromatic silkscreen. Adopting the incendiary rhetoric of contemporary news coverage, he labeled the peaceful demonstrators “rioters.” Race Riot reflects the artist’s own reckoning with the contradictions at the heart of American life: His obsession with celebrities and mass consumption give way to the sensationalized images of death and violence that belie it, like the mangled cars and electric chairs that also feature in his “Death and Disaster” series. Viewers are left to consider whether the relentless circulation of violence sharpens public outrage or gradually dulls our empathy.
For Willis Thomas, Warhol’s Birmingham silkscreen paintings function as “postcards to the future.” By transforming them from documentation to works of art, Warhol has made a case for their continued relevance. Nearby, Willis Thomas’s photo-based Black Survival Guide, or How to Live Through a Police Riot (2018) revisits the same era to recover another history largely omitted from public memory. While researching the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, he discovered a typewritten pamphlet offering practical advice to Black residents of Wilmington, Delaware, during the nine-month National Guard occupation in 1968. Onto retroreflective vinyl, Willis Thomas printed excerpts from the pamphlet—advice on how to staunch bleeding or communicate during a power outage, for example—atop archival News Journal photographs of confrontations between armed soldiers and the city’s Black communities. Installed in a darkened gallery, the black-and-white images are invisible until a flash of light illuminates them. Rather than merely encountering the past, the audience actively aids in its recovery. “In some ways the observers become the researchers,” he said.
Histories of state-sanctioned violence and resistance movements similarly converge across a nearly eleven-foot-wide canvas in Mickalene Thomas’s 2021 mixed-media painting The Charnel House (Resist #5). Reworking Picasso’s 1944–45 masterpiece of corpses heaped beneath a table made in response to news footage of liberated Nazi concentration camps, Thomas collages photographs and placards from the Civil Rights and Black Lives Matter movements with the modernist’s fragmented anatomical forms. A poster advertising the Black Panther Party’s free breakfast program appears beside a portrait of Angela Davis and the names of Freddie Gray and Alton Sterling, both killed during encounters with police. Here, grief and trauma are paired with resistance and community building.
The language of dissent assumes a subtler register in Ligon’s Narratives (1993), a suite of nine sepia-toned etchings that mimic the ornate typography and florid prose of 19th-century slave narratives. Ligon replaces accounts of enslavement and escape with details from his early education at a predominantly white private school, his desire for other men, and the circumstances of his career as an artist. In his hands, a literary form that freed Black people used to demonstrate their humanity becomes a medium for contemporary self-portraiture and self-determination.
Museums, of course, too, play a role in shaping public records. Over the past five years, the Broad has acquired work by 26 artists previously unrepresented in its collection, many of whom are of a younger generation and, like Rosales, actively working in LA. Heyler sees these acquisitions as part of an ongoing effort to better reflect the multiplicity of the communities that surround the institution. “We’re not telling one story but many,” she said. “We’re always striving to strengthen the connective tissues between them.”
The exhibition offers an opportunity to showcase many of the newly acquired artists and to extend an art-historical conversation that Heyler traces to exhibitions like “A Forest of Signs: Art in the Crisis of Representation,” a landmark 1989 survey at the Museum of Contemporary Art, just across the street. Bringing together works by 30 American artists, from Jeff Koons to Jenny Holzer, that show examined the unstable boundaries between reality and representation in an increasingly media-saturated society. But the terrain has evolved, Heyler noted. Where artists of that period often exposed the ideologies concealed by authoritative and commercial imagery, audiences today, immersed in social media and generative AI, navigate what she called a “stew of falsehoods and truths.”
Even so, curator Vanegas Rocha hopes her exhibition inspires something more generative than cynicism, in which artists can be seen as the “architects of better futures.” She locates the potential for systemic change in the power of an individual aesthetic encounter. “It can teach you about the world, about others, about yourself,” she said. “That single moment can have a ripple effect, leading to a collective difference.” Rosales, likewise, hasn’t relinquished hope. Citing José Esteban Muñoz’s 2009 queer theory book Cruising Utopia, she described hope as an ever-receding horizon that we must continue to endeavor toward. “We are a people that don’t give up,” she said, noting that her mother also took her to protests from an early age. “Standing up for each other, even when you don’t see it right away, does pay off.” Progress, she suggests, may not be linear or inevitable, but that doesn’t make it an illusion. In her mirror, the unresolved question—“Has the Myth Been Shattered?”—is cast back onto the people who might yet determine the answer.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Tighten your corsets! Pass the smelling salts! It’s the greatest period dramas ever made
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Michael Hogan, Zoe Williams, Lucy Mangan, Chitra Ramaswamy, Gwilym Mumford, Stuart Heritage, Hollie Richardson, Rebecca Nicholson, Mark Lawson, Phil Harrison ,Lucy Knight and Rachel Aroesti
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Lace up those corsets and wriggle into those breeches … it’s time for a huge new TV retelling of Pride and Prejudice. Jane Austen’s classic romance will come to life once more with writer Dolly Alderton’s glitzy Netflix version, starring Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet and Jack Lowden as the self-proclaimed “first ginger Mr Darcy”.
As a new generation of fans are set to fall in love with Lizzy, Darcy and the whole Bennet clan, it’s only right to celebrate all the incredible shows that have transported us back in time. Colin Firth’s wet white shirt might fly the flag for great period drama, but there are whole other old worlds spanning all centuries out there ready to stream. Our writers share some of the very best …
Brideshead Revisited
A floppy-fringed fop in cricket whites and stripey blazer, carrying a teddy bear named Aloysius? Count me in. Granada’s 1981 adaptation of Evelyn Waugh’s novel pretty much invented an entire TV genre. Like Saltburn 40 years later (but without the grave-humping), it saw an Oxford student form a homoerotic friendship with an eccentric toff and get sucked into the drama of his dysfunctional aristocratic family.
There had been great period pieces before – most notably I, Claudius – but they were stagey affairs, filmed on wobbly sets. Brideshead was a giga-budget game-changer, bringing in the cinematic scope and lavish locations we take for granted today. Poster boys Jeremy Irons and Anthony Andrews were supported by a West End’s worth of luvvies, including “Larry” Olivier and “Johnny” Gielgud. Over 11 stately episodes, it set the gilded template for ye olde dramas ever since. Michael Hogan
Pride and Prejudice
Pride and Prejudice was sometimes painful to watch, as Austen’s brute romantic realities – five pillars of next-generation Bennet, consigned to shrivel in genteel destitution unless they can get someone to fancy them, and fast – met the callous 90s, where the sisters have to laugh at their desperation or else they’re a killjoy. Andrew Davies’s script was fabulous but not kind. The great houses of the English aristocracy brought an elegantly tense, here’s-what-you-could-win atmosphere; like Location, Location, Location meets Squid Game.
Consequently, there was much more riding on Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle than a plain will-they-won’t-they: their unbearably slow though entirely predictable passion (even if you’d never met the book!) had to rescue the family, the society, the viewer, the very blades of grass all around, from the stress of a world in which the stakes were both impossibly high and pitiably trivial. And they really, really delivered: Ehle’s expression, as she’s almost winded by genuine feeling, is exquisitely evocative. Firth, of course, was never able to erase the cultural mark he made by jumping into a lake with his shirt on. The pair had a brief fling during and after filming, almost (one imagines) as a courtesy to the cultural fervour they created. It didn’t last, but it would have been rude not to. Zoe Williams
Wolf Hall
Technically, it can’t be done. You cannot take over a 1,000 pages of the most luminous, intricately woven prose ever written, put them on screen and lose nothing in translation – or at least nothing you don’t gain back tenfold elsewhere.
But that is what writer Peter Straughan and director Peter Kosminsky, plus a handful of actors at the top of their game, did when they adapted the first two volumes of Hilary Mantel’s trilogy about the rise and fall of Thomas Cromwell, and how he oversaw Henry VIII’s split from Rome, marriage to Anne Boleyn and eventually resolved on a scaffold at dawn the king’s Great Matter once and for all. There’s simply nothing like it – for beauty, for delicacy, for horror, for heartbreak. Every line, every frame, every fleeting expression on an actor’s face does double, triple duty as an engine of story and creator of an experience that allows you to watch the past unspool as if for the first time and stands as a testament to human creativity and the power and refuge of art. Lucy Mangan
Bleak House
Bleak House is the celestial moment when BBC period drama, the baronet of its adaptation for the screen Andrew Davies, the enormous cast of characters, and Charles Dickens himself were all at their very best. The outcome is 15 exquisitely taut, tense, addictive, fog-ridden half-hour episodes (except the first one which was an entire glorious hour), restoring Dickens to the serial format that made him so famous, broadcast twice weekly with cliffhanger endings so finely judged even the Victorians would have approved. Anna Maxwell Martin, in her first lead role, delivers an astonishing performance as Esther Summerson. Gillian Anderson’s haunting (and haunted) Lady Dedlock is unforgettably sombre and devastatingly sad. Charles Dance’s Tulkinghorn is the most terrifyingly serpent-like family lawyer known to the profession, all hooded eyes and hissed threats. And there will never be a more comically spot-on Mr Guppy in televisual history than Burn Gorman. Millions tuned in every week to see how Jarndyce and Jarndyce would pan out (badly, of course). I still rewatch it every single year, hanging on every perfectly-paced word. The benchmark of grip-the-nation British period drama, then and now. Chitra Ramaswamy
Mad Men
Period dramas are so firmly associated with bonnets and windswept moors that suggesting anything that doesn’t fit that description feels faintly sacrilegious. But despite depicting an era maybe even your mum can just about remember, and being [drops monocle into snifter in horror] American to boot, Mad Men is a proper period drama. And not just because the costumes are on point – though they are, with every last Sterling Cooper employee’s pocket square positioned just so.
No, what makes Matt Weiner’s ad industry saga so great is its ability to make its chosen age – buttoned-down late 50s giving way to the charged, chaotic 60s – both alien and achingly close to home. After all, nostalgia, as Don Draper reminded us in the show’s most memorable sales pitch, translates as “the pain from an old wound”. It’s a show that both seduces and repels you with its vision of the not-so-distant past – capitalism starting to curdle, sexism and racism both casual and deeply ingrained. But like an appealing if inadvisable Old Fashioned, you can’t help yourself from drinking it down. Gwilym Mumford
The Crimson Petal and the White
In truth, I have always struggled with period dramas, since it’s as if all the fun stuff – the characters, the plot, the identifiable human behaviour – is obscured behind a thick screen of frills and waffle. But Lucinda Coxon’s 2011 adaptation of Michel Faber’s novel cuts straight through all that. It’s a queasy, bilious four-parter that heaves with fury from the outset. Romola Garai plays Sugar, a sex worker fuelled by hatred for all the men who casually abused her and her friends. Chris O’Dowd plays William Rackham, an ineffectual rich kid who wants to be a writer but has no talent for it. He falls for her, despite having a mentally ill wife at home, and invites her to become the governess to his daughter. Sugar gets to see all the opportunities afforded to the upper classes and maximises upon them, while William stumbles into a trap of his own making. The Crimson Petal and the White represents period dramas at their nastiest. If only more would follow suit. Stuart Heritage
To Walk Invisible
Any Brontë fan who has walked around the tiny, rickety rooms of the sisters’ Haworth home will have spent hours imagining the young women huddled together, scratching away with pens to tell their stories. Leave it to Sally Wainwright to put her ideas of them on screen in this exquisite feature drama about Charlotte, Emily and Anne – and their brother Branwell, whose alcoholism deeply affected their lives and works. It shows not just their fight to get published, using pseudonyms, but their increasingly desperate need to earn money as unmarried women. Filmed in a replica of the Brontë parsonage and on the surrounding Penistone Hill Country Park, it’s like living daily life and walking the moors with the sisters – played almost precisely how I picture them by Finn Atkins, Chloe Pirrie and Charlie Murphy. Forget Margot Robbie in red latex! This is the real Brontë experience. Hollie Richardson
Tipping the Velvet
It has been almost 25 years since it aired on BBC Two, and in many ways, Andrew Davies’ adaptation of Sarah Waters’ debut novel does look and feel of its time. It told the story of fictional Victorian music hall star and male impersonator Nan Astley, whose lesbian awakening dragged her through the highs and lows of London’s bohemian society. It was raucous, camp and surprisingly sexually frank. It may have cast pretty, overtly feminine women in roles that would, today, demand a more butch presence, but in the early 00s, it was a rare case of a period drama, or any drama for that matter, that did not skirt around its queerness. As such, it deserves its place in TV history. Also fun to spot Benedict Cumberbatch and Sally Hawkins and Monica Dolan in early roles, and to wonder how “Monsieur Dildo” ever made it on to the screen in 2002. Rebecca Nicholson
Our Friends in the North
We tend to think of period drama as telling stories from a century or more before and coming from a dead writer’s book. Peter Flannery’s nine-parter was adapted from his own stage play with a narrative starting 32 years before the transmission date and ending just one year before. Yet all other qualifications of the genre are met: the popularisation of distant history (in this case, civic corruption in the north east), spectacular work by the costume and wig departments, characters of Dickensian richness that four young actors – Gina McKee, Daniel Craig, Mark Strong, Christopher Eccleston – made glorious calling cards: the show’s alumnae include a James Bond (Craig) and a Doctor Who (Eccleston) and the four share a heavy shelf of Bafta, Emmy, Olivier and Tony wins and nominations. Mark Lawson
The Red Riding trilogy
“To the North. Where we do what we want!” In period terms, this three-part adaptation of David Peace’s titular trilogy is riveted tightly to Britain in the 1970s. The original novels were loosely inspired (if that’s the right word for the ambient horror they conjure) by the hunt for the Yorkshire Ripper. These dramas pick up that deadly trail and run with it, into purgatory and beyond. The police station resembles the inside of a smoker’s lung. Straight-dealers end up in metaphorical and sometimes literal ditches. And around every corner, there’s a moral dead end waiting. The cast – which includes Andrew Garfield, Rebecca Hall, Sean Harris, Daniel Mays, Maxine Peake and Paddy Considine – is extraordinary and taken as a whole, Red Riding represents a relentlessly claustrophobic suite of desolation and corruption. Bodices and frilly frock coats are conspicuous by their absence. Phil Harrison
Parade’s End
Parade’s End, a sumptuous adaptation of Ford Madox Ford’s quartet of novels of the same name, aired on BBC Two when I was 16, just at the point when my TV tastes were becoming refined enough for meaty, sexy fare. I was blown away by Tom Stoppard’s expert take on Ford’s twisty story, which follows righteous aristocrat Christopher Tietjens as he serves in the first world war. And what a cracking cast: Benedict Cumberbatch plays Tietjens, Adelaide Clemens is excellent as Valentine Wannop, the young suffragette for whom he develops feelings, while Anne-Marie Duff and Stephen Graham appear in supporting roles. It’s Rebecca Hall, though, as Sylvia, Tietjens’s mesmerising and manipulative – but ultimately miserable – wife, who steals the show. Being closeted at the time, I put my teenage obsession with the show down to a crush on Cumberbatch, but I knew deep down it was actually Hall I fancied, with her long tailored coats and ability to express five emotions with the smallest raise of an eyebrow. I defy anyone watching Parade’s End not to fall in love with her. Lucy Knight
Life on Mars
“It’s 1973, almost dinner time. I’m havin’ ‘oops!” growls DCI Gene Hunt (Philip Glenister) as he pins bewildered noughties metrosexual DI Sam Tyler (John Simm) against a filing cabinet in the first episode of the BBC’s still mindblowing police procedural Life on Mars. I generally find costume drama a bit too much like homework. For Life on Mars, I make an exception. That’s mainly because it’s a show about suspension of disbelief. Has Simm’s detective really time-travelled from 2006 or is he comatose, dreaming? Could his subconscious have cobbled together a vision of the past this credible? This is a show that encourages you to question every little detail of the seductive 1970s setting – a deconstruction of the period drama that reflects on nostalgia, the nature of reality and the strangeness of the past. Now, 20 years on, it’s technically a relic itself – but this postmodern masterpiece is far from dusty. Rachel Aroesti
Pride and Prejudice is on Netflix from Thursday 3 December

Several Palestinians beaten and detained in Israeli raids across occupied West Bank
Raids and attacks by Israeli forces and settlers across the occupied West Bank on Friday left at least three Palestinians injured and several detained.
Three Palestinians were injured and another, identified as Muhammad Daifallah Arara, was detained on Friday night after Israeli occupation forces raided his home north of occupied Jerusalem and assaulted those inside.
The three sustained injuries to their shoulders, limbs and abdomens after being beaten by Israeli soldiers, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.
Earlier, a group of Israeli settlers attacked the family's home, attempting to break down its entrance and storm its courtyard, before Israeli forces intervened and raided the house.
Israeli forces raided a residential cave in the village of Khirbet Khallat al-Daba'a in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, on Friday evening, assaulting its owner, detaining his family members and vandalising property inside, Wafa news agency reported.
The cave belongs to activist Jaber al-Dababseh, who was beaten by Israeli soldiers while his family members were detained.
On Friday evening, Israeli forces fired tear gas at Palestinian residents in the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, during a raid. Israeli soldiers forced shop owners to close their stores.
In the village of Jayyus, east of Qalqilya, Israeli forces detained seven Palestinians after raiding their homes and ransacking their property.
Israeli settlers also continued their attacks across the occupied West Bank throughout the day. They attacked Palestinian vehicles in the Wadi al-Shaer area in the Salfit governorate, damaging at least two, locals told Wafa.
In the town of Za'tara, east of Bethlehem, settlers set up tents, raising fears among Palestinian residents that they could pave the way for a new Israeli outpost there.
Separately, a group of Israeli settlers dumped waste near a Palestinian home in the Turmus Ayya Plain, north of Ramallah.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/omans.author: Sean Mathews
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/omans.text:
Oman's stock market on track to beat all Gulf states in 2026
Oman’s stock market is on track to be the best performer in the Gulf region in 2026, with its economic growth pulling ahead of neighbours, in a sign of how it is reaping gains from distancing itself from the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The MSX30 Index, which tracks the performance of Oman’s stock exchange, has soared 22 percent year-to-date.
Dubai's stock market, the Dubai Financial Market General Index, the region’s second-best performer, is up 8.7 percent year-to-date. Saudi Arabia’s Tadawul market is down 3 percent year-to-date.
For comparison, in the US, the SP500 index is up 6.4 percent year-to-date after a sharp selloff in AI and technology.
Both the Saudi and Dubai stock markets have clawed back the steep losses of earlier this year after the US and Israel launched a war on Iran.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
But Oman's success is more interesting when one considers the anger US President Donald Trump directed at it during negotiations with Iran over the way to manage traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which is comprised of Iran and Oman's territorial waters.
Trump threatened to “blow up” Oman, where his family real estate business has licensed its name for use on a golf resort.
Oman: From outlier to trailblazer
Tensions are still simmering between the US and Iran. The US has launched strikes on Iran and its vessels, while Iran has attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf countries.
Kuwait blamed Iran for a strike on Thursday that killed two Italian soldiers at a military site. Iran denied responsibility, but in recent weeks has launched strikes on Kuwait and Bahrain, both of which host US military bases.
Oman’s economic performance is due in part to its posture in the Iran war, experts say. Middle East Eye reported in June that Oman’s geography, diplomacy and business acumen would put it at the forefront of a new order emerging in the Gulf where Iran is emboldened and the US’s security umbrella clouded by distrust.
Muscat was a mediator between Tehran and Washington in the months before the war. Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi made a rare public plea for diplomacy just before the US-Israeli attack, which was ignored in Washington.
Despite lobbying against the war, in relative terms, Oman is attracting more interest from investors and companies as they look for a safe haven that has not come under intense Iranian attack.
Geography and US bases
Oman also sits outside the Strait of Hormuz and boasts a large Indian Ocean coastline.
Oman’s two main ports experienced an unprecedented surge in traffic during the war. Sohar port saw a 1,766 percent surge in ship destination change requests in March, while Salalah saw an 800 percent increase, according to maritime intelligence firm Windward.
Oman is also being eyed as a corridor to bigger neighbours like Saudi Arabia.
One of the most obvious reasons Oman has not borne the brunt of Iranian strikes is its decision not to join the US and Israel in attacking Tehran. It also has a different approach to basing the US military, which resembles that of some European countries.
Oman is the US’s oldest treaty partner in the Gulf, going back to 1833. But Oman hosts no permanent US military facilities or troops, unlike Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Instead, the US has an “access agreement” to use Omani ports.
Albusaidi said earlier this year that the US was pursuing the war on Iran in the interest of Israel, and that Iran’s strikes on Gulf states hosting US military bases were ”inevitable”.
The International Monetary Fund estimates Iran’s economy to grow 4 percent this year, whereas every other Gulf economy is expected to contract, with the GCC overall shrinking 4.8 percent.

Eisenkot says Netanyahu dragging out coalition talks as deadline nears
Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli opposition leader who is tasked with forming the next Israeli government, said on Friday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been dragging out the negotiations, even though his Yashar Party is willing to agree on key points, Haaretz reported.
A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.
According to Haaretz, sources close to Eisenkot's bloc expect Netanyahu to make a significant offer next week to prevent the government Eisenkot is planning from being sworn in.
Yashar and Likud met five times over the past two weeks to negotiate. Eisenkot said that Likud had refused on several days to schedule meetings as frequently as his party proposed.
"Two weeks and five meetings are a sufficient period in which an agreement could already have been reached, if they had wanted one," he said.

Israeli attacks across Gaza kill four Palestinians
Israeli attacks killed four Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Friday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Several others, including a child, were wounded in a series of attacks across the strip.
In the southern city of Rafah, Gaza's civil defence crews recovered three bodies. They also rescued two wounded people after an Israeli strike near the Muawiya Mosque on al-Bahr Street, in the west of the city.
Wafa reported earlier on Friday that an Israeli drone struck a vehicle in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp, killing a Palestinian man and wounding several others, some seriously.
Medical sources and eyewitnesses said Israeli forces stationed near the so-called "Yellow Line" repeatedly opened fire on tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the area.
The so-called "Yellow Line" is a military boundary imposed by Israeli forces inside the Gaza Strip following the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Since the ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, more than 1,600 Palestinians have reportedly been killed and 5,833 injured.

Israeli real estate company holds ‘Black Friday’ land sale in Brooklyn
An Israeli real estate group held a "Black Friday" event in Brooklyn on Wednesday, advertising property sales and promoting what activist group Pal-Awda termed "illegal settlement on stolen Palestinian land”.
Firecrackers, smoke bombs and eggs were thrown at protesters by pro-Israel demonstrators outside the real estate event.
Israel's CapitIL real estate agency held the event, selling property in Essen NY Deli in Brooklyn. CapitIL’s website advertises several properties in and around Jerusalem. None publicly advertised is in the occupied West Bank. Middle East Eye was not able to verify which part of Jerusalem the land being promoted was located in. East Jerusalem is occupied according to international law.
Pal-Awda, an organisation that advocates for Palestinian refugees' right of return to their homeland, organised the protest outside the real estate event.
A spokesperson for Pal-Awda called the event "discriminatory" and said they would protest the land sales “no matter where in Palestine the stolen land is located” and that “all of it was taken from dispossessed Palestinians, as part of the ongoing Zionist ethnic cleansing”.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
A spokesperson for the group said that these land sales are only open to vetted Jewish Americans who often have no previous or familial ties to Israel, arguing that CapitIL has ties to land sales happening in the occupied West Bank.
“Whether advertised or not, CapitIL and the event's other Israeli real estate cohosts like First Israel Mortgage have consistently offered or financed properties in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem during these events.”
The group says that these land sales violate several state and federal laws, including “New York Property Law, New York Human Rights Law, and state and federal real estate and housing laws”.
Chaos at the protests
Outside the event, it was chaos.
On Avenue J, 200 pro-Palestine protesters were kenneled in with lines of New York Police Department (NYPD) officers on either end and pro-Israel protesters sandwiching them in on both sides. NYPD drones loomed overhead, monitoring activity in the area. Newsweek reported that around 200 pro-Israel demonstrators were present, citing the NYPD.
Protesters chanted: “Palestine is our demand. No peace on stolen land.”
Pro-Israeli agitators threw at least three firecrackers and a red smoke bomb into the crowd of pro-Palestine protesters.
NYPD told MEE that three people had been arrested, processed and released, but did not specify which group they were from.
“We are being confronted by a racist mob of bigots who believe that Palestine does not belong to Palestinians, but belongs to settlers from all over the world. The people of Gaza are being bombed and murdered for the crime of being Palestinian in the land of Palestine, while these greedy companies are selling their Palestinian land to prosperous Americans who have no connection to Palestine whatsoever,” Pal-Awda activist Bill D told MEE.
MEE has reached out to CapitIL and NYPD for further comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.
Protesters' Demands
Athena, a protester, was holding a sign depicting New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani pointing a gun with the words “Chief Executive of the SRG”, referring to the police department's Strategic Response Group.
Athena isn’t happy with Mamdani’s handling of Israel real estate land sale events in the city.
“We have a mayor who says that he's pro-Palestine and that he stands against the genocide. Yet he sends his police officers to defend Zionists selling stolen land in the United States,” she said.
Pal-Awda has four demands for the mayor. They are asking that he advance calls to the NY Attorney General Leticia James to investigate and audit "illegal Palestinian land sales" in the city; remove tax-exempt status from religious and educational institutions that host occupied West Bank land sale events; fire NY Police Commissioner Jessica Tish. They also want the mayor to “fully disband the Strategic Response Group (SRG) and its replacements that allow for the NYPD's ongoing brutalisation of our community”.
Mamdani announced the disbandment of the controversial SRG earlier this month, but officers in riot gear at the protest kenneling the demonstrators still wore shirts that said "Strategic Response Group".
The armour-clad SRG is made up of 500 highly trained NYPD officers who have become infamous for their “crowd control tactics” and mass arrests during protests in the city, where they use batons, tear gas, pepper spray and other “de-escalation” weapons on disruptive protesters.
The group came under particular scrutiny due to their crackdown on pro-Palestine protests at the height of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, particularly campus protests led by the student movement that started at Columbia University.
"The irony of the timing of Mamdani's announcement regarding the disbandment of the SRG is not lost on us tonight," a Pal-Awda representative said in a statement.
"We have no faith in the mayor's lofty words, when it is his NYPD that is trampling, strangling and brutalising those calling for the end of Zionist land theft in our city.
"Time and again, it becomes clear that all levels of city and state government - from Attorney General Letitia James, who allows illegal land sales to go unchecked, to Mayor Mamdani, who oversees the brutalisation of New Yorkers - remain deeply complicit in the sale of stolen Palestinian land."

UN rights chief voices concern as Costa Rica bars Francesca Albanese
Costa Rica denied entry to Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, drawing criticism from UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday.
Turk said he was "deeply concerned" by Costa Rica's decision to bar Albanese from entering the country and urged authorities to reconsider after she was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport, which serves the capital San Jose.
Albanese, an Italian national, had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica.
The UN human rights office said on X that Albanese was denied entry on "claimed national security grounds".
The government of Costa Rica asserted that Albanese was the subject of an "international alert over links to terrorist acts".
An Italian lawyer, Albanese is the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory, which has been occupied by Israel since 1967. She has been sanctioned by the United States since 2025.
"I am deeply indignant that the government of Costa Rica has spread false information that links me to terrorism," Albanese said from the airport, adding that she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision.
Israel's UN ambassador, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica's decision in a post on X.
Under President Laura Fernandez, Costa Rica has deepened cooperation with the United States on security and moved closer to Israel. It signed a free trade agreement with Israel last year.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/canad.title: Canada's Supreme Court upholds law banning hijabs in Quebec public sector
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/canad.author: Yasmine El-Sabawi
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/canad.text:
Canada's Supreme Court upholds law banning hijabs in Quebec public sector
The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday upheld Quebec's highly contested 2019 law that bans religious symbols in the public sector.
It was, more than anything, seen to be targeting Muslim women in the province who wear the hijab, but also impacted Catholics, Sikhs and other minorities.
Quebec's population is 5 percent Muslim, according to the last census carried out in 2021. That figure is second only to Ontario.
Amira Elghawaby, who was Canada’s first and only special representative on combatting Islamophobia, until her office was shut down earlier this year, called the verdict "devastating".
"The promise of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been broken, and could be broken again and again. It means that religious freedoms, equality and the rights of all Canadians are no longer guaranteed," Elghawaby said in a statement released by the organisation she founded this year, the Muslim Communities Research Observatory.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
“This ruling will instantly further impact the lives and livelihoods of Quebecers, particularly Muslim women who wear the hijab. In one study, 71% of Muslim women surveyed had considered leaving Quebec, with the province standing to lose an estimated $3.2 billion in income. It may also open the door for further violations of rights and freedoms," she added.
Technicality
Oftentimes rulings by the highest court come down to technicalities.
What the court was looking at in this case was the application of Section 33 of the constitution, known as the "notwithstanding clause", which shields Bill 21 from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms itself.
It was until recently rarely used, and even seen as taboo to invoke.
Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said in 2022 that Canada's charter "cannot become a suggestion".
The Canadian Department of Justice acknowledges that it is a "unique" provision among constitutional democracies, because it allows the Canadian parliament or a provincial legislature "to derogate from certain sections of the Charter, namely section 2 (fundamental freedoms), sections 7 to 14 (legal rights) and section 15 (equality rights)".
Section 333 does not apply to voting, mobility or language rights.
"Once invoked, the notwithstanding clause prevents a court from declaring that legislation covered by a section 33 declaration is of no force or effect, despite any inconsistency in the legislation with the rights or freedoms under the listed Charter sections," the justice department says.
The notwithstanding clause is valid for a renewable five years.
"In short, Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society," Supreme Court Chief Justice Richard Wagner said in Friday's ruling.
Impact
It was in 2019 that Quebec first passed the contentious law that bans public sector employees from wearing religious symbols - the Jewish kippah, Sikh turban or Muslim hijab, among others - on the job.
Bill 21 passed in a 73-35 vote at the time.
The rightwing Coalition Avenir Quebec government, which held a majority in the provincial legislature, invoked the notwithstanding clause to limit debate on the bill.
After it passed, Quebec's then-premier, Francois Legault, called it "a moment that Quebecers have long been waiting for".
"It's very clear, when we talk to Quebecers, that they want us to ban religious symbols for people in positions of authority," he added.
Within 24 hours, advocacy groups moved to challenge the law in court.
Among them were the National Council of Canadian Muslims and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, who asked the Quebec Superior Court for an injunction to bar the province from implementing the law.
The groups said in a statement that Bill 21 "is unconstitutional and will cause irreparable harm to religious minorities" in the French-speaking province.
Nearly two years later, in a 242-page ruling, the Quebec Superior Court ruled that while Bill 21 has "serious and negative consequences for all those who wear religious symbols in public", it ultimately does not violate "the Canadian constitutional architecture".
Still, the court struck down parts of the bill, saying that English schools in the French-speaking province would be exempt from the ban.
It also said that members of the National Assembly, the provincial legislature, were allowed to wear religious symbols that covered their faces, such as the niqab.
Quebec has long had debates over the issue of secularism and the protection of minority rights.
In 2017, it passed Bill 62, which barred individuals from giving or receiving public services with their faces covered.
It was met with widespread public protests and was later suspended after a Muslim woman in Quebec who wears the niqab filed a legal challenge against the law, arguing it violated her constitutional rights.
Trudeau later called it "unthinkable" to "legitimise discrimination against citizens based on their religion".
