How Gaza Broke the Art World
David Velasco
22.12.2025Essay
There are lines as I arrive at the Neue Nationalgalerie – long ones, snaking across the vast concrete plaza from which the museum, a squat glass pavilion, protrudes. On the façade, in bright neon scrawl, is the title of Nan Goldin’s show: This Will Not End Well. I landed in Berlin a few hours ago. It’s late on a Friday, November 2024. I meet up with Nikki Columbus, a friend from New York who is writing a piece about the night for The Nation, and we scout the perimeter, looking for familiar faces. We try our luck at the entrance. The museum’s director, Klaus Biesenbach, is outside. He shouts my name and grabs my shoulder, then waves us in.
Six large temporary pavilions swathed in black curtains are scattered in the sparse atrium. Each pavilion houses one of Nan’s penetrating videos or slideshows: early masterpieces like The Ballad of Sexual Dependency and The Other Side, plus more recent works like Sirens, an elegy to addiction. The show’s proposition is that Nan, one of our greatest living artists in any medium, merits recognition, specifically, as a filmmaker. The slideshows are not films in a traditional sense; mostly they are magnetic pictures of magnetic people drawn from the artist’s life, alchemists who have wrung beauty from desolation. The images are composed and ordered according to her singular sensibility, alert to pacing – dactyls of resemblance, resemblance, difference – and fastened together with music you might put on a mixtape to a lover: Marianne Faithfull, John Kelly, Rosalind Hunt. I think about how art is more or less a talent for putting one right wrong thing next to another to make something new, and how Nan knows this better than anyone.
I stake a spot in front of a stage near the museum’s entrance. I know what’s about to happen. Everyone does. It’s why we came. Klaus arrives and nervously asks where Nan is. A crowd collects in front of the platform – mostly young bodies in black clothes. She finally shows up, 20 minutes to eight, garnet curls, black tuxedo, trailed by a minder. The air crackles. Klaus stumbles as he walks to the lectern.
“Good evening. Good evening. My name is Klaus Biesenbach, and I’m the director of the Neue Nationalgalerie, and I’m really honoured that you’re all here tonight. I wish… I had a camera, I’d photograph you, it’s very beautiful. Thank you, thank you.”
The crowd is unmoved.
He continues: “As you might have heard, [Nan and I] decided to disagree. We decided to agree to disagree – you see, that was a Freudian… Um, I treasure the freedom of expression here and now in Berlin in 2024, to allow the Nationalgalerie to be such a place that you can do that. That sounds great, but I mean it.”
Nan ascends to the podium. I feel the holy tingle through my arms.
“I’m starting with a period of silence, in honour of the dead,” she begins. “Please put your phones away and join me.”
My mind runs a familiar montage – horror, depression, boredom, anger, helplessness. Here we are, for what it’s worth, feeling these things together.
“Why did I feel I have to talk tonight?” Nan asks. “This is my lifetime retrospective, but there is nothing in it from the past year, and that’s missing. The museum has kept its promise to allow me to talk, and I thank them. But they claim that my activism and my art are separate, even though that has never been the case. The last year has been Palestine and Lebanon for me. Since October 7th, I have found it hard to breathe. I feel the catastrophe in my body, but it’s not in this show.”
Germany has been consumed by a moral panic over antisemitism, and expressions of solidarity with Palestine have been demonised by the custodians of the state’s “memory culture”. Nan speaks of the more than 180 cancellations of pro-Palestine artists and teachers in Germany, the need for diverse strategies of resistance and cooperation inside the movement. She speaks of Islamophobia and the weaponisation of antisemitism, the consensus over the term “genocide” among members of the UN, even the pope. She speaks of the horror of watching the land grabs and domicide, the murders live-streamed to our phones.
“Antizionism has nothing to do with antisemitism.” Nan permits a smile as the crowd erupts in applause. “What I see in Gaza reminds me of the pogroms that my grandparents escaped. Never again means never again for everyone.” A bigger smile as the crowd cheers, and she pats her chest. A large black banner reading “ARMS EMBARGO NOW” unfurls behind her.
“The more of us there are, the more of us there are.”
Nan passes Klaus as they trade places on the platform. Neither acknowledges the other.
“As I mentioned in my introduction earlier,” Klaus begins, but his words are overwhelmed by the crowd’s chants of “Free, Free Palestine!” “As I mentioned in my introduction earlier,” he tries again, “I disagree with your opinion. Still, I stand for your right to express yourself freely.” A group outside, visible through the Mies van der Rohe building’s glazed façade, pulls open a large banner behind him: “STAATSRÄSON IST GENOZID”, referring to Germany’s official policy – its “reason of state” – of unflinching support for Israel. Museum staff arrange their bodies in a comical attempt to block the sign while Klaus pushes on, eventually conceding to the chants emerging from the canopy of keffiyehs and Palestinian flags.
He will return later, when the crowds have dispersed, with a puzzling speech describing how he turned 20 in Israel, how he met Nan in 1992, how he was a caregiver for Susan Sontag in 2004, how Susan taught him to “be unafraid”.
I think it takes a certain blinkered arrogance for a museum director to give a rebuttal to an artist’s remarks at their opening – an unprecedented act, as far as I know. I’m not sure this is the fearlessness Sontag had in mind. It is perverse for the person representing the state institution to claim that he, and not the artist speaking truth to power, is modelling courage. Or for him to describe Nan’s fury at the genocide in Gaza, and her call for introspection and action, as “opinion” – as if this might be dismissed as simple disagreement.
There are people who will go on to claim that the audience is silencing or even “censoring” Klaus by shouting him down, but I think that Klaus is not speaking so much as parroting the senescent propaganda of Staatsräson, the version of history that floats undisturbed through the technocratic ventilation systems, a malevolent spirit seeking new host bodies. I am aware on some level that Klaus has also done something unique and acted as an institutional buffer so that Nan could speak at all, so that the show could go on. I am aware that the protesters’ shouts are an incantation against the spell of the state.
Nan and I and a few friends slip away and take an elevator down to an empty loading dock behind the museum.
“How was it?” she asks, her voice trembling as she offers me a cigarette. “I hate talking in public.” She lights hers, takes a drag. “I usually don’t show up. You know that?”
“You’re a hero, Nan.”
“Oh man,” she says, dragging again. “I’m going to be in a lot of trouble after this one.”
I was in Berlin because Nan asked me to be there. She asked me to be there, I think, because I understand something about the shape of the situation. She had been preparing her remarks for weeks, and this is not the kind of thing you do alone. I’ve found myself in trouble alongside Nan before, trying to change things that seem impossible to change until you do, and I feel bonded to her. It’s strange enough to be a screen for others’ projections, which we are all the time in daily life. It is stranger still to know the queasy feeling of exposure that comes when you’re briefly shot into the vertiginous penumbra of history.
From October 2005 until October 2023, I worked at Artforum, the glossy, monthly scripture of contemporary art. For many, the magazine was the North Star of criticism – a peerless instrument of canonisation. For an artist, landing the cover was a consecration. People collected them: a row of the magazine’s totemic spines on a bookshelf signalled sophistication. (An Artforum on Edward Cullen’s Barcelona couch in the movie Twilight quickly establishes his urbanity.) I was editor-in-chief for the last six of those years, and during that time I witnessed history’s quickening: a #MeToo scandal at the magazine that resulted in the resignation of a disgraced publisher; protests at the Whitney Museum that provoked a rare surrender of a board member; the global standstill of Covid-19; the flash of white consciousness around Black oppression in the summer of 2020; Israel’s assault on Gaza during the Unity uprising in May of 2021; Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022. A sympathetic friend dubbed me the “crisis editor”. I took for granted that Artforum’s project was imbricated with the politics of the left, and ran the magazine on that basis; as a result, I sometimes heard people call it “Wokeforum”.
The fact that I refer to Artforum’s “project” at all reveals the grandiosity that is one of the art world’s key features, the soil for its spectacular financialisation – its unparalleled ability to transform radicalism into capital. This grandiosity was inflected in much of the bright and lofty material that we published. The stakes were high; we believed we were writing history, and we often were. Compared with my predecessors, my tenure as editor-in-chief was marked by a greater appetite for protest, for using our position to intensify pressure on institutions, to force real structural change. In some ways, this was a continuation of strategies of protest and institutional critique among artists we admired, from Adrian Piper and Hans Haacke to Andrea Fraser. But as time went on, our targets were becoming clearer, our tactics more refined.
I thought I knew how to move within the contradictions. I was not fired when I published, in my first issue as editor, the portfolio that launched Nan’s campaign targeting the Sackler family – prominent art-world patrons whose names were inscribed at the Metropolitan Museum, the Louvre and the Guggenheim – for their role in the opioid crisis. I was not fired when I commissioned “The Tear Gas Biennial”, a fiery polemic that cinched the departure of Warren Kanders, CEO of the weapons manufacturer Safariland, as vice-chairman of the Whitney Museum’s board. I was not fired in June 2020 when I posted calls on Artforum’s social media channels to donate to bail funds and defund the police.
There has been plenty of controversy in Artforum’s history. In 1974, the artist Lynda Benglis presented an ad featuring herself nude and holding a double dildo between her legs, a gesture that inspired a split in the editorial department and the subsequent founding of the journal October. A decade later, Thomas McEvilley’s article “Doctor Lawyer Indian Chief”, a searing critique of the “Primitivism” show at the Museum of Modern Art, occasioned an impassioned back-and-forth between the curators and the critic about art history’s colonial underpinnings, instigating a new phase of critical discourse. (As one of the magazine’s publishers was fond of telling me, we didn’t report the news, we were the news.) Controversy, the invigorating expression of oppositional positions, telegraphs health. We were modernists, after all. Risk and dissent were our sun and moon. Editors didn’t just survive controversies; they made their names with them. We knew that conflict is the engine of that eternal hysteria called “relevance”. As far as I know, prior editors left when they got bored or ran out of things to say. I was the ninth editor in the magazine’s 60-plus-year history, and the first to be fired for something I did. It is no surprise that this something concerned Palestine.
On 19 October 2023, I authorise the publication of an open letter from culture workers in support of Palestinian liberation and a ceasefire in Gaza. Twelve days have passed since Palestinians broke through the heavily fortified border walls surrounding the Gaza Strip, killing around 1,200 Israelis and kidnapping 251. Already, more than 3,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s retaliation.
I am in Paris for the opening of a major art fair, and I have spent the past week-and-a-half reaching out to contributors I hoped could rise to the occasion. I am experiencing profound alienation. In the art world you become accustomed to cognitive dissonance, but I am running up against my limits. At the fair, everything is proceeding as normal – invitations to dinners and parties, the rich swapping stories and resources. Almost no one speaks about Gaza. Those who do mostly take Zionist sympathies for granted: of course your passion is for the murdered and kidnapped Israelis, of course you condemn Hamas.
The letter is drafted by a group of anonymous individuals who decide not to take these sympathies for granted. When a colleague shares it with me, it feels obvious that the magazine should respond with solidarity instead of analysis. It feels obvious that we should do so quickly. We know that we are in one of those strange and extraordinary periods when collective action has more purchase. My colleague asks if they can use my name when approaching Nan about signing the letter, and I say yes, and sign it as well. In no time at all, the group collects some 8,000 signatures – many of whom are major artists and contributors to the magazine – which they cap just prior to publication.
As I am negotiating the letter, a missile hits a courtyard of al-Ahli Arab Hospital in Gaza City, killing hundreds of people who were sheltering there. Later we will find it quaint to recall that, at the time, Israel claimed that a failed Palestinian rocket launch caused the explosion, and that most newspapers take the word of the “most moral army in the world”. In the months to come, Israel will kill tens of thousands of Palestinians and demolish nearly all the hospitals in the Gaza Strip. We will find it hard to imagine a time when anyone could believe that Israel wouldn’t target civilians and hospitals. We will find it hard to imagine that, at the time of the letter’s publication, the principal objection was that it focused on Palestinian suffering, and that it refused to invoke or condemn Hamas.
Shortly after we publish the letter, all hell breaks loose. My phone, once a conduit for benign distractions, acquires the menacing nimbus of a grenade. In the car from Newark airport, I take a call from the head publicist of Penske Media, the company that acquired Artforum a year earlier, who implores me to do something acknowledging “the other side”. Our Instagram post about the letter becomes a flashpoint, generating more than 15,000 likes in a handful of hours – far more than any other post in our history. The comments feed is flooded with emojis of Palestinian flags, but also accusations of antisemitism and calls to unsubscribe. In an unprecedented move, the publishers go above the heads of the editorial department and take down the Instagram post. They remove the letter itself from the magazine’s homepage and briefly make it invisible in the search function, so that to find it you need a direct link. Shortly afterwards, they stop responding to my messages.
We begin to receive texts and emails from artists and curators asking to have their names removed from the list of signatories. There are some predictable figures – major artists with less experience in activism – as well as a few sad surprises. Some explain that they can’t be associated with anything that doesn’t explicitly condemn Hamas; others say they’re afraid for their jobs and careers. Each lost name is another chink in the armour of collective action. Some have the dignity to write to me directly; others employ expensive art PR teams. (“_____’s name is apparently still on the signatory list. He is asking that his name be removed immediately.”)
Some collectors are calling up individual artists who signed, threatening to sell off their works or stonewall exhibitions by refusing to lend to museums. Gallerists tell me and my artist friends that patrons are threatening not to fund exhibitions or buy work from anyone who signed. Messages from a WhatsApp group of Zionist collectors and gallerists called “Art World for Israel” are leaked, revealing an organised strategy of intimidation targeting artists who signed the letter. There seems to be a particularly vindictive ire toward the Jewish artists who spoke up to support the Palestinian cause – Goldin, Tai Shani, Candice Breitz, Nicole Eisenman. Museum board members pressure institutional leaders to distance themselves from the letter and raise the idea of deaccessioning works of Palestinian artists. A team of dealers and collectors writes a counter-letter, which is signed by artists such as Marina Abramović and Richard Prince, and publishes it in full-page ads in The New York Times, Le Monde and The Wall Street Journal. I have never seen anything like this. If this is the response, then the letter must really matter.
On the day that I am fired, I am offered a choice. It’s a little before noon on 26 October when I meet with Jay Penske, the youthful CEO of Penske Media. We are at the company’s New York headquarters, an airless sepulchre of corporate banality in a prewar office building on Fifth Avenue. Jay is friendly as we speak, a practised inquisitor. “You have good friends,” he says with some amusement, referring to a letter, composed by the filmmaker Laura Poitras and signed by some big names, petitioning to keep me on board.
He asks me to walk him through my decision, which I do, carefully. I tell him that I felt, and still feel, that the magazine needed to respond to the moment. I had consulted the editorial staff and had reached out to contributors. No one felt they had the authority to write about 7 October and its aftermath. I had watched the agile responses of several magazines that I trusted, and the clumsy nonresponses of nearly every other publication. I contemplated various savvy “art world” takes, all of which seemed specious. In Paris, one of our contributors brought the letter to my attention, and I told them we would publish it, which, as editor-in-chief, is literally my prerogative. I did this swiftly, in consultation with the web team and our international reviews editor, who were entirely on board.
Jay asks me why I signed the letter, and I explain that we’re not a newspaper, but a leftist art publication. People should know where we stand on genocide, and why not? What kind of interest are we protecting? He tells me about the tricky situation the publishers are in. We’ve all been spammed with threatening calls and emails, many from people we’ve never heard of. (“The artists and other persons whose names appear as signatories and supporters of this shameless letter have no soul in their hearts,” preaches Gil Brandes from Tel Aviv.) The art dealer Marianne Boesky writes a letter: “This is appalling to me as a Jew and I need Artforum to remove all Boesky ads from Artforum’s platforms immediately.” I am told that the Chanel Culture Fund has demanded that we stop the presses in order to pull their ad from our November issue. (We didn’t comply.) The gallery Lévy Gorvy Dayan has written a rebuttal, which I agree to publish online because it seems worth having a public record of the surreal moral universe it represents.
I am aware that much of the sentiment is divided by class: the letters’ signatories are mostly artists, the letters’ detractors are mostly their dealers and collectors. This is not a new rift in the art world, but Palestine seems to have deepened it beyond repair. Jay tells me that the magazine’s publishers are putting together a statement, and he asks me to write something describing my missteps, something I could post on Artforum’s website and to my personal Instagram. “And if I say no?” I ask. “Hopefully it won’t come to that,” he tells me.
I walk downtown to clear my head. What can I say? I don’t like the barely veiled threat, and I’m not sorry. Two weeks earlier, I cringed watching Samira Nasr, the editor of Harper’s Bazaar, post an apology for an Instagram story stating that Israel cutting off Gazans’ access to water and power “is the most inhuman thing I’ve seen in my life”. To me it’s simple: my job is to position the magazine correctly in the current of history. We have done the right thing.
My phone rings. It’s Jay. He sounds panicked. “Someone has tipped off The New York Times,” he says. “We need to accelerate your statement.”
“I can’t produce something on this timeline,” I reply.
“I’m very disappointed to hear that,” he says. “I had really hoped this would work out.” He hangs up.
A colleague at the magazine calls next. “Are you really going to throw everything away?” he asks. “Over this?”
“I’m not the one doing the throwing,” I say.
“The letter wasn’t even a success,” he says. “Look, it’s divided the art world.”
“I think we have different ideas of success.”
That night, at 7:39 PM, I am at home when I receive an email from one of the two publishers with the subject line “Your Employment”. The phrasing is evasive, but the message is clear: “Dear David, I was disheartened to learn that you did not respond to Jay this afternoon, we are therefore assuming that you have decided to leave your role.” I start to respond that I most definitely have not “decided to leave my role”. A minute later, the magazine’s website posts a statement from the publishers saying that the letter’s publication “was not consistent with Artforum’s editorial process”. Few people know “editorial process” better than I do – the “process”, after all, ended at my door. The sudden invention of phantom procedures is one of the more despicable attempts to disguise my firing as a matter of protocol rather than politics.
My termination is immediate; there is no settlement. I will be paid through the week and no more. It is 18 years to the day since I began at the magazine. Later that night, The New York Times publishes a story about my firing, kicking off another media storm. Nearly a third of the Artforum editorial staff resigns and 700 writers sign on to a boycott of the magazine. More editors will follow in the coming weeks. In every way that counts, the magazine as we knew it is over. The era of Vichy Artforum begins.
Of course, I’m not alone. Shortly after my firing, Jazmine Hughes, a prominent contributor to The New York Times Magazine, is forced to resign after signing an open letter condemning the genocide. Gabriella Karefa-Johnson, a Black editor-at-large at Vogue, resigns after an Instagram post condemning Israel as an apartheid state. Michael Eisen, the editor-in-chief of eLife, a prominent science journal, is let go for retweeting a satirical article from The Onion: “Dying Gazans Criticized for Not Using Last Words to Condemn Hamas”. The actress Melissa Barrera is fired from Scream 7, Susan Sarandon is dropped from her agency for speaking at a rally, and CAA agent Maha Dakhil apologises and endures a Stalinesque “re-education” after reposting an image stating, simply, “You’re currently learning who supports genocide.” Two years later, the fever of this repressive moment will largely be forgotten.
Billionaire donors run “doxxing trucks” around campuses featuring faces of people who protested Israel’s assault, and state officials study lists generated by the Canary Mission, a ghoulish conclave that targets student activists. The presidents of major universities are called before congress to testify. Their limp acts of contrition fail to satisfy the establishment’s thirst for blood, and Harvard’s Claudine Gay and the University of Pennsylvania’s M. Elizabeth Magill resign. We’ve been quick to label all this “McCarthyism”, but in truth, the fallout, which outrages the popular conscience, signals a vaster and more insidious repression.
The crackdown is international: across Europe, there are whispers and then headlines about artists, writers and curators losing residencies, sales and even jobs. An awards ceremony at the Frankfurt Book Fair for the Palestinian author Adania Shibli is cancelled in the weeks following 7 October. The city of Bremen and other sponsors of the Hannah Arendt Prize withdraw their support when its recipient, the Russian-American writer M. Gessen, publishes an essay in The New Yorker comparing Gaza to the Jewish ghettoes of Nazi-occupied Europe. Friends in Berlin in particular report an atmosphere of absolute censorship and policing, and across Germany, foreign nationals are threatened with deportation for showing solidarity with Palestine. The stealth punishments are perhaps the most pernicious: the jobs not offered, the sales not made. They contribute to an ambient fear that persists in people’s minds. The resulting silence is the only sign of its efficacy.
I don’t know why I thought we were an exception. Maybe because sometimes we were. Artforum, for many years, was about as leftist as an elite publication could get. We really did play a role in holding weapons manufacturers and the engineers of the opioid crisis to account. We really did give jobs and bylines to some singular and brilliant people. We really were a brainy refuge of weird glamour married to principle, and sometimes I wonder if mine is the last generation to grow up thinking of the art world as a place for ungovernable outsiders and talented eccentrics, which doesn’t hear the word ‘art’ and think immediately of commerce.
For me, and for many of my friends, art once seemed to offer a kind of promise. I grew up poor, brown and queer in Oregon, but I was still privileged enough to make it to a fancy college, where I looked for ways to orient myself amid unfamiliar codes of inclusion and exclusion. A young gay friend – an artist who made careful, exquisite paintings and sculptures, and whose ambition eventually yielded to his anarchic politics – exposed me to Portland’s small but vivid art scene. Here you could open a gallery or independent-minded bookstore, encourage strange and talented people to pursue their passions, and invite revolutionary thought into your life. I began to consider art a home for ideas and rebellion, a way to be yourself outside the stultifying halls of academia.
Those were the years when I encountered Adrian Piper, the Black conceptual artist who made politically incisive work with heart, who in 1970 withdrew a piece from the New York Cultural Center to protest against the US invasion of Cambodia, and in the early 1980s taught “funk lessons” to college students to exorcise xenophobia. I read the words of artists like David Wojnarowicz, who enraged senators with his scathing communiques about our genocidal indifference to AIDS. I learned about Felix Gonzalez-Torres, the sentimental minimalist who, in 1988, made a work called “Forbidden Colors”: four solid-colour paintings – red, black, green and white – installed side by side, evoking the Palestinian flag. (At the time, the colours were banned from being displayed together in the occupied territories.)
In New York, I fell in love with an artist who showed me Nan Goldin’s honest depictions of beautiful, untamed people who we believed shared our DNA. I learned to write about art to impress him, and in 2005 I landed a job as an editorial assistant on Artforum’s website. I discovered a fortunate alchemy: qualities that were liabilities in my early life could be transformed into clout through the magic of identity politics. My leftist orientations were tolerated and sometimes even rewarded. I was paid for my ideas, and flown to faraway places to write about biennials with themes inspired by Marx, Fanon and Aimé Césaire. I pictured cracks in the corridors of power.
I’m not yet cynical enough to think that the cracks were simply illusions. In the wake of what quickly came to be known as the “Artforum letter”, some of us were surprised to find that we were being asked to sacrifice something. For years we had been signing petitions for all kinds of social causes, calls for liberation – feminism, queer rights, climate justice, abolition – that were often taken up by the institutions that housed us. Until 2025, nearly every museum had a gay pride celebration. When George Floyd was murdered in May 2020, a parade of museums frantically marshalled committees of sacrificial minorities, staged unctuous exhibitions and asserted their commitments to “diversity, equity, and inclusion”.
Palestine is different. Even with broad public support, no major museum has taken up the genocide in Gaza. No large institution I know of has put on an exhibition about Palestinian artists or Palestinian lives. Instead, the opposite: in June 2025, the Whitney Museum “suspended” its 57-year-old Independent Study Program after some of its members dared to host a performance critical of Israel. The art world, with all its progressive scaffolding and humanist ornamentation, practically designed to celebrate and aestheticise every rebellion, couldn’t metabolise Palestine. It still can’t.
It’s October 2025, nearly a year after Nan’s “scandal” at the Neue Nationalgalerie, and she is in Milan to celebrate the penultimate stop of her retrospective at the Pirelli HangarBicocca, an old manufacturing plant retrofitted into a vast exhibition space. The chilly claustrophobia of the Berlin show is replaced with a warm sense of possibility. In the streets, more than a million Italians are striking in solidarity with the people of Gaza and the Global Sumud Flotilla. A tentative ceasefire is on the horizon, and Nan meets supporters everywhere she goes.
She has spent the past year making the most of every available platform. In July, during the opening of the prestigious Rencontres d’Arles photography festival, she and the writer Édouard Louis spoke about Palestine activism in front of 2,500 well-heeled attendees in an ancient Roman amphitheatre. The Milan version of This Will Not End Well includes a brutal montage called Gaza: Notes on a Genocide 2023-2025, a “work in progress” comprising unsparing footage from friends and journalists of explosions, starvation and forced displacement.
Nan’s persistence has won her many fans, but it has come with a cost. “Personally, my career tanked,” she told Mahmoud Khalil in an interview with Dazed in September. “My market tanked from one day to the next because of my support of Palestine.” The German press responded to her speech with universal savagery. The conservative daily Die Welt called it “undoubtedly the saddest, most undignified, and most shameful moment in the 56-year history of the Neue Nationalgalerie”, and Klaus Biesenbach told Der Spiegel the night was a “horror”, and the artist’s words were “hard to bear”. “I never thought Nan would be so cold,” he said.
The past two years have given the lie to any wisdom that the art world constitutes the progressive avant-garde. I can count acts of bravery from less-visible artists, but a fog of silence continues to dominate the field: few expressions of solidarity forthcoming from institutions, and too few artists willing to speak out via social media, much less their own work. What do we make of this depressing amalgam of fear and apathy? How many will it take to break the art world’s attitude of mute acquiescence?
I am struck by the fact that major celebrities seem more likely than major contemporary artists to publicly express support for the Palestinian cause. The musician Lorde lights the stage at Madison Square Garden in red, white and green. The actress Jennifer Lawrence tells reporters: “What’s happening is no less than a genocide and it’s unacceptable”. Joaquin Phoenix, Olivia Coleman and thousands more sign a boycott of Israeli film groups “implicated in genocide”. Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem make regular statements, and Hannah Einbinder shouts “Free Palestine” as she accepts her Emmy. These are not simply symbolic gestures, but meaningful demonstrations of solidarity.
“The more of us there are, the more of us there are,” Nan said at the end of her speech. She understands that we pierce repression with a surplus of reparative and disruptive actions. More voices, more collective, louder, riskier. She understands that we make change not through holding ideologically correct or coherent beliefs, but through an uneven accretion of strategic and local decisions. Not everyone has to make the same choices. Certainly not everyone has to agree. But we all have to act.
I have spent the past two years on unofficial hiatus from the official art world. Its ceremonial sound and fury feel remote to me. Speculation has been hollowing art out for decades, and we might simply have passed a threshold where price is the only measure of worth. But I’m alert enough to know that the era of unbridled conspicuous consumption might be ending. The proverbial bubble has burst. Collectors are disposing of their minions and concierges. Galleries are closing, or having less lavish parties. Artists at every level are feeling the burn. It’s only appropriate, now that the uneasy truce between the market and its playthings has been scuttled. Brute reality tore the mast from the boat.
None of this is “complicated”, as the boilerplate from strategic wafflers would have you believe. As I write this, dim leaders celebrate the supposed end to this “war”. Those who couldn’t admit to a genocide now begin to speak of it in the past tense. We’re roughly 11 weeks into a supposed ceasefire, which Israel breaks daily with routine barbarism. As I write this, IDF soldiers continue their enduring project of annexation and extermination in the West Bank. A politics of wilful ignorance and escalating stupidity keeps the killing machines going. The writing can’t keep pace. Every minute there’s another atrocity tidily packaged as a sedate number in a headline. At least 70,000 Palestinians have been murdered, but these are the underreported official counts. Around 30 percent of these have been children, with an estimated average of 28 children killed each day since October 2023. More than 98 percent of Gaza’s cropland has been damaged or made inaccessible, or both. It’s increasingly hard to hold in mind the scale of devastation. It’s increasingly hard to care about the fate of an art world narcotised by money and self-regard. We had a chance to at least try and make a difference. We had a chance to not sell ourselves out. We had a chance, and we blew it. This did not end well, and still we can choose to begin again, tilting – collectively, contingently – toward the pitch of liberation.

Archive selection
In response to the student protests, the French government has initiated a public consultation via a digital platform. If that sounds familiar, it could be because it’s exactly what it did, in 2019, in response to the Gilets Jaunes protests. ‘Right at the outset they warned they would only consider contributions submitted online,’ Magali Della Sudda and Grégory Rzepski write in this month’s edition. ‘But, in fact, the authorities never responded to the exercise at all.’ Pretending to listen has a long history. Even the idealistic Estates General of French Renewal, a huge public consultation exercise organised in 1945 by the National Council of the Resistance (CNR), was quickly sidelined by Charles de Gaulle.
Elsewhere, Italy’s far right is being outflanked by an even further right; Pierre Daum reports from the Algeria-Morocco border; in Cameroon, the AI revolution looks more like poorly paid, precarious work for Western firms. The Enemies List
The Trump administration’s war on the Left is designed to suffocate dissent.
Alberto Toscano
One year ago, in the wake of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, the White House ramped up its campaign against left-wing dissidence.
The government weaponized the legally dubious category of “domestic terrorism” when, on Sept. 22, 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order against “Antifa,” designating it as a domestic terrorist organization. Three days later, Trump issued a national security memorandum declaring that the “‘anti-fascist’ lie has become the organizing rallying cry used by domestic terrorists to wage a violent assault against democratic institutions, constitutional rights and fundamental American liberties.” It instructs federal agencies to devise a national strategy to preempt, disband and prosecute those “networks” and “conspiracies” that supposedly seek to undermine and overthrow the U.S. government.
This strategy framed the prosecution in the “Prairieland” case, in which nine activists were charged in relation to a solidarity noise protest outside an ICE detention center at which an officer was shot, in circumstances that remain disputed.
But as Adam Federman reported for In These Times and Type Investigations in March, FBI records obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request show that the bureau investigated an alleged Dallas-area antifa group years earlier, in 2018, and closed that investigation after finding it posed no threat to national security.
In June, eight of the Prairieland defendants were sentenced to a cumulative 450 years in prison. The sentences were largely for actions deemed “material support” for terrorism. Perhaps most egregiously, Daniel Rolando Sanchez-Estrada, who was not present at the demonstration, was given 30 years for moving a box of anarchist zines, which was construed as conspiracy to corruptly conceal documents.
The same month the protesters were sentenced, antifa was again invoked in the federal charges levied against 15 members of Direct Action Minnesota for their role in anti-ICE protests. Just as Prairieland prosecutors depicted black clothing at demonstrations as evidence of terroristic intent, the use of the messaging app Signal was understood as proof of conspiracy in the Minneapolis case.
These cases demonstrate the grievous effects of applying the legal and ideological arsenal of counterterrorism to left-wing activism, imagined as a vast conspiratorial network (“Antifa”). They are also one front in something larger: a counterterrorism crusade that functions as a miniature version of the economic warfare that has been deployed against nation-states such as Cuba, Iraq and Iran. Its aim: to suffocate any opposition — abroad and at home.
The Trump administration’s efforts to repress opposition have always been international in scope. While domestic terrorism is not covered as such by any existing law, designation as a foreign terrorist organization or specially designated terrorist group has momentous consequences — not least for U.S. citizens or residents accused of providing material support. The desire to paint antifa as an heir to the fantastical Soviet-managed “terror network” that preoccupied the CIA in the 1980s explains the decision to designate four marginal European groups as terrorists in November 2025.
The economic siege against Cuba has also been accompanied by an effort to link the U.S. Left to nefarious foreign puppet masters. In an improbable regurgitation of high Cold War propaganda, contemporary Cuba has been reimagined as America’s dystopian nemesis.
The State Department released a 100-page report, widely suspected to have been produced by the AI platform Claude, under the bombastic title “Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism.” The transparent aim is to tie the effort to turn Cuba into a docile dependent through economic (and eventually also military) warfare to the mounting campaign to persecute political dissidence at home.
Turning history on its head, the report’s first lines declare: “For nearly seven decades, the Cuban regime has waged a sustained campaign of subversion against the United States.” The conspiratorial imagination is on overdrive: despite its poverty and almost total asymmetry of power vis-à-vis the United States, Cuba has orchestrated “a vast hemispheric network.” It has infiltrated “the highest reaches” of the United States and established “a revolutionary infrastructure designed to turn America against itself.” This infrastructure has co-opted everyone from Karen Bass to Barack Obama, the Black Panther Party to the People’s Forum, Amy Goodman of Democracy Now! to myriad university departments and civil society organizations.
As scholar Charisse Burden-Stelly has argued, this pastiche of red scares past is a form of “anti-communist governance” — one that combines public authority and self-censorship “to penalize, regulate, censure and criminalize ideas and beliefs that challenge racial oppression, economic inequality and class antagonism by labeling them ‘communist.’”
These increasingly delirious declarations are not trying to consolidate or manufacture consent; they seem meant for internal consumption within the echo chambers of the White House Situation Room and the MAGA mediasphere.
Unfortunately, without commensurate resistance, force without consent can go a long way. Behind the fantastical façade is the as yet unimpeded project — nationally and regionally — to maximize the impunity of capital while suppressing any alternative vision of collective life and welfare.
That international reach was on full display at the “Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism,” a conference hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington, D.C., in July. In his keynote remarks, Rubio lambasted a media and academic establishment that he presented as treating left-wing violence as a “protected class unto itself” and declared: “It is time to crush this evil forever.” He launched into a vituperative portrait of violent leftists as resentful enemies of Western greatness and civilization.
For Rubio, the menace to be snuffed out is “a revolt of the worst against the best, a revolt of the weak and the cowardly against the strong and the good … perpetrated by those who cannot build, who cannot create, who cannot achieve great things, and take their revenge upon the world for their own inadequacy by seeking to destroy those who can.”
The sentiment was echoed with characteristic shrill hyperbole by White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, who asked the audience to reflect on why no one attending antifa protests looks “normal”. His answer contained a familiarly fascistic theory of leftist ideas manifesting as physical degeneracy: “Every one of them … has scarred their body and their appearance in many different ways, to the point in which their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred.”
But behind the rhetoric about the revolt of the weak — which, like the anti-communist pastiche of the Cuba report, is of very old vintage — lies a focused, and terribly contemporary, strategy of repression. Miller emphasized the need to “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest, and prosecute” the nodes of the new terror network.
This counterterrorism architecture projects any single act of so-called left-wing violence as linked to all others both ideologically and materially. Its latest target is the Italian anti-fascist hacktivist collective and digital service provider Autistici/Inventati (translated as Autistic/Invented), also known as A/I.
A/I was founded in 2001, in the context of the antiglobalization movement and the mobilization against the G-8 in Genoa, and provided services like blogs, mailing lists, email and website hosting to groups and individuals with whom it felt a broad political affinity.
On August 26, A/I was named a specially designated terrorist group by the State Department, alongside Palestine Action — the direct action group whose designation as a terrorist group by the UK government has been the object of sustained protest and challenge — and the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement (Masar Badil). But the designation does not concern any actions the collective has carried out. There are no indictments pending against it in either the United States or Italy. Rather, the State Department alleges that its digital infrastructure facilitated acts of “left-wing violence,” from railway sabotage in Europe to the resistance against Cop City in Atlanta, as well as communications among groups ranging from Rose City Antifa to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party.
The designation’s effect, as intended, was swift and drastic. In Italy, where a U.S. designation has no legal standing, A/I was debanked by Banca Etica. The bank declared that notwithstanding its opposition to this campaign against its client, it could not risk the consequences to its other 130,000 accounts should the Treasury Department’s secondary sanctions affect the bank’s access to Visa, Mastercard, Nexi and dollar exchanges.
The outsize power of the U.S. government and the dollar in the international financial system, specifically in monetary transactions, means banks exercise anticipatory overcompliance to avoid risk. The effect is to turn any opponent into an economic nonperson, with all the social and political consequences that entails.
A/I disbanded to shield its former clients from persecution. Shortly before, the collective said the Trump administration had targeted it in a kind of “hybrid warfare.”
Perhaps the most worrying aspect is the absence of any concerted effort by Italian or European institutions to defend the collective’s right to free expression, which is also a right to the digital infrastructures that make it possible. As the collective Sabot Media observed, U.S. sanctions create a “perimeter of fear” around those they target, one that operates in advance of and in lieu of the law.
This crusade builds upon the anti-Palestinian, anti-migrant and anti-Muslim legal provisions that were crystallized by the so-called “war on terror” — when the terror lists were born.
As the academic Lisa Bhungalia rightly notes in her work on the “asphyxiatory violence” of contemporary imperialism, the current wave of repression is “a depository of past decades that build one upon the other rather than … a radical departure from that which came before.”
To face this moment, an internationalist Left must maintain and repair the infrastructures of resistance. The threat is not only a frontal assault or Trump and Miller’s fascist verbiage, but also the kind of suffocation that uses the silent violence of money and law to snuff out any liberatory alternative to the status quo.
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
ALBERTO TOSCANO is the author of Late Fascism: Race, Capitalism and the Politics of Crisis (Verso) and Terms of Disorder: Keywords for an Interregnum (Seagull). He lives in Vancouver.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/woke-on.title: Woke 1 Was Not “Crazy,” but Needed
https://inthesetimes.com/article/woke-on.author: Calvin John Smiley
https://inthesetimes.com/article/woke-on.text:
Woke 1 Was Not “Crazy,” but Needed
When progressive politicians disavow the politics of 2020, they erase a legacy of Black political thought—and the policies it built that are quietly working today.
Calvin John Smiley
In August, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) stated, “Woke 1 was crazy,” on ABC’s “This Week” news show. She borrowed the phrase from her New York colleague City Councilman Chi Ossé, who had used it in a May post on X (formerly Twitter).
Soon after, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said this about AOC’s statement: “What you believe can change, it can develop, it can grow. … I’ve made very clear that I do not believe in defunding the police, that I will not be defunding the police.”
Woke 1 — which, according to the Internets, refers to cultural and social activism in and around 2020 — was not “crazy.”
These statements by progressive elected officials sparked criticism. Some labeled AOC an opportunist. Others gave Mamdani a bit more grace, arguing he was being strategically cautious. (As the person who must now work directly with the NYPD, he could be hoping to avoid the antagonism that plagued former Mayor Bill de Blasio’s police reform efforts.)
Yet the exhausting part of this debate is the seemingly endless pattern of people running on progressive or radical ideas only to retreat to the center once elected. Woke 1 was not crazy. It was an important moment in a longer legacy of struggle. To claim it was just a clumsy blip is disingenuous at best and dangerous at worst.
Wokeness is not a new concept. It has origins dating back to both Garveyism in the early 20th century and more recently to Erykah Badu’s 2008 song “Master Teacher,” in which she repeats the phrase “stay woke.” But for many of the hip-hop generation, the term was inspired by Black movements such as the Nation of Gods and Earths, which uses the term “woke” to refer colloquially to knowledge of self. The idea of being woke was then popularized further by 1990s hip-hop groups such as Brand Nubian and Wu-Tang Clan. It became cemented in my mind by the Black Star song “K.O.S. (Determination),” in which Talib Kweli and Mos Def rap the chorus: “With that — what? (Knowledge of self.) Determination.”
It took another 25 years for white conservatives to learn the term and co-opt it into a watered-down social media buzzword.
Despite this, wokeness is part of Black history. Knowing one’s history — the people, collectives, organizations and movements that came before us — is what helps many Black people navigate and endure a world that subjugates us.
As a teenager in the 2000s, I was reminded by Black elders to “stay woke,” meaning not only to learn this history but to remember it and use it. To dismiss wokeness is to dismiss the importance of this kind of self-knowledge.
When Mamdani tweeted “#DefundTheNYPD” in 2020, he was responding to the murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer. People around the globe similarly responded to the ideas of #defundthepolice and what they meant. Some will counter that it was too vague a demand. However, as I write in my book Defund, mainstream Republicans and Democrats alike attempted to appropriate or dismiss the phrase, respectively.
Former Georgia representative and loyalist turned enemy of Donald Trump, Marjorie Taylor Greene, tweeted “DEFUND THE FBI” in the aftermath of Trump’s Florida home being raided in 2022. During his State of the Union speech that same year, President Joe Biden exclaimed, “We should all agree: The answer is not to defund the police. It’s to fund the police.” Both parties clearly understood the power of this phrase and feared its influence on an electorate saddled with bloated police budgets and inadequate social services that actually help keep people safe. As I write in Defund, this fear was justified: “Defund gives us a platform and pathway to reimagine a society with less police, more care and services that meet the needs of all.”
The irony is that tenets of defund continue to shape progressive policy today. The Mamdani campaign made an ambitious promise to create a $1.1 billion Department of Community Safety. While this has not come to full fruition, he did create the Mayor’s Office of Community Safety by executive order with a budget of $260 million. This office plans to offer non-police responses to mental health crises and become a blueprint to combat gun violence — a defund strategy. According to the research hub Interrupting Criminalization’s toolkit, “The Demand Is Still #DefundPolice,” over $840 million was reallocated from police department budgets to other community needs in the months after the nationwide Black Lives Matter protests.
Outside NYC, cities around the country have rethought approaches to public safety in the aftermath of Defund Summer 2020. For example, Albuquerque, N.M., has started a community safety department that dispatches social workers, counselors and other community members to nonviolent crises. In a December 2025 report, the Center for Policing Equity found that more than 100 other localities implemented their own non-police crisis response programs between 2020 and 2024 (including Denver, Austin, Texas, and Oakland, Calif.) — a direct reflection of social movements advocating for defund and Black Lives Matter.
Last year, Baltimore saw its lowest homicide rate in nearly 50 years. Researchers have attributed this to Mayor Brandon Scott’s continued millions-of-dollars investment in violence interrupters and other community outreach workers — specifically taking a public health approach to gun violence prevention rather than solely relying on police. These efforts also build on the success of Baltimore programs like Safe Streets, which was established in 2007 as an evidence-based strategy to reduce gun violence. The program asks outreach professionals to mediate conflict and use de-escalation methods. In New Jersey, the Newark Community Street Team has invested in evidence-based and trauma- informed approaches to violence, reducing overall crime by 19% in 2025.
And according to the Council on Criminal Justice’s 2025 year-end report, overall national violent crime has begun dropping significantly, including a 21% drop in homicides from 2024 to 2025 across 35 large American cities. While we cannot say definitively that the sole reason is alternative or innovative approaches to crime, we can infer that these approaches are, at the very least, contributing to these declines and that officials inspired by summer 2020 to look beyond “arresting our way out of crime” have played a pivotal role.
Is there room for reflexive critiques of movement strategies? Absolutely. But that is done within organizing collectives to sustain momentum — not publicly in counterproductive wholesale dismissals. If Woke 1 is a cultural war around language, taking a reactive position only supports and retains the status quo and fuels reactionaries. Revolutions are not born in comfort but rather by creating contentious positions that challenge current conditions and offer the possibility of change. Defund has and continues to inspire challenges to capitalism, and that cannot be erased.
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.

And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.

Calvin John Smiley is a professor of sociology at Hunter College and author of Purgatory Citizenship: Reentry, Race, & Abolition, Defund: Conversations Towards Abolition and the new book Prison Hashtags: Incarceration, Reentry, and Digital Identity.

https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.title: Living in Normaltown and Feeling Anything But
https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.author: Chris Wiley
https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.text:
The photographer Tim Davis spent his early childhood, in the nineteen-seventies, in a bohemian community in Saratoga Springs, New York. “You could go into a giant Victorian mansion with no running water, and there were hippies and their kids living in there and welding a statue of a giant pterodactyl inside,” he recalled recently when I sat down with him in his studio, in upstate New York. His parents were beatniks who’d served in the Peace Corps, and the family had previously lived in Malawi and, briefly, in a hippie commune in Oregon. Then, when Davis was seven, his parents split up, and his mother took him and his younger sister south, to the unfamiliar city of Athens, Georgia, leaving their father behind. Davis recalls the period as “full of personal pain and tragedy.” Ironically, he found himself living in a neighborhood called Normaltown.
The town’s name serves as the title of Davis’s newest book, which collects pictures taken in Normaltown and elsewhere in Georgia between 2019 and 2024. (He had not been back since his family left, in 1980.) In the course of a twenty-five-year career, Davis has never approached his work so autobiographically. “It was never about my inner world,” he told me. “It was always about what was out there, and ideas.” Indeed, with the exception of a few seminal projects—including “Permanent Collection,” in which sections of the glossy surfaces of old paintings are obliterated by reflected light, and “Retail,” a group of nighttime pictures that show corporate signage reflected in the windows of suburban houses and apartment blocks—Davis has always been part of the peripatetic breed of picture-makers who find inspiration simply by walking out the door with a camera, and seeing what happens. “The best day in my life,” he told me, “is a day when I can photograph all day, from the second I wake up.”
For the Normaltown project, Davis didn’t jettison his exploratory shooting style, which he compares to “foraging.” In 2017, he switched from a cumbersome four-by-five-inch view camera to a more nimble digital 35-mm., and if anything he has become more freewheeling. (Sometimes this can be to his disadvantage—the book, which runs to nearly two hundred images, might have benefitted from a harsher editor’s hand.) But whereas comparable recent work, such as Davis’s 2021 book of pictures from Los Angeles, had a surreal, cinematic, gee-whiz quality, the pictures in “Normaltown” are more sombre, lonesome, even haunted. In one image, the rusted-out body of a car hangs miraculously from the top branches of a leafless tree, as if Davis had arrived in the aftermath of a Biblical deluge. In another, a jellyfish-like blob of melted ice cream leaks onto the sidewalk in the raking light of sunset. A row of uniformed boys stands on a baseball field, their shadows stretching long across the turf like the tines of a pitchfork. That picture is taken from the high-bleachers vantage of an outsider, a sort of camera-wielding ghost.
By many metrics, Davis didn’t have it too hard in Normaltown. His family was poor, but they had a semblance of a support system. He got his first camera—a Mickey Mouse Instamatic—on a post-divorce trip to Disney World that was facilitated by some friends of his mother’s who worked in the park. In school Davis was well-liked, a class clown, though he noted when we talked that his humor, like his camera, was a sly way to engage with people while keeping his distance. Some of this reticence stemmed from his disconnect with the people of Normaltown, who seemed trapped inside what he described as a “cartilage of politeness,” which he experienced as a kind of acute culture shock. He and his family were, in his memory, the only Jewish people for miles. He was never, in his memory, the target of antisemitism, but in other ways Normaltown was where he first met America proper, in all of its troubled contradictions. He had little awareness of racism, for instance, before the move. In Normaltown, he began noticing that Black people’s world “was different from mine (just as I was feeling differently).” His pictures favor a kind of ramshackle egalitarianism, in which all of his subjects, both Black and white, are forced to make the best of their relatively bleak surroundings.
Here and there, moments of connection and compassion sneak through Davis’s photos: a doting mother smiles at her stunned-looking baby as his drool runs in twin rivulets over her arm; a boy hoists a girl into his arms and gazes into her eyes with goofy glee. You can’t help but feel that some of the children pictured might be stand-ins for Davis himself, or for some fantasy of a life he did not live: a kid with a splinter in his palm captured as his father gently plucks it from his flesh; a boy on a miniature motorbike posted up beside a church, his face tilted skyward as if he were awaiting a revelation. Like many outsider observers of America before him—Robert Frank, for example—Davis simultaneously captures the American everyday and bends it around the poetic armature of his inner life. His pictures are documents not only of his own childhood struggle but of our collective disquiet.

Hello!
As the lords of chaos (see Monireh’s cartoon here above) continue to wreak havoc, we use the tools at our disposal (pen and paper, or tablet) to keep the chaos at bay.
In this newsletter we share the comic about humor and democracy we’ve been working on for the past couple of months. We also have an upcoming webinar and we show cartoons from the frontlines in Ukraine. Ukrainian cartoonist Ruslan Pikhota serves in the Ukrainian army, and captures the reality of war with pencil on paper as he fights for freedom. And, as our regular feature, we share the most popular cartoons of the month.
You can check out our other, daily newsletter, (featuring our daily editor’s choice) here:
Comic: Humour and Democracy
As some of you might know, Cartoon Movement is a consortium partner in Horizon Europe project DELIAH (Democratic Literacy and Humour). In addition to researching humour, part of DELIAH’s mission is to raise awareness about the role of humour in our democracies. We try to do this in various ways: by writing about it, by giving workshops and now also by making a comic about it.
Over the last few months, we have worked with the renowned cartoonist Pedro X. Molina to create a four-page comic that explains what we currently know about how humour works in a democracy.
Depending on your device, you can choose to read the mobile version or the desktop version.
We also have the comic available as a PDF and a slideshow. All formats of the comic are freely available to download and use, provided DELIAH and the artist Pedro X. Molina are credited when the comic is published.
Cartoons from the front lines
Ruslan Pikhota is a Ukrainian frontline cartoonist and an active-duty officer in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Before the full-scale invasion, he spent 15 years working in children’s publishing in Kharkiv. He volunteered in February 2022, served as an infantryman on the Donetsk and Kharkiv fronts, and was wounded near Bakhmut. He now serves with an unmanned systems unit.
Since the spring of 2022, he has created more than 550 drawings in trenches, dugouts, ruined buildings, and between military duties. We asked him to select what he considers to be his ten most telling drawings made at the front lines.
Webinar: how can humour inspire action?
Join a webinar led by Dutch cartoonist and CM editor-in-chief Tjeerd Royaards to learn more about how humour works and how it can be used to make people take action. Insights are based on scientific research done by our research project DELIAH.
The webinar is part of the 8th Cartoon Africa International Biennal and will take place via Google Meet; the session is open to all and can be accessed via this link. However, we would appreciate it if you register, so we have an idea how many people will attend:

https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.title: Deze impact had Apache in oktober
https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.author: Redactie Apache
https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.text:
Van Reynders in steeds nauwere schoentjes tot privérusthuizen die subsidies wegsluizen. Onderzoeken van Apache rolden in oktober over de tongen. Zo woog Apache de voorbije maand op het debat en het beleid.
- Het op een schandaal zonder weerga afstevenende fraudeonderzoek naar Didier Reynders – met nu ook smoking gun-bewijzen dat de ex-Eurocommissaris zaken waarin zijn naam viel in de doofpot liet stoppen – waarbij een “geklasseerde” zaak uit 2014 heropend werd na onthullingen van Apache.
- De financiële doorlichting die uitwees dat drie op de tien private rusthuizen in Vlaanderen en Brussel niet kunnen uitleggen waar hun zorgsubsidies naartoe gaan. Die kwam er nadat Apache in 2020 beschreef hoe private zorggroepen dat geld met slinkse truken wegsluizen naar hun aandeelhouders.
- De zogezegd “onaanraakbare” bevroren Russische miljarden bij Euroclear die dan toch al bleken te zijn aangesproken, niet om Oekraïne te steunen maar om Europese investeerders wiens geld vastzit in Rusland te compenseren. Een onthulling waarmee Apache ook in Kyiv de krant haalde.
Het zijn maar drie van de meer in het oog springende vormen van impact die Apache in oktober had. Ze illustreren hoe onze journalistiek niet alleen bewustzijn creëert, maar ook het beleid achter de veren zit en het gerecht een handje toesteekt.
Wegen op het beleid
Wegen op het debat én het beleid: dat probeerden we in oktober ook te doen met stevige argumenten voor een stop op het bouwen van datacenters, of om de kerncentrales niet holderdebolder te nationaliseren. Maar ook met een gouden tip voor de regering-De Wever over 15 miljard euro die zomaar voor het oprapen ligt. En met harde cijfers over beroepsziekten veroorzaakt door pesticiden – waarvan België er in tegenstelling tot meerdere buurlanden niet één erkent.
Weg van Amerikaanse big tech
De impact van datacenters en big tech onder de loep nemen, dat kun je moeilijk zonder conclusies te trekken over je eigen technologiegebruik. Daarom ruilde Apache de diensten van een Amerikaanse bigtechreus in voor Europese opensource-oplossingen, voor onze digitale werkplek, onze cloudopslag en onze redactionele chat. Dat vergde enig aanpassingsvermogen en had een zekere impact op de geoliede machine die we doorgaans zijn, maar daar heb jij als lezer hopelijk niets van gemerkt. Niettemin kunnen we iedereen aanraden om zelf de switch te maken – ook de Vlaamse overheid.
Klacht ongegrond, toch op kosten gejaagd
Impact van het minder leuke soort creëert onze journalistiek helaas ook van tijd tot tijd. Zoals voor de rechtbank of de Raad voor de Journalistiek gedaagd worden. En ook als zo’n klacht ongegrond wordt verklaard – omdat je aan niets schuldig bent behalve aan waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving – word je op kosten gejaagd. Ook daarom is journalistiek zoals die van Apache niet goedkoop, en de steun van onze leden onbetaalbaar.
Meer directe en indirecte impact van ons werk, maar ook kanttekeningen van onze redactie bij de dagelijkse actualiteit, vind je voortaan in de nieuwe rubriek Opgepikt.
Niets van het bovenstaande hadden we kunnen uitzoeken of onder de aandacht brengen zonder financiële steun van onze betalende leden.
Ben jij nog niet aangesloten bij Apache? Neem dan vandaag nog een betalend lidmaatschap, en geef ons meer middelen om te schrijven wat iedereen moet weten. Om kritische vragen te blijven stellen – hoe hardnekkig sommige politici ze ook negeren.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.title: Big Tech’s Millions Backfired in the Midterms
https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.author: Maegan Llerena and Theo Oshiro
https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.text:
Big Tech’s Millions Backfired in the Midterms
Big Tech companies and their executives poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the midterm elections to both Democrats and Republicans—and, in large part, they lost.
Maegan Llerena and Theo Oshiro
Big Tech billionaires tried to buy our elections — but the millions of dollars in political contributions they made largely backfired. In a number of high-stakes races, rejecting Big Tech money helped deliver wins to candidates that ran on an anti-Big Tech platform. Why? In the recent midterms we witnessed a popular uprising that cut across traditional political fault lines to build new political power that overcame Big Tech’s millions.
We’ve had a first hand look at how voters are coming together to reject Big Tech’s undue influence. At Make the Road Action, we knocked on hundreds of thousands of doors and have organized in some of the communities where popular rejection of Big Tech is at its highest — Lehigh Valley, PA, Lansing, Michigan and Reno, Nevada, to name a few. On the doors, we saw that voters — across party lines and demographic differences — consistently shared concern over skyrocketing utility bills, fears around job replacement, and the role of Big Tech surveillance firms in ICE enforcement.
For example, in Northeastern Pennsylvania, which is quickly becoming one of the epicenters of the data center boom, working class Latino voters in Reading and Hazleton — once strongholds for President Doanld Trump — expressed increasing concern about spikes in utility costs and the rise of data centers. More than 77% of voters we surveyed in the area told us they were worried about the growth of data centers, especially as it impacted their electric bills. Nationally, the Wall Street Journal reported that 56% of the voters they polled cited data centers as a key issue in determining who to vote for in Congress. Pennsylvania Republican Reps. Ryan MacKenzie and Rob Bresnahan — both of whom took large sums from Big Tech executives — lost re-election, in part due to their pro-data center, pro-AI stances.
Rejection of data centers and a broad based fight around AI also powered Will Lawrence’s long shot win in the deep purple 7th congressional district in Michigan. Voters we spoke with were deeply skeptical of his opponent, sitting Rep. Tom Barrett, a Republican who took substantial campaign contributions from Big Tech executives and voted to stop states from regulating AI. Lawrence flipped the seat on an AI accountability platform that spoke to the pocketbook concerns of voters as well as the more pervasive fears of AI job replacement and safety.
In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, the top recipient of Palantir donations in Congress, lost her race, as did Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina, who lost despite substantial support from data center companies. Democrats that cozied up to Big Tech also lost: Jimmy Gomez, a California pro-tech Democrat lost to a progressive in an “AI proxy battle.”Our analysis shows that about half of all incumbents that took money from Palantir Technologies lost their races this year — six out of the top eight recipients of money from Palantir executives lost. And in a shocking twist, one of the largest AI Super PACs, Leading the Future, run by Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale and OpenAI CEO Greg Brockman, pulled back their investments just weeks before the midterms because of concern their support would hurt, not boost, candidates. 
Across the country, voters came out to demand a say in what happens in their neighborhoods and towns, and an America they can afford, where rights are respected, kids are safe, and local economies are thriving. Where technology makes life better, not worse. And where elected officials are not in the pockets of corporate giants.
As Democrats take back control of Congress, now is the time to set a vision and comprehensive plan for AI in our country. We are at a critical juncture. Democrats must use their investigatory powers to bring AI CEOs before Congress to demand answers on safety breaches, out of control surveillance, and the impact of AI on workers and families. 
Now is the time to advance a vision for AI safety and regulation that includes public oversight and real public enforcement, a jobs guarantee for workers who fear being left behind by automation, and a plan to tax AI companies so that working people can share in the increased productivity. 
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.

Thank you.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.title: Trump Intel Pick Calls $1 Million Bribe for a Pardon a “Complicated Legal Question”
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.text:
Asked at a Wednesday confirmation hearing whether the law allowed people to give the president a $1 million bribe in exchange for a pardon, a White House attorney up for a major intelligence job said it was a “complicated legal question.”
Gary Lawkowski, who advised President Donald Trump in office and on the campaign trail, faced tough questioning from Democrats during his Wednesday hearing to serve as general counsel to the Office of Director of National Intelligence.
The hearing came as Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., sought to rush Lawkowski’s confirmation to the top intelligence posting before the end of the year, when Democrats take over Congress.
Although Lawkowski drew no hostile questions from Republicans, Democratic senators were concerned about Lawkowski’s role in Trump’s pardon spree, as well as his involvement in controversial executive orders that directed federal law enforcement to crack down on the left and designate antifa as a domestic terror organization.
“We’re looking for judgment here,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “And I understand: You were just the lawyer. But so many times, ‘I was just the lawyer’ kind of becomes the default answer.”
Lawkowski’s current position is deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president. He was little known outside the White House before Trump nominated him earlier this month to serve at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, a Cabinet-level department where he would coordinate legal advice for the 18 different agencies making up the intelligence community.
According to a questionnaire, Lawkowski has not held jobs at intelligence agencies before. His prior national security experience involves advising Trump on classified matters over the past two years.
He also has a long-standing relationship with Trump. During Trump’s time out of the White House, he helped provided legal advice to the president’s reelection campaign and defended him from lawsuits brought by people harmed during the January 6 insurrection.
Questioning His Record
During the Senate hearing, Warner criticized Trump’s pardons for January 6 rioters and for crypto mogul Changpeng Zhao. The crypto tycoon’s company Binance was involved in a transaction that benefited one of the Trump family’s crypto ventures.
Lawkowski suggested that prior reporting in the New York Times had exaggerated his role in the pardon process.
“My main focus was litigation and policy,” he said. “I’m actually not our primary pardon counsel. I have worked on some pardon issues.”
Sen. Angus King, an independent from Maine who caucuses with the Democrats, pressed Lawkowski on whether it would be illegal for someone to walk into the Oval Office and hand the president a $1 million bribe for a pardon.
“That’s OK?” King said.
“Well, bribery itself would be a separate statutory crime. How that would interact with presidential immunity would be a complicated legal question that I think the court kind of reserved in that case,” he said, referring to a 2024 Supreme Court decision that granted the president broad immunity from prosecution for official acts.
Another senator zeroed in on Lawkowski’s role in crafting National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, commonly known as NSPM-7, the executive order directing federal law enforcement agencies to target “antifa” and other boogeymen of the far right.
In the written questionnaire, Lawkowski said he was involved in “communications” regarding that order and another that purported to designate antifa — the loose-knit anti-fascist movement — as a domestic terror group. He declined to explain further, citing the confidentiality of his legal conversations with the president.
“There is no basis in law to designate a domestic terrorist organization, but you have claimed the president can just do it anyways based on some magical constitutional authority,” said Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. “Once he’s operating outside the law, are there any limits to how Donald Trump can persecute Americans?”
“I don’t agree with the premise that the president is acting outside of the law,” Lawkowski said. “Of course, the president is constrained by the limits of the Constitution.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
