Share This Article
“When he was running for mayor, Mr. Mamdani said he’d work on collecting fines the city was owed as part of finding funding for policy proposals like universal childcare. The time is here.”
Many times over many years, I have pointed out—to mayors, the City Council, state elected officials, at Charter Commission and city agency hearings, community board and Civic Association meetings, even in letters to editors—that there are hundreds of millions in unpaid Department of Buildings and Environmental Control Board (DOB/ECB) fines. I found this out via freedom of information requests to the City’s Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) several years ago. Nothing has been done.
With the recent, tragic building collapse on Brooklyn’s major Flatbush Avenue attracting so much attention, perhaps it’s finally time to wake up.
In fact, there is this clause in NYC’s Charter chapter 45A, re. “Environmental Control Board” section 1049-a(d) (1)(i): “A judgment entered pursuant to this paragraph shall remain in full force and effect for eight years.” I have argued for its repeal—finding that many officials are unaware of it.
I have not been able to find out exactly when, how and why this sentence came to be in the City Charter. Keep in mind that real estate developers are prime donors to campaigns for candidates running for city and state office. Indeed, imagine a candidate for, say City Council, asking developers for campaign contributions one day and the next introducing a bill to collect on their long-overdue violations?
If you check the city’s Buildings Information Systems site and enter the address of a building with a history of violations, you are bound to come across the phase “written off” for fines levied more than eight years ago, even where a dangerous condition existed.
While recognizing that real estate development is an important sector, and does contribute to the economy in many ways, I submit that it should not hold so much influence that it is able to control elected officials in order to get whatever it wants—or ignore “Stop Work Orders” at construction sites.
While more affordable housing clearly is needed, I have seen Brooklyn neighborhoods become unaffordable with the creation of high-end condos and “starter castles” (a term borrowed from former City Councilman Tony Avella when he visited us).
Whether it’s former Mayors Bill de Blasio’s Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (MIH) and Zoning for Quality and Affordability (ZQA) or Eric Adams’ “City of Yes” initiatives, they actually are developer dreams. Ask homeowners and you’d learn that the initiatives do nothing for preserving the character and safety of neighborhoods.
So, now my question: will the attention to and investigation of this Flatbush building collapse force Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the City Council, along with NY State Assembly and Senate oversight committees, to finally push the City’s Department of Finance to stop making excuses and aggressively pursue owed fines, and the Department of Buildings to assure that accompanying violations are fully addressed?
Furthermore, besides—very importantly—trying to prevent more avoidable tragedies like this building collapse, imagine adding nearly hundreds of millions to the city’s budget?
After all, when he was running for mayor, Mr. Mamdani said he’d work on collecting fines the city was owed as part of finding funding for policy proposals like universal childcare. The time is here.
Ed Jaworski is president of the Madison-Marine-Homecrest Civic Association and co-founder of the Brooklyn Neighborhood Congress.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.title: Just Rinse It Off, Army Says Before Blowing Up Five Tons of Lead Compound
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.author: Austin Campbell
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.text:
When the U.S. Army blows up nearly five tons of unstable lead azide in southeastern Iowa on Friday, blanketing communities in lead-containing particles up to 100 miles away, it has a simple solution for concerned Iowans: Just rinse it off.
“The good thing is, if people have concerns about it being on their property, all they have to do is hose that off, and it’s gone,” Army spokesperson Justine Barati told Radio Iowa earlier this week.
This won’t be sufficient to mitigate the harm of the toxic plume the Army plans to release, environmental health experts based in Iowa told The Intercept. And, while the Army’s publicly released dispersion modeling shows that airborne lead particles could travel northeast from the detonation site near Burlington, Iowa, as far as Maquoketa, the experts found the Army’s modeling incomplete.
Burlington is in southeastern Iowa, just west of the Mississippi River and the Illinois border. Because the Army’s plume modeling is a prediction based on anticipated weather conditions, changes in wind speed or direction could carry lead-containing particles into neighboring Illinois, even if the published projection does not show that path.
“They put out this plume model, which is basically a colored blob, so to speak, on a map,” said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa. “What they didn’t show was the projected or estimated concentration of settled dust within that plume.”
That settled dust will come from lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive commonly used in detonators. The Army has been storing the material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in a water-and-ethanol solution intended to keep it stable, but dangerous crystals formed during storage, according to an Army environmental assessment The Intercept found using the military’s Digital Visual Information Distribution System. Army officials determined that the resulting instability made the material too hazardous to move or transport, leaving an in-place detonation as their best option for disposal.
Now, the Army is warning residents and workers within the areas identified on its projected airborne exposure map to remain indoors, close windows and doors, and adjust air conditioning systems to prevent outside air from entering their homes “until the plume passes.” Children and pregnant individuals are among those specifically warned to avoid outdoor exposure.
O’Shaughnessy said the airborne plume could dissipate within hours, potentially ending the immediate inhalation hazard by Friday evening. But residents may not know how long they need to take precautions.
“Should I stay indoors all weekend? You know, the public doesn’t know, and no fault of theirs,” he said.
The Army environmental assessment shows that military officials considered several alternatives to Friday’s detonation, including chemically neutralizing the explosives or transporting them to an existing demolition facility, both of which were rejected as too dangerous. The Army also warned that leaving the explosives in storage could leave them to blow up by accident — and indefinitely disrupt the installation’s ability to make new ammunition.
The assessment does not establish how long the explosives had been stored, whether their deterioration was detected before March, or whether earlier intervention could have prevented them from becoming too dangerous to handle.
The Environmental Protection Agency, which issued an emergency permit authorizing the detonation, said the risk of an accidental explosion presented an “imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.”
“The Army, which has unparalleled expertise in matters concerning explosives safety, concluded that this material cannot safely be handled or moved and therefore, cannot be treated by any method other than in-place detonation,” an EPA spokesperson told The Intercept.
The permit requires the Army to notify potentially affected communities, conduct environmental sampling before and after the detonation, clean up contaminated areas, and report its findings to the EPA. At the University of Iowa, which is 60 miles away and not in the predicted pathway, researchers hadn’t gotten details about how that monitoring would be conducted, O’Shaughnessy said.
“We don’t know where it’s going to be conducted. We don’t know what instrumentation they’re going to use or how they’re going to report the information,” he said. Researchers there are preparing to assess the consequences independently, including by measuring potential lead contamination and conducting their own plume modeling.
The Army’s environmental assessment also acknowledges that contaminants from the detonation could enter waterways through stormwater runoff or seep into groundwater.
It’s clear, said Peter S. Thorne, professor emeritus of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, that washing away lead dust would not eliminate the contamination.
“Hosing lead dust off of cars and other surfaces will indeed move it to the soil or into surface water,” he told The Intercept. “This could lead to human and animal exposure beyond inhalation of the generated lead dust plume.”
Asked what scientific evidence supported the advice to hose lead dust off residential property, the Army did not provide any studies or technical analysis. Instead, it said the EPA had provided cleanup guidelines as a condition of the emergency permit.
In an environmental handout prepared for an Oct. 15 community open house, the Army acknowledged that the detonation could damage nearby homes and contaminate surrounding property. The military said it would conduct environmental sampling on private property with homeowners’ permission and clean up lead contamination exceeding regulatory thresholds. It also acknowledged that cleanup operations could temporarily disrupt agricultural leases.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has found that no safe blood lead level in children has been identified. Even low levels of exposure can harm children’s brain development and ability to learn.
Asked what concentrations of airborne lead it expected in surrounding communities, the Army did not provide specific projections. Instead, it pointed to naturally occurring lead in soil and contamination associated with leaded gasoline, lead-based paint, and hazardous waste sites. Asked about plans to monitor potential long-term health effects, Barati, the Army spokesperson, said only: “We do not anticipate long-term health impacts.”
O’Shaughnessy recommended testing surfaces in communities affected by the plume, including playground equipment, every three or four days for approximately a month to determine whether lead contamination persists after airborne particles have settled. “You can’t just sugarcoat this,” he said.
The Army’s assurances come against a documented history of lead contamination at military installations, including cases in which officials failed to address known hazards.
A 2018 Reuters investigation found that children living in Army housing had been exposed to hazardous lead paint, with military medical records documenting more than 1,000 elevated blood lead tests among young children processed by one Army medical center between 2011 and 2016. The investigation also found failures to report some test results to state health authorities.
Additionally, a 2024 investigation by The Intercept found that the Army National Guard had failed to adequately remediate lead contamination at armories used by soldiers and civilians, including children. A 2020 Army audit obtained by The Intercept found that 73 of 83 indoor firing ranges examined in New Jersey, North Carolina, and Ohio had not undergone thorough remediation or the required evaluations of lead hazards.
At New Jersey armories, officials had used high-pressure washing to remove lead contamination, despite a 2020 Army audit warning that the method was prohibited because it could embed lead throughout facilities and generate hazardous waste.
Asked whether earlier intervention could have prevented the explosives from deteriorating to the point that detonation became the safest available option, the Army did not answer directly. Instead, it referred The Intercept to previously published information about the operation.
“It strikes me that this is a case of neglect leading to only bad choices available to avoid a catastrophe,” Thorne said.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

Trump’s Man on the Inside
Before the balance of power shifts in Congress, the president hopes to ram through the appointment of a MAGA crony to federal office.
One of the more unsightly traditions on Capitol Hill is what might be called the lame-duck end run. As congressional power prepares to shift to a new majority, the executive branch seizes on its fleeting influence in the national legislature to ram through a regress of high-priority bills and nominations to ride out the balance of its term.
With historic new Democratic majorities poised to take power, and with the Trump administration being the Trump administration, Congress’s lame-duck session has become subject to a singularly ghoulish and unrestrained power grab. There is, just for starters, the unseemly rush to ram through the mendaciously titled Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—a deregulatory bonanza for AI data centers, gas and oil interests, and real-estate fiefdoms, which claimed pride of place in the Project 2025 governing blueprint for the right. There’s been a cluster of truly abhorrent and unqualified nominees to the federal bench, gaveled through to hasty confirmation. There’s also been the preemptive campaign on the part of recess-appointed US Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz to browbeat incoming Democratic committee chairs in Congress with entirely bogus threats of prosecution for doing basic oversight of White House malfeasance and abuses in the 120th Congress.
But perhaps the most outlandish lame-duck putsch from the Trump White House is its wonkiest one: In a bid to permanently throttle the critical appropriations process it has completely subverted while in power, the Trump administration is seeking to ram through the nomination of Eric Ueland, Russell Vought’s deputy at the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), to be head of the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
I realize that this cluster of bland and noun-heavy agency names is a prompt to close this tab with a heavy sigh. But this appointment would be highly consequential; in the warrens of federal budget oversight, the GAO holds enormous influence. It’s the bipartisan body that Congress chartered in 1921 to ensure that the money it spends is fairly and competently dispersed. Even as the process of funding the government has descended into rudderless ideological bloodsport, the GAO has managed, against all odds, to bring reliable oversight and accountability to bear on the main activity of the government—redistributing resources in the interests of the common good. It called out risks of fraud in Obamacare health exchanges, tracked abuses in Covid loan programs, and documented repeated failures to properly disburse funds approved by Congress in the second Trump White House. Its track record, in other words, bespeaks a rarity in American governance: a body of dedicated and genuinely nonpartisan guardians of the public interest, documenting fraudulent practices and demanding accountability for them.
Which is why, of course, the Trump administration hates the GAO. Throughout his nihilist tenure dating back to the first Trump White House, Ueland’s former boss, Russell Vought, has been on the warpath against the GAO, calling it a “quasi-legislative independent entity” that shouldn’t exist at all. Last year, he issued a memo to OMB staff to stop deferring to GAO requests and oversight initiatives—a directive that basically sidesteps a 1982 law holding that White House agencies must formulate accounting and budgeting protocols in conjunction with the GAO.
It’s not hard to see where Vought’s animus comes from. Since the second Trump administration came to power last year, the GAO has conducted at least 46 investigations into improper impoundment of appropriated funds by the White House, and documented several actionable abuses. The agency is the only body empowered by Congress to sue the executive branch on its behalf, but its former chief comptroller, Gene Dodaro, resigned at the end of last year, and his interim successor, Orice Brown, hasn’t initiated any legal proceedings in her caretaker regime. The GAO also denounced Vought’s illegal decision to take down OMB’s apportionment Web page, which tracks how much money Congress appropriates, on the flimsy and decidedly nonstatutory pretext that such spending disclosures inhibit federal deliberations over matters of national security—arguably the most phoned-in rationale for an executive branch action since the heyday of Elon Musk and Big Balls in the DOGEsphere.
Ueland’s nomination as the next chief comptroller is thus a clear escalation of the White House’s crusade to continue steamrolling the budget process out of all reach of congressional accountability. As a nominee who’d previously served in a Republican White House—in addition to his present post, he was policy adviser and legislative director in the first Trump administration—Ueland would represent a firm break with the GAO’s scrupulously nonpartisan leadership profile. In the questionnaire he completed for his OMB post, he endorsed Vought’s deranged impoundment mandate, and he has proven a loyal lieutenant in the broader MAGA war on governance. Just last week at a public administrators’ conference, he announced that the Trump administration’s reshaping of the federal government was “long overdue.” Ueland would basically take over with the same de facto agenda as Education Secretary Linda McMahon: to effectively dismantle the agency under his direction. His first order of business would doubtless be to squelch any pending legal actions against Trump administration officials (first and foremost Vought) for improperly impounding funds appropriated by Congress.
As with the other sketchy nominees thrust into this lame duck, Senate Republicans have put Ueland forward with a scandalous lack of basic due diligence. By law, the Senate chair of the Committee on Homeland Security and Government Affairs—Kentucky GOP Senator Rand Paul—is required to convene a bipartisan panel of 10 members to put forward nominees and weigh their qualifications ahead of scheduled confirmation hearings. None of that happened in Ueland’s case; instead, Paul shared a short list of prospective nominees, including Ueland, with the Senate panel on last week’s Veteran’s Day holiday, giving members until 8 pm that day to respond. Democratic members decried the rushed presentation as a “sham”—an altogether generous designation for a White House–ordered hit job on the GAO. This procedural chicanery has prompted the last two comptroller generals to call for a suspension of Thursday’s Ueland hearings, so that Paul’s committee can go back to square one in identifying and vetting a viable candidate field, while 21 former inspector generals have submitted a letter to Paul and his committee’s ranking member, Gary Peters, opposing Ueland’s nomination.
It’s also little wonder that Paul himself has stopped short of any formal endorsement of the nomination, telling reporters only that “I think it’s important to find someone who’s honest and objective.” (Memo to Paul: If you think these criteria apply to Ueland, you are on the verge of a colossal self-own.) Pressed for details about the nomination process, Paul conceded that he put Ueland forward at the White House’s request; when asked if he’d pushed back in any way, he offered this peremptory brush off: “That’s all I’ve got for you.”
Paul’s weary disclaimer is a broader admission of across-the-board noncompliance from today’s MAGAfied GOP as it prepares to sink into legislative irrelevance. If Ueland were to be confirmed, he’d serve a 15-year term—the comptroller’s de facto lifetime appointment representing, ironically in this case, the position’s stolidly nonpartisan mandate. For an American electorate that voted out Trump’s party on grounds of rampant corruption in the 2026 midterms, placing Gary Ueland atop the GAO would be a crowning “fuck you” from the same sold-out political formation that gave us Russell Vought, appropriations thief and aspiring science-grant denier. As an ardent Christian nationalist, Vought anticipates that a new millennium will bring his punitive social vision to pass, but the Trump administration and the lame-duck Congress are working overtime to hand him a 15-year Reich.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/freedma.text:
A Seat of One's Own
Their company has collected millions in public support and touts its second-chance hiring. But workers at Freedman Seating Company—which makes seats for Chicago trains and buses—say the jobs leave them stuck. They want a binding agreement that gives them a real voice and a seat at the negotiating table.
J. Patrick Patterson
CHICAGO—On the city’s deindustrialized West Side, the more-than-century-old Freedman Seating Company is one of the largest remaining manufacturing firms, employing more than 700 workers to make seats for city buses and trains.
But despite the company’s storied past — and millions of dollars in public support and contracts — labor advocates say it’s failing to provide real economic opportunity for community members.
On Oct. 21, a group of labor organizers and allies tried delivering a letter to Freedman’s leadership, demanding they sit down and negotiate a deal for workers.
After a few knocks at the door, a company representative answered but refused to accept the letter. She did, however, agree to reach out within 10 days, according to Edie Jacobs.
Jacobs, director of Get to Work, an organization that connects West Side residents with local jobs, was at the front of the group. “If we don’t hear from them in 10 days, then we got to come back,” she told In These Times in the parking lot.
The letter asks Freedman to negotiate a community benefits agreement (CBA), a legally binding deal between a company and community and labor groups.
“We want to make sure Freedman is a real opportunity for workers on the West Side of Chicago, an area where too few of our people are able to access stable, gainful employment,” the authors write.
Freedman has a reputation in the community for hiring people coming out of prison. Organizers, researchers and workers say that reputation conceals a harsher reality: People from disadvantaged backgrounds — ones with records, in particular — have few places to go, and that makes them easy to exploit.
About 35 people had assembled that afternoon in Augusta Park, on the West Side, to announce a campaign to win a CBA for Freedman workers. Many belong to the Good Work Coalition, a group of local community organizations, religious leaders and labor groups.
Freedman’s workers “are subjected to low wages and hazardous working conditions with no voice to fix it,” said Leone Jose Bicchieri, founder of Working Family Solidarity, at the rally. “We want a binding agreement that creates real partnership with the community for local hire, training and for workers to have a fair process to organize a union without fear of retaliation.”
Lippert Components bought Freedman in April 2025. Federal antitrust regulators are now reviewing a proposed merger between Lippert’s parent company, LCI Industries, and Patrick Industries. The Justice Department requested additional documents from both companies on Oct. 9, a step beyond initial review that extends the waiting period. Shareholders of both firms are scheduled to vote on the deal Nov. 18. 
LOW WAGES, SAFETY ISSUES, NO VOICE
The march followed the release of a report from Jobs to Move America (JMA), a national policy and research organization. The report, published in October, documents low wages, hazardous working conditions, limited opportunities for growth and lack of employee voice.
JMA’s research — completed in collaboration with the University of Illinois at Chicago’s Center for Urban Economic Development — includes survey responses from 116 Freedman manufacturing workers.
“You have to work overtime nonstop and slave yourself to be able to afford living,” says Max, a current Freedman worker who spoke with In These Times outside the facility. He asked to use a pseudonym to protect him from employer retaliation.
The factory is located on Chicago’s West Side, a largely Black and Latino area affected by historic disinvestment. Its workforce includes welders, polishers and sewers, among other positions.
Max works with metal to help make seats for the company’s transit market. As a grinder and polisher, he’s exposed to airborne metal dust and debris, including carbon, silica from the abrasive belts and “hex chrome six,” or hexavalent chromium, an extremely toxic chemical applied to metal to prevent rust.
“There are filter machines,” says Max, “but since I’ve started working in that department, I’ve been told that they don’t even work.”
In 2019, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration issued two serious citations to the company for failing to provide adequate chemical hazard training, including how to safely work with hexavalent chromium. Initial penalties of $11,366 were reduced to $7,000 in an informal settlement, according to public records.
Working with hexavalent chromium without proper training or safety gear can lead to serious long-term health issues, including lung cancer, eye damage, liver and kidney damage and asthma attacks.
Some workers surveyed by JMA also reported that the lack of air conditioning in the summer makes it difficult to wear masks. Eighty-one percent noticed at least one hazard in the past year, such as water reaching electrical equipment and welding machine cords held together with “many, many layers of electrical tape.” A polisher quoted in the report spoke of “worn out tools” that make it difficult to hit requested quotas. “Superiors don’t listen to concerns we voice to avoid complications ahead of time,” the worker said.
Freedman did not address specific questions about safety from In These Times, but said in a statement that, “Safety remains a top priority, supported by robust training, reporting and environmental health and safety programs.” The company also says it encourages “open communication” and provides “multiple avenues for employees to raise questions, share feedback and voice concerns without fear of retaliation.” 
PUBLIC MONEY, PRIVATE OWNERS
Freedman has benefited from millions in state and local subsidies. In January 2024, the company received $11 million in tax credits from the Chicago Development Fund to buy and improve a 263,400-square-foot building and expand its manufacturing operation. In November 2024, it won renewed Cook County property tax relief and a state tax credit agreement tied to 50 new jobs and 676 retained ones.
“As a major Chicago manufacturer that serves public-sector customers and has benefited from taxpayer-supported incentives and financing,” the report’s author writes, “Freedman has a particular responsibility to provide jobs that deliver meaningful economic opportunity to workers and the surrounding community.”
The company has kept its doors open throughout several waves of plant closures that have swept the city. “But is that the best that we can expect from them for the public contracts and the tax incentives that we dole out? That they just stay open and exist?” asked Marcos Feldman, senior researcher at JMA and author of the report, at the rally. “All of that public support makes the quality of the jobs back here at this factory a matter of public concern.”
Feldman says the community would also benefit from more scrutiny of Freedman itself as it enters this new phase of ownership. “Public support for manufacturing shouldn’t just preserve those jobs, but also has to improve, monitor and enforce job quality,” he says. “Continued public support has to be tied to clear, enforceable commitments around the quality of those jobs.”
Freedman workers tried organizing in 2019, but the company’s campaign helped defeat the effort, Feldman told In These Times. Department of Labor filings show Freedman signed a May 2019 agreement with LRI Consulting Services for “pre-petition campaign consulting,” a service whose stated goals included preventing petitions for a union election. Freedman reported paying LRI nearly $65,000 that year.
The company did not respond to specific questions about previous organizing efforts, but said in its statement that it “has been a committed member of Chicago’s West Side business community for more than 30 years, and JMA’s recent report does not accurately reflect our workplace culture, values or the experience of our employees.” 
A SECOND CHANCE?
Freedman is widely recognized for its long-standing “fair-chance” or “second-chance” programs, through which it hires formerly incarcerated people. Around 30% of the workers surveyed by JMA were formerly incarcerated or involved in reentry or parole programs.
“Consistent with our longstanding commitment to local hiring and fair-chance employment, we invest in our people through competitive wages and benefits, training and opportunities for advancement,” Freedman told In These Times.
“It sounds great,” said Jacobs at the rally, “but what’s the real story?” A retired probation officer, she’s spent years finding jobs for West Siders. “It’s not a real chance if you can’t even pay people enough to live.”
Felix, another pseudonym, has worked for Freedman for more than a decade and says his $21/hour pay is not enough to get by. “People are basically trying to make ends meet. They’re living paycheck to paycheck. Sometimes the paycheck doesn’t even last a full week. Mine doesn’t.”
Managers have brought up workers’ records on the factory floor, according to Felix: “They’ll tell them, ‘Good luck trying to find another job. You have a record.’” He says he has gone to HR about comments like this and was dismissed. 
“They make it so very obvious that we’re not listened to.”
Feldman says that vulnerability is actually the point. A stigma attached to records limits where people can work, he says, weakening their bargaining power and keeping them trapped in low-wage work. “And they kind of take advantage of that,” says Feldman. “We know that they get tax breaks for hiring formerly incarcerated folks as a federal program, so they have their incentive to hire these folks, but they can’t go anywhere else.”
“Your wages, according to the data we collected, really only go up $1 or $2, which is nothing compared to inflation,” he adds. “There’s no forward advancement in your career, and you’re kind of stuck. … It doesn’t seem like a real second chance.”
Research on the federal subsidy behind many fair-chance programs points in a similar direction. A 2025 Brookings Institution report found that the Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC), which pays employers up to $2,400 per qualifying worker, does not meaningfully influence who gets hired. “Large employers regularly hire lots of workers for low-wage jobs, and in the process, hire WOTC qualifying workers totally by accident,” the report found. In other words, a handful of corporations receive millions of dollars for employing workers they would have hired anyway.
Legal scholar Noah Katz writes in Inquest that “carceral labor is not a problem confined to the prison.” He describes a “carceral labor continuum” in which the prison system’s influence extends into the conventional labor market. For Felix and his coworkers, that influence has shown up in offhand managerial warnings on the shop floor.
FIGHTING FOR A BETTER DEAL
Workers and organizers across the country have benefited from CBAs, and the coalition points to some of them as models.
In Chicago, a coalition signed a 2016 CBA with CRRC Sifang America, a railcar manufacturer that was building a plant on the city’s Southeast Side to assemble train cars for the Chicago Transit Authority. As part of the agreement, the company created a hiring pipeline for residents facing barriers to employment.
In Alabama, community and labor groups negotiated a 2022 agreement with bus manufacturer New Flyer. The company committed to hiring at least 45% of new workers from historically disadvantaged groups, including people with criminal records. New Flyer agreed to stay neutral during unionization efforts. In 2024, workers at the Anniston, Ala., plant ratified a first union contract providing for raises of 15 – 38%, more paid time off, improved parental leave and better retirement benefits, among other wins.
Chicago built its reputation on steel, rail and meatpacking and on fights for workers’ rights. It was here, in 1886, that a strike for the eight-hour day led to the Haymarket affair, an event that gave rise to International Workers’ Day, or May Day.
“Behind the walls of Freedman Seating, there are men and women who show up every day and do what working people have always done in this city,” said Bret Rocchietti, organizer for Sheet Metal Workers’ Local Union 73, at the rally. “They build. They weld. They fabricate. … Today we are here because the people who build those products are asking for something every worker deserves: a voice, a fair shot and dignity on the job.”
After being ushered away from the office by a security guard, the group walked a few blocks around the corner to where workers arrive for their shift. They set up an inflatable Fat Cat, a cousin of Scabby the Rat, holding money in one fist and choking a worker with the other.
Organizers passed out flyers as workers came and went. Cars, trucks and fire engines honked while passing by. People gathered on either side of the driveway in front of chain-link fences topped with barbed wire, and others crossed Chicago Avenue to line the sidewalk with their signs from the rally.
Some cars sped away, eager to leave the lot, but many accepted a flyer explaining the CBA demand.
As of publication, a spokesperson for JMA says Freedman has made no effort to meet with the coalition. 
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/deat.title: After Democrats’ Midterm Romp, What’s Stopping Governors From Commuting Death Sentences?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/deat.author: Liliana Segura
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/deat.text:
Grace Hanna was preparing to drive from Tallahassee to the Florida State Prison in Raiford when she got an email sharing momentous news from across the country: California Gov. Gavin Newsom had announced he would commute the sentences of everyone under a death sentence in his state, sparing the lives of 548 people — roughly a quarter of the nation’s death row population.
It was Thursday, November 5, just hours before Florida was scheduled to kill 63-year-old Jesse Guardado, the 19th person put to death in the state’s death chamber this year. Hanna was going to stand outside the prison for the execution night vigil, as she has done repeatedly since becoming executive director of Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty.
News of the commutations capped off what Hanna called “a complicated week.” The “blue tsunami” that transformed the electoral map across the country just two days earlier stopped short of the Sunshine State, where gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, who supports the death penalty, narrowly beat a Democrat who backed a moratorium on executions. In a number of other active death penalty states, voters elected new governors and flipped legislatures, opening new pathways toward curbing the death penalty that seemed previously beyond reach. Even Texas, the death row capital of the country, was now about to be in the hands of a Democratic governor on record as opposing executions.
“It’s a hard night to be on death row in Florida right now,” Hanna later told vigil attendees after Guardado was declared dead at 6:13 p.m. The disconnect between Florida’s assembly-line executions and the week’s events made the prospect of progress seem painfully elusive.
Florida was not alone in this regard. Guardado’s execution was one of three carried out in the U.S. on November 5. Just after midnight, Indiana killed Jeffrey Weisheit at the state penitentiary in Michigan City, the fourth person put to death since the state resumed executions in December 2024. And within an hour of Guardado’s execution, Alabama killed Michael Taylor, with Republican Gov. Kay Ivey releasing a pointed statement aimed at Newsom. “California may let their criminals escape justice, but not Alabama,” she said. “Here, we enforce the law and always will.”
The executions were largely overlooked amid the frenzy of the midterms. Most Americans ignore the death penalty “except when something happens that’s big enough to get attention,” said Abe Bonowitz, head of Death Penalty Action. A veteran organizer who has helped steer successful legislative campaigns to abolish the death penalty in five different states, Bonowitz was driving back home from Indiana after leading a vigil during Weisheit’s execution when he got a text notification about Newsom’s commutations. “My focus really that day was making sure that the world was aware that there were three executions going on,” he said. The commutations cut through news coverage of the midterms in a way the executions had not.
The commutations also offered an important counternarrative to what has seemed like an American reembrace of capital punishment in the last several years. After a steady downward slide since a peak in 1999, when 98 people were put to death across the U.S., executions reached a historic low of 11 in 2021. In the following years, executions creeped back upward. Then the number of people put to death nearly doubled, jumping from 25 in 2024 to 47 in 2025. Although the total for 2026 will be lower, with 37 executions carried out so far, two more people are set to die tonight — and at least three additional executions are scheduled to be carried out before the end of the year.
The recent jump in executions can be largely traced to Florida, which accounts for more than half of the people put to death this year. Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis restarted executions in 2023, just before his failed presidential bid; Florida gives the governor far more power to set execution dates than other states. As death penalty lawyer Maria DeLiberato told me last year, “He just picks somebody, and then 30 days later they’re dead.”
DeSantis’s ongoing killing spree paints a distorted picture of the death penalty as a whole. Florida is an outlier, not an emblem, of the state of capital punishment, argues veteran attorney Robert Dunham, who has tracked death penalty trends for decades. In his view, Newsom’s commutations, coupled with the “seismic change in the political landscape in the midterm elections,” should empower other politicians to take more decisive actions that reflect this reality.
“The Trump administration and other vocal extremists have created this smokescreen suggesting that capital punishment is on the rise,” Dunham said. “Sometimes seismic explosions create more smoke, and sometimes they clear it away. And I think the elections may have cleared away that smokescreen.”
Indeed, last week a new Gallup poll found support for the death penalty below 50 percent, a drop from recent surveys. Conducted immediately after Tennessee’s botched lethal injection of Christa Pike — which was followed by backlash to Trump’s now-cancelled plans to livestream a military execution — the new poll was almost certainly shaped by the controversies. But such high-profile events can have lasting impacts. “Once something reaches the public consciousness, and it reaches it in a way that is so devastating, it’s hard to undo that,” Dunham said.
Viewed from afar, Newsom’s commutations seemed instantly emblematic of a new era, in which Democratic leaders might take bold actions that might have been previously unthinkable. While a campaign urging him to grant commutations had been underway for years, to critics, Newsom’s announcement was seen as plainly political — a maneuver designed to suit his presidential ambitions.
The idea that granting clemency to hundreds of people on death row might help, not hurt, a political campaign is itself a break from conventional wisdom, however. Since Bill Clinton famously witnessed the 1992 execution of Ricky Ray Rector in Arkansas while on the campaign trail, Democrats have either embraced capital punishment or run away from the issue. Although the party’s 2016 platform declared that “we will abolish the death penalty, which has proven to be a cruel and unusual form of punishment,” the Democrats’ 2024 platform eliminated any mention of capital punishment.
Until recently, the most significant mass commutation was carried out by a Republican: Illinois Gov. George Ryan, who in 2003 spared the lives of 167 people on death row and granted pardons to four. It would take more than two decades for anything remotely equivalent. In 2024, outgoing president Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 people on federal death row, leaving three people facing execution. Soon afterward, Democratic North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper commuted 15 death sentences on his final day in office (a relative fraction of the state’s condemned population). And in Oregon in 2025, Democratic Gov. Kate Brown commuted the sentences of 17 people in the state.
The commutations by Cooper and Brown came out of states in which executions had not been carried out in many years. Likewise, Newsom’s actions were undoubtedly made easier by the fact that California has not executed anyone since 2006. Although the governor has a long history of opposing the death penalty — and imposed an official moratorium in 2019 — his actions certainly took electoral politics into account. “The governor has made no secret that he’s thinking about running for president,” said veteran activist Natasha Minsker, the head of the California Anti-Death Penalty Coalition, which spearheaded the campaign for commutations.
The result was both monumental — the single largest commutation in U.S. history — while also cementing the status quo. In a state where the death chamber itself was dismantled nearly eight years ago, even the term “death row” is a misnomer in California. Over the last few years, condemned men and women have been moved out of the housing units that once kept them separated from the rest of the prison population and into the general population.
Still, Newsom’s commutations are not yet a done deal. Under the state constitution, the governor cannot unilaterally grant clemency to people with multiple felony convictions. Two-thirds of the commutations must be approved by the state Supreme Court. Dueling press conferences over the past two weeks have featured victims’ family members speaking to both sides of the issue, while many of California’s elected district attorneys have decried the commutations.
But the reality is that many people — inside and outside California — are likely only vaguely aware of the significance of Newsom’s actions. “If you were to just ask the person on the street, they would say we don’t have the death penalty,” said Minsker. “I have had numerous legislators say to me, ‘But we don’t have the death penalty in California.’ Some of them even think Governor Newsom already got rid of it.”
The sense that capital punishment exists more in theory than in reality is prevalent in much of the rest of the country. While the death penalty remains the law of the land in 27 states, many have not carried out executions for years. Some of these include places with the largest death row populations. In Pennsylvania, for example, where the last execution took place in 1999, the Department of Corrections counts nearly 100 people still on death row.
In theory, a governor like Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro should be an ideal candidate to follow in Newsom’s footsteps. Shapiro, a Democrat who is also rumored to be considering a presidential run, extended a moratorium imposed by his predecessor and has repeatedly expressed opposition to the death penalty, including during his reelection race. But his powers are limited. Pennsylvania governors can only grant clemency with the unanimous support of the state’s five-member Board of Pardons, which includes a standing slot for the state attorney general. The current attorney general, who came into office in 2025, supports the death penalty. “So you have the chief prosecuting officer of the commonwealth holding veto power over commutations,” said Dunham. It is no coincidence that “there has never been a commutation of a death row prisoner’s sentence in the modern history of Pennsylvania’s death penalty.”
By contrast, in Ohio, where more than 100 people remain on death row, Republican Gov. Mike DeWine has made clear that he plans to commute at least some death sentences before leaving office. Once the state’s attorney general, DeWine took office in 2019, less than a year after the botched execution attempt of an elderly man named Alva Campbell — the second time Ohio tried and failed to set an IV to carry out lethal injection. In February 2019, DeWine stopped an execution after a federal judge expressed concerns over evidence that condemned people were being tortured to death as a result of the state’s lethal injection protocol. After that, DeWine repeatedly exercised his clemency power, granting temporary reprieves to every person with a scheduled execution date. This had kept executions on hold for the entirety of his eight years in office. In June, he announced that he no longer supports the death penalty at all.
DeWine has fairly wide latitude to grant commutations. While he can technically only act after a recommendation by state Parole Board, the board’s decisions are not binding. Earlier this week, DeWine confirmed that he’s in the process of carefully reviewing death penalty convictions, telling the Ohio Capital Journal that he might be willing to act in cases where condemned people have been unfairly blocked from relief in the courts. “The governor has additional authority to look at that and maybe see something else that is in there,” he said, “that maybe the jury legally couldn’t have looked at or the judge legally couldn’t have looked at.”
Until recently, a governor also enjoyed latitude to grant clemency in Kentucky, where, despite ongoing attempts by the attorney general to resume lethal injections, no one has been put to death since 2008. Local anti-death penalty activists have long planned to pressure Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, another possible presidential candidate who is leaving office at the end of 2027, to commute the sentences of all 23 people on death row. But a new amendment passed as part of the midterm elections could complicate things.
The amendment was authored in response to a major scandal, after Beshear’s predecessor handed out more than 400 commutations and pardons before leaving office in 2019, including to relatives of campaign donors. Bipartisan backlash led to efforts to constrain executive clemency power; under the new amendment, Beshear is forbidden from granting commutations within 60 days of a gubernatorial election — or for 35 days afterward. The change sharply narrows the window for him to act. “It definitely gives us a sense of urgency,” the head of the Kentucky Coalition to Abolish the Death Penalty told Bolts last week.
Activist campaigns are also underway in states with smaller death penalty populations, like Kansas, which has not put anyone to death since 1965. “Kansas has not been plagued by crime despite conducting no executions over the past 61 years,” a former secretary of corrections wrote in an op-ed calling for Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly to commute the death sentences of all nine people on the state’s death row. Such an action “would simply acknowledge the reality we have lived with for decades.”
Campaigns for commutations are not limited to states the Democrats recently flipped. In Alabama, one of the country’s leading death penalty states, a new coalition is calling on outgoing Gov. Kay Ivey to grant clemency to people sentenced to death through judicial override, in which a trial judge disregards jurors’ vote for mercy to send someone to death row. Although it may seem like a long shot, Ivey herself signed legislation banning judicial override almost a decade ago — and this year she commuted the sentences of two men, sparing the life of Sonny Burton just days before he was set to die.
Still, the potential for change is perhaps even more compelling in a place like Georgia, where Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Black woman who has been critical of capital punishment, will now preside over an active death penalty state. Although Georgia’s pardon and parole board is uniquely powerful — one of a handful of state clemency boards with the sole authority to grant commutations — its five members are appointed to seven-year terms by the governor. As of now, the earliest vacancy will not be until the end of 2027, which means it will be a long time before Bottoms can choose new members who might be more inclined to show mercy to people facing execution.
But there is no state where such a change could be more transformative than in Texas, long known as the belly of the beast of capital punishment. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, a former civil rights attorney, has long said she is against the death penalty — a shattering change in itself. While Hinojosa can’t act unilaterally to grant commutations, she, too, can appoint members of the board of pardons and paroles, a body that until recently was little more than a rubber stamp for executions. Of the seven-member board, three people’s terms are set to expire in 2027, giving her the power to remake the body in a way that could turn the death penalty on its head.
For Reinaldo Dennes, who faces execution in Texas tonight, any such change will be too little too late, however. The same is true for Thomas Overton, who is set to die tonight in Florida. He will become the 20th person executed this year — a new record for the state.
Although Gov.-elect Donalds says he supports executions, abolitionists hope that he will, at the very least, slow down the pace set by DeSantis. Like people all over the country, Grace Hanna points out, Floridians are turning away from capital punishment more generally — and, as in all death penalty states, new death sentences are rare compared to what they used to be. “The reality is that juries in Florida are not sentencing people to death at nearly the rate that they were historically,” Hanna said. “The death penalty cannot sustain itself the way it’s going right now.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Jamaal Bowman’s Memoir Is Revealing About the Cost of Conviction
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Anthony Conwright
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Jamaal Bowman’s Memoir Is Revealing About the Cost of Conviction
Why we still need to rebuild the infrastructure of care.
Several lessons emerge from former representative Jamaal Bowman’s memoir, Unpolished. Chief among them is that there is a price to be paid for being Black and to the left of the Democratic Party. By early 2020s Democratic political standards, Bowman was the apotheosis of Black representation. A Black man raised by a single mother in a low-income Manhattan neighborhood, Bowman earned a doctorate in education and founded a public middle school. After his time as a school leader, Bowman entered politics. He described his 2020 political platform as “anti-poverty and anti-racist,” and supported Medicare for All and the Green New Deal, a platform that garnered endorsements from Senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren and the New York Times editorial board.
Bowman’s 2020 election followed the murder of George Floyd and the Democratic Party’s full tilt toward theatrical vows of racial solidarity. Yet when his political convictions extended beyond the borders of domestic racial justice, leading him to cosponsor legislation prohibiting American aid from supporting the murder of Palestinian children, the limits of Black representation became apparent. In 2024, as AIPAC marshaled a record-breaking, multimillion-dollar effort to unseat Bowman after his second term, Democratic leaders offered endorsement but little meaningful resistance to AIPAC’s financial onslaught, a deluge of spending and racist advertising Bowman could not overcome.
Unpolished arrives two years after Bowman’s lost bid for a third term, but Bowman does not cast AIPAC as his chief adversary. Instead, AIPAC, unlimited campaign spending, poverty, white supremacy, and unfettered free-market capitalism are manifestations of an American leviathan Bowman calls “The Hunger.” “The Hunger is a disease of the mind that inflicts all of us,” Bowman told me during an interview. “Even if you’re a white man with means at the top of that caste system, that wrote the Constitution of America, if you accept the belief that you are superior to everybody else, you’re afflicted with that disease too, and it stops you from reaching your full potential.”
Put differently, The Hunger does not consume adherents along party lines, nor does it need Republicans or white supremacy as a primer. Bowman’s memoir makes clear that one need not be a white supremacist to further an economic and political system that harms Americans in general while disproportionately harming Black Americans—one can just be a conservative Democrat.
No scene in Unpolished captures the intersection of Bowman’s life and The Hunger’s indiscriminate corruption more than a meeting between Biden and the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) on Friday, November 5, 2021, when the House was set to vote on Build Back Better and the bipartisan infrastructure bill. “Build Back Better was a reparative piece of legislation that Americans needed,” Bowman told me. “I’ve always supported truth and reconciliation for all, and reparative policy because through repairing those harms, we can unlock the full potential of the country, socially, politically, and economically.”
The bipartisan infrastructure bill would fund roads, bridges, transit, and broadband. Build Back Better would expand childcare subsidies, universal preschool, establish paid family leave, and invest in affordable housing and clean energy. House progressives had been withholding their votes for the infrastructure bill to keep pressure on Senate Democrats to pass Build Back Better.
Reading episodes of Bowman’s childhood in Unpolished, it is easy to understand why he was a stalwart supporter of Build Back Better. Bowman was around 7 years old when his grandmother, one of his primary caretakers, died of a stroke at 54. Bowman is 50. “It just hits different when you get older yourself, and you realize 54 is young as hell,” Bowman told me. Bowman’s grandmother suffered headaches for weeks and was unable to obtain and take medicine to treat high blood pressure.
“My grandmother’s story is not unlike millions of stories across America,” Bowman said. “A political system that ensures dignity and well-being of the people who pay into that system would provide universal healthcare. They’ll make sure you have your meds. They make sure those meds are delivered to your home.”
After his grandmother died, Bowman moved from the East River Houses to live with his mother in Yorkville. She had a union job as a postal worker, and the Mitchell-Lama housing program helped her obtain a rent-stabilized apartment in Knickerbaker Plaza. “Moving from East River to Yorkville felt like moving to a different universe even though the neighborhoods were only thirteen blocks apart,” Bowman writes. “The projects were confinement. Yorkville was freedom.”
Although Bowman moved, the trauma of confinement in Manhattan’s redlined East Harlem neighborhood followed. At around 19 years old, Bowman lost a childhood friend, Paul Black, to suicide. “When schools are underfunded,” Bowman told me, “they are less likely to have a mental health professional on staff.” Bowman wondered what help might have been available to Paul if his school had had the resources to offer it. Other losses followed. Another friend, Poochie, was stabbed to death. Years later, Poochie’s younger brother, Bubbles, was shot and killed. “Everything I’ve done since, I’ve tried to carry the friends I’ve lost with me,” Bowman writes.
By the time Bowman faced the infrastructure vote, he had already spent the first two decades of his professional life as a teacher and school leader, “scouring the earth for answers” to policy violence. Pain was not absent from Bowman’s learning, and as a dean of students during former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s era of punitive disciplinary policies, Bowman was tasked with enforcing measures that perpetuated harm. “My biggest frustration is that we often punish, scold, and suspend,” Bowman writes. “We never hold the system accountable. It’s the system and people within the system that create the conditions that lead to stress, hopelessness, and violence. This remains the norm in America.”
Frustrated with being a part of an academic structure that perpetuates trauma, Bowman founded CASA Middle School in the Bronx. As the founding principal, Bowman led the school to record-breaking outcomes and adopted restorative practices instead of zero-tolerance policies.
Having seen the possibilities of structural change, Bowman decided to run for Congress to hold the system accountable and advocate for the policy answers he had long sought. “Universal childcare is a major answer. Paid leave is a major answer. Affordable housing and rent stabilization—that’s a major answer,” Bowman told me. “That was all Build Back Better.”
The Senate had already passed the infrastructure bill. If the House passed it that Friday, it could go straight to President Biden’s desk. Build Back Better would still need Senator Joe Manchin’s vote in the Senate. Bowman expected to vote on both bills that day, but suddenly a group of moderate House Democrats said they wanted a Congressional Budget Office estimate before voting on the legislation. Bowman recalled feeling “hoodwinked.”
Bowman sought a coalition to vote on both bills together, only to find the consensus had largely ruptured. First, he met with the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC), but the CBC recommended decoupling the bills, passing infrastructure that day. By the time Bowman met with the Progressive Caucus (CPC), he heard colleagues in the CPC make the case for passing the infrastructure bill and coming back to Build Back Better later. That Friday was eye-opening for Bowman. “You think that if you do the right thing and you win the policy arguments and you’re coming from a human rights perspective and you’re on the right side of history, that that’s enough. But it’s not enough.”
President Biden called into the meeting to urge progressives to back the bipartisan infrastructure bill. Representative Cori Bush, Bowman recalls, challenged the president on whether he could get Manchin to support Build Back Better. “The only pushback when Biden was talking was Cori Bush,” Bowman said, recounting that Bush told Biden, “We don’t trust Joe Manchin. We don’t think you can get him on board.”
“Biden was pissed,” Bowman told me. “I could tell by his tone of voice; he sounded pissed that Cori would even question that. I want to emphasize Cori’s bravery and courage in that moment—questioning the president of the United States was palpable. I felt that in my bones because when he called, even I froze.”
After the phone call with Biden, Representative Pramila Jayapal moved toward a show of hands on taking up infrastructure separately. Representative Ilhan Omar asked for more time with her team. Bowman informed his staff he would vote no. Vice President Kamala Harris called, Bowman said, after he made up his mind. “The goal was to get me to a ‘yes’ on the infrastructure bill without Build Back Better,” Bowman told me. Still, Bowman held firm, telling Harris, “I’m gonna be a no.”

“It didn’t make sense to me,” Bowman told me. “This bill had cutting childhood poverty in half permanently. What are we talking about?”
“Why can’t we just vote on both bills? It doesn’t hurt anybody. It hurts no one except the corporate elite, and the Big Money elite,” Bowman continued. “My first term in Congress was learning that Big Money controls the House of Representatives; the corporate lobby controls the House of Representatives. When all of this was happening, I realized we’re doing this because of the money people because it made no sense that we would even decouple them.”
After the call, Bowman joined the other five members of the Squad in Representative Ayanna Pressley’s office. When they returned, Bowman recalls, Democratic colleagues in the Congressional Progressive Caucus still urged them to vote yes, but all six voted no. The bipartisan infrastructure bill passed. Two weeks later, the House passed Build Back Better with its childcare and paid leave provisions intact. Manchin announced his opposition in December, and the Senate never held a final vote. Several months later, a considerably watered-down set of social-welfare provisions cleared the Senate, with Manchin’s support, in the Inflation Reduction Act—and many of those outlays were promptly reversed by executive orders in the first days of the second Trump administration. Meanwhile, both Bowman and Bush were defeated in primary challenges—with AIPAC handpicking and delivering enormous funding advantages to their opponents.
The bruising intraparty conflicts that claimed the political careers of Black progressives in the last Democratic house majority now stand out in especially high relief after a landmark midterm vote that saw AIPAC ostracized in many high-profile House races, alongside major Democratic surges in the Black vote. While Bowman and Bush are now on the outside looking in, the new Democratic majority is under greater pressure than ever to distance itself from Israel’s genocide in Gaza, while also delivering meaningful remedies for the country’s deeply racialized system of sociopolitical inequality. It’s hard not to think that Democrats would be in a far better position to address the challenges now if the Biden White House had stood its ground on Build Back Better.
It’s likewise difficult to read Unpolished without thinking of the pending transfer of power on Capitol Hill—returning the modern Democratic Party to its seemingly perennial dilemma of weighing ambitious legislative agendas against the prerogatives of senior leadership often resistant to far-reaching change. Bowman’s experience suggests that part of The Hunger, perhaps its most insidious mechanism, is that it keeps people closest to the experiences of American rot from positions of power—thereby forestalling many prospects for meaningful reform in advance. If Black progressives continue to be treated as marginal-at-best players in the party’s governing coalition, why should they go on deferring to the inert mandates of big-tent leadership—especially when voters themselves are demanding that the circus masters start pulling up stakes?

https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-ide.title: If We’re Paying for Rockets to the Moon, We Should Set the Terms
https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-ide.author: J. Patrick Patterson
https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-ide.text:
If We’re Paying for Rockets to the Moon, We Should Set the Terms
A self-growing city needs people to pour the concrete, stock the shelves and sort the packages. Luckily, the moon offers everything the modern employer craves: no inspectors, no local press and no air that isn’t the company’s.
J. Patrick Patterson
lun·ar de·vel·op·ment
noun
1 . the construction of private settlements, factories and data centers on the moon, funded in part by public money
Why is everyone suddenly going to the moon?
Last year, Elon Musk called the moon a distraction; this year he’s promising a “self-growing city” there. What changed, as best as anyone can tell, was the business case. A Martian city could take more than six months to reach, while the moon is just a few days away, which is practically a commute for a wealthy man with an exit strategy. Jeff Bezos, meanwhile, suspended his space tourism business to focus on a lunar lander, then answered Musk’s moon posts with a picture of a tortoise. Slow and steady wins the race to abandon the planet.
The richest men in history have spent decades telling us the future is offworld, and who are we to stand in the way of people who’ve worked so hard to leave?
Who’s paying for it?
We are. SpaceX and Blue Origin are building their lunar landers with billions of dollars in NASA funding. We aren’t just waving goodbye from the dock; we’re buying the tickets, packing the bags and keeping the light on in the house they’re leaving. When you’ve decided the future doesn’t have room for everyone, you start building a bunker for the few. Even the AI satellites could get a lunar launchpad, so at least the data centers will have a future on the moon.
Sounds like a lot of work.
A self-growing city needs people to pour the concrete, stock the shelves and sort the packages. Luckily, the moon offers everything the modern employer craves: no inspectors, no local press and no air that isn’t the company’s. Safety complaint? Take it up with the vacuum.
Should we care?
Let them go. Truly, bon voyage. But if public money is buying the rockets, the public should set the terms: labor protections for anyone who works up there, public ownership of whatever gets built with our dollars and no oxygen subscription tiers.
Better still, we could spend those billions on the planet that already has air, water and people and whose residents, unlike passengers, are not planning to leave. The moon will still be there when the billionaires get bored. So will we.
This is part of “The Big Idea,” a monthly series offering brief introductions to progressive theories, policies, tools and strategies that can help us envision a world beyond capitalism.

https://apache.be/2026/11/20/open-brief-.title: Open brief: “Kinderrechten hoef je niet te verdienen”
https://apache.be/2026/11/20/open-brief-.author: Netwerk Kinderrechten
https://apache.be/2026/11/20/open-brief-.text:
Op 20 november 1989 maakten wereldleiders samen een belofte aan alle kinderen: kinderen hebben rechten. Vandaag, 37 jaar later, zien de ondertekenaars van deze open brief dat die belofte steeds meer onder druk komt te staan. Kinderrechten kunnen niet gegarandeerd worden als overheden sociale rechten afbreken en besparen op dienstverlening.
Dagelijks zien onze organisaties honderden kinderen, jongeren en gezinnen. We zien wat het betekent wanneer rechten gewaarborgd en gerealiseerd worden. Maar we zien ook wat er gebeurt wanneer ondersteuning afhankelijk wordt gemaakt van steeds meer voorwaarden.
Kinderen die opgroeien in een onzekere woonsituatie. Kinderen voor wie geen plaats is in de kinderopvang. Kinderen die maanden wachten op een plek in de jeugdhulp. Kinderen met een ouder in detentie. Kinderen met een handicap die soms jaren moeten wachten op gepaste ondersteuning. Kinderen die niet welkom zijn op school, of die niet op kamp kunnen omdat het te duur is. En dit is slechts een greep uit heel veel voorbeelden.
Het is aan overheden om inspanningen te leveren voor kinderen die, vanwege hun omstandigheden, bijkomende noden hebben
Deze kinderen betalen de prijs voor omstandigheden waar ze geen controle over hebben. Dat mogen we als samenleving niet normaliseren. 
Niet elk kind en elk gezin beschikt over gelijkwaardige mogelijkheden, middelen of kansen. Minderjarigen hebben bovendien minder controle over hun eigen leven en zijn, meer dan anderen, afhankelijk van de acties en beslissingen van volwassenen. 
Het Kinderrechtenverdrag, dat ontstond vanuit de internationale politieke wil om kinderen te beschermen, schrijft voor dat de kansen van kinderen niet mogen afhangen van omstandigheden waar zij zelf geen vat op hebben. Daarom zijn overheden verplicht om de rechten van alle kinderen te waarborgen, zonder discriminatie. Dat betekent dat de realisatie van rechten niet afhankelijk mag zijn van inkomen, handicap, afkomst of andere omstandigheden van het kind of de ouders. Integendeel: het is net aan overheden om inspanningen te leveren voor kinderen die, vanwege hun omstandigheden, bijkomende noden hebben. 
Wanneer toegang tot rechten afhankelijk wordt van steeds meer voorwaarden, dreigen rechten in de praktijk gunsten te worden. Extra voorwaarden voor sociaal wonen, zoals lokale binding, werkbereidheid en voldoende taalkennis, zetten een rem op het recht op wonen. De besparingen bij De Lijn dreigen vervoersarmoede te vergroten, waardoor ook meer kinderen en jongeren moeilijk op school, bij de dokter of op vrijetijdsactiviteiten raken. Daarnaast maken de snellere sancties binnen het Groeipakket bij problematische schoolafwezigheden gezinnen en kinderen in een kwetsbare situatie nog kwetsbaarder. 
Die evolutie is niet onschuldig. Als voorwaarden de toegang tot rechten onmogelijk maken voor wie die het meest nodig heeft, versterken we onrecht. De verantwoordelijkheid voor structurele 
ongelijkheid verschuift dan van de samenleving naar individuele gezinnen en kinderen. Zo duwen we wie al kwetsbaar is nog dieper in de put. De gevolgen voor kinderen zijn voelbaar thuis, op school en in hun gezondheid. Kinderrechten waarmaken is een collectieve verantwoordelijkheid. 
Individuele inzet kan niet opvangen wat structurele beleidskeuzes onmogelijk maken
Heel wat mensen zeten zich in voor kinderrechten: middenveldorganisaties, leerkrachten, jeugdwerkers, leefgroepbegeleiders, jeugdadvocaten, vrijwilligers, onderzoekers en ambtenaren. Hun engagement maakt dagelijks het verschil voor kinderen, jongeren en gezinnen. Maar wat zij kunnen betekenen, wordt begrensd door de beleidskeuzes van politici. Individuele inzet kan immers niet opvangen wat structurele beleidskeuzes onmogelijk maken.
Op Internationale Kinderrechtendag roepen wij beleidsmakers op om de belofte na te komen die in 1989 werd gemaakt: kinderrechten zijn geen gunsten, maar fundamentele rechten voor elk kind. We vragen hen om maatregelen systematisch af te toetsen aan hun impact op kinderen en jongeren. Om voldoende te investeren in collectieve voorzieningen die rechten daadwerkelijk waarmaken. En om actief te luisteren naar de ervaringen van kinderen, jongeren en gezinnen.
Beleid dat kinderen armer, onzekerder of minder kansrijk maakt, is geen goed beleid. De vraag is niet of kinderen hun rechten verdienen. De vraag is of wij als samenleving bereid zijn ze te garanderen.
De dertig lidorganisaties van Netwerk Kinderrechten namen het initiatief voor deze open brief. Nog eens 60 andere organisaties, 21 personen verbonden aan hogescholen en universiteiten en 26 andere 
individuele ondertekenaars schaarden zich achter de oproep. Hieronder ziet u de volledige lijst.
