https://theintercept.com/2026/11/20/faa-.author: The Intercept Briefing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/20/faa-.text:
A week after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop — disrupting 12,000 flights for an estimated 1.5 million passengers — there are still no answers on what exactly went wrong.
Transportation Secretary and former Real World Star Sean Duffy initially claimed that the incident was the result of “instability with air traffic communications and radar feeds,” but has since backtracked. With zero answers to one of the biggest aviation communication crises in recent memory; some speculated that the incident could be the result of the recent implementation of a new artificial intelligence air traffic control program, SMART. The FAA has denied any connection between the new program and the ground stop, and there is no reporting to indicate a connection.
However, questions remain about the AI program’s safety moving forward — and the Trump administration’s ability to manage one of the most complex and potentially deadly functions of our government.
“These are deeply unserious people in charge of a highly complex system in which the stakes could not be higher,” says Wise, referring to both President Donald Trump and Secretary Duffy. “Hundreds of thousands of people’s lives are in the hands of this system that is being maintained by people who have no idea or interest in how it works.”
This week, host Jessica Washington speaks with Jeff Wise, an aviation journalist who writes frequently for New York magazine, Wired, and others and the host of “Finding MH370,” an investigative podcast about the 2014 disappearance of an Malaysia Airlines flight. He explains why the nationwide ground stop wasn’t unprecedented at all, that the air traffic control system isn’t as antiquated as you might think, and that the skies of the United States might soon be taken over by delivery drones, if Amazon and Walmart have their way.
Washington also speaks with Intercept reporter Noah Hurowitz who was temporarily trapped in Denver during the ground stop along with other attendees of the “What’s Next!” conference, a who’s who of moderate Democrats discussing the future of the party. “It was funnier to witness than to be part of,” jokes Hurowitz.
He says the moderates at the post-midterms summit were “crafting themselves as the maverick middle,” adding, “What’s interesting is that they were also saying that we have to listen to voters. And the lack of any talk of Israel, for example, I think, is evidence of perhaps a selective idea of listening to voters.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.
Transcript
Jessica M. Washington: Welcome to The Intercept Briefing. I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter for The Intercept.
Noah Hurowitz: And I’m Noah Hurowitz. I cover politics, federal law enforcement, and immigration at The Intercept.
JMW: Noah, last week I know you attended the “What’s Next” conference, which was a two-day summit in Denver, Colorado, hosted by the Majority Democrats PAC, where moderates debated the future of a party that appears to be slipping from their grasp.
Both Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, and Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer for majority leader in the next Senate, spoke at the conference, sharing their visions for the party.
Noah, what is next for Democrats? Was there a winning vision that emerged?
NH: That was the question: What is next? It was interesting because the conference was scheduled sometime in advance, and so of course, what’s next could be a question for if they lost and if they won. It just so happened that this came on the heels of just this massive wave of wins for Democrats. And Democrats of all stripes, really.
Obviously, there’s an ascendant DSA left in New York and the [Senate] candidate in Maine, Troy Jackson, is relatively of the left. But there were also a number of more moderate, more centrist wins around the country. So this party, it really was a party because the “what’s next” here is, “OK, what do we do with these wins?” rather than, “How do we stop losing?” [laughs]
JMW: Nice change of pace.
NH: It did seem like a nice change of pace. There was an effort to craft both a reading of the midterm elections and a strategy for what’s next that elevated the wisdom of what I would call a centrist or a moderate vision. That’s not exactly the words that they used.
I had a conversation with one of the conference organizers, Lis Smith, who is a very prominent spokesperson for the moderate wing of the Democrats. She was saying, we don’t see Majority Dems as a centrist or an establishment group.
They’re crafting themselves as the maverick middle. They’re calling for flexibility. They’re calling for different strategies in different places, but there were a few themes that came up a number of times. I didn’t hear anything about Israel at all, but I did hear a number of calls for an end to the Iran war. I did not hear anything about abolishing ICE, but there were calls for a humane but secure immigration policy.
If you’re looking at it strictly from a popular standpoint, part of the reason that the Democrats likely lost, especially along the border in Texas in 2024, was that there was an experience of chaos on the border. With that gone, that was less of an issue here. I do see some of where they’re coming from — it’s not like saying a secure border is an unpopular opinion.
JMW: The maverick middle is a really, really funny way of putting it. But obviously issues like Israel, ICE anger and a desire for people to do more than what Democrats have been doing played into the midterm races, particularly in the primaries.
Was there any pushback on the fact that that wasn’t discussed more? Did you hear anything from people in the room that they wanted to hear on anything on these issues?
NH: We heard from some unsanctioned visitors to the conference during the speech by Hakeem Jeffries. A number of protesters stood up and called for a Green New Deal. They called for an arms embargo. They yelled, “We don’t trust you.” That was perhaps the most contentious instance of dissent or disagreement that I saw. For the most part, this was a fairly self-selected group of people — big group of people. There were more than 3,000 people there. There were a lot of elected officials there, including a number of candidates backed by this PAC, Majority Dems.
But one interesting fact is that this conference was co-signed by or done in close coordination with this group called the Searchlight Institute, which is a think tank formed by a former John Fetterman staffer, Adam Jentleson, which has really made its thing about pushing back on the so-called groups, pushing back on the left wing of the party who they blamed for perhaps going too far with some of the messaging in 2024. Woke 1.0, if you will. The tone was really set by just tuning out what they view as the groups’.
But what’s interesting is that they were also saying that we have to listen to voters. And the lack of any talk of Israel, for example, I think, is evidence of perhaps a selective idea of listening to voters.
JMW: The groups telling you not to listen to the groups because they’re the only group you should listen to is always funny. And I have to say, I’ve really enjoyed your little dispatches in our group chat from the conference. There’s a lot that’s in your story that people should read and also your social media.
But something else really funny happened. Funny is maybe not the right word, but you were —
NH: It was funnier to witness than to be part of. [Laughter.]
JMW: That makes sense. It was funnier to watch from the group chat. But you were also among the politicos stranded in Denver after the FAA — the Federal Aviation Administration — issued a nationwide ground stop. What was that like? Did you get to share a beer with anyone interesting?
NH: So on Friday afternoon, news broke of the FAA ground stop, and this obviously had very immediate logistical complications for most of the conference because it was ending Friday night, and everyone was flying home Saturday morning. And indeed, a lot of people got stuck.
I had a flight home the next morning at 7 a.m., which was canceled that night, and I booked some complicated itinerary for later in the day, which ended up also getting canceled.
When I was at the airport on Saturday, late morning/early afternoon, the departures terminal at the Denver International Airport was a very bizarre mix of normal stranded travelers and very high-powered stranded travelers.
Over here was Lis Smith, who was one of the conference organizers; she’s holding a Shake Shack bag. Over there, we have Mayor Jacob Frey of Minneapolis. I tried to talk to Sen. Raphael Warnock, but I think he had such a bad time of it that he didn’t want to talk; he told me that his flight had been canceled, then he had been deplaned from another flight.
It was a mess. This kind of aviation fiasco is bad for the people in charge no matter what, but it was certainly on the nose that a significant portion of the D.C. press corps and senators and representatives and politicos were all also stranded.
JMW: I have to say, when I was looking at the fact that you all got stranded there from a sourcing perspective, I was a little jealous. Then I thought about it, I was like, “Oh, they’re all trapped in one space. That’s ideal.” Then I thought about actually having to deal with that, and I was like, “You know what? I’m pretty happy I’m in D.C. right now.”
NH: That’s what I’m here for, taking one for the team.
JMW: You do a great job with that. [Laughter.] Obviously there is a lot more that we could get into, and I will be asking you about it offline.
Airport hijinks aside, the nationwide ground stop was obviously a massive crisis for Transportation Secretary and former “Real World” star Sean Duffy. The entire fiasco opened up a ton of questions about Duffy’s tenure as secretary, and how the administration’s embrace of AI could impact future air travel.
Joining me now to talk about all of that and more is Jeff Wise, an aviation journalist who writes frequently for New York magazine, Wired, and others. He’s the host of the podcast “Finding MH370,” an investigative podcast about the 2014 disappearance of a Malaysia Airlines 777.
Jeff, welcome to The Intercept Briefing.
JW: Thanks for having me.
JMW: Jeff, as you know, we’re entering one of the busiest travel seasons of the year, about a week after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights. To be exact, more than 12,000 flights were canceled and thousands more were delayed. Initially, the FAA said the issue stemmed from “instability with air traffic communications and radar feeds,” which was then traced back to a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.
On Tuesday, though, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the root cause has yet to be determined. To get us started, what do we know at this point about what caused the ground stop last Friday? What do you make of the explanations given so far? And just how unprecedented was that stop?
JW: It wasn’t unprecedented at all, actually.
One of the crazy things about this is that in 2009 there was a ground stop. It was more limited, it was shorter in duration, but it was caused by the same company doing the same thing — replacing copper wiring with fiber optic — and they had a problem with a router going haywire. This was in 2009. This was 17 years ago.
I keep seeing these quotes like, “they’re replacing antiquated copper wire with new fiber optic.” They’ve been replacing copper wire with fiber optic forever. So the fact that they still haven’t gotten it right after all these years, and the fact that, as you alluded to, there were all these explanations being given over the weekend, and then on Tuesday, Duffy comes out and says we don’t actually know what is causing this. What do we know? I don’t even know what we know!
JMW: Essentially, we don’t know what’s happening, but there has been some new reporting. According to CNN, on Monday, the FBI took possession of the router and other equipment the FAA says was behind the meltdown. Now, of course, now they’re saying they don’t know what was behind the meltdown — but is it normal for the FBI to take possession of equipment like this?
JW: The Department of Transportation called in the FBI, apparently out of concern that there might be a malicious actor involved, there might be some kind of hacking attack.
Sean Duffy: I’m concerned about what do the American people think? Which is why Kash Patel has sent his team to us from the FBI.
JW: Kash Patel? Right-wing podcaster Kash Patel is seizing equipment under the authority of an investigative agency? Look, nothing is normal. Nothing is normal.
I think the context that’s important to understand is that our government is being run by people who don’t know how anything works, are deeply incurious about how everything works, and we have seen a drumbeat of malfunctions, rule-breaking, and just general screw-ups, frankly, agencies working at cross-purposes to one another.
It’s truly a clown show, and I think, we can talk in all seriousness about this malfunction, that malfunction, but I think we do the the audience a disservice if we don’t point out that these are deeply unserious people in charge of a highly complex system in which the stakes could not be higher.
Thousands of people’s lives, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of people’s lives are in the hands of this system that is being maintained by people who have no idea or interest in how it works.
Obviously, a lot of the noises that were made over the weekend about this was a malfunction caused by an installation crew somehow misconfiguring a router. Apparently, we’re back to square one. We have no idea what’s going on.
The best case scenario, I guess, is that this is all being done out of an abundance of caution, that they’re pretty sure that it was just an unfortunate error on the part of the installation crew, and that they just want to rule out the possibility that it’s a hack.
But these are not people who have a very good track record based on the last two years of this administration. There has been one screw-up after another. And yeah, I think confidence is lacking. The one thing that you do not want to have lacking in an air transport system is confidence.
It’s really tragic because for decades, thousands of hard-working people have tried really hard to do their best to apply their professional expertise to make sure that this system is as safe as it can be. A lot of money has been spent, a lot of time has been spent to instill confidence in the American public.
But they always say it’s hard to build trust, and it’s really easy to lose trust. And unfortunately, we’re in the second part of that equation right now.
JMW: To your point about confidence, it’s not even just confidence in air travel, which is obviously a hugely scary thing that we partake in on a somewhat regular basis.
But there’s bigger issues happening as well. The FAA ground stop followed a Microsoft outage, and then this week several large banks also reported widespread service outages. Then the NSA, the National Security Agency’s internal communication was also reportedly down. All of these have been reported to be unrelated and isolated incidents, though on Tuesday, The Washington Sun reported that bank CEOs and the NSA have told Congress that AI-driven patches were behind their outages.
These combined incidents have obviously sparked concern from the public and online that they’re related. What do you make of the string of technological malfunctions and the public’s reaction to them?
JW: I see two main threads. One is that the public is deeply distrustful of AI. Everybody, I think, at this point has used AI. They know that AI can generate incredible images, music. They can give really sophisticated answers to highly technical questions, but they are not reliable. They make stuff up. They hallucinate. They lie, whatever you want to call it. So that’s part one, public distrust of AI.
Secondly, we are counting on our government ultimately to protect us. That’s one of their jobs, is to protect us. We have an elected leader who was primarily chosen for his entertainment value, and who has selected his Cabinet based on how telegenic they are and how good they are on TV, whether they come from central casting or not. So we have deeply unserious people who frequently lie to us.
There’s something really interesting about being in an era of AI and of Trump, because we both have these entities with enormous power that lie to us shamelessly. Then there’s another part of it, which is Trump coming out and saying that he takes no responsibility.
Reporter: What responsibility do you take for the ground stop on Friday, given that you’re the president?
Donald Trump: I don’t take any responsibility. They did a great job.
JW: So we are counting on this person to protect us, and he takes no responsibility.
JMW: Transportation Secretary and former “Real World” star Sean Duffy has been making rounds on TV blaming the ground stop on an archaic system that he says is in need of major upgrades, one that he inherited and claims that past administrations and Congress have failed to sufficiently fund.
Sean Duffy [On “Face the Nation”]: One of the problems I have is I need more money.
Sean Duffy [On “Meet the Press”]: The president was able to get $12.5 billion in One Big Beautiful Bill.
Sean Duffy [On Fox]: I need new software, Sean.
“Meet the Press”: Is $50 billion the total ask?
Sean Duffy: Let’s not let it happen again. Let’s make sure we keep the American people safe. Yeah, $50 billion.
JMW: President Donald Trump blamed Pete Buttigieg, the former Transportation Secretary under Joe Biden, who then threw the blame right back.
Buttigieg responded on X saying, “We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents.” He then went on to question the Trump administration’s execution of the work he started to transition copper wire to a more modern network, and asked why under Duffy they “triggered the worst FAA communications breakdown this century.”
Jeff, can you help us make sense of all of this finger-pointing? Who is really to blame, and how did we get here?
JW: I think to answer that question, we’d need to find out who was president over the last two years, and what party was in charge of Congress, and what party is in charge of the Supreme Court.
If we could find out the answer to that question, we might be a good way to answering who’s responsible. Because I think whoever holds political power in this country has to bear responsibility for the things that are done. So that would be the investigative path that I would pursue.
But, all this finger-pointing, nobody wants to take blame — that does not instill confidence. If something goes wrong, you don’t want just to hear, “Oh, it’s somebody else’s fault, it’s not my fault.” Or again, as the president said, “I bear no responsibility,” or “I accept no responsibility.” So it’s frustrating, and in the context of, we just don’t know what’s happening, it’s not the kind of noise you want to hear.
JMW: When we look back at Congress, at the White House, do past administrations, does Congress bear any responsibility? Is the FAA underfunded? Is there any truth to what Duffy is saying, essentially?
JW: My understanding is that money was allocated that Russ Vought just X-ed out and did not spend. We know that they fired a bunch of people when they came in at the FAA. They did not cut air traffic controllers. That is true.
There’s been a really bipartisan, ongoing long-term struggle to staff air traffic control towers and facilities. That is the structural nature of the job. It’s a very demanding job, requires very strict screening, so it’s just hard to fill those positions. I wouldn’t say it’s gotten dramatically better or worse in recent years, but that’s not really the issue here.
The issue is the other parts of what the FAA does, like this communication facility network that failed on Friday. I don’t think people want to find out who’s to blame. They want a sense that someone is in charge and knows what’s going on and is taking steps, and that’s not what we’re perceiving right now.
JMW: As a journalist, I’m always interested in who’s to blame, but as a consumer of air travel, I’d want to know that the airplanes are safe. To your point, that’s what most people who aren’t in our profession and whose job it isn’t to nitpick and assign these things, that’s what people want.
I am curious how other countries run their air traffic control system. How does the U.S. system of air traffic control compare to other countries? Why has it taken decades to upgrade our system, a system that, to my understanding, handles the most flights in the world?
JW: I recently did a deep dive into the history of American air traffic control, and I was interested to find that at every single moment in its history, there have been people complaining that it’s out of date and inadequate and needs more funding and needs to be better.
There’s never been a time when people have been happy with the condition of air traffic control in this country. I also think it’s interesting to look at, if you’ll recall, there was a major disruption at Heathrow back in, I believe it was early September. My wife was actually coming back from London at that exact moment.
She got lucky because her flight was not affected, but many flights were canceled because apparently a military flight had tried to enter some information into the system, and they had entered some bad data. I never heard the whole story about how it went down. But this kind of problem is not unique to the United States, and other countries have other kinds of problems.
Air traffic control is a difficult problem. You’re trying to make sure that all of these planes are taking off at the same place at not exactly the same time, and landing and taking off. The stakes couldn’t be higher, of course. It’s a tricky challenge, and there’s always going to be a need for more money and more expertise, and people are going to always have to make do with what they’ve got.
[Break]
JMW: I want to pivot to the future of aviation and the road that we’re currently heading down in the U.S. Immediately after the flights were grounded last week, there was obviously a lot of speculation that it could be linked to the implementation of a new AI-infused air traffic control system that was expanded nationwide a few days earlier called SMART.
I just want to play a clip of a produced video that Duffy shared on X about it really quick for you.
Sean Duffy: We are going to show you what we call our SMART system, which is Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories. We are actually able to use predictive data to see where flights are going, where weather is not just right now, but where weather is going to be in the future.
JMW: Government officials said the new AI system was not responsible for causing the ground stop last week. But obviously timing of the rollout, general concerns about the use of AI, as you’ve mentioned, and public trust in the Trump administration has raised questions. What do we know about how this new SMART AI system is supposed to work with air traffic control? And are other countries implementing anything similar?
JW: I’m not aware of any other country doing this. This is brand-new stuff, and as you say, it was just fully implemented. It was only partially implemented a couple months before, and so there was a very limited test of it in the Washington, D.C., airspace.
Of all places, Washington, D.C., has been on the receiving end of a lot of crazy activity on the part of the U.S. government. I don’t know why they choose this as their test bed, because it’s a very important, busy airspace. Anyway, they tested it out there for a couple months, then they decided, “OK, good enough. We’re going to roll it out to the whole system.”
The idea is that this is going to be essentially helping air traffic controllers plan the routes. It can take in hundreds of streams of data and integrate it and find patterns and find out the best route. One of the examples that they gave in one of the videos that I saw was if an initial route was going to have to go around weather and delay by 30 or 35 minutes, then the system would say, “Oh, actually, you can do this other thing. You can go over the weather instead, and you save all that time.” So one of the things that they took pains to underline when they were rolling this out is, this is not going to directly interact with flight crew. It’s not going to directly be communicating. There’s going to be a human in the loop who’s going to be able to review everything and sign off on it.
Whether that is an adequate safeguard, I think each of us can form our own conclusion, but there is some worry that these systems have a tendency to hallucinate. They can make up solutions that aren’t so good. What if this system hallucinates a danger where there isn’t one or just doesn’t see a major danger that needs to be avoided? Merely having a human in the loop is only partial protection because how is the human supposed to know that this information was hallucinated?
JMW: I have to say, I was not incredibly pleased as someone who lives in D.C. when I found out that they were doing the test here. It was not the best news I’ve ever gotten.
I did want to point to some of your reporting on this. I know that you spoke to an FAA employee about SMART who told you, “They’re pushing through all this new technology without any understanding of the complexity of the National Airspace System.” Can you talk to us a little bit about that complexity? What is the actual job of an air traffic controller? And, what are the implications of this new AI program at a time when there’s already a shortage of workers?
JW: Their hope is that by having this system that will be able to give them advice and kind of act in lieu of a human, that they will be able to reduce their staffing levels still further.
You asked: What does an air traffic controller do? They are tasked with looking at what’s happening, where the planes are coming in. Looking at the routes that they’ve been assigned, seeing how other traffic is coming in and taking off, looking at weather, looking at unexpected events.
Like in Washington, D.C., one of the unexpected events that can happen is the president’s helicopter taking off, and they’re supposed to give a three-minute warning. There was just an incident this past year where they just took off. They didn’t give the warning, or they said they tried to give the warning, but it wasn’t picked up. They did not establish that affirmative contact that is required, and so they just took off into airspace, and all of a sudden now all these other planes have to stop what they’re doing or go around it, or what have you. So it’s a very dynamic environment, and of course, the stakes are very high. Each of these planes has hundreds of people on it potentially, and it’s highly stressful, and it’s typically understaffed. So it’s quite a lot.
JMW: For Wired, you wrote this piece titled “No Pilots, Few Air Traffic Controllers, What Could Go Wrong?” And you got into these various commercial endeavors to create more, “robot-friendly skies” from making drone deliveries to electric air taxis ubiquitous.
What exactly is the vision here of some of these companies, and how does the FAA factor in? How exactly is all of that supposed to work safely and not kill or injure people?
JW: That’s a great question. It’s a big question. We hear a lot of talk lately about the “antiquated” air traffic control system. And that kind of rubs me the wrong way because I got my ticket, my pilot’s license, in 2002, and at that time, they were just ramping up a major overhaul of the entire airspace and the whole air traffic control system.
It was called NextGen, and a lot of the features of planes and aviation today are a result of that. It was a major buildout. It started around 2009, 2010. Billions of dollars were spent. Lots of capabilities were added. So antiquated, I guess I’m really antiquated because I’m 60 years old, and we’re talking about equipment that’s 15, 16 years old, and they’re like, “It’s antiquated.” And if that’s antiquated, I am definitely super antique.
This first renovation of the airspace, as it were back then, back in those days, already we were starting to see a really dramatic increase in the capabilities of drones. You were starting to see DJI, these Chinese drones starting to really multiply, and you can buy them off the shelf, and everyone’s flying drones.
The FAA was worried. In the future where we’re going to have lots of drones and other things of this nature flying around, how are we going to prevent them from colliding into other things? One of the FAA’s major, major jobs is to prevent planes from crashing into each other, and that’s basically what air traffic control is tasked with doing.
They realized that they had to introduce new capabilities, and over the intervening years, they’ve spent a lot of time generating new rules that will allow drone delivery, the use of drones for other purposes as well, and also what’s called eVTOLs, or flying taxis. These are going to be sort of like mini helicopters.
Imagine a helicopter that’s really a drone or vice versa. It’s got like many whirring blades, and it can carry you from point A to point B, usually a few people a short distance. Eventually, for that to be economically feasible, it’s going to have to be pilotless. These drones are pretty much pilotless.
I don’t think a lot of people really understand the scale of the ambition that companies like Amazon and Walmart have to transform the U.S. retail economy. They want to not have people driving up to your house in a van. They want to have the stuff dropped off in your backyard from a drone. Like tens of thousands of stations dotted around the country where you’re going to have sort of robot systems loading up these drones which will automatically take off, drop off the stuff, go back and get more.
So the skies of the United States, if these plans of these major corporations come to fruition with the help of the FAA, there’s going to be drones constantly buzzing overhead all the time.
JMW: Sounds lovely.
JW: Sounds nice, right?
JMW: Sounds perfect. Sounds ideal. I have to say, as a nervous flyer, this has not been the best episode for me.
I do want to get into Sean Duffy’s role in this whole thing. He has been described as much more business-friendly than his predecessor, Pete Buttigieg, a Democrat who the Wall Street Journal says “took a more consumer-focused approach that carriers viewed as adversarial.” What has Sean Duffy’s approach been when it comes to this vision of a more robot-friendly skies? Can you talk about how he’s helped accelerate the use of AI in aviation?
JW: This shift toward making American skies more friendly for robots is something that has been going on for many years. Both Obama and Trump 1.0 and Biden and Trump 2.0, even before that, I’m sure its roots go back to Bush.
This is something that a lot of very important, powerful people and corporations want to do. It’s the kind of future, like a physical world manifestation of the information technology revolution that has transformed so many parts of our lives.
It’s going to make it super responsive to your needs. You need a tube of toothpaste doo-doo-doo, buy it on Amazon, boop, boop, boop. It’s like, two seconds later, it’s dropped in your backyard.
So the consumer’s desires are fulfilled instantly. That’s the ultimate desire of capitalism, right?
JMW: I wanted to talk a little bit more about Duffy, and you already brought this up earlier, but he asked for more money from Congress. He’s now going on television saying he needs $50 billion to fully upgrade the air traffic control system, and he says he needs it by the end of the year. The FAA has already been allotted $12 billion, which hasn’t been fully spent. Do you think the FAA actually needs more money overall, and what do you think of Sean Duffy’s tenure as transportation secretary?
JW: I don’t think it’s about the dollar figure. He had that very morning asked for $30 billion, and then everything came a cropper, and he went back on air and asked for $50 billion. Listen: A highly, highly complex system requires the interplay of many different agencies, corporations, unions, customers. The interplay is mind-bogglingly complex.
What it requires above all is patience, steadiness of funding, and the willingness to be boring. Complex systems are boring. It’s really dull, and it requires pages and pages of regulation. And you can’t just come in and scoop up a bucket of money and just dump it on the problem and hope that it’s going to do better.
It’s probably going to make it worse, honestly. How can you just, out of thin air, come up with $20 billion worth of spending? It just doesn’t really make any sense.
I find that there’s a really useful metaphor in air crash investigation, and one of the reasons that flying is so safe is because of the approach that air crash investigators take. Which is, something bad happens, you go out and you meticulously document every single thing you can find out about it, and you don’t draw a conclusion until it’s done.
Only then do you lay out what you think to be the root causes. You’re not laying blame. You’re saying, “These are the root causes, and then these are the steps we could take to reduce the risk of this happening again.” You do that over and over again, and you wind up with a set of regulations and best practices, training protocols, and so forth, that make the system bit by bit a little bit safer.
Again, takes a lot of time, takes a lot of patience. It’s frankly pretty boring to go through that kind of meticulous detail.
If you then just tear up regulations, this idea that it’s pro-business to just tear up the regulations — if your business is founded on the trust that you’ve carefully inculcated in the public, you’ve carefully earned by years and years of not having accidents, by following this rigorous procedure, and then you’re going to start tearing it up and asking for money? What isn’t needed is, it’s not money by itself. You need rigor. To say, I only need $30 billion. No, wait, I need $50 billion. There was $20 billion. There’s no program that that’s attached to. It’s just noise, really.
What we’ve seen is time and time again, the administration doing things like there was recently an example where in order to have some giggles, they sent a fighter jet flying really low over people on a beach; it made great viral video footage. This is incredibly dangerous. There’s a reason why you don’t fly planes over civilians like that. It is an accident waiting to happen. The administration’s response to complaints about this, as with other things, is just like to laugh it off, to say, “Oh, you’re a stick in the mud. Can’t you have fun?”
That’s not how it’s supposed to work. Then we had the example with Kid Rock. Some helicopters flew past Kid Rock, and it violated regulations, and the powers that be said, “Ha, ha, ha, suck it,” basically.
So, much better than having an extra $20 billion pouring out of some hose somewhere would be to have people in charge of the aviation system who understand aviation culture, who understand how it came to be so safe in the first place. And it didn’t happen by flouting regulations.
JMW: If I’m understanding you correctly, what we need in this position is someone who is interested in doing the boring nitty-gritty, who is excited potentially by the boring nitty-gritty.
JW: Yeah.
JMW: And how would you overall rank Sean Duffy’s tenure as transportation secretary?
JW: Tragic. I know that’s not a letter grade. But this whole thing, it’s been really weird watching the country sleepwalk into this state of just absolute absurdity.
And how is Duffy as an administrator? He’s a reality star. What do you want? This whole thing is a joke.
If this happened in any other country, we’d be laughing at it. And now, listen, I don’t think I’m speaking out of turn in talking like this because I think the country, the penny has dropped. And I keep thinking about that Abraham Lincoln quote about, you can fool some of the people some of the time. I think you can’t fool all the people all the time. And I think enough people have realized what an insane situation we’re in right now.
Sean Duffy is a deeply unserious person in charge of a very, very serious project which he is in the process of running off the rails.
JMW: To your point, these are deeply unserious people doing what is supposed to be a deeply serious job.
Even earlier this year, Duffy returned to his reality TV roots, filming a cross-country road trip with his family called “The Great American Road Trip.” This was a seven-month road trip that followed his wife and nine children and was funded in part by companies, the agency he oversees and regulates, including Toyota, Boeing, and United Airlines.
JW: It wasn’t even a TV show, it was a YouTube channel. And I don’t want to piss on YouTube, I’ve got a YouTube podcast myself. God bless them. But this was all in service instead of being the secretary of transportation, which sounds boring, frankly — he’s off doing his YouTube channel for seven months or whatever.
And meanwhile, after all this breaks, and the air traffic system is desperately trying to unsnarl itself from five hours of being ground-stopped, we have Markwayne Mullin, who flies off on a government jet to go attend a football game and is in a booth with a corporate person who’s doing business with the government, et cetera.
To call it unserious is really not even strong enough.
JMW: Truly ridiculousness on top of ridiculousness. And by the way, you were referencing Markwayne Mullin, the secretary for the Department of Homeland Security. Jeff, we’re going to have to leave it there. Thank you so much for joining me on The Intercept Briefing.
JW: Thanks for having me.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Why the Midterms Were So Painful for Trans People
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jessica Kant
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Why the Midterms Were So Painful for Trans People
We watched politician after politician sell us out. Then we were demonized for getting mad about it.
It is hard to articulate the complexity of the feelings that I and other trans people in my life have been sorting through in the weeks since the Democrats’ crushing victory in the midterm elections.
The stakes for us were high; in many ways, it felt like our very survival was on the ballot. So, like many of us, I watched the results come in with bated breath, and breathed a sigh of relief as Republican after Republican was defeated. However, while the Democratic sweep will no doubt help begin to stop the ongoing decimation of trans rights in many places around the country, it’s impossible for us to look too optimistically to the future without acknowledging the danger that remains.
True, there has been a sudden wave of accurate postmortem analyses about the GOP’s decision to put far too many eggs in the proverbial basket of transphobia. But it wasn’t long ago that many people were passionately arguing that the Democrats needed to follow suit—and in the wake of the election, we need to reconcile with the fact that a lot of them did.
While the GOP made transphobia a central organizing principle for years, this was the first time that so many Democrats decided to join in. Like many trans people, I watched with increasing dismay throughout the midterm campaign as a wave of Democratic candidates—like Amy Acton, Nancy LaCore, Josh Turek, and Annie Andrews, to name just a few—offered us up as sacrifices, releasing statements or ads directly promising to curtail trans rights. Although it’s a stiff competition, the most rhetorically egregious was probably Ohio’s Marcy Kaptur, who boasted that she “voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools.” Hers was far from the only one to use incendiary language that would have been indefensible only a few years ago.
Josh Turek’s anti-trans messaging in his Iowa Senate campaign went even further than Republicans’ in some cases, particularly when it came to his position on gender-affirming care. In an ad released a week before the election, Turek opens by telling the audience about his personal motivations for opposing discrimination, which he inexplicably follows by stating his opposition to transgender girls—whom he calls “males”—participating in girls’ sports. Almost as an afterthought, he adds “I’m against taxpayers paying for sex changes too,” in a perfect mirror image of the flippant tone and regressive language that has become central to the modern GOP. (Turek was not the only Democrat adopting anti-trans messaging in Iowa. Congressional candidate Sarah Trone-Garriot, for instance, ran an ad in August stating she opposed “letting men in women’s locker rooms.”)
The toll this all took on trans people was very real. I know several people, most of whom live hundreds of miles from Iowa, who didn’t sleep for days after Turek’s ad. To them, he was a harbinger ushering in a Democratic Party that, while not yet wholly intolerant, is increasingly tolerant of those who are. They see a party on the verge of mimicking the British Labour Party, which, after a landslide victory over the Conservatives in 2024, ushered in the most draconian anti-trans laws the country has ever seen. And after the experience of the 2024 election—when hosts of columnists and consultants blamed us, falsely, for Kamala Harris’s loss—not a single one of the hundreds of trans people I spoke to in the weeks before the midterms was confident that we wouldn’t be scapegoated again if things went badly.
Perhaps more to the point, we all became acutely aware that either electoral result would be leveraged against us. The readily available narratives were telegraphed in advance: Either the ads were successful in drawing voters from ready pools of centrist moderates, and therefore should become central to the Democratic strategy for 2028—or, if the results were bad, they would have been successful had it not been for those of us who had the temerity to object. This is even though candidates like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed refused to turn their backs on us and still pulled off important victories.
It has become familiar terrain we navigate in our nightmares. Despite the fact that the 2 million or so voting-eligible trans adults are statistically some of the most politically engaged members of any given constituency—and vote Democrat more than nearly any other demographic—somehow we continue to be seen as an electoral net negative. It is difficult to reconcile with the fact that in a country where elections are often decided by margins smaller than the total population of trans adults, we are always the first to be cast aside.
As someone who publicly called for candidates to consider that we are not merely political chips to be cashed when the moment is right but real living, breathing people who have watched 70 years of hard-won rights virtually vanish overnight, it’s been truly astonishing to witness how little our betrayal has registered outside of our own circles. We are alone on an iceberg of indifference, and it’s a deeply fearful place to be.
I have been emotionally leveled by the invective thrown our way for asking for the basest amount of empathy. How ungrateful were we to a party that had carried us like an albatross across several elections, despite our alleged general objectionableness to the public? To this latter belief, they point to the several ballot measures attacking trans rights which passed—although they say nothing about the many which failed, including one in Missouri that doubled as an abortion ban. How could we not vote “blue no matter who” despite the fact that Josh Turek famously didn’t? (Unlike Turek, I did vote straight Democrat, as I have in every election. Had I been in Iowa, I would have left his name blank.)
The stranger who called me a “dumb c*nt” on social media did so after I’d told her that I was posting about Turek’s ad because I was afraid for my community. I assured her we were on the same side. She assured me we were not. Every trans person I know saw an influx of slurs and threats from self-described liberals just before the election was called. I and many people I know were told we deserved the camps into which we would eventually be herded if the GOP retained power.
Surely, they argue, we understood that there was a broader strategy at play? I was assured that Annie Andrews was “extremely careful” with her choice of words when I tried to engage the liberals in my life in conversation about why her ad troubled me so much. But when someone who only three years ago was using her power as a pediatrician to vocally stand with transgender youth suddenly runs an ad using “biological men” —a phrase popularized by the right—I am not interested in whether she believes she was being precise in her language. If she does not believe that transgender women and girls fall under the auspices of this category, she should have said so—and she didn’t. Nor did she make any overtures to the young trans girls who’ve watched as politicians abandoned them and participated in their ostracization.

My biggest fear now is not necessarily how our lawmakers will vote. My fear is that you—cis people—will forget. My fear is that once everyone is done having a good laugh at the fact that even Ron DeSantis now says the GOP overspent on anti-trans messaging, that people will file the past few years away as mere silliness—and that they will let further attacks on us float by. Most of all, I fear that the unholy amount of money spent on manufacturing public animus towards trans people to sow the seeds for our eradication will be understood as true bellwethers of public opinion.
An anti-trans ballot initiative in Washington, which will incomprehensibly require a physical examination of girls hoping to participate in school sports, passed not because we are unpopular. These initiatives did not even pass because the objection to trans participation in sports, using bathrooms or locker rooms, and accessing medical care are widely held objections. In actuality, where they did pass, they passed because in states like Washington, despite the objection of the state teacher’s association, the Washington Educational Association, proponents of the bill outspent trans rights groups by three and a half times. Nearly $8 million went into promoting that single initiative, and it was far and away not the largest nor most contentious issue this election. Suffice to say, while no exact count exists for every trans athlete in the state of Washington, it is likely that for every one that exists, more than a million dollars were spent lobbying against their inclusion. How that gets understood, and the relentless, mendacious nature of a decade-long blood libel against a vulnerable community, will determine if we are at all prepared to meet such a threat in the future.

https://www.propublica.org/article/aquab.title: Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon
https://www.propublica.org/article/aquab.author: Anna Clark
https://www.propublica.org/article/aquab.text:
When a biotech company named AquaBounty Technologies announced plans to farm genetically engineered Atlantic salmon at a new plant in Ohio, local and state officials eagerly provided it with incentives. Not long after, the company paused construction and auctioned off “new” and “unused” equipment. Now, the state’s private economic development arm wants its $1 million back.
JobsOhio has requested repayment from AquaBounty by Sunday, according to a company filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing also notes that, at the end of September, AquaBounty was down to three employees and $122,255 in cash.
AquaBounty said that its salmon could thrive in indoor freshwater farms and help feed the world. Announced in 2021, the new development in Pioneer, Ohio, was supposed to be its first large-scale production facility.
The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for schools and infrastructure. It was believed to be the largest investment ever in rural Williams County.
But AquaBounty, which had never made a profit over its 30 years in business, faced a tangle of regulatory challenges and pushback from environmentalists.
Locals were also suspicious of how the village mayor’s personal interests were tied up in the project. Among other moves, Pioneer Mayor Ed Kidston bought land that AquaBounty wanted to build on. He then sold it to the company for $1.5 million more than he’d paid.
AquaBounty’s plan was unproven, but, as ProPublica reported last year, the company was buoyed by state and local resources — including the million-dollar grant from JobsOhio. The company received the money in August 2021, according to financial filings, shortly after the project went public.
“Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling,” said Sherry Fleming of Williams County Alliance, a grassroots environmental group. While AquaBounty had genetic engineering know-how, she said it seemed to have limited experience in production.
In response to ProPublica’s queries, a press contact for AquaBounty said it shares what it can in its SEC releases and filings, and that it’s still in discussion with JobsOhio over the repayment demand. AquaBounty’s filing said that “there can be no assurance that JobsOhio will agree to any payment schedule or other accommodation.”
“Any collection or legal action by JobsOhio could result in additional costs and management distraction,” it added.
Kidston didn’t respond to requests for comment. He said at the time that his actions involving the plant were intended only to help the community. The village administrator referred ProPublica to AquaBounty and its website.
JobsOhio operates privately but has a funding mechanism set up by the state and a board appointed by the governor. Matt Englehart, a spokesperson for JobsOhio, said in an email to ProPublica that it “operates with transparency and accountability,” but its limited disclosures have long been a sore point for Ohioans.
On its website, JobsOhio says its funding model for specialized grants is “independent” and accommodating of “unique needs.” Qualifications include, but aren’t limited to, “job creation, additional payroll, fixed-asset investment commitment, project return on investment, and project location.”
The AquaBounty grant depended on not only the creation of jobs, but also $222 million in capital investment and a payroll of more than $5.4 million by the end of 2026. It had to maintain those commitments through the end of 2028.
Less than two years after it got the money, construction stalled. Roughly 30% built, the site languished at the end of Kexon Drive, a smooth new road that Pioneer had extended for its benefit.
AquaBounty sold equipment intended for the Ohio farm in 2024 and 2025. It also sold its intellectual property for genetically engineered salmon. By the end of September, according to its filing, its primary remaining assets were unsold equipment, the land in Pioneer and the incomplete build.
JobsOhio and other economic development boosters should “take a good look at this because they’re putting taxpayer dollars at risk when they advertise to bring these industries in, and they haven’t done their homework to protect the community,” Fleming said.
Englehart told ProPublica that he can’t discuss a situation that may result in litigation. But with any company, he said, “when metric commitments are not met, we work closely with those businesses” to help them overcome challenges.
If all options are exhausted, he added, “we will claw back some or all of our dollars so they can be used for future economic development projects to benefit Ohioans.”
JobsOhio’s demand notice came in September, the financial filing said, informing the company that its equipment sales and consideration of acquisition offers for the Ohio farm were a breach of the grant agreement.
AquaBounty “provided additional information” to JobsOhio in October, the filing said, but the agency upheld its demand and requested repayment this month. If it doesn’t come, the filing said, JobsOhio may refer the matter for collections and “pursue the remedies available” under the grant agreement.
With an onerous process and uncertain outcomes, it’s “pretty rare” for JobsOhio to try to claw back money, said Kristan Wong Karinen, a research analyst with the nonprofit Good Jobs First, which tracks public subsidies in economic development. More commonly, she said, it and other agencies will renegotiate the contract — extending the time period for a company to meet commitments, perhaps, or lowering requirements.
“In this case, with AquaBounty,” Wong Karinen said, “because they haven’t done anything, they haven’t fulfilled any of the requirements, I feel like JobsOhio is being forced into this.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/could-rodneyse-b.title: Could Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn Actually Pull This Off?
https://hellgatenyc.com/could-rodneyse-b.author: Jessy Edwards
https://hellgatenyc.com/could-rodneyse-b.text:
The reign of Assemblymember Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn, the Brooklyn Democratic Party's outgoing chair, is not over. Repeat: It is not over!
The second-largest county-based Democratic party in the country has been engaged in an ever-escalating intramural battle since the June primary, when its reformist faction won enough district leader seats to vote out Bichotte Hermelyn as chair and wrest control of the party's comms and finances. 
But the assemblymember, who's been mentored by some of Brooklyn's wiliest power players, is not going down without a fight. In August, she passed last-minute rule changes to expand the party's voting rolls before it elected a new chair, thus diluting the newly elected district leaders' power to the point of insignificance and allowing Bichotte Hermelyn and her cadre to retain power in perpetuity. Under those rules, which Dems across the state called a "power grab" and which the reformists immediately filed a lawsuit challenging, the old guard claimed to elect Assemblymember Nikki Lucas as chair. 
On September 29, a bevy of judges up to the appellate division decided the changes were unlawfully pushed through, and the courts ruled the dodgy late-night Zoom call in which Lucas was "elected" didn't stand.  
But on Thursday, a state Supreme Court judge made a shocking decision, doubling down on a surprising order that requires the party to go back in time and relive a now-legendarily chaotic September organizational meeting.
For some reason, even though no one asked for it—not even the establishment Dems who stand to benefit—Judge Peter Sweeney has ordered the Brooklyn Democratic Party to reconvene the County Committee meeting and hold another vote on some of the most controversial rule changes in party history before they elect a new leader. 
If these rule changes pass before the party holds its next vote for chair, the reformist faction that won a majority in the June primary will be diluted to the point of being nullified, as well as the will of Brooklyn voters who wanted party leadership to change—and Bichotte Hermelyn and her allies will retain power.
Even the outgoing chair seemed surprised by the ruling.
"From the Godfather: Just when I thought I was out, they pull me back in. 🤷🏾♀️," Bichotte Hermelyn mused in a text to Hell Gate, quoting mob boss Michael Corleone in that iconic scene of the "Godfather III" when it dawns on him that he will always be dragged back into the mafia game.

https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.title: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.author: Cassandra Garibay, Eli Hager
https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.text:
When Kelly Joly swiped her electronic benefits transfer card at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, she was trying to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son. Joly had worked for decades as a waitress. The day before her grocery run, she’d received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamp, benefits, she said. But now, her EBT card was being declined. She tried swiping again and began to cry. The cashier told her that this had been happening a lot recently and suggested she report the issue. Joly stepped to the side and called Texas Health and Human Services as her food sat bagged up on the belt.
The representative at the agency that oversees SNAP in Texas told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds, Joly recalled. Her benefits were gone, likely stolen by fraudsters. Joly said her account showed transactions from the day before at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California.
“I don’t understand why they wouldn’t replace [our food assistance] if they can see that it was fraud,” she said. “And on top of that, how am I going to feed me and my son this month?”
Read More
If you receive SNAP benefits, Joly’s experience may sound all too familiar. Last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by card scammers, affecting about 990,000 households.
ProPublica recently published an investigation into why Congress and the Trump administration have failed to crack down on SNAP theft despite promises to tackle fraud and waste in safety-net programs. As part of this reporting, we gathered detailed accounts from more than 50 people across 18 states who’ve had their benefits stolen in the past five years and reviewed dozens more messages, comments and social media posts from people who said they were targeted.
Many of the victims we heard from had similar questions: How did this happen? How can I prevent it from happening again? Why am I not being reimbursed? And why does it seem like little is being done to prevent these crimes in the first place?
We spoke with dozens of federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials, caseworkers, food security advocates and other experts to help answer these questions for you.
How does SNAP theft happen?
Much of this crime is the work of low-level street operatives for transnational criminal organizations who install “skimming” devices on card readers at local grocery stores and bodegas. When you swipe your card, these devices capture your data off the magnetic strip on the back, as well as your PIN. That data is either picked up later or transmitted via Bluetooth to thieves waiting nearby.
Skimming is largely preventable via microchips and tap-to-pay technology, which have been greatly successful in reducing fraud in credit and debit card transactions for over a decade. But efforts to install these chips in EBT cards have moved much more slowly.
In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal people’s card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check your SNAP balance and deposit date. In other instances, corner store owners themselves are in cahoots with these scammers, ringing up fake grocery purchases in exchange for cash. And in at least one prominent case, a federal SNAP employee gave sensitive data to criminals for them to be able to steal benefits.
What can I do to protect my benefits?
Unfortunately, due to the government’s inaction, the burden of protecting benefits from being stolen has largely been left up to you, the individual SNAP recipient. And the options are less than ideal.
Phone apps, like ebtEdge or Propel, allow you to keep careful track of your card balance, monitor your transaction history for any suspicious purchases and lock your card when it isn’t in use. These apps may also allow you to change your PIN and block out-of-state or online transactions.
But these aren’t always practical solutions, many victims told us. Remembering new PINs all the time, for example, isn’t easy, especially for older beneficiaries.
Cynthia Clark, a 63-year-old retired special education teacher in Jackson, Tennessee, said she has several health conditions that affect the dexterity of her hands, her vision and at times her speech. After her SNAP benefits were stolen in May, she was advised to lock her card every time she wasn’t using it. But she said her disabilities make using a cellphone incredibly difficult. On more than one occasion, she has locked herself out of her SNAP account trying to access her benefits.
“I was simply unable to do whatever the steps were, no matter how hard I tried,” she said.
Besides card locking and changing PINs, the Secret Service has suggested that people may be able to spot evidence of tampering with card readers at grocery stores. For example, if you look closely at the reader and see a noticeable gap between the keypad and the rest of the device, or if you see that something is blocking the light from under the keys, there may be a skimming device there.
What can I do after my benefits have been stolen?
If you’ve had your SNAP benefits stolen, you can report the theft to your state or local social services office — the agency where you applied for SNAP — or to the EBT card customer service line on the back of your card to receive a new card and change your PIN so thieves can’t continue to access your benefits.
You can also report the crime to local law enforcement and to the agency within your state in charge of investigating SNAP fraud — for example, in Texas, SNAP theft victims are advised to report it to the Texas Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. (This map shows where to report SNAP fraud for each state).
A representative for Texas Health and Human Services said, “HHSC takes the security of our client’s benefits very seriously. SNAP card skimming has been a persistent problem across the country, including Texas.”
While there have been some large-scale investigations into SNAP theft, individual reports don’t often lead to an arrest. More than 40 of the victims we heard from said that they had reported their stolen benefits to a SNAP office, the EBT card customer service line, the police or all of the above. A handful also called the stores where they’d noticed unrecognized transactions on their card history, and two said they contacted the FBI. Most were told nothing could be done.
“I was told that I will receive another card in the mail and that I will not get the money back,” one person wrote us. “They took my statement but said they couldn’t help,” wrote another. “No one ever followed up,” said a third.
The main benefit of reporting these thefts is that doing so keeps the issue on the radar of SNAP officials. Many program administrators and caseworkers told us that they feel the urgency of this crisis precisely because so many people have been calling in about it.
Will my stolen benefits be replaced?
In all but two states (California and Maryland), your benefits will not be reimbursed.
The federal government had been reinstating stolen SNAP funds in all 50 states starting in late 2022. However, at the end of 2024, an effort to extend that reimbursement system was quashed after Elon Musk posted more than a hundred social media messages opposing legislation that included it, as the Department of Government Efficiency era began. (Musk did not reply to a previous request for comment.)
Democrats in Congress have proposed legislation to restart the reimbursement program. Following the recent midterm elections, they will take power in January.
How does law enforcement investigate SNAP theft?
As ProPublica has reported, the Secret Service devotes a lot of investigative resources to this issue, with teams going store to store around the country to manually check card readers for skimming devices. But that’s not a very efficient approach — it’s a little like playing whack-a-mole, multiple Secret Service agents told us.
Local cops and state prosecutors, meanwhile, are often overmatched, having neither the jurisdiction nor the technical chops to catch scammers who are constantly crossing county, state and international lines. And the feds, who do have the capacity to bring interstate conspiracy charges, haven’t always shown an interest in doing so, given that these are considered relatively low-level cases compared with the other types of crime that federal prosecutors work on.
As for caseworkers, most can’t offer concrete help. Several said that all they can do is provide a list of local food banks.
Will chip cards help prevent theft?
If your benefits were stolen, there’s a good chance they were skimmed. And the best solution to skimming appears to be tap-to-pay EBT cards with microchips.
In California, where chip cards were implemented independent of federal efforts, reported theft of SNAP and other benefits decreased by more than 80% within two years.
Following ProPublica’s reporting in October, the federal Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP, announced plans to require all 50 states to adopt more secure card technology. But overhauling the SNAP payment system could take years, as well as additional funding from Congress.
The chip card transition comes at a time when social benefits are being drastically cut and more of the financial weight of SNAP is being shifted to the states. Issuing these new cards is likely to cost states millions, involving complicated negotiations with EBT card companies like FIS and Conduent, which are essentially the Visa and Mastercard of SNAP. Grocery stores, bodegas and any places that accept EBT will also need to update their card reader systems. It will be mostly up to states to notify local stores about this and help them with it, which some, like California, Alabama and Oklahoma, have already tried to do.
Do You Administer SNAP or Medicaid Benefits? Help ProPublica Report on America’s Safety Net.
While ProPublica is no longer gathering information about people’s experiences with SNAP theft, we are still interested in learning more about America’s changing safety net. If you work to administer SNAP or Medicaid, we want to know how the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill is shaping your work and what you are seeing and hearing from the communities you serve.

Ten countries in the European Union have urged the European Commission to keep Russia out of Venice’s 2027 architecture biennale. The effort is led by Poland and includes Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden. The countries say that allowing Russia to participate normalizes its actions in Ukraine.
Russia participated in this year’s Venice Biennale for the first time since 2022, despite financial pressure from the European Commission and protests from several EU countries and activist groups like Pussy Riot and FEMEN. The EU terminated a €2 million grant to the Biennale because of Russia’s involvement. The Biennale said in a statement at the time that it “rejects any form of exclusion or censorship of culture and art.”
The EU is preparing its twenty-second package of sanctions against Russia, expected before the end of the year. EU foreign ministers have called for it to include even tighter visa restrictions for Russians and a ban on Russian athletes competing in sporting events in the EU. The group of ten countries wrote a diplomatic note laying out its concerns ahead of a November 19 meeting of EU culture ministers.
“In light of the current geopolitical realities… there should be no room for ‘normalization’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” the countries said in the note. The architecture biennale will take place from May to November of next year. The Venice Biennale has not yet said whether Russia is expected to participate.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Officials Defend Response to Deadly Lithium-Ion Battery Fires
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The City Council is once again debating a slate of bills to step up safety and rein in the sale and distribution of uncertified lithium-ion batteries commonly used for powering e-bikes that have led to a surge in deadly fires across the city.
The Council has already approved a raft of reforms granting the Fire Department greater power to crack down on illegal battery sales and to speed up inspections. On Thursday night, the U.S. Senate unanimously approved a bill sponsored by New York Sens. Chuck Schumer and Kristen Gillibrand to stem the sale of unsafe e-bike batteries.
But the rate of fires has continued a steady climb across the five boroughs since 2022 in spite of local reforms. At the hearing on Friday, officials from the Fire Department defended its record to the palpable frustration of Julie Menin, the Council speaker.
“I asked for an emergency hearing because we are in an emergency. The numbers in terms of fatalities, injuries are just completely unacceptable. This is a crisis of epic proportions,” said Menin. “The Council has passed bill after bill after bill and yet the problem is getting worse, not better.”
Calls for Public Education
Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said that without curbing illegal sales, there is little officials can do to prevent fires without greater education for the public about how to safely vet, charge and store lithium-ion batteries.
“We do understand how big a problem this is, but this is a technology that more people are now starting to engage with,” said Bonsignore. “So I think we have to accept that this is a changing technology and it’s putting us in a very difficult place as it emerges and standards start to become something that will make it safer. But education is by far, I think, one of the most important things we can do — and we need to do this in every language.”
Fire officials testified alongside representatives from the housing and buildings departments. While previous hearings on the issue of lithium-ion battery safety have attracted large crowds eager to speak directly to lawmakers, on Friday only about two dozen members of the public were in attendance at the Council’s main chambers in City Hall, a handful of app-based delivery workers among them.
Faulty lithium-ion batteries have ignited 408 fires resulting in nine deaths so far this year, including a fire at a South Bronx public housing development that killed four people and another weeks later at a Sunset Park home that killed six. The cause of the latter fire has not yet officially been determined, but fire officials confirmed at the time that two charred e-bikes were removed from the burnt structure.
The Council heard seven bills on Friday to restrict the sale, distribution and possession of lithium-ion batteries that do not meet existing federal standards and to step-up the Fire Department’s investigation and reporting capabilities.
The only bill that fire officials explicitly endorsed on Friday, sponsored by Brooklyn Councilmember Susan Zhuang, lowers the threshold for the city’s consumer watchdog agency to shut down stores that sell the illegal batteries. The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection currently shut down stores after three violations; Zhuang’s bill would reduce that threshold to two strikes.
Stores that sell, store, and maintain e-bikes and related equipment cater mostly to the city’s vast community of app-based delivery workers, many of whom are immigrants living in the outer boroughs. The main group representing these workers, Los Deliveristas Unidos, have long said their own members are the ones most at-risk by the technology, a reality that fire officials have long acknowledged.
The fire department and worker groups have long taken pains to address proper safety measures for storing and maintaining e-bikes and e-bike batteries — including by hosting training sessions, battery swaps, and lessons on how to identify UL-certified equipment.
On Thursday, Councilmember Shaun Abreu introduced a bill, with the mayor’s support, that would make companies like UberEats and DoorDash responsible for ensuring workers use safe equipment.

https://citylimits.org/advocates-sue-ove.title: Advocates Sue Over Federal Rule Threatening Aid for Mixed-Status Immigrant Families, And What Else Happened This Week in Housing
https://citylimits.org/advocates-sue-ove.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/advocates-sue-ove.text:
Share This Article
A NYCHA residents’ association is among the plaintiffs challenging the federal rule, which advocates say could force thousands of families to separate or lose their housing assistance.
A coalition of public housing residents and immigrant advocates filed a federal class action lawsuit Thursday challenging a Trump administration rule that could force thousands of families with mixed immigration status to choose between staying together and keeping their federally subsidized homes.
The lawsuit, filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts, seeks to block a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule scheduled to take effect Dec. 14. The plaintiffs argue that the regulation violates federal housing law and constitutional protections.
Plaintiffs include the Alfred E. Smith Houses Resident Association, representing tenants at a New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) development in Lower Manhattan. According to the complaint, 16 of the development’s 1,876 households have mixed immigration statuses and could face displacement under the rule.
The legal challenge follows HUD’s announcement of the final regulation on Nov. 10, which would require members of households that receive federal housing assistance through programs like Section 8 and Section 9 to verify their U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status.
Under existing law, mixed status households can receive reduced federal rental assistance based on the number of eligible family members. Those who do not qualify for subsidies can still live with eligible relatives, including children who are U.S. citizens.
The new rule would end the longstanding arrangement allowing mixed status families to receive prorated assistance indefinitely, potentially forcing households to separate or give up their rental aid. As City Limits previously reported, approximately 2,500 New York households could be affected by the changes.
Among those challenging the rule is a Honduran woman identified in the complaint as Jane Doe #2, who has lived in the United States since 2009. She resides in New York City with her husband, a lawful permanent resident, and their three U.S. born daughters.
The family has lived in a federally subsidized Section 8 apartment for nine years. Although the woman has been authorized to live and work in the country since receiving U nonimmigrant status in 2022, it does not qualify her for federal housing assistance under the law cited in the complaint.
According to the lawsuit, the family cannot afford market rate housing in New York City. The plaintiffs argue that the rule could force the woman to leave the apartment or cause the entire family to lose their home.
The lawsuit also challenges new documentation requirements that would apply to recipients of federal housing assistance, not just mixed status households. The plaintiffs argue that the requirements could disrupt benefits for eligible tenants, particularly elderly and disabled residents who may have difficulty obtaining the necessary records.
Nationwide, roughly 80,000 people, including approximately 36,000 eligible children, could face displacement under the regulation, according to estimates cited in the complaint.
In a statement provided to City Limits, HUD Secretary Scott Turner defended the change saying it fully implements the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980.
“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD funded housing,” Turner said.
He added that the change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million in housing assistance to eligible Americans currently on waiting lists.
The plaintiffs dispute HUD’s interpretation of federal law, arguing that Congress explicitly authorized reduced subsidies for mixed status households. They are seeking a court order declaring the rule unlawful and preventing its implementation next month.
Housing lawyers who spoke to City Limits earlier this week urged households potentially impacted by the change to stay put.
“People need to know that until it goes into effect, nothing has changed,” said Lucy Newman, the supervising attorney of Legal Aid Society’s public housing unit. “They should not move, or evict out of fear.”
Here’s what else happened this week in housing—
ICYMI, from City Limits:
- For the first time, NYCHA is using a federal program called Section 32 to repair 91 single-family to four-family houses—opening a path for public housing residents to buy their homes.
- A career training program for the city’s public housing residents is getting $1 million from an unusual source: Kalshi, the prediction market company recently sued by New York State for allegedly operating as an illegal and unlicensed gambling platform.
- All but one building in a portfolio of properties that recently went to foreclosure auction failed to receive any bids, raising alarm about the health of the city’s rent-stabilized housing. Tenants, and the mayor’s office, hope to steer the buildings to a buyer they say will work to preserve them.
ICYMI, from other local newsrooms:
- The city is suing a landlord for evading fines and failing to make building repairs under a local fraud law, what City Hall described as a novel tactic to hold bad property owners accountable, according to Gothamist.
- Astoria residents are opposing proposals for three new apartment buildings on Steinway Street, the Queens Eagle reports.
- The city is billing 7,500 households under the new pied-à-terre tax on expensive second homes, what officials say will raise $500 million, according to The City Reporter.
- The Mamdani administration shuttered its last remaining migrant shelter in the Bronx this week, potentially stymying a a subpoena from the Trump administration demanding the city disclose the names of undocumented immigrants with criminal records who lived there, the New York Times reports.
