https://hyperallergic.com/is-gta-vi-the-.title: Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?
https://hyperallergic.com/is-gta-vi-the-.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/is-gta-vi-the-.text:
Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?
Miami-based artists Leo Castañeda and misael soto join Hyperallergic in a conversation about the tensions of a game that portrays a changing city locked in time.
“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.
The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.
To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.
Our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.
Hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?
Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to New York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.
I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.
misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.
It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.
H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in New York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.
And on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, users say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?
LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that says something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.
So it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the company. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?
H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?
MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?
It ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I said, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.
H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, said that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?
MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the company has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.
H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the company actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?
MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.
LC: Of course, I have to play more to fully understand it. There's the ads of the game and the game itself. I would say that the Netflix special did feel like it was perpetuating some of the stereotypes of the Haitian community. But at the same time, having played, or seen the range of minority characters so far in the first couple hours, it feels like they have a wide range of personalities, body types, and interests. It's not like they're all criminals. And I also found out that local Haitian muralist Serge Toussaint has his work featured in the game, which I think is an amazing thing. But in terms of artworks in other mediums that really relate to this, this is kind of like, let's say, South Park, or Euphoria — shows that are a mirror to the world that's very explicitly showing you both the best and the worst, and it's making fun of and critiquing everyone. But then how does it flip to show a new perspective or a solution?
I've seen a lot of people, especially women game critics and game developers, celebrating the relationship of Jason and Lucía being a central situation in the game, as opposed to a cast of different men from different backgrounds, or, in GTA IV, the Eastern European guy in the seedy underground. Having the relationship and the cultivating of the relationship be a core mechanic, almost in a Sims-like way — and even the learning of emotional labor, or doing kind things around the house, or the game having a really interesting reward mechanic for the nonviolent interactions ... At least in my experience so far, three hours in, I haven't shot a single shot.
H: Wait, how did you save Donnie in the first mission without shooting people?
LC: Oh, by hiding. It was saying, “Crouch around to make sure no one sees you.”
H: I think it's fascinating how different players can make these different decisions. I'm not very good at gaming, so I gave my husband the controller. I was like, “Get us out of here as quickly as possible. I want to get to Vice City!”
LC: Yeah, and usually my criticism of Rockstar Games and also Naughty Dog, two big companies that have these cinematic, movie-like games, is that the story missions often have a path where you fail if you don't take a violent action. The emergent gameplay — which happens just by walking around, the dynamic gameplay that's not in a story mission — is usually extremely layered and nuanced and can go in any direction, violent or not. Again, I'm only three hours in with GTA VI, but so far I appreciate that it is giving the choice of not using violence, and kind of rewarding it. There's something interesting about that. Because usually in those Rockstar games, I'm like, okay, there's this emotional tale, and now there's a mission, and I have to kill 20 minions.
MS: Leo, I'm thinking about your work and playing your pieces, immersing oneself in these worlds that you create, and there's a kind of mystery in the expansive potential that you create in your installations that at first can be a little overwhelming, but you have to just dive in. And this is the nature of games, or video games. There's a kind of trust fall. And I'm thinking about — let's just go there — the emancipatory potential of that. Because video games, to me, the potential in them as works is the building of awareness, the fostering of empathy, literally embodying someone who has a different way of life or a different body, a different perspective. Especially in our era of political correctness, and a lot of it is warranted, we're asked to speak from our own perspective and not assume things of others. And so this allowance — I wonder how you see the potential in that, especially in something like this game that is so immersive.
LC: I think games as artworks are, to a certain extent, some of the most affordably accessible. Yes, you need to have a PC or PlayStation or Switch or something, but they could be pieces of art that are globally accessible in an immediate way, and they really can affect culture. In terms of empathy, you're controlling a being that you identify as “I”: “I” drove the boat today, or in my game, “I” was camouflaging with the environment to gain energy. There's something there about the mutability of the body, or how one could shift one's self-identity into multiple beings, that is interesting in games, and also interaction and choice as a place that could be art, in a way that performance art also does, and maybe theater. And visual arts in general, maybe in a less touch-based way. But in terms of the empathy, I've been seeing a lot of reviews of GTA VI saying it's actually leading people towards that. Perhaps it is through the romantic relationship [between Jason and Lucía], or maybe by having so much freedom to do whatever you want and kill whoever you want, but then developing these characters and NPCs to a level where they feel like real people.
H: There is one moment in the game that was very emotive in a way that might provoke empathy, and it certainly did for me. At the very beginning — so this is not really a spoiler — we're shown the backstory of how Lucía gets arrested. She's been sitting at a cafe, a little Cuban cafecito, and she's just ordering ice water. The server keeps coming up to her and asking if she wants something else, and she's like, “No, no, just ice water for me.” It's clear that she just can't afford anything else. So in an act of true desperation, and from a place of deep poverty, she decides to rob a payday loan store nearby, and she gets caught. At one point, you can hear the cops saying, “She's saying she left something at the cafe.” And then we see the owners of the coffee shop taking care of her baby, who is then taken by social services.
We're not shown Tomás, her little baby, at the beginning. It's something that the game surprises us with. To me, it was such a thoughtfully articulated moment.
LC: The beginning is so strong. And then having the tutorial on how to walk and use the camera be her nine months later in prison. Out of overcapacity, the prison is letting some people who have lower sentences perhaps have probation, so she's gonna be let go, but the woman who works there says she doesn't know if or when Lucía will see her baby again. That works as a narrative tool, a teleology, giving purpose to the game beyond, “Oh, she's just a digital girlfriend.” Now there's this question of what the rewards of behavior are that the game's gonna have when one is part of the criminal underworld, but there is a child in foster care that could be taken back or not. That's gonna be so interesting if that ends up being a fork in the road within the narrative, because many of these games have multiple endings.
MS: This is so fascinating to me in regards to something we were talking about earlier — whether reality is informing the simulacrum and vice versa. It makes me think of how, living in Miami, it continuously feels like maybe the most neoliberal city I've ever lived in. But in so many ways, it oftentimes feels like when you're on the road or when you're at a cafe, you're alone. You really have to fend for yourself in this city. Of course, there are these moments where you break through, or if you're a regular at Enriqueta's, you know who to talk to, this and that. It makes me wonder how the game might change the way that we see ourselves. And, following that thread, how might it actually make us more united?
I don't know if that's a bit of a stretch, but there are just so many people playing this game. And I think over time it's really going to show, as visitors come and reflect their years of gameplay back to the city. In the same way that folks experience Paris syndrome, what will the GTA Miami syndrome be? How might that change us? I was thinking about it for the worse, but how might it change us for the better? Because I don't know a Miami where that childcare situation in the GTA story would happen. Of course, I'm not a caregiver. I'm not a parent. But I don't know that Miami — and I've been here long enough and I have a lot of family here, chosen family. So that makes me, in a weird way, hopeful.
LC: I think it's interesting, let's say with Pop art and conceptual art — if you use a urinal or a fluorescent light, you think of urinal, Duchamp; fluorescent light, Dan Flavin, etc. These artists are claiming this thing from the world. And it's interesting to have this very fluid cycle of, let's say, the Only in Dade Instagram account becoming almost a live feed of GTA, or us within Miami filtering our experience — when there's a very special or odd moment, it being a rehearsal for the game, or the game getting reflected back in the world.
If the game is marketing itself as this debauched, wild place, and that lures millions and millions of people in, but then it ends up being this profound story that actually shows how South Florida has issues of income inequality and climate change ... There's a hurricane system in the game, so there's a very strong chance that there will be flooding. Will that situation, where violence and comedy, or things that are not explicitly telling people what the values should be, actually make them more subtle and implicit? Does that create change or not?
H: We've been speaking over an hour, we could probably talk for two more hours. This feels like a beautiful note to end on. But I want to ask if there are any burning observations you want to share.
MS: I feel like we should speak about the takeover of Miami in the real world, physically. Anybody trying to do anything — F1, Art Basel, all these people who come in and take over the city, as they've done for decades — if they want to gain favor with locals, just look at what they did with GTA. Because the amount of free advertising — I mean, I went to this GTA VI-themed drag night, and it was not sponsored by them. It was at Las Rosas. They had a pool table and some neons, and they had the beer from the game available for purchase, but the event itself was fully done just to hop on the bandwagon, and everybody was lapping it up. Morphine Love Dion was playing the video game while people were dancing. It layered some uncanny feelings for me. But at the same time, I'm just very, very impressed, and scared, by the power of putting it everywhere to the point where it was inescapable. It's been inescapable for the last week. It's very impressive.
LC: Yeah. I've met at least two or three people who have been working on some of the release parties. So they're employing local artists and local musicians and local businesses, as opposed to, as misael was saying, these people arriving out of nowhere, renting a place for really exaggerated prices, and not giving back to the local community. At least through employment. We'll see over time if and how it leads to other forms of sustainability locally. I have a photographer friend who, similarly to that drag show, started doing GTA-style photos in front of one of the new signs and probably made some money through that, unofficially. So that's interesting.
MS: I think there's many ways to be a capitalist, or to do this kind of thing and take over the city in this way. And I've never seen something so thoughtful. It honestly reminds me to some degree of the first couple years of Art Basel, when they would do a lot of public programming and free concerts and they really seduced us ... But that's another conversation. I'll stop there.
H: Well, it's a perfect aperitif for Miami Art Week and the Basel boycott and everything else. And then the G20 summit hosted by Trump in Miami the following week.
MS: Wow, I forgot about that.
H: Yeah, we're going from GTA VI to G20. It's just a perfect pipeline, really.
MS: It doesn't get any more Miami surreal than that. Truly Vice City.

Hail to the Squash King
Hilma af Klint painting shatters records, new Edward Said documentary, the politics of pigment, and how should we memorialize the Trump era?
Swimming in a Peter Bradley color field. Leaping from dot to dot on a Howardena Pindell speckled canvas. A Peter Jemison horse prances toward me. A Pepsi Cherry truck pulls over as I’m having deep thoughts about authenticity.
In the morning glow, a pretty woman walks down the sidewalk with a carton of a dozen eggs. A faded black-and-white Marilyn Monroe poster greets customers at the Organic Deli. A photo in the paper shows the presidents of the United States, China, and Russia against a giant painting of the Great Wall. A Madonna song whispers, “Express yourself, express yourself.”
A well-dressed man cycling to work is nice to look at. A Hilma af Klint painting sells for $12.7 million at auction, 16 times its highest estimate. Meanwhile at the supermarket, just three small items set me back $100. How could that be? If the middle class had any guts, they’d be out there on the streets burning effigies of Adam Smith and Sigmund Freud. But they’re not; they’re waiting 40 minutes in line across the street just to buy a bagel.
At the Ace Hotel, I read something I’ve written for the new edition of The Other Almanac. I wear my heart on my sleeve in front of strangers. The next speaker is a whale necropsy expert. At the end of the evening someone is crowned “Squash King.”
A golden sunset falls over the glass towers of Long Island City. The Kosciuszko Bridge is lit with cotton candy colors. Fog in Downtown Brooklyn, or is it smoke? I can’t really tell. In Chelsea, I follow a group of people into an art gallery just to see what they’re into. It turns out to be a big mistake.
—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief
Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever
In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi

What It Looks Like to Parent Without Gender
My queer partner and I are raising our new baby in unconventional ways. It’s going to frustrate people on the right and the left.
In 2022, my partner, Wes, and I deposited three embryos in a fertility clinic freezer, where they sat for the duration of the pandemic. We wondered if we would ever see them again. It doesn’t matter where the embryos came from, or whether Wes and I are genetically linked to them. What matters is that we’ve wanted this for a long time, and our plan is bound to make people uncomfortable.
Physically speaking, neither of us can carry a child. In 2024, we started looking for a gestational surrogate—someone to carry our implanted embryo—which is different from a traditional surrogate, who contributes a portion of the genetic material. Surrogacy is altruistic in Canada where we live, meaning that surrogates do it simply because they want to help. Although they can be reimbursed for pregnancy-related expenses, it’s illegal for them to be paid for their services. That doesn’t mean it’s free: Laboratory, legal, notarial, and agency costs guarantee a five-figure project.
Because of this altruism, surrogates are relatively scarce in Canada: chimeras who mustn’t be scared off. It’s considered poor form to reach out to potential surrogates directly, so the best hope Wes and I had was to cast our line in private Facebook groups where intended parents can match with surrogates and… wait for a bite. We had decided on an independent search instead of the more costly method of using an agency.
We posted shy photos of ourselves in the salt flats of Bolivia’s Uyuni desert and explained what kind of parents we would be: loving, somewhat equipped, and interested in taking a little one to the strangest places on earth. We didn’t have to wait long. A reply came the next day, while we were watching the Opening Ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympics, just before the mechanical horse glided across the Seine. A few calls later, Em had volunteered to carry our baby. A gift of that magnitude is incomprehensible. What if we hadn’t posted that day, or if horses didn’t tread water?
Roadblocks came up as soon as we started the process. Wes is nonbinary, yet most of the forms required for surrogacy offer only binary options. A notary got our names wrong on the surrogacy agreement. Our lab results were contaminated four times somewhere between our home province of Quebec and Arizona, which delayed our family planning by several months. Quebec fertility laws changed when we were mid-process and our lawyer had to scramble to figure out the differences. Our first embryo transfer didn’t work out. But we forgot many of these troubles the minute we got news of the positive pregnancy test earlier this year.
This was Em’s second time being a surrogate, so they coached us through the steps. If at first the journey felt slow, soon we could hardly keep up. Our life became a diorama of midwife appointments, prenatal classes, and yes, even phone calls to prospective daycares, because with a baby, the future is always on your heels. I got a PhD in how to clean an umbilical stump with a cotton swab—theoretical knowledge, of course, until I could put it into practice in the real world on a real baby. There would be no time to read all our parenting books; babies operate on their own schedules.
Em became a friend, and we can never thank them enough for making this journey possible. Our baby crew is extensive, from casual supporters online to the professionals involved in drafting Quebec’s fertility laws. For expert opinions on the legislation, the province consulted our lawyer, as well as the community support group where we attended our very first workshop on becoming parents through surrogacy. Several queer folks in our orbit are waiting for us to make them aunts and uncles and ancles. I’m in a polyamorous relationship with two partners; Mark, my other partner, has agreed to be the child’s legal guardian in case anything happens to Wes and I. We have support from most within our circles, many of whom feel indignant that families like ours face so many hurdles to having a child.
Many on the right view surrogacy as a violation of natural law and a way to exploit vulnerable women who in the United States are paid for carrying children that aren’t theirs. The theocracy has never wanted women to have bodily sovereignty, much like they don’t want queers to have kids. (If they only knew that our surrogate is a self-described witch.) Wes and I aren’t in touch with many conservative religionists, but we have still received pushback online and in person from people we know when discussing our plan to have a kid—not in the form of outright objection, but rather as questions that reveal their true feelings: Who could give up a baby that way? What do you mean your kid will have no mother?
Just as likely to anger those on the right is our plan not to gender our baby. Growing up with an assigned gender, my nonbinary partner felt that it was a kind of violation of their informed consent. I’m a cis guy, have always used “he,” and am fine with the pronoun. To both of us, it’s crazy to squint at a blurry ultrasound photo to determine the presence or absence of an appendage, then use that observation to lay out the rest of someone’s life. It feels like astrology, which is to say, limiting. Biological essentialism is a dangerous ideology for how reductive it is. The vast range of human experience can never be encapsulated in the binary of pink versus blue.
When someone asks about the gender of our baby, we reply: “We’ll tell you when the kid tells us.” Good news: We found out that we’re able to request a birth certificate with an X marker in the sex category. Our kid will have a mix of given names, some gender-neutral and some that skew more masculine or feminine. Later in life, they can order those names in whatever way feels best to them, in the same way that many people choose to go by their middle name. Our kid can identify their gender when they’re ready, and it’ll be the most beautiful moment, more meaningful than a thousand infant gender reveals.
At the same time, we also understand how our baby plan can be alienating for some fellow queer people. Having and raising children is usually something straight people do, so it’s easy to read parenting as heterocentric, no matter the circumstances. There’s also so much privilege embedded in who gets to have a baby by surrogacy, including who can afford it, so it’s unsurprising that some of my friends might feel resentful. They’re right that the way some queer parents have children reinforces the primacy of biological ties, when those same ties have often failed the queer community. For many people, a chosen family can be a better way to live—one of the great lessons that queer people have gifted the world.
The beauty of having a baby is that we’ve learned how much doing so, as with forming a chosen family, can organize adults in meaningful ways. Suddenly, our friends and family are all providing materially, spiritually, and artistically for the babies in their lives. They’re also buying material objects at a level I’m not exactly comfortable with. But when Wes brings home a onesie that reads, “My daddy is an author” I weep for a week. If having spawn forces us into heteronormative models, we find ways to queer the process. We fight against what remains exclusionary, like government forms that assume there must always be a mother in the equation. Changing these norms can only start with people like us.
We surprised our surrogate, and perhaps even ourselves, when during the second trimester anatomy scan, we expressed openness to seeing our child’s genitalia on an ultrasound. To us, it didn’t make sense to avoid seeing any part of our baby during a scan designed to check on health and development just because of where the part was. Delaying the moment seemed to place even more emphasis on whether it was important if they had a vulva or a penis. We wanted to see the entirety of our child’s body as soon as possible because it’s not a big deal. I’ll never get over the debasement of people asking me, “What are you having?” What am I having? A baby. Let’s make a deal: Don’t reduce my child to a single body part, and we’ll teach them not to do the same to you.

Like we plan to reject the tradition of gendering a child, we plan to zap the gender out of parenting, too. We’ll both caretake, cook, discipline, and provide financially. Both of us will take the little one snowboarding and teach them to catch snowflakes on their tongue. Both of us will bottle feed. Neither of us will delegate teaching them how to pee in the toilet, because it won’t matter what genitals they pee with. They’ll grow up always knowing how to use the singular they. We have support for this, but there’s a lot more education to do. The parenting-industrial complex is hinged on a binary gender worldview, so we’re preparing for battle. Making sure all their personal documents match their gender identity, or lack thereof, is an agon unto itself.
Understanding any of this means acknowledging the existence of trans people and their rights. At London Trans+ Pride this summer, I marched in a crowd of 150,000 carrying homemade signs with all manner of provocative messages on them. I bought a posterboard from a stationary store, wrote a note about transphobia and fascism on it, and made sure to show passengers on every passing double-decker. Among the legendary slogans that day were “It’s raining them,” “Imagine making bathrooms your entire personality,” and “Throat goats, not scapegoats.” Special mentions go to the “I’m so fucking angry” cape, and “Human rights terrorist” beside a photo of J.K. Rowling.
We headed south down Regent Street, thrusting our fists, flags, and flowers into the bright July sky. The butch dykes in the crowd reminded us that trans rights aren’t an erasure of women or gay public life. The kids reminded us that the future we want is worth fighting for, even (especially?) if it means horrifying the tourists clustered at Trafalgar Square. There’s no greater statement than 10,000 trans people swarming the National Gallery looking for a place to pee. Except, of course, the staff at His Majesty’s Theatre waving to us from the windows, proof that the Phantom himself is onboard.
With the latest wave of anti-trans legislation in the UK, it’s a time for protest signs to be blunt. It’s also a time to provoke from within, because some of the gays just aren’t getting it. This year—during pride month, no less—multiple papers of record in the US published op eds calling for gay assimilation at the expense of queer and trans people. “My sexuality doesn’t require me to reject all that’s ‘normal’ and ‘legitimate’,” writes Ben Appel in “I’m Gay, but That Doesn’t Make Me Queer.” What Appel forgets is that basic gays like him aren’t safe; legitimacy is defined by the straight world, which can delegitimize you whenever it likes. (And “I’m gay” should never be followed by a “but.”)
The odds are that my kid will turn out cis and straight, but that’s beside the point. In every sense, having this baby with Wes is a way to remake the world. It’s a chance for me to discard whatever elements of gender performance are broken for us and for society and to replace them with something better. Our plan will always be too traditional for some and too progressive for others. That won’t stop us. Wes and I will do it with the help of those we love.
One day, we want our kid to research their genesis, starting with an Excel spreadsheet I made that documents the five years it took to bring them about. Their own personal creation myth. We want them to see how we navigated transphobia and queerphobia to make space for them to exist. How we rebounded after every setback. How their no-gender-assumed-at-birth existence explodes the universe into a million possibilities.
We got the call on a Monday morning that Em had gone into labor. We sped through farmlands in a car share to get to the birthing center in time, low on gas but high on adrenaline. In the final stretch, as we crossed a bridge over the Saint Lawrence river, I got visions of the horse on the Seine: all waterways somehow leading us to our child.
The baby was born in a clawfoot bathtub 15 minutes before we arrived, but it didn’t feel like we’d missed anything, because suddenly we were warming them on our bare chests, and everything that led to this moment melted away. We synchronized our breathing and counted our luck. They gradually opened their eyes and looked right through us, and their first name came to us in a shiver of insight. Love-drunk and sleepless, we inscribed it on a form so maladapted to our situation that we had to write outside the boxes. A problem to sort out another day.

https://www.propublica.org/article/carbo.title: Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology?
https://www.propublica.org/article/carbo.author: Katie Worth
https://www.propublica.org/article/carbo.text:
You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics and grocery aisles: “Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.” “Climate pledge friendly.” Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away.
Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated how the world came to rely so heavily on this premise, particularly in the technology known as carbon capture and storage. CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface, where, ideally, it stays put. The oil industry has long favored the idea.
At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.
Over the last two weeks, world leaders and negotiators met in Antalya, Turkey, for the U.N.’s annual flagship climate summit, where nations hash out global commitments to curb warming. A central foundation of these negotiations — and many of those carbon-neutrality labels and climate pledges — is the expectation that we can bury billions of tons of CO2 a year, an operation that would rival today’s entire global oil industry within just a couple of decades.
Yet our reporting found that expectation rests on thin evidence. After three decades of development, only 12 large-scale geologic storage projects have ever been built, and at least seven have underperformed or failed. Last year, the world buried less CO2 underground than a single large power plant emits annually.
Why do world leaders keep staking climate policy on a technology that remains unproven?
Because the models they all rely on to guide their approach have already presumed that it will work.
I spoke to more than 100 experts for this series, including several members of the wildly powerful group of people who build and run those models. Their simulations of the economy and environment map out how specific choices, like retiring coal plants or electrifying vehicles, could prevent warming catastrophic enough to submerge cities like Miami. Which means that if they’re wrong, Miami could pay the price.
One chart laid bare to me exactly how wrong they’ve been about CCS. It compares one prominent model’s projections for CCS with their projections for solar power, a technology so abundantly tested and proven that you can likely spot a panel out the nearest window:
Carbon Capture Capacity Has Never Come Close to Projections
Meanwhile, solar electricity production has grown rapidly, far outpacing projections.
I wanted to understand what could possibly account for such a disparity. But the problem is the models are opaque: Unlike most scientists, who trade in public, peer-reviewed studies, modelers aren’t required to document every assumption they build into their influential simulations.
So I tracked down the leaders of the world’s three most influential climate models — one based in the Netherlands, another in Germany and a third in Austria — and asked. Here’s what I learned:
Climate models assume it’s easy and efficient to capture carbon. It’s not.
Public data is hard to come by, but several analyses have found the real capture rates are far lower than the industry has promised. Yet the models calculate as much as a 92% success rate. When I pointed out this discrepancy to Keywan Riahi, who leads the Austrian model, he insisted that capturing concentrated CO2 from industrial emissions “is not high-tech, this is very easy to do.” Riahi told me the models assume a high rate of capture because they factor in incentives such as payouts from carbon taxes and large government subsidies. Add those incentives, he argues, and the capture rates would increase.
They don’t account for problems that come up in real-world practice.
In project after project, operators have struggled to inject as much carbon into the earth as they say they can. For instance, at Chevron’s Gorgon natural gas processing plant in Australia, billed as the largest CCS operation on Earth, clogged wells and pressure spikes have forced operators to release most of their CO2 straight into the air. As it stands, only the German model, led by Jessica Strefler, assumed there’d be any limit to how much CO2 operators could inject underground at once. But, she told me, there is no good data to work from, and she pegged the limit based on “expert interviews” with people in the industry.
They assume the Earth is a bottomless geologic landfill.
Modelers took that cue from a rosy 2005 U.N. report, which I’d learned had been written at the behest of Saudi Arabia and allied petrostates, that portrayed underground storage space as practically limitless. (The U.N.’s climate science body has said it stands by the report. Scientists who contributed to the report also defended their work. Authors and editors from Saudi Aramco, Chevron and Shell joined scientists in writing it; the companies did not respond to requests for comment.) Yet just last year, a paper in the journal Nature warned that the earth’s capacity to absorb CCS could be far more limited once you rule out pumping the gas beneath cities, into earthquake zones and under the deepest parts of the oceans. If CCS ever worked at the scale modelers imagine, the paper found, the Earth could run out of room as soon as early next century. Riahi, himself a co-author on that paper, conceded that although his model presumes the earth’s capacity for carbon storage is literally infinite, the real potential may be “smaller.”
They assume that stored CO2 will stay put.
Scientists warn that even tiny annual leak rates over longtime horizons could undermine a storage site’s climate benefit. Our investigation found two large-scale sites that have leaked, one all the way to the surface. Surely the models all factor in this risk? I asked Detlef van Vuuren, leader of the Dutch model, if his did so. His one-word answer: “Nope.”
The models all assume CCS gets more affordable over time, though real-world costs have steadily climbed.
When I asked Strefler if it makes sense to assume our children and grandchildren will pay big bucks to suck CO2 out of the air, even though today governments won’t spend pennies to avoid emitting that pollution, she said: “If a country is not willing to do that, I don’t see how they would be willing to” pay for CO2 removal.
In short, the modelers overlooked decades of underperformance, inflated capture rates, evidence of leaks and finite underground storage, all while assuming future generations will willingly bankroll an increasingly expensive industry. They pointed to a mix of legitimate studies to support those assertions. They also pointed to unreviewed white papers, casual chats with industry insiders and the 2005 U.N. report — of which van Vuuren was an author. Van Vuuren said his team is working to revise some of its assumptions, but he generally sees no technical reason why CCS cannot work, or should be excluded from the possibilities his model considers. He said it is a policy decision whether countries wish to invest the dollars and effort to make it happen.
One way to look at the model projections is as recipes for the future. Seen this way, the modelers’ argument is that their job is to assemble a cookbook, not tell us how each recipe tastes. In other words, the models merely show that if CCS works and is used at an extraordinary scale, it is possible to hit climate targets. And the modelers told ProPublica and Drilled that the delay in climate action has left few other tools to do so — and so they include CCS.
A good recipe, though, cannot rely on imaginary ingredients. If we’re making unrealistic assumptions, why not include the possibility that aliens will appear and hand us a solution to climate change, I asked Riahi, half joking.
“You can quote me that I think carbon dioxide removal is more likely than an alien,” Riahi said.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/21/trum.title: An Air Force Major Is Being Held in Solitary Confinement for Criticizing Trump on CNN
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/21/trum.author: Seth Stern
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/21/trum.text:
Seth Stern is the director of advocacy for Freedom of the Press Foundation.
Government lawyers on Tuesday played a video in court of a CNN interview where an American citizen called for President Donald Trump’s impeachment, arguing that the video alone proves the interviewee must remain in solitary confinement until his February trial.
“Not only is [Trump] a failure as president, he is flagrantly violating the Constitution, breaking the law, engaged in rampant corruption, and is killing Americans,” the now-defendant told CNN host Erin Burnett in August. “I believe we can defeat this government if we just take a stand.”
This view of the current presidential administration is hardly controversial, as this month’s midterm elections proved, let alone criminal.
The catch is that the interviewee is an Air Force officer, Maj. Jason Watson. In July, he was arrested during a protest on the steps of the U.S. Capitol where he wore his military uniform and held a sign calling for Trump to be impeached and removed from office.
He was subsequently charged under the Uniform Code of Military Justice over the protest and the CNN and other media interviews, including for “contemptuous words” against the president, failing to obey orders or regulations, and conduct unbecoming of an officer.
The military, unfortunately, has been afforded significantly greater leeway by the judiciary to punish speech than civilian courts.
But not that much leeway. As we’ve seen before, when the law gives the Trump administration an inch, it takes a mile. Watson’s case is the latest example of the administration plucking low-hanging fruit to suppress — and harshly punish — dissent.
The administration took advantage of purported ambiguities in immigration law to try to deport noncitizens for protesting and writing op-eds and posting on social media. It believes its broad authority to fight terrorism empowers it to make up a domestic terror organization, antifa, and prosecute and convict protesters — or people who merely read radical literature — as conspirators. It has used the archaic Espionage Act to harass journalists and their sources for exposing its incompetence.
Now, it’s weaponizing military law to retaliate against soldiers who talk to journalists.
The Trump administration is far from the first to try to justify punishing whistleblowers, and like its predecessors, it claims, based on flimsy or no evidence, that leaks of newsworthy classified documents threaten national security. But like the noncitizens the administration targets for their political speech, Watson leaked nothing. He simply spoke his mind, and for that he’s being held in extreme isolation for 24 hours a day, as if his freedom poses a danger to Americans.
The conditions of Watson’s confinement are further proof of the government’s vengeful motives. The charges against him cite the July 1 protest and his anti-Trump comments to a Substack blog in June in addition to the CNN interview, but he was placed in pretrial solitary confinement after the cable news appearance, where he’s been ever since. That interview was also used to justify his conditions at the recent hearing.
The Air Force says the CNN interview establishes probable cause of “continued misconduct.” But “continued misconduct” implies an initial misconduct, and according to military defense attorney Cody Harnish, who has followed the case closely, the order that Watson reportedly violated by talking to Burnett had expired weeks earlier.
But what kind of “continued misconduct” does the military fear enough that warrants keeping a decorated officer in conditions the United Nations considers torture? Is the prospect that he might give further interviews (despite his attorneys offering assurances he won’t pending trial) so terrifying that Watson must be caged for months?
Even those who agree that the military should be able to punish political expression in ways that civilian courts cannot should be alarmed by this escalation.
Watson has been convicted of no crime. Military law says a service member awaiting trial cannot be punished, and confinement may not be any more rigorous than the circumstances require.
According to Watson’s legal team, the government’s own witnesses testified Watson is not a flight risk. The military has not argued he is dangerous to anyone. Watson offered to resign in lieu of being court-martialed, an offer his attorney said in court that the government declined within a day.
Watson’s attorney, Christopher Mutimer, says Watson is the first major in the history of the military to be charged for “contemptuous words.” Harnish counts only three modern “contemptuous words” cases against service members of any rank. He has noted the offense is aimed at personal attacks, not advocating for legal processes like impeachment.
Yet the government is so committed to keeping Watson in solitary confinement that it’s willing to spend additional taxpayer funds to do so. Watson sits in a Maryland civilian jail because Joint Base Anacostia–Bolling, where he is stationed, has no confinement facility of its own. That means the government is contracting to hold Watson in jail, at your expense, for speaking his mind about the current presidential administration.
The government has claimed Watson is allowed to leave his cell for recreation and library visits. But the defining characteristic of solitary confinement, under the U.N. Nelson Mandela Rules, is solitude rather than space constraints.
His lawyers say he spends 20 to 22 hours a day alone in a small cell, where the lights are on around the clock. But as Mutimer told CNN, “Even if he gets an hour to eat or to exercise, he’s alone.”
Conditions are only getting worse. With the weather getting colder, he reportedly has to wear thermal underwear in his cell to keep warm. Guards have suggested jumping jacks to keep his body temperature up. That will, presumably, be less effective come January.
Mutimer told NPR that even soldiers who have been arrested for sexual assault and other violent crimes are not held in solitary confinement.
Watson’s case is selective enforcement at best and lawless retaliation at worst. Americans — whether they’re military or civilian, immigrant or citizen — should not be held in torturous conditions for months at a time, without having even been convicted of a crime, merely because they criticized the president or his policies.
A ruling in Watson’s case should come down soon, but even if he succeeds in being freed from solitary confinement, the administration will have succeeded in making an example of him.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://hyperallergic.com/hank-willis-th.title: Hank Willis Thomas’s Sleight of Hand
https://hyperallergic.com/hank-willis-th.author: Hrag Vartanian
https://hyperallergic.com/hank-willis-th.text:
Hank Willis Thomas’s Sleight of Hand
The artist makes us supremely conscious of being spectators in a society that streams out images faster than factories churn out products.
Hank Willis Thomas has the rare ability to turn the everyday into a spark, all informed by a mashup of ad-man and bro aesthetics that flips through magazines, dabbles in sports, and repurposes the trappings of nationhood and masculinity. In a seemingly effortless way, he makes us supremely conscious of being spectators in a society that streams out images faster than factories churn out products.
His skill excites us with the idea that art can communicate to the rest of the world an inner reality negotiated through medium, history, and word play. Sometimes those elements feel meme-like, harvesting popular discourse in a way that frames it for more rarefied spaces like the art museum — his playfulness with All Lives Matter is a prime example. Other times he’s tapping historical veins for conceptual moments he can elevate or criticize with a little tweak, like the I Am a Man series (2012) that riffs on the Civil Rights protest sign.

Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture reported on November 20 that Russian strikes had damaged cultural heritage sites in the cities of Kyiv and Odesa. According to the online newspaper Kyiv Independent, the hours-long series of attacks killed at least nine people and injured around 30.
Russian drone attacks damaged St. Volodymyr’s Cathedral, which is a national monument located in Kyiv. Ukraine’s Minister of Culture Tetyana Berezhna wrote in a Facebook post that the cathedral houses paintings “by famous artists such as Mykhailo Hrubely, Mykola Pymonenko, Serhiy Kostyantyn, Viktor Zamyriy, and others.”
The Ministry of Culture noted that the cathedral’s windows and window frames were broken in the course of the attack, with some cornices and carvings also suffering damage. Most of the cathedral’s structural elements and paintings remain intact although the total damage is still being assessed.
In addition, the National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War had its entrance and Hall of Glory damaged during the attacks. Damage was also reported in other sites across Kyiv, including the historic Embassy of the Netherlands, St. Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral, Yevhen Paton Bridge, the main building of the Mykhailo Drahomanov Ukrainian State University, and the Nechayev estate, among others.
The strikes caused damage in 12 cultural heritage sites within Odesa. The city’s historic center was inscribed on UNESCO’s list of World Heritage sites in danger back in January 2023. The Ministry of Culture stated that a total of approximately 212 sites in the city were damaged as a result of the recent shelling. This included architectural monuments such as the Kallio Palace and the Roman Catholic Cathedral of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
As of October 2025, Russian attacks have affected 2,185 cultural sites and 2,686 cultural institutions. In a statement, UNESCO condemned the recent strikes, adding that: “Damage to such institutions deprives communities of access to culture, education and shared spaces that are essential for recovery and social cohesion.”
