https://jacobin.com/2026/11/holmes-evans.title: Billy Evans’s You Can See Everything Deal Is the Real Story
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/holmes-evans.author: Stephen Lurie
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/holmes-evans.text:
Billy Evans’s You Can See Everything Deal Is the Real Story
You Can See Everything’s directors say no one in the documentary was paid, but The Hollywood Reporter says Billy Evans’s share is being paid out to a children’s charity. Either way, the film was made under a profit-sharing deal with its villain.
In just over a month in theaters, the new A24 film from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim has grossed over $93 million at the domestic box office, more than twelve times its $7 million budget. Had things gone as originally planned, a meaningful share of that money would now be flowing to Billy Evans — Elizabeth Holmes’s partner and the film’s de facto antagonist — under the profit-sharing deal he negotiated on camera in exchange for the couple’s participation. Evans has since told CBS News that his share would have been worth tens of millions of dollars.
We came close to living in that timeline: one in which moviegoers became, without knowing it, funders of the man now running what he himself dubs a “Theranos 2.0,” his blood-testing startup, Haemanthus. We have Evans — or Evans and A24 — to thank that we don’t. A title card at the end of the film tells us he “relinquished his negotiated share of the film’s profits and would not receive backend compensation.” That turns out to be incomplete. The Hollywood Reporter (THR) has since reported, citing two sources, that Evans’s representatives negotiated for that share to be paid out after all — to an unnamed children’s charity. At a Q&A last weekend, the directors disputed THR’s framing and, according to Semafor, said none of the film’s subjects were paid; a studio source told Semafor that Evans and A24 agreed to send the proceeds to charity, with Evans giving up his own participation as part of the arrangement. Neither the charity nor the amount has been disclosed. THR’s editor in chief, Maer Roshan, told Semafor the outlet stands by its reporting, calling A24's position “a pretty semantic argument.” Either way, money owed under the deal is leaving the film’s coffers — just not for Evans’s pocket.
What we do know is that A24 and the directors initially agreed to pay Evans a portion of the proceeds, that everything we see on-screen was produced under the auspices of that deal, and that there’s no reason to believe they would have backed out of it themselves.
In this light, alongside the critical appreciation the film has earned for its transcendent creativity and virtuosity, You Can See Everything should also be understood as something both more base and familiar: a deception practiced on its audience — a fraud in all but the legal sense. And as a wildly successful one, it may also push documentary filmmaking, as a whole, further toward crisis.
The film is seemingly transparent about the compromise at its foundation. From what’s shown on screen, we can conclude that the filmmakers, the studio, and Evans agreed — with or without Holmes’s knowledge — to make a film where at least one core subject would be paid in proportion to its earnings, while the film would be sold to the public as vérité documentary. That is what we see in the first half of the film. The arrangement unravels only when Holmes casually mentions to Fielder that she isn’t participating for money, raising the possibility that Evans had cut her out of the deal. It is entirely reasonable to suspect that had this discrepancy remained quiet — rather than metastasizing into the film’s second act — none of the parties would have disclosed the compensation agreement to the public.
“Pay-to-Play” Documentaries Are Becoming the Norm
What complicates matters is that arrangements like this have become commonplace. As Evans himself argues, documentary subjects are sometimes now paid for their participation — though invoking Harry and Meghan’s $100 million deal with Netflix was probably not the most persuasive benchmark for his negotiations. This phenomenon is an outgrowth of the genre’s ascendance in the streaming era. As streamers recognized how cheap documentaries are to produce and latched onto growing demand, the genre exploded — and is expected to continue to grow. Commercialization set off a competition for subjects, and the subjects, in turn, gained unprecedented leverage for money and control.
Crime documentaries and other fare about unsavory characters, which have increasingly dominated the streaming space, are no exception. Fyre Festival founder Billy McFarland shopped his participation to dueling productions from Netflix and Hulu — Netflix declined to pay him, but Hulu paid. Amazon MGM paid a reported $40 million to license Melania, and Donald Trump himself reported a $10.7 million licensing fee from the film on his financial disclosure. Most ordinary people receive no money for their appearance on reality TV, while some high-profile cast members, like those on the Real Housewives franchises, reportedly earn hundreds of thousands of dollars or more per season. There is enormous public demand to watch bad people doing bad things. And while paying subjects remains controversial among documentarians — some prominent directors and studios maintain their own opposition to the practice — it is neither illegal nor barred by Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences eligibility rules for awards, nor is disclosure of such payment required by documentary festivals.
In this sense, You Can See Everything sits closer to the center of current documentary trends than to the margins: it has celebrity, crime, and a production team ready to cross all kinds of norms to get the story. But even if the film fits in, its attempted profit-sharing scheme should still stand out. Many celebrity-driven documentaries are open about their subjects’ financial stakes, often crediting them as producers. Here A24 would have every incentive to keep quiet about this deal, with this recipient, and in a film about this subject matter. Public knowledge that proceeds would be going into Evans’s pocket could have crushed enthusiasm for the opening; moviegoers out to witness a retrospective on a scam would instead be unwitting investors in the subjects’ current venture. That the money is now bound for a children’s charity rather than Evans doesn’t mean the attempt carries no consequences. After all, conspiracy to commit fraud on investors — one of Holmes’s four convictions — does not require successful completion of the fraud. Plenty of other damage can be done by the attempt alone.
The Rise of Billy Evans
Everyone involved in the attempt will benefit from the effort. Billy Evans, despite his unsavoriness, has been granted a stratospheric rise in publicity. Our attentional economy will allow him to leverage this attention into power, at the very least among his fellow aggrieved, right-wing tech bros. With critical and financial success and talk of becoming the first documentary to be nominated for the Best Picture Oscar, Fielder and Oppenheim have made the jump from cult favorites to top-tier stars. A24 cements its status as a studio capable of commanding national attention. But most consequentially, perhaps, Elizabeth Holmes has received an astonishing rehabilitation courtesy of a sympathetic portrait that elides the Holmes described in prosecutors’ filings outlining the full extent of her crimes, and in the many accounts of the darker side of her character.
Where does that leave the audience? Aesthetically, we are rewarded. Calling the film a kind of fraud does not contradict its excellence as art: rather, the fusion of its subject matter and form underscores its slipperiness. That slipperiness is essential to its success, both exploring and embodying our modern fascination with the scam. The film enters the glut of podcasts, books, television shows, and movies about scams, frauds, and crimes of this millennium and then jumps to another dimension. The traditional structure of this genre is a reconstruction of a magic trick: we saw the result, and now we get to learn the methods of our deception. You Can See Everything is yet another illusion presented as the reveal. Judging by the pleasure, debate, and thought the film has provoked, viewers absorb this duplicity — we are both the mark of the scam and included as a beneficiary.
But if we are to judge You Can See Everything as a documentary — which the makers insist we do — artistry isn’t enough. Truth matters, too. A generous defense of the filmmakers would be that they believed moviegoers would have prior knowledge sufficient to engage the material from a responsible perspective. But presenting a misleading narrative — say, that the crux of Holmes’s innocence is whether “can” really meant “eventually capable of” — is not acceptable simply because facts elsewhere demonstrate her guilt was far broader. Moreover, as we know from many other stunning documentaries, truth and drama are plenty compatible. In fact, both could have been harmonized quite easily here, too. On a recent episode of the podcast Search Engine, host PJ Vogt and Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz discuss the chasm between the representation of Holmes on screen and reality — and how the public has fallen into it. They ask why the film couldn’t have a coda that put the artistic experience in its proper context, something like a supercut of Holmes’s many lies and wrongs. To disclose such a reality after the film has so successfully worked its magic, after Holmes has charmed Fielder and Fielder has charmed us, would only make the film’s effect even more powerful.
The filmmakers and studio must have discussed and rejected this option, choosing instead an epilogue that reveals Evans had given up his share — while leaving out that, it now appears, the share is being paid to charity. Viewers should wonder why. Perhaps, given the intimacy granted to them by the financial arrangement, they wanted to provide a sympathetic vision of Holmes. Or perhaps they just didn’t feel that genuine representation was their responsibility. Neither seems like a good precedent for documentary filmmaking.
We may have missed the timeline in which moviegoers paid Billy Evans millions of dollars, but the popularity and acclaim of You Can See Everything may carry other costs. What does it mean for the most successful nonmusical documentary of the decade to be made under a financial arrangement with its subject and to value story over reality? It could force a needed reckoning with the financialization of the genre. More likely, it will push the field further away from journalistic norms. A lesser production might have been widely condemned for its complicity, but Fielder and Oppenheim have faced no concerted backlash from critics or peers. There will apparently be no consequences for the pay-to-play arrangement that made this film possible and made it what it is. With enough charm, they seem to have learned, you really can get away with anything.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: State Education Officials Can’t Say Why Reading Scores Dropped Significantly Last Year
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Amy Zimmer, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
After reading test scores for New York students in grades 3-5 dropped significantly last school year following big gains the year before, state education officials promised to investigate.
They shared their findings this week, saying they found no errors in the testing process but could not pinpoint the cause of the swings, deepening the mystery.
“We are pleased to report that [our] review found no errors in the calculations or processes used and confirmed that all established analysis plans and industry standards were adhered to,” J.P. O’Hare, spokesperson for the state Education Department, said in a statement.
Several testing experts previously said such sharp swings were unusual. In New York City, for instance, third grade reading scores fell nearly 14 percentage points last year. Fourth grade scores fell nearly 6 points and fifth grade scores fell 13 points. Those declines essentially erased big gains made the year before, when city officials heralded the results as an indication that the city’s literacy curriculum mandate was paying off. But in both years, the trends were mirrored across the state, even in districts without such mandates.
Across grades 3-8, about half of New York City students were proficient in reading, a decline of 6 percentage points from the year before.
To investigate the results, the state Education Department worked with its technical advisory committee, a panel of experts paid by the state to oversee the testing process, as well as the test vendor, NWEA, and a third-party validation team. (Experts on the panel declined to discuss the investigation, citing a nondisclosure agreement.)
“The Department has not identified a specific reason for the changes in scores from one year to the next. It is necessary to point out that assessment results can be influenced by many factors — including but not limited to instruction, curricular materials, and administration conditions,” O’Hare wrote. “Because of this, it’s important to look at assessment results over multiple years, rather than draw conclusions from a single year’s scores.”
Parents and educators pointed to possible explanations for the unusual swings, including the transition to computer-based testing. The state previously said it conducted extensive reviews of the switch to online tests and that the change was not a factor. Still, the Education Department has not ruled out allowing New York City students to return to pencil-and-paper tests, following mounting pressure from local lawmakers to reduce screen time.
Some testing experts are still trying to understand what happened.
Andrew Ho, a testing expert at Harvard’s Graduate School of Education, said that while swings like New York’s are striking, they’re increasingly common.
“Since the pandemic, we’ve seen more anomalies like this. Trends depend on changes in population, motivation and administration,” Ho, who is on the state’s technical advisory committee but was speaking in a personal capacity, wrote in an email. “If tested populations change more, or kids and teachers care more, or administration conditions change, we see swings that don’t represent real changes in average achievement.”
He added: “The testing industry needs to improve its equating procedures or risk public trust.”
To help the public better understand the results and improve transparency, EdTrust-New York, a statewide education policy and advocacy group, called for an independent audit of the last three years of the state’s reading tests after officials released their findings without a public presentation or detailed analysis of the results.
Emily Oster, a Brown University education economist who closely follows test scores nationwide, has been vocal about her skepticism of the anomalous scores. She continues to question why reading scores for grades 3-5 plunged after soaring the year before, while grades 6-8 and math scores showed no similar changes.
“The changes are enormous, implying an increase of about 2/3 of a year of learning, and then a subsequent loss for the same children year-on-year,” Oster wrote in an email to Chalkbeat. “It’s very unlikely that these reflect changes in learning, or curricular changes. They happened at the same level for basically every racial group, both disadvantaged and advantaged students, and across the entire state. This is just really difficult to explain with learning gains.”
Oster raised the possibility that something may have gone wrong in calibrating test questions from year to year — a process that allows test makers to compare an individual’s score to those of peers — but acknowledged she had no firm evidence.
State Education Department officials did not provide further information on the investigation’s findings or on Oster’s theory.
Amy Zimmer is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat New York. Contact Amy at azimmer@chalkbeat.org.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/23/geo-.title: Private Prison Told ICE Its Jail Was Worth $67 Million. ICE Bought It for Nearly Half a Billion.
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/23/geo-.author: Jacqueline Stevens, Andrew Free
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/23/geo-.text:
As it eyed a sale of a jail in Tacoma, Washington, the private prison giant GEO Group valued the facility in March 2026 at $67 million, according to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement records obtained exclusively by The Intercept.
The federal government just paid GEO almost seven times that — $453 million — when it purchased the facility, the Northwest ICE Processing Center.
The chasm between GEO’s March 2026 asset appraisal and the sale price just eight months later represents a “massive increase,” according to Michael Wriston, co-founder of the government watchdog Project Salt Box, which tracks ICE spending and contracts.
“ICE should explain how it arrived at $453 million and release the appraisal behind that price,” Wriston told The Intercept.
“I think this is what happens when you move too fast without sufficient internal controls,” John Roth, the former inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, told The Intercept. “You’re going to waste a lot of money. And that assumes everyone has the best intentions and hasn’t got some sort of side deal or corrupt motive.”
Neither ICE nor GEO responded to requests for comment about the sale. Without answering questions about the sale price, the Department of Homeland Security told The Intercept the purchase was “to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations.”
With Democrats set to take control of Congress, ICE’s real estate purchases are already coming under intense scrutiny on Capitol Hill.
“This new report is worthy of serious investigation and is part of a pattern of Department of Homeland Security purchases of detention facilities for hundreds of millions of dollars more than they seem to be worth,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, told The Intercept in a statement. “These deals raise serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and corruption at DHS.”
Hassan opened a probe earlier this month into ICE’s $495 million purchase of a detention center the private prison giant CoreCivic previously offered to the state of Minnesota for $75 million — a sale the state’s corrections commissioner told the news site Punch Up was being discussed for $3 million.
GEO Group’s March 2026 valuation for Northwest ICE Processing Center, which the company purchased in 2005 as part of its acquisition of another private prison firm, was submitted to the Department of Homeland Security in accordance with its contract with ICE.
According to a chart in the document, GEO calculated the current $67 million value of the detention facility, which is not the same as its market value, by subtracting annual depreciation figures from its original value of $109 million.
Roth, the former Homeland Security inspector general, expects scrutiny into the nearly half-billion-dollar sale’s paper trail.
“I’d be curious to know,” he said, “what sort of due diligence they did before they put that number down.”
Cost of Avoiding Regulations
ICE officials told Government Accountability Office investigators that their robust plans for purchasing existing immigration detention facilities was not to save money, but to avoid issues with local governments.
“Officials noted that while they do not expect this effort to result in cost savings, it will help ICE fulfill its mission in locations where state governments may resist expanded detention efforts,” said a Government Accountability Office report released this month.
Like other private prison firms across the country, GEO’s efforts to build and operate facilities it owns have met obstacles in local rules and regulations.
In some cases, state-level regulators have gone after GEO for violations of labor laws like minimum wage and occupational safety regulations. Earlier this year in California, the company paid a $100,000 fine and agreed to extend worker protections to immigrant laborers over alleged violations of California worker safety standards.
One of the cases focused on the Northwest ICE Processing Center, the Tacoma facility that GEO just sold to ICE. In 2021, a judge ordered GEO to pay $26 million to former detainees and the state of Washington for, among other allegations, state minimum wage violations. (Andrew Free, one of the authors of this article, was an attorney for the ICE detainees in the lawsuit.)
The verdict was upheld by a federal appeals court in 2025 after GEO sought the same immunity from state minimum wage laws enjoyed by the federal government. The Supreme Court is currently deciding whether it will hear GEO’s appeal.
In a May earnings call, GEO chair George Zoley noted the problem in areas with Democrats in charge of regulation.
“I think the logical solution to much of that is federal ownership of the facilities,” Zoley told the earnings call, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer.
Lucibeth Mayberry, the CEO of CoreCivic, told investors during the company’s most recent earnings call that ICE should “move quickly” to complete several more purchases before the end of the current Congress’s term.
Taking federal ownership of the facilities could lead to massive new expenses for the government — and not only due to the enormous sticker prices, according to the Government Accountability Office report.
“ICE did not manage detention facility investments in accordance with DHS acquisition practices, which include the development of life-cycle cost estimates,” the report said.
According to the Government Accountability Office, ICE violated its own guidelines by failing to update its spending plans to account for the costs of a plan to purchase warehouses to convert them into immigrations jails, as well as its acquisitions of existing detention facilities.
“In purchasing facilities like the one in Tacoma, the administration is not only sticking the American taxpayer with the massive bill — but also escalating costs for operating them for years to come,” Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is slated to resume his perch atop the House Homeland Security Committee in January, told The Intercept. “DHS must answer for its actions.”
“Laughing to the Bank”
After the sale of the Northwest ICE Processing Center to ICE, GEO plans to use the $340 million net profits from the sale to buy back shares of stock, thus increasing their value, the firm told its shareholders.
“I am deeply concerned by what appears to be a gross misuse of taxpayer dollars to pad the pockets of the GEO Group, a private, for-profit company that has overseen real mistreatment and abuses of detained people across the country,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., the ranking member of the House Judiciary’s Immigration subcommittee, told The Intercept. “It is unfathomable that GEO has announced it intends to use the net proceeds from this sale for stock buybacks, in yet another move to put profits over the safety and health of the people it detains.”
The sale of the immigration jail is just the latest means by which GEO is extracting super-profits from public funds.
Days before announcing the nearly half-billion-dollar deal that would turn the Northwest ICE Processing Center into a federally owned property, ICE also awarded GEO a $1.5 billion contract to continue its detention services there, according to Project Salt Box.
While eye-popping ICE contracts are nothing new for major private prison firms, ICE’s purchase of the companies’ facilities at such high prices is raising eyebrows among government accountability advocates.
“Someone needs to come clean about why ICE is paying hundreds of millions for facilities that are worth a fraction of that amount,” said Scott Amey, general counsel of the Project on Government Oversight, a government watchdog.
“Who is minding the store and is anyone conducting market research or talking to commercial realtors to figure out the fair price?” asked Amey. “I don’t think so, and the public is now on the hook for years to come while the companies are truly laughing to the bank.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://hellgatenyc.com/lyft-mamdani-far.title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani Forced Lyft to the Negotiating Table—And Citi Bike Riders Won
https://hellgatenyc.com/lyft-mamdani-far.author: Max Rivlin-Nadler
https://hellgatenyc.com/lyft-mamdani-far.text:
After years of rapid price increases that netted the Citi Bike operator Lyft tens of millions of dollars in profits, City Hall announced Monday that it has ironed out a deal that will put fees for the city's booming bikeshare system much more in line with other forms of rapid transit. 
Starting in January, Citi Bike members will only pay $3.65 to ride for up to 45 minutes on the system's gray e-bikes (on which 70 percent of Citi Bike rides are taken), and the system's annual membership fee, which has skyrocketed 77 percent since the program's inception in 2013, will also be capped at $239 through 2029, when Lyft's current contract with the City to operate the bike share program runs out.

https://citylimits.org/it-feels-like-we-.title: ‘It Feels Like We Don’t Matter’:  NYCHA Residents Live With Dust From Nearby Waste Site as State Decision Looms
https://citylimits.org/it-feels-like-we-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/it-feels-like-we-.text:
Share This Article
Residents at NYCHA’s Redfern Houses say the state is dragging its feet on whether to allow the nearby Inwood Materials Terminal, which crushes leftover construction debris, to keep operating. Officials just extended the deadline for their decision by more than three months.
Public housing residents of Redfern Houses in Far Rockaway, Queens, say they’ve long documented the dust from an industrial waste site, which sits roughly 150 feet away, gathering inside in their homes, and covering playgrounds and cars.
“All the dirt blows over here, comes in through our windows and covers surfaces in our apartments,” said Kimberly Comes, who’s lived at Redfern Houses for about 36 years.
“It feels like we don’t matter,” Comes said.
Managed by the Haugland Group, Inwood Materials Terminal crushes construction and demolition leftovers, like concrete, asphalt, brick and rock, into recycled material.
It’s been operating near Jamaica Bay, at the tip of Inwood in on the border of Nassau County and Queens, since 2015, taking over the site of an oil terminal that had operated there for decades prior.
In 2023, the state adopted stricter laws governing solid waste management sites, requiring companies like IMT to submit applications for additional permits, which the state Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) can approve or deny. The new laws also require DEC to consider the impact of pollution on surrounding communities in its permitting decisions.
But neighbors at nearby Redfern Houses, a New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) development home to over 1,400 residents, say both IMT and the state agency have been dragging their feet on the re-evaluation process—noting that IMT has been submitting incomplete applications for over three years.
The company submitted its first complete application in August, which the DEC accepted public comments on this fall. Now the agency has extended its decision deadline by more than three months—to Jan. 30, 2027, according to an announcement earlier this month—to allow for a more thorough review of the feedback it received.
Now, residents are calling on DEC to hold a public hearing for community members to share how the site affects them, saying the state agency hasn’t yet met with residents directly to hear their concerns.
In public comments, residents are also calling on the DEC to deny the application, or strengthen requirements for IMT to protect the neighborhood from dust it releases.
Incomplete applications and delayed deadlines
Damon Gilbert, a staff attorney with New York Lawyers for the Public Interest (NYLPI) working with community members, described the DEC’s extension as another delay from the agency.
“There was an Oct. 28 deadline for them to make a decision on the permit application, and that deadline came and went,” Gilbert said. Still, he said, the extension “underscores the extent of community concern” over the project.
But as residents await a decision, the site is still crushing debris—and filling their homes with dust.
Gilbert explained that “it’s not unusual for companies like IMT to continue operations without proper permitting, because they’re usually given a grace period to transition onto the new track,” adding that the company’s earlier, incomplete application submissions allowed them to drag the process out.
Until now, IMT has “essentially been applying and getting denied over and over again, while operating under a general registration that is no longer what those types of facilities require,” Gilbert explained.
IMT’s applications, Gilbert said, were “incomplete in a number of ways, including how they are analyzing their impacts on the community, dust emissions, as well as the state’s Environmental Justice Siting Law, which requires that the state can’t make any actions that would add further harm to an identified disadvantaged community for environmental justice purposes.”
Redfern Houses is in one of those identified communities.
Public comments submitted to the DEC describe industrial activity at the site “six days a week, beginning early in the morning and regularly extending into overnight hours.”
“For residents, IMT’s operations have tangible consequences,” one read.
“The wind and the dust don’t care if we’re an impoverished community,” said Comes, who also serves as the president of the resident council at Redfern Houses. “Our health is just as important, especially if we’re poor.”
She said she’s been cleaning dirt that covers surfaces of her bathtubs, windows and car several times a week for years.
“I get the dirt every morning,” Comes said. “I can feel the grit on the bottom of the tub.”
Commenters also point to a community-led survey of about 436 nearby residents, which documents their experiences “rinsing layers of dirt from bathtubs before bathing, and repeatedly cleaning household surfaces and vehicles, only to find them coated again the next morning.”
Of the residents who responded to the survey, about 86 percent identified as Black or African American, and 46 percent identified as having a disability.
Public comments also argue that IMT’s existing burden report doesn’t determine how much pollution in the surrounding community is caused by dust from its operations, which include crushing, screening and stockpiling materials.
Additionally, community comments argue that the company’s proposed harm mitigation methods—which include extending walls and 15-foot limitations on open-air 24-hour stockpiles—are inadequate.
A spokesperson for IMT told City Limits that “while we meet all DEC operational regulations, we also continue to take community concerns seriously.”
“We continue to collaborate on further improvements with community leaders and residents on items such as additional dust controls through filtration fencing, additional water cannons and sprinklers, and enhanced cleaning,” the spokesperson added.
But Comes said that’s not enough.
“I would hope that they dome the place, or they move to where there are no people,” she said.
But IMT’s current waterfront location allows the facility to transport shipments of waste materials, like concrete and rock, on the water—which helps reduce traffic and congestion on local roads.
“Through barge transportation, the facility takes thousands of trucks off local and regional roads annually, while the materials it recycles support many critical local infrastructure and coastal resiliency projects,” a spokesperson for the company said in a statement.
Gilbert explained that an outcome where the operation is shut down or moved would require “an incredibly long process,” that “may not reflect a reality,” but explained that residents are hoping for a “cleaner operation that gets rid of the dust issues.”
“They’ve been living through this for over a decade now, and they just want change in the conditions they have to live with,” he said.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Week That Was: A Cavalcade of Catastrophes Across Air Travel and Workplace Technology
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Katrina vanden Heuvel
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Week That Was: A Cavalcade of Catastrophes Across Air Travel and Workplace Technology
America’s infrastructure crisis can no longer be ignored.
After nearly a decade, it seems that the Trump administration’s fabled “Infrastructure Week” finally materialized.
Except, instead of renewed investment in the tools and structures that make work and life possible, the nation was treated to a cavalcade of catastrophes—across air travel, banking, and workplace technology.
As Americans deboarded planes and scoured e-mail inboxes in vain, as account holders faced error messages while attempting to access their own money, as rescue workers searched for survivors of New York’s fatal apartment building collapse—it all added up to a sinking feeling. (And not just because, not long beforehand in Massachusetts, a 125-year-old pipe caved and created a literal sinkhole.)
In a time when Americans are already struggling to meet basic needs, the physical and digital systems we are meant to take for granted are crumbling. And while the timing of these crises may be coincidental, Dumb Infrastructure Week surfaced an alarming truth. Daily life in America hinges upon a patchwork of inadequate public and private infrastructure being maintained largely by a shrinking number of oligarchs and their hand-picked goons.
Over a third of America’s bridges need major repairs. It will require $625 billion of investments in pipe replacements, treatment plant maintenance, and other upgrades to sustain our clean water supply. And on the digital side, over 10 million Americans still lack high-speed Internet—even as the lightning-fast AI buildout strains power grids to further line a handful of well-padded pockets.
And all of these crises were well underway before the Trump administration canceled billions of dollars’ worth of EPA funding and cut staff at the Department of Transportation, before DOGE shrank regional FEMA offices and slashed the federal IT workforce. Public health infrastructure has been similarly undermined, to the tune of 5,412 measles cases and counting in 2026.
It is a self-fulfilling prophecy that Republican administrations have demonstrated again and again: claim government does not work, actively sabotage it while in power, then point to the resulting failures as evidence that government does not work. It is no wonder that the National Review’s proposed solution post-ground-stop is to privatize air traffic control.
So the federal government—led by an executive who has chosen to live out the remainder of his term in an endless episode of This Old House—is unlikely to meaningfully address any infrastructure needs outside of the ballroom sector.
But this vacuum of leadership offers an opening for progressives—to underscore the damage done by Trump’s disinvestment in civil service, and to propose bold, alternative solutions to the creeping privatization that has cheapened just about every facet of American living. Already, a number of leading voices in Congress are doing just that.
In an effort to avert blame for the nationwide ground stop, the Trump administration has claimed that full modernization of the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure would require as much as $50 billion in additional funding from Congress.
In response, Democrats have rightly pointed out that Republicans have cut FAA funding under Democratic presidents, eliminated a number of roles from an already understaffed FAA through DOGE, and have yet to spend much of the $12.5 billion that was allocated to the agency’s modernization through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Even Republicans in Congress have called for more fiscal transparency from The Real World: Boston alumnus Sean Duffy’s Department of Transportation. As Senator Thom Tillis said: “If you want $30 billion or $50 billion, you better damn sure have a long list of initiatives and planning that went into it versus ‘give me a number and I’ll figure out how to spend it.’”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
As it turns out, progressives have a long list of initiatives and planning of their own.
In Congress this year, Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY) and Greg Casar (TX) and Senator Ed Markey (MA) reintroduced their Connect the Grid Act, which would join Texas’s electric grid with national systems, making power more reliable. And in another AOC partnership—this time with Illinois Representative Delia Ramirez and Bernie Sanders—the Green New Deal for Public Housing Act, which seeks to modernize and maintain the nation’s stock of public housing, has also been reintroduced.
And it happens that funding for the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021—which helped the US earn its highest grade yet on the American Society of Civil Engineers’ 2025 infrastructure report card—expired on September 30, with some provisions temporarily extended until December 11. There may now be political will for the IIJA’s proposed successor—called the BUILD America 250 Act, because of course it is—to be improved before passage.
As newly empowered Democrats rev up their investigation apparatus, they can also shine a spotlight on the ways that Trump’s gutting of the federal government has contributed to the string of recent breakdowns, and the consequences yet to come if those cuts are not reversed.
In a nation that’s feeling every one of its 250 years, the next Democrat in the White House will have to recommit to strengthening our foundations—safe housing, bridges, and roads, reliable telecommunications, affordable and dependable green power. And they’ll also have to recommit to the dedicated civil service members, long maligned by Republicans and destabilized by DOGE, who make those fundamental services possible.
After all, as Everett Kelley, president of the American Federation of Government Employees, has said, “Federal employees treat our veterans and support our military, safeguard our food and air, process retirement and disability payments for tens of millions of Americans every month and so much more.” Without them, the nation would truly be grounded.

https://empire.streetsblog.org/transit-a.title: New York Transit Advocates Push Back on $68B Highway Industry Wish List
https://empire.streetsblog.org/transit-a.author: Austin C. Jefferson
https://empire.streetsblog.org/transit-a.text:
Advocates for mass transit and walkable cities are pushing back against a recent road builders’ report that urged New York state to nearly double its next five-year transportation capital plan — warning that the industry call to pour as much as $68.8 billion into aging highways will starve far more urgent transit, biking and pedestrian needs.
The October analysis — prepared by the American Road and Transportation Builders Association for the Long Island Contractors’ Association and its New York Roadway & Infrastructure Coalition partners — framed highway and bridge maintenance as a looming crisis requiring an extra $4.3 to 6.9 billion per year in state funding, even as New York’s non-car infrastructure faces a deeper funding hole.
Doubling down on a highway-first budget ignores what residents actually need to lower their daily expenses, according to critics of the $68-billion highway funding ask.
“With car and gas prices setting records, we need our leaders to invest in transportation projects that give us safe and affordable options for getting around, regardless of where we live, what we earn, how old we are or whether we have a disability,” said Danny Pearlstein, policy and communications director at the Riders Alliance.
Before lawmakers rush to bankroll a massive highway reconstruction blitz, they should ask a more basic question, one policy expert suggested — whether New York even needs all of its aging roadways in the first place. 
“We have this legacy system that we are abusing in ways that it never was even intended or designed to withstand,” said Rachel Weinberger, vice president for research and policy strategy at the Regional Plan Association. “Think about the opportunity cost of $60 billion.”
Rather than reflexively spending roughly $60 billion to rebuild every crumbling highway segment, the state should consider tearing down underutilized urban highways to eliminate permanent maintenance liabilities, Weinberger said.
Weinberger pushed back against the idea that New York must keep the highway pipeline going in order to preserve unionized construction jobs. Inventing road projects just to keep crews busy locks the state into a carbon-intensive system that has outlived its usefulness, she said; those same workers could build schools, public transit and hospitals instead.
Highway repair costs aren’t going down: Americans’ increased affinity for heavier passenger vehicles, like oversized SUVs, means more pavement damage and more frequent street repaving. At the same time, the shift towards electric vehicles cuts into state gas tax revenues meant to fund road repairs, Weinberger said. The surest way to rein in costs is to have fewer highways to maintain.
“We are making heavier and heavier vehicles. That’s more and more expensive to maintain. We are, for very good reasons, making more fuel-efficient vehicles, but that means our gas tax revenues, which are not in fact indexed to inflation, are eroded even further,” Weinberger said. “If I used to have to repave my roads every 10 years, but now because I have heavier vehicles, I have to repave every five years, I want to really think about, do I want to put a tax on heavy vehicles? Your Chevy Suburban maybe should pay more than my Honda Civic.”
The road builders’ own numbers underscore just how car-centric New York’s capital spending already is. 
Under the current $34.5 billion FY 2023–2027 plan, more than 96 percent goes toward state and local roads and bridges, leaving just $1.32 billion — or 3.8 percent — itemized for “other” modes. That tiny sliver goes to non-MTA transit capital assistance ($968 million), freight and passenger rail ($230 million) and aviation ($140 million).
Pedestrian, bicycle and accessibility upgrades, meanwhile, aren’t broken out as standalone priorities in either the budget or the industry’s proposal.
To make the case for doubling highway spending, the report points out that construction bid inflation has eroded the current plan’s real purchasing power by 26 percent compared to the previous two-year plan, degrading the state’s highway quality rating. 
New York directs 51 percent of its combined road and bridge contract awards to bridges — roughly double the 25 percent national average — yet 8.3 percent remain structurally deficient and 39 percent of state DOT-maintained lane miles rate in poor or fair condition, according to the industry report. In 2022, the state estimated it funded just 35 percent of its highway repair needs per year on average.
Those numbers may sound dire, but transit and street-safety advocates note that government has left non-driving modes even further behind: The state’s last 20-year long-term needs assessment in 2007 identified $6.5 billion in non-MTA public transit capital needs and $2 billion for pedestrian, bicycle and ADA improvements.
Even if lawmakers wanted to grant the road builders’ wish list, New York’s traditional highway funding sources are tapped out. Dedicated Highway and Bridge Trust Fund tax receipts have plateaued, with 80 percent of the fund’s disbursements now swallowed up by debt service and state operations rather than capital projects, accordingto state figures crunched by the highway group.
At the same time, state-supported debt is projected to hit 3.99 percent of personal income by FY 2031, leaving just $177 million in borrowing capacity beneath the statutory 4 percent cap set by the Debt Reform Act of 2000. To bankroll a $68.8 billion plan, the report floats raising the state gas tax, enacting new electric vehicle registration fees or implementing statewide road usage charges.
Washington isn’t offering an immediate bailout, either. Following the Sept. 30 expiration of the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, Congress passed a stopgap extension through Dec. 11 that effectively imposes a 13 percent annualized cut to federal highway and bridge funding until lawmakers pass a full reauthorization.
For organized labor and the construction sector, however, delaying road and bridge work to rethink the state’s transportation footprint is a nonstarter. Patrick Purcell, executive director of the New York State Laborers-Employers Cooperation and Education Trust, a labor-management partnership, told Streetsblog that policymakers cannot afford to pause for a top-down overhaul right as the next five-year capital cycle approaches.
“I’m always in favor of reviewing the transit system, and because things like transit, like everything else in the world, things change. So I believe in taking a look at it top down, but you can’t start that now when we’re about to start another five-year plan,” Purcell said.
Purcell expressed optimism that a friendlier incoming Congress will break the federal logjam and help fund major projects like the Gateway Tunnel. Pointing to the more than 600 structurally deficient bridges across New York, he warned that waiting for a catastrophic collapse before acting would hurt both working families and the state economy.
“My suggestion is let’s deal with it now. Let’s not wait for that disaster, let’s put money into it, let’s let the economy benefit from it. Let average New Yorkers benefit from it, and then let’s take a look at maybe a relook at how we do this with our transit system going forward.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ‘I want the experiences I had to be available forever’: arts figures and scientists hit out at proposed job cuts at Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Tim Stone
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
More than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution. The signatories include the former Tasmanian premier Lara Giddings and the 2014 Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan, along with 44 leading-scientists representing universities in the UK, Europe, Canada, USA, Russia and Australia.
TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium. Its “science collections are really critical on a global scale for research around climate change and species extinction,” explains Ian Terry, the chair of Friends of TMAG and the museum’s former senior curator of cultural heritage (2006-2017).
Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.
Staff at the TMAG were briefed in August that up to 19.7 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs, or roughly 30% of its workforce would be axed to rein in government spending. The government has disputed the claim that the scale of the required cuts has been confirmed; a spokesperson is quoted in ABC News as saying “TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30%”.
However, since news of cuts were made public Tasmanian MPs, TMAG’s executive and its board have received more than 25 letters from prominent European scientists that have decried the government’s planned cuts, and warned its decision to axe the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, Gintaras Kantvilas, an internationally renowned biologist, would have “consequences far beyond Tasmania”.
This week’s letter called for the Tasmanian government to recognise its “statutory obligation to care for approximately one million objects of inestimable value” and “reconsider the proposed job cuts with their unintended deleterious consequences on the Tasmanian economy.”
“I want TMAG properly funded. I want the life-changing childhood experiences I had at TMAG to be available to all Tasmanians forever,” David Walsh, the founder of Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art (MONA), and one of the letter’s signatories, wrote in a separate letter that was published in Hobart’s Mercury newspaper this week. “I put stuff on Mona’s wall because TMAG put stuff in my heart,” he added.
The proposed job losses are part of wide-ranging cost cutting initiatives being rolled out by the state Liberal government, as part of an attempt to rein in the state’s ballooning debt, which is projected to reach A$9.9bn (£5bn) by 2027-28. These initiatives include a plan to slash up 1700 public sector jobs by 2032.
Although the government disputes the scale of the proposed staff reductions, when a new organisational chart was shown to staff in late September it identified “seven positions that were definitely to be cut,” Terry says. Those positions included two positions at the herbarium, a biologist, a graphic designer, a photographer, the museum’s only exhibitions officer, as well as the amalgamation of the vertebrate and invertebrate zoologist into a single role.
Asked about the government’s dismissal of the claims about a higher number of staff losing their jobs, Terry explains that over the last 12 months the museum has already lost “quite a lot of staff” through natural attrition and redundancies. “I suspect some of those positions were included in the 19.7 figure,” he says.
TMAG and the Tasmania state premier’s department has been approached for comment by The Art Newspaper.
Funding cuts
According to independent budget analysis provided by the Friends of TMAG, the proposed changes under the broader cost-cutting initiative would also see TMAG move under the control of a new government agency called Building Tasmania and lose up to 27% of its funding for 2027-28 while its targets for physical visitation increase by 6.4%. TMAG is already “seriously underfunded”, says Terry. Its current exhibition Becoming Modern: Mid-century Australian Art has a 16-month run. “That's unheard of,” Terry continues, adding he thinks that “locals will be going less often because you're not going to go back many times to look at the same exhibition”.
A state government spokesperson says there is no correlation between the cost cutting measures and a new A$1.13bn (£573m) football stadium planned for Macquarie Point, a location that was once earmarked for a truth-and-reconciliation art park proposed by Dark Lab (a subsidiary of MONA). However, the independent MP Peter George asked in a statement issued on 25 September: “where’s the money [for that stadium] coming from?”
The proposed cuts to staff numbers are currently under review by the Tasmanian Industrial Commission and Tasmania’s Upper House is voting on calls to reverse cuts to TMAG’s budget. Decisions on both issues are expected on Tuesday 24 November.
At the time of writing both Gintaras Kantvilas, the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium and Simon Grove, a zoologist and curator of invertebrates, have said they have had their positions reinstated after they had been under threat due to the proposed cuts.

https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/italy-str.title: Italy's general strike
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/italy-str.text:
‘ Abbassate le armi, alzate i salari ! ’ (‘Down arms, raise wages.’)
On Friday 20 November, Italy’s largest trade union, the General Confederation of Labour (CGIL), organised its fifth general strike since 2022 in opposition to Giorgia Meloni’s budgets. In more than a hundred cities across the country, unions demanded more resources for wages, pensions, hospitals and schools from a government bent on austerity and rearmament.
Since the autumn of 2025, solidarity with Palestine has also fuelled the protests. In Genoa, dockworkers threatened to block the port if Israel intercepted the humanitarian flotilla bound for Gaza. On 22 September 2025, the Unione Sindacale di Base trade union (USB) called a general strike to condemn the Gaza genocide and Italy’s economic and military ties to Israel. From student marches to the docks of Genoa a single rallying cry rang out: ‘Blocchiamo tutto!’ (‘Let’s block everything!’)
In Italy, as in France, there has been a noticeable hardening of public order policies. The Meloni government has criminalised road blockades and authorised preventive police detention ahead of protests. Since October, ‘violent participation in a demonstration’ has carried a potential five-year prison sentence, and measures have been introduced to make it easier to place minors in detention. The prime minister has also deployed five hundred soldiers to Milan, where they will remain until the end of the year. Meanwhile, the minister of infrastructure and transport and deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini has repeatedly taken action to curb strikes. On 20 November, the CGIL was forced to exclude the rail and air transport sectors from its strike notice.
With an election just months away, leaders of the Italian left have joined the protests. Last Friday, they marched alongside the CGIL against austerity, precarious working conditions and handouts to the wealthy – a bold move, since that it was their own shift towards ‘extreme centrism’ that deprived the working classes of political representation and paved the way for the far right. For now, Meloni enjoys a solid parliamentary majority; yet opposition to her compromises with Brussels and the European economic order is emerging from her own right.

https://www.propublica.org/article/dc-me.title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
https://www.propublica.org/article/dc-me.author: Alec MacGillis, Andy Kroll
https://www.propublica.org/article/dc-me.text:
Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.
Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.
In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.
Do You Have a Tip for ProPublica?
If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.
The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.
Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.
Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s departure as head of the Smithsonian, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.
Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”
The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.
At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.
The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.
The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)
As recounted by ProPublica in September, the American history museum has faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in 2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-reckoning.
By the time of Trump’s return to office in 2025, there was no shortage of fodder for the new administration to seize on. The July report noted a recent exhibit on Ben Franklin that speculated about whether he had used enslaved members of his household as subjects of his experiments with electric shocks. And it chastised the museum for having trained staff using the “Museums as a Site for Social Action Toolkit,” a 200-plus-page tract on how to “truly transform the museum space,” which it says is linked “with white supremacy, hetero-patriarchy, abuse of labor, colonization, imperialist theft of art and artifacts, destruction or absencing of alternative ways of interpreting or representing art and artifacts, structural racism and other oppressions.”
The White House report emphasized that the museum should not whitewash blights on the nation’s history such as slavery and Jim Crow, but argued that it was failing to give visitors any sense of how it developed into the country that it is. “It should tell the whole story of a nation,” the report stated, “including the good and the bad, so Museum visitors can understand the development that led our nation to where it is today.”
The report was released with symbolic fanfare on the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding. The administration’s announcement of its next move on this front may have less pop, given its soft rollout on the Orange Line.

https://hyperallergic.com/for-some-artis.title: For Some Artists, Residency-Hopping Is a Form of Survival
https://hyperallergic.com/for-some-artis.author: Angelica Villa
https://hyperallergic.com/for-some-artis.text:
For Some Artists, Residency-Hopping Is a Form of Survival
Artists are increasingly turning to the programs as sites of refuge as they navigate precarity, commercial pressures, and burnout.
For Paul Maheke, a French-born performance artist in his 40s, a year of funding, a sunlit studio in a sixteenth-century palatial estate in Rome, and ample time alone represented a new phase in a career that has long been shaped by transience. Over the last decade, before landing at the Villa Medici, he’d completed more than 14 artist residencies.
By 2015, after graduate school, he began moving between residencies every few months, relocating to remote locations in France, Vienna, and Canada. He sought distance from London’s commercial gallery circuit, a networking scene he described as populated with “opening-rats” and an environment he felt was depleting his focus. “Residencies were a way around that,” he told Hyperallergic, four months into his stay at the Italian complex. “I think I’ve never been sedentary. I tend to think better when I’m in movement. As I’m traveling, it’s always shifting my way of working.”
As his ideas developed, Maheke said that the pressure to hold down a studio space better suited to a painter no longer made sense. His work had outgrown a conventional studio, encompassing choreographed performances with professional dancers and drawing on autobiography. He described enmeshing an “Afro-descendant European perspective” with ideas about queerness, memory, and the body as a vessel for social experience.
Across countries and career stages, artists like Maheke have found themselves increasingly turning to residencies to navigate precarity. In interviews with Hyperallergic, artists reported using residencies as alternatives for permanent studios and refuges from the commercial pressures of major cultural centers. What were once considered philanthropic sites for creative retreat or intellectual leisure have become for many a workaround for periods of economic volatility and increased pressure to sustain artistic output.

The Museum of Contemporary Art Australia (MCA) in Sydney has announced Sophie O’Brien as its new senior curator of exhibitions. O’Brien joins the institution from the Bundanon Art Museum in Illaroo, Australia, where she is head of curatorial and learning. She succeeds Jane Devery, who departed in August after four years in the role. In her new job, O’Brien will shape the museum’s exhibition platform with an eye to luring a broad audience.
O’Brien brings more than two decades of experience to the MCA. Before coming to Bundadon about six years ago, she was head of exhibitions and collections at the Govett-Brewster Art Gallery in New Plymoth, New Zealand, senior curator at the Serpentine Galleries in London, and curator of contemporary British Art at Tate Britain, also in London. Earlier curatorial positions include those at Artspace Sydney and the Art Gallery of Western Australia in Perth. She led exhibition teams for the Australian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale (2005–2007) and for the Biennale of Sydney (2003).
“Sophie brings a breadth of curatorial experience working with artists, and an outstanding track record of delivering ambitious and engaging exhibitions,” said MCA Australia director Suzanne Cotter in a statement. “Her international perspective, leadership and commitment to artistic excellence will be invaluable as we continue to build on the MCA’s reputation as Australia’s leading contemporary art museum.”
