https://jacobin.com/2026/11/stella-lefty.title: Stella Lefty: Data Center Music
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/stella-lefty.author: Nikil Soto
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/stella-lefty.text:
Stella Lefty: Data Center Music
Stella Lefty’s billionaire father has attracted more attention than her songwriting. Listen to her debut, Long Way Home, and you start to suspect she’s getting off easy.
When Stella Lefty wrote the chorus to “Boston,” she was waiting in Nashville for a boy from outside Atlanta. Why Boston? She had a gig coming up there, she told Taste of Country. A month later she noticed it was also the name on the piano.
Lefty posted the chorus on TikTok before there were verses to go with it. “Boston,” the breakout single from her debut album, Long Way Home, reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and number one on country radio. Try saying “I like it when you’re nice to me” aloud. Now hear how her bright, raspy voice tumbles into it over the acoustic guitar, pleased and a little embarrassed at what she’s admitted. Two verses would seem ample opportunity to give us one example of the guy being nice.
Much of the case against Lefty rests on her birth certificate. Born Stella Lefkofsky, she grew up in Glencoe, on Chicago’s North Shore, went to Tulane University, and moved to Los Angeles. Her father, Eric Lefkofsky, cofounded Groupon and runs the health tech company Tempus AI. A billionaire’s daughter singing in a Southern accent about boys in pickup trucks was always going to take some grief.
What’s worth resenting is how few of the people who build those pickups can afford to give their kids a few years to find out whether they’ve got a song in them. Give somebody an instrument and years to get good at it without having to earn a living, and now and then you get Gram Parsons. The grandson of a Florida citrus magnate, Parsons could sing about the riches he’d enjoyed and make you feel how badly he wanted to be up in a South Carolina oak tree again. Lefty put her own advantage nicely when she told Vanity Fair, “I didn’t have a stopwatch.”
Country owes a great deal to people who worked by the clock for a wage. Southern millhands played some of its earliest dance music. Jimmie Rodgers learned from the black crews he worked alongside on the railroad. Even Trisha Yearwood’s gloriously juvenile “She’s in Love With the Boy” turns on what a boy can afford. Tommy proposes outside the Tastee-Freez with his high school ring. When Katie’s father objects, her mother reminds him what a catch he was as a penniless farm boy. By the last chorus, you’ve met four people and taken sides in a family fight.
On Long Way Home, you can spend fourteen songs trying to get to know two people that well. In “Whiskey,” Lefty is so taken with the way a man talks that she’s struck dumb. We learn roughly as much about him as the bartender does — he likes his drinks on the rocks. I prefer “Missing You,” where she’s already nostalgic for the relationship while she’s still at his place wearing his T-shirt. He’s one door away. It’s funny and a little mortifying, which is how a person in love occasionally ought to sound.
The plagiarism complaints are harder to shrug off. In “Boston,” you can hear the little hop in the melody of Noah Kahan’s “Stick Season,” right down to the way the singer comes back and does it again on the next line. It’s the only part of “Boston” you can hum to. Lefty told Vanity Fair she hadn’t been thinking about Kahan when she wrote it. She had, however, covered “Stick Season” on TikTok. Kahan got a writing credit after his team flagged the resemblance, shortly before the single came out.
“Summer You Were Mine” deliberately borrows from the Chicks’ “There’s Your Trouble.” Rolling Stone verified that the interpolation was cleared before release. The original writers, Tia Sillers and Mark Selby, get their due. The tune fares worse. In the Chicks’ song, a woman has to explain to a lovesick man that the right girl is standing here talking to him. In Lefty’s song, what came between the lovers was September. Listeners heard Blake Shelton’s “I’ll Name the Dogs” in the album closer, “Why Wouldn’t We.” Both choruses itemize what each partner brings to the relationship. Lefty has at least reassigned the job of telling the jokes.
In October, after Lefty played an unreleased song called “Badly” at Nashville’s Bluebird Cafe, Shaylen and TAELA put it side by side with their own “WATCH THIS.” TAELA singled out the vocal phrasing and cadence. Allow for coincidence, unconscious imitation, and every last one of the credits, and you still have a debut filled with hooks from somebody else’s back catalog. That’s a poor return on fourteen chances to introduce yourself. There’s no need to believe in castigating people for their inherited privilege, but they should at least take advantage of all the time and security it affords.
What explains Stella Lefty’s sudden rise, then? By August, the trade publication Hits was touting more than half a million videos using “Boston.” It had the feeling to many of an “op.” But the kids singing every word at CMA Fest settle the question of whether Lefty has real fans. Labels pay for clips that look like ordinary recommendations and have long helped manufacture demand for their artists. How much of that happened here, if any, remains an open question. You can forgive a listener a little skepticism the fifth time her phone invites her to discover a billionaire’s daughter.
Lefty and her team tested takes on TikTok to see which songs to pursue, according to Crain’s Chicago Business. Once “Boston” took off, her label moved the album’s release from September to August. Here was a young woman with the means to take as much time as she liked, suddenly rushing to finish a record. Turns out somebody did have a stopwatch.
Take “Something to Lose,” her duet with Vincent Mason. Their voices fit beautifully together. On the record, they meet at 2 in the morning in “a Southern state.” In life, they met at Schulman’s in East Nashville. She brought three friends as chaperones. Her producer remembers drinking Chartreuse. Her cowriter Grace Enger got a burger inside while Lefty and Mason flirted outside. All those songwriters at the bar, and somehow the burger and the Chartreuse didn’t make the cut.
For all I know, the person who poured that Chartreuse has a worse country record in them than Stella Lefty. I’d happily run the risk of hearing it. A billionaire’s daughter gets the time off first and a chance to find out how good she is. The results turned out to be derivative and mediocre.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC, State Sue To Block Trump Rule on Public Housing Families With Undocumented Members
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
A coalition of nearly two dozen plaintiffs including New York City sued the Trump administration Monday to stop a rule barring families with undocumented members from living in public housing or receiving certain rental vouchers from taking effect next month.
The lawsuit, which was filed in Massachusetts federal court, argues the rule from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development would harm the plaintiffs and thousands of mixed-status families composed of undocumented people and those with legal status or citizenship. Those suing include other cities, counties and public housing agencies.
“We will not stand by while families are put at risk,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. “New York City is proud to join our peers across the country in fighting this cruel and unlawful rule.”
New York Attorney General Letitia James in the same court Monday filed a separate suit on behalf of more than 20 states also seeking to block the rule on similar grounds.
“This rule runs counter to our nation’s values and the very purpose of these housing programs,” she said in a statement, citing a national “housing crisis.”
HUD did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In recent weeks, HUD Secretary Scott Turner has said the rule would prevent “illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens” from benefiting from government-funded programs.
That’s not how the programs have worked. Mixed-status families have for years been allowed to live in subsidized housing, though only eligible individuals in the household receive a rental subsidy that is prorated based on who is eligible rather than the full household size.
HUD’s new rule — which the Trump administration proposed in February and is set to take effect on Dec. 14 — would no longer allow that to happen.
If implemented, about 20,000 households across the country would be at risk of losing their homes if they live in public housing, receive Section 8 project-based rental assistance or participate in the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program.
Those households consist of nearly 80,000 people, most of whom are eligible for HUD housing assistance, according to the lawsuits, which cite HUD figures.
The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development assists more than 350 mixed-status families made up of about 1,280 people, according to the city complaint. Even more mixed-status families live in NYCHA housing, though the authority did not respond to questions about how many.
‘Impossible Choice’
Monday’s lawsuits challenging the rule follow another lawsuit that a group of housing advocates filed Thursday, also in the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts. One of the plaintiffs in that suit is the Alfred E. Smith Houses Resident Association, which represents tenants of a NYCHA development in Lower Manhattan. There are 16 mixed-status families at risk of losing their homes in the Smith Houses, according to the suit.
Another plaintiff, named as Jane Doe #2, is a Honduran woman living in a project-based Section 8 apartment in New York City with her husband, who is a U.S. permanent resident, and their three daughters, all of whom are U.S. citizens. According to the lawsuit, Doe #2 is the primary caregiver for her children, including her middle daughter, who has autism. Doe #2’s husband is the family’s sole provider, as she is unable to work because of pain from an accident on a job.
The lawsuit states that if the rule takes effect, Doe #2 would have to leave the home — and because she takes care of her daughters, her family would lose their apartment or else be separated from her. But the family, who pays $1,830 a month for rent, would be hard-pressed to find anywhere else they can afford.
Lucy Newman, an attorney for the nonprofit Legal Aid Society who is working on the suit filed last week, said mixed-status families should not voluntarily move out of their homes before the rule kicks in. But she said it would force families to make an “impossible choice.”
“If implemented, this rule inhumanely compels mixed-status families to choose between staying together and losing critical rental assistance or separating to allow eligible members to maintain it,” Newman said. “If implemented, this rule will cause the mass displacement of thousands of mixed status families in New York City from their homes.”
The new lawsuit by New York City and the coalition of municipalities makes a similar argument. It highlights the city’s low housing vacancy rate and relatively high asking rents. Sheltering the families affected by the rule would cost the city about $156 to $277 per day per household, depending on the number of family members, according to the complaint.
The suit also argues the rules’ requirements for housing agencies would increase delays and burden them financially and administratively.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/23/alas.title: Losing to the Mud: Feds Drag Their Feet as an Alaskan Village Sinks
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/23/alas.author: Austin Campbell
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/23/alas.text:
The place where the village of Nunapitchuk remembers its dead is disappearing.
Vincent Wassilie remembers pointing it out to his adult nephew while bringing memorial flowers to their relatives’ graves, which sit on a cemetery hill overlooking the Indigenous Alaskan village.
“Look at that,” he recalled saying. “We used to play on it.”
Wassilie’s nephew looked over and did a double take. The hill beneath the graves, which the two men remembered towering over the surrounding tundra, had sunk by what they estimated to be nearly 10 feet since they were children.
In fact, almost all of Nunapitchuk’s roughly 7 square miles of land is sinking. Government records and scientific assessments obtained by The Intercept via a Freedom of Information Act request reveal sinking homes, damaged infrastructure, thawing permafrost, and growing flood risks across the village of approximately 620 Alaska Native Yup’ik people. One federal analysis found that almost the entire village could be inundated during a 100-year flood under projections for 2030 to 2050.
The federal government has been aware of this for almost a decade. The documents show that tribal leaders have spent years navigating proposed studies, unimplemented scopes of work, and funding constraints. They aren’t asking the government to somehow fortify their land or stop the thaw of permafrost. They just want its help to pick up the village and move it about a mile uphill, where higher ground would keep residents safer from increased risks of flooding and erosion.
“Every spring, my parents’ house turns into an island,” said Tia Tobeluk, who grew up in the village and has since moved to Utah. Tobeluk, now 25, started noticing the devastating effects of climate change when she was 14 or 15, and she remembers moving her parents’ fish racks, traditionally used to smoke and preserve wild-caught fish, up to higher ground.
Nunapitchuk tribal leaders formally warned the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers that the community was “highly vulnerable to environmental hazards” and “may not be habitable in the future” in 2018. They asked the Corps to help identify a safer place for the village and determine whether it could withstand future flooding, erosion, and thawing permafrost. But the village faced an obstacle from the beginning: Nunapitchuk was considered economically distressed, and the Army Corps imposes cost-sharing requirements that the village could not afford.
The Corps produced no records showing it conducted any relocation planning in response to the tribe’s 2018 request, suggesting that the federal entity did nothing. The request was the start of a maddening multi-agency pursuit that has forced tribal leaders to repeatedly ask for help, search for funding, and wait on federal studies and proposed plans, even after selecting where they want to move and documenting why the new site is safer.
Part of the problem is that there’s no single agency responsible for relocating a threatened village like Nunapitchuk. For all its issues, the Federal Emergency Management Agency at least has a clear mandate to help communities rebuild after disaster strikes. In the case of climate relocation, there’s a patchwork of more than 20 federal agencies that could have some role, according to previous reporting by The Guardian, including the Army Corps, FEMA, Bureau of Indian Affairs, Department of Housing and Urban Development, and Denali Commission. The Government Accountability Office has repeatedly recommended that the federal government establish clearer leadership for communities facing climate-driven relocation.
“It’s up to the tribe to kind of bring together all these different resources to try and get relocated,” said Sheryl Musgrove, until recently the climate justice director at the Alaska Institute for Justice. “There’s no central funding source.”
Nunapitchuk’s isolation compounds those challenges. The village is inaccessible by road, and reaching it requires air travel into remote western Alaska. There are days when changing conditions make travel difficult even within the village, keeping children from safely crossing the Johnson River to school and complicating residents’ access to the airport during medical emergencies. Hundreds of miles away, in Alaska’s larger tourist destinations, museums and souvenir shops market the state’s proud Alaska Native culture.
“You’re talking about Alaska Native tribes that have subsisted on these lands for thousands of years,” Musgrove said. “To say that we can’t afford to help them is wrong. The federal government has a trust responsibility to them to protect them and their lands. And the federal government isn’t doing that.”
Nunapitchuk is not alone. The Guardian, citing a 2020 Bureau of Indian Affairs report, noted that 144 Alaska Native villages face potential relocation because of infrastructure damage associated with the changing climate. Estimates placed the cost of relocating Nunapitchuk alone at approximately $230 million.
Wassilie wonders whether the federal government will act before the village experiences the kind of disaster residents are trying to avoid.
“Maybe they’re waiting for something catastrophic to happen before they do anything,” Wassilie said.
The Johnson River splits Nunapitchuk between its west side and its east, or “main,” side, where the village’s school and businesses are located. Historically, winter transformed the river into a route between the two sides once the ice became thick enough to bear a person’s weight.
Older generations, including his mother, remember it freezing quickly every winter, Wassilie said. Sometimes, a single cold Arctic night was enough for the river to become safe to walk across.
“Nowadays, it takes a week or more, depending on how the weather is going,” Wassilie said. Often, the river thaws again quickly after the freeze. “During spring and fall, kids miss school due to unsafe river conditions when it’s freezing up.”
In one instance, a resident needed urgent medical attention while the Johnson River was unsafe to cross. The village’s airport sits beyond the river on the west side, leaving residents to improvise a way to get the patient across.
“They had to figure out a way to bring that patient to the airport because the river wasn’t safe to walk on,” Wassilie said. “One solution was to put that patient in a boat and push the sick person in the boat across the river to the west side.”
Even after crossing the river, residents have historically relied on a wooden bridge to reach the airstrip. Wassilie said the bridge’s pilings shifted and several large wooden boards broke, leaving that route unusable as well.
And at the school, an employee was walking near a back entrance when the structure beneath her gave way, causing her to fall and break her leg. While Wassilie said he did not know whether thawing permafrost contributed to the collapse, researchers have documented extensive thaw beneath the village — extending from roughly 1.5 feet to more than 7 feet below the surface, according to a 2023 permafrost vulnerability assessment cited by the Woodwell Climate Research Center.
The Yup’ik have already determined where else they would like to go. Tribal leaders wrote again to the Army Corps in December 2022, warning that the existing village was “no longer sustainable” and again seeking federal assistance with relocation planning. By November 2023, the village had confirmed its preferred relocation site, and federal officials were exchanging data covering the proposed community site, barge landing and river access.
At the proposed relocation site, which sits approximately 50 feet higher, scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center measured substantially shallower thaw, ranging from 14 to 31 inches, with an average of 19 inches.
But the community’s attempts to move there have stalled.
By June 2024, the Army Corps’ own documents reflected both how far the process had advanced and how little ambiguity remained about what the village wanted. An internal presentation stated that Nunapitchuk had “resolved relocation to new site” and identified the community’s goal as being “moved within 5 years.” The presentation documented sinking houses, damaged boardwalks, melting permafrost, and flooding at the village airport while identifying a relocation site on higher ground.
Yet the engineering assistance needed to begin developing that site never materialized. Musgrove said the Corps proposed multiple scopes of work, but none were finalized, and the assistance under discussion became progressively more limited.
“It just kept getting narrowed down,” Musgrove said. Eventually, the ambition was limited to “OK, maybe we can build the road.”
In June 2025, more than a year after the Corps documented the village’s goal of moving within five years, Musgrove emailed officials asking when they would provide a proposed scope of work discussed during a meeting that March. The Corps proposal included a survey of the riverbed to determine where barges could safely land, an assessment of flooding at the relocation site, an investigation into possible drinking-water sources, and an effort to identify gravel needed for construction.
Musgrove noted that the work needed to remain within a $658,000 budget so the economically distressed tribe would not trigger a federal cost-sharing requirement it could not afford.
She did not receive a reply.
Two months later, she followed up again.
“I wanted to reach out again to see if you have made any progress on your scope of work,” Musgrove wrote in August 2025.
Despite years of studies, proposed scopes of work, scientific assessments, and planning meetings, no active relocation has begun.
In a statement to The Intercept, the Army Corps of Engineers acknowledged receiving the village’s 2018 letter and said it had worked with the community to develop potential technical assistance through its Planning Assistance to States and Tribes program. Discussions included possible site assessments and support for a relocation master plan, the agency said, but they didn’t have a final request on the books.
The Corps did not say when it began working with Nunapitchuk following the 2018 warning or explain why years of discussions had failed to produce a finalized scope of work.
“The Alaska District remains ready to assist our partners with their needs,” the agency said.
In Anchorage, a city of nearly 300,000 about 420 miles east of Nunapitchuk, tourist shops sell carvings and decorations depicting ravens, salmon, and whales in the vivid red, green, and black associated with Indigenous artistic traditions of Alaska and the Pacific Northwest.
Some sellers can identify the Alaska Native artists behind individual pieces and connect their work to the communities they came from. Others offer inexpensive imitations. In shops throughout Anchorage and surrounding cities, The Intercept repeatedly encountered Native-inspired souvenirs that, when turned over, bore small labels showing they had been manufactured thousands of miles from Alaska, including in Indonesia.
For many visitors, those commercial corridors are among their most accessible encounters with the cultures Alaska uses to represent itself. But Nunapitchuk residents told The Intercept that each village is distinct, with its own history worthy of preservation. “It’s sort of like our own unique story,” Wassilie said. “There are different traditions in every village.”
Alaska’s economy has long depended on extracting value from its enormous landscape, with exports of oil, fish, minerals, and timber. But the state’s marketing of Indigenous culture while the federal government neglects Indigenous requests for support presents an uncomfortable version of Alaska’s extraction economy: The imagery and traditions of Alaska Native people can be packaged, reproduced and carried away by visitors, even as some of the communities from which those cultures emerged struggle to secure the infrastructure necessary to survive.
The disparity is visible just outside the stores.
In Anchorage, Alaska Native people account for 53.5 percent of people experiencing homelessness, according to the Anchorage Coalition to End Homelessness, which has warned that Alaska Native residents are “not receiving timely or equitable solutions to address their needs.”
In many cases, the threat of poverty drives people away alongside the changing environment. Tobeluk eventually left Nunapitchuk, long before the village became physically uninhabitable.
“There’s no housing, not a lot of jobs,” she said. “I didn’t want to become a cashier for the rest of my life.”
Today, Tobeluk, a Yup’ik woman who grew up surrounded by the wet tundra of western Alaska, is raising her family in the high desert of Utah, thousands of miles from the village where generations of her family lived. In addition to the lack of housing and economic opportunities, she described a decline in the use of the Yup’ik language among people of her generation.
“There’s a handful of people who still speak Yup’ik,” she said. “But the language is dying, so it’s mostly English.”
Her parents, she noted, don’t want to relocate. “They love the village right now,” Tobeluk said. “Even if it’s sinking.”
But moving just a mile away would allow residents to escape increasingly unstable ground without abandoning the community itself. Families could remain together rather than dispersing across Alaska and the lower 48 states, while preserving a way of life tied to the surrounding land and water.
For some residents, that choice is already disappearing.
“There’s no more room to build infrastructure here anymore,” Wassilie said. “So some people are forced to move into bigger cities.”
Others have nowhere to go. Wassilie described two houses inundated by flooding in 2020 whose occupants continued living in them years later. Some homes, he said, have developed large gaps as their structures shift. But the inhabitants “have no choice but to live in those houses,” Wassilie said.
While the ground sinks beneath them, Wassilie said, “We just keep going forward.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Cathedrals of sound: the secret universe inside musical instruments – in pictures
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Photography by Charles Brooks, words by Emma Joyce
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Cathedrals of sound: the secret universe inside musical instruments – in pictures
Photographer and former cellist Charles Brooks creates optical illusions with minuscule cameras. He threads endoscopes inside instruments to capture thousands of images, which are then combined: a clarinet becomes a dark tunnel, a yidaki becomes a cave, a Steinway piano is a futuristic train station: ‘You’re also looking inside the history of these instruments … All the marks you’re seeing are from them being cleaned or repaired, or by the maker themselves’
- Brooks’s latest exhibition, Architecture in Music, is on at Adelaide’s Immersive Light and Art until 5 December
‘I’m very careful with the instruments. They’re never modified at all,’ Brooks says. The minuscule lens he uses can only capture a small area in focus at any one time. ‘So what I’m having to do is take anywhere between a few hundred and sometimes many thousands of images, moving that focus point, rotating the lens a fraction of a millimetre at a time, until I have enough to run them through a software.’ Photograph: Charles Brooks
Photography by Charles Brooks, words by Emma Joyce
Musicians couldn’t perform during Covid lockdowns, so Melbourne-based photographer Charles Brooks seized on the opportunity to capture instruments in repair at the time. ‘The effect was sort of immediate,’ he says. ‘The moment I saw these photos coming together I realised there was something special here. I had to get into other instruments’
Brooks uses modified endoscopes – tiny lenses just a few millimetres thick – as well as Lumix cameras to take thousands of photos of each instrument. This Muramatsu 14k rose gold flute is owned by flautist Jessie Gu of Orchestra Victoria. It was handmade in Japan and the fine abrasions seen inside are from cleaning it. ‘You can see these thousands of lines going down the middle of the barrel from cleaning every day, many times, because all of these are living instruments. They’re not sitting in a museum. These are the marks of them being played,’ Brooks says
‘It’s a very long, slow, drawn-out process to take any one of these shots – just taking the photo can take at least eight hours and then putting all the components together can take a couple of weeks,’ he says. As he takes thousands of photos per instrument, he adjusts the lighting and uses temperature monitors to make sure instruments are not damaged in any way. This particular guitar is played by Nick Granville, who has used it in concerts and musicals with the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra
‘People say it’s a bamboo forest or hair follicles,’ Brooks says. ‘This one really does mess with your sense of scale.’ The 48-year-old photographer, who was born in New Zealand, had to climb into the tower of St Mark’s church in Auckland to capture these tiny organ pipes, which measure less than a centimetre across
Photographed with a Laowa Probe lens on a Lumix S1R, this yidaki looks like a deep red cave. The ridges you see are caused by termites, not human hands, with ochre from the mouthpiece finding its way into the instrument over time. ‘It’s so unlike any other instrument because it’s not uniform. With the light coming through the end, it looks like a nebula, and that to me is really special’
You’re looking at the wippen, spoons and springs of a Steinway grand piano. ‘I think a piano is probably the most complex wooden thing that’s still handmade anywhere,’ Brooks says. They’re made from thousands of parts ‘almost entirely created by hand and, by the time they’re all strung up, the strings are putting about 20 tons of pressure on this frame … I find that level of craftsmanship just mind-blowing really’
‘I knew these bellows might look like a zigzagging form, but instead it looks like you’re walking up stairs inside a European opera house or up a red carpet into a theatre. It’s so dramatic,’ Brooks says. A cousin of the accordion, the bandoneón, is made in Germany. It is used in tango music and has become inseparable from the music of Argentina
Loaned to Brooks by the principal timpanist of Orchestra Victoria, Guy du Blêt, the percussion instrument gave the photographer a pause. ‘How do I photograph the inside of something that doesn’t have an inside?’ he says. ‘What look like enormous discs are actually the size of a coin. They’re roughly beaten but that’s critical to the sound they produce and, when you put them on top of each other, look through them and see the light filtering through the drum skin, it feels like you’re looking at modernist architecture’
Brooks held off from photographing guitars because he thought they’d all look the same. Also, you could peer into the belly of one without a camera. But this Martin D-35, owned by New Zealand-born, Melbourne-based musician Peter Mrkusich, proved how different a guitar can look from another angle. ‘I still used my endoscope to go through other openings. Typically a guitar will have a strap that’s held on by a little peg and you can slide it out and get different angles and little effects.’ The instrument’s Madagascar rosewood makes it feel like a warm expansive concert hall
‘I hesitated to photograph cymbals for a long time because I’m known for photographing inside instruments, and cymbals don’t have an inside, but then I realised what if I had them in that moment before they crashed together?’ Brooks had the 17-inch Zildjian K symphonic cymbals placed flat on top of each other, with just a tiny gap between. ‘They’re from the oldest musical instrument company that’s still running,’ he says. ‘The hand-hammered surfaces look like a seascape or a sunset’
Brooks photographed this Fazioli grand piano with a Lumix S1R and a Laowa Probe lens. One hundred images of various focal distances have then been stacked together for sharpness. ‘What you’re seeing are the wooden levers behind the keys translating the key places into hammer strikes on the strings of the instrument,’ Brooks says. ‘By making it totally in focus from back to front, your brain doesn’t think it’s small’
This Buffet Crampon Prestige Low C bass clarinet is made of African blackwood, ‘which normally looks jet black to the eye’, Brooks says. Blown up to this scale, ‘you start to see all the grain in it which is flecked with these incredible whites and browns’. There’s a brass bell at the end of what looks like a tunnel: ‘I’m bouncing the light through that – that’s how the instrument is lit up’
Owned by the Stringed Instrument Company of New Zealand and currently being restored, this Lockey Hill cello was made in England about 1780. You can see its original tool marks and repairs. ‘With the violins, the cellos, the guitars especially, they have to be cleaned [before being photographed] because specks of dust look as long as an arm,’ Brooks says. ‘You pour dry rice in and swill them around and the static electricity binds all the dust to it and you can just shake it out. That’s the way they’ve been cleaning these instruments for hundreds of years’
Made by Bret Gustafson in Adelaide, the instrument played by Ben Anderson with Orchestra Victoria in Melbourne merges two bass trombones. Its two bells create different tones. ‘What I’ve photographed is all of the intricate valves that were made so that he can easily slide and move from one sound to the other,’ Brooks says
Brooks’s photographs are on display at Architecture in Music, an exhibition at Immersive Light and Art gallery in Adelaide, until 5 December. For the first time in Australia, visitors will see the images at monumental scale. ‘You see them on a screen that’s three metres high and about eight metres long and curves around you – suddenly you’re not just looking at a picture of a space, you are standing physically inside the belly of a Stradivarius violin or a magnificent Steinway piano,’ Brooks says

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: We’re Ready to Love Hot Democrats Again
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Mathew Rodriguez
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
We’re Ready to Love Hot Democrats Again
Politician-related thirst levels are reaching heights not seen in decades. Why is America’s longing for lusty legislators spiking so much?
In the sixth season of Sex and the City, public relations expert Samantha Jones instructed her soon-to-be-movie-star beau Jerry “Smith” Jerrod in the art of cultivating a fandom. The secret to widespread popularity, it turned out, was getting people to ogle you. “First come the gays, then the girls, then the industry,” she quipped.
Replace “industry” with “electorate,” and you have a maxim that somewhat explains the post-Bluenami Internet fanfare over the yet-to-be-sworn in 120th Congress and its crop of incoming (and returning) Hot Democrats.
Ever since the first “CNN projects!” on Blue Wave Night, an AI rendering of once-popular teen-heartthrob rag Tiger Beat has been going viral. The mock-up has a few variations, but all of them feature Abdul El-Sayed smoldering, James Talarico smiling, and Jon Ossoff smizing. They sport denim jackets and exude a comforting aura. Some incoming politicians who didn’t make the cut, such as US representatives-elect Manny Rutinel and Sam Forstag, have still been lusted over. The message is clear: We, the American electorate, have creamed our jeans.
These faces represent a sharp contrast to the legislative body they will be entering—or, in Ossoff’s case, reentering. The 119th Senate has an average age of 64, meaning the typical senator was born at the tail end of the boomer generation; the average House member is a relatively youthful, though still firmly Gen X, 57.
Beyond all being millennials—sorry, Gen X!—each of these newly minted Hot Dems possess a handsomeness that has seemed to cause a collective regression to doe-eyed teenagedom. Group chats I’m in—full of other gay men—feature unpublishable texts about Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s butts, both of which have garnered quite a bit of online attention. Even TMZ seems to have caught the Bluenami Boy Crazies, asking Ossoff whether he has #BDE—short for “big-dick energy”—prompting him to laugh and respond, “Come on, my brother.” One viral tweet re-upping the video adorned the clip with the hashtag #needdat.
To those for whom politics is their business, none were surprised that the candidates’ handsomeness had taken center stage in the postelection discourse.
“They used to say, ‘I want to vote for a guy I could have a beer with, but that’s a very boomer notion,’ Ryan Adams, a progressive political consultant, told The Nation. “The millennial notion is ‘I want to vote for a guy I can thirst after.”
While everyone loves a handsome face, it’s clear that the fervor for these hot candidates has stretched beyond normal bounds of thirst, especially in the political arena. We’ve had plenty of models for hot politicians—Barack Obama and John F. Kennedy come to mind, of course—but never so many all at once and with such an Internet-ready response to their good looks.
Part of the reason the candidates’ looks seem to be front and center in the aftermath of this election cycle is purely that, given the last 10 years of our political landscape, the American citizens are ready for some eye candy in office again.
“After going through the Biden and Trump administrations with these two old guys who are shuffling along, losing their place and rambling, voters are looking for energy and competence,” says Steve Grand, a veteran Republican media consultant. But, more than good looks, Grand says, the 2026 Bluenami was a “backlash to the last two presidents.” Thirst-driven accounts saturating the Internet with pictures of El-Sayed’s butt while rock climbing are certainly calling attention to his plump assets, but also, such an image is the visual antithesis of the past decade of electoral politics.
Compare El-Sayed’s rock climbing to visuals of Biden or Trump, who “can barely get up the stairs on Air Force One,” Grand says. “That’s a real visual contrast for the voter.”
Certainly El-Sayed or Ossoff are a contrast to Trump and Biden, but are the American people so shallow as to just vote for a hot person?
“People still want to vote for you on policy,” Grand says. “Hotness is kind of a plus at the end.”
Gallup polling in the lead-up to the election proved that a usual suspects list of issues worried voters as they headed to the ballot box: the economy, healthcare, the worsening situation in Iran, gas prices, and income inequality. No pollster would’ve asked whether hotness played a role, but it’s hard to imagine it didn’t.
“Democracy revolves around human beings and what human beings want,” says Mitchell Jackson, a communication strategist and the founder of DCC Communications. “Human biology revolves around that. It’s just an animalistic thing.”
While hotness appeals to our most basic instincts, it has also, for millennia, been seen as a stand-in for all the attractive qualities one wants in a statesman: competence, leadership, acumen. Greek philosopher Aristotle laid out the beginnings of these beliefs—later called physiognomy—in his treatise Prior Analytics.
“It seems to me that soul and body affect each other sympathetically,” he wrote, per one 2020 translation. “A changed state of the soul changes also the appearance of the body; and again, a changed appearance of the body changes the state of the soul.”
In the second century CE, Roman sophist Polemon praised Emperor Hadrian by complimenting his eyes, which Polemon described as “clear and shining are good, unless other signs corrupt them. Of this type surely are the eyes of the Emperor Hadrian…gleaming, moist, keen, large, full of light.”
Researchers in 1972 coined this phenomenon the “what is beautiful is good” stereotype, which has also been called the “halo effect,” a cognitive bias wherein one positive trait, such as handsomeness, spurs people to assume other positive qualities, such as kindness or intelligence. Research has also shown that when it comes to leadership, countenance counts, and people prefer to vote for candidates they consider good-looking. Another 1999 study even showed that digitally altered versions of famous politicians could make them read differently—more honest, more cunning, less warm—to everyday Americans.
“We tend to impute to attractive people a level of competence that we don’t necessarily impute to people who are less attractive,” says Monika McDermott, a professor of political science at Fordham University. “That’s human nature.”
Of course, not every hot politician gets the keys to the Oval Office—sorry, John Edwards—and less-attractive politicians can prosper. No one is digitizing Sherrod Brown onto a Tiger Beat cover, but he still bested Jon Husted, whose rear end was the subject of many a Trump rally.
Even the agreed-upon pick for Best President of All Time was no looker. Abraham Lincoln may have predated mass media, but news of his face reached the people via newspapers. The Houston Telegraph called Lincoln the “leanest, lankiest, most ungainly mass of legs, arms and hatchet face ever strung upon a single frame. He has most unwarrantably abused the privilege which all politicians have of being ugly.” British journalist Edward Dicey poked fun at Lincoln’s “coconut-shaped” head and his pockmarked face—”furrowed, wrinkled, and indented, as though it had been scarred by vitriol.” Even his nose and ears, “which have been taken by mistake from a head of twice the size,” weren’t safe.
Logically, the question then becomes: If looks matter so much to the average American voter, then how did we get the current president in office? Though many Trump sycophants, including recent convert Nicki Minaj, have called Trump handsome, the rest of us have eyes. Despite being known to scrutinize women’s looks, he has also been ridiculed for his wispy hair, his signature ocher complexion, his sedentary paunch, and his “neck vagina.” Surely an electorate obsessed with artifice wouldn’t elect such a creature.
“It’s not just about hot,” says Jackson. “Donald Trump is not hot, but he has a look.” He added, “He has a look the same way that a drag queen has a look.”
Trump’s own form of bloviating masculinity downplayed physical fitness; he even believes that each person has a finite amount of energy that exercise can drain.
Trump himself has, of course, complimented many men on their good looks, including Zohran Mamdani, whose 2025 ascent to New York City Hall primed us all for more Hot Dems.
“I do think it was kicked off by Mamdani,” McDermott says. “And I do think it’s continuing in the fact that people are just saying, ‘Hey, look at these people—they look so different from who we’re used to.”
Our current Hot Politician era probably started in 1960, when John F. Kennedy bested champion debater Richard Nixon in the first televised presidential debate. You already know the lore: To those who listened on the radio, Nixon was the victor, but TV viewers favored the dashing Kennedy over the sweaty, awkward Nixon.
“Between the bleak gray walls and the bright floodlights of the television studio, [Nixon’s] gray suit and heavily powdered jowls looked flabby and pallid beside Kennedy’s dark suit and healthy tan,” biographer Theodore Sorenson wrote about the September 1960 debate.
Nearly 70 years later, hotness still matters.
“Attractiveness is not the end-all, be-all,” McDermott said. But “in a tight race it can make a difference.”
Of course, the right candidate has to come at the right time. And the left was ready. “Oh my God, I want a hot president,” wine mom par excellence and I’ve Had It host Jennifer Welch said in an interview in March. A week later, The Bulwark published an article claiming that Democrats were using hotness as an electoral strategy.
“Democrats remembered that people like hot people,” Jackson says.
Both Grand and McDermott agreed that the embrace of the incoming senatorial class is a generational issue and that people are ready to see fresh-faced people in government. Such a call, of course, brings us back to Obama, not only because of his looks but also the role his ascendancy played in the rise of 2010s-era millennial optimism.
Obama’s 2008 election victory has become the quintessential moment associated with Gen Y’s particular brand of hope, change, and unity, and his looks were a key part of his electability. (Readers of a certain age will remember when, in June 2007, a still-in-its-infancy YouTube became the site of a level-five nuclear hot-drogen bomb: “Crush on Obama,” the earworm that solidified him as the youthful, and handsome, alternative to the fumbling, unsexy lame duck George W. Bush and eventual Republican candidate John McCain.)
But if Obama emphasized that it helps to be hot, his presidency also showed another obvious truth—that good looks don’t necessarily make you a great leader. His presidency began with notes of hope and change, but his ties to plutocracy ended up launching the Occupy Wall Street movement and paving the way for Trump. His tenure has only soured further in the collective rearview mirror.
That souring is proof that while hotness can put on temporary blinders, it doesn’t last forever. People fall out of love with hot politicians all the time: Justin Trudeau’s popularity eventually plummeted and even Mamdani has encountered some stumbling blocks in transition from candidate to mustachioed mayor. Visual appeal can be an initial boon, but the novelty wears off; just as politicians campaign in poetry and govern in prose, the handsomeness of a person seeking office often feels less novel once the American people have begun to sign their checks.
“Attractiveness only matters on the margins,” McDermott says. “It’s unlikely to blind voters to issues that opponents and the media raise.”
If voting is like dating—we want a candidate who meets a laundry list of requirements, such as smart, handsome, and empathetic—then this 2026 class represents our first time trusting candidates after being spurned by our crush on 44.
“There was this feeling of letdown,” says Emily Keegin, a photo editor and creative director, who pointed to a “despondency” among millennials who put their faith in Obama. “There was like, ‘Can we ever love again?’”
Ossoff, Talarico, and El-Sayed might represent a Democratic voting body with a healed heart, ready to get back on the market with a new guy.
If Obama was the last time that love entered the equation, a new math has emerged since his time as a candidate. While Obama’s campaign is widely recognized as the first to effectively use the Internet to its advantage, the Bluenami occurred at a time when the Internet is now just a fact of political life. Not only must candidates adapt to it—they must fight for eyeball time in the attention economy, in which concentration is a currency.
That is a new opportunity and a new reality for handsome candidates.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
“JFK would have never admitted he was trying to sell sex. Obama and his campaign would have never admitted that they were trading on his handsomeness,” says Rachael Kay Albers, a brand strategist. She says that while campaign strategists may not admit it, they are stoking the fires of thirst. “In order to participate in the conversation, you have to find your angle.”
Complicating this, of course, is that the same news outlets that cover these candidates are also prey to the realities of the doomscrolling citizenry.
“This is also profitable for publishers, to turn Mamdani or El-Sayed into thirst traps,” she said. “To play into that, because it’s getting people clicking.”
Albers, as well as many others who spoke about these hot Democrats, underscored that hotness is never a primary concern for voters. Albers added that hotness is often only focused on after a candidate has “proven their competence in other ways.”
These hot new Dems are not just an alternative to an electorate primed to embrace a new generation; they are also entering an arena in which people are tired of the MAGA manosphere. (Even the manosphere is tired of its association with MAGA and a certain brand of masculinity; it turned away from Trump in the last election.) With the culture souring on the red-pilled podcasting Pepe the Frog walking memes, it’s searching for a healthier masculinity, a void that these Dems seem to have filled.
“There’s a craving for youthful vitality and a hope that, for the future, we’re gonna do things different,” Albers said. “They are the foil to the old guard, Pete Hegseth, the manosphere.”
If you haven’t noticed yet, almost everyone who has benefited from this discussion of hotness has been male; there hasn’t been the equivalent meme for the youthful Gina Hinojosa, for instance. Part of that is certainly that it is less socially acceptable to objectify professional women than it is to ogle Ossoff’s butt. Current cultural gender dynamics in the United States, and especially in electoral politics, also make it much more complicated when it comes to discussions of the hotness of women running for office.
Research on attractiveness in female candidates is a mixed bag: While Sarah Palin’s past as a pageant queen helped drum up interest, research seems to say that her beauty worked against her and ultimately cost the ticket votes. And while we do ascribe good qualities to people who are attractive, some research has shown that objectification makes women be perceived as less competent and human. Conversely, one Dartmouth study found that pretty female candidates do experience an electoral boon.
The question of whether hotness matters when it comes to women will be put to the test if New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez does run for the presidency in 2028, as some progressive fundraisers already want her to do.
“When I say that she could win if she ran for president, people go, ‘No, the electorate’s too sexist. They’ll never vote for a woman,’” Adams said, of course referring to the fact that two female Democrats have already lost when vying for the presidency. “And I say, ‘No, they will vote for a hot woman.’”
Ocasio-Cortez, who Jackson says is doing “what works” when it comes to her social-media routine and how she speaks to voters, has already found that playing up her glamour is no easy road for her. Her appearance at the 2021 Met Gala with a “Tax the Rich” dress spurred several news cycles’ worth of coverage, outstripping attention paid to many other frocks.
If hotness continues to be a strategy for Democrats, then it’s not one that can come to bear too soon. In politics we’ve experienced what Vogue editor Andre Leon Talley once called a “famine of beauty.” To an electorate with its mouths open and its jowls drooling, this crop of Democrats is a welcome sight. While looking at Ossoff or El-Sayed’s butt might be titillating, it’s also a very different visual from watching Republican Senator Mitch McConnell sitting on the Senate floor, Weekend at Bernie’s–style, barely speaking and not contributing in any way to find solutions to the many problems currently besieging America.
“Republicans are wheeling out Mitch McConnell and he can’t even walk or talk. What does that say to voters?” Adams said. “You don’t deserve a living body. You deserve however we tell this corpse to vote.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: International photography museum Fotografiska opens in Shenzhen
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Hokhang Cheung
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The international photography museum Fotografiska has recently launched in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023. “The strategy was always to self-fund the first space in Shanghai, and then expand through strategic partnerships for subsequent locations,” says Christian Devillers, the managing director for Fotografiska China.
The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also currently has locations in the Swedish capital, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.
“Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers says, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals. Fotografiska Shenzhen is replicating Shanghai’s late hours and lifestyle offerings, which draw office workers commuting to the city centres, and its first public day on the 1 October national holiday drew more than 1,000 paying visitors.
The project opened with exhibitions across the 5,300 sq. m facility, including a Shi Guowei solo show and Toiletpaper, showcasing Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari’s titular magazine (both until 14 March 2027). They have joined a show of photography award Prix Pictet (until 29 November), the six-artist group show Transcendent Realities (until 1 October 2027) and a Michael Najjar solo exhibition (until 17 January 2027). Subsequent planned events include a show of Hong Kong photographers featuring, among others, Ho Fan (1931-2016).
In Shanghai, even with Fotografiska’s busy traffic, admissions and memberships account for only around 20% of total revenue, Devillers says. The museum instead depends on commercial partnerships, and retail and food and drink sales. Fotografiska Shenzhen’s six-year partnership agreement with landlord China Resources Land aims to draw a profit by year three. The institution has set an initial target of 70,000 visitors for 2027.
Fotografiska Shenzhen is located in the upscale retail complex Shenzhen Bay MixC, which is also home to a new immersive art concept called Base. They join several new and forthcoming cultural projects in the city, which is making a concerted push to raise its artistic profile, such as the recently-opened Shenzhen International Art Museum and Shenzhen Bay Cultural Plaza. This month will also see the long-running Hong Kong fair Fine Art Asia relocate to the mainland city (26-29 November).

https://www.propublica.org/article/immig.title: If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be Deported?
https://www.propublica.org/article/immig.text:
About a dozen women chitchatted in Spanish between forkfuls of a tres leches cake. They spoke about their hopes and dreams — learning to drive, speaking English, visiting a son who had been deported. Some brought their young children, who scurried around them, circling the tables and tugging at their shirts, before the older kids nudged them into a nearby playroom, giving the women space to talk. The women were from Mexico and Guatemala, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador. Some settled here in west Michigan decades ago and had already become U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Others were more recent arrivals, with pending asylum cases. All of them said they had been abused by their current or former partners. And they had gathered at this informal support group, hosted by a local nonprofit, to talk.
I’m a ProPublica reporter in Detroit, and my colleague Melissa Sanchez is in Chicago. We each drove over 100 miles last summer to be in this room because we were working on a story. It published in mid-October, and it’s about how the immigration policies of President Donald Trump’s administration have made life more perilous for victims of domestic abuse. While reporting, we had heard about the pervasive presence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in west Michigan, and we wanted to hear from immigrant women there who were living through domestic abuse. How did they weigh whether it was safer to stay with an abusive partner or to seek help from law enforcement, knowing they might be detained — and even deported?
That night, a young woman with a toddler told us that she called 911 about a year earlier, after her boyfriend slapped her when he was drunk. If he hit her today, she said, she wouldn’t dial that number again. With arrests by federal immigration officers constantly in the news, she said, the risk is too great.
None of the others in the room said they were currently living with an abusive partner. Those women were out there, the group’s facilitators told us. But they were too afraid to even leave their homes.
After the meeting, as empty paper plates were cleared from the tables, the facilitators told us about E. She was once a regular at the meetings, they said, but hadn’t been around in a while. They worried about her. We asked if E. might be open to talking with us and, after a few texts, we learned that she was — if we could be ready to talk in about 20 minutes.
We hurried back to our nearby lodgings, dialed E.’s number and put her on speakerphone. In Spanish, Melissa explained what we were reporting on, why it was so important to hear from somebody like her and the kinds of questions we wanted to ask. Then we began the interview.
E., who asked not to be fully identified, told us that she avoids going out unless it’s absolutely necessary. She’d heard harrowing stories about women at the immigration detention center in Michigan where other women we’d interviewed were locked up. As we described in our story, several had been arrested here in Kent County when local police responded to domestic violence calls. E. doesn’t want to end up in ICE custody herself or, worse, deported.
For the sake of her kids, E. said, she tolerates her husband’s abuse in silence.
When he tells her she’s “nobody here” and to “go back to your country,” she said she puts her head down. When he pulls her hair in bed and says she belongs to him, she said she pretends it’s a joke. When he asks for the money she makes from selling food at a local factory, she said she hands it over.
A filing in E.’s immigration case says her husband is a U.S. citizen who has been “verbally and financially abusive” and has threatened to take away the child they share. E. said that, except for the hair pulling, he isn’t physically abusive.
(Like the other women we interviewed, E. asked that ProPublica not interview her alleged abuser because she’s afraid he will retaliate against her, take away her children or call ICE. To report these women’s stories, we interviewed attorneys, advocates, family and others who interacted with them. When available, we also reviewed text messages, and records from law enforcement and immigration court.)
E. said her husband doesn’t overtly threaten her with calling ICE. But she said she found a hotline number for the agency written in his journal, alongside a description of his ideal woman: obedient and submissive.
That reminded us of what a local immigration attorney, Catherine Villanueva, had told us: “We have this idea that we’re deporting these really bad people,” she said. “What we’re doing is we’re empowering the bad people who are already here.”
We asked E. if she had ever called the police to report her husband’s abuse. Her answer came quickly: No. Her husband is frail. She worries police officers will look at both of them and decide that he’s the victim. “They won’t see me as the abused one,” she said. “If I called the police, the one who would wind up losing is me.”
When we reached out to federal officials for our story, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.” As part of our reporting, we examined the backgrounds of the women we interviewed. Most had no criminal records we could find.
People in law enforcement and the prosecutor’s office in Kent County told us that they wanted everybody to feel safe reaching out to report crimes, regardless of their immigration status. Kent County Prosecutor Chris Becker said that he and a Spanish-speaking assistant prosecutor met with local advocates for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence “to try and lower that barrier, to make people understand that we see them as victims and want to serve them as victims.”
“But,” he added, “we can talk all we want, and still, I think it’s still difficult.”
Indeed, Angelica Ferrer, the victim witness coordinator in Becker’s office, said she used to be able to tell victims that if they came to court, “we’re not going to have ICE here.” She doesn’t say that to them anymore. “That is a choice that you have to make,” she said. “I can’t guarantee that you won’t be stopped on the way to court.”
Providing support for immigrants who are domestic abuse victims has long been extraordinarily difficult. But over five months of reporting, Melissa and I kept coming up against the same pervasive fear: In the current climate, nobody can really keep them safe.
Yet we heard from a lot of folks in Kent County who are trying to reach people like E., whether from positions in law enforcement, via social service agencies or as volunteers. Mary Sue Stegehuis, a retired teacher, is involved with a grassroots group called Hope for Neighbors. Even though she doesn’t know Spanish, she visits women in ICE custody, usually with a bilingual friend, and she stays in touch with them through a messaging app. She prints their stories — many involving domestic abuse — on homemade prayer cards, with an image of Mary, Joseph and Jesus migrating from Egypt on one side. Sharing the cards with others in the community, she told us, is meant to ensure that their stories don’t disappear, even if the women aren’t in the room to tell them.
We are still reporting on immigration and domestic abuse. If you have a tip or expertise, or you just want to share something you know, please get in touch. I’m at 313-310-6592, on both cell and Signal, and [email protected], and Melissa is at 872-444-0011, on both cell and Signal, and [email protected].

https://hyperallergic.com/something-stra.title: Something Strange at Maggie Ellis’s Thanksgiving Table
https://hyperallergic.com/something-stra.author: Rebecca Schiffman
https://hyperallergic.com/something-stra.text:
Something Strange at Maggie Ellis’s Thanksgiving Table
In Ellis's world, you can never be quite sure whether you've stumbled into a dream, a nightmare, or someone else's very strange family gathering.
It’s fitting that Maggie Ellis’s exhibition opened the day before Halloween. Her canvases teem with creatures, graveyard scenes, and all manner of ghoulish debauchery, making for a spooky and thoroughly entertaining show.
There is, yes, another iteration of Ophelia from Hamlet, which feels a bit overdone, but I’ll forgive it for the rest of the wacky scenes she has going on.
There’s a forest fire rendered in bright red, complete with snakes, a lizard the size of a human wearing a dress, a severed hand, and a woman leaning against a tree doomscrolling on her phone.

Amsterdam’s Eye Filmmuseum has named Brazilian artist Jonathas de Andrade the twelfth winner of the Eye Art & Film Prize, an annual €30,000 (about $35,000) award established in 2015 to support artists whose practices span film and the visual arts. Previous recipients of the honor include Francis Alÿs, Meriem Bennani, Wang Bing, Sohrab Hura, Kahlil Joseph, and Hito Steyerl.
Born in Maceió, Brazil, in 1982, De Andrade lives and works in Recife, in northeast Brazil. He is known for work centering marginalized communities and exploring themes including race, class, gender, and identity through the lens of Brazilian sociocultural norms. Working across photography, film, and installation, he frequently collaborates with local workers and unhoused people to create works that blend documentary and fiction.
“In de Andrade’s work, which traverses the porous line between aesthetic research and sociological investigation, the search for faces and bodily impressions assumes an important role,” wrote Alexandre Melo in a 2023 Artforum review of an exhibition by de Andrade. “The artist creates an idea of community—religious, cultural, social—through an aesthetic mediation based on images that give form to abstract notions.”
The prize jury praised de Andrade for his “deeply human and interdisciplinary practice, which moves seamlessly between film, photography, installation, performance and archival research,” further noting that “he is closely connected to the place where his work is set and, at the same time, he addresses wider questions about identity, memory and social history.”
In addition to the monetary prize, to be put toward the creation of new work, de Andrade will receive a solo presentation at Eye Filmmuseum sometime next year.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ea-tech-ai-s.title: Effective Altruism Is Increasingly Just Funding Itself
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ea-tech-ai-s.author: Jacob Davis
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ea-tech-ai-s.text:
Effective Altruism Is Increasingly Just Funding Itself
Effective altruists say they want to widen the circle of moral concern to include distant strangers. Follow the money, and the circle increasingly ends at other effective altruists.
The basic pitch for effective altruism (EA) is simple: charitable giving is an investment, whose return is in others’ well-being rather than your financial betterment. Given that it’s an investment, it makes sense to look for a strong, measurable return from wherever you choose to donate. After all, if you really care about others being well-off, you should be at leastas conscientious about these investments as you are about your retirement savings.
This is, to say the least, a controversial approach to charity. It has many detractors: those who argue that the approach flattens value to numbers in a spreadsheet, or that it ignores the place of solidarity and political organizing. But the ethic also has its undeniable appeal. Among effective altruists, the standard example of effective giving is usually the Against Malaria Foundation (AMF), which distributes insecticide-laced bed nets in sub-Saharan Africa to combat mosquito-borne illness. It is hard to argue that AMF is not a better place to give your money than many competing organizations, like various sketchy “voluntourism” outfits or microloan creditors.
Where many critiques of EA miss the mark is in taking this pitch at face value. In reality, as measured by volume of money flow, EA is more a means of cultivating a self-selecting, insular subculture based around the tech industry. The biggest objection that can be laid against it is not that its founding principles are misguided, but that they have come to play third or fourth fiddle to building a playground and safety net for a small, privileged portion of the global population.
Short-Term vs. Long-Term EA
Within EA, a distinction is sometimes drawn between “long-term” and “short-term” effective altruism. Classic poster children like AMF almost all fall on the “short-term” side of the split: concrete, clearly specifiable interventions to promote measurable goods in the present or near future. “Long-term” cause areas are generally more nebulous or speculative: preparations for future pandemics, the eventual curtailment of wild animal suffering, or (above all) artificial intelligence safety.
Long-term cause areas generally, and AI safety specifically, have come to dominate EA organizing. One measure of this is the recent spending decisions of Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), the dominant EA grant-making body. In 2025, nearly $490 million of Coefficient Giving’s roughly $840 million in grants were dedicated to “long-term and existential risk,” overwhelmingly in AI safety. This is in contrast to the approximately $150 million spent on global health and development, the classic “short-term” general cause area.
This spending strategy is puzzling, under traditional EA principles. As Coefficient Giving states on its funding page, effective altruists deliberately focus on funding for problems that are important, neglected, and tractable. Without prejudice to the issue’s importance, there is a growing consensus among concerned parties that AI safety is not currently tractable: there is widespread recognition that no robust technical road map to safe AI has been, or will likely soon be, forthcoming. And leading AI safety organization Anthropic just opened its initial public offering (IPO) at around $1.5 trillion — prompting disillusionment even within EA. Rarely in human history has any problem been less economically neglected.
Anthropic, like OpenAI before it, highlights the double-edged nature of much technical AI safety research. In the eyes of most effective altruists, developing AI capabilities is directly opposed to the goal of AI safety. And yet most avenues of technical safety research go hand-in-hand with capabilities development; indeed, this is a criticism lobbed against AI safety initiatives by many effective altruists. Research projects on interpretability, reinforcement learning with human feedback, and thinking traces have all failed to realize the elusive dream of AI “alignment” but have provided considerable returns to sheer performance levels.
What AI safety funding does offer is an opportunity to spread money around a self-selecting community of EA researchers and activists. A dizzying number of conferences, think tanks, and fellowships have sprung up to study the topic, backed by funders like Coefficient Giving. Much as a liberal-interventionist foreign policy makes for “a full-employment strategy for the foreign policy establishment,” so the focus on AI safety provides the AI safety community abundant opportunity for remunerative work and stimulating play.
Effective Altruism for Profit
Perhaps no organization better illustrates these tendencies than Manifund, a San Francisco–based fundraising body closely tied to the EA community. Whereas Coefficient Giving has historically acted mainly as a channel for the philanthropy of billionaire couple Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna, Manifund is designed to invite funding from a range of interested onlookers. Much of this fundraising is conducted through Manifund’s “impact certificate ecosystem,” which they describe as “like Kickstarter meets the stock market.” The organization also subscribes to a principle of full transparency, making its grant-making process unusually accessible.
Many of its grant choices are atypical, to say the least. In a recent blog post, for example, Manifund CEO and cofounder Austin Chen explains a number of routes the organization uses to funnel donor money into for-profit ventures — in spite of Manifund’s status as a 501(c)3 tax-exempt non-profit. These range from the relatively innocuous (commissions for specific services) to the legal but abnormal (outright investment).
Manifund has adopted more indirect means of supporting for-profit entities, as well. For example, it is responsible for funding and running Mox, an EA workspace and community hub in Downtown San Francisco. In addition to offering work space for individual paying members, Mox — which shares Chen as head — plays host to several EA-affiliated small businesses. And this summer, Mox and Manifund co-organized Surplus, a software start-up incubator offering generous seed funding and pitch opportunities to successful applicants.
Similarly unorthodox have been the charity’s recent hiring decisions. Against considerable uproar, Manifund recently hired effective altruist and convicted fraudster Caroline Ellison to serve on its administrative staff. In 2024, Ellison was sentenced to two years’ incarceration in connection with her roles at cryptocurrency trading firm Alameda Research and sister company FTX. She has since July played a major role alongside Chen in approving and directing grant decisions at Manifund, as well as contributing to the charity’s Substack.
This decision prompted considerable backlash from the EA community. Complaints stemmed partly from concerns about optics, given the extremely negative attention Ellison had already attracted to EA. But there were also more direct concerns about her trustworthiness and competence, especially in a financially responsible role, as well as resentment from victims of fraud connected to FTX and Alameda Research.
Chen defended the decision in the September blog post announcing the hire, offering among other reasons a sense of indebtedness to FTX:
I felt a keen debt to the FTX Future Fund. They provided seed funding for Manifold. They funded the retreat which drew me into the EA community, and the conference where I met my wife. Much of Manifund’s work today is directly inspired by the Future Fund’s approach.
The Future Fund was the philanthropic wing of FTX, which at the time was linked to fraudulently acquired funds siphoned from the exchange’s account holders. In addition to Manifund, the Future Fund supported a number of EA-related causes, primarily related to AI safety and pandemic prevention.
The Transfer of Wealth
In all of these capacities, Manifund has consistently deprioritized “short-term” EA work of the sort exemplified by AMF. Often, this has been in favour of recognizable “long-term” cause areas, like AI safety. But sometimes its beneficiaries have not even clearly fit this more extensive mold and instead have been connected to EA more through cultural and ideological affinity.
An easy indication of this is the official breakdown of Manifund grants by cause area. Best-funded is “Technical AI Safety” at over $8 million, coming out ahead of similarly AI-dominated causes like “AI Governance” ($5.2 million) and “Global Catastrophic Risks” ($4.7 million). All of these come out ahead of “Global Health and Development,” which clocks in at a comparatively meagre $436,000. (Cause areas are not mutually exclusive, so some of these funding amounts overlap.)
The immediate net effect of this outsize investment in technical AI safety is a transfer of wealth to the EA-dominated AI safety research community. Existing technical AI safety initiatives are effectively all research- or education-oriented: given the lack of any widely recognized way of implementing AI safety, the main place for funding to go is to researchers either currently trying to develop strategies for AI safety or learning what is needed to do the same. EA-affiliated AI governance initiatives, in turn, are carried out in close coordination with technical researchers and draw from a similar subcultural pool.
Many non-AI projects with heavy support from Manifund similarly circulate the EA cash pool among other effective altruists. For example, Manifund has raised $132,000 in funding for “human intelligence amplification @ Berkeley Genomics Project” — an attempt to breed a new generation of hyperintelligent humans through genomic engineering, in the hopes that they may be better suited to design safe AI systems. Setting aside any ethical considerations, the project is unlikely to generate immediate fruit. Rather, the main immediate impact is the opportunity to conduct highly speculative bioengineering research much in vogue among effective altruists.
The same tendency is even more directly on display in the “EA Community” category ($1.6 million). Best-funded of all projects in the category, after Mox, is Lightcone Infrastructure — the common funding and governing body of LessWrong and the EA hotel turned event venue Lighthaven. Lighthaven, acquired by Lightcone in 2022 (reportedly with the substantial financial assistance of FTX), has subsequently hosted a number of conferences, programs, and parties associated with the EA community in the Bay Area.
More indirect support from Manifund, such as through Mox, continues this trend. Some of the start-ups using Mox’s office space, for example, are only very dubiously philanthropic ventures. They include The Relationship Company (a dating app “making AI systems that understand who you are and find people you’d genuinely connect with”) and Stardrift (an AI-based travel agency).
Expanding the Circle
A common metaphor used to explain EA to outsiders is the “circle of concern.” Moral progress, in this story, is largely a matter of expanding this “circle:” the range of people, animals, and things about which one cares. At the center of your circle is you, whom you will care about even if you are maximally greedy and selfish. Beyond that lie family, neighbors, countrymen, humanity writ large, and the animal kingdom, at ever wider removes. Effective altruism, at its best, is about maintaining a wide circle of concern, in a self-consciously rational way.
The irony in this tale is that EA has often had the opposite effect. Where charitable donations might otherwise have gone to distant victims of poverty, illness, and disaster, many EA organizations have instead channeled them primarily to one another. Rather than expanding its devotees’ circle of concern, effective altruism has come to consist largely in narrowing that circle to effective altruists.
