https://jacobin.com/2026/11/piketty-glob.title: A Global Socialism Built on Shared Prosperity
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/piketty-glob.author: Lucas Chancel, Jonas Dietrich, Cornelia Mohren, Rowaida Moshrif, Moritz Odersky, Thomas Piketty
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/piketty-glob.text:
A Global Socialism Built on Shared Prosperity
Writing in Jacobin, Thomas Piketty and his fellow Global Justice Report coordinators argue that every country can reach today’s richest living standards by 2100, with rewards for workers in the Global North too.
All countries in the world can converge to the income levels of today’s richest regions by 2100 while staying within the 2 degrees Celsius climate target. That is the central finding of the Global Justice Report, published by the World Inequality Lab in June 2026 and drawing on the work of more than two hundred researchers. It holds under three conditions: a rapid energy transition; a shift in what economies produce (shorter working hours and less material consumption in rich countries); and substantial redistribution within and between countries. None of these conditions is enough on its own.
Virgilio Urbina Lazardi’s recent review of the report, published in Jacobin, argues that this scenario offers too little to workers in the Global North. But it leaves a fundamental question unanswered: Who or what pays for even faster growth in the North? The implicit answer is the Global South, the climate, or both.
An internationalist working-class movement can hardly accept this trade-off. The Global Justice Report proposes another path. It brings development and the ecological crisis into a single framework, combining four dimensions that today’s debates usually treat separately: a radical transformation of energy systems, substantial shifts in work time and consumption patterns, global redistribution, and a deep reform of the international financial and economic order. Unlike most climate scenarios, including those of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), it places inequality, class structure, and sufficiency at the center of the analysis.
The challenges of this century are global. Today the average income in sub-Saharan Africa is one-sixteenth of that in North America, and the world’s richest eighty thousand individuals own three times as much wealth as the poorest half of humanity. At the same time, current policies put the world on course for potentially more than 4 degrees Celsius of warming by 2100. Any serious discussion of future growth trajectories and the climate crisis must therefore acknowledge the legitimate demand of countries in the Global South to raise their living standards to the level of today’s rich countries.
In developing a new progressive vision, the report draws inspiration from two sources. The first is the great social movements of the twentieth century, which, through collective mobilization and legislation, cut working hours by more than a third, strengthened workers’ rights, and made progressive taxation a core pillar of modern welfare states. The second is today’s internationalist initiatives from the Global South: the African Group’s push for a United Nations tax convention, the Barbados-led Bridgetown Initiative to reform the international financial order, and the G20 initiatives of Brazil and South Africa on international taxation and global inequality. Building on these proposals, the report aims to offer a positive vision of the future from the left, in sharp contrast to the techno-autocratic narratives that dominate today’s public debate.
Putting Class Structure at the Center of Climate Scenarios
In the report’s central scenario of “Sustainable Convergence,” average monthly income per person converges to €5,000 in every country by 2100. This implies annual growth rates of 3–4 percent in today’s poorest regions and close to zero in the richest, as convergence at higher levels would likely exceed the 2 degrees Celsius carbon budget.
Such a trajectory is possible only if the transformation rests simultaneously on three pillars. The first is the rapid — and unprecedented — decarbonization of energy systems. The second is a major shift toward sufficiency: a sharp cut in working hours to shrink the material footprint, along with profound changes in consumption patterns and diets, land use, and forest cover. The third is a drastic reduction in inequality of income, wealth, and power, both between and within countries.
This transition requires massive investment in sustainable development, including education, health, and low-carbon energy systems. As part of a new international order, the report proposes a Global Justice Fund, financed by progressive taxes on income and wealth, that would raise around 10 percent of world GDP per year over the coming decades. The fund is a key building block of a broader reform of the international financial and trade system, which would abolish the current plutocratic voting rules in international organizations such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where voting power depends largely on economic size and gives rich countries outsize influence.
The result is a profound change in the global social structure. The share of world wealth owned by the bottom half rises from 2 percent to 30 percent, while the billionaire class’s share falls from about 6 percent to 0.05 percent. Nearly 90 percent of the world’s population doubles its income while working roughly half as many hours as today. Warming reaches 1.8 degrees Celsius by 2100, compared with more than 4 degrees Celsius if current policy trends continue.
The projected rise of the bottom 50 percent wealth share from about 2 percent today to over 30 percent represents a particularly striking shift. Together with the collapse of top wealth shares, this would amount to a major transformation of the social structure and power relations. This is especially true for today’s most unequal countries, such as the United States, where the working class would benefit enormously.
Do We Project Too Little Monetary Income Growth in the Global North?
Urbina Lazardi’s core objection is that doubling the average income of the bottom 80–90 percent in rich countries between 2026 and 2100 is far too little for the North’s working class to accept. This critique overlooks three fundamental points. First, projecting faster growth in the North comes at a price: abandoning the 2 degrees Celsius target, abandoning the South’s catch-up, or relying on wishful techno-optimism about emission decoupling. Second, income is not the only measure of well-being: workers in the North would also gain more leisure time, more equal societies, better public services, and a habitable planet. Third, given the North’s historical responsibility for climate change and colonial damages, our convergence plan may ask too little of rich countries, not too much.
More Income for the Global North?
Whether the working class in the Global North could enjoy higher income growth rates depends on the answers to two questions: how large the world economy can become, and how its income is shared.
The first question is whether a larger global economy is compatible with planetary boundaries. In our core scenario, all countries converge to an average per capita income of €60,000 a year (€5,000 a month), and the world economy grows fourfold by 2100. With seven of nine planetary boundaries already breached today, this growth must go hand in hand with a profound transformation that makes production far less emission-intensive, wasteful, and extractive. Our modeling focuses on greenhouse gases, with the aim of limiting warming to below 2 degrees Celsius. This lies at the upper end of the Paris Agreement’s goal of keeping warming “well below 2 degrees Celsius” while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees Celsius, a goal set because even 2 degrees Celsius of warming is expected to cause severe climate impacts and great human suffering.
The Jacobin review suggests that we are too pessimistic about technology and underestimate future gains in reducing emissions per unit of output, so-called decoupling. Yet our Sustainable Convergence scenario relies on the most ambitious decarbonization scenario of the International Energy Agency’s World Energy Outlook 2025, and our decoupling rates are similar to those of the most optimistic Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). For the world economy, we model annual decoupling rates of more than 6 percent over the next twenty-five years and even faster decoupling after 2050. In recent years, the world economy decoupled at less than 2 percent a year, so the pace would have to triple almost immediately. We consider this barely feasible under the proposed new international order in which global progressive taxation raises around 3–4 percent of world GDP each year for the necessary climate investment. Even so, €60,000 may prove too high once other planetary boundaries, such as critical-mineral extraction and fresh water use, are considered. We therefore see no credible path to even faster global growth without unrealistic techno-optimism.
Once the size of the economy compatible with 2 degrees Celsius is set, the second question is how its income is shared. If the Global North grows faster, the Global South has less environmental space. The resulting persistent inequality between regions beyond 2100 is built into most climate scenarios in use today: even in the most egalitarian SSP (SSP1) used by the IPCC, the richest regions remain three times richer than the poorest in 2100. But we are convinced that any vision of a desirable global future spanning several generations must take seriously the ambition of the Global South to catch up. Our scenario therefore starts from the principle of convergence. Given convergence between countries, the working class in the North could gain more only through even more radical redistribution within countries. However, our scenario is already very egalitarian: the income ratio between the richest and poorest falls to five-to-one, far below the eleven-to-one of the Nordic European social democracies in the 1970s, which were among the most equal societies in Western history.
Calls for more income growth for workers in the North must therefore spell out what they imply for low-income countries, for the climate, and for assumptions about technology. Moreover, as we argue next, our vision is desirable for the workers of the North too, once we look at well-being rather than income alone.
Well-Being Is More Than Income
If faster growth in the North is incompatible with global convergence within 2 degrees Celsius, the question becomes whether the gains our scenario does offer are really as meager as the review suggests. We do not think they are. In purely monetary terms, the gains for most workers in rich countries are modest. A doubling of income over seventy-five years corresponds to annual growth of just under 1 percent. That is roughly the pace at which median incomes grew during the neoliberal period. However, that growth came at great environmental cost, and a narrow focus on income leaves out much of what makes life better or worse.
The first additional gain, compared with growth-focused scenarios, is free time. In our scenario, the doubling of income comes with a sharp decline in working hours, so income per hour worked roughly triples. That is the opposite of the neoliberal period, when global working hours largely stopped falling after their steady decline during the rise of the welfare state before 1970. It would be a return to the long historical trend: societies have commonly used a large share of their productivity gains to work less rather than to consume more, and shorter workweeks, free weekends, and more holidays were some of the labor movement’s greatest victories. More free time means more time for family, friends, culture, and political life, and it makes a fairer division of domestic work between women and men easier to achieve.
The second gain is a healthier planet. Keeping warming below 2 degrees Celsius, rather than somewhere around 4 degrees Celsius under high-growth and slow-decarbonization scenarios, means cleaner air, more stable harvests, restored forests, and far fewer heat waves, floods, and forced displacements that would otherwise become a regular part of life in the North as well as the South. Workers and poorer households, who have the fewest means to protect themselves from such shocks, stand to gain the most.
The third gain comes from lower inequality itself. A large body of research suggests that more equal societies tend to do better on health, life expectancy, social and economic mobility, trust, and social cohesion, and that status anxiety and the sense of falling behind weigh less heavily on people’s lives. What matters for prosperity is not only how much people earn but also how unequal their incomes are.
Historical Responsibility and the Scale and Speed of Reform
The core scenario of the Global Justice Platform rests on a universalist principle: convergence of all countries to equal living standards by 2100. Yet we firmly believe that such a platform must also take seriously the historical responsibility for colonial and climate damages, which adds another powerful reason to support the Global South.
What matters most for global warming is the historical stock of carbon emissions, and the Global North has already used up far more than its fair share of the global carbon budget. Equally important are the colonial damages imposed on large parts of the Global South, including (but certainly not limited to) the costs of the transatlantic slave trade, fiscal transfers such as the “home charges” imposed on India by Britain, and the debts and indemnities imposed by colonial powers, for example by the Netherlands on Indonesia or by France on Haiti. These historical climate and colonial damages are very large: conservative estimates presented in the report put them at more than 200 percent of today’s world GDP. The argument that this is not the responsibility of today’s generations is unconvincing: people in rich countries today inherit the wealth, infrastructure, and education that historical emissions and colonial extraction made possible.
If anything, once we take these historical responsibilities into account, the Global Justice Platform does not go far enough. The notion of justice built into the platform is a “universalist, forward-looking” vision. Global income and wealth taxes are defined based on one’s position in the global income and wealth distributions, not on place of birth or residence. Similarly, country dividends from the Global Justice Fund are to be distributed on an equal per capita basis to all countries, implying equal per capita dividends for all global citizens. We chose this approach because a platform based on historical compensation would require a shared narrative about the past between North and South, which does not yet exist. Nonetheless, given that the vast majority of the ultrawealthy and rich live in countries of the Global North, the global wealth and income taxes would result in North-to-South transfers of about 0.8 percent of world GDP a year over 2026–2100. But these transfers are still nowhere near the 3.2 percent of world GDP that would be needed to fully compensate for our estimate of historical colonial and climate damages, which would require a Global Justice Fund four times larger than the one we propose.
We reach a similar conclusion if we assess the scale and speed of the Global Justice Platform from a different perspective. In particular, even under our benchmark scenario, it would take the entire rest of the century to equalize per capita education and health expenditures across regions. In other words, we will have to wait another seventy-five years before equality of opportunity with regard to health and education access can be achieved. A more ambitious scenario would involve faster implementation of the principle of equal access to education and health. This would require an annual budget that is up to four times larger than the one proposed in our benchmark scenario (about 40 percent of world GDP rather than 10 percent). Therefore, from at least two perspectives, some readers will find the Global Justice Platform too gradualist or moderate. We recognize this limitation of the platform and hence strongly support all strategies to scale up the size and scope of the Global Justice Fund and to complement the platform with other policies, including country-specific transfers and reparations.
Toward Postcolonial and Ecological Democratic Socialism
Let us conclude by stressing that the Global Justice Report has limitations and that we very much welcome all contributions and suggestions that could help us improve this work. In particular, our description of what living standards could look like in the future needs improvement. It is arguably more precise than that of existing climate scenarios (thanks to more detailed sectoral decompositions and inequality analysis), but it is still far too crude. We use eight core sectors to decompose economic activity, together with up to fifteen energy subsectors. In the future, we would like to develop a more disaggregated analysis, for instance to explore in greater detail the possible transformations of consumption and production patterns within food/agriculture, manufacturing, construction, and so on. In our view, this disaggregation is crucial, especially to move away from one-dimensional income categories and focus on actual material indicators of well-being.
Next, it is critical to do more work on the class alliances, political coalitions, and collective organizations that could support the “Sustainable Convergence” trajectory. The basic tenet of the Global Justice Platform is to reconcile the interests of the working classes of the North and the South. It is clear, however, that such a perspective requires much more collective work and strategic thinking — in particular regarding the relationship between this platform and the agenda for democratic socialism.
In the current version of the Global Justice Platform, we mostly emphasize the role of the Global Justice Fund (financed by sharply progressive wealth and income taxation) and the democratization of the international order (including the end of GDP-based plutocratic voting rights in international organizations and the creation of a UN currency). We also make clear that our own preference would be to combine these institutional transformations with an ambitious reset of the property regime, including a radical extension of workers’ rights and the rise of worker-managed firms, but we do not make it a precondition. One option would be to give workers’ representatives 50 percent of the voting rights on the boards of all companies (small or large, and independently of any equity ownership by employees), together with a 10 percent cap on the voting rights of individual shareholders in large corporations (with a gradual cap for smaller firms).1 There are many other possible options that should be discussed, including the use of Meidner-type labor-managed funds to gradually transform capitalist firms into worker-managed entities.2
Generally speaking, our own preference would be to move as far and fast as possible toward worker-managed organizations and participatory governance, within a broader process of decommodifying the economy. But this is also an area where much can be learned from the diversity of countries’ policy experiments, and there is little reason to restrict in advance the directions this collective learning process should take. There are many possible roads toward democratic socialism, and there are also some countries and actors who do not recognize themselves in this label (at least for the time being) but who might nevertheless be ready to participate in the Global Justice Platform (or a similar platform). These are important strategic issues that deserve extensive discussion.
In the end, the central message of the Global Justice Report is a positive one. We find that it is possible to combine shared prosperity for all with planetary habitability. But this would require a shift away from material consumption, a reduction in working hours, rapid decarbonization of energy systems, and a sharp compression of inequality within countries. The report puts forward a new vision for global progress in the twenty-first century, grounding human development and equality in planetary habitability. Yet there is a wide range of possible futures, and with the climate crisis looming over our heads, it is more urgent than ever to democratically debate the kind of shared future we collectively aspire to.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: US affordable artists' housing initiatives hobbled by uneven regulation and oversight
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kealey Boyd
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
“Affordability” is on the lips of every American. In Colorado, over 35% of residents spend more than 30% of their income on housing, which is considered a cost burden by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (Hud). The state is responding by allocating $300m annually to the State Affordable Housing Fund. A niche area of this investment is the development of affordable housing for artists and creative districts.
National non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort. Both non-profits market affordable housing for artists, but in the absence of artist certification programmes such as those in Boston, New York and now San Francisco, restricting available affordable housing to artists could run the risk of violating fair housing laws. There are also few mechanisms for cities and states to ensure their public funding delivers long-term solutions for artists’ housing and creative spaces.
“We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border. The artists used around 152 miles of yarn to bring the famous children’s book to life in a 2023 exhibition.
“We started our RV-life, one-year road trip experiment,” Chapin says. “We were on our way to Santa Fe, and went through Trinidad”—and they never left. Goodnight Moon and another project by Odeile debuted at Space to Create, a state-led initiative to produce creative workforce housing and studios in rural Colorado.
Trinidad was the first municipality identified by the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade (OEDIT) for public investment through the establishment of a creative district, in 2015. Today, 37 creative districts exist across the state. Next door to Space to Create on Trinidad’s historic Main Street, Artspace manages residences for artists.
Artspace develops and operates workforce housing across 23 states, including seven projects in Colorado. Each project markets itself “for those in the creative sector” and offers residential space that “prioritises creative use”. But without a formal certification programme to identify artists in Colorado or any of the local municipalities it operates in, it is unclear how Artspace can legally give preference to artist applicants over members of the general public.
Poet and editor Michele McDannold lived in Artspace’s complex in Michigan City, Indiana, for nearly four years and at the organisation’s Honolulu location for seven months. She arrived in Trinidad in 2020, but noticed a substantial difference in the artist preference process at that location compared to the properties she had been in previously. In Michigan City, she says, “I had to give a presentation to a board of practicing artists and participate in an interview.” In Trinidad, she was only asked to submit information for income eligibility. McDannold has only encountered five artists across the property’s 40 units during her three-year stay. The result of not prioritising artist applicants appeared to be that there were almost no artist residents.
“When it came time to organise or participate in something like [open studios or a gallery night],” McDannold says, “neighbours were like, ‘What? Why are you bothering me?”
Artspace did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s multiple requests for comment. The Artspace Trinidad leasing office stated that it does not track the number of artist residents at that location.
A tangle of laws, requirements and funding
Affordable housing is a broad term that lives on a spectrum of interpretation and regulation. According to the federal government, household affordability is based on the regional or area median income (AMI). What a property owner can charge a tenant is determined by Hud’s AMI calculations, but a lender can set the contractual terms of the tax credit, loan or grant, whether private or public. Under US Treasury regulations, a housing unit generates a low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) only if it is available for general-public use. However, in 2008 the Housing and Economic Recovery Act added a provision to the Internal Revenue Service’s tax code stating that general-public use is not violated if preference is given to tenants involved in artistic or literary activities. Even so, some cities maintain their own artist certification programmes for affordable housing.
A 2023 affordable housing audit by Denver’s Department of Housing Stability expressed concerns that priority access to housing could violate the federal Fair Housing Act. While the report specifically focused on the Denver city council’s move to prioritise displaced households or people at risk of displacement, it highlighted the fact that prioritising seniors and veterans also requires better systems for monitoring and evaluation. Each time a person, such as an artist, is prioritised for affordable housing access, the county must track data such as the number of units allocated, eligibility requirements, types of document accepted as evidence of eligibility, the selection process, and the parties responsible for implementation and monitoring the property and rent levels.
Municipal governments are concerned about incurring fair housing lawsuits, especially if state and county laws contradict or fail to reaffirm the 2008 tax code revision. Cities considering allocating affordable housing units for artists can be faced with having to develop significant compliance procedures. This patchwork of rules, requirements and compliance regimes helps explain why creating and maintaining affordable housing for artists can be very complicated, costly, and look different in different cities and regions. According to the Center for an Urban Future, US cities have created just 2,804 units of dedicated housing for artists in the last decade.
Artists’ housing, for whom?
The soaring windows of 210 East Street in Trinidad must have caught the eye of the developer Dana Crawford when she first visited the elegant century-old school building. Crawford, who died in January 2025, was a celebrated preservationist in the region, known for saving Denver’s historic Larimer Square and redeveloping the city’s Union Station. There were minimal requirements attached to the $4m community revitalisation grant Crawford received for the redevelopment of 210 East Street into 17 affordable live-work spaces for artists. An open records request reveals the terms of the grant for the property only ask for progress reports on the number of housing units and jobs created.
For the 210 East Street project, Crawford procured three different tax credits, the $4m community revitalisation grant and $1.8m in private financing, but the most restrictive terms were attached to last-minute funding from the city of Trinidad. In 2022 Crawford applied to the city’s Housing Now incentive programme to help cover the $125,000 cost of redesigning five units. The city approved the request on the condition of a two-year workforce housing deed restriction, requiring rent rates to be limited to 80% of AMI starting in 2023.
Crawford also sought $1.9m in funding from an impact investor, Greenland CDF. The funding from Greenland was contingent on signing a Community Benefit Agreement (CBA), a binding contract that requires the borrower to produce a social benefit with enforceable penalties. The details of the agreement are not public and expired earlier this year.
Less than five years after Crawford received a total of $7.5m in public funding for 210 East Street, the property was acquired by Cast. There are no existing public terms that legally require Cast to deliver affordable housing to artists, or even general housing.
Cast operates a non-profit real estate development strategy around creative spaces and affordability. Recently, the organisation expanded that strategy to housing in Colorado.
“Our model as a non-profit is to reset the floor of affordability,” says Ken Ikeda, Cast’s chief executive. “If we could do that without debt, through grants, then that would keep it that way in perpetuity.”
Currently, Ikeda adds, Cast is only required to deliver the private terms of the $1.9m grant the organisation received from the Colorado Health Foundation to acquire 210 East Street. Rent at the complex is currently between 55% and 80% of AMI, and according to a spokesperson for the organisation, five current residents are artists. The Art Newspaper was only able to verify that one resident is an artist, and that person said they know of no others.
Half a mile from 210 East Street are three properties that have received significant public funding in exchange for affordable artists’ housing. In 2019 ownership of two addresses on Main Street and one on Elm Street were transferred to Artspace by the city of Trinidad. In exchange for that real estate and a $715,000 promissory note by the Colorado Housing Finance Authority in 2022, Artspace must deliver housing units within or below 40% to 60% of AMI for 35 years, and preserve the historic facade of the Main Street properties for 15 years. If it fails to maintain this commitment, it must repay the borrowed funds.
The vastly different requirements for the Artspace and Cast properties in Trinidad, and the strings attached (or not) to their public and private funding reflect the wildly different standards and requirements for organisations creating and operating affordable artists’ housing.
Cities sustaining artists
A vibrant art and culture scene boosts local businesses and helps create jobs, according to the Denver Downtown Development Authority (DDDA), a city initiative to revive a downtown core where the vacancy rate has remained at or above 30% since the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2025 and 2026 the DDDA awarded $114.5m in financing for new housing and $4.45m for art-related initiatives—including a $1.35m grant to Cast to convert 6,300 sq. ft of vacant office and retail space into affordable artists’ studios, a cinema and gallery. The city council approved the terms of the property’s sale to Cast in September.
“We are going to make it affordable no matter what, because that is our aim and objective,” Ikeda says of the project in Denver, which has been vacant since 2021. Cast estimates the art space will open in the summer of 2027.
Representatives for the city did not clarify how it defines “affordable” in the context of commercial real estate, but noted that the city has the first right to purchase the property for $1 for the next ten years if Cast decides to sell. In the meantime, municipal support will be released in phases as Cast reaches a series of build-out milestones.
While Denver finds its footing on affordable housing for artists and New York has not added any units in a decade, San Francisco’s first dedicated affordable artists’ housing is on track to open in 2028. The Artist Hub on Market, at 1687 Market Street, will have 94 units of housing, rehearsal space and a theatre. Rent will be set between 30% and 80% of the AMI, depending on the size of the unit and number of occupants, which equates to annual income of between $46,440 and $167,120 for tenants.
Launching alongside the Market Street property is a new artist certification programme for San Francisco, facilitated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development. Artists can achieve certification by documenting at least $10,000 in annual income from their art practice, showing proof of a public art commission or grant in the previous three years, or submitting a portfolio of work for review. Once certification is awarded, artists can enter the lottery for units at Artist Hub on Market; any units unclaimed by artists in the lottery will be opened to general-public use through the city’s affordable housing system.
Of the Artist Hub on Market project’s $140m in funding, $100m came from a single anonymous donor and, according to a source familiar with the terms of the deal, implementing the artist certification programme was a condition of the funding.
The inconsistent regulation of properties that receive public funding for affordable artists’ housing and cultural spaces risks undermining such projects’ longevity and disappointing the communities they were meant to serve. Recently, a $400,000 low-interest loan from the DDDA to Denver Immersive Repertory Theater (Dirt) went into default after Dirt’s alleged failure to make rent payments less than a year after it was awarded the loan and before its project ever opened to the public. According to reporting by Denverite, the loan’s rate surges from 3% to 15% when loan proceeds are shown to not be used for their intended purpose, though it is unclear what assets the city will be able to claw back from the project’s founders.
Affordable housing for artists is an emerging sector entangled with various local governments’ goals, which include attracting business, lowering housing costs by adding units and retaining creative workers. Ikeda describes every affordability project as a funding “butterfly” due to the unique risks and complexity of the capital and terms assembled. But, he adds, they are worth the trouble: “There is something magical about artist-only housing and live-work environments.”

https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/a.title: ‘All-Out Assault’: Crucial Federal Transit Grants Could Go Up in Smoke If Congress Doesn’t Act Now
https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/a.author: Kea Wilson
https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/a.text:
‘All-Out Assault’: Crucial Federal Transit Grants Could Go Up in Smoke If Congress Doesn’t Act Now
One of America's most critical sources of transit funding has been under sustained attack from the White House for more than a year — and a new rule could finally send it up in flames unless Congress wakes up.
The Trump administration is hobbling the program America relies on most to grow its public transit networks — and unless Congress takes back its power, long-awaited expansions could grind to a halt, advocates warned.
A massive phalanx of transportation organizations, thought leaders and lawmakers sounded the alarm this month about Trump’s latest attack on the Capital Investment Grants program — or CIG, as it’s colloquially known — for which countless agencies across the country compete to secure the dollars they need to launch new rail, bus and streetcar lines.
The Federal Transit Administration’s proposed new guidance would move the goalposts for project eligibility so far that almost nothing would qualify, according to critics. Worse, the new rules would also apply retroactively, putting at risk nearly all of the 47 projects at various stages of the notoriously arduous CIG pipeline, including those its final stages.
Because transit has so little guaranteed money from other sources — in sharp contrast to highways, which benefit from heavily-subsidized federal trust funds whose expenditures are subject to far less scrutiny — local agencies will struggle to find new funding for rescinded grants and be forced to cancel projects, experts said.
“The new guidance is a part of the Trump administration’s systematic campaign to reduce or eliminate funding for new transit projects,” said Yonah Freemark, principal research associate at the Urban Institute. “It’s basically a crisis for transit agencies.”
What CIG is — and How The Trump Administration Has Been Functionally Dismantling It
Since it was first launched in the 1970s, the Capital Investment Grants program has been both a critical and deeply challenging fixture of the nation’s transit landscape.
Even before the Trump administration’s new guidance raised the bar into the stratosphere, the American Public Transportation Association compared the program to a “bureaucratic maze” freighted with statutory and regulatory requirements that can stall projects by decades and make costs balloon. Because there’s so little money for major transit projects anywhere else, though, many agencies have no choice but to run that rat-race if they want to even modestly expand their footprint.
“[Without CIG], you could do small advancements, but you would never be able to provide even the levels [of new transit service] we’re providing today — which [themselves] are wholly insufficient,” said Ward McCarragher, vice president of public affairs for APTA.
America caught its first glimpse of what a world without the CIG would look like when the President Trump returned to office in 2025 and proceeded to make history by failing to advance even a single grant under the program for a staggering 20 months — longer than any other president in recent memory. To date, only one project has been released from limbo so far: a bus rapid transit route that’s key to mobility plans for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and has drawn controversy for omitting bike lanes.
The White House didn’t say why it’s kicked the CIG can so far down the road, and neither the Federal Transit Administration nor the Office of Management and Budget responded to a request for comment from Streetsblog. But the conservative movement’s notorious Project 2025 initiative proposed eliminating the program entirely.
Of course, CIG isn’t the only transit program that Project 2025’s authors encouraged Congress to slash — and it’s certainly not the only one that the Trump administration has stonewalled since.
A swath of other federal transit programs have faced similar clawbacks and soft cancellations in the form of rescissions, illegal pocket rescissions, failure by Congress to extend advanced appropriations, failure by the Office of Management and Budget to allocate funding and a dizzying flurry of other legislative tricks that even the most engaged advocates struggle to follow.
All of those gambits, though, have had the same result: the administration abusing the complexity of the legislative process to hold transit projects hostage, until costs balloon out of reach and the mobility options Americans want most finally go pop.
“All of this evidence is pointing in one direction: A systemic effort within the administration is underway to undermine the CIG program,” wrote Kristina Curtiss of Transportation for America.
How the new ‘guidance’ makes all this worse
Trump and Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy have dealt blows to the CIG program for almost two years, but advocates fear the proposed new guidance could functionally deal it a knock-out punch — particularly when you take a hard look at the specifics.
While Duffy’s focus on marriage and birth rates drew headlines last year, the new guidance actually proposes giving “cost effectiveness” five times more weight in project selection. It also adjusts the “break points” at which, for instance, a project’s costs per trip are no longer considered worth spending taxpayer money, as well ratcheting up the level of non-federal dollars communities would need to secure to get higher levels of federal funding to match them.
Given rampant inflation and soaring transportation costs, those wonky moves would be more than enough to shove most projects off the CIG eligibility list, Freemark said.
“The reality in our economy is that costs are only going up and up,” he said. “But that’s not the fault of the transit agencies … The cost effectiveness guideline change is by far more damaging [than] the marriage and birth rates stuff. That stuff is stupid, and has no relationship to the performance of transit agencies, but it will have much less of an effect on whether projects are able to get funded.”
Many advocates say that the executive branch making these kinds of sweeping changes that Congress never requested is flat-out illegal, particularly when it comes to projects that played by the old rules and are now stuck in CIG purgatory.
McCarragher of APTA said that dozens of member agencies he’s spoken to are terrified they could be forced to start from scratch — and many won’t be able to.
“This is contrary to law and it exceeds the agency’s authorities,” he said. “It makes fundamental changes to the program that move the goalposts for all of the projects that are in the pipeline today. It will result in massive delays and uncertainty, increased cost to taxpayers, and in essence, stop these projects in their tracks and threaten their future.”
What to do about it
To stop CIG from going up in smoke, advocates say Congress must finally stand up to Trump and defend the program it created — and then take steps to insulate future transit dollars from similar attacks.
At the bare minimum, lawmakers could include a line in the next appropriations bill they’re set to pass in December, essentially blocking the new guidance from going into effect — something they actually did in response to past proposals to make CIG harder to qualify for back in 1989, 2007, and 2018, when Trump was last in office.
“For better or worse,” Freemark said, Congress might even “just ignore the CIG program entirely and give these projects the money that they need … because right now, waiting for the Trump administration to do something doesn’t seem to be working.”
While that sort of pork-barrel spending can set a bad precedent, some advocates argue it may be necessary to protect transit dollars that agencies earned fair and square under the normal process — and to send a signal that if the executive branch is going to steal their power of the purse, Congress will do everything in its power to take it back.
“Folks need to be contacting their Congress members and telling them that the Trump administration is on an all-out assault against transit investment — and it’s not just these regulations,” Freemark added.
More importantly, though, all the advocates who Streetsblog interviewed for this story said Congress must finally confront the root reasons why federal transit programs like CIG are so vulnerable to executive interference — and take steps to give shared modes the kind of durable, guaranteed funding that highways already enjoy.
As the next reauthorization looms, Freemark noted that few road projects are subject to any meaningful “cost effectiveness” or other potentially-disqualifying evaluations, despite decades of evidence and widespread public knowledge that adding lanes doesn’t decrease traffic jams – and that states can’t afford to maintain the overbuilt roads they already have.
Notably, the American Association of State Highway Transportation Officials — an organization which, despite its name, is supposed to represent all all transportation modes including transit — did not object strongly to the proposed new CIG guidance in its comment, except to argue that existing projects should be grandfathered in under the old rules. The Association did not reply to a request for comment from Streetsblog.
“Transit projects have to go through this years-long, or sometimes decades-long intensive, competitive process to get federal support for their new transit lines … [But] highway projects don’t have that at all,” Freemark added. “And that’s part of the reason why we have so much more highway construction than transit construction in the U.S.”
Kea Wilson is Senior Editor for Streetsblog USA. She has more than a dozen years experience as a writer telling emotional, urgent and actionable stories that motivate average Americans to get involved in making their cities better places. She is also a novelist, cyclist, and affordable housing advocate. She lives in St. Louis, MO. For tips, submissions, and general questions, reach out to her at kea@streetsblog.org, or on Bluesky @keawilson.bsky.social.

https://citylimits.org/court-upholds-new.title: Court Upholds New York Law Protecting Housing Voucher Holders From Discrimination
https://citylimits.org/court-upholds-new.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/court-upholds-new.text:
Share This Article
The decision was hailed a win for voucher holders, who may have faced fewer housing options if a lower court’s decision stood.
New York State’s highest court upheld protections for housing voucher holders in New York State Monday morning, in a win for voucher holders who may have faced fewer housing options if a lower court’s decision stood.
Hundreds of thousands of low-income New Yorkers use housing vouchers to pay a portion of their rent—but finding an apartment to rent with them can be challenging due to a tight housing market and discrimination from landlords.
The state’s human rights law prohibits discriminating against renters searching for housing with a voucher. But a ruling by a lower court in March said that compelling landlords to take federal Section 8 vouchers would violate constitutional protections from illegal search and seizure.
Monday’s ruling upholds the state’s anti-discrimination protections.
“Housing is a human right, and all New Yorkers deserve a home they can afford regardless of how they are able to pay for it. Today’s ruling by the Court of Appeals protects that right and affirms that landlords cannot deny housing to New Yorkers simply because they are using Section 8 to pay rent,” said Attorney General Letitia James, who brought the case, in a statement.
The landlord who won in a lower court, Jason Fane, owns an Ithaca housing complex called “Commons West.” His attorney, Curtis Johnson, said they “disagree with the decision and are considering their next steps, which may include seeking a review by the U.S. Supreme Court,” in written comment to City Limits.
With housing vouchers, families pay 30 percent of their income in rent while the city, state, or federal government picks up the rest. Voucher holders, who are all low-income and disproportionately Black and Hispanic, face significant discrimination in the housing market. Finding a home with a voucher can take months, if families are able to use them at all.
“This is just the latest obstacle. And so that discrimination sadly existed before this decision, and it will continue to exist after it,” said Even Henley, staff Attorney at the Legal Aid Society. “My hope is that with this decision, the agencies who are responsible for enforcing this law redouble their efforts, and they move forward with any cases that are on hold, and that they see this as a sign that we need to invest more resources.”
The lower court’s decision in favor of the landlord had paused all voucher discrimination claims in the state, and inspired more challenges from landlords in New York and around the country, City Limits reported in August.
Monday’s ruling now “means that the state of New York can open up its doors to taking complaints from tenants about discrimination against them,” said Diane Houk, a partner at Emery Celli Brinckerhoff Abady Ward & Maazel LLP.
More challenges ahead
Landlords’ main issue was with a different law than the one they sought to strike down in New York.
The suit in Commons West threatened to strike down part of the human rights law that protected discrimination by “source of income”—like a housing voucher. But the landlord’s “extraordinary and unprecedented” theory, wrote Chief Judge Rowan Wilson for the majority, argued that the state human rights law mandated searches because of apartment inspections required under federal law through the Section 8 program.
Judge Michael Garcia, in dissent, argued, “compelling ‘consent’ in this way results in a violation of the landlord’s Fourth Amendment rights.”
While federal Section 8 vouchers require regular inspections, “the [Human Rights Law] itself contains no search requirement,” said Wilson for the majority.
Legal advocates warn that even though the broad challenge to the law failed, landlords may still argue that inspection requirements from voucher programs require unlawful searches in certain circumstances.
“The landlords can’t just hold this up as a large shield, but instead must actually engage with the Section 8 program… accept applications by Section 8 voucher holders, consider those applications fairly, and engage with the program requirements,” said Henley.
Other challenges to source of income discrimination laws, lawyers say, would have to break the precedent set in New York, or show the specific circumstances of the search violated the landlord’s constitutional rights.
“The dissent is a challenge for the HUD administration and for Congress to think about whether to make modifications to the federal Section 8 programs so that states are able to protect its citizens from discrimination,” said Houk.
Increased collaboration for city and state enforcement
In a separate move Monday morning, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that the city’s Commission on Human Rights, which enforces the city’s own voucher discrimination laws, will refer brokers who violate source of income protections to the Department of State, which controls licenses for real estate brokers.
New Yorkers can already submit discrimination complaints with New York State, but direct collaboration between the agencies is a first, the mayor said in a statement, helping the city crack down on brokers who repeatedly flaunt source of income discrimination laws.
Amy Blumsack of Neighbors Together, a group that advocates for voucher holders, hopes that it will encourage more people to make complaints, and improve coordination between the city and state agencies.
“My hope is that this will help [voucher recipients] access housing and move into a stable home faster and I hope that it will give them a sense of justice,” said Blumsack.
The city’s Commission on Human Rights, which was facing a budget haircut earlier this year, has faced funding challenges for years that have slowed down housing discrimination cases.
“I think that they will make the most of this new policy,” said Blumsack. “I also was excited to see that [the Commission] was not included in the November savings plan,” referring to the Mayor’s call for city agencies to rein in spending.
Still, housing discrimination can be hard to prove, and owners, brokers, and landlords use tactics like “ghosting”—where they simply don’t respond to housing voucher holders—to evade the laws.
William Diaz Rivera says he was connected with a CityFHEPS voucher within days of entering the shelter system in June. “From that day, I have been searching,” he said, saying he’s inquired about “more than 2,000 apartments around New York,” to no avail. “When I say I want this [unit], suddenly the landlord went to another person.”
The move could have a chilling effect on repeat violators and encourage more people to file complaints with the city and the state, advocates suggested.
“It’s not hard to make the report. The question is: Is there a concerted effort to focus on the discrimination?” said Stephanie Rudolph, an attorney at the Legal Aid Society who used to run the Commission’s housing discrimination unit.
Not every discriminator is actually a registered broker, Rudolph said, making the enforcement strategy critical.
“There’s nothing that the Department of State can do if they’ve either already taken the license or the person never had a license in the first instance,” said Rudolph.

https://hyperallergic.com/trump-staffer-.title: Trump Staffer Unwittingly Reveals Smithsonian Takeover Plan
https://hyperallergic.com/trump-staffer-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/trump-staffer-.text:
With no sign of ceasing its attacks on the Smithsonian Institution, the White House could further upend the museum and research network, according to a supposed Trump staffer's documents for a tentative overhaul strategy, which were photographed on a Metro train in Washington, DC.
The photos, which a commuter took and dispatched to ProPublica, outline 25 items under the "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan," including the firing of National Museum of American History (NMAH) director Anthea Hartig, planned exhibitions on American nationalism, a redesigned logo and brand, and new institution-wide guidelines. If implemented, the measures could give the White House unparalleled authority over the Smithsonian's operations.
While the identity of the staffer has not been confirmed, ProPublica's report from today, November 23, speculates that it was Sam Bock, an associate policy adviser for the Trump-appointed Domestic Policy Council, which produced a draconian 162-page report in July that accused museum leadership, including Hartig, of promoting “extreme political activism."

Revisiting the artist's complications of authorship and replication in the digital age
In 1981, Sherrie Levine debuted “Untitled (After Walker Evans)” at Metro Pictures, a series in which the artist identically reproduced photos by New Deal–era photographer Walker Evans as her own. The works quickly gained a reputation among critics as “the example of postmodernist dismantling of authorship and originality,” that forever associated the artist with the tactic of appropriation. Nearly thirty years later, Levine contributed a seven-image portfolio titled “After Walker Evans Negative, 1981–1990” to the September 2009 issue of Artforum, coinciding with the display of the original series at MoMA’s “The Pictures Generation, 1974–1984.”
As Johanna Burton explains in an introduction to the portfolio, Levine began conceiving another version of the photographs while making the “After Walker Evans” series. This new body of work consisted of “‘negative’ images based on the first, quite literally taking the black-and-white pictures she had previously chosen from Evans’s oeuvre and printing them on reversal paper.” The negatives, a term that usually refers to the original “source” of photographic reproductions, are here copied from copies, heightening what Burton calls the “eeriness” of Evans’s subjects while emphasizing Levine’s deconstruction of originality.
The images published in Artforum are born from these negatives, but were produced at yet another degree of removal—while Levine made her earlier appropriations of Evans’s work by taking her own photos of the photographer’s prints, in this series she found images of the photographer’s work online and inverted the colors with a photo editing program. They are “neither reproduced from Levine’s own work nor even reshot again from Evans’s,” offering a colder, more impersonal approach than her initial Evans facsimiles, adapting her prior interests in authorship and replication to the emergent frontier of the internet.
Read “Sherrie Levine: Portfolio” from the September 2009 issue of Artforum.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Right Has Stopped Pretending to Care About Meritocracy and Is Openly Embracing Racism
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Kali Holloway
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Right Has Stopped Pretending to Care About Meritocracy and Is Openly Embracing Racism
Apparently grit and diligence are only virtues when they’re being portrayed as something Black people lack. Once Indian Americans demonstrate them, they’re suspect.
For decades, the right claimed that it opposed racial equity efforts not because of a belief in white supremacy but because of its commitment to “merit.” Given Asian-Americans’ success, how could racism—if it even still existed—be a hindrance to getting ahead? Under this theory, racial remedies were portrayed not just as an unfair “racial preferences” for Blacks and Hispanics, but a leg up for the least qualified. And conservatives could sell legal rollbacks and other attacks—on hard-fought Civil Rights Act protections, affirmative action, and the Voting Rights Act, among so many other regressive actions—not as attempts to reassert their commitment to a racial hierarchy but as demands for “the principles of meritocracy and individual achievement.”
That’s precisely how the conservative activist Edward Blum framed his successful campaign to overturn affirmative action. For years, Blum brought dozens of lawsuits arguing that the policy was unfair to white students. After repeatedly coming up short, Blum realized he should change tack: “I needed Asian plaintiffs,” he said in a 2015 speech. In the following years, Blum recast his attack on Black and Latino advancement as the defense of a community of color whose excellence was being punished. Other conservatives embraced the community for cynical ends as well. While whipping up the social panic over “critical race theory” in 2021, Christopher Rufo lauded Asian Americans for supposedly opposing CRT and “related ideological programs,” crediting their “commitment to the meritocracy” and their understanding that “if you work hard, you study hard, you have a little bit of luck, you can succeed.” Rufo was also candid about their tactical value, noting that they were “almost immune to the criticism of being white supremacists.”
Related Article
But the right’s support of Asian-American success sure looks different from the vantage point of this moment. It seems to be a vestige of a quainter time when conservatives felt the need to cloak their white supremacist goals in the language of meritocracy and colorblindness, lest they be called what they were. Now that fear seems to have been largely mitigated by the very political successes all that “colorblind” talk and “meritocracy” subterfuge enabled. A whole series of black Civil Rights Era achievements have been undone, and the confidence and swagger gained from so many W’s has yielded a right that says what it means, no longer feeling the need to justify itself, much less trouble itself with alibis and respectability. Especially now that the right’s idea of meritocracy is turning out to be not so great for white supremacy.
In recent years, there has been a surge in anti-Indian racism on the right, and certainly since Trump’s reelection, which ushered in a swell of xenophobia and racism that found a ready target in H-1B visas, just over 70 percent of which are held by Indian citizens, according to the Migration Policy Institute. Examples are too numerous to name, but if you are a very online person, it’s been impossible to miss the increase in Indian slurs and videos of poverty in India across social media especially on the platform formerly known as Twitter, where racism had been allowed to flourish under Elon Musk’s ownership. A recent report from the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found that between January 2024 and June 2026, anti-South Asian posts on the platform increased by 240 percent. In September, the Trump Department of Homeland Security tweeted an AI image of a South Asian man, identified only as “Mr. Singh”—a common Indian surname—with the warning to “get off our roads” and “self-deport or find out.” Conservative provocateur Nick Fuentes, who has spent a fair amount of the last two years ranting about Indian immigrants, recently expanded his vitriol to “race traitors” Brandon Gill, a US House member from Texas, and JD Vance, both of whom are married to Indian women. (Gill himself had created a campaign ad stating his desire for his kids to “grow up in a country that they recognize” that featured himself and his children, but conspicuously missing his wife, Danielle D’Souza, the daughter of Indian-born right-wing commentator Dinesh D’Souza.) Former presidential candidate and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy—who late last year even wrote a New York Times op-ed calling for people to stand against anti-Indian racism—has since abandoned all social media, noting that his accounts “are littered with hundreds of slurs, most from accounts that I don’t recognize, about “pajeets” and “street shitters” and calls to deport me “back to India.”
If one incident captures where things stand, it’s Texas Republican Bo French, who just lost to a Democrat in the statewide race for Railroad commissioner, posting a very real photo of a big group of jubilant University of Texas students—nearly all South Asian—in the stands during a football game, writing, “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” To be fair, a handful of Texas Republicans, including Sen. John Cornyn and Governor Greg Abbott, responded disapprovingly, along with national figures including Karl Rove. But there was open approval, The Bulwark notes, from “Federalist CEO Sean Davis, Blaze Media’s John Doyle, and Turning Point USA show host Jack Posobiec.” Trump tacitly sided with them in a post that chastised Rove, by name, for being “completely wrong so often.” Later that week, the Department of Education tweeted an AI depiction of football stands brimming with white fans under the words “MAKE COLLEGE FOOTBALL GREAT AGAIN.”
Then Rufo and his podcast partner Jonathan Keeperman dropped an episode titled “The Indian Question” in which he openly disavowed the right’s embrace of meritocracy. Rufo declares the H-1B program “radically unfair” not because it exploits Indian workers with lower wages but because it “undercuts native born” salaries; complains that high-achieving Indians are “another compounding factor” for “whites in university settings” who apparently still can’t cut it with affirmative action scrapped; and even has an eye roll for Indian kids who “grind on spelling-bee words [for] unlimited hours.”
“The right always says, “Oh, meritocracy, meritocracy, meritocracy.” You morons,” Rufo scolds. “You actually don’t want ‘meritocracy’”—he actually puts the word in scare quotes—because it rewards the grinders, and “perverts these unspoken cultural assumptions,” and offends “an essential component of the national character.”
And there it is. Not a complaint that Indians are failing but an admission that their success is unsettling to the racial and cultural hierarchy Rufo wants preserved. Rufo readily acknowledges that “Indian Americans are a very successful group,” adding, “That’s exactly the rub.” Keeperman is blunter, stating, “It’s important even to preserve a white majority and preserve this white, Anglo-Protestant sort of character. That actually is essential to who we are.” By the time they get to Keeperman saying that the real American hero is “the kid who is the fullback on the high-school football team, who puts his head down and is willing to run through a freaking wall on behalf of his teammates and then spends the night drinking beers at the kegger and wakes up in the morning and gets a 1500 on his SATs,” we’re so into racist cope-land that it’s almost parody. I have listened to right-wingers tell Black people that the cure for inequality is to pull up their pants, shut up about racism, study harder, and stop making excuses for as long as I can remember. I have seen an endless parade of conservatives claim, despite studies that consistently contradict them, that Black culture doesn’t prize education. Now the movement is put off by the kids and families who are doing that, and pretty openly stating it’s because they’re brown. I guess grit and diligence are only virtues when they’re being portrayed as something Black people can be told they lack, but once Indian Americans demonstrate them, they are suddenly suspect. The bootstrapping whiplash is astounding.
Conservatives in America have always sought to conserve whiteness. The idea of America as an ethnonationalist project runs directly through the right’s history, from Father Charles Coughlin and Charles Lindbergh to the John Birch Society and the “Southern strategy,” and Donald Trump has mainstreamed all that stuff again. But I have a particular interest in Rufo’s abandoning the bit because I cannot think of anyone in recent memory who has acted in such transparently bad faith and still been treated like a serious thinker and not an actor whose racial intentions were always more apparent than he admitted. This is a man who once once denied identifying as a white, insisting that he didn’t “buy into the framework that the world can be reduced into these metaphysical categories of whiteness and Blackness”; who spent years denying his crusade against even the most esoteric equity efforts had anything to do with race. Now he’s telling his audience Indians have “a tendency toward nepotistic hiring,” calling “cultural and racial sorting…natural,” and nodding in agreement as his podcast partner calls white resentment toward Indians “legitimate.”
Even the name of the episode, “The Indian Question,” echoes the horrifying history of groups of people being reduced to problems that need to be solved. Today’s very online Nazis often refer to the “JQ,” a nod to “The Jewish Question” raised by Adolph Hitler, whose movement decided the answer was genocide. I suspect few are aware that the Jewish Question was preceded by America’s own “Negro Question,” which dominated American discourse from the end of Reconstruction onward, as white Americans debated what to do about the troublesome newly emancipated Black citizens and their claims to democratic rights. W.E.B. Du Bois turned the question around, asking what was wrong with a country that would make its own people a problem. The question remains unanswered.
Meritocracy as a value only served to the right when it could be wielded against Black claims to equality while presenting itself as race-neutral. Now that meritocracy’s outcome is too many browns in America’s upper echelons—and a threat to white supremacy—the right is abandoning the idea. There are people claiming the right-wing, Groyper-influenced fringe has dragged people like Rufo rightward, but I think people like Fuentes just moved the Overton window enough that his rhetorical window dressings became unnecessary. The racial project has expanded so much it no longer needs “meritocracy” as cover—we’re beyond the need for respectable euphemisms. White supremacy has no need for disguises anymore. And to be clear: The argument is now that Indian success is itself a problem, that Indian striving and reaching is somehow anathema to Americanness itself. Because this was always about race. The right has just stopped pretending it’s about something else.
It’s not unlikely that the right—still smarting from major losses incurred in the midterms—may decide its electorally unwise to go around making the movement’s most overtly racist aims public. (It’s also just as likely that they’ll double down on the explicit white supremacy that got us here. You really never can be sure at this point.) Only time will tell. That said, the racial project that was always at American conservatism’s core has been made plain. And whatever softened language the right might opt to use, the ends will surely remain the same.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Efforts to save I.M. Pei’s Dallas City Hall likely headed to referendum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James M. Russell
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
When the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M. Pei’s city hall in 1978, he called it “a monument to the city’s pride, a symbol of a first-class city that’s reaching for greatness”. The seven-storey inverted pyramid slopes over a large plaza with site-specific sculptures like Henry Moore’s Vertebra in Three Pieces (1978, also known as The Dallas Piece) and Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973), which sits in a reflecting pool.
Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers. They have cited the prohibitive costs of renovating the building, which ballooned within a matter of months from $81m according to an initial estimate for a basic infrastructure upgrade to $1.4bn for massive upgrades over two decades.
In recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor. He has called the building “obsolete”. Architecturally significant or not, moving the municipal headquarters “would make this location available for development, which I would also support. I believe that will be a very, very big part of the future of downtown and its revitalisation.” Spokespersons for the city did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s questions.
The current mayor is in alignment with the “Say Yes to Downtown” campaign group led by former mayor Mike Rawlings. With developers and other former leaders, the campaign argues that city hall must be demolished to create an entertainment district, including a new arena for two of the city’s professional sports teams, the Dallas Mavericks basketball team and the Stars hockey team. When the teams announced plans to move out of the city’s core, both considered relocating to the city hall site. They ultimately chose other locations.
Amid the uproar over the possible demolition of Pei’s modernist complex, few have questioned the fate of Pan’s and Moore’s sculptures. Both were gifted to the city and are part of the municipal public art collection. But the future of Moore’s, which has required previous renovation, in part with help from the artist’s London-based estate and foundation, is a particular concern. The large grouping of organic forms was meant to complement Pei’s rigidly angular structure. It was also a gift to the city from the philanthropist W.R. Hawn in memory of his wife Mildred Hawn, whose favourite sculptor was Moore. Both sculptures are part of the preservation plan for the building; representatives for Moore and Pan’s estates did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries.
The non-profit Save Dallas City Hall, an ideologically diverse grassroots coalition, has been among the loudest voices opposed to moving the facility. It is led by president Bruce Richardson, a musician, artist and former political candidate, and vice-president Zaida Basora, an architect and former city employee who oversaw maintenance of properties, including city hall, and currently serves as the executive director of the American Institute of Architects Dallas.
Basora and her colleagues have proposed a ten-year phased plan that, even factoring in inflation, is estimated to cost between $70m and $100m, and would not require municipal staff to move. The cost of simply demolishing the building—to say nothing of the expense of building something in its place—has been estimated at $60m.
Deferred maintenance and a looming referendum
The Dallas city council gave Tolbert a deadline of 26 August to present relocation options for city hall, which she missed. Inflation has also increased the cost of relocating. The same month, Save Dallas City Hall sued the city, arguing that it was committing “demolition by neglect”.
“Dallas city hall has at least one failed generator, active parking garage leaks and is due for roof maintenance,” Richardson said in a statement. “Instead of tackling these problems with millions in available funds, the city halted repairs, wasting money and time to explore a move.”
On 2 October, the Save Dallas City Hall coalition started an effort to gather signatures to create a ballot referendum on the fate of city hall, which would be put to residents for a vote in May 2027. In early November, the group announced it had gathered around 25,000 signatures—well over the minimum 20,000 signatures needed for a ballot referendum. If the group’s proposed amendment to the city charter passes next spring, the municipal government will be required to continue operating from Pei’s city hall.
During elections earlier this month, 56% of Dallas voters opposed a $443m bond package. That package had included funding to move emergency operations out of city hall, which, according to advocates of preserving Pei’s building, would have been a first step toward abandoning it.
For the local activist Stephanie Drenka, a co-founder of the Dallas Asian American Historical Society who has spoken at nearly every public hearing since she learned of the building’s significance, preserving city hall is essential to recognising Pei’s contribution to Asian American history.
“The stakes are beyond our city alone,” she says. Less than 1% of historic markers in the US acknowledge the contributions of Asian Americans, according to the national non-profit Asian & Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation.
“This also makes demolition of city hall an issue of further erasure of Asian Americans in history,” Drenka says. “It’s not just Pei’s legacy, but we’re defending ourselves. Everything in our community is embodied in this building.” She adds: “If we can’t save city hall then what threat can we stop?”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/24/t.title: Tuesday’s Headlines: Another City Bike Edition
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/24/t.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/24/t.text:
Som Ray and David Krawcyzk of Clip show off their new product, the Neon (theirs are well-worn; yours will be sparkling clean). Photo: Gersh Kuntzman
For a minute, it looked like I’d picked the wrong day to check out the latest bike accessory that promises to “turn-your-regular-bike-into-an-e-bike.” After all, hours earlier on Monday, Mayor Mamdani announced that the price of a 45-minute electric Citi Bike ride would be capped at $3.65.
The price cap seemed like a game-changer to me … until I realized that it wasn’t: Sure, $3.65 is a decent price for a 45-minute electric bike ride, but it still means that a Citi Bike member who likes to commute on Lyft’s white bikes would pay about $2,000 a year (including the annual $239 membership). And it’s likely going to mean slightly worse service for all of us, as more people sign up to use the same finite supply of bikes and docks (docks that are often full when you want to drop off, or empty when you need a bike after work).
Full disclosure: I’m a Citi Bike annual member, but I haven’t used the electric bikes because they are just too damn expensive. But as my age rises in indirect proportion to my muscle tone, I confess that I’m jealous of the electric horsemen who get a little boost to get over the East River and up the hill that the name “Park Slope” doesn’t do justice.
So that’s how I ended up in the Brooklyn Navy Yard on Monday talking to Som Ray and David Krawczyk, the CEO and chief of product, respectively, of Clip, the e-bike accessory company. You may have read about the company’s first product, the Clip, (in these pages, even), but now Ray and Krawczyk are hawking an entirely new e-bike concept that threatens to take some wind out of Mamdani’s Citi Bike announcement:
It’s called Neon — and it comes in two options:
- For $365 (once), you get a new front wheel with a hub motor built in that’s easy to install on your existing bike, plus the 3.5-pound Neon battery pack that clips on and off for easy portability. The electric boost is controlled via Bluetooth from a small button that clips to your handlebars (no wires). The UL-certified battery pack isn’t going to take you to White Plains and back, but it’ll get you to work, where you’ll recharge it for the ride home.
- For $49 a month, you can lease a new bike with the Neon wheel and battery, aka “Neon Fleet.” Repairs and replacement batteries are covered. There’s no per-minute charge. That’s about $600 per year for all the e-bike rides you want.
Either option ends up less than commuting on Citi Bike e-bikes, even once the price is capped (which was covered extensively on Monday in The Times, in Streetsblog, in the mostly negative New York Post, mostly positively in Hell Gate, and in Gothamist).
Now, look, I have no financial interest in Clip and no personal relationship with anyone who works there (though they seem nice). As a newsman who bikes, I just wanted to share info about a different way to get around (plus I thought it would be fun to test the Neon — which I did, and it was). The Neon provides more than enough boost to get you up hills, but it only adds about five pounds to the weight of your regular bike, so your bike rides normally when you don’t need the boost. And the battery clips off easily, so you can toss it in your backpack when your ride is over.
And best of all: No empty docks when you need an e-bike and no full docks when you want to return one.
In other news:
- Speaking of e-bikes, the Pope looks like he’s violating at least two of the seven deadly sins as he lusts after this gorgeous two-wheeler:
- They finally un-paved paradise! Gov. Hochul announced a plan to turn the parking lot next to Tavern on the Green (reminder: it’s inside Central Park!) into a soccer field. (Westside Rag)
- No one has covered the Council’s battle with Amazon better than our own Sophia Lebowitz (archives here), but more and more outlets are noticing what oligarchy looks like. (Jacobin)
- Great minds think alike: Streetsblog USA and the NY Times both looked at the Trump administration’s latest attempt to gut public transit.
- We enjoyed the Daily News’s editorial about lithium-ion batteries (including a link to our coverage), but it also raised one thought: Is there no accountability for Sen. Ted Cruz? The Texas Republican blocked — for like two years! — a federal bill to set up battery standards only to finally yield before the bill passed unanimously. So does anyone ever go back and say, “Yo, Cruz, what was that bullshit all about anyway?” Interested, Greg B. Smith?
- And, finally, how about a map of all the detours on all the bike lanes? (Two Pedals)
Tabloid legend Gersh Kuntzman has been with New York newspapers since 1989, including stints at the New York Daily News, the Post, the Brooklyn Paper and even a cup of coffee with the Times. He's also the writer and producer of "Murder at the Food Coop" (NYC Fringe Festival, 2016) and “SUV: The Musical” (Fringe, 2007). On Jan. 1, 2027, he will step down as editor in chief of Streetsblog and remain as senior editor. His Cycle of Rage column is archived here.
