Days before the Venice Biennale opened, the Golden Lion jury resigned amid calls to exclude Israel from the festival. Dozens of artists and pavilions took themselves out of the running in solidarity. Now, as the exhibition draws to a close, the Biennale is ready to present its visitors’ choice awards — a “poisoned chalice,” in the words of the Art Not Genocide Alliance (ANGA), that “few want to win.” ANGA reflects on a historic year of organizing against attempts to artwash Israel’s assault on Palestine in an opinion piece today.
As gamers everywhere pore over Grand Theft Auto VI, Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia sits down with Miami-based artists misael soto and Leo Castañeda to make sense of the game’s many tensions and complexities, while Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar tracks down its various art references. In another form of uncanny valley, Associate Editor Phillip Pyle wanders through empty corporate offices in Midtown Manhattan, transformed by artists who dismantle the systems of technocracy from the inside out. More to start your week below.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
The Venice Biennale’s Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide
Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. | Art Not Genocide Alliance

A nine-month restoration of El Greco’s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion (1580–82) has removed more than four hundred years’ worth of varnish, dirt, and repainting and revealed the composition’s vivid colors and striking details.
Housed in the Royal Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial near Madrid, the monumental painting was restored at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery by Rafael Alonso, an eighty-one-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, according to Artnews. Alonso, who has worked on El Greco’s paintings for decades, originally projected a four-month timeline, but quickly found that the damage and neglect accumulated over 444 years would require a much longer process.
“When I put the cotton to the painting, my heart sank,” Alonso told El País. Varnish and overpainting dulled El Greco’s colors and flattened the overall composition. After removing reinterpretations made over damaged areas in the nineteenth century, Alonso and his team restored areas where the original paint had been lost using soluble materials that could be removed later.
King Philip II of Spain commissioned the altarpiece from El Greco, but when he saw the completed painting in 1583, he was dissatisfied. It depicts Maurice in a bright blue breastplate over a red tunic surrounded by his officers and legion of soldiers. Philip wanted the execution of Maurice and his Christian soldiers to be foremost in the painting as a statement of Catholic faith, but El Greco set the martyrdom in the background, anticipated by a host of angels above.
Commissioned for the king’s monastery and palace outside Madrid, the painting was instead relegated to another room, and El Greco did not receive the permanent position as a court painter that he had hoped for. The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion remained at its original site until 1999, when it was transported to Madrid for an exhibition.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Peter Kornbluh

Henry Kissinger’s Reputational Management
Barbara J. Keys’s new book, Super K, reveals Kissinger’s ceaseless efforts to burnish his bloody legacy.
Henry Kissinger’s Reputational Management
Barbara J. Keys’s new book, “Super K,” reveals Kissinger’s ceaseless efforts to burnish his bloody legacy.
On November 7, 2002, I attended a lunch meeting with Henry Kissinger’s personal lawyer, William D. Rogers, at a tony Spanish restaurant in downtown Washington, DC. Rogers was concerned about my forthcoming book, The Pinochet File—what it would reveal about Kissinger’s documented roles as chief architect of US efforts to undermine Chile’s democratically elected president, Salvador Allende, as well as lead enabler of Gen. Augusto Pinochet’s consolidation of his vicious dictatorship. Based on advance access to my manuscript, a year earlier 60 Minutes had broadcast a hard-hitting segment that tied Kissinger to the CIA’s violent plot to neutralize Chile’s commander in chief of the armed forces, Gen. René Schneider, who had opposed a preemptive coup to prevent Allende’s inauguration. On Henry’s behalf, Rogers had cause for concern.
Nevertheless, our conversation was civil; we discussed our differences on key points of the dark history of US intervention in Chile and agreed that we would debate each other in a special event when the book was published on the 30th anniversary of the Chilean coup.
Somewhat naïvely, I agreed to give him an advance galley of the book so he could prepare.
Rogers’s mission, as he reported to Kissinger via e-mail, was “to head off [Kornbluh’s] book or diffuse it.” I later learned that he had a team of associates pick apart the galleys to refute the evidence the book would present. Rogers drafted a 14-page rebuttal to share with those in the media who could counter my arguments. When he received a tip that I planned to write an opinion piece in The Washington Post on the 30th anniversary of the coup, he pressed editors there for “equal time and ink” and advised Kissinger to reach out to his friend senior associate editor Lally Graham Weymouth. In what became the biggest “project” to countermand the book, Rogers enlisted conservative academic Mark Falcoff to write a major article on what Rogers called “the powerful and pernicious myth” of US involvement in Chile. “Mark and I met yesterday for some extensive editing of his paper,” Rogers reported to Kissinger in mid-August 2003, as the anniversary of the coup approached. “I told him I would not—unless I heard otherwise from you—be sending you the draft beforehand. Thus, we can all say that the appropriate niceties of authorial independence were strictly observed.”
Their plan was to publish Falcoff’s attack article in Foreign Affairs, the prestigious journal of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), where Kissinger wielded tremendous influence by bringing in big donors to support the “Henry A. Kissinger Chair for U.S. Foreign Policy.” But that plan fell through when the editor James Hoge rejected the Falcoff article as “too narrow a defense of Kissinger.” Instead, the CFR’s Latin America specialist, Kenneth Maxwell, wrote a lengthy and moderately favorable review of The Pinochet File, sending Kissinger into a complete meltdown.
For Kissinger, “being attacked in Foreign Affairs was like being mugged in his own living room,” writes historian Barbara J. Keys in her compelling and damning new book, Super K: The Making, Breaking, and Remaking of Henry Kissinger’s Legacy. As Kissinger told his colleagues, Foreign Affairs had been used “to smear a former secretary of state closely associated with the Council for fifty years in a manner comparable to those of the most radical journals.” In addition to trying to get the entire Foreign Affairs issue pulled from circulation and threatening to resign from the Council and take the endowed chair along with its wealthy donors with him, Keys recounts, Kissinger “briefly contemplated a libel lawsuit before launching into a monthslong campaign to discredit the review.”
As a target (along with Ken Maxwell) of Henry Kissinger’s wrath, one of the great rewards of reading Super K was to learn that mine was not a special case. When William Shawcross published his meticulously documented Sideshow: Kissinger, Nixon, and the Destruction of Cambodia, Kissinger fired off a long letter to The Economist (reprinted in The New York Times) denouncing the book as “based on omissions, inaccuracies and inventions.” He tasked his assistant, Peter Rodman, with drafting a 17-page “independent examination” to be distributed to journalists and editors attacking the book as “a compendium of errors,” “shoddy,” and “deceitful.” Keys describes how Kissinger also halted the prepublication process of his forthcoming memoir, already in galleys, to rewrite the chapter on Cambodia; he added complete falsehoods about the secret bombing campaign in a damage-control effort against Shawcross’s book, which, as Keys points out, “tether[ed] Kissinger to one of the twentieth century’s worst genocides.”
In the case of investigative reporter Seymour Hersh’s The Price of Power: Kissinger in the Nixon White House, Kissinger launched his counteroffensive even before the book was published. He tracked Hersh’s interviews with former colleagues to ascertain whom he was talking to, what issues he was researching, and what evidence he was seeking. “His lawyers used the Freedom of Information Act to get copies of Hersh’s own FOIA requests,” Keys reports. They also sent prepublication letters of intimidation to Hersh’s publisher, Simon & Schuster, threatening libel lawsuits. Kissinger’s office developed a “dirt file” on Hersh to challenge his integrity as a reporter. When The New York Times gave The Price of Power a positive review, Kissinger sent a bitter 22-page letter to the executive editor, A. M. Rosenthal, excoriating Hersh and claiming that books like his would deter “people who value their reputations” from pursuing public office, thus doing damage to US national security. In a damning episode that Super K describes in detail, Kissinger collaborated with one of his most influential mainstream media buddies, Ted Koppel, to use his popular ABC News program, Nightline, as a platform to trash Hersh and the best-selling book he had written.
And when then–Nation magazine columnist Christopher Hitchens published The Trial of Henry Kissinger in 2001, Kissinger did his best to attack him as well. In her chapter titled “War Criminal,” Keys recounts how the history-changing arrest of Gen. Augusto Pinochet in London in October 1998 for human rights crimes offered a legal foundation on which Hitchens built his case for prosecuting Kissinger. If the international legal community could breach Pinochet’s immunity, it could do the same with Kissinger and hold him accountable for the thousands of human lives lost to his immoral foreign policies.
“Not since Hersh’s The Price of Power in 1983 had a book so enraged and provoked Kissinger,” Keys notes. Hitchens’s was “a far smaller book,” thinly researched with no new revelations. “Yet thanks to a propitious climate it inflicted more damage to Kissinger’s reputation,” not to mention threatened his very freedom.
Kissinger understood that Pinochet’s predicament could quickly become his own. He enlisted his media mogul friends in Britain, Conrad Black and Rupert Murdoch, to use their news outlets to demand the release of the former Chilean dictator. He began researching the powers of the International Criminal Court and wrote an article in Foreign Affairs condemning universal jurisdiction—the legal concept used to detain Pinochet—not mentioning that he himself was likely to become a target.
Nevertheless, the Pinochet precedent would haunt him. Not long after The Trial of Henry Kissinger was published, French policemen showed up at the Ritz hotel in Paris, where Kissinger was staying, with a summons for him to testify on his knowledge of Pinochet’s human rights crimes. Soon thereafter, judges in Chile and Argentina sought him for questioning. As Kissinger prepared to travel to Brazil to receive a prestigious award, a special prosecutor announced a plan to interrogate him; he promptly canceled his trip.
To attack Hitchens, Kissinger’s office compiled a 1,000-page rebuttal to his 160-page book. Kissinger hired a defamation lawyer in London to sue The Guardian, which had published excerpts. In the end, however, the suit did not move forward. “A lawsuit would have played into Hitchens’s hands, allowing the critic to subpoena documents and witnesses, from Kissinger and third parties, that might bring new, damning material to light,” Keys writes. “More documents would expose more issues and invite new lines of inquiry, without any guarantee of interpretive control—exactly what Kissinger wanted to avoid.”
Kissinger’s aggressive quest for guaranteed “interpretive control” of his legacy after he left government service is the central subject of Super K. The title is drawn from the many “mythologizing monikers” bestowed on Kissinger during his time in office—in this case, the June 1974 cover of Newsweek magazine, which depicted a soaring secretary of state with six-pack abs, red cape flapping in the wind, under the banner “It’s Super K!” The Superman image encapsulated the way Kissinger saw himself—and wanted to be seen. “Like the comic book superhero, in this telling, he possessed special powers: a strategic mind that grasped what eluded others and diplomatic skills that could unlock any impasse,” as Keys writes in her ultra-engaging introduction. “He was, it seemed, indispensable.”
Kissinger’s Super K persona was, of course, a myth—one that he assiduously cultivated through constant “reputation management.” When he left government, he built a self-promotion machine to protect and burnish his image, as Super K reveals, and “he spent the next forty-seven years of his life defending, explaining, and justifying his record.”
Sometimes Kissinger’s aggressive efforts backfired spectacularly. In the case of my book, as Super K recounts, Kissinger’s campaign to discredit the review in Foreign Affairs led to Ken Maxwell’s high-profile resignation—and his publication of a 30-page exposé of how Kissinger had bullied top officials at the Council on Foreign Relations to censor honest discourse on his own role in Chile. The scandal inside America’s preeminent foreign policy institution generated significant publicity: The Nation published a substantive article; The New York Times published two articles; and The Washington Post ran a three-page spread (with a half-page photo of a smiling Kissinger shaking Pinochet’s hand). The media coverage was negative for Kissinger’s reputation but positive for book sales.
But often Kissinger’s efforts to cast himself as the indispensable statesman and savior of humankind proved quite effective. His master manipulation of the media kept him in the public eye on his own terms; his close friendships with celebrity reporters such as Koppel and Barbara Walters, and top officials at The Washington Post, Time magazine, NBC, and ABC News, among other major outlets, provided a steady supply of positive press and ready channels for Kissinger’s self-promotional information warfare when needed.
But to truly secure his eternal legacy, Kissinger needed a like-minded, kindred-spirit biographer. In the final chapter of her book, “Kissinger’s Last Battle,” Keys tells the story of how he recruited a young, fiercely conservative British historian named Niall Ferguson to write the definitive, authorized history of Henry Alfred Kissinger.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
“Kissinger sought to bind his biographer with ties of friendship and intimacy,” Keys reports, plying Ferguson with access to “the rarefied world of power and money that Kissinger inhabited.” This courtship of hospitality succeeded. “I’m in Henry Kissinger’s swimming pool talking about his meeting with Mao Tse-tung, thinking I must be dreaming,” Ferguson exclaimed. The first of his two-volume biography, Kissinger: 1923–1968: The Idealist, was published in 2015, covering Kissinger’s pre-government life. The second volume, which will address Kissinger’s years in the Nixon and Ford administrations, is reportedly finished but yet to be released.
Keys, however, seems to have obtained an advance sneak peek. “He will say that Kissinger made the entire globe more stable, and that the suffering of millions unlucky enough to live outside strategically vital regions was the necessary price for this stability,” she reports. “In the end, much of what Hersh and Hitchens wrote about is trivial,” Ferguson told Keys dismissively. Three years after his death at age 100, it seems, Kissinger’s efforts at reputation management continue from the grave.
But regardless of what Kissinger’s handpicked biographer publishes in the future, the man that Newsweek dubbed “Super K” will forever be vulnerable to the kryptonite of history. As Keys’s book reminds us, the historical record haunted Kissinger’s many attempts to spin, falsify, or simply fabricate the true history of his role on the world stage when he was alive. And that historical record will continue to offset efforts to rewrite the past since his death.
William Shawcross used the Freedom of Information Act to obtain declassified Pentagon records that exposed Kissinger’s mendacity on Cambodia; Sy Hersh obtained troves of TOP SECRET records from various secret sources to write The Price of Power. Super K features my late (and great) colleague at the National Security Archive, William Burr, who was the first to obtain the declassified memoranda of conversations Kissinger held with leaders of the Soviet Union and China and publish them in The Kissinger Transcripts. And through legal efforts that Keys describes, the National Security Archive was able to force Kissinger to return some 30,000 pages of telephone transcripts that he illicitly took with him when he left office, precisely so he could control the historical narrative as he fostered his legacy.
Super K itself is evidence of how the effort to excavate the historical record on Kissinger’s true legacy continues. To write the untold history of how Kissinger sought to salvage and shape his enduring reputation, Keys has obtained access to many of his private papers, including letters and communications he himself wrote after he left office.
As her important book demonstrates, those records provide a powerful indictment of Kissinger’s insidious efforts to create a false legacy and cover up the true history of his rampant abuses of power. In the end, it is not just historians and reporters who have exposed the myth of Super K. It is his own words.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/m.title: Mamdani Won’t Guarantee More Citi Bike Service As Lyft Commits to Fare Cap
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/m.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/m.text:
Citi Bike e-bikes will become cheaper, but will the system be able to hold up? File photo
Mayor Mamdani would not commit to increasing Citi Bike service as part of his new plan to slash the cost of a ride — even as experts warned lower costs would increase demand and add strain to the already strained system.
On Monday, the city and bike share operator Lyft agreed to immediately freeze Citi Bike’s annual subscription at $239 and cap e-bike rides for members at $3.65 for the first 45 minutes starting on Jan. 19.
The announcement garnered praise from lawmakers and advocates who have amped up their fight in recent months for more affordable fares from the largest docked bike system in the Western hemisphere.
The deal will be in force until the current bike share contract expires in 2029, but the price cuts could strand riders as more and more New Yorkers choose to ride — but only if officials don’t push the tech company behind Citi Bike to deliver more service as well, according to a former city transportation leader.
“There’s tunnel vision on price, and not on operation or quality of experience,” said Jon Orcutt, director of policy at DOT during the Bloomberg and de Blasio administrations, who spearheaded the launch of Citi Bike in 2013. “It could create some more stresses on the system if more people use it.”
Mamdani said the city recently completed an expansion of the network to 3,700 stations in parts of Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx — but that work dates back to an Adams-era plan from nearly two years ago.
The mayor added that the Department of Transportation will work with utilities to make it easier for Lyft to electrify 130 docking locations next year, though officials did not share a specific plan. Dock electrification reduces the necessity of manually swapping out batteries, a process that requires workers to drive vans around the city.
“We have been working with Lyft on increasing supply across the network,” Mamdani told Streetsblog at a press conference in Prospect Lefferts Gardens. “And in early 2027, we’re going to be delivering new charging stations that will also help to keep [up] with growing demand.”
Hizzoner said the price cap will also allow riders more time to search for open docks without incurring extra charges. “I also think it will reduce in anxiety… for New Yorkers who have ended their ride, and yet are then looking for a place to dock it, and know that the price is going up,” he said. “Now you have through 45 minutes to find that dock.”
Orcutt disagreed. “That’s still not helpful to someone who’s missing a doctor’s appointment they waited six months to get,” he said.
Citi Bike ridership surpasses 200,000 daily trips during the warmer months — on par with the PATH train — but both completely full and completely empty docks continue to plague New Yorkers. This problem is particularly acute in high-demand areas, such as Downtown Manhattan, and the edge of the system in neighborhoods such as Red Hook in Brooklyn. Moving bikes around to ensure availability — a process known as “rebalancing” — plummeted after Lyft took over the bike share contract in 2018.
One rider told Streetsblog that he often has trouble finding a bike for his commutes between Brooklyn and Lower Manhattan, and urged officials address those shortages before they open the floodgates to more users.
“I think they have a logistical issue,” said Morgan, who declined to give his last name, at a dock at Broadway and Reade Street in Tribeca “There’s hardly any open docks when I need a bike in Brooklyn.”
Rebalancing will always cost time and money, Orcutt said, but the city should also pressure Lyft to station more valet attendants to handle overflow bikes. “That’s the answer, really, is staffing a set of key nodes where you know those tidal flows are really bad,” Orcutt said. “That costs money, so that’s one of the questions that’s always gonna be out there with bike share operations in a big city.”
Lyft representatives attend, but did not speak at, Monday’s press conference. Company spokesperson CJ Macklin said the company is working with DOT to “add incremental docks” to hotspots like Midtown, where many of its valet-staffed stations operate, and that they will evaluate demand patterns monthly.
Both Lyft and Mamdani touted the addition of 130 charging docks starting next year, which will be installed by early 2028, according to the company. But Lyft already committed to hooking up at least 160 docks back in August, which is about that same number of supposedly new docks on top of the existing 33 in operation.
Those docks will still account for only 4 percent of the network. Lyft previously told Streetsblog that it would need to electrify between 10 and 20 percent of its busiest stations to “materially reduce” its costs.
Indeed, DOT officials and Lyft set a 20-percent electrification target in a 2023 amendment to its current contract. That would amount to around 740 stations in today’s network. The city said at the time it would engage in “good faith negotiations” to reach that goal and discuss possible public subsidies, but that never happened. The city has not published any updated contract amendments relating to Mamdani’s latest announcement.
Unlike other cities, New York City’s bike share runs without a public subsidy, and Lyft’s largest expense is field operations, which includes fleet maintenance, charging, redistribution, and renting space, which made up $87 million out of its $203 million in total expenses last year.
To make up for lost income, the Mamdani administration agreed to ditch an annual $1 million reimbursement fee the city has charged bike share operators for lost parking meter money, and allowed Lyft to keep more of its earnings under its revenue sharing agreement.
“When it comes to revenue share, we’re saying that the city will be paid whatever exceeds $5.25 million a year, and that threshold will be modified annually according to the consumer price index,” Mamdani explained at the Monday press conference.
The price cap came with other changes. Lyft will no longer provide 60 free e-bike minutes to members who renew their membership. The city will also allow Lyft to install more advertisements on docks and bikes.
“We’re likely going to make less [money] on this system. Hopefully volumes increase to make up for it, but who knows. It’s worth a try,” Lyft CEO David Risher shared on X.
Bike share experts had previously warned that Lyft was gaining enough leverage to dictate the terms of its 2029 contract renewal. The San Fransisco-based rideshare giant absorbed the company that builds the Citi Bike fleet and has amassed more bikeshare systems across the globe.
The company’s rep noted the new agreement will deliver good service and system growth, despite the lower fares.
“Reliable service is what makes an affordable fare worth having, and we’re investing to keep up with demand as more New Yorkers ride,” Macklin told Streetsblog in a statement. “Charging at the dock keeps more ebikes available, especially at the busiest stations and during peak commutes, and means fewer vans on city streets. Citi Bike also operates without taxpayer funding, so this agreement was designed so the system can deliver lower fares while continuing to grow and improve.”
Kevin Duggan joined Streetsblog in October, 2022, after covering transportation for amNY. Duggan has been reporting on New York since 2018, starting at Vince DiMiceli’s Brooklyn Paper, where he covered southern Brooklyn neighborhoods and, later, Brownstone Brooklyn. He is on Bluesky at @kevinduggan.bsky.social and his email address is kevin@streetsblog.org.

https://hyperallergic.com/inside-edward-.title: Inside Edward Said’s World
https://hyperallergic.com/inside-edward-.author: Hyperallergic
https://hyperallergic.com/inside-edward-.text:
‘Tis the season for great documentaries. Twenty years after the death of Palestinian literary critic and theorist Edward Said, a new film revisits his life and legacy. Moustafa Bayoumi, a student of Said himself, posits that it offers a new generation a glimpse of Said’s indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight.
The lovely Eileen G’Sell takes a look at Trisha Ziff’s latest documentary, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, which screened recently at DOC NYC. The film considers the commercial afterlife of Frida Kahlo, asking how the artist’s personal history has been whitewashed even as her image circulates endlessly through retail culture. What happens when an artist’s legacy becomes as much a consumer product as a creative one?
And finally, if you haven’t seen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, what are you waiting for? It may be the best film I’ve seen all year, full of unexpected twists, turns, and glorious awkward pauses. Though billed as a documentary, the film raises what I think is a more intriguing question: Is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian? Not to toot my own horn, but I explore that possibility and more in my recent review, though be warned: spoilers abound.
—Rebecca Schiffman, associate editor
Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise
As an art historian, it’s hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything. I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one? | Rebecca Schiffman

https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/f.text:
Artists are continuing to speak out against the soulless flood of AI slop that’s appearing in our timelines (and in various other places) these days. And not only artists; even a lot of non-creatives are complaining about the emptiness they feel when looking at a computer-generated image that’s trying to pass itself off as art.
As most of you (hopefully) know, here at Cartoon Movement we do our best to keep everything as AI-free as possible. Why? Because AI-generated visuals are based on the biggest art theft in history, the environmental impact of the wide-spread use of AI is enormous, and the people running the AI companies are the sort of greedy evil bastards that motivated most of us to become political cartoonists in the first place, so we could use our art to fight back with satire.
One cartoonist that has decided to fight back is CM-member Piet from France. Using the most powerful tool he has at his disposal, his pencil, Piet has created a series of stickers for people to publicly show what they think about AI ‘art’. Better yet, the stickers are free to download and can be used freely (under a Creative Commons license).
They are available in English and French; to download them, click the big red button:
And if you’d rather like to have ready-made stickers, you can purchase them in Piet’s Redbubble shop.
We hope we’ll see Piet’s stickers in a lot of places! If you decide to download/order them and use them, please send us some photos so we can share them on our socials and get even more people to use these stickers!

https://citylimits.org/opinion-survivors.title: Opinion: Survivors Are Not Less Deserving of Safety Just Because They Don’t Have Children
https://citylimits.org/opinion-survivors.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-survivors.text:
Share This Article
“New York’s domestic violence shelter system operates under a complex, outdated set of rules that deprioritizes single survivors in favor of those with children.”
When people fleeing violence and abuse seek safety in a shelter, it’s not a decision they’ve made lightly.
Leaving an abusive relationship of any kind—whether it’s a romantic partnership, a family living arrangement, or exploitation such as trafficking—can be incredibly dangerous. Sometimes, abusers become more violent in response, like in the recent case of a woman in Queens who was murdered by her estranged boyfriend.
Survivors may be dependent on their abusers for money or housing, and leaving can be incredibly destabilizing. Survivors fleeing trafficking may face difficult immigration hurdles. In all these cases, when survivors make the risky decision to leave, it’s because the risk of staying is even worse.
On top of all that, some single survivors in New York State face another hurdle you might not expect: shelters that reject them because they don’t have kids.
New York’s domestic violence shelter system operates under a complex, outdated set of rules that deprioritizes single survivors in favor of those with children. Most of these shelters were designed for families, and the system pays shelter operators based on the number of individuals they serve, not the number of rooms they use.
That means that when a single adult stays in a room with two beds, the shelter provider only receives half of the funding designated for that room. In other words, single survivors often struggle to get a room because shelters face a financial penalty for serving them.
This creates tough decisions for domestic violence shelter providers, who are already grappling with cuts in a turbulent funding landscape. Reductions in funding directly impact the shelter’s ability to pay rent, staff, utilities, and services. In the worst-case scenarios, providers are forced to choose between survivor safety and the viability of the shelter itself.
But a lack of children doesn’t mean a lack of need. Single survivors tend to be older adults, pregnant people, LGBTQ+ folks, men, and trafficking survivors. And in today’s heightened immigration enforcement climate, survivors who can’t find safe shelter are more susceptible to detainment and deportation. These New Yorkers are being left behind even when space is available—New York’s domestic violence shelter system is only at 70-80 percent occupancy.
For survivors being turned away and told to try again later, the impact can be draining, demoralizing, and even traumatic. We’ve seen from our clients and constituents firsthand the urgent need for shelter. When single survivors don’t have a safe place to go, they’re more likely to stay in an abusive relationship, remain with their trafficker, or become homeless, exacerbating already dire conditions.
That’s why we’ve advocated for the Securing Access to Fair & Equal (SAFE) Shelter Act, a bill to make it easier for single survivors to access the shelter they need. By signing this bill into law, Gov. Kathy Hochul would ensure shelter providers are fully reimbursed for sheltering singles, even if their room is configured for a family. This would increase statewide capacity for shelters to serve single survivors of domestic violence, improve single survivors’ chances of accessing lifesaving resources, and help keep shelters open.
The need is greater than ever. Since 2020, the number of single survivors seeking shelter across the state has increased by 6 percent, while successful placements have dropped by 14 percent. Legislators and service providers have been advocating for the SAFE Shelter Act for years. Now’s the time for Gov. Hochul to listen and to take these survivors’ needs seriously. They’re New Yorkers, after all.
Survivors of violence and abuse shouldn’t be penalized just because they are alone, and a broken system shouldn’t inflict more trauma on people already struggling. With the SAFE Shelter Act, we can ensure no New Yorker is left behind.
Kelly Coyne is chief program officer at Safe Horizon, the nation’s largest victim service organization.State Sen. Andrew Gounardes represents New York’s 26th State Senate District and is the SAFE Shelter Bill sponsor.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/rosa-luxembu.title: Rediscovering Rosa Luxemburg’s History of Ancient Rome
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/rosa-luxembu.author: Serena Unzueta, Ian Tewksbury
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/rosa-luxembu.text:
Rediscovering Rosa Luxemburg’s History of Ancient Rome
Rosa Luxemburg’s writings have long been a touchstone for socialist theory, but her work as an ancient historian remains almost entirely unknown. We can now see the importance of the slave revolts in ancient Rome for her understanding of Marxist theory.
More than a century after her death, Rosa Luxemburg is renowned as a revolutionary socialist and leader of the 1919 Spartacist Uprising in Germany. Her writings have long been a touchstone for socialist theory. But her work as an ancient historian remains almost entirely unknown.
Luxemburg’s political writings, especially her work on political economy, were full of historical references, and indeed she often stressed the importance of history to the project of political economy — and revolution itself — in her major works. These references offered a tantalizing glimpse into a rich archive of study on Luxemburg’s part, but there was a frustrating lack of further elaboration on historical topics and the study of history itself.
That remained the case until 2001, when Professor Narihiko Ito discovered lost documents in Moscow of Luxemburg’s unpublished lectures and notes. One of the texts discovered is a manuscript on Greek and Roman slavery. This text, titled “Slavery,” survives because it was saved by her former student Rosi Wolfstein and biographer Paul Frölich from being destroyed after her murder in 1919. It was likely to have been a lecture she composed for her courses at the working-class night school in Berlin, where she began teaching in 1907.
It has been over a decade since this text was made available in English for the first time in the first volume of Luxemburg’s complete works. However, Luxemburg’s ideas on ancient slavery have not yet received the attention they deserve. We can now see what place the role of Greco-Roman history in general and the Roman slave revolts in particular had in her understanding of Marxist theory.
Ancient Roman Slavery
Luxemburg opens “Slavery” by taking issue with the argument of Friedrich Engels that slavery arose in antiquity after the advent of private property. She uses examples from Greek history, and even the Inca empire in Peru, to argue that certain types of exploitation already existed in ancient societies that were communal in nature. She refers to societies of this kind as “the mark community,” a concept she takes from Georg Ludwig von Maurer’s 1854 work Introduction to the History of the Mark, Manor, Village and Town Constitution (which also greatly influenced Engels).
In contrast to the early communal forms of social organization, ancient Greece and Rome developed the full alienation of the land from the people, creating a new form of exploitation and slavery. Instead of one society dominating another from the outside by exacting tribute, the dominant actor now incorporated the populations of dominated societies into its own structures and exploited their labor power for trade.
For Luxemburg, two further developments arose from this shift. Firstly, trade expands from a purely external practice to an internal one as well. Secondly, “slavery and trade evolved at the same time as the aristocracy,” creating the conditions for a split between a laboring class in the countryside and an intellectual class in the cities.
She believed that the Greek city-states had already maximized the cultural potential of this economic system:
Greek philosophy, art, and everything that could be achieved on the basis of the slave economy of antiquity had already been perfected by Greece. Rome merely had to borrow it, appropriate it, take possession of it. From then on Rome lived, one could say, as a sponger or freeloader.
For Luxemburg, Rome went further than Greece by stigmatizing all forms of labor: “Rome arrived at this conclusion: everything related to work is slave work, physical and mental. In Greece only physical labor had been regarded as slave work.”
The high point of slavery in antiquity came during the late Roman Republic and Empire. It was achieved through a combination of Rome’s wars of expansion abroad and the displacement of peasant farmers from their lands at home. As Luxemburg puts it: “In the depths of Roman society radical changes began to take place around the third century BC. It began with Rome’s struggle to establish an empire on a world scale.”
The peasant farmers accounted for the majority of Rome’s military forces. This resulted in the collapse of peasant agriculture, as many of these farmer-soldiers lost their lives or went into debt because they could not afford the taxes required to sustain the wars. Without their land, peasant farmers could only offer their labor power to the new, large agricultural estates that the Roman nobility had established, which were called latifundia.
This was a precarious position, Luxemburg notes, as there were not enough peasants available to hire for the labor required on the estates, and the peasant farmers themselves could be called back to war at any moment. She identifies the consequences of this labor shortage: “The great proprietors thus had to bring in more slaves. And the wars provided them in great quantities.” This created new antagonisms between citizens and slaves but also led to extreme wealth inequality, as the elite used more slaves to boost their capacity for territorial expansion and production.
The Roman Proletariat and the Slave Revolts
Without a home or gainful employment in agriculture, peasant farmers were forced to move to the cities. Luxemburg refers to this group as the proletariat, quoting the observation of Jean Charles Léonard de Sismondi: “There was in Rome a proletariat as there is today. But whereas the proletariat today supports society, the Roman proletariat lived at the expense of society.”
Ultimately, she observes, this social tendency corroded the Roman commonwealth, because the poor free citizen farmers lost their land to the rich and subsequently lived at the expense of the Roman welfare state. Part of this expense was the amount of grain needed to feed Rome’s new urban proletariat. The Roman authorities reduced the cost by moving grain production out of the Italian peninsula and importing the necessary supplies from Africa, Spain, and Sicily instead.
Two revolutionary consequences arose from these conditions. First, the Roman proletariat began to demand land redistribution and rallied behind magistrates such as the Gracchi brothers who took up their cause. Second, there was a massive concentration of slaves in agricultural production who would later rise up and revolt. Luxemburg insists that slavery could still be of fundamental importance even if slaves were a minority of the population: “It is not the numbers that are definitive, but the sum total of the tendencies that result from them.”
The latifundia intensified agricultural production. As well as changing the way of life for displaced peasant farmers, this also changed the nature of slavery itself, according to Luxemburg:
Now of course the living conditions of the slaves had to undergo a change. They were now completely reduced to the status of naked labor power. In agriculture they were labor power that was applied for the purposes of trade. In this entire institution, or configuration, everything worked toward a single purpose: to extract the maximum possible from the slaves.
For Luxemburg, “these relations inevitably led to slave revolts, particularly because the slaves had previously been free.” She goes on to list seven slave revolts that took place on the Italian peninsula and in Sicily. The Sicilian revolts are the most famous, in part due to the colorful descriptions that have been passed down from ancient accounts. It is at the bottom of this list that we find the legendary Spartacus, whose name would come to represent Luxemburg and her allies in the German workers’ movement until the time of her death.
Spartacus
Before the publication of “Slavery,” we did not know that Rosa Luxemburg had written about ancient history and Rome’s slave revolts, including the historical figure who became the legendary symbol of the Spartacus League. This text demonstrates that before Luxemburg called upon Spartacus to represent her current of revolutionary socialists, she was interested in the place he held within the larger context of ancient Roman slavery and the history of class struggle.
At this point in the text, Luxemburg does not offer a dramatic narrative about the life of the Roman slave who Karl Marx once described, in a letter to Engels, as “the most splendid fellow in the whole of ancient history.” Such narratives were widely available in the historical works that we know Luxemburg read and studied.
For example, Luxemburg read the famed German historian Theodor Mommsen closely and cites him in her work. Like many historians of his time, Mommsen had a tendency to sympathize with the ruling-class perspective on history. His account of the Spartacus uprising between 73 and 71 BCE depicts its figurehead as a “gang-leader” with an army of “half-savage herdsmen.”
Mommsen came up with further colorful epithets for Spartacus and his men as he recounted the crisis they precipitated for the rulers of Rome, referring to them as “banditti” and “robbers.” He accused the rebels of inflicting “atrocities” on “defenseless civilized men,” and attributed their final defeat to internal discord, “lack of a common foe,” and a “barbarous” demand for “plunder.”
For Mommsen, the only redeeming quality of Spartacus appears to be the fact that he died the death of a free man at the hands of the Roman General Marcus Licinius Crassus, whom Mommsen calls one of “the great capitalists” of Rome. The differences between Luxemburg’s account and that of Mommsen could hardly be starker.
In “Slavery,” Luxemburg deals with Spartacus matter-of-factly as the final representative of the great slave revolts of ancient Roman history. She refers to “the third Sicilian slave revolt, led by the famous Spartacus” within the broader landscape of all the documented revolts in ancient Rome, with an assessment of why they happened and why they failed.
In this way, Luxemburg follows the example set by Marx, who put heroic narrative and literary detail aside when seeking to understand and explain ancient history. The ancient Spartacus uprising was born from a sequence of uprisings that came before it: “The slave revolts were the first immense, world-historical class struggles against the exploiters. Not the free peasants, not the proletarians in Rome.” However, they did not lead to a transformation of Roman society:
The slaves wanted to return to their homelands; they wanted to break loose and get away from society entirely. They were only partly successful, to the extent that they escaped, some to their homelands, some joining robber bands or becoming pirates. The slave revolts remained without consequence, because any further development of them was not based on any trend of economic development.
She presents internal decay resulting from the economic logic of slavery as the main factor behind the eventual demise of the Roman Empire rather than external pressure from invading forces: “It was not only the Germans who brought about the destruction. Rome was already ripe prey for foreign conquest after such consequences had been arrived at as a result of its own development.”
In her own time, Luxemburg believed that the modern proletarian revolution would succeed where the great slave revolutions of Rome had failed. In the Introduction to Political Economy, she says:
In the end, this great proletariat in ancient Rome was simply maintained by the state. Capitalist commodity production, accordingly, is the first economic form in the history of humanity in which the lack of occupation and resources of a large and growing stratum of the population, and the direct and hopeless poverty of another stratum, is not simply a result of this economy but also a necessity for it, a condition of its existence.
Unlike Rome’s proletariat, she argues, the modern working classes have no incentive not to unite in the struggle against capitalism. Solidarity between “wage slaves” at the national and international level is possible in order to accomplish this goal.
The Spartacus League
The discovery of Luxemburg’s “Slavery” text provides us with a new understanding of what “Spartacus” meant to her political works. She began teaching political economy and history in 1907. The following year, she signed her article “The Epic of Łödź” with the pen name “Spartacus.” This anticipated the formation of the Spartacus League during World War I, and it was under the banner of Spartacus that Luxemburg herself would be sacrificed after the failed uprising in January 1919.
Spartacus was for Luxemburg a symbol of hope for the liberation of the international proletariat, a hope that lay not in the patrons of bread and circuses, but in the hands that reaped the wheat and baked the bread. The founding members of the Spartacus League chose an apt historical figure to represent them. But they believed that the modern proletariat possessed advantages over the slaves of antiquity that would enable it to prevail over the capitalist class.
In the 1950s, the preeminent classical historian M. I. Finley, who was blacklisted during the McCarthyite Red Scare, noted that the question of ancient slavery had been “a battleground between Marxists and non-Marxists, a political issue rather than a historical phenomenon” since the time of the Communist Manifesto (if not earlier). All historians of ancient slavery, Finley argued, inherit the polemics of this history. The most prominent defender of Marx’s concept of class for the study of the ancient world was the Oxford scholar G. E. M. de Ste. Croix.
In a field long dominated by male figures, it is exciting that we can now include Rosa Luxemburg’s voice in long-standing debates about ancient history. For example, we can identify two essential differences between the analysis of ancient slavery and class in de Ste. Croix’s work and that of Luxemburg in “Slavery.”
The first difference is methodological. Rosa Luxemburg used the study of prehistory, comparative anthropology, and colonial ethnography in order to explain the development of slavery. De Ste. Croix, on the other hand, was hostile to the integration of prehistory and classical history.
The second is theoretical. While Luxemburg identifies the cleavage between free and enslaved labor as the central class division of ancient Greek and Roman society, de Ste. Croix instead treats free peasant labor and enslaved labor as two elements of a single class. It is an important distinction that informs their respective views on the relevance of ancient history to the development of class struggle from the conditions of ancient slavery to the modern working class.
The addition of Luxemburg’s voice is timely, as there is a renewed interest in Marxist theories of ancient history. Luxemburg’s “Slavery” asks us to look anew at the history of class through the history of slavery. She proposes reexamining the roots of exploitation, on the one hand, and its corrosive effects on society, on the other hand. Overall, Luxemburg offers a new and valuable perspective on the lessons of ancient history for the socialist left today.

The City Government in Oslo, Norway, has announced the appointment of Thorsten Sadowsky as director of MUNCH, a museum dedicated to the Norwegian modernist Edvard Munch. He will begin his new role on May 1, 2027.
Thorsten comes to MUNCH with extensive experience leading European institutions. He currently serves as museum director and CEO of the Stiftung Schleswig-Holsteinische Landesmuseen Schloss Gottorf (Schleswig-Holstein State Museums Foundation Schloss Gottorf), a German organization comprising six museums, including the Jewish Museum Rendsberg and the Archaeological Museum Schleswig. He previously held positions at the Museum Kunst der Westküste, the Kirchner Museum Davos, and the Museum der Moderne Salzburg.
“I am delighted that MUNCH will be led by a director with such strong international experience and outstanding expertise in the arts,” said Mehmet Kaan Inan, Oslo’s Vice Mayor for culture and business development. “Sadowsky has … demonstrated a strong talent for audience development, collaboration, and engaging broad and diverse audiences. His exceptional interest in Edvard Munch’s artistic legacy also provides an excellent foundation for leading MUNCH into the future.”
MUNCH, which first opened in 1963, houses more than 28,000 works of art, including 26,724 by Munch himself. The artist bequeathed all the artworks still in his possession to the City of Oslo on his death in 1944, as well as original photographs, printing plates and lithographic stones, letters, and personal belongings. The museum also holds a substantial number of work by the artists Amaldus Nielsen and Ludvig O. Ravensberg as well as the private collection of Rolf Stenersen.
“Being entrusted with the leadership of MUNCH is a responsibility that I approach with great enthusiasm and respect. Edvard Munch’s art possesses a unique ability to speak to fundamental human experiences across time and cultural boundaries. This gives the museum both a special responsibility and significant opportunities to bring this artistic legacy into a living dialogue with our own time,” Sadowsky said in a press release.
He replaces Henrik Svalheim, who has served as interim director since Tone Hansen departed for Stockholm’s Moderna Museet last month. She had led MUNCH since 2022.

https://hellgatenyc.com/why-mta-bus-time.title: Here's Why the MTA Sucks at Predicting When Your Bus Will Arrive
https://hellgatenyc.com/why-mta-bus-time.author: Téa Kvetenadze
https://hellgatenyc.com/why-mta-bus-time.text:
You arrive at the bus stop and open up the MTA app on your phone. The next bus is four minutes away. Then one minute. Then zero minutes. The bus that never arrived has somehow already departed. Now it's disappeared from the map entirely.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani made "fast and free" bus service a cornerstone of his campaign, and in doing so highlighted a complicated, long-neglected problem for the 1.4 million New Yorkers who ride the bus every day: bogus bus arrival times.
"Riders shouldn't have to wonder if they'll make it to work, school or a doctor's appointment on time," Mamdani said at a press conference last month announcing new arrival time displays across the city. "Real-time bus information puts that uncertainty to rest and gives riders the information they need to plan their day."
The expansion is part of the joint "bus action plan" between the MTA and the City's Department of Transportation to improve overall service.
But neither the new displays nor the revamped MTA app can fix the problem of inaccurate estimated bus arrival times. That's because they're built on a beleaguered underlying system known as Bus Time.
First rolled out in the 2010s, Bus Time is the MTA's real-time information system that provides bus ETAs. Onboard GPS hardware pings the MTA's server every few seconds, and the bus' location gets combined with route, stop, and schedule data. Then an algorithm comes up with predictions for when the bus will reach subsequent stops, and this information is fed to the MTA app and website, the separate Bus Time website, and the passenger information signs at bus stops.
And it's a mess.
Four current and former MTA employees with knowledge of the bus data—all of whom spoke to Hell Gate on condition of anonymity because they were not allowed to discuss their work publicly—attributed Bus Time issues to a combination of tough technical problems and a lack of institutional will to fix them.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-thanksgiv.title: NYC Thanksgiving travel: Trains, buses, traffic will be busy, so get on the road now
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-thanksgiv.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-thanksgiv.text:
Before the turkey, there’s the travel.
Tuesday and Wednesday will be among the busiest travel days of the year in New York City and around the country as people head to their destinations ahead of Thanksgiving on Thursday. The AAA expects major metro areas like ours could see double the normal traffic congestion, especially in the afternoon and early evenings.
The city’s Department of Transportation has designated Tuesday, Nov. 24, a Gridlock Alert Day — one of the busiest traffic days of the year when the DOT makes real-time adjustments to traffic signals as needed. That’s when Thanksgiving travel headaches really ramp up — though it might not be quite as bumper-to-bumper as years past, said Sam Schwartz, chair of the Transportation Research Program at Roosevelt House at Hunter College.
“It's a busy traffic week. It'll be a little lighter than last year, I predict, because gas prices in New York are up by 86 cents from $3.15 a gallon average to $4.01 average,” said Schwartz, a former city traffic commissioner whose claim to fame is popularizing the term “gridlock.” But he said there will still be “plenty of traffic.”
The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade, expected to happen under rainy skies, will make things even hairier in Manhattan.
We’ve compiled information from agencies around the metro area to help you get to your destinations as smoothly as possible this week.
Thanksgiving Day Parade Road closures
Whether you’re hoping to watch the parade or avoid it, you’ll want to take note of the route if you’re traveling through Manhattan. Barriers will be going up as early as Wednesday for balloon inflation.
The parade itself heads south on Central Park West from 76th Street to Columbus Circle, loops around the circle, then goes east on 59th Street to Sixth Avenue, before turning south on Sixth Avenue to 34th Street and then turns west to end at Herald Square. Major road closures will run along the route, with adjacent streets closed for formation and dispersal zones.
For a full list of closures, check the DOT’s notice here.
Behind the wheel
If you’re not reading this from the road (presumably and hopefully as a passenger), you’re probably leaving the city too late. Schwartz said the best time to leave the city, if you’re driving, is Tuesday before 1 p.m. But you’ll get another lighter traffic window Wednesday morning, when again, “the earlier you leave the better,” according to Schwartz, with heavy traffic starting at 1 p.m. and lasting through 6 or 7 p.m.
“A number of people will try to get out early,” Schwartz said. “We are expecting a lot of traffic after 2 [p.m.], and that'll affect the Van Wyck, the Belt Parkway, the Grand Central, BQE, New Jersey Turnpike.”
Travel won’t be easy for anyone — but at least those heading to JFK will have a smoother time this year because of the recent completion of the Van Wyck Expressway, which included a new HOV lane for multi-occupant vehicles, according to Schwartz.
“Not telling you to leave too late, but there is an extra lane if you're taking a taxi cab or you if you have two or more people, so that's good news,” Schwartz said.
Things will ramp up again on Sunday as everyone heads back into the city — and again, trying to get back sooner rather than later will allow drivers to avoid the worst traffic, according to Schwartz.
In the skies
The Port Authority anticipates about 3.1 million passengers will travel through John F. Kennedy International, Newark Liberty International, LaGuardia and New York Stewart International airports during the eight-day Thanksgiving travel period from Monday, Nov. 23 through Monday, Nov. 30.
Wednesday, Sunday, and this coming Monday are projected to be the busiest travel days, according to the agency.
The numbers represent a 3% decrease from the 2025 Thanksgiving travel period, which broke previous high records at 3.3 million passengers.
Last-minute travelers whose flights depart Thursday might have the easiest time, according to Schwartz.
“I find the best time to fly is the morning of Thanksgiving, so just 12 hours will make the world of difference, between 8 o’clock in the evening on Wednesday versus 8 o’clock in the morning on Thursday,” he said.
On the subway and PATH
On Wednesday, the subway and the Staten Island Railway will operate on a regular weekday schedule, according to the MTA. On Thursday, they will operate on a Sunday schedule.
Those headed to the Upper West Side for the parade or otherwise should take note of service changes on the B and C lines on both days, because of the Macy's Balloon Inflation Celebration on Wednesday and then the parade on Thursday. Those involve some intermittent closures of the 72nd and 81st Street stations on those lines.
The MTA is asking people to consider taking the 1, 2 and 3 lines to the area. For more information, check the MTA’s advisory.
On the buses
MTA buses will also operate on a Sunday schedule on Thanksgiving Day, with many expected to experience delays, affected by reroutes, detours and frozen zones, particularly those on routes operating near the parade route in Midtown Manhattan.
Then on Friday, most buses will operate on a reduced weekday schedule, with the majority of routes running, but coming less often. Limited-stop service will not run on some routes in Manhattan and most routes in Staten Island; for more information, check the MTA’s advisory.
For regional bus travel, bus commuters may experience intermittent departure delays during weekday afternoon peak periods due to new traffic patterns in place because of the construction of the new Midtown Bus Terminal, according to the Port Authority advisory.
NJ Transit is increasing bus capacity to Newark Airport on Wednesday, and then also adding extra buses to the schedule Thursday morning and early afternoon hours for those getting to and from the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. On Friday, NJ Transit will be providing buses to shopping centers throughout New Jersey. For more information, check the NJ Transit advisory.
On the rails
The MTA is adding extra service to and from Manhattan on the Long Island Rail Road Babylon, Port Jefferson, and Ronkonkoma branches before and after the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. It’s also adding extra service to the Metro-North Railroad’s Hudson, Harlem, and New Haven lines.
On Friday, the LIRR will run on a weekday schedule, and the Metro-North will run on a Saturday schedule, and off-peak fares will be valid on both. For more information, check the MTA’s advisory.
Amtrak added two additional Northeast Regional round trips between Washington, D.C. and New York Penn Station for Nov. 24-25 and Nov. 28-29.
NJ Transit is stepping up train routes throughout the holiday weekend as well. On Wednesday, trains will operate on a weekday schedule on all lines, with the additional “early getaway” service from Penn Station, New York, Newark Penn Station and Hoboken Terminal starting at 2 p.m. on the Northeast Corridor, North Jersey Coast, Raritan Valley, Morris & Essex and Port Jervis lines. Newark Light Rail, Hudson-Bergen Light Rail and River Line Light Rail service will operate on a weekday schedule.
On Thursday, NJ Transit trains will operate on a weekend/major holiday schedule, with extra trains on the Northeast Corridor, North Jersey Coast, Raritan Valley, Morris & Essex and Port Jervis lines to accommodate people heading to the parade.
On Friday, NJ Transit trains are on an enhanced weekend/major holiday schedule on all rail lines with additional trains accommodating shoppers during the morning and afternoon peak periods on the Northeast Corridor, North Jersey Coast, Raritan Valley, Morris & Essex, Gladstone, Montclair-Boonton and Port Jervis lines.
For more information, check the NJ Transit advisory.
Oh, and one more thing …
Schwartz really wants to remind all New Yorkers that while Friday might be a work holiday for many, it isn’t a parking holiday.
“Friday is the biggest shopping day of the year, and it's also the day traffic agents write the most parking tickets because people feel like it's a holiday, and it is a holiday for many people. They're off from work, but traffic agents are not off from work, and all rules are in effect on the Friday after Thanksgiving,” he said.

https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.title: Jensen Huang's Restoration Farce
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.author: David Futrelle
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.text:
Jensen Huang’s Restoration Farce
Donald Trump leaned on Nvidia’s board to return the disgraced CEO to power, but the real scandal here is just beginning.
There is perhaps no better symbol of the elite impunity that currently infects our body politic than the meme President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social Monday celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to his position as CEO and de facto king of the chipmaker Nvidia. It’s a doctored version of the famous photo of Trump taken after the assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, blood on his face and fist in the air, except in the new, faux photo Trump has been replaced with Huang, his face similarly caked with blood, holding in his raised fist a scarlet bra, suggesting that his return to Nvidia in the wake of as many as three extremely questionable affairs was as much a triumph over sexual propriety as it was a victory over accountability. Trump, as I hardly need to remind anyone, is himself a serial cheater and adjudicated rapist in civil court who has largely escaped consequences for nearly every terrible thing he has ever done, and presumably he takes a special pride in his successful attempt to broker Huang’s return by intervening with the company’s board.
As tasteless as the meme was, it could have been worse. X is awash in awful Huang memes that Trump could have picked from, including a seemingly endless array of AI slop videos depicting a leather-clad, boorishly triumphant Huang returning to the company he cofounded, with vengeance (and dancing) on his mind. In one, he’s a smug rapper spitting bars at a terrified board; in another, he returns to work as a vigilante of sorts, splattering various employees with bursts from a paintball gun, including a woman meant to represent the Nvidia vice president he’s alleged to have slept with. Another AI video, presented from Huang’s own POV, shows him scanning a conference room packed with beautiful, busty Asian women in low-cut tops smiling suggestively at the returned patriarch.
Elsewhere on X, accolades from his tech-bro fans poured in. “GPU Jesus has risen!” declared loudmouth investor and podcast host Jason Calacanis. “Return of the King,” posted Palmer Luckey, the goateed founder and CEO of the military tech company Anduril. “It is done,” remarked Elon Musk, with relative restraint for once.
In the markets, animal spirits prevailed. Giddy investors (and rattled short-sellers closing their positions) sent Nvidia stock shooting skyward by more than 30 percent; the S&P 500 ended Monday up nearly 5 percent, recovering the value lost in the tech-led rout at the end of last week. (On Tuesday, the market opened with major losses for Nvidia, suggesting that we’re in for much more volatility than Trump and Huang foresee.) Yesterday, I read through an assortment of quotes from stock analysts and other market watchers; at times, it was a bit like studying the minutes of a cult meeting. “Overall, it brings a lot of confidence,” explained Andre Bakhos of New Jersey’s Ingenium Analytics. “As far as stocks go, it adds confidence, in the sense that the AI leader is, on the surface, at least for now, things are going to be okay, that the company is going to be okay. It just makes everyone feel a little more confident that the right guy is back.” As Pee-wee Herman might say: The day’s secret word was “confidence.” A self-described “reputation management consultant” named Eric Schiffer, who also chairs a private equity firm called, no lie, The Patriarch Organization, declared that “Jensen is bigger than Elvis for tech investors.” Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote that while Nvidia is “not out of the woods in terms of investigations, accounting investigations and political theater—no one is more focused than Jensen.” Really? Focused on what? Making sure he doesn’t schedule dates with two mistresses on the same night?
In the midst of the market’s celebration on Monday morning, a somewhat giddy Trump held court for nearly an hour in a CNBC interview, assuring the world that all was well in the house of Nvidia. Trump told CNBC’s Eamon Javers that his administration had done “a study. They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he himself was, was exonerated.” When Javers pointed out that Jensen’s gal pal Alice Huang had been “in contact” with the Chinese Ministry of State Security, Trump replied, “Well, who isn’t in contact?… I think probably China speaks to everybody.… That doesn’t make them bad. But I can tell you, the bigger threat would be losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen. That would be a threat to me.”
It’s all a bit surreal, not to mention grotesque. Some commenters rushed to conclude that Huang’s astonishing return, and the stock rally that followed, means that we’re still stuck in the “lol nothing matters [era] in American politics and technology,” as Charlie Warzel of The Atlantic put it in a newsletter yesterday. I’m not so sure. Yes, Trump has gotten away with murder for years (at first figuratively but now arguably quite literally, considering episodes like the boat strikes he’s ordered in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific and the bombing attack on an Iranian school). And Huang seems to have gotten away with multiple affairs and possibly a bit of treason. But the story isn’t over yet for either man, and what we’re seeing in the stock market and on X may mark the death throes of an era of extreme impunity rather than the depressing continuation of the lol era.
The midterms made abundantly clear that a solid majority of American voters are thoroughly sick of Trump’s bullshit—his war, his tariffs, his cruelty, his corruption, his utter obliviousness to the needs and concerns of Americans who don’t happen to be billionaires, even his goddamned ballroom. His Teflon coating is starting to look a little chewed up.
Meanwhile, there are currently at least half a dozen open investigations of Huang and Nvidia, and the heat on both will presumably rise considerably when the Democrats take control of Congress in January. Huang’s affairs aren’t the real story driving these inquiries; the company could be in serious trouble if it’s found to have been complicit in, or at least to have averted its eyes from, the smuggling of billions of dollars of prohibited chips to China. Even if literal treason isn’t on the menu, there may be accounting fraud.
And even with Huang back in charge, it’s not clear that the company will be able to continue to pump up the already partially deflated AI bubble in its role as the “central bank of AI” underpinning a vast system of circular finance that helped to gin up demand for its chips in the first place. The Nvidia scandal, which may also turn out to be very much a Trump scandal, isn’t over. It’s really just beginning.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/hake.title: Hakeem Jeffries Can Live With “Medicare for More”
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/hake.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/hake.text:
After years of being able to hide behind Republicans’ blatant mismanagement and intentional sabotage of the healthcare system, Democrats will now have to put forth their own plan to save our crumbling healthcare infrastructure. Whether the party can agree on what that plan is remains to be seen.
The middle path has been dubbed “Medicare for More.” It’s been framed variously as a first step toward Medicare for All and as a half-measure to relieve the pressure to pass the more expansive healthcare agenda. Now backed by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the presumed next speaker of the House, the policy would lower the eligibility age for the public retiree health system; expand dental, vision, and hearing care; and provide universal coverage for children.
But the plan would maintain the status quo for people ages 26 to 55 — many of whom saw their Affordable Care Act healthcare premiums spike after December 2025, when enhanced subsidies expired for an estimated 22 million people as a result of Republicans’ so-called Big, Beautiful Bill.
“We’re in the wealthiest nation on Earth, and we’re running out of excuses for why Americans don’t have universal healthcare,” Rep. Summer Lee, D-Penn., wrote in a statement to the Intercept. “The mandate from voters is change. The American people literally cannot afford to return to the status quo.”
Progressives have vowed to pass Medicare for All, a sweeping proposal to establish a national public health insurance program sponsored by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash. Backers of the full Medicare for All package argue that systemwide change is necessary — and that half-measures are not what voters asked the party to do.
Polling suggests broad support for Medicare for All, particularly among Democratic voters. A Kaiser Family Foundation poll found that 94 percent of registered Democrats support the policy — and roughly 79 percent of all adults polled favor the federal government doing more to help provide health insurance.
Despite Medicare for All’s growing popularity, Jeffries, a New York Democrat, remained skeptical of the policy throughout the midterms. In August, he told “Meet the Press” that he did not support it, emphasizing that since joining leadership he has declined to co-sponsor Medicare for All legislation.
Jayapal, who has reintroduced her signature legislation every session since 2019 and plans to do so again in the next Congress, said wins from candidates who ran on Medicare for All in this year’s midterm elections have helped to push leadership on this issue. She specifically cited the success of purple-state candidates like Sen.-elects Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, who invoked the policy again and again on the campaign trail — and won.
At a meeting of the Congressional Progressive Caucus last week, the Washington congresswoman said that Jeffries agreed to two out of three of the caucus’s requests on Medicare for All. First, he agreed to support the initial phase-in of the Medicare for All Act, which Jayapal says she has been pushing him on for “the last couple of months.” The plan would greatly expand access to healthcare for most Americans by simultaneously lowering the Medicare eligibility age and covering everyone under the age of 18.
Second, he agreed to get a Congressional Budget Office score on the full Medicare for All act. The CBO score estimates the cost of any given legislation, which gives members a chance to weigh the financial impact of a bill before casting their vote.
But Jeffries declined to support their third request: a markup of the full “Medicare for All” bill in committee. Markups allow committees to make amendments to a bill before it gets voted on in front of the full House — making it substantially easier to pass.
Still, Jayapal believes there is a path forward for her bill. She said that she has spoken with both new members and incumbents “who haven’t been on it before” and now say they want to co-sponsor the bill, and she believes that with more of the caucus’s support, Jeffries could support a bill markup in the future.
It appears that attacks on the policy have become less effective with voters over time. Private insurance companies have long supported anti-Medicare for All messaging, Jayapal pointed out.
Opponents of the public healthcare proposal argue it will create longer wait times, raise taxes, and separate people from their preferred doctors. But as the state of healthcare in the United States has degraded and become more dystopian, Jayapal said, “none of those attacks work when people are already experiencing $20,000 in premiums, when they’re already being told they can’t have care by an AI model or by a private insurance company.”
Regardless of what the public wants, and even if Democrats can agree on a vision, the mercurial commander-in-chief remains an obstacle. The Democrats’ 56-seat Senate majority is significant but not veto-proof, and President Donald Trump has previously called Medicare for All a “socialist takeover.” On Saturday, he told Fox News there’s a “chance” he would work with Democrats on healthcare — but it would not be the legislation Democrats “want.”
Jayapal says she’s not holding out much hope for collaboration.
“I don’t think much about Trump in this particular moment,” she said. “I think we just need to do the thing that we know Americans deserve and want, and then let’s send it to his desk. And if he signs it, great. And if he doesn’t, he will be the one that is not allowing Americans to have healthcare, and then we can sign it when we have the trifecta.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
