https://www.propublica.org/article/cop31.title: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
https://www.propublica.org/article/cop31.author: Katie Worth
https://www.propublica.org/article/cop31.text:
A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.
Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.
Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found.
The role of carbon capture was just one cause of discord in Turkey at the 31st annual U.N. climate summit, known as the Conference of the Parties. But it reflects a culmination of decades of effort by fossil fuel companies, and the nations most dependent on them, to slow a transition away from oil, coal and gas in part by pressing for methods like carbon capture, which theoretically allow for the use of their products and cleaning up carbon pollution at the same time.
Over the course of two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, drafts of the summit’s main political accord were stripped of language encouraging such a transition even as specific targets were added to expand carbon capture and storage, or CCS.
One draft released Nov. 16 included language encouraging a transition from fossil fuels alongside a recommendation to scale up carbon capture — where greenhouse gases are caught from industry, or filtered from the air, and injected underground — so that it removes at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide a year by 2035.
Currently, however, the carbon capture industry buries only a sliver of that amount and has struggled for three decades to meet even the lowest-end projections, leading many climate experts to conclude that it will never be a practical solution to climate change.
“The effort by bad faith petrostate actors to block any agreement at #COP31 on fossil fuel phaseout in favor of (hypothetical future) carbon capture is the best evidence yet that moral hazard FUNDAMENTALLY compromises carbon capture as a climate solution,” wrote Michael Mann, a prominent climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, in a Bluesky post Sunday.
As it stands, most CCS is used to squeeze additional oil from aging fields, so critics say setting global goals for it would lead to further subsidy of oil production, rather than limit or reduce the amount of CO2 that reaches the air.
Behind the scenes in Antalya, some 700 carbon capture lobbyists were registered as attending, up from 531 at last year’s summit in Brazil and more than the combined delegations of all 14 Pacific Small Island Developing States, according to an analysis of U.N. participant lists by the Center for International Environmental Law. Forty-five of those representatives were granted entry to closed-door negotiating sessions. The center has not completed a similar analysis of lobbyists for other technologies.
By Thursday, as formal climate talks continued, drafters had entirely stripped out mention of a transition away from fossil fuels while leaving the aggressive carbon capture benchmarks intact. When a final draft was proposed Sunday — two days after negotiations were scheduled to conclude — the CCS targets had been made less specific but remained, described as a nonbinding “gigatonne scale” goal.
The agreement — and its emphasis on CCS — “really had the fossil fuel industry’s fingerprints all over it,” said Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead for the nonprofit Oil Change International, a research and advocacy group pushing for a phaseout of fossil fuels.
A coalition of nations, including the European Union, rejected the proposal outright.
For years, tensions at the annual climate talks have tended to break down to three camps: Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states — at times with tacit U.S. support — which argue for an approach that prioritizes slow changes in the energy system in service of economic stability; the wealthy, industrialized nations, which push for an energy transition but resist measures to pay for both the transition and damages caused by warming; and the low- and middle-income nations, which will sign on to fossil fuel phaseout only if other powerful economies commit to supporting the cost of their transition.
Carbon capture remains just one part of that larger debate, which included other ways to clean up energy sources. But its weight in this year’s talks reflects long-standing efforts to tie climate action to its success, as well as a failure to enact any other meaningful agreement that would slow the rate of CO2 emissions in the first place.
For more than a year, ProPublica and Drilled have investigated the history of carbon capture and storage and the decades-long effort by oil companies to validate it in the scientific community and at the U.N. Our reporting has found that industry funding contributed to influential CCS research at universities, petrostates pressed the U.N. to validate the technology without supporting evidence and climate modelers have assumed it can work at an enormous scale, despite the technology’s troubled real-world track record.
In the closing session, a delegate from Panama explained that the country could not support the language in the final COP31 text in part because “it wagers too much” on CCS “instead of calling for deep changes.”
Vanuatu, a small island nation in the Pacific that is especially vulnerable to rising sea levels, warned that the text “risks legitimizing continued fossil fuel dependence” and that carbon capture must not become “an excuse to prolong the fossil fuel era.”
But Saudi Arabia, speaking on behalf of the 22 countries in the League of Arab States, insisted CCS was an essential part of a “package of solutions” to address climate change.
“If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important,” the Saudi delegate said, “it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions, which is what this COP was meant to represent, will be taken off the table.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Exploitation or Opportunity? The Fight Over Amazon’s New York Drivers
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte, Greg David
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The multimillion-dollar battle over a bill that would disrupt Amazon’s delivery operations in New York City and make it easier for workers to unionize reached new heights when the retail giant rolled out a stark warning to customers.
“ATTENTION: NYC Council could add up to $5 per order,” a pop-up notice on the Amazon app and website said, threatening higher costs if the City Council passes a bill that would ban the retail giant from using subcontractors to deliver packages across the five boroughs.
A bright yellow button below the message urged customers to “Make your voice heard today.”
It’s the latest escalation in the company’s more than $5 million crusade to block a bill by Councilmember Tiffany Cabán (D-Queens) that seeks to force Amazon to directly employ thousands of drivers it currently subcontracts to a constellation of independent “delivery service partners.” Cabán says her bill would make it easier for workers to organize and file wage and safety complaints against the company.
Amazon, in turn, has threatened for months that if the bill succeeds, it will be forced to move its delivery operations outside of the city and fire thousands of workers, while shuttering its delivery service partners — many of whom it describes as minority-owned small businesses.
Here’s what to know about the battle pitting Mayor Zohran Mamdani, much of the City Council and the Teamsters union against Amazon, the city’s business community, and dozens of local delivery businesses. 
What Is the Delivery Protection Act?
Depending on who you ask, the bill that’s going before the City Council is either a major step towards protecting thousands of New York delivery workers, or an overreach by labor-friendly lawmakers that will result in massive job losses and higher costs for consumers.
At its core are claims that the people delivering packages for Amazon in New York are employees in all but name, wearing Amazon uniforms, following routes set by Amazon, and adhering to Amazon policies, all while on the payrolls of small independent delivery businesses.
Proponents of the bill say that direct employment by Amazon will give workers greater protection from abrupt layoffs and better protection from, and compensation for, on-the-job injuries. Delivery owners say that the same laws and workplace rules that would apply to Amazon already apply to them.
Objections to Amazon’s arrangements echo longstanding efforts around the country by unions and progressive politicians to make the parent companies of franchise operators, like McDonald’s, responsible for their franchisees. All such efforts up to now have failed.
Conflicting Claims on Workers
The city’s position is clear.
“These workers are being exploited,” Samuel Levine, commissioner of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection said at a conference last month.
Defenders of the companies paint a very different picture.
“These are true entrepreneurs who have worked very hard to build legitimate businesses that do follow the rules and they should be allowed to continue,” said Jessica Walker, president of the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce, who is vocal in her support of the delivery companies.
The battle has pit Amazon against the City Council and the Mamdani administration, but also worker against boss. Operators of the more than 40 delivery service partners that zip across the city on trucks, bicycles and on foot say that the Council’s efforts would destroy their business, while some workers say the current model is exploitative and their jobs are already unstable.
Amazon has rejected claims that its model makes these entities little more than — as the mayor and some top aides have called them — “shell companies” that shield the online behemoth from accountability.
“These aren’t shell companies — they’re 4,500 entrepreneurs across 22 countries who’ve built real businesses, generated $75 billion in revenue, and created hundreds of thousands of jobs,” said Amazon spokesperson Steve Kelly, citing nationwide numbers.
“The vast majority are running profitable, growing operations — and profitability has improved year over year,” he said.
Small Business, Big Business
Among them is Rudy Cazares, a former Marine Corps officer who said his company, Cazar Logistics, will go out of business if the City Council gets its way.
“Delivering packages for Amazon has given opportunities for individuals like myself to be successful and provide an opportunity for individuals who wouldn’t have this opportunity if they applied to corporate America,” he said.
Owners of delivery companies say they don’t recognize the way Mamdani and proponents of the bill have portrayed them.
One owner left a job in finance to start a company that pays its drivers more than $27 an hour and offers a $5,000 tuition reimbursement. A driver for another company left FedEx because, he says, his Amazon delivery company pays better. Other workers say their companies offer chances for advancement that they can’t get in the corporate world because they lack college degrees.
“I think that small businesses have a purpose and they certainly offer a benefit for me as a person with not a huge intellectual background but a breath of lived experience,” said Shannon Lindley, a high school graduate who is general manager at a Midtown logistics hub. “I can get somewhere in this small company.”
While Amazon has threatened to shut down delivery operations in New York City should the bill pass, workers say the company already regularly yanks jobs away. In August, the Teamsters charged Amazon and 13 subcontractors with violating the state’s WARN Act by failing to give the approximately 1,300 workers at least 90 days’ notice of their impending terminations, according to a complaint filed to the state labor department.
Earlier this month, Amazon severed its contract with a Delancey Street-based subcontractor that provided same-day delivery on electric cargo bikes. Two hundred workers were laid off overnight. Notice of the impending layoff does not appear on the state’s WARN notice dashboard, in another apparent violation of state law, Streetsblog reported.
“They have these random ads, talking about ‘We care so much about Black and brown entrepreneurship’ — they just fired 200 black and brown workers in a company owned by a Black man,” one of the laid-off workers, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The City Reporter. The worker says he supports the Delivery Protection Act because it would allow workers like himself to directly hold Amazon accountable.
One expert compared Amazon’s forceful objection to the bill with Uber’s push to block a measure that raised drivers’ minimum pay rates. Just as Amazon warned of higher delivery costs, Uber said it would have to pass on fees to its passengers as well — and at one point threatened to shut down operations in New York.
“Amazon gets away with making claims that are just totally false,” said Elizabeth Pancotti, vice president of policy, advocacy and research at the Groundwork Collective, a left-leaning think tank. “Uber made the same empty threats and look at that — it is easier than ever to get an Uber ride in New York City.”
From the Trenches
Jorge Arias, who until recently worked at a Maspeth-based delivery service partner, said he and his coworkers were pulled into a meeting on the dangers of the Delivery Protection Act. He still supports the bill.
“They said if the Delivery Protection Act passes, we’re going to be like the UPS drivers: ‘They don’t have new vans, but you have new vans,’” recalled Arias. “And I’m thinking, you know, most Prime vans are broken.”
Local delivery companies say they’re providing good, flexible jobs at good wages.
Logistics veteran Christine Chen set out two years ago to take advantage of Amazon’s enormous market share. While Amazon says it costs about $30,000 to establish a delivery company, Chen put in more than $60,000 to get Highgate Logistics off the ground — money well spent, she added. She uses bikes to deliver packages in Harlem.
Staffing up for the holiday season, Chen now employs about 220 people earning $21 an hour, or $4 more than the city’s minimum wage. She offers health care, dental and vision insurance, plus a 401K match.
Devon Smith, 23, a dancer with the Alvin Ailey Dance Theater, has been working for Chen since June. He works mornings so he can attend rehearsals in the afternoon, earning about $700 for 30 hours a week.
“As artists, we work hard but it costs money to survive in the city,” he said. “Artists are terrible at jobs, but this is something we can do. It’s not the same thing every day and people interact with you — which is rare in New York City.”
The Media War
Council Speaker Julie Menin is reportedly moving to finally put the bill up to a vote on Dec. 3. The speaker, a former city consumer protection commissioner, has not taken kindly to Amazon’s tactics.
“To put out an ad that falsely claims that if you purchase something on Amazon you’re gonna get socked with a $5 fee apiece, every single time, is completely misleading and deceptive, and it does not add to the negotiation we’re trying to have,” Menin said on Thursday in response to questions from The City Reporter.
“I have made very clear from the start that we are not going to do something that will cause us to lose those jobs in New York City,” Menin said.
The Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a longstanding business group, spent $2.3 million on anti-DPA ads between September and October. Amazon bankrolled that group to the tune of $5 million in the first six months of 2026, New York Focus reported.
Meanwhile, Mayor Mamdani hasn’t been shy about using his physical and digital bully pulpit in support of the bill. On Monday, he said there was “a worker safety crisis” and that the DPA would “put in place some basic guardrails to regulate what is an expanding last-mile industry.”
Is This Going to Become Law?
The bill’s passage is still not guaranteed.
In its current version, the bill has enough supporters in the Council to ensure its passage, and Mamdani has endorsed the measure as it stands today.
But Menin is reportedly weighing changes before it is put for a vote, including a compromise that would still allow third parties to handle package deliveries so long as they are “true independent contractors,” City & State reported.

Vandaag (24/11) klagen 1.400 omwonenden het chemiebedrijf 3M in de Antwerpse haven aan na jarenlange lozing van PFAS in de bodem. https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-stall.title: I Play Rocky Is Undeniably Charming
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-stall.author: Eileen Jones
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-stall.text:
I Play Rocky Is Undeniably Charming
I Play Rocky depicts Sylvester Stallone as a battered underdog fighting all of Hollywood for his big break. It’s a crowd-pleasing myth that is built on the working-class grit of the great 1970s cinema that made Rocky possible.
I Play Rocky goes for earnest meathead sentimentality in the most shameless way, which is presumably why it’s undeniably a crowd-pleaser. It makes Song Sung Blue (2025) — another heartwarming underdog story of working-class American dreamers making good against all odds — look like the height of sophistication.
But whereas Song Sung Blue was about delightfully “Midwest nice” characters wearing sequined outfits in a Neil Diamond tribute band who find unlikely fame, I Play Rocky is the semi-fictionalized story of how Sylvester Stallone got Rocky made. The sleeper hit of 1976, Rocky was produced on a shoestring budget, spawned a zillion-dollar Hollywood franchise, and made Sylvester Stallone an overnight star. Stallone wrote the script and starred, though he was a relatively unknown actor at the time. According to I Play Rocky, it was his incredibly stubborn insistence on playing the title role that nearly torpedoed the project again and again — and that gives this movie its name.
Screenwriter Peter Gamble and director Peter Farrelly (Green Book) go for the obvious crowd-pleasing approach, making Stallone’s story virtually identical to Rocky Balboa’s, with almost no daylight between them, except that Stallone reads a lot. Rocky’s a boxer whereas Stallone’s an actor trying to break through by writing himself a good film role, but both are essentially lonely, bighearted laboring lugs given no chance in life, working bottom-of-the-barrel jobs and barely getting by, who chance upon one big flukey opportunity to prove their worth. This involves “going the distance,” putting everything they have on the line when all they have is their mental endurance and — especially — their endlessly tested, repeatedly wounded, ultimately exhausted bodies.
Such suffering becomes the keynote of Stallone’s star persona; he’s the sad-eyed hulk getting tortured and railroaded by everybody but enduring what nearly kills him and then coming back stronger in the end. Stallone’s other hit franchise, Rambo, would only intensify the cyclical martyrdom of a muscle-bound saint who slurs his words.
The Myth vs. Reality
I Play Rocky pushes Stallone’s hardships to the limit, several levels beyond what they were in real life. Luckily, newcomer Anthony Ippolito has a fairly light touch with his Stallone impersonation, making it possible to stay in your seat for two hours of melodramatized working-class striving and deep-voiced mumbling. Stallone was a struggling twentysomething actor and writer when he came up with the script for Rocky, sure, but in real life, he was not a total nobody in the entertainment industry. He was actually getting traction as an actor — you can see him in a small but notable part in a mainstream Neil Simon comedy, The Prisoner of Second Avenue (1975), which came out the year before Rocky. In it, Jack Lemmon’s character, getting steadily driven mad by the challenges of life in New York City, becomes convinced Stallone’s character is a mugger stalking him and, in an irrational rage, chases him relentlessly through Central Park. Finally, Stallone collapses and hands his wallet over to Lemmon, because he’s a perfectly innocent guy now convinced that Lemmon is a mugger.
Stallone is quite effective in the part. He also had one of the leads in The Lords of Flatbush (1974), an independent ensemble film full of rising talent like Henry Winkler and Armand Assante — not the negligible background role I Play Rocky suggests.
Plus, he wasn’t sitting on a pile of unsold scripts before he hit it big with Rocky — Stallone had already sold one, Hell’s Kitchen (later Paradise Alley), and he had agents who fought hard to keep him on as the lead. There was no conspiracy to make the low-budget production of Rocky so grueling and impossible that director John Avildsen (Jay Duplass) would be sure to fall behind, giving the studio an excuse to replace Stallone in the lead, as I Play Rocky depicts. Keep in mind that it was the 1970s, and studios had been giving young up-and-coming talent terrific early career opportunities since the late 1960s when it became clear that Hollywood business as usual wasn’t cutting it anymore.
Stallone did run miles in beat-up sneakers during the first few days of shooting Rocky, winding up with shin splints and presumably some pretty bad blisters. But there’s no evidence he had a torn tendon and a grave doctor telling him he mustn’t walk at all for several weeks or else suffer some mysterious, unstated, forever crippling consequences.
There are tidbits of cool info in Rocky, such as the experimental use of the Steadicam operated by inventor Garrett Brown. Though I Play Rocky makes it seem as if the only way to complete Rocky on its absurdly tight schedule was to shoot the entire movie using the Steadicam, which is definitely not what happened; not even close. But people making biopics never know when to stop.
The movie is angled so hard toward a naively idolizing view of Stallone and his all-or-nothing gamble, you might find yourself laughing out loud at certain points. I know I did when, during the early scenes of the Rocky shoot, Stallone starts running all out, and two formerly jaded Philadelphia crew members, tough blue-collar guys, watch him with wide eyes. “Jesus, that guy is fast,” murmurs one reverently, as if he’d just witnessed the Second Coming.
The best parts of the film are either the funny parts or the slightly edgy parts, which figures, given Peter Farrelly’s history as one of the Farrelly brothers responsible for crass and riotous comedies Dumb and Dumber (1994) and There’s Something About Mary (1998). Stephan James is energetically funny as Carl Weathers, the football player turned actor who struts into the audition to play Rocky’s prizefight opponent, a supreme Muhammad Ali–like boxer, as if Weathers himself were a master in the ring, which it turns out he definitely is not.
The tendency of actors to lie in order to get cast becomes an amiable running gag in I Play Rocky, giving Kiki Seto as Talia Shire, who’s playing Rocky’s love Adrian Pennino, a nice comic moment when she’s supposed to do the skating scene and can’t skate. Tracy Letts is also amusing as the embittered, grousing Sandy Maddox, a composite of several United Artists executives — though colorfully awful Hollywood types make for pretty easy laughs. And Matt Dillon is quite good as Stallone’s malevolent father, Frank Sr, a man who became a hairdresser to support his family but never reconciled himself to his fate and takes his bitterness out on his son.
The Understandable Nostalgia for 1970s Cinema
A nostalgia for the gritty 1970s is inevitably part of the movie’s appeal, especially when little shards of the unvarnished reality of the era stab through, such as the 1975 boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner that supposedly inspired the Rocky script. Stallone is shown watching the actual fight — which is riveting — on one of those small, chunky old TVs hanging over the bar in a local New York City dive. We get to see key moments such as when Wepner, a hulking white fighter shambling around the infinitely quicker and more formidable Ali, nevertheless manages to get in a surprise punch and knock Ali flat on his ass. Realizing he’s underestimated his opponent, Ali commences to batter Wepner relentlessly, but Wepner somehow stays on his feet into the fifteenth round before the fight is stopped and Ali wins on a TKO.
Like a lot of movies in the recession-era 1970s, Rocky was all about working-class struggle and the blind hope that some miraculous chance would allow the protagonists to escape their bleak fates or at least redeem their thwarted lives in some sort of meaningful way. A solid number of these movies were centered on sports, whether they were comedies or dramas — see the darkly hilarious hockey movie, Slap Shot (1977) as the perfect example. These narratives often played out against an all-too-realistic backdrop of government and corporate corruption in the United States, the collapse of the industrial economy, the crumbling of infrastructure, the rising of unemployment, and the general impoverishment of the American population.
I Play Rocky obviously preserves some of the lower-class misery these films emphasized, but all in the sweetening context of what we know is a success story so huge it’s like a fairy tale. The most dangerous edge of 1970s films, so many of which were remarkably grim and unsparing, has all been softened and planed away by a lot of hokum and an avoidance of the more harrowing aspects of Rocky. There’s no depiction, for example, of Rocky’s brutal beating in the ring at the hands of Apollo Creed as he loses the fight, or his raw screams for Adrian at the climactic moment of the film. This is notable because, in I Play Rocky, there’s a whole subplot featuring director John Avildsen’s old-pro wisdom about the one memorably emotional scene in a film that can make it a success even if the rest of the movie isn’t so hot, and his urgent advice to Stallone to dig deep and do the best acting of his life in such a scene. It turns out not to be the “Adrian!” scene you might be expecting.
The Biopics Won’t End
I Play Rocky is a bit like another recent hit biopic, Michael, which also focuses, even more worshipfully, on the early life of a hugely successful star — in that case, Michael Jackson. As with the Sylvester Stallone story, the all-purpose villain of the piece that both scars and motivates Michael Jackson is his abusive father. And both films end at the point before the star’s life becomes darkly messy and very hard to sanctify.
Consider what any sequels to I Play Rocky would potentially have to deal with. Ten years after Rocky made him a star, Stallone is divorced from his wife Sasha Czack, who’s played by AnnaSophia Robb in I Play Rocky and represents his stalwart true love and devoted wife and mother of his first child.
In 1985, not long after the divorce from Sasha, Stallone swiftly married model and actor Brigitte Nielsen, who played a role in Rocky IV (1985), written and directed by Stallone. The couple’s short union and ugly divorce began an extended roiling period of Stallone’s personal life that made him a favorite of the tabloid press. His tangled involvements with various models — Janice Dickinson, Angie Everhart, and Jennifer Flavin, whom he married in 1997 — kept supermarket aisle readers entertained for years. Various unsavory accusations of physical and sexual abuse against Stallone by romantic partners that allegedly occurred from the mid-1980s through 2000, including allegations by his own half sister, have kept his lawyers busy through the years. (Stallone denied, and continues to deny, all of the allegations.)
As for all the inspirational bonding between Stallone and the tough but ultimately mensch-like producers of Rocky, Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff (played by P. J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell in I Play Rocky), Stallone’s hatred of Winkler has long been on the record, though he claims to have loved Chartoff. At various points over the years of the franchise, Stallone has called out the elderly Winkler in the media as “remarkably untalented and parasitical,” and accused Winkler’s “moronic vulture children,” Charles and David, of “picking clean the bones” of the Rocky franchise.
This feud is based on the original contract that gave the producers an equity stake in a potential franchise but deprived Stallone of one, though he continues to reap other forms of profit from Rocky movies and, of course, is very, very rich. Still, he could always be a bit richer, and it’s a fair enough point — Hollywood contracts are notoriously cutthroat. In I Play Rocky, Stallone doesn’t even read the contract before signing it, much less get a lawyer or agent to look it over.
But in I Play Rocky, Winkler and Chartoff go from tough, dismissive Hollywood producers to schmaltzy, huggable slobs, and the film ends with everyone beaming over their shared success. That’s a recognizable emotional trajectory of filmmaking — lots of temporary sentimentalists in the film business giving bear hugs right before the shiv goes in — and it should be noted that both producers really did put up their houses as collateral in order to get studio funding for Rocky. But there’s no indication of the sharp dealing going on or Stallone’s vengeful fury to come.
In short, I Play Rocky takes a slightly unusual approach to the biopic — focusing just on the story of Sylvester Stallone getting Rocky made and becoming a star — but otherwise it’s completely typical of the genre. That’s not a compliment, but it hardly matters; audiences love biopics regardless. It’s a shame the biopic isn’t formally classified as a subgenre of fantasy. That would clear up a lot about how these films get made.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Film anything in NYC and people will watch it. Even if it's boring.
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Monica Melton
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
As I arrived at Samuel Donner’s brightly decorated Manhattan apartment, I was greeted with a warm hug. Books like “Meet Cutes” and “Dear New York” adorned a glass coffee table, and a sea otter plushie nestled among throw pillows brought home the hygge feel. I was over for lunch; I’d asked him to cook for a change.
Donner, who is from Los Angeles but moved to New York a year-and-a-half ago, hosts “Cook With Me,” a social media series where the premise is to document strangers cooking him a meal — and sharing their life stories — in exchange for $100. The number is a significant one for Donner, 29, who had an earlier series where he attempted to get 100 strangers — mostly around the UCLA campus where Donner studied mechanical engineering — to become his friends. The series culminated with everyone who said “yes” having a large picnic in a park.
As he prepared us an herbaceous and tomatoey shakshuka, he explained that the goal of "Cook With Me" is to “show the shared humanity of every person.”
On the show, Donner approaches strangers on the street and asks them to make him a meal and share their life story with him. In one short video with 49 million views on YouTube, he approached a young woman with his go-to line, “Would you cook for me, for $100?” while flashing cash. She accepts, and later, when back at her apartment, we learn she’s a nurse named Mary whose family immigrated from Italy to New York. She says she keeps her grandmother’s memory alive through recipes and spoon-feeds Donner some pesto.
In another video, as he approaches a woman on the street, her daughter recognizes Donner. Back at her home, the Puerto Rican mother of five makes meaty, Sazon-laced quesadillas and shares the story of how she came to live in New York, after her mother went into labor with her shortly after traveling to the city. The video, which was sponsored by plant-based meal manufacturer Daily Harvest, ends with Donner presenting the cash as usual, except it’s $1,000, which is met with shrieks of excitement.
Social media videos dedicated to the particularities of New Yorkers’ lives have struck a chord with online audiences (and subsequently with brands eager to engage this audience). Videos of people doing things that usually elicit yawns are suddenly interesting because of where they’re set and who they feature: New York and New Yorkers. The videos become a sampling of the kinds of people and experiences found here.
"New York is one of the densest cities in America,” Donner said. ”When you have that density with that level of diversity, the random person you approach on the street ends up being extremely interesting.”
As if to up the ante on New Yorkers’ watchability, another NYC-based social media show casts its characters in the dullest situations.
The “Errands” show — with about 200,000 Instagram followers as of November — follows (sometimes famous) locals running – as the name suggests –errands. The city has a plethora of world-class cultural activities, art and entertainment, yet for most New Yorkers, simple things like doing laundry require schlepping to a coin-operated laundromat, or moving awkward furniture through the subway because you don’t have a car. Why not gawk at New Yorkers taking care of dumb little things on their to-do list? In one episode, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Curtis Silwa, wearing his signature red beret, are seen making their way into an NYC clinic, where, along the way, Mamdani stops to pose with medical staff who ask for pictures. As a needle jabs his arm, he jokes that he won’t be sore after his flu shot since he doesn’t have much muscle.
Meanwhile, a whole host of influencers use the typical man-on-the-street interview style to ask passersby the perennial “How much do you make?” question to get at what it takes to survive in one of the country’s most expensive cities. Influencer Caleb Simpson gets apartment tours from strangers, showcasing brownstones and walkups alike.
But as popular as this content is, who is watching? City dwellers who want to see their existence and experiences reflected? Or faraway lurkers who want to live vicariously in NYC — or dunk on it? The popularity of these videos could reflect the current iteration of a shift in media.
“In the 2010s it was extremely distasteful to be an influencer in New York. They were sort of seen as extremely gauche,” said Ryan Broderick, founder of internet culture publication Garbage Day. He says NYC influencers were initially met with suspicion but that this began to change with the “professionalization” of platforms like TikTok and Instagram.
Influencers following ad dollars, coupled with the familiarity and recognition that New York City evokes in viewers, set the stage, even for the most monotonous content. People like to see New York on screens, and it follows that people who used to watch the city on TV and film would migrate to phones.
“ New York also is more of a character, a presence in these videos because New York is famous,” Broderick said. “You're not really seeing the same thing in, like, Cleveland or D.C. or whatever.” New York City, as both the perfect backdrop and a character in this less polished content, lets this genre flourish. Donner says his show has garnered 1 billion views in the past year across platforms.
Amid our chatting, I cautioned Donner to turn down the burner. Though his show is centered around the kitchen, Donner himself seemed unaccustomed to cooking. He eventually plated the eggs, heaping the whole half dozen onto a plate, then took down another to plate one for me. He centered the stiff egg and its tomatoey stew on the plate before wiping the rim clean. From a plastic clamshell of herbs, he tore off a few parsley leaves to top off the eggs; the pop of green would make for a nicer photo. Naturally, he took out his phone to snap a picture of his creation before handing me a fork.
“The kind of people that watch the videos, I think, initially might watch for the food. That's like the gateway, but it's really not about the food,” said Donner. “And it's really not even about the apartment. It's more about the person, right? It's like these are just windows into the soul.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Munch museum appoints Thorsten Sadowsky as new director
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexander Morrison
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Munch museum in Oslo, dedicated to the work of the Modernist artist Edvard Munch, has appointed Thorsten Sadowsky to be its next director. Sadowsky, who joins Munch from Stiftung Schleswig-Holsteinische Landesmuseen Schloss Gottorf (Schleswig-Holstein State Museums Foundation Schloss Gottorf) in northern Germany, will begin his new role on 1 May 2027.
Sadowsky arrives with experience leading several prominent European institutions. His current position involves the management of multiple museums in the Schleswig-Holstein area, including the Museum of Art and Cultural History Schloss Gottorf and the Jewish Museum Rendsburg. Previously he has also directed the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, Museum Kunst der Westküste in Alkersum and the Kirchner Museum Davos, which is focused on the life and career of the German Expressionist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner.
“My experience at the Kirchner Museum Davos has taught me that the distinctive strength of a museum dedicated to a single artist can also be its greatest challenge,” Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper. “Such a museum offers an exceptional opportunity to engage with an artist’s oeuvre with a degree of intensity and depth that is rarely possible in an art museum with a more broadly based collection. The challenge, however, is to ensure that the focus on a single artist does not lead to intellectual or curatorial narrowness.”
Sadowsky adds that his task is therefore “to continually open up new perspectives, reveal unexpected connections and bring the artist’s work into dialogue with other artistic practices, historical experiences and contemporary concerns”.
The Munch museum, which opened in a sprawling new home on Oslo’s Bjørvika waterfront in 2021, houses nearly 27,000 works of art by Munch. Alongside its permanent displays, the museum hosts a temporary exhibition programme that has brought Munch’s work into dialogue with that of contemporary artists such as Tracey Emin, Katherina Grosse and Alice Neel, as well as events such as concerts and conferences. It has welcome more than 700,000 visitors so far this year, according to a release.
Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper that he first encountered Munch’s work at the Hamburger Kunsthaller, while he was a university student. The opportunity to direct the museum, he says, is exciting thanks to "the extraordinary richness of [Munch’s] artistic legacy. Beyond the familiar image of Munch as a painter of anxiety, loneliness and existential uncertainty, there is still much to discover. His work speaks equally of vitality, human relationships, our experience of nature and the social transformations of modernity.“
“Few artists have succeeded so convincingly in transforming individual experiences into images of universal human significance,” he adds. “In the realm of sculpture, Alberto Giacometti is another artist who achieved something similar.”
In his previous role as director of the Museum der Modern Salzburg, Sadowsky spoke about the importance of widening the scope of the programme and collection. He told the Austrian art magazine Parnass in 2022: “During my tenure as director, a major focus has been on broadening our perspective beyond the Western European canon and incorporating more postcolonial viewpoints.”
In his new role, Sadowsky says his immediate priority will be to “listen, to learn and to develop and deeper understanding“ of the institution and its people. “Over the coming years, I would like to further strengthen the Munch Museum as the world’s foremost centre of expertise on Edvard Munch, while continuing to develop it as an internationally minded, intellectually vibrant and socially relevant cultural institution,” he adds.
The Munch museum is owned by the city of Oslo. Mehmet Kaan Inan, Oslo’s vice mayor for culture and business development, says in a statement: “I am delighted that Munch [museum] will be led by a director with such strong international experience and outstanding expertise in the arts. Sadowsky has headed several highly respected art museums and has demonstrated a strong talent for audience development, collaboration, and engaging broad and diverse audiences. His exceptional interest in Edvard Munch’s artistic legacy also provides an excellent foundation for leading Munch [museum] into the future.”
Sadowsky takes over from Henrik Svalheim, who has served as interim director since Tone Hansen departed in October. Hansen left to lead Moderna Museet in Stockholm.
The Munch museum directorship runs as a six-year term, with the potential for one renewal.

https://www.propublica.org/article/ambet.title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
https://www.propublica.org/article/ambet.author: Max Blau, Brandon Roberts
https://www.propublica.org/article/ambet.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Delayed and Denied: Ambetter, the Affordable Care Act marketplace’s most popular health plan, has among the worst track records of rejecting prior authorization requests, our analysis found.
- Paying the Price: Customers said the consequences of Ambetter’s prior authorization denials have resulted in delayed tests and postponed treatments.
- More Scrutiny Needed: Four former insurance commissioners who reviewed our findings said Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that current regulators should examine further.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.
In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.
A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.
Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”
“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.
A veteran health insurance executive who had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, Counihan conceded on the call that Felicia’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” But he assured her that “we really want to get you what you” and your doctor “think is the most appropriate medication for you.”
“I’m working on it as fast as possible,” said Counihan.
Counihan’s call was a rare acknowledgment from the company’s top brass of a pervasive problem. Ambetter, the most popular plan on the ACA marketplace, has one of the worst track records of delaying or denying medical coverage by refusing to cover the costs.
ProPublica has found that Ambetter last year denied these kinds of requests — known as prior authorization — at a higher rate than any other large insurer on the ACA marketplace. Our analysis of Ambetter’s own data, along with interviews with more than two dozen recent customers, sheds new light on the vast and sometimes illogical nature of how the company can block access to care.
Our analysis is based on data that federal regulators required marketplace plans to report and publish for the first time this year. The requirement is intended to offer greater transparency into how often insurers restrict care by denying prior authorization for treatment.
Since the ACA marketplace launched in 2013, there has been little transparency around how often insurers request — and deny — prior authorization. Insurers use prior authorization to limit spending on treatment, equipment and prescriptions. They say it is also intended to ensure that doctors try less expensive and less invasive treatments before pricier ones. Health insurance experts said that the process of how or when prior authorization gets used is largely a black box.
U.S. Rep. Craig Goldman, a Republican from Texas, sponsored a bipartisan bill that would require marketplace plans to disclose more information about their use of prior authorization. “These companies represent these individuals — and yet denying them coverage and not being transparent with what they will be able to cover,” he said. “They’re just not there for the best interest of the people.”
Four former heads of state insurance departments who reviewed ProPublica’s findings said that Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that current regulators should examine further.
“This is stunning — and not in a good way,” Mila Kofman, a former insurance superintendent in Maine who now oversees the District of Columbia’s ACA marketplace, said of Ambetter’s denial rate. “This is something insurance regulators need to understand. There’s a huge opportunity for regulators to address the improper use of prior authorization.”
We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your Health Insurance Denial.
ProPublica is looking into the ways health insurers’ use of prior authorization impacts patients. We need your help to figure out if the process is still leading to delayed or missed treatments, tests, medical equipment or medication.
Sarah London, CEO of Ambetter’s parent company, Centene, recently said in a statement on its website that it was “creating a more predictable and transparent experience” for its customers. That statement followed growing backlash against the industry and a push to limit the practice of prior authorization.
Last year Centene joined America’s largest insurers in vowing to rely on prior authorization less often. Industry representatives have said that the collective efforts of those insurers will decrease their use of prior authorization across all of their plans by 11% in 2026. (Health plans aren’t required to publish 2026 data until next year.)
ProPublica sent Centene a detailed list of questions about its use of prior authorization and the impact it has on its customers. ProPublica also provided Ambetter with signed releases from customers, including Felicia, waiving their right to privacy, so that Centene representatives could speak with ProPublica about their specific denials. Centene didn’t respond to ProPublica’s questions. In a statement, a spokesperson for the company said that Ambetter is “committed to help ensure patients receive safe, appropriate, evidence-based care, and we continue to work to simplify the prior authorization process and reduce administrative burden for members and providers.”
Reached by phone, Counihan told ProPublica that he retired this year and declined to comment due to “contractual commitments” with the company that prevent him from doing so.
Listen to Ambetter’s Then-CEO
Kevin Counihan tells a customer he can’t approve coverage of the treatment her doctor sought.
For some Ambetter customers, the consequences of prior authorization denials were particularly stark, leading to delayed tests and disrupted treatments. A small fraction of those customers got Ambetter to cover their care after complaining to powerful politicians. One Ambetter customer who was denied routine bloodwork complained to a state agency. Another who had been denied cancer treatment asked a U.S. senator for help.
Even though Felicia’s complaint made it all the way up to powerful politicians — and she had pressed Centene’s C-suite to get in touch — she was disheartened by what Counihan ultimately would have to say.
Felicia had lost track of all the hours spent on curbing her weight, going so far as to try three different anti-obesity medications. During the follow-up call, Counihan explained that didn’t actually have the authority to help with the fourth.
“Do what you need to do,” Counihan responded. “Escalate it in any way that you can.”
This spring, as Richie Jones recovered from having his tumor-filled prostate removed, he received some troubling news. The cancer was still in his body.
The 49-year-old drummer from Atlanta’s suburbs was willing to do anything to get more time with his wife and daughter. His oncologist said the best option was to shoot a pencil-sized beam of protons at the cancer that remained, zapping it out of existence. That kind of therapy can cost far more than standard radiation but inflicts far less damage to the rest of the body.
First, though, his oncologist had to confirm that Ambetter would cover proton therapy. He asked the insurer to approve it in advance, as it required. Ambetter denied the request based on a recommendation from an oncologist working with the insurer.
Insurers have varying policies on whether to cover proton therapy for patients with prostate cancer. In recent years, insurance researchers have found that patients with commercial plans who are facing a denial for proton therapy for a variety of cancers have a good shot of getting it overturned on appeal.
Jones’ oncologist appealed. That, too, was denied. Ambetter explained its decision in a letter to Jones, claiming he did “not have a type of cancer this treatment is used for.”
What angered Jones most was that there was a different doctor advising Ambetter on the denial of the appeal, and that doctor didn’t specialize in proton therapy, let alone cancer. It was an OB-GYN.
Fearful that his cancer would spread more, Jones emailed Ambetter’s support department, hoping to break through to whatever human was on the other end. “You have the power to allow my child to have her daddy around for years to come,” he wrote.
When people actually fight prior authorization denials, they have a good shot at winning. ProPublica’s analysis found that more than half of Ambetter customers who contested their denials had them overturned. But the vast majority of the time, denials go uncontested. Only 7% of prior authorization denials by Ambetter were challenged last year, the analysis found.
Marketplace plan holders told ProPublica that they didn’t appeal because they didn’t know about their rights or how to navigate the process. Insurance experts and advocates say that patience and persistence are required to fight a denial.
Ambetter Customers Have a Good Shot at Overturning Their Denials. Few of Them Try.
Most prior authorization denials are never appealed. More often than not, Ambetter customers who appeal get approved after going through a complex process.
On the other side of metro Atlanta from Jones, 48-year-old artist Travis Christopher was trying to get treatment for his liver cancer last year. After getting so sick that he left his job — and lost the insurance that came with it — he bought an Ambetter plan on the marketplace.
It covered a specialized treatment by his oncologist, who placed a wire of irradiated beads in his liver to precisely target his tumor. But to know if the radiation worked, his oncologist needed CT scans.
Ambetter denied three different requests for prior authorization for the scans. After a month of delays, Christopher complained to his state senator, saying that he was “stuck waiting until Ambetter decides whether or not I live or die.” The state senator passed it along to Georgia’s insurance commissioner. Soon after, Ambetter overturned the denial and agreed to cover the care.
Every day of delay can increase the odds that cancer spreads. No one can say how much the wait affected Christopher’s prognosis. What is certain is that Christopher’s health got worse in the months ahead. He died this past winter, shortly after his daughter was born.
Jones was able to get care in time. Like Christopher, he worked to draw attention to Ambetter’s denial. He contacted local journalists, wrote to the office of the U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, and filed a complaint with Georgia’s insurance commissioner. In late June, after getting in touch with staffers in both officials’ offices, Jones received a call from Emory Healthcare: Their oncologists were ready to start.
Ambetter had decided to reverse its denial.
Over the course of his nearly 40 rounds of proton therapy, Jones realized that he wanted others to know the importance of fighting back. So he granted permission to Ossoff to publish what had happened in a report on prior authorization denials. In a statement to ProPublica, Ossoff said that he has “heard from too many Georgians who get a cancer diagnosis, and then instead of being free to fight their cancer, they have to fight their insurance company.”
“We need to ban health insurance companies from denying or delaying needed health care,” Ossoff said in the statement.
Several months later, Jones stood in the lobby of Emory’s cancer center. Surrounded by his family and friends, he rang a ceremonial bell hanging on the wall, marking the end of his treatment.
It was only after he was in remission that Jones would begin to see just how much his complaint had mattered.
With Jones’ permission, ProPublica obtained records this month that shed light on why Ambetter changed its decision about the proton therapy. The records include a letter Ambetter sent to Georgia’s insurance commissioner’s office that explained the rationale for each of its denials. In the letter, the insurer wrote that it had decided, two days after Jones filed his complaint, to consult clinical guidelines used by America’s leading oncologists in determining how to proceed with covering his treatment. Ambetter previously had relied on a more restrictive guideline from a contractor that handles its prior authorization requests for cancer treatment.
“Why wasn’t that their guideline in the first place?” Jones said. “Why does it take being a squeaky wheel to have them change their mind?”
In June 2025, following a meeting with U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Centene and other large insurers promised to reduce the volume of medical services subject to prior authorization. Centene has since touted “measurable progress” toward fulfilling that promise. The company didn’t answer ProPublica’s questions about whether Ambetter’s prior authorization use has gone down this year.
But insurance experts, consumer advocates and lawmakers question how far those promises go.
Wendell Potter, a former Cigna executive turned consumer advocate, recently wrote that these commitments rely on “an impressive-sounding number to mislead.” For instance, he said that UnitedHealthcare promised a 30% drop in prior authorization requirements, but only 2% of covered medical services are eligible for the more relaxed requirements. (UnitedHealthcare spokesperson Eric Hausman told ProPublica that the insurer has been “transparent” about its efforts to reduce the use of prior authorization and has already enacted some of them.)
Brit Vanneman, a staff attorney for the National Health Law Program, wrote that these commitments “may simply be a strategic attempt to deflect growing public criticism” regarding prior authorization.
“The commitments are vague,” Vanneman told ProPublica. “There’s a lot of fluff.”
What isn’t vague: the continued impact of prior authorization denials since the industry’s pledge.
Two women got their denials overturned by Ambetter only after posting about them on social media. One, a Florida mother, told ProPublica she bought an Ambetter plan because her previous insurer stopped covering autism therapy for her 6-year-old son. The Ambetter plan she chose had covered other children seen by the providers who’d treated her son for the past two years. But Ambetter denied the request for his treatment this year, and her son’s care was put on pause.
The other, a Kansas woman, said Ambetter denied a drug infusion to treat her Crohn’s disease last year. She said this was shocking to her, since for the previous two years Ambetter had covered the infusion, which worked better for her than anything else she tried.
Both women’s social media posts prompted Ambetter reps to reach out to them directly, saying they wanted to address their problems. And indeed, the ordered treatments were provided.
Felicia wasn’t as fortunate. After Ambetter’s CEO expressed sympathy and encouraged her to fight for her obesity treatment, she moved forward with the final step in the process: asking an independent company to review her appeal.
At that point, Felicia had spent two years on three different weight-loss drugs that were covered by Ambetter, including the popular GLP-1 drug Ozempic. But those drugs had caused side effects, such as insomnia and migraines. When she was prescribed samples of tirzepatide, another GLP-1, by her doctor in 2023, everything finally clicked: She lost a significant amount of weight over two months without any side effects.
But Ambetter was not willing to cover Zepbound, the tirzepatide her doctor prescribed.
As a way to keep costs down, health insurers tend to deny requests for GLP-1s not listed on their formularies. When that happens, a customer can appeal and seek a formulary exception.
In September 2024, she asked her endocrinologist to support her appeal. He explained in a letter that a denial of this particular GLP-1 “could significantly hinder her progress and potentially lead to worsening of her condition, which could result in more intensive and costly interventions in the future.” As he saw it, this GLP-1 was “the most appropriate and potentially life-saving medication,” especially given Felicia’s other overlapping medical conditions.
But that November, the company overseeing the independent review declined to consider her appeal, writing that an appeal involving a medication that wasn’t on a health plan’s approved drug list was “outside of our scope of review.” In other words, Felicia had hit a dead end.
Felicia has continued struggling with obesity ever since the Zepbound denial. She’s also experienced worsening symptoms for several other chronic conditions, including persistent migraines. Felicia said she has nine each month on average, and medical experts say that obesity is a strong risk factor for migraines. But Ambetter has denied prior authorization for numerous migraine medications prescribed by her doctors.
Ambetter is the only insurance Felicia had ever bought. By this fall, she had become so fed up with the denials that she contacted an insurance broker to help her find another marketplace plan during open enrollment. But the quotes she received for various plans were either much higher than Ambetter’s or didn’t provide access to her doctors. If she wanted to clear the hurdles she’d faced, the cost would be far more than she could possibly afford.
It left her with a sinking feeling: Ambetter might be her only viable option.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-netany.title: The US-Israel Relationship Is Shifting. Not Nearly Enough.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-netany.author: Gilbert Achcar
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-netany.text:
The US-Israel Relationship Is Shifting. Not Nearly Enough.
Benjamin Netanyahu says the end of US military aid to Israel marks a move “from dependency to an alliance of equals.” But ending military aid won’t stop the arms pipeline between Israel and Washington.
On November 3, the very day of the midterm congressional elections, Donald Trump announced that the United States would cease its annual military aid to Israel at the end of this year. That aid, amounting to $3.8 billion annually, was provided under an agreement signed by the Obama administration in 2016, covering the ten years from 2019 through 2028. Trump cannot end it on his own — the money is appropriated by Congress — but the announcement was no surprise: it had been signaled before, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, now leading a caretaker government after Israel’s October election, said he was fine with it (or pretended to be), arguing that the Zionist state no longer needs this money and is perfectly capable of purchasing US weapons at its own expense.
The truth is that US military aid to Israel, as to other countries — regional states like Egypt and Jordan in particular — consists essentially of funding those governments’ purchase of US weaponry. In other words, it is an old and familiar method of using American taxpayers’ money to fund and enrich the military-industrial complex, one of the largest sectors of American capitalism.
The regular annual aid to Israel, moreover, is only a floor: Washington readily raises the amount when circumstances call for it. A report published last year found that the United States provided Israel with $21.7 billion in military aid during the first two years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, under the Biden and then the Trump administrations. That is but one measure of Washington’s full complicity in the genocide.
Still, the talk of ending the annual aid is significant, particularly given the timing. Everyone understood that, by making the announcement on Election Day, the president was attempting to mitigate the considerable damage done to his party by his enthusiastic support for Israel and his constant praise of Netanyahu at a time when the war on Gaza has shifted American public opinion, which is outraged at the spectacle of Israeli cruelty toward the Palestinians.
A Public That Has Turned
A Washington Post–Ipsos poll conducted last July revealed that 55 percent of the public now considers US military aid to Israel excessive, including 29 percent who support ending it completely, while 26 percent wish to see it reduced. According to another poll conducted last September, the proportion of those favorable to Israel in US public opinion has plummeted to 29 percent, its lowest level to date, while 59 percent declare holding an unfavorable view. And another recent poll, published last July, shows that 58 percent of young Americans under thirty (including 72 percent of young Democrats) sympathize with the Palestinian people nowadays, compared to 32 percent who sympathize with their Israeli oppressor.
These figures make inevitable a shift in the relationship between the Zionist state and its US godfather. The question is, what will be the nature of this shift? Netanyahu has boasted that the end of the funding marks a transition from dependency to an alliance of equals. The truth is that Israel would benefit from reducing its dependence on Washington, freeing itself as much as possible from the looming prospect of US pressure. That concern is all the more pressing for Israel given the shift in American public opinion and the Republicans’ debacle in the midterms, which cost them control of both houses of Congress.
One should not, however, be overly optimistic about the future of the relationship. The share of leftists among congressional Democrats has grown to an unprecedented degree, but the Democratic majority does not share their principled position: refusing to supply the Zionist state with US weapons at all, even at its own expense — or at least restricting the kind of weapons supplied and imposing strict conditions on their use, on Israel’s conduct in the Palestinian territories occupied in 1967 and, more generally, on its aggressive and expansionist regional policies.
The Liberal Zionist Ceiling
A glimpse of where the Democratic majority’s position on Israel might be heading, should current trends continue, is offered by a policy agenda that J Street, the liberal Zionist lobby, published this November. Founded in 2008 as a rival to the much older, right-wing American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), whose origins date to 1954, J Street has gained significant influence at its rival’s expense over the past two years. Its proposal calls for treating Israel like any other wealthy ally — selling it weapons rather than subsidizing them. It still supports supplying Israel with defensive missiles like the Iron Dome, the product of cooperation between the US and Israeli military-industrial complexes, a collaboration J Street sees no problem with — so long as Israel pays.
As for the political conditions J Street would impose on the Israeli government, they include support for “elements” of the Gaza “peace plan” that the Trump administration produced last year — with an emphasis on disarming Hamas on the one hand and freezing the expansion of Zionist settlements in the West Bank on the other. The document also calls on Israel to commit to the prospect of a “State of Palestine” alongside it. That has nominally been Washington’s policy for years, including Trump’s: the plan drafted by Jared Kushner and unveiled by the president in January 2020, the final year of his first term, in Netanyahu’s presence and to his effusive praise.
Pressure From Below
Of course, even a shift in US policy in such a direction, should it occur, would have a beneficial impact despite its obvious limitations. But US foreign policy is primarily managed by the president, meaning that Trump will continue to shape it for the remaining two years of his term. Left-wing pressure for a radical change in US policy toward Israel must continue and grow, in public opinion and in Congress, building on the ongoing momentum — to stop the United States from arming Israel and to force a fundamental change in its treatment of the Palestinian people.
Deepening the shift in US policy toward Israel is a prerequisite for a change among Israeli Jews, and reversing the drift to the far right that has dominated their society since the turn of the century and accelerated dangerously after the Hamas-led operation of October 7, 2023. Without that change, there can be no relief for the Palestinian people from the unbearable suffering inflicted on them and no real prospect of their achieving their fundamental, inalienable right to self-determination — without which no durable peace is possible in the Middle East.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Charlotte Jansen
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour.
It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something.
The works here also bring out the insouciance and humour in Sory’s portraits. In a wall of selected studio photographs, reprinted from negatives in his archive, the poses are sometimes gloriously over the top: fingers pointing skywards, a fake phone held to the ear, an imitation of Grandmaster Flash. It’s all about the mash-ups: a girl in a traditional pagne paired with Nike Air Slants. Sory seems to encourage his subjects to take their fantasy roles as far as they can – the bolder, the better. Driving a motorbike into the studio? No problem. One man is almost transformed into a sculpture, draped in ceremonial, traditional and western fabrics, a religious portrait held tightly to his chest and one clenched fist raised. But Sory can be understated, too: a young man in a leather-shoe shop in the market, one leg kicked out to the side as he holds up one of the shop’s models.
It’s thought that Sory has taken more than one million portraits; at Volta Studio’s peak, 250 people would come to be photographed every day. In the 1970s, Sory had his subjects stand against specially commissioned painted backdrops – an Ivory Coast beach setting, an aircraft boarding bridge, a generic north American city – familiar but fantastical, for his clients to project themselves into. A few of those examples are included here, in black and white, too. In the colour studio portraits here, the backdrops are replaced with a simple brown curtain, and prismatic patterned rugs, shifting the focus back to the people in front of the camera, to the here and now. If they wanted, Sory loaned his clients clothes or props; but what he couldn’t give them is the attitude. In a vitrine in the back room, there’s a small collection of original prints given to clients who came to the studio – their album-size scale totally changes the picture, and reminds you of the purpose of these keepsakes: private souvenirs for personal histories, loved ones. Enlarged and displayed on the gallery walls, they become something else – something that reaches beyond the individual.
At night, the buzz of the studio blurred seamlessly into long nights on the dancefloor. As well as creating record sleeves for groups such as Dafra Star, Orchestre Volta Jazz, and Echo Del Africa, Sory was also an organiser of DIY raves around Bobo-Dioulasso, known as bals poussières (dust balls). As he recounts in his 2017 book, Sanlé Sory: Volta Photo 1965-85: “I would drive down to some remote village in the bush and set up a player, a few records, some loudspeakers and a few lights and get the party going. We started around 8pm and people would tell me, ‘Sory, you need to set the place on fire!’ It would go on until 5am.” Of course, the party became a Sory photoshoot, too. Like Malian master Malick Sidibé or Ivorian photographer Paul Kodjo, Sory was attracted to photographing people when they were at their loosest and most free. Liberation looks like people dancing. Sory photographed like a jazz musician, improvising, feeling, riffing off the energy in the room.
The move to colour, which began in the 1980s, amplifies every compositional and stylistic element of Sory’s portraits. It brings yet more life, if that were possible, to pictures already bursting at the seams. This was also the iconic era of Thomas Sankara in Burkina Faso: the revolutionary, Marxist and pan-Africanist, who was also a jazz musician, came to power in 1983 before being assassinated in a coup led by his former comrade Blaise Compaoré. Sory’s images of this period seem to embody Sankara’s messages of pride, self-reliance, courage and non-conformity. You can hear the echoes of Sankara’s famous slogan: “La patrie ou la mort, nous vaincrons!” (Homeland or death, we will overcome!)
The biggest problem with this exhibition, really, is its size. It offers a tantalisingly small taste of the six-decade long Sory story. Around 20,000 negatives survive, as Sory had begun burning parts of his archive when he was rediscovered in 2011. A slideshow projection running in the back room attempts to give more of a sense of its scale, but it is no substitute for spending time with the photographs themselves. The colour pictures offer an entirely fresh perspective on this exuberant, intoxicating body of work. But you leave wanting more.

https://hellgatenyc.com/creative-courts/.title: New Yorkers Get to Play Pick Up Basketball on an A$AP Ferg Artwork
https://hellgatenyc.com/creative-courts/.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/creative-courts/.text:
A special mini-episode of the Hell Gate podcast dropped yesterday. Make sure you never miss an episode by subscribing here or wherever you get your podcasts, or by tuning into our YouTube channel.
In this particularly basketball-forward era of New York's history, it's a shame for everyday New Yorkers to have to play on busted-up, dilapidated, and depressing courts. So, for the past 10 years, the City's Parks Department has revitalized local basketball courts and other recreational spaces with murals, from Pan-African flags to a rather sus-looking Bugs Bunny. On Thursday in Hell's Kitchen, the Parks Department unveiled its 58th mural, a bright color-blocked design inspired by Canadian Mexican painter Arnold Belkin, who painted an anti-gentrification mural in the park in the '70s.
Parks launched the first of its "Creative Courts" project in Sara D. Roosevelt Park a decade ago, with an Elmo-based mural by (ahem) Kaws, who, to be fair, is almost from New York. It was also sponsored by Nike, and the tradition of sponsorship has carried through to the present day, with Parks partnering with brands like Glossier, Mountain Dew, the National Guard, and most recently at the Matthews-Palmer playground in Hell's Kitchen by Project Backboard, a 501(c)3 that does this kind of thing around the world. Thankfully, the branding is usually kept to a tasteful minimum. (The Parks Department partners with brands as often as philanthropic organizations these days. If you don't like it, maybe we should increase their budget. If you do like it, maybe apply for a grant sponsored by Uniqlo.)
Project Backboard has also worked with the City to install murals across the five boroughs, like in Pelham Bay Park and in Jackson Heights with help from students from nearby Voyages Prep High School. Personally, I think it's best when they keep it simple and geometric, like Na Chainkua Reindorf's "Gaze," in Tompkins Square Park (sponsored by Glossier), which looks like a diamond-shaped eye, or Jeff Sonhouse's "Harlequin," a blue and orange motley in St. Nicholas Park.
