https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.title: The “Petroleum Mafia” Takes On COP31
https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.author: Mark Hertsgaard
https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.text:
The “Petroleum Mafia” Takes On COP31
How consensus decision-making doomed yet another UN climate summit.
Breakdown. Collapse. Failure. Those were some of the words that media coverage used to describe last week’s COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. The talks ended in acrimony and finger-pointing after the nearly 200 participating nations could not reach consensus on how to advance the official mission of these annual summits: to protect humanity from “dangerous” amounts of man-made global warming.
Most news coverage also identified the main reason for the lack of consensus. As Reuters reported, Saudi Arabia “was at the forefront of resisting language on reducing reliance on fossil fuels,” even as “the European Union, several small island states, and other nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the oil, gas, and coal that scientists say drive global warming.”
Coming on the heels of a summer that featured 50,000 excess heat deaths across Europe and a glacial collapse in Nepal that killed at least 7,000 people and wiped out 10 percent of the country’s gross national product in the space of minutes, the failure to highlight fossil fuels’ role in the climate emergency unleashed both derision and dismay. “A climate deal that leaves out fossil fuels is like a plan to quit smoking that never mentions cigarettes,” commented Katharine Hayhoe, the chief scientist at the NGO The Nature Conservancy.
Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister and COP31 copresident, opened the final day of talks by declaring that “a historic decision” was in the offing. What followed was historic, alright, though not in the way Kurum hoped. This COP marked only the second time in the 31-year history of these summits that no final agreement (known in COP parlance as a “cover decision”) was published.
Yet a strong case can be made that COP31 was not a total failure but rather a much-needed turning point toward more effective climate diplomacy going forward. “No deal is better than a deal that locks in failure,” said Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser and global engagement director for the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative. Bill Hare, chief executive at Climate Analytics, wrote in The Guardian that “the failure of COP31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no.”
COP31 vividly demonstrated what has been evident for years: Petro-states—including the United States, which boycotted these talks for the second year in a row—will never willingly agree to leave fossil fuels behind. And they will exploit the COP tradition of consensus decision-making to delay action as long as possible.
By refusing at COP31 to keep playing along, the vast majority of the world’s countries were, to borrow from Beckett, no longer “waiting for Godot”—no longer waiting for petro-states to help rather than hinder the fight against climate breakdown. Instead, many of these countries are moving ahead on their own to do what both science and justice call for.
One of the few bright spots at COP31 was further growth of the Santa Marta coalition of countries that is committed to a global phaseout of fossil fuels. The coalition first took shape at COP30, where 87 countries wanted the final agreement to endorse developing a global “road map” to phase out oil, gas, and coal. But when Saudi Arabia and Russia led a handful of petro-states in refusing to consent, consensus decision making meant that the endorsement of a road map was excluded from the agreement.
Undaunted, many of those countries met in April 2026 in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin developing a road map themselves. Collectively, the countries that met in Santa Marta—a group that included Germany, the world’s third-largest economy; France, the sixth-largest; the UK, the seventh-largest; Brazil, the 10th-argest; and The Netherlands, the 18th-largest—amount to the biggest economic superpower on Earth. Combine their GNPs and the total is larger than that of the United States. Include California, whose governor, Gavin Newsom, said at COP31 that he backed the Santa Marta effort “100 percent”—and the coalition’s GNP is nearly as large as that of the US and China put together.
If these countries can implement credible plans for transitioning away from fossil fuels to solar, wind, batteries, and other forms of clean energy, it would put governments and financial markets on notice that staying invested in fossil fuels will be a risky proposition that could leave them with trillions of dollars of stranded assets. This scenario became more plausible at COP31, as the coalition expanded to include not only California, the world’s fourth-largest economy, but also Spain, Ireland, Belgium, Finland, Denmark, Norway, Luxemburg, and Pacific island nations.
Petro-states’ obstructionism at COP31 also led to renewed calls to reform the decision-making process at future COPs. “COPs are designed to fail,” Juan Carlos Navarro, the minister of the environment for Panama, said in an interview with Covering Climate Now. Minutes earlier, Navarro had delivered the summit’s most piercing sound bite, telling a press conference that, “We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.” In the interview, he explained that consensus decision making means that “all it takes is one idiot to torpedo the entire process. If we don’t change direction, by the time we have COP61 the world will be 5 degrees [Celsius] warmer.”
Panama plans to press this issue at the UN General Assembly, Navarro said. “Decisions at the COP should be made by simple majority, just like at the General Assembly,” he said, adding that “more and more countries” are coming around to this view. An effort within the UN to update the operating rules for COPs is another potential avenue for reform.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Such reform is not as unlikely as some observers seem to think. Chris Bowen, the climate minister of Australia and the copresident of COP31, acknowledged after the talks ended that consensus decision-making was partly to blame for the outcome. But Bowen misstated the relevant history when he asserted that “when COPs were created…[decision-making] was made consensus only.”
Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research, walked through the history in a LinkedIn post during COP31. How COPs would make decisions was initially discussed at the very first COP, held in 1995. A proposal was made to make decisions by consensus if possible, but if “all efforts have been exhausted and no consensus reached,” then a two-thirds majority vote would serve as a last resort. “But oil producing countries opposed this, with support from US oil lobbyists,” Rockström wrote.
The issue was left unresolved. Nevertheless, Rockström said at a CCNow Press Briefing, in subsequent years “a culture took hold…to operate under consensus,” though in fact “there is nothing hindering…the COP process to have majority voting today.”
How the various efforts to reform decision-making at UN climate summits unfold is a story worth watching—and covering. There would seem to be enough time to fix the process before COP32 takes place next November in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Doing so could make a world of difference.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Conflict without end: grief, fear and resilience in Kashmir – in pictures
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Conflict without end: grief, fear and resilience in Kashmir – in pictures
Robert Nickelsberg has been photographing the plight of the Kashmiri people for more than 20 years – his images reveal how trauma has settled into the fabric of everyday life
‘The picture remains unchanged’ … Women grieve over the body of Kashmir law minister Abdul Ghani Lone, 2000
Photographer Robert Nickelsberg visited Kashmir repeatedly for more than 20 years, witnessing how a political uprising evolved into one of the world’s longest unresolved conflicts – and how its consequences have settled into the fabric of everyday life. In this image, a Kashmiri man suffering from temporary loss of eyesight is treated with prayers and curative koranic verses. Kashmir, the Valley is available to purchase from Kehrer Verlag
An Indian schoolteacher stands near a sign at a closed public high school. The armed uprising in favour of Kashmiri independence from India began in 1989. ‘For me, as a photojournalist, the Kashmiris’ plight was the essence of the story,’ says Nickelsberg. ‘This work is my personal commitment, over two decades, to recording the deadly tactics deployed by both Pakistan and India. Twenty years later, tragically, the picture is unchanged’
The uprising was triggered by a rigged state election, and with material and political support from neighbouring Pakistan. After 18 years of conflict and violence the population’s mental health has been severely affected. Figures of Kashmiri dead vary from 10,000 to 45,000. In this image a widow, Farida Sunderwani, whose husband was killed in crossfire between Kashmiri militants and Indian army soldiers in 1992, is treated by psychiatrist Dr Arshad Hussain (right), at the outpatient department of the state-run Sri Maharaja Hari Singh Hospital in Srinagar
Moderate and militant Kashmiri separatists take part in a heated discussion at a mosque in Anantnag. Following the allegedly rigged Jammu and Kashmir state legislative elections in 1987, a call for independence and armed resistance began by the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front’s armed wing
Mourners raise clenched fists at the funeral for a Kashmiri woman killed in crossfire between Kashmiri militant separatists and Indian security forces at Eid Gah, a space reserved for Muslim prayers
Robert Nickelsberg: ‘On most trips I made to Indian-administered Kashmir, I made an effort to visit the Shah-i-Hamdan shrine in Srinagar’s old city. Inside, I could quietly observe Kashmiris as they appeared to momentarily drop their fears and experience a period of calm, a sense of peace, either in deep thought or prayer, to recharge themselves, replenish their spiritual sides and find strength for their daily encounters with the conflict outside the walls of this historic site with an intricately decorated interior’
Women grieve over the body of Kashmir law minister Abdul Ghani Lone in Sogam. Lone was assassinated by a gunman during a campaign rally as a candidate in an upcoming state election. Lone, a moderate, had been in favour of dialogue with the Indian government
Nickelsberg: ‘The expressions on the two Kashmiris’ faces and the Border Security Force soldier are indicative of the tension that existed between Kashmiri property holders and the Indian security force. The BSF soldier was patrolling houses on a weapons search. What I knew from other house searches was that private citizens, although they may not be active in the conflict, could have their house used by Kashmiri militants to hide weapons and ammunition. If searches found either, they could face serious interrogation, torture and possible disappearance’
Indian tourists sightsee from a traditional Kashmiri boat, known as a shikara, on Dal Lake, Srinagar. Nickelsberg’s photographs stay close to the people living within overlapping political realities. Muslim families, Hindu Pandits, soldiers, local politicians, children and pilgrims inhabit the same visual field. The photographs resist easy hierarchies of victimhood or heroism; what holds the work together is a sustained attention to lived experience
A pro-Pakistan Kashmiri militant, brandishing a Kalashnikov rifle, marches in a street demonstration against Indian authorities and security forces, on Pakistan’s Independence Day
Two Pakistani army soldiers, one pointing and the other looking through a pair of binoculars, stand behind a rock wall at Mumtaz base camp, near the Line of Control border during the Kargil conflict. They were looking down a valley to where they’d made a direct artillery hit on a passing Indian Army convoy, five to six kilometres away. The conflict, which eventually lasted slightly over 11 weeks, began after Pakistani forces occupied Indian army positions that had been abandoned during the preceding winter months
Kashmiris visiting the Makhdoom Sahib shrine tie a ‘desh’, or a piece of cloth, to wish for a positive outcome during a time of stress, trauma, sickness or sorrow. Shrines in Kashmir provide a space for spiritual solace, comfort or prayer

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: UK government blocks export of 17th-century British landscape painting
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The UK government has placed an export bar on a 17th-century painting of the Welsh estate Llannerch Park in Denbighshire, northeast Wales, thought to be the earliest known British country-estate landscape painting.
The export ban, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the work, will initially expire on 19 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £550,000 (plus VAT of £11,000), followed by a second deferral period of four months.
The painting, made around 1662 by an unknown artist, gives a bird’s-eye view of the house and Italian-style gardens at Llannerch Park which “contained a series of marvellous watery innovations: pools, fountains, sculpture, cascades and hydraulic surprises all set off by Baroque architecture, staircases and planting”, says Pippa Shirley, a member of the reviewing committee on the export of works of art and objects of cultural interest which advises the government. The fact that the garden is now lost makes the painting more important, she adds in a statement.
The Llannerch Park garden was created by the landowner Mutton Davies following a tour of France and Italy; according to Sotheby’s, which offered the painting in a sale in 2014 in London, Davies also commissioned the landscape painting in the 1660s, and had remained in the family since. The work failed to sell at the 2014 auction, where it was estimated to sell at £400,000-£600,000. A government spokesperson declined to provide further details regarding the painting's ownership. A slightly smaller version of the painting is housed at the Yale Center for British Art in Connecticut.
“If the painting remains in the UK, researchers will be given the opportunity to explore how people and culture were spreading between Wales, England and the European continent in the seventeenth century. It could also reveal new details about how the artistry of country-estate landscapes developed in Britain,” according to the UK Department for Digital, Media, Culture and Sport.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Iliana Hagenah
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
The Deportation Influencers
A growing group of US deportees is documenting their new, post-deportation lives on social media, revealing the human cost of our Kafkaesque immigration system.
Laymone Khambounleung pulls up on a scooter along a gravel road and flips his camera into selfie mode. “I’m out here in Laos, man, I don’t know what village I’m at,” he says, in a thick, unmistakable Louisiana accent.
He turns his camera on an albino buffalo. A tropical landscape surrounds them.
“Look. This is the type of thing you see here.”
This video could pass for a travel vlog. Khambounleung, who goes by Mones, is, after all, exploring an unfamiliar place. But he didn’t come to Laos by choice. After spending nearly his entire life in the United States, he was deported at the beginning of Donald Trump’s second presidency.
“I don’t know how to read or write or speak the language. It’s still a shock to me,” Mones told me in a WhatsApp call. “When I started posting, I was getting a lot of support. It helps [my followers] to see how we’re doing after deportation.”
Mones is one of a growing group of US deportees who are documenting their new, post-deportation lives on social media. Their videos run the gamut from travel vlogs to food challenges. But they also reveal the human cost of a Kafkaesque immigration system that deposits thousands of people in unfamiliar countries—whether a country they left as infants or a “third country” they’ve never known. The videos offer a glimpse of the lives often flattened by political agendas and a media landscape that either temporarily thrusts them into the spotlight or forgets about them completely.
Mones left Laos when he was a baby. His family fled to refugee camps in Thailand during the Lao communist takeover in the 1980s that led to civil unrest. But he doesn’t remember any of this. He can only place his life in Louisiana, where he calls home. His family had refugee status in the United States, but he never thought to apply for US citizenship amid spending his adult years in and out of jail for a string of nonviolent crimes.
In 2025, the Trump administration pressured Laos to accept deportees after its long reluctance to repatriate them. Mones never thought that would happen. By the summer, Mones was among thousands sent back to countries they aren’t even citizens of anymore. While he lives with his extended family who embraced him and gets financial support from back home, his day-to-day struggles are mostly absent from his social-media videos. It’s also not the point.
“I’m showing them, like, we’re not all bad people,” he told me. “All they see is that they’re ‘bad.’ But they don’t know; they’re not the same as they were 20, 30, 40 years ago, and people can change.”
On any given day, what Mones finds interesting enough to post isn’t too different from what a travel vlogger would. Sometimes, he devours a popular Lao meal like grilled dried squid or kapoon, a spicy noodle soup. He can be exploring a new restaurant, a backroad region he traveled by scooter, or a beautiful waterfall draping the mountains. He’s almost always making jokes about the mundane and idiosyncratic sides of Laotian culture, like his cousin climbing up a coconut tree or waking up in the middle of a monsoon.
Humor is Mones’s intention. “The more I post, the more my family gets to see me, and they know that I’m doing good,” he said. His commenters are mostly supportive, often asking questions about Lao life and his deportation experience, which he enjoys answering.
“It’s a lot of smiles and laughs and everything. But there is also the sad part too,” Mones told me
Along with Mones, I spoke to four other deportees making similar kinds of content. All five told me they wanted to challenge the “dangerous immigrant” stereotype that eclipses their stories. That’s important, said Sarah Tosh, a sociologist focusing on immigration enforcement who teaches at Rutgers, because we usually know very little about what happens to people after they’re removed from the US.
“The United States doesn’t do anything to keep records of people post-deportation. There is no overarching picture of the deportee experience,” Tosh said.
The US government keeps records of removals, but not what happens after. We don’t know how many deportees find work or housing, reconnect with family, or safely remain in their destination country. Tosh said that researchers have tried to study what happens to specific communities. But the expansion of deportation, particularly following sharp increases in enforcement in the 1990s and the creation of the Department of Homeland Security after September 11, has outpaced efforts to understand its long-term effects.
This information gap has consequences. It can shape immigration court cases, where attorneys and researchers rely on limited studies for expert testimony to explain why someone faces persecution upon removal. It can also influence public opinion.
“People are like, ‘Oh, like, yeah, it’s a crime. Deport them,’” Tosh said. “But it’s like they don’t know what these cases look like.” (In 2025, public support among people who said some immigrants should be deported was near-universal at 97 percent for deporting individuals with violent criminal records, though much more divided when it comes to nonviolent offenders and individuals with no criminal record.) For a start, Tosh said, the public generally doesn’t understand that many deportees already served their sentences. “People have an opportunity to connect and see these people that in so many ways are just like us, and they shouldn’t have to be in order to be humanized,” she said.
Chris Edwards’s videos offer a lens into what deported life looks like 15 years later. Edwards is a dark-skinned man of Tamil descent with face tattoos, a set of gold teeth, and a Prince George’s County, Maryland, dialect. On a Zoom call, he explained to me his life in India since 2011, when he was caught up in the wave of Obama-era deportations.
“They still think I’m Black,” he laughed, talking about his life in Bengaluru, India, “But I learned a couple of words here and there so I can get by. I figured out the ins and outs, even though they get surprised.”
He gradually built a new life there, growing his streetwear business and his music, which sometimes blends southern “Tollywood” music with rap. He also told me he had a daughter who was born there. He calls the country home and now sees it through her eyes.
Similar to Mones, Edwards shows different facets of Indian life from street food to women milking donkeys on the side of the road, under the account name indian777_perico.
He told me he started talking about his deportee experience more last year. “I think now there is more of an interest because of the amount of people getting deported. They are curious about what’s going on with people,” he said. Like Mones, he hasn’t gotten a payout for any of his videos yet, but he’s hoping it can happen with the increase in interest.
The algorithm has the ultimate say in who sees these stories. To reach an audience, people often need to package their lives into recognizable formats. And in the case of the genocide in Gaza, we’ve seen how platforms can seemingly suppress content, such as with shadow banning.
But people have used the algorithm to their advantage to call attention to a crisis. Tosh said that, with anti-immigration AI videos surging online, these deportee videos offer an opportunity to shift the balance of immigration content. “For people to put back real narratives from real people going through these systems in these same forums in subversive ways…and if people do watch these videos and repost them…that’s so powerful.”
One account demonstrates the potential impact of deportee content. I spoke to Yasmany Moreno de Armas, a Cuban national, on a Zoom call while he was in a detention center in the Central African Republic. He told me that he got there in July and can leave for only two hours a day, sleeping on a floor mattress and eating barely edible food.

Moreno de Armas is among a group of detainees, many with no criminal record, who have been sent to “third countries”—in other words, countries they have no ties to—under the Trump administration. These include Ecuador, Honduras, Russia, and Vietnam. Moreno de Armas was apprehended in Florida and stayed in a detention center for years. Then he was placed on a flight in shackles and told he was going back home. Five hours into the flight, he learned he was going to Africa, not Cuba.
“I didn’t believe any of it until I saw the plane landing in an airport in Senegal, where you could see colorful lands and disorderly houses. That moment changed me,” he told me. “Seeing Africa in a movie is the same as seeing it in person.”
Ever since that flight, Moreno de Armas has documented his life on Instagram and TikTok channels (his handle is yasmany255) like a citizen-journalist. He has almost 40,000 followers on Instagram, where he shows the living conditions in detention and, when he’s allowed to see it, the world outside. He urges viewers to support his videos to raise awareness of what life looks like after deportation and the more than 25,000 people sent to over 30 so-called ‘third countries’ in the past year.”
“This has helped me a lot in my immigration process, to allow the world to see what is going on,” Moreno de Armas said.
He told me he also received donations from Instagram and money from news channels that publish his videos to buy food and supplies for him and other deportees.
“I think there is just this natural instinct towards people wanting to tell their story,” Tosh told me when I asked her how deportees shared their experiences before social media.
Deportees sharing their life stories is nothing new. But before social media, most had to turn to journalists and academics to tell their stories. While the storyteller’s role is changing to vlogger, food challenger, or citizen-journalist, the audience’s role is also morphing. We can be the casual viewer, the patron, the amplifier, or the commenter. For those watching, the question is not only what these videos reveal about life after deportation but also what we choose to do with this knowledge.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: From the margins to the mainstream: the growing market for illustration art
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Daniel Grant
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”. Some six decades later and the apotheosis of that market has arrived with the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the $1bn creation of film-maker George Lucas (Star Wars and Indiana Jones) devoted to children’s book art, fantasy art, cartoon images, movie posters, film stills and magazine illustrations, as well as works distinguished as fine art by the likes of Paul Cadmus, Diego Rivera and Carrie Mae Weems.
Rockwell’s success has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the whole field seriously
Lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up. Today, the interest in works by Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, J.C. Leyendecker, Howard Pyle, Maxfield Parrish, Jessie Willcox Smith, John Held Jr and Charles Dana Gibson, among many others, has mushroomed—and in some cases prices have shot up from almost zero to millions of dollars.
“A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” says the New York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”
Certainly, one doesn’t hear that at the major auction houses where works by Rockwell, Parrish, Wyeth and Leyendecker frequently bring the highest prices in American art sales. Norman Rockwell (1894-1978) leads the pack, with his 1951 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover, Saying Grace, fetching $46m at a 2013 Sotheby’s auction and his 1957 oil painting The Rookie (Red Sox Locker Room) sold for $22.5m at a 2014 auction at Christie’s. The 1922 painting Daybreak by Maxfield Parrish(1870-1966) earned $7.6m at a Christie’s sale in 2006, while a 1943 tempera on panel, Portrait of a Farmer, by N.C. Wyeth (1882-1945) brought $5.9m at Sotheby’s in 2018. Football Hero, the 1914 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover by J.C. Leyendecker (1874-1951), brought $4.1m at a Heritage Auctions sale in 2021, and the 1907 painting Captain Keitt by Howard Pyle (1853-1911) for the frontispiece of his novel The Ruby of Kishmoor earned $702,000 at a 2004 sale at Sotheby’s.
“There’s definitely a hierarchy,” says Aviva Lehmann, the deputy chair of fine art at Heritage Auctions, which sold Rockwell’s 1943 work So You Want to See the President! in 2025 to the White House Historical Association for $7.2m.
However, “Rockwell’s success has not been at the expense of these other illustrators”, says Skye Lacerte, an illustration art specialist at Swann Auction Galleries in New York. “Rather, it has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the entire field seriously.” She notes that “immediately recognisable” images from magazine covers and illustrations from famous books like Alice in Wonderland, The Wind in the Willows, or L. Frank Baum’s Oz books are highly sought after, as well as advertising art for “companies like Coca-Cola, TWA and Cadillac because those images have become part of American cultural experience”.
Lucas and beyond
Besides the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, there is the Brandywine River Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in Amherst, Massachusetts; and the National Museum of American Illustration in Newport, Rhode Island. That last museum was founded in 1998 by Judy Goffman Cutler, the owner of Manhattan’s American Illustrators Gallery, who claims to have sold Lucas “hundreds” of original paintings by the top book and magazine illustrators. “I sold him his first Rockwell—it was called Going Out,” she says—a 1933 painting that was used on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post. For reasons of “client confidentiality”, she declines to say how many works in the illustration field she has sold to Lucas, only noting that “I built his collection”.
Other museums that aren’t wholly devoted to illustration or storytelling art also have collections of this type of work, most notably the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut and the Delaware Art Museum in Wilmington. The New Britain Museum has almost 1,800 works in its Sanford B.D. Low Illustration Collection, named in honour of the institution’s first director who himself had been an illustrator and invited illustrators he knew to donate works for a collection. They include such artists as Willcox Smith, Everett Raymond Kinstler, Stevan Dohanos, Walter Wick and William Steig.
“Interest in illustration art doesn’t begin and end with Rockwell, and the awareness of illustration art as art is definitely increasing,” says Lisa Williams, head of curatorial affairs at the New Britain Museum.
Others agree. “I have no doubt that the collective appreciation for the category will continue to grow thanks to its elevation by these museums,” says Quincie Dixon, head of sale in Christie’s American art department. She adds that “private collectors make up the bulk of this market, but perhaps that will change now that there are museums on both coasts dedicated to the category”.
Working against segregation
Specialised museums and collections reflect a growing prominence, but they might also be keeping these works segregated. Goffman Cutler states that it is her “goal to have museums include American illustration art in their American art galleries”, which the occasional museum has done, but not many and not too often.
A spokesperson for the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, notes that the “collection includes art from American artists of many backgrounds, including quite a few who have worked as illustrators, among them Winslow Homer, Childe Hassam, William Glackens, Joseph Leyendecker, Charles Sheeler” and some others. Having worked as illustrators doesn’t mean that their illustration work is what the museum shows, and the Leyendecker is not currently “on view”. Both New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, own paintings by Parrish that are not displayed in their American art galleries, but the Art Institute of Chicago has hung its Rockwell, The Dugout (1948), in one of the Arts of Americas galleries, and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, has hung Rockwell’s 1943 work Rosie the Riveter (which the museum purchased from a private collector in 2009) next to Charles Willson Peale’s George Washington (around 1780-82) and works by John Singleton Copley and James Peale Sr in its Visions of America galleries. “In the same section of the gallery as Rosie the Riveter,” says a museum spokesperson, “are Susie J. Lee’s Johnny [2013], Kerry James Marshall’s Our Town [1995] and a new commission by artist Teri Greeves.”
It seems the greatest test for illustration art is no longer garnering record prices, but if it can enter—and hold its own within— the art historical canon.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Can’t-Miss Way to Prove That Democrats Have Solutions to Americans’ Problems
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Kali Holloway

The Can’t-Miss Way to Prove That Democrats Have Solutions to Americans’ Problems
A single-issue bill strategy will either force Trump to veto enormously popular legislation—or sign bills that would actually benefit all Americans.
Republicans are good at declaring they’ve been given a mandate, even when they lose the popular vote or win by the absolute slimmest of margins. (See Trump, 2016 and 2024.) They also can’t be beat in the category of taking credit for things, and that includes legislation they had nothing to do with—or even voted against. (See the many congressional Republicans who voted against Biden’s Chips and Science Act or infrastructure bill, then quietly requested the money and showed up to ribbon cuttings.) Democrats are, quite notoriously, bad at doing both. Now voters have given them large majorities in the House and the Senate, and put them in control of most state legislatures—providing an authentic mandate to govern that demands real follow through. But with a Republican President and congressional minority whose only plan for the next two years seems to be obstruction, how can Democrats show their voters, many of whom are not partisans but frustrated with Trump and the GOP, that their party can get things done?
The answer is single-issue bills, which are as uncomplicated as they sound, and the centerpiece of the almost embarrassingly intuitive strategy that I’m begging Democrats to undertake. For the next two years, congressional Democrats should focus on putting forward short bills, each addressing one of the many critical proposals that would make Americans’ lives better and more secure and are wildly popular with Americans overall and Democratic voters, but which—offering no discernible way to make rich people even richer—Republicans oppose. For example, Medicare for All, which more than 65 percent of Americans told pollsters they support just weeks before the midterms. Or a bill that restores reproductive freedom, which national polls throughout 2026 proved 60 to more than 70 percent of Americans support. Or raising the $7.25 minimum wage to $15, which 77 percent of Americans, including 75 percent of Republicans, support after 17 years without a raise.
Let’s see a bill for a congressional stock trading ban, which well over 80 percent of Americans support. Congressional Republicans claim that they support it, too, but earlier this year—according to one of their own—they intentionally tanked a stock trading bill. “Congress is not serious,” GOP Representative Thomas Massie wrote on social media in July. “We are voting on a stock trading ban for members of Congress… BUT Republicans added voter-ID in the legislation. Not to get Dems to vote for voter-ID, but to get them to vote against the stock trading ban, so they can use it in the Nov. election.” The Stop Insider Trading Act consequently died in the Senate, with every Democrat and independent voting no and every Republican voting yes—then rushing out press releases and social–media posts feigning self-righteous indignation toward Dems for opposing it. (The media deserves a side-eye, too, for stories that led with Democrats blocking the bill, and headlines that obligingly elevated Republicans’ cynical framing, yet again demonstrating how the media is complicit in the same political manipulation it’s supposed to be reporting on.) “This is the Republican M.O.,” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said. “The public wants something done, and what they do is put in a bill that does virtually nothing, because they want to try to assuage the public but not solve the problem.”
A single-issue bill will clear that problem right up! House Democrats in the incoming Congress should write an easy to read, three-page-maximum bill that does one thing and one thing only—outlaw stock trades by Congress members. Senate Republicans can shoot it down—but this time, out in the open, where everyone can see. No hiding behind unrelated tack-ons, no forcing all-or-nothing votes on proposals that seemingly sanction one thing but try to smuggle in something altogether different. If congressional Republicans want to use their votes to let Americans know that they do not oppose the kinds of government corruption a majority of voters cited as one of the key motivating forces behind their midterm choices—the ones that cost Republican power in a post-Watergate-level wipeout—have them say it with their chests, as the saying goes.
Of course, there’s a nonzero chance that some bills will put forward solutions so popular—and potentially politically disastrous to oppose—that even the GOP’s most reliable obstructionists might reconsider blocking them. As of this writing, Senate Democrats have 56 seats, which means they need only four Republicans to break ranks to override any filibusters. That would move bills out of the Senate and onto this president’s desk, where he’s kept, since the midterms, a prominently displayed baseball cap stitched with the word “VETO” in all caps. Even before the election, Trump promised that in response to Democratic wins, he’d “become Mr. Veto.” All this to say, if the president should decide to veto a moratorium on data centers—which damn near 90 percent of Americans oppose near their homes and even more than 90 percent of public comments review unfavorably—it’s in the public record. Make him wear the veto like a brand logo, since he’s already treating it like one, and whenever possible, have fun with it. Appeal to his infamously fragile ego and insecurity by naming proposed legislation after him, as Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed did recently, pitching the president on Medicare for All rebranded as “Trumpcare,” complete with a picture of a gold card featuring the name. (Trump reposted El-Sayed’s tweet on his Truth Social platform.) In a follow-up video post, the incoming senator playfully addressed Trump as “habibi” and suggested that the way back from the “rough” midterms is for him to back healthcare for all.
“You want to be the most popular president in the history of America—there’s one way to do that. Trumpcare for All,” El-Sayed says. “You can put your name all over it! You can even give them a gold card!”
But Kali, I can hear you almost shouting, what about all the brazen grifting and corruption, the shameless self-dealing and looting of public resources, the public abuses of power and outright lawlessness we’ve witnessed from this administration and its many allies, enablers, and co-conspirators? What about all that?!?!?? Way ahead of you here. Democrats can, should, and even must investigate, hold hearings and hold the guilty accountable. But hearings and single-issue bills aren’t separate strategies—they’re one and the same. Incoming House Oversight Committee chairman Robert Garcia—whom you may know from such post-midterms social-media classics as “Lawyer Up”—has promised to look into the Trump family’s corruption, ICE’s abuses and DHS mismanagement, corporate pay-to-play and graft, and—the pièce de résistance—the Epstein files. Every form of corruption revealed in the hearings should inspire a categorial response via single-issue bill—a lovely sort of call-and-response that will demonstrate Democrats’ commitment to righting this administration’s wrongs and their commitment to an anti-corruption agenda that prevents the next autocrat from ascending.
For example, Elizabeth Warren, who’s expected to be the next Senate Banking Committee chair, is reportedly focused on Trump-family crypo schemes. If the hearings reveal that the family profited from policy decisions the president made, the single-issue bill basically writes itself, in the form of a bill that closes the loophole that allows presidents and vice presidents—let’s throw their family members in for good measure—from making money off ventures that involve government decision-making, just like every other executive office official. (“Trump owns ~$1 billion in cryptocurrency. Meanwhile, his administration shapes crypto policy. The President shouldn’t be getting rich off his own policy decisions,” Warren tweeted back in August, which suggests she’s long been thinking about it.) Or take hearings on Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which has refused to open its records, claiming that it was never an agency but instead a mere “government adviser,” despite having broad, agency-level authority. That deserves a bill declaring that any body vested with governmental powers, regardless of what the White House and said group call it, must keep its records and release them to the public. (The administration is, as I write this, trying to get a complicit Supreme Court to help it hide those records.) Again and again, the pattern should be that when hearings root out abuse, the loophole that allowed it is identified and a short and sweet bill is written that closes the loop, forcing a vote.
This seems like the moment to mention that Democrats might want to reconsider the filibuster, which under the single-issue strategy becomes an even more compelling consideration. After all, they’re up against more than just Trump and his “VETO” hat—others in Republican leadership seem to be in no mood to learn from what voters are demanding. Republicans’ newly elected minority leader is Jim Jordan—once dubbed a “legislative terrorist” by a former GOP speaker—who campaigned for the role as “battle-tested” and declared that “offense, not defense, wins elections.” Party whip Tom Emmer recently stated that House Democrats “will regret ever putting your name[s] on a ballot.” In an open letter to Representative Garcia, White House attorneys pushed further, going so far as to suggest that Democratic investigations qualify as “threats to executive branch officials” and amount to congressional overreach that “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” Taken together, it suggests that Republicans are on the warpath, fully committed to refusing attempts at accountability and blocking even the most popular policies. In that case, Democrats may want to ditch a procedural rule that prevents their majority from governing and allows for tyranny of the minority. (Not to mention—without getting too into the historical weeds—that the filibuster was created by accident during a decluttering of the rules in 1806, and has a history steeped in racism.) Just because the Senate is known as the place where good legislation goes to die, and former Republican power brokers like über-ghoul Mitch McConnell delighted in being declared the “grim reaper,” doesn’t mean that’s just the way we ought to live. Democrats could scrap the filibuster with a simple majority vote, using the so-called nuclear option, and with 56 seats they can afford to have five defectors. Senator John Fetterman and incoming Senator-elects Adam Hamilton and Roy Cooper have all defended the procedure. There’s also the option of reforming the filibuster, including lowering the 60-vote threshold for cloture or, as Jamelle Bouie suggests in the The New York Times, “requir[ing] 41 members on the floor to continue debate, rather than 60 members to end it,” flipping the script and making the obstructionists do the work to stop it. Should Republicans who want to block a bill restoring the Voting Rights Act—which 55 percent of voters recognize that we need, and which they absolutely will, judging from recent Senate history—they should have to do more heavy lifting than a lazy non-talking filibuster. Democrats owe the black voters who delivered their majorities a real try.
Let’s also remember that Democrats have made huge gains at the state level, being now in control of a majority of statehouses and with trifectas in 22 states. While some bills may be vetoed at the federal level, there are all kinds of opportunities for wins at the state and local levels. If states enact paid family leave, expand Medicaid, protect reproductive freedom, or block corporate bullying, those wins should be touted by their Democratic partners in Congress. It’s not only a PR move to counter the news of federal-level vetoes—it’s a chance to show what Democratic governance looks like when it’s not thwarted by Republicans.
Americans want to know that Democrats are doing stuff, and a single-bill strategy will show them that they are. Vetoes aren’t losses in these cases, and they’re nothing to run from. One 2023 New York University study even found that voters feel far more positive about politicians they agree with who at least try to legislate on the issues they care about—even if the chances for success are slim—than they do about politicians who don’t put in the effort. Favorability ratings, on a scale from 1 to 100, for politicians who chose not to submit a bill averaged around 40, but if they introduced a bill, that rating went up to 61. It also correlated with voter support in the future, with the estimated probability of casting a ballot for that legislator rising from 42 percent, up to 64 percent after the politician submitted a bill. (In 2028, alongside the presidency, there are 19 Republican Senate seats on the ballot. Just sayin’.) “Voters appreciate it when politicians take action, even if their efforts do not lead to any concrete policy change,” one study author wrote. When voters “already agreed with the politician on an issue”—like the super popular policies mentioned—putting up a fight counts.
That’s why voters have to know the effort is happening. Consider the Inflation Reduction Act, a massive 2022 omnibus bill that not a single congressional Republican voted for—and which they even held votes to piecemeal repeal. It should have been one of Biden’s signature pieces of legislation. A Politico investigation would find, one year later, that “roughly two-thirds of the major projects are in districts whose Republican lawmakers opposed” the bill, although many were taking credit for the new works going up. A 2026 study from Harvard researchers ultimately found that nearly half of survey respondents thought their governor was “at least partly responsible.” But just 41 percent cited Biden’s involvement. Another example is Biden’s Covid stimulus package, aka the American Rescue Plan. Although it was incredibly popular with every stripe of voter, every Republican in both chambers voted against it. A Newsweek analysis found that “nearly one-third of Republican voters believe that GOP lawmakers in Congress backed President Joe Biden’s $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan—even though not a single Republican voted for the massive relief legislation.” Similarly, one NBC News headline read, “Republicans trumpet elements of Covid-19 relief bill they voted against,” while the Associated Press blared, “Republicans promote pandemic relief they voted against.”
Popular

The single-issue plan helps remedy some of this, by keeping bills short and easily understandable. But none of this works unless Democrats also spread the word. Create a central, interactive website—something separate from the dry congressional bill sites—where people can read bills, look at FAQs, find information about the longer-term benefits, track how their representative votes, and see what happens when the legislation hits the Resolute Desk. If a bill gets vetoed, make sure everyone hears about it. New York recently reported that Representative Garcia’s Oversight Committee will have a fully stocked communications staff that’s already considering how to promote its work “for an audience that would never watch a hearing on C-Span but might encounter a clip from one while scrolling through TikTok.” (The congressman is already a talking-head fixture on news and podcasts.) Pundit Adam Mockler had the great idea that popular figures, including Senator Jon Ossoff, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Senators-elect James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed, and a bunch of other incoming soon-to-be stars, should be sent out to the media—including their own socials—to spread the word about the legislation being considered. The process includes relentlessly pushing the story until a media that sometimes needs prodding asks Republicans to explain why they’re voting against policies supported by the people who voted to be represented by them in Washington. And repeat, literally. Democrats need to bring legislation for those policies to the floor, in one single-issue bill at a time.
This isn’t just my idea—there are Democrats who are already big proponents of single-issue bills. Senator Warren has urged Democrats to deliver “popular, meaningful legislation to Trump’s desk and then dare him to veto it.” During a post-midterms appearance on Pod Save America, Colorado Representative-elect Melat KirosI said she “would like to force Donald Trump to veto Medicare for All. I would like to force him to veto a data center moratorium. Or childcare or elder care for all. And the threat of a veto should not stop us from putting that forward.” Senator-elect El-Sayed complained about Democrats’ putting forth omnibus bills “with obscure names like Inflation Reduction Act” that are too overstuffed for anyone to realize what they actually have in them. “What I want us to be doing is spitting out new bills, and putting them on the President’s desk, that brand on what they’re doing,” he proposed as an alternative. And Representative Ro Khanna told USA Today that single-issue bills are the way to go “so that people know Donald Trump’s not for raising your wage, or he is.”
It’s a matter of playing the political game as aggressively as Republicans do. Democrats can use the single-issue strategy to prove to voters that they have solutions—and they can make them real if Republicans get out of the way. That would to make this midterm victory more than just a temporary changing of the guard. Maybe kick things off this Congress with a succession of single-issue bills that restore cuts to, respectively, Medicaid, ACA subsidies, and SNAP/food stamps, which a majority of Americans of every stripe support. Unlike the “One Big Beautiful Bill” Act—a 1,037-page monstrosity that slapped together all kinds of legislative horrors into a single omnibus bill that multiple Republicans admitted regretting voting for without reading it—and that nearly all voters hated. Trump should don his “VETO” hat as he vetoes it, proving just how little this president and administration care about Americans, including their voters. That, or he’ll pass it, and Americans will benefit.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Exhibition celebrates Delftware, the Dutch art form that became the ‘Ikea of its day’
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Joanna Moorhead
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
On a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark new Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people. “There was no one there because ceramics can feel cold and distanced,” she says. “They can be hard to bring alive, because the makers are anonymous, and [the objects are] often displayed in glass cases.”
But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different. The result, Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, opens this month at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague, where she is the curator of decorative arts. It will, she says, be “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever”. Equally importantly, she promises it will be captivating and enjoyable.
“Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she says. “We want to show the love craftspeople put into these pieces. It has inspired, and it continues to inspire, so many craftmakers—we’ll give them a platform.”
Around 1,000 objects, including vases, teapots, plates, wall plaques and tiles, will be on display at the Kunstmuseum, which has one of the largest collections of the art form that is perhaps the best-known cultural export of the Netherlands. Also on show in Blue Loves You will be Delftware-inspired pieces, including the blue dress worn by Queen Máxima of the Netherlands for her husband’s 2013 investiture, its bodice embroidered with Delft-derived flowers. “There’s a lot more to it than blue and white fridge magnets,” Lambooy says.
Although the porcelain is known for its characteristic colouring, the show will include examples of both white and multicoloured Delftware. It will explore its history, dating back to the 17th century. The form was originally a high-end Chinese import, displayed in the wealthiest homes. But when factories started to make their own version of it in Delft, it was transformed.
“It became an on-trend, functional brand that was affordable for every home and on every budget: it was the Ikea of its day,” says Lambooy, whose co-curator for the long-term show is the television presenter Janny van der Heijden (who is also a judge on the country’s version of The Great British Bake Off).
The quintessential Delftware piece was the tulip pyramid, some of the best examples of which were made for King William III, born in The Hague, and his English wife Queen Mary II, who were the joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland in the late 17th century. “Mary exported Delftware to Britain—she was the most important woman in its history,” Lambooy says.
The porcelain’s connections to Dutch colonialism will also be explored, with exhibits including an installation of sugar flowers by the floral artist Natasja Sadi, whose family are originally from the former Dutch colony of Suriname and whose ancestors were enslaved.
• Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, Kunstmuseum, The Hague, 28 November-31 December 2029

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: At Cornell, Students Are Still Seeking Answers
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Jeannine Chiang
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
At Cornell, Students Are Still Seeking Answers
Amid faculty votes of no confidence and perceived administrative mishandling of sexual assault allegations, Cornell students are still searching for accountability.
Accusations that university leaders were evading questions filled a Cornell University community forum on November 16, as approximately 100 students confronted president Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators over the university’s handling of sexual assault.
The gathering came two months after a former Cornell student, identified as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and gang-raped by members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024. The allegations, along with questions about Cornell’s investigation and disciplinary response, drew national attention and a wave of student-led protests demanding changes to the university’s sexual assault policies and leadership. On November 6, the Faculty Senate passed a vote of no confidence in the administration’s ability to address sexual assault. And on November 19, the Student Assembly passed Resolution 37 to hold an undergraduate vote of no confidence, with voting open through December 7.
The forum, intended to rebuild trust and transparency after weeks of outrage, instead showcased growing frustration with Cornell’s leadership. Inside Call Auditorium, students questioned the independence of the New York attorney general’s ongoing investigation into the rape allegations, challenged disciplinary double standards, and demanded accountability from the officials promising reform.
“The atmosphere was very tense. No one was there to defend Kotlikoff’s actions. We were all there to voice concerns or get some kind of information out of the administration, and the students were very united in demanding answers,” said student John Hartnett.
For many students, the forum was an opportunity to hear from a president whose administration has spent months dodging responsibility. But the exchanges revealed a greater divide between what Cornell considered progress and what its students considered accountability.
“Kotlikoff said he wants to build trust between the student body and administration, but when he was asked a question, he either deflected or said, ‘We will talk about it later,’” said Saya Taylor.
Taylor questioned Kotlikoff about the school-wide October protest and the faculty vote of no confidence, asking “why administrators have not been held accountable” when “two major constituents have lost trust in the administration.”
Kotlikoff directed Taylor to an ongoing independent review led by former US deputy attorney general Sally Yates, who is examining Cornell’s handling of the Chi Phi allegations and its broader sexual misconduct policies. He told students that the investigation would determine whether mistakes had been made and identify necessary reforms.
But for students who had already spent months demanding action, the promise of yet another investigation proved far from satisfactory. “Admin is always outsourcing responsibility in this investigation,” Hartnett said.
That mistrust became even more apparent when Jack Huber questioned whether Sally Yates, who was retained by Cornell’s Board of Trustees, could conduct a truly independent investigation given her institutional ties.
Huber cited the trustees’ earlier probe into a May 2026 incident in which Kotlikoff drove into two students with his car. The board found him innocent, and now the same governing body is responsible for another high-stakes investigation.
But Hartnett’s demands for accountability went beyond the investigation. He challenged the disparity between Cornell’s Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards (OSCCS), which handles student conduct violations including protest-related cases, and its Title IX process, which addresses allegations of sex-based misconduct.
Both systems are in place for imposing suspensions when “student safety” is at risk. Yet Hartnett questioned why the university has been able to move at “same-day speed” against student protesters while allegations of sexual violence have not resulted in similarly immediate consequences.
“In order to be suspended from OSCCS, you need to threaten safety, and the same is true for Title IX. Someone accused of rape is undoubtedly a threat to safety,” Hartnett said.
According to Hartnett, Kotlikoff answered that the university would “think about the issue,” a response he saw as emblematic of the administration’s reluctance to commit to specific policy changes.
Sol Schoenbach-Lee confronted the president with an analysis of university data published by USA Today: Cornell received 1,216 reports of sexual violence between 2018 and 2024, but only 14 cases resulted in suspensions, while seven resulted in expulsions or dismissals. Schoenbach-Lee asked how Cornell could continue to encourage students to pursue Title IX proceedings when so few reported cases resulted in serious disciplinary action.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
“There is disingenuity from the university’s framing of Title IX being the right thing for students to do because statistically, it shows that it underserves and doesn’t help victims seek justice,” Schoenbach-Lee said.
Kotlikoff initially responded, “I don’t know,” to his question.
“It’s disappointing that the administration is approaching the town hall from a recognizable tactic of damage control instead of genuine interaction with the students. The university sort of attempts to twist questions into inspirational messages of ‘We know things are bad’ and ‘We want to do better’ without actually making changes,” Schoenbach-Lee said.
At several points, according to Hartnett, the president criticized students for being disrespectful during some of the exchanges.
“When Kotlikoff said something deflective, the audience would question him directly, which kept happening, and he would say, ‘You guys need to stop being so disrespectful’ to the students,” Hartnett said.
“The audience laughed at Kotlikoff’s response to Jack’s question about the trustees and Yates investigation, and people were laughing because he kept saying absurd things. If we didn’t laugh, we would be in rage,” Taylor said.
The November 16 gathering revealed that the growing crisis of confidence is no longer just a disagreement over which policies should change; for the students who confronted Kotlikoff, the question is whether those responsible for the university’s existing failures can be trusted to lead the reforms themselves.
“This is just another example of Cornell admin not listening to students,” Taylor said. “A whole town hall built on student anger, and they’re still here deflecting.”

https://gothamist.com/news/4-year-old-bo.title: 4-year-old boy dies, 2 others injured in NJ house fire
https://gothamist.com/news/4-year-old-bo.author: Phil Corso
https://gothamist.com/news/4-year-old-bo.text:
A 4-year-old boy died and two other people were injured in a house fire Tuesday afternoon in Union Township, New Jersey, near Newark, fire officials said.
Firefighters responding to a two-alarm blaze just after 4 p.m. at a single-family home at 1129 Liberty Ave. encountered heavy flames coming from the front of the house, according to Union Fire Department official Raul Malave III.
Residents outside the home alerted firefighters that a child was missing. Crews searched the house “under extreme heat and advancing flames” and found the boy in a rear bedroom, Malave said.
The boy was taken to a hospital in critical condition and later died, officials said.
A 12-year-old boy and a 39-year-old woman were also taken to hospitals with injuries that were not considered life-threatening, Malave said. No firefighters were injured.
Authorities said an investigation was underway to determine the cause of the blaze.
It wasn't the only major fire in Union Township on Tuesday, authorities said. Mayor Patricia Guerra-Fraizer said an earlier fire on Stuyvesant Avenue near Axton Avenue damaged at least seven businesses, including Here's the Story Bookstore and Conca D'Oro Bakery.
