https://www.propublica.org/article/donal.title: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
https://www.propublica.org/article/donal.author: Robert Faturechi, Aaron C. Davis
https://www.propublica.org/article/donal.text:
In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.
The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.
The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.
If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.
A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed.
Do You Have Information We Should Know About Donald Trump Jr.?
We’re still reporting. If you know anything about Trump Jr. or his businesses, please get in touch with our reporting team.
Robert Faturechi
Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses.
The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.
According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.
The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.
The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan.
Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show.
The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.
Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it.
Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”
A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.
In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”
Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said.
Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment.
In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.
1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year. That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new factory in Arizona.
This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy, which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half million dollars, campaign filings show.
1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of financing that included participation from institutional investment managers. “This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in a LinkedIn post about the funding round.
It’s unclear when the Pentagon began considering Hadrian for the loan. But defense documents cite the August funding round that Trump Jr.’s firm was part of. It’s also not clear if the White House played any role in Hadrian’s being considered, though defense documents about the deal mention the “White House and DoW leadership’s expressed need for advanced manufacturing” — which Hadrian specializes in.
In response to questions to the White House, an administration official said Hadrian reached out to the Pentagon proposing a loan and that “It is at an extremely early stage.” (The documents ProPublica reviewed show specific terms being considered by the Pentagon for the loan and discussions of its merits and risks.)
At the March ribbon cutting for the first of three factories to be built for submarine parts and systems for the Navy, Hadrian’s Australian-born founder, Chris Power, promised a radical change to defense manufacturing. “The number-one problem that the Navy’s identified is we can’t find enough skilled workers, so we have to automate our way out of this problem,” he told reporters. The factory will be run on its artificial intelligence software, called Opus, which Power said would make his production line more efficient and nimble.
The Navy “can’t hire enough people and the primes can’t hire enough people because there aren’t enough trained people to do it,” he said, referring to major defense contractors. “We need to automate and have people running multiple robots in a new way of doing things versus replacing jobs.”
Venture capital firms are betting heavily that the marriage of AI and robotics will lead to major upheaval in manufacturing sectors, investing $33 billion — more than all of last year — in just the first half of 2026, according to data from PitchBook.
When it comes to defense contracting, analysts have said that they expect only a handful of companies will succeed, with a wave of consolidations to follow. A mega Defense Department contract for Hadrian could position it as just such a winner — even as the company has shared few details publicly about what its AI-powered factories have so far been able to produce. In testimony before Congress last year, Power said only that the company had successfully fabricated parts for “missile systems, fighter jets, spacecraft and naval vessels.”
Power started the company in 2020, saying he moved to the U.S. with just $6,000 and began cold-calling manufacturers looking to develop an idea to understand their operations and probe for bottlenecks. Much of the aerospace and defense industries, he found, relied on small shops with experts who were close to retirement. The solution, he decided, was automation.
Hadrian executives told Forbes in 2024 that the company spent its first two years trying to replicate components for two companies using its automation software in a small demonstration factory in California. It never named the companies or said which components it was able to replicate. It hired employees away from Elon Musk companies SpaceX and Tesla. It also hired employees from defense contractors Anduril, Raytheon and Palantir. Hadrian has also drawn investments from high-profile Silicon Valley funds, including Andreessen Horowitz and Altimeter Capital. The company has not released a recent employee count, but outside estimates put it at a few hundred.
This year, Hadrian has announced openings of new plants faster than outside analysts have been able to assess how well its operations are working. Mesa, Arizona, officials celebrated opening the company’s third factory in January. The ribbon cutting for its fourth, in Alabama for the Navy, took place in March, with Hadrian saying full production would begin in a couple of years.
A multibillion-dollar investment in Hadrian could push the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital far beyond the purpose for which it was approved and funded by Congress, some former defense officials said.
The office was created during the Biden administration to fill holes in the country’s industrial base so that the U.S. can stop relying on China, its top rival, to equip its own military. Under Trump, the lending unit has greatly expanded and focused on issuing loans to private companies to develop production of rare earth minerals and other technologies that have both commercial and military applications. That need has been elevated as the president’s tariff wars have heightened concerns that China could cut off the flow of critical minerals needed to produce high-tech weapons. The firms receiving loans generally make their money by supplying both defense contractors and other private-sector businesses.
But the idea of loaning money to Hadrian in hopes that it grows to become a major source of military munitions has sparked concerns within the Pentagon that the company would become reliant largely on the federal government.
When Congress created the Office of Strategic Capital, it included language prohibiting the OSC from making loans for projects with only military applications. A Pentagon document describing the proposed Hadrian loan indicates that the firm’s new factories would expand the U.S. capability to manufacture munitions and precision components for military use. The document states that Hadrian factories could “pivot rapidly to commercial applications.”
The former defense officials said the U.S. government might face allegations that it would be giving a distinct advantage to Hadrian over potential competitors. Other businesses could challenge whether the company is winning bids or subcontracting work on its merits or so that taxpayers do not lose on their capital investment.
David Lorch, a political appointee who heads up OSC, would have to sign off on the loan. Lorch previously worked at Cerberus, the private equity firm founded by Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg. It’s unclear if Feinberg or others in the Trump administration would also have to approve the deal because of its size.
A former defense official familiar with the OSC said a Hadrian loan of that magnitude could put the lending unit’s credibility in jeopardy with the incoming Congress, which would likely have to approve additional funds to allow it to continue issuing new loans.
“OSC is clearly a powerful tool to advance national security. But its ability to invest and access to long-term funding are tenuous,” the official said. “Some senior leaders seemingly want to use it as a pot of money for deals that exceed its mandate.”
Read More
In the past, Trump Jr. and his firm have said he does not discuss the companies he invests in with federal officials. In his public comments, he has shown a personal interest in defense tech and has criticized cronyism in defense spending.
The Office of Strategic Capital was also behind the decision to give hundreds of millions of dollars in loans to Vulcan Elements just months after Trump Jr.’s venture firm invested in the company.
Of the dozens of companies the Pentagon was considering funding at the time, Vulcan’s was the only deal brought forward by a top aide to the president, ProPublica previously reported. After defense officials got the White House request, they asked Pentagon staff to move at an unusually rapid pace, and staff worked late nights and with little sleep to get the loan through in a matter of weeks.
The Pentagon denied any preferential treatment, and Trump Jr. said he played no role in the deal.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Grand Theft Auto VI takes over Miami, including its art destinations
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Douglas Markowitz
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, a massive marketing campaign for the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI has transformed Miami—and the city’s art scene is coming along for the joyride.
On 13 October, the street art-focused Wynwood Walls museum unveiled a collaboration with the game’s developer Rockstar Games, inviting ten artists to create GTA-themed murals in and around the museum property. The museum also announced the partnership would include merchandising and free admission for all Miami-Dade County residents until the end of 2028, reversing a pandemic-era policy that saw tickets sold at the attraction for the first time.
The art-centric campaign is part of a massive marketing push around the game, which was released globally on 19 November to universal critical acclaim. Set in a satirical version of Miami called “Vice City”, the game world is an incredibly detailed virtual replica of the real city and the surrounding state of Florida (“Leonida”), complete with areas such as “Stockyard” replicating Wynwood with its street art and graffiti culture.
Demonstrating an extreme dedication to realism, Rockstar has even painstakingly replicated and renamed local landmarks such as the nightclub Club Space (“The Vault”), the beloved regional casual dining chain Flanagan’s (“Uncle Jack’s) and local art institutions such as the Pérez Art Museum Miami ("Future Leonida Art Museum", or "Flam") and the Wolfsonian–Florida International University design museum ("Hicksonian Museum of Art and Design"). Miami Beach’s Bass Museum of Art (“Vice City Museum of Art”) had its iconic Ugo Rondinone sculpture Miami Mountain (2016) turned into a monumental stack of emojis inside the game. (Unfortunately the current exhibition at the "Vice City Museum of Art", Karl Bergstrom: Diaspora, cannot be visited as the building is not currently accessible within gameplay.)
According to Jessica Goldman Srebnick, the Wynwood Walls museum’s chief executive and curator, Rockstar commissioned in-game murals from around 50 artists, many of whom have exhibited at the museum before. When the developer approached the museum to suggest a collaboration, it was a no-brainer. “Street art and gaming have a lot of shared cultural DNA, and they’ve influenced each other,” she says. The game’s creators “share our commitment to creativity, to supporting artists. They share our commitment and deep appreciation for the city of Miami. And I’m just really grateful that they are supporting something that provides more access to the arts.”
The murals in Wynwood, which will be on display until 1 January 2027, are similar to those featured in the game itself. A mural by the artist Queen Andrea, for instance, reads “Welcome to Vice City” in a curvy, neon-like font, while another by Ron English features a design with grenades in the shape of lightbulbs and the slogan: “There’s nothing more dangerous than a good idea.”
The project, as well as GTA’s larger presence in the city, has not been without controversy. The local newspaper Miami New Times reported on 10 November that one of the GTA murals had covered up a piece by the late artist Alex “Rect” Reyes, who finished the work shortly before his death in 2022. The wall had been considered a memorial by Reyes’s family and friends, who say they were not informed about its replacement. Goldman Global Arts, which owns the wall and museum, said in a statement to the New Times that it had offered Reyes’s crew a different wall to make amends.
Meanwhile, a joint partnership with Miami-Dade County and the Miami Heat professional basketball team has resulted in everything from player uniforms to the Kaseya Center arena in Downtown Miami being rebranded with “Vice City”. Massive crowds turned out for a Heat game on 18 November, the eve of the GTA VI’s release, to purchase custom merchandise that was only available at the arena. The total package, which includes lighting and signage inspired by the game at Miami International Airport and PortMiami, is valued at $3.9m according to a press release from the county government. Some officials have expressed alarm at the collaboration, with one county commissioner worried that the game is “depicting Miami like a murder capital”, according to the Miami Herald.
As for the benefits for the local art scene, perhaps gamers who visit GTA VI’s virtual “Vice City Museum of Art” will be inspired to seek out the Bass on their next visit to Miami Beach.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/trum.title: Court Orders Trump Media to Hand Over Truth Social Records in The Intercept Lawsuit
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/trum.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/trum.text:
The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation won a crucial victory against the Trump administration in court on Tuesday in a case challenging the president’s right to sell early access to his social media posts on Truth Social.
The ruling by Judge J. Paul Oetken in the Southern District of New York allows both organizations to seek limited discovery, offering a chance to peel back the layers on the president’s scheme to enrich himself through his public office. The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation can request records from the president’s private media company on both the operation of its six-figure early-access model and whether other media companies have purchased a subscription.
Truth Social is owned and operated by Trump Media & Technology Group, a company in which the president holds the largest stake in a trust controlled by his son, Donald Trump Jr. The early-access model, known as Truth API, requires subscribers to pay $60,000 to $100,000 a month. The service offers a first look at Trump’s posts — where, as the White House has acknowledged, he often makes official policy announcements.
The lawsuit argues that the premium service violates the First Amendment rights of the public and the media to enjoy equal access to official government information. According to the lawsuit, Trump has published about 11,000 posts or reposts on Truth Social since returning to office.
The ruling will allow the plaintiffs “to get some answers about how this scheme works,” said Nikhel Sus, chief counsel at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, who is representing the plaintiffs. The subscription service, he added, was “rolled out with minimal transparency as to how the actual functionality works and who has been subscribing to the service thus far.”
In October, The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation requested a preliminary injunction arguing that the president should be barred from posting on his personal platform, Truth Social, as long as the premium service is in effect.
Oetken has not ruled on the preliminary injunction. But his decision on Tuesday is a “positive step forward,” Sus said. “The court didn’t explicitly say that it thinks our claims have merit, but the fact that it ordered discovery, we think, indicates that the court doesn’t think our complaint is non-meritorious because otherwise it wouldn’t have granted discovery.”
David Bralow, The Intercept’s chief legal officer, agreed.
“We are grateful that the Court is allowing us to proceed with uncovering the nature of the scheme that violates our First Amendment rights,” Bralow wrote in a statement. “By continuing to allow President Trump to exclusively post official government announcements on Truth Social’s API, the President and the other defendants continue to provide preferential access to those who pay up to $100,000 a month to increase Mr. Trump’s personal wealth.”
Despite the initial victory, Sus noted, the court still has not ruled on the government’s motion to dismiss the case, nor the initial motion for a preliminary injunction. “So we still have to wait and see,” he said.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://citylimits.org/eight-months-afte.title: Eight Months After Policy Change, NYPD Still Doling Out Criminal Summonses to City’s Street Vendors
https://citylimits.org/eight-months-afte.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/eight-months-afte.text:
Share This Article
Despite changes in the law, the NYPD continues to issue violations as criminal fines—sending people to court, where immigrant street vendors are increasingly afraid to appear.
A street vendor who manages two halal food carts in the Midtown area says he’s received more than five criminal summonses since March of this year, when a city law decriminalizing certain fines for this sector took effect.
The vendor—who, for fear of retaliation from police, asked to go by the pseudonym “Samy,” a common name in Egypt where he’s from—said one of his new workers even quit after receiving a summonses, asking them to appear in one of the city’s criminal courts for operating the cart too close to a fire hydrant.
“He was brand new,” Samy, 59, said in Arabic through a translator, explaining his workers tend to be asylum seekers scared of any interaction with the criminal court. “He received only one ticket, one criminal ticket, and he never showed up again to work. He turned off his phone. He was not even responsive.”
Last year, the City Council took steps to decriminalize some street vending violations, recognizing the “severe collateral consequences” that a criminal summons can have on workers in the sector, which is largely powered by Black and brown immigrant New Yorkers.
However, on the streets—and in practice—implementing Local Law 122 has been more complicated. Eight months since it went into effect, NYPD officers are still issuing criminal summonses to vendors. According to the New York Office of Court Administration (OCA), about 180 of these citations have appeared in their records after the law was enacted in March.
According to the new law, those violations should instead be handled by the city’s venues for civil offenses, such as the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH).
The Street Vendor Project, an advocacy group that helped pass the Council’s decriminalization bill, estimates the numbers are even higher, with more than 350 of these criminal tickets.
“We are so tired,” Samy said. “We fought so hard for these changes to happen, for these laws to pass.”
The new law was supposed to eliminate misdemeanor criminal penalties for mobile food vendors and general vendors, reducing violations to civil penalties for infractions such as vending near building entrances, crosswalks, or prohibited streets.
It also removed imprisonment terms and capped fines. At the same time, violations of what’s known as “time, place, and manner” rules—like failing to wear or display a license, failing to produce books, among others—should now be considered civil infractions.
When asked, an NYPD spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the department “is continually training officers on the change in the law and which offenses are no longer eligible for a criminal summons.”
The law didn’t change NYPD’s powers to issue criminal court summonses for unlicensed vending in general.
“We are not criminals,” Samy said. “We are hard workers. We run the smallest businesses in the city. We should never be treated as criminals. We should never go to criminal court.”
Fear of appearing in court
The street vending industry in the city is mostly made up of immigrants, including many Latinos. A criminal fine can have serious consequences, especially as the federal government aggressively cracks down on immigration enforcement.
Some vendors getting criminal tickets are recent immigrants who are applying for asylum, according to advocates with the Street Vendor Project, who are too scared to appear in Criminal Court for fear of arrest.
On one recent occasion, the organization said, a street vendor left New York City altogether because he was afraid that the charge could follow him and he’d be deported.
According to vendors and their advocates, when vendors appear in court, judges usually dismiss their tickets. Still, the summonses carry not only an emotional burden—with potential immigration implications—but also an economic impact.
“It is really a big obstacle for a lot of people because for them to go to the court, they have to lose a whole day of work,” Samy explained. “So when they lose a shift, when they lose a day, they lose the pay for that one day. So there is a big loss of money and wages that happens.”
Mohamed Attia, the Street Vendor Project’s director, called on City Hall to ensure the new law is being implemented properly. The mayor’s office did not respond to a request for comment.
“The Mamdani administration made it clear throughout the campaign trail—and all the way to their first days in office at City Hall—that they support the street vendor reform; they support decriminalizing street vending, and the local law 122 that passed in 2025,” Attia said.
“We’re expecting City Hall to fulfill this promise, but also go above and beyond and remove the NYPD from street vendor enforcement and make sure that we have fair, equitable enforcement for street vendors, our smallest businesses.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-unifo.title: Amazon Workers Have Won a First North American Contract
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-unifo.author: Adam D. K. King
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-unifo.text:
Amazon Workers Have Won a First North American Contract
The binding agreement reached by British Columbia Amazon workers is a historic breakthrough after the company fought it tooth and nail. The union’s next task: build rank-and-file strength to enforce their contract and organize beyond the warehouse.
Amazon has spent years and enormous resources trying to prevent its North American workforce from unionizing. Even where workers have successfully organized, the retail giant has used everything from legal challenges to warehouse closures to frustrate their efforts to secure a first contract. Now, for the first time, workers at an Amazon facility in North America have a collective agreement.
On November 13, an independent arbitrator issued a three-year contract covering approximately eight hundred workers at Amazon’s YVR2 fulfillment center in Delta, British Columbia, a suburb of Vancouver. The workers are represented by Unifor Local 114, part of Canada’s largest private sector union.
The agreement represents an important breakthrough in the struggle to organize Amazon.
Unlike workers at Amazon’s Staten Island warehouse in New York, who remain without a contract, workers in British Columbia benefited from provincial labor laws that provide stronger remedies against employer interference and bargaining obstruction.
Yet the victory also presents a challenge. Having secured both union recognition and a first contract through labor board intervention, Unifor must now ensure the rank-and-file organization necessary to sustain its bargaining relationship with Amazon. Legal victories are essential, but they cannot substitute for organized worker power.
How Amazon’s Union Busting Backfired
The road to a first contract began with an organizing campaign launched in 2023. By May 2024, Unifor had applied to the British Columbia Labour Relations Board (BCLRB) for certification at YVR2. Amazon responded with a sophisticated anti-union campaign. According to the board’s subsequent decision, the company deployed a specialized management team, subjected employees to extensive anti-union messaging, and deliberately increased hiring to dilute union support.
The board found that Amazon had hired unnecessary additional workers with the purpose and effect of undermining the union’s organizing drive. It also concluded that the company’s pervasive anti-union campaign made it impossible to reliably determine employees’ wishes through a representation vote.
In July 2025, the board took the extraordinary step of granting Unifor remedial certification, recognizing the union as the workers’ bargaining representative without counting the ballots from the previously conducted vote.
Under the province’s Labour Relations Code, the board can certify a union when employer misconduct has made a fair representation vote impossible. The provision recognizes that traditional remedies, such as ordering employers to cease unlawful conduct or rerunning elections, may be insufficient to reverse the effects of union busting. Remedial certification effectively prevents employers from profiting from their own illegal interference.
Though Amazon’s challenge to the certification decision proved unsuccessful, its resistance did not end there.
In February 2026, the BCLRB ordered Amazon to provide what is likely to be over $1 million in back pay after finding that the company had unlawfully withheld wage increases from unionized employees while granting raises at other regional facilities.
Yet even after these defeats, Amazon continued resisting meaningful collective bargaining.
Negotiations began in late 2025, but ten bargaining sessions and subsequent mediation failed to produce an agreement. A central obstacle was Amazon’s insistence that Unifor surrender its ability to challenge the company’s productivity expectations.
According to the mediator’s findings, Amazon demanded that the union permanently waive its right to contest how quickly and intensively employees were required to work. The company indicated that it would never abandon this position. Brown concluded that the parties were unlikely to reach an agreement voluntarily and recommended binding arbitration.
Here, another distinctive feature of British Columbia labor law proved decisive. Section 55 of the province’s Labour Relations Code establishes a first-contract mediation and arbitration process. Where bargaining has broken down, the board can direct the parties toward a binding resolution rather than allowing an employer to indefinitely drag out negotiations.
In August, the BCLRB ordered the dispute be resolved through arbitration. Amazon challenged that decision as well, unsuccessfully seeking to halt a standard labor relations process it continues to characterize as “unfair.”
The resulting collective agreement demonstrates the importance of labor laws that do more than formally recognize workers’ right to unionize. While Amazon sought to thwart workers at every turn, crucial legislative protections ensured workers a defense.
A Contract That Challenges Amazon’s Control
The agreement provides tangible improvements for workers, including wage increases bringing the top hourly rate for regular warehouse employees to approximately C$29 by 2028, additional vacation for long-serving employees, enhanced severance protections, and guarantees concerning existing benefits. It gives the union a formal role in handling grievance procedures and access to binding arbitration to resolve disputes.
But the most consequential achievement may be the union’s ability to challenge Amazon’s control over the organization and pace of work.
Amazon’s business model depends on intensive surveillance and algorithmic management. Workers’ movements and productivity are continuously monitored through scanners and software, while management uses this information to evaluate performance and impose discipline.
At YVR2, Amazon employs a system called Structured Productivity Performance Review, which compares individual workers’ output against that of their peers. Employees falling within the bottom 5 percent of productivity can become subject to corrective measures, potentially culminating in termination.
Such systems create powerful incentives for speedup. Even without fixed production quotas, workers face pressure to continually increase their output to avoid falling behind their coworkers. The resulting competition can undermine workplace solidarity and encourage unsafe working practices.
Unifor sought to replace this approach with a more transparent work-measurement system incorporating ergonomic considerations, fatigue, and the physical demands of warehouse work.
The arbitrator declined to impose that alternative, concluding that insufficient evidence had been presented to establish that Amazon’s existing productivity system was unsafe.
Nevertheless, he also rejected Amazon’s attempt to insulate its productivity standards from union challenges.
Under the agreement, Amazon must provide advance notice of material changes to its productivity, quality, and inactive-time management systems, explain those changes, and meet with union representatives upon request. Such changes must also be safe.
Combined with contractual protections against unjust discipline and access to grievance arbitration, these provisions create opportunities to challenge how Amazon’s productivity expectations are applied and enforced.
The union has not won collective control over production, and Amazon retains considerable managerial authority. But the company can no longer treat every aspect of its productivity regime as an exclusively managerial concern beyond scrutiny.
The contract creates an enforceable mechanism through which workers can collectively contest decisions that previously confronted them as isolated individuals.
For a corporation whose labor-management strategy relies heavily on individualized monitoring, automated decision-making, and direct employer–employee communication, this represents an important breach in its system of workplace control.
Winning the Contract Is Only the Beginning
Amazon has made clear that it does not consider the matter settled.
In a November 13 statement, the company denounced the agreement as unfairly imposed, objected to mandatory union membership and dues, and complained that workers had not voted on the contract — all of course ignoring the litany of labor law violations that precipitated the “imposed” contract.
Amazon also continues to pursue legal challenges, while a separate employee application to decertify the union remains unresolved.
This ongoing decertification dispute raises a potential pitfall for Unifor’s victory.
Because certification and the first agreement were secured through labor board orders rather than a successful representation vote followed by a negotiated contract, the union faces the additional task of demonstrating its value to workers and building durable workplace power.
This in no way diminishes the legitimacy of the legal remedies; they operated to redress employer violations exactly as they should. But legal recognition alone cannot produce an active, democratic union capable of defending its members.
Unifor will need to develop strong workplace leadership, recruit and train stewards, involve members in enforcing the agreement, and demonstrate that collective representation can deliver improvements in their daily working lives.
The new grievance procedure will be particularly important. Challenging unjust discipline, unsafe productivity expectations, and arbitrary management decisions can help workers experience the practical benefits of union membership while building confidence in collective action.
This is especially important at Amazon, where employee turnover, workplace surveillance, and sophisticated anti-union messaging present formidable organizing challenges.
Unifor’s victory has created an institutional foothold inside one of the world’s most powerful corporations. Whether that foothold becomes the basis for a wider breakthrough will depend on workers’ ability to turn contractual rights into collective strength.
Amazon has lost an important battle. But its war against unionization is far from over. The next task is to ensure that this first contract becomes not simply a legal victory but the foundation of a durable, militant workplace union capable of challenging Amazon’s power from below.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Has Pedro Sánchez’s Luck Finally Run Out?
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Sebastiaan Faber, Bécquer Seguín
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Has Pedro Sánchez’s Luck Finally Run Out?
Spain’s progressive prime minister has defied political gravity over and over again. But this Sunday’s election might be his last act.
On November 13, two weeks before the elections that could spell the end of Spain’s progressive government, the YouTuber and podcaster Jordi Wild—known as the “Spanish Joe Rogan”—began releasing a series of long-form video interviews with the leading candidates vying to be the country’s next prime minister after votes are cast this Sunday.
First up was Ada Colau, the 52-year-old housing activist and former mayor of Barcelona, who heads up the Frente Amplio (FA), a newly created 15-party progressive front. “My son watches your videos all the time and said I absolutely have to go on your show,” she told Wild. Next was Alberto Núñez Feijóo, 65, the leader of the conservative Popular Party (PP), who agreed with Wild that any leader of a European country should speak English—only to add that he hadn’t “made any effort to learn it.” Wild finished his series with sitting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, the 54-year-old leader of the Socialist Party (PSOE), who for the past eight years has steered Spain through the Covid crisis, dared to defy Trump, NATO, and Israel on defense spending and Gaza, and managed to turn Spain into the highest-performing of Europe’s largest economies.
There was one candidate Wild did not interview: Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party. (When Wild asked him to succinctly define each of his political opponents, Sánchez called Colau “activist” and Feijóo “conservative.” Meanwhile, Abascal, he said, “should find a new tailor because his jackets are too tight.”) Wild explained that Abascal had canceled at the last minute, but not before his team had imposed demands that were as arbitrary as they were ridiculous, including exclusive proprietary rights over the interview.
This obsession with controlling all aspects of public appearances is standard fare for right-wing populist parties in Europe, who are quick to accuse other politicians of cowardice but wince at the possibility of a curveball. But Abascal’s attitude felt particularly bizarre for a program like Wild’s, whose followers—young, disenchanted men between the ages of 18 and 24—are catnip for the far right. And sure enough, Abascal paid a price for his miscalculation; over the next couple of days, Vox dropped nearly two points in the polls.
In another election year, Abascal’s podcasting choices might not have mattered so much. But this year, how Vox does could determine whether one of Europe’s last progressive governments hangs on to power—or whether the Spanish far right enters national government for the first time since the days of Franco.
As things stand, it looks like Vox will triumph, even without that podcast appearance. The final polls predict that the party will receive close to 18 percent of the vote, which will translate to some 60 representatives in the 350-seat Congress. Feijóo is projected to reach 31.5 percent—approximately 130 seats. While this is not enough for the conservative leader to govern on his own, a coalition with Vox would yield an absolute right-wing majority.
Sánchez, who for the last three years has presided over a precarious progressive coalition without a parliamentary majority, has a 25 percent chance to win the elections, but only a 10 percent chance of continuing on as prime minister. That’s because the parties to Sánchez’s left have imploded. Colau’s Frente Amplio is expected to get only around 10 seats, while Podemos, led by Irene Montero, will be lucky if it gets a single seat—a far cry from the 31 seats obtained in 2023 by Sánchez’s current coalition partner Sumar, led by Labor Minister Yolanda Díaz.
The elections this Sunday are seen by many as a referendum on Sánchez, who became prime minister in 2018 after ousting a conservative government via a no-confidence vote—a first in Spanish history. Until recently, he long seemed determined to serve the full four years of his term that the Constitution allows. Yet, in late September, Sánchez changed his mind as the country became awash in protest following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to the Vox leader), an elderly resident in Madrid who became the poster child of the housing and affordability crisis that has many Spaniards desperate—and furious. Housing prices in Spain have gone up by nearly 91 percent over the past decade, and nearly 31 percent since the beginning of 2024 alone, making the crisis especially acute for anyone looking to buy a home, renew their lease, or sign a new one. (Maricarmen was in many ways the exception that proved the rule: Though she was evicted because she couldn’t pay her rent, which skyrocketed after her apartment building was bought by a corporate landlord, only 8 percent of homes in Spain are owned by businesses. The overwhelming majority are owned by fellow Spaniards, many of whom were, up until the 2008 financial crisis, incentivized to purchase second or third homes.)
These cascading problems would seem to spell doom for Sánchez. But he is a political chameleon and skilled tactician who has often been described as the continent’s ultimate comeback kid. In 2023, he was down by more than eight points when he called for snap elections. To everyone’s but Sánchez’s surprise, he cut that lead by three points during the campaign and by another four on election day, winning just enough seats to cobble a coalition together and prevent the PP and Vox from forming a governing majority.
Now Sánchez is hoping that he can pull one more electoral rabbit out of the hat. In 2023, Sánchez mobilized voters’ fear of a far-right national government, and exploited the substance-free mediocrity of Feijóo’s campaign. He is trying to do the same in 2026, and is treating the campaign like a very high-stakes game of chess.
During his lone face-to-face debate with Feijóo on November 19, Sánchez appeared unusually measured, even meek, while an aggressive Feijóo pummeled him with false accusations and half-truths. (According to the Spanish fact-checking site Newtral, which analyzed more than 100 statements made during the debate, Feijóo made six false and four misleading statements and Sánchez only five misleading statements.) Confronted by his disappointed supporters, Sánchez later explained that his calm demeanor, allowing Feijóo to interrupt him time and again, was designed to appeal not to his base but to the large segment of voters who are still undecided.
However, Sánchez is facing a deeper level of anger at politics in general than he did three years ago. The protests that erupted in late September were unusual in that they were highly political but not associated with any one party. Behind them was a so-called “renters’ syndicate” (sindicato de inquilinas), a national network of local collectives organized in a loose federative structure that sought to defend their members’ interests by achieving political and economic reform from outside the party system. “The most important thing is that this be understood as the beginning of a period of struggle,” their 33-year-old Madrid spokesperson, Alicia del Río, a high school counselor and union organizer, said to the digital outlet El Salto. “With the idea of generating increasing economic harm to those who stockpile housing, to those who increase the price of our groceries, to those who want to lower our pensions or take away our time off.”
In addition to marches through central Madrid, the renters’ protests took the form of a weeks-long encampment occupying the city’s iconic Puerta del Sol plaza. The déjà-vu was unavoidable. Several of Spain’s parties to the left of Sánchez, including Podemos, emerged from a similar mass protest, the indignados, that took place 15 years ago. Since then, its promise of political reform has run aground in a quagmire of petty infighting, top-down decision-making, party splits, and tactical errors. Sumar, the party formerly led by Labor Minister Díaz, is one of the indignados movement’s most recent incarnations; but now, several years after its founding, the party has lost most of its political capital. And its most intelligent and visionary young star, the 43-year-old Pablo Bustinduy, who is currently the country’s minister of social rights, has declined to step into a leadership position—in no small part thanks to the extraordinary wear and tear that comes with that role. What’s left of Sumar has joined the Colau-led Frente Amplio. Podemos, meanwhile, has not. Now led by Montero (whose partner is Pablo Iglesias, the party’s cofounder), Podemos still claims the political mantle of the indignados. But while 10 years ago the party seemed poised to overtake Sánchez’s Socialists, this time around it may not make it into parliament at all.
The mass protests in response to the housing crisis were also unusual because they were not necessarily directed against the sitting government. In fact, when the renters’ syndicate called for a general strike on November 11, the first in the country since 2012, Sánchez openly supported it. (Although Spain’s Constitution protects the right to strike, the country’s top business lobby argued the protest was illegal because it was not related to labor rights. Feijóo, for his part, dismissed it as a “camouflaged campaign event.”)
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The irony of a sitting government’s supporting mass protests is symptomatic of this strange moment in Spanish politics. Although Sánchez and his left-wing coalition partners nominally govern the country, they often behave as though they are in the opposition. Part of public opinion seems to operate under the same assumption. Sánchez’s parliamentary weakness—he hasn’t been able to pass a new budget in years, for example—helps explain that paradox. So, too, does the fact that the political right still holds many levers of power. Hard-line conservatives control key parts of the judiciary, including the Supreme Court. The right also currently governs 14 of Spain’s 19 autonomous territories and dominates large swaths of the media. (In an attempt to correct the balance—and preemptively provide a progressive outlet should the right return to government—a new national TV channel, La Séptima, launched on November 5.)
The tactical advantage that Sánchez gained in early October by unexpectedly announcing new elections was shattered three weeks later when the country saw its second high-speed train wreck in a year, reaching a combined death toll of 115, with more than 300 injured. The causes of these accidents were, in many ways, structural: The partial liberalization of Spain’s high-speed rail has led to a 74 percent increase in passengers since 2019; meanwhile, maintenance costs have exploded, and repairs, as well as security system updates and redundancies, have lagged. The political aftermath was unavoidable: Óscar Puente, Spain’s transport minister and a Sánchez loyalist, resigned several weeks later.
During the two weeks of official campaigning, Sánchez has provided a slow drip of new policies he would pursue if reelected. He has proposed creating a public housing stock of 100,000 units and extending rent freezes, as well as providing €200 a year each for dental care and young adult sports vouchers. He has also proposed new taxes on the AI industry, luxury travel, and the “ultrarich.” Yet, when it comes to passing legislation and implementing policy, Sánchez’s track record, especially over the past three years, has been, at best, uneven. The progressive measures he has been able to pass during his eight years in power have resulted from pressure from his left-wing coalition partners and their constituencies in the street. With the parties to his left projected to be dramatically weakened on Sunday, that internal pressure will evaporate overnight. Sánchez’s other main vulnerability with voters includes a handful of corruption cases affecting several of his closest collaborators and party icons, and, dubiously, his wife and brother.
The parties to Sánchez’s right have seen a weak campaign and political program buoyed by the Europe-wide wave of anti-immigration sentiment. Feijóo, who tries to project moderation and centrism, has been compelled to don a populist outfit so as not to be outdone by his party’s right wing, which includes Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz-Ayuso as well as Oxford-trained aristocrat Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo. Beyond championing tax cuts and housing deregulation, Feijóo’s proposals include new anti-squatting legislation, stricter border controls, and cutting back sick leave benefits. Meanwhile, Abascal, who, in recent years, has purged many of Vox’s economic conservatives in favor of Milei-style libertarians, has landed on clearer and more disciplined messaging: “National Priority, Deregulation, Remigration.”
Whatever happens on November 29, the result of Spain’s elections will echo far beyond its borders. Sánchez’s ouster would be read as an ominous sign for France, Poland, and Italy, all of which will have national elections next year that far-right parties are poised to win. If Sánchez beats the odds again, however, his victory, alongside Lula’s in Brazil and the recent wave of Democrats in the United States, will signal, for many, just how useful social-democratic messaging is for stopping the advance of the far right.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-panel-set.title: NYC panel set to vote on $8 billion Queens casino design Monday
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-panel-set.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-panel-set.text:
A New York City panel is set to vote Monday on the proposed design of the Metropolitan Park and Hard Rock Hotel and Casino complex in Queens.
The city's Public Design Commission is scheduled to consider preliminary and final design approval for the more than $8 billion development adjacent to Citi Field in Willets Point. The project already has a state casino license.
New renderings for the planned casino were released last month. The designs drew more than three hours of public testimony in October before the panel postponed its vote, citing a need for more information about the project's stormwater management plan.
Supporters praised the project's potential to create tens of thousands of union jobs, add green space and improve the nearby 7 train station. Opponents, including the group Queens Anti-Casino, argued the development would strain local infrastructure and raise environmental justice concerns.
The Metropolitan Park project is one of three downstate casino projects licensed by the New York State Gaming Commission last year. Resorts World in Queens is undergoing an expansion at Aqueduct Racetrack, and a Bally’s casino is planned for Ferry Point Park in the Bronx.
Monday's meeting is scheduled for 2:30 p.m. at City Hall and will be livestreamed on the commission's YouTube channel. The public testimony period for the project has closed.
Metropolitan Park did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Gothamist.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Why are people captivated by this photo of a crowded Chris Bowen scowling? Is it the negative space?
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Blake Sharp-Wiggins explains it to Graham Readfearn
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Blake, I was at the back of the huge plenary hall in Antalya on Sunday at the end of the UN climate summit that overran by two days. For about 20 minutes, you could see from the panic on the stage that it wasn’t going well.
I only had an old iPhone, was a long way back, and remember thinking: “I’d love a long lens to see the expression on their faces.”
  
Then came this incredible picture of Chris Bowen looking like all his Christmases had come at once and every present was a jumper he hates. Why can’t I stop looking at it?
It’s about the natural geometry and negative space in the frame.
It’s tragedy and resignation. On reflection my Christmas jumper analogy probably wasn’t the best. It’s planet-defining stuff, all of this. Sorry, what? Negative space?
That’s the area above his head with nothing in it. It’s shaped like a V and it’s drawing your eyes down to this amazing expression that I’ve actually seen Bowen make before. He does it occasionally.
So it might just be a lucky shot?
Yes and no. Not many other photographers have that frame. If the photographer, Murad Sezer, had been a few metres to one side it would have been really different. But he made choices about where to be and what to focus on. Technically, though, it’s not perfect. The lady on the far left …
She is Australia’s head of international negotiations.
Well, she’s cropped in half. That’s not perfect. And there’s a guy with the top of his head chopped off.
 
This is starting to sound bad.
Not really. Murad wasn’t lucky. He would have been looking at body language and the people behind Bowen and then shooting in bursts. I’ve seen the other frames and there’s only a few that catch that expression. We can forgive the cropping because it perfectly tells the story of the moment and what Bowen must have been thinking.
 
That it’s all gone to shit and can this all be over?
 
Well, yes. But the people above him look as though they’re still trying to work things out, actually. So there’s intrigue. Was everything lost at that point?
 
Maybe. The picture was taken before the plenary had started properly. I remember thinking, this looks as though the Australians know they don’t have consensus.
Consensus?
Bowen was president of negotiations and the little sign in front of him seems perfectly placed for the picture. He had to get more than 190 countries – rich and poor, petrostates, fossil fuel producers and low-lying countries that are being particularly smashed by the climate crisis – to agree not to disagree and to accept a pact.
Those of us in the room only knew for sure they hadn’t reached consensus once the meeting got going and countries started interjecting. It was high drama. Consensus is not quite the same as unanimity but it’s close.
So those people behind Bowen?
I thought you were explaining this to me? They’re political and department staff from Australia. Negotiators, department experts and there’s a senior media adviser in there – she’s second from the right. All exhausted after two weeks and days of all-night negotiations. With so much on the line, I don’t think I would have fancied being any of them.
There’s another brilliant frame from the same day from Khalil Hamra for Associated Press. Again Bowen is wearing an unfortunate expression but this time he’s being chased by a crowd of people with their microphones out, as though he’s Britney Spears. The frames seem to reflect the sentiment that Cop didn’t deliver for the planet.
Well, like the climate, it did all get a bit “toxic”. But we can’t end this on a bad pun. There’s going to be some serious questions asked about how these meetings are run so we secure better climate agreements and don’t have more pictures of ministers who just got lost in the game. Oops, I did it again.
Stop now.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Frida Kahlo-inspired health initiative and Ukrainian veterans exhibition among winners of prize celebrating innovative cultural projects
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Rachel Kubrick
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The charity Art Explora has revealed the five winners of the 2026 edition of its Académie des beaux-arts European Award, which recognises innovative work by non-profit arts and culture organisations in Europe. They are Polish performing arts foundation Jazdaa Polska!, Spanish art and health organisation Cultura en Vena, the French library charity Bibliothèques Sans Frontières, UK literary organisation London Writers Centre and Slovakian theatre company RAMAGU. The organisations were awarded funds ranging from €30,000-50,000, shared from a total £180,000.
The winners were announced at an award ceremony at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London on the evening of 24 November. Each of them, apart from RAMAGU—which won an audience choice award—was selected by an international jury, which included several members of the Académie des beaux-arts in Paris, such as the illustrator Emmanuel Guibert and the sculptor Eva Jospin; Vanja Kaludjercic, the director of the International Film Festival Rotterdam; and Antonija Letinić, a cultural development consultant in Croatia. Frédéric Jousset, the French entrepreneur and founder of Art Explora, was also a juror.
Cultura en Vena, who has been awarded €40,000, will puts the funds towards its Arte Ambulatorio project, which brings reproductions of works of art and other forms of creative programming into hospital spaces. The new phase of the project will involve an exhibition inspired by the work of Frida Kahlo, as well as live music sessions and creative writing workshops for children. Previous Arte Ambulatorio interventions focused on the work of the Spanish artists Francisco Goya and Joaquín Sorolla.
According to the organisation, “Frida Kahlo’s artistic universe offers a powerful entry point into themes closely connected to the hospital experience: the body, pain, vulnerability, identity, resilience, emotional expression and care.”
“Cultura en Vena takes art as seriously as care,” Jousset tells The Art Newspaper. He says the jury was convinced by “their rigour”. “They measure their impact and keep improving each exhibition based on patients’ and staff feedback,” he continues. “With over 23,000 peopkeople reached last year, they are one of the leading voices in arts and wellbeing in Spain.”
Bibliothèques Sans Frontières, meanwhile, will put its €50,000 award towards its L’autre retour project. The initiative involves workshops within which Ukrainian veterans are invited to draw, read and write with members of their community outside of a clinical environment, in an effort to help with reintegration after the military. The charity then plans to tour some of the works in Ukraine, as well as show them at the European Commission in Brussels.
“This project shows art as an act of rebuilding,” Jousset says.
The additional funded projects include developing touch-based choreography with blind and partially-sighted people in Poland (Jazdaa Polska!), making Lewisham in London the UK’s first “Borough of Literature” (London Writers Centre), and creating documentary theatre with minority groups in rural Slovakia (RAMAGU).

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/icc-.title: Why a Case Against ICC Sanctions Is a Major Victory for Palestine Human Rights Work
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/icc-.author: Noah Hurowitz
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/24/icc-.text:
A federal judge on Monday ruled that the Trump administration may not punish Americans for sharing evidence of Israeli war crimes with the International Criminal Court. The ruling also blocked the administration from meting out punishments for sharing information with three sanctioned Palestinian human rights groups and a prominent United Nations official.
The Monday ruling is the broadest challenge yet to an executive order issued by President Donald Trump in the early days of his second term that has been used by U.S. officials to issue sanctions against the ICC; the Palestinian groups al-Haq, al-Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights; and U.N. special rapporteur Francesca Albanese.
The order, which came as a result of a lawsuit filed in July by Democracy for the Arab World Now, or DAWN, and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, is the latest setback to efforts by the Trump administration to undermine the efforts by the ICC, Albanese, and others to hold Israel accountable for crimes against humanity.
“This landmark ruling dismantles a core part of Trump’s ICC draconian sanctions regime,” said Omar Shakir, executive director at DAWN. “The court has affirmed that every American has the constitutional right to advocate for justice on Palestine without fear of reprisal.”
While previous rulings against Trump’s executive order applied more narrowly — including an October preliminary injunction in the ICC case that prevented punishments against the plaintiffs — this is the first ruling against the sanctions that protects all Americans.
“The main difference is that this was expanded to be universal, meaning it doesn’t just protect the people who filed the lawsuit in the first place,” Michael Schaeffer Omer-Man, the Israel-Palestine director for DAWN, told The Intercept. “It was kind of expected that they would make the preliminary injunction permanent, but the universal part is huge.”
A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a legal filing earlier this month, attorneys for Trump argued that his original executive order did not represent a restriction on free speech.
Another previous ruling that applied narrowly came in a case brought by a pair of university professors who challenged the administration’s prohibition on working with the ICC. Joseph Pace, a lawyer for DAWN and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, said this ruling also helped overcome some of the limitations in the professors’ successful case.
“It didn’t stop the administration from enforcing the sanctions against anyone else,” he said, of the decision in the professors’ case. “Nor did that decision say anything about the Palestinian NGOs or Albanese” — neither of which had been sanctioned yet at the time of the ruling.
“The permanent injunction, though, is what’s called a ‘universal injunction,’” Pace told The Intercept. “That means the government can’t penalize anyone for providing (or receiving) First Amendment-protected services to or from ICC, Albanese, and the NGOs.”
“Challenging These Crimes”
In his ruling, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman found that the so-called services provision of Trump’s order — which threatened penalties for anyone “providing services” to the ICC, Albanese, or the three Palestinian NGOs — was unconstitutional because it undermined the First Amendment rights of people seeking to provide non-financial services to human rights advocates.
In a statement, Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide co-founder Anna Marie Stenberg said the ruling by Furman provided immediate clearance for her organization and others to resume work with the ICC, Albanese, and the three Palestinian organizations.
“We challenged Trump’s Executive Order on the ICC because we refused to let his regime intimidate us into silence while it used our tax dollars to fund crimes against humanity,” Stenberg said. “This victory means that others can join us in challenging these crimes without fear of punishment for exercising their First Amendment rights. Ordinary people have a right to seek justice, and our government cannot take that right away.”
Trump’s Executive Order 14203, issued in February 2025, called for financial penalties against the ICC under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. It barred Americans from providing financial assistance or services to further the court’s activities. Trump’s order explicitly cited the court’s investigations into Israel as a justification for the sanctions.
The order led to sanctions by the Trump administration against Albanese, who has consistently drawn the ire of pro-Israel officials for pursuing investigations into Israeli war crimes. The sanctions barred her from entry to the U.S. and froze her assets in the country. Albanese challenged the sanctions and a judge threw them out in May, but they were reinstated later that month.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://citylimits.org/east-harlem-resta.title: East Harlem Restaurant Reopens After Two Months Amid Subway Construction Woes
https://citylimits.org/east-harlem-resta.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/east-harlem-resta.text:
Share This Article
Los Panteras Negras, which serves classic Mexican food, reopened on Nov. 15. But the owners say they had no income during the two months they were closed, and that the incident cost them around $60,000 in repairs.
Los Panteras Negras, a family-run restaurant in East Harlem, was forced to close for two months after Second Avenue Subway construction broke a gas line in front of the eatery—and its owners say they were left to cover roughly $60,000 in repair costs.
Bonifacio Cortés and Valentín Cortéz—who are brothers, despite the slight spelling difference in their last names—have run the restaurant together since 2018. They say workers building the second phase of the Second Avenue Subway ruptured the gas pipe serving their building on Sept. 11.
“We arrived and found out there was no gas, that the pipe had been broken,” Cortés said to City Limits. The brothers say they asked the construction crew what had happened and were told only that it would be fixed later.
The pipe was repaired that same weekend, but the problems didn’t end there. When a technician came to reconnect the gas that week, he detected a leak at another point in the building’s system and refused to approve it. The building’s gas lines then had to be repaired, and the plumbing work and inspections added weeks to the closure.
In a statement to City Limits, an MTA spokesperson said excavation crews discovered a second pipe in front of the restaurant and believed it to be abandoned, since records showed only one active gas line in front of the building.
“That turned out to not be the case, and the live gas line was accidentally struck,” the spokesperson said, saying the MTA worked with Con Edison to resolve the issue on Sept. 14, and that subsequent delays to restoring service were due to “advanced long-standing corrosion of the interior gas line.”
“The extended closure is because of the poor condition of the building, which was not a result of MTA work,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
Still, the snafu has cost the brothers, who said they paid for much of the repair work themselves. “It was my own savings, which I’ve worked for my whole life,” Cortés said.
The Second Avenue Subway’s second phase will extend the Q line about 1.5 miles north along Lexington Avenue from 96th Street to 125th Street, with new stations at 106th, 116th and 125th Streets. The project is expected to cost nearly $7 billion and open in 2032, and will serve an estimated 300,000 commuters each day, according to the MTA.
Merchants and community leaders have worried for years about what the construction would do to Second Avenue. City Limits reported in 2018 on how residents feared East Harlem shops would suffer as many on the Upper East Side did during the first phase of the project, which extended the Q line from 63rd to 96th Street.
While the extended train line has provided a boost to businesses now that it’s up and running, years of construction were disruptive, and many local businesses closed or relocated. Businesses that stayed open saw revenue fall by as much as 30 percent, then-Councilmember Ben Kallos said at the time.
Work on the second phase of the subway expansion further north kicked off last year.
Los Panteras Negras, which serves classic Mexican food, reopened on Nov. 15. But the brothers say they had no income during the two months they were closed, though the building’s costs continued. They have built up a loyal customer base over eight years, and Cortés said patrons kept calling to ask when the restaurant would reopen.
Two local City Council members who represent Harlem, Shanel Thomas-Henry and Elsie Encarnacion, published an op-ed in September calling for the MTA to establish a fund to support small businesses impacted by the ongoing construction.
Cortés said he has looked for financial help but found little. He said city agencies keep sending him to other departments to see if he qualifies for assistance. “There’s nothing,” he said.
