https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: “Grand Theft Auto” Is the “Mona Lisa” of Video Games
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Grand Theft Auto Is the Mona Lisa of Video Games
It is technically perfect in its rendition of imperfection, evocative in a way that can’t be explained and must be experienced. And it can be experienced on many different levels.
“Grand Theft Auto” Is the “Mona Lisa” of Video Games
It is technically perfect in its rendition of imperfection, evocative in a way that can’t be explained and must be experienced. And it can be experienced on many different levels.
Grand Theft Auto VI, the sprawling new video game released last week by Rockstar Games, is the latest edition of the most lucrative media franchise on Earth. How lucrative? It made an estimated $3.8 billion on its first day. That’s bigger than the Avengers. It’s bigger than Harry Potter and the Transphobic Author. It’s bigger than the Super Bowl. It’s the biggest single thing in culture right now. And that appears to be confusing a lot of people who don’t play video games. For the uninitiated, GTA is essentially a sandbox crime simulator. It allows you to steal cars, sell drugs, and run over pedestrians as you flee from the cops you haven’t yet shot. It allows you to stick up a Waffle House, drag an ATM through the streets until it breaks open, and murder every civilian in an only lightly fictionalized rendition of the state of Florida.
The fact that this is the most popular thing on the planet seems to be scrambling many brains. I keep seeing the same question from non-gamers: Why? Why has this video game broken containment and landed in the center of American and even global public discourse? Why does it make so much money? Why is it everywhere?
I feel like I am well situated to answer these questions, because, while I’m a normal American dad with a wife and children and a full-time job and all the other indicia of normal adult responsibility, I’m also an avid gamer. Most people who play video games will buy only one or two a year; I probably buy a new game (often on sale) every six to eight weeks. I generally find at least 10 hours a week to play them—though really, the weeks when I only play 10 hours are, like, “election week” or “a week when a hurricane knocked out my power for days.”
So, with my bona fides out of the way: the first thing I tell non-gamers about GTA, or any video game, is that “it’s art.” Thinking about GTA as art helps to explain everything else that’s happening around it, because GTA is the Mona Lisa of this art form. It is technically perfect in its rendition of imperfection. It is evocative in a way that can’t be explained and must be experienced. And it can be experienced on many different levels. Some people want to see the Mona Lisa just to say that they’ve seen it. Some people will see it and not get what all the fuss is about (the French call those people “Americans”). Some people will see it and feel moved to their core. The same thing happens with GTA: It has a fairly linear “Bonnie and Clyde” type of story with a couple of different endings, but no two people will experience GTA in exactly the same way.
Of course, the Mona Lisa isn’t going to pull out a gun and start shooting paintballs at the other portraits. Nor is she going to remove her top and start shaking her money-maker. So let’s get into that. Yes, GTA is violent and hypersexualized. There is a lot of shooting, there are a lot of boobs and penises, and all the violence and sex is delivered with a steady stream of foul language and crude humor. If you want to be mad at the game, the game will give you something to be mad about, no matter your politics. Indeed, right now the people who are most mad at the game are the white-wing manosphere. The game tracks the relationship between the two main characters (who are in a cis-heteronormative relationship) and essentially encourages you to be a “good boyfriend/girlfriend.” The notion of being nice to a woman has made the manosphere lose its mind. Oh no, the game gives you the option to buy flowers for your girlfriend as part of a quest! Men are doomed! You can also not buy her flowers, or you can, I assume, murder the flower-shop guy and take the flowers (but I didn’t try to do that because I am a normal freaking person whose masculinity is not threatened by showing affection).
Just like the sex—or, in the case of the manosphere, the “acknowledging that a woman is a human being”— the violence in GTA is going to turn a lot of people off. But here’s the thing I think most non-gamers do not understand: GTA isn’t the most violent video game on the market. It’s not in the top 10 violent video games that are broadly popular right now. I wouldn’t even rank GTA VI as the most violent video game I’ve played this year. It’s also not the most sexually explicit game I’ve played recently: Baldur’s Gate 3 (a role-playing game that won Game of the Year in 2023) allows you to play with your characters fully nude, if you want to. It famously lets you have sex with a bear.
GTA is not popular because of the violence or sex. The thing that makes GTA popular is the agency you have over the violence. Yes, you can run over pedestrians, but you can also not do that. You can shoot all the cops in the head as you blast your way out of a bank with cash stuffed in the duffel bag, or you can carefully plan your heist so that you trip no alarms and get away without firing a shot. You can’t play the game as a pacifist (you are a criminal; you will be committing crimes; the authorities will try to stop you from committing crimes; this will often lead to violence), but your ultimate body count is your own and reflects your choices, not the game’s.
It’s that agency that makes GTA a totally different experience from other games that are facially far more violent and bloody. If you put me in an average mission in the popular first-person shooter Call of Duty, I’m going to kill a lot of people. The game will call those people “terrorists” because I’m not supposed to feel bad about killing them, but it will give me no success condition other than murdering every terrorist in the compound. In GTA, by comparison, there was an early mission where my friend was kidnapped by odious redneck pig farmers. They were coded as rednecks so that a certain type of person (namely me) wouldn’t feel bad should violence become necessary. Once I freed him, the game gave me the option of
- Quietly sneaking away,
- Stealing their drugs and sneaking away, or
- Stealing their drugs and their heavily guarded money stash, and murdering every redneck in the compound.
I went with option 3. GTA is popular not because option 3 exists—option 3 exists in pretty much every video game. GTA is popular because options 1 and 2 also exist, so when you choose option 3 you feel it. It makes the killing more of a personal choice than a gameplay mechanic. Most games allow you to kill; GTA is a success because you don’t have to.
Choice and consequence over murder or mercy is not unique to GTA. In fact, I’ve played a lot of games with far more difficult and engaging murder choices than “kill rednecks, yes/no?” But what makes GTA truly special, and a cultural phenomenon rather than simply a very good video game, is that it is a satirical take on us: America in the 2020s. The game is not set in medieval Europe. There are no dragons or witches. It is set in only lightly fictionalized Florida. If you walk down the street in the GTA’s main city (called “Vice City”), you will feel like you’re walking around Miami.
The game cost well over a billion dollars and 13 years to make, and part of that budget went toward sending game developers to Miami and around Florida to just watch, observe, and report back. It’s reactive in a way never before seen: Random characters will be having random conversations that don’t involve you, and react as one might expect them to if you pull a gun on them: most will run; some will fight; some will just shrug and be like “joke’s on you, I’m broke.”
You will see every body type, fashion choice, race, color, or creed in the game that you might see on any street in America. You’ll hear music blaring out of certain stores. You’ll see car accidents that don’t involve the player at all. One random character tried to steal my car (it didn’t work out well for him).
All of this detail allows GTA to do what only the best art or satire can do: hold a mirror up to our society and allow us to look at it. The game reminded me of the very first popular movies: They weren’t silent films or mime acts; they were slices of real life. Somebody would put a camera on a busy street corner for three minutes, and then show the footage in a theater. People would flock to see these “moving pictures,” because people are always fascinated to see what we look like to others. Thousands of technological revolutions later, and GTA is essentially doing the same thing: They’ve basically plopped a camera on the state of Florida, and allowed players to be dropped in the middle of it and drive around. The game is not about committing crimes. The game is about America, from the perspective of outsiders (Rockstar, the developers, are a Scottish company). It might be the equivalent of a funhouse mirror, but it’s still a mirror. The game is a cultural phenomenon because it’s about the culture in a way that Star Wars or Avatar can never be.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
And it might be the last game of its kind. First of all, no other game can be like GTA, because no other game studio has essentially infinite money and resources to spend 13 years and a billion dollars making a single-player video game. Only Rockstar can do this financially, and only Rockstar has the talent to put those near-infinite resources to good use, because of its experience making past GTA games. While Rockstar will certainly make GTA VII someday, I think by the time it does, artificial intelligence will have changed the industry to the point that the cultural verisimilitude will be lost. Rockstar “hand-crafted” this game: If there is a dildo on somebody’s bedside table, it’s because some developer placed it there to give the character who owns the bed a little more flavor. If there are two randos on a stoop complaining about menopause, it’s because a human writer wrote out a menopause conversation and then human voice actors performed the scene.
I fear that AI will take that personalization away from future games, even GTA. I fear that the next GTA game will be an AI’s vision of the culture, not the vision of the 4,700 or so people who work for Rockstar. (Rockstar also appears to be on the cutting edge of… union busting, so I can’t imagine that the company will resist the siren’s call of AI for long.) I fear that the next game in 2040 or whenever will be an AI parody of a human parody of real life, and while I’m sure that GTA VII will be as technically groundbreaking as GTA VI, I worry that a copy of a copy can never be that good.
But that’s a problem for 60-year-old me. Forty-eight-year-old me is lucky enough to have this piece of art and to understand its value in real time. If you have the means to play GTA VI (and at this point having the means involves spending upwards of $600 on a console and $70 bucks on a video game, which I acknowledge is a rapacious cost for “an experience”), I honestly encourage you to give it a whirl. I mean, if you’re going to buy a plane ticket to Paris, you’re going to go to the Louvre, right?

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-l.title: NYC Council looks for colleges to testify about sexual assault procedures
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-l.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-l.text:
The New York City Council is calling on the presidents of the city’s 10 largest colleges and universities to testify under oath about their handling of sexual assaults on campus at a hearing next month.
Council Speaker Julie Menin said the lawmakers will be taking an investigative approach at the Dec. 8 hearing, questioning school leaders on sexual assault reporting procedures, how schools investigate allegations, what disciplinary actions are taken against those found responsible and other issues. The Council is also inviting New Yorkers to testify at the hearing about their experiences.
“The point of the hearing is to help inform our decision-making in terms of legislation,” she said. “We believe legislation is needed, but in terms of what those legislative fixes are, that is the point of the hearing, to basically hear relevant testimony, to take that back and then work on some legislative solutions.”
There were 1,100 sexual assault complaints reported in across the city's 10 largest schools in 2024 — a figure Menin called “unacceptable” — according to data gathered under the New York State “Enough is Enough” law, which requires that colleges adopt standardized policies regarding sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence and stalking. The 10 largest schools are Columbia University, NYU, City University of New York, Fordham University, St. John's University, Pace University, Touro University, The New School, Mercy University and Yeshiva University.
The hearing comes nearly three months after a former Cornell University student, known as Jane Doe in court filings, filed a lawsuit alleging she had been gang raped by members of a fraternity while attending the school, and that Cornell had mishandled the case.
“This is an urgent issue,” Menin said, citing state data. “The fact that there are 1,100 complaints just at these 10 largest universities alone in one year, is shocking. And so it's very deeply concerning, and so we really wanna get to the bottom of what can be done about this.”
Menin said there’s been an “unbelievable amount of sign-up and interest from current students, former students, women’s groups,” and others. A finalized list of which school presidents will be testifying will be published next week, she said.
Spokespeople for the presidents of the New School and Mercy University confirmed to Gothamist they plan to testify. Messages to spokespeople for the other schools had not yet returned messages sent Tuesday afternoon asking if they plan to participate in the hearing.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Frieze Los Angeles reveals 102 exhibitors for 2027 edition
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The eighth edition of Frieze Los Angeles will welcome 102 exhibitors under the sprawling white tent on the grounds of the Santa Monica Airport. The exhibitor list, as in previous years, includes heavy local representation—with more than one-third of participants operating a space in Los Angeles.
The roster includes established Los Angeles galleries such as Jeffrey Deitch, Regen Projects, David Kordansky, Château Shatto, Commonwealth and Council, Anat Ebgi, Night Gallery, the Pit and Roberts Projects. Four younger Los Angeles galleries will make their debuts in the Focus section for emerging galleries: Megan Mulrooney, Rajiv Menon Contemporary, House of Seiko and Zodiac Pictures. Erin Christovale from the Hammer Museum will curate this section.
International blue-chip galleries returning to Frieze Los Angeles include Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Pace, White Cube, Perrotin, Gladstone, Almine Rech, Thaddaeus Ropac and Sprüth Magers. First-time exhibitors include Gallery Wendi Norris from San Francisco, Franklin Parrasch in New York, G Gallery in Seoul, Newchild in Antwerp, and Yehudi Hollander-Pappi and Danielian in Brazil.
A handful of prominent galleries will not be returning after taking part in recent editions, like Berggruen Gallery from San Francisco, Ortuzar and Tina Kim Gallery in New York, Mendes Wood DM and Nara Roesler from Brazil, Southern Guild from Cape Town and Timothy Taylor from London. Turnover year-over-year remains around 28% for a second consecutive year, amid stable overall exhibitor numbers.
Visitors to the fair will be greeted at the entrance by a new work by the Los Angeles-based artist rafa esparza called Queercancha, painted across two adobe panels mounted on chrome steel, drawing on Southern California’s culture of lowrider cruising.
Amid a boom following the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic, art dealers from all over the world began setting up shop in the Los Angeles area. However, many of those outposts have since closed alongside local dealerships—most recently, the Landing on Jefferson Boulevard. Along with a global market downturn, many local businesses were hurt by the devastating 2025 wildfires that nearly saw that year’s edition of Frieze Los Angeles cancelled. A handful of galleries have closed their local spaces and shifted their attentions to New York, including Southern Guild and Pietro Alexander.
This may be one of the final years the fair will be held at the Santa Monica Airport; the facility is scheduled to close permanently to aviation at the end of 2028 for conversion into a public park.

https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-body.title: Brooklyn body shop owner charged with bilking drivers in illegal tow truck scheme
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-body.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-body.text:
A Brooklyn bodyshop owner preyed on car crash victims for years, using a fleet of unlicensed tow trucks to haul wrecked vehicles that he held hostage while charging thousands of dollars in bogus storage fees, prosecutors charged Tuesday.
The Brooklyn district attorney charged Steven Ventura, 35, with running the operation out of State to State Automotive on Atlantic Avenue, which closed last year after several people filed complaints to police about the shop. Prosecutors say he equipped illegal tow trucks with police scanners to find crashes across Bedford-Stuyvesant and Crown Heights in 2024 and 2025.
When one of the company’s drivers would find a crash victim, the tow truck operator would allegedly urge the car’s owner to send their vehicle to the Atlantic Avenue shop for repairs. Once there, Ventura and his team would hold onto the car and illegally demand the vehicle’s owner pay $150 in daily storage fees that would often add up to more than $10,000, prosecutors said.
Ventura was arrested in Osceola County, Florida, on Nov. 13. He and his business face 29 counts, including grand larceny, scheming to defraud and illegally equipping a motor vehicle with a radio that scans frequencies used by police. Prosecutors allege at least 12 people fell victim to the scheme.
Ventura pleaded not guilty and was released with orders to come back in February. He smiled at a TV camera as he left the building.
His arrest is law enforcement's latest effort to clamp down on the growing ranks of illegal tow truck drivers in New York City.
A Gothamist investigation published in February identified more than 700 unlicensed tow trucks operating on city streets. In 2024, the owner of another illegal tow truck company, Christian Lugo, ordered a shooting that led to the death of a rival tower. Lugo is serving 19 years in prison. Last month, the driver of a tow truck that lacked a medallion or company information, which is required by law, ran a red light and crashed into two children crossing a Queens street. The children survived the crash, according to police.
It’s not clear how many unlicensed tow truck drivers worked for Ventura, though Gothamist routinely spotted unlicensed tow trucks and other vehicles with Florida license plates coming and going from State to State Automotive.
Sara-Lee Ramsawak, one of the victims identified in a criminal complaint against the shop, alleged Ventura towed her car after she crashed on Pacific Street in 2024. He promised to repair her ride within three weeks, according to prosecutors. Instead, he stalled for more than six months while charging $150 a day in storage fees, leading to a bill of $30,000.
Ramsawak confronted Ventura at the shop as police radio frequencies blared from the speakers.
"I wasn't really that scared,” she said. “My preference to try to get my vehicle back and then try to get justice probably overtook any sort of fears that I may have had.”
Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said more tow operations could face criminal penalties for towing schemes like Ventura’s.
"This case is indicative of wider lawlessness in the towing industry and should put unscrupulous operators on notice: the NYPD and my office are watching and attempts to defraud motorists will lead to consequences," he said in a statement.
Councilmember Justin Sanchez of the Bronx, who chairs the city's sanitation committee, said that unlicensed towers are also openly operating in his borough.
"Just as it's felt in Brooklyn, we see dirty work by towing companies every day in the Bronx. It's time for our city to get it under control and clean it up," Sanchez said.
Sanchez said he plans to introduce legislation stripping towing oversight from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which employs a small team of civilian inspectors. He wants to turn over control to the Business Integrity Commission, which has law enforcement authority and was formed to regulate the once notoriously corrupt and deadly private waste-hauling industry.
A spokesperson for the commission said it would review Sanchez’s legislation once it’s introduced.

https://gothamist.com/news/goodbye-kitty.title: Goodbye Kitty: Preparation underway for a windy Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in NYC
https://gothamist.com/news/goodbye-kitty.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/goodbye-kitty.text:
It could be Goodbye Kitty for Macy’s Centennial Thanksgiving Day Parade.
The National Weather Service is forecasting a tempestuous Thanksgiving Day in New York City, with rain, flooding and strong winds. The agency issued a high wind watch for the metro area from 10 a.m. until after midnight. Weather conditions could affect the parade, which marks its 100th anniversary, especially for the event’s roughly 100 inflatables.
“It’s going to be a stormy Thanksgiving Day,” National Weather Service meteorologist Bryan Ramsey said.
While a few inches of precipitation could dampen the parade starting in the morning, rain hasn’t stopped crowds in past years. The serious issue is the wind.
The weather service predicts wind speeds of up to 35 mph, with gusts reaching up to 60 mph. Winds at those speeds can blow down trees and power lines and make travel very difficult.
”With the high wind watch in effect, it's not a warning yet, but that means damage is likely and strong winds,” Ramsey said.
While marching bands, dancers, performers and floats can go on rain or shine, the weather conditions could be bad news for Joe Cool and Woodstock, and the many other character inflatables. As a safety precaution, if winds exceed 23 mph or wind gusts are more than 34 mph, giant balloons are grounded or flown lower.
The wind speed precautions are the result of an incident nearly 30 years ago when high winds caused the Cat in the Hat balloon to collapse after running into a lamppost, resulting in four injuries, with one paradegoer in a coma for 24 days, as the New York Times reported at the time.
The final call won’t be made until the morning of the parade, when organizers check conditions and consult with city agencies. Ramsey said that even two days before the event is still too early to tell how the weather will manifest.
The 2.5-mile parade is scheduled to step off from West 77th Street at 8:30 a.m., then march along Central Park West to Columbus Circle, where the procession will moves east to continue south down Sixth Avenue and finish at Macy’s Herald Square.

https://gothamist.com/news/queens-driver.title: Queens drivers give thanks as Van Wyck work wraps ahead of busy season at JFK Airport
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-driver.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-driver.text:
The state transportation department has wrapped up its long-awaited expansion of the Van Wyck Expressway, just in time for Thanksgiving travel at JFK Airport.
The six-year, $1.4 billion project came after decades of other construction work on the notoriously traffic-choked Queens highway. Crews added new lanes, entrance and exit ramps, and replaced or restored 23 bridges in an effort to reduce gridlock.
“I thought I was never going to see this,” Sandy Contreras, 36, who works at JFK Airport said on a recent afternoon. Contreras said the new roadway has shaved 30 minutes off his hour commute. “I'm glad I finally got to witness this.”
A new HOV lane on the highway open only to buses, taxis and cars carrying at least two people could reduce driving time by up to 25 minutes, Gov. Kathy Hochul declared at a ribbon cutting last week.
The governor’s promise was at least partially true last Friday afternoon when the expressway’s southbound lanes were relatively clear of traffic. The northbound lanes were still congested with vehicles leaving JFK Airport.
Ramnauth Kush, who lives in South Jamaica, was a child when construction began. The 18-year-old commutes to college on Long Island.
“ I would say there's not as much traffic anymore,” he said as he filled his gas tank up at a station right off the highway. “I mean, rush hour's still always going to be a mess, but I do feel like it has changed for the better, and it's finally done.”
But critics of the project said the wider highway will actually make traffic worse. The research group TransitCenter noted that Hochul’s victory lap over the Van Wyck ignored the well-documented phenomenon of “induced demand,” where expanded road capacity creates more traffic.
“Those benefits will likely be temporary because of induced demand, which isn’t accounted for in the project’s environmental impact statement,” TransitCenter wrote in a blog post.
The group argued that more than half of the residents who live near the Van Wyck take public transit, and the money spent on the highway improvements should’ve gone to mass transit.
“Rather than sink more than $1 billion for at best, temporary time savings, New York State DOT should cancel the Van Wyck widening and apply over $500 million of flexible funding to improve nearby transit instead,” the TransitCenter report argued.
Rolando Infante, a spokesperson for the state DOT, wrote in a statement the department "stands by the integrity of the data outlined in the EIS."
The state's work also included upgrades to the sewer system to prevent flooding in Southeast Queens.
Hochul quipped at last week’s ribbon-cutting about the Van Wyck highway’s terrible reputation. She cited a 1991 episode of “Seinfeld” where Elaine Benes drove recklessly to the airport after oversleeping so an unwelcome house guest could catch a flight, only to be thwarted by a five-car pile-up on the Van Wyck. Hochul said Benes’ guest would have made their flight if they had driven on the new Van Wyck.
“ It's been a long time in coming, but Elaine, if you're out there, and you need to get to JFK, try it again. It's gonna be incredible,” Hochul said, making a double Seinfeld-entendre.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/trum.title: Trump’s Imperialist Fantasy for Latin America Is Already Failing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/trum.author: Sam Carliner
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/trum.text:
The U.S. “Backyard”
It would have been unimaginable for the United States and longtime U.S. adversary, Venezuela, to enter into a military alliance just one year ago. But that’s exactly what U.S. “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth announced from its capital, Caracas, on November 18, as part of a surprise meeting with Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez.
The new military agreement — which will include joint training, intelligence sharing, and defense equipment capabilities — and an oil deal signed in August, which even Bloomberg has called a reprise of the industry’s “neocolonial past,” is the most significant achievement of President Donald Trump’s aggressive “Donroe Doctrine” to strengthen U.S. control over Latin America. “In the last year, the country that previously sent its oil wealth to Cuba or to China, from rigs built by Venezuelans and Americans, has now signed a historic oil deal with the United States, through the Department of War,” Hegseth boasted at a press conference last week.
That same day, however, the New York Times reported that Colombia rejected a plan to conduct joint military operations with the United States. This led Hegseth to cut a visit to Colombia short; he had originally planned to discuss military cooperation with the country’s new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella. Both he and Hegseth took to X deny the Times’s claims. But de la Espriella, who campaigned by aligning himself with the Trump administration and calling for military action against drug cartels and gangs, did not have sufficient support in Colombia’s Congress to ink a military agreement with the United States that would have allowed U.S. troops to conduct counter-cartel operations inside Colombia.
The military agreement with Venezuela and the lack of one in Colombia showcase the contradictions of the Trump administration’s aggressive Latin America policy. On the one hand, the administration has greatly expanded operations in the Western Hemisphere over the past year. But a recent series of setbacks, of which Colombia’s snub is only the latest, show the limits of U.S. power projection even in a region it has treated as its backyard for hundreds of years.
The Donroe Doctrine in Action
One year ago this month, the Trump administration published its National Security Strategy, which candidly advocated for a “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, invoking the policy that the United States historically used to treat Latin America and the Caribbean as the country’s exclusive sphere of influence. Just two months after releasing the NSS, on January 3, the administration carried out a coup in Venezuela, which removed its president, Nicolás Maduro, from power. A U.S. strike in southern Venezuela in June reportedly killed a leader of the Tren de Aragua gang. And last month, U.S. aircraft attacked a camp of supposed Colombian guerrillas operating inside Venezuela, killing more than two dozen people.
With the cooperation of remaining regime officials, headed by Rodríguez, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also effectively dictated significant shifts in Venezuelan domestic and economic policy, including the oil deal which gives the United States a direct stake in more than 17 strategic oil fields and the resumption of U.S. embassy operations in Caracas.
Rubio’s influence over Venezuelan policy also enabled him to escalate an economic offensive against Cuba, which has long been a target of Rubio’s staunch anti-communist crusade. Venezuela had been Cuba’s largest oil supplier, but after the coup, Venezuela quickly cut off its supply of fuel to the island nation. The Trump administration then threatened tariffs against any country that sold oil to Cuba. By February, the United Nations was warning that Cuba faced “humanitarian collapse” from the embargo. Trump officials have also repeatedly threatened to carry out regime change on the island. As recently as November 13, Trump told reporters: “I want to get Cuba done before I leave you.”
Since last September, the United States has also conducted scores of attacks on supposed drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean. By alleging that these boats are suspected of “narco-trafficking,” the Trump administration has carried out lawless operations that have killed more than 240 civilians.
The administration had even bigger plans for Latin America. The NSS envisioned a region run by subservient governments willing to play their part in advancing policies favorable to U.S. interests. As the document put it:
Our goals for the Western Hemisphere can be summarized as “Enlist and Expand.” We will enlist established friends in the Hemisphere to control migration, stop drug flows, and strengthen stability and security on land and sea. We will expand by cultivating and strengthening new partners while bolstering our own nation’s appeal as the Hemisphere’s economic and security partner of choice.
Shifts in the region would favor this policy, with recent Latin American elections bringing U.S.-aligned, right-wing leaders to power in several countries that had previously been governed by left-wing administrations. Bolivia, Chile, and Honduras elected right-wing heads of state in 2025, followed by Costa Rica, Colombia, and Peru this year. These new governments joined staunch Trump allies Javier Milei in Argentina, Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, and Daniel Noboa in Ecuador.
On March 7, 2026, Trump and Rubio brought 13 of these allies together at a summit of Shield of the Americas, a multinational security initiative created by the administration earlier this year. The main result of the summit was the creation of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, which Trump described as “a pledge from military leaders and representatives from 17 countries demonstrating that the region is ready to operationalize hard power to defeat these threats [cartels and terrorists] to our security and civilization.” At an October meeting, the coalition (which has grown to 19 countries) “committed to expand information sharing, increase bilateral and multilateral cooperation, and conduct combined operations that deter and dismantle those networks, secure borders and critical infrastructure, and protect law-abiding citizens,” according to a U.S. Southern Command press release.
New Partnerships and Human Rights Concerns
Under Noboa, Ecuador has been at the forefront of advancing U.S. military operations in Latin America, offering a glimpse of what might be in store as the United States seeks to expand military cooperation across the region.
In March, U.S. Special Operations forces began joint operations with Ecuador’s military against alleged drug cartel facilities. The partnership was established despite a referendum in Ecuador which saw voters overwhelmingly reject a proposal to host a U.S. military base. A New York Times investigation found that at least one of the facilities targeted in these joint operations was a civilian dairy farm. A Human Rights Watch report — based on extensive interviews and analysis of data including satellite imagery, judicial documents, and medical records — found three separate incidents implicating the U.S.–Ecuador security partnership in subjecting civilians to torture, drone strikes, and arbitrary detention. The report argues:
From a human rights perspective, this partnership is a perilous one. The two countries’ security relationship is deepening at a moment when both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fueled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organized crime groups as a kind of war.
On November 6, Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García and 12 other members of Congress sent a letter to Rubio urging him to suspend military assistance to Noboa, noting “Ecuador has seen the repression of opposition actors across the political spectrum, attacks on judicial independence, and restrictions on the freedom of the press.”
While the plans to expand military cooperation in Colombia suffered a setback, the Colombian and U.S. militaries have nonetheless made efforts to deepen their relationship. This month, 350 U.S. military personnel were in Colombia training alongside 400 local troops as part of a military exercise dubbed Southern Vanguard 2027. Panama and Honduras have also hosted training exercises with U.S. troops in the past year.
A recent U.S. Army press release also announced that U.S. and Colombian military leaders met for bilateral discussions about the two countries’ partnership. Even under left-wing President Gustavo Petro, who was a vocal critic of Trump and the war on drugs, U.S. military personnel were deployed to Colombia and the two countries shared intelligence.
Historically, U.S. military partnerships with Latin American leaders have been linked to human rights abuses, including the Guatemalan military’s massacre of Indigenous Maya civilians during the country’s 36-year-long civil war, and Peru’s government, under the 10-year rule of Alberto Fujimori, carrying out forced disappearances of dissidents. Considering the civilian toll of the administration’s boat strike campaign, as well as the abuses being carried out in Ecuador, it is likely that the Donroe Doctrine will lead to further human rights violations.
The administration has also increasingly meddled in the political affairs, and even the sovereignty, of various Latin American countries, including conditioning a $20 billion bailout of Argentina’s economy on the success of Milei’s party in the country’s legislative elections, pressuring Bolivia’s government to arrest its own attorney general and other officials who were investigating a Trump-friendly political strategist, and attempting to sway Brazil’s presidential election in favor of Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro.
Has the Donroe Doctrine Peaked?
Despite the seemingly unrestrained advance of the Donroe Doctrine this past year, Trump’s influence over the region is already teetering. Even before Colombia rejected deeper cooperation, Trump had encountered several other key setbacks across Latin America.
Despite Trump’s efforts to sway Brazil’s presidential elections in October, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva pulled off a stunning defeat of Bolsonaro, securing another term leading the largest country in Latin America. Bolsonaro’s loss, bolstered in no small part by the Brazilian public’s outrage at U.S. interference, dashed the Trump administration’s hopes of having an entirely subservient ally at the head of the largest and most politically influential country in Latin America.
This month, outrage over a banking scandal in Paraguay led to the impeachment of Trump-aligned President Santiago Peña. In Chile, right-wing President José Antonio Kast’s approval rating has plunged to new lows after just eight months in office. And in Argentina, where Milei, one of Trump’s most subordinate allies, has been carrying out sweeping neoliberal reforms, the country appears to be entering a recession just ahead of next year’s presidential election.
This year has also seen significant protests and increased left-wing activism challenge the region’s right-wing governments. In May, a peasant-led rebellion in Bolivia over austerity and government ties to the Trump administration brought the country to a standstill for over a month. President Rodrigo Paz has since enacted a state of emergency, enabling him to use the military and police to suppress dissent. Despite this, Bolivian teachers launched a strike last month over efforts by the government to privatize education. In Chile, the country’s student movement has held several national days of protests, facing off against police armed with tear gas and water cannons. Recently, Chilean truckers also entered the fray, setting up roadblocks to protest fuel price hikes.
In Argentina, Trotskyist congresswoman Myriam Bregman has rapidly grown in popularity. Recent polling has shown that Bregman, a vocal critic of Milei and U.S. influence in Argentina, now has the highest favorability rating of any political figure in the country, foreshadowing an electoral environment in which the far left is becoming a serious contender against the right and the country’s more mainstream Peronist opposition. All these trends further signal a landscape less conducive to Trump’s agenda of continued U.S. intervention.
This surge of left-wing populism across Latin America doesn’t mean that the administration will cease aggressive interventions in the region. Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff may signal the opposite. Miller was highly involved in planning the coup in Venezuela and the boat strike campaign. But following the Republican Party’s historic defeats in the U.S. midterm elections, the administration will have to contend with a new Congress elected by a public that is souring on constant military interventions. Hegseth, competing with Miller in his zeal for employing military terror in the region, has already become the target of an impeachment effort which is likely to carry over into the next legislative term.
As the Iran war has shown, military might alone is not enough to make countries, let alone entire regions, submit to U.S. dictates. The Trump administration may well continue its efforts to revive the Monroe Doctrine, but the long history of U.S. intervention in Latin America is also a history of the region’s people defending their sovereignty from U.S. empire and local quislings. This year has been another chapter in that history.
“To the narco-terrorists who have used this as a safe haven, your time is up. We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you,” Hegseth announced last week in Caracas. Standing outside the U.S. Embassy, Hegseth praised Venezuela’s transformation from an enemy to a “compliant security partner.” But repeating the success in Venezuela may prove to be very difficult.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Thelma Golden will step down as leader of the Studio Museum in Harlem after 21 years
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Benjamin Sutton
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her role at the end of 2027, after a successor has been hired. Announcing the impending leadership transition on Tuesday (24 November), the chair of the museum’s board Kathryn C. Chenault said Golden “is now passing on the leadership of the museum she helped build, entrusting it to a new generation she helped foster”.
News of Golden’s decision comes almost exactly a year after a moment of personal and institutional triumph: the opening of the Studio Museum’s new six-storey, 82,000-sq.-ft home at 144 West 125th Street. That project had been a focus of much of the past decade of her tenure, including helping to raise a total of $322m as part of a capital campaign supporting construction and growing the museum’s endowment from $5m to $95m. The museum now has significantly more public areas, more galleries for special exhibitions and displays of its public collection, more centrally located studios for its residency programme, a rooftop terrace and a number of key front- and back-of-house amenities it previously lacked.
“It allows us to fully explore our ambitions, institutionally,” Golden told The Art Newspaper last year at the time of the opening. “The limitations of our two former spaces never stopped this museum from making important, historic, significant work, it never stopped people from coming and making this a place that was important to them, it never made it so that artists didn’t want to work or engage or show here. However, what it meant to do those things in those spaces often required incredible effort and ingenuity because they weren’t spaces made to be museums, they weren’t spaces made for art. What this space does is it not only increases our physical space, but it allows us to work in ways that we could only dream of in those former spaces.”
Golden’s history at the Studio Museum spans not only her 21 years as its director, but stretches back to her years as an undergraduate student of art history and African American studies at Smith College in Northampton, Massachusetts, during which time she had an internship at the museum. After graduation she stayed on as a curatorial fellow.
Her career then led her to the Whitney Museum of American Art, where she was initially a curatorial assistant, then the director of its off-site programme in Midtown Manhattan, and later an associate curator. During her time there she co-curated the influential 1993 Whitney Biennial (with Elisabeth Sussman) and curated Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art (1994-95), a landmark examination of the construction of Black masculinity through post-war art.
Golden returned to the Studio Museum in 2000, when she was hired as the deputy director for exhibitions and programmes, collaborating with then-director Lowery Stokes Sims. Golden took over the top job in 2005, when Sims stepped down. In addition to her curatorial projects—including a major Chris Ofili show in 2005 and a survey of figuration in African American Art (2002)—Golden became increasingly focused on building the Studio Museum’s future.
When preparations for demolition of its longtime home on 125th Street required the Studio Museum to close in 2018, Golden pursued partnerships with cultural and community organisations in Harlem. Building on a crucial professional development programme created with the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in 2015, she helped launch a multi-year partnership with MoMA and MoMA PS1 in 2019. This led to exhibitions of the Studio Museum’s collection and showcases for the participants in its renowned artist-in-residence programme at those institutions while construction was underway on the new building.
Construction of the Studio Museum’s new home was complicated by both the Covid-19 pandemic, which brought activity to a standstill, and by accusations of sexual harassment and misconduct made against its architect, David Adjaye (he has denied all the allegations). The site’s eventual completion and reopening, in November 2025, was seen as a triumph, creating a vastly expanded, purpose-built home for Black art that is equal to the museum’s ambitious programming and stellar permanent collection. The collection wassignificantly expanded during Golden’s tenure.
“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to new projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors, and professional colleagues; the long line of directors, trustees, and donors who established the Studio Museum and made it thrive; half a century’s worth of endlessly dedicated staff members, audiences and beloved Harlem neighbours; and above all the generations of artists who have enlightened us.”
As important to Golden’s legacy at the Studio Museum as her leadership in the building project is how her work has elevated a new generation of curators and institutional leaders, and championed artists of the African diaspora who had historically been overlooked. In her work at the Studio Museum and elsewhere, she has provided crucial support for artists including Amy Sherald, Lorna Simpson, Mark Bradford, Simone Leigh, Njideka Akunyili Crosby.
“She has nurtured the careers of countless artists; she has impacted the arc of art history; she has overseen the construction of a world-class facility in Harlem; and she has transformed the way the public thinks about art of the African diaspora,” Darren Walker, the former president of the Ford Foundation, told The New York Times. (The Ford Foundation endowed the Studio Museum's director position through a $10m grant in 2024.)
In addition to her role at the Studio Museum, Golden serves on the board of directors of the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation and the Obama Foundation.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/c.title: Cycle of Rage: Pols Who Don’t Support ‘Stop Super Speeder’ Bill Will Attend Lots Of Funerals
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/c.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/c.text:
Some politicians (including, from left, David Carr, Inna Vernikov, Joann Ariola and Chris Banks) are living under a rock when it comes to super-speeders. The Streetsblog Photoshop Desk
Congratulations, Council Member Joann Ariola — the roads in your district are the most dangerous in town.
On that latter topic, Ariola notably hasn’t signed onto the “Stop Super Speeder” bill that would require the city to set up a program to require drivers with 16 or more speed-camera tickets in 12 months to install speed-limiting devices inside their cars. It follows a state law passed earlier this year that allowed city lawmakers to create such a program.
Such devices would prevent drivers from exceeding the speed limit, which is a main cause of crashes and catastrophic injuries. As the Department of Transportation has long said, super speeders are far more likely to get in a crash — with drivers who get 20 speed-camera tickets four times as likely to hit something. Once a driver gets to 25 tickets — as so many drivers you’ll read about below rack up — they’re 15 times as likely.
The fact that Ariola (R–Ozone Park/Rockaways) isn’t on the stop super-speeder bill suggests that she’s either unconcerned with the number of reckless drivers on her roads or that she simply doesn’t know the extent of the problem.
Let’s be charitable and say it’s the latter. So I called up Michael Freedman of Crashcount, the seminal crash and reckless driving mapping site, and asked if he could computer the number of super-speeders who drive through Ariola’s district.
Freedman did not disappoint.
First, he calculated how many drivers got 16 or more camera-issued speeding tickets in the 12 months between Oct. 1, 2025 and Sept. 30, 2026. It was about 18,000! (Reminder: these are drivers who exceeded the speed limit by 11 or more miles per hour 16 or more times in just one year.)
Then, he plotted where they got their tickets. He found that 4,778 of the 18,000-odd super-speeders had racked up 21,542 tickets in Ariola’s district! In one year! That’s 60 tickets a day — just from the super-speeders, let alone all the other drivers speeding through school zones.
Friedman also provided a map, right, depicting all the speed-camera tickets written to the five worst drivers in the district. The map, even more than the numbers, should make someone like Ariola realize that this problem is closer than the house next door. (Ariola declined to comment for this story.)
But let’s not single out Ariola — she’s one of 26 Council members who have yet to sign onto their colleague Kayla Santosuosso’s legislation. Other Council members have similarly dangerous districts — districts that will remain unsafe until the Council passes, and the Mamdani administration implements, the “Stop Super Speeders” bill.
Freedman has a theory why Council members are slow to co-sponsor the bill.
“People think, ‘Oh, this is somebody else’s problem’ or ‘These bad drivers are in someone else’s district,’ but these speeders are everywhere,” Freedman said. “So that’s why we need to solve this problem on a citywide basis. If we don’t, Council members are responsible for the next traffic death is their district. They’ll need to go to the funeral to explain themselves to the grieving family.”
Fortunately, the bill is starting to gain momentum. When I started reporting this story on Friday, there were only 19 co-sponsors, leaving 31 Council members in the “no” column. But after I sent emails to the 31 seeking comment on why they would oppose this life-saving measure, five members — Chi Ossé and Susan Zhuang of Brooklyn; Shekar Krishnan and Nantasha Williams of Queens; and Elsie Encarnación of the Bronx and Harlem — quickly signed onto the bill.
At this rate, I’ll get this bill passed in a week. So you’re welcome, New York.
Nonetheless, a majority of the Council’s 51 members remain off the bill; let’s call them the Timid 26. Hopefully, they’ll look at the rest of Freedman’s numbers and sign onto the bill before the week is out:

https://www.propublica.org/article/ectop.title: An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset
https://www.propublica.org/article/ectop.author: Agnel Philip
https://www.propublica.org/article/ectop.text:
For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the ongoing impacts of abortion bans since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of abortion bans has become politicized and federal agencies have been gutted under the Trump administration.
For example, last year my colleagues uncovered a dramatic rise in sepsis rates since Texas instituted its abortion ban, which carries the strictest penalties for healthcare providers. The number of blood transfusions during emergency room visits for first-trimester miscarriage spiked in the state as well.
Most recently, my colleagues Andrea Suozzo, Sophie Chou, Kavitha Surana and I examined pregnancy-related deaths on a national level. We turned our attention to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The agency collects information from death certificates and publishes totals based on variables like location, demographics and cause of death. It’s a commonly used resource for journalists and academics who want to learn more about trends in mortality.
Pretty soon a trend leaped off the page: Almost 200 women died after ectopic pregnancies between 2020 and 2025, nearly twice the number of deaths compared with the previous six-year period.
The increase was particularly stark in states that had banned abortion.
This was a significant and serious finding. And as far as we could tell, the fact that the number of women who died from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled after abortion bans came into effect hadn’t been reported before.
A death from an ectopic pregnancy should be a “never event,” according to Dr. Alice Abernathy, an OB-GYN in Philadelphia. And yet, as we later confirmed, more than a dozen leaders in the field of maternal health were unaware of the spike. Neither state governments nor the federal government, whose own dataset we were using, had publicly identified this trend.
How could it be that seemingly no one was aware of this but us?
The answer, as it turns out, is multifold and begins with the nature of the condition itself. Ectopic pregnancies occur when an embryo fails to properly implant in the uterus and begins to develop elsewhere, most commonly inside a fallopian tube. The pregnancy grows until it causes the organ to rupture, triggering catastrophic bleeding.
It is a rare condition, estimated to impact up to 2% of pregnancies, but it is incredibly dangerous.
“I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Kyleigh Thurman, whose right fallopian tube ruptured after she struggled to get ectopic care in Texas in 2023.
“There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” Leitaea Lowrimore of Oklahoma said in an ongoing lawsuit challenging an abortion ban, after being denied treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at multiple hospitals in February. “I kept thinking about our kids.”
Even before ectopic pregnancy deaths began rising, the condition was noted as the leading cause of death in the first trimester of pregnancy. Yet it has received little research attention. For example, the CDC doesn’t track how many ectopic pregnancies occur a year and doesn’t require healthcare providers to report them. The most recent nationwide study we could find examined data only through 2013.
The U.S. doesn’t conduct national maternal mortality reviews in the same way as countries like the United Kingdom, which responded to a similar spike in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic by instituting changes to emergency services and promoting awareness of ectopic pregnancy symptoms. Instead, in our country, much of the work of investigating pregnancy-related deaths is left to state committees.
This creates a large potential knowledge gap. In individual states, the number of ectopic deaths is small and subject to a lot of variation, making it harder to spot a trend. After our story was published, we reached out to maternal mortality review committees in states with abortions bans; many of them responded that they didn’t identify an increase in ectopic deaths and that, despite the findings of our reporting, they had no plans to examine this issue further.
We realized the fact that nearly double the number of women are dying from ectopic pregnancies is visible at only the national level.
It is unclear why the CDC and other federal agencies across two administrations have failed to publicly respond to the increase in deaths despite having access to the same information ProPublica analyzed. We reached out to the CDC to ask what the agency has done to investigate or address this trend. It has epidemiologists who review death and birth records and has in the past done its own investigations and analyses. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, didn’t provide a direct answer to that question but said the agency continues to track maternal mortality trends, investigate their causes and provide funding for research.
Maternal experts agree that the government’s capacity to respond to this trend has been significantly reduced as a result of the staffing cuts initiated by the Trump administration since the beginning of last year. The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health, for example, lost most of its 100 employees, according to a lawsuit filed by more than a dozen states’ attorneys general last year.
This lack of awareness surrounding ectopic pregnancy deaths is imperiling women’s lives.
We asked several experts why death rates were going up, but there was no consensus. And while our analysis can’t establish whether there is a causal link between abortion bans and the worse outcomes in the states that have them, there is no evidence that officials are stepping up to examine this question or offer solutions. Even professional organizations, such as the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, have yet to provide specific guidance to doctors about how to adequately treat women with suspected ectopic pregnancies in states with abortion bans.
But experts say the trend we uncovered is unacceptable and requires a response. As Courtney Schreiber, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology, told us, our work “raises concern that young women are dying from a preventable cause at an increasing rate. That is not what we should be seeing in the United States of America.”
We hope you’ll read our recent investigation, which includes more details on potential explanations for this trend and stories from women in states with abortion bans who faced delays in care. We plan to continue reporting on maternal health and the impact of abortion bans for the foreseeable future.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: State Probes Alleged Amazon Safety Violations at Staten Island Warehouse
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The state Labor Department is investigating a sprawling Amazon distribution center on Staten Island known as JFK8, The City Reporter has learned, over allegations that the megaretailer is ignoring rules that mandate transparent productivity quotas and ergonomic training for employees.
Amazon employs approximately 6,000 people at the 855,000 square-foot facility. In 2022, JFK8 became the first Amazon shop to unionize anywhere in the United States, and its workers have since voted to affiliate with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which also represents a number of drivers around the country who deliver packages for Amazon.
Sherri Raponi, a top official at the Labor Department’s occupational safety division, sent the Teamsters and other groups who submitted complaints on behalf of workers a letter on Nov. 3 informing them that it was launching an official probe of potential violations of a law known as the Warehouse Worker Protection Act at JFK8.
MORE: Exploitation or Opportunity? The Fight Over Amazon’s New York Drivers
“Please be advised the Safety and Health and Essential Rights (SHER) program of the Division of Occupational Safety and Health (DOSH) has received the complaints you referenced in your letter,” wrote Raponi. “Please be assured SHER has opened an investigation of this facility regarding compliance with the above provisions of the New York State Labor Law.”
Though the letter does not go into detail over what exact claims the agency is following up on, workers have sent numerous written complaints to the agency over Amazon’s alleged refusal to comply with rules governing the warehouse logistics sector.
According to the complaints, Amazon has not submitted ergonomic safety plans known as “worksite evaluations” or provided workers with productivity quotas in writing, while refusing to work on safety issues with the union.
“We comply with all laws and legal requirements, including the Warehouse Worker Protection Act, and we don’t use fixed quotas,” Amazon spokesperson Sam Stephenson said.
Warehouse Laws
The claims stem from a patchwork of laws — the Warehouse Worker Protection Act, the Warehouse Worker Injury Reduction Program and the New York HERO Act — all approved by lawmakers in the years since the COVID pandemic. The most recent of those laws, the WWIRP, went into effect last summer.
That law requires managers to create and implement injury reduction programs to identify and minimize the risk of ergonomic on-the-job injuries, which JFK8 workers claim the company has not done.
When staff presented a proposed safety plan this summer, managers refused to meet with them and did not respond to written requests for a meeting, according to several complaints reviewed by The City Reporter.
“I have had supervisors tell me I need to maintain a rate of 150 units per hour in shipdock, but I have seen in internal communication and managers that 250 units per hour is the ‘new normal,’’” one worker wrote. “None of this is ever explicitly communicated with us in writing.”
“In June 2026, JFK8 workers requested several documents from Amazon that the company must provide including the written evaluation of the on-site medical program and summary of treatment protocols,” wrote another employee. “To date, Amazon has NOT given us these documents…”
Department of Labor spokesperson Jack Lamson confirmed the Raponi letter’s accuracy and declined to comment further, saying the agency “does not comment on open investigations.”
State Sen. Jessica Ramos (D-Queens), the labor committee chair, was the lead senate sponsor on both the WWPA and the WWIRP, and she made warehouse worker safety a signature issue. Ramos, who was the subject of a recent New York Times investigation into complaints of alleged campaign finance violations related to her doomed 2025 mayoral campaign, could not be reached for comment on Tuesday.
The slate of laws regulating depots like JFK8 were meant to address the kind of injuries that are most common in warehouses — sprains, fractures and aches resulting from repetitive movement, heavy lifting and a fast-paced environment with high productivity quotas.
First Test of New Labor Rules
“No matter what your strength is, your size, your gender, no matter what your physical makeup is — if you are working at full speed, doing the same task day in and day out, you are going to have some kind of physical ramifications for doing so,” said Charlene Obernauer, executive director of the New York Committee for Occupational Safety and Health.
The Labor Department probe is the first major test for the relatively new rules governing warehouse worker safety, said Obernauer.
There are no federal standards governing ergonomic safety and warehouse injury prevention, said Debbie Berkowitz, a former policy chief at the Occupational Safety and Health Administration during the Obama administration. Rather, states are left to come up with their own rules. The law in New York was the subject of fierce debate before lawmakers ultimately approved the WWPA in 2023, and the Warehouse Worker Injury Reduction Program two years later.
Berkowitz, a worker safety and health policy fellow at Georgetown University, applauded the Labor Department’s decision to investigate safety concerns at JFK8. “This is exactly how things should work,” she said.
The law is far from perfect, advocates say. Some point to the relatively low penalties — the WWPA tops penalties at $3,000 for each repeat violation — which they say won’t deter companies like Amazon, which is valued at $2.7 trillion.
“As we test these laws, one of the questions that’s going to come up is the penalties, and whether they are enough to prevent the employer from breaking the law,” said Obernauer. “And if they are not enough, then what would be enough — is it the court of public opinion? Is it issuing press releases?”
MORE: Teamsters Hit Amazon Over Delivery Worker Layoffs, With Millions at Stake
JFK8 workers who spoke with The City Reporter said they had not received on-the-job injury prevention training at all.
Whenever workers walk in to seek treatment for stress injuries and other ailments they are, at most, given an over-the-counter pain medication like ibuprofen and allowed a few minutes to lie down, JFK8 employees said.
But most troublingly, workers say, is what they describe as Amazon’s apparent failure to provide a safety plan as required by the 2025 law. Anthony Sparrow, the union’s grievance director at JFK8, said management has “not acknowledged” the union’s requests for a written safety plan.
Sparrow and Xavier Villaroel, a shop steward, have said that when workers experience sprains, strains or other stress fractures, they are told to “walk it off.”
Villaroel said staff are told to stretch for a few minutes at the beginning of each shift, which helps prevent injuries — but workers routinely get hurt on the job anyway. Amazon and the JFK8 facility have been in the crosshairs of workplace safety watchdogs and federal regulators for years.
A 2022 study commissioned by the Teamsters and other groups found the Staten Island facility ranked among the workplaces with the highest number of injuries in the state, and federal prosecutors in Manhattan are investigating “potential fraud” related to claims that Amazon keeps its injury data artificially low.
A 2024 investigation by the U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, then chaired by Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, found that nationally Amazon discouraged workers from seeking medical care.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘As much joy as I could find’: a splash of colour – in pictures
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Sarah King
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘As much joy as I could find’: a splash of colour – in pictures
From bright green kebab shops to a flash of red stocking, photographer Niall McDiarmid is constantly on the hunt for antidotes to our muted beige and monochrome world
Scottish photographer Niall McDiarmid’s work is a joyful antidote to the greyscale tones predominant across architecture, interiors, fashion and cars. Of this image he says: ‘I’m sure interior design for kebab shops is a niche profession but I salute whoever led this project. The addition of replica coloured Jacobsen dining chairs is genius. If only Christine Keeler had sat for that famous Jacobsen chair portrait in a green kebab shop in south Wimbledon.’ Niall McDiarmid’s Colour is available via RRB Photobooks. All quotes: Niall McDiarmid
For over 15 years, McDiarmid has been documenting the inherent colour of life as he finds it. ‘I was drawn into this kaleidoscope of colourful commuters,’ he says. ‘I suspect with over 2,000 trains passing through Clapham Junction every day these random colour moments happen regularly. But waiting around never seems to work for me in photography. I have to keep moving’
‘I set out with the project to photograph as much colour as I could. Frames that were full of colour from edge to edge, from corner to corner. I was looking for vibrancy, saturation, brightness, joy – and as much of it as I could find. The images were an antidote to the overwhelmingly diﬃcult times that our family were going through at that time. In some ways finding colour helped me get through those days. This shot was taken in an ice-cream shop in Covent Garden on a late September afternoon’
‘The entrance to Liberty’s department store is always awash with flowers and colours. Green and purple seems like a perfect combination here. I have a strong aﬀection for Liberty’s. As a family we came down to London for our first visit from our home in Highland Perthshire in the late 1970s. We lost my younger brother Calum in a lift mix-up in the store. He was about six. Panic ensued. He showed up pretty quickly but every time I walk by the building I remember the episode and chuckle’
‘Red stockings have been a constant inspiration for photographers. They are so vibrant and distinctive. Fred Herzog, who documented the streets of Vancouver, and French fashion photographer Guy Bourdin both had memorable shots that featured red tights. This shot was taken at the entrance to the Royal Academy on Piccadilly’
‘A woman in a yellow dress, reading a blue book, drinking orange juice, with a red rose on the table, all against a pink wall. Sometimes the gods of serendipity, luck, chance – call it what you like – just come good for you. This was shot in a coﬀee shop just oﬀ the Strand in London’
‘Although most of the images in the book were from London I did a number of trips to other towns in search of colour. This was taken in Folkestone, which has a burgeoning artistic scene. Luckily this enthusiastic fellow carrying a bright red box walked into the frame as I headed up to the town centre’
‘One of the earlier shots in the book, this was taken on a bright Sunday afternoon in February. I drifted into town from my home in south-west London with no particular mission in mind. I ended up wandering along the South Bank and came across this girl with wonderful hair browsing the secondhand book stalls. Six or seven shots taken on this day started a portrait odyssey that firstly took me all across London and then across the whole of Britain resulting in several books and exhibitions’
‘Bring up Tooting, the south London neighbourhood, and the most common response usually leads back to Wolfie Smith and his Popular Front [in BBC sitcom Citizen Smith]. “Freedom for Tooting!” But I’ve never watched the programme and I never have an adequate response. Tooting has always been a vibrant and exciting place to photograph for me and I’ve visited many times over the years. This was taken in the busy indoor market, now a big draw for street cuisine’Photograph: Niall McDiarmid
‘Like many photographers I’m drawn to greasy spoon cafes. Combine some warm evening light with Formica table tops and faded lampshades and the desire to drop in and photograph is irresistible. But then again, maybe that’s just an excuse for a full English breakfast at four in the afternoon’
‘A bright yellow umbrella will punch colour through even the wettest of days. This is the most recent shot in the book, taken early this year in Hoxton in the pouring rain’
‘Chris Oﬃli’s memorial to the victims of Grenfell Tower dominates the west stairwell in Tate Britain. In particular it commemorates the photographer and artist Khadija Saye whose career was cut short by this tragedy. I caught this yellow-clad visitor as he headed into the main gallery with the mural behind through the frosted glass’

Jacobin is seeking a full-time senior video producer to make video about socialist politics and ideas.
Location: Hybrid. New York metro area candidates; at least two days a week in our Brooklyn office
Salary: From $68,150.03 per year
Reports to: Director of Communications
Position: Full-time
Start date: As soon as possible, no later than January 7, 2027
Jacobin is seeking a Senior Video Producer to make thoughtful, engaging video about socialist politics and ideas, with a focus on YouTube and long-form work.
The producer will develop, produce, and edit videos; commission projects in consultation with the Director of Communications; work with contributors and freelancers; and coordinate video coverage of Jacobin events. They will collaborate with the Editor and incorporate feedback into their projects.
We’re looking for someone with experience producing and editing video, strong editorial judgment, familiarity with YouTube, and the ability to manage projects independently. During the interview process, applicants will be asked about their familiarity with the theory and practice of socialism, including the thought of historical and contemporary Marxist thinkers.

Jacobin is an equal opportunity employer. We consider applicants without unlawful discrimination based on any protected status and provide reasonable accommodations during the hiring process. https://www.artforum.com/news/thelma-gol.author: Polly Watson

The Studio Museum in Harlem, New York, has announced that longtime leader Thelma Golden will depart the institution in late 2027. Golden, who has served as the museum’s director and chief curator for twenty-one years, is practically synonymous with the institution, which she helped shape into an international force showcasing work by artists of African descent. Most recently, she spearheaded the construction of the museum’s first purpose-built home, which opened last year to great fanfare. Golden has left an indelible impact as leader of the Studio Museum, developing the institution’s collection, exhibition history, and storied artist-in-residence program.
“For more than twenty years, Thelma Golden has defined the vision and identity of the Studio Museum in Harlem,” said Kathryn C. Chennault, board chair of the Studio Museum in a statement. “She has elevated and strengthened this institution in every way, helped move Black artists into the center of the cultural landscape, and mentored countless Black museum professionals across the country. She is now passing on the leadership of the museum she helped build, entrusting it to a new generation she helped foster.”
Golden, a native of Queens, interned at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art as a teenager. She first arrived at the Studio Museum as an intern, while studying at Smith College, before returning after graduation as a curatorial fellow. She began her career as a curatorial assistant at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1988, rising to associate curator in 1993. That same year, Golden co-curated an iteration of the Whitney Biennial that proved controversial for its focus on diversity and inclusion. In 1994, she curated the landmark show “Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art” at the Whitney. Golden returned to the Studio Museum in 2000 as deputy director for exhibitions and programs before being appointed to her current roles in 2005.
Chennault revealed that the board has begun the search for Golden’s replacement, and that Golden would remain onboard until that person was in place, assisting with the transition.
