https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/h.title: How The MTA Plans To Build Up America’s Bus Manufacturing Base
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/h.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/h.text:
The MTA wants to buy a small number of buses from international bus manufacturers in order to encourage them to set up shop in America — an ambitious “try before you buy” strategy that could give the agency more options when it acquires thousands of buses in the near future.
Earlier this year, the MTA explained its struggle to find reliable zero emissions buses built in the United States, and paused an order for almost 500 electric buses from New Flyer until the manufacturer could ensure the company’s buses could consistently complete a day’s service. But instead of twiddling their fingers, agency executives are recruiting international firms in an attempt to develop a more competitive manufacturing environment while still taking advantage of federal help for bus purchases.
“Buy America” rules incentivize American transit agencies to purchases buses made in the United States, because the federal government will subsidize 80 percent of their cost. According to a recent study by the Eno Center for Transportation, the average price tag of an American zero-emissions bus is approximately $1 million.
The same Eno study found American bus manufacturing has dwindled to only two main firms: Gillig and New Flyer. Gillig does not bid on requests for proposals from large transit agencies, which means the MTA has little choice but to continue buying New Flyer buses even as transit companies around the country reported similar problems with its electric buses.
Now, in order to better understand the global bus market, the MTA will purchase a small number of buses from overseas manufacturers without any federal subsidy. It will then stress-test those buses by running them on city streets. By doing so, the agency hopes to learn more about the rolling stock from new companies and how they work in the Big Apple.
The pilot will place a major emphasis on electric buses, which are popular and widely used in Europe but have yet to gain traction in the United States.
Transit officials are currently racing to replenish the MTA’s bus fleet with new buses so and take older, less reliable buses off the road. Last month, the MTA published a request-for-proposals for 650 new buses that run on compressed natural gas.
But the scale of the entire bus replacement program goes far beyond last month’s RFP. According to an outside engineering firm that monitors the MTA capital plan, the agency must purchase 500 new buses per year, and MTA executives say the agency needs to order 4,500 buses over the next few years.
The agency hopes the pilot, and the knowledge it gains from stress-testing, will help it lure non-American manufacturers who make buses that satisfy the agency’s needs. The idea is to provide the chosen firms with the promise of immediate business, to accomplish the monumental task of keeping the MTA’s bus fleet in a state of good repair. It’s plenty of desirable work for the right firm, but also so big that the MTA is skeptical a single new entrant to the American market will suffice.
“The size of our orders are very interesting to these companies that are making service and delivering a great product in Europe and Asia,” said Jessie Lazarus, the MTA’s head of rolling stock procurement. “But they’re deterred a bit by the scale, which is sort of the irony around it. We need so many buses, so we obviously need to think really broadly about who those partners can be, or cast a really wide net as we’re doing that market outreach because we can’t rely on just one new partner. We need to think about bringing in a few more. But I think for any new manufacturing relationship, we need to de-risk this for both sides.”
In this case, Lazarus explained that the small orders take the risk out of both sides of the relationship: the MTA doesn’t over-commit to a single company, and can learn about new bus designs used around the world, while bus manufacturers don’t need to navigate the process of establishing factories in America without the certainty of future business.
“We are going to run several pilot fleets,” Lazarus said. “Think of the fleet size as five to 10 buses. We’re going to run those buses for 52 weeks. We’re gonna put them into service and at depots, we are gonna give those manufacturing partners an opportunity to learn more about the New York City operating environment, and we’re going to give our teams an opportunity to learn more about a design that is unfamiliar to us but not unfamiliar to bus service globally.”
European and Asian manufacturers bring certain challenges: some are unaccustomed to placing the operator booth on the left side of the chassis, while others and may not be suitable for dense urban environments. But Lazarus noted that the MTA’s fact-finding mission is receptive to designs that differ from the expectations of the MTA and its bus passengers, if the design is still familiar enough to drive in America.
“If we get close on those dimensions, then we look really closely at [the manufacturer’s] technical specifications, what does this bus look like,” she said. “And if it’s pretty different than what we have, but it’s working really well in a lot of urban areas with varied weather conditions, we think it it would be a good fit to to at least try it in New York.”
MTA leadership has struggled to reconcile two important and seemingly competing goals: completing the transition to a fully zero-emissions bus fleet by 2040, and also ensuring the buses the agency owns are able to stay on the road.
Although those goals are not in natural competition, the central roadblock to the MTA’s effort to acquire more zero-emission buses is New Flyer — the only manufacturer from which the MTA can buy electric buses and still enjoy federal matching funds that cover 80 percent of the cost of new buses under the Buy America program. As a result, the MTA owns a handful of New Flyer electric buses that continue to suffer from major problems with battery charging and equipment failure. That makes it impossible for these buses to complete their runs without breaking down.
Understandably, the MTA has held off on acquiring more rolling stock from New Flyer. But that also means the agency is running hundreds of buses that are more than 12 years old — the effective lifespan of a bus before breakdowns become more frequent.
Another difficulty stems from the companies that make parts for electric buses, such as batteries, seats, doors and HVAC systems. These firms have experienced the very same kind of consolidation and industry shrinkage that destroyed American bus manufacturers. Lazarus said the MTA hopes that overseas companies who make bus components will follow bus manufacturers to the states.
“The constraints on low and no emissions busses in the U.S. have been in part on the [original equipment manager] side, but also on the supplier side,” she said. “Buses have lots and lots and lots of subsystem components, and unfortunately, the story in the subsystem supplier market is pretty similar to that in the [original equipment manufacturer] side, which is a ton of consolidation and not a lot of competition.”
Lazarus continued: “My hope here is that our work to bring in new bus manufacturers will also demonstrate to their suppliers, that if we’re able to prove that those components work for our operating folks and work in our operations, and we generally like our relationships with the the bus manufacturers, we might also be able to encourage some of their subsystem suppliers to come to New York State also and hang a shingle.”
The MTA’s not-so-secret weapon: a well-funded capital plan
The MTA’s plan to engage foreign manufacturers and put their buses on the road is a decidedly non-traditional strategy that its peer agencies in other cities and states would likely struggle to pull off. But the MTA has a not-so-secret weapon to lure manufacturers here: its fully-funded and very large capital plan, which sets aside a big chunk of money for rolling stock.
“Having a funded capital program with $12 billion set aside for rolling stock and very specific commitments on bus replacement and bus purchase is the biggest tool that we have, and the one and the biggest tool that we would need,” Lazarus said.
“We looked initially in the United States for how to spend this money and how to get these buses as quickly as we need them,” she added. “We don’t have the the option to to do that, and so we’re investing these dollars in relationships with new manufacturers that we can bring to the United States and to New York State, hopefully specifically.”
A bus manufacturing company won’t show up in America out of the goodness of its executives’ hearts, and it certainly won’t do so if there’s any chance the MTA will decide its products don’t work in the five boroughs. The pilot fleets allow the MTA and the bus builders to avoid that initial risk.
Tariffs pose another challenge. President Trump has repeatedly applied the import taxes as an unpredictable cudgel. MTA Chairman and CEO Janno Lieber has bemoaned how they have forced the MTA to scrounge up an additional one billion dollars for rolling stock, because the federal government doesn’t exempt parts purchased overseas even if firms used them to build trains and buses in America.
Lazarus echoed her boss’s concern but also suggested the Republicans’ recent midterm losses could relieve the situation.
“The major elephant in the room for all of these companies selling to North America and setting up shop here right now is the tariff environment,” she said. “The biggest obstacle that I’m talking to folks about. We can overcome a lot, but we can’t really overcome the current volatility of the tariff environment. That’s a major deterrent, and I hope we’ll start to see something change on that.”
Environmental advocates praised the MTA’s new strategy.
“Cities around the world successfully run transit bus fleets that are majority electric,” said Rachel Spector, the deputy managing attorney of Earthjustice’s northeast office. “New York City shouldn’t be left behind, and it’s great that MTA is pursuing new vendors. Electric buses can work for New York City and are critical to cleaner air and meeting our climate targets. Especially in light of surging diesel prices, it’s never been clearer that electrification and defending healthy transit budgets go hand in hand.”
Lazarus hopes the pilot will benefit other American transit agencies who need reliable buses, and potentially revive the country’s bus manufacturing sector.
“If we’re able to issue a request for proposals for hundreds or thousands of new buses, that plus the collective demand from other public transit agencies will be attractive enough for [manufacturers] to set up shop in North America,” she explained. “This is really aimed at how can the MTA put these dollars to work to support the health and diversity of the bus ecosystem in North America. We don’t want to be buying from abroad once we solve the problem, we’re trying to solve the problem so we don’t have to do that.”
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: MTA Seeks ‘Millions and Millions’ Over Bungled OMNY Rollout
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Jose Martinez
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The MTA is pumping the brakes on doling out “millions and millions” of dollars to the tech giant overseeing the troubled rollout of the MetroCard’s replacement.
Nearly a decade after awarding a $573 million contract to Cubic Transportation Systems to develop OMNY, the tap-and-go technology that pays for subway and bus trips, the country’s largest mass transportation authority has paused some payments to the company for repeatedly failing to meet its marks.
Saying “we have a problem with our software developer,” MTA chief Janno Lieber last week confirmed that the authority is following through on threats made at the authority’s October board meeting to withhold money over OMNY software shortcomings.
“We have to keep working with Cubic,” Lieber said. “But they have been a disappointment in many respects and we are holding them aggressively to their contract obligations and withholding payment of millions of dollars to make sure they make good on these commitments.”
An MTA spokesperson declined to specify how much Cubic is being docked on a contract that has ballooned to more than $700 million since it was first awarded. The penalties come as the company is facing financial woes that include getting downgraded by credit rating agencies, with the latest coming last week — and after the MTA officials had hoped OMNY would be “good to go” by the time the MetroCard reached the end of the line at the end of 2025.
According to the MTA, more than 5 billion trips have been via OMNY since it was introduced in 2019 as the MetroCard’s eventual replacement. The fare-payment system pays for rides via mobile devices, contactless credit and cards and MTA-issued fare cards.
But its rollout has been plagued by technical glitches and repeated rider complaints about delays in processing bank card payments, getting double-charged for transfers and having to go online for information on trip history and card balances.
Eileen Robbins, 80, said she has been frustrated for months after her OMNY account stopped automatically replenishing via a credit card once it dipped below $10.
“I found out the hard way,” she said. “But the bus driver let me on.”
After multiple calls to OMNY’s customer-service line, Robbins said she was frustrated enough to take Access-A-Ride from her home in Astoria to an MTA board meeting in Lower Manhattan to complain.
“They seem to be throwing good money after bad, even though they’re withholding some of it,” Robbins told The City Reporter. “In the meantime, they are infuriating their customers, whether it’s the students with their cards or the Access-A-Ride users or the general public.”
Lieber acknowledged the long-running rider frustrations.
“All of those features that people want from OMNY, they’re right,” he said. “We want to deliver those features where there’s more transparency and predictability and people can be confident that they’re getting those transfers and so on.”
MetroCard sales ended at the end of 2025, with the MTA saying almost all paid transit trips are now processed via OMNY.
“The underlying issues from a technology standpoint have made the rollout extremely problematic,” said Brian Fritsch, associate director of the Permanent Citizens Advisory Committee to the MTA. “From my understanding, the system architecture has not been where it needed to handle the number of transactions and the speed at which they need to be computed at the scale that New York City Transit requires.”
Riders who have been caught up in OMNY’s issues said they have been flustered by issues with the new fare-payment system.
Frederic Klein complained to the MTA board that in the last six months, the OMNY card that he has used since 2023 no longer automatically reloads $50 at a time.
“They’ve been paying them a lot of money for, what, nine years now?” the 35-year-old Washington Heights man told The City Reporter. “I think it’s disappointing that it’s taken so long for the MTA and its board to get on the same page with where riders are at and the frustrations with the system, but I am glad that they are finally taking notice and are starting to withhold money.”
Eric Schmidt, said his own problems with OMNY — which centered around being repeatedly double-charged a few years back for transfers — drove him back to using the MetroCard until its retirement.
“It’s wild,” said Schmidt, 41, of the Upper West Side. “OMNY is obviously more convenient because you can tap your card or your phone instead of loading money on a MetroCard, but in almost every other way, it’s worse.”
Cory Shields, a spokesperson for Cubic, told The City Reporter that the company is “committed to working closely with the MTA” to boost the OMNY experience for commuters.
“We take feedback seriously, and that input helps guide our joint efforts to strengthen the system, enhance reliability and incorporate the latest advances in fare-payment technology,” Shields said in a statement.
Fritsch of the PCAC — which last year issued recommendations on how to improve OMNY — said Cubic’s financial struggles compound its problems with the MTA.
Just last month, the company named Lee Sander, a former MTA CEO and executive director, as its new chief executive.
“Cubic can’t really afford serious financial penalties from the MTA,” Fritsch said. “Hopefully, that means they will do everything in their power to make good on their end of the contract in short order.”

https://gothamist.com/news/community-boa.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/community-boa.text:
The calisthenics-enthusiasts fighting to preserve the beloved, '90s-era pull-up bars in Tompkins Square Park lost a battle last night.
The Manhattan community board that represents the East Village voted to support the New York City parks department's plan to demolish the pull-up bars and other calisthenics equipment and replace them with new materials. The nearly $10 million renovation project also includes reconstructing the adjacent basketball courts and improving the miniature, kids-only swimming pool.
The vote comes after regular users of the outdoor fitness area pleaded with the parks department for months to repair the aging equipment, rather than demolish it. Some fans told Gothamist that they moved to New York solely to be near the Tompkins Square Park pull-up bars and the community of people who use them.
“We think that those bars, the way they've been built…somehow we struck gold with this equipment of how versatile, how sturdy, how open-ended they are,” said Salo Coslovsky, an associate professor of urban planning at NYU who is at the forefront of the preservation fight and fears the new equipment won’t be the same.
The plan the community board approved was designed as a compromise for the pull-up bar advocates’ request to preserve the existing equipment and to keep the park open during any necessary construction. The pull-up bars and calisthenics equipment will be replaced with new, high-quality material, according to the parks department's plan, and will be reconfigured in the exact same way as it is now, barring changes that will make the equipment more accessible for all users.
Construction will follow a phased schedule that, according to the community board’s resolution, will keep the outdoor fitness area open while the pool and basketball court are under construction, which is expected to take 15 months.
The resolution states that the fitness area will be closed for an anticipated nine-month construction period, but that the parks department will wait until the nearby East River Park fitness area – which is currently under construction – is reopened, so that locals have an alternative space for exercise.
“We at Parks have a long-standing tradition of soliciting and honoring community input and remain committed to creating an inclusive, fully accessible exercise area at Tompkins Square Park while minimizing disruptions to the fitness community,” Parks Commissioner Tricia Shimamura said in a statement. “We look forward to moving this project forward and working with our partners to enhance this beloved public space.”
Members of Manhattan Community Board 3 did not respond to requests for comment in time for the publication of this article.
The fight over Tompkins Square Park is far from over. The preservationists told Gothamist they are now thinking of creative ways to help the city understand why the pull-up bars and the community that surrounds them are so special.
That includes inviting Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who recently tore his Achilles tendon, to come out to the park for physical therapy.
Accessibility concerns were of top concern for the community board and the parks department when advancing the proposal.
The community board “believes that compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act and other applicable accessibility standards is a baseline, not the limit of public investment, and that NYC should strive to exceed minimum requirements,” the resolution states. “NYC Parks has identified deficiencies involving accessible routes and maneuvering space, overlapping equipment activity and fall zones, signage and maintenance.”
But Coslovsky said that he and other people fighting to preserve the bars agree that the area needs to be made more accessible.
“ That's not only a legal mandate, but a moral imperative. So we are on the same page,” Coslovsky said.
Still, accessibility concerns are being used as an excuse to demolish the existing equipment, he said.
The community board’s approval is just one of many backstops required before the city can begin construction on the park. Those fighting for its preservation said they have no plans to give up.
“ There’s a procedural kind of sequence that Parks has to go through,” Coslovsky said. “Wherever they go, we’re going to be there.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Judge Tosses Lawsuit Against Mamdani’s Signature NYC Rent Freeze
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Rent freezes for stabilized tenants across roughly 1 million New York City apartments will remain in place after a Manhattan judge on Wednesday dismissed a lawsuit brought by landlords challenging the policy.
The decision marks a major win for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, one of whose signature campaign promises was to freeze rents for stabilized units as an affordability measure. Neither City Hall nor a spokesperson for the plaintiffs immediately responded to requests for comment. It was not clear if the plaintiffs will appeal.
In his ruling, Manhattan Supreme Court Judge Brendan Lantry called Mamdani’s campaign pledge to freeze rents “reckless and irresponsible” because the mayor cannot unilaterally do so. But Lantry wrote that the plaintiffs failed to establish the freeze enacted by the city’s Rent Guidelines Board in June was “unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious.”
The judge said the freeze, which affects one- and two-year stabilized leases and took effect on Oct. 1, “has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid.” Still, he warned the policy could negatively affect the residential real estate industry.
A group of several landlords, who are represented by former Mayor Eric Adams’ first deputy Randy Mastro, sued in July to try to overturn the freeze. Pointing to Mamdani’s campaign pledge, they alleged the Rent Guidelines Board, which sets allowable rent increases for stabilized units, “ran a sham process with a predetermined outcome.” 
Throughout the lawsuit, the board maintained its independence from City Hall and said it voted to freeze rents after examining official data. Three previous rent freezes were in place under Mayor Bill de Blasio.
While Mamdani could not direct a freeze, he appointed six of the board’s nine members when he took office. Adams appointed three of the members, including one who resigned just hours before the board voted on how much stabilized landlords could raise rents.
Tenants and some housing advocates have long said many stabilized tenants cannot afford to keep up with rent increases.
Landlords and housing analysts have argued rents must increase so owners can keep up with rising operating costs, including for insurance and fuel.
Sumathy Kumar, director of the advocacy group New York State Tenant Bloc, celebrated the judge’s decision.
“Today’s decision affirms that tenants won the rent freeze fairly and secures relief for millions of tenants,” she said in a statement.

https://www.propublica.org/article/fda-p.title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
https://www.propublica.org/article/fda-p.author: Naisha Roy
https://www.propublica.org/article/fda-p.text:
The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply.
About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate.
Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study.
The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way.
“All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica.
A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards.
ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector, a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made.
Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer. All but one passed every test.
The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.”
In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns.
In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.”
Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense.
“It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.”
ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness.
“I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-rockstar.title: Grand Theft Auto Grew Up. America Didn’t.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-rockstar.author: Ryan Zickgraf
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-rockstar.text:
Grand Theft Auto Grew Up. America Didn’t.
The United States under Donald Trump has turned into a parody of itself, descending further and further into juvenilia. Grand Theft Auto VI, meanwhile, has turned more darkly serious and morally complex.
Early in Grand Theft Auto VI, you and your girlfriend drive to the local branch of Fleeca bank on an errand that, by the franchise’s standards, is something of a novelty. Your job is not to rob a bank but to open an account at one.
Lucia Caminos, fresh out of prison, needs somewhere to deposit her check from her mandatory reentry job, and since her boyfriend, Jason Duval, has made it this far in life without a checking account, they’d like to open one. But after a quick financial review, the manager wonders whether they’ve considered maybe downloading an app instead, and you leave empty-handed.
There are any number of teenagers who could, with a few shakes of a PlayStation 5 controller, get these two out of a police pursuit and across three counties of South Florida without putting a scratch on the car. None, however, can get Jason approved for a checking account. As in real life, the credit score — not brute force or cunning — is the god of this universe.
It’s a telling moment, because the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) that I grew up with was two things at once. It was an adolescent male power fantasy, a sandbox where you could steal a sports car, mow down a crowd, and outrun the police with no lasting consequence beyond a few hundred dollars docked from your wallet. And it was a South Park–style satire of American life, all fake radio ads for penis pills and televangelists and talk-radio cranks. The jokes were broad, and the violence was cartoonish, and the upshot was that nothing meant anything, so everything was permitted. GTA III let you hire a prostitute and beat her to get your money back. GTA V let you torture a man with a car battery and then play golf. It all had a weightless quality.
Yet in the thirteen years since Grand Theft Auto V came out, something peculiar has happened: Rockstar, the studio that produces the game, and its subject have switched places. The United States has turned into a parody of itself, while GTA VI has turned more darkly serious. It plays less like a theme park and more like prestige television, something like HBO’s The Wire or Task crossed with It’s Florida, Man.
In VI, you alternate between the two leads: Jason Duval, an Army veteran doing errands for drug runners, and Lucia Caminos, his girlfriend and partner in crime, recently out of prison. Their relationship is the spine of the game, and a score is kept. If Jason behaves like a sociopath, Lucia notices. Push it far enough, and the game will decide you are, in its own words, “Irredeemable,” and you will be saddled with the suboptimal happy-never-after ending.
Protagonists for the 2020s
Perhaps even the idea of a happy ending is laughable. Jason and Lucia are not mafia dons or retired bank robbers in shiny new Miami mansions; they are among South Florida’s ever-growing lumpenproletariat, Karl Marx’s term for the drifting, disorganized underclass that sits below the working class and outside its institutions. They’re the deinstitutionalized, dealigned masses who hold no union card, no pension, no political loyalty, and often no permanent address. Together they must navigate the gig-work and shadow economy with one hand on their guns and one eye over their shoulders for a probation officer who could help take their young son away from them forever into the foster care system.
So, yes, you can still be a monster, and there are plenty of mindless action sequences and shoot-outs. But they’re tempered by real-world obligations (your son’s crib isn’t going to build itself) and the moral weight of your misdeeds.
Likewise, the world of Leonida, Rockstar’s faux Florida, is much more than a virtual crime laboratory. For twenty-five years, GTA’s pedestrians were furniture with legs. They walked, they screamed, they died. In GTA VI, if you accidentally bump into a man outside a gas station, he’ll square up and may throw a punch. Cut someone off on the highway, and they’ll chase you down in their own bout of road rage. Try to make small talk with a stranger, and there’s a decent chance she’ll tell you to go to hell — or worse — because in a place like this, hardly anyone talks to strangers.
The city is no longer a collection of victims waiting for you to beat up or exploit them. It’s a collection of people with their own short fuses, and many of them are as broke, as frightened, and as intoxicated as you are.
Because the city seems to have a soul, however shrunken, it’s striking what isn’t in Leonida. There are no churches, an observation by British critic Peter Hitchens, who once called GTA the Devil’s Bible. There are also no schools, no community centers, no food pantries, no nonprofits. To be fair to Rockstar, there were never caring institutions of any kind in Grand Theft Auto; the series has always been a portrait of America with the heart surgically removed. But in the older games, the absence read as a joke, a deliberate cartoon of a godless consumer wasteland.
Here, in a world rendered with photographic fidelity, that absence feels like a statement. Every building you can enter exists to extract something from you — your money, your labor, your time. Pawnshops, payday lenders, strip clubs, car washes that launder cash. The only god in Leonida is the market, and you are a free agent navigating its moods, which are capricious and rarely in your favor.
For half a century, Florida has been where America goes to see its own fever dreams, from glamorous to gonzo. In the 1980s, it was cocaine-cowboy Miami: Scarface and Miami Vice, pastels and shoulder holsters, an image so seductive that Rockstar lifted it wholesale for Vice City in 2002. Later came Carl Hiaasen’s crooked developers and his hit man with a Weed Eater for a hand, Tom Wolfe’s Back to Blood, Harmony Korine’s Spring Breakers, the “Florida Man” headline construction, and Tiger King. From high culture to low, it all seemed insane and fun.
Not here. There were stretches early on when GTA VI made me queasy. Rockstar doesn’t open with the postcard Florida of South Beach sunsets or champagne-soaked nightlife, but with the ugly, uncinematic Florida: trash-strewn trailer parks, run-down motels with hourly rates, drug dealers too strung out to count their own money, and skeezy strip club owners who talk to Lucia like she could be part of the inventory. It’s Sean Baker’s The Florida Project, minus the Magic Kingdom glowing on the horizon. I’ve played every GTA since the series went 3D, and this is the first one in which I occasionally wanted a shower, as if the scum from the swamps I was wading through had rubbed off on me.
We’re at a strange moment in the culture wars. In 2026, the people defending Grand Theft Auto VI’s honor are largely progressives — even though one of its leads is a violent white man devoted to his straight, monogamous relationship — while it’s MAGA types who seem to want more anarchy and amorality in their games.
For a quarter-century, hating on Grand Theft Auto was one of the few things Washington could agree on. In 2005, Hillary Clinton demanded a federal investigation after the Hot Coffee scandal in GTA: San Andreas. After Sandy Hook, Joe Biden called video game executives in for a meeting. In 2018, after Parkland, Donald Trump held his own meeting: “The video games, the movies, the internet stuff is so violent. It’s so incredible,” he said. A year later, after El Paso, he blamed “gruesome and grisly video games” for glorifying violence.
Blaming Rockstar Games was once the bipartisan comfort food of American politics: cheap, filling, and nobody ever had to touch a gun law.
So you’d expect Grand Theft Auto VI, the biggest entertainment launch of the decade, to set off the mother of all moral panics. The timing could hardly be better: Republicans were just routed in the midterms and lost both chambers of Congress. Why not change the subject to a video game where you can rob a liquor store in a neon-soaked Florida?
Instead, we’ve mostly heard crickets, with a couple of notable outliers. Tennessee Congressman Tim Burchett told TMZ the game is “more of a how-to video” for stealing cars and shooting cops and said those who let their kids play it are bad parents. But he immediately added, “We’re not going to legislate it.” On Fox & Friends Weekend, Rachel Campos-Duffy said she was “gonna push back a little,” because she didn’t think the game was good for our culture and asked whether Lucia, one of the coprotagonists, was “the hooker.” (Surprise: sex workers are gone from this version.) Fox News Digital’s big GTA story last week was about the dangers of sleep deprivation from playing games all night.
Liberals? They gave up the video game hate beat years ago. Since the Gamergate wars of the 2010s, progressive game criticism has mostly asked who gets to be the hero and how women are depicted. How many cops you can run over hasn’t been the question, and a game with a Latina colead has largely inoculated itself on that front.
So why has the Right gone soft? Perhaps because the Trump White House is like a parody that Rockstar’s writers’ room would have rejected in 2013 for being too on the nose.
The day before GTA VI launched, the official White House account posted a montage of Donald Trump striding past fighter jets, rendered in the game’s signature font, set to Dire Straits’ “Money for Nothing” and captioned “WELCOME TO MAGA CITY XLVII.” This wasn’t shocking, because for more than a year the White House’s social media team has embraced a strategy of appealing to gamer bros.
Consider the back catalog. In September 2025, the account cut footage of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests to the Pokémon cartoon’s opening theme, then closed on fake trading cards bearing detainees’ faces under the tagline “Gotta Catch ’Em All.” When the bombs started falling on Iran in March, the White House opened its war montage with a Call of Duty killstreak animation, as if the strikes were a reward for thirty kills without dying. Then, in September this year, came Arcade.gov, a set of retro browser games in which you can build the wall and deport people.
The Pokémon Company objected; Halo’s cocreator said a Halo-themed ICE recruitment post made him sick. The White House’s response? More or less its mission statement: “Nowhere in the Constitution does it say we can’t post banger memes.”
That line tracks with an administration that has governed as if life were a nihilistic M-rated game, with the president living out an adolescent male power fantasy: parading young blonde female aides on his arms, staging an Ultimate Fighting Championship fight card on the South Lawn for his eightieth birthday, and floating Nicki Minaj as press secretary after the previous one lasted five days in the job. Alligator Alcatraz might sound like a sick joke from GTA, but indeed, it was all too real: a dehumanizing makeshift immigration detention center in the Florida Everglades, complete with Florida Republicans selling branded merch to chuds.
Even outside of Mar-a-Lago, there are signs everywhere that America has hit a midlife crisis, descending into juvenilia — or, worse yet, psychosis. Grown men trade cartoon apes or dogs on the blockchain and lose their savings, while Hunter Biden gets in on the action with a $LAPTOP coin; bets on Jesus Christ returning for the Rapture in 2026 on Polymarket turn out to be a better wager. Even Las Vegas is dying, because everywhere in America is becoming like Las Vegas, a casino and a vape pen in every pocket.
One of our nation’s biggest young celebrities, sadly, is Clavicular, a twenty-year-old famous for smashing his own face with a hammer to “improve” his bone structure. Out on bail for rape charges, which he denies, stemming from an alleged assault shortly after a live stream, he’s complained about GTA VI being too “cucked” because it wants you to be kind to your virtual girlfriend.
The politicians and pundits worried about GTA corrupting America have it the wrong way around. These days, the game is the one that should worry about being corrupted by us.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Preserving Henry Ford’s failed Amazonian empire
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Deep in the Amazon Rainforest, in the Brazilian state of Pará, lies the dilapidated settlement of Fordlândia. A once bustling—albeit highly exploitative—village, it was established by the US industrialist Henry Ford in the 1920s. Fordlândia’s sole purpose was to serve as a rubber-tapping enterprise that would provide materials for the Ford Motor Company. But less than a decade after its founding, the rubber crops failed. With the development of synthetic rubber following close behind, Ford abandoned the project in 1945, and the village along the Tapajós River fell into severe disrepair.
Earlier this year, almost a century after Fordlândia was built, a federal court ruled that it must be protected as a heritage site under the Brazilian constitution. Local and national authorities have until the end of this month to come up with a conservation plan.
Ford’s company originally acquired the land for what would become Fordlândia in 1927. He envisioned building a Midwestern-style village as a hub for latex extraction, supplying materials for his factories in Michigan. Ford hoped to upend the dominance of British-controlled rubber plantations in Southeast Asia, which had left US manufacturers dependent on foreign suppliers.
Fordlândia, beyond giving the Ford Motor Company control over its supply of raw materials, was imagined as a self-sufficient settlement for around 10,000 people in the Amazon. Ford himself viewed Fordlândia as a sociological experiment intended to “Americanise” the local population, although the tycoon never visited his dystopian village. Workers there, many of them Indigenous people and migrants from northeastern Brazil, endured cultural subjugation and often faced dangerous conditions—including having to work through the hottest part of the day. Hundreds of people died during the short-lived project.
Workers organised a mutiny in 1930 after unreasonable restrictions were imposed in Fordlândia, including the prohibition of alcohol and tobacco, as well as the requirement of US customs like square dancing and a diet of wholewheat bread, brown rice, oatmeal and canned peaches. Shortly afterwards there was a full-scale riot, in which workers chased their American managers and the village cook into the jungle. The Brazilian army was brought in to restore order. The company subsequently fired a number of workers and appointed a new manager to complete Fordlândia’s infrastructure. (An agreement on serving different food to the workers was also reached.)
Ford’s social experiment unfolded alongside agricultural problems. Without the consultation of local experts, the rubber trees had been planted too close together. This made them vulnerable to disease and pests, and the growing conditions along the river were unsuitable. In 1933, at the recommendation of the American plant pathologist James Robert Weir, a second plantation was established downstream at Belterra, where conditions were more appropriate. Although it fared better than Fordlândia, production remained costly and it never became commercially viable.
No usable latex was ever produced in Fordlândia. After investing millions of dollars with no return, Ford sold the land back to the Brazilian government. The population dropped by more than 90% in the following years, but squatters and families moved back into the decaying structures in the 2000s. Around 3,000 people live in Fordlândia today, even as the village remains unconnected to paved roads.
A unique historical moment
The federal process for the designation of Fordlândia as a heritage site has been unresolved since the 1990s, when the move was first suggested by local advocates. In 2015, Brazil’s federal public prosecutor’s office filed a lawsuit stating that the site had “unquestionable” cultural value. In 2024, the National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage (Iphan) countered that Fordlândia lacked the criteria required for federal heritage listing, pointing to the loss of its original characteristics and the site’s deteriorated condition.
But in May 2026 a federal court ruled that, even without formal heritage status, the site should be protected. This decision was based on a 1988 constitutional article that mandates the conservation of both material and immaterial assets connected to Brazilian communities. The court added that uncertainty over ownership of the site had been used repeatedly as justification for inaction, and that the state of Pará and the municipality of Aveiro (which administers Fordlândia) had previously signed an agreement to begin conservation measures that never materialised. It also alleged that some interventions had been carried out without authorisation.
The court ruled that Iphan must now work with the state and municipality to deliver a plan by the end of November 2026, outlining the responsibilities of each government entity and the needs of each site in Fordlândia—including emergency measures for structures at imminent risk. Once approved, conservation work must begin within 30 days. If deadlines are not met, the court will impose a daily fine of $2,000 (10,000 reais) on the federal government and Iphan, and a $1,000 (5,000 reais) fine on the state and municipality. Iphan must also begin the administrative process to recognise Fordlândia as a heritage site.
In a statement to The Art Newspaper, a spokesperson for Iphan says the agency does not comment on ongoing legal proceedings. It remains unclear if Iphan plans to counter the court’s decision. “In May 2024, Iphan’s cultural-heritage advisory council denied Fordlândia’s designation as Brazilian cultural heritage,” the spokesperson says. “Iphan reiterates that it remains committed to the preservation of Brazilian cultural heritage, as mandated by the constitution.”
The sites to be reviewed include the former Fordlândia Hospital, designed by the Detroit architect Albert Kahn; the long-abandoned industrial and port warehouses; the houses of the American Village, where the company’s American managers lived; the workers’ village; the Henry Ford School; the Cine Patinha, a cinema whose roof has recently collapsed; and a convent on a cliff overlooking the Tapajós River, built in the post-Ford era and active until the early 2010s. All these structures have been exposed to the Amazon’s heat, humidity and heavy rainfall for years.
TripAdvisor-approved
Fordlândia remains highly remote, receiving few outside visitors and requiring a minimum six-hour trip to reach via high-speed boat. Still, there is evidence that intrepid travellers have made the journey. A company specialising in tours of the Amazon is currently offering a five-day visit to the region, including a stop in Fordlândia, for approximately $3,000 (16,000 reais) per person. Reviews for “Fordlândia Ghost Town” on TripAdvisor average 4.7 out of 5 stars, with one reviewer in 2016 calling the site “historical, magical and melancholic”, and another saying it tells a story of “hubris, determination, paternalism and ultimately failure”.
Although Fordlândia is unlikely to be commercialised as a tourist destination, the village’s surviving infrastructure has come to represent an unusual and failed attempt to Americanise and industrialise the Amazon. The remnants of the settlement also tell the story of the Brazilian workers who lived there, and those who have continued to inhabit it. The Brazilian government maintains that Fordlândia has “unquestionable historical, cultural and architectural value”, and that it represents “an American attempt to break the British monopoly on rubber and bring modern infrastructure to the middle of the Amazon”.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Dave Zirin

There’s Nothing “Crazy” About Wanting to Abolish Prisons
A recent New York Times article argued that “wokeness,” including calls for prison abolition, is a political liability. That’s simply not the case.
There’s Nothing “Crazy” About Wanting to Abolish Prisons
A recent “New York Times” article argued that “wokeness,” including calls for prison abolition, is a political liability. That’s simply not the case.
In a recent op-ed for The New York Times, Jacobin editor Meagan Day offered a pointed critique of the ways that identity politics can be weaponized to muzzle dissent. On its face, this could have been a valuable contribution to larger conversations about how the powerful co-opt anti-oppression language to silence and discipline their critics. Instead, Day punches down.
In his indispensable 2022 book Elite Capture: How the Powerful Took Over Identity Politics (And Everything Else), Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò explains how those in power deploy the politics of identity to entrench their own class or managerial positions, a method we have seen utilized in breathtakingly cynical fashion with the recent push to secure the speaker of the House position for Representative Hakeem Jeffries. According to Al Sharpton, Van Jones, and Jeffries himself—not to mention centrist fossils like Paul Begala and James Carville—opposing Jeffries is “racism of the left,” an accusation that undercuts any principled objections to his centrist politics, his commitment to funding the war on Iran, and his fealty to Israel and AIPAC.
It would be extremely valuable to introduce the concept of “elite capture” to a New York Times audience. But that’s not the op-ed Day wrote. Instead, starting with a headline that could comfortably appear as a chyron on Newsmax—“Woke 1 Was Crazy—and It’s Still Here”—the article rehashes what I’m sure Day would agree has been a well-trod argument across the political spectrum: that the “wokeness” of the “crazy” left is pushing people away from progressive politics. (Before reckoning with Day’s argument, it’s worth saying that her pejorative use of the word “woke”—a linguistic attack coined by the nationalist right to mock the phrase “stay woke” in the Black community—is an unfortunate choice.)
In the op-ed, Day argues that for democratic socialists to move forward, they must reject “wokeness,” which she argues has devolved into a “crusade against personal transgressions” built on the performance of empty absurdities. She explains the “crazy” of “wokeness” by telling the story of an almost-two-decade old experience she had in 2009 at Oberlin College, involving confusion over whether a frat was throwing a racist party and the ensuing uproar. What her disdain for these overzealous, painfully earnest college students (and don’t we want our college students to be overzealous and painfully earnest?) has to do with the actual titanic challenge plaguing the left—namely, how to organize this generational thirst for socialist politics—is left unclear.
In its last paragraphs, the op-ed gets at what seems to be its real intent. Here, Day calls for the “woke” brigade to stop attacking those in the DSA who say that the only way to build a mass party is to accept some degree of law-and-order politics—an idea that Day and other DSA thought leaders are calling “carceral minimalism.”
“Carceral minimalism” is a pithy label for a socialist position that makes strategic peace with the prison-industrial complex. Instead of advancing the century-old socialist principle of calling to abolish this country’s system of mass incarceration, they argue that such a demand is “not a viable road to social justice.” Police and prisons effectively reduce crime, they argue (although criminologists differ on this point), making them a necessary part of society, one that actually “protects the weakest.” Instead of abolishing this system, they argue that we should focus on jailing fewer people.
But the proponents of “carceral minimalism” never say how many human beings have to be locked away to meet their criteria. Currently, the United States has the largest prison population on earth, with 2 million people behind bars. Would 1.5 million incarcerated be the goal? That certainly would be better than our current nightmare. And decarceration reforms—like eliminating prison terms for nonviolent offenses or drug abuse and bail reform—have long been demands of the prison abolitionist movement. But this country would still be jailing more people per capita than anywhere on earth. Statistically, we know who would continue to get locked away: overwhelmingly the poor, some wrongly accused, few with decent legal representation, and disproportionately Black and Latino. Calling for “carceral minimalism” amounts to playing a racialized lottery with people’s lives. It’s about as far as a person can venture from the tradition of socialist prison abolitionists like Angela Davis and Howard Zinn. It is also a rebuke of the great socialist leader Eugene Debs’s thunderous declaration: “While there is a criminal element I am of it. While there is a soul in prison I am not free.”
Day and her cohort advance these politics in order to separate themselves from the “crazy” identitarian dead-enders and, in their telling, fully seize the power and opportunities that come with DSA’s unprecedented presence within the Democratic Party. This could come, however, with the price of unnecessarily dividing or pushing away the many in DSA who are joining in droves in order to build a multiracial organization that can effect radical change. There are no easy answers for how to accomplish this mammoth task, but history tells us that the organizations that did the most successful work in building multiracial coalitions—like the Communist Party in the 1930s or the Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee in the early 1960s—were able to do so because they threw themselves into explicitly anti-racist work.
To abandon that and support, even tactically, our racialized prison-industrial complex doesn’t seem like a feasible path to that goal. If anything, it recalls the early-20th-century Socialist Party’s terrible position on race, summed up best in Debs’s regrettable assertion, “We have nothing special to offer the Negro, and we cannot make separate appeals to all the races.”
Debs’s position, in addition to undercutting the Socialist Party’s ability to build in Black communities, also gave cover to the party’s outwardly racist, hyper-nationalist right wing, led by Representative Victor Berger. The Wisconsin congressman supported the Chinese Exclusion Act, promoted white-supremacist race science, and was not a fan of organizing Black and white workers together. As W.E.B. Du Bois wrote in 1911: “So long as the Socialist movement can put a ban upon any race because of its color, whether that color be yellow or black, the negro will not feel at home in it.”
Berger’s views changed for the better in subsequent decades, but the harm caused by a Socialist leader taking those positions caused irreparable damage to the reputation of socialism—one that lingers. It also played a role in the eventual split and near-total destruction of their organization, as socialists inspired by the 1917 Russian Revolution and those who became disgusted by the right of the Socialist Party split off to build the Communist Party of the United States.
Today, some thought leaders on the right of DSA have been publishing a great deal in praise of Victor Berger—his later years, of course—as a model for socialist organizers today. That the praise for Berger is happening alongside arguments for “carceral minimalism” feels more like a concerted branding rollout than a coincidence.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
What a time, in a moment so bursting with possibility, to choose to stand with the political establishment and join their exhausting “war on woke.” But even more harmful, what a time to introduce “carceral minimalism” to a mass New York Times audience as an aim of the socialist movement. This only serves to undermine those trying to organize in the best traditions of the movement and not its most regrettable.
Decades ago, Howard Zinn made it plain: “I am convinced that imprisonment is a way of pretending to solve the problem of crime. It does nothing for the victims of crime, but perpetuates the idea of retribution, thus maintaining the endless cycle of violence in cruel and useless substitute for the elimination of those conditions—poverty, unemployment, homelessness, desperation, racism, greed—which are at the root of most punished crime. The crimes of the rich and powerful go mostly unpunished.”
Is it “crazy woke” to want to tear down the prison-industrial complex? If so, it beats dreaming that the path to socialism is paved with the discarded remains of anti-oppression principles in the name of electoral expediency.

Sotheby’s withdrew a painting by Wade Guyton valued at $1 million from its Contemporary Day Auction in New York on November 17 after a collector notified the auction house that it might be a fake. Guyton confirmed that the work was not his, according to Artnet.
The untitled painting, dated 2006, was on view in a presale exhibition, where it was spotted by the collector, who noted its similarity to a work by Guyton in their private collection. The artist and his gallery, Matthew Marks, were contacted and arrived to inspect the work. They concluded that the work was not authentic, and it was withdrawn from the show.
The work in question was listed as an Epson ultrachrome inkjet on linen measuring 89 ½ by 53 inches. The canvas depicts two uneven columns of black with flames at the bottom of each and a red U shape in the right column that echoes the shape of the flames at left. An untitled work by Guyton sold at Sotheby’s in 2014 for nearly $6 million, a record for the artist.
The Contemporary Day Auction included postwar, Abstract Expressionism, Minimalist, and contemporary art by artists such as Helen Frankenthaler, Mark Rothko, Alice Neel, Wayne Thiebaud, Faith Ringgold, and Christopher Wool. Some works arrived from private collections, but it is not yet clear where the fake Guyton originated.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/sena.title: It’s Time to Ditch Kirsten Gillibrand
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/sena.author: Eoin Higgins
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/sena.text:
Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”
The stakes in 2028 couldn’t be higher for Democrats. Americans see the party as likely to win the White House after another two years of Donald Trump, especially given his historic unpopularity, and Democratic leadership will look to further expand their majorities in Congress.
How the Democratic Party selects candidates and develops strategy is going to have an outsized effect on the overall results — and the direction of the country.
After Senate Democrats elect their leader for the next two years on December 1, Chuck Schumer or Chris Van Hollen will have the opportunity to name the next head of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. It’s a powerful role: Whoever’s chosen will have an outsized voice in what kind of candidates run in 2028 and how much support they get.
New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a close ally of Schumer and a loyal member of the party’s pro-business wing, is making her case to remain DSCC chair for a second two-year term. On the face of it, she has a lot to commend her record: nine flipped seats in the 2026 midterms and a new majority that is likely to extend to 2030. It’s inarguable that under her leadership, the DSCC saw major gains.
Yet Gillibrand’s political instincts have, at times, threatened electoral success. Her tenure at DSCC has been marked by pushing ideological preferences, and candidate choice from her and Schumer has been a mixed bag.
While Gillibrand and the DSCC can point to real success stories like James Talarico in Texas and Mary Peltola in Alaska, they also backed Haley Stevens in Michigan, a charisma void who turned on the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, in the last days of the race allegedly over his views on Israel.
In Maine, the DSCC and establishment Democrats recruited Gov. Janet Mills, a 78-year-old with little interest in running, whose campaign against progressive upstart Graham Platner failed to launch. That was true even despite the many glaring deficiencies that ultimately doomed Platner’s candidacy and saw him replaced with ultimate general election winner Troy Jackson (whom Mills declined to endorse outright).
Even in cases when her instincts are right, Gillibrand struggled to exercise her influence for material effect. In Florida, left-wing Democratic Socialists of America member Angie Nixon came within 2 percentage points of winning the state’s Senate seat. Gillibrand, alongside Schumer, donated $5,000 each from their own leadership PACs and urged other senators to do the same — but couldn’t get the party overall to commit cash when it could have mattered.
The Democratic Party is not a monolith bringing together moderates and progressives into a general left-of-center umbrella. There are, necessarily, compromises for those in the tent, as Third Way Democrats are in coalition with DSA members.
After a blue-wave election, it’s important for party leaders to keep both sides happy as much as possible — within reason. The current push and pull and jockeying for position is leading to some dubious assertions of success metrics that the next DSCC chair will need to keep a clear head about.
Polling decisively showed Americans want action on the economy, healthcare, and the war with Iran. Over and over again, the public has made its priorities clear about accountability: Many voters in Texas were motivated this year because of the brutality of the administration’s immigration crackdown; voters also named “corruption” as a top concern.
Given those concerns, a role in leadership for someone like Gillibrand raises questions. The senator’s coziness with the crypto industry has drawn criticism as sector heavy-hitters poured over $196,000 in campaign donations to her in 2026 alone, by far the most for a candidate or officeholder in New York state.
This summer, Gillibrand’s son, Theo, started a financial exchange at age 22. He quickly took on investments from powerful financial operatives like crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, among others.
Gillibrand has legislated in lockstep with industry interests and repeatedly publicly defended crypto —even, in 2022, analyzing the feasibility of investing retirement plans in the currency market. As The Intercept reported in July, she was a lead negotiator in the crypto industry-favored legislation known as the Clarity Act, which would have allowed Wall Street to directly invest in the currency. The bill stalled out in the Senate in September despite her best efforts.
It’s hard to see a context in which it makes sense to send the message that corruption will continue, just as long as it’s our team doing it. But with Gillibrand at the head of the DSCC, that’s exactly what voters will hear in the next election cycle. The New York senator simply isn’t the right leader for the moment.
DSCC vice chairs Adam Schiff, Lisa Blunt Rochester, and Mark Kelly seem to be the three most likely alternatives, and all bring with them their own baggage. But they can plausibly claim a break with the existing do-nothing-Dem approach aimed more at personal enrichment and out-of-touch ideological commitments than Gillibrand can.
Newly elected Democrats understand the need for change and have almost uniformly rejected calls to continue the status quo by backing stale leadership in the Senate. Whether their efforts to change the face of the party in the chamber succeed or not, first-term Democrats are going to be more attuned to the concerns and priorities of the voters who sent them to Washington.
Senate leaders should listen to them. Democrats have an opportunity to show the public they heard the change message on Election Day.
Sticking with Gillibrand won’t help get that across to voters.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
