https://gothamist.com/news/driver-charge.title: Driver charged with killing Brooklyn nurse crossing Third Avenue
https://gothamist.com/news/driver-charge.author: Liam Quigley, Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/driver-charge.text:
The driver accused of fatally mowing down a nurse as she crossed a notoriously deadly Brooklyn roadway in August has been arrested, police said, and records show his vehicle was repeatedly cited for speeding on the day of the hit-and-run.
Staten Island resident Justin Mercado allegedly blew a red light on Aug. 29 and plowed into 28-year-old nurse Jiayi Zheng as he flew down Third Avenue at 55 mph, more than double the speed limit, authorities said. Officials said that Zheng, who had just finished a shift at nearby NYU Langone Hospital, was rushed back to the same hospital, where she died.
Authorities said Zheng was walking in a marked crosswalk when she was hit. In 2020, another nurse, Clara Kang, was killed by a motorcyclist while riding her bike home on the same stretch after an overnight shift.
City transportation department data shows there have been 17 deaths on the roadway in the past decade.
The NYPD said Mercado turned himself in on Wednesday after detectives identified him through surveillance footage.
He pleaded not guilty to manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide, leaving the scene of a crash, assault and reckless endangerment.
Mercado’s 2014 Cadillac, which had Pennsylvania plates, was captured flying through Brooklyn on the day of the crash. On the morning of her death, the sedan was clocked speeding through a school zone in Lower Manhattan just 30 minutes before he plowed into Zheng, data shows.
The Cadillac was cited for another speed camera violation on Third Avenue minutes after the crash. The car received two more school zone speeding violations in Brooklyn eight minutes after the crash.
Weeks before the crash, the car received a school zone speeding violation on Staten Island.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani restarted plans to make Third Avenue safer following Zheng’s death. Traffic lanes in both directions will be replaced over a 2.1-mile stretch beneath the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway with bike lanes, and the street’s pedestrian crossings will be shortened.
A call to Mercado’s lawyer was not immediately returned.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Rikers Monitor Details 14-Hour Delay in Finding Overdose Victim, Slams Slow Pace of Reforms
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The body of a Rikers Island detainee who overdosed wasn’t found for about 14 hours, according to a report by a court-appointed monitor overseeing the Department of Correction, as wider long-delayed jail reforms move at a “glacial pace.”
“The glacial pace of reform has been frustrating to all stakeholders and is far less than the urgency of the situation demands,” said monitor Steve Martin, noting violence is still far above levels the jail system reported in 2016, when he was first appointed.
“The high risk of harm is ongoing and pervasive,” the 432-page report said.
The report is the most recent oversight document detailing negligence and excessive use of force by corrections officers amid efforts to close Rikers and build new jails closer to courts.
The status update comes a week after Mayor Zohran Mamdani detailed the city’s latest plan to shut down Rikers, which will begin gradually as the first new jail in Brooklyn is expected to be complete in about three years and extend until 2032. The report did note some positive developments. Martin, who is based in Texas, said the Correction Department and the federally appointed remediation manager, Nicholas Deml, and his team “have made some important forward progress.”
Martin credited them with establishing a reliable baseline of staffing practices for the first time in more than a decade, reorganizing the Correction Department’s deeply flawed investigations division, and winning court approval for a comprehensive action plan to guide reforms.
Jail staff appear to have curtailed some of the most extreme uses of force, the report said. But Martin described that as a baseline expectation, not proof of compliance, and wrote that the city’s jails reflect “a system that is generating avoidable force events and then responding to them.”
The report, which covers January to June 2026 (and all the deaths since), is Martin’s 23rd status update. It echoes many prior failed efforts to improve conditions for detainees and staff, including a deeply flawed disciplinary system, officers too quick to use force, and hundreds of broken cell doors.
Conflict Over Solitary Confinement
The monitor also raised new concerns about a City Council law sharply restricting the use of solitary confinement, arguing that the legislation — currently on pause due to mayoral override — could make an already volatile jail system more dangerous if implemented before the Department of Correction addresses its underlying problems.
Martin and Deml said the city’s jails lack the operational foundation needed to safely implement key provisions of what is known as Local Law 42.
They warned that eliminating managerial discretion in certain situations could increase the risk of harm. Martin also flagged potential conflicts between the law’s requirements and existing court orders governing jail operations.
Still, the city and the monitoring team are continuing to develop a pilot program for restrictive housing where detainees who act out would be placed as an alternative to solitary. That includes finding a location, the right staff, security protocols and rehabilitative programming.
Martin and Deml’s concerns come after city lawmakers spent years crafting the new rules following the death of Layleen Polanco. The 27-year-old transgender woman was in the ninth day of a 20-day solitary confinement sentence when she was found lifeless inside her Rikers cell. She was being held in lieu of a $500 bond for misdemeanor sex work and drug possession charges.
Overall, Martin’s review used almost identical language from his prior report, in January, to describe the slow pace of meaningful changes.
“The reform effort continues to progress at a glacial pace,” he said, citing entrenched resistance and “pervasive poor practices.”
Martin and his team, led by Anna Friedberg, a lawyer with no previous jail experience, have billed the city $22 million since 2024, the latest year of available data. Martin rarely visits Rikers himself and primarily relies on Friedberg and some city jail staffers assigned to assist.
For all the damning findings in his reports, Martin has seldom pressed U.S. District Judge Laura Swain, who oversees the case, for immediate action. Instead, he has repeatedly chided jail officials for ignoring his advice and dragging their feet.
The review was made public late Tuesday night before the Thanksgiving holiday weekend. Several of Martin’s prior reports have also been published right before holiday stretches when the public is less focused on news.
Violence and Mayhem
In the latest report, Martin cites one eight-day stretch, Oct. 1 to 8, as an illustration of the ongoing danger. Over those days, the Correction Department reported 148 uses of force by correction officers, six stabbings and slashings (including two attempts), seven fires, 42 incidents of detainees hurting themselves, and 35 assaults on staff. There were also 16 serious-injury reports from fights or reported assaults, seven incidents in which Narcan was administered, 38 discoveries of contraband, and 28 emergency lock-ins.
The report also describes two incidents in a two-week span in late August and early September when staff at the Otis Bantum Correctional Center used pepper spray on men who had tied sheets around their necks and attached them to holding pens.
In both cases, staff hit the men, who were trying to take their own lives, with pepper spray.
Martin called the incidents “especially troubling” because the department’s own directive expressly prohibits using chemical agents on someone trying to hang themselves. The department revised that directive in 2025, but Martin wrote that his team “continues to identify incidents” in which staff use pepper spray in those dire mental health crises.
In one July 5 incident at the West Facility on Rikers, the report says an officer grabbed a detainee by the neck, pulled his hair, kneed him in the head and struck him with a chemical-agent canister. The officer then sprayed him while he was restrained and also used racially charged language during the violent encounter, according to the report.
A captain had to order the officer to step away. He was suspended for 30 days and resigned in September while facing formal charges.
The 14-Hour Delay
As for deaths in custody, nine people have died behind bars this year so far.
That includes Barry Cozart, 39, who was found unresponsive inside the George R. Vierno Center on March 25.
Cozart had a history of substance abuse and was seen on surveillance video looking intoxicated the night before his death, according to the report.
Staff repeatedly failed to conduct proper tours, left their posts unsupervised for extended periods, and a logbook entry falsely recorded that a tour-tracking device was working. Cozart’s body wasn’t found until roughly 14 hours after he was last seen moving, the report said.
The Medical Examiner said the cause of death was acute intoxication from the combined effects of methadone and gabapentin.
The area captain and floor officer were each suspended without pay for one month.
Another detainee, John Price, 49, suffered from clear signs of medical distress as he waited for roughly 3 ½ hours in a clinic holding pen without being seen because jail officers didn’t tell medical staff he was having a medical emergency inside the Eric M. Taylor Center on March 28.
No jail or medical staff have been disciplined but the investigation is ongoing, Martin said.
“The deaths of people in DOC custody are tragic and continue to expose the serious consequences that occur when basic security, supervision, and correctional health practices break down,” Martin wrote.
Martin urged better communication between DOC and Correctional Health Services, which oversees medical care, “to improve prompt identification of people in distress, and improve emergency response times.”
The Correction Department did not respond to an email seeking comment.
The Legal Aid Society, which brought the class action case that has led to the monitor and remediation manager, said the report showed how little progress had been made despite a decade of court oversight.
“The conditions at Rikers Island remain dangerous and unacceptable,” said Mary Lynne Werlwas, director of the group’s Prisoners’ Rights Project, and Debbie Greenberger, a partner at the law firm Emery Celli, who issued a joint statement.

https://www.propublica.org/article/smith.title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
https://www.propublica.org/article/smith.author: Andy Kroll
https://www.propublica.org/article/smith.text:
A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.
In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”
Read More
Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.
In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure.
“No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.”
Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public.
“We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said.
Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year.
Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.
The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story.
Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”
Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence.
Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.”
“The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote.
Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media.
“Over my dead body,” he wrote.

Generally I don't mess around with food pop-ups and limited drops and such. I don't think there's anything wrong with them ethically or, like, strategically, but unless you're my personal friend (for whom I will go anywhere and do anything!), the irreplicable nature and inherent scarcity of the model usually requires jumping through more hoops, and causes more anxiety, than I care to handle.  
Sometimes though, I'm happy to make an exception, especially on a lovely day weather-wise, at a location that's an enjoyable bike ride from my apartment, and most importantly, for something that's rarely offered anywhere else and when prepared well, hits me exactly right. Which is why I was delighted to spend last Saturday morning with Mikey Deegan and his partner Susie Thomas as they hurriedly prepared their weekends-only, holiday-season takeover of the Screen Door in Greenpoint. They're calling it Mikey's Pies.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economi.title: Charles Koch Has a Dystopian Plan for How to Control Workers
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economi.author: Henry Snow
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economi.text:
Charles Koch Has a Dystopian Plan for How to Control Workers
Ultraconservative billionaire Charles Koch likes to style himself as a champion of individual liberty. But his phony science of workplace management created an atmosphere that Koch’s workers compared to living in a totalitarian state.
At a conference in Orlando, Florida, in 2005, the American billionaire Charles Koch gave a speech explaining how he and his audience could protect “freedom and prosperity in the world.” While accepting an award named after potato chip magnate Herman Lay, Koch explained that he had conceived a “science of liberty,” which he described as “the study and practice of sustainably advancing liberty to create prosperity and social progress.”
The solution lay, Koch said, in economic analysis — treating every interaction between people as a market exchange. He claimed this “Market Process Analysis” helped him build not only his fortune but also his family life and interpersonal interactions.
Out of it, he created what he called Market-Based Management (MBM), a theory for managing workers and his business. The science of liberty he outlined in Orlando applied those same principles to government — in America and around the world.
Playing God
Workers at Charles Koch’s web of companies felt differently. One anonymous Koch employee in Wichita wrote that their colleagues were “walking around like they are in the George Orwell book, ‘1984,’” terrified of the Koch family, the “only major employer in the area,” who used their power “to control the employees and their movement within the other Koch entities.”
Another, in Atlanta, called Koch’s extensive training in MBM “brainwashing.” The atmosphere, others reported, was “cult-like,” and employees were “noticeably unhappy,” with fifty-hour workweeks as well as mandatory overtime and weekend work. A software engineer in Bangalore wrote that at Koch’s companies “managers are GOD. . . . They can play with anyone’s life.”
Some of these disgruntled employees, hoping to convince management to change their ways, insisted they were not “practicing what they preached” — that MBM’s values were good and simply being misapplied. But Charles Koch had worked on the system for decades.
He personally cultivated its materials, and his company forced employees to study them for upward of five hours a week, according to one review. Some of the values in Koch’s system of MBM were simply anodyne — “respect” is its ninth “guiding principle.” But the underlying purpose of the philosophy was to extract maximum profit from employees.
Science of Control
The science of liberty seemed more like a science of control. Koch’s “science” relied on four connected claims about human behavior that structure economic and political life across the globe today.
First, that we should analyze society as merely a collection of individuals, an idea known as methodological individualism. Second, the claim that individuals are motivated only by self-interest, generally though not exclusively in the form of material incentives — or psychological egoism.
Third, an insistence that deliberate planning cannot be trusted: humans are too selfish, and too limited, to make or execute grand plans for society. We should trust the competitive evolution of markets over the cooperative intention of democracy.
And fourth, the belief that everything is — and should be — a market. The world consists of competing individuals, and social science exists to figure out how to structure that competition so prosperity arises out of it. This paradigm is known as market fundamentalism.
Proponents of these ideas present them as inescapable truths about the world, like gravity. If we know how human beings will act, there is no need to speak of how they should act. Thus, “there is no alternative,” as the Victorian philosopher Herbert Spencer put it, to these cruel calculations: they are an inescapable truth about human action.
Political Visions
But these ideas are not scientific truths that experts have discovered. They are political visions that ideologues have created. There are other ways we can live and work, and generally most people prefer those alternatives when asked and frequently pursue them when we are not.
From Samuel Bentham’s program of mechanized and precarious shipbuilding labor to Frederick Winslow Taylor’s floundering efforts to optimize pig iron loading, supposedly optimal methods for manipulating workers have generally failed — until their architects relied on political and economic force to impose their ideas anyway.
Four hundred years of elite scheming have failed to produce either the technocratic control that utilitarians like the Benthams wanted or the pure competition advocated by market radicals like Ludwig von Mises. Every country in the world, even those with little or no political freedom, has major movements that demand better. Those movements do not always win. But every victory builds a foundation for the next.
Today we have labor rights, voting power, and political freedoms — where we have them — because of the hard work of those who came before us. Building on their legacy, we can continue to make a better world now and to create conditions for yet more advances after we are gone.
Control science is not “human nature.” It is not “how the world works.” It is not just orthodox economics or economic common sense or advanced political discourse. Identifying the different intertwining strands that give control science its strength and naming the total result, helps us take it on. Labeling control science — and labeling it accurately as a matter of control — is all the more important because of how it works.
Rule Without Rulers
The irony of control science is that it is ultimately not a theory of control by anyone at all. Control science respects no kings, no presidents, and no gods but what one of Herbert Spencer’s followers called “that awful One to whom it is profanity to pray.” This is an ideology for control by no one, of everyone. Its advocates call this freedom.
The science of control is an attempt at rule without rulers, an abstract authoritarianism, an art of excuses: centuries of elites finding themselves in positions of power and scrambling to justify that power to themselves and the world. This vast program of institutionalized apathy has been developed through, and always relies on, the forceful control of workers themselves.
Identifying this program does two things for us. First, it makes clear that cynical claims about “human nature” are social and political constructions, not an objective truth discovered by capitalists. Second, then, this intellectual history of economic thought reveals how much it has always been about control of us, not by us. We can rally against it accordingly: control science is fake, and it is wrong.
Ideas alone will not be enough, of course. Control science has succeeded by embedding itself in the legal, political, and economic structures of the world around us. It does not describe actual human nature, but it does describe how many people do, and must, act, precisely because of the way capitalists have made the world.
Selfishness is embedded in the real material relations we have with each other: the most responsible strategies for investing, for example, may include investments in oil companies. The cheapest products are produced under the worst labor conditions. Buying better or investing differently as an individual will accomplish little, and it is difficult to build collective movements around doing something that makes us, temporarily, worse off, in a world of economic scarcity and against constant competition by the preachers of selfishness.
We cannot defeat control science as individual consumers. But we can as workers, as voters, and as full human beings. Over the last four centuries, many of the greatest victories for justice, equality, and freedom have relied on mass movements of working people, from the revolutions of the eighteenth century to the New Deal and decolonization in the twentieth century.
Workers’ Control
The twenty-first century has been, in much of the world, a period of defeat and retreat for working-class left-wing politics. But it does not have to be that way. The science of control was made in the workplace. It can be unmade there as well. Labor organizing forces idealistic progressives to ground our projects in material incentives: better wages, improved working conditions, more free time.
This is particularly necessary in the cynical world control science has made. We have been told that everyone is selfish and that an alternative world is impossible. This makes it all the more difficult to believe rousing appeals to empathy and ethics alone. Organizing within workplaces must become part of a broader movement for democracy and equality at work — control by workers, not of them.
Most of us recoil at the idea of an absolute monarch or a dictator. Yet we spend a good portion of our days, and our lives, doing the bidding of bosses over whom we have little power. We should abhor authoritarian company “presidents” and company boards the way we do dictatorship and monarchy. Working people should wield power through robust and assertive democratic unions to force our bosses to take our needs and desires and dreams into account.
A powerful labor movement alone will not end the science of control. And an economy of competing democratic cooperatives would still be one driven by markets and competition. Thus, we also need to aim for democratic control of the economy writ large. Human needs and collective desires, not the movement of markets, should determine what we make and do.
A market is a forever skewed democracy: your voting power is proportional to your wealth, and the most exploitative actors are therefore the most powerful. We should find this an offense against democracy, and we should act accordingly. Rule by market rules has only succeeded in leading us to a world that satisfies no one.
Mass working-class movements, wielding the power of democracy, can build an intentional and deliberate world that reflects our most meaningful and deeply held collective wants, democratically aggregated, rather than our individual purchasing choices, scaled by our wealth. We can build our moral principles and our material needs into the legal structure, social fabric, and collective ideals of our societies so that acting in the common good, instead of against it, becomes easier and more obvious every day.
A Collective Program
We know collective effort can outcompete nihilist competition, because it has done so before: an imperfect fraction of this program of economic democracy saved the world from fascism. Imagine what a full-fledged collective program could do for living standards, economic growth, and climate change.
Through public housing authorities, we can determine where housing is built and how much it costs based on our need for comfortable homes, instead of the political demand to keep housing prices up for those already locked into an expensive mortgage. With utility nationalization, we can replace hated telecommunications monopolies with less expensive, more functional infrastructure that we control.
All of this requires no promises of or belief in a socialist utopia (though it will help us move toward one). Right now, it is right-wing economics that is in the way of lower rent, higher wages, shorter hours, full employment, and economic dignity, for all of us. If we take control of our work and our lives, we can secure a better life together.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Artist Nick Cave and India pavilion win Venice Biennale prizes following controversy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James Imam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Venice Biennale has named the American artist Nick Cave and India’s national pavilion as the winners of its top art prizes this year, following a controversy that saw the competition’s jury resign and several artists and pavilions withdraw from the running.
In previous editions of the Biennale, an international jury has selected the artist and national pavilion to receive the prizes, traditionally known as Golden Lions. This year, however, the awards were renamed Visitors’ Lions and awarded on the basis of votes cast by visitors to the exhibition.
The new voting system was introduced following a dispute over the inclusion of Russia and Israel in the 2026 Biennale. In a statement in April, the five-person jury announced that it would not award prizes to national pavilions or artists from countries whose leaders were charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The International Criminal Court had issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin, Russia's president, in 2023, and for Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, the following year.
The jurors resigned days later, saying they were doing so “in acknowledgement” of their previous statement.
Dozens of artists then ruled themselves out of the contest in solidarity with the jury, though they remained on the ballot. The Biennale clarified that votes for withdrawn entries would not be considered.
It is unclear whether Cave and the India pavilion received the most votes of all entries on the ballot, including withdrawn entries. The Biennale declined to provide The Art Newspaper with a breakdown of the results.
“The Venice Biennale does not publish rankings or detailed voting results, as the regulations do not provide for this,” a Biennale spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper. “This applies to the Visitors’ Lions, just as it has always applied to the decisions of the international juries.”
Cave is best known for work that combines fashion, sculpture and performance. His exhibition at Venice’s Arsenal includes seven works, among them Amalgam (Origin) (2024), a monumental bronze sculpture of a figure with branches growing out of its body and birds nestling among twigs. Each of the seven works address a stage of grief.
"On the eve of Thanksgiving, I feel an even deeper sense of gratitude, for the friendship that bound me with Koyo Kouoh, and for the fact that she decided to include my work in the In Minor Keys exhibition," Cave said in a statement. "This project is a synthesis of my wider artistic research: it recognises the history of violence and oppression that Black people have endured and continue to endure in the United States, and it pays tribute to the beauty created by that very community, expressing the possibility of growth towards a different future."
India's exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance, features works by five artists including clay sculptures, dried flowers and plants hung from the ceiling, and a demolished family home reconstructed in white thread. Curated by Amin Jaffer, the exhibition reflects on the rapid expansion of cities in India, according to the Biennale's website.
On Wednesday, when this year's winners were announced, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, the Biennale’s president, praised the new voting system.
He said in a statement: “The public of the Exhibition embraced this recognition—the Visitors’ Award—as an opportunity to bring Pablo Picasso’s practice to life: a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it".

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Trump Wants to Quiet Quit the Iran War—but the War Won’t Let Him
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: David Faris
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Trump Wants to Quiet Quit the Iran War—but the War Won’t Let Him
The president’s senseless war of choice has left him without any good choices.
Despite the GOP’s historic drubbing in November’s midterm elections based at least in part on the fallout from America’s disastrous war of choice in Iran, President Donald Trump seems to have no new ideas about how to end the conflict, apart from randomly declaring that it’s already over. He likewise is at a loss to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and return the global economy—upended by the war’s shocks to the supply chains for oil, fertilizer, and other essentials—to normalcy.
If anything, Trump appears determined to “quiet quit” the war, simply by declaring the status quo to his liking and pushing new attacks into the next calendar year. This move stands athwart his repeated vows during the midterm campaign to renew an aggressive bombing campaign in Iran after the election. But Trump won’t be able simply to walk away from his war of his choice, because no amount of flimflam and media manipulation can make this problem go away.
A diminished Trump, just back from his embarrassing hang-out session with the brutal autocratic leaders of Russia and China, shuffled slowly to the podium at the White House last Friday and mumbled that he would “absolutely” launch the war again. “Well. I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year,” he said about the possibility of new hostilities, as if the war is a work project to be circled back to when it’s convenient. You can’t send a war home for the holidays.
This latest effort to kick the can down the road is very much of a piece with the countless ultimatums Trump has issued and then walked back in the weeks and months since this pointless and ill-conceived war failed to achieve its objectives. The president finds himself mired in an open-ended standoff that not only strengthened the Iranian regime and its resolve but has also sent catastrophic ripple effects through the global economy. And with both sides seemingly eager for a pretext to move on to the next, and potentially much more destructive, round of fighting, the Iranian stalemate has become a catastrophic setback in a year already overstuffed with them.
For months, the United States has been leading an end-run around the Strait of Hormuz, escorting mostly Saudi and Emirati tankers to safety. This policy has succeeded in the short-term goal of bringing prices down somewhat—but its costs are staggering. There are now three aircraft-carrier battle groups in the Persian Gulf, along with dozens of support vessels, all working around the clock to sustain the expensive illusion that oil exports are back to prewar levels. Operating a carrier group runs about $8–9 million a day, which means that keeping three of them in the region is running taxpayers upwards of $27 million a day, to say nothing of the munitions and opportunity costs. The United States may be spending as much as $42 million a day on naval operations in and around the Strait of Hormuz alone.
Yet it is hard to know exactly how well this gambit is going even on its own logistical terms, because the Pentagon has descended into Vietnam-era degrees of lying and misdirection, even allowing for the impressive levels of mendacity reached by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his minions. Classified briefings are provided only to Trump’s Republican quislings, while tallies of killed and wounded have been altered and updated without explanation. And cost estimates are almost certainly fanciful.
What is actually happening in and around the Strait of Hormuz is likely much uglier than what we have thus far been told. On Monday, for example, two tankers reportedly hit Iranian mines in the strait and caught fire. Last week, New York Times columnist Thomas Friedman, a longtime enthusiast of the Gulf monarchies, went to the Gulf to perform his decades-old shtick of mixing metaphors and quoting cab drivers. But this time, Friedman may have inadvertently relayed the truth about what’s really happening.
From an unnamed “senior Emirati oil official,” Friedman claimed that, far from carrying out the perfectly calibrated petroleum-exfiltration scheme detailed in credulous news reports, the escort convoys are subjected to relentless Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks. These salvos, Friedman wrote, result in a “bull’s-eye every time,” disabling tankers and forcing them to be towed back to port. This is “happening every day” according to Friedman’s source. If this is even remotely true, American war planners will eventually run out of ships to carry oil in and out of the Gulf and possibly people willing to operate them. Are people dying in these attacks? We certainly won’t be getting this kind of information out of the Pentagon anytime soon.
Hegseth’s strategy of deception and diversion simply won’t work in the long run. Remember that it wasn’t a string of dramatic sinkings of tankers that forced the Strait of Hormuz to close in the first place—it was shipowners and maritime insurance underwriters who found the threat of catastrophe to be far too high and effectively halted operations in the area. If the mighty American military, working day and night with its closest regional partners, cannot avert nightly precision strikes that disable countless tankers or permanently eliminate Iran’s capacity to harass shipping, then the forces of economic gravity will once more overtake the rhetoric of Trump administration jingoists.
Even if American political leaders were willing to continue to indefinitely foot the bill for this fool’s errand, it won’t return oil markets to the prewar status quo or ease the pain of diesel prices that are still close to $6 a gallon. And if there is no deal in place, the whole edifice will collapse in five minutes when the United States pulls the plug, just as it did when America jettisoned its occupations in Afghanistan and Iraq after 20 years.
So what’s the plan here? Iran has spent decades in an economic straitjacket imposed by the United States and its allies, and yet the regime persists. Neither economic isolation nor months of punishing attacks from the US and Israel have made them crack. Still, even though Tehran is willing to impose almost limitless hardships on its citizens so that its authoritarian system may endure, it’s unlikely to sit back and let America choke off its oil exports forever. This dangerous moment is made potentially more combustible by both a radicalized Iranian leadership and an American president who habitually threatens war crimes and escalation as a negotiating tactic.
A reckoning may come sooner rather than later. The Institute for the Study of War warned on Sunday that Iran “will likely attempt to run the US naval blockade in the coming days” in an effort to break it. Tehran has reportedly positioned 14 tankers around the export hub of Kharg Island and intends to use them to test US resolve—perhaps by setting China as a destination and daring the United States to stop them.

“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
If the United States moves to interdict or disable the tankers, Iran may choose to retaliate by hitting targets it has thus far deemed off limits, including vital Gulf energy infrastructure or the multitude of unhardened civilian targets across the region. This threat is why, almost nine months into the war, America has chosen not to strike vital facilities of the Iranian oil industry or critical civilian infrastructure, despite Trump’s continued threats to do so.
Last week, CNN reported that Iran may be planning to target Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb attack in Washington DC. Based on unnamed sources, the report reeked of the kind of media manipulation and errant fearmongering that led to the Iraq War more than 23 years ago. Zeteo’s Asawin Suebsaeng asked his own intelligence sources about the threat, which they deemed “total horseshit.” Both the contents of the report as well as its timing are disturbing—in the same way that alarmist accounts of new terrorist plots fed pro-war sentiment prior to the invasion of Iraq.
Meanwhile, as Tehran and Washington signal their intent to renew widespread hostilities, Iranian leaders are openly contemplating reversing their long-standing claim that the country’s nuclear program is for civilian purposes only. This would, of course, reverse the ostensible rationale for Trump’s war—and confirm the many warnings from regional experts that a military confrontation with Iran presents Tehran with a powerful incentive to build up its military nuclear capacity. It’s a problem Trump has been on a collision course with since his rash 2018 decision to pull out of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action that stemmed the development of nuclear weapons in Iran.
American intelligence sources claim that they’ve pinpointed the location of Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile beneath a bomb site in Isfahan—but officials from the International Atomic Energy Agency say they can’t confirm these claims. For all we know, there are centrifuges spinning day and night deep inside Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain as the emboldened junta of Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps leaders who seem to be making the day-to-day decisions in Iran race toward a nuclear weapon.
Trump is, therefore, stuck exactly where he has been for months—desperate to be finished with a war that is far from finished with him, with the worst seemingly yet to come.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Fishing in Goa before tourism made taxi-drivers of everyone: Karan Kapoor’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Charlotte Jansen
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
I was born in India in 1962, the year after Goa was liberated from Portuguese rule. My mother was English and my father was Indian. My maternal grandparents worked in a theatre company and toured the east doing Shakespeare plays. My father, Shashi Kapoor, was an actor who worked for my grandparents’ theatre company and met my mother – Jennifer Kendal – there when he was 18. He then became a very successful movie star in India. They had a remarkable, unusual life. I thought it was normal.
In 1970, my parents decided to take a family holiday in Panjim in Goa. We stayed at the Mandovi hotel, an amazing place. I remember it vividly. We discovered a restaurant on the beach in a village called Saunta Vaddo, run by a seafarer, Anthony, who made incredible food. We fell in love with Saunta Vaddo. There was no electricity or running water back then. We went out exploring every day – there was always something to do. We swam, went fishing and read a lot. We rented a house called the Love House, because of the white heart painted on the roof – a shack on the beach that was previously inhabited by hippies and was full of books.
From then on, we spent every holiday there – Diwali, Christmas, Easter. Back then, if you took a ship to Goa from Mumbai it took 24 hours, and there were often no cabins left so you slept out on deck. But sometimes we drove and once my grandfather, who was a very bad driver, took us there. You couldn’t use headlights because of the war in the east, so we used torches from the backseat to light the road. The whole family would come at Christmas, and my dad would appear with a turkey on Christmas Eve, and fried fish and prawns from Anthony’s.
We became part of the village and we knew everyone. Eventually I started to record and photograph the people around me – our friends, weddings, ceremonies – characters I had known since I was eight. Then I started travelling to other parts of Goa with my brother, first on bikes, then motorbikes.
For me, this image of a big boat is very symbolic of everything that was amazing about Saunta Vaddo at that time. The whole village was involved, all the men were launching the boats out to sea to catch mackerel. A scout would look out for the schools, millions of them would come down the coast. There was a lot of excitement and shouting because, if they missed the catch, the next village further down would get them, so it was all a bit competitive.
As a child it was the most exciting thing, screaming and pushing this massive boat out, held together by tar and rope, and made the same way boats were made a century ago. The villagers would sing songs and drink feni, a local liquor; it was a way of life we had that doesn’t exist any more. In many ways, that boat held the whole village and the old slow Goan way of life together. Then tourism hit and the fishers became taxi drivers and waiters – they could make a better living that way. Things changed.
I continued photographing Goa until about 1996. You can’t recognise these places now, they’re so built-up. I’ve made a book of the photographs as a tribute to my parents, and will exhibit them in Panjim next month. I like to romanticise that the picture shows the last time they fished like that.
I went around on my Royal Enfield motorcycle with my Nikon FM and Hasselblad, stopping in tavernas to have a beer and some fried fish. I was drawn to the Portuguese influence in Goa, a legacy of more than 450 years of colonial rule. I photographed religious festivals, tiatr (musical theatre) and dhirio (a traditional bullfighting sport native to the state). I do remember the hippy era in the 1960s and 70s in Goa very well but it never interested me. I never photographed it.
Music was always a very big part of life in Goa: serenading, singing, playing instruments – and drinking. And the amazing fish curry rice is the best. I still go there every year, but I don’t go back to Saunta Vaddo – it’s been devastated. At first it made me sad but now I just feel fortunate to have had this experience, to have lived like that and known what it was like. It was incredible. I’m still looking for places like it.
My Goa 1976-1996: Photographs by Karan Kapoor is at Serendipity arts festival in Panjim, Goa, 13-20 December.
Karan Kapoor’s CV
Born: Mumbai, 1962
 
High point: I am just grateful that I have been able to have a successful career that provided for me and my family, doing what I love most
 
Top tip: Work with what is most personal and closest to your heart

https://gothamist.com/food/inside-the-th.title: Inside the Thanksgiving pie rush at the Brooklyn bakery Four & Twenty Blackbirds
https://gothamist.com/food/inside-the-th.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/food/inside-the-th.text:
At the Brooklyn pie shop Four & Twenty Blackbirds, Thanksgiving prep begins in August. That’s when Ben Heemskerk, director of operations, said he starts to think about the massive amount of dough needed to fulfill an influx of orders for meticulously baked desserts. In September, he puts a team together to make that dough, which is kept frozen until much closer to the holiday.
“It’s like a roller-coaster where you’re just gradually going up,” Heemskerk said. “You feel the ch-ch-ch-ch-ch-ch and you know the time is coming. You know November is on its way.”
When November hits, the roller-coaster drops. Because everything other than the pie dough at Four & Twenty is made fresh for Thanksgiving orders, Heemskerk said the two weeks leading up to that Thursday are full of confectionery madness. Tensions rise with the oven temperatures as staff members work around the clock to bake pies for pickup and delivery orders, along with larger batches for wholesale shipments to places like Butterfield Market, Union Market and the Park Slope Food Coop. This year, according to Heemskerk, Four & Twenty will have produced something like 30,000 pies in the run-up to Thanksgiving.
“I’m really proud of [that] fact,” he said. “This year is actually the biggest year yet.”
Four & Twenty co-founders Melissa and Emily Elsen (they’re sisters from South Dakota) started custom-baking pies in their Crown Heights apartment in 2009. They opened a brick-and-mortar location on Third Avenue in Gowanus in 2010 and, within a couple years, had started to bake out of a nearby facility on Sackett Street as well. I swung by that roughly 3,000-square-foot facility earlier this week, hoping to catch a glimpse of the Thanksgiving sugar rush.
Melissa had warned me ahead of time that some employees might be stressed out, given the demands of baking this many handmade desserts: “When we’re only making a few hundred or even a thousand [pies], it’s doable,” she said. “When we scale up to this volume, you realize that it’s slow. Making things by hand takes a lot of time.”
But the facility turned out to be a pretty calm environment. By mid-Tuesday morning, all of the wholesale orders were out the door, and the bakers vibed to pop music while whisking custards and carefully folding pie crusts for local pickup and delivery orders. A warm buttery scent greeted me upon entering the space.
Four & Twenty hired several seasonal employees to join a dozen (or so) staff bakers during the Thanksgiving scramble. One of those staff members, Rufus Read, told me Tuesday that he had worked 12-hour shifts three days in a row. During that time, he oversaw the production of custard fillings for three of the four pies Four & Twenty offered customers for Thanksgiving orders: bittersweet chocolate pecan, salty honey and brown butter pumpkin. (The fourth and most popular pie of the bunch, the salted caramel apple, doesn’t involve custard.)
“We try to keep morale up,” he said. “It’s a long shift, but it could be way worse.”
Read estimated that he had made close to 50 rounds of pumpkin pie filling by the time I talked to him. “There’s 6,000 grams per batch, so you guys do the math,” he said. This would explain the massive stack of Libby’s canned pumpkin I saw resting against a wire storage rack.
Heemskerk talked me through some other Thanksgiving purchase orders, many of which were negotiated with suppliers over the summer. Four & Twenty ordered six pallets of 40-pound apple bushels from the Hudson Valley; three 1,700-pound pallets of medium-sized Georgia pecans; about 1,200 pounds of flour; and “lots and lots of butter” (specifically, Cabot’s European-style butter with 83% butterfat).
I walked around the facility to observe these ingredients in action. The bakers seemed to have reached a flow state, each one bouncing between different stages of the process. Rica Borich, a former Four & Twenty kitchen manager who returned to help with the Thanksgiving rush, told me she was working on a brown butter butterscotch for the pumpkin pie while also helping a colleague make chocolate ganache to spread across the bottom of the pecan pie.
The Four & Twenty employees working on the packaging side of things were a little more frantic, given that the unparalleled logistics of Thanksgiving pie delivery remains a headache. The completed wholesale orders had included 3-inch and 8-inch pies, which required a separate packaging process. Now, at least, all the pies were the traditional 10-inch size. (Thanksgiving orders have closed, but the same pies will be available afterward.)
McKale Goodwin, a fulfillment lead working his fifth Thanksgiving with Four & Twenty, said he had worked eight days in a row “trying to keep things going as smoothly as possible.” His job is to make sure the pies are packaged correctly and sent to the right destinations, lest someone not receive what they paid good money for (the 10-inch pies run $46 each). On Tuesday, Goodwin flitted about the facility to make sure his team had removed pies from the racks quickly enough for everyone in the kitchen to replenish the supply.
Four & Twenty scaled up operations as its client list grew over the past couple years. The company now works with Baldor, a food distribution service that Heemskerk said stretched the pie delivery zone from Maine to Washington, D.C. He told me about an email he received that morning from a loyal customer in Virginia who worried that her Thanksgiving would be ruined if she didn’t receive her Four & Twenty order in time. (She had nothing to be worried about, per Heemskerk.)
“People get really stressed out about their Thanksgiving dinners, and they want to be amazing hosts,” he said. “Whether you buy 5,000 pies for your company or one apple pie for your dinner table, it’s the same importance. It’s the same priority for those two customers.”
Heemskerk has a far more relaxed attitude toward his own Thanksgiving celebration. He said he planned to take a Four & Twenty pie to the house of friends who are hosting his family.
I asked which flavor he would bring. “Good question,” he answered. “At that point, it might just be whatever’s left. Don’t tell my hosts that.” (Sorry, hosts, if you’re reading this.)
Read, the custard czar, assumed he would end up in the kitchen on Thanksgiving, as per usual, but noted that there’s a lot less pressure when you’re cooking at home and can “wave my drink around and say hi to everyone and make some food.” Maybe someone else will bring the pie.
“That’s what I’ll be doing at some point on Thursday,” he said. “Might have to sleep in first.”
That rest is well deserved. Heemskerk said he encourages his staff to take the work seriously, given how much these pies mean to their customers — especially those like the woman in Virginia, who said that she’s ordered Four & Twenty pies for the past 10 Thanksgivings.
But Heemskerk also acknowledged that these aren’t life or death matters.
“I love my job,” he said. “It’s an important thing … but it’s just pie, right?”

https://www.propublica.org/article/orego.title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
https://www.propublica.org/article/orego.author: Rob Davis
https://www.propublica.org/article/orego.text:
When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning.
The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.
Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”
Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.
Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency.
JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.
A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show.
Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm.
JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue.
Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.”
“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”
Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.
Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.
“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.”
De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.
“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said.
Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.
Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.
After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.)
Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing.
ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.
Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy.
ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and said the state agency director was receptive to talking further.
The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018 voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional government.
Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical” to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment.
Behind the Aloha 209th discussion was the way that Oregon awards its housing subsidies. Since 2024, Oregon has given the money on a first-come, first-served basis. When funding runs out, Bell’s agency places applications on a waitlist in the order received.
Bell spoke with Washington County officials about Aloha 209th during a 45-minute Zoom meeting in August, records show. Internal notes summarizing the conversation say that the county would send an updated report to the state agency to “inform movement of 209.” The summary said the groups involved would have a follow-up conversation about the project.
Bell went on to discuss the project with regional government officials in early September. About two weeks before the meeting, she emailed her deputy with two possible ways to get the project funded: a legislative “carve-out” or Metro consolidating its subsidies so it could fully pay for the project. “I want to do everything we can to help the metro projects be successful and the resources, like ours, are nearly depleted,” Bell wrote. She acknowledged that Metro might not find the solution appealing.
Bell told ProPublica that she met with Metro and Washington County at the other agencies’ request. She said her agency “does not have and is not pursuing a ‘legislative carve out’ for any project.”
“My approach is to listen to partners’ concerns and explain our funding process,” she said in an email. “I have no role in deciding whether projects should receive funding as part of this process, and I do not advocate for individual projects. Characterizing these routine discussions and legitimate concerns as something improper fundamentally misrepresents their purpose and context.”
A spokesperson for Washington County’s housing authority told ProPublica that Bell did not make any commitment to alter the prioritization of Aloha 209th. Another Washington County spokesperson said the August meeting with Bell was mainly focused on the housing authority’s desire for “clearer criteria” for how projects on the state’s waitlist get funded.
A Metro spokesperson said the regional agency requested the September meeting with a goal “for the two agencies to strengthen our working relationship and coordination.”
“Metro does not, and did not, advocate for any specific project,” the spokesperson said. “We clearly indicated this at the meeting and in writing ahead of the meeting.” The agency has advocated for a group of remaining projects, including Aloha 209th, to get money so Metro can fulfill commitments made as part of its affordable housing bond, the spokesperson said.
Oregon’s Government Ethics Commission has until early December to complete its preliminary review of the complaint over Bell’s financial disclosure, which will help the agency decide whether to open a full investigation.
Bell said she will “continue to remain responsive to the Ethics Commission” as it completes its examination.
Kotek’s office, provided with a list of ProPublica’s latest findings, said in a statement that the governor “holds all agency leadership to consistent and high ethical standards” and that her office “is closely following” the ethics panel’s review.
