https://jacobin.com/2026/11/lawsuit-amaz.title: Pregnant Workers Say Amazon Is Violating Their Rights
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/lawsuit-amaz.author: Jenny Brown
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/lawsuit-amaz.text:
Pregnant Workers Say Amazon Is Violating Their Rights
Amazon now faces a class-action lawsuit on behalf of its pregnant workers, many of whom say their rights to accommodation have been violated. They describe a pattern of being refused chairs, additional bathroom breaks, and relief from strenuous work.
Willamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat. . . . He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit.
But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations — a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting.
Amazon — a company known for fast delivery — had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. Even after Barclay provided it, Amazon still refused most accommodations, permitting her four breaks a day but no chair. She was moved to a different position but still required to lift heavy packages.
Amazon counted her new breaks against her unpaid time off (UPT), a leave bank that workers accumulate at five minutes per hour and that maxes out at eighty hours. She went to Human Resources several times to try to rectify the situation but stopped, because they were also counting those visits as UPT, the lawsuit says.
The heavy lifting led to sharp pains. At one point she left the warehouse in a wheelchair headed for the hospital. Amazon also counted that time against her unpaid leave bank. On another occasion, she had to leave due to uncontrolled vomiting. Despite a doctor’s note, that was also counted against her. Her UPT thus used up; Amazon fired her.
Under the law, workers cannot be penalized for taking pregnancy-related leave.
Barclay’s ordeal is detailed in a lawsuit filed September 8 by A Better Balance, a nonprofit focused on work policies affecting families. It’s a proposed class action on behalf of all US workers whose rights under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) have been violated by Amazon.
Systematic Violations
Barclay’s harrowing experience is common, said Sultana Hossain, recording secretary of the Amazon Labor Union (ALU) on Staten Island: Under the law, “pregnant workers don’t have to give in paperwork,” she said. “They only have to verbally say, ‘I’m pregnant and I need to be accommodated.’ But we’re seeing Amazon systemically violate that.
“Even if workers get an accommodation eventually, it can take several weeks,” said Hossain. “So people really don’t have any choice but to keep working in their regular role, which is really dangerous if they actually need an accommodation.”
Key’Asia, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center near Wilmington, Delaware, said that Amazon management twice rejected a note from her doctor, once because it had an e-signature, and then again when she got an ink signature. (For privacy to discuss medical matters, some workers asked that last names not be used.)
Managers said the signature looked fraudulent and still refused to accommodate her pregnancy, Key’Asia said. “They are making you do the things that your doctor told you that you’re not supposed to be doing,” she told attendees at an online Jobs With Justice event in October. “They’re making you do things that are putting yourself and your baby at risk.” She said Amazon fired her twice, both times when she was pregnant.
Pattern of Illegality
Workers have noticed a pattern: When they request accommodations, Amazon managers ask if they are “safe to work.” If they say yes, they are forced to continue to work without accommodations. If they say no, Amazon puts them on unpaid leave, which rapidly runs out.
Marissa, who worked at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rossford, Ohio, said that after her accommodations were denied, she was forced out on unpaid leave, and she ended up losing her apartment. “I was out $1,700. . . . I couldn’t pay for my vehicle. I couldn’t afford to eat.
“Amazon doesn’t care about whether or not you’re in pain,” she said. “They care about whether or not you can get their packages out on time.”
Hossain said it was typical for workers to get fired for “job abandonment” because “they ran out of time-off options because they were just not given the accommodation.” (A Better Balance has also sued Amazon for this practice on behalf of a disabled worker.)
Tragic Results
Hayat Bzezi was working at Amazon’s Staten Island JFK8 warehouse during the busy holiday season of 2024, when all workers were required to take an additional weekly ten-hour shift. She had asked for lighter duty, and management said she could use a chair, but then she was denied it.
She was “lifting heavy products, climbing up and down the stairs, despite having a high-risk pregnancy,” said her husband Wajdy, an elected ALU trustee who works at the same warehouse.
Hayat worked through pain, but it got worse and finally she had to go to the hospital, where she miscarried. It was the second time she had miscarried while working at Amazon. After that the couple decided to speak out. Since then, she has stopped working at Amazon and has been able to bear a child.
Law Reduces Miscarriages
When the PWFA went into effect in 2023, a study found that it reduced miscarriages by 9.6 percent. This suggests that many more miscarriages could be avoided if Amazon, the country’s second-largest private employer, started following the law.
But there is every indication that Amazon is ignoring it. Last year, New Jersey’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against Amazon after reviewing thousands of worker requests for accommodations. Amazon is New Jersey’s largest private employer, with around fifty thousand workers.
“When Amazon’s pregnant workers and workers with disabilities request accommodations, Amazon stonewalls them,” the suit charges. “It forces them through a byzantine accommodations process, imposing rigid and unnecessary paperwork requirements and subjecting workers to unexplained weeks-long delays.”
Rosa, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Akron, Ohio, said she asked for pregnancy accommodations because she was working in Ship Dock, a role that requires heavy lifting, pushing, and pulling. She was hospitalized for dehydration four times, but managers still kept her in that role, she said.
“Eventually my symptoms became so severe that I had to take an unpaid leave of absence,” she said. “I found out afterwards that I could have done paid short-term disability leave, but these options weren’t told to me.”
Amazon denies this. “The suggestion that we routinely deny or don’t support pregnancy accommodations is simply untrue,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. She said “99.9 percent” of pregnancy accommodation requests this year had been approved.
But New Jersey investigators found that Amazon regularly fired workers for requesting accommodations, in violation of New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination and the PWFA. New York State has also sued Amazon for this.
Hossain said the medical forms that Amazon requires for pregnancy, injury, and disability accommodations are so comprehensive and invasive that doctors have objected that they violate medical privacy laws.
Amazon wants such detailed medical documentation, Hossain said, because “they want to claim that if workers ever get injured, it’s because of conditions they came to work with, and it’s not workplace injuries.” Asked about this, an Amazon public relations representative declined to respond.
Pace Drives Injuries
The worker justice group Warehouse Life has been tracking and protesting Amazon’s health and safety record since 2023, and helping injured workers who have to “fight through a lot of misinformation and lies that they received from [Amazon] managers about workers’ comp,” said Chloe Sigal, campaign manager for the group.
Sigal said Amazon’s rate system, along with “time off task” (TOT) policies, make the work unsafe: “Amazon is pushing people to work as fast, as hard as humanly possible — or really outside what is humanly possible. That’s what’s driving this injury epidemic.”
In 2021 the California legislature found that injuries in Amazon warehouses were driven by its rate system. Workers were forced to work faster and faster because if they fell into the lowest 25 percent they could experience discipline, and the bottom 5 percent risked termination.
California passed a law requiring warehouses to publish stable quotas and not constantly accelerate them. In 2024 the state fined Amazon $6 million for violating it.
Workers also accumulate TOT when surveillance detects a pause in their package scanning. Fear of too much TOT pushes workers to cut short their breaks, skip bathroom breaks (and reduce liquid consumption to match), and push on through pain. Dehydration is particularly risky during a pregnancy. “The reason that people are miscarrying at Amazon is because of this rate system,” said Sigal.
Doctors agree. Jenny Fish is a Santa Rosa, California, physician who provides prenatal care. “Prolonged standing, going the whole shift without water, lifting more than 15 to 20 pounds, working night shifts regularly,” she said, “all of this has been irrefutably linked to higher risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, increased maternal fatigue, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and just in general adverse birth outcomes.” Preeclampsia is potentially fatal.
Is There a Policy?
Sigal said that soon after Warehouse Life started, several Amazon workers came to the group reporting pregnancy issues. But when the group put out a call on social media for experiences working at Amazon while pregnant, it was flooded with stories. Two thousand women from forty states responded, and eighty-one described loss of a pregnancy. (Get more info on Warehouse Life here.)
Now some of these workers are leading the charge to get changes at the company. They have put pressure on New York City’s Mount Sinai Health System to terminate Amazon board of directors member Edith Cooper as a hospital trustee, given Amazon’s dismal safety record.
Warehouse Life members have also met with Amazon management. Sigal said that during those meetings Amazon claimed to have a policy on pregnancy that was only available to workers. But no workers were able to access it. “Nobody has it. We’ve heard from managers that they don’t have it either, that they don’t receive training on what to do,” Sigal said.
When Labor Notes asked Amazon for its pregnancy policy and any training materials, no documents were forthcoming. Warehouse Life counters that the company’s real pregnancy policy is “Delay. Deny. Discipline.”
March on HR
The Amazon Labor Union organized on Staten Island in 2022, and in 2024 affiliated with the Teamsters. But Amazon refuses to negotiate with the union at the five-thousand-worker warehouse, despite being ordered to do so by the National Labor Relations Board in April.
The union can still help, though. “Just a few weeks ago a pregnant worker came to our union hall saying she wanted help getting an accommodation at work,” said ALU’s Hossain. The worker had already told her manager that she was pregnant.
The union sent several workers to accompany her to HR, saying “that should be enough, and Amazon needs to start the process of accommodating her,” Hossain said. “And they actually did listen, but only because a group of workers accompanied her.” A contract could provide additional protections.
The union isn’t waiting for workers to seek it out. Union activists distribute fliers with a QR code to a reporting form that goes to the union. Half of the reports “are unfair discipline, the other half is workers who are dealing with injuries or the accommodation process or need workers’ comp or whatever,” said Hossain. “It’s such a big issue.”
“It really does feel like we’re all just numbers,” said Rosa in Akron. “I want them to take more accountability. They make it so hard when it comes to a life-changing thing.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: What is at stake for Spain’s art sector as snap election approaches?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexandra F. Coego
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Spain’s snap elections, due to take place on 29 November, have left several long-awaited new measures and legislation for art and culture hanging in the balance. These include regulations on AI, intellectual property and artist welfare. With a coalition between the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party looking increasingly likely, here is what the vote could mean for the country’s art and culture sector.
Reduced budget and censorship fears
The future of the ministry of culture has been a subject of debate in the lead-up to the election. PP has argued in favour of maintaining it, albeit merged with other portfolios, but Vox will only support the ministry’s existence if cultural powers currently held by Spain’s autonomous communities are transferred to the central government.
The prospect of such a transfer has raised concerns over censorship, particularly in the light of a wave of cancelled art festivals and plays in PP-Vox-led regions since the 2023 regional elections. At a party meeting on 22 November, Vox’s secretary general, Ignacio Garriga, stated that they will support cultural professionals who “create quality national products” and “highlight the value of the country's culture”.
Even if the ministry of culture continues, the sector expects budget cuts under a PP-Vox coalition. The PP has pledged to quickly pass a new patronage law with tax and legal incentives to encourage private businesses and individuals to fund cultural projects, arguing that healthcare and defence spending will leave culture underfunded by the state. The PP's proposals for culture also include auditing working conditions, exhibition standards and security protocols across national museums.
Long-awaited legislation up in the air
The Status of the Artist bill, a welfare package designed to improve working conditions of those in the cultural sector, will enter into force in 2027 regardless of the election results, after being approved by the Council of Ministers in July. However, the inclusion of visual artists—who, unlike other types of artists, were entirely left out of the bill and continue to face prohibitive self-employment quotas—remains up in the air.
Earlier this year, the Union of Contemporary Artists of Spain launched a campaign to push for their inclusion with the support of the ministry of culture, but the decision stalled in the ministries of social security and finance. Gloria Reguero, the president of the union, says that they have been waiting since 2018 for painters, sculptors and photographers to be recognised as artists. “Just when it seemed we were going to start negotiating our terms, the elections came along, and with them, another setback,” she tells The Art Newspaper.
Meanwhile, a separate draft bill regulating the use of generative AI in the arts is not getting off the ground at all. The legislation was put out for public consultation in late September and it marked the government’s third attempt to regulate AI in the arts following two failed royal decrees. The draft bill sought to prohibit the use of generative AI to exploit an artist’s image, voice or work without their express consent and specific remuneration and, like the Status of the Artist, it left out the visual arts.
Major museum projects in the balance
Both PP and Vox have strongly opposed plans by Ernest Urtasun, the current Spanish culture minister, to review state museum collections—specifically the Museum of the Americas and the National Museum of Anthropology—to “move past a colonial framework”. When the initiative was first announced in early 2024, the PP dismissed the push for decolonisation, in a statement, as “a false debate, imposed and manufactured to create division among Spaniards”.
In November 2025, the ministry formally presented a €13.6m project to overhaul the permanent exhibitions and narratives of both institutions through an “anti-racist and gender perspective”.
Ahead of the elections, the project has reached different stages: while the National Museum of Anthropology has already moved through its public tendering process for the remodelling of its permanent exhibition, the Museum of the Americas remains at an earlier stage, with major works still pending. If a new government takes office, the initiative’s long-term completion, scheduled for 2028, faces significant uncertainty—with a risk that yet-to-be-contracted tenders may be halted or that curatorial direction may be revised. A spokesperson for the Museum of the Americas declined to respond to The Art Newspaper's request for comment, “especially now that we’re on the eve of the elections and everything is so uncertain”, they say.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: A new NYC Thanksgiving tradition: Stocking up at the legal weed dispensary
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
For many Americans, Thanksgiving promises two things: a feast on the table and an extended cast of relatives seated around it.
And for some, there’s one substance that can enhance the experience of both.
“I can't be around my family sober,” said Campbell Saverein, who was picking up weed at the SoHo dispensary Mighty Lucky before heading to Long Island for the holiday.
“It really helps me, personally,” she said. “ We get into political arguments — someone's mad at some skirt being too short on Instagram.”
The “cousins walk” — wherein the young people (or any other down-to-clown relatives) go outside before dinner and smoke weed — is a long-standing Thanksgiving tradition. But now, four years into New York’s rollout of legal cannabis dispensaries, the once illicit pastime is not only less stigmatized — it’s also marketable. (Enter: “Green Wednesday” sales.) So we stopped by Mighty Lucky on Bowery to see how the shop, and its customers, were gearing up for the big day.
“As somebody who's been selling cannabis illegally, then legally, Thanksgiving specifically was the biggest sales holiday for me in the entire year — bigger than 4/20,” said Beau Allulli, the store’s co-owner.
Veteran stoners, we learned, know their way around a Thanksgiving high. Pre-rolls. Edibles. Volcanoes. Dabs. A lemony bud that one customer said pairs well with her mashed potatoes.
“I have a recipe where I make it kind of like patatas bravas style, so lemony and spicy,” said Stephanie Villavicencio, who popped into the store while visiting from Miami, where recreational weed is illegal. (“I carry it in smell-proof things.”)
William Diaz, who celebrates Thanksgiving with his family in the Bronx, said there’s no need for a sneaky walk at this point — all the adults, ranging in age from 23 to 75, take part.
“We smoke first, before the turkey. And then pray. And then eat,” he said.
Hmac, an artist and weed delivery driver, said she’s “definitely getting high on Thanksgiving,” but the party starts even before the walk.
“The morning of any holiday in our family, we have killer-dillers and cinnamon rolls,” she said.
A killer-diller?
“It's like Orange Julius mixed with vodka,” she explained. “It's, like, game over. Starts your day off right. We get goofy, for sure.”
Getting goofy, if you can handle it, sounds fantastic. But say you’re an uninitiated cannabis user — surely you’d want to avoid paranoia, drowsiness or absently staring into the bowl of cranberry sauce. Is there a way into this for the uninitiated?
“If I was going to curate something for you, you'd start out with probably a low-dose sativa,” Allulli said, walking me through a case of products.
“And then maybe, right before dinner, go for a little bit of a CBG-combined edible. That will increase the appetite,” he said. “ And then, after dinner, for me, it would be smoking some sort of fat indica. Really something that's gonna just sort of, like, totally mellow me out.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/wind-warning-tha.title: Will the Wind Ruin the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade… Again?
https://hellgatenyc.com/wind-warning-tha.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/wind-warning-tha.text:
It's Wednesday, you deserve a treat, like an episode of the Hell Gate Podcast! Listen here or watch here.
In its 100-year history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has never been canceled due to bad weather.
But as of Wednesday morning, event officials are closely watching forecasts for a fearsome nor'easter to decide whether 100 gloriously oversized balloons should be grounded, disappointing some 32 million expected parade-viewers.
While it sucks to take the air out of what is objectively the coolest thing about the parade—especially on the event's 100th anniversary—Macy's and the Mamdani administration certainly do not want a repeat of November 27, 1997.
Students of New York City history will know that the 1997 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was, categorically speaking, an absolute shitshow. As gale-force winds peaked at 43 mph that year, the vicious gusts turned balloons representing some of New Yorkers' favorite characters into ghastly comic weapons.
Barney the Dinosaur tore down a tree in Central Park, before being disemboweled by a lamppost. The Pink Panther had to be stabbed into submission by the NYPD. Sonic the Hedgehog's head was torn off by the sleigh of the Grinch. And, by the end, a six-story Cat in the Hat had taken down a lamppost at 72nd Street—with falling debris sending Kathleen Caronna, then 33, into a coma for 24 days with a head injury. (She sued for $395 million and settled for an undisclosed amount.)
Two million people watched the event from the streets, the chaos etched in City kids' memories forever. "Stray Cat!" the NY Post screamed the next day. "One critical, 3 others hurt as wicked wind blows balloon into lamppost."
After that parade fracas, then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani set new rules: No giant balloons may fly in our city when sustained winds exceed 24 mph, or gusts exceed 34 mph.
Now, meteorologists are forecasting abysmal weather for Thursday, with a high-wind warning in place starting at 10 a.m. Gusts are projected to reach up to 60 mph, with sustained winds hitting up to 35 mph, Bryan Ramsey, a meteorologist for the National Weather Service, told Hell Gate. "These winds are going to be damaging," Ramsey said. "We're anticipating numerous downed tree limbs, scattered downed trees and power lines. Power outages are likely."
The question is when, exactly, the highest winds will hit—and will it be while the balloons are meant to be flying? The forecasters aren’t quite sure when the winds will reach their peak, but they couldn’t rule out the possibility of them roaring through the parade, which starts at 8:30 a.m. and finishes midday.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/books-weimar.title: The Weimar Republic Still Haunts Our Political Imagination
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/books-weimar.author: Andrew Bonnell
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/books-weimar.text:
The Weimar Republic Still Haunts Our Political Imagination
Political commentary that draws contemporary parallels with the fall of the Weimar Republic can be glib and superficial. But the readiness of capitalist elites to ditch democracy in a crisis is still a danger today, just as it was in Germany a century ago.
There has been a wave of books recently on the Weimar Republic and its fall. While publishers love centenaries, and it’s now a hundred years since the “roaring twenties,” there may be more to the current Weimar wave than that. Are we currently living in a “Weimar moment”?
The current crop of books on the end of Weimar includes Timothy W. Ryback’s Takeover: Hitler’s Final Rise to Power, the German historian Volker Ullrich’s Fateful Hours: The Collapse of the Weimar Republic, and French historian Johann Chapoutot’s Les Irresponsables (“The Irresponsible Men”), not yet translated into English.
These accounts focus on the end of the republic and the choices that members of Germany’s conservative elite made that enabled Adolf Hitler to become chancellor on January 30, 1933. They also suggest parallels with the rise of the far right today: Donald Trump and MAGA in the United States, the Alternative for Germany, and the National Rally in France.
Now we also have Katja Hoyer’s Weimar: Life on the Edge of Catastrophe and Victor Sebestyen’s Weimar Germany: Death of a Democracy to add to the shelf on the Weimar Republic.
On the Edge
Katja Hoyer has recently become one of the best-known commentators on Germany and German history in Britain, where she now lives. Born in East Germany in 1985, she achieved prominence with a book on the German Democratic Republic (GDR) entitled Beyond the Wall, which was dedicated to the unsurprising but apparently still controversial proposition that there was more to life in the GDR than the Berlin Wall.
Hoyer’s new book tells the story of the German town of Weimar, which lent its name to the newly founded German Republic after its founding constituent assembly was held there in 1919. The book covers the history from that year to 1939 and the outbreak of World War II, and there is an epilogue that deals with the wartime years.
Writers on German history have often remarked on the incongruity of the images with which Weimar is associated. Having been famous for its connections with German classical humanist high culture and figures such as Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller, the town also hosted one of Nazi Germany’s most notorious concentration camps, Buchenwald, on its outskirts. Today a number 6 bus can transport visitors from the Goetheplatz in the center of town to the Buchenwald memorial site in about twenty minutes.
It will be clear to readers of Hoyer’s book that the simple binary opposition of German high culture and Nazi barbarism is not as clear-cut as is sometimes assumed. Members of Weimar’s cultural elite, such as Carl von Schirach, the former director of Weimar’s Grand-Ducal Court Theater (later the National Theater), supported the Nazi Party. Schirach joined the party as early as 1926, when the Nazis were still on the fringes of German politics. His son, Baldur, later became the national leader of the Hitler Youth.
Then there was Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, sister of the late philosopher Friedrich, an admirer of Benito Mussolini. She had reservations about Hitler, but came to accept the patronage of his regime. When the Buchenwald concentration camp was opened in 1937 to enforce Heinrich Himmler’s plans for the “racial” and social reshaping of Germany’s population, the respectable, cultured bourgeois citizens of Weimar could observe the arrival of brutalized prisoners at the town’s railway station.
Of course, Weimar has already attracted the attention of many historians, and Hoyer clearly draws on their work. Her achievement is to provide a highly readable narrative, often full of novelistic incidental detail and local color, that describes the twenty years in the life of the town through the eyes of a selection of its citizens.
Finding Lessons
The figure she follows most closely, thanks to his voluminous and detailed diaries, is one Carl Weirich, a bookbinder and owner of a stationer’s shop in Weimar. It is often said that history is written by the victors, but if you leave good diaries behind, you have a better chance of being quoted in it. Hoyer describes the privations of Weirich’s family in World War I, when the British blockade caused widespread malnutrition in the civilian population. This resulted in the death of his infant daughter, and his first wife also died from tuberculosis after the war’s end.
Having seen his small business narrowly survive both the hyperinflation of the early 1920s and the Great Depression that followed with just a few years’ respite in between, Weirich voted for the Nazis. For a while, he was even a paid-up “sponsoring member” of the SS. But he later became disillusioned with the Nazi regime, especially when he learned that his house was scheduled to be demolished to make way for a grandiose new Nazi Party building project.
The Weimar Republic’s most celebrated diarist, Count Harry Kessler, also gets frequent mentions in Hoyer’s account, partly because of his friendship with Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, another regular character who left a rich paper trail. Kessler was a famously liberal aristocrat and a well-connected patron of the arts (and gay). He died in exile in France in 1937.
For more political balance, Hoyer also traces the life of a local Social Democratic Party leader, Kurt Nehrling, who sought to stay in contact with former comrades in order to maintain some capacity for resistance after 1933. He was executed in Dachau in 1943. In addition, there is a moving description of the fate of one of Weimar’s Jewish families, the hotel-keeping Schmidts, torn apart in the Holocaust.
Another figure who Hoyer follows is Walter Gropius, whose Bauhaus school for architecture and design found a home in Weimar until 1925, when a right-leaning government of the state of Thuringia cut its funding. The legacy of the Bauhaus in Weimar includes the surprisingly modernist lettering on the concentration camp gate of Buchenwald, which bore the slogan: Jedem das Seine — “To each his own.” It was the handiwork of Bauhaus alumnus Franz Ehrlich, who was detained there.
Hoyer’s narrative is consistently readable but light on analysis. Her history is the sum of decisions by individuals and she aims to help her readers see events through the eyes of those individuals to make those decisions more comprehensible. Such an understanding of individuals and their interaction with society and the events of the time may, she hopes, help the reader to “find lessons to safeguard democracy and freedom in our own time.”
The Compromise of November 1918
Victor Sebestyen’s Weimar Germany: Death of a Democracy is also primarily a narrative history for a general readership. Sebestyen is a journalist and author of several books on Hungary and Eastern European history, and his book is packed with entertaining anecdotes and vignettes.
Weimar Germany leans heavily into what some scholars have characterized as the “glitter and doom” vein of writing about Weimar — Otto Friedrich’s 1972 Before the Deluge is an acknowledged influence. The diaries of the indefatigable Count Harry Kessler are (inevitably) regularly quoted. Unfortunately, his book also contains a large number of factual errors (after the first hundred pages I stopped counting).
Sebestyen’s book gives much more space to the genesis of the Weimar Republic and its early years than to its decline and end, which are telescoped into the last few chapters. He deals with the extent of big business support for the Nazi Party in two short paragraphs. Still, it is hard to disagree with his characterization of President Paul von Hindenburg, who chose to appoint Hitler as head of government in 1933, as “one of history’s guiltiest men.”
Narrative accounts of the collapse of the Weimar Republic that focus on the decisions of individuals in key positions of power during its last couple of years omit important structural factors. The republic was founded on an unstable compromise between the right-wing leadership of the German labor movement and the essentially antidemocratic surviving elites from the Kaiser’s regime. This included a social compromise between the trade unions and heavy industry.
The unions won recognition as legitimate bargaining partners in industrial relations, as well as the eight-hour day, a cherished goal of the labor movement since the founding of the Socialist International in 1889. The bosses of industry escaped the popular demand for socialization, especially of the mining, iron, steel, and armaments concerns that were widely viewed as war profiteers.
For heavy industry in particular, the republic was a historical aberration. These interests had been closely identified with the Imperial German state order: when there were major strikes in the Ruhr in 1905 and 1912, the authorities obligingly sent the army in to quell them. They saw the social compromise of November 1918 as merely an expedient and temporary truce with the representatives of their workers.
Industry Against Democracy
The first nail in the coffin of the social compromise was the abolition of the mandatory eight-hour day at the end of the hyperinflation in late 1923. After a few years of post-inflation stabilization and rationalization enabled by American loans, heavy industry went on the offensive against organized labor even before the onset of the Great Depression in 1929. In early 1928, industrial conflict in the metalworking industry in Saxony saw industrialists locking out some 150,000 workers.
Later that year, the bosses of heavy industry in Germany’s Ruhr industrial region locked out 250,000 workers in a concerted attack on both organized labor and the state arbitration system. The coal, iron, and steel barons of the Ruhr banded together in an organized cartel to prosecute their interests vis-à-vis the unions and the republic. Industrialists like Paul Reusch increasingly sponsored extreme-right, antidemocratic activists.
At this stage, only a few individual big businessmen were giving significant financial backing to the Nazi Party, which was still on the political fringes, with just 2.6 percent of the national vote in 1928. This changed after the Great Depression set in, unemployment rose, and the ranks of the Communist Party started to swell with unemployed young workers calling for revolution on the model of the Soviet Union.
The offensive of heavy industry against democracy was followed by the radicalization of the middle classes and the traditional right wing. The mainstream nationalist-conservative German National People’s Party became more militant under its new leader, the multimillionaire media mogul Alfred Hugenberg (Chapoutot gives a good account of this).
Under the strain of the intensifying class tensions during the depression, amid widespread disillusionment resulting from the failure of the legacy middle-class liberal parties to alleviate Germany’s economic crisis, the voting bases of the established liberal parties melted away. At the same time, those parties themselves abandoned liberal precepts for more nationalistic and authoritarian politics. Chapoutot’s characterization of Germany’s economic elites as “liberal-authoritarian” is a little hard to follow, as most of them were not liberal on any level — the term seems to be aimed more at today’s neoliberal tech oligarchs.
Under these conditions, the Nazis made a concerted effort to forge an alliance with big business and sections of the German elites. They captured the leadership of the peak German agrarian lobby group, the Reichslandbund, which represented the interests of Prussia’s large landowners, who counted President Hindenburg as one of their own.
Guilty Men
These nationwide developments fall outside the scope of Hoyer’s local study, absorbing as it often is. Nor does Sebestyen’s colorful narrative do them justice. But narratives that focus on the decisions of a few guilty men do offer some timely lessons about the potential gravity of political decisions, and remind us that far-right parties have only ever come to power through deals with the ruling conservative elites.
Conditions today are very different from those of Weimar — we are not (yet) in a great depression, and there is no mass revolutionary working-class movement marching in city streets. But the capacity of wealthy elites to turn on democracy when they perceive it is opportune to do so, and the willingness of sections of the middle classes to abandon liberal ideas when they feel under economic stress, are both recognizable across the span of almost a hundred years.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Christie’s acquires British auction house Dreweatts
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Christie's announced today it has acquired the British auction house Dreweatts, a move that confirms the enduring appeal of antiques and older collectibles, particularly as profits in other parts of the auction sector remain squeezed.
Both businesses will run as before, Christie’s confirms, with no staffing changes expected as a result of the deal. Dreweatts will retain its name and continue to be run “independently” by its chief executive, Henry House, and chairman Will Richards, according to a Christie's statement. Dreweatts will continue to operate from its salesroom at Donnington Priory in Newbury, Berkshire, with no sales expected to move to London.
Dreweatts, founded in 1759, is best known for country house and estate sales, and its specialist departments covering furniture, Old Masters, ceramics, jewellery, silver, clocks and wine. It holds around 70 sales a year. In 2025, it posted a record total auction turnover of £37.56m (£47.3m with fees)—a 26% increase from its 2024 results. Both Christie’s and Dreweatts are privately owned and do not disclose their profits.
The acquisition in some ways sees Christie’s backtrack its 2017 decision to close its South Kensington venue, known as Christie's South Kensington or CSK, which specialised in antiques and other traditional collecting categories. This decision was taken as the market for postwar and contemporary art was at its peak, and as the trade chased global expansion and billionaire tastes at the expense of localism and connoisseurship.
Today, auctions of Modern and postwar trophy lots might generate more glamour and headlines than high-volume and lower-value antiques sales, but the overheads for winning these prize consignments devours profit margins. Indeed, many leading industry figures criticised Christie’s decision to close CSK as a shortsighted one that haemorrhaged valuable strongholds of specialist knowledge and alienated potential new buyers.
Christie's president Bonnie Brennan says in a statement that Dreweatts possesses “particular strength in a part of the market that is highly complementary to our own. Most importantly, our clients collect across categories and at every price point, and together we have the opportunity to provide them with an even broader and more complete level of service.”
This marks the second major acquisition of a smaller auction house by Christie’s in recent years, following the 2024 buyout of the classic car vendors Gooding & Company.
Christie’s acquires Dreweatts from the advisory firm Gurr Johns, which bought the regional auction house in 2017 for £1.25m, as The Art Newspaper reported at the time. “I believe that Christie’s is the only business with the capacity, experience and shared culture to fulfil the further potential of Dreweatts,”, Gurr Johns chief told the Financial Times.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Does Spain’s Leftist Government Stand a Chance?
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Pablo Castaño Tierno
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Does Spain’s Leftist Government Stand a Chance?
Pedro Sánchez’s coalition has been an exception to Europe’s reactionary turn. What went wrong?
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez reaps more successes abroad than in his own country. At least that is what the polls suggest, which foresee a joint victory for the right and far right in the November 29 general elections. If the forecasts hold, it will be the end of the coalition government formed by the Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) and the leftist coalition Sumar—which has aroused the admiration of progressive sectors around the world for its strong stance against Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, but has struggled to concretely improve the lives of the Spanish working class.
Spaniards’ main concern is the meteoric rise in housing prices, a surge the government has not been able to contain. Rents have risen 43 percent in a decade, and in large cities the cost of renting an apartment already amounts to 100 percent of the average income of a young person. The last years of coalition government have been a permanent tug-of-war between the PSOE—reluctant to regulate the housing market—and its Sumar partners, aligned with tenant unions that demand curbing speculation and a legal and effective price cap.
The housing crisis became a political crisis following the eviction of Maricarmen, an 87-year-old Madrid tenant expelled from her home by a real estate company. Her case gave a face to the more than 40 daily evictions, provoking a wave of social protests and an encampment in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol public square. Pushed by the mobilizations, the government presented two decrees aimed at protecting tenants and limiting real estate speculation, but Congress rejected them, leading Sánchez to call early elections. Tenant and workers’ unions called a general strike for November 11 for the right to housing, which partially halted Spain’s economic activity, with mass demonstrations all over the country. The protests for housing have placed the issue at the core of the electoral campaign, although the concrete state response to it will depend on the election results.
The current government has been more successful with labor, approving a labor reform in 2021 that strengthened the unions’ bargaining power and reduced temporary employment—a perennial scourge of the Spanish economy—from 25 to 15 percent of workers. The government has also approved successive increases in the legal minimum wage, which has gone from €858 gross per month in 2018 to €1,500 in 2026.
But the increase in wages is not enough to make ends meet, particularly in in large cities where rents have soared. In addition to housing, the prices of basic products such as food and clothing have risen: Inflation is above 4 percent. Consequently, the purchasing power of millions of workers is stagnant.
The elimination of tax exemptions and the drop in unemployment—at its lowest level since 2008—has increased the state resources, which has made it possible to finance new social policies such as the Minimum Vital Income. This is a minimum revenue scheme that intends to alleviate poverty, which remains at a rate of 25 percent despite the good macroeconomic figures. Bureaucratic obstacles are such that this benefit only reaches one in every five households in poverty, and its provisions are insufficient to offset the rise in rent. Another major policy achievement is the equalization of maternity and paternity leave at 16 weeks.
Pedro Sánchez came to power in 2018, amid the rise of the Spanish feminist movement, and women’s and LGBTQ rights became one of the coalition government’s banner issues. Their main advance was a law that strengthened the prevention of sexual violence and reformed the criminal code to clarify the definition of consent, in reaction to a history of sexist judicial rulings. They also managed to pass a law recognizing the right to gender self-determination without the need for psychiatric or medical reports.
Beyond the laws, the Spanish state has increased resources to fight gender-based violence through a state pact that allocated an extra €1 billion to prevent and combat violence against women.
As in the rest of Europe, the Spanish far right has turned immigration into its main electoral focus. But while the governments of the United Kingdom, France, or Germany have hardened their migration rules in a vain attempt to stop the rise of the far right, Sánchez’s government has opted for the opposite path, approving an extraordinary procedure to regularize the administrative status of hundreds of thousands of migrants. The decision was the response to a campaign led by migrant and anti-racist movements, which gathered more than 700,000 signatures in favor of regularization.
The number of immigrants in Spain increased by more than 2 million between 2021 and 2025, with the foreign-born population reaching 20 percent of the total. Sánchez remains favorable to immigration, for both ethical and utilitarian reasons, highlighting the benefit that it represents in an increasingly aging labor market. His rhetoric coexists with the reality of Spain’s immigrant detention centers, often criticized by human rights organizations, and with the daily police persecution of immigrants and racialized people. According to the NGO Sos Racisme, foreigners are three times more likely to be identified by the police than Spaniards.
Spain is one of the European countries most exposed to the effects of the climate crisis, as the deadly floods in Valencia in 2024 painfully underscored. In 2021 the Spanish Parliament approved a climate change law that envisions emissions neutrality by 2050, although it does not reach the ambition levels of the Paris Agreement. Spain’s great success has been the multiplication of wind and solar energy, which already generate more than half of the electricity produced in the country, which has allowed some reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. However, the decline stalled in 2025, largely due to the lack of decisive actions to electrify transport, and Spain is far from the 32 percent reduction committed for 2030.
Sánchez came to power thanks to a motion of no confidence against then-President Mariano Rajoy, due to his conservative Popular Party’s involvement in a corruption network. Therefore, the corruption conviction of Sánchez’s former deputy, José Luis Ábalos, and the charging of Santos Cerdán, another important PSOE leader, have dealt a hard blow to the president’s popularity.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
There are other less straightforward cases—including charges against Sánchez’s wife and brother—that many commentators describe as examples of lawfare by a judicial elite close to the political right. The conviction of the coalition government’s attorney general for disclosure of secrets remains controversial. The legal doubts about these cases do not prevent them from casting a long shadow of doubt over the president’s honesty.
Sánchez has acquired a powerful international image thanks to his firm stand against Trump and Netanyahu. This stance responds to the Spanish population’s broad majority support for the Palestinian cause, which became visible when hundreds of demonstrators interrupted the Vuelta a España cycling race in 2025 to protest the participation of an Israeli team.
But Sánchez’s decisions on the international stage have not gone uncriticized. Although he announced an arms embargo against Israel, Spain has continued buying Israeli weapons. In a similar vein, Sánchez rejected Trump’s demand that NATO countries devote 5 percent of their GDP to defense, but Spanish military spending grew 50 percent in 2025, exceeding 2 percent of GDP.
Sánchez’s coalition government has been an exception to the reactionary turn in Western politics, in key areas such as immigration and opposition to the aggressive imperialism of Trump and Netanyahu. However, recognizing the example that he has represented for progressives around the world is compatible with pointing out the failure of his government to tackle the housing crisis and translate the good macroeconomic figures into an improvement in the living conditions of the Spanish working class. These will be the first challenges that the next government will face, regardless of its ideology.

https://gothamist.com/news/judge-upholds.title: Judge upholds NYC rent freeze, marking win for Mamdani and his affordability agenda
https://gothamist.com/news/judge-upholds.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/judge-upholds.text:
A Manhattan judge has upheld a city board’s decision to enact a two-year rent freeze for roughly 1 million New York City apartments after landlords sued to reverse the first-of-its-kind directive.
In an order Wednesday, Judge Brendan Lantry rejected the bid to block the rent freeze for stabilized apartments approved by the city’s Rent Guidelines Board in June. The pause in rent increases fulfills of Mayor Zohran Mamdani's campaign pledges. Lantry wrote that although the freeze “may have detrimental impacts on the New York City residential real estate industry,” the court did not have the authority to overturn the decision.
A group of landlords represented by Randy Mastro — a former first deputy mayor under previous Mayor Eric Adams — argued that the board had conducted a “sham” process that ignored owners’ rising expenses in order to deliver on one of Mamdani’s signature campaign pledges. Mastro asked a judge to order the board to hold a new vote.
Mamdani and city lawyers denied any interference in the process and countered that the board arrived at its decision independently.
City Hall and Mastro did not immediately respond to requests for comment and Mastro did not say whether he planned to appeal.
Legal Aid Society attorney Ellen Davidson, whose organization intervened in the case on behalf of tenants, said she was pleased with the ruling but not surprised.
“The law is clear that courts do not have the power to override the decisions of the Rent Guidelines Board,” she said.
The closely watched decision reflected the unusual attention paid to the board over the past year, after Mamdani made a rent freeze a key plank of his victorious campaign. The board’s nine members are each appointed by the mayor for multiyear terms, but the panel is considered an independent body that analyzes data on landlord and tenant expenses and listens to public testimony before holding its annual vote.
Mamdani named six of the board’s members, but stopped publicly calling for the rent freeze after taking office in January.
In an effort to find evidence that City Hall swayed the board’s decision, Mastro requested communications between top city officials, including Mamdani, and the board members and staff. Lantry granted the request and ordered officials to turn over emails and texts.
Mastro released roughly a dozen of those exchanges. They largely showed City Hall officials informing new members of their appointments, coordinating meeting dates and planning a presentation on a new “true cost of living” report not previously considered by the board.
Mastro said the materials were “shocking” in a letter to the judge. Top city lawyer Steven Banks said there was nothing “improper” about the communications.
At an unrelated news conference Oct. 1, Mamdani sought to turn the tables on Mastro and cited reporting from Gothamist that revealed how Mastro himself has attempted to influence the board’s vote during his time as top deputy to Adams in 2025.
Former Rent Guidelines Board Chair Doug Apple told Gothamist that Mastro had spoken with him by phone last year and “advocated for a low vote” when the board was considering an increase up to 4.75%.
Mastro confirmed that he had spoken with Apple, but only to say how he and Adams “disagreed” with the board’s eventual decision to raise rent by 3% that year.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: A brush with... Zanele Muholi—podcast
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ben Luke, David Clack, Aimee Dawson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Content warning: this episode has some discussion of sexual and homophobic violence.
Muholi was born in 1972 in Umlazi, Durban, South Africa and lives today in Cape Town. They are a self-described visual activist, who, since the mid-2000s, have used photography to document the lives of LGBTQ+ people, initially in South Africa, where they were born.
They have since expanded their project around the world and work in discrete, often ongoing series that have a common aim: to respond to violence and discrimination against queer and trans communities, to reflect their defiance and resistance, and to expand their visibility in visual culture in South Africa in particular but also far beyond.
The people they depict have, since the start, been far more than sitters or subjects; they are collaborators, participants who help define the way they are represented. A crucial factor is that Muholi turns the lens onto themself. “When I position myself in my own frame,” they have said. “I do so on my own terms attempting to articulate my own way of seeing and wanting to be seen.”
And whether it is their unflinching and tender portraits of their collaborators or their imaginative and improvised self-portraits Muholi’s photographs are always beautiful objects, with a fastidious attention to the properties and possibilities of their medium.
They discuss the influence of their mother, who was a maker herself, and was a profound influence on one of their most notable works, Somnyama Ngonyama (2012). They reflect on the enormous impact of photographers including Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Lola Flash and Joan E. Biren, writers including Audre Lorde, and musicians including Brenda Fassie. Plus, they answer our usual questions, giving insight into their daily practices and the rhythms of their work, and reflecting on the ultimate question: what is art for?
- Faces and Phases: Zanele Muholi, MACK, $80, £65
This podcast is sponsored by Bloomberg Connects, the arts and culture platform.
Bloomberg Connects offers access to a vast range of international cultural organisations through a single click, with new guides being added regularly. They includeseveral guides to institutions that have shown and collected Zanele Muholi’s work, including SFMOMA in San Francisco, Tate in the UK, the Center for Visual Arts in Denver in the US, and MEP, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris. On the guide to the MEP, you will find features on its current exhibitions. They include Penn and Fashion, exploring the photographer Irving Penn’s long association with the fashion world, in which his stripped-back style has had a lasting influence on generations of photographers. You can hear audio features on all the sections of the exhibition, from his early years at Vogue magazine in the 1940s to the photographs made when Penn was in his 90s of Karl Lagerfeld, John Galliano and Christian Lacroix. You can also explore the related exhibition in La Petite Galerie, called Everyday Clothing, which allows young visitors and families to explore the creative process through works from the MEP’s collections.

https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.title: How Congress’s Permitting Bill Doubles as an AI Bailout
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.author: Dylan Gyauch-Lewis, Matthew Scherer
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.text:
How Congress’s Permitting Bill Doubles as an AI Bailout
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is loaded up with giveaways to the AI sector—part of the Trump White House’s broader plan to shield AI from economic reality.
Bailouts come in many forms. For the financiers and tech moguls who’ve been inflating the AI bubble, the seeds of a federal rescue are sown in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The massive bill, which the Senate approved last week and is now before the House, needs to be understood as part of a multifront deregulatory push to embed the AI industry’s policy preferences into law. There’s no explicit language in BAAJA charging taxpayers to bail out AI companies—but there doesn’t really need to be.
After the 1980s savings-and-loan crisis, law professor Cheryl Block offered a taxonomy of modern government bailouts, dividing them into two classes: overt and covert. The overt bailout is the more familiar: direct cash infusions, credit guarantees, and so on. Covert bailouts also prop up distressed businesses, but are structured so as to mask their purpose and beneficiaries. Instead of directing public funds to failing companies, a covert bailout typically assists them through subtler measures such as looser regulations, tax relief, or protection from competition.
Tech lords and financiers, through their Trumpist cronies, have already sought to obtain covert bailout protections in piecemeal fashion, from promoting favorable legislation on transmission line siting to diluting SEC oversight of corporate accounting to shield AI platforms from basic consumer liability. BAAJA represents their crowning bid to secure deeper and more durable protection before a new Democratic majority is seated in Congress next January.
BAAJA would codify many of the industry’s preferred energy policies while also abetting the massive buildout of AI data centers. If it wins passage in the House, the bill would help place AI development beyond the basic forces of market discipline, and set the stage for indemnifying the corrupt and cronyist tech sector from any meaningful responsibility for promoting the largest investment bubble in human history. Without pledging taxpayer funds outright, BAAJA bears all the hallmarks of a covert bailout.
This de facto mandate stands out in especially high relief if you examine the manic push to pass BAAJA in the context of the Trump White House’s other flagrant giveaways to the AI sector. Some involve the use of taxpayer funds, such as the many government contracts that the Trump administration has doled out to the industry. The growing role of the public sector in financing the bubble similarly serves as a slow-roll cash injection that would buffer AI concerns from the impact of a full market collapse.
But most of the Trump administration’s AI giveaways have come through policy changes at federal agencies. This summer, the SEC signaled that it was effectively exempting certain data center debt from key regulatory requirements—a key concession that makes it easier for risky AI-linked debt to be packaged and sold throughout the financial system. The regulatory carve-outs kicked into high gear this month as investors began to flee AI stocks. On November 12, the White House urged federal agencies to place limits on liability for cybersecurity incidents—a measure disingenuously presented as an overdue initiative to update “aging” cyber liability regulations. In reality, the new rule serves to protect AI model developers from damages arising from high-profile hacks like the notorious release of AI bots in the Hugging Face incident. In fact, Trump assured AI moguls and their backers that his administration would continue shilling on their behalf, sternly announcing that his administration wouldn’t “allow” any “robust regulation” of AI, a statement that serves as a nice capsule summary of the Trump administration’s AI policy.
The most recent and starkest example of the Trump administration’s alignment with AI billionaires was, of course, the unprecedented pressure campaign from Trump and Vice President JD Vance to get Nvidia’s corporate board to restore Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO after he resigned in disgrace for conducting an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. That effort had the desired effect on Monday, when tech stocks soared on the announcement that Nvidia had brought Huang back—though Nvidia’s subsequent performance on Wall Street suggests that these gains may not amount to much more than a dead cat bounce.
The bailout that AI interests are on the verge of procuring in BAAJA, which the White House also strongly backs, is somewhat better disguised. The bill’s headline provisions seem at first glance as though they’re designed to benefit ordinary people and their communities. BAAJA’s new rules on “ratepayer protection,” for example, are advertised as guarantees that data-center developers cover the cost of building out new infrastructure for energy generation, grid transmission upgrades, or other commitments that utilities face in providing power and other services to data centers.
But the devil is in the details. BAAJA does not require data center developers to pay upfront for the infrastructure and transmission costs they impose on utilities. Instead, the bill only stipulates that utilities obtain “reasonable financial assurances” that they would be able to “recover” those costs from the data center’s “owner” or “operator.”
We know from bitter experience how such riders play out in reality. When the dot-com bubble burst in the early aughts, many companies that devoted themselves to building Internet and mobile telecoms infrastructure, such as Global Crossing and Worldcom, went bankrupt. If that pattern repeats when the AI bubble bursts, many utilities—together, in all likelihood, with the households and small businesses they continue to serve—would find themselves saddled with the full cost of infrastructure improvements. What’s more, the owners and operators of record for AI data centers typically are not the megacorporations behind the projects but shell companies set up in part to shield those megacorporations from liability.
These are questions of grave concern, given how the financial house of cards underpinning AI capital expenditures has been teetering. Revenues for AI companies have utterly failed to keep pace with the massive investments in new data centers—and in a financial crisis, that means much of the industry’s vast economic power could vanish. (For another early-aughts cautionary tale, see the fate of the massively overleveraged accounting firm Enron, which also brought many energy companies and utilities to the brink of oblivion.) The Trump administration’s blind support for the data center building spree is a ploy that essentially triples down on the bet that AI will spur a historic productivity boom and result in an infusion of real cash to replace the circular financing network that’s currently propping up the industry. But that productivity boom has not yet appeared, and until and unless it does, the AI sector will continue to more closely resemble a Ponzi scheme than a sustainable industry.
It’s true that BAAJA’s permitting provisions would extend to most energy infrastructure projects—yet their benefits will flow disproportionately to the companies racing to build AI data centers. The AI Now Institute, a nonprofit research organization, warned as the Senate was preparing to consider the bill that “BAAJA weakens or removes essential environmental protections and democratic levers that preserve clean air and water and allow communities, states, and Tribes to decide whether and on what terms data centers are built in their communities.” The language of the bill also helps to preemptively open up federal lands for data centers. The Southern Environmental Law Center notes further that BAAJA will likely spur the continued siting of on-site or “behind-the-meter” power sources, like the roughly three dozen methane gas turbines that Elon Musk’s xAI was operating largely without oversight in Memphis.
What makes BAAJA a bailout rather than just another good-old-fashioned corporate giveaway is the plainly distressed condition of the AI industry. AI companies are collectively spending more than a trillion dollars this year alone on infrastructure to train and run generative AI models, but those models are only bringing in a small fraction of that amount in sales of generative AI products and services. Despite their enormous revenues, the cash flows of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft—the biggest spenders on AI infrastructure—are all either already negative or soon will be. As a result, the AI industry has been forced to accumulate a staggering amount of debt over the past year, most of it hidden from public companies’ balance sheets.
Lenders are starting to heed these distress signals. Many “neoclouds”—newer companies that focus on leasing data centers and access to AI chips to model developers—have to pay double-digit interest rates when they borrow. Even bonds tied to tech giants like Microsoft and Meta now often carry high interest rates closer to those of junk bonds than those of typical blue-chip companies.
Interest rates across the rest of the economy, in turn, are rising in no small part because of the pressures that the AI buildout exerts on supply chains and bond markets. Additional rate hikes are expected in the coming months—another indicator, as was the case in the dot-com bust, that the bubble is poised to burst.
Popular

These pressures make implementation of BAAJA and the Trump administration’s recent slew of covert bailouts an urgent priority for AI companies so that data center construction and model development can continue to race ahead. Delayed or canceled data centers can’t produce the revenues that AI companies need to pay down the trillions of dollars in debt they have accumulated.And potential liability for cyberhacking incidents could make the industry’s eventual market reckoning worse. Dismantling industry regulations and protecting AI companies from lawsuits might seem like wonky and technical fare, but they represent enormous boons for Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
More bailout proposals are no doubt in the works. In its IPO S-1 filing, Anthropic hinted that AI might need to be exempted from standard consumer product safety and even criminal liability, writing, “Any determination that we are liable under such theories, or any judicial or regulatory expansion of tort, product liability, or consumer protection law, or criminal liability” would unfairly “require us to change how we design and offer our models, platform, and applications”—and, yet again, pose an unthinkable risk to the business. The company’s pitch to essentially operate above the law came as watchdog groups and state attorneys general had begun to sue for major public harm. Meanwhile, the financing mechanics of the AI boom threaten to embed a covert bailout in the bubble itself. The private credit firms doing the lion’s share of lending to AI infrastructure are deeply intertwined in life insurance markets—a position that could open the door to state government insurance guaranty funds serving as a backstop to company failures. This would be a kind of institutionalized bailout that both increases the risk of contagion and socializes the cost of reckless AI lending.
Anthropic has also pushed for Silicon Valley model developers to be protected from global competition by pressing Washington to ban or restrict (mostly Chinese) open-weights models, which are priced far lower than Anthropic’s offerings.
While none of the steps taken so far have been as dramatic or financially costly as the overt bailouts of airlines, banks, and Silicon Valley billionaires over the past quarter century, they reveal a pattern of assistance that has accelerated as the strain on the AI industry has continued to mount. Moreover, covert bailouts have often set the stage for far larger overt bailouts. When the savings-and-loan sector began teetering in the early 1980s, the federal government first responded by loosening regulations. That spurred years of reckless lending by emboldened S&Ls, all but guaranteeing the much bigger S&L crisis that hit when defaults started to pile up on S&Ls’ risky loans. Eventually, Congress stepped in with a $160 billion taxpayer-funded bailout ($380 billion in today’s dollars).
BAAJA, alongside the Trump White House’s supine regulatory posture toward the industry, would produce much the same effect, allowing the speculative frenzy behind the AI buildout to continue building in defiance of both political oversight and a market that was finally showing signs of restraint. These covert bailouts bespeak a shocking disregard for the will of voters, who loudly expressed their opposition to data centers in this year’s elections, while also ignoring the interests of the communities sure to be saddled with stranded and underwater assets in an AI collapse.
To begin steering a viable path toward the regulation of AI in the public interest, Congress needs to completely jettison the Trump White House’s model of appeasing the sector at all costs. A necessary first step in that direction is ensuring the defeat of BAAJA—an overdue signal that we need to stop bailing out the AI sector and the lords of Big Tech, and start acquainting them with real accountability for their reckless actions.

https://gothamist.com/news/thanksgiving-.title: Thanksgiving Day forecast upgraded to a high wind warning ahead of parade
https://gothamist.com/news/thanksgiving-.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/thanksgiving-.text:
Tie your turkey bonnets tight; the National Weather Service has upgraded its forecast to a high wind warning for Thanksgiving Day, and that spells trouble for balloon enthusiasts.
High winds will begin to pick up in the late evening Wednesday and continue to increase throughout Thanksgiving morning before peaking in the afternoon. Meteorologists forecast a very rainy parade with up to 2 inches of precipitation and coastal flooding. If weather conditions manifest as predicted, the Macy’s Centennial Thanksgiving Day Parade will likely still go on but without its more than 100 iconic inflatables.
“They should be concerned,” said Joe Pollina, a National Weather Service meteorologist. “Overall, it’s going to be a very windy day tomorrow.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch are expected to give a parade update on Wednesday evening.
Winds will begin to pick up at sunrise on Thanksgiving Day, with speeds up to 20 mph and gusts that can reach 30 mph, forecasters say. The high wind warning goes into effect at 10 a.m. just as the parade is in full swing, with forecasted wind speeds of nearly 30 mph and gusts that could exceed 40 mph.
During these windy conditions, the National Weather Service highly recommends securing or bringing in any loose outdoor objects, such as holiday decorations, which could become dangerous projectiles. The gusts could bring down power lines and tree limbs. The service also warns paradegoers to stay clear of trees.
“ When we issue a high wind warning like this, that means we have an 80% confidence level at least that these conditions will occur,” Pollina said. “Don't go outside during the peak of the storm, which is during the afternoon tomorrow.”
While the floats, dancers, and performers could still take to the streets, the giant character balloons such as Mickey Mouse and his gal pal Minnie may have to be grounded. As a safety rule, if winds exceed 23 mph or wind gusts surpass 34 mph, giant balloons are grounded or ordered to fly lower than usual.
Pollina said New York City wind is unpredictable and this is a concern for giant inflatables hovering in the canyon of streets. Because of the city’s vertical geometry, there could be spots of higher wind.
“You could have higher winds around a certain corner,” Pollina said. “It's very much a microclimate.”
In addition to the gales, weather predictions include moderate to heavy rain with widespread flooding that could be major at some of the city’s typical flood-prone spots.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Tate Liverpool to reopen with Surrealism survey after two-year delay
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Tate Liverpool will reopen next autumn following an extensive four-year redevelopment costing around £30m. The relaunch programme includes a major show dedicated to Surrealism along with the first major retrospective for the Liverpool-based artist Chila Kumari Singh Burman. The key regional UK gallery, located on the city’s Royal Albert Dock, closed in October 2023 and was initially due to reopen in 2025.
Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds, which will run until spring 2028, will include work by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray, among others. “The show will reveal the important role of Surrealism in the history of theatre and dance, from experiments with masquerade, character and role play to major commissions for stage sets and costumes,” says a Tate statement. Works featured include Claude Cahun's photograph of Sheila Legge’s 1936 performance Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal, when the artist wore a Dalí-inspired costume in London's Trafalgar Square.
For the overhaul, Tate Liverpool received £18.6m from the Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund, which is awarded by the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. It also received philanthropic donations from the Garfield Weston Foundation (£3m), the Wolfson Foundation (£1.25m) and the Ross Warburton Charitable Trust, alongside other trusts and individuals.
The UK Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government also awarded £10m to the gallery, which it secured through a combined £20m bid with National Museums Liverpool. “We have raised more [than £30m] because there are other costs associated with reinstalling and reopening the museum,” a Tate spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper.
According to a Tate statement, the designs for the new gallery, drawn up by 6a architects, “open up spaces to display the incredible variety of Tate’s collection and host world-class exhibitions. These galleries will sit alongside new public spaces for play, relaxation and learning with views across the Mersey, helping to connect the gallery with the city and the communities that surround it.” The New York and Berlin-based artist Asad Raza will create the first major commission for the gallery’s Art Hall.
Tate Liverpool, which opened in 1988, was designed by James Stirling who converted the northwest corner of a seven-story warehouse standing on the Royal Albert Dock into the five-storey gallery. It received 405,000 visitors in 2022, its last full year, and 660,000 in 2019, before the Covid-19 pandemic.
Helen Legg stepped down as Tate Liverpool director earlier this year, with Jemima Pyne taking over in the interim; a new director will be recruited after the new director of Tate, Jessica Morgan, is in post next year, the spokesperson confirmed. Tate comprises four galleries: Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives.
