https://gothamist.com/news/530-press.title: NYC postpones Thanksgiving parade to Saturday as wind gusts threaten disaster
https://gothamist.com/news/530-press.author: Rosemary Misdary, Kaya Laterman
https://gothamist.com/news/530-press.text:
The balloons of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will live to fly another day — two days after Thanksgiving, to be precise.
City officials announced Wednesday that the iconic parade, which is marking its 100th edition this year, will be postponed until Saturday as a powerful storm barrels toward New York City. Both New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said there were no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time.
The National Weather Service predicts high winds will begin to pick up late Wednesday evening and continue to increase throughout Thanksgiving morning before peaking in the afternoon.
“This will be a heavy storm,” Mamdani said at a Wednesday night press conference. “There is no destination worth risking your safety.”
The National Weather Service said the forecast calls for a very rainy Thursday with up to 2 inches of precipitation and coastal flooding.
“Overall, it’s going to be a very windy day tomorrow,” said Joe Pollina, a National Weather Service meteorologist, on Wednesday.
In a statement, Macy’s said the parade is expected to kick off at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday.
Will Coss, the vice president and executive producer of Macy’s Studios, said organizers were “heartbroken that our parade was postponed.”
Coss said the balloons will be deflated on Wednesday night, taken back to a facility in New Jersey and brought back out to be inflated before Saturday's parade. There will not be another traditional public balloon inflation event on Friday, he added.
Coss described getting the balloons ready again as a “weeks-long process that’s going to get condensed to about 24 hours.”
“It’s the only inflation we support here in New York City,” Mamdani said.
Thousands of police officers will be deployed Saturday, with an increased police presence along the parade route, officials said.
Tisch said more than 1,000 officers who were scheduled to be off on Saturday will now have to work.
Mamdani said sustained winds of 30 to 40 mph were expected on Thanksgiving Day, with gusts potentially reaching 65 mph. The NWS’s high wind warning goes into effect at 10 a.m., when the parade would have been in full swing.
The weather forecast for Saturday is mostly sunny, with a high near 55, according to the NWS.
The last time the parade’s giant balloons were grounded was in 1971, when high winds and rain kept characters like Donald Duck and Snoopy out of the skies, according to a New York Times account. The rest of the parade went on. The parade was canceled from 1942 through 1944 because materials, including rubber and helium, were needed for the World War II effort, according to the Macy’s website.
Because the mayor is scheduled to have surgery to repair his torn Achilles tendon on Friday, he said he will not attend the rescheduled parade.
Tisch said the parade will start from the corner of West 77th Street and Central Park West. The route will head south on Central Park West, turn left onto Central Park South and then turn right onto Sixth Avenue. The parade will end on 34th Street in front of Macy’s Herald Square.
Street closures will begin Friday and continue into Saturday, Tisch said. They include Central Park West from West 88th to West 59th streets, restrictions on Central Park transverse roads and closures along Sixth Avenue and surrounding streets down to 34th Street.
There will be no crosstown vehicle traffic through the parade route and streets will reopen in phases throughout the afternoon, she said.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: An archaeological take on ancient rituals in the heart of a legendary Berlin nightclub
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sarp Kerem Yavuz
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
“The world is changed. I feel it in the water. I feel it in the earth. I smell it in the air. Much that once was is lost, for none now live who remember it.” Cate Blanchett, as the high elf Galadriel, spoke these opening lines in The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), and in darkened cinemas around the world, her delivery set the tone for the wonder that followed. Not since my first viewing of that film 25 years ago had I felt that sense of being dwarfed by mythology, and to re-experience it in Berlin’s famous nightclub Berghain of all places was a delight.
Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, an artist duo hailing from Iran and Canada, respectively, expertly blended archaeology, artificial intelligence (AI), acoustics, chemistry and sculpture to create a profoundly multi-sensory experience in A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads earlier this autumn (2-18 October).
Situated inside Halle am Berghain—a gargantuan former power station that, yes, was reminiscent of J.R.R. Tolkien’s Khazad-dûm—the installation was presented by the Berlin-based contemporary art initiative House, helmed by Juliet Kothe, who co-curated with Nadim Samman. The exhibition was co-presented by the Autotelic Foundation, whose whimsical take on AI art in Venice had been one of the standout digital presentations during the most recent Biennale.
At the centre of A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads was a towering, eight-minute-long, 4K video installation that slowly panned through a digitally rendered, 4,000-year-old Mithraic cave temple, created based on 3D scans of the ancient site. Originally made for an exhibition in Lausanne in 2025, the installation was expanded to take advantage of the Halle am Berghain’s size.
As the “camera” floated through the ancient temple in the looping video, visitors were encouraged to position themselves in the center of the installation, where they would be encircled by human-height black monolithic speakers. Each speaker featured a different voice, all chanting in an AI-generated, speculative Proto-Indo-Iranian (PII). PII is the ancestor of the Indo-Aryan and Iranian language families, including Sanskrit and Avestan. There are no historic documents or written texts in PII, let alone documented Mithraic chants from that period.
To realise the vital sonic component of the installation, the artists worked with the University of Toronto, drawing on comparative linguistics to reconstruct plausible linguistic forms. AI then allowed them to bring the speculative language to life. One of the speakers, Roushan said, was based on her own mother’s voice, which had been used to train one of the AI chanters.
"Mithra…" the chant began, referring to the ancient solar deity, a kind of lesser-known Ra, and as the incense burning in the hall filled one’s nostrils it was difficult not to feel transported by the sheer scale and the acoustic prowess of the installation. Near the ceiling, graffiti of the Eye of Horus that pre-dated the exhibition oddly contributed to the compounding of ritualistic symbols that have accumulated in the hall.
There is an inherent futility in worshipping an ancient sun god for any kind of wish-fulfillment. But ritualistic production and devotion have persisted through millennia and in our lives today, be it in our fascination with our illuminated, hand-held screens, or our commitment to attend public dance events that encourage abandon—such as the one that took place the weekend of Roushan and Stankievech’s opening, several metres and a few layers of concrete away. Objects scattered throughout the exhibition space included replicas of Bronze Age bells and reliefs, objects of ritual and religious significance that adorned the space and further contextualised the spiritual dimension of the installation, although none so potent as the ever-burning incense.
“We are all subject to digital change in society, economy, politics,” Nadim Samman, the Autotelic Foundation’s director, says. “These changes are massive, they are abrupt and they are intense. Making sense of it needs to come from below. Artists offer important ways to understand what this change means. Without artists, we are just stuck with the narratives and the images supplied by the companies that make the technology. Digital change impacts culture, and artists can help us understand what that impact actually feels like, and how we can think it through."
Since we have no recordings of PII, it is hard to refute that AI contributed a vital component of the installation. The exhibition’s thoughtful and archaeological approach to incorporating technologies that help us to speculate on the past was a welcome counterpoint to many digital art exhibitions in recent memory.
Roushan and Stankievech’s ambitious undertaking stands as one of the highlights of what has been a busy year for digital and AI-generated artistic presentations. The rather romantic gesture of leveraging AI to take us back several thousand years, to a time of fascination with nature and solar worship, and the decision to do so within the Brutalist context of a power-station-cum-nightclub, cleverly brought together many disparate threads.
- Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech: A Shroud Woven of Solar Threads, 2-18 October, organised by the Autotelic Foundation and House, Halle am Berghain, Berlin

https://gothamist.com/news/rikers-detain.title: Rikers detainees were routinely strip-searched in violation of policy, monitor finds
https://gothamist.com/news/rikers-detain.author: Ryan Kost
https://gothamist.com/news/rikers-detain.text:
Detainees held in restrictive housing on Rikers Island were routinely strip-searched when leaving and returning to their cells — in violation of the Department of Corrections’ own policy — according to a new report from the federal monitor overseeing reforms at the jail.
The practice was being carried out under a 2023 security memo issued by the department, the monitor, Steve J. Martin, found.
The unit, known as the Rose M. Singer Center Enhanced Supervised Housing, or RESH, holds people accused of serious violence while in custody. In its most restrictive level, detainees spend their out-of-cell time in individual recreation pens or at restraint desks.
Though department policy requires strip searches when a person enters or leaves the unit, the memo, issued in July 2023, went further, instructing correction officers to search detainees whenever they moved between their cells and the dayroom or restraint chairs.
Martin’s team only learned of the memo in October, even though it had been circulating for more than three years, according to the report. Under federal court orders, the department should have consulted the monitor before establishing the policy. The department told the monitor that various leaders had not been aware of the memo, according to the report.
Nicholas Deml, the court-appointed remediation manager tasked with driving reforms in the jails, joined Martin in asking the department to rescind the memo and issue new guidance in line with existing department policy. The department has agreed, according to the report.
Allegations that staff have used strip searches “to intimidate, harass and/or demean” detainees in the unit also come up in the report, along with concerns that some searches included visual body cavity inspections when not necessary or permitted. The correction department’s internal investigation team has opened an inquiry into the unit's use of strip searches, according to the report.
Detainees held in RESH have complained about routine strip searches before, including in written testimony posted on the Board of Correction’s website, which is routinely anonymized.
One person said they would sometimes stay in their cells for days “so that I don’t have to get strip-searched.” Another person described the setting: “You are strip-searched in front of the officers: the officer desk is right there, so there are multiple officers walking by.”
“I understand you have a job to do, but we shouldn’t be strip-searched every single day,” they added. “People aren’t animals.”
Natalie Fiorenzo, a senior corrections specialist with New York County Defender Services, said the finding “was not shocking.” She’s heard from detainees across the island — and in the new Bellevue Hospital medical facility — that they are “getting strip-searched excessively or seemingly randomly.”
The discovery of a memo that department leaders did not know about also fits a familiar pattern, she added. “I do think that there's probably a lot more where that came from, unfortunately,” she said. And while she noted the memo would be rescinded, Fiorenzo was surprised that Martin and Deml did not recommend informing detainees about the correct policy.
The Department of Correction referred a request for comment to the mayor’s office. City Hall spokesperson Sam Raskin said the Mamdani administration remained “committed to working alongside the Remediation Manager and Federal Monitor to deliver the urgent improvements our jail system needs.”
These findings all appear in the latest report filed this week in the long-running federal case over violence in the city’s jails. The more than 400-page report covers the first half of the year and states that the city’s jails remain both dangerous and dysfunctional. The monitor once again used the term “glacial” to describe the pace of change.
At least nine people have died in the Department of Correction's custody this year. After reviewing the circumstances of those deaths, Martin wrote that long-standing security lapses appeared to contribute to many of them. The report describes officers skipping tours or leaving their posts, drugs moving openly through housing units, and detainees exhibiting distressing symptoms for hours before anyone noticed.
The Correction Officers’ Benevolent Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Yonah Zeitz, advocacy director at the Katal Center, a reform group, called the searches “just one of many examples of violations that have been recurring over and over and over across many years.” He noted that the jails are now overseen by a federal monitor, a remediation manager, a reformist mayor and commissioner and both the Board of Correction and the State Commission of Correction.
“[They] are all responsible for oversight, yet these types of violations continue to persist,” Zeitz said. “And it's clear that left alone, these violations will continue to happen again and again and again.”
Still, the monitoring team wrote that the arrival of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s correction commissioner, Stanley Richards, and Deml’s team earlier this year has “altered the dynamics within the agency,” allowing for better cooperation.
A consultant working for Deml has also produced what the monitor described as the first reliable census of staff posts across the department in more than a decade. Martin said the count was critical for figuring out how to properly staff the city’s jails.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Comment | A missed opportunity for a full accounting of cultural cleansing
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Robert Bevan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
It is always gratifying to see one’s work referenced—especially 20 years after the fact. The exhibition Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, at the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine in Paris (until 3 January 2027), traces attacks on material and intangible culture in conflicts beginning with the dynamiting of the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001 and ending in Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza.
The vast exhibition spans art, digital re-creations, photography and filmed interviews. It is conceived of as an investigative report organised into sections on erasure, resistance and repair.
A wall text references my 2006 book The Destruction of Memory: Architecture at War, which first set out systematically why such targeting happens. The exhibition credits me with coining the term “cultural cleansing” in respect of the Bosnian War to explain the pattern of heritage erasure that can accompany, or presage, ethnic cleansing and the persecution of populations. It notes that Unesco adopted the term from 2012 to describe “the destruction of World Heritage Sites by terrorist groups”.
Except that book says much more than that. It talked about this same process in other places such as the Israel-occupied West Bank. It examined cultural genocide (like cultural cleansing, this still has no definition in international law) witnessed in instances ranging from the Ottoman Empire and Native American populations to the Holocaust and Tibet. I would now add the experiences of the Uyghurs in China, the Rohingya in Myanmar, the Yazidis in Iraq and the Palestinians in Gaza to that dreadful list. I argue that patterns of heritage destruction can evidence genocidal intent. Other genocides, such as that in Rwanda, did not have a pronounced material culture component.
These are matters that the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine exhibition unacceptably skirts. As in Germany and the UK (where a talk at London’s Building Centre including Architects for Gaza was cancelled following an intervention by Lawyers for Israel this summer), the French state and its institutions are censoring pro-Palestinian voices.The crucial work of Forensic Architecture in documenting destruction, for example, is not present after a dispute over the group’s use of “the G word”. How can you explain what has happened to Gaza’s cultural heritage unless you are at least prepared to discuss possible intent and patterns of destruction?
As an investigative report, the show obfuscates as much as it reveals. Institutions and governments shield themselves behind the argument that it is up to the courts to determine genocide. They forget the Genocide Convention’s duties of prevention—as litigated in the 2007 International Court of Justice (ICJ) case, Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, or South Africa’s inclusion of attacks on culture when considering Palestinian “conditions of life” at the ICJ.
There is an impression that heritage destruction in conflicts has got worse over recent decades and that the propaganda impact of destruction is actually exploited by some groups. The jury is out on this. As reflected in the show, however, the international heritage community has had an almost singular focus on actions by terrorist groups, whereas over the past decades (Islamic State and its affiliates aside) it has been the firepower of United Nations State Parties that has been overwhelmingly responsible for the devastation to material history—including but not limited to the United States, Russia, China, Israel and Saudi Arabia. Isis iconoclastically wrecked religious sites in Mosul, but it was the liberating forces that comprehensively flattened the historic city.
Does loot support terrorism?
Looting, too, is problematically covered in the Paris exhibition. This is a serious issue in war zones where security vanishes. But the myth repeated here that the sale of looted artefacts is a meaningful source of terrorist funding “on a par” with resources such as oil is simply unevidenced. (Recovered Isis documents show something quite different.)
The exhibition is sponsored in part by the French office of Unesco. No surprise then that the organisation’s manifest failure to protect heritage in conflicts is absent from the walls. Unesco is celebrated—as it should be in some cases—for its work in Timbuktu, where the International Criminal Court brought the first (and, to date, only) successful prosecution for the targeting of monuments as a war crime. Less convincingly, the show argues that this episode was a turning point after which Unesco formulated a more grassroots approach to preserving culture by working with local people on local priorities.
It was Unesco that disgracefully praised Putin for liberating Palmyra despite the terrible damage Russian forces allied with Assad inflicted on Syria’s people and heritage. Unesco has been just as partial since: while it “strongly condemns” Russian attacks on heritage in Ukraine and Israel’s on Lebanon, it does not offer the same degree of pressure in its statements on heritage destruction in Gaza or Iran. Even then, unlike other UN agencies, Unesco never names Israel. Unesco has not invoked the 1954 Hague Convention in relation to Gaza, despite citing it in virtually all similar instances. Unesco did not seek urgent action by the UN Security Council or the General Assembly to protect cultural sites there as it did in respect of Isis.
The Paris show is more subtle in its understanding of the ways that post-war heritage reconstruction can be problematic and not necessarily healing, but is just as silent on Unesco’s move away from the centrality of authenticity to reconstruction work. Whereas the notion of rebuilding the Bamiyan Buddhas was deemed unacceptable, Unesco promoted building a brand-new Mostar Bridge in Bosnia and Herzegovina as peacebuilding—despite community relations actually deteriorating in the city. And then the agency had the temerity to declare the facsimile bridge a World Heritage Site, undermining its own scientific tenets to bolster a failed symbolic gesture. All this bad-faith is set out in my follow-up book, Monumental Lies (2022).
One is left to read between the lines for hints at the full curatorial mindset. Once through the exhibition doors, the first large-scale works displayed are photographs by the Palestinian artist Taysir Batniji of Gazans’ retrieved housekeys, with their heartbreakingly quotidian fobs—a friendship bracelet, a cheap carabiner clip, a Minnie Mouse figure. The unknown fate of their owners is pencilled in below.
In its silences and voids, Heritage in Resistance at least accurately mirrors failures of international institutions and laws and the partiality and misinformation that surrounds responses to contemporary heritage destruction. Ultimately, the show offers false hope about successful resistance via digital surveying, reconstruction and Unesco work. What we should be feeling is despair.
- Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, until 3 January 2027, Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine, Paris
- Robert Bevan is a journalist, author and heritage consultant

https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-envi.title: Brooklyn environmentalists sue to block Greenpoint waterfront development
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-envi.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-envi.text:
Environmental activists are suing New York City to stop plans for a waterfront residential complex of more than 1,300 units in Greenpoint that they say sits in a floodplain and will endanger residents.
Friends of Bushwick Inlet Park, a nonprofit that advocates for a public park on the North Brooklyn waterfront, and local environmental activists say in court papers that the city’s environmental review of the Monitor Point project relies on outdated climate projections.
The lawsuit is the latest chapter in a decadeslong disagreement over how the land near the East River’s Bushwick Inlet should be used. A sweeping zoning change in 2005 made way for skyscrapers across swaths of Williamsburg and Greenpoint, but also promised public parkland on the nearly 30 acres surrounding the inlet — heavily polluted land that was historically home to fossil fuel companies. More than 20 years later, according to Friends of Bushwick Inlet Park, only a third of the promised parkland is open.
“Using public land and funding to put people in harm’s way without a thorough, science-based environmental review is just reckless,” said Ari Feldman, a spokesperson for Legal Services NYC, which filed the lawsuit, in a statement. “This project would place hundreds of affordable housing residents, including seniors, in a high-risk floodplain without adequate protections.”
The City’s legal department has yet to file a response to the petition, but told Gothamist it stands by its decision to approve the project.
“We are reviewing the suit and are confident in the integrity of the City's environmental review,” said Nicholas Paolucci, the director of public affairs in the city’s law department, in a statement. “We will be responding further in the litigation.”
Monitor Point, set to be built right next to a narrow edge of the parkland, includes two predominantly market-rate residential towers up to 640 feet tall and a third building intended to be entirely income-restricted. Part of the project will be built on land owned by the MTA, which has agreed to lease its property to the real estate developer Gotham Organization.
The Article 78 petition — a legal filing that challenges the decisions of government agencies — which was filed against New York City, the Department of City Planning, the City Council, the MTA, Gotham Organization and other city agencies, argues that the proposal should not have been approved.
The review process “downplayed and ignored the true costs and climate risks of a project that will deepen the climate dangers for the surrounding community and endanger the fragile Inlet ecosystem, the neighborhood, the Project’s own residents, and people who already reside, work or recreate nearby,” the lawsuit states.
The properties at 40 and 56 Quay Street were rezoned again this summer to make way for the development. In doing so, the environmental review process, according to the lawsuit, relied on outdated climate and flood projections from 2015 that do not include what’s called “compound flooding,” the combination of heavy rainfall with other flood sources like rising groundwater runoff, river levels and storm surges. Doing so “severely underestimated flood risk,” according to the lawsuit.
The New York Panel on Climate Change released new metrics in 2024 that do consider the risks of compound flooding, and, according to the lawsuit, those updated metrics should be incorporated into the city’s environmental review process.
Opponents of the project said that the area where Monitor Point is planned has flooded before. Hurricane Sandy left it 12 feet underwater, according to the lawsuit, noting that risks from climate change have since increased.
Katherine Conkling Thompson, president of Friends of Bushwick Inlet Park and one of the Article 78 petitioners, told Gothamist she is particularly concerned about flooding risks because the Monitor Point proposal touts 662 affordable units, including more than 160 deeply affordable units for seniors and 110 for formerly homeless New Yorkers.
“The city would be investing… hundreds of millions of dollars in housing for particularly at-risk people,” Thompson said. “These are formerly unhoused people and elderly… in a very flood-prone location. We think that’s unwise and needs more scrutiny.”
Ron Shiffman, a city planner and professor emeritus at the Pratt Institute, filed an affidavit supporting the lawsuit against the city agencies. More affordable housing in New York is paramount, he argued to the court, but it should also be done right.
“New York urgently needs more housing, and especially more housing affordable to very low, low- and moderate-income households,” Shiffman stated in the legal filing. “But affordable housing production cannot be treated as a substitute for planning and community development.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Smithsonian leader defends institution's independence after leak of White House’s draft overhaul plan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Elena Goukassian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Lonnie G. Bunch III, the outgoing leader of the Smithsonian Institution, sent a letter to staff on Tuesday (24 November) in an attempt to quell fears of a political takeover after photos leaked of a Trump aide working on an overhaul plan while riding the city's metro.
“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote of “The Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan” that the staffer was seen editing on his laptop on a crowded train in late October. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programmes.”
Photos of the staffer working on the plan—in full view of fellow passengers on public transit—had been published by ProPublica the previous day (23 November). Formatted as a 25-item to-do list, the draft focused largely on the beleaguered National Museum of American History (NMAH), a recent focal point in the White House’s attempts to rewrite US history.
The list included firing NMAH’s director and a dozen other administrators and curators, opening a new permanent exhibition centred on “Western civilisation inheritance”, erecting a new “colossus statue” of George Washington for NMAH’s entrance and overhauling its online curriculum for schoolchildren to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology”. The plan also called for a review of Smithsonian grants to “woke third parties” like the American Alliance of Museums.
Given that it was in process prior to the midterm elections—which resulted in a landslide for Democrats, who gained a majority in both houses of congress—it remains unclear if this plan for the Smithsonian is still in the works. However, congressional Democrats are ready to fight.
“I intend to investigate these matters in the 120th congress and vigorously defend the Smithsonian’s independence,” Chellie Pingree, the ranking member of the congressional subcommittee that funds the Smithsonian, wrote in a letter to the institution’s Board of Regents after the ProPublica leak. “This reporting is extremely concerning, but not surprising given this administration’s previous attempts to illegally impound Smithsonian Institution-appropriated funding, use federal agencies to spread misinformation about the Smithsonian, and release a demonstrably false report accusing the Smithsonian Institution of systemic bias in its curatorial decisions.”
US President Donald Trump has been steadily attacking the Smithsonian ever since he took office for his second term, with a goal of realigning the institution to complement his own political agenda. Last year, Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, over her support for diversity, equity and inclusion programmes. She later resigned and now heads the Milwaukee Art Museum in Wisconsin.
In July, NMAH director Anthea M. Hartig was summoned to appear before congress and interrogated by Republican lawmakers after a White House report concluded the museum was not “proudly patriotic” with leadership having “denigrated and displaced whites, males, Christians and Americans”. A few days later, Trump ordered that signs be placed outside the NMAH, warning visitors of "ideological capture" and "inaccurate information" inside. (The signs have yet to be erected.)

https://gothamist.com/news/woman-at-rive.title: Woman at Riverside Park with self-inflicted stab wounds gave a false account, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-at-rive.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-at-rive.text:
New details have emerged in the case of a woman who told police she was stabbed by a stranger in Riverside Park this week — with NYPD officials now saying her wounds were self-inflicted.
Police initially said they responded to a 911 call from the woman around 7:40 p.m. Monday, saying she had been stabbed in the torso near West 96th Street by a man wearing all black. First responders took the 26-year-old woman to Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital in stable condition.
But on Wednesday, NYPD officials said detectives had determined that the story was a lie. Police said the woman admitted to having stabbed herself, and police obtained surveillance video of her purchasing a knife before the incident.
Police said the woman was still hospitalized and recovering, and her motives were still unclear. Officials said they were no longer searching for a suspect. Police did not disclose the woman's identity or say whether she will face charges in connection with the incident.
The case follows the fatal stabbing of Brooklyn jogger Katie Suarez last month.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Mariana of Austria, royal art patron who saw power in portraiture, explored in Prado exhibition
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Karen Chernick
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Mariana of Austria’s position in the 17th-century Spanish court was not an easy one. She became queen of Spain in 1649 after marrying Philip IV, and then when he died in 1665, she assumed the role of regent, governing for over a decade on behalf of their three-year-old son, Charles II. Her authority was challenged, repeatedly. She was also the last woman of the Habsburg dynasty to exercise governing authority within the Spanish court. Even after her regent years were over, Mariana of Austria remained a significant figurehead until her death in 1696.
The Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid is taking a closer look at the Spanish monarch as it opens its first exhibition devoted to a female patron of the arts. Titled Mariana of Austria, the show reflects the museum’s efforts in recent years to re-examine historic women artists, benefactors and subjects. It includes around 100 objects, from paintings to prints and medals to manuscripts, building up a comprehensive picture of the iconography that Mariana used to curate her own public persona.
“The exhibition reveals a sovereign who was not simply the subject of some of the most celebrated portraits of the Spanish Golden Age, but who understood the political power of images and actively used them to assert and legitimise her authority,” says the exhibition curator Noelia García Pérez, a professor of art history at the Universidad de Murcia.
The Prado is poised to host such a presentation since it holds the most comprehensive collection of portraits of Mariana of Austria, representing every stage of her life from her youth as an Austrian archduchess up until her late years as queen mother. A full-length portrait of her by Diego Velázquez, within the Prado collection, was the model for her official image during the early years of her reign.
Mariana of Austria was in good company among other European royals who understood that authority needed a visual translation, to be communicated both domestically and across Europe. Some of the iconographic devices used by her court painters had precedents elsewhere, including among other queens. Such strategies include the use of the seated portrait, which was traditionally associated with ruling princes, and portraits in which she held a document as a reference to her governing ability.
Preparation of the exhibition has led to both a different understanding of such iconography, and a deeper knowledge of the works themselves, thanks to restorations and a reassessment of dates, identifications and attributions of several works. The exhibition also reunites rarely seen and never before exhibited works, such as a double portrait of Mariana of Austria and Charles II, on loan from the Bečov nad Teplou Castle in the Czech Republic, and a bust attributed to Nicolás de Bussy, which was recently identified as a portrait of the queen.
Shifting meanings
Another section of the exhibition is devoted to portraits of queens, regents and other female governors who held power within the Spanish monarchy over the course of roughly two centuries. “Seeing these works together reveals how attributes such as the book and the column were passed down and acquired new meanings from one generation to the next,” Garcia Pérez says, “gradually shaping a shared visual language in which piety, dynastic legitimacy and the exercise of power were closely intertwined.”
Mariana of Austria culminates a year of focusing on three queens at the Prado—Elisabeth Farnese, Christina of Sweden and now Mariana of Austria—exploring not only their tastes but also how they used the arts as a means of asserting their authority. This focus is part of the Prado’s commitment, over the past decade, to highlight the multifaceted roles of women in art history. These initiatives have evolved into the long-term programme called The Female Perspective, which will investigate the influence of Europe’s ruling women on the arts in collaboration with the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.
The next exhibition in the works will focus on female patrons of the 19th century, highlighting figures such as Spain’s Isabella II. “Ultimately, the ambition of The Female Perspective is not simply to add women’s names to an established narrative,” Garcia Pérez says. “But to enrich and, where necessary, rethink that narrative.”
• Mariana of Austria, Museo Nacional del Prado, Madrid, until 28 March 2027

https://gothamist.com/news/some-nyc-rest.title: Some NYC restaurants worry they won't be ready for year-round outdoor dining this winter
https://gothamist.com/news/some-nyc-rest.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/some-nyc-rest.text:
Dining al freeze-co?
Restaurants can now opt to keep their roadway cafes up year-round — but as colder weather approaches, restaurateurs are still waiting for finalized guidelines from the city on how to make the structures warm enough to eat in this winter.
When the City Council loosened restrictions on the city’s dining program, Dining Out NYC, in August, it was a win for participating restaurants. Under the new law, they can now, for a fee, avoid taking down and storing roadway cafes for the winter months as previously required. Now as temperatures drop, the city’s Department of Transportation, which oversees the program, is still working to update the rules and guidelines for winterizing the dining sheds.
Thousands of restaurants first built makeshift dining sheds in 2020 under a then-emergency COVID-19 relief program with few restrictions. The administration of then-Mayor Eric Adams formalized the program in 2024, making roadway cafes permanent but seasonal — allowing them from April through November. The program also had strict design rules, which didn’t account for colder months.
“They’re still waiting on the standards and specifications of how they are going to enclose that roadway cafe, what kind of materials they can use, and all these other really important details,” said Andrew Rigie, the NYC Hospitality Alliance's executive director. “The challenge is, once those details are finalized, it's going to take time for restaurants to design their enclosures, to contact a company and have them fabricated and then installed. So, unfortunately, at this pace, it seems like many restaurants will not be fully able to take advantage of the new laws until later in the winter, in the new year.”
Manny Colon, owner of Manny’s Bistro on the Upper West Side, said he isn’t sure the guidance will arrive in time for him to take advantage of it this winter. Colon said he was relieved when the program became year-round in August, since finding storage for the set-up can be costly. But his current roadway cafe — which features a simple border of plastic water-filled barriers topped with planters on three sides of a rectangular seating area — will take considerable adjustments to winterize.
"If they say tomorrow, ‘This is what you can use, this is what you can do,’ it may take me 30 days just to order the materials and maybe longer because we don't know what the materials are going to be,” he said. “ I think it's taking too long.”
Will Livingston, a DOT spokesperson, said the agency "began working as quickly as possible to finalize the rules and create a process for restaurants to opt into year-round roadway dining" after the council approved the program in August. New rules are subject to a mandated rule-making process, which typically takes 75 to 90 days after a rule is published to finalize.
Under the proposed rules, which have already gone through the public comment period, the DOT would allow restaurants to install “retractable, non-rigid, transparent covering installed vertically” on their roadway cafes, which would be permitted “on all sides of a year-round roadway cafe for weatherproofing purposes, provided that clear visibility is maintained.”
While they wait for the rules to be finalized, some restaurateurs are already taking action and making their roadway cafes winter-ready in advance. On a recent afternoon outside Friend of a Farmer on the Upper West Side, workers were already attaching clear plastic wrapping to the roadway cafe and installing heaters inside. Co-owner Rose Morabito said it’s important for sales that the space be usable during colder days, and they will reassess its design once the DOT finalizes the rules.
“We're just keeping it simple for now and then seeing how the winter goes and if we can add more to it, but I am under the impression it has to be more, like, bare bones,” she said, adding that the restaurant’s Gramercy location had already winterized its roadway cafe. “We'll find out if we get another fine, but for now it seems okay.”
Noncompliant roadway winterization coverings are among the dozens of new reasons restaurants can be fined under the new rules and regulations proposed by the DOT — $200 for the first offense and $500 for the second. Others include “failure to maintain a sidewalk cafe or roadway cafe in a ‘service-ready’ condition, and failure to install required reflective strip on roadway cafe.”
Still, some restaurants with roadway cafes are avoiding the winterization headache altogether and opting out of the year-round program.
Rigie said the slew of new rules piqued concern in the small business community about penalties cutting into restaurants’ bottom lines.
“We want to just make sure that an inspector comes out to a restaurant, if they see there's some technical violation that's being made, they explain why it's a violation, how the small business can correct it, and they give him an opportunity to cure it before simply issuing a violation and issuing a fine,” he said. “ We've had a history of New York City really just issuing far too many fines for small businesses, and I'd say even exploiting them and using them as an ATM. And that is not right.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-searches.title: NYPD searches for 6 sewer spelunkers seen exiting a Manhattan manhole
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-searches.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-searches.text:
Police have released pictures of six people wanted for climbing out of a Manhattan manhole last week — the latest in a series of similar incidents that have captivated public attention and raised questions for investigators.
NYPD officials said the latest incident happened just before 5 a.m. on Nov. 18, when a witness saw five people exiting the city’s sewer system through a manhole on 2nd Avenue and East 17th Street in Gramercy Park.
The group then got into a red sedan driven by a sixth person, and they all drove west on East 17th Street, officials said. No one was injured, and police said the group’s motives were still unclear.
On Tuesday, police released photos of the two women and four men they are looking for. Most appear to be carrying various tools, including sledgehammers.
The manhole mystery has gripped the five boroughs since at least last May, when two groups of people were spotted climbing out of manholes in different parts of Brooklyn. Additional sightings followed near Penn Station, at an intersection on Long Island, and in September on the Upper East Side when the U.N. General Assembly was meeting. Two men were arrested and charged with trespassing in connection with that incident, and told police they were looking for gold and other valuables washed away into storm drains.
The sightings didn’t stop in October, and police arrested five more men who allegedly meddled in manholes in Inwood.
NYPD officials have said some of the sewer spelunkers appear to be motivated by treasure hunting. But they warn that the city’s manholes can be dangerous and unpredictable places: a 56-year-old woman died after falling into an open Con Edison manhole in Midtown last spring.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://gothamist.com/news/queens-da-kat.title: Queens DA Katz seeks to block prosecutor watchdog investigating wrongful convictions
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-da-kat.author: Graham Rayman
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-da-kat.text:
After taking office as a reformer, Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz is seeking to block a new state watchdog from investigating the wrongful convictions of three men who spent decades in prison for the murders of a check cashing store owner and an off-duty detective.
In the suit filed under seal, Katz argues the Commission on Prosecutorial Conduct “suffers from a fatal constitutional defect.” Gothamist obtained a copy of the lawsuit, which centers on the commission’s demands for records tied to the wrongful convictions of George Bell, Rohan Bolt and Gary Johnson.
The verdicts against the men were thrown out after it emerged prosecutors under former DA Richard Brown knowingly withheld key evidence that would have proved their innocence.
Legal observers pointed to Katz’s suit against the prosecutorial watchdog as evidence she’s become more resistant to wrongful conviction cases in recent years.
“Katz won her election based on a promise of transparency and review of prosecutorial misconduct — two commitments she has abandoned,” said Ron Kuby, a lawyer who represents clients with wrongful conviction claims.
“She has consistently rejected transparency when it would embarrass the office and she has consistently defended corrupt prosecutors even when she agreed to vacate the convictions they wrongfully caused.”
Katz’s lawsuit, filed earlier this month, was first reported by the Queens Daily Eagle. The nature of the commission’s probe into the Bell, Bolt and Johnson case is unclear.
When Judge Joseph Zayas tossed the men’s convictions, he wrote that the case “was not an isolated instance of misconduct, but part of a larger pattern of behavior that was calculated to deprive the defendants of fair trials.”
Katz touted the exoneration of the men in 2021, saying in a press release that “There can be no true justice, in Queens County or anywhere, unless we hold ourselves to the highest standards facilitating the process by which justice is sought.”
The men were paid nearly $50 million in settlements with the city for their wrongful incarcerations. But accountability for the wrongful convictions has been elusive.
No prosecutors were ever disciplined in connection with the Bell, Bolt and Johnson case. In August, a state grievance committee found “insufficient evidence” prosecutors violated rules or law governing attorney conduct.
Katz argues in the lawsuit that the prosecutorial conduct commission has no authority to investigate prosecutors who have left the DA’s office or died. The suit also states grievance committees have authority over attorney discipline — not the commission.
Russell Neufeld, a former attorney-in-charge of the Legal Aid Society’s Criminal Division, described the Bell case as “one of the most egregious examples of prosecutor misconduct in the past 30 years.”
“The DA’s office is doing everything they can to stop the inquiry. It means they will do whatever they can do to protect the misconduct,” he said.
“The entire reason the commission was set up is because the grievance committees don’t discipline prosecutors for misconduct.”
Brendan Brosh, a spokesperson for the Queens DA, defended the office’s record.
“District Attorney Katz is deeply committed to righting the grave injustices of wrongful convictions and imprisonment,” Brosh said.
Then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo signed the commission into law in 2018 after years of alarm across the state over cases of prosecutorial misconduct that sent men to prison for decades for crimes they did not commit.
The state’s District Attorney Association sued twice over the commission’s mandate and powers, which resulted in legislators reforming the law that created the watchdog.
Katz’s suit states the commission only began operations in 2024.
So far, the commission has released just two annual reports and one public finding — censure of Monroe County DA Susan Dooley for ignoring a police traffic stop.
But in recent months, the commission has been ramping up its inquiries.
Last week, the commission sued the Suffolk DA Ray Tierney and police in state court alleging they were violating the law by refusing to comply with the subpoenas.
On Monday, Orange County DA David Hoovler sued the commission, alleging its subpoenas to his office are improper. It’s not clear what cases the commission is investigating in both counties.
“This appears to be a coordinated effort by the prosecutors to undermine an entity that the legislature found was a necessary response to the problem of prosecutorial misconduct,” Ross Firsenbaum, a lawyer for the commission, said. He emphasized he was only commenting on the Suffolk and Orange County disputes due to confidentiality rules covering the Queens case.
The District Attorney’s Association of the State of New York, which is led by Tierney, says the commission is exceeding its authority.
“We support the Queens DA’s efforts to ensure that proper disciplinary procedures are followed,” Tierney said in a statement to Gothamist.
“The association’s position is that all attorneys practicing in New York are subject to the authority of [the courts system's] grievance committees, which are justly empowered to censure, suspend, and disbar. We respect that jurisdiction and those processes to improve the profession of law.”
Katz was elected in 2019 under a banner of reform following the 29-year tenure of Brown, a tough-on-crime DA whose office was exposed in a series of reversed homicide convictions and multimillion-dollar settlements for bending and breaking rules.
Katz promised “dramatic and immediate change” and created the borough’s first Conviction Integrity Unit.
From 2020 through 2022, the unit backed exonerations in nine cases, including Bell, office press releases show.
Since Katz won re-election in 2023, the unit's output has appeared to slow. The unit has not put out a press release since that year.
Brosh, the Queens DA spokesperson, countered that across her nearly seven-year tenure, Katz has vacated 17 convictions based on evidence pointing to innocence or other errors that had been overlooked.
He said 100 additional convictions have been vacated based on unreliable evidence provided by law enforcement officers.
Allen Porter, who was convicted in 1992 of a Queens double homicide, and his lawyers say they had a frustrating experience with Katz’s office. After they had a decadelong battle with the DA for records, Katz's Conviction Integrity Unit agreed to take the case in 2021.
Porter’s team said the probe inexplicably stalled two years later. Porters attorneys said they grew so fed up they withdrew from the Conviction Integrity Unit process and instead filed a motion with a judge to vacate Porter’s conviction.
Katz’s office was compelled to turn over key documents, and in January Judge Michelle Johnson ordered Porter be released from prison after more than three decades.
“It is not just the amount of undisclosed evidence that is alarming, it is the people’s continued attempts to justify it and explain it away,” Johnson said from the bench. “The cumulative violations cannot be understated.”

https://gothamist.com/news/no-bench-no-p.title: No bench, no problem: Things to do at Moynihan Train Hall
https://gothamist.com/news/no-bench-no-p.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/no-bench-no-p.text:
Hordes of New Yorkers and out-of-towners are traveling by train over the Thanksgiving holiday amid ongoing air travel headaches, including a rare nationwide ground stop earlier this month.
Thanksgiving is Amtrak's busiest travel season, with more than 380,000 people using the national railroad to travel through Moynihan Train Hall and Penn Station last year, according to a spokesperson. There’s so much demand for train travel to and from New York City over Thanksgiving that Amtrak said it has added extra trips between Penn Station and Washington D.C.
Moynihan Train Hall, which opened Jan. 1, 2021, offers an alternative to Amtrak’s notoriously dingy areas of Penn Station across Eighth Avenue. It’s also a place for Long Island Rail Road riders to board. (NJ Transit doesn't have entrances at the newer station, which means Garden State train commuters are stuck at old Penn.)
With so many people passing through Moynihan and Penn, Amtrak spokesperson Jason Abrams recommends that riders arrive 30-45 minutes before their scheduled departures.
The Midtown commuter hub is infamous for its lack of benches, but there’s no shortage of ways to spend your wait if you find yourself with extra time. Here are some recommendations:
Browse the stacks of the Strand
The beloved indie bookstore has a selection of books and merch at the Gotham News on the concourse Moynihan Train Hall. Get a book for your ride or a souvenir for a literary aficionado in your life.
Buy a gift
If you need a gift, you’ve got options.
You can buy a bouquet, a greeting card, a notebook or skincare products. There are also plenty of options for sweet treats, including Magnolia Bakery, known for its banana pudding and its cupcakes, which Carrie and Miranda famously devoured on an episode of Sex and the City.
Grab a bite
There’s basically a full-on food court in the train station. Several local restaurants have stalls inside the train hall, including Jacob’s Pickles and Pastrami Queen. You can also nosh on a salad, sushi, pizza, ramen or a classic H&H bagel. There are even more food stalls on the lower level.
For travelers who need a caffeine fix, there are multiple coffee shops and a Cha Cha Matcha. Or if you’re looking for a different kind of drink, you can sip on a beer at Threes Brewing.
Take a seat (if you have a ticket)
While there are no benches on the main concourse, there are some places to sit. Amtrak and Long Island Rail Road ticket holders can rest their legs in waiting rooms, where there are lightly padded seats and a smattering of outlets to charge your devices.
Amtrak has a lounge on the mezzanine level, but it’s only open to select riders, including those with first-class tickets. You can also buy a day pass for access to the lounge if you’re willing to shell out $50.
If you need to get some work done or want to pass the time with your favorite TV show, you can connect to free Wi-Fi throughout Moynihan Train Hall.
Hit the restroom
If you need to go before you go, you can find public restrooms in the concourse and on the first floor of the station. There are also bathrooms in the ticketed waiting room and the Amtrak lounge.
Beware that the restrooms do occasionally close for cleaning, which can put riders in a pinch if time is running out before boarding. But if you don’t make it before your train arrives, don’t sweat. There are also bathrooms on the train.
Anxiously await your track assignment
For Amtrak customers, boarding is often the most chaotic part of a trip to the train hall. As soon as a track assignment is announced — and sometimes even before — travelers swarm.
Lining up early can help to secure a better spot on a sold-out train, especially if you’re hoping to sit with someone else or have a lot of bags to lug around. But track assignments aren’t announced until moments before departure, making it tricky to find out where to go before a massive queue has already formed.
There are a few clues to look for if you want to get a good spot in line. If you see train staff setting up retractable belts to form a line, it might be a good cue to check if they’re preparing for your train to board. If you see a small line already starting to form, you can ask and see if the other commuters are heading toward the same destination — with the caveat that sometimes people line up without actually knowing if they’re in the right place.
There are boards around the station that list the status of upcoming trains and track numbers once they are available. As your departure time approaches, keep an eye on those boards. You may also be able to catch an announcement in the ticketed waiting area.
Abrams, the Amtrak spokesperson, recommended that travelers download the Amtrak app and follow the railroad operator on social media for updates on their trip, including gate assignments.
Need help? Find a red cap
Amtrak employees in signature red caps are available to help people navigate the station and board the train. The Red Cap service offers assistance for people with disabilities, seniors and big groups, as well as solo commuters. Red Cap employees can also help to carry luggage and load it onto the train.
Red Cap service is free, but tips are welcome, according to Amtrak’s website.

https://gothamist.com/news/fowl-weather-.title: Fowl weather alert: Thanksgiving Day in NYC to bring cornucopia of wind and rain
https://gothamist.com/news/fowl-weather-.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/fowl-weather-.text:
Break out the Scrabble board. Thanksgiving Day will be an indoor affair this year in New York City.
The National Weather Service is warning New Yorkers to stay inside for much of the day, especially in the afternoon, when winds and heavy rain reach their crescendo.
City leaders announced that Macy's would postpone its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day parade to Saturday and Mayor Zohran Mamdani warned families they may be hunkered down together for longer than planned this holiday.
"You may have to stay late," he said during a briefing alongside NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch. "There is no destination worth risking your safety."
The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning that goes into effect at 10 a.m. and runs until 1 a.m. Friday. The wind will begin howling Wednesday evening and will steadily intensify through Thanksgiving Day when it could reach gusts of 60 mph. Winds will be stronger on bridges and elevated locations, according to city officials.
Heavy rains are expected to accompany the strong winds. The downpour could begin late Thursday morning and may last through the night, forecasters say, dropping as much as 2 inches of rain.
Minor to moderate flooding is likely in coastal and flood-prone areas, officials warned, especially during the high tides at around 9 a.m. and 9 p.m. on Thursday.
"The worst conditions are expected later in the day," Mamdani said Wednesday evening, urging drivers to stay off the roads. "Winds will be strong enough [Thursday] to down tree limbs and power lines."
He warned people living in basement apartments to be especially vigilant.
"Make sure you know your exits and move to a higher floor," he said. "Never stay in or go back to a flooded basement."
There is a silver lining. The parade rain date on Saturday has a forecast that is mostly sunny and could reach highs in the mid-50s.
David Giambusso contributed reporting.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Pair accused of murdering South African artist and curator Tamlin Blake appear in court as art scene mourns
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Charles Leonard
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Two men accused of the murder of the South African mixed-media artist and curator Tamlin Blake appeared in the Riebeek West magistrate’s court on Wednesday (25 November). Blake was found killed on Sunday at her home in Riebeek-West, a small town 80km northwest of Cape Town. The 51-year-old artist was a well-loved member of the town’s prominent community of artists, among whom she lived for the past 20 years.
The two suspects, Pedro Fraser and Ronnie Von Wielligh, both aged 32, have been charged with murder and possession of stolen goods and will appear in court again on 1 December where they are expected to respond to the charges.
Angry protestors gathered outside the court, demanding justice with some chanting “no bail!”, reported the South African digital news platform, News24.
A representative for the state told the court that the murder was a Schedule 6 offence, which is one of the most serious categories of crime, according to News24. Prosecutors reportedly said she was attacked with a sharp object. Fraser and Von Wielligh will remain in prison until their appearance next Tuesday.
The police tracked down the suspects after tracing Blake’s cellphone, which was allegedly stolen during the attack, a source told another news platform, IOL Media.
“One suspect was arrested in possession of the cellphone. During police questioning, he admitted that he did not commit the offence alone. He then took police to his co-accused,” IOL Media’s source said.
“The gentlest person and a quiet thought leader”
The residents of Riebeek West and neighbouring Riebeek Kasteel are “completely shell shocked” by the news of Blake’s death, a fellow local artist and close friend of Blake’s, Kevan Moses, tells The Art Newspaper. He describes the area as home to many artists, “international, established as well as new” and that it is a “very nurturing creative environment”.
Blake, who was born in Johannesburg, obtained a master’s in fine arts at the University of Stellenbosch in 2001. She has exhibited extensively at home and abroad and is represented by Everard Read Gallery, which has locations in South Africa and London.
Blake was, according to her website, instrumental in developing beading techniques which are now used by various South African artists. Her recent works include tapestries woven from recycled hand-spun newspaper. She was also the chief curator for the Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based organisation dedicated to building sustainable careers for professional artists. There Blake oversaw the acquisition of works of art for diverse collections and lead initiatives that supported artists at pivotal stages of their careers.
“Tamlin was a remarkable artist whose work reflected a deep sensitivity to the natural world and an unwavering commitment to her creative practice,” Everard Read Gallery said in a statement. “Through her distinctive voice and vision, she built a respected career and touched the lives of collectors, colleagues, and fellow artists in South Africa and abroad.
“We are grateful to have worked with Tamlin over many years, and to have shared her work with our audiences. Her contribution to contemporary South African art will be remembered with admiration, gratitude and affection.”
Spier Arts Trust described Blake in a statement as a “visionary artist” who “possessed the rarest gift: a boundless, ego-free generosity that put other people’s growth and dignity at the centre of her life’s work”.
“Those of us fortunate enough to have worked alongside her will forever remember her sharp eye, her quiet grace, her advocacy for authentic, exceptional expression, and the warmth she brought into every studio conversation,” the trust said.
Her friend Moses said: “Tamlin was a great artist, the gentlest person and a quiet thought leader. She was a mentor for many artists. She will be truly missed.”
Blake leaves behind her husband and two daughters, aged 18 and 20.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: FDR’s Thanksgiving Proclamations Made the Moral Case for Taming Capitalism
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
FDR’s Thanksgiving Proclamations Made the Moral Case for Taming Capitalism
When Abdul El-Sayed attacks the “corporate capture of our politics,” he recalls Roosevelt’s rejections of “greed and selfishness and striving for undue riches.”
Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who will join the United States Senate in January as part of a dynamic new class of congressional changemakers, is already shaking things up with proposals to work across party lines in order to establish a national healthcare system. He’s even caught the attention of President Trump, with an offer to name the initiative “Trump Care” in the event that the embattled executive might actually be willing to sign a Medicare for All bill into law.
That’s unlikely to happen. But the president did share an El-Sayed post on the proposal, and Vice President JD Vance’s office reached out to the new senator to arrange a meeting.
All of this is ironic, because, of course, El-Sayed was frequently attacked by Trump, Vance, and other Republicans during the 2026 election campaign as a socialist. The president even labeled the Michigander a “communist.”
That has never been the case. “I believe in capitalism, and I think capitalism works well to allocate resources in a market. And I think if you look at where we are right now, we don’t live in capitalism. We live in corporatism,” El-Sayed told reporters during his Senate campaign. In a late-summer interview with The Nation, El-Sayed explained that “what we have right now is a level of corporate capture of our politics, in every single part of American society,” where the political system and the government that extends from it “acts as a handmaiden to the richest and most powerful, accelerating the inequality that we have in our society”
El-Sayed brought this savvy economic critique into his campaign, describing his belief that a corrupted form of capitalism harms Americans “in every part of our lives: whether it’s the food system, which is controlled by a couple of very large corporations and agribusiness, [or] our healthcare system, which is captured by a few pharmaceutical and health insurance companies.”
With his Senate victory, El-Sayed has instantly become one of the nation’s leading advocates for a flexible, efficient and humane “Medicare for All” system. He proposes a “Break Up Big Medicine Act” to tackle the monopolistic profiteering of private-sector healthcare corporations, and he backs similar initiatives to address other concentrations of power in the hands of predatory corporations that neglect the needs of working Americans, as part of a headlong rush to turn billionaires into trillionaires.
What distinguishes El-Sayed in this moment is that he recognizes the importance of putting the economic and social reforms he seeks in perspective. That requires speaking not only in technical terms but also in moral language that voters can connect with. Ordinary people may not know the ins and outs of health policy, but they know what El-Sayed means when he argues, “No one should have to choose between getting the care they need or going into debt in the richest, most powerful country in the world.” El-Sayed is determined to employ every opportunity to drive forward the project of ensuring that capitalism serves working Americans rather than corporate bottom lines and the fever dreams of the billionaire class.
No one doubts El-Sayed’s dynamism or his potential. He will be a central figure in policy debates going forward; and, yes, he could even transform our economic discourse. Yet his approach is not new. It channels the ambition of the populist and progressive movements that took on the robber barons of the Gilded Age, and more particularly of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt.
Like El-Sayed, FDR sought to advance his New Deal agenda by offering a critique of capitalism as it had come to operate in the years leading to the Great Depression. Roosevelt declared in his first inaugural address, “Practices of the unscrupulous money changers stand indicted in the court of public opinion, rejected by the hearts and minds of men. The money changers have fled from their high seats in the temple of our civilization. We may now restore that temple to the ancient truths. The measure of the restoration lies in the extent to which we apply social values more noble than mere monetary profit.”
This critique of capitalism was a constant theme of Roosevelt’s presidency. He claimed as his mission “the liberation of the exploited” and announced that “there must be an end to a conduct in banking and in business which too often has given to a sacred trust the likeness of callous and selfish wrongdoing.”
FDR, a master communicator, recognized that this agenda could not be truly understood, or accepted, if it were merely delivered through addresses to Congress and in political debates. Like El-Sayed, FDR knew that his critique needed to permeate American life. So it was that the 32nd president used his Thanksgiving Proclamations to speak not just of bountiful harvests and prayers of gratitude but also of moral certainties that were at odds with unrestricted capitalism.
“May we ask guidance in more surely learning the ancient truth that greed and selfishness and striving for undue riches can never bring lasting happiness or good to the individual or to his neighbors,” read Roosevelt’s first proclamation, in 1933. A year later, he wrote: “Our sense of social justice has deepened. We have been given vision to make new provisions for human welfare and happiness, and in a spirit of mutual helpfulness we have cooperated to translate vision into reality. More greatly have we turned our hearts and minds to things spiritual. We can truly say, ‘What profiteth it a Nation if it gain the whole world and lose its own soul.’”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
By 1935, with the New Deal project fully in swing, the president wrote: “We can well be grateful that more and more of our people understand and seek the greater good of the greater number. We can be grateful that selfish purpose of personal gain, at our neighbor’s loss, less strongly asserts itself.”
And after his landslide reelection in 1936—following a campaign in which he said, “We know now that Government by organized money is just as dangerous as Government by organized mob”—FDR encouraged Americans “to fulfill our obligation to use our national heritage by common effort for the common good.” That same year, he found cause for thanksgiving in the fact that labor organizing guaranteed “the toiler in shop and mill receives a more just return for his labor.”
The socialists of the 1930s would have had Roosevelt go further. But, as with El-Sayed, FDR was more than ready to echo the left’s condemnations of greedy oligarchs and self-serving autocrats. Nor did he hesitate to speak of economic democracy. Toward the end of his presidency, FDR would use his 1944 State of the Union address to outline an Economic Bill of Rights that demanded healthcare, housing, education, and living wages for all Americans.
As with his 1939 Thanksgiving Proclamation, which celebrated the fact that “[o]ur Nation has gone steadily forward in the application of democratic processes to economic and social problems,” FDR’s speech near the end of his long tenure in the White House argued, “We have come to a clear realization of the fact that true individual freedom cannot exist without economic security and independence. ‘Necessitous men are not free men.’ People who are hungry and out of a job are the stuff of which dictatorships are made.”
Conservative critics claimed that FDR’s vision was “socialist.”
But Franklin Roosevelt understood then, as Abdul El-Sayed does now, and as we all should in this season of reflection and sharing, that capitalism needs both regulatory guardrails and humane ambitions—because, as the nation’s longest-serving president taught us, “greed and selfishness and striving for undue riches can never bring lasting happiness or good to the individual or to his neighbors.”
