Sols pollués : Dix sites identifiés à Bruxelles
L’inventaire officiel de la pollution des sols à Bruxelles est très incomplet. La preuve, Médor a déterré dix sites à risques qui n’y sont pas repris. Ils ont été présentés avec des expert·es et en public, le 9 novembre dernier.
Forcément, la carte officielle de la région, réalisée par Bruxelles Environnement (BE), a été au cœur des échanges lors de cette soirée organisée pour faire suite à notre enquête sur la pollution sous-estimée des sols de la capitale (septembre 2026).
François Antoine, chef de service aux Archives de l’État, a tenu à rappeler le caractère innovant de cet outil, « qui fonctionne assez bien par rapport à toutes les procédures actuelles ». Mais l’arriéré lié aux données anciennes reste problématique. On le disait, de nombreux documents précieux n’ont pas été pris en compte. Par exemple, les anciens permis d’environnement, conservés depuis 1810, qui encadrent les établissements insalubres, incommodes et dangereux en Belgique. Ces documents sont stockés aux Archives de l’état, sans avoir été incorporés dans l’inventaire de l’état du sol, comme tant d’autres.
Est-il seulement possible d’intégrer toutes ces archives existantes à l’inventaire des sols ? La quête de l’exhaustivité se heurte assez vite à la disponibilité des fonds d’archives, et aux moyens financiers nécessaires pour les exploiter. Marie Tielemans, archiviste-historienne, rappelait que le bureau d’étude mandaté pour construire la base de données de l’inventaire avait pourtant relativement bien fait son travail : « Ils ont prospecté, ils sont allés interroger différents intervenants, différents pourvoyeurs potentiels d’archives, mais la plupart du temps, ils se sont heurtés à l’indisponibilité des archives par manque de moyens ». Parce que ces données sont loin d’être prêtes à l’emploi. François Antoine est revenu sur « le mirage digital », qui laisse penser que ces fonds sont accessibles en l’état. « Chez nous, seulement un dixième des documents administratifs est conservé et c’est seulement 1 % de ce dixième qui est numérisé. Et encore, il n’est pas interopérable, on ne sait pas le mettre dans les bases de données », détaille-t-il.
Quelles pistes pour la dépollution des sols ?
La dépollution des sols est une entreprise complexe, puisqu’elle suppose de travailler avec un support qui est muet. Quand on dépollue, on procède de la même manière que lors d’une prise de sang : il faut définir les polluants recherchés pour pouvoir vérifier leur présence. Le sol ne parle pas de lui-même, il faut d’abord savoir ce qu’on y cherche. Ce qui rend la tâche ardue lorsqu’on travaille sur un sol dont on ignore tout des usages passés. D’où l’intérêt des archives, qui nous renseignent sur les polluants potentiellement laissés par les activités industrielles passées.
L’étude et la dépollution d’un sol ont aussi un certain coût. Pour un carottage seulement, comptez entre 2000 et 4000 euros. Francisco Davila, chercheur en agroécologie, a heureusement pu développer quelques pistes de solutions et d’actions concrètes.
Dans le projet CiDéSol, des terres polluées ont pu être assainies via la phytoremédiation, une technique plus douce que l’excavation. Elle utilise le « tabouret bleu », ou Noccaea caerulescens, une petite plante qui accumule le cadmium, le zinc et le nickel. Les résultats sont encourageants : « On a réussi à dépolluer certains potagers collectifs. On n’était pas vraiment loin au-delà des seuils (de pollution, ndlr), on n’a pas fait un bond spectaculaire, mais on est passé en dessous des seuils pendant les trois ans de travail de recherche », explique Francisco Davila.
Le chercheur a également mentionné l’existence du projet ECHO, avec la commune de Saint-Gilles, où des kits d’analyse sont à disposition des citoyens, qui peuvent prélever des échantillons de sols et les faire analyser gratuitement. De son côté, Bruxelles Environnement propose un « test maison », à renvoyer à l’administration pour une centaine d’euros.
Si ces solutions ont le mérite d’exister, les intervenants étaient toutefois unanimes : elles ne remplaceront pas une prise en charge globale de ces enjeux. Il est nécessaire d’amender l’ordonnance « sol » pour rouvrir l’inventaire, considéré comme clôturé pour l’industrie d’avant 2000. Permettre l’intégration des archives et des données historiques est la voie vers une gestion intégrée des sols.
Les dix sites identifiés
Lors de cette soirée en public, les archivistes de l’État François Antoine et Marie Tielemans ont présenté dix sites problématiques passés sous les radars de l’administration régionale lors de l’élaboration de sa cartographie.
Quatre imprimeries, un dépôt de pétrole, une blanchisserie, une fabrique de produits chimiques, quatre usines à gaz… Autant de sites oubliés qui constituent une menace pour l’environnement comme pour la santé publique et qui sont développés ci-dessous :
1. Uccle, quartier du Bourdon : ancien dépôt de pétrole
Au 20e siècle, cet ancien site industriel abrite un dépôt de pétrole de 40 000 litres, ainsi que sa raffinerie. C’est une activité à risque, puisqu’on y stocke et utilise des produits dangereux : substances dégraissants, huiles et graisses minérales, les hydrocarbures, liquides inflammables… La zone est blanche sur la carte.
2. Uccle, quartier du Bourdon : ancienne blanchisserie
En activité à partir de 1810, d’abord blanchisserie de lin mais grossit grossit jusqu’en 1873. Disparaît en 1894, on rase tout et on installe trois petites maisons. D’une entreprise à moindre impact environnemental, on passe au chimique vers 1850 (acides, solvants, huiles minérales). Longe le potager voisin de la décharge, au n°206. Dans la zone, plein de potagers de jardins et surtout, une école. La zone est blanche sur la carte.
3. Saint-Gilles, quartier de la Barrière : ancienne fabrique de produits chimiques
Ce grand site, très connu dans le monde de l’industrie à l’époque, s’établit dès 1835. Il s’agrandira ensuite avec le transfert de chambres de plomb pour permettre la production d’acides, sulfurique notamment. L’activité est considérée comme à risque, en raison des produits utilisés, stockés et fabriqués. La zone est blanche sur la carte.
4. Woluwe-Saint-Lambert, quartier Montgomery : ancienne imprimerie.
Établie dès 1953 et pendant une trentaine d’année, cette industrie est active durant une longue période pour l’époque. Les imprimeries sont considérées comme des activités à risques, puisqu’elles utilisent des huiles, des métaux lourds, des solvants, des acides. La zone est blanche sur la carte.
5. Woluwe-Saint-Lambert, quartier Rodebeek : ancienne imprimerie
En activité dès 1985 et ce, pendant quinze ans. Les imprimeries sont considérées comme des activités à risque, puisqu’elles utilisent des huiles, des métaux lourds, des solvants, des acides. La zone est blanche sur la carte.
6. Woluwe-Saint-Lambert, quartier Rodebeek : ancienne imprimerie
Ce site industriel demande un permis en 1931 pour quinze ans, mais continuera son activité jusqu’en 1984. Les imprimeries sont considérées comme des activités à risques, puisqu’elles utilisent des huiles, des métaux lourds, des solvants, des acides. La zone est blanche sur la carte.
7. Ixelles, quartier Petite Suisse : ancienne imprimerie
Actuellement peu d’information sur la période d’activité. La commune prévoit d’y construire une crèche, où les enfants auraient un accès à l’extérieur. Les imprimeries sont considérées comme des activités à risques, puisqu’elles utilisent des huiles, des métaux lourds, des solvants, des acides. La zone est blanche sur la carte.
8. Bruxelles-Ville, quartier Yser : ancienne usine à gaz
Rentrée dans l’histoire comme la « première usine à gaz du Continent », la fabrique s’établit dès 1818, en intérieur d’îlot, proche de la Senne. Sur la cartographie, les gazomètres sont bien repris, mais toute une partie de l’usine passe sous les radars, notamment les bâtiments où avaient lieu la combustion. Considérées comme très polluantes, les usines à gaz stockent et utilisent des produits dangereux, en émettant aussi de nombreux déchets toxiques.
9. Saint-Josse, quartier Nord : ancienne usine à gaz
Certaines données indiquent la présence de l’usine et de ses quatre gazomètres dès 1873. Sur la carte, la zone est bien reprise comme étant un site industriel, mais seule la dernière activité est reprise. La première couche d’information, qui mentionnerait la présence de l’usine à gaz, est donc manquante. Puisque le sol est déjà cartographié, il est peu probable que de nouveaux tests soient effectués. La zone apparaît en jaune sur la carte, en catégorie « potentiellement polluée ».
10. Koekelberg, quartier du Sippelberg : ancienne usine à gaz
Dès 1930, certains fonds d’archives démontrent déjà la présence de trois gazomètres, ainsi que la présence de deux bâtiments industriels, qui y semblent liés. Entre 1935 et 1944, tout est rasé sauf les gazomètres, qui semblent être à l’abandon, et les bâtiments ont disparu. En 1953 déjà, des jardinets sont aménagés sur la zone. En 1977, une route se crée et sépare deux gazomètres, à gauche, du troisième à droite. Aujourd’hui, la cartographie reprend correctement le site où l’on trouvait les deux gazomètres de gauche, mais passe à côté du troisième, de l’autre côté de la route, ainsi que des bâtiments industriels où devaient être stockés les produits.
Réécouter la rencontre du 9 novembre 2026
Avec Lou Janssens (journaliste autrice de l’enquête), François Antoine (archiviste-historien, chef de services des Archives de l’état), Marie Tielemans (archiviste-historienne), Francisco Davila (chercheur en agroécologie) et modérée par Olivier Bailly (pilote et co-fondateur de Médor).
Rencontre séquencée en 5 partie :
- présentation
- carte et archives
- risques pour la santé
- pistes de solution
- questions du public

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bill-woul.title: NYC bill would give crash victims online access to NYPD investigation updates
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bill-woul.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bill-woul.text:
New Yorkers seriously injured in traffic crashes and certain family members could get online access to updates about police investigations under a bill the City Council's public safety and transportation committees are set to consider at a joint hearing in December.
The bill would require the NYPD to operate a secure website where victims of serious crashes and eligible family members or representatives could check the status of an investigation and whether police have issued summonses, made arrests or identified witnesses. The department would have to make information about qualifying crashes available within 72 hours and update it within 72 hours of receiving new information.
The proposal aims to make it easier for people affected by serious crashes to get information from police while navigating injuries, insurance claims or the loss of a loved one.
It would not change how police investigate crashes or require the department to post police reports online, according to the bill text. The NYPD could also withhold information that would interfere with an investigation or prosecution or that is exempt from disclosure under state public records law.
Tomasina Byron said she supports the bill.
Her mother, Judith Byron, 75, was killed in a hit-and-run crash in Sunset Park in October 2025. Police arrested a 33-year-old man more than a year later and charged him with leaving the scene and failing to obey a traffic signal, according to the NYPD.
Byron said the detective handling her mother's case was caring and always responded to her messages. But she said she had to keep contacting him for updates.
“I’d call him every day. I’d call until he answered the phone or I’d leave a text message or voicemail,” she said. “In my case, someone killed my mom, so I was relentless.”
The investigation into her mother's death was handled by the NYPD's Collision Investigation Squad, which investigates fatal crashes and certain crashes involving critical injuries.
An NYPD spokesperson did not respond to multiple messages seeking comment on the legislation.
Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse, who sponsored the bill, said constituents come to her office struggling to obtain information after crashes.
“For someone that’s dealing with all the anxiety, they don’t know what to do and how they go to the next step, having that information can be a game-changer,” she said.
Transportation Alternatives spokesperson Alexa Sledge called the proposal a “huge step forward” for crash victims.
Corey Hannigan, 36, the organization's policy director, said he was riding an electric Citi Bike in a bike lane on 42nd Street in Sunnyside on Nov. 6 when a driver struck him and left the scene. He spent the night at Elmhurst Hospital.
Hannigan said police told him his crash report would be ready within 72 hours. He said it wasn't available by then and that a detective didn't contact him until about six days after the crash.
“Unless I pester the detective and I don’t want to annoy him, I don’t know what he’s finding,” Hannigan said, adding that he went from store to store looking for surveillance footage himself. “All I know is what I found and what I sent him. And it goes into a black box.”
Hannigan said he went to his precinct on a cane to obtain his police report. He said the delay also complicated his efforts to arrange an MRI through no-fault insurance.
Narcisse said the bill does not currently require police reports to be posted on the proposed website, but she wants to add that provision and expects resistance from the NYPD.
The legislation would also require the city Department of Transportation to create a guide explaining how crash victims can obtain police reports, access insurance information and apply for no-fault benefits. Officers would have to distribute the guide to people involved in crashes, and it would be available at police precincts and on city websites.
Kate Brockwehl, co-chair of Families for Safe Streets New York, was struck by a driver while crossing Houston Street in SoHo in 2017. Weeks later, after obtaining a paper police report and filing for no-fault coverage on her own, an MRI revealed injuries that required knee surgery.
Brockwehl said having information about crash investigations and victims' rights more readily available would help people navigate the aftermath of a collision.
“Being hit by a car pushes you into this administrative hurricane that you’re in for years,” she said. “This bill would really restore some dignity and give back some time to people hit by cars.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘The streets were alive with sonic vibrations’: music and protest in Black London – in pictures
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Photography by Ian Watts
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘The streets were alive with sonic vibrations’: music and protest in Black London – in pictures
From booming sound systems at Notting Hill carnival to defiant marches against the National Front, Ian Watts’s images capture Black lives in the capital across two pivotal decades
‘Unplanned encounters’ … Chrystal Rose and Her Sisters, circa 1985, by Ian Watts.
I-Roy and His ‘Nice, Nice’ Car, west London, circa 1984
Bafta award-winning photographer Ian Watts’s images capture the people, culture and lived experiences of Black communities in Britain across two pivotal decades. Of this image, Watts says: ‘A casual remark led to an unexpected photographic opportunity with one of Jamaica’s most distinctive and influential reggae deejays.’ The two-book series Black Britain 1976-1996 is available from Cafe Royale. All quotes by Ian Watts
A Young Deejay Takes to the Mic, Notting Hill carnival, 1982
Ian Watts: ‘Carnival was an important platform for music lovers, aspiring performers and established artists to showcase their talents. For singers and deejays, these gatherings offered an opportunity to make a name for themselves and potentially launch a musical career. Reputations could be made or broken in these spaces, depending on how well performers connected with the audience. More than anything, performers wanted to be that singer or deejay who people were still talking about long after carnival had finished’
Reggae Sunsplash, Crystal Palace football ground, London, 1985
‘This was an immensely popular music festival traditionally held in Jamaica, but in 1985 the organisers brought the event to Britain, staging it at Crystal Palace football ground in south London. The event was a big success, attracting a large audience and featuring performances by some of the biggest names in reggae and African music, including Dennis Brown, Gregory Isaacs, Sly and Robbie and Black Uhuru, among many others’
Linton Kwesi Johnson and Vin Gordon Backstage at the 100 Club, London, 1981
‘This photo was taken backstage while British reggae group Aswad were performing at the 100 Club, Oxford Street. Linton Kwesi Johnson had become an influential voice in dub poetry, using words and performance to explore Black British experiences and social realities, while Vin Gordon was an accomplished Jamaican musician whose saxophone playing featured on numerous reggae recordings’
A Small Sound System Enjoying the Moment, Notting Hill carnival, 1984
‘There was something spontaneous about this encounter. The sound system’s operators and followers are clearly enjoying the music with nobody putting on a performance for the camera. They were simply celebrating carnival in their own way. It is these unexpected encounters that make photographing carnival so rewarding. This image captures a small but genuine moment of the musical freedom, camaraderie and infectious enjoyment that made Notting Hill carnival so special in the 1980s’
‘I had been visiting Time Radio, a local community radio station in Harlesden. Afterwards, I unexpectedly bumped into television presenter and music promoter Chrystal Rose, along with her sisters. We stopped to take this photograph nearby, quite spontaneously. Looking back now, I suspect it was taken in the goods lift! Unplanned encounters like this capture a moment in time, and offer a glimpse into the social networks, personalities and cultural connections that helped shape London’s Black community and entertainment scene during the 1980s’
Notting Hill Carnival, Acklam Road, Beneath the Flyover, 1976
‘My first Notting Hill carnival in 1976. The streets were alive with the sonic vibrations of static sound systems, colourful costumes and dancing revellers celebrating Caribbean music and culture. However, the festive atmosphere was overshadowed by a substantial police presence that year, creating an increasingly tense and confrontational environment. This erupted into disturbances and rebellion, which became a defining feature of the 1976 event’
‘Two brothers pose nonchalantly together in the garden of their north London home, happy to oblige when I took their photograph. This image captures a simple but meaningful moment of everyday family life. There is something special about photographing people in familiar surroundings, where they can relax and be themselves naturally, providing a valuable glimpse into family and community at the beginning of the 1980s’
‘The central figure is a family friend who was well known for his beautifully maintained afro hairstyle and immaculate appearance. Fashion has always been an important part of identity and self-confidence among young Black people. My friend understood this, but he was also a talented deejay with a deep passion for reggae music. Sadly, he died in 2026, so this photograph is a personal reminder of a friend whose passion for music, style and love of reggae reflected so much of the spirit of Black British youth culture in the early 1980s’
‘In 1977 I was living in a youth hostel in Harlesden, London, and beginning to develop my interest in photography. I was learning my craft by photographing events, activities and everyday occurrences within my local community. At the time, the far-right National Front party had a significant presence, and their activities and growing influence generated considerable concern among residents. Anti-racist demonstrations and protests were organised in response, as communities came together to oppose racism and challenge the activities of the far right’
Jesse Jackson Visits a North London Housing Estate, 1986
‘In 1986, while living in north London, I heard that American civil rights leader and political figure Jesse Jackson was due to visit the housing estate where I used to live. I managed to photograph Jesse as he met and interacted with members of the local community, including his guide, Labour councillor Russell Profitt. It was an opportunity to capture an important public figure away from the usual political platforms and in a more personal setting, in a community I knew and used to call home’
Sound System Vibes into the Night, Notting Hill carnival, 1984
‘This photo, taken in 1984, captures a time of greater musical freedom, when music could be played late into the night with a sound system and deejay, with no obvious police presence or interruptions. This created a positive atmosphere which was all about the music, dancing and having a good time. People came together to enjoy the rhythms and the lyrical skills of the deejay through the infectious energy of the sound system. It was a celebration of music and community’ More of Ian’s work can be found at www.ianwatts.org

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Museums finding new ways to measure wellness initiatives' value
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Pamela C. Samaniego
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Museum programming in the US has been branching out recently, much of it in the direction of connecting art to health and wellbeing. As part of this trend, institutions have been creating programmes for people living with memory loss. But these present unique challenges, particularly when it comes to evaluating their success.
The qualitative data from a caregiver's perspective does not necessarily include the point-of-view of the person struggling with cognitive decline. This is why institutions like Seattle’s Frye Art Museum try to do a lot of in-the-moment observations and feedback rather than relying exclusively on formal surveys.
The Frye is at the forefront of art and health initiatives. Each quarter, the museum offers a special programme for medical residents, students and teaching professionals from nearby hospitals, designed to develop perspective-taking and empathy. Meanwhile the museum recently expanded its Creative Aging initiative, gallery-based experiences and hands-on artmaking in partnership with the University of Washington's Memory and Brain Wellness Center.
Located in Seattle’s First Hill neighbourhood and surrounded by medical centres and senior living facilities, the Frye has served older adults experiencing memory loss for 17 years. Its Creative Aging programme began with a former employee’s experience caring for her mother with dementia, and has since expanded to reach broader communities of older adults.
The Frye's experience in the field highlights a broader challenge facing museums as arts-and-health programming expands. The Lancet medical journal recently published a call for translating growing evidence of the arts’ health benefits into more equitable access, stronger healthcare partnerships and research into how programmes work in practice. For museums, a big question is how to evaluate these initiatives while responding to community needs.
Susan Magsamen, the founder and executive director of the International Arts + Mind Lab at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, sees this kind of programming as an opportunity for museums to expand their public roles. She describes art as “a superpower that we have forgotten” and museums as institutions that contribute to “human thriving and flourishing”.
Magsamen compares the growing integration of health and wellbeing into museum missions with the emergence of education as a core museum function in previous decades. “Beyond things like attendance, revenue and membership, we need to think about a scorecard,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “What is the institutional performance and public benefits?”
The Frye has been using the Art Bridges Foundation’s Art + Wellness Toolkit, which includes validated measures across four areas of wellbeing: social, emotional, cognitive and physical. The museum is currently evaluating four programmes, incorporating the toolkit's terminology into its materials and developing surveys using its standardised measures.
“This common language has been valuable as we grow programmes under art and wellbeing," says Lea Lovelace, the Frye’s associate director of creative aging programmes.
Jill Sonke, a co-author of the Lancet study, underscores the importance of measuring behavior and patterns of engagement, so that the most vulnerable can access the arts and their underlying health benefits. “Institutions need to also measure who’s not coming,” she says, “why they don’t see themselves in the programming.”
In the quickly developing field, Sonke cautions museum staff to move ahead carefully. Enthusiasm for evidence can create its own problems. If institutions set out primarily to prove that their programmes work, evaluation instruments can inadvertently be designed to confirm the outcome they hope to find. “We need to make sure that we’re designing objective, open measures that will allow us to really understand the experiences of the people we’re seeking to serve,” she says.
Sonke also questions whether additional assessment is always warranted: “If the evidence exists already, if it’s not really necessary, then it’s not ethical to put people through the burden of assessment."
The Frye has experienced these tensions firsthand. "It's a balancing act," says Tamar Benzikry, the museum’s director of learning and engagement. "We are careful about 'survey fatigue', because we realise you might not get the information requested because our audience is burnt out from surveys."
Sonke, despite her caution, underscores the importance of “making relationships and normalising the idea that museums should be talking to public health folks, and public health folks should absolutely be talking to museums”.
The Frye is always working with community leaders to identify barriers to participation and create programmes that strengthen connections between the museum, public health and healthcare. The team plans to share experiences at a convening of museum professionals next May, while incorporating arts and health more deeply into its 2027 exhibition programme.
Activities will include gallery-based creative movement inspired by works of art and led by a physician who is also a trained dancer. There are also plans for folklore-inspired slow-looking and storytelling sessions led by a professional storyteller with training in gerontology.

https://gothamist.com/news/every-day-is-.title: Every day is Turkey Day in Battery Park for fans of Astoria the bird
https://gothamist.com/news/every-day-is-.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/every-day-is-.text:
Stories about New York wildlife can captivate even the city’s most hardened residents. Tales of a Bengal tiger raised in a Harlem apartment and a rat that dragged a slice of pizza down a subway staircase have become part of the city’s folklore.
At Battery Park in Lower Manhattan, another wild animal has charmed New Yorkers. Her name is Astoria, and she is a wild turkey who, according to birdwatchers and fans, was first spotted in her namesake Queens neighborhood, spent a formative year on Roosevelt Island and has now settled in the bustling downtown business district.
“I love it. She brings me so much joy,” said Lauren McPhate, a local resident and partner at a nearby wine merchants. “I guess it’s because it’s so unexpected. You don’t expect to see a turkey in the middle of the city and she’s just kind of doing her thing.”
Wild turkeys have nested and roamed in parks across the five boroughs for decades. Hunters nearly wiped them out of the Northeast United States in the 1800s, according to Jessica Wilson, the executive director of NYC Bird Alliance. Today, hundreds of turkeys are currently settled in parks in the Bronx and on Staten Island, where they’ve occasionally made headlines for blocking traffic. But as far as birdwatchers are aware, Astoria is the only turkey who currently calls Manhattan home.
“She rests at night in the trees in Battery Park. And as long as folks leave her alone, give her a lot of space, she's really happy and successful there,” Wilson said of the wild bird.
From Queens to Manhattan
New Yorkers first noticed Astoria in Western Queens in the spring of 2024, according to the NYC Bird Alliance, a nonprofit that works to protect the city's birds and their habitats. Like many New Yorkers, she moved frequently before finding suitable digs.
In the spring of 2024, she flew across the East River and landed in Midtown, but didn’t stay long. She left for the more affordable Roosevelt Island, just across the river, where locals nicknamed her “Rosie.”
For Astoria, though, the lure of Manhattan remained. She flew the coop once more in the spring of 2025, soaring from Roosevelt Island back to the city. She eventually made her way downtown to The Battery, where she remains to this day, foraging for food and roosting in trees at night.
“She's finding ample food sources, seeds and nuts, but also little insects and occasionally small amphibians. She eats everything, probably, like most turkeys do,” Wilson added.
On a recent morning, Astoria blended in with the crowd in the park, which was bustling with New Yorkers out for pre-work exercise.
“Each morning I sort of cross my fingers that I’m going to see Astoria,” said Arvind Jaggi, 65, a Lower Manhattan resident who was out for a walk in the park. “It is incredible that this small little oasis has become the chosen home of this bird which would otherwise be in the woods."
“It’s so out of place. It makes it weirdly attractive and cute that in the midst of this concrete jungle, we have this creature of wildlife feeling at home,” Jaggi added.
Jessie Attard, another Manhattan resident who was out for a walk, said like other wild birds in New York, Astoria has adapted to city life.
“[She’s] just like a pigeon, but a bigger bird,” Attard said.

https://gothamist.com/news/v.title: NYC’s true Thanksgiving Day heroes: Greyhound bus drivers
https://gothamist.com/news/v.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/v.text:
This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
The tight turns, winding ramps and intense traffic Port Authority Bus Terminal make it a great training ground for Greyhound.
The four-story building is used by more than 200,000 passengers on a typical weekday, making it one of the busiest bus stations in the world. But that number soars over Thanksgiving, America’s busiest weekend for interstate travel.
And with airlines facing so many issues — like this month’s nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration due to tech issues — more people are turning to the trusty old bus to get home for the holidays.
Greyhound reports its bookings are up 17% this holiday week compared to last year. And that means the company needs to make sure it has enough drivers for the busy season.
Earlier this month, drivers-in-training were at the Midtown bus terminal learning the rules of the roads in the labyrinthine facility. One of them, Shakari Mahfood, said he was ready to hit the road. He felt a sense of pride and responsibility ahead of his Thanksgiving shift.
“I honestly haven’t thought about that before this job, how I might be missing my own events with my own family, but then again, I have 50 passengers in my bus,” Mahfood said, adding, “So I’m making a whole bunch of other people happy and making sure they get off at the destination in a safe manner so they can be with their families.”
During training, drivers practice steering 45-foot buses around the loops and ramps of the Midtown bus terminal. Drivers also perfect parking at one of the 183 gates.
Daouda Kone, a new hire at Greyhound, had to navigate the facility and park at a gate while his instructor, Carlos Santiago, sat right behind him. After Kone put the bus in park, Santiago checked the alignment of the wheels.
He gave Kone top marks.
“This is part of their practice technique. The more time behind the wheel and they’re going to get better and better,” Santiago said. “This is actually really good for a start.”
Kone, 32, was jubilant. Asked if he was ready to drive for the holiday season, he replied with a smile: “Honestly, yes.”
Greyhound’s training process for new bus operators can take up to eight weeks, according to Matt Maglio, the company’s northeast regional vice president who works out of the Port Authority Bus Terminal. In addition to handling the bus, trainees get schooled on customer service and safety rules.
In order to be hired, drivers need a commercial drivers license that allows them to operate large vehicles like buses, trucks and trailers.
“We want people who like to work with people, people who enjoy driving the bus,” Maglio said. “And it’s a pretty rigorous training program. We do a lot of in-classroom instruction, followed by a lot of instructor-led, almost one-on-one instruction, and then a lot of road time with a senior driver instructor.”
NYC transportation news this week
Mamdani inks new deal with Lyft to cap Citi Bike member rides. Under a new agreement between Mayor Mamdani’s administration and Lyft, Citi Bike members will soon pay less for electric bike rides. Starting Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for e-bike rides lasting up to 45 minutes. The cap also applies to reduced-fare members and shorter rides that already cost less will remain at their current price.
Traveling to JFK Airport just got a little easier. Just in the nick of time before holiday travel, the state department wrapped its six-year, $1.4 billion expansion of the Van Wyck Expressway.
Brooklyn body shop owner charged in swindling scheme. Prosecutors say a Brooklyn bodyshop owner preyed on car crash victims for years, using a fleet of unlicensed tow trucks to haul wrecked vehicles that he held hostage while charging thousands of dollars in bogus storage fees.
Could a fare hike keep cab drivers out of poverty? A new report found that costs for maintaining yellow cabs have increased since the last fare hike in 2022 and that regular fare hikes could help cabbies better avoid poverty.
Curious Commuter
Have a question for us? Use this form to submit yours and we may answer it in a future newsletter!
Jon from Brooklyn asks
Will NYC buses and busways ever be free? Why can’t congestion pricing and other funding streams be used to pay the fare?
Answer
We can’t say for sure whether the city’s buses or subways will ever be free, but we can say it’s unlikely to happen any time soon. While Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned on eliminating the bus fare, the leaders of the state-run MTA have pushed back against the idea. The agency collects about $600 million a year from bus fares, and more than $3 billion in bus fares. Making either service free would require lawmakers to sign off on a source of revenue to replace all that money, which would likely mean more taxes for everyone else. The MTA’s congestion pricing tolls, which rake in more than $500 million a year, are required by state law to finance the MTA’s construction budget, not its day-to-day operations — so that money isn’t available to subsidize a free fare.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-vi-gamin.title: GTA VI Takes Capitalism Seriously
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-vi-gamin.author: Tim Brinkhof
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-vi-gamin.text:
GTA VI Takes Capitalism Seriously
The Right is furious that Grand Theft Auto VI swapped macho wish fulfillment for heart. They’re missing the bigger shift: Rockstar is taking working-class struggle seriously.
In the first twenty-odd hours of playing Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited latest installment in developer Rockstar’s open-world simulations of contemporary America, I chased a hovercraft with a helicopter, raced Jet Skis around a superyacht, and shot my way out of a hospital in a wheelchair — though not before spending all my stolen cash on medical bills. I also fixed the leaky roof of my apartment, bought flowers for my incarcerated girlfriend when I learned she was about to be let out on parole, and wiped an unexpected tear from my eye as I watched her jump into the arms of a friend who — for a moment — seemed to be on the brink of tears herself.
The blockbuster game’s more slice-of-life-oriented gameplay and sentimental, relationship-focused story are relatively new additions to this franchise, especially compared to the detached and bombastic satire of its immediate predecessor. But while journalists have given GTA VI perfect or near-perfect reviews, many right-wing gamers are outraged. To audiences of millions, they complain that Rockstar has replaced the testosterone-fueled wish fulfillment of previous games with what pro-MAGA streamer Zack Hoyt (Asmongold) called a “cuck simulator” and, by doing so, become the latest company in this once exclusively and unapologetically masculine industry to go woke.
Responding to this outrage, progressives like Hasan Piker were quick to point out that — actually — the franchise has always been woke. I agree but also believe that such responses shut the door on another, equally interesting discussion. By focusing on GTA VI’s portrayal of masculinity, public discourse has yet to appreciate how the game engages with another topic central to its identity: capitalism. In line with today’s circumstances, Rockstar has ditched the more overtly comedic parodies of games past, opting instead to portray the everyday struggles of its working-class protagonists in a more serious and sympathetic light. As a result, the gap between its world and the real one has never been smaller.
A Franchise Built on Parody
Grand Theft Auto became both famous and infamous for the way it enabled and even encouraged its (often young) players to engage in violent, antisocial behavior, from stealing cars and robbing stores to creatively and indiscriminately murdering the AI-generated NPCs — non-player characters — that populate the franchise’s increasingly lifelike cities. What recurring moral panics around the corruptive influence of these games never seemed to grasp, though, is that the developers deliberately matched this gameplay with stories that explored how violence isn’t just random or personal but integral to the structure and functioning of neoliberal society.
In each game, the violence committed by its usually marginalized main characters is placed in favorable contrast with the violence committed by their cop, politician, and billionaire opponents. The ensuing conflicts show that the line separating legal from illegal is mostly arbitrary, and wealth impossible to accumulate without a willingness to hurt others. Every new installment approaches this conceit from a slightly different angle. Inspired by hood films and hip-hop, GTA: San Andreas (2004) is steeped in black street culture, while GTA IV (2008) tells the story of an immigrant who comes to Rockstar’s version of New York in search of a better life, only to find things almost as bad as where he came from.
While GTA IV is remembered for having a darker, more cinematic tone, both games were fundamentally parodies, critiquing reality by exaggerating it to such a degree that — despite their ever-increasing immersiveness — there always remained a distance between player and player-character. This approach reached its undisputed zenith with GTA V (2013), whose unprecedentedly interactive open world went hand in hand with Rockstar’s most comedic, absurd, and cynical story yet. One of its three protagonists, an unhinged maniac, was specifically designed to serve as a superconductor for the audience’s ability to create carnage and chaos but offered little in the way of reflection. As with The Wolf of Wall Street, released the same year, the game’s excesses were intended to nauseate. Instead they mostly proved either addictive or desensitizing.
From Satire to Sincerity
The over-the-top, larger-than-life energy that was everywhere present in GTA V can still be found in its sequel, only it is now relegated to a supporting role. One side character — an erratic drug runner — quickly gets the player into trouble when he starts a turf war with swampland rednecks. His actions lead to some exciting and explosive early missions, but unlike in GTA V, they are not without consequence. Toward the end of the game’s opening act, this emblem of the franchise’s more carefree and lighthearted legacy is — spoiler alert — literally fed to the pigs. It’s a subtextual warning for the rest of the game, as well as the setup for a genuinely touching moment of mourning for a death that previous games would have simply laughed off.
GTA V was developed during the optimism and relative stability of the Obama administrations, when — for many middle-class Americans — the perils of capitalism were far enough away to be mostly spiritual rather than material, manifesting in a vague desire for meaning and authenticity. GTA VI’s thirteen-year-long development, by contrast, spanned both Donald Trump terms: a period during which the struggles of its characters — their inability to find stable employment, unfair treatment by institutions, and lack of upward mobility — have become more relatable than ever, imbuing them with a gravity and intimacy they did not possess before.
GTA VI’s move from satire to sincerity corresponds with a broader trend in mass media. As the hosts of the Critics at Large podcast at The New Yorker discussed in an episode released in April, more and more of today’s mainstream entertainment — from Hollywood films to reality TV shows — is shedding the trademark cynicism and irony of postmodernism in favor of a post-postmodern embrace of earnestness and empathy. Not just because, in times as precarious as now, escapism is a luxury that people can no longer afford, but also because we turn to art to feel emotions that regular life doesn’t readily provide.
A New Front in the Culture War
GTA VI is not the first game to be turned into a major battleground of the culture wars. Another long-standing franchise, God of War, about a Spartan general who fights and kills gods, has likewise angered conservatives for reinventing its nihilistically sadistic protagonist as a caring father and thereby distancing itself from the gratuitous violence and sex appeal of older games. Rockstar, too, has chosen reformation. Not simply for the sake of profit, but also because its developers realize that GTA bears great responsibility for creating the persistent notion that games are and should remain a space where toxic masculinity and political incorrectness are perfectly okay.
Studying the right-wing response to GTA VI helps us understand how culture war controversies around media properties are shaped by, and in turn shape, politics. Many criticisms of the game verge on the conspiratorial, with content creators and commentators believing gaming journalists are in Rockstar’s pocket, while Rockstar itself is brainwashing gamers on behalf of the woke elite. At the same time, they also echo populist and fascist narratives of nostalgia and decline: the franchise’s original creators have been pushed out by foreign agents and corrupted GTA from the inside, feeding a longing for a lost golden age of originality and excellence.
Though currently dismissed as fringe, the reactionary backlash to GTA VI — the single biggest media event in recent memory — could well fuel a conservative resurgence in the future. At the same time, if the game is truly the cultural barometer that everyone says it is, it also gives plenty of reason to be hopeful. Reflecting, and to some extent perhaps even explaining, recent left-wing electoral victories, Rockstar’s vision of the country is one in which the oppressed choose solidarity and compassion over despair or alienation, and the desire for a better, more equitable future is worth taking seriously.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Hoor Al Qasimi to curate Venice Biennale in 2028
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James Imam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Hoor Al Qasimi, one of the preeminent figures of contemporary art in the Middle East, has been named curator of the Venice Biennale's next art exhibition, the Biennale has announced.
Following this year's edition, which was curated by the late Cameroon-born curator Koyo Kouoh, the appointment of Al Qasimi, from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), marks the second consecutive edition in which a woman from outside the Western art world has been chosen for the role.
Al Qasimi was born into the royal family of the port city of Sharjah and is the daughter of Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, the current leader of the emirate of Sharjah.
She has been involved in the Sharjah Biennial since 2003, when she curated the exhibition's sixth edition after completing her undergraduate studies at the Slade School of Fine Art in London. In 2009, she founded the Sharjah Art Foundation, a public art organisation that promotes and funds contemporary art collaborations in the emirate and internationally, including organising the Sharjah Biennial.
She holds board positions for numerous other arts organisations, including the International Biennial Association, Sharjah Museums Authority, Sharjah Architecture Triennial and University of the Arts Sharjah. She has also curated major exhibitions including the Lahore Biennale in 2020, the Aichi Triennale in Japan in 2025, and this year's edition of the Biennale of Sydney.
Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, president of the Venice Biennale, says in a statement that Al Qasimi's work gives “voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected”.
He adds: “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people...These are qualities that we feel are particularly close to La Biennale’s vision”.
Buttafuoco, a right-leaning journalist and intellectual who was born and raised in Catania in Sicily, reportedly converted to Islam in 2015, adopting the name Giafar al-Siqilli (“Jafar the Sicilian”) in a reference to the Arab-Sicilian general associated with the Fatimid conquest of North Africa.
Since becoming president of the Biennale in 2024, he has sometimes championed art from the Middle East. In 2025, under his watch, Qatar announced it would launch a national pavilion at the Biennale. A temporary structure was used for the most recent architecture and art biennales; the completed pavilion building will be the first permanent addition to the Giardini, one of the Biennale’s two main venues, in 30 years.
In a statement, Al Qasimi says that the Biennale “continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators”, adding that she was “honoured” to be appointed as curator.
Al Qasimi could not immediately be reached for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘A window into imagination’: the magic of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade – in pictures
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Briana Ellis-Gibbs
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘A window into imagination’: the magic of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade – in pictures
Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade is the first book from Aperture Kids, which aims to create community and understanding through photography. The book celebrates the historic 100th anniversary of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade with images by EA Kahane, illustrations by The New Yorker cartoonist Tom Toro and a story by Doro Globus
‘For the past 28 years, I’ve photographed the Thanksgiving Day Parade from my perch in our third-floor window. I like to call it my Miracle on 64th Street!’ says EA Kahane. ‘Ever since our son Harry was little, that window has been a gathering place for his friends, their families and generations of children … I hope children looking at that window will imagine themselves sitting right there, watching the giant balloons float past, close enough to almost touch. The window is more than a frame for the parade; it’s a window into a child’s imagination’Photograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
‘Harry captured that feeling beautifully in an essay he wrote for my first book, Come Join The Parade! 25 Years From My Third-Floor Window. Somehow, even though I was only a kid in a window, I was a part of the parade. I belonged inside the spectacle; I owned a little piece of it’Photograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
When cartoonist Tom Toro made these illustrations, he noted that he let Kahane’s photographs guide him. ‘Her unique vantage point on the parade balloons, capturing them at eye-level, created a wonderful sense of intimacy,’ he writes in Between The Balloons. ‘It brought the characters to life in fantastic ways. I followed the feeling of an expression here, or a gesture there, and sketched out ideas until I found moments and stories that stitched the pages together’Photograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
‘Funnily enough, I’ve never been to the Thanksgiving Day Parade in person, so the photographs were my own window onto that world. But I think this allowed me to treat it as a space of pure, unbounded imagination,’ Toro saysPhotograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
‘It’s really a story about creativity and all the different layers of imagination that go into the parade, from the original characters and giant balloons to the photographs, illustrations, and ultimately the readers themselves,’ writer Doro Globus saidPhotograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
Toro made a deliberate choice to make his drawings black and white. ‘I wanted the illustrations to stand out and be legible against the rich, colorful photographs, so drawing them in black-and-white made perfect sense,’ he says. ‘Then it dawned on me that I could also incorporate the child’s perspective by making the illustrations feel sketchy and unfinished, as if drawn quickly by an excited but untrained hand. The final result is whimsical and spontaneous, airy and light. It even had an unintended benefit: kids can use the illustrations as a coloring book!’Photograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
‘That is exactly the feeling I hope children will experience when they open Between the Balloons. That wonderful sense of being part of something magical, where imagination has no limits,’ Kahane saysPhotograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
Toro wants the reader to remember the power of their imagination. ‘The world is full of joy, humor, and magic. Surprising connections exist between everything around us. All it takes to discover them is imagination’Photograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
Kahane wants the book to bring children ‘pure, unadulterated joy’! She added: ‘I hope that Doro’s wonderful storytelling, together with my photographs and Tom’s delightful illustrations, will unlock the boundless imagination of a child. I want young readers to feel as though they’re sitting right there in the window, watching those enormous character balloons, colorful floats, clowns, cheerleaders and marching bands pass by. Most of all, I want them to have FUN!’Photograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade
Doro said that ‘more than anything, [she hopes] the book reminds children (and adults!) to keep their imaginations alive and to always ask, ‘What if?’’ Photograph: From Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade

https://gothamist.com/news/travel-treach.title: Travel treachery: The Thanksgiving holiday travel outlook is grim
https://gothamist.com/news/travel-treach.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/travel-treach.text:
Traveling home after a Thanksgiving feast tonight could be a treacherous ordeal.
New York City officials warn travelers to prepare for strong winds up to 65 mph, heavy rain and flooding that could plague the region until late evening. According to the National Weather Service, the worst of the storm will come late afternoon through the evening. The National Weather Service advises waiting until after 10 p.m. or the next day to return home.
“If you're traveling, give yourself extra time, and remember, no destination is worth risking your safety,” said Mayor Mamdani in a public service announcement. “If winds pick up, get indoors. This wind is strong enough to knock down tree limbs and power lines.”
The National Weather Service forecasts the storm will be at its worst from around 4 p.m. until 10 p.m. on Thanksgiving. During this period, meteorologists predict the heaviest rains and strongest winds will descend upon the New York City metro area. According to the city’s emergency management agency, six inches of moving water can knock over a pedestrian and one foot of water can sweep away a car.
“It’s definitely downhill from here,” said National Weather Service meteorologist Matthew Wunsch. “There will be locally damaging wind gusts which could bring down trees and some power lines as well.”
The evening could be cataclysmic because strong winds and heavy rains will coincide with the high tide, which will roar along the coastline between 7 p.m. and 10 p.m. The chaotic trifecta could result in flooding. Wunsch warns that wind will also cause lots of leaf litter to collect in drainage areas, which could worsen flooding. City officials warn people who live in basements to seek higher ground during the storm. New Yorkers should move any vehicles parked in a flood-prone area or near the coast.
“Never walk, bike, or drive through flooding,” Madani said. “If you live in a basement apartment or your home floods often, make a plan now. Move to higher ground before flooding starts.”
Even as the storm begins to subside by the late evening, travel conditions will still not be ideal. High wind warnings are in effect past midnight, and rain may persist through Friday.
If traveling on Thanksgiving is unavoidable, city officials said to allow more time, especially for public transportation.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/li.title: Lisa Marei Schmidt Appointed Director of Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/li.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/li.text:
Lisa Marei Schmidt, the director of the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, is leaving her post to take over as director of the Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern, Switzerland, starting August 1, 2027. She will also chair the management board of both institutions and be responsible for their artistic direction. The Renzo Piano-designed Zentrum Paul Klee holds the world’s largest collection of works by Klee, while the Kunstmuseum Bern is Switzerland’s oldest fine art museum.
Schmidt has been at the Brücke-Museum since 2017 and has orchestrated many exhibitions, including Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019), Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22), and Confiscated and Forgotten: The Female Artists Targeted by the Nazi ‘Degenerate Art’ Campaign, which opens April 30 to July 25, 2027. The Berlin museum is currently exhibiting Swedish Modernism until February 28, 2027, with a focus on the artist groups De unga (The Young Ones), De åtta (The Eight) and the Gothenburg Colorists. “To me, museums are places where art and people meet. They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society,” said Schmidt, in a statement on Thursday. “I very much look forward to getting to know the two remarkable institutions, the teams and the people in the City and Canton of Bern. Together, I hope to build on the Kunstmuseum Bern’s and Zentrum Paul Klee’s distinctive qualities and shape their future development.”
Schmidt was chosen out of 97 candidates who applied for the position. Jonathan Gimmel, president of the umbrella foundation of Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee, said in a statement that Schmidt brings “remarkable professional expertise, international experience and a deep understanding of people” as she shapes the next “development phase of our museums.”
Before joining Brücke-Museum, Schmidt was a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and a curator at the Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. She studied art history and modern German literature in Marburg, Amsterdam, and Berlin before graduating from the Royal College of Art.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/thanksgiving.title: The Socialist History Behind Thanksgiving’s Most Iconic Image
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/thanksgiving.author: Liza Featherstone
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/thanksgiving.text:
The Socialist History Behind Thanksgiving’s Most Iconic Image
Norman Rockwell’s Thanksgiving painting is classic Americana. Less well-known about the painting: it was commissioned as a depiction of FDR’s “Freedom From Want” and accompanied by a socialist’s essay on the working class as the “creators of abundance.”
An older woman, still wearing her apron from all her work in the kitchen, brings a large turkey to a table set with cranberry sauce and fruit and full of family, friends, and neighbors, who are smiling, talking, enjoying one another’s company. Her husband stands beside her at the head of the table, surveying the scene with pride.
The 1943 Norman Rockwell oil painting has become perhaps the most iconic and ubiquitous image of Thanksgiving in our modern era. It looks like a classic piece of kitschy, complacent Americana. Yet the image has a surprising political history. With so many in America going hungry this year, it’s a good time to remember that the painting was commissioned in honor of Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s bold call for “Freedom from Want” and released with a much bolder critique of New Deal America for failing to deliver that freedom to everyone.
“Freedom from Want” was one of the “Four Freedoms,” values set forth in FDR’s 1941 message to Congress on the need for continued US involvement in World War II, which the US would officially enter eleven months later. In our post–Ronald Reagan world, the very idea sounds revolutionary, especially since FDR said he was describing “the kind of world attainable in our own time and generation.” He argued the entire project of America’s domestic order was an ongoing “peaceful revolution.”
The Four Freedoms speech didn’t make much of an impression on the American public when FDR first delivered it. Two years later, the war underway, The Saturday Evening Post commissioned Rockwell to illustrate each of the Four Freedoms, and the artist delivered this image of an abundant Thanksgiving feast to represent “Freedom from Want.”
Along with the illustrations, the Post assigned essays to accompany them. “Freedom from Want” was assigned to Carlos Bulosan, a Filipino socialist activist, trade unionist, and writer. Bulosan was born in the Philippines to a peasant family, did not receive a formal education beyond third grade, and grew up picking coconuts and selling them to wholesalers to pay his older brothers’ school fees. He came to the United States at seventeen and worked in a fish cannery in Alaska, eventually becoming organizer and an elected official with the longshoreman’s union. In Washington and California, he worked as a dishwasher, a farm laborer, and in other low-wage jobs.
Despite his life’s hardships, he spent many hours in public libraries. Once, during a two-year battle with tuberculosis, he claimed to have read a book a day, including the works of Karl Marx and Walt Whitman. During this same bedridden period in the late 1930s, he began writing, contributing to publications like The New Yorker and Harper’s Bazaar — and The Saturday Evening Post.
Bulosan embraced the “Freedom from Want” assignment with a paean to America’s working class, whom he called “the creators of abundance.” His description of that class is rich and expansive:
If you want to know what we are, look upon the farms or upon the hard pavements of the city. . . . We cut timbers in Oregon just as the wild flowers blossom in Maine. We are multitudes in Pennsylvania mines, in Alaskan canneries. We are millions from Puget Sound to Florida. In violent factories, crowded tenements, teeming cities. . . . We are factory hands, field hands, mill hands. . . . We are the living dream of dead men. We are the living spirit of free men.
He emphasized the working class’s role in driving history forward, seeing that class as the engine of progress, not only through its labor but through its political struggles:
We are bleeding where clubs are smashing heads, where bayonets are gleaming. We are fighting where the bullet is crashing upon armorless citizens, where the tear gas is choking unprotected children. Under the lynch trees, amidst hysterical mobs.
Bulosan celebrates the progress of such struggles, including the right to organize unions. Yet because of the barbarities and inequalities of capitalism, Americans were still suffering deprivation:
We are not really free unless we use what we produce. So long as the fruit of our labor is denied us, so long will want manifest itself in a world of slaves. It is only when we have plenty to eat — plenty of everything — that we begin to understand what freedom means. . . . Our march to freedom is not complete unless want is annihilated.
Bulosan’s writing is heavy with disappointment that this vision hadn’t already been realized, emphasizing that the New Deal hadn’t gone far enough. Yet with an end to hunger, he wrote, democracy could be fully realized. He imagined a polity of plenty:
When we have enough to eat . . . then we have the time and ability to read and think and discuss things. Then we are not merely living but also becoming a creative part of life. It is only then that we become a growing part of democracy.
Rockwell’s painting was originally titled Freedom from Want, though since then, reflecting how this political context has been lost to history, it’s also been called I’ll Be Home for Christmas or simply The Thanksgiving Picture. As many observers have noted, the people around the table are enjoying their time together and are not looking at the turkey; the guests have the luxury of taking the food for granted as they revel in one another’s company.
Although Rockwell reportedly worried that his painting didn’t match Bulosan’s radical essay, it’s not hard to see how it does: both envision an America in which the conditions of plentiful comfort support a robust and lively social world. Just about everyone in America would recognize this Thanksgiving painting, but the socialist demand for food abundance that accompanied it has been forgotten.
That demand is more timely than ever. The cost of a typical Thanksgiving feast for ten this year has increased by 6 percent since last year, according to the American Farm Bureau.
And if you live in a neighborhood with a food pantry, as I do, you are probably seeing long lines around the block. With the increase in grocery prices and millions thrown off the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) by the Trump administration’s work requirements, food banks are seeing even more hungry people than during the pandemic years, with a dramatic increase in first-time visitors. Damningly, the Trump administration has discontinued the US Department of Agriculture’s annual household food security survey, but the New York Federal Reserve, in a national survey earlier this year, found what it called a “remarkable” increase in food insecurity from 2025 to 2026, especially in lower-income households and in households with young children. The New York Fed noted at the time that food insecurity was diminishing Americans’ confidence in the future; it seems certain that this increase in hardship contributed to the recent election results.
As so many go hungry in America, even as we elect more leaders in FDR’s tradition, Bulosan’s exhortation to American workers calls to us to push beyond the frame of what seems possible under US capitalism, to make the promises of its democracy real by feeding everyone.
“What do we want?” Bulosan asked, invoking the beginning of a timeless protest call and response:
We want to share the promises and fruits of American life. We want to be free from fear and hunger.
If you want to know what we are — we are marching!

https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-stat.title: New York State and local police out at sobriety checkpoints all Thanksgiving weekend long
https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-stat.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-stat.text:
State and local law enforcement are on high alert during the long Thanksgiving holiday weekend.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced a statewide increase in patrols to target drunk and reckless drivers from Thursday through Sunday, Nov. 29. According to the Governor’s office, Thanksgiving in particular has a lethal combination of increased vehicle traffic and alcohol use.
“As we gather with friends and family to celebrate Thanksgiving, I want to ensure that everyone gets where they are going safely and not have what should be happy memories marred by a preventable tragedy,” Hochul said. “I urge drivers to stay alert, stay sober and move over when you see vehicles stopped on the side of the road. If you’re in a vehicle, you should wear seat belts or use proper restraint. I thank our law enforcement for sacrificing their time with loved ones to work on Thanksgiving and throughout the holidays to help keep New York’s roadways safe.”
During the 2025 Thanksgiving weekend, police officers statewide arrested 2,236 drivers under the influence of alcohol or drugs. Over the same period last year, law enforcement issued nearly 12,500 speeding tickets and more than 3,000 tickets for seat belt violations. In total, more than 62,000 tickets were issued over the four-day holiday weekend.
“Please think twice before getting behind the wheel of a vehicle if you’ve been drinking,” said New York State Police Superintendent Steven G. James. “If you have had alcohol, there are several options available that will provide you with a safe ride to your destination.”
State officials said millions of drivers are on the road during the holiday. Police presence will increase statewide, including sobriety checkpoints and unmarked patrols to spot distracted drivers, especially drivers who are texting on the road.
To promote a safer roadway and minimize traffic congestion and delays, lane closures and construction zones for roads and bridges on state highways will be suspended until 6 a.m. Monday, Nov. 30.
All 27 rest stops along the New York State Thruway are open 24 hours a day during the holiday weekend.
Travelers can check road and traffic conditions by visiting the 511 website.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Lisa Marei Schmidt appointed to lead Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Anzhela Khachaturova
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Lisa Marei Schmidt has been appointed as the new director of two major museums in Bern: Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee. The board of trustees of the foundation that oversees both institutions selected Schmidt from 97 applicants following an international search, according to a release. She will lead on artistic direction and also chair the museums' management board.
Schmidt has directed the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, home to the world’s largest collection of works by artists from the German Expressionist group Die Brücke, since 2017. During that time she has co-curated exhibitions exploring complex and sometimes dark aspects of the history of German Expressionism, such as Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019) and Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22). Under her direction, the museum has also strengthened its work in provenance research, restoration, art education and digitisation. The German Association of Art Critics (AICA) named the Brücke-Museum as its museum of the year for 2023.
Born in 1978, Schmidt studied art history in Marburg, Amsterdam and Berlin, and curating contemporary art at the Royal College of Art in London. Before joining the Brücke-Museum, she worked as a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and served as a curator at Berlin's Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. In 2020, she curated Bonzo's Dream by Swiss artist Vivian Suter, which received AICA's Special Exhibition award.
“To me, museums are places where art and people meet,” Schmidt said in a statement. "They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society." She said she looked forward to getting to know the teams in Bern and building on the distinctive qualities of the two museums, which have shared strategic leadership under the umbrella foundation Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee since 2015.
Schmidt will also inherit a pressing challenge at Kunstmuseum Bern. In June, voters in the canton rejected a CHF15.7m (£14.4m) planning credit, or budget allocation, for a project to renovate the museum's historic building and replace its 1983 extension, with 51.8% voting against it. The museum says its ageing buildings still urgently need repairs.
Schmidt succeeds Nina Zimmer, who led the institutions for a decade and will become director-general of Vienna's Belvedere in January 2027. The foundation’s commercial director Thomas Soraperra will serve as interim director until Schmidt arrives.

https://gothamist.com/news/fate-of-long-.title: Fate of long-stalled NY bills could be decided by 27 new Democrats
https://gothamist.com/news/fate-of-long-.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/fate-of-long-.text:
This column originally appeared in The Politics Brief, our weekly newsletter on the people, power and policies that shape New Yorkers' lives.
Sign up to get the full version where you can ask questions, share news tips and weigh in on the conversation. Hits inboxes on Wednesdays.
The big blue wave certainly didn’t miss Albany.
When New York state lawmakers return to the Capitol in January, Democrats will control at least 158 of the 213 total seats in the Legislature — up from 144 at the start of 2024.
The state Assembly, in particular, is gearing up for a large freshman class. Add in a handful of retirements and seats that flipped in primaries, and the chamber’s Democratic majority will have a whopping 27 new members. Roughly one in four Democrats will be new.
All those fresh faces present a major opportunity for supporters of bills that have long stalled in the Legislature’s lower house. With 27 new majority members, that’s 27 new opportunities for advocates and their lobbyists to pick off votes for their cause.
“I started talking to some of the people who won Democratic primaries a few weeks after the primaries,” said Judith Enck, founder of Beyond Plastics. “We have to educate every incoming member and just see if we can get our numbers up.”
Enck, a former regional administration for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, has spent countless hours working the halls of the state Capitol in support of a bill that would force many companies to dramatically reduce their plastic packaging. The state Senate has passed the bill more than once, but the Assembly has never put it on the floor for a vote. She’s hoping 2027 is finally the year that changes — perhaps with the support of many of the Assembly’s new members.
Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie, a Bronx Democrat, says he picks which bills come to the floor for votes based on whether there are enough Democratic votes to pass them. A bill needs 76 votes to pass in the chamber — but, Heastie told WNYC’s “The Brian Lehrer Show,” he likes to have a bit of a buffer. And he won’t rely on Republican votes, either.
“People say, ‘Well, 76 sponsors can pass a bill,’” Heastie said earlier this month. “Yeah, that's great. But what happens if that one person is not there? People change their mind. So yeah, I usually like to have a little bit of a cushion.”
A bill to change state sexual assault laws to make it easier to prosecute cases in which victims knowingly consumed drugs or alcohol has also drawn renewed attention in recent months.
In September, a Cornell University student filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was gang raped at a frat house. The local district attorney claimed current New York law — which, as in 18 other states, only considers someone incapacitated if they’re drugged or became drunk without their consent — was an impediment to bringing charges.
That bill also passed the Senate but failed to get an Assembly vote. Heastie said Assembly Democrats discussed the bill in private twice. There weren’t enough Democratic votes either time, he said.
Now, with 27 new Democrats, supporters of the measure are hoping they can convince enough of the new lawmakers to tip the scale their way. But opponents have the same opportunity. Public defenders, in particular, have long argued the bill is overly broad, unconstitutionally vague and would lead to arbitrary enforcement, which helped derail efforts to pass the bill in years past.
Assemblymember-elect Brian Romero, a Queens Democrat, said he supports adding a voluntary intoxication clause to the sexual assault law, so long as there are protections in place to protect any one community from being disproportionately affected. He’s one of the 27 new Assembly Democrats taking office next year.
“I have to see what the bill looks like that is introduced in session next year,” he said. “It is very true that anything on the penal code will likely disproportionately impact Black and brown New Yorkers — and we have to figure out a compromise and solution because campus sexual assault and sexual assault in general is horrific and deeply traumatizing.”
In hopes of striking a compromise, Heastie tapped a group of 14 Assembly Democrats to examine the issue earlier this year. It’s due to deliver its recommendations to the speaker before the end of the year.
Soon-to-be-former Assemblymember Jessica Gonzalez-Rojas, a Queens Democrat who is heading to the state Senate next year, said she’s hopeful the working group will come up with a solution that all lawmakers can support.
“ I do think it's critical that we pass something and that we get to a place where maybe not everyone's going to be happy, but we're addressing the horrors that came out of Cornell and that happen all the time,” she said.

https://gothamist.com/news/nj-agency-eye.title: NJ agency eyes housing along the highways in Central Jersey
https://gothamist.com/news/nj-agency-eye.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/nj-agency-eye.text:
Forget park and ride. New Jersey wants you to live and ride.
The New Jersey Turnpike Authority is proposing to develop housing and commercial properties on five tracts of land it owns near busy interchanges along both the New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway. It’s a strategy Kris Kolluri, the Turnpike Authority’s executive director, said will encourage new development in areas that are also accessible to mass transit.
“Transit-oriented developments have been happening worldwide for a very long time,” Kolluri said. “But I think it's kind of unusual for a toll authority to look at its property and see how it can basically build live-and-ride facilities close to its asset, and then also tie it into mass transit.”
The plan, unveiled Monday, calls for commercial or industrial development focused in Central Jersey — in South Brunswick, Tinton Falls, East Windsor and Robbinsville. It moves the Turnpike Authority toward Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s goal of building housing on as much state-owned land as possible. Sherrill’s administration estimates that more than 40,000 housing units could be built on state property. It follows a similar plan unveiled by NJ Transit — which Kolluri also leads — earlier this year.
“To bring down housing costs, we need to build more homes and make better use of property the state already owns,” Sherrill said in a statement. “We’re advancing new housing near transit so families can more easily get around. The Turnpike Authority’s Land Plan builds on that progress, creating opportunities to expand housing and support local businesses while generating revenue for our transportation system.”
Kolluri said developing these properties could create new revenue streams for the Turnpike Authority, and mitigate soaring construction costs due to tariffs and supply chain challenges. He described it as complementary to the 3% toll increases that have hit in each of the past five years and are set to occur again in the new year.
Two of the five properties would be in South Brunswick. The first of those is a roughly 30-acre site on Friendship Road. Under the plan, that property could become 13 single-family houses or multifamily townhomes.
The other South Brunswick property is the park-and-ride currently operating at Turnpike Exit 8A. It’s a nearly 19-acre parking lot that is currently a stop for commuter buses to midtown and Wall Street. The Turnpike Authority’s plan envisions mixed-use development at the site. Commuter bus service at the site would continue, Kolluri said.
Kolluri had especially high praise for the Exit 8A park-and-ride.
“I can't think of a better site for a development, a housing development or an apartment development,” Kolluri said. “Literally steps away from the development you have a mass transit service to New York and other places.”
The other properties would be at land along Asbury Avenue in Tinton Falls, off Exit 102 on the Parkway; about eight acres on Franklin Street in East Windsor, off Exit 7 on the Turnpike; and an industrial site in Robbinsville near where I-195 intersects with the Turnpike.
The Turnpike Authority next plans to solicit proposals from developers for each property. Kolluri said the Turnpike Authority would work with municipal authorities to make sure any development aligns with local planning.
Kolluri said more land along the Turnpike and the Parkway in North Jersey may be made available for development in the future.
“There certainly may be, especially on the Parkway as you're going up north and maybe even on the Turnpike, opportunities for us to monetize and put some of these properties into play,” Kolluri said.
