https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Comment | Cop31 may have faltered but all is not lost
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Louisa Buck
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The fact that Cop31 failed to reach a final agreement on tackling climate change is obviously cause for grave concern. Despite the talks in Antalya, Turkey running over by two days as delegates struggled to achieve a consensus, they were ultimately derailed by the refusal by a group of oil producing states—led by Saudi Arabia and including Russia—to allow any mention of fossil fuel in the conference’s final agreement. This despite an agreement already made at Cop28 in 2023 to “transition away” from coal, oil and gas. As a result, more than 130 countries, including the European Union (EU) and the UK, refused to sign off a deal which omitted any reference to the main cause of climate change.
“We will not accept a Cop that greenwashes fossil fuel”, declared the EU representative Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, environment and energy, also stating that a climate pact which makes no mention of fossil fuel was “unconscionable” and “failed to meet the moment.”
Much of the art on display at Cop also seemed out of kilter with the urgency of the times. The centrepiece of the official CopArt programme, which was installed across the Cop site and curated by art advisor and contemporary art curator Nagihan Ozel, was an extensive installation of 18 mirror panels installed in the Green Zone and created by veteran artist Heinz Mack who has been making similar work since the 1960s. Other conspicuous pieces included Anselm Kiefer’s giant seascape bearing a pair of metal scales, Für Rabbi Löw (2010-12) and a forest made from recycled cardboard from Eva Jospin. Two monumental bronze sculptures by Belgian artist Koen Vanmechelen, one of an ape standing on a mirrored glass sphere balanced on a human thumb and another of a child struggling to hold an iguana, are described by the artist as “exploring our relationship with the natural world.”
Also on show in the Cop Green Zone and an especially jarring symbol of the deep schisms and incompatible agendas that characterised this latest Conference of the Parties were five animal sculptures created from discarded electronic and industrial defence waste materials. These were part of the “Upcycling a Future Vision” art collection launched by Aselsan, Turkey’s largest defence contractor to demonstrate its “commitment to a circular economy”, according to Turkish state-run media, as well as to celebrate the company’s 50th anniversary and “future of more efficient, innovative and sustainable production.” In a further irony, the defence giant—which is majority owned by the Turkish Armed Forces Foundation and produces electronic warfare technology and naval and air defence missile systems—was awarded a Green Transformation certificate from the Turkish authorities in tribute to its sustainability efforts. These apparently include a five-year road map to maximise energy, water and raw material efficiency whilst reducing carbon emissions and recycling 87% of total waste.
But amidst the chaos and anomalies within Cop some consolation can be gleaned from the fact that, while the oil-producing countries united to derail proceedings (undoubtedly spurred by the absence of an official US delegation and the Trump administration's overt hostility to the global fight to combat climate change), nonetheless 193 countries plus the EU remain committed to the Paris Agreement. Collectively these nations account for around 85% of global emissions. And while not wrapped up in a final deal, a number of significant agreements were made at Cop31 which included countries backing faster electrification and clean energy, drawing up measures to cut methane emissions and passing measures to protect the planet’s forests and oceans and strengthen support for communities impacted by climate change.
Power to the people
Beyond the Cop negotiating rooms, there are also glimmers of progress. In the UK greenhouse gas emissions have fallen by more than 50% since 1990 (although this much-vaunted statistic doesn’t include international aviation, shipping and imports and exports, which makes it more like 24%, according to the Office for National Statistics). Solar panels now provide 28% of Pakistan’s power while France and Denmark have announced roadmaps to phase out all fossil fuel by 2050, with Spain, Portugal and other countries planning to do the same. While these shifts often have as much to do with the fall in the cost of renewable technology and its resilience to market swings as a desire to hit climate goals; nonetheless an incremental frustration at the Cop consensus model means that countries are increasingly going it alone in naming what needs to be done and in identifying how they will tackle it.
Case in point was last Monday (16 November) when, as Cop31 was rumbling on, an important milestone was reached in the UK as Parliament debated a nearly 139,000 strong petition which called for the government to hold a UK-wide emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis. The petition had been generated by the National Emergency Briefing (NEB), a public information campaign consisting of an influential group of leading experts and fronted by the British naturalist and BBC TV presenter Chris Packham. It was asking for a “prime-time Covid-style briefing across all channels” which would be introduced by the Prime Minister and delivered by independent experts in order to spell out the extent and risks posed by climate change and nature loss, along with the action—both public and governmental—that needs to be taken. More than seventy members of parliament from across the political spectrum attended the three-hour debate which ended broadly in favour of the proposed televised emergency briefing, although not officially agreed. Speaking for the government, climate transition minister Katie White MP did go on record to state that she and her colleagues would meet with the leaders of the NEB campaign and “explore opportunities to work together”, and work on public engagement within the government's climate and nature security taskforce.
Just as Westminster was being galvanised by the NEB campaign, so too was the art world. Two days after the briefing debate, Tate Modern hosted a packed screening of The People’s Emergency Briefing, a 50-minute documentary film made by the NEB and presented by Packham. An articulate panel of nine experts starkly presented the urgent threats that climate and nature breakdown pose to food security, nature, the economy, national security and public health. This film, which anyone can freely register to screen, has been responsible for fueling much of the groundswell of both public and parliamentary support for the NEB’s petition. Since its release in April last year, The People’s Emergency Briefing has been shown more than 5000 times across myriad sectors and in venues large and small throughout the UK, from church halls, offices and hospitals, with many more scheduled for the forthcoming months. As Katie White declared at the Parliamentary debate, “a film has become a movement.”
However—with a few notable exceptions—the People’s Emergency Briefing has not had much airing in the art world. But now this seems set to change thanks to the art world environmental charity the Gallery Climate Coalition (GCC), who organised the screening and the following panel discussion. This was chaired by Frances Morris, the former director of Tate Modern and nowthe GCC's chair, speaking with artist Heather Ackroyd and Peter Lefort, the green futures network manager at the University of Exeter.
Among the two-hundred strong audience of artists, including Cornelia Parker and Marcus Coates, academics and art workers from across both the public and commercial sectors, there emerged a strong determination to galvanise action. Many declared a commitment to lobby their MPs, to organise screenings of the People’s Emergency Briefing in their galleries and generally to be more courageous in both acting individually and collectively to help instigate what Peter Lefort compellingly described as “positive tipping points.”
As Lefort explained, these tipping points occur when cumulative changes in behaviour, policies, expectations and attitudes reinforce each other and gather momentum to accelerate change and achieve transformative impact. As politicians falter and our systems for joining forces globally become increasingly dysfunctional and inflexible, it now seems increasingly clear that these new forces for change—such as the NEB, with allied activist groups and screenings occuring across Europe—are coming from the grassroots up, and that the creativity of the art world needs to be applied to shift ossified, seemingly intractable structures and open up new ways of thinking.
After all, it was back in 2019 that, on the instigation of artist duo Heather Ackroyd and Dan Harvey, a procession of bell ringing artworkers headed by a woman wearing a coat of living grass and riding a white horse, occupied Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. The event from the Culture Declares Emergency movement inspired then-director Frances Morris to make the institution of Tate declare a climate and ecological emergency, helping set in motion an increased environmental awareness that is now common currency throughout the art world. In the words of one attendee at last week’s Tate Modern gathering, “we may be small compared to other sectors but we can be LOUD!” So now let’s brush ourselves down after Cop and make our voices heard, before it is too late.

https://taz.de/Lobbyismus-bei-der-Bundes.title: Lobbyismus bei der Bundesregierung: Alle zwei Wochen ein Bänker
https://taz.de/Lobbyismus-bei-der-Bundes.author: Jana Laborenz
https://taz.de/Lobbyismus-bei-der-Bundes.text:
Lobbyismus bei der Bundesregierung: Alle zwei Wochen ein Bänker
Mindestens 35 Mal trafen Vertreter der Bundesregierung Mitglieder der Deutschen Bank. Was sie in den Treffen besprachen, ist nicht dokumentiert.
Die Bundesregierung hat sich seit Beginn ihrer Amtszeit mindestens 35 Mal mit Vertretern der Deutschen Bank getroffen. Das geht aus einer schriftlichen Frage der Linksfraktion an das Finanzministerium hervor, die der taz vorliegt. „Für die Sorgen und Nöte der Durchschnittsbevölkerung ist dann natürlich keine Zeit mehr“, wirft die Vorsitzende der Linksfraktion, Heidi Reichinnek, der Bundesregierung vor.
Die Deutsche Bank ist in den vergangenen Wochen in die Schlagzeilen geraten, weil ein Datenleck fragwürdige Geschäftspraktiken und mutmaßliche Probleme bei den Kontrollen der Bank offenbarten. So berichtete ein internationales Recherchenetzwerk unter anderem aus Spiegel, ZDF und New York Times, wie die das größte deutsche Geldhaus noch bis kurz vor Beginn des Ukrainekriegs das Geschäft mit Russland ausbauen wollte.
Die Dokumente enthielten außerdem Details über Geschäfte mit dem Sexualstraftäter Jeffrey Epstein und dem US-Präsidenten Donald Trump. Zudem zeigen die geleakten Dokumente, wie die Verlegerin Friede Springer dem Chef des Medienkonzerns Axel Springer, Mathias Döpfner, im September 2020 Aktien im Wert von rund einer Milliarde Euro schenkte. Auf diese Schenkung musste er offenbar kaum Steuern zahlen, weil die Deutsche Bank dafür sorgte, dass Döpfner zum Zeitpunkt der Schenkung über keine Liquidität verfügte.
Das Leak sorgte nun für eine Debatte um die Erbschaft- und Schenkungsteuer. Die Konzerne, die Kunden der Deutschen Bank seien, hätten nur das Ziel, „die Allgemeinheit um die eigentlich fälligen Steuereinnahmen zu bringen“, so Linkenpolitikerin Reichinnek. Jedes Jahr gingen schätzungsweise über 100 Milliarden an Steuereinnahmen durch Steuerhinterziehung verloren. Im Bundeshaushalt fehle derweil „das Geld für Investitionen in Infrastruktur, klimafreundlichen Umbau der Industrie oder Bildung“.
Etwa alle zwei Wochen ein Treffen
Die Linke fordert ein Unternehmensstrafrecht und verstärkte Sanktionsmöglichkeiten gegenüber Vorständen und Managern. Zusätzlich müsse die Verschonungsbedarfsprüfung bei der Erbschaftsteuer sofort abgeschafft werden. Auch Politiker von SPD und CDU forderten nach den Recherchen zur Deutschen Bank schärfere Regeln bei der Erbschafts- und Schenkungsteuer.
Bei 35 Treffen zwischen Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz oder Mitgliedern seines Kabinetts und Vertretern der Deutschen Bank kam es im Durchschnitt etwa alle zwei Wochen zu einem Treffen. Was dort besprochen wurde, geht aus der Antwort des Finanzministeriums nicht hervor. Informelle Gespräche und Telefonate fallen außerdem nicht unter die 35 Treffen, da die Regierung nicht verpflichtet sei, diese zu dokumentieren, so das Ministerium.
2026 trafen sich unter anderem Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil, Digitalminister Karsten Wildberger oder Bundesumweltminister Carsten Schneider mit Vertretern der Deutschen Bank. Schneider hatte demnach im November ein Treffen zu einem „Austausch zur Kreislaufwirtschaft“, Bundeskanzler Merz im Oktober zum „Allgemeinen Austausch zum Wirtschaft- und Investitionsstandort Deutschland“ oder zuvor „zu Fragen des Investitionsstandorts“. Bundeswirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche traf sich zum „Austausch mit der Initiative Made in Germany“.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Thanksgiving meal in Florida leads to ‘mass casualty’ food poisoning incident
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A Thanksgiving meal in Florida triggered a bout of food poisoning so bad that local emergency officials said it was a “mass casualty” event as numerous stricken diners were sent to hospital.
Local media reported that 18 people at the Leon Medical Center headquarters in Doral fell ill due to possible food poisoning after attending the center’s annual Thanksgiving lunch on Wednesday.
Miami-Dade fire rescue crews who received reports of the possible food poisoning said the call was upgraded to a “mass casualty incident” after 15 of those who fell ill required hospitalization, the Miami Herald reported.
In a statement to NBC Miami Leon Medical Center said: “Some of the staff began to experience gastrointestinal symptoms shortly after the luncheon and required treatment.”
“We continue to work with the caterers to determine, if possible, the cause and continue to provide support to our staff and their families.”
No patients at the center were affected. Investigations are continuing as to the exact cause and nature of the food poisoning.

- Kommentare
- Plattformökonomie und Amazon-Streik
Versagen auf der letzten Meile
Kommende Woche läuft die Frist einer Richtlinie der EU zum Schutz von Lieferdienst-Mitarbeitern ab. Es gibt noch keinen Gesetzentwurf. Ein Kommentar.
Die Kampagne »Make Amazon Pay« (Deutsch: Lasst Amazon zahlen) gehört inzwischen zum Black Friday wie Rabattschlachten und Betrugsmaschen. Dabei geht es nicht nur um gute Löhne und Tarifverträge. Der Großkonzern soll zahlen, auch für die Belastung des Planeten durch seine Emissionen und Rechenzentren sowie die digitale Überwachung von Arbeiter*innen.
Dieses Jahr bestreikt Verdi elf Amazon-Standorte in Deutschland. Die Gewerkschaft kritisiert niedrige Löhne der 40 000 Beschäftigten, gravierende körperliche Belastungen und die Überwachung ihrer Arbeit durch digitale Tracker. Letztere gibt es laut Sprechern des Versandriesens nicht. Die streikenden Beschäftigten arbeiten in der Logistik, Verwaltung sowie Forschung und Entwicklung und fordern den Abschluss rechtsverbindlicher Tarifverträge.
Schlechter sieht es bei der Zustellung auf der »letzten Meile« aus. Diese organisiert Amazon über digitale Plattform- und Subunternehmerstrukturen. Die Plattformökonomie ist jener informelle Arbeitsmarkt, in dem zeitlich befristete Aufträge flexibel und kurzfristig über Onlineplattformen vergeben werden – und der bekannt ist für auf ganzer Linie prekäre Arbeitsverhältnisse.
Die Plattformrichtlinie der Europäischen Union soll die Situation der Arbeiter*innen verbessern. Diese müsste die Bundesrepublik bis zum 2. Dezember umsetzen. Aktuell liegt aber nicht einmal ein Referentenentwurf vor. Ein Gesetzgebungsverfahren dauert selbst im Schnelldurchlauf mehrere Wochen, dementsprechend unwahrscheinlich ist die fristgerechte Umsetzung. Aktuell zahlt also nicht der Großkonzern – es sind die Lieferant*innen.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/27/midt.title: How the Gaza Encampments Unleashed the Blue Tsunami and Helped Spark a Worldwide Movement
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/27/midt.author: Safia Southey
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/27/midt.text:
Safia Southey is an international lawyer and writer who focuses on how societies reckon with wartime abuses.
The Hidden Backstory of the Blue Wave
Students at Columbia University set up tents on the lawn at the center of campus in April 2024 and said they would stay until the university divested from Israel’s war on Gaza. Within weeks, encampments had spread to campuses across the country, and soon around the world.
I was a law student at Columbia that spring and spent much of it in the encampment. I remember the cold nights and the teach-ins on the grass, the food that kept arriving from strangers, a Passover seder held on the lawn, and students praying in rows beside the tents.
Those who watched from a distance may remember a different set of images: riot police dragging students across their own campuses, an Emory economics professor thrown to the ground by officers, and a spring in which more than 2,000 people were arrested at protests nationwide. By the summer, the tents were gone. The bombing of Gaza continued.
In the 2024 presidential race, these same young people who had spent the spring organizing were asked to support a ticket that would not break with the policy they had protested. They were told that their objection was a luxury the country could not afford. Months before the encampments, more than 100,000 Michigan Democrats had voted “uncommitted” to warn the party about Israel’s onslaught, but the warning went largely unheeded. Many of us voted that November with dread, and some could not bring themselves to vote at all.
Donald Trump won the presidency, and within only a few months, federal immigration agents had detained Mahmoud Khalil (who had negotiated on the encampment’s behalf), and Columbia had agreed to pay more than $200 million to the administration that was punishing its students. By then, much of the commentary class had decided the protests had alienated voters and might even have helped elect Trump.
The midterm election results told a very different story. Darializa Avila Chevalier, who was arrested alongside students at Columbia’s encampment in 2024, won the congressional seat that includes the university, after unseating a five-term incumbent in June’s primary. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who ran openly against his own party’s position on Gaza, won a seat in the Senate. Democrats took back both the House and the Senate, and they did it by winning in places the party had stopped imagining it could compete: Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, to name a few, while also flipping Senate seats in Ohio and Maine. When Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York City a year ago, plenty of commentators treated it as a local story, one that could only happen there; the midterm results show they were wrong.
This election was enormous, and the encampments belong at the center of the story of how it happened. Gaza was the source of the anger: For two years, a generation watched the genocide on their phones in real time, while the people they had been raised to trust explained why nothing could be done. The encampments and the wider student movement gave that anger somewhere to go, taught people how to organize, and even more importantly, showed them the institutions meant to protect them simply would not. If young people wanted to be represented, we realized we would have to build that representation ourselves.
Learning From the Encampments
Many of the students who joined the encampments had never organized anything before. Within days — especially after the original organizers were arrested — they were running a small town: rotating security shifts, feeding hundreds of people, coordinating legal observers and jail support, holding meetings late into the night to decide by consensus what to do next, and negotiating with administrators who had far more power than they did.
Students learned how to bring a demand to an institution, how to build a coalition across groups that did not always agree, and how to keep people together after arrests and suspensions. Jewish, Muslim, Arab, Black, and Latino students, graduate workers, faculty, and neighbors from Harlem and Morningside Heights in New York City learned to work beside one another. Political campaigns run on those same skills, and plenty of people who staffed jail-support lines in 2024 were staffing phone banks two years later.
Socialist organizers were part of that education from the start. Members of the Young Democratic Socialists of America helped set up encampments from the University of California, Berkeley to New York City’s Hunter College, and the culture there — with mass meetings, shared labor, and decisions made together — already resembled the organizing that the Democratic Socialists of America had been practicing in tenant unions and on picket lines for years.
The students also learned what their universities would do when tested. Columbia presented itself as a place for open debate and then called the police on its own students, suspended and expelled them, and later settled with the federal government to restore its funding while one of the encampment’s negotiators sat in immigration detention. Students who had been taught that their schools existed to protect free inquiry watched those schools choose their endowments and their relationships with power instead. Many of them had already watched law firms withdraw job offers from students who had signed statements about Gaza in the fall of 2023. The lesson was harsh and clarifying: No institution was coming to save them.
The Democratic Party gave them no reason to think otherwise. Even after Biden withdrew and Kamala Harris became the nominee, the policy stayed where it was, and at the party’s convention that August, organizers rejected the Uncommitted delegates’ request to have a Palestinian American speak on the main stage.
For a generation already disillusioned with their universities, this confirmed that if Gen Z wanted their voices heard in the halls of power, they would need to knock on the doors, recruit the candidates, raise the money through small donations, and build the organizations themselves.
From the Lawn to the Ballot
Mamdani’s mayoral campaign was the first clear sign that they had started that work. He grew out of that energy, and his campaign gave it a direction. His primary victory in June 2025 rested on years of organizing by tenants, socialists, workers, and Palestine solidarity groups, and much of it ran through New York City DSA, whose electoral organizers described the coalition behind him as young New Yorkers becoming politically active, tenants, and voters drawn to both his affordability agenda and his support for Palestinian rights.
Sociologist Heba Gowayed traced the protest movement’s contribution to his win within days of the result. More than 50,000 people signed up to volunteer during that primary. Many of them were young people who had never knocked on a door for a candidate before, and they learned to canvass the way they had learned to run an encampment: quickly, from one another, and because no one else was going to do it for them. A campaign that talked about both affordability and Palestinian rights gave them a reason to give up their evenings and weekends. When he won the general election, more than 2 million New Yorkers had voted, the most in a mayoral race since 1969.
Mamdani’s victory changed what seemed possible for everyone watching. Candidates who had been warned that criticizing Israel would end their careers could now point to New York. Reps. Rashida Tlaib and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, currently the only members of DSA in Congress, will be joined by a record number of DSA-endorsed candidates, at least six. Claire Valdez, a state assembly member who had joined protests calling for an arms embargo on Israel, won the open seat in New York’s 7th Congressional District. In Colorado, Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old lawyer who lost her job after refusing to take down a social media post criticizing law firms over their positions on Israel and Palestine, unseated Rep. Diana DeGette, who had held the seat for three decades.
Avila Chevalier remains the clearest line from the lawn to the Capitol. She is a Columbia alumna who stood with students through arrests and threats of expulsion, and who had spent years in immigrant rights and community organizing before that spring. She ran with the backing of the same democratic socialists who had helped elect Mamdani. After her primary, Maryam Alwan, who protested at Columbia in 2024 (and with whom I am proud to have studied at Sciences Po Menton in France), told Al Jazeera what it meant to see “Darializa, a former leader and organiser of the encampment, represent the school that arrested her.” Gowayed, the sociologist, put the connection more bluntly: “This does not happen if those students don’t encamp; it just doesn’t happen.”
In Michigan, the state where the uncommitted vote first registered the party’s Gaza problem, Seed the Vote organized Jewish, Muslim, and Arab volunteers to knock doors for El-Sayed together, alongside IfNotNow and Bend the Arc. El-Sayed spoke directly to voters’ anger over the party’s position on Gaza and asked them to elect someone who shared it.
For anyone who had been in the encampments, those canvasses would have looked familiar. Khalil, who was released from detention in June 2025 and is still facing deportation, pointed to El-Sayed and Mamdani a week before the election as evidence that politics was shifting. “The American public is finally changing, is finally looking at the Palestinian as an equal human,” he said.
Anger at Trump, the cost of living, and organizations with decades of history all helped produce the blue tsunami, and no election return can isolate the share owed to the encampments. For people who had already concluded that their leaders were willing to fund devastation in Gaza while claiming there was no money for housing or healthcare at home, the war with Iran confirmed the judgment.
By October, polls compiled by Responsible Statecraft found voters were more worried about the war than about immigration or crime, and 6 in 10 opposed U.S. military action against Iran. The candidates who won on Election Day week treated rent, healthcare, and war as one argument about whose lives the government is willing to sacrifice, and young voters answered them.
Lessons for Serbia and India
Americans were not the only ones to see a student movement reach the ballot this fall. In November 2024, the canopy of the Novi Sad railway station collapsed and killed 16 people, and Serbian students, blaming the corruption they believed had made the disaster possible, blockaded their faculties and demanded accountability. Inside the blockades, they ran themselves through plenums and open assemblies with no leaders; every decision went to a vote. In March 2025, they invited the rest of the country to do the same, and within 10 days, citizens had formed their own assemblies, called zborovi, in neighborhoods and towns from Niš to Novi Sad. That same month, roughly 300,000 people filled Belgrade for the largest protest in Serbia’s history, but a moment of silence for the victims ended in panic when the crowd scattered from what protesters and analysts said was a sonic weapon; the government denied using one.
In May 2025, the students began calling for snap parliamentary elections. Serbian opposition politics had long concentrated on the cities and left smaller towns and villages to the ruling party, so the students went there, knocking on doors in places where the state media had branded them terrorists. On October 25, almost two years after the collapse, the Students’ List group won 140 of Parliament’s 250 seats and ended Aleksandar Vučić’s party’s hold on government. The plenums had taught them how to make decisions together, keep thousands of people moving in the same direction, and earn trust one conversation at a time — skills they carried over into election campaigning. Few people would have predicted that outcome during the first winter of the blockades, when the students were being dismissed as naïve.
In India, young people organized under the banner of the Cockroach Janta Party have been in the streets since September, together with student groups and opposition parties, protesting a revision of the voter rolls that has removed more than 130 million names. Police have detained thousands of them, and it would be easy to judge that movement by what it wins this month. Two years from now, we may have a better sense of what it set in motion.
What Comes Next
Nothing that happened on Election Day can repair what was done to Gaza, and the encampments’ original demands remain unmet. The students were protesting the killing of Palestinians and their own institutions’ complicity in it, and electing a former organizer to Congress will not change American policy toward Israel on its own. The organizations that carried these candidates into office will need to stay independent enough to press them once they arrive, and the voters who returned to the Democratic Party this year came back on conditions. Officials who forget this should expect the same organizers to come for their seats.
For those of us who felt crushed in 2024, though, the midterm victories deserve to be fully absorbed and celebrated. We were told that the protests had failed, that we had cost the party an election, that our anger was a liability. The people who had every reason to give up kept meeting instead. They recruited friends, built campaigns, found candidates they could believe in, and spent two years knocking on doors in neighborhoods where no one expected them.
While the news cycle may measure movements in weeks, it wrote this one off before most of its participants had graduated. The verdict came on Election Day, two years late, and it was written by the same people who had been dismissed. We did it, or at least we started to. The work ahead is harder, and it will take longer than anyone would like, but it starts now, with the wind at our backs.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

Image of the week
After a 10-year, £437m transformation, the glorious cathedral-like Smithfields market is the new home for the Museum of London. Our architecture critic entered a world of jewels, axes, DJs and dog races and was astonished. Read the full story
What we learned
Live data from a Spanish farm is directing sound and light for Philippe Parreno’s Sydney show
Marc Chagall’s lifelong passion for the circus animates a bewitching new exhibition
A Nan Goldin retrospective proves she is as great an American artist as Warhol
Theaster Gates explained why he’s bought a 60,0000 sq ft Chicago porcelain factory
Ron Athey, creator of famously extreme live art, explained why being naked isn’t enough

Masterpiece of the week
London: Interior of the Rotunda at Ranelagh by Canaletto, 1754
One of London’s vanished wonders is magically preserved in this masterpiece of perspective painting by an artist better known for his views of Venice. The Rotunda gave 18th-century revellers at Ranelagh Gardens, Chelsea, somewhere to promenade when it was raining or cold outside. Canaletto captures the flirtations, gossip, games and fashionable posing under this spectacular structure in the mid-1750s. It’s a high class, consciously sophisticated urban haunt. There are tables to dine at, privately located in their own arched alcoves, and a full orchestra is playing. The building itself is richly decorated in the rococo style, with a relaxed mix of classical grace and gilded ornament. It looks very European: a grand architectural expression of the rational, science-inspired era known as the Enlightenment. This is not a distorted view of London by Canaletto, but a reminder that the British capital was seen as the Enlightenment’s leading city, its science, coffee shops, commerce and comparatively free speech and satire the envy of continental visitors. The orchestra might be playing Handel, for instance, who worked in London and whose Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks reflect the lifestyle we see here.

https://gothamist.com/news/the-achieveme.title: The achievement gaps in NYC's public schools, stat by stat
https://gothamist.com/news/the-achieveme.author: Joe Hong
https://gothamist.com/news/the-achieveme.text:
It’s the height of high school and middle school application season in New York City. Applications are due Dec. 4 and Dec. 11 respectively.
Students are writing earnest application essays, preparing art portfolios and recording drama audition videos. It’s a complicated, stressful process for both students and parents. Critics say it can worsen existing educational inequities.
The city has the largest school system in the country — and one of the most segregated. The Mamdani administration has come under growing pressure to address racial imbalances across the city’s roughly 1,800 public schools.
Gothamist crunched a wide range of education data, which shows that yawning achievement and opportunity gaps still plague the school system.
Black students have left the city’s schools at disproportionate rates and are far less likely to get an offer from one of the city’s highly competitive specialized high schools. Test scores and graduation rates are significantly lower for Latino and low-income students. And students who are white, Asian and Pacific Islanders or from more affluent families are more likely to be in gifted and talented programs and get into their preferred high schools.
Nicole Brownstein, a spokesperson for New York City Public Schools, said the city will continue investing in standardized, research-backed literacy and math programs to help close these gaps. She pointed to higher test scores for Latino and Black students in eighth grade as signs of progress.
“We know this work has just begun and is far from over,” Brownstein said in an emailed statement.
Here’s Gothamist’s deep dive into the city’s education stats:
Overall enrollment decline
Let’s start with who’s actually in the system.
For close to a decade, the number of students in public schools has been shrinking in the city and across the country, largely the result of low birthrates and more families choosing private schools or homeschooling, according to one study by Brookings.
Here in the five boroughs, enrollment has dropped 9% since 2016, but some students have left the city’s public schools more than others. Black enrollment has plummeted 22% over the past 10 years. White enrollment has only declined by 15% over the same period.
The number of students living in low-income families has also dropped but at a slower pace. They now make up a slightly bigger share of the student population, as rents and other costs have soared and the city has become less affordable. In 2016, those children made up 71% of overall enrollment. Today, that number stands at 73%.
A 2026 study by the advocacy group Available to All found that New York City has the most segregated school system in the United States. Black students are more likely to go to majority Black schools. And the accelerated decline in Black enrollment means those schools are losing the funding that’s tied to enrollment. Less funding means schools are less equipped to support the students who remain.
The drop in students has led to calls for closing some under-enrolled schools. But because low enrollment is more likely at schools in low-income Black and Latino neighborhood, school closures would disproportionately affect those parts of the city.
“Historically there’s been a lot of divestment in Black communities,” said Kathy Hill, an education researcher at NYU. “It affects a lot of institutions, including the schools.”
3-K and pre-K enrollment
While overall enrollment has shrunk, the number of the city’s youngest learners has continued to grow. Enrollment in 3-K has increased since the program launched as a pilot in fall 2017 and has since expanded to every school district in the city. The number of students in 3-K is 13% higher this year compared to 2021, even as Pre-K enrollment for 4-year-olds has shrunk slightly over the same period.
Neither program is compulsory in New York. But education research shows that early childhood education programs can significantly boost cognitive development and academic achievement. One 2020 study found that students living in poverty can especially benefit.
But not all groups are signing up at the same rate. While Pre-K enrollment has increased among Asian and Pacific Islander, Latino, white and economically disadvantaged families, according to city data, fewer Black students are now enrolled in pre-K compared to five years ago.
Halley Potter, an education advocate and a former policy director at the Century Foundation, said that decrease is likely due to the disproportionate decline in Black student enrollment overall.
“A lot of it has to do with Black families moving out of the city because it’s unaffordable,” Potter said. “It might also intersect with the exodus of families with young children.”
In an effort to address inequities in early childhood education, the Mamdani administration earlier this year doubled the initial expansion plan of 3-K, adding 2,000 more seats.
Standardized test scores
Students in grades three through eight are required to take standardized tests each year in math, English language arts and science. Test scores have long fluctuated, but the data shows a persistent gap between white and Asian and Pacific Islander students on one side, and Black and Latino students on the other. As of 2026, white elementary-school students had the highest test scores for English language arts, with pass rates that were 25 points higher than Black students and 30 points higher than Latino students.
Aaron Pallas, an education professor at Columbia University’s Teachers College, said he’s grown disillusioned over the public education system’s failure to close achievement gaps for test scores, both nationwide and in the city. He said educational disparities take time to address and require a level of political will that is rare to find in most elected representatives.
He said closing the gap would require officials to play the long game and remedy poverty through affordable housing and lowering the overall cost of living. However, Pallas said elected officials often need quick wins, and short-term agendas don’t amount to long-term systemic change.
“Most things change slowly,” he said. “But politicians are often being pressured to show immediate results.”
Middle school admissions
New York City students typically attend an elementary school close to their homes. But as they near promotion into middle school, fifth graders and their families have some choice in where to go next.
Students get priority admissions in their neighborhood middle schools, but they can also apply to any school city wide, including gifted and talented programs and magnet schools. Admissions are largely based on grades earned during fourth grade.
Asian and Pacific Islander students are least likely to be placed in one of the three schools at the top of their lists. In 2026, 88% of Asian and Pacific Islander students got an offer from one of their top three. Compare that to 96% and 97% of Latino and Black students and 92% of white students.
Low-income students also matched to their top picks at a slightly higher rate than those from more affluent households.
For many students and parents, staying close to home is a priority. Some kids may help with family childcare responsibilities. Competitive middle schools are largely concentrated in Manhattan, which makes them less of a viable option for families living farther away in the outer boroughs.
High school admissions
High school admissions outcomes follow similar patterns. At 69%, Asian and Pacific Islander students again had the lowest rate of matching with one of their top three choices in 2026. Black and Latino students had higher match rates of 88% and 89%, respectively.
Asian and Pacific Islander students, Potter said, likely had lower match rates because, as data shows, they’re more likely to apply to selective programs.
But for students from low-income families, the trend is reversed compared to middle school admissions. Those kids were less likely to match with one of the top high-schools on their lists. This year, 73% of students living in poverty matched with one of their top three choices, whereas the rate was 85% for students not living in poverty.
The city’s high school application process is complex and, for some families, includes a grueling schedule of school tours to find the right fit. The city is home to over 400 high schools with over 700 different programs, according to the Department of Education.
Students receive a lottery number that, in part, determines their chances of getting into a program of their choice. They’re also relegated to tiers based on their grades in seventh grade. Kids can also sit for essays as part of the admissions process. And some submit portfolios and audition videos for art, drama, dance and other programs.
The complexity of applying to high school has come under considerable criticism for contributing to existing inequalities in the education system. Hill and Potter said the city’s admissions process disadvantages working class families who may not have the time and resources to make the most informed decisions.
Potter added that making it easier for Black and Latino students to attend more selective high schools could help integrate schools.
“A system with as much choice as New York City’s also creates more segregation,” she said.
Gifted and talented programs
Disparities are starker for admissions to gifted and talented programs, especially at the five K-8 and K-12, gifted and talented schools that accept students from across the city, including NEST+m, or New Explorations into Science, Technology, and Math, on Manhattan's Lower East Side.
These five schools serve more white students and fewer economically disadvantaged students compared to the city’s overall student population, according to city enrollment data.
Standardized test scores at these schools are also significantly higher. According to Gothamist’s analysis, over 94% of students at the city’s five gifted and talented schools met or exceeded standards in English Language Arts and over 96% met or exceeded standards in math in 2026.
Mamdani has signaled a willingness to phase out gifted and talented programs. Former Mayor Bill de Blasio had also proposed phasing them out in 2021. De Blasio's successor, Eric Adams, suspended that plan indefinitely.
Specialized high schools
The most blatant disparities can be seen in who gets into the city’s specialized high schools. In 2026, 26,000 students competed for 4,000 spots by taking the Specialized High School Admissions Test, or SHSAT.
White and Asian and Pacific Islander students who took the test were offered spots at much higher rates in 2026, but Black students were disproportionately less likely to receive an offer.
Among those who took the test, 17% were Black. But Black students only made up 3.5% of the offers. Stuyvesant High School, one of the largest specialized high schools, accepted only three Black students in 2026.
The city education department does not publish SHSAT or offer numbers for specialized high schools by socioeconomic status.
In response to these long-standing inequities in selective programs, Mamdani has suggested using other factors, instead of just a single test, to consider students for admissions.
AP exams
Pass rates for Advanced Placement courses offer a snapshot into how well students are prepared for college. Those who pass more AP exams are more likely to finish college, according to some research.
Black, Latino and economically disadvantaged students were less likely to pass an AP exam in 2025. White and Asian and Pacific Islander students were more likely to score higher.
Students from low-income families had a pass rate of 58%, while students from more affluent households passed 75% of the time.
Graduation rates
The same achievement gaps we see across the city for test scores, high school admissions and AP enrollment are reflected in graduation rates. In 2025, Asian and Pacific Islander students had the highest graduation rate with 92%. Latino students had the lowest with 77%.
Since 2021, the city has made little progress in increasing graduation rates, especially for historically disadvantaged students. The disparities for Latino, Black and economically disadvantaged students have grown since the pandemic. Last year, all three groups, as well as white students, reached a five-year low in graduation rates.
But compared to 20 years ago, the city has made considerable progress. In 2006, Asian and Pacific Islander students’ graduation rate was 10 percentage points lower than it was in 2025. Rates for Latino and Black students were both more than 15 points lower.

Why Abolition Is Essential to Reproductive Justice
A landmark gathering brought together activists on the inside and outside of a women’s prison fighting for reproductive justice for everyone.
In early October, I had the opportunity to attend the first-ever convening on reproductive justice and abolition held, in part, inside a women’s prison. The event, called RJ Across Walls, gathered participants at the California Institution for Women in Corona on the first day—enabling 100 people who are currently serving sentences at CIW to attend—and outside at Riverside City College on the second day. It was a remarkable experience to facilitate a conversation about abortion with my coauthor Renee Bracey Sherman on the first day. But what I took away from the convening went well beyond gaining a deeper understanding of the reproductive injustices inside the carceral system; the event underscored why abolition is essential to our fight for bodily autonomy.
The California Coalition for Women Prisoners, in close partnership with a subcommittee composed of people “inside” at CIW, organized the two-day gathering. The coalition formed 31 years ago in the wake of a class-action lawsuit, Shumate v. Wilson, which documented the medical injustices inside CIW and the Central California Women’s Facility. As the number of women in California’s prisons surged in the 1990s, organizers inside and outside of prisons understood pressure would need to be applied across prison walls in order to improve the conditions. Shumate was the catalyst for organizers to form CCWP, and in the years since that case was decided in the plaintiffs’ favor, its advocates have continued to fight for justice for those being harmed behind bars while seeking to end the systems that make this abuse and medical neglect possible.
Related Article
What I remember most about stepping out of our rental car and onto the grounds of the California Institution for Women was the smell. My nose was completely blocked from a cold, but I felt the foul odor, which Renee confirmed, without being able to inhale it. CIW is located almost 50 miles east of Los Angeles on former farmland. Arid fields surround the facility, backdropped by scenic mountain views. Soon after our arrival, we joined about 50 other attendees to have a police dog check all of the food and meeting supplies we were bringing into the prison. Then CCWP organizers gathered our group, before we entered the front security building in small groups. No electronic devices were allowed, though CIW did permit Courtney Hanson to bring in her camera and document the day (the photos she took were reviewed by the facility before her departure).
The inside portion of the convening was held in a huge hall that the inside sub committee had turned into a meeting room, with armed officers stationed outside the building. It was easy to forget they were there as you entered the hall, which was divided into four sections, each with foldout chairs forming a circle around a white board listing the upcoming workshop.
CCWP organizers and the inside folks they have worked with over the past three decades have long understood that abolition is essential in order for people trapped in the prison industrial complex to experience or exercise reproductive freedom, but this convening allowed them to bring these conversations to the forefront. “Welcome to the solution,” CCWP organizer and MC for the day Elizabeth “Leesa” Normura said as she addressed the 100 inside attendees who sat among the 50 outside attendees, referring to the convening’s mandate:
- To imagine new visions for care and community beyond California’s carceral institutions.
- To collectively strategize how to best support incarcerated people facing reproductive justice issues in California prisons, and mobilize efforts to dismantle carceral institutions.
- To share collective wisdom, expertise, and ideas across prison walls, with an aim of developing reproductive policy and practice interventions grounded in reproductive justice and abolition.
The day consisted of three blocks of workshops, 12 in total, covering a range of topics, from parenting while incarcerated to pregnancy and postpartum separation, to sexual violence and forced sterilization. One workshop on toxic prisons and environmental racism would directly address the very apparent air quality concerns surrounding the prison, emanating from the former dairies, as well as issues of extreme temperatures and unequal access to bottled water. And Renee and I guided a discussion on abortion stigma and how it operates in tandem with the carceral system to criminalize people for their pregnancy outcomes and control reproductive decisions.
Women are the fastest-growing prison population, and thanks to the Supreme Court’s ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the number of people facing pregnancy-related prosecutions is only growing. But the prison system was not designed to meet their medical needs, nor set up to ensure women—the majority of whom have survived sexual abuse—would be safe in the custody of prison staff. The same can be said for incarcerated trans people.
Paige Linville, one of the subcommittee organizers, explained in her remarks that upon setting foot in prison, “we immediately learn that our bodies no longer really belong to us. From the first strip search when every inch of our body is examined by a stranger, we are constantly reminded that other people are in complete control of us.”
And it’s not just the loss of bodily autonomy. The reproductive justice framework also demands the right to have children, or not have children, and the right to parent the children you have in safe and sustainable communities. But prisons, by design, make exercising those rights impossible, as Kwaneta Harris, a mother and former nurse who is incarcerated at a Texas state prison, explained in her pre-recorded keynote address. I met several women who had spent the majority of their reproductive years behind bars, and did not have children but not by choice. Reproductive justice and abolition are intertwined because, “you cannot dismantle reproductive oppression while leaving cages standing, because the cages ARE reproductive oppression, wearing a badge,” said Harris. “You can’t have bodily autonomy on the outside while there are women in here who can’t choose when they use the bathroom, see daylight, eat, and whether they get to hold their newborn for more than a few minutes before the shackles come back on.”
“Think about it this way,” Harris added. “If your movement fights for the right to parent, but doesn’t fight the system that snatches parents away and cages them for surviving abuse, poverty, or a broken safety net—that ain’t full justice. That’s justice with an asterisk. And if your movement fights to close prisons but doesn’t center the specific ways that gender, race, pregnancy, and violence against women funnel us into those prisons in the first place—that ain’t full abolition either. That’s abolition with a blind spot.”
The organizers of the convening spent six months thinking deeply about how to shape this convening around a vision for full justice, without asterisks or blind spots. In the spring, CCWP had published a booklet—in collaboration with the advocacy nonprofit Unapologetically HERS, researchers at the University of California San Francisco, and incarcerated researchers at the Central California Women’s Facility—titled Know Your Reproductive Rights in Prison. This convening marked the next stage of CCWP’s RJ work, creating “an opportunity to harness wisdom inside, to really be thinking critically about not only how do we protect folks who are there now, but how do we work with them to envision a world without prisons,” said sociologist Jennifer James, a CCWP organizer who runs the PhD Sociology Program at UCSF and contributed to the booklet. “So many of the reproductive harms, the reproductive oppression, that comes through prison, is not stuff that can be reformed away.” Reforms that have increased access to period products, breastfeeding, or have eliminating shackling during childbirth are important, James noted, but “the critical harms of people not being able to create their families the way they want to, not being able to raise the families they have, concerns about their overall reproductive health, sexual abuse and assault and violations of body autonomy, are features of prisons themselves.”
In other words, reforms can hide structural problems that aren’t going away.
The organizers wanted to highlight those tensions and invite attendees to imagine ways to shrink the carceral system, not expand it. What attendees came up with on day one—expanded upon on day two with outside attendees, including folks who weren’t able to attend the inside portion—is a list of priorities across each topic. For example, menopause continues to be an issue area where there’s “real excitement and energy to help us think critically about the impact of aging…on women’s chances of getting out,” James explained. Women who are behind bars while experiencing perimenopause and menopause, without the resources or support to treat their symptoms, may experience changes in their mood or how they engage in their community, which “might be a hindrance [when it comes to] getting board approval,” said James. “So how can we really advocate around considerations and menopause and helping people come home when they’re eligible?”

There’s also been a lot of progress around expanding access to doulas in prisons. On day two, I sat in on the breakout session focused on supporting pregnant and birthing people, and doula programs are central to this work. (The topics for the breakout sessions were based on the most paramount issues that developed during day one’s conversations.) Pregnant people represent 4 percent of people in jails and prisons. Very little information is known about their experience behind bars, though medical anthropologist Carolyn Sufrin has worked incredibly hard to change that. Doulas can empower incarcerated pregnant people, who may not be familiar with their rights or have all the information they need about pregnancy behind bars or the forced separation from their newborns shortly after giving birth, when they are returned to prison. And while California has gone further than most states in improving maternal healthcare in prisons and jails, not everyone is able to access the care or treatment they need. But ending the incarceration of pregnant people would be the only way to ensure they are removed from this system that by design treats them unfairly and subjects them to medical neglect and, often, to forced C-sections. However, there are some efforts advocates can take to improve the conditions of incarcerated pregnant people, like increasing doula training and ensuring state institutions are following the rules outlined in policies like California’s Reproductive Dignity for Incarcerated People Act, which offers protections for pregnant people behind bars, when the law is actually followed.
CCWP is currently gathering the priorities outlined over the two days and strategizing around ways to build on the momentum, including potentially organizing a followup session with inside attendees this winter. Already, inside attendees have shared with the organizers that the convening gave them a voice, making them feel heard. Others declared that “abolition is possible and necessary” and demanded we “FIGHT” because “we got each other, forever.”
In many ways, the convening pulled together different threads of discussions happening across the state. An event at CIW earlier in the year, hosted by the Oakland-based nonprofit Impact Justice, addressed gaps in menopause care and information within the prison. Not long after, the US Department of Justice concluded its investigation into sexual violence at California’s two women’s prisons and found the facilities had an “unbroken pattern” of staff sexual assault over the past 20 years. And, the women at CIW are still reckoning with California’s history of involuntarily sterilizing tens of thousands of people, from 1909 to 1979, in its institutions because they were “unfit to produce.” According to the 2020 Belly of the Beast documentary, nearly 1,400 sterilizations occurred between 1997 and 2013. A Reveal News investigation found “the state paid doctors $147,460 to perform the procedure” during that period. Some who participated in the RJ Across Walls gathering are survivors, while others there reported that these coerced sterilizations—an internationally recognized form of genocide—have not stopped despite the state passing a ban in 2014.
The convening reaffirmed for me why abolition is essential to reproductive freedom. It also confirmed why it’s crucial for those of us on the outside to be sure to elevate the voices of those on the inside when we make any demands for reproductive justice from our elected officials. If our demands do not reach everyone, they are not going far enough.

https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/f.title: Carroll Dunham Calls His Filthy Formalism “Abstraction with a Hard-On”
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/f.author: Emily Watlington
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/f.text:
I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.
“I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie, the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade.
The spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for.
Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses in varying states of specificity, usually attached to the bodies or the faces of humanoids engaged in sex or violence. This scenery belongs to a tradition of ridiculous bodily extremes, from Greek vases to Thomas Rowlandson to Gustave Courbet to Nicole Eisenman. His style, meanwhile, belongs to the black outlines and dropped-in colors of cartoons. That graphic clarity seems to ask us to read his bodily subjects loud and clear, without any of the technical seduction of peers like Lisa Yuskavage or John Currin.
Although his loud and lusty scenarios committed no real transgression (Peter Saul took care of that in the ’60s, then Robert Mapplethorpe in the ’80s), what may genuinely surprise the uninitiated is the academic remove that characterizes the writing about Dunham. His work is discussed—and discussed primarily by those born before 1975—almost exclusively in the specialist language of form or space or paint application, with little reference to the subject matter. It seems that the writers in Camp 1 understand the shock factor that attends men dildoing their rectums with pistols, or angrily ejaculating on each other from enormous penis-noses, as ammunition against the claim that subject should dictate one’s opinion of a painting. As if to deny the charge of prudery, some of them describe moments of rapture. On a Dunham painting made between 2006 and 2012, of a giant woman spreading her anus and vagina above a landscape like a parade float, the artist Paul Chan wrote of feeling transported: “When I entered the room where it hung [at the Whitney], I gasped. The painting was at once exuberant, provocative, and entrancing. It literally took my breath. I quickly glanced at the other people in the room. Was anyone else having an asthma attack looking at this?”
Representing Camp 2 are John Yau (The Brooklyn Rail, 2007: “Saul is an iconoclast and Dunham is a wannabe.”) and a young man in a basketball jersey I met at the Chicago show. This man was examining a pencil scribble from 2020 of a fist clasping an erection, the balls parted and meatus shaped like a teardrop. I asked him what he thought, and he said, “I feel like I’m being pranked.”
Dunham walked me to the “other studio,” a smaller room reserved for painting, where acrylic tubes lay neatly on a table in gradients, labels down. A canvas he had just finishedstood on sawhorses. It showed a man with long black hair down on all fours in a sculpture studio. The painting is called Looking for Something, and its protagonist’s pants are on the floor. His skin is white, and a woman, who is purple, kneels behind him, her head thrown back in a wail or moan. With her hand, she does something to the man’s ass that is not visible to us. In the foreground, another purple person, a Peeping Tom, watches them through a window. Nine of these most recent “Sculptor” paintings, from about Covid to now, were to go up at the Matthew Brown gallery in Manhattan in September as a sort of appetizer for the Miami show.
I asked where these recent purple/white folks come from. “They come from my work,” Dunham explained. “And I don’t mean that to be glib. They really do. So to even answer that question, I would have to go, ‘Before I was doing these paintings, I was doing these paintings, then these paintings,’” he continued, miming with his hands successive leaps into the past.
BORN THE FIFTH IN A line of Carrolls to a Connecticut poultry farmer who turned to real estate, Dunham went to Phillips Academy (Andover), class of 1967. The sculptor Mel Kendrick was his roommate. “Tip was doing Rapidograph drawings,” Kendrick recalled as we spoke by phone, using Dunham’s nickname. “Almost hippie drawings, very fine sketches.” (Of “Tip,” Dunham said, “It’s a WASP thing.”) Kendrick also recalls Dunham’s appetite for science fiction. (Face-down on his studio table, I spotted James L. Cambias’s Darkling Sea.) Dunham took darkroom classes. In the school’s literary magazine, his finely exposed photograph of a pouting and rotund lady in a playground swing illustrates a poem by Anthony Grafton, the historian-to-be. “Anything he did, he always had a touch,” Kendrick said. “Tip is very specific. And that’s something I don’t know if people know about his paintings, even now.”
After a year at the University of Rochester, Dunham followed Kendrick to Trinity College, in Hartford, where they worked in a small studio art department. “That meant smoking a lot of dope and reading Artforum,” said Dunham. On weekends, Dunham and Kendrick would drive down from Connecticut in Dad’s (Carroll IV’s) pickup truck, Kendrick recalled, to sample the new galleries in Soho—Bykert, Paula Cooper, Sonnabend, OK Harris—and to feast on spaghetti and jug wine at the apartment of their Trinity teacher Terence LaNoue.
LaNoue made almost three-dimensional combine paintings with poured latex and molds. He “was a great teacher, but I always had a kind of resistance to what he was making,” Dunham said. “And I’ve been that guy. I know that I’ve had good experiences between students and me where it really didn’t have to do with them being that turned on about my work.” Dunham never followed, either, in the footsteps of the artist with whom LaNoue installed him for a formative internship. Dorothea Rockburne produced—and still does, at 97—large, clean panes of paper or vellum, lined geometrically or coated in graphite. But the two got on, and still do. “Brighter than almost anybody around,” Rockburne said of him by phone.
What attracted Dunham was the planning implied by Rockburne’s planes—she taught him and Kendrick “how to handle a T-square and other basic things,” she said. He was also drawn to the repetitious text paintings of Mel Bochner (who lived with Rockburne), and to the heaps of raw material arranged by Barry Le Va and by Richard Serra. On graduating, he moved into a loft on Thomas Street shared with Kendrick and Peter Wheelwright, the architect. His 1970s and ’80s in New York were “isolation lite,” he told me. Dunham was part of no scene, he said, but befriended the photographers of the so-called Pictures Generation, and married one: Laurie Simmons. For seven years he worked in a frame shop, then for another seven at Time magazine, as a layout artist, all the while plotting his entrance into the art world.
DUNHAM’S ’70s ART BEGAN with single-line squiggles on canvas or paper. Some are elegantly coiled springs, while others resemble long strings dropped to the floor, their loops filled with ground colors of fast-drying casein or acrylic. He debuted with them at Artists Space in 1981, the Chicago survey was their first time on view since. Rockburne sees little of herself in Dunham’s famous later work. “It had that kind of [Sol] LeWittian, instructional aspect,” said the artist John Newman, another Dunham confederate from those days, by phone. “In the ’70s, drawing was sort of raised to a new place,” Newman explained, “as a much more immediate and idea-oriented kind of territory that wasn’t so laden with the history of painting and sculpture.”
The string-loops soon became blobs. When Dunham found the lid of a shipping crate on the street, around 1980, and used that for his surface, the almost sculptural grains and knots of the plywood veneer became guidelines for even more specific and conflicting blobs all mashed together—amoebas, geysers, wilting donuts, kinked tubes, beans, ripples, Froot Loops—in palettes ranging from medical textbook to clown paint. It is with these plywood paintings that the Miami survey begins. From 1984 to ’88, they appeared in three shows at the Baskerville + Watson gallery, with the middle show limited to monochromes.
“When the veneer things came out,” Newman recalled, it was amazing. “Think about the first time you ever read James Joyce. You really had to step up to it, participate in it. It was new information.” The art dealer David Nolan “hated them” at first, he said by phone: “I thought these garish, psychedelic colors were just there to shock me, and I just wasn’t interested.” But after a while, he began “to peel away the layers and see how they’re put together. And once I understood that, I thought, Oh God.”
The third show sold out before even opening, scoring acquisitions by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney, and the Brooklyn Museum. Dunham quit his magazine job. Gestural painting had been deemed safe again by young galleries, and although Dunham used a brand of biomorphism that didn’t quite fit with the headliners—Basquiat, Baselitz, Schnabel—he was made. Instead of buying up pallets of plywood and sticking safely to what worked, however, Dunham pivoted again. By the ’90s, his veneer paintings migrated to stretched linen, this time as single forms. They began to elongate into screaming fish-lipped mouths, nugget bodies, wincing faces, and undeniable penises. “They weren’t until they were,” Kendrick said of these organs. Nolan noticed them, too. But since they were untitled, Nolan said, “I thought he was avoiding what was right in front of our noses. They are bodily explosions. Come on.”
DUNHAM HAD BEEN PLENTY aware. He described the ’90s work to me as “abstraction with a hard-on.” But he seemed as bewildered as I about its origin. He spoke with plainness about sex and aggression as if he were a social worker, treating his own work as a sort of passive conduit for those realities. This tone did not seem to me like an act. I asked if he had tried to be provocative with his art, then or now. He said no: “It doesn’t interest me very much … The entire enterprise was provocative.” He spoke of Duchamp’s urinal.
Into the new century and his large survey at the New Museum in New York from 2002 to 2003, which was his last show of that scale until this year, his canvases begin to carry entire buildings and shiploads, colonies and planets full of hateful little nugget people with their penises, guns, and hideous gourd breasts. The exceptions from sex—lumpy tree scenes and landscapes—became the transgression. From there, he went more humanoid. In the past 20 years, his nuggets have grown up, first into suited G-men with fedoras and angular suits, then into cleanly clarified cartoon nudes, their globe buttocks outlined in elegant black and set in plain landscapes or rooms. They wrestle, fight, bathe, masturbate, copulate, and blind each other. They examine their gaping anuses, their big labia like bike tubes, and their nipples like air-hockey pushers.
These characters occupy about half the Miami paintings. In one, Horse and Rider (My X), 2013–15, a woman holds her arms up in a “Why me?” pose on the back of a horse. The lines of her reach continue south into a stand of flowers and a broken tree branch, dividing the canvas into a perfect X, which Dunham has left visible in pencil beneath the paint. At the geometric center is the woman’s anus, as if to say “Look here.” Just beneath, the horse’s anus gapes, too. He turns back at us with a look like “Excuse you.” (No human or humanoid, however, has eyes in a Dunham work.)
Dunham said of this X composition, “I was very excited when I figured out that that would work.” He explained: “It’s two layers of truth. There’s the subject and whatever that requires to be plausibly rendered.” (He counted “breasts, genitalia, asshole, some notion of limbs, and hair.”) “Then the geometry of the canvas has this other kind of truth, and the two things have to become one thing.” And the woman? “I honestly do not remember why I thought it would be interesting to put a woman on a horse in the paintings.” He thought. “It’s nice to have a black dot in the center of a painting. And it’s even nicer when that black dot is a woman’s ass, you know?”
Nolan was the only one I spoke to who saw strategy in Dunham’s turn to hyper-figuration. He saw the artist “dealing with his own demons or faults about the world.” But he described the work as Dunham did, composition-first. “If you try to forget there’s a face in there, the compositions are very strong.” He advised me to view the paintings upside down, pointing out convincing similarities to Aztecan decoration and adding that recently he, Nolan, had refused to sell one—for a lot of money—until the potential buyer flew to New York to see the shapes in person. “That is a problem with the younger generation. They will lose all of the subtleties.”
WHAT DOES THE YOUNGER generation think? The Miami show this winter (and the Chicago catalog forever) will give them the chance to see Dunham’s career as a single entity and to decide if the evolution of blob to aggression to anus stands up to the hindsight of a more literally minded era. In the purple alien characters on view at Matthew Brown this fall, from the series Dunham calls “Studio on Another Planet” (2022–26), one was hard-pressed not to read a narrative about artists at work in a culture that will misunderstand them: a solitary white male surrounded by voyeurs (critics? dealers? posterity?) as he quietly molds his clay on their land, incurring their sinister attentions. In the last of those canvases, Finished (2019–2025), the aliens have had enough. They’ve dragged the artist outside and are now quartering him to death.
“You’re not supposed to get it,” Newman said of Dunham’s pictures. “Art is about having an experience.” Newman speaks, Darwin-like, of Dunham’s characters emerging from the primordial soup of the plywood paintings. “Younger people probably don’t know the early work. And I actually think if they did, it would help them understand his later work better.” In my conversations with Camp 1, I began to wonder if there has ever been a generation more permissive, more game, than the one that had Dunham as a sort of living symbol of egress: out of the hermetic tasks of Minimalism, through pure shape, into a future where human fictions of any extreme can live without excuse or embarrassment. And I began to envy them.
I asked Dunham if he believed pure abstraction existed. He said yes, adding, “And I think that when I started my work, I was doing it. And then I think at a certain point I realized that it fascinated me to try to add some really literal aspects of just being a human being incarnated, or incarcerated, however you think about it, in a body.”
But I didn’t fully buy Dunham’s hermetic account of his own work as “always in some way self-referential.” There seems to be plenty of lived Artist v. World in his pictures and posture, and plenty of visual breadcrumbs leading to the culture at large. I asked, for instance, which cartoons he watched with his two children, who were born in 1986 and ’92. His eyes widened. “Ren & Stimpy was good,” he said of John Kricfalusi’s unhinged and influential program. “But the masterpiece of ’90s cartooning as far as I’m concerned was Angry Beavers,” which he watched with his son. I was fishing. The affinities between Dunham’s ’90s work and the prevailing depravities of Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network are inarguable; and in those affinities, a new generation may see homage to the last golden age of a truly transgressive child-absurd.
Speaking of his younger child, Dunham flashed back: “He came into my studio a lot. He would pick up on things I was drawing and then he would draw stuff of his own that was kind of like that. So I got a lot of, you know, 6- and 7-year-old energy coming back at me about my own work.” Dunham smiled. “It definitely encouraged a certain kind of energy. It’s very sweet to think about actually.”
