https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Brussels’s expansive, €230m Kanal art complex set to open in former Citroën garage
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sarah Belmont
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The much-anticipated Kanal, billed in press materials as Europe’s largest museum development, opens tomorrow (28 November) in a former Citroën garage and showroom on the banks of Brussels’s Charleroi–Brussels Canal. The institution aims to establish Brussels as a major international centre for Modern and contemporary art, and also to provide new truly public, inclusive institution for the city’s residents.
The Brussels-Capital Region acquired the site, which dates back to 1934, in 2015 with the intention of creating a major cultural centre. The work was then carried out by an international team featuring noAarchitecten, EM2N and Sergison Bates. The resulting complex spans 40,000 sq. m.
Three new structures, called “houses”, have been inserted into the former garage. Upon entering from the Quai de Willebroeck, visitors find on their left the “Rassembleur”, as the team calls it, which is home to an auditorium and offices. Opposite, on the right, is Kanal Architecture, which is intended to house the CIVA architecture centre and its archives. The transfer of the archives has been delayed following a fire in July. Further along on the right is Kanal-Centre Pompidou, a museum dedicated to modern and contemporary art. This latter space will feature work from the collection of Paris’s Centre Pompidou, with which Kanal signed an agreement in 2017. The agreement, valid until 2031, gives Kanal access to works from the Paris museum's collection, alongside curatorial expertise and support with exhibitions and programming.
More than 20,000 sq. m within the broader Kanal project is devoted to freely accessible public space. The complex also includes creative studios, observation points, a rooftop bar, a bakery, a restaurant and Carrosserie (French for bodywork), a bistro whose counter is made from shaped car-body sheet metal, finished with a chameleon-effect paint. Work on the site is complete, though construction related to the redevelopment of Place Sainctelette surrounding it is still under way and scheduled to continue until the end of 2027.
Questions over funding
The run-up to Kanal’s opening has not been without controversy and challenges. Kanal’s managing director, Yves Goldstein, announced earlier this year that he would step down and he is due to leave his position on Monday (30 November). A statement from the Brussels-Capital Region, the executive body that established the museum, said in September: “The parties acknowledge a difference of opinion regarding the future of Kanal.” His replacement is yet to be announced.
There have meanwhile been years of debate over the institution’s cost, funding and institutional partnerships. The initial investment budget of €150m (€125m for the works and €25m for studies), set out by the Brussels-Capital region in 2017, rose to around €230m. In May 2026, the region granted the Kanal Foundation, established in 2017 to operate the institution, a €60m loan to help complete the construction works and ensure the museum could open as planned. The budget provided for the ongoing operating of the museum, initially projected at €35m a year, was reduced to €28m in 2026 and is projected to fall to €24m in 2027, €22m in 2028 and €10m in 2029. Brussels’ regional government has previously told The Art Newspaper that private investors will be needed from 2028.
The five-year partnership with the Centre Pompidou will cost around €2m a year. Critics have questioned the expense and the decision more generally of partnering with a Paris institution rather than with Brussels-based organisations. Regional politician Benjamin Dalle has described Kanal as a “top-down political project”, arguing that it should have started with local artists and communities. The Fédération des arts plastiques has raised concerns about the place of Belgian artists in the programme, acquisitions and support for emerging practitioners. Kanal has been approached for comment.
Redzisz, however, has defended the museum’s role as a cultural resource for Brussels and its community. “This museum has an obligation to speak as much to locality as to contribute to global debate,” she told The Art Newspaper in October. That approach is reflected in Kanal–Centre Pompidou’s main inaugural exhibition, in which loans from Centre Pompidou mix with others from international institutions as well as works from the Kanal Foundation. The foundation has a particular focus on contemporary artists connected to Belgium—such as Sammy Baloji, Edith Dekyndt and Aglaia Konrad.
The show, titled A Truly Immense Journey, features 350 works across three levels. Marcel Duchamp’s Boîte-en-valise, lent by a Belgian private collector, is placed in dialogue with a version of Alberto Giacometti’s L’Homme qui marche I. Kader Attia’s Untitled (Ghardaïa) (2009), a model of a city made from couscous, borrowed from Tate, is shown alongside two portraits of Leonie Ngoie, a Belgian woman of Congolese descent, photographed by the Belgian artist Chrystel Mukeba against an Art Nouveau backdrop by the Belgian architect and designer Victor Horta.
Other exhibitions and projects are spread across the Kanal-Centre Pompidou house. No Show, orchestrated by the Brussels-based artist duo Deborah Bowmann and musician Maoupa Mazzocchetti, brings together around 20 artists from the Belgian capital, all of whom are under 40. Clémentine Deliss’s Department of Traps features 70 objects and paintings, including nets, snares, decoys and trompe-l’œil works, deriving from 11 Brussels museums.
A key part of the museum’s strategy is to involve the public directly in its programme. The Antwerp-based Nigerian artist Otobong Nkanga, for instance, has created an installation of wooden looms in Hall 2, inviting participants to weave together and contribute to a collective work of art. Nearly 200 pupils from four neighbouring schools have, meanwhile, contributed to writing exhibition labels. “Inclusivity is the best way for the public to make the place their own,” Kasia Redzisz told The Art Newspaper in January.
By 2030, Kanal expects to attract 550,000 visitors a year.

https://taz.de/Nach-Rauswurf-von-Vanessa.title: Nach Rauswurf von Vanessa Emde: Fahrplan Richtung Rot-Grün-Rot
https://taz.de/Nach-Rauswurf-von-Vanessa.author: Stefan Alberti
https://taz.de/Nach-Rauswurf-von-Vanessa.text:
Nach Rauswurf von Vanessa Emde: Fahrplan Richtung Rot-Grün-Rot
Die Bedingung von Grünen und SPD für eine Koalition mit der Linkspartei in Berlin war Vanessa Emdes Fraktionsausschluss. Und jetzt?
Zwei Monate. So lange dauert es auch bei einem – aus Sicht der beteiligten Parteien – bestmöglichen Verlauf, bis Elif Eralp in Berlin erste linke Regierende Bürgermeisterin sein könnte. Nach dem Fraktionsausschluss der Linken-Abgeordneten Vanessa Emde, die das Existenzrecht Israels verneint, richtet sich der Blick nun tatsächlich wieder auf den Tag, an dem Eralp Regierungschefin einer rot-grün-roten Koalition werden könnte: am 28. Januar, wenn es schnell läuft, oder mit einer Sondersitzung des Parlaments sogar schon eine Woche früher.
Ohne den Fraktionsausschluss von Emde hätten weder die Grünen und noch weniger die SPD mit der Linkspartei koalieren wollen. Auch für den Fall weiterer als antisemitisch empfundener Äußerungen sagte SPD-Landeschef Steffen Krach am Mittwoch: „Dann wird es wieder Ausschlüsse geben, das ist klar vereinbart.“
14 Facharbeitsgruppen haben seit Anfang November über alle Bereiche der Berliner Landespolitik, von Wohnen über Kultur und Verkehr, verhandelt. Der entscheidende Schritt ist, daraus einen stimmigen Koalitionsvertrag zu machen. Diese Aufgabe wird ab dem 1. Dezember der sogenannten Dachgruppe vorbehalten sein, einem 24-köpfigen Gremium mit allen Partei- und Fraktionschefs.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Bis Weihnachten, und wenn nötig auch über die Feiertage sollen sie ausverhandeln, was bei extrem leeren Kassen möglich ist, ohne zahlreiche Wahlversprechen wieder einkassieren zu müssen. Denn im Berliner Landeshaushalt fehlen ab dem Jahr 2028 fast 5 Milliarden Euro, was rund ein Achtel des gesamten Haushalts ausmacht.
Das bedeutet, dass auch die Linkspartei womöglich nicht um Kürzungen bei den Sozialausgaben herumkäme – was der Basis nicht leicht zu vermitteln wäre. Über einen Koalitionseintritt entscheidet bei der Linkspartei die Basis, bei SPD und Grünen ebenfalls.
Während bei den Grünen ein deutliches Ja zu erwarten ist, wirkt die Lage bei Linkspartei und SPD weniger klar. Teile des binnen zwei Jahren sprunghaft von knapp 8.000 auf rund 20.000 Mitglieder gewachsenen Linken-Landesverbands könnten sich wegen des Ausschlusses von Emde und drohender Haushaltskürzungen verärgert zeigen. Ihnen wird die Parteiführung Anfang Januar deutliche Vorteile eines Koalitionsvertrags präsentieren müssen.
Bei der SPD wiederum stemmt sich in einem bundesweit so noch nicht erlebten Szenario das bekannteste Gesicht des Berliner Landesverbands als amtierende Ministerin gegen ein rot-grün-rotes Bündnis. Wirtschaftssenatorin Franziska Giffey mag wegen antisemitischer Tendenzen, Verbindungen zur organisierten Kriminalität und auch einem eher ablehnenden Verhältnis zur Polizei nicht mit der Linkspartei koalieren.
Giffey schwebt eine links-grüne Minderheitsregierung vor, ohne die SPD. „Dann sollen Linke und Grüne in einer Minderheitsregierung eben zeigen, welche Versprechen sie wirklich halten können“, sagte Giffey jüngst im taz-Interview. Ob sie mit ihrer Argumentation Erfolg hat, wird sich Mitte Januar zeigen, wenn das über zwei Wochen laufende digitale SPD-Mitgliedervotum endet.
Noch nicht fest terminiert, aber für den gleichen Zeitraum anvisiert ist der Mitgliederentscheid bei der Linkspartei. Die Grünen erheben online nur ein sogenanntes Meinungsbild und entscheiden – Stand jetzt – offiziell bei einer Landesdelegiertenkonferenz am 16. Januar. Dieser Parteitag ist nach dem Selbstverständnis der Berliner Grünen – „Basis ist Boss“ – klar angehalten, das Onlinevotum zu übernehmen.
Gibt es bei allen drei Parteien Zustimmung, wäre der Einzug von Elif Eralp ins Rote Rathaus, die Berliner Regierungszentrale, in zweifacher Hinsicht eine Premiere: Noch nie besetzte die Linkspartei dort den Spitzenposten. Und es gab noch nie jemanden mit Migrationsgeschichte in diesem Amt.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.title: Free Jazz | Trespassing Rooms: Ich packe meinen Tourkoffer
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.author: Robert Mießner
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.text:
- Kultur
- Free Jazz
Trespassing Rooms: Ich packe meinen Tourkoffer
Die Bassistin Isabel Rößler und der Drummer Samuel Hall sind Trespassing Rooms. Ihre Platte »Stimultan« ist der perfekte Start in den Tag.
Neulich hatte die Berliner Bassistin Isabel Rößler einen begeisterten Hifi-Nerd an der Strippe. Beide waren sich auf einer Tontechnik-Messe begegnet. Sie hatte ihm eine Schallplatte mitgegeben. Diese sei das »Salz in seiner Sammlung« geworden, sagte er über »Stimultan«, das Debüt Isabel Rößlers und des Drummers Samuel Hall im Duo Trespassing Rooms.
Rößler und Hall spielen Jazz und Impro, also eine Musik, die gemeinhin nicht so einfach runtergeht. Aber, meinte der neugewonnene Fan, ihm hätten Trespassing Rooms das Tor zu dieser vertrackten Musik erst richtig geöffnet.
Was eine Platte von gerade einmal 22 Minuten Spieldauer mit fünf Songs vermag! »Stimultan« kommt in einem heutzutage ungewohnten Format, ist als Zehn-Zoll-Vinyl keine Single mehr, aber noch keine LP. Dabei ist das ein höchst eleganter Knicks vor der Jazzgeschichte: Das Zehn-Zoll-Format half Ende der 40er, Anfang der 50er Jahre beim Übergang von den Schellackplatten zum Mikrorillenvinyl und bot mehr Spielzeit. Beispielsweise sind die legendären Dial- und Savoy-Sessions des Bebop-Pioniers Charlie Parker, mit denen der Jazz hörbar Zähne zeigte, zuerst auf zehn Zoll erschienen.
Rößler hat noch mehr Argumente für das Format. Das eine ist praktischer Natur: »Die Platten passen besser in den Tourkoffer.« Tatsächlich liest sich ihr Konzertkalender, als seien sie und ihr Kontrabass ununterbrochen quer durchs ganze Land unterwegs.
»Weshalb tut man sich das an, schleppt das dicke Ding durch die Gegend und ist immer nur der Sideman, die Sidewoman?«, fragt sie sich schon mal und fährt doch wieder los. »Stimultan« könnte dabei noch mehr Tore öffnen. »Die Zehn-Zoll ist nicht zu langatmig, dafür prägnant«, meint Rößler und fügt hinzu: »Durch die kompakte Länge machen wir Impro zugänglicher.«
Nun ist »Stimultan« nicht Free Jazz to go, hat aber das Zeug zum Start in den Tag, wenn es einmal nicht das Morgenmagazin sein soll. Der Auftakt »Sleeper Hold« ist noch ganz behutsam. Samuel Hall lässt Glöckchen Roulette drehen, Rößler spielt einen hypnotischen Pendelton auf dem Bass. Dann gehen die Geräusche auf. Im »Echokessel« wechselt Rößler zwischen gezupft und gestrichen, Hall traut sich Breaks, die man vom Hardrock zu kennen meint. »Bones In The Curtains Wake The Sleeper«, toller Songtitel, eröffnet die B-Seite als Ruhepol. Durch die »Funkmulde« geht es zum Titelstück »Stimultan«, einem bewegten und bewegenden Panorama.
Das Duo Rößler und Hall kann innerhalb weniger Momente von der Intimität eines Kammerkonzerts zur Wucht einer Band wechseln, ohne dabei vor den Kopf zu stoßen. Die Besetzung Bass und Schlagzeug mag wie eine weitere Ungewöhnlichkeit anmuten, kommt aber aus einer Tradition. So haben Charles Mingus und Max Roach die »Percussion Discussion« eingespielt. Das irre Duett des Bassisten und des Drummers ist 1955 auf dem Album »Mingus At The Bohemia« erschienen. Das dazugehörige Label Debut Records darf übrigens als eines der ersten Independent-Labels in Eigenregie der Musiker gelten. Zum Thema Vorbild und Geschichte wirft Rößler ein: »Nur weil jemand das vorher schon gemacht hat, ist dein eigener Gedanke weniger deiner?«
»No Trespassing« steht im Englischen übrigens für »Zutritt verboten«. Rößler sagt, sie wolle »Räume durchstreifen«. Auf dem Albumcover geschieht genau das. Es zeigt ein Raumkaleidoskop des Künstlers Christoph Kühl. Das Original hat exakt die Größe eines Zehn-Zoll-Covers. Und auf diesem Weg geben Trespassing Rooms ihrem antielitären Free Jazz noch ein erschwingliches Kunstwerk mit in die Welt.
Trespassing Rooms: »Stimultan« (Ma Records)

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/27/yell.title: The Far Right Wants to Kill Wolves Whenever and However They Please
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/27/yell.author: The Intercept Briefing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/27/yell.text:
The reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the 1990s is one of the most celebrated conservation comeback stories in history, thanks to the Endangered Species Act. Recently, however, wolves became a political football in a time of shifting politics in Montana.
“It’s a barometer. What somebody feels about wolves might tell you what they feel about many other aspects of American political life,” says investigative journalist Ryan Devereaux.
This week on The Intercept Briefing, senior editor Ali Gharib and Devereaux discuss the reporting in his new book, “The Hunt: A True Story of Resurrection and Retribution in the West,” which documents how a 2021–2022 hunt became one of the deadliest assaults on Yellowstone’s wolves since the animals were completely wiped out around 100 years ago.
“These were groups who gathered around the idea that reintroduction was not only a mistake, but that extirpation was correct and that we should return to the days of a wolf-free West,” says Devereaux.
The successful passage of environmental protections in the ’70s had “also spawned a counterrevolution,” he adds. In Donald Trump’s second presidential term, many of those same anti-Endangered Species Act and anti-federal regulation figures now hold powerful positions in the agencies tasked with protecting wildlife and public lands.
“A lot of what they planned to do was laid out in Project 2025, the planning document that laid out the blueprint for what Trump 2.0 would look like,” notes Devereaux. “In fact, if you go back and read the Department of Interior section of that document, you’ll see that the reintroduction of wolves under the Clinton administration is held up as the shining example of the way in which a network of liberals and environmentalists have ruined the West and the federal government has overstepped its bounds.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.
Transcript
Ali Gharib: Welcome to The Intercept Briefing. I’m Ali Gharib, a senior editor at The Intercept.
Today on The Briefing, we’re going to be talking about — drum roll — politics. But it’s a different type of politics than we’ve discussed here before. It’s the politics of wolves in the lower 48 states. A book on this very subject, “The Hunt: A True Story of Resurrection and Retribution in the West,” recently came out from Avid Reader Press. Its author, Ryan Devereaux, will be joining us to talk about ground zero in the political war over wolves: Yellowstone National Park.
Wolves were reintroduced into the park in the 1990s in what’s largely considered to be the greatest conservation success in history. But they became a political football as their presence was assailed, often with deadly violence by the far right.
The 2021–2022 hunt itself was the deadliest assault on wolves around Yellowstone National Park since the animals were completely wiped out around 100 years ago. Some 25 Yellowstone wolves were killed, about a fifth of the park’s population, with an entire pack wiped out completely. Hunting is illegal in national parks, of course, so most of this hunting came right along the edge of the park in the public land surrounding it.
The investigative story that gave rise to Ryan’s book was published by The Intercept in 2022, the year the hunt concluded. The article revealed that a park ranger had shot and killed the last wolf taken in the hunt himself, right at the knife’s edge by mere minutes of the end of the official hunt. In The Intercept article, Ryan also revealed a major probe by the Park Service’s internal investigative wing into this kill.
The investigative report, though, was largely redacted. Since that article was published in 2022, Ryan and The Intercept won a lawsuit to release much of the file. The book is chock-full of new, never-before-seen material on the hunt, on the ranger’s kill. Fascinating stuff. I couldn’t recommend this book more highly. It’s informative, it’s exciting, and like all great journalism, it tells the gripping story of this hunt, which illuminates much larger truths about the world we’re living in today.
Ryan was a longtime investigative reporter at The Intercept, but today he’s doing his work at ProPublica, where you can read his latest material as it comes out.
Ryan, welcome to the Intercept Briefing.
Ryan Devereaux: Thanks so much for having me.
AG: Let’s get right to it, Ryan. As we’ve talked about before, and as you’ve written, this is really a story that’s as old as all the myths about the big bad wolf that Europeans brought with them to what would later become known as the Americas.
But the episode of wolf history in the U.S. that you write about really starts to kick into high gear in the 1990s, when wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone Park. Can you tell us about why there were no wolves in the park and just touch on the program about how to get them back?
RD: The story is a long one, but I’ll try to keep it brief.
When Europeans arrived here in North America, they brought with them a lot of cultural, spiritual, and religious baggage from the Old World relating to wilderness, and this idea that wilderness was a kind of space that needed to be tamed, conquered, and made productive.
And to do that required moving out of the way the Native folks that they encountered when they got here, as well as much of the native wildlife, especially predators and wolves in particular — having featured prominently in the Bible and lots of European mythology as a symbol of evil and Satan — were right at the top of the list for extirpation.
As the settlers marched West, they wiped out wolves wherever they found them. But the system was sort of ad hoc up until the early 1900s, when the federal government got involved and undertook a massive targeted killing program across the Lower 48 that resulted in extirpation by the 1920s and 1930s, including in Yellowstone National Park.
As this was unfolding, new understandings of the role that species play vis-a-vis one another in ecosystems was beginning to flourish. A new field of ecology was being born. By the 1960s, Americans were starting to have much different understandings of the roles that predators played in ecosystems.
By the 1970s, you had the environmental movement in full swing, and the passage of a whole bunch of new critical federal laws, including the Endangered Species Act. The ESA is what paved the way to wolf reintroduction in the 1990s. So it happened in January 1995 in Yellowstone National Park, as well as the wilderness of Idaho just to the west.
Dozens of wolves captured in the Canadian Rockies were transported to Yellowstone National Park. They were welcomed with schoolchildren on the side of the road there in Gardiner, which is the northern gateway to the park in southwest Montana, but also a ton of controversy. This was unfolding in the mid-1990s. 1994, the year before, was the Republican revolution, the first time that the GOP had taken control of Congress in decades, a flowering of culture-war battles in American political life. And this issue — this initiative — in the West became the touchstone symbol of the growing divide between segments of the population in the Northern Rockies.
AG: That was the backdrop of the changes in politics, sort of proto-MAGA era, right? These changes in Montana really came to fruition in this century, when Montana went from being a purple state with eclectic politics to being much more in the kind of MAGA evangelical stronghold world, which led to the rise of one of the central figures of your book, the governor of Montana: Greg Gianforte.
Can you talk about, briefly, the shifts in Montana politics and how Gianforte came to power?
RD: Yeah, it’s a fascinating story, and in many ways, Gianforte is representative of the changes that Montana in particular has experienced over the last three decades. He arrived in the state in 1995, in fact, the same year that the wolves were reintroduced — and he came amid this larger wave of new arrivals to the region.
They’re sometimes known as the “modem cowboys.” These were well-to-do individuals who realized that they could do their jobs free from the coastal environments that they had historically lived in because technology was allowing them to do so. Gianforte has spoken about this specifically.
He was a tech executive who made his money in software development in the Bozeman area. He was extraordinarily successful in doing so, and he came in at this time in the late ’90s, into the 2000s, into the 2010s, making a lot of money in tech, and then deciding he wanted to move into politics after he sold his company.
He spent a lot of his own fortune in attempts to run for office as a governor and in Congress. Some folks might remember a few years back, Gianforte first broke into the national spotlight when he choke-slammed a journalist who had asked him a question about healthcare — and then he won his special congressional race the next day. This was just after Trump had come in the first time.
[Gianforte] manages to successfully run for governor in the Covid, racial justice protest summer of 2020, and he takes office in 2021. What that does is change a tradition of ticket-splitting that had held firm in Montana for about a decade and a half. The state hadn’t had a Republican governor since the Bush administration.
What that allows, with respect to wolves, is Republican lawmakers who had been fighting ever since the 1995 reintroduction for a much heavier hand in wolf management to put forward a number of bills that would really aim to slash the state’s wolf population dramatically and see them green-lit by the governor. That’s essentially what happens over the next several months in the 2021 legislative session.
There’s also an incident involving Gianforte’s own interest in hunting a wolf that kicks off that year — I can talk about that as well, if it sounds interesting. But that’s the backdrop to how all of this began to unfold in 2021 and led to the hunt that I write about in the book.
AG: Yeah, Ryan, I’d love to hear you talk about the incident involving Gianforte. It was just within a month of him taking office, right?
RD: That’s right. The governor, shortly after taking office, killed a Yellowstone wolf, a radio-collared Yellowstone wolf.
Not only that, he killed a Yellowstone wolf on the property of a campaign donor who owns a mega-ranch in the Paradise Valley, which is this extraordinary valley that runs from around the Livingston area down to the park’s gateway, the sort of setting of “Yellowstone,” the TV show.
Word spread in the state that this had happened. The governor had killed a wolf. The state’s fish and wildlife department – whenever somebody kills a wolf legally, they have to register with the state. Game wardens have to check out the situation, sign off on it. Gianforte called his wolf in. And I write about the head of wildlife law enforcement for the state realizing it’s going to be up to him to check in the governor’s wolf kill.
There is an alleged attempt by the governor and his partner in the wolf hunt to shift responsibility for the kill from the governor to his hunting partner. It was discovered during the course of looking into things by the fish and wildlife department that the governor had failed to take a requisite trapping course prior to killing this wolf.
The governor and his buddy have insisted that everything that they did was aboveboard here, but this killing of a park wolf — a radio-collared wolf, no less — right at the beginning of his tenure, set the tone in many ways for what was to follow. The alleged attempt at a cover-up didn’t come out until much, much later. I had discovered it early in the course of my reporting. But yeah, that was the big opening event.
After that you saw Gianforte sign a number of bills with respect to wolves that would allow a whole host of new measures, including night hunting, hunting over bait, hunting with night-vision goggles, and most critically, as it pertains to this story, the elimination of hunting quotas north of Yellowstone.
There’s two districts north of the park. The quotas before the governor came in were one in each district, and after he took office and after this legislative session, there were no limits whatsoever.
AG: This is crucial to your book, and one of the reasons I love this Gianforte story is that there were these meager regulations, and he, according to the citation that he got, wasn’t even able to follow them for this wolf that he trapped himself in early 2021.
By late 2021, the entire ground has shifted, and even these regulations that he wasn’t able to follow are gone, and everything has been undone.
There are these proposals that come from the laws that Gianforte signed, and they have to pass through the Fish, Wildlife, and Parks Commission in Montana, which is the regulatory body for protecting wildlife in the state, including administering all the hunts. This is not a model unique to Montana, but the bureaucracy of FWP is overseen by a commission. The commission is assigned by the governor.
But FWP itself was storied, not only in the region, but across the country for being extremely rigorously based in science in Montana. That was something that just in the span of a very short time from Gianforte taking office was completely turned on its head, and instead we had a very anti-science perspective that we’re still seeing with regard to the politics of endangered species in the country.
But can you talk about FWP and how, and the options they were presented with, and how Gianforte’s FWP went whole hog on wiping out regulations?
RD: The story with wildlife governance, like so many bureaucracies, it has a deep history. In the West, it has something to do with our settler expansionist roots.
As settlers moved West, there’s this mass killing of wildlife along the way. It’s not just wolves, and it’s not just bison killing, which were killed by the tens of millions. As settlers put down roots in what would become these western states, they tore into local game populations.
They created game markets where the meat and hides of wildlife were sold by the ton. It became evident fairly early on in the late 1800s, early 1900s, that this was not sustainable. Wildlife was starting to disappear, including in states like Montana. Nascent government bodies were formed to address this issue.
States created state fish and wildlife departments, and as you described, they created these game commissions, these fish and wildlife commissions, to set the rules and regulations for those departments. The model’s pretty much the same across the country, and especially in the West. These commissions tend to be populated by, often, folks who’ve contributed to the governor who appoints them. In many cases, they serve at will.
Across the country, the qualifications for serving on these commissions vary, but it’s actually somewhat rare for commissioners to be required to have any background in wildlife management, biology, and science. Typically, historically, they’ve represented industries that have a stake in wildlife. That’s big game hunting industries, livestock production, that sort of thing. That trend has remained a constant throughout history and throughout the West.
Montana as a state and its Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks —everybody knows as FWP — as you described, became a model in the mid-1900s of progressive, science-based wildlife management.
Because the new arrivals to the state dug so deep into the wildlife populations, the fish and wildlife department took it upon themselves to start reintroducing different types of huntable species. They were pretty successful with this, actually quite successful. They were among the first departments in the country to require that their biologists have a master’s degree.
It was the kind of place where if you were interested in doing high-quality scientific wildlife management work at the state level, Montana was the place to be. You had this incredible range of species, and you had a department that was serious about its science. The folks who went to work there prided themselves, especially the biologists, on their ability to be self-sufficient, to be in their communities, to know what their communities needed, what they wanted, and what they expected from wildlife management policy in their area.
I’m getting all of this based on a number of people who I interviewed who devoted their careers to this department, and what they described as a change — the political change — in Montana were new rules that prohibited them from speaking directly to their commissioner about policy decisions. A feeling that they were being muzzled and that their actual views on what policies should look like weren’t being heard, and that those decisions were instead being made in Helena, the state capital, by lawmakers.
This was particularly pronounced and particularly evident in the way that the policy was formed around wolf management in 2021. You had lawmakers, mostly from Northwest Montana, which is a different scene ecologically, socially, politically, economically than Southwest Montana, creating wolf policy for the entire state based on arguments that were frankly pretty flimsy.
Those arguments were turned into law, which were turned into policy that the department had to implement. And this was deeply frustrating for career biologists who worked in some of these places in Southwest Montana, where the issues with wolves, livestock, elk were different than they are in Northwest Montana. It was a really deep and, in many cases, profoundly upsetting experience for a lot of career biologists in the state.
AG: OK, so Ryan, the climactic action of this bureaucratic wrangling to deregulate wolf hunts happens with a vote by the Fish and Wildlife Commission.
On a personal note, Ryan and I have spent a lot of time in Southwest Montana and especially camping in Yellowstone Park. And on the day this vote was held, we were actually in a parking lot on Slough Creek, this area northwest of the park, the Lamar Valley, known as one of the best wildlife spotting places in the country, if not the world, with a Ford van that wouldn’t start — and a bunch of wolves running around.
This wasn’t like spotting scopes from 300 yards. This was like, we were looking at them with our naked eye, crossing rivers. It was really a remarkable thing. What had happened that summer was that one bison had gored another to death, and the park rangers had moved the carcass a little bit further from the road, but still close enough that it was within full view, and it just became — what longtime wolf observers have said — was the best wolf viewing time in their lifetimes.
Incredible numbers of people got to see these wolves. We were camping in the area. We heard them howl at night. We didn’t even care that the van wouldn’t start. We were just sitting there enjoying the sights and sounds of these wolves, and it was really a remarkable scene.
On that same day we were sitting there, the FWP commission was voting from three different options of what would be allowed — the extreme methods that would be allowed, less extreme to more extreme of wolf hunting. Can you talk briefly about that vote and what the different categories of regulations were?
RD: I’ll just add that was an extraordinary moment in time to be in the park. The park’s largest and most famous wolf pack. It was known as Junction Butte. They had 18 pups survive from the previous season, which is basically unheard of.
So the pack was going into this season with big numbers. Just the year before, the biologists involved in the reintroduction had written a book collectively marking the 25th anniversary of the reintroduction and all its achievements. They wrote about it describing how the story of reintroduction, the story of how the United States government went from a policy of wolf eradication to wolf reintroduction, was a story of a change of heart. It was a book that had this tone of accomplishment and a joy and a hard-won victory. All of that was about to come crashing down with the vote that you were describing.
Over the summer, the Fish and Wildlife Commission had put forward a slew of different ideas for how the hunt that winter could take shape. There were these hearings that were held, and members of the public came out in huge numbers. Wolf hearings in general bring out a lot of people. But there was a ton of public pushback against this direction that the commission was clearly drifting, which was toward extraordinarily heavy-handed wolf management.
On the day in question, there were, like you said, three options that were put forward — basically a light, medium, and hard wolf management regime. Biologists in the department felt like, after many years of conflict, they had settled on a suite of policies that was maintaining a steady population. People who wanted to hunt wolves were getting the opportunity to do so; a lot of the rancor over this issue had quieted down.
So their light option was basically keep the status quo. We’ll make a couple tweaks to satisfy new laws that were passed during the legislative session that we have to make because they’re legally required, but by and large we’ll stay the course.
The medium option incorporated, as you might expect, some of the heavy-handed measures that I described before that lawmakers were interested in implementing.
The heavy option was everything: Bring all of the tools to bear in an effort to reduce the state’s population to the greatest degree possible.
It was a heated hearing. The hard-liner, anti-wolf faction was roundly outnumbered by a whole host of local Montanans, including hunters, people from around the country who didn’t think that this was scientific and had no basis or justification based on the state’s own analysis.
Because a lot of these measures were justified on the basis of the claim that wolves were decimating the state’s elk population, when in fact there were more elk in Montana than there were at the time of reintroduction in 1995. According to some population biologists, there were probably as many there as were there in the past couple centuries.
In Paradise Valley, just north of the park, ranchers consistently complained about there being too many elk and the problems that that created for their line of work. In fact, even Gianforte, when he was running for governor, described how the overabundance of elk in southwest Montana was a problem.
So the core basis for the argument for going as hard as possible, it didn’t have a leg to stand on, and yet at the end of the day, the commission green-lit the most heavy-handed suite of wolf management options possible. That included all of the measures I described, as well as the elimination of quotas on Yellowstone’s border.
What that signaled to the relatively small but extraordinarily motivated cohort of hunters and trappers who live around the park was that it was “go time” and an opportunity that they had been waiting for a quarter century was finally there, an opportunity to punch back the wolf population in the park and everything it represented.
[Break]
AG: This is really crucial to your story, because this is part of the 2021 hunt. It was this extraordinary number of wolves killed, and much of it happened in the two districts north of the park, and half of those wolves that were killed were taken by just four people who are pretty known figures in this area as being extreme anti-wolf ideologues.
Which brings us to the titular hunt of your book. It’s an extraordinary moment, and it’s gone from this day you and I were watching the greatest wolf-watching experience, the culmination of 25 years of reintroduction — wolves just jaunting around in plain view of tourists like us in the park — to the winter of 2021–2022.
Can you just run down some of the devastating consequences for Yellowstone wolves of the hunt itself?
RD: To your point about the relatively small number of people who were participating in the hunt, it’s absolutely true. This is a small-town community, Gardiner, Montana, an unincorporated community.
Everybody knows everybody, and to a large degree, everybody knows what everybody else feels about wolves. It’s a barometer. What somebody feels about wolves might tell you what they feel about many other aspects of American political life. The most motivated of these guys, they didn’t keep their feelings about the reintroduction secret.
When Gianforte was running for governor, one of these guys posted photos of dead wolves in front of a “Make America Great Again” yard sign. On social media, their accounts abounded with photos of dead wolves; it was often couched in the language of saving elk and basically sticking it to the libs.
But while it was a rather small number of people doing the actual killing, the way that they would do it is cluster around a couple of key wildlife migration corridors that empty out of the park. Same places where hunters hunt other species, wolves follow their prey species through these corridors into the Gardiner area.
These are wide-open territories. These are wolves that could grow up in a national park. It’s not an area where you have to engage in some multi-day backpacking journey to get yourself a wolf. They’re coming out in the open, and they don’t know any better around people. These areas, one known as Beattie Gulch and another called Deckard Flats, became shooting galleries for wolves.
But to the point about, a small number of people engaging in that kind of activity, that is true. At the same time, however, it didn’t take a lot of research on my part to find online communities that were fairly substantial in number really rooting for this hunt to be absolutely as deadly as possible. Social media groups devoted to wolf hunting and trapping, not because they saw it in the way that some hunting groups devoted to other species like revel in the challenge or procuring their own meat for the winter. These were groups who gathered around the idea that reintroduction was not only a mistake, but that extirpation was correct and that we should return to the days of a wolf-free West.
When Gianforte and the Republicans in Montana gave the green light to this hunt, those groups were rejoicing and demanding the highest body count possible, and it started right away. Within the first week of the hunt, there were two pups and a yearling taken from that Junction Butte pack that you and I had watched right north of the park.
From there, it took a little time to get going through the fall, but by the winter, the rate of killing was starting to pick up. By the end of the year the season had already surpassed the previous deadliest season, in which I believe around a dozen wolves were killed, and there were still many weeks to go.
AG: I edited the original long investigation that you did for The Intercept. You got to talk about the park ranger who was involved in the hunt and what happened there. This was Beattie Gulch, this is the area right outside the park. The proximity plays a crucial role here in the last, literally, the last moments right at the edge of the legal territory of the wolf hunt and the subsequent National Park Service investigation.
Can you give us a quick rundown with leaving a little bit to pique readers’ interests of what happened with the park ranger?
RD: As this hunt was escalating and reaching its crescendo, there was one commissioner on Montana’s Fish and Wildlife Commission who was a holdover from the previous governorship, and he was responsible for the region that includes Yellowstone in southwest Montana.
He actually called for an emergency meeting about the extraordinarily high death toll resulting from the hunt and said, “We got to call this off.” Long story short, that effort was ultimately unsuccessful. And within a couple days, the biologists at Yellowstone National Park, the wolf team, had gotten word that a radio-collared wolf had been reported killed in the Beattie Gulch area.
That was not unusual. That’s how things had been going the entire season. But without giving away too much, there were some unusual elements to this situation. The wolf’s collar had indicated that it was inside the park when legal hunting hours in Montana closed that night. The route that the collar took after the hunting hours closed was somewhat suspect.
What ultimately came to light was that the wolf was taken by a veteran Yellowstone Park law enforcement ranger, perhaps the most veteran working in the park at the time, a ranger who had been in Yellowstone since 10 years before the wolves were reintroduced and was actually among a cohort of rangers who were assigned to protect the wolves when they were returned to their to the park.
This set off a series of events, which included a serious investigation executed by what is effectively the National Park Service’s equivalent to an FBI unit. What they call a “Tier 1” investigation was started, to look into the possibility that this ranger had been sharing the location of wolves to hunters outside of the park throughout the season, and also into the specifics of his hunt specifically.
I managed to obtain a large investigative file through a public records request when I first got this tip, and it confirmed the existence of the investigation. It included a couple maps, including where the wolf was taken, and confirmed that a Yellowstone ranger was the subject of the investigation.
But everything else in this nearly 300-page report was blacked out, redacted, as though it were some national security file. That was unusual to me, having reported in those contexts before, to see that level of secrecy around a wolf kill was surprising, to say the least.
I managed to speak to this ranger at length in a couple of interviews, and he spoke to me on the record in detail about what happened that night — the night of his kill. He denied that the wolf was taken after hunting hours, and in fact the state game warden confirmed his account, recording his hunt as having been completed just a few minutes before the hunting hours closed. The wolf was definitely taken outside of the park. I later visited the location where the wolf was killed.
It was right on the border, but nobody, as the ranger told me, knew that border better than he did. He was never charged with a crime. He retired as this investigation was running its course, but as this news started to percolate around Gardiner, among people in the know, especially in the park, especially among his now former colleagues [were] deeply, deeply upset. Because this wasn’t the first or second wolf killed in a normal hunting season. It was the 25th in the deadliest season that the park had ever seen, in a season that had pit Gianforte, the governor, against the manager, the superintendent of Yellowstone.
It was a decision made consciously. The ranger told me, look, I purchased a hunting license just like anybody else, I took advantage of an opportunity that was there. Wolves should be managed like any other species, and I chose to exercise my right to do so.
But to folks inside the park, it felt like something deeper and more painful. We published this investigation in the summer of 2022, and I still had a ton of questions about what was under those redactions, how truthful the ranger had been with me, how exactly was this investigation experienced by people who were working inside the park at the time.
Through collaboration with The Intercept, we filed a federal lawsuit seeking to repeal — remove some of those redactions — and we had a lot of success with that. I was able to unearth some new details that I’ll leave for readers to check out. But it added a lot more complexity and layers to this whole episode.
AG: We should shout out our attorney here, David Bralow, who helped out on that lawsuit, and I know is super, super proud of getting that stuff out there. It just adds, from the story we did to the section of your book that deals with this particular part of the wolf hunt, it’s just the rich detail there, it really reads like a thriller. It’s a lot of fun to pick it up, even having worked on the initial story.
That was the hunt. It was devastating. It was a sign of these changing politics. There’s a reason it’s the title of your book, right? It’s really at the heart of telling this story. But this is a much, much broader story. It’s a broader story about politics, and it’s a broader story about wildlife management. I have two questions to wrap up here that are throwing the story forward a little bit.
What’s happened since then with the wolf hunt? That was the 2021–2022 hunting season. What’s going on with wolves in Montana and Yellowstone; what’s the latest with the regulations? Has there been a come-to-Jesus moment? Is the course being stayed?
Then the other question — and this is a huge question — but this is one piece of a much larger battle about the roadless rule, about building new roads in Forest Service public lands, and about wilderness areas, about extractive industries in these public lands, about hunting, grazing, selling off public lands. The whole thing.
Public lands and wild spaces and wildlife are all being assailed from so many different directions. This is to say nothing of the dismantling of the Endangered Species Act and other large predators like the grizzly bear and what’s happening with their listing under the Endangered Species Act.
What set all this off was the delisting of the wolf as populations recovered from having the highest levels of protection from the ESA. Now we’re facing that with grizzly bears as well. Can you put this in the context of the broader fights happening over public land right now in the U.S.?
RD: To answer the first question, what’s going on with wolves in Yellowstone National Park and what happened with rules and regulations after the hunt. There are a number of organizations, companies, individuals whose livelihoods are built around the wolf population that recovered post-1995 in Yellowstone.
There’s an enormous wildlife watching industry that has cropped up and in some ways has supplanted or is supplanting the guided hunting industry that dominated that region when Yellowstone’s northern range was free of its native predators.
After the hunt, a coalition was formed of wildlife watching groups, hospitality industry folks, even some outfitters who aren’t hardcore anti-wolf to say that we care about this ecosystem being intact. It affects our livelihoods. Their group, Wild Livelihoods, commissioned a study to look at just how much wolf watching contributes to the local economy, and the estimate that they found was somewhere in the ballpark of $82 million a year going to the local economy. There is some trepidation among these folks in terms of using an economic argument to rein in overly aggressive wolf management policy.
These folks would rather be making an argument for the intrinsic value of these animals, but they also recognize that they live in a capitalist society, and money does talk. They took these arguments to the Fish and Wildlife Commission for the following season, and they were able to reinstate quotas north of the park.
They were not the 1 in 1 — the low 1 in 1 — quotas that existed prior to Gianforte’s election, but there was some level of restriction implemented. However, everything else, all of the other measures, the night hunting, snaring, baiting, all of that stuff still remained in place.
Across the rest of Montana, very little change. Year to year, legislative session to legislative session, the same actors who advocated for this ultra-aggressive hunt are showing up year after year in Helena, putting forward new bills.
They would like to see wolves across the state classified as a predator, which in the sort of parlance of wildlife governance has nothing to do with what an animal eats. It has everything to do with the kind of protections that they receive under the law. An animal classified as a predator, like a coyote, can be killed any time of year in any number by any means necessary. They’re also fighting for a yearlong hunting season, which would allow for the hunting of pups — which is critical if you want to really make a dent in a wildlife population. It’s already happening in Idaho.
As for the wolves themselves, in the park’s boundaries, there was a major disease outbreak over the past year that took out a big chunk of the population. So in terms of the number of wolves on the ground, it’s significantly lower than it was that year that you and I visited. So it’s a complicated story. Some wins for wolf advocates, some losses.
As for the bigger picture, one of the core threads that I chart in this book is how the 1970s environmental movement led to this slew of new federal environmental laws, the Endangered Species Act kind of being the shining example, and the shining example of Endangered Species Act initiatives being the reintroduction of wolves in the West.
But that moment in history also spawned a counterrevolution. It’s known as the Sagebrush Rebellion. But it also goes deeper than the Sagebrush rebels, where there was a coalescence of industry actors and conservatives in the West who saw these new federal regulations as constraining the power that they had over the region for generations. And they’ve been organizing and fighting back ever since.
[In] the 1980s, under the Reagan administration, they had the upper hand for quite a while. There’s a reason it took 20 years after the ESA was passed, after initial wolf recovery plans were kicked around, that it took before they were actually reintroduced.
There was an intense fight, and a lot of the figures who have been deeply involved in that anti-federal regulation, anti-ESA world have been vying to return to power ever since. With Trump’s second election, a number of those actors have assumed powerful positions in the federal government, the Department of Interior, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
A lot of what they planned to do was laid out in Project 2025, the planning document that laid out the blueprint for what Trump 2.0 would look like. In fact, if you go back and read the Department of Interior section of that document, you’ll see that the reintroduction of wolves under the Clinton administration is held up as the shining example of the way in which a network of liberals and environmentalists have ruined the West and the federal government has overstepped its bounds.
It is held up as an example of the kind of overreach that needs to be reined in. What we’ve seen since Trump has returned to office is a kind of attack on this whole suite of laws passed in the 1970s, the ESA right at the top of that list. This law, which has historically passed with huge bipartisan support and has historically remained one of the more popular environmental laws in the country, is under threat like never before. You see initiatives and species that are associated with that law also under threat, and that is certainly the case with wolves, also the case with public lands. All of these things are very interrelated, especially in the West.
AG: Ryan, we’re going to leave it there. Thanks for joining us. This is such a huge and important story for the world we’re living in. Everybody should go out and read this book. I loved it so much. It’s called “The Hunt: A True Story of Resurrection and Retribution in the West.” It’s available everywhere, but you should probably go pick it up at your local bookseller.
Thanks again, Ryan, for speaking to us and joining us on The Intercept Briefing.
RD: Thanks so much for having me.
AG: That does it for this episode. This episode was produced by Laura Flynn. Ben Muessig is our editor-in-chief. Maia Hibbett is the managing editor of The Intercept. Chelsea B. Coombs is our social media producer. Nara Shin is the copy editor. Will Stanton mixed the show, and the legal review, as always, is done by David Bralow. Slipstream provided our theme music.
The show and reporting at The Intercept doesn’t exist without you, our listeners and readers. Your donation, no matter the amount, makes a huge difference for us. Keep our investigations free and fearless at theintercept.com/join.
If you haven’t already, please subscribe to The Intercept Briefing wherever you listen to your pods, and please leave us a rating or a review. It really helps other listeners find us. Let us know what you think of this episode, or if you’d like to send us a general message, you can email us at podcast@theintercept.com. Someone will read it.
Until next time, I’m Ali Gharib. Thanks for listening.

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
Dans la sélection de « l’Humanité » cette semaine : un étonnant voyage de bovins Normands, une histoire d’amour et celle d’un écrivain passionné.
« Le voyage en Uruguay » : un petit troupeau sur l’océan
Voilà une étrange histoire agricole qui se déroule sur les océans. Avec deux vaches, trois taureaux, un veau et un garçon vacher. Telle est la trame de ce récit poétique merveilleux et intime écrit par Clément Hervieu-Léger, aujourd’hui administrateur général de la Comédie-Française. La pièce, créée en 2014 et reprise cet automne, est mise en scène par Daniel San Pedro.
Sur la scène, trois bottes de paille, quelques planches pour dire le pont d’un cargo mixte, c’est-à-dire transportant passagers et marchandises, des sceaux, des guindes (on ne dit jamais corde au théâtre). Nous voilà dans les années 1950 avec Philippe qui raconte, détaille, mime, explique. Il est incarné par le comédien Vincent Breton...

https://gothamist.com/news/next-on-the-p.title: Next on the Park Slope Food Coop agenda: lifting a COVID-era mask mandate
https://gothamist.com/news/next-on-the-p.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/next-on-the-p.text:
Members of the Park Slope Food Coop are wrestling with whether it’s time to finally lift a pandemic-era policy that requires shoppers to wear masks two days of the week.
On one side are members who argue the rule, which is in place on Wednesdays and Thursdays, is outdated and results in thousands of discarded surgical masks. Supporters of the mask mandate say the policy helps older and immunocompromised members feel safe, especially during cold and flu season.
The issue is up for discussion at the co-op’s next general meeting on Dec. 1. Previous gatherings have garnered national headlines over debates about whether the co-op should have Israeli tahini on its shelves as its government wages war in Gaza.
“It's stupid. It's wasteful,” co-op member Meredith Davis said Wednesday as she put on her mask. “It's just a holdover. It feels, like, slightly woke. It's bad.”
But many shoppers on the mask-mandatory day said they supported the policy.
“There's a lot of diseases in winter to worry about,” said Zach Gage, a Park Slope local, as he loaded Thanksgiving groceries onto his bicycle. “I have two kids. We're always thinking about dodging the flu. It just doesn't seem like a big deal to have masks two days a week.”
In fact, “ we should probably mask more places,” he said as he pedaled away.
The historic Brooklyn grocery store with more than 16,000 members has gone through several iterations of the mask mandate since the darkest days of the pandemic.
Like many businesses, co-op leaders required staff and shoppers to wear masks in 2020. The co-op lifted the policy in March 2023 after surveying about 5,000 members. The poll found 68% of respondents favored making masks optional, while 32% wanted to keep the mandate in place.
But some members pushed back, arguing for a mask requirement during specific days or shopping hours. At the co-op’s October 2023 general meeting, a majority of attendees voted to mandate masks on Wednesdays and Thursdays to support “immune-compromised or medically vulnerable members.”
Free surgical masks are now provided at the door. As shoppers leave, they discard the blue masks in a cardboard trash bin marked “mask recycling."
But that practice has raised concerns among some co-op members about the amount of litter generated through the mandate.
“There’s a massive environmental impact,” said Larry Linsey, a retired lawyer who’s one of the sponsors of the measure to make masking fully optional. He said the term recycling is inaccurate, and that the masks are disposed of like any other medical waste. “This single establishment throws away almost a quarter-million masks a year,” he said.
The co-op has purchased 188,000 masks since December 2025, according to Park Slope Food Coop General Coordinator Ann Herpel. She said it’s not clear how many were thrown out. The masks cost $7,800 to purchase, and another $2,500 for specialized disposal.
In addition to concerns about waste, Linsey argues recent studies have challenged the efficacy of universal masking as a public health measure. Studies also show that N95-style masks provide much better protection than the thin surgical masks provided by the co-op.
Linsey said he and his co-sponsors filed their proposal eight months ago and it’s just coming up for discussion. Under the co-op’s governing structure, policy changes require a discussion period before an official vote.
“I personally don't think that encouraging a policy that doesn't really protect anybody is being kind to them,” Linsey said. “I just think it's kind of pointless, honestly.”
Others disagree. On a Reddit thread that’s generated hundreds of comments, some users chided those advocating for ending the mandate.
“For most people it’s a slight inconvenience,” said Redditor cheesus_christ. “For disabled people, it’s an important and effective accommodation.”
Katrina Dodson, who joined the co-op this summer, agreed.
“I think it's nice to have at least one fixed period when people who are more sensitive can be guaranteed that everyone's going to mask,” she said.
Elijah Sivin, who was working a co-op shift, said he doubted the policy’s efficacy as a public health measure but supported it in spirit.
“I think what they're doing is an awkward and not very effective compromise,” he said. “It probably annoys more people than it helps.”
Retired member James Schlefer counts himself among the annoyed. “ It's unnecessary. The pandemic was three years ago,” he said.
Schlefer said he doesn’t usually go to co-op meetings but was planning to attend next week to voice his opinion.
“It is an imposition. I don't like wearing a mask unnecessarily, and if somebody is worried about that, they should wear a mask,” he said. “Or maybe not come to the co-op.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Scotland’s Wealthiest University Is in Crisis
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Henry Fernandez
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Scotland’s Wealthiest University Is in Crisis
The University of Edinburgh’s £140 million cuts threaten the institution’s intellectual life and Scottish identity. Students and staff are fighting back.
This fall, lecture halls that once held hundreds of students at the University of Edinburgh sat empty. LED screens outside large theaters and modest conference rooms glowed brightly with a daily calendar of lectures and tutorials that would not take place.
Scotland’s largest and wealthiest university ground to a halt following strikes led by its chapter of the University College Union (UCU), a group representing more than 100,000 higher-education workers across the United Kingdom.
The Edinburgh strike began on September 28 to protest a proposed £140 million in university cuts. The austerity measures will lead to the shuttering of close to 100 degree programs, and the union’s leadership calculates that around 1,800 of the university’s close to 18,000 employees stand to be axed. A reported £90 million of the cuts will come from slashing wages and staff.
Of the programs being eliminated, several deal with subjects core to Scotland’s cultural identity. The University of Edinburgh boasts the oldest Celtic and Scottish studies department in Scotland. Yet courses in Scottish literature, ethnology, and Celtic have admitted their final students. These cuts are part of necessary financial restructuring, according to university principal Sir Peter Mathieson, the head of the school.
The strike by lecturers, staff, and students reflect some existential questions with which universities across the world are contending. In an era of increasingly expensive higher education, wilting job markets for new graduates, and the looming threat of artificial intelligence taking our jobs (if not our lives), just what is a university for?
On September 24, before faculty were to strike, a deluge of students and staff stuffed two lecture halls—not for class, but for the first meeting of the Student and Staff Assembly. The assembly laid out the argument for why faculty were striking, and why the union opposed cuts. The crowd ranged from scraggly brunettes in keffiyehs to business students in rib-knit quarter-zips.
“We spend a lot of money on shiny buildings. We spend very little money on increasing staff pay,” Ben Goddard, a member in the mathematics department told the audience. “Staff costs are not to blame. Staff are the people who run the university, keep everything going, and give you your education. You do not learn from shiny buildings.”
In step with its contemporaries across the United Kingdom and broader Europe, Scotland’s universities are facing serious financial strain. In Scotland, drops in public funding, rising inflation, and diminishing international student populations have created a gap in funding of over £200 million. This problem is coalescing into a potentially existential threat for smaller schools. But Edinburgh, unlike its peers across Scotland, is not in an obviously dire position.
James Grey, the university’s chief financial officer, said during an April 2026 university business committee meeting that Edinburgh had an operating surplus of £20 million.
Grey stated that the surplus was primarily the result of “non-core activities, including better returns on investments.” What didn’t cause the surplus? “Core activities related to teaching and research.” In fact, according to Grey, teaching and research are “closer to break even or in deficit,” and there is a “pressing need to improve their financial performance.”
The real problem, according to the UCU, is irresponsible spending and opaque financial practices. Particularly puzzling to the union is that the university continues increasing capital expenditure to purchase and maintain its hundreds of properties rather than prioritizing the preservation of entire programs and potentially hundreds of staff members.
A £140 million slash would generate more capital for investment and operating costs, keeping the institution alive. But as university management stared down the barrel at these purportedly vital cuts, their spending jumped by a third.
A few dozen people huddled before Edinburgh’s Gordon Aikman lecture theatre, beneath a muddled gray sky, to recite Scottish poetry. Students and lecturers read from William Dunbar’s court writings to Norman MacCaig’s paean to an aunt who spoke Gaelic.
Over a dozen programs in Scottish and Celtic studies are being shut down by the university. After the current crop of first-years graduate, these programs will cease to exist. Before then, some staff in Celtic and Scottish studies are likely to be cut.
Part of the union’s strategy is to host alternative learning sessions to provide some educational content for students while lecturers strike. The reading was coordinated by the union in conjunction with the Scottish student’s association.
Edinburgh is one of Scotland’s four ancient universities, institutions that have survived from their inception in medieval, and in Edinburgh’s case, Renaissance-era Scotland into 2026. These institutions are world-class, with the universities of Edinburgh and Glasgow landing top-100 spots in the Quacquarelli Symonds global university rankings.
Scotland’s universities are tuition-free for students who grew up in Scotland, meaning there are thousands of guaranteed spots the government funds every year for Scottish students.
One of these students is Dana Freimute. Freimute immigrated to Scotland as a young girl, following Latvia’s financial crisis in 2008. Freimute grew up on a council estate—social housing—after her parents, once successful business owners in Latvia, left to give their children a steadier future.
Freimute describes education being a large part of her upbringing—her mother always read to her and engaged her intellectually, pushing her to be a top student. Now, Freimute is pursuing a joint degree in Spanish and art history at Edinburgh—becoming one of the few students in her community to study at the university.
Many of the programs the university is cutting are joint degrees, including Freimute’s. These programs allow students to study two subjects at one time, at the cost of one degree. The university says low enrollment is the major reason these programs are being cut; according to The Herald, a fifth of the programs on the chopping block had no enrollment. Freimute’s belief is that the slashing of joint-degree programs is a way for the university to make more money off students with more interests.
“If I’m a student who wants to study both Spanish and history of art, I would do a degree in Spanish first, so I would pay them for that degree and then I’d have to come back to university to study history of art again and pay them more,” Freimute said. “So they’re essentially getting double the income out of me.… The university is now looking more like a business than an educational institution…. I think it will just completely cut off the ladder for social mobility.”
The amount of funding Scotland gives its universities has not kept pace with inflation, according to a report by the Institute for Fiscal Studies. Many Scottish universities, especially the University of Edinburgh, heavily recruit international and English students to increase tuition revenue. The University of Edinburgh has the second-lowest population of Scottish students proportionally among Scottish universities.
The comparatively small number of Scottish students has led to a cultural stereotype that many Scottish students tend to be working-class in comparison to the posh English and internationals whom the university relies on for funding. The Scottish Society on Edinburgh’s campus started in 2024 as a response to Scottish students’ experiences of cultural and economic discrimination.
Dani Brady’s life has been shaped by Scotland’s past. A first-year student at Edinburgh, Brady grew up in Dunfermline, the nation’s ancient capital. The abbey in town holds the skeleton of Scottish king Robert the Bruce—or Braveheart. Brady’s father had a brief stint as a tour guide, and after he finished work she would sit and listen to him tell her about Scotland’s folklore, history and people. This led her to pursue a degree in Scottish ethnology and history.
So, on her first day, when the croons of bagpipes barreled across the university’s welcome ceremony, everything felt appropriately Scottish. But, when she heard about the cuts, the idea of Edinburgh as one of the Scottish institutions she’d grown up revering, changed.
“They were trying to give this impression of Scottishness without committing to the Scottish degrees, Scottish students, and Scottish traditions that came before all this,” Brady said. “No matter how small a course is, things should still continue. Universities used to only teach religious studies, and now they’re so expansive and teach so much. Why would you want to make something less inclusive, and less broad?”
Dr. Duncan Sneddon, a large man with long, dark hair, is a Celtic lecturer at Edinburgh. He told me the cuts are potentially lethal to Scottish fields of study. “Where will the next generation of scholars that carry us forward, carry our field of inquiry in new directions be?” he asked. “Where are they going to get the training and the expertise that they need if we’re not here to teach them?”
Sneddon says that he finds these cuts “baffling,” placing blame on the financial ideologies of university leadership that stand in direct contrast to what he sees as the purpose of a university. “A university is an intellectual community, where ideas can be pursued for their own sake, and where we remember things instead of actively choosing to forget them,” Sneddon said.
In a union office with a small boardroom cluttered with picket-posters, papers, and tea biscuits sat Courtney Stafford-Walter and Marion Lieutaud, vice presidents of Edinburgh’s chapter of the UCU.
Stafford-Walter, a lecturer in education studies, has the charm and style of a whimsical American schoolteacher—when I met her, she was wearing rainbow glasses. Lieutaud holds a steelier demeanor, but kindly offered me a cup of lemon tea before our interview.
They said this strike feels different from ones that have happened in years prior. Stafford-Walter told me that senior management, under the guidance of Sir Peter Mathieson, has refused to seriously negotiate with them about halting or minimizing staff cuts.
“We said, ‘If you make any movement on any of our demands, we will bring that to our membership,’ because we are so desperate to avoid the strike…and yet they said they had no flexibility,” Stafford-Walter said.
Mathieson became the university’s principal in 2014. Under his leadership, Edinburgh’s endowment has grown by tens of millions of pounds. The institution is now the third-wealthiest in the United Kingdom, behind Cambridge and Oxford.
“If you look at wealth, it’s very clear the university has never been wealthier than it is now. If you look at disposable income…we’re still in a very healthy place,” Lieutaud said. “If they continue to invest as much as they have been, eventually we’re going to have too much capital expenditure relative to income. The very simple answer is capital expenditure. They don’t need to make further capital expenditure.”
“It’s exactly the kind of moment where you should be using your reserves,” Lieutaud said. “We have three billions worth of them and they’re refusing to touch it.”
Mathieson went on BBC Radio to accuse the union of weaponizing students against the university, framing it as the enfant terrible, anti-establishment behavior of college students.
“It’s really disingenuous because we are the ones who spend all the time with the students. We are the ones who love our students,” Stafford-Walter said about Mathieson’s view. “This is not a moment where they can continue to pit the students and staff against one another. Because the truth is we are united in the same fight. Our working conditions are their learning conditions.”
“If Peter Matheson doesn’t come to work for five weeks, our students would never notice,” Stafford-Walter continued. “But if we don’t come to work for five weeks, they notice.”
Mathieson announced his resignation a few days after my interview with Stafford-Walter and Lieutaud. He will leave his post as principal and vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh in 2028.
By Tuesday October 20, a new activist group, “Students Against Scabs,” had occupied Gordon Aikman Lecture Theatre, jamming the revolving entrance doors with bins, chairs, and even a sack truck. They’d peppered the theatre with large banners demanding that the university divest from Israel, stop the program and staff cuts, and for the resignations of Sir Mathieson and the university’s provost, Kim Graham.
A notice from the local sheriff’s court, addressed to “the unauthorized occupiers,” ordering the protesters to leave was plastered on a side door.

“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
A lone security guard watched silently as some of the occupiers, clad in dark garb and balaclavas left through a side entrance. He counted four. I counted six. The guard told me he had just started the job a few days ago.
“Talk about a trial by fire,” I said.
He told me that the students would be allowed to hold the building for a few days, and if they were still there then they’d be physically removed. I tell him I’m shocked that any student group, especially those hanging up Palestinian flags, would be allowed to occupy an academic building for so long.
“You’re American. You guys probably would’ve had SWAT in there by now,” he said, chuckling.
Since the strike’s end on October 30, little has been resolved.
Students returned to class. The University of Edinburgh student newspaper uncovered that the university circumvented its democratic decision-making body, a Senate of 300 academic staff members, administrators, and students, to make the cuts. Students and staff dressed up as cows for a protest, accusing the university of treating its students as “cash cows.” The union and its student supporters effectively barred the university’s provost from an appointment to the board overseeing and advising on tens of millions in Edinburgh’s tourism taxes. The university is trudging along with its cuts anyway.
On November 18, the Student and Staff Assembly had its final meeting of the semester. The room was emptier than its standing-room-only first meeting, students and staff now occupying the front-end of the room. Lieutaud and Stafford-Walter ran the meeting.
A lecturer at the college of medicine and veterinary medicine announced that cuts in the college were further along than other schools. Teaching duties will be passed on and research ended. Union organizers announced that the university has still not come to the bargaining table with them. Next term is when many of the university’s cuts are thought to come into effect, changing the university’s scale and scope of study and leading to the unemployment of hundreds.
But still, for people in the room, there was hope. The meeting’s primary focus was to organize protests and events for next term. Organizers were told their tactics had frazzled senior management, and French student protesters currently blazing through Paris had pledged their support for the Edinburgh UCU’s actions.
“We’re dealing with management that’s incredibly stubborn,” Lieutaud said. “They have to feel like they’re being kicked on all corners and not getting a break.”
After the meeting, I sat with Stafford-Walter to ask about whether she thought this term’s strikes had been successful. “They refused to meet with us to negotiate throughout the entire five weeks,” she said. “We’ve taken a massive action, we’ve taken a huge pay cut, and those kinds of very clear and tangible goals like getting an agreement to to pause compulsory redundancies, didn’t happen. I think that’s been difficult for us to grapple with.”
But, she said, they’ve grown the size of their movement—increasing student participation in a way she hadn’t seen before. “Even though we don’t know what we can win, we do know what we can lose if we don’t fight.”
