https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.title: Batima Zaurbekova’s Textiles Meld Traditional Kazakh Techniques with Modernist Influences, Defying Easy Categorization
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.author: Maximilíano Durón
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.text:
How does an artist sustain five decades of artistic production while remaining faithful to her cultural heritage? For Batima Zaurbekova, one of Kazakhstan’s most respected artists, the answer seems to be an unrelenting commitment to her craft. “You can’t be lazy,” the 80-year-old artist told me during a recent conversation.
That maxim is borne out in “Threads of Heritage,” a retrospective of more than 80 works at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Her largest exhibition to date, it features the textiles she is known for as well as drawings and paintings. Curated by Alina Fedorovich, a curator at the Museum of Moscow, the exhibition traces a career in which tapestry becomes both a repository of cultural memory and a vehicle for artistic reinvention.
Rooted in traditional Kazakh textiles, her practice is also shaped by the influences of modernist painting and music, moving fluidly between abstraction and figuration and in turn, defying easy categorization. Her tapestries hold seemingly disparate influences, transforming traditional motifs into a distinct visual language. Ornamental Rug (1969), for example, revives motifs associated with horses, spiritual symbolism, and petroglyphs depicting mountain goats. Completed just after her graduation and the earliest work in the exhibition, Ornamental Rug provides a recognizable reference to the country’s landscape via the distinctive horns of the wild argali, a local mountain goat, while distilling these forms into rhythmic, stylized arrangements. The work’s title foregrounds the relationship between ornament and abstraction, suggesting how decorative forms can become a vehicle for modernist experimentation.
Zaurbekova grew up in the mountainous Zhambyl region of Kazakhstan, where textile-making was part of everyday life. She remembers watching older women create syrmak, traditional felt rugs, and kurak-korpe, patchwork quilts meaning “stitched from scraps.” Neighbors gathered to work, sing, cook, and share food, embodying the Kazakh tradition of asar, in which a community joins forces to help a household undertake a task, be it making a carpet or building a home.
Textile-making was as much a social practice as a technical one, transmitting skills and cultural knowledge across generations. This collective spirit is evoked in In the Yurt (1985), a weaving in which a maternal figure presides over the dastarkhan, the table prepared for guests. The yurt, a traditional felt dwelling associated with Kazakh nomadic life, becomes a symbol of hospitality, family, and belonging. Its ornaments merge with the surrounding figures, establishing a visual language equally rooted in the formal and the domestic.
In her youth, Zaurbekova had alternative ambitions for herself. “I really loved music, so I wanted to become a musician,” she recalled. However, her seamstress mother encouraged her to pursue painting instead. She is equally accomplished in oil painting and tapestry, and occasionally the same image is translated in both mediums.
Nevertheless, music has remained central to Zaurbekova’s life and practice, in which her visual compositions are animated by repetition, variation, and rhythm—the basic structure of music. This way of working is best observed in one gallery showing three works, each titled Composition and made in 1980, 2019, and 2024. Their stained-glass aesthetic, contrasting color planes, and rhythmic linear forms evoke Henri Matisse’s celebrated “Jazz” series. Undulating figures and vegetal motifs merge within an ornamental field, dissolving the distinction between figure and ground.
“Threads of Heritage” is being exhibited in dialogue with the museum’s collection of Kazakh decorative and applied art. Traditional felt objects, carpets, and ornaments establish the historical context out which Zaurbekova’s work emerges, while the installation reinforces the relationship between inherited forms and contemporary expression. Here, custom-built walls reference the architecture of the Khoja Ahmed Yasawi Mausoleum, an important historical monument whose forms recur in the artist’s imagery, like the monumental Antiquity (1993). The display also evokes the balbal, ancient stone monuments that connect contemporary life with earlier cultures.
The exhibition’s largest gallery showcases Zaurbekova’s technical mastery and evolving visual language. Each tapestry offers a dazzling array of color that boggles the mind. How, exactly, does she coax such subtle gradations from a seemingly limited collection of threads? “Selecting the right colors is a big part of the work—and it takes me a long time,” Zaurbekova explained. During the Soviet period, artists often dyed threads by hand, painstakingly creating transitions from darker to lighter shades. Although commercially produced threads from Belarus expanded her palette in the 1990s, Zaurbekova has continued to experiment, combining those threads and ones she has dyed to create colors all her own. “Kazakhstan, our land, is very rich, and this is represented in the rich colors of my work,” she told me.
Zaurbekova’s textiles are woven over several weeks to multiple months, and the artist still works for up to 18 hours a day. The vertical threads form the foundation of a given work, she explained, while horizontal threads of different colors construct the image. Through subtle variations in their combinations, Zaurbekova achieves tonal effects that can make woven surfaces appear almost painted. She is also deft at making alasha, a traditional yet simple Kazakh carpet.
Rather than presenting national identity as a fixed collection of symbols, her compositions transform familiar motifs through color and pattern. In keeping these traditions alive, Zaurbekova said she thinks “all of my work reflects our nationality and national pride.” Kazakhstan (1977) depicts themes of agriculture and collective labor. To make it, Zaurbekova used threads sourced from a Kazakh carpet manufacturer, working within the limitations of an existing palette to achieve subtle distinctions of tone. Her exacting yet delicate manipulation of the threads’ colors gives the woven surface a gentle vibration and shimmering quality. A work like this makes visible the precision and patience necessitated by such a craft.
A centerpiece of the exhibition is Vastness (1975), a large tapestry from the museum’s collection showing a bride associated with spring and Nauryz, the celebration of the spring equinox and new year. Around her, women gather at tables and a young man on horseback appears among the birds. Elsewhere, figures emerge from the surrounding forest, creating a dense tableau that feels as abstract as it is narrative. The exhibition’s final gallery focuses on the shanyrak, the circular wooden crown at the top of a traditional Kazakh yurt. A symbol of home and family, it serves an architectural motif representing womanhood. In Mother Earth (1984), connections between generations of women evoke the continuity of life and inherited knowledge. Zauberkova’s achievement lies not only in her sheer technical mastery, but in her ability to reinterpret Kazakh textile traditions through a vision that is unmistakably her own, creating work that is deeply rooted in its cultural origins while remaining formally inventive and alive.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ‘Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element’: Yuko Mohri on her exhibition of found objects at London's Barbican
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Vivienne Chow
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
After picking up the 2025 Calder Prize, the multidisciplinary Tokyo-based Yuko Mohri artist has been on a recent roll, opening institutional shows from Santander in Spain and her first US solo show in Miami Beach to bringing her 2024 Venice Biennale presentation home to her native Japan.
What you see is not stable: water leaks, gravity and the audience’s presence will change elements
Among the highlights is In Concert (until 24 January 2027), her solo exhibition at the Barbican Centre’s The Curve gallery in London. At the show’s core is a series of site-responsive kinetic and sound installations made with objects she found at the Barbican. These objects, either stored away or nearly tossed out, embed the history and memories of this famed cultural centre, which will be closed for a year from June 2028 for a £191m revamp ahead of its 50th anniversary in 2032. According to Mohri, the pieces represent an ongoing process that may lead to imperfection, which she finds more profound than a picture-perfect scenario.
The Art Newspaper: How did your Barbican residency come about?
Yuko Mohri: When I was approached for a project at The Curve, I discussed with Inês Geraldes Cardoso, the curator of this exhibition, the possibility of researching the Barbican Centre.
The Curve is a unique and challenging space, and they accept experimental projects with artists. I am not the kind of artist who needs to work within a white cube. I understand why they chose me to create something unique. I am, however, the kind of artist who needs time to understand the environment and identify interesting elements that already exist in that context. A research residency is necessary.
But rather than focusing on just this curved gallery space, I wanted to see what the Barbican really is. It is a huge centre involving many different departments and activities. Thousands of people are also living here in the attached residential complex.
After rounds of negotiations, I was offered a two-week residency to look for objects and meet the people living and working here. I got a temporary studio at The Pit, a small theatre space located in the basement.
What were your biggest discoveries?
The centre has many departments, but they seem very separate from each other and don’t have a lot of communication between them. But since they are going to have a major renovation, they want to revamp the centre’s system, too, and strengthen communication.
We started researching different departments and looked for objects across all the spaces. I wanted to collect objects from here that resonate with the space.
Among the most iconic ones are the original Barbican lamps featured throughout this exhibition. These were once used as street lamps surrounding the centre and also in the building. But as time went on, they were replaced with those of a new design. They were dusty and strange, but I immediately knew that I wanted to use them for my installation. So I spent a lot of time washing these lamps in my temporary studio.
The speakers that I use for the new iteration of the ongoing Decomposition series (begun 2021) located near the entrance to The Curve are old speakers from the Barbican. The found cables that I use to connect the fruit with the lamps and the sound are also very important to me. I also found these metal junk pieces that were discarded in a workshop, and I reappropriated them as triggers for the lamps in the installations in the middle part of the exhibition.
Throughout this project I met many people outside the gallery space, from engineers to the caretakers of the parking space. The extensive communication helped me connect with a lot of open-minded people who accept me and my work.
How do you relate the centre’s characteristics with your practice?
The Barbican has many water leaks. There’s also a leak of sound because The Curve wraps around the concert hall. So these leaky elements resonate with my practice, especially my ongoing Moré Moré (Leaky) series (begun 2017), which was inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations and how the staff contain these water leaks with temporary fixes using everyday items. I presented a version of this in Venice.
This time at the Barbican, I created a large-scale installation located towards the exit of The Curve, using found objects such as a pot, an umbrella, plastic bottles, Wellington boots, traffic cones and old water sinks designed for the Barbican apartments.
I also keep the space open and transparent by removing the covers on the entrances and the back so that people can see what’s going on there from the outside. I also exposed the inner layers of the walls to give people a peek into what is behind them.
Are you building an ecosystem within the Barbican that makes the inaudible heard and the invisible seen?
Instead of building, I see it as repairing. Inspired by attending concert rehearsals at the Barbican, I chose the title In Concert, which mirrors the Latin root consertare. It carries the meaning of repair and adjustment, resembling the process of making an organisation.
The process is also similar to making an installation. When I started, I had no idea how it would turn out eventually. I constantly make adjustments to the elements of my installations, like a conductor making adjustments to the tempo or the volume of the musical instruments. The title also reflects that what you see is not stable. Water leaks, gravity and the audience’s presence will change even some very tiny elements. It is not a finalised show. It’s an ongoing process.
Would you say that you are in control and at the same time you also let go?
I am a human being and I have a desire for a certain outcome. But somehow, it doesn’t always work. This trial and error process is a very learnable process for me.
We all have our expectations, but our society and environment have become increasingly unstable. For example, this summer Tokyo rained non-stop for a record 36 consecutive days. We need to adjust our lives. It’s also a necessity when we are based in Tokyo, constantly facing natural disasters like earthquakes. Japan has long been isolated, but now we have many immigrants. Our society is changing. I see this as a kind of training and accept these changing forces. It’s not necessarily about making things perfect. Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element.
Biography
Born: 1980
Lives and works: Tokyo
Education: 2004 BFA, Tama Art University; 2006 MFA, Tokyo University of the Arts.
Key shows: 2026 The Bass, Miami Beach; 2026 Yokohama Museum of Art; 2026 Centro Botín, Santander; 2025 Pirelli HangarBicocca, Milan; 2024 Japan Pavilion, Venice Biennale; 2023 14th Gwangju Biennale
Represented by: Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, New York; Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tokyo; Mother’s Tankstation, London; White Space, Beijing; Project Fulfill Art Space, Taipei
• Yuko Mohri: In Concert, Barbican Centre, London, until 24 January 2027

https://taz.de/Thinktank-Konferenz/!6233.title: Thinktank-Konferenz: Wenn die Rüstungsindustrie zur Debatte bittet
https://taz.de/Thinktank-Konferenz/!6233.author: Malte Steinmüller
https://taz.de/Thinktank-Konferenz/!6233.text:
Thinktank-Konferenz: Wenn die Rüstungsindustrie zur Debatte bittet
Ein US-Rüstungskonzern sponsert eine Berliner Sicherheitskonferenz. Vor Ort: Spitzenpolitiker und Lobbyisten, die sich bei der Aufrüstung einig sind.
Ist Europa bereit für Krieg? Auf einer von der Rüstungsindustrie gesponserten Konferenz in Berlin ging es unter anderem um diese Frage. Am 25. und 26. November trafen sich deutsche und internationale Politiker*innen mit Lobbyist*innen und Ökonom*innen, um über dieses und weitere Themen zu sprechen. Sie sprachen – und diskutierten nicht, denn größtenteils herrschte Einigkeit.
Die Veranstaltung organisierte der britische Thinktank Chatham House. Er finanziert sich unter anderem durch Mitgliedsbeiträge von Rüstungskonzernen und dem britischen Verteidigungsministerium. Im Lobbyregister des Bundestags hat die Denkfabrik einen Eintrag als Lobbyorganisation.
Speziell diese „Chatham House Berlin Conference 2026“ sponserten laut eigenen Angaben des Thinktanks zwei Partner: der US-Rüstungskonzern Northrop Grumman (drittgrößter Rüstungskonzern weltweit) und die Interessengemeinschaft Deutsche Luftwaffe – ein Verein, der von diversen Rüstungskonzernen gefördert wird.
Hochkarätige Politiker*innen vor Ort
Zu den Gesprächen erschienen deutsche Politiker in teils relevanten Positionen. Darunter Nils Schmid (SPD), parlamentarischer Staatssekretär des Bundesverteidigungsministeriums, Thomas Röwekamp (CDU), Vorsitzender des Verteidigungsausschusses, und Roderich Kiesewetter (CDU). Auch der ehemalige Grünen-Vizekanzler Joschka Fischer (heute Lobbyist) nahm an einem Podiumsgespräch teil.
Philip Steeg von Greenpeace würde die Veranstaltungen solcher Thinktanks als „erweiterte Lobbyarbeit“ bezeichnen. Er ist Investigativ-Rechercheur in der Nichtregierungsorganisation und beschäftigt sich seit Jahren mit Aufrüstung. Für eine Studie von 2023 recherchierte er viele fragwürdige Verbindungen zwischen der Politik, der Rüstungsindustrie und den Lobbyorganisationen. Erweiterte Lobbyarbeit definiert er als den Versuch von Rüstungskonzernen, die politischen Einstellungen, Stimmungen und Diskurse in der Bevölkerung und Politik langfristig zu beeinflussen.
Zu Beginn der Veranstaltung unterhält sich Staatssekretär Schmied mit einer Unterstaatssekretärin aus dem finnischen Außenministerium sowie den litauischen und bulgarischen stellvertretenden Außenministerinnen. Eine Moderatorin stellt ihnen die Frage, ob Europa bereit für Krieg sei und was die EU von den Ländern an der Nato-Ostgrenze „lernen“ könne über „gesamtgesellschaftliche Resilienz“.
Als positive Beispiele der „Resilienz“ dienen die allgemeine Wehrpflicht für Männer in Finnland und die hohen Verteidigungsausgaben in Litauen, welche bei über 5 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts liegen. Staatssekretär Schmied sagt dazu: „Was wir von unseren baltischen und nordischen Freunden lernen können, ist die enge Verflechtung und Einbindung des Militärs in die Gesellschaft.“ Alle sind sich einig, die EU-Bevölkerung müsse „resilienter“ werden. Damit das passiert, müsse die Politik immer wieder über die Bedrohung aus Russland sprechen, so Schmied auf Nachfrage aus dem Publikum.
Philip Steeg, Greenpeace-Rechercheur
„Ein Staatssekretär im Verteidigungsministerium hat einen erheblichen Einfluss auf das politische Tagesgeschäft der Bundesregierung“, sagt Greenpeace-Rechercheur Steeg. Deshalb sei es für Thinktanks sinnvoll, einen solch hochkarätigen Politiker einzuladen. Dabei gehe es nicht nur um die Podiumsgespräche: „Hintergründig findet mutmaßlich weiterer intimer Informationsaustausch statt und der ist ganz klar auch im Interesse des Thinktanks.“
In einem weiteren Panel sprechen Ökonom*innen mit dem Moderator Sir Simon Fraser über Europas angebliches wirtschaftliches Potenzial, wenn Bürokratie und Regulierung gesenkt würden. Fraser selbst ist Mitgründer einer Lobbyorganisation. Sein Unternehmen Flint ist im deutschen Lobbyregister verzeichnet und hat auch eine Sparte für Rüstungsberatung.
Darüber hinaus behandelt die Konferenz künstliche Intelligenz und mögliche strategische Verbündete Europas. Ein deshalb eingeladener Vertreter der Türkei wird mit keinem Satz für die langjährigen völkerrechtswidrigen Angriffe durch die Türkei in Nordostsyrien kritisiert. Im Gespräch mit einem usbekischen Vertreter erwähnt niemand das autoritäre politische System des Landes, das sich laut dem Demokratie-Index der Universität Würzburg kaum von Iran unterscheidet.
Northrop Grumman meldet sich direkt zu Wort
Im letzten Podiumsgespräch des ersten Tages spricht der Verteidigungsausschuss-Vorsitzende Röwekamp mit einem Vertreter des Nato-Hauptquartiers und Stephanie Willmann, der Landesleiterin von Northrop Grumman. Die sagt gleich zu Beginn: „Wir müssen bereit sein, heute Abend zu kämpfen. Um heute Abend zu gewinnen.“ Deshalb solle Deutschland mehr auf US-Rüstung setzen, da diese technologisch fortschrittlicher sei.
Zum Abschluss des ersten Tages veranstaltet Chatham House ein privates Galadinner für die Konferenzteilnehmer*innen. Das sieht Steeg besonders kritisch: „Da ist ein Moment, der aus zivilgesellschaftlicher Sicht fragwürdig ist. Denn üblicherweise dürfen dabei auch Geldgeber auftreten.“ Das sei eine hervorragende Möglichkeit für die Privatindustrie, ihre Interessen gegenüber politischen Entscheidungsträger*innen zu platzieren.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Bigfoot enthusiasts hope government’s US sightings files are ‘just the beginning’ of proving the creature real
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adam Gabbatt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
When the Forest Service, one of the US government’s less sexy departments, quietly posted three documents to its website in mid-October, it was probably hoping to avoid a fuss.
It didn’t succeed. The files were about Bigfoot, after all, and their publication sparked interest from around the globe, with Bigfoot enthusiasts hopeful that this could be a key step step in the road to proving the creature is real.
“It’s going to help normalize the conversation that the people in this community have been having for decades,” said Tami Grimes. She’s a director at the North American Wood Ape Conservancy (Nawac), which investigates sightings of Bigfoot (the organization prefers the term ‘wood ape’, as it is less mythical-sounding). Nawac collects reports and, if Bigfoot encounters are deemed legitimate, sends out volunteers to gather, or attempt to gather, evidence.
“The release of these papers shows that there have been government reports done to document it. It shows that there was enough to the incidents that the Forest Service took the incidents seriously.”
Grimes, 59, has reason to be invested. She said she has seen Bigfoot several times – the first when she was four-years-old. Her family lived close to Green Swamp, in central Florida, and Grimes recalls looking out of the bedroom one night and seeing a bipedal creature, covered in dark brown-to-back colored hair, staring back at her. It was 7ft tall, and powerfully built.
“The best way to describe the physique is that it was like Lou Ferrigno,” Grimes said, referring to the bodybuilder-turned-actor who was crowned Mr Universe in 1974 and later played the Hulk in the CBS TV show The Incredible Hulk. 
“It was broad across the shoulders, incredibly muscular,” she said.
The creature, which Grimes believes was a Bigfoot, was not impeded by its bulky frame. It ran off at a “rapid speed”, Grimes recalls. She had nightmares for 25 years after the event. She then had another run-in with a Bigfoot in December 2003, when she and a friend went looking for one in a swamp in Florida. She saw a figure standing in the woods, swaying from side to side. It turned to look at her, Grimes said, then it tried and failed to hide behind a pine tree: “Its face and its backside was still sticking out from behind the tree,” before running off into the woods.
Grimes had been watching the figure through a thermal camera, but unfortunately she had only recently purchased the camera and did not know how to press record, so no footage was captured.
Bigfoot, or Sasquatch, has captured American imaginations for decades. Believers say the creature inhabits forests in the US and Canada, being particularly common in the Pacific north-west. Commonly described as tall, strong-looking and foul-smelling, there have been thousands of reports of sightings submitted to amateur Bigfoot tracking organizations like Nawac and the Bigfoot field researchers organization.
Yet Bigfoot is considered by many to be a myth, its alleged existence attributable to folk tales and whimsy, and governmental discussion of it is rare. The White House, the US Department of Defense and the US Department of the Interior all declined to comment on Bigfoot to the Guardian.
The Forest Service did reply. In a statement, a spokesman said: “Stories of Bigfoot, Sasquatch, and other legendary beings have long been part of the cultural fabric of many regions, reflecting a rich tradition of folklore, oral history, and storytelling that surrounds our public lands. While the Forest Service does not endorse or make any claims regarding the existence of such creatures, we appreciate the public’s enthusiasm for exploring and learning about our public lands.”
Other sources were more forthright. A chatbot on the National Park Service website said there “is no scientific evidence that Bigfoot exists as a real animal”, while Encyclopedia Britannica said “most scientists do not recognize the creature’s existence”. Bigfoot does not feature in the National Wildlife Federation’s database of fauna found in the US.
The amount of Bigfoot hoaxes likely hasn’t helped boost its credibility. In one case, two men said they found a Bigfoot body, but when they handed it over to researchers it turned out to be a rubber gorilla suit. A 2014 study of 30 hair samples alleged to be yeti or Bigfoot found that all the hair was from extant species, including a black bear, a cow and a human.
Still, there was plenty of excitement when the forestry service quietly released those Bigfoot-related documents, even if the content was a little underwhelming. One of the files was merely a copy of a newspaper article, which reported that mysterious tracks had been discovered in Montana. Another was a 1980 essay written by someone called Leo Kinney, in which Kinney wrote that he and three others had encountered something in the woods: a creature “that walked on its hind legs that altho [sic] there wasn’t actual sightings, tracks, a strong odor and a gruntling sound were observed”.
The file that received the most attention was probably a report which had been commissioned by the US Department of Agriculture. In the report, Rodney Johnson, a wildlife biologist, said the USDA had asked him to accompany a group in the Umatilla national forest, in Portland, to investigate a reported finding of Bigfoot tracks – suggesting that at least someone at the department thought Bigfoot worthy of further study.
Johnson made plaster casts of four different foot or paw prints at two locations in the forest. He examined them, but found that the tracks “were made by something other than a 300 pound plus two-footed being” – aka, not Bigfoot. Johnson listed eight reasons for his conclusion, finding that the tracks did not extend deeply into the mud, that the stride length did not change even when they tracked uphill, that “forest litter”, like leaves, had been brushed aside prior to making the track, and that the tracks came to an abrupt end in the forest.
Some Bigfoot theories, however, account for that last point.
“It sounds more and more like alien or extraterrestrial than it does animal,” said Ronny LeBlanc, who starred in the Travel Channel show Expedition Bigfoot, which saw him and other experts search for Bigfoot at various locations. LeBlanc believes Bigfoot, or the creature known as Bigfoot, may be inter-dimensional or may use telepathy – or both – to evade capture.
“We’re hearing about UFOs coming in and out of the water. We’re hearing about underwater bases and all this stuff,” LeBlanc said, echoing claims made by UFO-curious Republican congressman Tim Burchett. Burchett, who has been a lead figure in demanding the government release information pertaining to UFOs, said last year that an admiral had told him about large unidentified craft “moving at hundreds of miles an hour underwater”.
“So for me, it’s not that far of a stretch that you have something running around in the forest,” LeBlanc said.
He has had his own Bigfoot experiences. He said he and another man once encountered an “orange orb” in a forest, which “split into two eyes” before taking on the shape of an 8ft tall Bigfoot. “We were with a clairvoyant medium, so I don’t know if that had something to do with it,” LeBlanc said.
He compared the relatively low lack of sightings of Bigfoot to the case of air force pilots who were reluctant to tell their commanding officers that they had seen UFOs. Several finally came forward and shared their experiences with the 60 Minutes news show in 2021, sparking an increased interest in a taboo subject, and prompting several congressional hearings.
“In that same vein, you have people [asking]: “How come hunters don’t see [Bigfoot]? or ‘How come loggers don’t see them?’
“They do. They’re just not talking about it,” he said. “Forestry workers are finding nests in tracks and having sightings, and they’re afraid to kind of pass it up the chain.”
LeBlanc said the Forest Service releasing the three reports could be “just the beginning” in terms of encouraging more conversation and disclosure.
“They’re going to start releasing more of these types of things, probably coming right from the US department of agriculture,” he said. “And I think some of the UFO files that are going to get dropped: they’re going to contain some Bigfoot stuff.”
Should a Bigfoot be discovered, it probably wouldn’t meet a happy fate. It’s easy to imagine it becoming a target for hunters or others who might wish it ill, and even Bigfoot friendly organizations pose a threat.
Asked what it would take to definitively prove Bigfoot’s existence, Tami Grimes, from Nawac, said it would essentially require the group killing one then hauling it off to some scientists for inspection.
“That is part of our mission. It’s uncomfortable, but it is what science demands,” Grimes said. She said Nawac has a small cadre of volunteer hunters who are prepared to shoot dead a Bigfoot, which Grimes said would likely be necessary, because capturing a live Bigfoot would be too difficult.
Whether mammal, or alien, or Lou Ferrigno in an elaborate costume, Bigfoot is probably better off not being found.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.title: Marzahn-Hellersdorf | Ostbezirk in Berlin: CDU-Kandidatin als Kompromiss gegen die AfD
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.author: Marina Mai
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.text:
- Berlin
- Marzahn-Hellersdorf
Ostbezirk in Berlin: CDU-Kandidatin als Kompromiss gegen die AfD
Um einen AfD-Vorsteher zu verhindern, wählen Linke, SPD und Grüne die scheidende Bezirksbürgermeisterin zur Leiterin der BVV in Marzahn Hellersdorf.
In Marzahn-Hellersdorf konnte am Donnerstag die Wahl eines AfD-Politikers zum Vorsteher der Bezirksverordnetenversammlung (BVV) verhindert werden. Die AfD, mit großem Abstand stärkste Partei in dem Ostbezirk, hatte ihren Verordneten Patrick Fritsch ins Rennen geschickt.
Als einer seiner Fraktionskollegen die Nominierung begründen wollte, wurde es laut im Saal. Rund ein Dutzend Antifaschist*innen aus dem Zuschauerraum warnten mit Plakaten und einem Kanon vor seiner Wahl. »Kein AfD-BVV-Vorsitz« stand auf dem selbst gefertigten Transparent, mit dem in der Hand die jungen Leute rund zehn Minuten lang im Kanon sangen: »Wehrt euch, wehrt euch, leistet Widerstand«.
Der AfD-Redner bat einen Bezirksamtsvertreter, das Hausrecht durchzusetzen. Bevor dazu die Polizei gerufen wurde, gelang der SPD-Verordneten Luise Lehmann aber eine Vermittlung: Sie vereinbarte mit den Sänger*innen, dass die Verordneten der demokratischen Fraktionen ihnen Applaus spenden würden und sie anschließend den Saal verlassen. So geschah es.
Der Protest der Gruppe M6 Antifa ging auf ein Video der Grünen zurück, mit dem auf das nach der BVV-Wahl im September drohende Szenario aufmerksam gemacht wurde: Den Aussagen der Grünen zufolge wollte die AfD einen Rechtsaußenmann nominieren und die CDU bei der Abstimmung geschlossen den Saal verlassen. Die Gegenkandidatin der Linken hätte dann mit den Stimmen von Linke, SPD, Grünen und Tierschutzpartei nur weniger Stimmen auf sich vereinen können als der AfD-Mann. Ausschlaggebend wäre dann das Abstimmungsverhalten des BSW gewesen. Ob die BSW-Fraktion sich auf eine Seite schlagen würde und wenn ja, auf welche, war ungewiss.
Doch darauf kam es am Ende doch nicht mehr an. Nach der Auftakt-BVV im Oktober, wo eine Vorstandswahl nicht einmal zustande kam, wurde hinter den Kulissen viel moderiert und verhandelt. Linke-Bezirkschef Kristian Ronneburg beschrieb es so: Seine Partei habe »in zahlreichen Gesprächen mit den demokratischen Parteien kontinuierlich darum gerungen, die BVV arbeitsfähig zu machen«. Gemeinsam mit SPD und Grünen habe man um eine »breit getragene Lösung« gerungen. Und die hieß: Linke, SPD und Grüne akzeptieren die Wahl einer CDU-Vorsteherin, obwohl die CDU hinter AfD und Linke nur drittstärkste Partei im Bezirk geworden war. Die Linke nominiert dann deren Stellvertreterin.
Nadja Zivkovic heißt die CDU-Frau, die gegen den AfD-Mann ins Rennen ging. Wem der Name bekannt vorkommt, liegt richtig: Aktuell ist Zivkovic Bezirksbürgermeisterin. Und das löste gleich eine Frage aus: Kann eine Bürgermeisterin gleichzeitig der BVV vorstehen, also dem Gremium, das das Bezirksamt kontrolliert?
Für SPD und BSW hatte das Ganze darum »ein Geschmäckle«, und ein SPD-Mann fragte Zivkovic, ob sie nicht nach ihrer Wahl als Bürgermeisterin zurücktreten könne. Denn, so hatten es die demokratischen Fraktionen auf Drängen der CDU vereinbart, das neue Bezirksamt wird erst im Januar gewählt. Voraussichtlich am 21. Januar und damit nach der geplanten Bildung der neuen Landesregierung. Das war der CDU wichtig. Und sie beruhigte: Sie verwies auf ein Rechtsgutachten aus einem anderen Bezirk, dem zufolge diese Konstellation für eine Übergangszeit zulässig sei.
Zivkovics Gegenkandidat Fritsch versprach eine überparteiliche Führung der BVV. Doch die SPD-Verordnete Luise Lehmann verwies auf seine Biografie: Ihren Recherchen zufolge sei er über Jahre in der Jungen Alternative aktiv gewesen, die vom Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz als gesichert rechtsextrem eingestuft wurde und sich im vergangenen Jahr aufgelöst hatte. Er habe an einem Aufmarsch der Identitären Bewegung in Wien und an Veranstaltungen des völkischen Netzwerks Idearium teilgenommen, unter anderem gemeinsam mit Björn Höcke. Darüber hinaus habe sich der AfD-Politiker an verschwörungsideologisch geprägten Demonstrationen während der Corona-Pandemie beteiligt. Fritsch selbst relativierte diese Recherchen und betonte, für ihn seien alle Menschen gleichwertig.
In der Abstimmung bekam Fritsch 19 Ja-Stimmen, eine weniger als AfD-Verordnete anwesend waren. Nadja Zivkovic wurde mit 29 Stimmen gewählt. Bemerkenswert waren vier Stimmenthaltungen. Das sind ebenso viele Stimmen, wie das BSW Mandate hat. Die Wahl erfolgte geheim.
Stellvertretende Vorsteherin wurde mit 27 Stimmen die Linke Regina Kittler. Die 71-Jährige war viele Jahre Bildungs- und Kulturpolitikerin im Abgeordnetenhaus und engagiert sich nun im Ruhestand in der BVV. Beeindruckend war, mit welch großem Respekt sich Zivkovic und Kittler begegneten: Sie wiesen auf ihre unterschiedlichen politischen Ansichten hin, hoben aber die Sachkunde, Gründlichkeit und Fairness der jeweils anderen Frau hervor. Beisitzerin wurde mit Martina Polizzi ebenfalls eine Linke mit langer politischer Erfahrung.
Mit der Wahl des Vorstands ist die BVV gut zwei Monate nach der Wahl endlich arbeitsfähig, auch wenn sie erst Ende Januar erneut tagen wird. Ausschüsse wurden eingesetzt, Arbeitsverträge für Mitarbeiter*innen können nun geschlossen werden.
Manuela Neubert von den Grünen freute sich, »dass die Wahl eines AfD-Vorstehers verhindert werden konnte und dass der Vorstand der BVV jetzt feministisch besetzt ist«. Doch das war erst der erste Streich. Ob es Ende Januar gelingt, einen AfD-Bürgermeister für Marzahn-Hellersdorf zu verhindern, ist völlig offen. Ebenso, ob die Wahl dann erneut mit Kanongesang begleitet wird.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: « Grandir entre plusieurs cultures, ça vaccine contre les nationalismes » : Serge Bloch, dessinateur de « Max et Lili »
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Lucie Servin
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
Récompensé par la Grande Ourse du Salon du livre et de la presse jeunesse de Montreuil (dont « l’Humanité » est partenaire) pour l’ensemble de son œuvre, le dessinateur de Max et Lili et de SamSam cultive la liberté d’un simple trait et le goût des histoires. Avec humour, ses dessins retracent le sens de ses engagements humanistes.
« Dessiner toute une vie, c’est marcher sur un fil », résume Serge Bloch, qui n’a cessé de promener son trait, en France comme à l’étranger, du papier aux écrans, dans les livres et l’espace. Né en 1956 à Colmar, rue de l’Ours (ça ne s’invente pas), cet artisan touche-à-tout se définit comme un « amateur professionnel ».
Affichiste, dessinateur de presse, l’auteur mondialement connu pour ses séries jeunesse prépare un livre conçu comme un méli-mélo, un « bric-à-Bloch », pour naviguer dans son œuvre fantaisiste, tout en modestie. Un fil de légèreté et d’humour relie les souvenirs de son enfance dans une famille juive alsacienne à ses engagements contemporains comme dans Eux, c’est nous, un livre récemment réalisé en soutien aux enfants de Gaza.
Que représente pour vous cette Grande Ourse que vous avez reçue au Salon du livre de Montreuil ?
Serge Bloch
Illustrateur
J’ai été très surpris. J’ai commencé ma vie de dessinateur en travaillant pour la jeunesse, mais, ces dernières décennies, j’ai fait beaucoup d’autres...

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Joanna Ruck
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Week in wildlife: ‘polar bear jail’, baby penguins and the turkeys’ revenge
This week’s best wildlife photographs from around the world
Sleep tight … an officer gives a sedated polar bear one final reassuring touch before it is airlifted to safety in Churchill, Canada. Photograph: @morenowildlifephotography/Caters News
King penguin chicks, still in the brown, downy feathers of infancy, huddle together against the cold wind in their rookery at Volunteer Point, Falkland IslandsPhotograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
A Swiss tourist was killed and British and American tourists were injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon. The elephants attacked the group, and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored. One of the guides was tossed into a ditch, while the others hid in trees. Cameroonian wildlife authorities believe the elephants may have perceived the hikers as a threat to their calvesPhotograph: CBS Radio
Roasters’ revenge … a woman was chased by a group of turkeys on Saturday in Newton, Massachusetts, days before the Thanksgiving holiday. She was rescued by two strangers who drove by and let her escape in their carPhotograph: Taryn LaPrade via Facebook
Elisa Mangione feeds a hedgehog at La Ninna wildlife hospital in Novello, Italy. Prolonged drought and unusually high summer temperatures linked to climate change have made the rescue centre in northern Italy’s Piedmont region busier than everPhotograph: Niccolo Lupone/AP
A monkey outside Swayambhunath Stupa, Kathmandu, Nepal. Hundreds of Buddhist devotees and monks gather at the historic temple to offer 84,000 flowers, praying for peace and harmony in the worldPhotograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA
A scarce silver-lines moth, UK. (Despite its name, it is quite common across the country, and can usually be found near an oak tree, since it feeds on the leaves.) Councils, town planners and homeowners are being urged to plant more native trees in urban areas to help insects. Marking National Tree Week, Butterfly Conservation says species such as apple, oak, silver birch, hawthorn, willow, poplar and elm can boost numbers of moths and butterfliesPhotograph: David Green/PA
San Francisco garter snakes born and raised in a zoo-based conservation program have been released into the wild for the first time as part of an effort to save what is considered one of North America’s most beautiful snakes Photograph: Courtesy of Vishal Subramanyan & Midpen Open Space
Changthangi goats – the breed that produces cashmere wool used for pashminas – graze near the Tso Kar lake in India’s northern Ladakh region. At an elevation of 4,500m, the wetlands are intensely cold, which explains the goats’ thick, warm coatsPhotograph: Mohd Arhaan Archer/AFP/Getty Images
Grizzly bear cubs follow their mother through sagebrush and green grass at the edge of a forest in Grand Teton National Park, Wyoming. USPhotograph: Richard Ellis/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Sleep tight … a conservation officer gives a sedated polar bear one final reassuring touch before it is airlifted to safety, far away from the town where it had become a potential danger to residents in Churchill, Manitoba, Canada. After spending time in the town’s holding facility, better known as ‘polar bear jail’, the animal is being relocated by helicopter to an area 70km to the northPhotograph: @morenowildlifephotography/Caters News

https://gothamist.com/news/its-officiall.title: It's officially Christmas season in NYC. Can you afford a tree?
https://gothamist.com/news/its-officiall.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/its-officiall.text:
As long as her fresh Christmas tree costs under $100, Nicole Norris said she can stomach it.
“ Anything under $100, we're like, ‘Oh my God. OK, great,’” she said as she picked a 7-footer at a Manhattan Whole Foods with her family for $99.99 that was “not too full” and had a top branch perfect for her Donkey Kong topper.
Gothamist is once again tracking the price of a fresh pine and asking readers to help us report the cost of Christmas trees in their neighborhoods. To participate, fill out this Google form, tell us what price you paid for your tree, and share photos of your shopping experiences.
Last year, after more than 400 submissions, we found the average price for a tree was $116. The cheapest tree our readers spotted was a footlong mini from Trader Joe’s going for $10. On the other end was a 9-foot-tall Fraser fir on the Upper West Side for $633.
Some tree sellers told Gothamist they’re raising their prices slightly this year because higher gas prices have pushed up transportation costs and inflation is just making everything more expensive.
“ We don't have no choice. The market's so hard,” said Ruibel Diyarza, who runs Diyarza Landscaping in Brooklyn. He said he’s raising prices by about 5% this year. ”We don't want to raise the prices, but they just keep raising everything else.”
While tree prices tend to be lower at box stores like Home Depot and Whole Foods, according to crowd-sourced data Gothamist analyzed last year, independent sellers said you don’t get the same level of customer service, or sometimes, quality.
“Even though we're more expensive, you know you're getting a good tree,” said Karl Wiesner, who sells trees at Wiesner Bros. Nursery on Staten Island, a family-run business that’s been around for 98 years. Wiesner said they’re raising their price by $5 on their larger trees that come from Canada.
“If you shake the tree, you don't want any needles to come off. Also, if you grab a branch and pull your hand down it, you shouldn't have any needles in your hand.”
Buying at his location, also comes with good advice: “My big tip would be to always make sure you use warm water in the stand, and it's typically gonna be the first few days that matter the most for watering the tree,” he said.
Even at Whole Foods, 6-foot to 7-foot trees are selling for $10 more than last year, when the national grocer sold them for $89.99.
Pricier pines were more common in Manhattan and were cheaper in the outer boroughs. Last year, the median price for a tree in Manhattan was $120, compared with $99 in Brooklyn and $75 in the Bronx.
“ I feel like it's par for the course with what's been happening. The big economic dirty word is inflation,” said Antonia Bats as she browsed the $99.99 trees at Whole Foods in Lower Manhattan.
“Compared to the other vendors, it's still a pretty good deal,” she said.
Diyarza said New Yorkers looking to save some money can opt for a balsam tree that tends to be cheaper, or, just get a smaller tree. And if you get your tree early in the season, opt for a Fraser that lasts longer.
“We got so many sizes, so we just try to make sure the customer will be OK and enjoy Christmas,” he said.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Finding Freedom When Your Body Becomes State Property
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Grace Coleman
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Finding Freedom When Your Body Becomes State Property
When you’re incarcerated, your name is replaced by a number, your self-worth stolen by a strip search. But serving time does not grant the state permission to deny your humanity.
What would happen if your body was no longer yours? And no, I am not talking about some sort of out-of-body experience, but losing your autonomy to an unworldly place: prison. Shackles weigh down your feet and your wrists are tightly cuffed to gut-wrenching waist chains. The discomfort screams your body is no longer yours. As women in prison, our bodies become property of the state. Our name is replaced by a number. Our self-worth is stolen by a strip search. In today’s terms, our health, our rights, and our bodies are canceled.
On October 1, 2026, the California Coalition for Women Prisoners (CCWP) Reproductive Justice Working group offered an antidote to the reproductive injustices incarcerated people face at the California Institution for Women (CIW). CCWP has maintained a relationship with women’s prisons for over 30 years. Beginning in response to witnessing people who died from medical neglect, CCWP still assists folks who currently live inside prison without proper medical care. At the convening, inside and outside advocates came together to gain a deeper understanding of abolitionist work. Keynote speaker Kwaneta Harris, who is currently incarcerated in a Texas women’s prison, made one thing very clear, “Nobody is free until the state has no cages and no chains left to put anybody in. Not on our bodies, not around our.… Not on our children or our future.”
Related Article
System-imposed trauma concealed for years, or even decades, was openly discussed amongst attendees, including women’s health professionals, OB-GYNs, lawyers, journalists, and advocates. CCWP advocate, and event host, Leesa Nomura, called out the levels of bodily harm caused by incarceration. While discussing a solution, she explained, “1t can’t just be policy work. It has to hold prisons accountable for not caring for needs, like postpartum depression.” Addressing postpartum needs was one of the many healthcare concerns advocates shined a light on.
Women’s reproductive rights are muted and, for some, removed during incarceration. For decades, marginalized women have been subjected to crimes eliminating their ability to have children. Not to mention, longterm punishment in itself prevents women’s ability to have children—and no, freezing eggs isn’t an option. While the past torture of giving birth chained to a hospital bed is infuriating enough, it gets worse. Imagine this, you walk into your OB-GYN appointment to have your fibroids removed and walk out without your ovaries.
While women in prison are responsible for committing serious crime, serving time does not grant medical professionals the right to endanger women’s health or reproductive rights. Nor should it subject families and children to undergo the pain of their hurt and absence.
Reproductive justice leaders used the convening to discuss the hurdles they must overcome in order to shift the shame culture that isolates and resists change. Because the Prison Industrial Complex has developed and implemented oppressive practices tor so long, great difficulty arises when trying to put less brutal policies into action.
The inhumane living conditions inside prison cells, such as extreme temperatures and metal bunks, force women into facing various health issues, including body aches, sleep deprivation, and early menopause. The therapeutic privacy of mental health becomes public. Ongoing stressors inside the toxic environment expose women to violence and sexual assault, and surveillance is often justified as safety.
So if reform isn’t the solution, then what is? Reproductive justice leaders say, “abolition.” In true abolitionist fashion, women walked out looking to identify root causes and create community to challenge systematic oppression.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Rare Marie Antoinette ‘Breast Bowl’ Hammers for $2.47 M. in Paris, Surpassing Top Estimate
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Devorah Lauter
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million), or €2,945 million with fees ($3.23 million), at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).
Legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts. While no documented proof of such a legend exists, the so-called “jatte-téton” or “nipple bowls,” painted in fleshy light pink with an areola and nipple at the tip, do have a surrealistic, convincingly realistic quality, despite a too-perfectly circular shape.
Made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC. It is one of four highly prized jatte-tétons delivered that year and in 1788, destined for the royal “pleasure dairy” in Rambouillet, near Versailles, that King Louis XVI gifted to Marie Antoinette. There, per the fashion of the time, nobility would gather to socialize and taste an assortment of fine milk, cream, and cheese delicacies prepared for them.
The rare breast bowl comes from the collection of French dealer Claude Meyer, who passed away in November 2025. His children happened upon it while going through boxes of storage, and learned that their late father, whose Paris gallery closed in the 1990s, had never offered it for sale. It is unclear how Meyer acquired the piece, which is known to have once belonged to the French Marquise de Chanaleilles.
Three of the four breast bowls made in 1787 and 1788 for the queen’s royal dairy dishes are housed in public collections today, including two at the Musée de Sèvres and one at the Museo Duca di Martina in Naples. The bowl that sold tonight is the last of that specific series. They are “the most celebrated and the most extravagant shape of the porcelain service,” by the royal Sèvres manufactory for the queen’s dairy, notes the auction house in its description.
With the bowl comes an intricately carved tripod stand decorated with goat heads in relief, as seen above. Indeed, the breast bowls require a pedestal to hold them upside down, as it were, so as to contain the milk and cream they were meant to serve.
Speaking to Le Journal des Arts about the bowl, auctioneer Alexandre de La Forest Divonne observed: “It has become something of a symbol of the queen; it is truly a totem.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Museum acquisitions round-up: a Simone Leigh monumental bronze and an atmospheric early Rothko
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Anna Brady
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Okwui (2024) by Simone Leigh
National Gallery of Australia, Canberra
The American Friends of the National Gallery of Australia bought this sculpture by Simone Leigh last year from Matthew Marks Gallery in New York. The monumental bronze, measuring 3.3m long and 1.5m tall, is named after the Nigerian American artist and actress Okwui Okpokwasili. It shows a reclining woman in a cast raffia skirt, exploring the resilience and cultural memory that merges the semi-abstract female form with the African vernacular. This cast is the second from an edition of two (with one artist’s proof). In 2022, Leigh became the first Black woman to represent the US at the Venice Biennale.
Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) (1934) by Mark Rothko
Cape Ann Museum, Gloucester, Massachusetts
Christopher Rothko, the son of the artist Mark Rothko (1903-70), says that while his father thought “all art was inherently of its time”, sometimes “even with a master of abstraction like Mark Rothko, art can also be inherently of its place”. He is referring to this painting—an atmospheric early watercolour-and-gouache work depicting the harbour in Gloucester—which Christopher recently donated to the Cape Ann Museum from his private collection. Mark Rothko frequently summered on Cape Ann, painting alongside two other New York artists: his mentor, Milton Avery, and his friend Adolph Gottlieb. This painting is included in Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea—a touring exhibition currently on view at the Phillips Collection in Washington, DC (until 24 January 2027).
Arc-en-ciel no. 5 (1913-14) by Robert Delaunay
Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
It may not be instantly recognisable, but the lilac spire behind the rainbow in this painting is the Eiffel Tower—the tallest building in the world when the work was painted by Robert Delaunay (1885-1941). The French artist was the husband of Sonia Delaunay, and in 1912 they co-founded the short-lived Orphism movement—an offshoot of Cubism that prized bright colours and geometric shapes. This vivid oil-on-canvas work, measuring 35cm by 40cm, is one of several variations of the composition and shows Delaunay moving away from strict geometry to a looser, more expressive and rhythmic style. The painting, which sold at Christie’s in 2025 for $317,500 (with fees) from the collection of Arnold and Joan Saltzman, was exhibited by the London-based dealer Willoughby Gerrish at Tefaf Maastricht in March—where the sale to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, was initially agreed.

https://taz.de/Trumps-Einfluss-in-der-Re.title: Republika Srpska: Das bleibt in der Familie
https://taz.de/Trumps-Einfluss-in-der-Re.author: Mathias Brüggmann
https://taz.de/Trumps-Einfluss-in-der-Re.text:
Republika Srpska: Das bleibt in der Familie
Milorad Dodik, der sanktionierte Langzeitherrscher der serbischen Teilrepublik Bosnien-Herzegowinas, hält seine Familie an der Macht. Was Trump damit zu tun hat.
Wladimir Putin hat keine Söhne, sonst wüsste man, wer sein Nachfolger einst wird. Nun hat einer seiner politischen Freunde, der Langzeit-Präsident der Republika Srpska, also des serbischen Landesteils Bosnien-Herzegowinas, seinen Sohn zum Regierungschef auserkoren: Der 37-jährige Igor Dodik soll als Ministerpräsident binnen spätestens eines Monats eine neue Regierung bilden.
Sein Vater Milorad Dodik hat diese serbisch geprägte Teilrepubik Bosniens seit 20 Jahren fest im Griff. Damals gründete sich die Partei Allianz der Unabhängigen Sozialdemokraten (SNSD), deren Chef Milorad Dodik bis heute ist. Sohn Igor hat beim Wahlsieg der Partei im Oktober ein Abgeordnetenmandat geholt und wurde Fraktionsvorsitzender. Nun beauftragte Savo Minić, der Präsident der Republika Srpska, ihn in Banja Luka mit der Regierungsbildung.
Milorad Dodik wurde von einem Gericht im Februar 2025 aus dem Amt entfernt und verurteilt, sechs Jahre lang keine öffentlichen Ämter mehr bekleiden zu dürfen. Denn er hatte für vom Hohen Repräsentanten für Bosnien-Herzegowina, einem zur Beendigung des Bosnienkriegs von der internationalen Gemeinschaft eingesetzten Oberaufseher, für illegal empfundene Gesetze in Kraft gesetzt. Mit diesen sollte die Republika Srpska vom Gesamtstaat Bosnien und Herzegowina abgespalten und die Region destabilisiert werden.
Der Langzeitherrscher wurde von Deutschland, Großbritannien, Österreich und Slowenien mit Einreiseverbot belegt. US-Präsident Donald Trump, dessen Familienangehörige und politische Freunde große Wirtschaftsinteressen auf dem Balkan verfolgen, hob die Sanktionen gegen den heute 67-jährigen Dodik voriges Jahr auf.
Dank an Putin und Trump
Im April war Trumps Sohn Donald Trump junior bei Igor Dodik in Banja Luka. Umstrittene Energiedeals des Trump-Umfelds in der Region belasten die Beziehungen zur Europäischen Union. Parallel war Dodik senior zusammen mit dem inzwischen abgewählten serbischen Machthaber Aleksandar Vučić ein politisch enger Weggefährte des Kremlchefs Wladimir Putin.
Die Inthronisierung von Dodik junior verspricht nun beiden Antieuropäern – Trump und Putin –, dass die Republika Sprska und damit das faktisch weitgehend unregierbare Bosnien-Herzegowina weiter eine politische Blackbox und Einfallstor für „Dealmaker“ bleibt.
Belma Zulčić, Direktorin der Gesellschaft für bedrohte Völker in Bosnien und Herzegowina, forderte bereits nach dem knappen Wahlsieg der Dodik-Partei Anfang Oktober: „Die EU darf nicht ignorieren, dass enge politische Berater Trumps für die Regierung der Republika Srpska arbeiten und Dodik Trump für den Wahlerfolg seiner Partei verantwortlich macht. Sie muss unmissverständlich klarmachen, dass die Souveränität, territoriale Integrität und verfassungsmäßige Ordnung Bosnien und Herzegowinas nicht Gegenstand politischer Deals oder wirtschaftlicher Interessen sein dürfen.“
Vater Dodik bedankte sich nach der Wahl auch bei Putin und Trump. Nun macht er seinen Sohn zum Premier. Tochter Gorica Dodik indes kommt politisch nicht zum Zuge. Sie hatte nach Verhängung von US-Sanktionen gegen die Dodik-Familie mit Vorwürfen der Selbstbereicherung 2025 ihr schickes und mit Schwiegertochter Ivana Dodik betriebenes Restaurant Agape in Banja Luka geschlossen.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Turkey again! Eight Thanksgiving leftover recipes you’ll actually look forward to eating
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Karen Yuan
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
There’s only so much turkey sandwich a person can eat. Luckily, Thanksgiving leftovers are a delicious excuse to make something entirely new. From crispy hoisin pancakes to a fragrant turkey pho to a golden, cheesy gratin, here are eight ways to give yesterday’s bird a second life – or explore more recipes in our huge collection.
Waste-not-want-not turkey stock (Giorgio Locatelli)
With a few vegetables and hours of gentle simmering, a turkey carcass becomes a golden stock for soups, pastas and anything you’re cooking in the weeks ahead.
1 cooked turkey carcass, with remaining skin and meat attached, stuffing removed
1 carrot
1 onion
1 celery stalk
2 bay leaves
Weigh the turkey carcass then put it in a large stockpot with the veg and bay leaves. Add about 2½ quarts of water for every pound of meat and bones. Put it on the lowest possible heat for a couple of hours. You’ll be left with a lovely stock for risotto, soups, or to freeze to use later.
Quick and easy turkey curry (Josceline Dimbleby)
Turkey meat is perfect for curries, and this recipe uses curry paste and quick-cook veg, so it takes no time at all to prepare and serve. Serve with a steaming mound of basmati rice.
Serves 6–8
2–2¼lb skinless cooked turkey meat
1lb zucchini
9oz grape or cherry tomatoes
2tbsp butter
2tbsp canola oil
3-5tsp tikka curry paste or mild curry paste
1 (13.5-oz) can coconut milk
A handful of fresh cilantro leaves
Cut the cooked turkey meat into smallish pieces. Trim the ends of the zucchini and slice across fairly thinly. Halve the tomatoes lengthwise.
Heat the butter and oil in a large, deep pan over medium-high heat. When the butter has melted, add the zucchini and tomatoes and stir for 2–3 minutes, until the zucchini begins to soften but hasn’t lost its bite.
Next, add the curry paste and the sliced turkey. Stir over the heat for another minute or so.
Lastly, pour in the coconut milk, stir and bring just up to bubbling. Remove from the heat, add salt, if needed, and more curry paste if you want a hotter curry. Before serving, roughly chop the cilantro leaves and throw them into the curry.
Warming turkey pho (James Ramsden)
Pho is pretty much the perfect tonic to overstuffed Thanksgiving palates. It’s fresh, lively and deeply nourishing.
Serves 6
For the broth
Turkey bones
2 onions halved and peeled
A few fat slices of fresh ginger
5 star anise
2 cinnamon sticks 
1tsp fennel seeds 
2 garlic cloves
1 Thai chili, chopped
3tbsp fish sauce 
1tbsp superfine or palm sugar
For the soup
10.5oz vermicelli rice noodles
10.5oz leftover turkey, shredded
A big handful of cilantro leaves
A big handful of Thai basil or mint leaves
1.75oz bean sprouts
6 lime wedges
4 Thai chilis, chopped
Sriracha hot sauce (optional)
A few hours ahead: To make the broth, put a large, heavy-bottomed pot over the highest possible heat. Add the onion and the ginger. Burn them. Really burn them. Add the star anise, cinnamon, fennel seeds, garlic cloves, chili, turkey bones, fish sauce and sugar. Cover with water and bring to a boil. Simmer for 2–3 hours, until reduced by half. Strain and leave to cool, then chill, or continue to the next step. Cook the noodles according to package instructions, then cool in a bowl of iced water before draining.
30 minutes ahead: Put the broth over a medium heat. When hot, add the turkey to warm through. Taste the broth and add salt if necessary. Warm some large bowls.
To serve: Divide the noodles between the bowls. Spoon over the broth. Garnish with the herbs, bean sprouts, lime and chilis, and serve.
Mum’s turkey, barley and vegetable soup (Jeremy Lee)
Winter on the east coast of Scotland can be bitingly cold. Hogmanay often saw our garden turned into an ice-bound realm beneath indigo skies. Going out was not much of an option, but there was little need as we devoured film after film, while the smells of Mum cooking turkey broth in the kitchen filled the air throughout the house.
While her brood hunkered under woolen blankets, Mum popped the carcass into a large pot with much chopped vegetables and a handful of barley, to be simmered for a fair few hours. The resulting broth was always the dish we craved most over the festivities.
Serves 6-8 with second helpings
1 roast turkey carcass
4 carrots
3 onions
6 celery stalks
1 small celery root (celeriac)
1 small rutabaga
4 slices bacon
4 bay leaves
2 sprigs each of thyme and savory
1 small bunch curly parsley, leaves picked and stems reserved
2 heaping tablespoons barley
2 large leeks
1 bunch scallions
Sit the carcass in a large pot. Peel and chop the carrots, onions, celery, celery root and rutabaga into smallish pieces. Cut the streaky bacon into small strips. Tie the bay leaves, thyme, savory and parsley stalks into a small bundle with twine.
Tumble all these into the pot with the turkey. Add the barley. Fill the pot with cold water and bring to a simmer over a gentle heat, spooning off any foam that rises to the surface. Leave the soup to tick over for 2 hours or so, until the barley and vegetables are tender. Turn the heat as low as can be and cook slowly for a further hour.
Trim the green part of the leek and chop into small pieces and chop the white of the leek into smallish squares also. Trim and slice the scallions thin. Wash these thoroughly and add to the soup 15 minutes before serving.
Chop the curly parsley leaves finely and add to the pot a minute before serving the soup. Bread and butter vital.
Crispy turkey pancakes with hoisin sauce (Tom Hunt)
This is a super quick way to upcycle even a small amount of leftover meat into a special last-minute meal. If you don’t have hoisin sauce in the pantry, it’s possible you might have the ingredients to make your own – garlic, soy sauce, sweetener, vinegar, chili of some sort and a blob of tahini or peanut butter are all you need to make it.
I really like the neutral flavor of Chinese-style pancakes, because it makes them a great carrier for other intense flavors, but if you can’t find them, regular wheat tortillas will work here instead.
Serves 4
For the hoisin sauce (or use store-bought)
1tbsp vegetable oil, or sesame oil
3 garlic cloves, peeled and minced
2tbsp soy sauce
2tbsp black bean paste, or more soy sauce
3tbsp sweetener – honey, sugar or molasses
3tbsp vinegar – rice, white wine or apple cider vinegar
1tbsp tahini, or creamy peanut butter
2tsp sriracha, or gochujang or chili flakes
½ tsp Chinese five-spice powder
For the pancakes
10.5oz cooked turkey, shredded
1tbsp vegetable oil, or sesame oil
4tbsp hoisin sauce, plus extra to serve
12 Chinese-style pancakes
3.5oz cucumber, cut into matchsticks
3 scallions, trimmed and cut into matchsticks
To make your own hoisin sauce, heat the oil in a frying pan, then gently fry the garlic until it begins to turn light brown. Stir in the soy sauce, sweetener, vinegar, tahini and sriracha, then add the black bean paste and the five-spice. Bring to a boil, simmer for three minutes, then season to taste and leave to cool.
Put the oil in a frying pan over medium heat, add the shredded roast turkey and leave to cook without stirring until it’s crisp underneath. Break up the meat, stir in 3-4 tablespoons of hoisin sauce to coat it evenly, and cook for another minute.
Set the table with a platter of the crispy turkey, 12 steamed Chinese-style pancakes (or small tortillas), a bowl each of cucumber and scallions, and the hoisin sauce. To assemble a pancake, spread a little hoisin sauce on one side, top with some turkey, cucumber and scallion, then fold or roll and tuck in.
Sweet and sour turkey salad (Yotam Ottolenghi)
Chicken or ham work just as well instead of the turkey, if that’s what’s left over from yesterday’s menu. If you have more leftover meat, add more to the salad and increase the amount of dressing as needed.
Serves 6
7oz cooked turkey, shredded
3.5oz flat rice noodles (or mung bean noodles)
½ red onion, peeled and thinly sliced
¼ iceberg lettuce, cut into ¾in thick slices
2 medium carrots, peeled and julienned
0.75oz Thai basil leaves (or regular basil), torn
0.75oz mint leaves
1.5oz cilantro leaves
3.5oz bean sprouts
3.5oz roasted salted peanuts, roughly chopped
3 red chilis, seeded and julienned
1oz store-bought fried shallots
For the dressing
1.75oz palm sugar, finely grated
1½tbsp fish sauce
2tbsp apple cider vinegar
2tbsp lime juice, plus the finely grated zest of 1 lime
1½in piece fresh ginger, peeled and grated
1tbsp soy sauce
2tbsp peanut oil
1 garlic clove, peeled and crushed
Whisk all the ingredients for the dressing until the sugar has dissolved, and set aside.
Cook the noodles according to the package instructions (they vary from brand to brand). Drain, then put in a large serving bowl with all the remaining ingredients apart from the fried shallots. Pour over the dressing, toss gently, then take to the table or divide between six individual bowls. Serve, with the shallots sprinkled on top.
Turkey gratin with stilton, walnuts and goat cheese (Josceline Dimbleby)
Normally, I prefer St Agur when cooking with blue cheese, but this recipe is perfect for using up stilton or any other leftover cheese. Walnuts combine deliciously here, as does the dash of brandy.
Serves 6–8
2.25lb skinless cooked turkey meat
3.5oz walnut pieces
3½tbsp butter
2tbsp chickpea flour
3¼cups whole milk
½ small glass brandy
6.5oz stilton or other blue cheese, crumbled
2 large garlic cloves, finely chopped
1.75oz hard goat cheese
Preheat the oven to 340F. Cut the turkey into pieces and arrange in a large, fairly shallow ovenproof dish. Scatter the walnuts among the turkey.
Melt the butter in a fairly large saucepan, then remove from the heat, sift in the chickpea flour and stir in with a wooden spoon. Gradually stir in the milk and return to the heat. Bring up to bubbling, stirring all the time until the sauce is thick and smooth.
Still stirring, let it simmer gently for another 2–3 minutes. Then stir in the brandy, the crumbled stilton and the chopped garlic. Stir until the cheese has melted. Remove from the heat and add salt and pepper, to taste.
Pour the sauce over the turkey and walnuts. Coarsely grate the goat cheese and scatter it over the top. Cook in the center of the oven for 35–40 minutes, until it has turned a nice, golden brown.
Turkey and ham pie with brussels sprout salad and cranberry vinaigrette (Felicity Cloake)
Stir in a couple of chopped leeks if you’re not making the accompanying salad – soften them in butter first. And a word on that salad: don’t knock it until you’ve tried it. After all, if raw cabbage can work in a coleslaw …
Serves 4
For the pie
14oz roast turkey
3.5oz ham
2tbsp butter
2tbsp all-purpose flour
⅔cup chicken or turkey stock, or leftover gravy
1cup milk
3tbsp cream (heavy or half-and-half, whichever you have left over)
8oz puff pastry
All-purpose flour, to dust
1 egg, beaten
For the salad
14oz raw brussels sprouts, trimmed
Handful of pecans, roughly chopped
6tbsp olive oil
2tbsp balsamic vinegar
3tbsp fresh cranberry sauce
Zest of ½ orange
Tear the turkey into evenly sized pieces, and roughly chop the ham. Preheat the oven to 356F.
Melt the butter in a medium saucepan over low heat, and stir in the flour. Cook, stirring, for a couple of minutes, then slowly whisk in the stock or gravy and the milk to make a smooth paste. Simmer gently for about 10 minutes until thickened, then add the cream and season to taste. Add the meat, and pour into a pie dish.
Roll out the pastry on a lightly floured surface until about ¼ inch thick, and brush the rim of the pie dish with beaten egg. Place the pastry on top, and press down around the rim, then trim off the excess – you can use these scraps to decorate the top of the pie if you like. Poke a hole in the middle to let the steam out, and brush with beaten egg.
Bake for about 30 minutes, until the pastry is golden and well puffed up.
Meanwhile, make the salad. Shred the sprouts finely, and place in a salad bowl with the pecans. Whisk together the oil and vinegar, then stir in the cranberry sauce and orange zest. Season well, and pour over the sprouts, then toss to coat. Serve alongside the pie.
