Pas dan is onafhankelijk toezicht verplicht. Het akkoord zelf hoeft niet openbaar te worden gemaakt. Garanties voor de mensenrechten ontbreken voorlopig, en geen garantie neemt de structurele risico’s weg.
Een Rwandees centrum is geen oplossing, maar verplaatst mensen uit ons zicht, naar een land waar ze taal noch familie hebben
Hoe vrijheidsberoving in een terugkeercentrum er dan uitziet, zien we trouwens al in België. Het Nationaal Preventief Mechanisme, het orgaan dat in België plaatsen van vrijheidsberoving bezoekt om mishandeling te voorkomen, bezocht in oktober 2025 het gesloten terugkeercentrum 127bis en publiceerde eerder deze maand zijn rapport. Wie er op een uitwijzingsvlucht wacht, wordt systematisch naakt gefouilleerd, de toegang tot psychiatrische zorg is ‘bijna onbestaande’ en een continu, wettelijk geregeld toezicht op de vrijheidsberoving ontbreekt. Deze Belgische vaststellingen tonen waarom vooraf helder moet zijn wie toezicht houdt, welke klachtenprocedure geldt en wat gebeurt wanneer een open model toch vrijheidsbeperkend wordt.
Open of niet, de kern blijft het niemandsland waarin mensen nu al vastzitten, en dat kennen wij maar al te goed. Een deel van de betrokkenen zit vast omdat identificatie, reisdocumenten of terugname door het herkomstland uitblijven. Uit zoveel uitzichtloosheid groeit zelden een duurzame beslissing. Een Rwandees centrum lost dat niet op, maar verplaatst ze uit ons zicht, naar een land waar deze mensen taal noch familie hebben en opnieuw in limbo dreigen te belanden of van daaruit verder worden teruggestuurd.
Voorwaardelijke steun
Wat in onze ervaring wél werkt, is begeleiding. Die rust op drie pijlers: sociaal-juridische oriëntatie en terugkeerbegeleiding in België en re-integratie in het land van herkomst. De eerste stap staat open voor iedereen, voor én na een negatief besluit. Omdat wij als ngo onafhankelijk en vertrouwelijk werken, weten mensen dat hun begeleider geen verkapte handhaver is. Pas dan leggen ze hun echte situatie op tafel en wordt duidelijk wat haalbaar en veilig is. Kiest iemand voor terugkeer, dan stopt het traject niet op de luchthaven: we bereiden de re-integratie voor het vertrek voor en lokale partners volgen ze bij aankomst op.
Zo’n proces vraagt tijd en rust. Volgens bronnen bij de onderhandelingen wil Duitsland de hub onder meer inzetten voor mensen die niet meewerken aan identificatie en wier herkomstland terugname bemoeilijkt: de “terugkeerhub” als breekijzer dus. Maar wie bang is voor de stok, klapt dicht. De Europese regels laten vanaf volgend jaar toe om terugkeergesprekken te verplichten en steun te verminderen bij een gemiste afspraak met terugkeerdiensten. Wij vragen België die weg niet in te slaan. Steun die afhangt van medewerking, dreigt de vertrouwensrelatie te ondergraven die begeleiding nodig heeft.
Perspectief
Duurzame terugkeer begint bij perspectief, niet bij een enkeltje Kigali
Een geloofwaardig terugkeerbeleid vraagt geen dure luchtbruggen naar Afrika, maar drie keuzes. Ten eerste, zorgvuldige procedures met een kwaliteitsvolle begeleiding zodat wie bescherming nodig heeft die snel krijgt en wie wordt afgewezen een besluit dat standhoudt. Ten tweede, gerichte diplomatie met herkomstlanden, op voet van gelijkheid en met respect voor de mensenrechten. Ontwikkelingssamenwerking is daarbij geen pasmunt. Ten derde, legale uitwegen − zoals bijvoorbeeld gezinshereniging voor wie aan de voorwaarden voldoet en regularisatie om uitzonderlijke humanitaire of medische redenen.
Daarnaast zijn er meer veilige en legale wegen nodig. Legale kanalen dichtknijpen helpt niet om irreguliere migratie terug te dringen.
Wie enkel percentages najaagt, kiest voor terugkeer tegen elke prijs. Dat wijzen wij af, ook omdat het niet standhoudt. Duurzame terugkeer begint bij perspectief, niet bij een enkeltje Kigali.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The explosion of extreme wealth is the major problem of our time | Bernie Sanders
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Bernie Sanders
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
We are at a pivotal moment in history. Never before in human history have so few people held so much wealth and so much power. And never before have we seen such an unprecedented level of greed, arrogance and irresponsibility on the part of the world’s ruling class.
Here is the good news: leaders from around the world are finally starting to wake up. This week, elected officials and economists from around the world – including four Nobel prize winners – came together in Paris for a “Summit Against International Oligarchy”. As the summit’s proclamation stated, “The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time … We are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.”
They are right. And that is exactly why I organized, along with other progressives, the Fight Oligarchy tour last year which brought out more than 340,000 Americans in 27 states.
As members of the summit point out, in 1987 the wealth of the richest 0.0001% amounted to the equivalent of 3% of global gross domestic product (GDP). Since then, these 3,000 households have seen their fortunes grow to 17% of global GDP.
At this moment, we live in a world where the top 1% owns more wealth than the bottom 95% of humanity and the gap between the very rich and the poor is growing wider and wider.
Think about it. After all of the wars and revolutions over the last 250 years, after all of the carefully drafted constitutions and hard-fought elections, after all of the wonderful speeches that politicians around the world have given, the top 1% owns more wealth than the bottom 95% of humanity.
In country after country, we are seeing unprecedented income and wealth inequality.
We see it in America today, where the top 1% now owns more wealth than the bottom 93% and one man, Elon Musk, owns more wealth than the bottom 53% of American households.
We see it in Russia, where the latest figures indicate that the wealthiest 500 people in that country control more wealth than the bottom 99.8% of their people.
We see it in France, where more than one out of five children live in poverty, while 53 billionaires own more wealth than the bottom half of the population.
We see it in Africa, where in recent years, nearly 850 million people have struggled with food insecurity, while just four men own more wealth than the bottom 50% of the people on that continent. Yes. Four men own more wealth than half a continent.
We see it in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar, where a handful of families have unbelievable wealth and power while most of the work done in those countries is performed by impoverished and powerless migrant laborers.
But it’s not just massive income and wealth inequality. It is oligarchs’ control over the global economy. It is oligarchs’ control over much of the media and what people see, hear and read. It is oligarchs avoiding taxes by stashing trillions of dollars in offshore tax havens around the world while the children in their native countries go hungry.
And what are the political implications when the very rich get much richer while working people struggle and feel more and more powerless?
The answer is clear. If people no longer believe that their government is responding to their needs, many of them will give up on democracy and move towards authoritarianism.
And it’s not just Trumpism in the United States. It’s the growth of extreme rightwing parties in Germany, France, the UK and elsewhere.
All over the world, people are asking a very simple question: why should I continue to vote for the same old, same old political parties when my job has been shipped overseas, my factory has been automated, my credit card interest rate is now 25%, I’m unable to retire with dignity, and my children will likely have a lower standard of living than I do – all while the top 1% have never, ever had it so good?
As the country the most billionaires, with a record 989, including 15 of the top 20, the US has a major role to play.
Bottom line: if we are going to improve the lives of working people and protect democracy, the new Democratic majority can no longer continue the failed status quo policies that have devastated so many of our people throughout our country.
This election was about change, real change, and that’s what Democrats must deliver. Now is the time to take on Big Money and fight for an economy that works for all, not just a few.
Yes. We need a wealth tax on billionaires to substantially reduce child poverty, build affordable housing, protect our seniors and invest in the needs of working families.
Yes. We need to guarantee healthcare as a human right by passing Medicare for All.
Yes. We must raise the minimum wage to a living wage – at least $20 an hour – and make it easier for workers to join unions by passing the Pro Act.
Yes. We must strengthen public education and make higher education available to all, regardless of income.
Yes. We must make sure that AI and robotics benefit working families and not just enrich a handful of big tech oligarchs.
Yes. We must ensure that everyone in America can retire with dignity by expanding social security, scrapping the cap on taxable income and restoring traditional defined benefit pension plans.
The new Democratic majority in Congress must act boldly and with an unprecedented sense of urgency. The crises facing our country and the world are much too dangerous to be ignored, or to be dealt with through tepid half-measures.
At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class.
- Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Why are families going hungry in northern Yemen even where food is on sale?
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Why are families going hungry in northern Yemen even where food is on sale?
Flour and oil still reach markets in Hodeidah and Sanaa. But rising costs, scarce work and loss of food aid put them out of reach.
Umm Sami, a widow raising four children in Yemen’s Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, sells household goods and takes on occasional domestic work to feed her family. Rising prices have changed how she shops. “Sometimes we buy a little flour or oil that lasts just one day because we cannot afford a whole bag,” she told Al Jazeera.
Food is still on the shelves. It was available in the markets that monitors could reach in September, but families had less money to spend, according to the Yemen Joint Monitoring Report, a humanitarian and food security assessment. Across Houthi-controlled areas like Hodeidah, a basket of basic foods cost about 7 percent, or $91, more that month than in August, its highest level in a year.
Families on both sides of the front lines are struggling, and prices are rising faster in the government-held south, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET). What sets the Houthi-controlled north apart is how little families there can earn and how little help is left.
Most households in and around northern towns find only five to 10 days of paid work a month, FEWS NET reported in October. The UN World Food Programme’s (WFP) food assistance in Houthi-held areas has been suspended since September 2025, FEWS NET said. By mid-September 2026, WFP had begun a distribution round in government-held areas that aimed to reach about 1.7 million people.
In the last nationwide hunger analysis by UN agencies and their partners, published in mid-2025, the only people projected to face catastrophic hunger, about 41,000, were in four districts of Amran, Hodeidah and Hajjah governorates – all under Houthi control.
On Friday, the WFP and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) named Yemen among its hunger hotspots of highest concern for the six months ending May 2027.
As fighting spreads and aid dries up, we look at why food on sale in northern Yemen is slipping out of reach of the families who need it.
Why are some families in Hodeidah buying food one day at a time?
Because a day’s work – when there is any – no longer pays for a day’s food.
Ahmed Arjash drives a rented motorcycle taxi near Hodeidah’s Othman market to support his family of six. Many of his former customers now walk to save the fare. “Now, my daily earnings barely cover the fuel or the rent for the motorcycle,” he told Al Jazeera.
Saleh, a construction worker paid by the day, said some days pass without anyone hiring him. “If I work one day, the wage is not enough to cover the family’s needs for several days with prices this high,” he said.
Fishing pays less, too. Salem, a fisherman in his 30s, said fuel, boats and equipment cost him more while fewer customers could afford his catch. “Many families no longer buy fish as they used to,” he said. On some trips, he barely earns back what it costs to go to sea.
Families are adjusting by eating less. In Hodeidah’s poorest neighbourhoods, many skip meals or go without meat, fish, milk and fruit, Al Jazeera found.
In Houthi-held areas, FEWS NET reported that higher taxes on street vendors and shops had already reduced demand for labour in September. In its outlook through May 2027, it expected more small businesses to close and those that stayed open to hire fewer workers.
How does food reach shops in northern Yemen, and what makes the journey more expensive?
Almost all of it comes by sea, and each step from ship to shop now costs more. Yemen imports about 90 percent of its food, according to WFP. Hodeidah is the main port supplying the Houthi-held north, including Sanaa.
Food has kept arriving – data shows imports into Houthi-held areas rose 10 percent between June and August compared with the previous three months and doubled year-on-year – but fuel has not.
Fuel imports fell about 85 percent year-on-year in August, with no recorded arrivals of diesel or petrol through northern ports, according to the FAO. In September, the Houthi authorities raised the price of petrol by about 10 percent, the first increase in four years, Al Jazeera reported. Bread prices in Houthi-held areas rose 25 percent that month, FEWS NET said.
The ports themselves have come under attack. On November 2, the Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said Saudi aircraft had hit a pier and a commercial ship at Ras Isa port, north of Hodeidah, the news agency AFP reported. On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had attacked “operational capabilities” in Hodeidah, and the Houthis threatened to retaliate against Saudi Red Sea ports. Hodeidah port remains open, Al Jazeera reported. How the latest attacks will affect deliveries remains unclear.
Moving goods inland has also become slower and costlier. A truck travelling between the south and the north “now takes up to a week to reach its final destination”, Saleh Abdullah, a shopkeeper in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera in September. Before the renewed fighting, the trip took three days or less. Customers pay the extra transport and fuel costs, he said. “Whether it is the flour, the baby milk, the fruits, the vegetables, or anything else.”
When families cannot afford food, what stops aid from reaching them?
In the north, the main source of food aid has been switched off. WFP suspended its activities in Houthi-controlled areas in September 2025 after the group detained UN staff. Last month, WFP said 73 UN personnel, 38 of them its own staff, remained in detention.
Other aid organisations still operate in the north, but funding cuts and restrictions limit their reach.
On Thursday, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) said a handful of overstretched and underfunded Yemeni and international organisations were the only remaining lifeline for millions there.
Funding cuts, sanctions and the UN’s pause in operations had all contributed to a collapsing humanitarian response, it added. The NRC said donors had provided just 16 percent of the money sought for food security across Yemen this year.
What does the UN’s new hunger warning tell us about northern Yemen?
The latest FAO–WFP report warns that fighting and economic hardship threaten to deepen hunger through May 2027. It names economic hardship among the threats, but it cannot say how many people in the north are going hungry. FAO and WFP said conflict, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather drove the risk in the five hotspots of highest concern, the Reuters news agency reported.
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), the UN-backed system for measuring hunger, has not published a recent analysis of Houthi-held areas. Its latest figures – 5.4 million people facing crisis levels of hunger or worse between October and December, including 1.8 million at the more severe emergency level – cover government-held areas only.
In June 2025, the IPC projected that 18.1 million people in Yemen would face crisis levels of hunger or worse between September 2025 and February 2026. That was 52 percent of the population covered by the nationwide analysis.
FEWS NET expects emergency levels of hunger to persist in Hodeidah and Hajjah through May 2027.
At that level, families face large gaps in what they eat, or must sell what they need to make a living to buy food. The network’s gravest warning concerns Taiz, a government-held city besieged by Houthi forces, where it sees a credible risk of famine between February and May if the siege is prolonged and tightened.
In Hodeidah, the market still has flour. For families like Umm Sami’s, the question is how little of it they can afford. “Even bread has become a burden,” she said.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: After nearly two decades, the Old Acropolis Museum in Athens re-opens
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melissa Gronlund
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Old Acropolis Museum, the first Greek museum to be built in modern times, re-opened on Monday after a major restoration project. It is the first time the museum, founded in 1874 and nestled into the rock of the storied Acropolis hill, has been accessible to the public since 2007.
The opening ceremony was a grand affair, with speeches by the Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and the country’s minister of culture Lina Mendoni, among others.
Once simply the “Museum”, the Old Acropolis Museum took its current name in 2009, when Athens built a newer Acropolis Museum 300 yards down the hill. This offered larger and state-of-the-art space in which to house the antiquities from the Parthenon and other Greek sites, as well as a viewing room designed for the Elgin Marbles—currently showing casts, but with the idea that one day the museum might one day welcome the real items.
The Old Acropolis Museum was left empty for years, and plans eventually developed to use it as storage and administrative spaces. But by 2019, the Greek state definitively nixed this idea.
“For us, it was inconceivable, almost an affront, that this historic building, with its unique location, should be converted into offices and storage facilities,” said Mendoni during her opening speech. “We therefore decided that the museum should reopen in accordance with its original purpose. However, it was not to become just another conventional museum, but rather a museum and exhibition space hosting exhibitions on the history, archaeology and culture of Athens, as well as contemporary art exhibitions inspired by Greek civilisation and innovative programmes incorporating cutting-edge technology.”
The museum will now host both a rotating selection of artefacts as well as a contemporary art programme. The first exhibition, Athens City Idea, focuses on Athens as a social, political, and economic entity, via tragic masks, statues, coins, and amphorae that have been in storage elsewhere across Athens, plus recent discoveries. A digital art component animated the Parthenon’s friezes and the history of the Acropolis Hill.
Part of the idea behind the temporary exhibitions is to keep the museum’s display current, a point also underlined by its commitment to contemporary art.
This includes the last of a trilogy of works commissioned for Athens from the American artist Michael Rakowitz, which is also the final project of Neon, the roving art foundation created by Dimitris Daskalopoulos that for 14 years has funded art and exhibitions across the city, and which announced its closure earlier this year.
“You could say that the first contemporary work here was Phidias’s statue of Athena in the 5th century BCE,” quipped Daskalopoulos, the Athens-born collector who founded Neon. Daskalopoulos also supported the refurbishment of the Old Acropolis Museum, which was funded by both private and public money. “But encouraging the coexistence of antiquity with the contemporary is a challenge we have embraced many times throughout our work at Neon.”
Rakowitz’s installation What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026), which was commissioned by Neon, and comprises a kiln and newly fired bricks, looks at a lesser-known episode in the Acropolis’s history.
“I realised that you could only tell the whole story of the site if you look through the lens of migration,” the artist told The Art Newspaper. He studied the population exchanges during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, when Greece and Turkey forced a combined total of around 1.5 million inhabitants to leave—Christian Turks to Greece and Muslim Greeks to Turkey. When the Turkish refugees arrived in Athens, they set up tents and encampments at the base of the Acropolis hill.
“Thinking about a ruin as being something that can renew itself to a population and become once again a shelter excited me,” he said. "When I found out about the tradition of the Asia Minor refugees who were able to go back to Turkey after some years, and then the Muslims who were uprooted from Greece, when those populations were able to visit their the departed homelands, they found oftentimes their buildings or towns in a state of ruin, and they would take a brick from that place and bring it back as a memento.”
Rakowitz has incorporated these original bricks alongside ones newly made with inscriptions and stamps that bear witness to more recent histories of displacement. For these he worked with survivors of the 1920s population transfers as well as women in the Melissa Network, a nonprofit organisation that supports migrant women in Greece.
“I wanted these bricks to become a foundation for a new kind of city that welcomes strangers and doesn't push them back at sea,” he said.

https://gothamist.com/news/forecast-impr.title: Forecast improves for Saturday's postponed Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade
https://gothamist.com/news/forecast-impr.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/forecast-impr.text:
Weather for the rest of the holiday weekend and Saturday’s postponed Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will be a breeze compared to Thursday’s mayhem.
The National Weather Service is predicting mild weather for the rest of Friday, with temperatures in the 50s, partly cloudy skies, brief passing showers in the afternoon or evening, and wind gusts up to 35 mph.
Clear and dry weather is expected on Saturday, with sustained winds reaching up to 15 mph and gusts up to 25 mph, according to the weather service, below the threshold that parade requires to proceed with its iconic giant balloons.
“Conditions are much better for a parade on Saturday,” said National Weather Service meteorologist David Stark. “The winds won't be anywhere near as strong.”
The weather was a different story on Thursday, when heavy rains caused flooding in coastal and low-lying areas, and strong winds downed trees and power lines.
Central Park recorded 2.18 inches of rain, topping the previous record of 1.91 inches for Nov. 26, set in 1996, according to the weather service. The Rockaways remained under a flood advisory into Friday morning.
More than 100,000 homes in the Garden State were still without power early Friday, down from 179,000 on Thanksgiving Day.
More than 15,000 Con Ed customers in New York lost power during the nor'easter, according to Con Ed. In Westchester County, more than 9,000 households lost power, and many still were still waiting for service to be restored.
On Long Island, at the height of the storm, more than 40,000 homes lost power and the total was 11,000 in Orange and Rockland. Only a few thousand customers were still without service Friday, according to the utility officials.
Only general flight delays were reported at the region's airports.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Anaadi faz roda de samba em Porto Alegre nas vésperas dos 40 anos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Carol Zatt
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Nome muito conhecido e elogiado da cena musical gaúcha, a cantora Anaadi tem dividido a vida entre Porto Alegre e Paris, já faz mais de cinco anos. Neste sábado (28) à noite, ela realiza seu primeiro show do ano aberto ao público na Capital.
Ao lado do percussionista Tuti Rodrigues e do violonista Max Garcia, parceiros de longa data e também reconhecidos pelo Grammy Latino entregue à artista em 2018, a cantora celebra a alegria dos reencontros neste mês de novembro com o espetáculo “Não Se Proteja da Felicidade”, a primeira edição de uma roda de samba que convida o público ao reencontro e à celebração da vida. Em um formato marcado pela proximidade e pela troca com a plateia, os artistas reúnem sambas consagrados e algumas canções autorais em um repertório vibrante, permeado por leveza, alegria e esperança no amanhã.
Os músicos Cabelinho Azevedo (cavaquinho) e Bruno Coelho (percussão) – outros dois nomes ilustres no cenário do samba no estado – também subirão ao palco do Grezz (Rua Almirante Barroso, 328, Floresta), a partir das 21h. Ingressos de R$ 20 (meia-entrada) a R$ 40 (inteira) estão à venda no Sympla e no local.
“Os preparativos são mais de 10 anos de amizade entre os realizadores desse projeto, que somos eu, Tuti Rodrigues, Max Garcia e Angela dos Passos, acompanhados também por grandes amigos e parceiros: Bruno Coelho e Cabelinho Azevedo. Esse show nasce da amizade e da luz que ela promove em nossas vidas. Por isso, o eixo dessa roda de samba é a celebração da vida, da alegria, da esperança e dos reencontros. Nós vamos interpretar samba, porque esse é o universo musical que melhor representa essa conexão e essa energia que nos une e que nos leva adiante. O samba é convidativo, agregador, amoroso, e assim será também a nossa roda. Que ela possa encorajar a todos a se deixarem levar pela energia positiva que vamos vibrar juntos”, conta Anaadi.
Para além de tanto tempo de parceria conjunta, ela explica que a ideia “nasceu de um desejo compartilhado por nós todos de revigorar as energias depois de um ano tão difícil pra nós brasileiros. Acreditamos que o samba vem como um convite à felicidade, à paz, à alegria, à solidariedade, à virtude. Fazer essa roda de samba no final do ano é a nossa forma de nos energizarmos após um período de muita luta e trabalho, pra nos prepararmos pras próximas aventuras!”. O objetivo é que a produção se fortaleça daqui pra frente como um espaço anual para “recarregar as baterias, exorcizar as mazelas e energizar o corpo e a alma”.
Para tal, o setlist reúne clássicos de Clara Nunes, Beth Carvalho, Dona Ivone Lara, Alcione, Paulinho da Viola, Jorge Ben Jor, Almir Guineto, Zeca Pagodinho, Arlindo Cruz, Xande de Pilares, Chico Buarque e Gilberto Gil, com algumas composições próprias. São canções do próximo disco da Anaadi, “Iluminar”, que tem como tema o samba e o cuidado de si, assunto da pesquisa de mestrado dela. “Todo repertório traz temáticas inspiradoras, esperançosas, convidativas à virtude e à felicidade”, diz.
O título da roda faz referência não apenas ao tema do evento, mas ainda ao primeiro single do próximo projeto fonográfico da artista, já disponível em formato de videoclipe. Composta em parceria com Allan Dias Castro, Eduardo Pitta e Rodrigo Allende, “Não Se Proteja da Felicidade” é um samba solar e acolhedor que encoraja os corações partidos a se abrirem às possibilidades, aos novos encontros e à felicidade.
“É essa a principal mensagem: que essa música afete as pessoas como um convite a aceitarmos que a vulnerabilidade é parte inevitável de uma vida feliz. Quando fechamos o coração, seja por medo, traumas ou decepções, achamos que estamos evitando apenas os eventos ruins. Mas o coração é um só. Se o fechamos para evitar afetos ruins, o fechamos também para os afetos bons, aqueles que nos fazem felizes. Portanto, se proteger da dor é também se proteger da felicidade”, destaca a autora.
Com apoio do estúdio Transcendental Audio e roteiro e direção de Leo Bracht, o clipe do single está disponível no YouTube desde setembro de 2025. A produção da Jasmine Music e Colateral Filmes contou com financiamento da Secretaria de Cultura de Porto Alegre e da Lei Paulo Gustavo.
Uma trajetória iluminada que abre caminhos
Ana Paula Lonardi de Souza nasceu em 17 de dezembro de 1986, na capital gaúcha. Desde sempre, por aqui, sua voz e sua forma de interpretar canções chamava a atenção, os olhares e os ouvidos. Em 2013, participou do programa The Voice Brasil, para ampliar sua carreira nacional. Em 2017, antes de lançar seu primeiro disco, “Noturno”, adotou o nome artístico ANAADI, assim mesmo, em letras maiúsculas. A palavra vem do hindi e significa “eterno”.
Então, veio o grande marco da trajetória. Com o álbum sendo o vencedor do Grammy Latino de Melhor Álbum Pop Contemporâneo em Língua Portuguesa em 2018, registro que já contava com a assinatura de Tuti Rodrigues e Max Garcia nos arranjos e performances em diversas faixas. Parceiros musicais de longa data, os três colecionam colaborações nacionais e internacionais representando a música brasileira. Os artistas se reuniram novamente para colaborações na Costa Rica, no Brasil e nos EUA, com destaque para uma gravação em Miami, onde co-criaram uma inspirada versão de “Mas Que Nada” ao lado da Raíces Jazz Orchestra e do produtor e percussionista vencedor do Grammy Latino Tony Succar. Nela, são Tuti e Anaadi os responsáveis por trazer a identidade musical brasileira para essa mistura de samba e salsa, que também contou com a contribuição de Max, e que conquistou mais de meio milhão de ouvintes ao redor do mundo.
O segundo disco, “Iluminar”, está com a pré-produção “toda planejada, com as composições prontas e o desenho do que queremos pra esse álbum. Tenho um desejo imenso de produzir esse disco! Não conseguimos o capital financeiro pra concretizar esse projeto, mas espero que consigamos esse apoio na hora certa. Nesse disco, reuniremos sambas em parceria com diversos amigos, entre eles Allan Dias Castro, Mario Falcão, Bianca Obino, Tuti Rodrigues, Rosa Franco, Eduardo Pitta, Rodrigo Allende e Leo Bracht. Ainda estamos estudando a ideia de uma participação nacional ou internacional. Mas o foco será em lançarmos luz a parcerias profundas, que nascem da colaboração contínua entre nós”.
Anaadi está radicada em Paris, já morando na capital francesa há 5 anos e meio: “Desde que fui pra lá, tenho tido o privilégio de passar uma temporada em Porto Alegre todos os anos. Seja por convites de trabalho ou por datas comemorativas da minha família. E pretendo seguir vindo pra minha cidade natal, ocupando esse espaço e me deliciando com os lugares e relações de amizade que cultivo por aqui”.
Às vésperas de completar 40 anos de vida, a artista admite que passa um compilado de memórias pela mente: “Como um filme que atesta hoje um sentimento de realização e de gratidão. Olho pra trás e vejo quantas coisas eu vivi, como mudei e aprendi, como cresci, entre erros e acertos, sempre numa busca por conquistar cada vez mais coerência entre o que penso, sinto e faço”.
Formada em Psicologia, ela lembra que também está completando 22 anos de terapia. “O que é muito transformador e potente, e só se realiza com o passar dos anos mesmo. Sou uma mulher que estabeleceu algumas relações de amizade, amor e parceria preciosas, e que realizou muitas coisas cedo, principalmente no trabalho, junto a essas parcerias. Essa bagagem tão consistente, que é ao mesmo tempo afetiva e profissional, me dá orgulho”, avalia.

https://taz.de/Erstes-deutsches-Supermod.title: Erstes deutsches Supermodel: Eine Kunstfigur ihrer Zeit
https://taz.de/Erstes-deutsches-Supermod.author: Jenni Zylka
https://taz.de/Erstes-deutsches-Supermod.text:
Erstes deutsches Supermodel: Eine Kunstfigur ihrer Zeit
Vera von Lehndorff ist mit 87 Jahren gestorben. Mit ihrer Hauprolle im Filmklassiker „Blow Up“ von Michelangelo Antionioni wurde sie weltberühmt.
In „Blow-Up“, Michelangelos Antonionis enigmatischem Meisterwerk von 1966, schießt Vera von Lehndorff den Vogel ab. Mit wenigen Szenen bildet die damals 27-jährige den Rahmen der Erzählung über einen blasierten Modefotografen, der denkt, zufällig einen Mord dokumentiert zu haben.
Lehndorffs Rolle entspricht ihrer damaligen Tätigkeit – sie spielt ein Model, das im auf der Höhe der Swinging Sixties in London angesiedelten Thriller zunächst versetzt wird. „Ich muss um 11 ein Flugzeug nach Paris kriegen“, beschwert sie sich, als Thomas (David Hemmings) zu Beginn des Films zu spät zum Fototermin kommt – ihm ist das egal.
Die folgende Choreografie beim von Jazz und Grenzüberschreitung geprägten Shooting parodiert einen Sexakt: Irgendwann kniet Thomas über der 1,90 großen, knochigen Frau, die unter dem glänzenden Fransenkleid nackt ist; er fixiert sie mit seinem Objektiv, seine „Yes, yes, that’s good, give it to me, make it come!“-Rufe werden lauter. Als er genug hat, steht er abrupt auf, und lässt sie in zeittypisch-männlicher Ignoranz gegenüber weiblichen Befindlichkeiten ohne ein weiteres Wort zurück.
Eine „furchtbare Märchengeschichte“
Am Ende des Films trifft Thomas wieder auf das Model – doch bei einer drogenschwangeren Party prallt seine Aufregung an ihr ab: Während er seinem Freund von seinem Erlebnis berichtet, übernimmt Veruschka den Fokus der Szene. Sie betritt den Raum in einem engen Jumpsuit mit Schlangenmuster, ein Gürtel betont ihre Hüfte, die toupierten Haare sind zerzaust, in der Hand hat sie einen Joint. „Du wolltest doch in Paris sein“, wundert sich der etwas konfuse Thomas. „Ich bin in Paris“, antwortet sie knapp.
Obwohl die sich später selbst mit dem Mononym „Veruschka“ bezeichende von Lehndorff damit den 60s-Lifestyle perfekt verkörperte, lässt sich an ihr auch deutsche Geschichte rekapitulieren. Geboren wurde die aus einem ostpreußischen Adelsgeschlecht stammende Malerei- und Tanzinteressierte 1939 in Königsberg, und eine „furchtbare Märchengeschichte“ nahm ihren Lauf, sagte sie in einem 2005 entstandenen Dokumentarfilm vom Andy-Warhol-Kollaborateur Paul Morrissey, durch den sie selbst mit tiefer, ruhiger Stimme führt.
Ihr Vater wurde 1944 wegen seiner Beteiligung am Hitler-Attentat vom 20. Juli hingerichtet, die Familie inhaftiert, die dritte ihrer Schwestern im Gefängnis geboren. Ihre Kindheit war geprägt von Flucht, Orts- und Schulwechseln. Veruschka studierte in Hamburg und Florenz Kunst und wurde schließlich als Model verpflichtet – ihr schönes, melancholisches, etwas abweisendes Gesicht mit den schläfrigen Augen und der lange, ultraschlanke Körper passten zum 60er-Jahre-Ideal der Kindfrau, die gleichzeitig Vergänglichkeit ausstrahlt. Dick sei sie einzig als „arischer Babyspeck im Schloss“ gewesen, erzählt sie.
Beine und „big hair“ als Markenzeichen
Trotz der misogynen Atmosphäre in der Modebranche der 60er-Jahre versucht sie die Inszenierung ihres Körpers früh selbst in die Hand zu nehmen. Das Handwerk und die Bedeutung des Lichts habe sie von Irving Penn und Richard Avedon gelernt, sagt sie und beschreibt, wie Beine und „big hair“ zu ihrem Markenzeichen wurden. Das Dasein als Model bezeichnete sie als Teufelskreis: „Es verlangt, immer perfekt zu sein, die Leute wollen dich anhimmeln und akzeptieren nicht, dass du auch Schwächen und Fehler hast.“
Dem mit „Blow-Up“ ausgelösten Hype folgen wenige Filmrollen. Offen spricht Veruschka nachträglich von Depressionen, Krankenhausaufenthalten und dem Weg heraus. Der emanzipatorische Gedanke war bei ihr stets präsent: 1971 posiert sie neben Romy Schneider und Senta Berger auf dem von Alice Schwarzer inszenierten Stern-Cover unter dem Titel „Wir haben abgetrieben“.
Gemeinsam mit herrenlosen Katzen lebte sie später in Brooklyn, New York; sie malte, fotografierte und organisierte Happenings, bei denen sie ihren Körper und ihr Gesicht bemalte – „Mode und Kunst gehen eine Fusion ein“, sagt sie, und stellte sich damit gegen die damals vorherrschende elitäre Ansicht, Mode sei gegenüber Kunst zweitrangig. 1984 spielte sie für Ulrike Ottinger die Figur des Dorian Gray; in der Foto- und Performance-Reihe „Emanationen“ zeigte sie in den 90ern Menschen in opulenten Kostümen mit Punkfrisuren.
Ein Lebensabend in Berlin
Nach Kollaborationen und Freundschaften mit Künstlern wie Blixa Bargeld und Alva Noto und einem Gastauftritt im James-Bond-Film „Casino Royale“ lebte sie in Berlin, wo man sie zuweilen in langen Handschuhen und flamboyanten Schleiern und „Head Pieces“ erleben konnte.
Vera von Lehndorff, die am 24. November in Berlin starb, erfuhr am Anfang ihres Lebens die Vereinnahmung ihres Körpers. Stark wie sie war, eroberte sie ihn unbeirrt zurück.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ru.title: Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ru.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ru.text:
All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.
Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.
The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.
Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.

Législatives anticipées en Espagne : l'extrême droite va-t-elle arriver au pouvoir ?
Publié le 27 novembre 2026
Dans la dernière ligne droite de la campagne, droite et extrême droite aiguisent leurs couteaux, convaincues qu’elles peuvent défaire dans les urnes le socialiste Pedro Sanchez et le gouvernement sortant de coalition de gauche. L’issue du scrutin des élections législatives anticipées du 29 novembre, présenté comme l’un des plus cruciaux depuis le retour de la démocratie, s’annonce très serrée.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.title: Bundeshaushalt | Nullrunde bei den Regelsätzen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.author: Sarah Yolanda Koss
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120419.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Bundeshaushalt
Nullrunde bei den Regelsätzen
Mit dem Bundeshaushalt friert die Regierung auch die Grundsicherungsbeträge bis Mitte 2028 ein. Linke bezweifelt Verfassungskonformität.
Bis Ende Juni bleiben die Regelsätze in der Grundsicherung so, wie sie derzeit sind: bei 563 Euro für Alleinstehende. Das beschloss der Bundestag am Freitag mit dem Haushaltsbegleitgesetz. Im kurzfristigen parlamentarischen Verfahren brachten die Koalitionsfraktionen von CDU/CSU und SPD eine »Einfrierungsregelung« ein. Diese sieht vor, dass die bisherigen Regelbedarfe unverändert bleiben. Auch wenn es neue Berechnungen gibt, die andere Beträge vorschreiben würden. Der Ausschuss für Arbeit und Soziales, der für die Regelsätze fachlich zuständig ist, wurde daran nicht mehr beteiligt.
Die Beträge, die den monatlichen Grundbedarf einer Person oder eines Haushalts zur Sicherung des Existenzminimums decken sollen, werden als Regelbedarfsstufen bezeichnet. Sie gelten für Millionen Menschen, unter ihnen Ältere, Erwerbsgeminderte, Erwerbslose und Beschäftigte mit kleinem Einkommen und richten sich nach dem Alter und der Lebens- beziehungsweise Wohnsituation.
Laut Regierungskreisen gibt es zumindest für eine Regelbedarfsgruppe bereits höhere Bedarfsberechnungen als mit dem Haushalt festgelegt. Welche das sei, erklärte das Bundesministerium für Arbeit und Soziales »nd« auf Nachfrage nicht. Ebenso wenig, warum die »Einfrierungsregelung« nachträglich eingereicht wurde.
Der Entwurf zum Regelbedarfsermittlungsgesetz werde derzeit innerhalb der Bundesregierung beraten. »Dies betrifft auch die Frage, in welcher Höhe die Regelbedarfe neu ermittelt und festgesetzt werden. Die Neuermittlung folgt den Vorgaben des Bundesverfassungsgerichts«, so eine Sprecherin des BMAS.
»Das Existenzminimum ist kein haushaltspolitischer Verhandlungsspielraum, sondern ein Grundrecht«, sagt Cansın Köktürk, sozialpolitische Sprecherin der Linksfraktion. Sie fordert eine vollständige Offenlegung der Neuberechnung. »Wir sprechen hier nicht über abstrakte Rechengrößen, sondern über Menschen, die darauf angewiesen sind, dass der Staat ihr Existenzminimum tatsächlich sichert.«
Durch das »Geheimhalten der aktuellen Daten« werde der Fachwelt die Möglichkeit genommen nachzurechnen, um wie viel Abschläge den Regelbedarf verkleinern, kritisiert auch der Paritätische Gesamtverband. In der Vergangenheit erschien beispielsweise willkürlich, dass Sozialleistungsbeziehende das Geld für Hundefutter, einen Weihnachtsbaum oder eine Woche Campingurlaub aberkannt wurde.
»Hier tritt eine politische Entscheidung an die Stelle einer transparenten und sachgerechten Ermittlung, wie sie das Bundesverfassungsgericht 2010 verlangt hat. Wir fordern, die Regelsätze zu erhöhen und die Preisentwicklung zeitnah auszugleichen«, so Katja Kipping, Geschäftsführerin des Paritätischen Gesamtverbands.
Das menschenwürdige Existenzminimum ist über die Verfassung geschützt. Der Gesetzgeber ist demnach verpflichtet, die Bedarfe realitätsgerecht zu erfassen, seine Berechnungen auf verlässliche Daten zu stützen und nachvollziehbar zu begründen. Dabei geht es auch darum, die Lebenshaltungskosten laufend zu prüfen. »Eine pauschale Festschreibung ersetzt diese verfassungsrechtlich gebotene Prüfung nicht«, erklärt Köktürk.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-sanche.title: In Spain, the Indignados’ Parties Are Dwindling Fast
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-sanche.author: Carlos Delclós
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-sanche.text:
In Spain, the Indignados’ Parties Are Dwindling Fast
Most Spaniards across the political spectrum agree that housing should be a right, not a commodity. But the radical-left parties who voice this demand are riven by infighting and seemingly unable to regain voters’ trust.
On September 23, Maricarmen Abascal was carried on a stretcher out of her apartment in the Retiro district of Madrid, where she’d been living since 1956. She was eighty-seven, disabled, and had limited mobility. Neighbors and members of the Madrid Tenants’ Union had formed a human chain to stop the eviction. This time, the police broke through it. As she was carried out, the crowd shouted that she was not alone. Two weeks later, she died in a hospital, before she could return to her home, under an agreement with her corporate landlords that arrived far too late.
Her case set off a massive wave of mobilization led by a confederation of tenants’ unions. On September 26, marches under the slogan “Not One More Maricarmen” filled the streets of some forty towns and cities. In Madrid, protesters pitched hundreds of tents in the iconic Puerta del Sol, the public square that the anti-austerity Indignados occupied in 2011, and encampments soon spread across Spain. But on October 2, after Pedro Sánchez’s center-left government proposed two emergency housing decrees, the conservative Partido Popular, the far-right Vox, and the right-wing Catalan-nationalist Junts joined forces to block the measures. Sánchez, who represents the Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE), responded by calling snap elections for November 29, this Sunday. With parliament dissolved, its standing committee revived the main decree by a single vote, extending the ban on evicting vulnerable households through 2030.
Pressure has been building in Spain’s housing system for two decades. In 2006, at the height of a speculative bubble, the V de Vivienda (“V for Housing”) movement summed up a generation’s prospects in its blunt slogan: “You’re not going to have a house your whole f — ing life.” After the bubble burst in 2008, dragging the economy down with it, some of its more prominent activists founded the Mortgage Victims’ Platform (PAH), which became a pillar of the broader Indignados Movement.
Today rents are at record highs, and housing has become a primary driver of inequality in Spain. According to the Spanish Youth Council, only 14.5 percent of Spaniards ages sixteen to twenty-nine lived away from their parents last year, the lowest share on record. But the cracks run deeper than young tenants’ case alone. Bank of Spain data show that the share of households headed by sixty-five- to seventy-four-year-olds owning additional real estate properties nearly doubled, to 62 percent, while homeownership among those thirty-five to forty-four fell dramatically. Increasingly, Spain’s class structure is dividing along the lines of rentiers and lifelong tenants, with inheritances largely deciding who ends up where.
The right-wing opposition criticizes the Left’s policy focus on rent control, noting that the supply of long-term rentals collapsed in Catalonia after price caps took effect in 2024. But much of that housing moved into temporary contracts, which the 2023 Housing Law left unregulated despite warnings from tenant unions and the PSOE’s left-wing coalition partners. Seasonal contracts in Catalonia rose 45 percent over the caps’ first year. The Socialists now back closing the loophole in the national legislation.
Sympathy for the evicted reaches well beyond the Left. In an early October survey by Spain’s state-run Center for Sociological Research (CIS), housing topped the list of national problems even among right-wing voters. Two-thirds of Partido Popular and Vox voters agreed that housing should be seen as a right rather than a commodity. Yet their parties had just voted down the decrees.
For now, the polls are unkind to the governing broad-left coalition. Most show the Partido Popular and Vox on course for a majority coalition. Hostility toward Sánchez is especially strong, bolstered by the corruption conviction of his former right-hand man, José Luis Ábalos, amnesty for Catalan separatist leaders, and July’s mass crossing of people into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, among other issues.
The Spanish Exception
This prognosis is especially striking since, for much of the past decade, Spain has stood out as a relatively progressive exception in European politics. After years of contentious mobilization, the energy of the Indignados’ anti-austerity protests was eventually channeled into government. Since 2018, Sánchez’s governments — supported by Podemos from the outside, before the Socialists and Podemos formed a coalition in 2020 — have raised the minimum wage by more than 60 percent, curbed temporary labor contracts, and opened a path to legal status for undocumented migrants. GDP growth has also outpaced most of the eurozone. Abroad Sánchez recognized a Palestinian state, imposed an arms embargo on Israel, and refused NATO’s new spending target, becoming a standard-bearer for left-wingers internationally. At home, however, he is seen as a polarizing figure.
Many observers read today’s situation as the end of an era. But in 2023, most polls similarly predicted a right-wing majority that didn’t materialize on Election Day, and even now a large share of voters remain undecided. What does seem to be ending is the political cycle that began in the squares in 2011 and entered parliament in 2015. Fragmented and consumed by personal hostilities, the Left’s most familiar faces will compete against one another on November 29.
Sumar, the coalition led by Deputy Premier Yolanda Díaz, won thirty-one seats in 2023. Podemos left the coalition early in the new term, citing its exclusion from the cabinet and its inability to operate inside Sumar’s parliamentary group. Sumar’s successor, the Frente Amplio, led by former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau, herself a founder of the PAH, is now competing against Podemos. The latter, in turn, has allied with regional parties in several provinces, most notably the pro-independence Esquerra Republicana in Catalonia.
Tellingly, the dispute began over process. Podemos insisted on an open vote to choose candidates while Frente Amplio demanded a prior political agreement on the lists. That two parties born of a movement for “real democracy” could not agree on how to make a democratic decision is the clearest symptom of a deeper failure, namely, a lack of proper mechanisms for deliberation between the coalition’s different currents. At its founding assembly in 2014, Podemos opted for a centralized structure designed to win elections quickly; the local circles that had given birth to it soon lost their influence. Internal democracy came to mean online votes, which some members criticized as simply ratifying decisions already made at the top. Without shared rules for settling disagreements, conflicts ended in splits: Íñigo Errejón’s departure in 2019, Podemos’s break with Sumar in 2023, and now this one. Sumar, for its part, was built around Díaz, with its internal structures assembled ad hoc only later.
What filled the vacuum was personality. Podemos was born at a peculiar moment in Spain’s media landscape, when political talk shows were booming on television and social media was beginning to set their agenda. Pablo Iglesias, a political scientist who had honed his style on a small online TV show, became a fixture of prime-time debates, and in 2014 the party put his face on the ballot. Few parties have exploited the personalization of politics so skillfully, or at such an opportune time. But a party organized around the visibility of its leaders has no way to resolve their conflicts other than a politics of personal brands, neglecting development of the internal mechanisms needed for movements to outlive their leaders.
New Generation
Yet even amid the apparent demise of these party vehicles, a new political generation is emerging: people who came of age after the 2008 crash, organized in tenant unions rather than parties, but also far less hesitant than the Indignados to situate themselves ideologically. The question that will shape Spain’s next decade is not only who governs but who participates in politics, and how. For the Indignados, participation was not just turnout but a broad set of radical democratic practices: assemblies in the squares, consensus-based decision-making, self-management, and civil disobedience. As they grew into their institutional roles, the parties that grew out of the squares left these practices behind.
The movements did not abandon such principles, but they have also changed. While the Indignados resisted ideological labels in their condemnation of the entire political class, today’s housing movement is explicitly left-wing. Part of it, most notably the fast-growing Movimiento Socialista, openly contests the PSOE’s claim to the word “socialism.” Meanwhile, they do not reject electoral strategy as aggressively as the movement did in 2011. Tellingly, an essay in one of its main outlets rejected abstention from voting as “antipolitics” and argued for a third position independent of both the (pro-government) progressive and reactionary blocs. If the Sánchez era is to end, its author Axel Altadill claimed, it should be brought down later by a working-class movement, not now by the reactionary right.
This position, and the issue of housing rights, is all the more relevant given recent research on political polarization. A study of forty-one elections in twenty countries, including Spain, by political scientists Mariano Torcal and Paul Beck finds that conversations across party lines rarely soften partisan hostility, and that polarized citizens tend to avoid them altogether. In the October CIS survey, about four in ten Partido Popular and Vox voters backed restricting home purchases by speculative investors, and as many or more wanted tighter rules on seasonal rentals. Over 40 percent of lower-income right-wing voters support banning evictions of vulnerable households. Yet only 9 percent of Partido Popular voters and 7 percent of Vox voters rated the government’s decrees on this issue favorably. It seems the more a policy is identified with Sánchez, the less its content matters to conservative voters.
In contrast, housing rights cut across party lines when they emerge as a bottom-up demand. Tenant organizing seeks to bridge the divides electoral spectacle tends to amplify. On November 11, Spain got a taste of what bottom-up organizing can achieve: its first general strike in fourteen years, a nationwide stoppage in which workers across sectors walked off the job for a day. It began as a demand from tenant unions, was taken up by the country’s main labor federations, and culminated in marches that drew millions into the streets. In practically all of Spain’s major cities, tenant unions led the marches, with the leaders of the largest labor unions gathering behind their banners. As Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, put it: “Whoever governs, we will not tolerate another four years without tackling this country’s biggest problem.”
In this context, Spain’s still-undecided voters will play a key role this Sunday. According to the CIS data from October, they make up about one-sixth of the electorate, and those among them who voted in the last general election in 2023 largely backed the Left over the Right. Half of these potential voters support at least eight of the eleven measures in October’s government housing decrees, but only 17 percent claim to trust Sánchez. So, while undecided voters want a comprehensive housing agenda, they don’t seem to trust anyone to see it through.
This pattern is most pronounced among the one-fifth of all undecided voters who are under thirty-five years of age. A massive 94 percent of this group say housing should be a right rather than a market good, yet only about half rate the Sánchez government’s housing decrees favorably. This new political generation has yet to find an electoral vehicle. The energy with which it comes to the ballot box may decide whether Sánchez’s coalition remains in office or whether the far right enters government. But whoever wins the elections will face a society with tenants organized in cities throughout Spain and unions newly willing to strike. Maricarmen’s neighbors were unable to save her home, but their promise echoes beyond her doorstep. It is becoming a mass movement with its own political program, ready to confront whoever governs Spain after this Sunday’s vote.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office
It comes a month after opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to Venezuela.
Venezuela will repeal a law that prohibits opposition figures from office, National Assembly Chief Jorge Rodriguez has announced.
The legislation, approved in 2024 and criticised for enabling political persecution, targeted those who promoted or supported sanctions against the country.
“That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through,” Rodriguez said on Thursday.
The law was passed just after fraught elections which the then-incumbent Nicolas Maduro ultimately won amid widespread allegations of fraud.
An interim government headed by Delcy Rodriguez, the parliamentary chief’s sister, has run Venezuela since Maduro’s abduction by US forces in January. Delcy Rodriguez promised in September during a speech at the United Nations that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.
Since then, the US-backed government has been in political transition talks with parts of the opposition selected by Washington. That dialogue had reached an agreement to review several laws, including the one up for repeal now, according to Jorge Rodriguez.
Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado shook up Venezuelan politics with her surprise return from exile last month. Machado won an opposition primary in 2023 to take on Maduro in the following year’s election, but she was legally barred from running. The Nobel Peace Prize laureate is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election, despite her exclusion from transition talks.
Despite being shut out, on Thursday Machado launched a system of neighbourhood assemblies aiming to gather proposals for a future government programme and democratic transition. The assemblies are expected to bring together over a million people over several months, according to Machado’s team.
“We listened to neighbours who are breaking down barriers that many thought were impossible, debating the issues that will lay the foundations for the Venezuela to come,” Machado said on social media on Thursday after the meetings. “We are designing the transition to democracy, the Venezuelan way.”
Around 2,000 meetings with residents were organised in Venezuela and abroad on the first day of the initiative, her team told the AFP news agency.
Nineteen questions are asked during the assembly, with responses fed into a digital platform. Issues of national interest range from dates for the presidential election to changes in the justice, education, health, wage and pension systems, as well as the role of the public and private sectors.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Argentina leads the way in repatriating Indigenous human remains, study says
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Mercedes Ezquiaga
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Driven largely by Indigenous activism, the repatriation of ancestral human remains in Chile and Argentina is pushing museums, universities and scientific institutions to re-examine longstanding practices of collection, research and display. A recent study by the Chilean researchers Jacinta Arthur and Patricia Ayala suggests that the movement has opened a crucial ethical debate in both countries, with key differences: while Chile has handled repatriation campaigns on a case-by-case basis, Argentina has emerged as a regional leader since passing a law specifically tackling the issue.
“Argentina is central to any discussion of this issue in South America, since it is the first country in the region with a law specifically aimed at the restitution of Indigenous human remains,” Ayala, an archaeologist at the Universidad de Chile, Santiago tells The Art Newspaper. “In Chile, by contrast, there is no legal framework of this kind. That is why it was both necessary and interesting to compare the two realities.”
The researchers’ article, “Indigenous Repatriation Movements in South America and Their Repercussions on Ethical Discussions on the Respectful Treatment of Human Remains: The Cases of Chile and Argentina”, was published on 11 September in the journal Latin American Antiquity. It emerged from Arthur and Ayala’s work with Indigenous communities in Chile, particularly the campaigns led by the Atacameño and Rapa Nui people, where demands for the respectful treatment of human remains include critiques of their scientific study, museum display, sample collection, repatriation and reburial.
Those efforts were underscored last July, when the Australian Museum in Sydney returned the remains of ancestors of the Rapa Nui people who had been removed from sacred burial sites at Rano Raraku during a German naval expedition in 1882, and acquired by the museum the following year. The institution’s director, Kim McKay, publicly acknowledged the circumstances under which the ancestors’ remains had entered the collection, and said: “Returning them is an act of moral responsibility.”
According to Ayala, despite the legal differences between Argentina and Chile, the treatment of human remains from an Indigenous perspective “has not yet become central to scientific concerns”. Indigenous activism, she says, has forced museums and archaeologists to confront “the exclusion of Indigenous voices” and “alternative knowledge and ontologies” linked to ancestral bodies and the materials associated with them. It has also brought renewed attention to the violence of looting, collecting and scientific research that helped shape colonial and national museums, where Indigenous ancestral remains have ended up since at least the 19th century.
“In this context, both museums and academic fields have begun to reflect on their practices and discourses,” Ayala says, “although much work remains to be done to fully integrate the rights of Indigenous peoples in both countries.”
Argentina’s groundbreaking law
Argentina passed a law in 2001 mandating that Indigenous human remains held in public or private collections must be made available to the peoples or communities that claim them. An implementing decree followed in 2010, making the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs responsible for surveying and identifying remains, and coordinating their return.
A recent case at the Museo Etnográfico Juan B. Ambrosetti, part of the Universidad de Buenos Aires, shows how such restitutions unfold in practice. Last May the museum returned the remains of an Inca child from Apu Chañi, along with his grave goods, to El Angosto and Sol de Mayo, two communities in the El Moreno area of Jujuy state. The child had entered the museum’s collection in 1905, after being brought down from a hill on Nevado de Chañi. Following the restitution, a mausoleum was built at the foot of the mountain to display the grave goods, while the child’s remains will be buried at high altitude when conditions in the freezing high Andes allow.
“What I think is missing here, above all, is getting ahead of restitutions, not waiting for communities to file a claim,” Andrea Pegoraro, the director of the Museo Etnográfico, tells The Art Newspaper. Pegoraro, says the return of the child from Apu Chañi shows that Argentina has a more developed legal framework than many neighbouring countries, but also exposes the limits of a policy based solely on responding to claims.
That, she says, is one of the challenges still facing Argentine museums: moving from responding to specific requests to actively reviewing collections, identifying provenance gaps, reconstructing acquisition histories and contacting the relevant communities. In the Apu Chañi case, she says, the museum reviewed archival and archaeological records to establish where the remains had been taken and to which community they should be returned.
At the restitution ceremony, Pegoraro said the museum was not handing over “a heritage object or an object of study”, but rather “an ancestor to his territory and his people”. The community, in turn, described the returned ancestor as “a guardian” connected to water and life in the Puna region of Jujuy.
For Pegoraro, the distinction between human remains and objects is crucial. “If they are human remains, I am fully in favour of returning them, and the community must decide what to do with them,” she says. Objects raise a different set of considerations, in her view: to whom they should be returned, what happens to them and how museums can ensure access for other communities.
Provenance research is key
Reconstructing provenance is essential to any restitution process, Pegoraro adds, because Indigenous territories do not always align with today’s political boundaries. “Communities inhabit territories that did not previously have the political or geographical boundaries we have today,” she says. Museums often rely on documentation archaeologists wrote at the time the remains entered a collection, even when the places they recorded no longer correspond neatly to current jurisdictions.
Pegoraro also warns that change cannot be limited to isolated restitutions. “The integration of Indigenous communities does not come only through rhetoric, or by carrying out a restitution or holding an exhibition once in a while, but by literally working side by side,” she says. She adds that collaboration must include the ongoing rewriting of exhibition narratives, as well as financial compensation.
In Pegoraro’s view, the current movement for repatriation of Indigenous remains and artefacts began in the 1980s, especially in the US, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. In Argentina and elsewhere in South America, she adds, those demands gained force with the return of democracy after dictatorships. In Europe, however, museums carry “a much stronger colonial history”, she says, and while some countries are beginning to talk about decolonising collections, returning objects or rewriting narratives, “they still have a long way to go. It must not remain just rhetoric.”

https://gothamist.com/news/advocates-vis.title: Advocates' vision for discounted NJ Transit fares could be an uphill climb
https://gothamist.com/news/advocates-vis.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/advocates-vis.text:
Jasai Howard-Wright has always relied on public transit to get around.
The Seton Hall University student lives on campus in South Orange without a car. So running errands, meeting friends or getting to activities outside the Essex County campus means hopping on an NJ Transit bus or train. It’s something he’s used to. Howard-Wright said he grew up in Somerville without a car, so taking the bus around the Central Jersey suburbs of Somerset County was a way of life.
But the bus isn’t free, and a cash-strapped college student can feel the costs add up quickly. Howard-Wright estimates at least a quarter of his expenses are transit-related.
“A lot of the money that I earned over the summer is going towards these transportation costs,” Howard-Wright said.
And that cost is constantly rising, with 3% automatic annual fare increases for NJ Transit.
“It used to only cost $10 to get from Somerville to Newark Penn Station. Now it costs almost $15 just to do it. You know, it's crazy,” Howard-Wright said. “It's a $5 increase, and other people might say, ‘Oh, it's only a $5 difference.’ But it adds up these days, especially when everything else is so expensive.”
Howard-Wright is just one of thousands of low-income New Jerseyans transit advocates say should have access to discounted rides on NJ Transit buses, trains and light rail lines.
A coalition of advocacy groups in the Garden State launched the Fair Fares NJ campaign earlier this year. Their goal is to convince state leaders to expand NJ Transit’s reduced fare program to make some people eligible based on income thresholds. It’s currently open to seniors, people with disabilities and military personnel, and offers half-price fares on trains, buses and light rails.
Howard-Wright said a discount would go a long way for him.
“It would just put less stress on our day-to-day lives and help us focus on more essential things such as tuition and, you know, food and stuff like that,” Howard-Wright said.
The campaign is backed by a coalition of more than a dozen transit, environmental and progressive advocacy groups, including the Regional Plan Association, New Jersey Policy Perspective, the New Jersey League of Conservation Voters and the New Jersey Environmental Justice Alliance.
They argue that making transit more accessible would spur other benefits in society.
“Transportation's the game board upon which all other games are played,” said Zoe Baldwin, the vice president of state programs for the Regional Plan Association, which advocates for improving public transit throughout the New York City region. “When you're talking about public health, if you can't reliably access or afford to get to healthcare, that's going to impact public health. It's going to impact unemployment. It's going to impact our traffic. It's going to impact our air quality.”
Many other transit systems around the country already offer reduced fares for low-income riders. New York City’s Fair Fares program offers a 50% discount on subways and eligible buses for people with incomes up to 150% of the federal poverty level. That program will expand to include people making up to 200% of the federal poverty level at the end of November.
More than 370,000 New Yorkers are enrolled in the city’s program, though about 1.3 million will be eligible under its new rules. To try and boost enrollment, the New York City Council passed a law allowing people to simply check a box and enroll in Fair Fares when renewing with SNAP.
Baldwin said the campaign has had talks with NJ Transit and Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s office about expanding New Jersey’s reduced fares program to include income-based eligibility.
NJ Transit President Kris Kolluri said he agrees with the general goal of expanding transit access. But he said if it were to come to fruition, he’d want to see another agency in charge of administering enrollment and handling the fare subsidy because NJ Transit is facing a structural deficit that fluctuates between $100 million and $200 million year-to-year.
“What I would not advise is for someone to impose this laudable goal onto the existing transit balance sheet because that doesn't do anything to help us get out of the hole,” Kolluri said. “But if it serves as a separate program organized by the Legislature, if they think it's the right thing to do, separate and apart from New Jersey Transit, I think it's something I'm sure everybody would be interested in at least hearing about.”
The Fair Fares NJ campaign is not advocating for specific eligibility requirements or administrative structures. Existing programs around the country may serve as models, but NJ Transit is unique as being the only statewide entity of its kind.
“We need to make sure that we're creating a program that works for how the agency works,” Baldwin said.
Alex Ambrose, a senior policy analyst for the New Jersey Policy Perspective think tank, said it's likely the state could tie enrollment in NJ Transit’s reduced fares with enrollment in other programs, like SNAP or utility bill relief efforts.
“There's lots of other programs that people qualify for, and this can be just one more thing we add on top of it,” Ambrose said.
The administration can expand the reduced fare program on its own. But actually funding such a move would likely require help from state lawmakers, either through appropriations in future state budgets or through amendments to dedicate revenue sources like the state’s corporate transit fee or Transportation Trust Fund.
The current version of the corporate transit fee — a 2.5% tax surcharge on large companies signed into law in 2024 by then-Gov. Phil Murphy — expires at the end of 2028. Baldwin expects that will trigger legislative discussions that could provide an opening for expanding reduced fares, as part of larger structural changes.
“We're going to have to discuss how transit is funded broadly,” Baldwin said. “I think that's the most likely vehicle.”
New Jersey is coming off a tight budget season that saw Sherrill pressure lawmakers to reign in spending across state government. Next year’s budget is expected to be similar. That’s a big hurdle for the Fair Fares campaign to overcome. But Ambrose said if state lawmakers are serious about making New Jersey more affordable, this is the kind of policy they need to find the political will to support.
“It could happen during the next budget cycle if our lawmakers were willing to actually raise revenue instead of just cutting programs,” Ambrose said. “We keep hearing that it's going to be a tough budget year, but it's only a tough budget year if they decide it's going to be. We can raise revenue by closing corporate tax loopholes, raising taxes on the wealthiest New Jerseyans and the wealthiest corporations without actually harming everyday working New Jerseyans.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Uma grande fábrica de celulose está por ser implantada nos arredores de Porto Alegre. É o megaprojeto que o grupo chileno CMPC deseja levantar em Barra do Ribeiro, município distante 61 quilômetros da Capital, com o beneplácito do governo estadual.
Seus números são altissonantes: investimento de R$ 27 bilhões, processamento de 12 milhões de toneladas de madeira por ano, matéria-prima proveniente de 74 municípios, sobretudo da metade sul gaúcha. É o que a CMPC chama de “Projeto Natureza”.
Mas será que o projeto faz jus ao seu nome? Embora a empreitada conte com o respaldo quase unânime dos entes públicos e da imprensa corporativa, há muitos reparos à proposta entre a sociedade civil organizada, que já levou o caso à Justiça.
Discute-se a veracidade dos números propalados pela CMPC quanto ao impacto ambiental e quanto à oferta de empregos. Os primeiros seriam imensamente mais graves do que os anunciados e as vagas oferecidas com a planta em operação muito inferiores à projeção da empresa.
Este será o centro da conversa com o professor e pesquisador Francisco Marshall, diretor do Instituto Latino-Americano de Estudos Avançados da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), uma das tantas entidades que confronta os planos da CMPC.
O podcast De Fato é uma produção do Brasil de Fato RS em parceria com o SindBancários de Porto Alegre e Região.
Todo sábado, um entrevistado ou uma entrevistada debaterá os principais fatos em destaque no Rio Grande do Sul, no Brasil e no mundo.
