https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-recov.title: Mamdani recovering after surgery to repair torn Achilles
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-recov.author: Jill Webb
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-recov.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani is recovering in Gracie Mansion after successfully undergoing surgery on Friday to repair an Achilles tendon injured on the soccer pitch last week, City Hall spokesperson said.
The procedure began at 11:33 a.m. and ended at 12:42 p.m., mayor’s spokesperson Joe Calvello said in a statement posted on social media. The statement did not disclose where the procedure was performed.
“The surgery was successful, and the mayor is expected to make a full recovery,” Calvello said in the statement. “He was discharged from the hospital and is now resting comfortably at Gracie Mansion.”
He added, “We are extremely grateful for the first-class care the mayor received from the medical staff today.”
Mamdani, 35, sustained the non-contact injury in a soccer match last week between City Hall staffers and members of the media. The injury is expected to limit the mayor's movement for months to come.
Mamdani arrived late to the Nov. 19 game at an indoor soccer field in the Financial District. He later told reporters he didn’t stretch before playing.
“I forgot that I was 35,” he said.
He said ahead of the procedure he expected to wear a protective boot for six to eight weeks and won’t be able to play soccer again for nine months.
First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan is leading day-to-day operations today, Calvello said.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Keira Knightley’s Emerald-Green ‘Atonement’ Gown Heads to Christie’s
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Devorah Lauter
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
The stunning emerald-green plunging-back gown worn by actress Keira Knightley in Atonement will be auctioned live in London on December 9 at Christie’s. It is estimated to fetch between £100,000 and £120,000 ($130,940 to $157,125). In addition, the sale titled Love & Lust: A Literary Guide, will offer a host of items “celebrating the many expressions of love, romance and desire,” per the auction house’s description. This will range from passionate letters and cinematic costumes behind famous romances played out on stage and in literature, including about 30 books, manuscripts, autographed letters and original works dating back centuries.
Knightley wore the silky green ensemble designed by Jacqueline Durran for her role as Cecilia Tallis in the 2007 film Atonement, adapted from Ian McEwan’s acclaimed novel, and directed by Joe Wright. The dress last went under the hammer in a charity auction in 2008 and fetched £35,000 ($46,000).
Also for sale are rare examples of early film poster art, including one of the influential film Metropolis, made in 1926 for its premiere, estimated at £100,000 to £130,000 ($130,940 to $170,220). Another poster for Dracula (1931), which marked a pivotal moment for early sound movies, is being offered for an estimated £80,000 to £120,000 ($104,750 to $157,125).
These lots are joined, among others, by early 19th-century love letters from the celebrated British Royal Navy officer Horatio Nelson to Emma, Lady Hamilton, estimated at £5,000 and £8,000, plus original sketches by Chris Foss for the publication of The Joy of Sex (1972), estimated at £6,000 to £8,000.
“Love and desire have inspired some of the most enduring stories in literature and art, and this sale brings together a wonderfully eclectic group of objects that capture their many facets…” jointly stated Thais Hitchins, associate specialist, and Mark Wiltshire, specialist, Christie’s London.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-wareh.title: In Europe, Too, Amazon’s Warehouses Are a Dystopia
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-wareh.author: Li Andersson, Johannes Anttila
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/amazon-wareh.text:
In Europe, Too, Amazon’s Warehouses Are a Dystopia
We visited Amazon warehouses in Germany and Poland. Managers told us workers were well paid and supported. Workers described a system of surveillance, relentless productivity targets, and pressure not to organize.
When you see it, it’s hard to believe that nobody, at any point from planning to installation, raised a hand to say how tone-deaf it was. But there it is, emblazoned in bright colors above the gates where workers enter an Amazon warehouse in Germany:
“Work hard. Have fun. Make history.”
The corporate Americana and hyperoptimistic bravado are enough to make us wince. In Germany, of all places, words about work above an iron gate also bring to mind a much darker time and another slogan about work and freedom. It’s a terrible look.
That gate was our introduction to a fact-finding mission to Amazon warehouses in Germany and Poland. On October 26 and 27, we joined a delegation from the European Parliament’s Committee on Employment and Social Affairs at the company’s sites in Mönchengladbach, Dortmund, and Sosnowiec, near Katowice.
The visit was long overdue. In refusing to take part in the European Parliament’s hearings on warehouse working conditions, Amazon showed disrespect for workers’ rights and for democracy. A planned visit fell through in 2023, and the Parliament revoked Amazon lobbyists’ access badges in 2024. This January, the committee finally held a hearing with Amazon representatives and workers. By October, members of Parliament could visit the warehouses without signing nondisclosure agreements and with few restrictions on taking photos or videos.
We knew what we were dealing with even before we saw the sign. Amazon workers and their unions have organized campaigns and taken strike action over digital surveillance, punishing work rates, reliance on temp agencies, and the company’s resistance to collective bargaining. Amazon has also been accused of rerouting packages to blunt the impact of strikes.
The sign captured much of what we saw and heard during the visit. From the slogans on the walls to the managers’ answers to our questions, we encountered an eerie, over-the-top optimism and a single overriding concern: productivity at any cost.
At times, it was nearly impossible to discuss our concerns with the managers who accompanied us. We asked about reports of worker surveillance and algorithmic management, and whether rising productivity targets put workers at greater risk of injury. The managers dismissed our concerns as a misconception.
They said they measured workflows, not individual workers. If someone fell behind, then of course it was a manager’s job to help them. Wouldn’t we agree? When we raised collective bargaining, they said they preferred speaking to workers directly. Everyone was earning more than the minimum wage, they told us, and getting good benefits. Wasn’t that a good thing?
It felt strange to move through the warehouses with these optimistic, evasive chaperones. At one station, we stopped to watch a worker who was intensely focused and moving very fast. She looked stressed. A manager hurried over to explain that our presence was probably the reason.
The next day, at the Polish warehouse, things seemed much calmer. A worker later told us that management had diverted packages away from the site, offered an unpaid day off to anyone who wanted one, and had many of the workers who came in wait in the canteen during our visit.
We met with workers and unions in the evenings after our visits. What they told us sounded like it came from a different world from the one the managers had described.
The workers described what sounded to us like a digital panopticon. We had been unable to get a clear picture of how Amazon used technology to monitor and discipline workers. The workers had little more insight into what data Amazon collected on them, how it used that data, or how it set their performance targets.
But they knew what happened if they fell short.
Workers told us that if they went a certain number of minutes without scanning a package, the system counted that time as a break. If they couldn’t keep pace, a manager would keep dropping by their station, smiling, telling them to do better.
The uncertainty, combined with constant pressure to go faster, made workers feel paranoid, they told us. If you think you’re always being watched and need to move faster to keep your job or avoid being seen as difficult, you go faster and faster.
That is the logic of Jeremy Bentham’s panopticon, which Michel Foucault used to explain how surveillance disciplines people. The threat of punishment gets inside your head and drives you forward.
Some workers told us they barely dared to speak to colleagues at the next station, for fear of making them miss a target neither of them could see. Keep your head down and carry on. With even a quick chat out of the question, workers went faster and faster, helping set ever-higher targets they still couldn’t see.
Workers and union representatives also told us how Amazon used technology and workplace practices to thwart collective resistance. Union busting and resistance to collective bargaining have been cornerstones of Amazon’s modus operandi in Europe, too.
In Italy, the public broadcaster Rai reported that Amazon managers received recordings from people who had infiltrated union meetings during a drivers’ labor dispute. Amazon told Rai it lacked details to comment on the specific allegations and said its TERA team monitors publicly available information for operational risks. In a separate inquiry, Italy’s data protection authority ordered Amazon to stop processing personal data on workers at its Passo Corese site, including information on their health and union activity.
This fall, internal documents disclosed in a British Columbia labor dispute described a tool called Atlas that used AI to assess the likelihood of union organizing and other labor activity at Amazon warehouses. The inputs included employee feedback from channels such as Amazon’s Voice of the Associate message board. Amazon told openDemocracy that the tool assessed activity at the site level and that it did not monitor individual workers’ opinions or union affiliations. When we raised the Italian and Canadian reports during our visit, Amazon representatives denied the allegations, with a smile.
The workers’ accounts of union busting went beyond technology. In our evening meetings, workers told us the company had deliberately held works council meetings before it had hired all the warehouse workers at some sites, leaving the councils dominated by management and support staff.
Workers active in unions said they feared Amazon would find out. They told us they’d seen colleagues passed over for promotions or moved to worse workstations. They said Amazon had hired workers just before a key vote on industrial action at some sites to dilute the vote. Strikers told us they had been met with music blasting from speakers outside the gates.
This falls far short of what workers in Europe should expect from employers, even when tensions are running high.
We left the warehouses with much the same concern we heard from labor inspectors. Without fuller access to Amazon’s systems, it’s hard to tell exactly how the company uses them to pressure workers.
We could see the effects, though. As one worker put it: “It is like modern day slavery, without the whip.” At Amazon, the whip has gone digital, built into an invisible algorithm. It works alongside union busting, making workers think twice before demanding their rights. And it comes with a smile.
Our delegation left determined to keep monitoring conditions and supporting Amazon workers.
As workers strike and protest this Black Friday in Europe and around the world, the question is how far Europe is willing to go to defend collective bargaining and workers’ right to act together. That means resisting the Americanization of Europe’s labor market and the idea that large employers alone should set pay and working conditions.

https://taz.de/Jeremy-Corbyn-ueber-linke.title: Jeremy Corbyn über linke Politik: „Wir haben einen Weg aufgezeigt“
https://taz.de/Jeremy-Corbyn-ueber-linke.author: Daniel Bax
https://taz.de/Jeremy-Corbyn-ueber-linke.text:
Jeremy Corbyn über linke Politik: „Wir haben einen Weg aufgezeigt“
Der britische Ex-Labour-Chef über den aktuellen Trend nach links, seinen Nachfolger Andy Burnham und sein „Gaza-Tribunal“, das er in Berlin vorstellt.
taz: Herr Corbyn, die US-Demokraten waren im November bei den Midterms mit klaren sozialpolitischen Forderungen und scharfer Kritik an Israel erfolgreich, mit einem ähnlichen Profil gewann Zohran Mamdani die Wahl zum Bürgermeister in New York. Kommt Ihnen dieses Erfolgsrezept bekannt vor?
Jeremy Corbyn: Ja, das tut es. Mamdani hat die Tür zu einem sozial gerechteren und ökologisch nachhaltigeren New York geöffnet und mit seiner Kampagne enorme Vorurteile gegenüber einem muslimischen Kandidaten überwunden. Ich war erst kürzlich in New York und sehr beeindruckt von den Veränderungen, die ich dort sah, sowie vom Erfolg demokratischer Kandidaten, die von den „Democratic Socialists of America“ unterstützt wurden. Aber sie haben ihre Ämter noch nicht angetreten. Ab Januar werden sie auf eine harte Probe gestellt werden, wenn es darum geht, Präsident Trump einzudämmen oder zu kontrollieren. Sie werden sehr, sehr entschlossen sein müssen.
taz: Als Sie 2017 in Großbritannien erstmals als Spitzenkandidat für die Labour-Partei antraten, forderten Sie eine klare Abkehr vom neoliberalen Kurs der Jahre zuvor sowie höhere Steuern für Großkonzerne und Spitzenverdiener. Ihr Motto lautete „For the many, not the few“. Warum war die Zeit damals noch nicht reif für diesen Slogan?
Corbyn: Das war schon damals richtig und heute noch mehr, denn die Ungleichheit hat seitdem enorm zugenommen. Wir haben europaweit mehr Obdachlose als damals, und der obszöne Reichtum einer sehr kleinen Zahl von Menschen wird immer schlimmer. Doch unter den Wirtschaftsberatern der meisten Regierungen herrscht immer noch die Meinung vor, eine kleine Zahl sehr wohlhabender Menschen würde der Wirtschaft insgesamt irgendwie zugutekommen. Dabei war diese Trickle-down-Theorie von Margaret Thatcher und Ronald Reagan schon damals völliger Unsinn, und sie ist es auch heute.
Jeremy Corbyn, 77, war von 2015 bis 2020 Vorsitzender der britischen Labour Party. 2025 gründete er die linke „Your Party“ mit, deren Mini-Fraktion er nun im Londoner Parlament vorsitzt. 2026 rief Corbyn das „Gaza-Tribunal“ ins Leben, um Großbritanniens Rolle in diesem Krieg zu untersuchen. Am Samstag, den 28.11., wird er es in Berlin vorstellen – bei „Zeit zu reden“ mit der Journalistin Kristin Helberg.
taz: Sie und Bernie Sanders haben das früh kritisiert. Warum drangen Sie damit nicht durch?
Corbyn: Unsere Argumente sind mittlerweile viel stärker im Mainstream verankert. Die Antwort der Parteien der Mitte auf das Erstarken der extremen Rechten in Europa war allzu oft, sich gegen Asylsuchende zu wenden und die brutalsten Formen der Einwanderungskontrolle umzusetzen. Auf der anderen Seite erstarken linke Kräfte, wie wir derzeit in Frankreich sehen. Ich denke, dieser Trend wird anhalten.
taz: Sie wurden damals von der „Momentum“-Kampagne getragen, die junge Leute in Großbritannien über soziale Medien mobilisierte, eine regelrechte Euphorie entfachte und zu Masseneintritten in die Labour-Partei führte. Beim Popfestival in Glastonbury wurden sie 2017 wie ein Star gefeiert, das Publikum sang ihren Namen. Was ist davon geblieben?
Corbyn: Die Labour-Partei unter Keir Starmer hat sehr viel Mühe darauf verwandt, Leute auszuschließen, die mich unterstützt haben und zum linken Flügel der Partei gehörten. Mir wollten sie untersagen, dass ich für Labour in dem Wahlkreis kandidiere, den ich 40 Jahre lang vertreten hatte. Also trat ich dort als unabhängiger Kandidat an und gewann das Mandat.
taz: Deswegen wurden Sie 2024 aus der Labour-Partei ausgeschlossen, nachdem man sie schon kaltgestellt hatte. Im vergangenen Jahr haben Sie eine neue Partei gegründet, „Your Party“. Warum hat es damit bisher nicht geklappt, ihrer alten Partei damit von links Konkurrenz zu machen?
Corbyn: Wir haben mittlerweile fast 100 Ortsverbände im ganzen Land und verfügen über eine beträchtliche Mitgliederbasis, die Beiträge an die Partei zahlt. Es war ein langer und schwieriger Prozess, das bedauere ich. Dennoch habe ich das Gefühl, dass wir die Wende geschafft haben und jetzt recht gut vorankommen.
taz: Viele ehemalige Labour-Wähler sind inzwischen zu den Grünen gewechselt, vor allem wegen deren Haltung zu Gaza. Haben die Grünen die Lücke gefüllt, die Sie schließen wollten?
Corbyn: Ich sehe uns nicht in Konkurrenz. Wir sind eine dezidiert sozialistische Partei, die soziale Gerechtigkeit und die Umverteilung in den Vordergrund stellt. Unsere Schwerpunkte liegen auf der Regulierung des Mieten, angemessenen Sozialleistungen sowie der Bekämpfung der Jugendarbeitslosigkeit. Und es gibt innerhalb der Grünen große Spannungen zwischen den eher traditionellen, gemäßigten Umweltschützern und den neueren Mitgliedern, die in wirtschaftlichen und anderen Fragen weiter links stehen.
taz: Seit Juli dieses Jahres ist Andy Burnham neuer Ministerpräsident und Labour-Chef. Er setzt sich für eine stärkere öffentliche Kontrolle über Bereiche wie Wasser, Energie und Verkehr ein, für einen bezahlbaren öffentlichen Nahverkehr und mehr Wohnungsbau. Rückt er seine Partei und sein Land wieder stärker nach links?
Corbyn: Burnham spricht nicht von öffentlichem Eigentum, sondern von öffentlicher Kontrolle, das ist nicht dasselbe. Regulierung gibt den Behörden ein gewisses Maß an Kontrolle, aber sie überträgt ihnen weder das Eigentum noch die Kontrolle über Investitionen. Daher glaube ich, dass noch ein langer Weg vor uns liegt.
taz: Tritt er in Ihre Fußstapfen?
Corbyn: Nicht wirklich, obwohl sein Kurs eine große Verbesserung gegenüber allem darstellt, was Keir Starmer getan hat.
taz: Ihnen wurden damals vorgeworfen, nicht genug gegen Antisemitismus in den eigenen Reihen unternommen zu haben. Haben Sie die Sorgen britischer Jüdinnen und Juden unterschätzt?
Corbyn: Es ist schwer zu sagen, was man anders hätte tun können, wenn eine große Lüge verbreitet und von Leuten aus der eigenen Partei verstärkt wird. Diese bösartigen Angriffe galten meiner Unterstützung für das palästinensische Volk. Aber ich arbeite viel mit jüdischen Gruppen zusammen und setze mich für sie ein. Tatsächlich stellen jüdische Menschen, gemessen an ihrem Anteil an der Bevölkerung, bei den Demonstrationen für die Rechte der Palästinenser die größte Gruppe.
taz: Haben Sie keine Fehler gemacht?
Corbyn: Jeder macht Fehler. Ich wurde damals auf einer enormen Welle der Unterstützung von Labour- und Gewerkschaftsmitgliedern zum Parteivorsitzenden gewählt. Das spiegelte sich aber nicht innerhalb der Labour-Fraktion im Parlament und schon gar nicht in den offiziellen Strukturen der Labour-Partei wieder. Es ist uns nicht gelungen, die Partei rasch so weit zu demokratisieren, dass die von mir verfolgte Agenda weitergeführt werden konnte. Außerdem sahen wir uns vom ersten Tag an in den Medien mit den absurdesten Angriffen gegen mich konfrontiert. Es ist sehr schwer, die Partei in Richtung sozialer Gerechtigkeit zu führen, wenn man sich gleichzeitig täglich und stündlich dagegen wehren muss.
taz: Hätten Sie entschiedener gegen den Brexit eintreten sollen, für den vor zehn Jahren eine knappe Mehrheit der Briten votiert hatte?
Corbyn: Das war ein schwieriges Thema, denn die Wählerschaft war in dieser Frage sehr gespalten. In meinem eigenen Wahlkreis waren etwa 70 Prozent für den Verbleib in der EU, aber in sozioökonomisch vergleichbaren Wahlkreisen im Norden Englands war es genau umgekehrt. Die Mehrheit der Mitglieder der Labour-Partei stimmte für den Verbleib, und auch unter den Labour-Abgeordneten war die Mehrheit dafür, aber es gab eine bedeutende Minderheit, die für den Austritt war.
taz: Andy Burnham versucht jetzt, sein Land wieder stärker an die Europäische Union anzunähern. Hat er recht?
Corbyn: Ich denke, dass Burnham sehr vorsichtig sein muss, denn die Einstellungen gegenüber der EU haben sich im Norden und Süden Großbritanniens nicht geändert. Ich glaube nicht, dass Großbritannien in naher Zukunft wieder der Europäischen Union beitreten wird oder will, und würde das zum jetztigen Zeitpunkt auch nicht unterstützen. Ich glaube jedoch, dass es in den Bereichen Handel, Reisen und Migration bessere Regeln braucht.
taz: Burnham hat sich für den Umgang der vorherigen Labour-Führung mit dem Krieg in Gaza entschuldigt und fordert mehr Druck auf Israel. Steht er für einen Kurswechsel?
Corbyn: Burnham sagte, wir hätten in Bezug auf Gaza falsch gehandelt, ohne jedoch zu präzisieren, was er damit meinte. Und Miliband hat Sanktionen gegen verschiedene Leute in der israelischen Regierung und ein Exportverbot für Waren aus den Siedlungen im Westjordanland verhängt. Ich persönlich halte das micht für ausreichend und auch unpraktikabel. Will man jede einzelnen Orange und jede einzelne Avocado überprüfen, ob sie aus einer der illegalen Siedlungen stammt oder nicht? Das geht nicht. Man muss Sanktionen gegen Israel als Ganzes verhängen.
taz: Sie haben im Juni 2025 im Parlament einen Gesetzentwurf eingebracht, der eine unabhängige Untersuchung der Rolle Großbritanniens im Gaza-Krieg forderte. Nach dem dieser von der Regierung blockiert worden war, haben Sie mit den beiden Wissenschaftlern Neve Gordon und Shahd Hammouri ein „Gaza-Tribunal“ ins Leben gerufen. Worum ging es da?
Corbyn: Uns stand die Untersuchung, die der damalige Premierminister Gordon Brown nach dem Irakkrieg einrichten ließ, als Vorbild vor Augen. Nachdem der Gesetzentwurf wie erwartet von der Regierung blockiert wurde, richteten wir ein zweitägiges Tribunal aus und hörten dafür 29 Sachverständige an. Die Protokolle aller Zeugenaussagen von Ärzten, Journalisten, Analysten und palästinensischen Bürgern aus dem Gazastreifen haben wir inzwischen in einem Buch veröffentlicht.
taz: Sie haben auch die Nutzung eines britischen Stützpunkts auf Zypern untersucht. Mit welchem Ergebnis?
Corbyn: Britische Flugzeuge sind von der Militärbasis der Royal Air Force in Akrotiri auf Zypern aus über Gaza geflogen, um Informationen zu sammeln. Uns wurde gesagt, dies sollte der Befreiung von Geiseln dienen. Ein Anwalt hat versucht, an diese Informationen zu gelangen, um den Mord an einem britischen Entwicklungshelfer in Gaza-Stadt aufzuklären und die Täter strafrechtlich zu verfolgen. Die Royal Air Force weigerte sich aber kategorisch, sie in irgendeiner Form freizugeben. Das bestärkt uns in dem Verdacht, dass sie im Rahmen einer umfassenden Sicherheitspartnerschaft an die israelische Armee weitergegeben wurden.
taz: Was fordern Sie von der britischen Regierung?
Corbyn: Wir fordern, alle Waffenverkäufe an Israel einzustellen. Der ehemalige Außenminister David Lammy hat zwar im Februar 2024 erklärt, man werde einen Teil der Waffenlieferungen aussetzen. Aber es war nie klar, welche genau. Und er fügte hinzu, man werden nichts tun, was Israels grundlegende Sicherheit gefährden könnte. Ich glaube, das bedeutet, dass sie den Informationsaustausch fortsetzen und weiterhin Komponenten und Ersatzteile liefern. Doch die Komponenten für F-35-Kampfflugzeuge mögen zwar selbst nicht unmitelbar tödlich sein. Aber natürlich sind sie Bestandteil einer mächtigen Militärmaschinerie, die in Gaza so viele Menschen getötet hat.
taz: Deutschland hat sich noch stärker an die Seite Israels gestellt als Großbritannien. Braucht es auch hierzulande ein Gaza-Tribunal?
Corbyn: Die deutsche Öffentlichkeit hat ein Recht zu erfahren, welche Waffen von deutschen Unternehmen an Israel geliefert werden und welche Zusammenarbeit es gibt. Wir haben einen Weg aufgezeigt, wie das geschehen kann.

https://www.humanite.fr/sports/bulgarie/.text:
Si l’OM a bien battu (1-0) chez lui en Ligue Europa le club bulgare de Levski Sofia, les deux clubs pourraient perdre beaucoup suite aux incidents survenus dans les tribunes du Vélodrome entre les supporters des deux camps, dans la soirée de jeudi 26 novembre.
L’avant-match, qui avait déjà été assez mouvementé entre supporters des deux camps, a connu une suite dans les tribunes juste avant le début de la rencontre. Des incidents ont eu lieu une dizaine de minutes avant le coup d’envoi de cette rencontre de Ligue Europa, dans la soirée de jeudi 26 novembre. Des centaines de supporters marseillais ont quitté le virage Sud pour se diriger vers la tribune Jean-Bouin où se trouvaient les supporters bulgares. Selon certaines images, ces derniers auraient provoqué les Ultra marseillais notamment par des saluts nazis et des cris de singes alors qu’ils étaient mélangés à des familles marseillaises.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120418.title: EU-Sondergipfel | Haushaltsverhandlungen der EU vorzeitig abgebrochen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120418.text:
- Politik
- EU-Sondergipfel
Haushaltsverhandlungen der EU vorzeitig abgebrochen
Ein Ende des Streits um den EU-Haushalt ist weit und breit nicht in Sicht. Nun soll es kurz vor Weihnachten mit einer Einigung klappen
Brüssel. Nach stundenlangen und weitgehend ergebnislosen Haushaltsverhandlungen haben die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU ihren Sondergipfel zur Finanzplanung bis 2034 vorzeitig beendet. Die Vorstellungen über Umfang und Verteilung der Finanzmittel würden noch »weit auseinanderliegen«, sagte Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz am späten Donnerstagabend. Man habe sich daher darauf verständigt, dass man das Treffen anders als ursprünglich geplant am Freitagvormittag nicht fortsetzen werde.
Ratspräsident António Costa beendete die Zusammenkunft, die am Morgen begonnen hatte, kurz nach Mitternacht. Er hatte den Gipfel für zwei Tage angesetzt, um die Verhandlungen über den nächsten langfristigen Haushalt endlich ein Stück weit voranzubringen – mangelnde Kompromissbereitschaft der Staats- und Regierungschefs machte ihm aber einen Strich durch die Rechnung. »Dieser Gipfel war ein notwendiger Schritt im Prozess«, verteidigte er sich anschließend.
Merz und die anderen Staats- und Regierungschefs hatten sich auf einen Aufenthalt in Brüssel bis Freitagabend eingestellt. Der Kanzler hatte sogar schon mit der CDU/CSU-Fraktion im Bundestag abgemacht, dass er nicht zu der für Freitagnachmittag geplanten Abstimmung über den Bundeshaushalt 2027 in den Bundestag kommen muss. Jetzt kann er unverhofft doch noch dabei sein.
Merz und Macron wollen nun Einigung im Dezember
Ein Durchbruch war vor dem Gipfel ohnehin nicht erwartet worden, alle hatten sich von Anfang an darauf eingestellt, dass es erst bei einem weiteren Treffen im Dezember zum Showdown kommen werde. Sowohl Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron als auch Merz betonten aber, dass es dann zu einer Einigung kommen müsse.
Für den Fall, dass auch dieser Gipfel ohne Ergebnis bleibt, hat Frankreich angedroht, dass die Verhandlungen erst nach der für April angesetzten französischen Präsidentenwahl weitergehen würden. Die Wahl könnte nach derzeitigen Umfragen die EU-kritische Nationalistin Marine Le Pen gewinnen, was eine Einigung wohl nochmals erschweren würde.
Österreichs Kanzler: »Ich habe hier keine Eile«
Der niederländische Regierungschef Rob Jetten machte aber klar, dass er sich nicht hetzen lassen will. »Es gibt immer irgendein europäisches Land, in dem gerade gewählt wird«, sagte er. Ähnlich äußerte sich Österreichs Kanzler Christian Stocker: »Ich habe hier keine Eile. Wenn die Bedingungen nicht stimmen, kann es auch keine Einigung geben.«
Wie andere Länder, die für Kürzungen plädieren, nahm auch Österreich nicht alle Einladungen zu den sogenannten Beichtstuhlgesprächen an, zu denen Costa Vertreter unterschiedlicher Gruppen einlud. Dies sei kein Boykott, betonte Stocker – und übte zugleich deutliche Kritik an der Verhandlungsführung des EU-Ratspräsidenten: »Für uns ist das ein Zeichen, dass wir mit der Art und Weise, wie der Prozess gestaltet ist, genauso wenig zufrieden sind wie mit dem Vorschlag, der vorgelegt wurde.«
Schon zu Beginn des Sondergipfels hatten mehrere Staats- und Regierungschefs deutlich gemacht, dass sie von ihren Positionen nicht abrücken wollen. Auf die Frage, ob es bei dem Sondergipfel überhaupt Fortschritte gegeben habe, sagte Merz: »Es gibt durchaus Bewegung Richtung weiterer Reduzierung dieser sogenannten Verhandlungsbox.« Gemeint ist der Umfang des Gesamthaushalts, den Costa vor dem Gipfel um 204 auf 1781 Milliarden Euro im Vergleich zum Kommissionsvorschlag reduziert hatte. »Das wird nicht bei 204 bleiben«, sagte Merz.
Er verlangt eine weitere Kürzung um mehrere hundert Milliarden Euro und hat sich mit gleichgesinnten Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus den Nettozahler-Staaten Niederlande, Österreich, Schweden, Finnland, Dänemark und Belgien zusammengetan, um das durchzusetzen. Die Gruppe nennt sich »Die vernünftigen Sieben« – »The sensible Seven«. Damit will sie deutlich machen, dass ein zu großer EU-Haushalt aus ihrer Sicht unvernünftig wäre.
Sie haben es mit einer großen Gruppe von Ländern zu tun, die keine weiteren Kürzungen wollen und hohe EU-Ausgaben für strukturschwache Regionen und die Landwirtschaft verteidigen. Viele dieser Staaten, vor allem in Süd- und Osteuropa, sind Nettoempfänger aus dem EU-Haushalt. Kritik kommt zudem von Ländern wie Frankreich und Italien, die auch Nettozahler sind, aber Einbußen für ihre Landwirte und Regionen vermeiden wollen. dpa/nd

Israeli strike on Doctors Without Borders clinic in Gaza kills two staff
MSF says Israeli attack on Gaza clinic a ‘direct hit’ and calls for those responsible to be held accountable.
Two staff members of Doctors Without Borders, the humanitarian relief agency known by its French initials MSF, have been killed in an Israeli strike on one of its clinics in Gaza City.
“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” MSF said on X on Friday.
It called the attack a “direct hit” and said the deaths bring the number of its staff killed in Gaza to 17.
The agency’s premises were “clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military”, the group said.
It called for those responsible to be held accountable.
In a statement following the strike, the Israeli military claimed, without providing evidence, that the two workers were members of Hamas.
World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the attack “outrageous and unacceptable”.
“Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked,” he wrote on X.
The Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor condemned the “attack on a clearly marked MSF clinic” and accused Israel of “systematic targeting of humanitarian personnel and facilities”.
A pattern of attacks
Israeli forces have killed more than 1,700 health workers in Gaza, including 15 MSF staff as of January.
In January, MSF said Israel had blocked its supplies and denied entry to all its international staff since the start of the year.
Israeli officials have alleged, without proof, that aid groups are linked to Hamas, while aid organisations say such accusations have helped normalise attacks on humanitarian workers.
Earlier this week, an Israeli strike in Gaza killed Adel al-Helou, who had worked for 35 years for UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees.
Al-Helou was supplying water to residents of the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza. Three other people were wounded in the attack, UNRWA and medics said.
The strike came despite a ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, which Israel has repeatedly violated.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Trump, Putin e Zelensky: o que mudou nas negociações para encerrar a guerra na Ucrânia?
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Serguei Monin
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A cúpula entre Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump e Xi Jinping, em Shenzhen, abriu espaço para novos desdobramentos diplomáticos em torno da guerra na Ucrânia. A expectativa de retomada das conversas trilaterais entre Rússia, Estados Unidos e Ucrânia, prevista para dezembro, indica uma tentativa de avançar nas negociações, embora persistam divergências sobre os termos de um eventual acordo.
O enviado de Donald Trump, Jared Kushner, em entrevista publicada em 25 de novembro de 2026 ao CEO do Axel Springer Media Group, Mathias Doepfner, disse que o conflito na Ucrânia se tornou uma “guerra por procuração”, apoiada financeiramente e militarmente pela Europa contra Moscou, reproduzindo uma visão semelhante à do Kremlin.
Em entrevista ao Brasil de Fato, o cientista político Oleg Ignatov aponta que os EUA modificaram sua abordagem, deixando de buscar concessões da Rússia em primeiro lugar, para priorizar aproximar Washington, Kiev e os governos europeus antes de novas conversas com Moscou. O objetivo, nesse contexto, seria consolidar uma posição comum entre ucranianos e europeus para levá-la à mesa de negociação com os russos.
“Os EUA mudaram um pouco a abordagem. Antes, diziam que estavam tentando negociar primeiro com a Rússia e obter algumas concessões deles, e só depois discutiriam com os europeus. Então, tudo está acontecendo em paralelo agora. Agora eles acreditam que não devem primeiro buscar concessões da Rússia, mas sim formular uma abordagem comum entre a Ucrânia e a Europa e discutí-la com a Rússia. E, consequentemente, tentar encontrar um meio-termo entre todas essas posições e forçar as partes a tomarem decisões políticas em relação a ideias específicas”, argumenta.
Um dos principais pontos de divergência permanece sendo a possibilidade de presença militar estrangeira em território ucraniano após um eventual cessar-fogo. Moscou rejeita a instalação de contingentes militares ocidentais no país, argumentando que a medida representaria uma ameaça à segurança russa.
O porta-voz do Kremlin, Dmitry Peskov, reiterou que a Rússia não aceita a presença de tropas estrangeiras na Ucrânia, mesmo em um cenário posterior ao fim das hostilidades. A posição russa mantém o tema no centro das discussões sobre garantias de segurança para Kiev.
“Para o lado russo, isso é completamente inaceitável e inadmissível. Nossa posição sobre o destacamento de qualquer contingente estrangeiro em território ucraniano foi reiteradamente declarada em vários níveis, inclusive pelo presidente Vladimir Putin. E também sabemos que, lamentavelmente, tanto das capitais europeias quanto de Bruxelas, têm ocorrido repetidas declarações sobre planos de envio de contingentes militares. Posso repetir mais uma vez: isto é absolutamente inaceitável para Moscou”, destaca.
Embora Moscou admita discutir mecanismos de segurança para a Ucrânia, o governo russo rejeita garantias que reproduzam, na prática, o modelo de defesa coletiva previsto no artigo 5º da Otan. A neutralidade ucraniana permanece entre as condições defendidas pela Rússia, enquanto Kiev e Washington buscam estabelecer compromissos que assegurem proteção ao país no pós-guerra.
Disputa territorial
As disputas territoriais também seguem como um dos principais obstáculos. Moscou reivindica o controle integral do Donbass e insiste na incorporação dos territórios que considera parte da Rússia, enquanto Kiev rejeita ceder áreas ainda sob seu controle.
Ainda em outubro de 2022, a Rússia anunciou a anexação de quatro regiões do leste ucraniano – Donetsk, Lugansk, Kherson e Zaporozhye –, incorporando estes territórios formalmente na Constituição do país. No entanto, Moscou não possui controle pleno sobre estas regiões, exigindo, assim, a retirada das forças ucranianas das áreas que elas ainda ocupam como condição para o fim da guerra.
O cientista político Oleg Ignatov afirma que a posição russa envolve não apenas a questão territorial, mas também o estabelecimento de condições políticas e de segurança que garantam o controle sobre a região. Segundo ele, Moscou busca consolidar sua presença no Donbass, enquanto as discussões diplomáticas tentam encontrar alternativas para acomodar as exigências dos dois lados.
“E as diferenças de interpretação em relação aos territórios permanecem as mesmas. Ou seja, a Rússia quer controle administrativo, controle administrativo completo sobre todo o Donbass. Vários compromissos são possíveis. Mas o mais importante é que, como dizem os ucranianos, a Rússia quer a bandeira russa hasteada em todos os lugares. Não importa se há forças militares ou não militares lá. Mas a bandeira russa deve estar em todo lugar. E a governança, os órgãos administrativos, também devem ser russos”, afirma.
Ao mesmo tempo, o cientista político aponta que as conversas também têm incorporado novas propostas norte-americanas que poderiam abrir espaço para algum tipo de compromisso. A possibilidade de concessões, entretanto, permanece condicionada às divergências sobre fronteiras, segurança e o futuro político da Ucrânia.
“O que mudou é que existem novas abordagens. Sim, os americanos estão propondo novas ideias, tentando de alguma forma fazer esse processo avançar. Eles estão trabalhando nisso; eles entendem que há um impasse na questão territorial; eles estão tentando de alguma forma expandir o horizonte das possibilidades de segurança na esperança de que, se as partes concordarem em avançar na segurança, isso lhes permita encontrar compromissos sobre as questões territoriais”, afirmou.
Outro elemento que Ignatov considera relevante é a ampliação da agenda diplomática. Segundo ele, Kiev passou a reconhecer que as negociações não podem se restringir exclusivamente às garantias de segurança ucranianas, mas precisam incorporar também as preocupações de Moscou e questões mais amplas de segurança europeia.
Para o analista, essa mudança representa um avanço na construção de uma agenda negociadora, ainda que não signifique, por si só, uma aproximação concreta entre as posições.
“A Ucrânia não queria discutir nada além de sua própria segurança, mas agora a Ucrânia está dizendo: sim, devemos discutir as preocupações da Rússia também. Zelensky reconheceu isso. Então eu diria que o que está acontecendo de positivo é que as partes estão entendendo cada vez mais qual agenda é necessária, qual agenda de negociação é necessária, qual agenda de negociação precisa ser discutida para, em última análise, alcançar a paz’, completa.
A próxima rodada de conversas deverá testar se a ampliação dos temas em discussão pode resultar em avanços efetivos. Território, neutralidade, garantias de segurança e o papel dos países europeus continuam sendo pontos de difícil conciliação, e a abertura de novas frentes diplomáticas não elimina as divergências estruturais entre os envolvidos.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Could New Zealand head back to the polls? The new centrist party on the block holds the power| Lara Greaves
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Lara Greaves
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
After a 20-day wait for the results, New Zealand’s election doesn’t have a clear winner. Several unprecedented events, including the success of a new centrist party and the looming threat of an election re-run, mean a definitive outcome could still be months away.
Election night revealed that parliament would have a substantial overhang: extra seats added to the house when a party wins more electorate seats than its party vote is entitled to.
The final results provide for a 130-seat house, where 66 seats are needed to govern. The current rightwing coalition government (National-Act-New Zealand First) secured 65 – not enough for a majority. The opposition left bloc (Labour-Greens-Te Pāti Māori) won 58.
The Opportunity party meanwhile won seven, meaning New Zealand has a hung parliament. The newcomers now need to choose between backing the right bloc or returning the country to an election.
The entrance of the Opportunity party is remarkable: in 30 years and 10 previous elections a new party has never entered the parliament, unless it was started by someone who was already a member of parliament.
The Opportunity party was founded in 2016 by businessman and economist Gareth Morgan, who was looking for evidence-based, centrist policy solutions.
But in 2017 Morgan caused controversy for describing Jacinda Ardern, who was then ascending to the Labour party’s leadership, as “lipstick on a pig” and making comments about restricting the number of pet cats.
After Morgan stepped away, the party persisted across the 2020 and 2023 elections, but with limited success and successive leaders.
Enter Qiulae Wong. In 2025 the party took the rather amusing step of listing their party leader as a job posting on various websites, as well as advertising it to party members, which Wong states is how she found the role.
At the time, many wrote this off as a stunt or joke, but it seems to have worked. Wong was widely praised throughout the campaign as a charismatic outsider, who assumed a fresh, conciliatory approach.
This centrist technocratic turn may seem strange in a world of populist right politicians gaining and holding power, although is perhaps akin to the “teal” independents in Australia. Opportunity has positioned itself through a series of “bottom lines” for coalition negotiations,with a focus on the environment and integrity of the political system.
Opportunity now faces challenging negotiations. National’s rightwing minor party allies have a larger share of the party vote than ever before with 25 seats to National’s 40.
An obstacle for Opportunity is New Zealand First, led by Winston Peters. Some party members, such as candidate Michael Laws, have sparked outrage for uncouth comments, including what an Opportunity candidate would look like after sex. Wong has said Opportunity would not govern with Peters returning as foreign minister, nor with the party if Laws remained.
Another big problem for Opportunity is that polling has showed 68% of its voters would preferit to support a left government. New Zealanders have booted out parties in the past that propped up governments their supporters did not want them to partner with, such as the Māori party in 2017 and New Zealand First in 2020.
Opportunity would need to balance their bottom lines, address issues with New Zealand First members, and secure enough policy gains for their voters to take this risk.
If the right cannot find some way of working with Opportunity – which could include a range of inventive arrangements – then the result could be a deadlock. At which point there are mechanisms for another election sometime in early-mid 2027.
- Lara Greaves is an associate professor of political science at Victoria University of Wellington

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/chuck-schume.title: Chuck Schumer’s Former Aides Now Lobby for Corporate America
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/chuck-schume.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/chuck-schume.text:
Chuck Schumer’s Former Aides Now Lobby for Corporate America
Chuck Schumer wants to lead the new Senate majority. His former aides now lobby for the companies it would have to take on, from health insurers and AI giants to Wall Street.
One of the quirks of Sen. Chuck Schumer’s (D-NY) bid to lead the incoming Democratic Senate majority is that delivering the change voters demanded in November would mean facing off against a small army of his own former staff.
Over his many years in Congress, Schumer has seen countless staffers cycle into his office and out into lobbying work for a broad swath of corporate interests: banks, credit card companies, health insurers, drugmakers, cryptocurrency firms, and the AI industry.
His former top health advisor lobbies for the American Medical Association, a longtime opponent of single-payer health care. His ex-chief counsel now leads a top lobbying firm’s AI practice as lawmakers weigh how to regulate the industry. Two former financial advisors now lobby for a crypto industry eager to win government-backed legitimacy while keeping the government off its back. Two former legislative directors have lobbied for the private equity industry on housing legislation.
A search of federal lobbying disclosures filed since the start of 2025 turns up upwards of a thousand reports naming former Schumer staffers.
For his rival for the leadership spot, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) — like Schumer, a decades-long creature of the DC establishment — the equivalent number is only a fraction of this. The disclosures show a different mix of clients: an airline, a major university, several local airport-related organizations, and a company that develops drones for delivering food and medicine, to name a few.
It’s all part of a Washington practice Schumer has excelled at: building a vast network of former staff whose careers he takes an interest in long after they’ve left his office.
“People come into Washington in their twenties and thirties, go to the private sector, but stay tethered to their former boss. And the rising tide lifts all boats,” says Jeff Hauser, executive director of the Revolving Door Project. Schumer’s current staff “get extra mentorship from the alumni who are strewn across DC lobbying for various industries,” Hauser says, sometimes simply about benign matters like how to handle their boss. But the resulting close network of loyal former staffers can also be a rich resource in a town that runs on who you know.
“These people are super valuable if you’re a corporate interest and looking for who to hire,” he says.
This is the fundamental conundrum of Schumer’s potential leadership: if elected majority leader again, the longtime New York senator will have to make good on a historic mandate for change by challenging the very industries that have hired some of his own former senior staff to represent them.
Medicare for Few
Take, for instance, Matt Fuentes, a partner at the Democratic lobbying firm Avenue Solutions, whose former role as Schumer’s senior health policy adviser for eight years is prominently advertised on the firm’s website.
Since 2025, Fuentes has been a lobbyist for the American Medical Association (AMA), a longtime opponent of single-payer health care that has fought national health insurance proposals for more than a century. The AMA has softened its stance in recent years, but its policymaking body voted in 2023 to retain its opposition to single payer.
Fuentes doesn’t just lobby for the AMA. His clients include a broad swath of the for-profit health care industry, including some of the large drugmakers Merck, Moderna, Takeda, and Amgen, as well as pharmacy services company HouseRx. His client list also features insurers Blue Cross Blue Shield and UnitedHealth Group (UHG). For the latter, he has lobbied on “prior authorization” — the widely disliked insurer practice of requiring advance approval for care, which can delay treatment and sometimes have deadly consequences.
Records show that, for both insurers, Fuentes lobbied on AI and its “correlation to prior authorization and utilization management policies.” UHG and other insurers have long come under fire for the controversial practice of using AI to deny care to and overcharge people, with UHG specifically the subject of a lawsuit alleging it used an algorithm to deny care to older patients. That is one kind of AI use the incoming Congress might seek to regulate.
Then there’s Reggie Babin, whose former role in Schumer’s office is prominently displayed on his page on Akin Gump’s website. Babin is co-lead of the firm’s federal AI policy practice. In practice, that means Babin — who worked for five years under Schumer, two of them as his chief counsel from 2020 to 2022 — has lobbied Congress on data centers and AI regulation for several companies, including Microsoft, Adobe, Dropbox, and data center operator STACK Infrastructure.
His clients also include OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and the Data Center Coalition, a trade group for data center operators whose board of directors includes executives from across the industry. A 2025 filing lists Babin as lobbying on the coalition’s behalf on “issues related to Section 232 investigations and investment,” a reference to the Trump administration’s trade investigations under Section 232. Tariffs threatened to raise the cost of the AI data center buildout.
The concerns about staffers-turned-lobbyists like Fuentes and Babin aren’t theoretical. As the American Prospect reported at the time, a package of antitrust bills aimed at tech giants had broad bipartisan and public support during Joe Biden’s presidency. Schumer, then Senate majority leader, never brought the bills to the floor.
“How did the enormous momentum against Big Tech that was developed at the end of the 2010s and built in the early days of the Biden administration fail to lead to significant legislative changes?” says Hauser. “Schumer’s daughters and many former staffers working in Big Tech is a popular explanation.”
The New York Post reported at the time that not only were Schumer’s two daughters an Amazon lobbyist and a Facebook product marketing manager, but eighty of his former staffers had gone on to take jobs at those and numerous other tech companies, including Google and Apple. That included Babin, who moved on after the 117th Congress to Akin Gump, which raked in millions of dollars in lobbying fees from tech firms.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who was championing the legislation, blamed unnamed members of Congress for “giving in to the dominant social media platforms,” while a former Senate staffer told HuffPost that “if Schumer wanted this to happen it would have already happened.” The Prospect reported that Schumer said the votes weren’t there, though he hadn’t conducted a private whip count.
Super Intelligence
Babin is just one of Schumer’s former senior staff who today lobbies for the AI industry. Another is Lucia Panza, Schumer’s former leadership counsel. She took a position lobbying for Amazon after leaving the Senate and now represents companies before Congress and other federal bodies at Crossroads Strategies. When Panza joined the firm, its CEO noted that “her time advising some of the most influential lawmakers and voices in Washington, D.C.” would be helpful to their clients.
During Trump’s second term, her clients have included AI companies and other businesses and trade groups that lobby on AI, such as Motorola and the Advanced Medical Technology Association. One of the AI firms Panza has represented is CoreWeave, a cloud computing firm whose bonds have come under pressure amid concerns about the AI data center buildout on which its business depends.
Like Babin, Panza also counts the Data Center Coalition as a client. Records show that Panza began lobbying on the Ratepayer Protection Act for both the coalition and CoreWeave in the third quarter of 2026. The bill would require state regulators and certain utilities to consider standards for recovering grid upgrade costs from large data centers. It passed the House 417–3 in September and met opposition in the Senate. A separate bill addressing data center costs passed the Senate in November, leaving the question of who pays for grid upgrades on the congressional agenda.
This is on top of several other Schumer connections knee-deep in the industry. Grace Magaletta, his legislative correspondent from 2019 to 2023, lobbied for Samsung on “artificial intelligence policy issues” as recently as 2025. Josh Vlasto, who worked for Schumer from 2004 to 2010, this election cycle co-headed an AI industry group funding Democratic and Republican super PACs to help elect candidates friendly to the industry. Throughout Trump’s second term, Schumer’s former communications director, Israel “Izzy” Klein — whose firm trumpets his “deep ties to congressional leadership” and who was appointed in October to the Congressional Award’s board of directors by Schumer — has lobbied for Cisco and Larry Ellison’s Oracle.
Resolution Public Affairs, whose principals included former Schumer legislative directors Heather McHugh and Meghan Taira, also employed a third former Schumer staffer. The three lobbied for chipmaker TSMC Arizona, a key part of the AI supply chain, and on AI issues for Oracle and the Murdoch family’s News Corp.
Maxwell Young, who served several stints in Schumer’s office over the past two decades, including most recently as his senior communications adviser in 2020, has since November 2025 been the head of policy communications for AI giant Anthropic. In September, OpenAI hired Schumer’s daughter away from Amazon to head its lobbying efforts at the state and local levels in the Northeast.
Not all of Schumer’s ex-staffers are simply doing the industry’s bidding. Carrie Adams, Schumer’s deputy digital director from January 2017 to June 2018, now lobbies for the AI Policy Network (AIPN). She lobbies Congress and, as of the third quarter of 2026, federal agencies including the State, Treasury, and Commerce Departments on a range of AI issues.
AIPN, which has gotten funding from ultrarich AI safety advocates and describes itself as independent, backs more regulation as well as export controls aimed at keeping the United States ahead of China in the AI “race.”
Political Currency
Former Schumer staffers also work for the cryptocurrency industry as it seeks mainstream legitimacy. One example is Jennifer Brown, a former financial policy adviser to Schumer.
After Brown left Schumer’s office in 2025, crypto investment firm Paradigm added her to its Policy Council. In announcing the new members, Paradigm said it wanted to “put the misguided era of anti-crypto policy firmly in the rearview mirror,” just months after the Senate leader — while being advised by her — had failed to extend the tenure of a crypto-skeptical SEC commissioner before Trump was sworn in. Brown joined BGR Group as a lobbyist in January 2025, focusing on financial regulation and tax policy. The firm highlighted her experience under Schumer when it announced her hiring.
Many of those issues involve cryptocurrency. Filings list Brown as lobbying for crypto clients including stablecoin issuer Circle, wallet provider Phantom, and crypto-focused investors Dragonfly and Digital Currency Group.
Brown also lobbied on crypto regulation in 2025 and 2026 for the Decentralization Research Center, which advocates for keeping cryptocurrency “decentralized” — in other words, free from the control of a single authority, including governments and banks. A Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) memo from September 2025 detailed how members of both the center and BGR (Brown wasn’t listed as an attendee) met with the SEC’s Crypto Task Force to discuss regulation of the crypto industry, and handed them reading materials about decentralization.
Brown also lobbied for venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, headed by billionaire Marc Andreessen, maybe best known as one of the first and most high-profile Silicon Valley oligarchs to shift his allegiance from Democrats to MAGA. Andreessen Horowitz employed Brown to lobby on AI and digital assets. It was one of several of Brown’s clients, like data center operator Galaxy Digital Holdings, that sit at the intersection of crypto and AI.
Brown is one of several former senior Schumer staffers who have lobbied for crypto-related clients.
That the crypto world will have the possible next Senate majority leader’s allies as its advocates in Congress comes at a pivotal time for the industry, which has sought to shed its reputation for facilitating scams and become a mainstream investment option while remaining as free from government oversight as possible. To get there, the industry has pushed for a Goldilocks-style regulatory regime: just enough to grant it legitimacy and reassure skeptical Americans that buying digital assets is safe, but not enough to seriously step on its toes.
But that effort has also aroused concern from experts, who fear the destabilizing effects of having digital assets under a light regulatory touch reshaping the balance sheets of banks and other financial institutions. The collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX in 2022 seemed to be a cautionary tale, an episode whose fallout was largely contained within the crypto sector. Under Trump, the industry has moved aggressively to deepen its links to the broader financial system.
One former Schumer staffer’s lobbying record illustrates the crypto industry’s push for legitimacy through regulation: Ryan Eagan, the Crypto Council for Innovation’s (CCI) director of US federal affairs, whose nearly decade-long stint advising Schumer on banking policy is the first thing mentioned in his official bio, along with his work with other members of Congress to “advance legislative priorities” like “cryptocurrency policies.”
In 2026, Eagan lobbied on a spate of bills for the CCI that illustrate the industry’s “just right” regulatory framework: bills extending established securities and commodities tax rules to digital assets or cracking down on fraud and terrorist financing in the industry, as well as a bill barring the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency, a measure criticized for potentially putting a straitjacket on monetary policy in a future economic crisis. One bill, the GENIUS Act, which Trump signed into law in July 2025, requires payment stablecoins to be backed by liquid assets such as dollars or short-term US Treasuries. A 2026 working paper argues that a growing stablecoin market could add to systemic risk by tying stablecoin redemptions to the functioning of the Treasury market.
A number of other bills Eagan lobbied on were similarly controversial. The CLARITY Act, along with several other pieces of legislation listed in the lobbying filings involving Eagan, would give the smaller Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority over trading in digital commodities and retain a role for the SEC in regulating securities.
The CLARITY Act passed the House in July 2025 with a large bipartisan majority. In September 2026, a Senate vote to advance it failed, 49–50 — but the industry is already planning to run it back in the new, Democratic-led Congress next year, with one expert observing that the midterm result doesn’t mean the bill is dead, but that it simply “changes the authors of the next draft.” Schumer’s fellow New York senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a prominent backer of crypto legislation, has drawn scrutiny for her ties to the industry.
The crypto connections do not end there. Filings show that Panza, Schumer’s former leadership counsel, has lobbied on the GENIUS and CLARITY Acts for fintech company Block Inc., credit card trade group Electronic Payments Coalition, and the Financial Services Forum, an industry group representing eight of the largest US financial institutions. (She also lobbied on general crypto issues for Visa and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association.) The trio of former Schumer staffers at Resolution Public Affairs likewise lobbied for these two bills for asset manager BlackRock and JPMorgan Chase.
Return of Wall Street
Meanwhile, several of these same former staffers now also lobby for a financial sector that has long stood in the way of reform in Congress and that many Americans associate with corruption in Washington.
The Resolution Public Affairs trio, for instance, lobbied throughout this year for the American Investment Council (AIC), a private equity trade group that fought Joe Biden’s proposed tax hikes in 2021. Among other things, they lobbied on the AIC’s behalf on housing legislation that included limits on purchases of single-family homes by large institutional investors. The federal government enacted those limits in July 2026. The Private Equity Stakeholder Project separately estimates that private equity firms own at least a tenth of US apartments.
Besides lobbying for both JPMorgan Chase and Mastercard on the matter of capping credit card rates, they also counted as a client the Investment Company Institute (ICI). They lobbied on a bill the ICI supported that aimed to make it harder to treat nonbank institutions as systemic risks to the economy that need extra regulatory scrutiny. Likewise, Panza has spent Trump’s second term lobbying for a number of finance clients on regulatory issues, including work for Morgan Stanley on the implementation of the Obama-era Dodd-Frank Act.
Some also represent the growing gambling industry, which has poured money into politics and lobbying.
Jennifer Brown, Schumer’s former banking counsel, has lobbied over the past two years for FanDuel on “federal gaming policy,” while Schumer’s two former legislative directors, Heather McHugh and Meghan Taira, lobbied in 2026 through Resolution Public Affairs for the prediction market platform Kalshi. The reason Taira, who spent a total of eighteen years in Schumer’s office, is no longer at the firm is because in October she cut out the middleman and went to work for Kalshi directly, heading its federal lobbying efforts. It was part of a hiring spree of former Democratic staffers that the company undertook in the lead-up to the GOP’s bloodbath this November.
Schumer vs. His Own Staffers
It would be easy to say this is simply what happens when you’ve been in Washington for a long time. Schumer’s rival, Van Hollen, has represented Maryland in Congress since 2003, and his former staffers’ lobbying work tells a different story.
Some former Van Hollen staffers do represent companies with a stake in the incoming Congress’s agenda. Cassandra Brzezinski, a Van Hollen policy adviser until January 2026, now lobbies for Allstate Insurance, the Financial Technology Association, and the London Stock Exchange Group, the latter on digital assets and AI. John Mitchell, his former legislative aide, lobbied in 2025 for Workday, which sells human resources software that uses AI. Alexander Simpson, a legislative correspondent for Van Hollen when he served in the House, now lobbies for American Airlines.
The Van Hollen alumni in the filings generally held less senior positions and represented a different mix of clients. Schumer’s alumni include a former chief counsel and multiple former legislative directors working for some of the biggest companies in health care, finance, and technology.
The next Democratic Senate majority leader will have a long to-do list, from expanding Medicare and regulating AI and crypto to lowering housing costs as large financial firms buy up more of the nation’s homes. If Schumer wins back the majority leadership, it may prove the most compelling test yet of just how much influence the Washington revolving door commands.

https://taz.de/Gesetzentwurf-zur-Rente/!.title: Gesetzentwurf zur Rente: Rentenstreit geht in die nächste Runde
https://taz.de/Gesetzentwurf-zur-Rente/!.author: Anna Lehmann
https://taz.de/Gesetzentwurf-zur-Rente/!.text:
Gesetzentwurf zur Rente: Rentenstreit geht in die nächste Runde
Der SPD-Arbeitsminister legt den lang erwarteten Gesetzentwurf vor. Die „Rente mit 63“ soll bleiben, aber modifiziert. Wie reagiert die CDU?
Die Kameras waren schon aufgebaut, als Arbeitsminister Alexander Schweitzer (SPD) am Freitagnachmittag um kurz vor 16.00 Uhr in den Lichthof seines Ministeriums trat. Schweitzer hat am Freitag überraschend den lang erwarteten Gesetzentwurf zur Reform der gesetzlichen Alterssicherung vorgelegt; sein Haus hatte kurzfristig zum Pressegespräch eingeladen.
Laut Entwurf des Arbeitsministeriums soll die sogenannte „Rente mit 63“ erhalten bleiben. Allerdings soll der Kreis der Anspruchsberechtigten kleiner werden. Mit dem Kanzleramt ist der Vorschlag nicht abgestimmt, was bedeutet, dass der Streit darum, ob Versicherte nach 45 Beitragsjahren ohne Abschläge in Rente gehen können, nun in die nächste Runde geht. Schweitzer sagte vor den Kameras, man müsse diesen Streit lösen. „Mein Vorschlag kann dazu geeignet sein, uns da zusammenzubringen.“
Laut Gesetzentwurf sollen Beschäftigte, die 45 Jahre in die Rentenkasse eingezahlt haben, weiterhin vorzeitig ohne Abschläge in Rente gehen können. Allerdings sollen Zeiten der Arbeitslosigkeit oder der Kurzarbeit, in denen die Versicherten geringfügig beschäftigt oder länger krank waren, nicht mehr angerechnet werden. Zeiten für Pflege und Kindererziehung zählen weiterhin. Der Kreis derjenigen, die vorzeitig in Rente gehen können, ohne Einbußen in Kauf zu nehmen, würde nach Berechnungen des Ministeriums um gut ein Viertel sinken.
Zudem soll die Altersgrenze auch für diese Frührentner weiter steigen, und zwar mit der gesetzlichen Regelaltersgrenze. Der Abstand soll fest bei zwei Jahren liegen. Das gesetzliche Rentenalter, so sieht es der Entwurf aus dem Arbeitsministerium vor, soll künftig an die Lebenserwartung gekoppelt sein. Das soll für alle Jahrgänge ab 1968 gelten. Mit jedem Jahr zusätzlicher durchschnittlicher Lebenszeit sollen die Beschäftigten ein halbes Jahr länger arbeiten.
Große Teile von der Rentenkommission übernommen
Menschen, die vor dem gesetzlichen Rentenalter in den Ruhestand gehen wollen, müssen künftig bis zum 64. Geburtstag warten und tiefere Einschnitte in Kauf nehmen. Wer drei Jahre früher in Rente gehen will, dem wird die Rente dauerhaft um 14,4 statt derzeit 10,8 Prozent gekürzt.
Der Entwurf aus dem Bundesarbeitsministerium basiert auf den Empfehlungen der Rentenkommission und hat viel davon übernommen. So betont es jedenfalls Schweitzer: „Der überwiegende Teil der darin enthaltenen Empfehlungen wird mit diesem Entwurf umgesetzt.“
Der Entwurf enthält tatsächlich viele Dinge, über die sich die Koalitionspartner bereits einig sind, etwa die Einführung einer Kapitalrente, das eigentliche Novum der Rentenreform. Aber auch bislang strittige Punkte hat das Arbeitsministerium von der Rentenkommission übernommen. So sieht Schweitzers Entwurf vor, dass auf Minijobs künftig Rentenbeiträge gezahlt werden müssen – nur Schüler und Beschäftigte in privaten Haushalten sollen auf Wunsch davon befreit werden können. Auch die Altersteilzeit in Blöcken wird abgeschafft – allerdings laut Entwurf erst in drei Jahren.
Warken: „Keine Verständigung“
Knackpunkt bleibt die Abschaffung der früheren Rente für besonders langjährige Versicherte, die die Rentenkommission ebenfalls empfohlen hat – und besonders der CDU wichtig ist. Die SPD will diese Rente hingegen mit Rückendeckung der Gewerkschaften beibehalten. Doch mehrere Verhandlungsrunden der sogenannten „Sherpas“ brachten keine Annäherung. Zuletzt trafen sich CDU-Kanzleramtsministerin Nina Warken, CSU-Innenminister Alexander Dobrindt, SPD-Finanzstaatssekretär Björn Böhning und Schweitzer am Donnerstag im Kanzleramt – und gingen ohne Ergebnis auseinander.
Ein Vorschlag von CDU-Sozialpolitikern, die „Rente mit 63“ nur noch für Beschäftigte mit niedrigen Löhnen anzubieten, war nach taz-Informationen nicht mehr Gegenstand der Verhandlungen. SPD-Sozialpolitikerin Annika Klose, die auch Mitglied der Rentenkommission war, hatte diesen Vorschlag öffentlich als „nicht hinnehmbar“ bezeichnet.
Nach dieser letzten Runde riss Schweitzer dann offenbar die Hutschnur und präsentierte „seinen“ Entwurf. Noch bevor der Arbeitsminister vor die Mikrofone trat, teilte Kanzleramtschefin Warken mit, ein Gesetzentwurf befinde sich in der Frühkoordinierung innerhalb der Bundesregierung. „Eine Verständigung darauf gibt es nicht“, sagte sie der Deutschen Presse-Agentur.
Soziapolitikerin Klose ist der Meinung, der Vorschlag des Arbeitsministers stelle einen guten Ausgleich der Interessen dar. „Die abschlagsfreie Rente nach 45 Beitragsjahren wird reformiert und bleibt im Kern erhalten“, sagte sie. Dafür sei die Forderungen der Unionsparteien nach höheren Abschlägen und für die Beibehaltung der Minijobs in den Gesetzentwurf aufgenommen worden. „Nun ist zu hoffen, dass dieser Kompromiss durchträgt und ein Beschluss im Kabinett zeitnah möglich ist.“
Danach sieht es jedoch nicht aus. Unionsfraktionschef Thorsten Frei (CDU) sagte den Zeitungen der Neuen Pressegesellschaft, er sei über das Vorgehen irritiert. „Wir sollten am bewährten Verfahren festhalten und vertrauliche Verhandlungsrunden auch vertraulich halten“, so Frei. Dem gemeinsamen Ziel, die Rente generationengerecht zu gestalten, komme man nicht näher, „indem wir an Maximalforderungen festhalten, die uns in Zukunft finanziell schwer belasten“.
Immerhin dürfte Schweitzer sich über gedämpfte Zustimmung aus den Reihen der Jusos freuen. Deren Bundeskongress begann am Freitag in Bochum, Schweitzer soll am Abend sprechen. Sein Vorvorgänger im Amt, Hubertus Heil, wird am Samstag zu Gast sein. Dieser bewirbt sich aktuell um den Parteivorsitz.
